note: Hammer bank as rewritten by Antigravity in v3.6.12 (imported by site/patches/v3613_import.py)

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old woman attends the breast clinic with a lump in her right breast. She noticed it 3 months ago and it has grown rapidly. She has no nipple discharge or family history of breast cancer.
There is a 6 cm smooth, mobile lump in the upper outer quadrant with no axillary nodes.
Ultrasound shows a solid mass; core biopsy reveals leaf-like stroma with high cellularity.
hq_q.w: Phyllodes tumours are rapidly enlarging fibroepithelial breast lesions presenting in women aged 40 to 50 with characteristic leaf-like stromal projections and stromal hypercellularity on biopsy. They require wide local excision with clear margins to prevent recurrence.
hq_q.f: A 2 cm smooth, rubbery mobile lump in a 20-year-old with low stromal cellularity -> fibroadenoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Hypercellular stromal overgrowth creates leaf-like clefts lined by epithelium that grow rapidly and recur locally if enucleated
tm.g: Rapidly growing large mobile breast mass with leaf-like hypercellular stroma -> phyllodes tumour
x: Occurs typically in women under 30 as a small (1 to 3 cm), stable rubbery lump with uniform hypocellular stroma.
Forms a hard, irregular, speculated mass with skin tethering and malignant epithelial infiltration rather than leaf-like stroma.
Appears as an anechoic fluid-filled sac with posterior acoustic enhancement on ultrasound rather than a solid stromal tumour.
Presents as a soft, doughy, slow-growing fatty lesion composed of mature adipocytes.
f: A 2 cm rubbery, mobile lump in a 21-year-old woman with uniform benign pericanalicular stroma on biopsy
A hard, irregular, tethered breast mass with spiculated margins on mammography and malignant ductal cells on biopsy
A fluctuant perimenopausal lump that is anechoic on ultrasound and disappears completely upon aspiration of clear fluid
A soft, doughy, mobile lump showing mature adipose tissue identical to subcutaneous fat on ultrasound

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old woman found a painless lump in her left breast 4 weeks ago that has not changed in size. She has no family history of breast cancer.
There is a 1.5 cm smooth, rubbery, highly mobile lump in the upper outer quadrant with no axillary lymphadenopathy.
Triple assessment with breast ultrasound and core biopsy confirms a benign fibroadenoma.
o: Wide local excision with 1 cm margins
hq_q.w: Biopsy-confirmed simple fibroadenomas under 3 cm in young women are managed conservatively with reassurance and discharge, as most remain stable or regress spontaneously. Surgical excision is reserved for lesions >3 to 4 cm, rapid growth, or patient preference.
hq_q.f: Fibroadenoma enlarging beyond 4 cm or causing persistent patient distress -> surgical excision.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: 1.5 cm smooth, rubbery, highly mobile lump
tm.m: Small fibroadenomas are benign hormone-responsive fibroepithelial lesions with a high rate of spontaneous regression
tm.g: Confirmed fibroadenoma <3 cm in a young woman -> reassurance without routine excision
x: Mammography is ineffective in dense teenage breast tissue and benign fibroadenomas require no radiological surveillance.
Selective oestrogen receptor modulator used for oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, not benign fibroadenomas.
Radical overtreatment for a benign 1.5 cm fibroepithelial lesion.
Wide margin excision is required for phyllodes tumours or breast carcinoma, whereas small fibroadenomas are left in situ.
f: A 42-year-old woman with a strong family history of breast cancer undergoing high-risk surveillance
Adjuvant endocrine therapy for premenopausal oestrogen receptor-positive invasive ductal carcinoma
Multicentric invasive breast carcinoma or extensive ductal carcinoma in situ unsuitable for breast conservation
A borderline or malignant phyllodes tumour requiring clear surgical margins to prevent local recurrence

hq_q.s:
A 23 year old woman has noticed a painless lump in her right breast while showering. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and has no family history of breast cancer.
There is a 2 cm discrete, firm, mobile lump in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, with no skin tethering or axillary lymphadenopathy. She attends the one-stop breast clinic for triple assessment.
hq_q.w: In women under 35 years of age, predominantly fibroglandular breast tissue appears radiodense on mammography, markedly reducing sensitivity. Targeted breast ultrasound is therefore the first-line imaging modality in triple assessment for women under 35.
hq_q.f: A 55-year-old woman presenting with a discrete breast lump -> two-view mammography plus targeted ultrasound.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation?

c: one-stop breast clinic for triple assessment
tm.m: High fibroglandular density in women under 35 obscures masses on X-ray mammography, whereas high-frequency ultrasound differentiates cysts from solid lesions
tm.g: Symptomatic breast lump in a woman under 35 -> breast ultrasound scan first
x: Used to stage distant pulmonary and nodal metastases in locally advanced breast cancer, not to image a primary lump.
Reserved for BRCA surveillance, lobular cancer sizing, or implant rupture assessment rather than initial triple assessment.
3D X-ray mammography technique limited by radiodense fibroglandular tissue and radiation exposure in a 23-year-old.
First-line imaging alongside ultrasound in women aged 35 to 40 and over, where fatty involution allows radiographic contrast.
f: Staging of newly diagnosed node-positive or locally advanced invasive breast carcinoma
Annual breast cancer surveillance in a 32-year-old woman carrying a pathogenic BRCA1 mutation
Further radiographic evaluation of an equivocal architectural distortion on a mammogram in a 58-year-old woman
A 54-year-old woman attending the breast clinic with a newly discovered breast lump

hq_q.s:
A 47 year old perimenopausal woman has had a tender lump in her left breast for 2 weeks. She has no family history of breast cancer.
There is a 2 cm smooth, well-defined, mobile lump in the upper outer quadrant.
Ultrasound shows a simple cyst. Fine-needle aspiration yields 6 mL of clear straw-coloured fluid, and the lump completely disappears.
o: Core needle biopsy of the cyst cavity
Surgical excision of the cyst wall
hq_q.w: When aspiration of an ultrasound-confirmed simple breast cyst yields non-bloody fluid and the palpable mass resolves completely, the fluid is discarded and the patient reassured. Cytology and core biopsy are required only if fluid is blood-stained or a mass persists.
hq_q.f: Residual mass palpable after aspiration or blood-stained aspirate -> core needle biopsy and cytology.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Complete resolution of a simple cyst with non-bloody fluid excludes intracystic carcinoma, making routine cytology low-yield
tm.g: Simple breast cyst with clear fluid and no residual mass after aspiration -> discard fluid and reassure
x: Indicated only when a solid mural nodule is visible on ultrasound or a residual mass persists after aspiration.
Routine cytology of clear cyst fluid has a very low diagnostic yield and is reserved for blood-stained aspirates.
Simple breast cysts are benign perimenopausal changes and do not require intensified mammographic follow-up.
Unnecessary for a simple cyst that resolves on aspiration.
f: A palpable mass remaining immediately after cyst aspiration or an intracystic solid mass on ultrasound
Aspiration of heavily blood-stained fluid from a breast cyst
Short-interval radiographic follow-up of a probably benign (BI-RADS 3) mammographic lesion
A complex cystic breast lesion showing atypical epithelial proliferation on core biopsy

hq_q.s: A 44 year old woman is seen in the breast clinic with a tender lump in her right breast. Ultrasound shows a simple cyst, which is aspirated. The fluid is clear and the lump disappears.
hq_q.w: Cysts arise from involuting lobules in the years before menopause. They are uncommon after menopause unless the woman takes HRT.
hq_q.f: A new cyst in a 75-year-old not on HRT → assess carefully for cancer.
hq_q.ql: In which group of women are simple breast cysts most common?

tm.m: Cysts form as lobules involute in the years before the menopause
tm.g: Simple cysts are commonest at 35 to 50
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Girls before menarche (Breast cysts are hormone-driven perimenopausal lesions and do not occur before menarche)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pregnant teenagers (Cysts are hormone driven in the years before the menopause, not in teenagers)
asked which group most often gets fibroadenomas
the presentation instead showed features specific to Women over 70 (Cysts are uncommon after the menopause unless on HRT; a new lump at 70 is cancer until proven otherwise)
x: Breast cysts are hormone-driven perimenopausal lesions and do not occur before menarche
Cysts are hormone driven in the years before the menopause, not in teenagers.
Ruled out here: requires asked which group most often gets fibroadenomas, whereas this patient has simple cyst, 44 year old woman.
Cysts are uncommon after the menopause unless on HRT; a new lump at 70 is cancer until proven otherwise.

hq_q.s:
A 39 year old woman has had aching pain and lumpiness in both breasts for 6 months. The pain starts about a week before each menstrual period and settles once menstruation begins. She has no nipple discharge.
On examination, both breasts are diffusely nodular and mildly tender in the upper outer quadrants, with no discrete mass, skin dimpling or axillary lymphadenopathy.
hq_q.w: Cyclical mastalgia with diffuse bilateral nodularity (fibrocystic change) is driven by luteal-phase hormonal stimulation before menstruation and resolves at menses. In the absence of a discrete lump or red flags, management is reassurance, a well-fitted bra, and simple analgesia.
hq_q.f: Discrete lump persisting after menstruation -> refer to the breast clinic for triple assessment.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: aching pain and lumpiness in both breasts
week before each menstrual period and settles once menstruation begins
tm.m: Luteal-phase oestrogen and progesterone surges cause transient lobular stromal oedema and ductal distension that subside at menses
tm.g: Bilateral premenstrual breast pain and diffuse nodularity relieved by menses -> cyclical benign mastalgia
x: Presents with a unilateral hot, erythematous, fluctuant mass and fever, typically during breastfeeding.
Causes rapid unilateral diffuse erythema, warmth, and peau d'orange skin oedema over weeks.
Presents as a discrete, smooth, fluctuant unilateral lump rather than symmetrical premenstrual nodularity.
Forms a firm, irregular, painless unilateral lump with skin tethering following blunt breast trauma.
f: A breastfeeding woman with fever and a 3 cm hot, red, fluctuant breast swelling
A diffusely swollen, warm, erythematous breast with peau d'orange skin pitting and a firm axillary node
A single 2.5 cm smooth, fluctuant lump in a 46-year-old woman showing an anechoic sac on ultrasound
A firm, irregular lump with skin tethering at the site of a seatbelt bruise 6 weeks after a collision

hq_q.s:
A 31 year old woman is breastfeeding her 6-week-old baby. She was started on oral flucloxacillin 5 days ago for left lactational mastitis, but her breast pain has worsened and she feels feverish.
Temperature 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg. There is a 3 cm tender, fluctuant swelling in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast with overlying skin erythema.
hq_q.w: Lactational mastitis that fails to resolve with oral flucloxacillin and develops a localised, tender, fluctuant swelling with persistent pyrexia has progressed to a lactational breast abscess, requiring ultrasound-guided needle aspiration while continuing breastfeeding.
hq_q.f: Painless, afebrile, fluctuant subareolar swelling containing milk after weaning -> galactocele.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: started on oral flucloxacillin 5 days ago
tm.m: Staphylococcus aureus mastitis liquefies lobular parenchyma into a walled-off purulent cavity requiring drainage
tm.g: Fever and a tender fluctuant breast mass despite antibiotics in a lactating woman -> lactational breast abscess
x: Presents in non-lactating women with diffuse peau d'orange skin oedema and axillary lymphadenopathy without high fever or fluctuance.
Occurs in perimenopausal women with green or cheesy nipple discharge and slit-like nipple retraction.
Forms a painless, non-inflamed, afebrile milk-retention cyst without erythema or systemic fever.
Produces a firm, irregular, non-fluctuant mass without fever following blunt chest wall injury.
f: An afebrile 52-year-old woman with a diffusely erythematous breast, peau d'orange skin, and a hard axillary node
A 56-year-old woman with thick green multi-duct nipple discharge and a transverse slit-like retracted nipple
An afebrile woman who stopped breastfeeding 1 month ago presenting with a painless fluctuant lump yielding milky fluid
An afebrile woman with a hard irregular breast lump at the site of previous seatbelt bruising

hq_q.s:
A 35 year old woman attends with a painful swelling beside her right areola. She has had two similar episodes in the past year that were treated with antibiotics. She is not breastfeeding, has never been pregnant, and smokes 20 cigarettes a day.
Temperature 37.6°C, pulse rate 82 bpm. There is a 2 cm tender, erythematous, fluctuant mass at the periareolar margin.
hq_q.w: Periductal (Zuska's) mastitis occurs predominantly in young women who smoke. Toxic tobacco metabolites damage subareolar duct walls and induce squamous metaplasia, leading to recurrent non-lactational periareolar abscesses and mammary duct fistulae.
hq_q.f: Older perimenopausal non-smoker with thick green multi-duct discharge -> mammary duct ectasia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying condition?

c: painful swelling beside her right areola
two similar episodes in the past year
tm.m: Cigarette smoke toxins damage subareolar lactiferous ducts, causing keratin plugging, anaerobic/aerobic infection, and periareolar abscesses
tm.g: Recurrent non-lactational periareolar abscesses in a young smoker -> periductal mastitis
x: Occurs during breastfeeding or expression in the postpartum period, whereas she has never been pregnant.
Presents as a persistent hard, irregular mass rather than recurrent self-limiting periareolar abscesses in a 35-year-old smoker.
Affects older perimenopausal women (typically >50) causing dilated ducts, cheesy green discharge, and slit-like nipple inversion.
Rare granulomatous infection presenting with chronic painless cold sinuses and constitutional symptoms in endemic exposure.
f: A 29-year-old woman 3 weeks postpartum with a painful red wedge-shaped breast area while breastfeeding
A 62-year-old woman with a progressive hard, fixed upper outer quadrant lump and axillary lymphadenopathy
A 58-year-old woman with bilateral thick green nipple discharge and slit-like nipple retraction
A chronic painless discharging breast sinus with caseating granulomas and acid-fast bacilli on biopsy

hq_q.s:
A 29 year old woman is breastfeeding her 3-week-old baby. She has had pain and redness in her right breast for 2 days that has not improved with frequent feeding, and she now feels feverish. As a child she developed widespread urticaria and facial angioedema after taking amoxicillin.
Temperature 38.2°C, pulse rate 96 bpm. There is a tender, red, wedge-shaped area in the right breast without fluctuance.
hq_q.w: Lactational mastitis is usually caused by beta-lactamase-producing Staphylococcus aureus. When a history of immediate penicillin hypersensitivity (urticaria and angioedema) precludes flucloxacillin, NICE recommends oral erythromycin or clarithromycin while continuing breastfeeding.
hq_q.f: Lactational mastitis in a patient with no penicillin allergy -> oral flucloxacillin for 10 to 14 days.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate oral antibiotic?

c: widespread urticaria and facial angioedema after taking amoxicillin
tm.m: Macrolide antibiotics cover penicillinase-producing Staphylococcus aureus safely in patients with IgE-mediated penicillin allergy during lactation
tm.g: Lactational mastitis with immediate penicillin allergy -> erythromycin (or clarithromycin)
x: Contraindicated due to immediate penicillin anaphylaxis/angioedema and inactivated by staphylococcal beta-lactamase.
Fluoroquinolones have poor Gram-positive activity against Staphylococcus aureus and are avoided during breastfeeding.
First-line treatment for non-allergic lactational mastitis, but strictly contraindicated in immediate penicillin allergy.
Used for uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections rather than staphylococcal lactational mastitis.
f: Acute otitis media or community-acquired pneumonia in a patient with no penicillin allergy
Acute Pseudomonas aeruginosa pyelonephritis in a non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding adult
Lactational mastitis in a breastfeeding mother with no history of penicillin allergy
An uncomplicated Escherichia coli lower urinary tract infection in a non-pregnant woman

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman has noticed small spots of blood inside her bra cup for 3 weeks. The discharge comes from her left nipple spontaneously without squeezing. She has no breast pain.
On examination, gentle pressure at the 3 o'clock margin of the left areola expresses blood-stained fluid from a single duct orifice. There is no palpable mass, skin dimpling or axillary lymphadenopathy.
hq_q.w: Spontaneous blood-stained or serosanguinous discharge from a single lactiferous duct with no palpable mass is most commonly caused by a benign intraductal papilloma. Urgent triple assessment is still mandatory to exclude papillary carcinoma or DCIS.
hq_q.f: Bilateral milky multi-duct discharge with secondary amenorrhoea -> hyperprolactinaemic galactorrhoea.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying cause?

c: spots of blood inside her bra cup
blood-stained fluid from a single duct orifice
tm.m: A benign fibrovascular papillary frond within a large subareolar lactiferous duct ulcerates and bleeds into the lumen
tm.g: Spontaneous bloody discharge from a single duct with no palpable lump -> intraductal papilloma
x: Produces bilateral multi-duct milky discharge accompanied by oligo-amenorrhoea rather than unilateral single-duct bleeding.
Produces thick, green or cheesy discharge from multiple ducts, often with slit-like nipple retraction.
Presents with a unilateral erythematous, scaly, crusted eczematous plaque starting on the nipple apex.
Presents in young smokers with painful periareolar inflammation, subareolar abscesses, and mammillary fistulae.
f: Bilateral milky discharge from multiple ducts with amenorrhoea in a woman taking risperidone
Thick green or creamy multi-duct nipple discharge with slit-like nipple inversion in a 58-year-old woman
A unilateral crusted, scaling, erythematous rash on the nipple apex that fails to respond to topical steroids
A painful, erythematous periareolar swelling in a 32-year-old woman who smokes 20 cigarettes daily

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman has had milky discharge from both nipples for 3 months and secondary amenorrhoea for 6 months. Over the past month she has developed daily frontal headaches. She takes no regular medications and her urine pregnancy test is negative.
Examination shows bilateral multi-duct milky discharge and no breast masses.
Serum prolactin is 4,200 mU/L (100–500); TSH is 1.8 mU/L (0.4–4.5).
o: Computed tomography of the adrenal glands
Ultrasound scan of the thyroid gland
hq_q.w: A serum prolactin above 2,000 mU/L in the absence of pregnancy, hypothyroidism, or dopamine-antagonist drugs is diagnostic of a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the pituitary fossa and formal visual field perimetry are required.
hq_q.f: Unilateral blood-stained single-duct nipple discharge in a 52-year-old -> breast ultrasound and mammography.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

tm.m: A lactotroph pituitary adenoma secretes excess prolactin, suppressing GnRH pulsatility and stimulating lactation
tm.g: Galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, headache, and prolactin >2,000 mU/L -> MRI of the pituitary
x: Bilateral milky discharge is an endocrine disorder rather than primary breast pathology, and mammography is avoided at age 28.
Used to investigate Cushing's syndrome, Conn's syndrome, or phaeochromocytoma, not hyperprolactinaemia.
Assesses optic nerve demyelination in multiple sclerosis, whereas chiasmal compression is assessed by visual field perimetry and pituitary MRI.
Evaluates thyroid nodules rather than pituitary lactotroph adenomas, and her TSH is normal.
f: Unilateral spontaneous blood-stained single-duct nipple discharge in a 55-year-old woman
Resistant hypertension with suppressed renin and elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio
Suspected subclinical optic neuritis in a young adult being investigated for multiple sclerosis
A palpable solitary anterior neck nodule moving on swallowing with normal TSH

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman has had secondary amenorrhoea and bilateral galactorrhoea for 8 months. Her serum prolactin is 3,800 mU/L (100–500) and pituitary MRI confirms an 11 mm prolactinoma confined to the sella with no optic chiasm compression. Confrontation visual fields are full.
She wishes to restore ovulatory menstrual cycles so she can conceive.
hq_q.w: Dopamine D2 receptor agonists (cabergoline or bromocriptine) are first-line medical therapy for both micro- and macroprolactinomas. Cabergoline normalises prolactin, shrinks the tumour, and restores GnRH pulsatility and ovulatory fertility more effectively than bromocriptine.
hq_q.f: Growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma causing acromegaly refractory to surgery -> octreotide.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug treatment?

c: wishes to restore ovulatory menstrual cycles
tm.m: Pituitary lactotrophs are under tonic dopamine D2 inhibition; cabergoline activates D2 receptors to suppress prolactin secretion and shrink lactotroph tumours
tm.g: Symptomatic prolactinoma -> dopamine agonist (cabergoline first line)
x: Typical antipsychotic D2 receptor antagonist that blocks dopamine inhibition and worsens hyperprolactinaemia.
Used for anovulatory infertility in polycystic ovary syndrome, not gonadotrophin suppression from a prolactinoma.
Somatostatin analogue used to treat growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenomas (acromegaly) and carcinoid tumours.
Selective oestrogen receptor modulator used for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer.
f: Drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia in a patient treated with a potent D2 antagonist for acute psychosis
Anovulatory subfertility with oligomenorrhoea, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound
Persistent growth hormone excess and raised IGF-1 following transsphenoidal surgery for acromegaly
Adjuvant endocrine therapy for premenopausal oestrogen receptor-positive breast carcinoma

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman stopped breastfeeding her second child 2 months ago. She has noticed a painless lump beneath her left areola that has remained unchanged in size. She feels systemically well.
Temperature 36.8°C, pulse rate 72 bpm. There is a 3 cm smooth, non-tender, fluctuant subareolar swelling with no overlying erythema.
Ultrasound-guided aspiration yields thick milky fluid and the mass resolves.
hq_q.w: A galactocele is a benign milk-retention cyst caused by obstruction of a lactiferous duct during or shortly after cessation of lactation. It presents as a painless, mobile, fluctuant subareolar lump; needle aspiration of milky fluid is both diagnostic and curative.
hq_q.f: Painful, erythematous, fluctuant breast lump with fever of 38.6°C -> lactational breast abscess.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: stopped breastfeeding her second child 2 months ago
painless lump beneath her left areola
tm.m: Inspissated milk plug obstructs a lactiferous duct after weaning, distending the proximal acinar segment with sterile milk
tm.g: Painless fluctuant breast lump after lactation yielding milky fluid on aspiration -> galactocele
x: Solid rubbery fibroepithelial tumour that does not fluctuate or yield milky fluid on needle aspiration.
Presents with spontaneous blood-stained or serous single-duct nipple discharge rather than a 3 cm milk cyst.
Causes severe throbbing pain, overlying erythema, warmth, and systemic fever, yielding purulent pus on aspiration.
Occurs in women aged 35 to 50 from lobular involution and contains clear straw-coloured or green serous fluid, not milk.
f: A solid, rubbery, highly mobile 2 cm lump in a 22-year-old nulliparous woman
Spontaneous blood-stained discharge from a single duct orifice with no palpable breast lump
A febrile breastfeeding woman with a hot, red, exquisitely tender fluctuant breast swelling
A 47-year-old woman with a tender fluctuant lump that yields clear yellow serous fluid on aspiration

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old woman has noticed a painless lump in her right breast that has been present for over a year without changing in size. She has no family history of breast cancer.
There is a 3 cm soft, doughy, mobile, well-defined lump in the upper inner quadrant, with no skin tethering or axillary lymphadenopathy.
Ultrasound and mammography show a radiolucent, encapsulated fatty lesion.
hq_q.w: A breast lipoma is a benign, slow-growing, encapsulated tumour of mature adipocytes. It feels soft and doughy on palpation and appears radiolucent with a thin capsule on mammography and ultrasound. Triple assessment confirms benignity.
hq_q.f: Hard, irregular, tethered breast mass after a seatbelt injury -> traumatic fat necrosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: present for over a year without changing
3 cm soft, doughy, mobile, well-defined lump
tm.m: Proliferation of mature white adipocytes within a thin fibrous capsule forms a soft, radiolucent subcutaneous breast mass
tm.g: Soft doughy mobile lump with encapsulated radiolucent fat on imaging -> breast lipoma
x: Contains a disorganised mixture of glandular epithelium, fibrous stroma, and fat ('breast within a breast' appearance), not pure fat.
Occurs in young women under 30 as a firm, rubbery solid fibroglandular mass rather than a soft radiolucent fatty lesion.
Presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, lobulated fibroepithelial mass rather than a stable soft fatty lump.
Follows blunt trauma or surgery and forms a hard, irregular mass with skin tethering and oil cysts/calcification.
f: A well-circumscribed breast mass showing mixed fibroglandular and adipose tissue ('breast within a breast') on mammography
A firm, rubbery, mobile 2 cm solid mass in a 20-year-old woman
A 6 cm firm breast mass that has doubled in size over 8 weeks with leaf-like stroma on core biopsy
A hard, irregular lump with skin tethering over an area of previous seatbelt bruising

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old woman underwent wide local excision of a benign breast lesion 3 weeks ago. She now notices a tender, tight line beneath the skin on the lateral aspect of her breast that pulls when she raises her ipsilateral arm.
Temperature 36.9°C. Examination reveals a subcutaneous, tender, cord-like band running vertically along the lateral chest wall, with no erythema, mass or axillary lymphadenopathy.
hq_q.w: Mondor's disease is benign superficial thrombophlebitis of the thoracoepigastric or lateral thoracic vein, often triggered by breast surgery, biopsy, or trauma. It presents as a tender subcutaneous cord that bowstrings on arm elevation and resolves with NSAIDs.
hq_q.f: Diffuse breast erythema, warmth, and peau d'orange skin oedema -> inflammatory breast carcinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: wide local excision of a benign breast lesion 3 weeks ago
pulls when she raises her ipsilateral arm
tm.m: Local endothelial trauma induces thrombosis and perivenous inflammation of the superficial thoracoepigastric vein
tm.g: Tender subcutaneous lateral breast cord accentuating on arm elevation -> Mondor's disease
x: Causes painful red cutaneous streaks spreading towards tender axillary nodes accompanied by systemic fever.
Produces diffuse breast enlargement, erythema, and peau d'orange dermal oedema rather than a linear venous cord.
Causes subareolar inflammation and periareolar abscesses in smokers rather than a lateral thoracoepigastric cord.
Presents as a focal hard, irregular parenchymal lump with skin tethering rather than a linear subcutaneous cord.
f: Fever of 38.5°C with erythematous linear skin streaks tracking from an infected nipple fissure to tender axillary nodes
Rapid onset of diffuse breast redness, warmth, and peau d'orange skin pitting over more than one-third of the breast
A recurrent tender, erythematous swelling at the edge of the areola in a young cigarette smoker
A focal hard, irregular breast mass at the surgical site mimicking carcinoma on palpation

hq_q.s:
A 61 year old woman has had a red, crusted, itchy lesion on her right nipple for 3 months. It has failed to improve after a 4-week trial of topical hydrocortisone butyrate cream prescribed by her GP. She has no history of atopy.
Examination shows a unilateral erythematous, scaling, oozing plaque covering the right nipple apex and extending onto the areola. The left nipple is normal.
o: Allergic contact dermatitis of the breast
hq_q.w: Paget's disease of the nipple is epidermal infiltration by malignant adenocarcinoma cells from underlying ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive breast cancer. It begins on the nipple apex before spreading to the areola and requires urgent punch biopsy.
hq_q.f: Bilateral itchy scaly plaques beginning on the areolae that respond rapidly to topical steroids -> nipple eczema.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: red, crusted, itchy lesion on her right nipple for 3 months
failed to improve after a 4-week trial of topical hydrocortisone
covering the right nipple apex and extending onto the areola
tm.m: Malignant ductal epithelial (Paget) cells migrate up the lactiferous ducts into the nipple epidermis, causing unilateral eczematous ulceration
tm.g: Unilateral crusted lesion starting on the nipple apex and refractory to topical steroids -> Paget's disease of the nipple
x: Affects both breasts symmetrically where clothing or detergent contacts the skin and resolves with allergen avoidance and topical steroids.
Typically bilateral, starts on the areolar skin while sparing the nipple apex, and responds rapidly to moderate topical steroids.
Causes thick green multi-duct discharge and slit-like nipple retraction rather than an ulcerated crusted nipple plaque.
Presents in younger smokers with a tender periareolar inflammatory mass or fistula rather than a scaly nipple plaque.
f: An acute symmetrical itchy vesicular rash across both breasts after wearing a new synthetic lace bra
Bilateral itchy scaling of both areolae sparing the nipple tips in a woman with flexural eczema that clears with topical steroid
Thick greenish nipple discharge and slit-like nipple inversion with intact nipple epidermis
A tender, fluctuant subareolar abscess at the areolar margin in a 30-year-old smoker

hq_q.s:
A 49 year old woman has had a swollen, red and heavy left breast for 3 weeks. She is not breastfeeding, and a 7-day course of oral flucloxacillin has made no difference. She feels systemically well.
Temperature 36.9°C. The left breast is diffusely erythematous, warm and enlarged with orange-peel skin pitting over half the breast and a firm left axillary lymph node.
hq_q.w: Inflammatory breast carcinoma is an aggressive cancer in which malignant emboli obstruct dermal lymphatic vessels, producing rapid diffuse erythema, warmth, and peau d'orange skin oedema over at least one-third of the breast without fever.
hq_q.f: Febrile breastfeeding woman with a tender erythematous wedge that responds to flucloxacillin -> lactational mastitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: 7-day course of oral flucloxacillin has made no difference
orange-peel skin pitting over half the breast
tm.m: Tumour emboli plug the superficial dermal lymphatics, causing cutaneous lymphoedema tethered by Cooper's ligaments (peau d'orange)
tm.g: Afebrile diffuse breast erythema with peau d'orange and axillary node unresponsive to antibiotics -> inflammatory breast carcinoma
x: Presents with systemic fever, rigors, and acute tenderness that responds promptly to beta-lactam antibiotics.
Forms a localised, tender, fluctuant collection rather than diffuse peau d'orange across half the breast with a hard node.
Causes focal subareolar inflammation and nipple retraction in young smokers.
Produces a discrete, firm, irregular mass after trauma rather than diffuse breast erythema and peau d'orange.
f: Acute spreading erythema with fever of 38.7°C and raised inflammatory markers that resolves on flucloxacillin
A localised 3 cm tender, fluctuant periareolar swelling yielding pus on ultrasound-guided aspiration
Recurrent tender periareolar inflammation and mammillary fistula in a 32-year-old cigarette smoker
A focal firm, irregular lump at the site of a previous seatbelt bruise with calcified oil cysts on mammogram

hq_q.s:
A 54 year old woman underwent wide local excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy for a 2 cm invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast. Her last menstrual period was 3 years ago.
Histopathology confirms a grade 2 invasive ductal carcinoma that is oestrogen receptor positive (Allred 8/8) and HER2 negative, with one micrometastatic sentinel node.
hq_q.w: In postmenopausal women with oestrogen receptor-positive invasive breast cancer at medium or high risk of recurrence, an oral aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole, letrozole, or exemestane) is first-line adjuvant endocrine therapy, blocking peripheral conversion of androgens to oestrogen.
hq_q.f: HER2-positive invasive breast carcinoma -> add adjuvant trastuzumab (Herceptin) with cardiac monitoring.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line adjuvant endocrine therapy?

c: last menstrual period was 3 years ago
tm.m: After menopause, peripheral aromatase in adipose tissue is the main source of oestrogen; inhibiting aromatase deprives ER-positive tumour cells of oestrogen
tm.g: Postmenopausal ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer -> aromatase inhibitor monotherapy (anastrozole)
x: Anthracycline cytotoxic chemotherapy agent rather than an endocrine therapy targeting oestrogen signalling.
GnRH agonist that suppresses ovarian function in premenopausal women; postmenopausal ovaries are already quiescent.
Adding ovarian suppression with goserelin is only required in premenopausal women who need an aromatase inhibitor.
Monoclonal antibody against the HER2 receptor, which is ineffective in HER2-negative breast carcinoma.
f: Adjuvant cytotoxic anthracycline chemotherapy for high-risk triple-negative invasive breast cancer
Reversible ovarian function suppression in a premenopausal woman undergoing chemotherapy
High-risk ER-positive breast cancer in a 36-year-old premenopausal woman requiring ovarian suppression plus an aromatase inhibitor
Adjuvant targeted biological therapy for HER2-overexpressing (IHC 3+ or FISH-amplified) invasive breast carcinoma

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old woman attends her GP because she is concerned about her risk of developing breast cancer. Her mother was diagnosed with unilateral breast cancer at age 40 and her sister was diagnosed with breast cancer at age 42. She has no breast symptoms.
Clinical examination of both breasts and axillae is normal.
o: Arrange a single screening mammogram today and reassure
Defer breast screening until she reaches age 50
Refer to a secondary care familial breast clinic
Start oral tamoxifen 20 mg daily in primary care
hq_q.w: Under NICE familial breast cancer guidelines, having two first-degree relatives diagnosed with breast cancer at an average age under 50 places a woman at moderate-to-high risk, warranting referral to a secondary care family history/genetics clinic.
hq_q.f: Single first-degree relative diagnosed with breast cancer over age 40 -> near-population risk; manage in primary care with routine screening from 50.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

c: mother was diagnosed with unilateral breast cancer at age 40
sister was diagnosed with breast cancer at age 42
tm.m: Two first-degree relatives diagnosed with breast cancer at age <=45 indicates high familial risk requiring specialist risk stratification, annual mammography/MRI from 40, and genetic testing
tm.g: Two first-degree relatives with breast cancer under 50 -> refer to a secondary care familial breast clinic
x: A one-off mammogram at 38 neither quantifies her hereditary BRCA risk nor establishes structured annual surveillance.
Risk-reducing surgery is considered only after formal genetic testing, risk calculation, and multidisciplinary counselling.
Women at moderate or high familial risk qualify for annual mammographic surveillance starting from age 40 (or MRI from 30).
Chemoprevention is initiated only after specialist risk stratification confirms high or moderate risk and counsels on thromboembolic risks.
f: A 52-year-old woman attending her routine triennial NHS Breast Screening Programme appointment
A confirmed BRCA1 mutation carrier who has completed genetic counselling and psychological assessment and requests prophylactic surgery
An asymptomatic woman whose only affected relative is a maternal aunt diagnosed with breast cancer at age 68
A premenopausal woman confirmed by a specialist genetics clinic to have high familial breast cancer risk who opts for chemoprevention

hq_q.s:
A 51 year old woman attends her GP after receiving her first routine invitation letter for the NHS Breast Screening Programme. She has no breast symptoms and no family history of breast cancer, and her clinical breast examination is normal.
She is anxious about being recalled to an assessment clinic after her initial screening mammogram.
hq_q.w: In the UK NHS Breast Screening Programme, about 4% of women (1 in 25) are recalled for assessment after a screening mammogram. Roughly three-quarters of those recalled have benign findings, and about 1 in 100 screened has cancer.
hq_q.f: Proportion of screened women actually diagnosed with breast cancer per round -> about 1 in 100 (8 to 9 per 1,000).
hq_q.ql: What proportion of women are recalled for further assessment after an NHS screening mammogram?

c: first routine invitation letter for the NHS Breast Screening Programme
tm.m: Screening mammography has a recall rate of approximately 4% (1 in 25) to maximise sensitivity for early preclinical lesions
tm.g: NHS breast screening mammogram recall rate -> about 1 in 25 (4%)
x: Represents the approximate proportion of screened women found to have breast cancer (around 8 to 9 per 1,000), not the recall rate.
Grossly underestimates the recall rate; 1 in 2,000 is closer to the rate of rare procedural complications.
Overestimates the recall rate fivefold; 1 in 5 (20%) is the approximate proportion of recalled women who turn out to have cancer.
Underestimates the recall rate twentyfold; approximately 1 in 500 women screened has a life saved from breast cancer death.
f: The approximate proportion of women attending NHS breast screening who are diagnosed with breast cancer
The approximate lifetime prevalence of male breast cancer in the general population
The approximate proportion of women recalled to the assessment clinic who are ultimately diagnosed with breast cancer
The approximate population prevalence of a pathogenic BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation in the general UK population

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman is reviewed in the genetics clinic after predictive testing confirms she carries a pathogenic BRCA1 gene mutation, identified after her mother developed high-grade serous ovarian cancer. She has no breast symptoms and clinical breast examination is normal.
She wishes to delay risk-reducing mastectomy until she has completed her family.
hq_q.w: NICE familial breast cancer guidelines recommend annual contrast-enhanced breast MRI surveillance from age 30 to 49 for women who carry a confirmed BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation, because young breast tissue is radiodense and X-ray radiation can induce DNA double-strand breaks.
hq_q.f: Woman aged 40 to 49 at moderate familial risk without a BRCA mutation -> annual X-ray mammography.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate breast imaging surveillance for her now?

tm.m: Contrast-enhanced MRI detects angiogenesis in dense young breast tissue without exposing BRCA-deficient cells to ionising radiation
tm.g: Confirmed BRCA1/BRCA2 carrier aged 30 to 49 -> annual contrast-enhanced breast MRI
x: Waiting until age 50 leaves a BRCA1 carrier unscreened during two decades of very high early-onset breast cancer risk.
Ultrasound has insufficient sensitivity for high-risk screening and a 5-year interval misses rapidly growing BRCA1 tumours.
Population-level triennial screening from 50 is inadequate for a woman with a 65 to 80% lifetime breast cancer risk.
Clinical palpation does not improve survival and misses subclinical early-stage tumours detected by MRI.
f: A woman aged 50 to 69 with a high familial risk profile where annual mammography is offered
Targeted diagnostic evaluation when MRI is contraindicated (such as a non-MRI-conditional metallic implant)
An asymptomatic woman who tests negative for her family's known BRCA1 mutation (true negative)
Routine physical check during pregnancy when contrast-enhanced MRI and mammography are deferred

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old warehouse worker has noticed a lump in his right groin for 2 months. It appears when he stands or lifts heavy boxes and disappears when he lies flat. He has no pain or vomiting.
On standing, there is a soft swelling located above and medial to the right pubic tubercle with a positive cough impulse that reduces easily when supine. Both testes are normal.
hq_q.w: An inguinal hernia emerges through the superficial inguinal ring above and medial to the pubic tubercle, whereas a femoral hernia emerges through the femoral canal below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
hq_q.f: Groin lump located below and lateral to the pubic tubercle -> femoral canal hernia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: appears when he stands or lifts heavy boxes
above and medial to the right pubic tubercle
positive cough impulse that reduces easily
tm.m: Peritoneal sac protrudes through the inguinal canal to exit at the superficial ring superior and medial to the pubic tubercle
tm.g: Reducible groin swelling above and medial to the pubic tubercle -> inguinal canal hernia
x: Protrudes through the femoral ring inferior to the inguinal ligament, lying below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
Forms a firm, discrete, irreducible nodule without an expansile cough impulse.
Sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle with a bluish tinge, a fluid thrill on coughing, and varicose veins.
Forms a fluctuant intrascrotal swelling surrounding the testis that transilluminates brilliantly and you can get above.
f: A firm, irreducible groin lump located below and lateral to the pubic tubercle in an elderly woman
A firm, tender, non-reducible groin nodule with no cough impulse in a patient with a foot infection
A soft, bluish groin swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle with a cough thrill and varicose veins
A painless fluctuant scrotal swelling that transilluminates and has a normal cord palpable above it

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old man attends his GP with a right groin swelling that appears when he lifts weights at the gym. He has no pain.
On examination, the swelling lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle and reduces easily when he lies supine. With the hernia reduced, firm pressure over the midpoint of the inguinal ligament prevents the swelling from reappearing when he coughs.
hq_q.w: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the inguinal canal through the deep inguinal ring (1.5 cm above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels), so digital pressure over the deep ring controls it.
hq_q.f: Hernia bulges forward medial to the finger despite pressure over the deep inguinal ring -> direct inguinal hernia.
hq_q.ql: Which type of hernia is this most likely to be?

c: above and medial to the pubic tubercle
firm pressure over the midpoint of the inguinal ligament
prevents the swelling from reappearing when he coughs
tm.m: Indirect inguinal hernias traverse the deep inguinal ring at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, lateral to the inferior epigastric artery
tm.g: Inguinal hernia controlled by digital pressure over the deep inguinal ring -> indirect inguinal hernia
x: Pushes directly through the posterior wall of Hesselbach's triangle medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, so deep ring pressure fails to control it.
Lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and is not reducible through the deep inguinal ring.
Traverses the obturator foramen in the pelvis without producing a visible groin lump.
Interpolates through the semilunar line at the lateral border of rectus abdominis well above the inguinal ligament.
f: An inguinal swelling that still bulges medially on coughing despite firm pressure over the deep inguinal ring
A groin lump located inferior to the inguinal ligament and below and lateral to the pubic tubercle
Small bowel obstruction and pain radiating down the medial thigh in a thin elderly woman with no groin lump
A tender interparietal swelling at the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle below the arcuate line

hq_q.s:
An 82 year old frail woman has had colicky abdominal pain and bilious vomiting for 2 days. She describes shooting pain down the medial aspect of her right thigh to the knee, worsened by hip extension.
Pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg. The abdomen is distended with no groin lump.
CT shows ileum incarcerated between the pectineus and obturator externus muscles.
hq_q.w: Obturator hernias occur in emaciated elderly women due to loss of protective preperitoneal fat in the obturator canal. Compression of the obturator nerve produces pain radiating down the medial thigh to the knee (Howship-Romberg sign) alongside small bowel obstruction.
hq_q.f: Tender irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle -> femoral hernia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: shooting pain down the medial aspect of her right thigh
incarcerated between the pectineus and obturator externus muscles
tm.m: Loss of pelvic preperitoneal fat allows small bowel to herniate through the rigid obturator canal, compressing the anterior division of the obturator nerve
tm.g: Small bowel obstruction with medial thigh pain (Howship-Romberg sign) and no groin lump in a thin elderly woman -> obturator hernia
x: Produces a palpable, tender lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle rather than herniating between pectineus and obturator externus.
Protrudes through a previous abdominal surgical scar.
Produces a visible swelling above and medial to the pubic tubercle.
Occurs along the lateral border of the rectus sheath in the lower abdominal wall and does not compress the obturator nerve.
f: Small bowel obstruction with a tender, irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle
A reducible or incarcerated bulge protruding through a previous midline laparotomy scar
A groin swelling above and medial to the pubic tubercle extending towards the labium majus
A localized swelling along the semilunar line lateral to the rectus abdominis below the umbilicus

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old man has noticed a painless pulsatile lump behind his right knee for 3 months. He has hypertension and is an ex-smoker.
Pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 138/82 mmHg. There is a 3 cm expansile pulsatile mass in the right popliteal fossa. Distal foot pulses are palpable.
Duplex ultrasound confirms a 2.5 cm right popliteal artery aneurysm.
hq_q.w: Up to 50% of patients with a popliteal artery aneurysm have a synchronous abdominal aortic aneurysm, and around half are bilateral. Ultrasound screening of both the abdominal aorta and the contralateral popliteal artery is mandatory.
hq_q.f: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is found first -> screen both popliteal arteries.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important additional investigation?

c: pulsatile lump behind his right knee
expansile pulsatile mass in the right popliteal fossa
tm.m: Degenerative arterial wall weakness affects multiple large vessels simultaneously, linking popliteal and abdominal aortic aneurysms
tm.g: Confirmed popliteal artery aneurysm -> screen the abdominal aorta with ultrasound
x: Used to investigate transient ischaemic attacks or amaurosis fugax, not synchronous aneurysms in popliteal disease.
Assesses venous reflux or deep vein thrombosis rather than synchronous arterial aneurysm formation.
Used when renovascular hypertension or flash pulmonary oedema is suspected, not routine popliteal aneurysm work-up.
Evaluates cardiac chambers and valves for an embolic source rather than screening for synchronous aortic dilatation.
f: Transient unilateral visual loss (amaurosis fugax) or hemispheric TIA requiring carotid stenosis assessment
Unilateral pitting calf swelling and tenderness where deep vein thrombosis is suspected
Resistant hypertension with a rise in creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor suggesting renal artery stenosis
Acute embolic lower-limb ischaemia in a patient with a new murmur where a cardiac source of emboli is sought

hq_q.s:
A 79 year old man has had sudden severe pain in his right foot for 3 hours. He is known to have a right popliteal artery aneurysm and is awaiting vascular surgical review.
His right foot is cold, pale and mottled. There are no palpable pulses below the right knee. Sensation in the toes is reduced. The left leg is normal.
hq_q.w: Unlike abdominal aortic aneurysms, popliteal artery aneurysms rarely rupture; instead, mural thrombus within the sac acutely occludes the vessel or embolises into the tibial runoff, causing acute limb ischaemia.
hq_q.f: Painful tense swelling in the calf with intact pedal pulses -> ruptured Baker's cyst or deep vein thrombosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?

c: no palpable pulses below the right knee
Sensation in the toes is reduced
tm.m: Turbulent flow within a popliteal aneurysm promotes laminated mural thrombus that acutely occludes or embolises into crural arteries
tm.g: Sudden white, pulseless foot in a known popliteal aneurysm -> acute thrombosis or distal thromboembolism
x: Popliteal aneurysms rarely rupture and rupture causes a tense, expanding, bruised popliteal haematoma rather than isolated distal pallor.
Causes neurogenic claudication on walking that eases with lumbar flexion, with warm feet and intact pulses.
Produces a warm, congested, swollen calf with pitting oedema rather than a cold, pale, pulseless foot.
Causes sudden calf swelling and bruising mimicking DVT in knee arthritis, with preserved pedal pulses.
f: A rapidly expanding, pulsatile haematoma in the popliteal fossa with bruising and haemorrhagic shock
Bilateral leg pain on walking downhill that eases when sitting or leaning forward on a shopping trolley, with normal pulses
Unilateral warm, pitting calf swelling and tenderness after recent immobility with normal arterial pulses
Sudden calf pain and swelling with crescentic ankle bruising below the malleoli in a patient with knee osteoarthritis

hq_q.s:
A 55 year old woman has noticed a swelling behind her right knee for 2 months. It is more obvious when she stands with her knee straight. She has osteoarthritis of both knees.
There is a 4 cm soft, non-tender, non-pulsatile swelling in the medial popliteal fossa. It becomes firmer with the knee extended and softer when flexed (Foucher's sign).
hq_q.w: A Baker's (popliteal) cyst is a distended gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa communicating with the knee joint, strongly associated with knee osteoarthritis. It is non-pulsatile and softens on knee flexion (Foucher's sign).
hq_q.f: An expansile pulsatile mass in the popliteal fossa -> popliteal artery aneurysm.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: non-pulsatile swelling in the medial popliteal fossa
firmer with the knee extended and softer when flexed
tm.m: Synovial effusion from an osteoarthritic knee extrudes posteriorly into the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa
tm.g: Non-pulsatile medial popliteal swelling with knee osteoarthritis that softens on flexion -> Baker's cyst
x: Causes diffuse tender pitting calf swelling rather than a discrete fluctuant medial popliteal cyst that varies with knee flexion.
Produces an expansile, pulsatile mass in the midline of the popliteal fossa rather than a non-pulsatile medial bursa.
Forms a doughy subcutaneous mass whose tension does not change between knee extension and flexion.
Presents as a firm, deep, progressively enlarging mass >5 cm that remains fixed in consistency regardless of knee angle.
f: Diffuse warm, tender, pitting swelling of the entire lower leg after long-haul travel
An expansile pulsatile swelling in the popliteal fossa in an older male smoker
A superficial, lobulated, doughy subcutaneous mass on the thigh that is unchanged by joint movement
A firm, deep, painless mass >5 cm in the thigh enlarging steadily over months

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old man with atrial fibrillation has had pain and coldness in his left foot for 5 hours. He is not taking an anticoagulant.
His left foot is pale and cold with absent pedal pulses. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. Sensation to light touch is normal and he can move his toes and ankle normally. Arterial and venous Doppler signals are audible at the ankle.
hq_q.w: In the Rutherford classification of acute limb ischaemia, a Category I (viable) limb has no sensory loss, no muscle weakness, and audible arterial and venous Doppler signals, allowing urgent imaging before revascularisation.
hq_q.f: Sensory loss beyond the toes with mild motor weakness -> Category IIb immediately threatened.
hq_q.ql: Which Rutherford category of acute limb ischaemia is this?

c: Sensation to light touch is normal
can move his toes and ankle normally
Arterial and venous Doppler signals are audible
tm.m: Rutherford staging grades acute limb threat by sensory deficit, motor deficit, and ankle Doppler signals
tm.g: Intact sensation, normal power, and audible arterial and venous Doppler -> Category I viable
x: Requires minimal sensory loss (restricted to the toes) and inaudible arterial Doppler signals, whereas sensation and arterial Doppler are intact here.
Requires sensory loss extending beyond the toes with rest pain and mild-to-moderate muscle weakness.
Features profound anaesthesia, paralysis with rigor of the calf muscles, and absent arterial and venous Doppler signals.
Describes chronic exertional calf pain relieved by rest rather than a 5-hour history of an acutely pale, pulseless foot.
f: Numbness confined to the toes, normal motor power, and an inaudible arterial Doppler signal with audible venous Doppler
Sensory loss extending proximal to the toes with mild weakness of ankle dorsiflexion
Complete anaesthesia, fixed skin mottling, paralysis of foot movement, and absent arterial and venous Doppler signals
A 6-month history of cramping calf pain after walking 200 metres that resolves within 5 minutes of standing still

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old woman with atrial fibrillation has had sudden severe pain in her right leg for 3 hours. She stopped taking her apixaban a week ago because of nosebleeds.
Her right leg is cold and pale with absent popliteal and pedal pulses. There is mild sensory loss in the toes but no weakness. The vascular team are preparing her for urgent surgical embolectomy.
o: Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel
hq_q.w: Immediate intravenous unfractionated heparin is given in acute limb ischaemia to prevent proximal and distal thrombus propagation in the stagnant arterial tree, and its short half-life allows rapid reversal with protamine during surgery.
hq_q.f: Long-term secondary stroke and embolus prevention after recovery in atrial fibrillation -> oral apixaban.
hq_q.ql: Which drug should be started immediately before theatre?

c: cold and pale with absent popliteal and pedal pulses
preparing her for urgent surgical embolectomy
tm.m: Intravenous unfractionated heparin halts thrombus extension immediately and is titratable and reversible perioperatively
tm.g: Preoperative anticoagulation in acute embolic limb ischaemia -> intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion
x: Oral factor Xa inhibitors cannot be easily titrated or reversed immediately during emergency surgical embolectomy.
Platelet inhibition does not halt fibrin clot propagation in acute cardiogenic arterial thromboembolism.
Systemic intravenous thrombolysis carries a high bleeding risk and is not used when urgent surgical embolectomy is planned.
Warfarin takes days to act and fondaparinux has a long half-life with no specific reversal agent for emergency surgery.
f: Long-term oral anticoagulation after successful embolectomy and haemostasis in non-valvular atrial fibrillation
Secondary prevention following percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent insertion
Massive pulmonary embolism with haemodynamic collapse and systemic hypotension
Subacute venous thromboembolism in a patient with a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia transitioning to warfarin

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man had an embolectomy for an acutely ischaemic left leg 6 hours after symptom onset. Four hours after surgery he develops severe, escalating pain in his left calf that is not relieved by intravenous morphine.
Pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 138/84 mmHg. The calf is swollen and tense, with exquisite pain on passive dorsiflexion of the toes. Pedal pulses are palpable.
hq_q.w: Ischaemia-reperfusion injury after delayed revascularisation causes capillary leak and muscle oedema within inelastic fascial compartments. Pain out of proportion to examination and pain on passive toe stretch mandate emergency four-compartment fasciotomy.
hq_q.f: Loss of previously restored pedal pulses with a cold, white foot -> acute arterial reocclusion.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely postoperative complication?

c: exquisite pain on passive dorsiflexion of the toes
tm.m: Post-ischaemic reperfusion generates oxygen free radicals and capillary permeability, raising intracompartmental pressure above capillary perfusion pressure
tm.g: Tense calf and severe pain on passive toe stretch after limb reperfusion -> acute compartment syndrome
x: Would cause loss of the restored pedal pulses and a cold, pale foot, whereas pedal pulses remain palpable here.
Causes moderate calf ache and pitting oedema over days rather than morphine-resistant pain on passive stretch 4 hours after reperfusion.
Takes days to develop spreading erythema and warmth around the incision, not tense muscle compartments 4 hours postoperatively.
Produces painless motor weakness and sensory loss rather than a tense swollen calf and severe pain on passive stretch.
f: Sudden disappearance of pedal pulses 4 hours after embolectomy with a cold, white, pulseless foot
Unilateral pitting ankle and calf oedema 5 days postoperatively with mild calf tenderness and a soft compartment
Spreading erythema, warmth, and purulent exudate around the groin incision 4 days after surgery with fever
Painless foot drop and numbness over the dorsum of the foot noticed immediately after hip surgery with a soft calf

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man has had cramping pain in his right calf for 6 months. It starts after he walks about 200 metres on the flat and resolves within 5 minutes of standing still. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and has hypertension.
His right pedal pulses are weak and the skin is intact. His right ankle-brachial pressure index is 0.65.
hq_q.w: An ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) between 0.9 and 1.3 is normal, 0.5 to 0.9 indicates mild-to-moderate peripheral arterial disease (intermittent claudication), <0.5 indicates severe/critical ischaemia, and >1.3 indicates arterial calcification.
hq_q.f: ABPI <0.5 with rest pain or gangrene -> critical limb-threatening ischaemia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of his ankle-brachial pressure index?

c: cramping pain in his right calf
tm.m: Haemodynamically significant atherosclerotic stenosis reduces distal systolic ankle pressure relative to brachial pressure
tm.g: ABPI 0.5 to 0.9 with intermittent claudication -> moderate peripheral arterial disease
x: Produces a falsely elevated ABPI above 1.3 (typically in diabetes or chronic kidney disease), not a reduced ratio of 0.65.
Has a normal arterial pressure ratio (0.9 to 1.3) alongside gaiter haemosiderin staining, varicosities, and oedema.
Corresponds to an ABPI below 0.5 accompanied by ischaemic night/rest pain, non-healing ulceration, or gangrene.
Corresponds to a resting ABPI of 0.9 to 1.3 with palpable pedal pulses.
f: An ABPI of 1.45 in a patient with long-standing diabetes and absent pedal pulses
An ABPI of 1.05 in a patient with aching legs, gaiter haemosiderin pigmentation, and varicose veins
An ABPI of 0.35 with nocturnal foot pain relieved by hanging the leg out of bed
An ABPI of 1.10 with strong dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses

hq_q.s:
A 67 year old man has intermittent claudication in his left calf at 300 metres. He has hypertension and stopped smoking a year ago. He takes amlodipine.
His ankle-brachial pressure index is 0.7 on the left. He has no rest pain and no ulcers.
hq_q.w: All people with peripheral arterial disease get high-intensity statin and clopidogrel as secondary prevention. Key discriminator: Every patient with PAD gets a high-intensity statin and clopidogrel.
hq_q.f: He is still limited after exercise → naftidrofuryl can be considered.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is recommended for every patient with this condition?

tm.m: Arterial disease anywhere carries high cardiovascular risk; statins reduce events
tm.g: Every patient with PAD gets a high-intensity statin and clopidogrel
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Cilostazol 100 mg (NICE does not recommend cilostazol for intermittent claudication)
still limited after a supervised exercise programme
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pentoxifylline (NICE does not recommend pentoxifylline for intermittent claudication)
an asymptomatic person in AF with no carotid stenosis
x: NICE does not recommend cilostazol for intermittent claudication
Ruled out here: requires still limited after a supervised exercise programme, whereas this patient has intermittent claudication, year old man has.
NICE does not recommend pentoxifylline for intermittent claudication
Ruled out here: requires an asymptomatic person in AF with no carotid stenosis, whereas this patient has intermittent claudication, year old man has.

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old man has had pain in his right foot at night for 3 weeks. It wakes him and he finds relief by hanging his leg over the side of the bed. He has claudication at 50 metres and smokes.
The right foot is pale when elevated and becomes dusky red when hanging down. There are no palpable pulses below the femoral artery. Capillary refill is 5 seconds.
hq_q.w: Rest pain eased by dependency and dependent rubor show critical ischaemia. Urgent vascular referral is needed.
hq_q.f: Leg pain on walking that eases with sitting and bending forward → spinal stenosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: hanging his leg over the side of the bed
no palpable pulses below the femoral artery
tm.m: At rest the foot is not getting enough blood; gravity helps it
tm.g: Rest pain eased by hanging the leg down with dependent rubor is critical limb ischaemia
f: burning pain in both feet with lost sensation and good pulses
a hot red big toe joint after a heavy meal
leg pain on walking that eases on sitting and bending forward, with good pulses
heel pain worst on the first steps in the morning
x: Ruled out here: requires burning pain in both feet with lost sensation and good pulses, whereas this patient has wakes him, hanging his leg over the side of the bed.
Ruled out here: requires a hot red big toe joint after a heavy meal, whereas this patient has wakes him, hanging his leg over the side of the bed.
Ruled out here: requires leg pain on walking that eases on sitting and bending forward, with good pulses, whereas this patient has wakes him, hanging his leg over the side of the bed.
Ruled out here: requires heel pain worst on the first steps in the morning, whereas this patient has wakes him, hanging his leg over the side of the bed.

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old woman has had an ulcer on her left lower leg for 4 months that causes a dull ache. She had a left deep vein thrombosis 10 years ago.
There is a 5 cm shallow ulcer with agranulating sloughy base just above the medial malleolus. Surrounding skin shows brown haemosiderin pigmentation and eczema. Pedal pulses are palpable and her ABPI is 1.0.
hq_q.w: Venous leg ulcers develop in the medial gaiter area above the malleolus with sloping edges, haemosiderin staining, and stasis eczema secondary to chronic venous hypertension. An ABPI >=0.8 confirms safe application of graduated compression bandaging.
hq_q.f: Deep, painful, punched-out ulcer on the toes or lateral foot with ABPI <0.5 -> arterial ischaemic ulcer.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: left deep vein thrombosis 10 years ago
tm.m: Post-thrombotic valvular incompetence causes sustained ambulatory venous hypertension, capillary fibrin cuffing, and gaiter skin breakdown
tm.g: Shallow medial malleolar ulcer with haemosiderin staining and ABPI 1.0 -> venous hypertension ulcer
x: Produces a deep, punched-out, severely painful ulcer on the toes or pressure points with absent pulses and low ABPI.
Presents as a chronic wound over many years that develops a raised, everted, nodular edge that bleeds on contact.
Occurs as a painless punched-out ulcer surrounded by thick callus over plantar weight-bearing pressure points in peripheral neuropathy.
Starts as a pustule that rapidly expands into a painful ulcer with violaceous, undermined edges, often associated with inflammatory bowel disease.
f: A deep, punched-out, severely painful ulcer on the lateral malleolus and toes with absent pulses and an ABPI of 0.45
A 15-year-old venous ulcer that develops a firm, everted, heaped-up nodular margin and inguinal lymphadenopathy
A painless punched-out ulcer surrounded by thick callus beneath the first metatarsal head with absent monofilament sensation
A rapidly enlarging, exquisitely painful leg ulcer with a purple undermined border in a patient with ulcerative colitis

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old woman has had a shallow ulcer above her right medial malleolus for 3 months, accompanied by haemosiderin staining and pitting ankle oedema. She smokes 15 cigarettes daily and has hypertension.
Her right pedal pulses are diminished. Her right ankle-brachial pressure index is 0.68. The ulcer base is granulating with no surrounding cellulitis.
o: Arrange urgent split-skin grafting to the ulcer
Prescribe oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily
Prescribe potent topical betamethasone to the ulcer bed
Refer to vascular surgery before applying compression
hq_q.w: Full four-layer compression bandaging requires an ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) of at least 0.8. An ABPI below 0.8 indicates concomitant arterial insufficiency (mixed aetiology ulcer), requiring vascular specialist assessment before compression.
hq_q.f: Uncomplicated venous ulcer with an ABPI of 0.95 -> apply four-layer graduated compression bandaging.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

c: shallow ulcer above her right medial malleolus
tm.m: High-pressure elastic compression on an artery with reduced perfusion pressure (ABPI <0.8) precipitates distal skin necrosis and limb loss
tm.g: Venous-pattern leg ulcer with ABPI <0.8 -> refer to vascular surgery before compression
x: Full compression is contraindicated when the ABPI is below 0.8 because it compromises arterial perfusion and risks gangrene.
A skin graft will fail while underlying arterial inflow is impaired and venous hypertension remains uncorrected.
Systemic antibiotics do not promote ulcer healing and are reserved for clinical cellulitis or spreading infection.
Topical corticosteroids applied directly to an ulcer bed impair keratinocyte migration and delay wound healing.
f: A medial malleolar venous ulcer with palpable pedal pulses and an ABPI of 0.95
A clean, well-vascularised post-excisional defect where primary closure is not possible and arterial supply is normal
Spreading erythema, warmth, tenderness, and pyrexia surrounding the leg ulcer indicating acute cellulitis
Severe surrounding varicose stasis eczema on intact peri-ulcer skin or biopsy-confirmed pyoderma gangrenosum

hq_q.s:
A 78 year old man has had a chronic venous ulcer on his right lower leg for 15 years. Over the last 2 months its appearance has changed: the lateral edge has become raised, heaped-up and nodular, and it bleeds easily on dressing changes.
There is a 6 cm ulcer above the medial malleolus with an everted, indurated edge and a firm right inguinal lymph node.
hq_q.w: Marjolin's ulcer is a malignant squamous cell carcinoma arising within a chronic venous ulcer, burn scar, or osteomyelitis sinus. Any chronic ulcer developing heaped-up, everted edges or contact bleeding requires urgent punch or incisional biopsy.
hq_q.f: Rapidly enlarging painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border -> pyoderma gangrenosum.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: chronic venous ulcer on his right lower leg for 15 years
tm.m: Decades of chronic inflammation and epithelial regeneration induce malignant squamous transformation at the wound margin
tm.g: Everted nodular edge and inguinal lymphadenopathy in a long-standing venous ulcer -> Marjolin's squamous carcinoma
x: Causes purulent exudate, spreading cellulitic erythema, and fever rather than a focal everted nodular tumour edge.
Presents on sun-exposed skin as a rapidly growing dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin plug that involutes spontaneously.
Forms a pearly, rolled edge with surface telangiectasia on sun-exposed skin and virtually never metastasises to inguinal nodes.
Develops rapidly with a violaceous, undermined border rather than after 15 years with an everted proliferative edge.
f: Increasing pain, purulent discharge, warm spreading erythema, and pyrexia around the ulcer over 48 hours
A dome-shaped skin nodule with a central keratin-filled crater that grew rapidly over 4 weeks on sun-exposed forearm skin
A slowly enlarging pearly nodule with rolled margins and arborising telangiectasia on the cheek
A rapidly expanding, painful ulcer with a purple, undermined edge in a patient with inflammatory bowel disease

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman has had aching varicose veins in her right leg for 5 years, worse at the end of her shifts as a hairdresser.
There are tortuous varicose veins along the medial thigh and calf. The skin above the right medial malleolus is indurated, tight and brown (lipodermatosclerosis). There is no ulceration and pedal pulses are strong.
o: Computed tomography venography of the pelvis
Plain radiograph of the right tibia and fibula
Venous duplex ultrasound of the lower limb
hq_q.w: Symptomatic varicose veins accompanied by venous skin changes (haemosiderin pigmentation, eczema, or lipodermatosclerosis) warrant vascular referral for venous duplex ultrasound to map superficial junctional reflux and confirm deep vein patency before ablation.
hq_q.f: Diminished pedal pulses or claudication symptoms alongside leg skin changes -> measure ankle-brachial pressure index.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation at the vascular clinic?

c: aching varicose veins in her right leg
tortuous varicose veins along the medial thigh and calf
tm.m: Venous duplex ultrasound locates incompetent superficial valves and confirms deep venous patency prior to endovenous intervention
tm.g: Symptomatic varicose veins with skin changes -> venous duplex ultrasound of the lower limb
x: Reserved for suspected iliac or inferior vena cava obstruction rather than primary superficial saphenous reflux.
Invasive catheter study superseded by non-invasive venous duplex ultrasonography.
Images bone and soft-tissue calcification rather than venous anatomy or valvular reflux.
Used to rule out acute venous thromboembolism in low-probability patients, not to map chronic varicose veins.
f: Suspected May-Thurner iliac vein compression or pelvic venous outflow obstruction
Complex congenital venous malformation requiring intraoperative catheter roadmap venography
Localised bony tenderness and inability to bear weight after an inversion injury of the lower leg
Acute unilateral calf swelling and tenderness with a two-level DVT Wells score of 1

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old woman has aching, heavy legs with prominent varicose veins along her left medial thigh and calf that interfere with her work as a ward nurse. She has no history of deep vein thrombosis.
Venous duplex ultrasound demonstrates truncal reflux at the saphenofemoral junction and along the great saphenous vein, with patent and competent deep veins.
o: Endothermal ablation of the saphenous vein
hq_q.w: NICE recommends endothermal ablation (radiofrequency or endovenous laser ablation) as first-line intervention for confirmed truncal varicose veins with reflux. Ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy is second line, and open surgery is third line.
hq_q.f: Endothermal ablation is unsuitable -> offer ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line definitive treatment?

c: aching, heavy legs with prominent varicose veins
truncal reflux at the saphenofemoral junction
tm.m: Endovenous thermal energy denatures the great saphenous vein endothelium, occluding the refluxing trunk with faster recovery than stripping
tm.g: Confirmed truncal saphenous reflux -> first-line endothermal ablation
x: NICE recommends against offering compression hosiery unless interventional treatment is unsuitable or declined.
Reserved as third-line treatment only when both endothermal ablation and foam sclerotherapy are unsuitable.
Venoactive drugs such as diosmin are not recommended by NICE for the management of varicose veins.
Offered second line only if endothermal ablation is anatomically or clinically unsuitable.
f: Symptomatic varicose veins in pregnancy or where the patient declines all interventional procedures
Confirmed truncal varicose veins where both endothermal ablation and ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy are unsuitable
A patient asking which oral venoactive supplement is not recommended in UK NICE guidance
Tortuous recurrent truncal varicose veins whose anatomy is unsuitable for endothermal catheter passage

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old woman has noticed a soft lump in her right groin that disappears when she lies flat. She has extensive varicose veins down her right medial thigh and calf.
On standing, there is a soft, compressible, bluish swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. It vanishes on lying supine, and coughing produces an impulse with a palpable fluid thrill.
hq_q.w: A saphena varix is a saccular dilatation of the proximal great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction. It sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, has a bluish tinge, empties on lying flat, and gives a cough thrill.
hq_q.f: Firm, tender, irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle -> incarcerated femoral hernia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Valvular incompetence at the saphenofemoral junction dilates the terminal great saphenous vein into a compressible venous sac
tm.g: Bluish compressible groin swelling with cough thrill and varicose veins -> saphena varix
x: Presents with a pulsatile groin mass and systolic bruit, typically after femoral arterial catheterisation.
Also lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, but is firm, non-bluish, irreducible, and lacks a venous thrill.
Forms a firm, discrete, non-compressible nodule that does not empty on lying supine or transmit a cough thrill.
Presents with fever, flank pain, and hip flexion deformity rather than a painless bluish venous varix.
f: A painful, expansile, pulsatile groin mass with a systolic bruit 24 hours after coronary angiography
A firm, tender, irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle with colicky abdominal pain and vomiting
A firm, mobile, tender groin nodule in a patient with an infected ulcer on the ipsilateral foot
Fever, night sweats, and a fluctuant groin swelling with pain on passive hip extension in spinal tuberculosis

hq_q.s:
A 16 year old girl has had painless swelling of both lower legs since menarche 2 years ago, worse by evening. She has had no surgery and has never travelled abroad.
There is firm, non-pitting swelling of both legs extending onto the dorsum of the feet and toes. The skin at the base of her second toe cannot be pinched (Stemmer's sign). Urinalysis is normal.
hq_q.w: Primary lymphoedema arises from congenital lymphatic hypoplasia and most commonly presents around puberty in young women (lymphoedema praecox). Involvement of the dorsum of the feet with a positive Stemmer's sign distinguishes it from lipoedema.
hq_q.f: Symmetrical tender fatty leg swelling that spares the feet (negative Stemmer's sign) -> lipoedema.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: extending onto the dorsum of the feet
tm.m: Congenital hypoplasia of subcutaneous lymphatic collectors causes protein-rich interstitial fluid accumulation and dermal fibrosis from puberty
tm.g: Adolescent-onset non-pitting leg and foot swelling with a positive Stemmer's sign -> primary lymphoedema praecox
x: Causes acute painful, pitting swelling with venous engorgement rather than a 2-year painless non-pitting swelling.
Causes symmetrical tender fat deposition from hips to ankles that strictly spares the feet, giving a negative Stemmer's sign.
Produces soft, pitting oedema with heavy proteinuria on dipstick and hypoalbuminaemia.
Follows pelvic malignancy, lymph node dissection, radiotherapy, or filariasis, none of which are present.
f: Acute painful pitting swelling of both legs with distended superficial veins from inferior vena cava thrombosis
Symmetrical tender, easily bruised fatty swelling of both legs that stops at the malleoli and spares the feet
Periorbital and pitting ankle oedema with 4+ proteinuria on dipstick and serum albumin of 18 g/L
Progressive unilateral leg swelling following inguinal lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for melanoma

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old woman had a left mastectomy and axillary node clearance for breast cancer 2 years ago. She now has persistent swelling of her left arm. She has had one episode of cellulitis in the arm.
The left arm is swollen from the hand to the shoulder, with mild skin thickening. There is no sign of infection. She asks how to stop it getting worse.
o: Rest the arm in a sling all day
hq_q.w: Skin care prevents cellulitis, and compression with exercise and lymphatic massage reduces swelling. Key discriminator: Lymphoedema: skin care and compression garments with exercise.
hq_q.f: She develops a hot red arm → treat cellulitis promptly.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate advice?

c: persistent swelling of her left arm
tm.m: Removed nodes leave lymph pooling; good skin care prevents cellulitis and compression pushes fluid back
