tm.g: Lymphoedema: skin care and compression garments with exercise
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Daily furosemide (Loop diuretics are ineffective for high-protein lymphoedema and only treat fluid overload)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Keep the arm hanging down (Dependent positioning increases hydrostatic pressure and worsens lymphoedema; elevation is advised)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Regular sauna sessions (Extreme heat causes vasodilation and increases lymph production, worsening lymphoedema)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Rest the arm in a sling all day (Immobilisation loses the skeletal muscle pump needed for lymphatic drainage)
x: Loop diuretics are ineffective for high-protein lymphoedema and only treat fluid overload
Dependent positioning increases hydrostatic pressure and worsens lymphoedema; elevation is advised
Extreme heat causes vasodilation and increases lymph production, worsening lymphoedema
Immobilisation loses the skeletal muscle pump needed for lymphatic drainage

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old man moved to the UK from northern Ghana a year ago. He has had progressive swelling of his left leg for several years, punctuated by episodes of fever and painful red streaks ascending the leg.
The left leg is grossly swollen from foot to thigh with hyperkeratotic, warty, fissured skin. He has no history of surgery or malignancy.
hq_q.w: Lymphatic filariasis (chiefly Wuchereria bancrofti, transmitted by mosquitoes) adult worms lodge in afferent lymphatics, causing recurrent febrile lymphangitis and gross elephantiasis. Diagnosis is confirmed by nocturnal thick blood film or circulating filarial antigen.
hq_q.f: Barefoot highland farmer exposed to red volcanic clay soil with negative filarial serology -> podoconiosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying cause?

c: episodes of fever and painful red streaks
grossly swollen from foot to thigh
tm.m: Mosquito-borne Wuchereria bancrofti adult worms obstruct lymphatics and trigger recurrent bacterial adenolymphangitis and elephantiasis
tm.g: Endemic West African exposure with recurrent febrile lymphangitis and elephantiasis -> lymphatic filariasis
x: Autosomal dominant VEGFR-3 mutation presenting at birth with bilateral lower-limb lymphoedema rather than adult-onset tropical elephantiasis.
Causes acute pitting venous oedema and cyanosis without warty hyperkeratosis or recurrent febrile lymphangitis.
Progresses over months in older patients with pelvic cancer and constitutional weight loss.
Occurs in barefoot farmers walking on irritant alkaline volcanic clay in highland East Africa and remains confined below the knee.
f: Non-pitting bilateral lower-limb lymphoedema present from birth with a family history of autosomal dominant inheritance
Acute painful, tense, pitting swelling of the entire left leg after pelvic surgery
Progressive unilateral leg swelling over 3 months with a hard pelvic mass and weight loss
Bilateral below-knee mossy foot swelling in a barefoot farmer from the volcanic highlands of Ethiopia with negative filarial tests

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old woman has had painful colour changes in her fingers in the cold for 5 years. More recently, the skin of her fingers has become tight and she has had difficulty swallowing solid food.
There is sclerodactyly with small calcified nodules on the fingertips. There are telangiectasia on her face and palms. The skin of her forearms and trunk is normal.
hq_q.w: Limited systemic sclerosis, CREST: calcinosis, Raynaud's, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly and telangiectasia. Key discriminator: CREST features with skin changes limited to the hands: anti-centromere.
hq_q.f: Diffuse skin involvement with lung fibrosis → anti-Scl-70.
hq_q.ql: Which antibody is most likely to be positive?

c: skin of her fingers has become tight
tm.m: Limited systemic sclerosis spares the trunk and is linked with anti-centromere antibodies
tm.g: CREST features with skin changes limited to the hands: anti-centromere
f: a malar rash with nephritis
the presentation instead showed features specific to Anti-Jo-1 (Anti-Jo-1 goes with myositis and lung disease, not limited skin thickening with calcinosis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Anti-RNA polymerase III (Anti-RNA polymerase III goes with diffuse systemic sclerosis and renal crisis, not the limited form)
skin thickening of the trunk with lung fibrosis
x: Ruled out here: requires a malar rash with nephritis, whereas this patient has skin of her fingers has become tight, difficulty swallowing solid food.
Anti-Jo-1 goes with myositis and lung disease, not limited skin thickening with calcinosis.
Anti-RNA polymerase III goes with diffuse systemic sclerosis and renal crisis, not the limited form.
Ruled out here: requires skin thickening of the trunk with lung fibrosis, whereas this patient has skin of her fingers has become tight, difficulty swallowing solid food.

hq_q.s:
A 36 year old woman attends her GP with a 4-month history of her fingers turning sharply white, then blue, and then red when exposed to cold weather. She has noticed painful sores at the tips of her right index and middle fingers.
Pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg. Radial pulses are normal, and there are two 3 mm pitted digital tip ulcers.
o: Digital tip ulceration or pitting scars
hq_q.w: Digital ulceration, tissue necrosis, onset after age 30, abnormal nailfold capillaries, or positive autoantibodies indicate secondary Raynaud's phenomenon (such as systemic sclerosis), where structural obliterative microangiopathy causes fixed digital ischaemia.
hq_q.f: Onset at age 18 with symmetrical attacks, normal nailfolds, and no ulcers -> primary Raynaud's phenomenon.
hq_q.ql: Which clinical feature in a patient with Raynaud's phenomenon points to a secondary cause?

c: turning sharply white, then blue, and then red
two 3 mm pitted digital tip ulcers
tm.m: Intimal proliferation and microvascular obliteration in connective tissue disease reduce baseline perfusion enough to ulcerate digital tips
tm.g: Digital tip ulceration or onset over age 30 -> secondary Raynaud's phenomenon
x: Typical of primary vasospastic Raynaud's phenomenon and does not indicate underlying structural vasculopathy.
Cold and emotional stress trigger vasospasm in both primary and secondary Raynaud's phenomenon.
First-degree family history is characteristic of benign primary Raynaud's disease.
Primary Raynaud's classically begins between ages 15 and 30, whereas secondary Raynaud's typically starts after 30.
f: A feature shared by typical primary Raynaud's when no tissue loss or asymmetry is present
The universal precipitating stimulus for both primary and secondary digital vasospasm
A feature supporting benign familial primary Raynaud's phenomenon in a young woman
Typical age of onset for primary idiopathic Raynaud's disease with normal nailfold capillaroscopy

hq_q.s:
A 50 year old man has had mild Raynaud's phenomenon for 10 years. Over the last month his attacks have become much more frequent and painful. He has hypertension and his antihypertensive medication was changed at his clinic review a month ago.
His hands are cool with intact radial pulses. Pulse rate 58 bpm, BP 136/84 mmHg.
hq_q.w: Beta-blockers such as propranolol block vasodilatory beta-2 adrenoreceptors in cutaneous arterioles and reduce cardiac output, leaving alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction unopposed and worsening Raynaud's phenomenon. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers improve it.
hq_q.f: First-line drug treatment to reduce frequency of Raynaud's attacks -> dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (nifedipine or amlodipine).
hq_q.ql: Which drug started last month is most likely to have caused the worsening?

c: attacks have become much more frequent
tm.m: Beta-adrenoreceptor blockade leaves cutaneous alpha-1 vasoconstriction unopposed and reduces digital perfusion pressure
tm.g: Worsening Raynaud's phenomenon with bradycardia (58 bpm) after antihypertensive switch -> beta-blocker (propranolol)
x: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that dilates peripheral arterioles and is used to treat Raynaud's phenomenon.
Thiazide-like diuretic that lowers blood pressure without causing peripheral cutaneous vasoconstriction or bradycardia.
Angiotensin II receptor blocker that reduces systemic vascular resistance and can mildly improve Raynaud's symptoms.
ACE inhibitor that causes arterial vasodilation rather than digital vasospasm or bradycardia.
f: An antihypertensive drug that simultaneously treats Raynaud's vasospasm or causes bilateral ankle oedema
An antihypertensive drug precipitating gout and hyponatraemia in an older patient
Avasodilator antihypertensive used as an alternative when calcium channel blockers are not tolerated in Raynaud's
An antihypertensive causing a persistent dry cough or hyperkalaemia

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old retired farmer has a flat brown patch on his left cheek. It has slowly spread over 10 years and his wife thinks it has darkened recently.
There is a 3 cm flat, irregularly pigmented macule on the left cheek with an irregular edge and several shades of brown. There is no raised area within it. The surrounding skin is sun-damaged. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy.
hq_q.w: Lentigo maligna is melanoma in situ on sun-damaged skin of older people. A raised nodule within it means invasion. Refer under the suspected cancer pathway.
hq_q.f: A stuck-on, warty, greasy lesion → seborrhoeic keratosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: flat brown patch on his left cheek
tm.m: Melanoma in situ spreads slowly along sun-damaged facial skin before invading
tm.g: A slowly enlarging flat irregular pigmented patch on the face of an older person is lentigo maligna
f: rough, scaly patches that feel like sandpaper
a raised nodule appears within it
a stuck-on greasy warty lesion
the presentation instead showed features specific to Superficial spreading melanoma (Superficial spreading melanoma usually affects the trunk or legs of younger adults and has a raised area)
x: Ruled out here: requires rough, scaly patches that feel like sandpaper, whereas this patient has retired farmer, flat brown patch on his left cheek.
Ruled out here: requires a raised nodule appears within it, whereas this patient has retired farmer, flat brown patch on his left cheek.
Ruled out here: requires a stuck-on greasy warty lesion, whereas this patient has retired farmer, flat brown patch on his left cheek.
Superficial spreading melanoma usually affects the trunk or legs of younger adults and has a raised area.

hq_q.s: A 47 year old woman had a changing mole excised from her back. Histology confirms a superficial spreading melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 0.6 mm. She asks what the number means and whether it is good news.
hq_q.w: Breslow thickness, from the granular layer to the deepest tumour cell, is the strongest predictor of outcome.
hq_q.f: Breslow over 1 mm → offer sentinel lymph node biopsy.
hq_q.ql: What does the Breslow thickness measure?

tm.m: The deeper the melanoma has grown, the more likely it has spread
tm.g: Breslow measures depth of invasion
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Distance to the margin (Margin distance is reported separately; Breslow is depth)
asked what the mitotic rate measures
the presentation instead showed features specific to Number of nodes involved (Node involvement is staged separately by sentinel node biopsy)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Width of the lesion (Width does not predict outcome; depth does)
x: Margin distance is reported separately; Breslow is depth.
Ruled out here: requires asked what the mitotic rate measures, whereas this patient has Breslow thickness of 0.6 mm, A 47 year old woman had.
Node involvement is staged separately by sentinel node biopsy.
Width does not predict outcome; depth does.

hq_q.s:
A 50 year old man of Black African family origin has had a dark area under his right big toenail for a year. It has grown and he does not recall any injury.
There is a dark brown longitudinal band under the toenail that widens towards the base, with brown pigment extending onto the proximal nail fold. The nail is not thickened.
hq_q.w: Acral melanoma is the commonest type in people with darker skin. Hutchinson's sign, pigment on the nail fold, is a red flag.
hq_q.f: A dark nail after trauma that grows out with the nail → subungual haematoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: pigment extending onto the proximal nail fold
tm.m: Acral melanoma grows under the nail and spreads onto the fold, Hutchinson's sign
tm.g: A widening dark nail band with pigment on the nail fold is acral lentiginous melanoma
f: a thickened yellow crumbly nail
a bleeding red friable nodule after minor trauma
the presentation instead showed features specific to Subungual glomus tumour (A glomus tumour is a small red-blue spot under the nail that is very painful and cold sensitive)
a dark nail after stubbing the toe that grows out with the nail
x: Ruled out here: requires a thickened yellow crumbly nail, whereas this patient has Black African family origin, widens towards the base.
Ruled out here: requires a bleeding red friable nodule after minor trauma, whereas this patient has Black African family origin, widens towards the base.
A glomus tumour is a small red-blue spot under the nail that is very painful and cold sensitive.
Ruled out here: requires a dark nail after stubbing the toe that grows out with the nail, whereas this patient has Black African family origin, widens towards the base.

hq_q.s:
A 75 year old man has had a slowly growing lump on his upper back for a year. It occasionally bleeds when he dries himself.
There is a 1 cm pearly nodule with rolled edges and telangiectasia on the upper back. There is no lymphadenopathy. Biopsy confirms a nodular basal cell carcinoma.
hq_q.w: Surgical excision with a margin is the standard treatment for most BCCs. It is curative.
hq_q.f: A BCC on the nose near the eye → Mohs micrographic surgery.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Excision with a margin cures most nodular BCCs
tm.g: Nodular BCC on the trunk: surgical excision
f: Genital warts in pregnancy: cryotherapy
a superficial BCC on the chest

the presentation instead showed features specific to Mohs micrographic surgery (Mohs surgery is kept for high-risk BCCs on the central face or recurrent tumours; a nodular BCC on the back is excised with a standard margin)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Watch and wait (Untreated nodular basal cell carcinoma continues to grow and ulcerate locally)
x: Ruled out here: requires Genital warts in pregnancy: cryotherapy, whereas this patient has pearly nodule with rolled edges, nodular basal cell carcinoma.
Ruled out here: requires a superficial BCC on the chest, whereas this patient has pearly nodule with rolled edges, nodular basal cell carcinoma.
Mohs surgery is kept for high-risk BCCs on the central face or recurrent tumours; a nodular BCC on the back is excised with a standard margin.
Untreated nodular basal cell carcinoma continues to grow and ulcerate locally

hq_q.s:
A 65 year old woman has had a pink patch on her chest for a year. It is occasionally itchy but has not responded to an antifungal cream.
There is a 2 cm pink, scaly, flat patch on the upper chest with a fine, thread-like raised edge. There is no ulceration. Biopsy confirms a basal cell carcinoma.
hq_q.w: Superficial BCCs look like scaly patches on the trunk and can be treated with imiquimod, photodynamic therapy or curettage.
hq_q.f: A scar-like waxy plaque with poorly defined edges → morphoeic BCC.
hq_q.ql: Which subtype is it most likely to be?

tm.m: Superficial BCC spreads along the surface of the trunk like a scaly patch
tm.g: A flat scaly pink patch with a thread-like edge on the trunk is superficial BCC
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Infiltrative (Infiltrative BCC is a firm scar-like plaque with poorly defined edges, often on the face)
a scar-like waxy plaque with poorly defined edges
a pearly nodule with rolled edges
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pigmented (Pigmented BCC contains brown or black areas; this patch is pink)
x: Infiltrative BCC is a firm scar-like plaque with poorly defined edges, often on the face.
Ruled out here: requires a scar-like waxy plaque with poorly defined edges, whereas this patient has pink, scaly, flat patch, fine, thread-like raised edge.
Ruled out here: requires a pearly nodule with rolled edges, whereas this patient has pink, scaly, flat patch, fine, thread-like raised edge.
Pigmented BCC contains brown or black areas; this patch is pink.

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old woman has had a basal cell carcinoma diagnosed on biopsy of a pearly nodule on her nose. She has been referred routinely to dermatology for excision.
Her daughter asks whether it can spread to other organs.
o: They grow locally and rarely spread
They spread to lymph nodes early
hq_q.w: BCCs invade locally and can destroy tissue, but metastasis is very rare. Routine referral is fine for most.
hq_q.f: A BCC near the eye that grows fast → urgent referral.
hq_q.ql: Which statement best describes how this cancer behaves?

tm.m: BCC invades and destroys tissue locally but almost never metastasises
tm.g: BCC grows locally and rarely spreads
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to They become melanoma (Basal cell carcinoma arises from keratinocytes and never transforms into melanocytic melanoma)
the presentation instead showed features specific to They often metastasise to lung (Basal cell carcinoma metastasis is exceedingly rare (<0.1%))
the presentation instead showed features specific to They regress after 1 year (BCCs do not regress; they slowly enlarge and can erode deeply if left)
asked how melanoma behaves
x: Basal cell carcinoma arises from keratinocytes and never transforms into melanocytic melanoma
Basal cell carcinoma metastasis is exceedingly rare (<0.1%)
BCCs do not regress; they slowly enlarge and can erode deeply if left.
Ruled out here: requires asked how melanoma behaves, whereas this patient has basal cell carcinoma, spread to other organs.

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old retired builder has a lump on the back of his left hand. It appeared 6 weeks ago and has grown rapidly. It is not painful.

A 30 year old man has had painful, swollen fingers for 4 months, mainly at the end joints. He has had scaly patches in his scalp for years.

hq_q.w: Psoriatic arthritis can affect the DIP joints, with nail changes and skin plaques. Key discriminator: DIP arthritis with nail pitting and psoriasis is psoriatic arthritis.
hq_q.f: Arthritis with urethritis and conjunctivitis → reactive arthritis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Psoriatic inflammation involves the entheses and nail bed next to the DIP joints
tm.g: DIP arthritis with nail pitting and psoriasis is psoriatic arthritis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Gout (Classic picture: Gout crystals vs CPPD crystals)
bony DIP swellings in an older woman with no psoriasis
arthritis with urethritis and conjunctivitis after an infection
symmetrical MCP and wrist swelling with long morning stiffness
x: Classic picture: Gout crystals vs CPPD crystals
Ruled out here: requires bony DIP swellings in an older woman with no psoriasis, whereas this patient has end joints, scaly patches in his scalp.
Ruled out here: requires arthritis with urethritis and conjunctivitis after an infection, whereas this patient has end joints, scaly patches in his scalp.
Ruled out here: requires symmetrical MCP and wrist swelling with long morning stiffness, whereas this patient has end joints, scaly patches in his scalp.

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old woman with chronic plaque psoriasis has had a severe flare over the last month. Her psoriasis had been well controlled with topical treatment for years. A new medicine was started by her psychiatrist 6 weeks ago.
There are widespread red, scaly plaques on the trunk and limbs.
hq_q.w: Lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials and NSAIDs can worsen psoriasis. Stopping steroids can cause flares. Key discriminator: Psoriasis flare after a psychiatric drug: lithium.
hq_q.f: Rapid flare after oral steroids stop → pustular psoriasis.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most likely to have caused the flare?

c: well controlled with topical treatment for years
new medicine was started by her psychiatrist
tm.m: Lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials and NSAIDs can flare psoriasis
tm.g: Psoriasis flare after a psychiatric drug: lithium
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amlodipine (Amlodipine is not a recognised psoriasis trigger and was not started by a psychiatrist)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Omeprazole (Omeprazole does not flare psoriasis)
NSAIDs contraindicated by a stomach ulcer, and he needs a weak opioid
Concurrent prescription of systemic fusidic acid or clarithromycin therapy
x: Amlodipine is not a recognised psoriasis trigger and was not started by a psychiatrist.
Omeprazole does not flare psoriasis.

Ruled out here: requires NSAIDs contraindicated by a stomach ulcer, and he needs a weak opioid, whereas this patient has well controlled with topical treatment for years, new medicine was started by her psychiatrist.

Ruled out here: requires Concurrent prescription of systemic fusidic acid or clarithromycin therapy, whereas this patient has well controlled with topical treatment for years, new medicine was started by her psychiatrist.

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old man has developed a widespread rash over 1 week. He had a sore throat 2 weeks ago that got better without treatment.
There are dozens of small, droplet-shaped, red, scaly papules and plaques over the trunk and upper limbs. The palms, soles and mouth are spared.
hq_q.w: Guttate psoriasis follows a strep throat. It often settles in weeks to months. UVB helps.
hq_q.f: A herald patch then oval patches → pityriasis rosea.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: A strep infection triggers many small psoriasis plaques at once
tm.g: Droplet scaly papules after a sore throat is guttate psoriasis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Chronic plaque psoriasis (Chronic plaque psoriasis gives fewer, larger plaques on elbows and knees, not dozens of small drops after a sore throat)
red scaly skin over 90% of the body
a herald patch then oval patches along skin lines
widespread sterile pustules after stopping steroids
x: Chronic plaque psoriasis gives fewer, larger plaques on elbows and knees, not dozens of small drops after a sore throat.
Ruled out here: requires red scaly skin over 90% of the body, whereas this patient has sore throat 2 weeks ago, droplet-shaped, red, scaly papules.
Ruled out here: requires a herald patch then oval patches along skin lines, whereas this patient has sore throat 2 weeks ago, droplet-shaped, red, scaly papules.
Ruled out here: requires widespread sterile pustules after stopping steroids, whereas this patient has sore throat 2 weeks ago, droplet-shaped, red, scaly papules.

hq_q.s:
A 23 year old woman has had acne since age 15. She has tried topical treatments and 2 courses of oral lymecycline with topical treatment, with little benefit.
There are multiple inflamed nodules and cysts on the face, chest and back with atrophic and hypertrophic scarring. She is distressed by her appearance.
hq_q.w: Severe acne with scarring needs specialist oral isotretinoin. Pregnancy must be prevented. Key discriminator: Scarring nodulocystic acne after failed antibiotics: refer for isotretinoin.
hq_q.f: Mild acne → topical adapalene with benzoyl peroxide.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Isotretinoin shrinks sebaceous glands and is the only drug that changes severe acne long term
tm.g: Scarring nodulocystic acne after failed antibiotics: refer for isotretinoin
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Combined pill (A combined pill helps hormonal acne in women but will not control scarring nodulocystic disease after 2 failed courses)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral doxycycline for a year (Oral antibiotics for acne should not be continued beyond 3 to 6 months)
mild comedonal acne
the presentation instead showed features specific to Topical clindamycin (Topical antibiotic monotherapy promotes bacterial resistance and is ineffective in cystic acne)
x: A combined pill helps hormonal acne in women but will not control scarring nodulocystic disease after 2 failed courses.
Oral antibiotics for acne should not be continued beyond 3 to 6 months
Ruled out here: requires mild comedonal acne, whereas this patient has 2 courses of oral lymecycline, nodules and cysts.
Topical antibiotic monotherapy promotes bacterial resistance and is ineffective in cystic acne

hq_q.s: A 19 year old woman has started oral isotretinoin for severe nodulocystic acne under a dermatologist. She is sexually active. She asks which monitoring and precautions matter most.
hq_q.w: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic. A pregnancy prevention programme is required. Key discriminator: Isotretinoin: pregnancy prevention matters most.
hq_q.f: Low mood on isotretinoin → stop and refer.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important safety measure?

tm.m: Isotretinoin causes severe birth defects
tm.g: Isotretinoin: pregnancy prevention matters most
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Avoid all dairy (Isotretinoin is better absorbed with food and dairy is not contraindicated)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Monthly ECG (Isotretinoin does not affect heart rhythm, so a monthly ECG is not needed)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Monthly hearing tests (Hearing loss is not a key isotretinoin risk)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Weekly kidney tests (Kidney tests are not part of routine isotretinoin monitoring; lipids and liver tests are)
x: Isotretinoin is better absorbed with food and dairy is not contraindicated
Isotretinoin does not affect heart rhythm, so a monthly ECG is not needed.
Hearing loss is not a key isotretinoin risk.
Kidney tests are not part of routine isotretinoin monitoring; lipids and liver tests are.

hq_q.s:
A 17 year old boy has had acne for a year. He has not tried any treatment.
There are many open and closed comedones on the forehead and cheeks, with about 15 inflamed papules and pustules. There are no nodules, cysts or scars.
hq_q.w: A topical retinoid with benzoyl peroxide, or a fixed combination with clindamycin, for 12 weeks.
hq_q.f: No response → add oral lymecycline with topical treatment.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate topical treatment?

tm.m: Retinoids unblock pores and benzoyl peroxide kills bacteria without resistance
tm.g: Mild to moderate acne: adapalene with benzoyl peroxide
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Clotrimazole 1% cream (Clotrimazole is an antifungal and does nothing for acne)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fusidic acid cream (Fusidic acid alone breeds resistant bacteria and does not treat comedones)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hydrocortisone 1% cream twice daily (Topical corticosteroids cause steroid acne and perioral dermatitis on the face)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Mupirocin ointment (Mupirocin treats MRSA carriage and impetigo, not acne)
x: Clotrimazole is an antifungal and does nothing for acne.
Fusidic acid alone breeds resistant bacteria and does not treat comedones.
Topical corticosteroids cause steroid acne and perioral dermatitis on the face
Mupirocin treats MRSA carriage and impetigo, not acne.

hq_q.s:
A 40 year old man has a lump on his forearm.
It is a raised, firm, solid lesion measuring 1.5 cm across that can be felt in the deeper layers of the skin. It contains no fluid.
hq_q.w: A nodule is a raised solid lesion over 1 cm, palpable deep in the skin. A papule is under 1 cm.
hq_q.f: A raised fluid-filled lesion under 1 cm → vesicle.
hq_q.ql: Which term best describes this lesion?

tm.m: Lesions are named by size, depth and whether they hold fluid
tm.g: A solid raised lesion over 1 cm felt deep in the skin is a nodule
f: a flat change in colour only
a solid raised lesion under 1 cm
a flat-topped raised area wider than 1 cm but not deep
a fluid blister under 0.5 cm
x: Ruled out here: requires a flat change in colour only, whereas this patient has 1.5 cm, deeper layers of the skin.
Ruled out here: requires a solid raised lesion under 1 cm, whereas this patient has 1.5 cm, deeper layers of the skin.
Ruled out here: requires a flat-topped raised area wider than 1 cm but not deep, whereas this patient has 1.5 cm, deeper layers of the skin.
Ruled out here: requires a fluid blister under 0.5 cm, whereas this patient has 1.5 cm, deeper layers of the skin.

hq_q.s:
A 44 year old woman has been admitted with toxic epidermal necrolysis affecting 40% of her body surface area after starting a new medicine. She is being transferred to a burns unit.
Temperature 35.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 96/58 mmHg. Large areas of skin have detached, leaving raw, weeping dermis.
hq_q.w: Loss of the skin barrier causes heat loss, fluid and protein loss and infection. Key discriminator: Acute skin failure: hypothermia and fluid loss.
hq_q.f: Many patients need burns unit care.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important risk from acute skin failure?

tm.m: Without the skin barrier, heat, fluid and protein escape and infection gets in
tm.g: Acute skin failure: hypothermia and fluid loss
f: an adjusted calcium of 3.2 with confusion
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hyperglycaemia and ketosis (Ketosis is not a feature of skin failure; heat and fluid escape through the raw dermis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hypertension and oedema (Massive trans-epidermal fluid loss causes hypovolaemic hypotension rather than hypertension)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Polycythaemia (Fluid loss concentrates the blood slightly but polycythaemia is not the danger; shock and hypothermia are)
x: Ruled out here: requires an adjusted calcium of 3.2 with confusion, whereas this patient has 40% of her body surface area, 35.6°C.
Ketosis is not a feature of skin failure; heat and fluid escape through the raw dermis.
Massive trans-epidermal fluid loss causes hypovolaemic hypotension rather than hypertension
Fluid loss concentrates the blood slightly but polycythaemia is not the danger; shock and hypothermia are.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman started carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia 2 weeks ago. She now has a painful widespread rash, sore eyes and mouth ulcers.
Temperature 38.8°C, pulse rate 112 bpm. There are dusky red patches with flaccid blisters over 35% of her body. The skin peels away with gentle lateral pressure. There are erosions on the lips and buccal mucosa.
hq_q.w: TEN: skin detachment over 30% of the body, linked to drugs such as carbamazepine and allopurinol.
hq_q.f: Skin detachment under 10% → Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: peels away with gentle lateral pressure
erosions on the lips and buccal mucosa
tm.m: A drug reaction kills keratinocytes so the epidermis sloughs off with mucosal erosions
tm.g: Drug-triggered detachment over 30% with mucosal erosions is TEN
f: tense blisters without mucosal erosions in an older person
target lesions after a cold sore
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pemphigus vulgaris (Classic picture: Flaccid blisters + mouth erosions + Nikolsky positive)
a febrile young child with no mucosal erosions
x: Ruled out here: requires tense blisters without mucosal erosions in an older person, whereas this patient has carbamazepine, over 35% of her body.
Ruled out here: requires target lesions after a cold sore, whereas this patient has carbamazepine, over 35% of her body.
Classic picture: Flaccid blisters + mouth erosions + Nikolsky positive
Ruled out here: requires a febrile young child with no mucosal erosions, whereas this patient has carbamazepine, over 35% of her body.

hq_q.s: A 49 year old man attends his general practice for an NHS Health Check. He feels well and denies polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision or unintentional weight loss. His father was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at the age of 58. On examination, his BMI is 31 kg/m2, blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg and waist circumference is 104 cm.
hq_q.w: An HbA1c between 42 and 47 mmol/mol defines non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (prediabetes) under NICE guidance. Patients should be offered an intensive lifestyle modification programme (such as the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme) and an annual HbA1c review. Impaired glucose tolerance and impaired fasting glycaemia can only be diagnosed using fasting or 2-hour oral glucose tolerance plasma glucose values.
hq_q.f: HbA1c of 49 on two tests → type 2 diabetes.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Peripheral insulin resistance in central adiposity -> mild chronic hyperglycaemia below the microvascular threshold -> HbA1c 42 to 47 mmol/mol
tm.g: Asymptomatic adult with HbA1c 42 to 47 mmol/mol = non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (offer lifestyle programme + annual HbA1c)
x: Diagnosed by a fasting venous plasma glucose of 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L rather than an HbA1c measurement
Requires a 2-hour post-75 g oral glucose tolerance test plasma glucose between 7.8 and 11.0 mmol/L
Presents with acute osmotic symptoms, weight loss and ketonaemia from autoimmune beta-cell destruction
Requires an HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol or above (confirmed on a second test when asymptomatic)
f: fasting venous plasma glucose of 6.4 mmol/L with a normal 2-hour post-load glucose
75 g oral glucose tolerance test showing a 2-hour venous plasma glucose of 9.2 mmol/L
19 year old with 3 weeks of polyuria, 6 kg weight loss, capillary glucose 22 mmol/L and blood ketones 3.8 mmol/L
repeat HbA1c of 51 mmol/mol 4 weeks later in this asymptomatic patient

hq_q.s: A 56 year old man attends the diabetes clinic for annual review. He has had type 2 diabetes for 6 years and was admitted with decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction 3 months ago. He takes metformin 1 g twice daily, ramipril, bisoprolol and furosemide. His blood pressure is 124/76 mmHg, pulse is 68 bpm and chest is clear. HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol and eGFR is 64 mL/min/1.73 m2.
hq_q.w: NICE NG28 recommends adding an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit (such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin) alongside metformin in any patient with type 2 diabetes and chronic heart failure or established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. SGLT2 inhibitors promote natriuresis and osmotic diuresis, lowering cardiac preload and reducing heart failure hospitalisations. Pioglitazone causes fluid retention and is contraindicated in heart failure.
hq_q.f: Weight is the main issue with no cardiac disease → a GLP-1 agonist may be considered later.
hq_q.ql: Which drug should be added next?

c: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
tm.m: Proximal tubular SGLT2 blockade -> glycosuria and natriuresis -> reduced ventricular preload and tubular hyperfiltration -> lower heart failure hospitalisation
tm.g: Type 2 diabetes + chronic heart failure or established CVD on metformin = add an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin)
x: Sulfonylureas promote weight gain and hypoglycaemia and provide no prognostic benefit in heart failure
Basal insulin causes weight gain and sodium retention and is reserved for severe symptomatic hyperglycaemia or later-line escalation
Thiazolidinediones increase renal sodium reabsorption, precipitating pulmonary oedema, and are contraindicated in any history of heart failure
DPP-4 inhibitors are cardiovascularly neutral and do not reduce heart failure hospitalisations
f: acute symptomatic hyperglycaemia triggered by a 2-week course of high-dose oral prednisolone
marked catabolic weight loss, polyuria and an HbA1c of 98 mmol/mol despite dual oral therapy
biopsy-proven non-alcoholic steatohepatitis in a patient without heart failure, bladder cancer or osteoporotic fractures
frail 84 year old with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m2) needing a simple weight-neutral agent without hypoglycaemia risk

hq_q.s: A 61 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with 2 days of nausea, vomiting and diffuse abdominal pain following viral gastroenteritis. She has type 2 diabetes and continued taking metformin and dapagliflozin despite eating very little. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse is 112 bpm, blood pressure is 104/66 mmHg and respiratory rate is 26 breaths/min. Her mucous membranes are dry and her abdomen is soft.
hq_q.w: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin) lower plasma glucose by increasing renal glucose excretion, while elevating the glucagon-to-insulin ratio and stimulating hepatic ketogenesis during fasting, dehydration or intercurrent illness. Consequently, diabetic ketoacidosis develops with a near-normal blood glucose (<14 mmol/L). Patients must be counselled on sick-day rules to suspend SGLT2 inhibitors during acute dehydrating illness.
hq_q.f: Glucose of 40 with no ketones and high osmolality → hyperosmolar state.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Persistent urinary glucose loss via SGLT2 inhibition during starvation -> suppressed insulin and raised glucagon -> unrestrained hepatic beta-oxidation and ketonaemia with near-normal blood glucose
tm.g: High blood ketones (>3.0 mmol/L) + metabolic acidosis + near-normal glucose (<14 mmol/L) on an SGLT2 inhibitor = euglycaemic DKA
x: Presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and a serum amylase or lipase over three times the upper limit of normal
Characterised by extreme hyperglycaemia (>30 mmol/L) and serum osmolality (>320 mOsm/kg) without significant ketonaemia or acidosis
Produces a high-anion-gap acidosis driven by lactate (>5 mmol/L) in severe renal impairment or tissue hypoxia, with normal blood ketones
Uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis does not explain Kussmaul tachypnoea, blood ketones of 4.2 mmol/L and venous pH of 7.21
f: severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with a serum lipase four times the upper limit of normal
blood glucose of 42 mmol/L, serum osmolality of 358 mOsm/kg, pH 7.36 and blood ketones of 0.4 mmol/L
eGFR of 14 mL/min/1.73 m2, serum lactate of 8.4 mmol/L, pH 7.18 and blood ketones of 0.5 mmol/L
normal venous pH of 7.41, bicarbonate of 24 mmol/L and capillary ketones of 0.3 mmol/L

hq_q.s: A 24 year old woman with type 1 diabetes was admitted to the Acute Medical Unit 1 hour ago with diabetic ketoacidosis after missing her basal insulin. She is receiving intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride and a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour. Her capillary blood ketones were 5.0 mmol/L on admission and are now 4.6 mmol/L. The bedside nurse asks what hourly rate of ketone reduction is required.
hq_q.w: Joint British Diabetes Societies (JBDS) guidelines specify three hourly metabolic targets during fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion for DKA: capillary blood ketones should fall by at least 0.5 mmol/L/hour, venous bicarbonate should rise by at least 3.0 mmol/L/hour, and capillary blood glucose should fall by at least 3.0 mmol/L/hour. If these targets are not achieved, pump lines are checked and the insulin infusion rate is increased by 1.0 unit/hour.
hq_q.f: Ketones fall too slowly → increase the insulin infusion rate.
hq_q.ql: What is the minimum target fall in blood ketones per hour during treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis?

tm.m: Continuous weight-based IV insulin suppresses hormone-sensitive lipase -> halts free fatty acid delivery to the liver -> blood ketones clear by at least 0.5 mmol/L/hour
tm.g: DKA hourly metabolic targets: ketones down >=0.5 mmol/L/h, bicarbonate up >=3.0 mmol/L/h, glucose down >=3.0 mmol/L/h
x: Represents an inadequate clearance rate (0.1 mmol/L/hour) that requires increasing the fixed-rate insulin infusion by 1 unit/hour
Below the JBDS minimum threshold of 0.5 mmol/L/hour needed to confirm suppression of ketogenesis
Exceeds the standard minimum hourly ketone reduction threshold of 0.5 mmol/L/hour
Represents the hourly target reduction for capillary blood glucose (or hourly rise in venous bicarbonate), not blood ketones
f: hourly increment (in units/hour by which the insulin infusion is stepped up when ketones fail to clear) divided by ten
weight-based fixed-rate IV insulin dose in units/kg/hour multiplied by two
capillary blood ketone threshold in mmol/L above which DKA ketonaemia is defined at presentation (divided by two)
minimum target hourly fall in capillary blood glucose (or hourly rise in venous bicarbonate) during DKA treatment

hq_q.s: A 22 year old man with type 1 diabetes is 2 hours into treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis on the Acute Medical Unit. He is receiving a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour alongside intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride. He is alert and passing 60 mL/hour of urine via a catheter. His pulse is 98 bpm and blood pressure is 116/72 mmHg. Repeat venous blood gas findings are shown.
o: Add 40 mmol/L potassium chloride to the next fluid bag
Halve the fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion
Stop the intravenous insulin infusion for 1 hour
hq_q.w: Insulin activates the Na+/K+-ATPase pump, driving potassium rapidly into cells and causing serum potassium to fall during DKA resuscitation. Once serum potassium is between 3.5 and 5.5 mmol/L and urine output is confirmed, 40 mmol/L potassium chloride must be added to the subsequent bags of intravenous fluid. Insulin is only temporarily withheld if serum potassium falls below 3.5 mmol/L while urgent senior-supervised replacement is given.
hq_q.f: Potassium above 5.5 → no potassium added to that bag.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate change to his management?

tm.m: Insulin stimulates cellular Na+/K+-ATPase uptake -> extracellular K+ falls as acidosis corrects -> add 40 mmol/L KCl once K+ is 3.5 to 5.5 mmol/L and passing urine
tm.g: DKA fluid potassium rule: K+ >5.5 = nil; K+ 3.5 to 5.5 (and passing urine) = 40 mmol/L; K+ <3.5 = pause insulin and get senior help
x: Routine intravenous bicarbonate causes paradoxical CSF acidosis, hypokalaemia and impaired tissue oxygen unloading
Oral potassium absorption is unpredictable during acute DKA with gastroparesis and nausea; intravenous replacement is mandatory
The insulin infusion rate must remain at 0.1 units/kg/hour until ketonaemia resolves (<0.6 mmol/L)
Stopping the insulin infusion when potassium is above 3.5 mmol/L rapidly restarts lipolysis and worsens ketoacidosis
f: refractory shock with arterial pH below 6.9 despite fluid resuscitation under intensive care supervision
mild asymptomatic hypokalaemia (K+ 3.2 mmol/L) in a stable outpatient taking bendroflumethiazide
capillary blood glucose falling below 14 mmol/L when ketones are still 2.4 mmol/L and 10% glucose is started alongside saline
repeat venous blood gas showing a serum potassium of 3.1 mmol/L before potassium replacement has been started

hq_q.s: A 30 year old man with type 1 diabetes has been on a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion and 0.9% saline for diabetic ketoacidosis for 6 hours. He is improving clinically.
hq_q.w: Once glucose is below 14, add 10% glucose so the insulin can clear ketones without hypoglycaemia.
hq_q.f: Ketones below 0.6 and eating → switch to subcutaneous insulin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate change?

tm.m: Insulin is still needed to clear ketones; glucose stops it causing hypoglycaemia
tm.g: Glucose under 14 with ketones still high: add 10% glucose and keep the insulin
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Give IV sodium bicarbonate (Sodium bicarbonate is not indicated for routine DKA acidosis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Increase the saline rate (More saline does not stop the glucose falling while ketones are still high; add glucose so insulin can continue)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Stop the insulin infusion (Stopping insulin before ketonaemia resolves will rapidly restart ketoacidosis)
ketones under 0.6, pH normal and eating
x: Sodium bicarbonate is not indicated for routine DKA acidosis
More saline does not stop the glucose falling while ketones are still high; add glucose so insulin can continue.
Stopping insulin before ketonaemia resolves will rapidly restart ketoacidosis
Ruled out here: requires ketones under 0.6, pH normal and eating, whereas this patient has year old man with, 1 diabetes has been.

hq_q.s: A 76 year old man with type 2 diabetes is brought to the Emergency Department after 4 days of progressive drowsiness, polyuria and intense thirst. He lives alone and has had a productive cough for a week. On examination, his mucous membranes are parched, pulse is 112 bpm, blood pressure is 102/60 mmHg and capillary refill time is 4 seconds. Laboratory results from admission are shown.
hq_q.w: Calculated serum osmolality in UK SI units (mmol/L) is given by the formula: 2 x [Na+] + [glucose] + [urea]. Substituting his values gives (2 x 148) + 40 + 30 = 296 + 40 + 30 = 366 mOsm/kg. A calculated serum osmolality of 320 mOsm/kg or greater, accompanied by marked hyperglycaemia (>=30 mmol/L) and absence of significant ketonaemia (<3.0 mmol/L) or acidosis (pH >7.30), confirms hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS).
hq_q.f: Sodium 140, glucose 10, urea 5 → 295, normal.
hq_q.ql: What is his calculated serum osmolality?

tm.m: Serum osmolality = 2(Na) + glucose + urea -> (2 x 148) + 40 + 30 = 366 mOsm/kg
tm.g: HHS osmolality formula: 2(Na) + glucose + urea (threshold >=320 mOsm/kg)
x: Calculated by doubling serum sodium (2 x 148) alone while omitting both glucose and urea
Calculated by doubling serum sodium and adding urea (296 + 30) while omitting the 40 mmol/L glucose contribution
Represents the effective osmolality (2 x Na + glucose = 296 + 40), which excludes freely diffusible urea
Results from mistakenly doubling plasma glucose as well as sodium
f: contribution of sodium and its accompanying anions alone (2 x Na)
patient with sodium 148 mmol/L, urea 20 mmol/L and normal plasma glucose of 10 mmol/L
calculated effective osmolality (tonicity) using 2(Na) + glucose without urea
patient with sodium 158 mmol/L, glucose 55 mmol/L and urea 35 mmol/L

hq_q.s: An 80 year old man was admitted 8 hours ago with hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state secondary to urosepsis and has been resuscitated with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride alone. He is now more alert and passing 70 mL/hour of urine. His plasma glucose has fallen from 52 to 34 mmol/L, his serum sodium has risen from 148 to 151 mmol/L, and his calculated osmolality has fallen from 362 to 352 mOsm/kg.
o: Expected shift of water back into cells
hq_q.w: During early fluid resuscitation of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS), falling extracellular glucose reduces extracellular osmotic pull, allowing water to move back into the intracellular compartment. This concentrates extracellular sodium, causing an expected transient rise in measured serum sodium (typically ~2.4 mmol/L for every 5.5 mmol/L fall in glucose). Provided calculated total serum osmolality is declining steadily (target 3 to 8 mOsm/kg/hour), 0.9% sodium chloride is continued.
hq_q.f: Osmolality falls by over 3 per hour → slow the fluids.
hq_q.ql: What does the rise in serum sodium over the first 8 hours most likely represent?

c: glucose has fallen from 52 to 34 mmol/L
sodium has risen from 148 to 151 mmol/L
osmolality has fallen from 362 to 352 mOsm/kg
tm.m: Extracellular glucose falls with IV 0.9% saline -> water shifts back into dehydrated cells -> extracellular Na+ concentrates while total osmolality steadily falls
tm.g: Rising Na+ while glucose and calculated osmolality fall steadily (3 to 8 mOsm/kg/h) in HHS = expected osmotic water shift into cells (continue 0.9% saline)
x: Cerebral oedema is triggered by an excessively rapid drop in osmolality (>8 mOsm/kg/hour) and causes deteriorating consciousness, headache and bradycardia
Worsening dehydration would cause calculated serum osmolality to rise rather than fall steadily by 10 mOsm/kg over 8 hours
Cranial diabetes insipidus causes hypotonic polyuria with normal plasma glucose rather than resolving extreme hyperglycaemia
Primary adrenal insufficiency causes hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia from aldosterone deficiency, not rising serum sodium
f: osmolality dropping by 15 mOsm/kg/hour after early high-dose insulin with new headache, vomiting and falling GCS
rising calculated serum osmolality (from 362 to 372 mOsm/kg) with persistent oliguria and worsening tachycardia
polyuria of 6 L/day with urine osmolality 110 mOsm/kg and plasma glucose 5.1 mmol/L after pituitary surgery
refractory hypotension with serum sodium falling to 124 mmol/L and potassium rising to 6.1 mmol/L

hq_q.s: A 78 year old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and sitagliptin is brought to the Emergency Department with progressive drowsiness after a week of productive cough and poor oral intake. On examination, her pulse is 116 bpm, blood pressure is 98/58 mmHg, respiratory rate is 20 breaths/min and capillary refill time is 4 seconds. Her mucous membranes are parched. Admission blood tests are shown.
o: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride with fixed-rate insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour
Oral rehydration solution via nasogastric tube
hq_q.w: In hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS), severe dehydration (typically 100 to 220 mL/kg fluid deficit) is the primary driver of hyperosmolality. Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride alone restores circulating volume, improves renal perfusion and lowers plasma glucose and osmolality safely. Fixed-rate insulin is withheld initially unless there is significant ketonaemia (>1.0 mmol/L), because early insulin drives glucose and water rapidly into cells, precipitating vascular collapse and cerebral oedema.
hq_q.f: Glucose stops falling on fluids → start low-dose insulin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate primary fluid and metabolic treatment in the first hour?

tm.m: Severe osmotic diuresis over days -> 10 to 20 L fluid deficit -> IV 0.9% saline restores renal perfusion and dilutes glucose without rapid osmotic shifts
tm.g: HHS without significant ketonaemia (ketones <=1.0 mmol/L): start IV 0.9% sodium chloride alone and withhold insulin initially
x: Hypotonic 0.45% saline is reserved for later only if osmolality stops falling despite adequate positive fluid balance
Starting DKA-dose insulin (0.1 units/kg/hour) before fluid resuscitation in HHS causes a precipitous drop in osmolality and circulatory collapse
Intravenous 5% glucose worsens hyperglycaemia and drops extracellular tonicity too rapidly
A drowsy, hypotensive patient with a 4-second capillary refill requires immediate intravenous crystalloid resuscitation
f: serum osmolality plateauing despite a positive fluid balance of 3 litres of 0.9% sodium chloride
blood ketones of 4.6 mmol/L, venous pH of 7.14 and bicarbonate of 9 mmol/L confirming mixed DKA/HHS
plasma glucose falling below 14 mmol/L later in HHS recovery while intravenous saline continues
alert child with mild viral gastroenteritis, normal capillary refill and normal blood glucose

hq_q.s: A 72 year old man is brought to the GP surgery by his wife after a week of recurrent morning confusion, clamminess and tremor that resolve within 20 minutes of eating breakfast. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and gliclazide 80 mg twice daily and has eaten poorly since a recent viral illness. His eGFR has fallen from 52 to 30 mL/min/1.73 m2. Neurological examination between episodes is normal.
hq_q.w: Sulfonylureas (such as gliclazide) bind pancreatic beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channels to stimulate insulin secretion regardless of ambient blood glucose. Because gliclazide metabolites and insulin are cleared renally, a fall in eGFR combined with reduced carbohydrate intake precipitates recurrent fasting neuroglycopenia and autonomic symptoms (sweating, tremor) that resolve with carbohydrate (Whipple triad). Gliclazide should be stopped or replaced with an agent that does not cause hypoglycaemia.
hq_q.f: Metformin on its own → rarely causes hypoglycaemia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of his morning symptoms?

c: resolve within 20 minutes of eating breakfast
tm.m: Glucose-independent beta-cell stimulation by gliclazide + reduced renal clearance (eGFR 30) and poor intake -> fasting morning hypoglycaemia relieved by food
tm.g: Morning confusion/sweating relieved by breakfast in an older patient on gliclazide with declining eGFR = sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia
x: Causes persistent lethargy, cold intolerance and bradycardia rather than acute morning sweating and confusion relieved within 20 minutes by breakfast
Produces a persistent focal neurological deficit (such as pure motor hemiparesis) rather than daily pre-breakfast episodes resolving with food
Causes sudden focal neurological deficits (unilateral weakness, dysphasia or amaurosis fugax) unrelated to fasting or carbohydrate intake
Produces persistent delirium with dysuria or fever rather than stereotyped fasting episodes resolving rapidly after breakfast
f: 4 months of progressive lethargy, weight gain, dry skin, slow-relaxing ankle jerks and TSH 42 mU/L
sudden-onset persistent right arm and leg weakness lasting 48 hours with no cortical signs
15-minute episode of right-hand weakness and expressive dysphasia at 3 pm unrelated to meals
2 days of continuous confusion, suprapubic tenderness, fever of 38.3°C and nitrite-positive dipstick

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old woman with type 1 diabetes is found unconscious at home by her partner. Paramedics are on the way. She is breathing normally and has a pulse.
Her capillary glucose is 1.9 mmol/L (4.0–7.8). She cannot swallow, and attempts at intravenous access have failed.
hq_q.w: If unconscious and no IV access, give IM glucagon. Nothing by mouth while unconscious. Key discriminator: Unconscious hypoglycaemia with no IV access: IM glucagon.
hq_q.f: IV access available → 10% or 20% IV glucose.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Glucagon releases liver glycogen and works by intramuscular injection
tm.g: Unconscious hypoglycaemia with no IV access: IM glucagon
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Buccal glucose gel (Gel in the mouth of an unconscious person risks aspiration; without IV access, give IM glucagon)
awake and able to swallow
the presentation instead showed features specific to Subcutaneous insulin (Insulin lowers blood glucose further and can be fatal in hypoglycaemia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Wait for IV access (Delaying treatment in severe hypoglycaemia risks seizures and brain injury)
x: Gel in the mouth of an unconscious person risks aspiration; without IV access, give IM glucagon.
Ruled out here: requires awake and able to swallow, whereas this patient has 1.9 mmol/L, cannot swallow.
Insulin lowers blood glucose further and can be fatal in hypoglycaemia
Delaying treatment in severe hypoglycaemia risks seizures and brain injury

hq_q.s: A 21 year old man with type 1 diabetes treated with a basal-bolus insulin regimen attends his diabetes clinic after passing his Group 1 car driving test. He has full hypoglycaemia awareness, has had no severe hypoglycaemic episodes requiring third-party assistance in the past year, and monitors his capillary blood glucose regularly. He asks what DVLA blood glucose testing rules apply whenever he drives a car.
o: Avoid driving after dark or on motorways
Check blood glucose after completing each journey
Check blood glucose only if he feels sweaty or shaky
Check blood glucose within 2 hours before driving and every 2 hours while driving
Drive without extra carbohydrate if blood glucose is between 4.0 and 5.0 mmol/L
hq_q.w: DVLA Group 1 (car and motorcycle) regulations for insulin-treated drivers can be remembered as '5 to drive': blood glucose must be tested no more than 2 hours before the start of the first journey and every 2 hours after driving has started. If blood glucose is 5.0 mmol/L or below, the driver must eat a carbohydrate snack; if it is below 4.0 mmol/L, they must not drive and must wait 45 minutes after recovery (>5.0 mmol/L).
hq_q.f: Glucose of 4.5 before driving → eat a carbohydrate snack first.
hq_q.ql: Which DVLA rule applies to his blood glucose monitoring for Group 1 car driving?

tm.m: Exogenous insulin risks unpredictable neuroglycopenia at the wheel -> mandatory pre-drive (<2 h) and 2-hourly in-journey checks ('5 to drive')
tm.g: DVLA Group 1 insulin rules: test within 2 hours before driving and every 2 hours while driving; snack if <=5.0 mmol/L; do not drive if <4.0 mmol/L (wait 45 min after recovery)
x: Insulin treatment alone does not restrict night or motorway driving unless severe diabetic retinopathy or laser photocoagulation impairs visual fields
Testing after a journey cannot prevent an in-journey hypoglycaemic collision; testing must occur before driving and every 2 hours during travel
Symptom-only testing is unsafe because cognitive impairment occurs before autonomic symptoms are recognised behind the wheel
When blood glucose is between 4.0 and 5.0 mmol/L, the driver must take a carbohydrate snack before setting off
f: extensive pan-retinal laser photocoagulation causing a binocular Esterman visual field defect
patient taking metformin and dapagliflozin alone for type 2 diabetes with no insulin or sulfonylurea
patient treated with lifestyle and metformin alone who asks whether routine pre-journey fingerprick testing is required
capillary blood glucose of 5.8 mmol/L checked 30 minutes before a 40-minute commute

hq_q.s: A 63 year old woman of Black African family origin attends her GP surgery after elevated clinic blood pressure readings at three consecutive appointments. She has had type 2 diabetes for 4 years and takes modified-release metformin 1 g twice daily. Her ambulatory blood pressure average is 146/92 mmHg. Her urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 1.4 mg/mmol (<3.0) and her eGFR is 78 mL/min/1.73 m2.
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG136 hypertension guidance, any adult with type 2 diabetes (regardless of age or ethnic family origin) starts Step 1 antihypertensive therapy with an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) because renin-angiotensin blockade lowers intraglomerular pressure. In patients of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin with type 2 diabetes, an ARB (such as losartan) is preferred over an ACE inhibitor because ACE inhibitors carry a higher rate of cough and angioedema.
hq_q.f: No diabetes and Black African family origin → amlodipine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive drug to start?

c: ambulatory blood pressure average is 146/92 mmHg
tm.m: Type 2 diabetes mandates Step 1 RAAS blockade for renoprotection -> ARB (losartan) preferred over ACEi in Black African family origin to avoid bradykinin-mediated angioedema
tm.g: Step 1 hypertension in type 2 diabetes + Black African/African-Caribbean family origin = ARB (losartan/candesartan) first line
x: Calcium-channel blockers are Step 1 first line in patients of Black African origin only if they do NOT have type 2 diabetes
Conventional thiazide diuretics impair glucose tolerance and are not Step 1 therapy in NICE hypertension guidelines
Alpha-blockers are fourth-line (Step 4) add-on agents when potassium is above 4.5 mmol/L or spironolactone is not tolerated
Low-dose spironolactone is reserved for Step 4 resistant hypertension when serum potassium is 4.5 mmol/L or lower
f: 63 year old woman of Black African family origin with Stage 1 hypertension and no history of diabetes or proteinuria
Step 3 hypertension requiring a thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide) alongside an ARB and amlodipine
Step 4 resistant hypertension on losartan, amlodipine and indapamide with a serum potassium of 4.9 mmol/L
Step 4 resistant hypertension on losartan, amlodipine and indapamide with a serum potassium of 4.1 mmol/L

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and known distal symmetrical polyneuropathy presents to the diabetic foot clinic with a 3-week history of a warm, swollen right midfoot. He denies trauma or fever. On examination, his temperature is 36.8°C, the right midfoot is erythematous, non-tender and 3.5°C warmer than the left, pedal pulses are bounding and skin is intact. Foot radiograph shows tarsometatarsal subluxation and bone fragmentation.
hq_q.w: Charcot neuropathic osteoarthropathy (Charcot foot) occurs in patients with severe diabetic peripheral sensory and autonomic neuropathy. Loss of protective pain sensation combined with autonomic hyperperfusion causes repetitive unrecognized microtrauma, inflammatory osteolysis, midfoot joint fragmentation and eventual rocker-bottom deformity. Absence of fever, intact skin without ulceration, bounding pulses and a >2°C inter-foot temperature difference point to acute Charcot foot, managed urgently with non-weight-bearing total contact casting.
hq_q.f: A deep ulcer with bone you can probe → osteomyelitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Sensory loss + autonomic arteriovenous shunting -> unperceived repetitive weight-bearing microfractures and osteoclastic resorption -> hot, swollen, painless midfoot collapse
tm.g: Hot (>2°C warmer), swollen, painless/mildly aching neuropathic diabetic foot with intact skin + midfoot joint fragmentation = Charcot foot (off-load with total contact cast)
x: Causes acute exquisite pain and tenderness, classically at the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra), with negatively birefringent urate crystals
Presents with spreading tender skin erythema, systemic inflammatory markers and no tarsometatarsal bony fragmentation
Almost always spreads from an overlying deep diabetic foot ulcer (positive probe-to-bone test) with elevated CRP and systemic features
Presents with an acutely painful, immobile joint, systemic fever and purulent synovial aspirate on arthrocentesis
f: sudden excruciating pain and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint waking him at 3 am after starting bendroflumethiazide
spreading hot tender erythema up the shin from macerated interdigital tinea pedis with normal foot radiographs
chronic plantar metatarsal head ulcer through which gritty bone can be palpated with a sterile metal probe
temperature of 38.9°C, rigors, inability to move the ankle joint and turbid synovial fluid containing Gram-positive cocci

hq_q.s: A 44 year old woman who was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 12 months ago attends her GP surgery for her annual diabetes review. She takes metformin 1 g twice daily, her HbA1c is 51 mmol/mol and her blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg. She has normal visual acuity (6/6 bilaterally) and no visual symptoms. Her baseline screening 1 year ago showed no retinopathy in either eye.
o: Annual direct ophthalmoscopy by the GP
Optical coherence tomography of the macula
hq_q.w: The NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme invites all people with diabetes aged 12 years and over for mydriatic digital two-field retinal photography (after tropicamide 1% pupil dilation). Digital retinal photography has far higher sensitivity and reproducibility than direct ophthalmoscopy for detecting microaneurysms, blot haemorrhages, hard exudates and neovascularisation. Since 2023, low-risk patients with two consecutive normal scans are screened every 24 months.
hq_q.f: Photos show maculopathy → refer to eye clinic.
hq_q.ql: Which modality is used for routine surveillance in the NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme?

tm.m: Asymptomatic microvascular retinal damage -> mydriatic two-field digital fundus photography detects early microaneurysms and new vessels before vision loss
tm.g: NHS routine diabetic retinopathy screening (from age 12) = digital mydriatic retinal photography
x: Direct ophthalmoscopy has a small field of view and poor sensitivity for early peripheral retinopathy or maculopathy
Automated perimetry assesses peripheral visual field loss in chronic open-angle glaucoma or chiasmal/retrochiasmal lesions
Invasive angiography using intravenous sodium fluorescein is reserved for hospital ophthalmology assessment of retinal ischaemia and neovascular leakage
Cross-sectional macular OCT is used in hospital eye clinics to quantify central retinal thickness when diabetic macular oedema is suspected
f: bedside inspection of the optic disc for papilloedema in a patient presenting with acute headache
monitoring peripheral arcuate scotoma progression in primary open-angle glaucoma
localising leaking retinal microaneurysms and capillary non-perfusion prior to focal retinal laser therapy
quantifying central subfield macular thickness prior to intravitreal anti-VEGF injection for diabetic macular oedema

hq_q.s: A 34 year old woman presents to her GP with 3 weeks of palpitations, heat intolerance, anxiety and a 4 kg weight loss. She delivered a healthy baby 4 months ago and is bottle-feeding. She denies neck pain or recent viral illness. Her pulse is 104 bpm regular, she has a fine postural tremor, and her thyroid is non-tender and mildly diffusely enlarged without a bruit or ophthalmopathy. Investigation results are shown.
hq_q.w: Postpartum thyroiditis is an autoimmune destructive lymphocytic thyroiditis (strongly associated with anti-TPO antibodies) occurring within 12 months of childbirth. Preformed thyroid hormone leaks from damaged follicles, causing a transient painless thyrotoxic phase (1 to 3 months) followed by a hypothyroid phase before recovery in most women. Because follicular synthesis is suppressed, radionuclide uptake is globally low (<1%) and TSH-receptor antibodies are negative; symptoms are managed with propranolol rather than carbimazole.
hq_q.f: High uptake with eye signs → Graves' disease.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: delivered a healthy baby 4 months ago
tm.m: Postpartum rebound of anti-TPO autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis -> leakage of preformed T4/T3 with suppressed TSH -> painless thyrotoxicosis with absent tracer uptake
tm.g: Painless thyrotoxicosis within 12 months of delivery + negative TRAB + diffusely low uptake scan = postpartum thyroiditis (treat symptoms with beta-blocker, not carbimazole)
x: Causes an exquisitely painful, tender goitre radiating to the jaw with a markedly raised ESR following a viral upper respiratory infection
Produces positive TSH-receptor antibodies, a thyroid bruit, orbitopathy and diffusely increased radionuclide uptake
Presents with chronic painless goitre and primary hypothyroidism (high TSH, low free T4) rather than acute thyrotoxicosis
Demonstrates a single hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodule with suppression of the remaining thyroid tissue on technetium uptake scan
f: exquisitely tender anterior neck swelling radiating to the ears 3 weeks after a viral illness with ESR 82 mm/hour
exophthalmos, thyroid bruit, positive TSH-receptor antibodies and diffusely increased technetium uptake
progressive lethargy, cold intolerance, weight gain, firm rubbery goitre, TSH 48 mU/L and free T4 5 pmol/L
palpable 2.5 cm left lobe nodule showing intense focal tracer uptake with suppression of the rest of the gland

hq_q.s: A 33 year old woman started carbimazole 40 mg daily 5 weeks ago for newly diagnosed Graves' disease. She attends an urgent GP appointment with a 2-day history of severe sore throat, painful mouth ulcers and fever. On examination, her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse is 106 bpm, blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg and her pharyngeal mucosa is erythematous with two shallow buccal aphthous ulcers.
o: Add levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily as block-and-replace
Continue carbimazole and prescribe oral phenoxymethylpenicillin
Halve the carbimazole dose and repeat thyroid function tests
Stop carbimazole immediately and perform an urgent same-day full blood count
Take a throat swab and review in 5 days
hq_q.w: Carbimazole and propylthiouracil carry an idiosyncratic risk (approximately 0.3%, highest in the first 3 months) of bone marrow suppression and agranulocytosis (neutrophils <0.5 x 10^9/L). Every patient starting a thionamide must be warned that if they develop a sore throat, mouth ulcers, bruising or unexplained fever, they must stop the drug immediately and have an urgent same-day full blood count checked before taking any further doses.
hq_q.f: Neutrophils normal → carbimazole can be restarted.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate action?

c: started carbimazole 40 mg daily 5 weeks ago
severe sore throat, painful mouth ulcers and fever
tm.m: Idiosyncratic anti-neutrophil/myeloid precursor toxicity from carbimazole -> agranulocytosis -> sore throat and mucosal ulceration
tm.g: Sore throat, mouth ulcers or fever on carbimazole/PTU = stop drug immediately + urgent same-day FBC (neutrophil count)
x: Levothyroxine addresses iatrogenic hypothyroidism during block-and-replace therapy and does nothing for life-threatening neutropenia
Continuing carbimazole while prescribing outpatient oral antibiotics risks fatal neutropenic sepsis
Thionamide-induced agranulocytosis is an immune-mediated idiosyncratic reaction requiring immediate complete cessation, not dose reduction
Delaying a full blood count for 5 days while awaiting throat swab culture can result in overwhelming Gram-negative sepsis
f: patient rendered biochemically euthyroid on high-dose carbimazole who is moving onto a 12-month block-and-replace regimen
afebrile patient not taking antithyroid drugs with Centor score 4 tonsillitis and normal neutrophil count
asymptomatic patient on titration carbimazole whose free T4 has fallen just below the lower reference limit with normal FBC
recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis in an immunocompetent child with normal white cell count

hq_q.s: A 29 year old woman with a history of Graves' disease attends the joint antenatal-endocrine clinic at 8 weeks' gestation after relapsing off treatment. She complains of palpitations, heat intolerance, anxiety and a 2 kg weight loss over the past month. On examination, her pulse is 108 bpm, she has a fine tremor and a small diffuse goitre. Blood tests show TSH <0.01 mU/L, free T4 36 pmol/L and positive TSH-receptor antibodies.
hq_q.w: Propylthiouracil (PTU) is the preferred antithyroid drug when conceiving and throughout the first trimester of pregnancy because carbimazole crosses the placenta and is associated with congenital malformations during organogenesis (aplasia cutis, choanal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula). Because PTU carries a risk of severe maternal hepatotoxicity, patients are often switched to titration-dose carbimazole in the second trimester. Block-and-replace and radioiodine are contraindicated in pregnancy.
hq_q.f: Second trimester → switch to carbimazole.
hq_q.ql: Which antithyroid treatment is preferred during the first trimester of pregnancy?

tm.m: Carbimazole causes first-trimester embryopathy (aplasia cutis, choanal atresia) -> use PTU in 1st trimester, then switch to carbimazole in 2nd trimester to avoid PTU hepatotoxicity
tm.g: Thyrotoxicosis in 1st trimester of pregnancy = propylthiouracil (PTU) monotherapy (switch to titration carbimazole in 2nd trimester)
x: Block-and-replace is contraindicated in pregnancy because carbimazole crosses the placenta far more readily than levothyroxine, causing fetal hypothyroidism and goitre
Carbimazole during first-trimester organogenesis increases the risk of aplasia cutis and choanal atresia; it is used from the second trimester onwards
Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding as it crosses the placenta and destroys the fetal thyroid
Subtotal or total thyroidectomy in pregnancy is reserved for severe thionamide allergy or non-adherence and is performed in the second trimester
f: non-pregnant adult with Graves' disease undergoing an 18-month medical course to prevent fluctuations in thyroid status
pregnant woman with Graves' disease entering her second trimester (14 weeks' gestation) to reduce maternal hepatotoxicity risk
non-pregnant 45 year old woman with relapsed Graves' disease who has completed her family and has no thyroid eye disease
pregnant woman at 18 weeks' gestation who developed agranulocytosis on PTU and severe hepatotoxicity on carbimazole

hq_q.s: A 67 year old woman attends her GP surgery to discuss routine blood tests taken for mild tiredness over the past 6 months. She denies cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain, voice change or low mood, and has no history of thyroid or cardiovascular disease. Physical examination is normal with no goitre. Blood tests show TSH 7.2 mU/L (0.3-4.2) and free T4 15.4 pmol/L (12-22), unchanged from 3 months ago; FBC, ferritin and HbA1c are normal.
o: Repeat thyroid function tests in 6 months without starting treatment
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG145 guidance, adults aged 65 years and over with persistent subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH between the upper limit of normal and 10 mU/L with a normal free T4) do not derive symptomatic or cardiovascular benefit from levothyroxine replacement, and over-treatment increases the risk of atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis. In asymptomatic older adults with TSH <10 mU/L, a watch-and-wait strategy with periodic TSH monitoring is recommended.
hq_q.f: TSH over 10 on two tests → consider levothyroxine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: free T4 15.4 pmol/L (12-22), unchanged from 3 months ago
tm.m: Age-related physiological upward drift in pituitary TSH setpoint -> TSH <10 mU/L with normal fT4 in patients >=65 years requires monitoring rather than thyroxine
tm.g: Subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH <10 mU/L, normal fT4) in an adult >=65 years without classic hypothyroid symptoms = monitor without levothyroxine
x: Thyroid ultrasonography is indicated only when there is a palpable thyroid nodule, asymmetrical goitre or cervical lymphadenopathy
TSH-receptor antibodies are measured to investigate hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease), whereas anti-TPO antibodies are used in hypothyroidism
Starting full-dose levothyroxine (100 micrograms) in an older adult with TSH <10 mU/L carries no proven benefit and risks atrial fibrillation
Liothyronine (T3) is not recommended by NICE for primary or subclinical hypothyroidism due to short half-life and arrhythmia risk
f: palpable firm 2 cm solitary nodule in the right thyroid lobe with normal TSH
32 year old woman presenting with weight loss, tremor, TSH <0.01 mU/L and free T4 39 pmol/L
42 year old woman with TSH 13.5 mU/L and normal free T4 on two occasions 3 months apart
hospitalised patient in intensive care with myxoedema coma requiring intravenous thyroid hormone replacement

hq_q.s: A 58 year old woman has taken levothyroxine 100 micrograms each morning for 5 years with a stable normal TSH. Her TSH is now 9.6 mU/L (0.3–4.2). She takes the levothyroxine at the same time as a new tablet started 2 months ago for heavy periods.
hq_q.w: Iron and calcium reduce levothyroxine absorption. Take them at least 4 hours apart. Key discriminator: Rising TSH after starting a tablet for heavy periods: ferrous sulfate.
hq_q.f: She takes omeprazole → can also reduce absorption.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most likely to have caused the rise in TSH?

c: at the same time as a new tablet
tm.m: Iron binds levothyroxine in the gut and blocks absorption
tm.g: Rising TSH after starting a tablet for heavy periods: ferrous sulfate
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amlodipine (Amlodipine does not affect levothyroxine absorption; iron taken at the same time does)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Paracetamol (Used for: Step 1 for all pain: 1 g four times a day, less if under 50 kg)
a tricyclic has not helped or is not tolerated
the presentation instead showed features specific to Simvastatin (Statins do not chelate levothyroxine or impair its gut absorption)
x: Amlodipine does not affect levothyroxine absorption; iron taken at the same time does.
Used for: Step 1 for all pain: 1 g four times a day, less if under 50 kg
Ruled out here: requires a tricyclic has not helped or is not tolerated, whereas this patient has at the same time as a new tablet, heavy periods.
Statins do not chelate levothyroxine or impair its gut absorption

hq_q.s: A 78 year old woman with a history of autoimmune hypothyroidism is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after her neighbour found her drowsy and confused in an unheated flat. Her blister packs show she stopped taking levothyroxine 2 months ago. Her core temperature is 33.2°C, pulse is 44 bpm, blood pressure is 96/58 mmHg and respiratory rate is 10 breaths/min. She has periorbital puffiness, coarse dry skin and slow-relaxing ankle jerks.
hq_q.w: Myxoedema coma is a life-threatening decompensation of severe hypothyroidism, often precipitated in older patients during winter by treatment non-adherence, infection or sedatives. Cardinal features are hypothermia, sinus bradycardia, hypoventilation (with hypercapnia), hyponatraemia (from impaired free water clearance), hypoglycaemia and depressed consciousness. Immediate management requires critical care support, passive rewarming, intravenous hydrocortisone (given BEFORE thyroid hormone to prevent adrenal crisis) and intravenous liothyronine/levothyroxine.
hq_q.f: High fever, tachycardia and agitation → thyroid storm.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: core temperature is 33.2°C, pulse is 44 bpm
periorbital puffiness, coarse dry skin and slow-relaxing ankle jerks
tm.m: Profound thyroid hormone depletion -> depressed basal metabolic rate, myocardial beta-receptor downregulation and impaired free water excretion -> hypothermia, bradycardia, hyponatraemia and coma
tm.g: Hypothermia + bradycardia + hypoventilation + hyponatraemia + slow-relaxing reflexes off levothyroxine = myxoedema coma (give IV hydrocortisone + IV thyroid hormone)
x: Brainstem stroke produces cranial nerve palsies, crossed long-tract signs and pinpoint pupils rather than periorbital myxoedema and delayed reflex relaxation
Typically causes tachycardia, bounding or vasoplegic shock and an infectious focus, although infection can precipitate myxoedema coma
Isolated hypoglycaemia causes sympathetic activation (sweating, tachycardia) and resolves immediately with intravenous glucose, though it can coexist with myxoedema coma
Presents in chronic alcohol misuse or hyperemesis with the triad of acute confusion, ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus/sixth nerve palsy) and gait ataxia
f: sudden-onset quadriplegia, pinpoint pupils and preserved vertical eye movements after a vertebral artery dissection
temperature of 39.1°C, pulse 128 bpm, BP 82/46 mmHg, warm peripheries and purulent urine in a catheter bag
capillary blood glucose of 1.6 mmol/L in a patient taking gliclazide who wakes completely 5 minutes after 150 mL IV 10% glucose
chronic heavy alcohol drinker presenting with confusion, bilateral sixth nerve palsies and a broad-based ataxic gait

hq_q.s: A 50 year old woman presents to the Endocrine Clinic with a painless anterior neck swelling noticed 6 weeks ago and occasional watery diarrhoea with facial flushing. Five years ago she underwent laparoscopic right adrenalectomy for a phaeochromocytoma, and her brother had thyroid surgery at the age of 34. Examination reveals a firm 2.2 cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe and palpable ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Serum calcitonin is markedly elevated and TSH is normal.
