hq_q.w: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from neuroendocrine parafollicular C-cells, which secrete calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA); high calcitonin can cause secretory diarrhoea and flushing. Around 25% of cases are familial due to autosomal dominant germline RET proto-oncogene mutations causing Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN2A: medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and primary hyperparathyroidism; MEN2B: mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus). Phaeochromocytoma must always be excluded before thyroid surgery.
hq_q.f: A lump in a young woman with spread to neck nodes → papillary carcinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: brother had thyroid surgery at the age of 34
tm.m: Germline RET proto-oncogene mutation (MEN2) -> neoplastic proliferation of parafollicular C-cells -> calcitonin-secreting medullary thyroid carcinoma + phaeochromocytoma
tm.g: Thyroid nodule + raised serum calcitonin + personal/family history of phaeochromocytoma (MEN2) = medullary thyroid carcinoma
x: Presents in patients over 70 as a rapidly enlarging, rock-hard fixed neck mass causing stridor and dysphagia over weeks
Arises from thyroid follicular cells (thyroglobulin-positive, calcitonin-negative), spreads haematogenously to bone and lung, and is not part of MEN2
Arises from follicular epithelium (Orphan Annie eye nuclei, psammoma bodies, thyroglobulin marker) and does not secrete calcitonin
Develops on a background of chronic Hashimoto's thyroiditis as a rapidly enlarging diffuse goitre with B symptoms
f: 78 year old woman with a rock-hard fixed thyroid mass growing over 3 weeks with stridor and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy
solitary encapsulated thyroid tumour showing capsular and vascular invasion on hemithyroidectomy with lytic bone metastases
28 year old woman with a thyroid nodule, cervical lymphadenopathy, normal calcitonin and Orphan Annie eye nuclei on FNA
68 year old woman with longstanding Hashimoto's thyroiditis developing a rapidly enlarging diffuse goitre, night sweats and weight loss

hq_q.s: A 79 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a neck swelling that has enlarged rapidly over the past 4 weeks, accompanied by a hoarse voice, dysphagia and shortness of breath when lying flat. On examination, there is a rock-hard, irregular 6 cm mass in the anterior neck that is fixed to the overlying skin and fails to move cleanly on swallowing, with audible inspiratory stridor and fixed cervical nodes.
hq_q.w: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is an aggressive, undifferentiated malignancy occurring primarily in elderly women (peak age >70 years), frequently arising from a pre-existing differentiated thyroid lesion or multinodular goitre. It enlarges rapidly over weeks, invading the trachea, oesophagus and recurrent laryngeal nerve to cause stridor, dysphagia and hoarseness. Because it does not concentrate iodine or express thyroglobulin, radioactive iodine is ineffective and management focuses on airway protection and palliation.
hq_q.f: A fast-growing lump in Hashimoto's → thyroid lymphoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: enlarged rapidly over the past 4 weeks
tm.m: Dedifferentiation of follicular epithelium (often TP53 mutation) -> explosive local invasion of trachea, oesophagus and recurrent laryngeal nerve -> stridor and hoarseness
tm.g: Elderly patient + rapidly enlarging rock-hard fixed thyroid mass over weeks + stridor/hoarseness = anaplastic thyroid carcinoma
x: Presents as a slow-growing painless solitary nodule in middle age with haematogenous spread to lung and bone
Presents as a firm nodule with raised serum calcitonin and cervical lymphadenopathy, often associated with MEN2
Enlarges slowly over many years with multiple smooth nodules and remains mobile on swallowing without recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion
Most common in young women (20 to 40 years), grows indolently and carries an excellent prognosis (>95% 10-year survival)
f: 55 year old woman with a slow-growing solitary thyroid nodule and a pulsatile lytic metastasis in the sternum
42 year old man with a thyroid nodule, raised serum calcitonin and elevated 24-hour plasma metanephrines
65 year old woman with a 15-year history of a slowly enlarging nodular neck swelling that moves upwards on swallowing with no voice change
31 year old woman with a 1.8 cm painless thyroid nodule whose FNA cytology shows psammoma bodies and nuclear grooves

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old woman noticed a lump in the front of her neck in the mirror. She has no voice change, no swallowing problems and no previous neck radiation.
There is a 2 cm smooth nodule in the left lobe of the thyroid that moves on swallowing. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy.
TSH is normal.
hq_q.w: Ultrasound grades the nodule, then fine needle aspiration if it looks suspicious. A scan is used if TSH is low.
hq_q.f: Low TSH with a nodule → radioisotope scan for a hot nodule.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first investigation?

tm.m: Ultrasound grades how suspicious a nodule looks before any needle test
tm.g: Thyroid nodule with normal TSH: ultrasound first
f: Severe acute symptomatic hypercalcaemia requiring rapid temporary calcium lowering
the presentation instead showed features specific to CT neck (Fatal delay in imminent airway obstruction from an expanding neck haematoma)
low TSH with a nodule
the presentation instead showed features specific to Thyroid antibodies (Antibodies support thyroiditis but do not assess a single nodule)
x: Ruled out here: requires Severe acute symptomatic hypercalcaemia requiring rapid temporary calcium lowering, whereas this patient has moves on swallowing, TSH is normal.
Fatal delay in imminent airway obstruction from an expanding neck haematoma
Ruled out here: requires low TSH with a nodule, whereas this patient has moves on swallowing, TSH is normal.
Antibodies support thyroiditis but do not assess a single nodule.

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old man presents with a 6-month history of a slow, spraying urinary stream, terminal dribbling and needing to strain to empty his bladder. Twelve months ago he required a urethral catheter for 5 days after emergency abdominal surgery.
Digital rectal examination shows a small, smooth prostate. Uroflowmetry shows a flat, prolonged, plateau-shaped flow curve with a maximum flow rate of 7 mL/s.
hq_q.w: Urethral strictures typically follow urethral catheterisation, endoscopic instrumentation, perineal trauma or urethritis. Fixed luminal narrowing produces a characteristic prolonged, flat plateau-shaped uroflowmetry curve with a normal-sized prostate, confirmed by flexible urethroscopy or retrograde urethrography.
hq_q.f: Man aged 70 years with nocturia and a large smooth prostate -> benign prostatic hyperplasia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Periurethral fibrosis following mucosal trauma narrows the urethral lumen and restricts peak urinary flow to a fixed plateau.
tm.g: Obstructive voiding symptoms after catheterisation with a small prostate and plateau flow curve -> urethral stricture
x: Benign prostatic hyperplasia typically affects older men and produces an enlarged prostate on rectal examination rather than a small gland.
Bladder neck stenosis is a post-operative complication of transurethral resection of the prostate or radical prostatectomy, not brief urethral catheterisation.
Detrusor underactivity produces an intermittent, fluctuating low-amplitude flow pattern from impaired contractility rather than a flat plateau from fixed outlet narrowing.
Locally advanced prostate cancer causing outflow obstruction produces a hard, craggy, nodular gland on rectal examination.
f: a 72 year old man with nocturia, hesitancy and a symmetrically enlarged smooth prostate on rectal examination
obstructive voiding symptoms developing 4 months after transurethral resection of the prostate
a man with long-standing poorly controlled diabetes, peripheral neuropathy and an intermittent saw-tooth uroflowmetry trace
progressive voiding difficulty with a hard, nodular asymmetric prostate and raised serum PSA

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man presents with a 12-month history of a weak urinary stream, hesitancy and nocturia twice nightly. He has taken tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily for 6 months with only modest symptom relief.
BP 134/78 mmHg, pulse rate 72 bpm. Digital rectal examination reveals a smooth, significantly enlarged prostate, and transrectal ultrasound estimates prostate volume at 60 mL. Serum PSA and creatinine are normal.
hq_q.w: NICE recommends offering a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor such as finasteride in combination with an alpha-blocker to men with bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms who have a prostate estimated above 30 g or PSA above 1.4 ng/mL.
hq_q.f: Predominant storage urgency and frequency after outlet treatment -> add an antimuscarinic or mirabegron.
hq_q.ql: Which drug should be added?

tm.m: 5-alpha-reductase inhibition blocks conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, shrinking prostatic glandular volume over 3 to 6 months.
tm.g: Persistent voiding LUTS on an alpha-blocker with prostate volume >30 mL -> add finasteride
x: Bethanechol is a muscarinic agonist that is contraindicated when bladder outlet obstruction is present because it increases intravesical pressure without relieving prostatic narrowing.
Mirabegron is a beta-3 adrenoceptor agonist used for overactive bladder storage symptoms rather than reducing large prostatic outflow obstruction.
Oxybutynin treats overactive bladder storage urgency and frequency but does not shrink an enlarged 60 mL prostate causing voiding obstruction.
Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor indicated for erectile dysfunction rather than combination therapy for prostatic enlargement.
f: post-operative non-obstructive detrusor underactivity after mechanical bladder outlet obstruction had been excluded
persistent urinary urgency and urge incontinence despite anticholinergic side effects in a patient with normal post-void residual volume
predominant urinary urgency and frequency without a large post-void residual volume
the patient primarily requested first-line pharmacotherapy for erectile dysfunction

hq_q.s:
An 80 year old man attends the emergency department unable to pass urine for 12 hours and reporting severe lower abdominal pain. He has had a slow urinary stream for 2 years and started over-the-counter chlorphenamine for hay fever 2 days ago.
Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 162/90 mmHg. He is distressed with a tender, dull suprapubic mass reaching halfway to the umbilicus.
hq_q.w: Acute urinary retention presents with a sudden, painful inability to void and a tender, palpable, percussibly dull bladder, frequently precipitated by anticholinergic drugs such as first-generation antihistamines in men with underlying benign prostatic enlargement.
hq_q.f: Painless palpable bladder >1 litre with nocturnal overflow incontinence -> chronic urinary retention.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: unable to pass urine for 12 hours
tm.m: Muscarinic blockade from chlorphenamine impairs detrusor contraction against a fixed prostatic outflow resistance, causing painful acute bladder distension.
tm.g: Sudden painful inability to void with a tender dull suprapubic mass -> acute urinary retention
x: Chronic urinary retention develops insidiously and presents with a painless, grossly distended bladder and overflow dribbling rather than severe acute pain.
Bladder cancer classically presents with painless visible haematuria rather than sudden complete anuria following an antihistamine.
A pelvic abscess causes swinging pyrexia, diarrhoea or mucous PR discharge and systemic sepsis after abdominal pathology rather than afebrile anuria.
A unilateral ureteric stone causes colicky loin-to-groin pain and microscopic haematuria but does not cause a distended palpable bladder or complete anuria.
f: a painless, non-tender suprapubic mass draining 1.5 litres on catheterisation with nocturnal overflow wetting
a 72 year old smoker presenting with recurrent painless frank haematuria and an irregular bladder wall mass on cystoscopy
swinging fever, pelvic tenderness and mucous diarrhoea 6 days after surgery for a perforated appendix
sudden colicky unilateral loin-to-groin pain with microscopic haematuria and an empty bladder

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer presents with a 2-week history of mid-thoracic back pain that is worse when lying flat at night. Since yesterday his legs have felt weak and difficulty walking.
Temperature 36.8°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 138/80 mmHg. There is tenderness over T8, bilateral grade 4/5 hip flexion weakness, brisk knee reflexes and reduced pinprick sensation below the umbilicus.
o: Isotope bone scan and outpatient oncology review
Oral morphine and GP review in 1 week
Plain radiographs of the thoracolumbar spine
hq_q.w: Suspected metastatic spinal cord compression is an oncological emergency. NICE recommends immediate high-dose oral or intravenous dexamethasone alongside urgent whole-spine MRI within 24 hours so definitive decompressive surgery or radiotherapy can be planned before irreversible paraplegia develops.
hq_q.f: Spinal pain suggestive of metastases without neurological signs -> MRI within 1 week.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: worse when lying flat at night
reduced pinprick sensation below the umbilicus
tm.m: Epidural vertebral metastasis compresses the thoracic corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts, causing upper motor neurone leg weakness and a T10 sensory level.
tm.g: Known cancer with thoracic back pain, UMN leg weakness and sensory level -> immediate dexamethasone and whole-spine MRI
x: An isotope bone scan identifies osteoblastic bone metastases but cannot visualise the spinal cord or epidural space in acute cord compression.
Delaying investigation for 1 week in evolving spinal cord compression leads to irreversible spinal cord infarction and permanent paraplegia.
Plain spinal radiographs miss up to 30% of vertebral metastases and cannot demonstrate epidural soft-tissue cord compression.
Spinal manipulation or physiotherapy is contraindicated when unstable metastatic spinal cord compression is suspected.
f: baseline staging of newly diagnosed high-risk prostate cancer without neurological deficit
stable chronic mechanical low back pain without red flags or neurological signs
suspected osteoporotic wedge compression fracture in an older patient without malignancy or neurology
uncomplicated mechanical sciatica with normal sphincter function and no history of cancer

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man with newly diagnosed metastatic prostate cancer and multiple sclerotic vertebral metastases on an isotope bone scan attends the oncology clinic to start androgen deprivation therapy with subcutaneous goserelin injections.
Pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg. He has mild lower back ache with normal lower-limb power and reflexes. Serum PSA is 86 µg/L (<4.5) and eGFR is 74 mL/min/1.73 m².
hq_q.w: GnRH agonists such as goserelin initially stimulate pituitary LH release, causing a transient testosterone surge for 1 to 2 weeks that can flare bone pain or cord compression. Oral bicalutamide is started first to block androgen receptors.
hq_q.f: GnRH antagonist such as degarelix started instead -> immediate receptor blockade without flare.
hq_q.ql: Which drug should be given first to prevent a tumour flare?

tm.m: Androgen receptor antagonism with bicalutamide prevents the initial GnRH agonist-induced testosterone surge from stimulating prostate cancer cells.
tm.g: Starting a GnRH agonist (goserelin) in metastatic prostate cancer -> cover flare with bicalutamide
x: Abiraterone inhibits CYP17 androgen synthesis in advanced prostate cancer alongside androgen deprivation rather than serving as short-term anti-androgen flare cover.
Dexamethasone reduces vasogenic oedema in established malignant spinal cord compression but does not block prostatic androgen receptors during a goserelin surge.
Finasteride inhibits 5-alpha-reductase in benign prostatic hyperplasia and does not prevent GnRH agonist-induced metastatic tumour flare.
Tamsulosin relaxes prostatic smooth muscle to ease voiding symptoms but has no hormonal activity against testosterone flare.
f: adding a CYP17 androgen synthesis inhibitor plus prednisolone to ongoing androgen deprivation therapy
acute upper motor neurone leg weakness and a sensory level from malignant spinal cord compression
symptomatic benign prostatic enlargement with a prostate volume over 30 mL
bothersome voiding lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old man is reviewed in the urology clinic after a serum PSA of 6.8 µg/L (<5.0). Multiparametric MRI demonstrated a small solitary peripheral-zone lesion, and targeted transperineal biopsy confirmed prostate adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score of 3+3=6 in 1 of 12 cores.
Staging confirms organ-confined T1c N0 M0 disease. He has hypertension and mild COPD and remains independent.
hq_q.w: NICE recommends active surveillance as the preferred option for low-risk localised prostate cancer (PSA below 10 µg/L, Gleason score 6 and stage T1-T2a), using serial PSA testing, repeat multiparametric MRI and biopsy unless disease progresses.
hq_q.f: High-risk localised disease (Gleason 8-10 or PSA >20 µg/L) -> radical prostatectomy or radical radiotherapy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: Gleason score of 3+3=6 in 1 of 12 cores
tm.m: Well-differentiated Gleason 6 acinar adenocarcinoma has a very low rate of metastasis, so surveillance avoids urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction.
tm.g: Low-risk localised prostate cancer (PSA <10, Gleason 6, T1c) -> active surveillance
x: Surgical castration is reserved for metastatic prostate cancer when rapid permanent testosterone suppression is required, not low-risk localised disease.
Systemic docetaxel chemotherapy is indicated for metastatic prostate cancer alongside androgen deprivation, not organ-confined Gleason 6 tumour.
Primary androgen deprivation monotherapy is not recommended for low-risk localised prostate cancer because it causes metabolic and bone toxicity without improving survival.
Immediate radical prostatectomy exposes men with low-risk Gleason 6 disease to incontinence and erectile dysfunction when active surveillance is equally safe.
f: metastatic prostate cancer in a patient declining medical LHRH therapy
newly diagnosed high-volume metastatic prostate cancer with visceral and skeletal deposits
symptomatic locally advanced or metastatic prostate cancer unsuitable for radical local therapy
a fit 62 year old man with high-risk localised Gleason 4+4=8 prostate cancer

hq_q.s:
A 60 year old woman presents to her GP after noticing frank, painless blood with small clots in her urine on two occasions over the past week. She has a 30 pack-year smoking history and takes ramipril for hypertension.
BP 132/80 mmHg, pulse rate 74 bpm. Abdominal examination is normal. Urine dipstick shows blood 3+ with negative nitrites and leucocytes, and midstream urine culture is sterile.
hq_q.w: Flexible cystoscopy under local anaesthetic is the gold-standard investigation for visualising the bladder mucosa and urethra in patients with unexplained visible haematuria, allowing direct inspection and biopsy of papillary or flat urothelial lesions.
hq_q.f: Cross-sectional imaging of the upper urinary tracts -> CT urogram.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is the gold standard for assessing the bladder?

tm.m: Direct endoscopic visualisation detects flat carcinoma in situ and small papillary urothelial tumours that cross-sectional imaging misses.
tm.g: Gold-standard assessment of the bladder lumen for suspected urothelial cancer -> flexible cystoscopy
x: CT urogram is the imaging modality of choice for the upper urinary tracts (renal pelvis and ureters) but cannot replace direct cystoscopic inspection of the bladder mucosa.
Ultrasound assesses the renal parenchyma and hydronephrosis but misses small papillary bladder tumours and flat carcinoma in situ.
Urine cytology has low sensitivity for low-grade urothelial tumours and is only an adjunct when high-grade carcinoma in situ is suspected.
Urine dipstick detects haem peroxidases to confirm haematuria but provides no anatomical visualisation of the bladder.
f: the question asked for the gold-standard imaging investigation to exclude an upper tract urothelial carcinoma
initial radiation-free imaging of the kidneys in a pregnant patient with loin pain
adjunctive testing for suspected high-grade flat carcinoma in situ after inconclusive cystoscopy
initial point-of-care screening for non-visible haematuria in primary care

hq_q.s:
A 54 year old man has had painless visible haematuria for a month. He grew up in rural Egypt and swam in the River Nile as a child. He has never smoked and has not worked with dyes.
Cystoscopy shows an irregular bladder mass. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
hq_q.w: Chronic schistosomiasis irritates the bladder and causes squamous cell cancer. Key discriminator: Squamous bladder cancer after Nile exposure is schistosomiasis.
hq_q.f: A dye worker with transitional cell cancer → aromatic amines.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?

c: squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder
tm.m: Schistosoma eggs inflame the bladder for years, causing squamous change and cancer
tm.g: Squamous bladder cancer after Nile exposure is schistosomiasis
f: a dye worker with transitional cell cancer
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cyclophosphamide (Used for: Vasculitis, lymphoma, breast cancer)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pelvic radiotherapy (Pelvic radiotherapy can cause bladder cancer, but he has had none; Nile swimming in childhood points to schistosomiasis)
a smoker with transitional cell cancer
x: Ruled out here: requires a dye worker with transitional cell cancer, whereas this patient has rural Egypt, River Nile.
Used for: Vasculitis, lymphoma, breast cancer
Pelvic radiotherapy can cause bladder cancer, but he has had none; Nile swimming in childhood points to schistosomiasis.
Ruled out here: requires a smoker with transitional cell cancer, whereas this patient has rural Egypt, River Nile.

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man attends the urology multidisciplinary clinic after transurethral resection of a 2.5 cm papillary bladder tumour. Histopathology shows high-grade pT1 urothelial carcinoma invading the subepithelial lamina propria with uninvolved muscularis propria present in the specimen.
Staging CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no nodal or distant metastases. His performance status is 0.
hq_q.w: For high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (high-grade pT1 or carcinoma in situ), NICE recommends adjuvant intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) immunotherapy induction and maintenance to stimulate a local T-helper immune response and reduce recurrence and progression to muscle-invasive disease.
hq_q.f: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer (pT2 or above) -> neoadjuvant cisplatin chemotherapy followed by radical cystectomy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate adjuvant treatment?

tm.m: Intravesical live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis (BCG) provokes a granulomatous urothelial immune response that destroys residual high-grade dysplastic cells.
tm.g: High-grade non-muscle-invasive (pT1) urothelial bladder cancer -> intravesical BCG
x: Systemic cisplatin-based chemotherapy is indicated for muscle-invasive (pT2+) or metastatic urothelial carcinoma rather than lamina-propria-confined pT1 disease.
External-beam pelvic radiotherapy with radiosensitisation is a bladder-sparing radical treatment for muscle-invasive (pT2+) bladder cancer, not non-muscle-invasive pT1 disease.
Immediate radical cystectomy is first-line for muscle-invasive pT2 bladder cancer or BCG-unresponsive disease, whereas intravesical BCG is tried first in pT1 tumours.
High-grade pT1 urothelial carcinoma carries a 30% to 50% risk of progressing to muscle invasion if managed without adjuvant intravesical therapy.
f: neoadjuvant systemic therapy before radical cystectomy for muscle-invasive pT2 urothelial carcinoma
definitive organ-preserving radical treatment for muscle-invasive pT2 bladder cancer in a patient declining cystectomy
histology showing invasion into the detrusor muscularis propria (pT2) without distant metastases
asymptomatic low-risk localised prostate cancer in a frail older man with limited life expectancy

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old man presents with a 6-week history of intermittent left loin ache and frank haematuria. He smokes 15 cigarettes daily, takes no regular medications and is euvolaemic.
BP 148/88 mmHg, SpO2 98% breathing air. There is a firm, ballotable left flank mass. CT abdomen shows a 7 cm left renal cell carcinoma. Haemoglobin is 190 g/L (130-175), with normal white cell and platelet counts.
hq_q.w: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma arises from proximal convoluted tubular epithelium and can ectopically secrete erythropoietin (due to constitutive VHL-HIF pathway activation), producing paraneoplastic secondary polycythaemia with isolated erythrocytosis and normal white cell and platelet counts.
hq_q.f: JAK2 V617F mutation with splenomegaly, thrombocytosis and low serum erythropoietin -> polycythaemia rubra vera.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of the high haemoglobin?

c: normal white cell and platelet counts
tm.m: Loss of VHL tumour-suppressor function stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), driving autonomous paraneoplastic erythropoietin transcription by the renal tumour.
tm.g: Renal cell carcinoma with isolated high haemoglobin and normal SpO2 -> tumour erythropoietin
x: Moderate cigarette smoking causes only a mild carboxyhaemoglobin-related rise in haematocrit and would not explain a haemoglobin of 190 g/L alongside a 7 cm renal mass.
He takes no medications and is clinically euvolaemic, ruling out relative polycythaemia from plasma volume contraction.
Primary polycythaemia rubra vera is a JAK2-positive myeloproliferative neoplasm typically accompanied by thrombocytosis, leucocytosis, splenomegaly and suppressed erythropoietin.
He takes no exogenous medications or androgens, whereas clear cell renal carcinoma is a classic cause of paraneoplastic erythropoietin secretion.
f: a heavy smoker with elevated blood carboxyhaemoglobin levels and normal abdominal imaging
haemoconcentration with normal red cell mass in a patient taking high-dose loop diuretics
aquagenic pruritus, splenomegaly, thrombocytosis, suppressed serum erythropoietin and a JAK2 V617F mutation
a bodybuilder using exogenous intramuscular testosterone esters with testicular atrophy and suppressed gonadotrophins

hq_q.s:
A 40 year old man presents with a 2-month history of occipital headaches and unsteady gait. His mother died from metastatic kidney cancer aged 45 years.
BP 136/82 mmHg. Examination shows right-sided dysmetria, past-pointing and horizontal nystagmus. Brain MRI demonstrates a cerebellar haemangioblastoma, and contrast abdominal CT shows multiple bilateral renal cysts and a 3 cm solid enhancing right renal mass.
hq_q.w: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by germline mutation of the VHL tumour-suppressor gene on chromosome 3p, predisposing to cerebellar and retinal haemangioblastomas, bilateral renal cysts, early-onset clear cell renal cell carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma.
hq_q.f: Bilateral renal angiomyolipomas, cortical tubers, ash-leaf macules and facial angiofibromas -> tuberous sclerosis complex.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: mother died from metastatic kidney cancer aged 45
3 cm solid enhancing right renal mass
tm.m: Inactivation of the VHL ubiquitin ligase complex prevents degradation of hypoxia-inducible factor, driving highly vascular haemangioblastomas and clear cell renal carcinomas.
tm.g: Cerebellar haemangioblastoma + bilateral renal cysts + early-onset renal cell carcinoma -> Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
x: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease causes bilateral renal and hepatic cysts and intracranial berry aneurysms, not cerebellar haemangioblastomas or solid clear cell carcinoma.
MEN 1 causes parathyroid hyperplasia, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours and pituitary adenomas rather than cerebellar haemangioblastomas or renal cell carcinoma.
Neurofibromatosis type 1 presents with cafe-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules and cutaneous neurofibromas rather than renal cell cancer and haemangioblastoma.
Tuberous sclerosis causes renal angiomyolipomas, subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, ash-leaf hypopigmented macules and epilepsy rather than cerebellar haemangioblastoma.
f: bilateral massively enlarged cystic kidneys, hepatic cysts and a family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage from berry aneurysms
primary hyperparathyroidism, recurrent peptic ulceration from a gastrinoma and a prolactinoma
multiple cafe-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch iris nodules and cutaneous neurofibromas
seizures, hypopigmented ash-leaf macules, facial adenoma sebaceum and bilateral fat-containing renal angiomyolipomas

hq_q.s:
A 6 year old girl presents after her mother noticed a painless swelling in her abdomen while bathing her. She is active and eating well but has passed pink-stained urine twice this week.
Temperature 36.7°C, BP 128/84 mmHg (above the 99th centile for age). Examination reveals a large, smooth, firm left flank mass that does not cross the midline. Urine dipstick shows blood 2+.
hq_q.w: Wilms' tumour (nephroblastoma) is the commonest childhood renal cancer, typically presenting under age 6 in a well child with a painless, smooth unilateral flank mass that does not cross the midline, haematuria and renin-mediated hypertension.
hq_q.f: Unwell child with an irregular calcified abdominal mass crossing the midline and raised urinary HVA/VMA -> neuroblastoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Embryonal metanephric blastema proliferates within the renal capsule, producing a smooth unilateral intrarenal mass with haematuria and excess renin secretion.
tm.g: Well child with a smooth unilateral flank mass not crossing the midline + haematuria -> Wilms' tumour
x: Congenital pelviureteric junction obstruction produces a soft, cystic, ballotable kidney typically detected on antenatal ultrasound rather than a firm solid tumour with frank haematuria.
Adrenal neuroblastoma presents in a systemically unwell child with an irregular, craggy retroperitoneal mass that crosses the midline and raises urinary catecholamine metabolites.
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease presents in neonates with bilateral symmetrical flank masses, Potter sequence and hepatic fibrosis rather than a single firm mass at age 6.
Renal cell carcinoma overwhelmingly affects adults aged over 50 years, whereas nephroblastoma is the classic childhood renal tumour.
f: an infant with antenatal renal pelvic dilatation and a soft cystic flank swelling without solid tissue on ultrasound
a systemically unwell 2 year old with periorbital bruising, an irregular abdominal mass crossing the midline and raised urinary VMA
a neonate with bilateral symmetrical flank masses, oligohydramnios-related pulmonary hypoplasia and congenital hepatic fibrosis
a 64 year old smoker presenting with painless visible haematuria, left loin pain and a solid renal mass

hq_q.s:
A 40 year old woman presents to the emergency department with a 3-hour history of sudden, severe colicky right loin pain radiating to her right groin and labia, accompanied by nausea. She is restless and unable to lie still.
Temperature 36.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 136/84 mmHg. There is right renal angle tenderness without peritonism. Urine dipstick shows blood 2+ and a urinary pregnancy test is negative.
hq_q.w: NICE recommends urgent low-dose non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder (CT KUB) within 24 hours as first-line imaging for non-pregnant adults with suspected acute renal colic, as it has over 95% sensitivity and specificity for urinary tract calculi.
hq_q.f: Pregnant woman or child with suspected renal colic -> renal tract ultrasound first-line.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line imaging?

c: colicky right loin pain radiating to her right groin
tm.m: Non-contrast helical CT visualises both radiopaque calcium stones and radiolucent uric acid calculi alongside secondary hydronephrosis and perinephric stranding.
tm.g: Suspected acute renal colic in a non-pregnant adult -> non-contrast CT KUB within 24 hours
x: Ultrasound has lower sensitivity than CT for mid- and distal ureteric calculi and is reserved as first-line imaging for pregnant women and children.
Intravenous urography has been superseded by non-contrast CT KUB, which is faster, avoids iodinated contrast nephrotoxicity and detects non-urological pathology.
MR urography does not directly visualise calcified stones well and is reserved as second-line imaging in pregnancy when ultrasound is inconclusive.
Plain KUB radiography misses radiolucent uric acid stones, small ureteric stones and overlying bowel gas shadows.
f: a woman at 24 weeks gestation presenting with acute unilateral loin-to-groin pain and microscopic haematuria
historical contrast study; in modern practice CT urogram is used when upper tract urothelial malignancy is suspected
persistent suspected ureteric obstruction in pregnancy after an inconclusive renal ultrasound scan
outpatient follow-up to check passage of a known radiopaque calcium oxalate stone previously mapped on CT

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old man is reviewed 2 days after presenting with acute right renal colic. Non-contrast CT KUB shows a 6 mm calculus at the right vesicoureteric junction with mild hydronephrosis and a normal left kidney.
His pain is well controlled with oral diclofenac. Temperature 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm. White cell count is 7.2 × 10⁹/L (3.8-10.0), CRP 3 mg/L (<5) and creatinine 82 µmol/L (60-120).
hq_q.w: For an uncomplicated distal ureteric stone under 10 mm where pain is controlled and there is no sepsis, acute kidney injury or solitary kidney, conservative watchful waiting with analgesia and medical expulsive therapy is appropriate as most stones pass spontaneously.
hq_q.f: Obstructed kidney with fever or urosepsis -> emergency percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stenting.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: 6 mm calculus at the right vesicoureteric junction
tm.m: Distal ureteric calculi smaller than 10 mm have a high spontaneous passage rate, facilitated by alpha-1A smooth muscle relaxation at the vesicoureteric junction.
tm.g: Uncomplicated distal ureteric stone <10 mm with controlled pain and normal renal function -> watchful waiting
x: Emergency percutaneous nephrostomy decompression is indicated for an obstructed infected system, acute kidney injury or solitary kidney, none of which are present here.
Open ureterolithotomy is obsolete for uncomplicated 6 mm distal stones and reserved for rare complex anatomical failures.
Immediate shock wave lithotripsy is unnecessary because most 6 mm stones at the vesicoureteric junction pass spontaneously with conservative care.
Ureteroscopic laser lithotripsy is reserved for stones over 10 mm, refractory pain, persistent obstruction or failure of conservative passage after 4 weeks.
f: a 6 mm obstructing ureteric stone accompanied by rigors, temperature 39.2°C and acute kidney injury
failure of both endoscopic ureteroscopy and percutaneous access in a patient with complex urinary reconstruction
a persistent 8 mm proximal ureteric or renal pelvic calculus that has failed to pass after conservative management
a 12 mm ureteric stone or a 6 mm stone with intractable pain despite analgesia

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old man attends the metabolic stone clinic after passing his third urinary calculus in 5 years. Infrared spectroscopy of the passed stone confirms pure calcium oxalate composition. He works as a long-distance lorry driver, drinks approximately 1 litre of fluid daily and eats salted processed meals.
Serum calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone and urate are normal. His 24-hour urine volume is 1.1 litres.
o: Add 6 g of table salt to meals daily
Drink 2.5 to 3 litres of fluid daily
Eat 2 portions of spinach and nuts daily
Limit dietary calcium under 300 mg daily
Take vitamin C 1000 mg supplements daily
hq_q.w: Increasing fluid intake to 2.5 to 3 litres daily to keep 24-hour urine output above 2 litres is the most effective way to prevent recurrent calcium oxalate stones, alongside reducing salt and keeping normal dietary calcium.
hq_q.f: Hypercalciuria persisting despite fluid and low-salt diet -> add a thiazide diuretic such as bendroflumethiazide.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important dietary advice to prevent recurrence?

c: drinks approximately 1 litre of fluid daily
tm.m: Increasing urinary volume lowers the supersaturation product of calcium and oxalate ions below the threshold for crystal nucleation.
tm.g: Recurrent calcium oxalate stones with low 24-hour urine volume -> drink 2.5 to 3 litres of fluid daily
x: High dietary sodium intake reduces proximal tubular sodium and calcium reabsorption, increasing calciuria and promoting stone formation.
Spinach, rhubarb, beetroot and nuts have high oxalate content, which increases urinary oxalate excretion and promotes calcium oxalate stones.
Restricting dietary calcium leaves free oxalate unbound in the gut lumen, increasing intestinal oxalate absorption and worsening hyperoxaluria.
High-dose ascorbic acid is metabolised endogenously to oxalate and excreted in the urine, increasing calcium oxalate stone formation.
f: the patient had salt-wasting adrenal insufficiency rather than recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis
dietary folate and magnesium supplementation in a patient without oxalate stones
never appropriate for stone prevention; normal dietary calcium (700 to 1200 mg daily) should be maintained to bind gut oxalate
treatment of clinical scurvy rather than prevention of calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old man presents to his GP with a 3-day history of burning dysuria and urinary frequency every 2 hours. He feels systemically well with no fever, rigors, haematuria or loin pain, and he has no indwelling catheter.
Temperature 36.9°C, pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 136/80 mmHg. His abdomen is soft and non-tender, and digital rectal examination shows a smooth, non-tender prostate.
o: Antibiotics without sending a urine sample
Culture and 3 days of oral antibiotics
Culture and 7 days of oral antibiotics
Urine dipstick testing to decide treatment
hq_q.w: Lower urinary tract infection in men requires a pre-treatment midstream urine culture followed by a 7-day course of trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin. Urine dipsticks should not be used to diagnose UTI in patients over 65 years.
hq_q.f: Non-pregnant woman under 65 with uncomplicated lower UTI -> 3-day antibiotic course.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: no fever, rigors, haematuria or loin pain
tm.m: Male lower UTIs carry a higher prevalence of anatomical outflow abnormality and prostatic involvement, requiring pre-treatment culture and a full 7-day antibiotic course.
tm.g: Symptomatic afebrile lower UTI in a man -> send MSU culture and give 7 days of antibiotics
x: All men presenting with symptoms of a urinary tract infection must have a pre-treatment midstream urine culture sent to guide targeted therapy.
A 3-day course is only sufficient for uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women; men require 7 days of treatment to prevent relapse.
PHE and NICE guidance state that urine dipstick testing is unreliable in patients over 65 years because asymptomatic bacteriuria and pyuria are common.
Symptomatic lower urinary tract infection in a man requires prompt antibiotic treatment after culture collection to prevent ascending pyelonephritis or prostatitis.
f: uncomplicated lower UTI in a non-pregnant woman aged under 65 years with classic symptoms
a 32 year old non-pregnant woman presenting with uncomplicated dysuria and frequency
a 28 year old woman presenting with only one equivocal urinary symptom
asymptomatic bacteriuria in an older nursing home resident without urinary symptoms

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman is 38 weeks pregnant. She has had dysuria and frequency for 2 days. She has no fever or loin pain and no drug allergies.
Temperature 36.9°C. Urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes. A sample has been sent for culture.
hq_q.w: Nitrofurantoin near term can cause haemolysis in the newborn. Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester as a folate antagonist.
hq_q.f: 10 weeks pregnant → nitrofurantoin is first choice, avoid trimethoprim.
hq_q.ql: Which antibiotic is most likely to harm the baby if given now?

tm.m: Nitrofurantoin near delivery can cause haemolysis in the newborn
tm.g: UTI at term: avoid nitrofurantoin
f: low-severity community-acquired pneumonia
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cefalexin (Avoid cephalosporins in immediate/anaphylactic penicillin allergy)
breastfeeding + urticarial rash and facial swelling after amoxicillin
12 days + getting worse rather than better
x: Ruled out here: requires low-severity community-acquired pneumonia, whereas this patient has 38 weeks pregnant, nitrites and leucocytes.
Avoid cephalosporins in immediate/anaphylactic penicillin allergy
Ruled out here: requires breastfeeding + urticarial rash and facial swelling after amoxicillin, whereas this patient has 38 weeks pregnant, nitrites and leucocytes.
Ruled out here: requires 12 days + getting worse rather than better, whereas this patient has 38 weeks pregnant, nitrites and leucocytes.

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman presents with a 2-day history of high fever, rigors, right loin pain and vomiting. One week ago she had untreated dysuria and urinary frequency. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago.
Temperature 38.9°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg. There is marked right renal angle tenderness. Urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leucocytes, and urinary beta-hCG is negative.
hq_q.w: Acute pyelonephritis presents with fever, rigors, vomiting and unilateral renal angle tenderness after ascending lower urinary symptoms. Send a midstream urine culture and treat with cefalexin, co-amoxiclav or ciprofloxacin for 7 to 14 days.
hq_q.f: Dysuria and frequency without fever, rigors or loin pain -> acute uncomplicated cystitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: high fever, rigors, right loin pain and vomiting
tm.m: Ascending uropathogenic Escherichia coli infection from the bladder into the renal pelvis and parenchyma triggers acute tubulointerstitial inflammation and systemic pyrexia.
tm.g: Fever, rigors and renal angle tenderness after dysuria with positive nitrites -> acute pyelonephritis
x: Acute appendicitis causes periumbilical pain migrating to McBurney's point in the right iliac fossa with local guarding rather than renal angle tenderness and nitrituria.
Uncomplicated lower cystitis causes dysuria, frequency and suprapubic discomfort without systemic fever, rigors, vomiting or loin tenderness.
Uncomplicated ureteric colic causes afebrile paroxysmal loin-to-groin pain and microscopic haematuria rather than high fever and preceded cystitis.
Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago and the urinary beta-hCG test is negative, excluding ectopic pregnancy.
f: central abdominal pain migrating to the right iliac fossa with rebound tenderness at McBurney's point
dysuria, urgency and suprapubic discomfort with temperature 36.7°C and no renal angle tenderness
sudden afebrile colicky loin-to-groin pain with blood 3+ on dipstick and negative nitrites
6 weeks of amenorrhoea, iliac fossa pain, vaginal bleeding and a positive urinary pregnancy test

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old man presents with a 3-month history of a dragging ache in his left hemiscrotum that worsens after standing all day. He and his partner have been trying to conceive for 14 months.
On standing there is a tortuous swelling above the left testis that feels like a bag of worms and empties completely when he lies supine. Both testes feel normal.
hq_q.w: A varicocele is a dilated pampiniform venous plexus, occurring on the left in 90% of cases because the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein. It feels like a bag of worms on standing and collapses supine.
hq_q.f: New non-emptying left varicocele in a man over 50 -> urgent renal imaging for left renal cell carcinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: dragging ache in his left hemiscrotum
empties completely when he lies supine
tm.m: Incompetent valves in the internal spermatic vein allow venous reflux into the pampiniform plexus, raising intrascrotal temperature and impairing spermatogenesis.
tm.g: Left scrotal 'bag of worms' swelling on standing that empties when supine -> varicocele
x: An epididymal cyst is a smooth, tense, brilliantly transilluminating globular swelling posterior to the testis that does not empty on lying flat.
A hydrocele is a smooth, fluctuant fluid collection within the tunica vaginalis that surrounds the testis and transilluminates brightly.
An inguinoscrotal hernia extends down from the inguinal canal so the examiner cannot get above it, and it has an expansile cough impulse.
A testicular tumour presents as a firm, solid, non-transilluminating mass within the body of the testis itself that does not empty when supine.
f: a smooth, fluctuant, transilluminating pea-to-grape-sized swelling palpable separate from and posterior to the testis
a smooth, fluctuant, transilluminating scrotal swelling through which the testis cannot be palpated separately
a scrotal swelling that you cannot get above on palpation and that has a palpable cough impulse
a hard, irregular, painless mass within the body of the testis that does not change with posture

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old man presents after noticing a painless lump in his right hemiscrotum for 6 months that has not changed in size. He has no urinary symptoms or trauma history.
Examination reveals a 2 cm smooth, fluctuant swelling superior and posterior to the right testis. The right testis is palpable separately and feels normal. The examiner can get above the swelling and it transilluminates brightly.
hq_q.w: An epididymal cyst (or spermatocele) is a benign fluid-filled dilatation of the epididymis presenting as a smooth, fluctuant, brightly transilluminating swelling situated superior and posterior to the testis, where the normal testis can be palpated quite separately.
hq_q.f: Transilluminating scrotal swelling surrounding an impalpable testis -> hydrocele.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: painless lump in his right hemiscrotum
superior and posterior to the right testis
tm.m: Cystic dilatation of efferent ductules in the head of the epididymis creates a discrete, fluid-filled sac separate from the testicular body.
tm.g: Scrotal swelling that transilluminates + examiner can get above + testis palpable separately -> epididymal cyst
x: A hydrocele accumulates within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis, so the testis cannot be palpated separately from the fluid collection.
An indirect inguinoscrotal hernia arises through the deep inguinal ring, so the examiner cannot get above the mass at the neck of the scrotum.
A testicular seminoma is a firm, solid intratesticular mass that does not transilluminate and is part of the testis itself.
A varicocele feels like a compressible bag of worms on standing, does not transilluminate and occurs predominantly on the left side.
f: a transilluminating right scrotal swelling that completely surrounds the testis so the testis cannot be felt separately
a reducible scrotal mass with a positive cough impulse where the examiner cannot get above its upper border
a firm, solid, non-transilluminating mass arising within the body of the testis
a compressible left-sided scrotal swelling feeling like a bag of worms that disappears on lying flat

hq_q.s:
A 25 year old man has noticed a painless swelling of his left scrotum over 6 weeks. He has had no injury or infection.
There is a smooth, non-tender swelling surrounding the left testis that transilluminates. The examiner can get above it. The testis cannot be felt separately.
hq_q.w: A new hydrocele in a young man can hide a testicular tumour, so ultrasound looks at the testis.
hq_q.f: A hydrocele in a newborn → usually resolves by 1 to 2 years.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important investigation?

tm.m: A tumour can produce a reactive hydrocele that hides it
tm.g: New hydrocele in a young man: scrotal ultrasound to exclude a tumour
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Blood cultures (Used for: Fever with a source unknown, sepsis, endocarditis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to CT abdomen (CT is used to stage a confirmed testicular cancer; ultrasound looks at the testis first)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Urine culture and sensitivity (Enterococcus links to the urinary tract, not this organism)
2 episodes this year
x: Used for: Fever with a source unknown, sepsis, endocarditis
CT is used to stage a confirmed testicular cancer; ultrasound looks at the testis first.
Enterococcus links to the urinary tract, not this organism
Ruled out here: requires 2 episodes this year, whereas this patient has 25 year old man, surrounding the left testis.

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old man presents with a 3-day history of right scrotal pain and swelling preceded by dysuria and frequency. He has benign prostatic hyperplasia and has not been sexually active for 5 years.
Temperature 38.1°C, pulse rate 92 bpm. The right epididymis is swollen and tender, and scrotal elevation relieves his pain. Urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes.
hq_q.w: Epididymo-orchitis has a bimodal aetiology: in men aged over 35 years without sexually transmitted infection risk factors (especially those with bladder outflow obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia), ascending enteric coliforms such as Escherichia coli are the commonest cause.
hq_q.f: Sexually active man under 35 years with urethral discharge -> Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely causative organism?

c: not been sexually active for 5 years
tm.m: Bladder outlet obstruction increases high-pressure voiding reflux of coliform-infected urine into the ejaculatory ducts and vas deferens.
tm.g: Epididymo-orchitis in an older man with BPH, positive nitrites and no STI risk -> Escherichia coli
x: Chlamydia trachomatis is the commonest cause of epididymo-orchitis in sexually active men under 35 years, not in a celibate 70 year old with nitrituria.
Mycoplasma genitalium is a sexually transmitted pathogen causing non-gonococcal urethritis and epididymitis in sexually active individuals.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is sexually acquired and typically presents with profuse purulent urethral discharge in sexually active men.
Treponema pallidum causes a painless indurated primary chancre and painless inguinal lymphadenopathy rather than acute coliform epididymo-orchitis.
f: a 22 year old man with a new sexual partner, mucopurulent urethral discharge and negative urinary nitrites
persistent non-gonococcal urethritis and epididymitis in a sexually active young adult with negative chlamydia testing
acute epididymo-orchitis with profuse purulent urethral discharge and Gram-negative intracellular diplococci
a single painless indurated genital ulcer with non-tender rubbery inguinal lymphadenopathy

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old man presents with a 3-day history of right scrotal pain, swelling and dysuria. He has benign prostatic hyperplasia, no sexual risk factors and no drug allergies.
Temperature 37.9°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 136/80 mmHg. The right epididymis and testis are swollen and tender with a normal testicular lie. Urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leucocytes, and urine culture is sent.
hq_q.w: In men over 35 years without sexually transmitted infection risk factors, epididymo-orchitis is usually caused by enteric coliforms from the urinary tract and is treated with oral ofloxacin or levofloxacin for 14 days.
hq_q.f: Sexually transmitted epididymo-orchitis in a man under 35 -> IM ceftriaxone stat plus oral doxycycline for 10 to 14 days.
hq_q.ql: Which oral antibiotic is most appropriate?

c: benign prostatic hyperplasia, no sexual risk factors
tm.m: Fluoroquinolones achieve high tissue penetration across the blood-epididymis barrier and provide bactericidal activity against uropathogenic Enterobacterales.
tm.g: Enteric coliform epididymo-orchitis in an older man without STI risk -> oral ofloxacin (or levofloxacin)
x: Azithromycin is a macrolide used as a second-line option in sexually transmitted infections and lacks activity against uropathogenic Escherichia coli.
Doxycycline targets Chlamydia trachomatis in sexually acquired epididymo-orchitis and does not reliably cover enteric coliforms in an older man with BPH.
Metronidazole only covers obligate anaerobes and protozoa such as Trichomonas vaginalis and has zero activity against aerobic Gram-negative coliforms.
Phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) has narrow Gram-positive streptococcal activity and cannot treat Gram-negative enteric epididymo-orchitis.
f: confirmed Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis in a patient with a documented true allergy to tetracyclines
a 23 year old sexually active man presenting with suspected chlamydial epididymo-orchitis
urogenital Trichomonas vaginalis infection confirmed on nucleic acid amplification testing
acute streptococcal tonsillitis with a high FeverPAIN score

hq_q.s:
A 14 year old boy presents with a 12-hour history of localised pain at the upper pole of his left testis that came on gradually during football. He has no vomiting or dysuria.
Temperature 36.8°C, pulse rate 78 bpm. The left testis lies in a normal vertical axis and the cremasteric reflex is brisk. A tender pea-sized nodule is visible as a blue dot at the upper pole.
hq_q.w: Torsion of the appendix testis (hydatid of Morgagni) peaks at 7 to 14 years and causes gradual upper-pole testicular pain with a paratesticular blue dot sign, normal vertical testicular lie and preserved cremasteric reflex.
hq_q.f: Sudden severe pain, vomiting, high horizontal testicular lie and absent cremasteric reflex -> testicular torsion.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: blue dot at the upper pole
tm.m: Ischaemic venous infarction of the pedunculated vestigial Mullerian remnant at the upper pole of the testis is seen through thin prepubertal scrotal skin as a cyanotic nodule.
tm.g: Localised upper-pole testicular pain with a 'blue dot' sign and intact cremasteric reflex -> torsion of the appendix testis
x: Bacterial epididymo-orchitis causes diffuse posterior epididymal swelling, fever and dysuria or pyuria rather than a discrete upper-pole blue dot nodule.
A strangulated inguinal hernia presents with a tense, irreducible inguinoscrotal mass that you cannot get above and features of bowel obstruction.
True spermatic cord torsion presents with abrupt severe pain, vomiting, a high-riding horizontal testis and an absent cremasteric reflex.
A varicocele causes a painless or dull dragging 'bag of worms' swelling superior to the testis on standing, not an acute tender blue nodule.
f: gradual diffuse posterior scrotal swelling with fever, dysuria and positive leucocytes on urinalysis
a tense, tender inguinoscrotal swelling extending from the inguinal canal with bilious vomiting
abrupt-onset severe hemiscrotal pain with vomiting, a high-riding horizontal testis and an absent cremasteric reflex
a dull left scrotal ache worse on standing with a compressible bag-of-worms venous plexus

hq_q.s:
A 15 year old boy attends the emergency department 3 hours after the sudden onset of severe right scrotal pain and vomiting. The right testis is high-riding and horizontal with an absent cremasteric reflex.
At emergency scrotal exploration, the right spermatic cord is twisted 720 degrees; after detorsion and warm packs, the testis becomes pink and bleeding from the tunica confirms viability.
o: Remove the right testis and fix the left
Untwist and fix the affected testis only
Untwist the cord and observe without fixation
hq_q.w: When a torsed testis recovers viability after detorsion, bilateral orchidopexy (fixing both testes) is mandatory because the predisposing bell-clapper tunica vaginalis anomaly is bilateral in over 80% of patients.
hq_q.f: Testis remains black and necrotic after detorsion and warming -> ipsilateral orchidectomy plus contralateral orchidopexy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate operative procedure?

c: becomes pink and bleeding from the tunica confirms viability
tm.m: High attachment of the tunica vaginalis (bell-clapper deformity) affects both hemiscrota, so fixing only one side leaves the contralateral testis at high risk of future torsion.
tm.g: Viable testis at exploration for testicular torsion -> untwist and fix both testes (bilateral orchidopexy)
x: The right testis is viable and the contralateral testis is normal; bilateral orchidectomy would cause unnecessary surgical castration and infertility.
Orchidectomy of the affected testis is only performed when the testis remains black and non-viable after detorsion and warming.
Unilateral fixation leaves the contralateral testis exposed to asynchronous torsion because the bell-clapper deformity is bilateral in most patients.
Detorsion without suture fixation to the dartos pouch results in a high rate of recurrent spermatic cord torsion.
f: never indicated in unilateral testicular torsion
the right testis remained black, necrotic and non-viable after detorsion and warming for 15 minutes
fixation of an isolated undescended testis without torsion
manual preoperative detorsion as a temporary bridge before definitive bilateral surgical orchidopexy

hq_q.s:
A 13 year old boy presents to the emergency department 5 hours after waking with sudden severe left testicular pain and two episodes of vomiting.
Temperature 37.0°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg. Examination reveals a swollen, tender, high-riding left testis lying horizontally with an absent left cremasteric reflex. The surgical registrar consents the family for immediate scrotal exploration without waiting for a Doppler ultrasound scan.
o: His fertility is lost in 1 hour
hq_q.w: Testicular salvage in spermatic cord torsion is strictly time-critical: salvage exceeds 90% when detorsion occurs within 6 hours of onset, falls to 50% by 12 hours, and drops below 10% after 24 hours.
hq_q.f: Symptom duration exceeding 24 hours with a hard, necrotic testis -> salvage rate falls below 10%.
hq_q.ql: Which clinical principle explains the urgency of immediate exploration?

c: without waiting for a Doppler ultrasound
tm.m: Rotation of the spermatic cord occludes venous drainage and arterial inflow, causing irreversible coagulative necrosis of seminiferous tubules after 6 hours of warm ischaemia.
tm.g: Suspected testicular torsion at 5 hours -> immediate surgical exploration because salvage falls sharply after 6 hours
x: Testicular torsion is an acute vascular ischaemic emergency rather than a bacterial infection, so pus formation is not the reason for 6-hour urgency.
Irreversible ischaemic necrosis of the affected testis begins after 4 to 6 hours rather than 1 hour, and the healthy contralateral testis maintains spermatogenesis.
Testicular tissue tolerates up to 4 to 6 hours of warm ischaemia with >90% salvage; complete necrosis does not occur within 30 minutes.
Untreated testicular torsion leads to ischaemic hemorrhagic infarction and subsequent testicular atrophy rather than spontaneous tunica albuginea rupture.
f: untreated suppurative bacterial epididymo-orchitis progressing to a scrotal pyocele over days
never accurate; the critical warm ischaemia window for testicular salvage is 6 hours
never accurate; complete testicular infarction typically occurs after 12 to 24 hours of untreated cord torsion
high-energy blunt scrotal trauma causing tunica albuginea disruption and haematocele

hq_q.s:
A term male infant born 6 hours ago by spontaneous vaginal delivery is found to have a swollen left hemiscrotum during his routine newborn examination. He is breastfeeding well, settled and shows no signs of distress on palpation.
Temperature 36.8°C, heart rate 132 bpm. The left hemiscrotum is enlarged, firm and dark bluish-red. The left testis feels hard and non-tender, does not transilluminate and has no inguinal swelling.
hq_q.w: Neonatal (perinatal) testicular torsion is typically an extravaginal torsion of the entire spermatic cord and tunica vaginalis occurring It presents at the newborn check as a firm, hard, painless, darkly discoloured hemiscrotum that does not transilluminate.
hq_q.f: Soft, painless, brightly transilluminating scrotal swelling in a newborn -> congenital communicating hydrocele.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Before the gubernaculum and tunica vaginalis adhere to the dartos fascia in the first weeks of life, the entire spermatic cord and tunica can twist extravaginally in utero.
tm.g: Painless hard dark-blue non-transilluminating hemiscrotum at the newborn check -> neonatal testicular torsion
x: A congenital hydrocele is soft, fluctuant, non-discoloured and transilluminates brightly because it contains clear peritoneal fluid.
An incarcerated inguinal hernia causes an irritable, vomiting infant with a tense mass extending from the inguinal canal that you cannot get above.
A neonatal scrotal haematoma typically follows traumatic breech delivery or neonatal adrenal haemorrhage, with a palpable normal-consistency testis inside bruising.
Varicoceles develop during puberty and adolescence and are virtually unseen in neonates.
f: a soft, fluctuant, normal-coloured scrotal swelling in a newborn that transilluminates brightly
an inconsolable, biliously vomiting neonate with a tense inguinoscrotal mass extending into the inguinal canal
superficial scrotal ecchymosis after a traumatic breech delivery with a normal-feeling testis on ultrasound
an adolescent boy with a left-sided compressible bag-of-worms swelling on standing

hq_q.s:
A 25 year old man presents to the rapid-access urology clinic with a 6-week history of a painless lump in his right testis and dull back ache.
There is a 2.5 cm hard, craggy, non-tender intratesticular mass on the right that does not transilluminate. Ultrasound shows a solid intratesticular lesion. Serum AFP is 620 kU/L (<10), beta-hCG is 340 IU/L (<5) and LDH is 410 IU/L (140-280).
hq_q.w: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is secreted by yolk sac and embryonal carcinoma elements and is NEVER elevated in a pure classical seminoma. An intratesticular mass with raised serum AFP is diagnostic of a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour (NSGCT).
hq_q.f: Solid testicular tumour in a 35-year-old with normal AFP and normal or mildly raised beta-hCG -> classical pure seminoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely histological diagnosis?

tm.m: Yolk sac tumour and embryonal differentiation within a mixed non-seminomatous germ cell tumour synthesise alpha-fetoprotein, whereas syncytiotrophoblasts secrete beta-hCG.
tm.g: Intratesticular mass in a young man with raised serum AFP -> non-seminomatous germ cell tumour
x: Pure classical seminoma never secretes alpha-fetoprotein; any elevation in serum AFP mandates classification and management as a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour.
Primary testicular lymphoma affects men aged over 60 years and is associated with normal serum AFP and beta-hCG.
Leydig cell tumours are rare stromal neoplasms that secrete androgens or oestrogens causing gynaecomastia or precocious puberty, with normal AFP and beta-hCG.
Sertoli cell tumours are benign-behaving sex-cord stromal tumours that do not secrete alpha-fetoprotein or beta-hCG.
f: a homogeneous lobulated testicular mass in a 36 year old man with strictly normal serum AFP and mildly raised LDH
a 72 year old man presenting with a painless diffuse testicular mass, night sweats and normal AFP and beta-hCG
a testicular mass associated with gynaecomastia, suppressed gonadotrophins and normal AFP and beta-hCG
an incidental small well-circumscribed testicular nodule with normal AFP and beta-hCG and tubular Sertoli histology

hq_q.s: A 27 year old man has a 3 cm hard lump in his left testis. Ultrasound and tumour markers suggest a germ cell tumour and he is listed for radical inguinal orchidectomy next week. He and his partner hope to have children in the future and ask what can be done before treatment.
o: GnRH analogue to protect the testis
hq_q.w: Surgery and chemotherapy can affect fertility, so sperm banking is offered before treatment. Key discriminator: Before germ cell tumour treatment: offer sperm banking.
hq_q.f: He has had an orchidectomy and is low → testosterone replacement.
hq_q.ql: Which should be offered?

tm.m: Surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy can all reduce sperm production
tm.g: Before germ cell tumour treatment: offer sperm banking
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Biopsy of the other testis (A biopsy of the other testis looks for germ cell neoplasia in situ in high-risk men; it does not preserve fertility)

the presentation instead showed features specific to GnRH analogue to protect the testis (GnRH analogues are tried to protect the ovaries during chemotherapy; there is no evidence they protect sperm production)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hormone therapy (Hormone therapy is not used for testicular cancer and does not preserve fertility)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Wait until treatment ends (Chemotherapy and orchidectomy impair fertility so banking must happen before treatment)
x: A biopsy of the other testis looks for germ cell neoplasia in situ in high-risk men; it does not preserve fertility.
GnRH analogues are tried to protect the ovaries during chemotherapy; there is no evidence they protect sperm production.
Hormone therapy is not used for testicular cancer and does not preserve fertility.
Chemotherapy and orchidectomy impair fertility so banking must happen before treatment

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old man presents with a 2-month history of progressive, painless enlargement of his left testis, drenching night sweats and 5 kg of unintentional weight loss.
Temperature 37.4°C. Examination reveals a firm, diffusely enlarged, non-tender left testis that does not transilluminate, plus bilateral rubbery axillary lymphadenopathy. Scrotal ultrasound shows a diffusely hypoechoic hypervascular left testis. Serum AFP and beta-hCG are within normal limits.
hq_q.w: Primary testicular lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) is the commonest testicular malignancy in men aged over 60 years, presenting with painless diffuse testicular enlargement, B symptoms and normal serum AFP and beta-hCG.
hq_q.f: Painless testicular mass in a 28-year-old man with raised AFP and beta-hCG -> non-seminomatous germ cell tumour.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: drenching night sweats and 5 kg of unintentional weight loss
AFP and beta-hCG are within normal limits
tm.m: Malignant B-lymphocytes infiltrate the immunoprivileged testicular interstitium in older men, causing diffuse painless enlargement and systemic B symptoms without AFP or hCG secretion.
tm.g: Testicular mass in a man >60 years with B symptoms, lymphadenopathy and normal AFP/hCG -> testicular lymphoma
x: Testicular choriocarcinoma is an aggressive germ cell tumour of young men that produces extremely high serum beta-hCG (>10,000 IU/L) and early lung metastases.
Classical seminoma peaks between 30 and 45 years of age and does not typically present at age 70 with axillary lymphadenopathy and B symptoms.
Testicular teratoma is a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour affecting men aged 20 to 35 years and showing cystic and calcified elements on ultrasound.
Yolk sac tumour is the commonest testicular tumour in infants and young children under 3 years and always produces markedly elevated serum AFP.
f: a 24 year old man with haemoptysis, cannonball lung metastases and a serum beta-hCG of 85,000 IU/L
a 35 year old man with an isolated painless solid testicular mass, normal AFP and no axillary lymphadenopathy
a 26 year old man with a heterogeneous cystic and calcified intratesticular mass
a 2 year old boy with a solid testicular mass and a markedly elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia is undergoing urethral catheterisation for acute painful urinary retention. After instilling lignocaine gel, a 14 Fr catheter is advanced halfway along the urethra and no urine drains.
The operator inflates the retention balloon with 10 mL of sterile water, and the patient immediately cries out in excruciating perineal pain with frank blood at the meatus.
o: Balloon slips safely into the bladder
hq_q.w: Never inflate a catheter balloon until the catheter is advanced fully to the bifurcation hub and urine flows freely. Inflating inside the urethra causes immediate severe pain, urethral mucosal tear and frank bleeding.
hq_q.f: Catheter advanced fully to the hub with free urine drainage before balloon inflation -> safe intravesical placement.
hq_q.ql: Which complication has most likely occurred?

c: inflates the retention balloon with 10 mL
excruciating perineal pain with frank blood at the meatus
tm.m: Distending a 10 mL retention balloon inside the narrow prostatic or bulbar urethra ruptures the urethral mucosa and corpus spongiosum.
tm.g: Balloon inflated before advancing to the hub or seeing urine flow -> severe pain and urethral tear
x: A 10 mL balloon inflated inside the urethra becomes trapped in the bulbar or prostatic lumen rather than slipping up into the bladder.
Halfway advancement leaves the catheter tip in the urethra below the external sphincter, so the bladder dome is not reached.
Catheter-associated bacteriuria develops over days of indwelling drainage rather than presenting as instantaneous pain and urethral bleeding during inflation.
Intra-urethral balloon inflation causes immediate excruciating pain and frank urethral bleeding at the moment of inflation, not painless haematuria a week later.
f: the catheter had been advanced to the bifurcation hub with free urine flow prior to inflating the balloon
high-energy blunt lower abdominal trauma in a patient with a distended full bladder
fever, cloudy foul-smelling urine and suprapubic tenderness developing 5 days after uncomplicated catheter insertion
secondary sloughing of prostatic eschar 7 to 10 days after transurethral resection of the prostate

hq_q.s:
An 84 year old woman in a nursing home has a long-term indwelling urethral catheter for neurogenic retention. Carers report that the urine in her drainage bag looks cloudy today.
She is eating and drinking well and is at her cognitive baseline. Temperature 36.8°C, pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 134/72 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and the catheter drains freely.
o: Change the catheter and start antibiotics
Use a urine dipstick to decide treatment
hq_q.w: Bacteriuria is universal in patients with a long-term indwelling catheter. NICE guidance states that cloudy or malodorous urine alone in a systemically well catheterised patient must not be tested with dipsticks or treated with antibiotics.
hq_q.f: Fever, rigors, acute delirium or loin pain in a catheterised patient -> change the catheter, send a sample from the new catheter and start empirical antibiotics.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Polymicrobial bacterial biofilm forms on all indwelling catheters within days; giving antibiotics for asymptomatic colonisation selects for multidrug-resistant organisms without clinical benefit.
tm.g: Cloudy urine in an afebrile, systemically well patient with a long-term catheter -> observe without antibiotics
x: Catheter replacement plus empirical antibiotics is indicated only when there is symptomatic catheter-associated UTI (fever, rigors, loin pain or new sepsis-related delirium).
NICE specifically recommends against routine antibiotic prophylaxis in long-term catheter users because it drives antimicrobial resistance without preventing symptomatic infection.
She has chronic neurogenic urinary retention requiring long-term bladder drainage, so removing the catheter without an alternative plan would precipitate retention.
Urine dipsticks are never used in catheterised patients because bacteriuria and pyuria are universally present from catheter biofilm.
f: she developed a temperature of 38.8°C, rigors and right renal angle tenderness
recurrent symptomatic UTIs in a non-catheterised woman after behavioural and non-antibiotic measures have failed
an unnecessary short-term post-operative catheter in a mobile patient with normal bladder function
a 25 year old non-catheterised woman presenting with mild dysuria alone

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old uncircumcised man had an indwelling urethral catheter inserted on the medical ward 8 hours ago for fluid balance monitoring. He now reports severe, throbbing pain at the tip of his penis.
Examination shows the foreskin retracted behind the coronal sulcus, forming a tight, oedematous constricting ring. The glans penis is tense, congested and swollen, and the foreskin cannot be drawn forward.
hq_q.w: Paraphimosis occurs when a retracted foreskin is left behind the glans after catheterisation and forms a tight oedematous constricting ring around the coronal sulcus. Urgent manual reduction is required to prevent glans necrosis.
hq_q.f: Tight non-retractile foreskin distal to the glans causing ballooning on voiding -> phimosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: urethral catheter inserted on the medical ward 8 hours ago
tm.m: The tight prepuce trapped proximal to the coronal sulcus obstructs superficial venous and lymphatic return from the glans, causing progressive glans oedema and arterial compromise.
tm.g: Retracted foreskin trapped behind a swollen congested glans after catheterisation -> paraphimosis
x: Infective balanitis causes diffuse erythema and subpreputial exudate over the glans without a retracted constricting ring behind the coronal sulcus.
Phimosis is the inability to retract a tight, scarred distal foreskin back over the glans, whereas here the foreskin is stuck in the retracted position.
Ischaemic priapism causes a rigid, tender erection of the paired corpora cavernosa with a soft glans, rather than isolated glans and preputial oedema.
A urethral stricture is a late fibrotic narrowing of the urethral lumen presenting months after catheterisation with a slow urinary stream.
f: erythema, pruritus and white curdy subpreputial discharge in a man with poorly controlled diabetes
a scarred, white fibrotic preputial ring distal to the glans that cannot be retracted behind the corona
a persistent painful erection lasting over 4 hours with rigid corpora cavernosa and a soft glans
a slow, spraying urinary stream and plateau uroflowmetry curve 6 months after catheter removal

hq_q.s:
A 55 year old woman has had gradual hearing loss in her left ear over a year, with intermittent tinnitus on that side. She has no ear discharge or vertigo.
Otoscopy is normal in both ears. Weber's test lateralises to the right. Rinne's test is positive on both sides.
hq_q.w: In unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, Weber's test lateralises to the unaffected (better) ear and Rinne's test remains positive bilaterally (air conduction louder than bone conduction). Asymmetric sensorineural loss requires MRI of the internal acoustic meatus.
hq_q.f: Weber to the left with negative Rinne on the left → left conductive loss.
hq_q.ql: Which type of hearing loss is it?

c: Weber's test lateralises to the right
Rinne's test is positive on both sides
tm.m: Cochlear or retrocochlear pathology reduces perception on the left while air conduction remains superior to bone
tm.g: Weber lateralises away from the deaf ear with bilateral positive Rinne -> sensorineural hearing loss in the deaf ear
f: Weber lateralising to the left ear with bone conduction louder than air conduction on the left
bilateral chronic otitis media with bone conduction louder than air conduction in both ears
right-sided muffled hearing with Weber lateralising to the right and a negative right Rinne test
progressive right-sided deafness with Weber lateralising to the left and bilateral positive Rinne tests
x: Left conductive hearing loss causes Weber's test to lateralise to the affected left ear with a negative left Rinne test.
Bilateral mixed hearing loss produces negative Rinne tests where bone conduction exceeds air conduction.
Right conductive hearing loss lateralises Weber's test to the right, but right Rinne's test would be negative and symptoms right-sided.
Right sensorineural hearing loss causes right-sided deafness and lateralises Weber's test toward the normal left ear.

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old man has had progressively worsening hearing loss and high-pitched tinnitus in his right ear for 18 months, with recent numbness over his right cheek and mild gait unsteadiness.
Otoscopy is normal. Weber's test lateralises to the left and Rinne's test is positive bilaterally. Right facial sensation and the right corneal reflex are diminished, with intact facial expression.
hq_q.w: A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) expanding out of the internal acoustic meatus into the cerebellopontine angle compresses the trigeminal nerve (CN V) early, causing ipsilateral facial hypoaesthesia and loss of the afferent corneal reflex before facial weakness appears.
hq_q.f: Bilateral schwannomas in a young adult → neurofibromatosis type 2.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Expansion of an eighth nerve schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle compresses the adjacent fifth cranial nerve
tm.g: Unilateral sensorineural deafness + ipsilateral trigeminal numbness and absent corneal reflex -> vestibular schwannoma
f: acute unilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness including the forehead with intact facial sensation
foul-smelling ear discharge, an attic retraction pocket with keratin debris and conductive hearing loss
progressive spastic weakness and hyperreflexia of the contralateral leg with normal hearing
recurrent 3 hour bouts of rotational vertigo with aural fullness and normal corneal reflexes
x: Bell's palsy causes acute lower motor neurone facial muscle paralysis over 24 to 72 hours without trigeminal sensory loss or chronic deafness.
Cholesteatoma presents with chronic foul-smelling otorrhoea, an attic keratinous crust on otoscopy, and conductive hearing loss.
A parasagittal falx meningioma compresses the medial motor cortex, causing contralateral lower-limb spastic weakness rather than cerebellopontine angle signs.
Meniere's disease causes episodic vertigo lasting hours with fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss and aural fullness, sparing the trigeminal nerve.

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman has had hearing loss in both ears over 2 years with tinnitus and unsteadiness. Her father had similar problems and needed brain surgery. She has no café-au-lait macules.
MRI shows bilateral masses in the internal acoustic meati and a small meningioma.
hq_q.w: NF2 is caused by a mutation on chromosome 22 and causes bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas.
hq_q.f: Café au lait spots and freckles in the armpits → NF1.
hq_q.ql: Which condition is most likely?

c: bilateral masses in the internal acoustic meati
tm.m: A chromosome 22 mutation causes schwannomas and meningiomas
tm.g: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas with a meningioma is NF2
