f: café au lait macules and axillary freckling
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sturge-Weber syndrome (Sturge-Weber gives a port-wine stain on the face with seizures, not bilateral deafness running in the family)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Tuberous sclerosis (Tuberous sclerosis gives ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas and seizures, not bilateral hearing loss)
haemangioblastomas with renal cysts
x: Ruled out here: requires café au lait macules and axillary freckling, whereas this patient has both ears, no café-au-lait macules.
Sturge-Weber gives a port-wine stain on the face with seizures, not bilateral deafness running in the family.
Tuberous sclerosis gives ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas and seizures, not bilateral hearing loss.
Ruled out here: requires haemangioblastomas with renal cysts, whereas this patient has both ears, no café-au-lait macules.

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man noticed this morning that the right side of his face has drooped. He has hypertension and smokes. He is examined to decide whether this is a stroke or Bell's palsy.
hq_q.w: In upper motor neurone lesions, the forehead is spared because it has supply from both sides of the brain.
hq_q.f: The forehead is weak too → lower motor neurone, such as Bell's palsy.
hq_q.ql: Which feature most suggests a stroke rather than Bell's palsy?

tm.m: The forehead gets supply from both hemispheres, so an upper motor neurone lesion spares it
tm.g: Forehead sparing points to a stroke
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Hyperacusis (Hyperacusis comes from a stapedius palsy in a lower motor neurone lesion such as Bell's palsy, so it argues against a stroke)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Loss of taste (Loss of taste on the front of the tongue happens in Bell's palsy because the facial nerve carries taste fibres)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pain behind the ear (Pain behind the ear often comes before Bell's palsy)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Reduced tear production (Reduced tears happen in Bell's palsy, a lower motor neurone lesion)
x: Hyperacusis comes from a stapedius palsy in a lower motor neurone lesion such as Bell's palsy, so it argues against a stroke.
Loss of taste on the front of the tongue happens in Bell's palsy because the facial nerve carries taste fibres.
Pain behind the ear often comes before Bell's palsy.
Reduced tears happen in Bell's palsy, a lower motor neurone lesion.

hq_q.s:
A 60 year old man has had severe pain in his right ear for 3 days. This morning the right side of his face became weak.
Temperature 37.5°C. There are vesicles in the right external auditory canal and on the pinna. There is weakness of the whole right side of the face, including the forehead. He has reduced hearing on the right.
hq_q.w: Shingles of the geniculate ganglion. Treat with aciclovir and steroids within 72 hours. Key discriminator: Ear vesicles with lower motor neurone facial weakness is Ramsay Hunt syndrome.
hq_q.f: Facial weakness without vesicles or ear pain → Bell's palsy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: severe pain in his right ear
vesicles in the right external auditory canal
tm.m: Zoster reactivates in the geniculate ganglion, affecting facial and hearing nerves
tm.g: Ear vesicles with lower motor neurone facial weakness is Ramsay Hunt syndrome
f: a red bulging drum in a child
facial weakness with no vesicles or ear pain
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cholesteatoma (Cholesteatoma gives painless smelly discharge over months, not acute ear pain with vesicles)
a diabetic with granulation tissue in the canal
x: Ruled out here: requires a red bulging drum in a child, whereas this patient has severe pain in his right ear, vesicles in the right external auditory canal.
Ruled out here: requires facial weakness with no vesicles or ear pain, whereas this patient has severe pain in his right ear, vesicles in the right external auditory canal.
Cholesteatoma gives painless smelly discharge over months, not acute ear pain with vesicles.
Ruled out here: requires a diabetic with granulation tissue in the canal, whereas this patient has severe pain in his right ear, vesicles in the right external auditory canal.

hq_q.s:
A 46 year old woman has had weakness of the left side of her face for 1 day. She has started prednisolone for Bell's palsy.
There is weakness of the whole left side of the face, including the forehead. She cannot close her left eye fully, and the eye is watering but not red. There are no vesicles in the ear.
hq_q.w: Impaired eyelid closure (lagophthalmos) in Bell's palsy risks exposure keratopathy and corneal ulceration. Protect the cornea with frequent daytime lubricating drops, night-time ocular ointment, and micropore taping of the eyelid shut during sleep.
hq_q.f: Within 72 hours of onset → prednisolone for 10 days.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important additional measure?

c: cannot close her left eye fully
tm.m: Paralysis of orbicularis oculi prevents blinking and lid closure, causing corneal desiccation and exposure ulceration
tm.g: Incomplete eye closure in Bell's palsy -> daytime lubricating drops, night ointment and lid taping
f: secondary mucopurulent bacterial conjunctivitis with sticky yellow discharge
persistent synkinesis and residual facial asymmetry during chronic recovery
painful vesicular lesions in the external auditory canal and conchal bowl indicating Ramsay Hunt syndrome
persistent unilateral muffled hearing with a dull retracted tympanic membrane
x: Topical antibiotics treat bacterial infection and do not prevent corneal desiccation from incomplete lid closure.
Facial muscle exercises do not protect the exposed cornea from overnight drying and ulceration.
Antiviral therapy alone is ineffective in idiopathic Bell's palsy without Ramsay Hunt vesicles.
Audiometry is not routinely required in uncomplicated Bell's palsy with normal otoscopy and no deafness.

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old woman has had constant spinning vertigo, nausea and unsteadiness for 2 days. It started a week after a cold. Her hearing is normal and she has no tinnitus, headache or weakness.
There is horizontal nystagmus beating to the right in all directions of gaze. The head impulse test shows a corrective saccade when her head is turned to the left. There is no skew deviation. Limb coordination is normal.
hq_q.w: Vestibular neuronitis follows a viral illness and spares hearing. An abnormal head impulse test points to a peripheral cause.
hq_q.f: Same symptoms with hearing loss → labyrinthitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve cuts input from one side
tm.g: Viral onset, normal hearing and an abnormal head impulse is vestibular neuronitis
f: brief attacks on turning in bed
the same picture with hearing loss
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ménière's disease (Ménière's attacks last hours and bring hearing loss and tinnitus; she has had 2 days of vertigo with normal hearing)
vertical nystagmus with a normal head impulse
x: Ruled out here: requires brief attacks on turning in bed, whereas this patient has a week after a cold, Her hearing is normal.
Ruled out here: requires the same picture with hearing loss, whereas this patient has a week after a cold, Her hearing is normal.
Ménière's attacks last hours and bring hearing loss and tinnitus; she has had 2 days of vertigo with normal hearing.
Ruled out here: requires vertical nystagmus with a normal head impulse, whereas this patient has a week after a cold, Her hearing is normal.

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with 6 hours of continuous, severe spinning vertigo, nausea, and vomiting. He has no hearing loss or tinnitus.
On bedside HINTS examination, the clinician evaluates his eye movements and vestibulo-ocular reflex to distinguish a posterior circulation stroke from vestibular neuritis.
hq_q.w: On bedside HINTS testing in acute vestibular syndrome, a central brainstem or cerebellar stroke is indicated by a normal head impulse test, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, or vertical skew deviation on alternate cover testing.
hq_q.f: Abnormal head impulse with fixed horizontal nystagmus → peripheral.
hq_q.ql: Which finding most suggests a central cause?

tm.m: Vertical nystagmus arises from central brainstem or cerebellar vestibular pathways rather than a single semicircular canal
tm.g: Acute continuous vertigo with vertical nystagmus -> central posterior circulation cause
f: asked which HINTS sign reassures that acute continuous vertigo is due to peripheral vestibular neuritis
asked which additional symptom distinguishes acute viral labyrinthitis from vestibular neuritis
asked which nystagmus pattern is classic for benign peripheral vestibular neuritis
asked which autonomic symptom is shared by both peripheral labyrinthine disorders and cerebellar infarction
x: An abnormal head impulse test with a corrective saccade indicates a peripheral vestibulo-ocular reflex deficit such as vestibular neuritis.
New unilateral hearing loss typically accompanies peripheral labyrinthitis or Meniere's disease, although anterior inferior cerebellar artery infarction is an exception.
Unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus suppressed by visual fixation is characteristic of peripheral vestibular neuritis.
Severe nausea and vomiting occur frequently in both benign peripheral vestibular neuritis and cerebellar stroke.

hq_q.s: A 42 year old man has had constant vertigo with vomiting for 1 day after a viral illness. His hearing is normal. A diagnosis of vestibular neuronitis is made. He cannot keep fluids down at home but has no neurological signs.
hq_q.w: Short-term prochlorperazine or cyclizine. Stop within 3 days to let the brain compensate. Key discriminator: Acute vestibular neuronitis: a short course of prochlorperazine.
hq_q.f: Ménière's to prevent attacks → betahistine.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most appropriate for a short course?

tm.m: A vestibular sedative eases vomiting but slows compensation if kept going
tm.g: Acute vestibular neuronitis: a short course of prochlorperazine
f: burning feet in diabetes
preventing attacks in Ménière's disease
Chronic burning neuropathic pain in feet persists after abstinence
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sertraline (Sertraline treats depression and anxiety; it does nothing for acute vertigo and vomiting)
x: Ruled out here: requires burning feet in diabetes, whereas this patient has cannot keep fluids down, short course.
Ruled out here: requires preventing attacks in Ménière's disease, whereas this patient has cannot keep fluids down, short course.
Ruled out here: requires Chronic burning neuropathic pain in feet persists after abstinence, whereas this patient has cannot keep fluids down, short course.
Sertraline treats depression and anxiety; it does nothing for acute vertigo and vomiting.

hq_q.s:
A 4 year old girl who has not had any childhood immunisations has had a sore throat and fever for 6 hours. She is now drooling and has noisy breathing.
Temperature 39.5°C, pulse rate 160 bpm, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute. She is sitting forward on her mother's lap with her mouth open and looks toxic. There is soft inspiratory stridor.
o: Examine her throat with a spatula
hq_q.w: In suspected acute epiglottitis, any distress, crying, cannulation, or pharyngeal examination can precipitate complete fatal airway obstruction. Keep the child calm on the parent's lap and summon senior anaesthetic and ENT specialists immediately.
hq_q.f: A barking cough and mild stridor with no drooling → croup.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Severe inflammatory oedema of the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds can acutely occlude the glottic inlet if provoked
tm.g: Unimmunised toxic child sitting forward drooling with soft stridor -> call senior anaesthetics and ENT without examining throat
f: a well teenager with sore throat, no stridor and ability to swallow fluids normally
after inhalational induction and endotracheal intubation have safely secured the airway in theatre
a haemodynamically stable adult without stridor where supraglottitis is uncertain and airway staff are present
a toddler with a barking seal-like cough, hoarse voice, no drooling and mild stridor
x: Inserting a tongue depressor in acute epiglottitis can trigger laryngospasm and immediate complete airway arrest.
Painful venepuncture before securing the airway causes crying and agitation that can precipitate complete glottic occlusion.
Delaying airway control or repositioning an unstable child for radiography risks sudden fatal airway obstruction.
Oral dexamethasone is first-line for viral croup, whereas forcing oral medication in epiglottitis risks acute airway obstruction.

hq_q.s:
A 46 year old man has had a severe sore throat for 1 day. He cannot swallow his saliva and his voice is muffled.
Temperature 38.8°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, SpO2 97% breathing air. He is drooling and leaning forward. There is no stridor. The tonsils and oropharynx look almost normal. There is tenderness over the front of the neck at the level of the hyoid.
hq_q.w: Adult acute supraglottitis presents with severe odynophagia, inability to swallow saliva (drooling), muffled 'hot potato' voice, anterior neck tenderness over the hyoid bone, and a strikingly normal-appearing oral cavity and tonsils on simple inspection.
hq_q.f: A swollen soft palate with the uvula pushed to one side → quinsy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Inflammatory oedema is confined to the epiglottis and supraglottic structures below direct oral view
tm.g: Severe odynophagia, drooling and muffled voice with a normal-looking oropharynx -> acute supraglottitis
f: a hoarse whispery voice after shouting and a viral cold with normal swallowing
bilaterally enlarged red tonsils covered in white exudate with no drooling or hyoid tenderness
fatigue, bilateral tonsillar exudate, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and a palpable spleen tip
marked trismus with unilateral peritonsillar swelling pushing the uvula across the midline
x: Acute viral laryngitis causes hoarseness and a whispery voice after a coryzal illness without drooling or severe odynophagia.
Acute bacterial tonsillitis reveals erythematous, enlarged palatine tonsils coated in purulent exudate on oral inspection.
Infectious mononucleosis causes prominent tonsillar pseudomembranes, palatal petechiae, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.
Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) causes trismus, unilateral soft-palate bulging, and deviation of the uvula away from the affected side.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman attends the emergency department with a 24 hour history of severe sore throat, painful swallowing, and a muffled voice.
She is sitting upright, haemodynamically stable with no stridor and SpO2 98% on air. While senior ENT staff attend for flexible nasendoscopy, a portable lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray is performed for suspected supraglottitis.
hq_q.w: On a lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph, oedematous enlargement of the epiglottis obliterates the vallecula and produces a rounded, thickened shadow resembling an adult thumb ('thumb sign'), characteristic of acute epiglottitis or supraglottitis.
hq_q.f: Steeple sign on a frontal X-ray → croup.
hq_q.ql: Which sign is most likely on the X-ray?

tm.m: Inflammatory swelling transforms the thin leaf-like epiglottis into a rounded thumb-like profile on lateral X-ray
tm.g: Supraglottitis on lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph -> thumb sign
f: acute left ventricular failure with perihilar alveolar oedema on an erect chest radiograph
bilious vomiting in a neonate with Down's syndrome on an abdominal radiograph
left lower lobe atelectasis forming a triangular retrocardiac density on a chest radiograph
subglottic tracheal tapering on an anteroposterior neck X-ray in a toddler with a barking cough
x: Bat's wing perihilar alveolar shadowing is seen on a frontal chest radiograph in acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
The double bubble sign on a neonatal abdominal radiograph indicates congenital duodenal atresia.
The sail sign on a frontal chest radiograph reflects left lower lobe collapse behind the heart or a normal neonatal thymus.
The steeple sign on an anteroposterior neck radiograph shows symmetrical subglottic narrowing in viral laryngotracheobronchitis (croup).

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old man has had a nosebleed from his right nostril for 30 minutes. He takes no anticoagulants.
Pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 146/88 mmHg. He has been leaning forward and pinching the soft part of his nose for 15 minutes but it is still bleeding. Anterior rhinoscopy shows a bleeding vessel on the anterior septum.
hq_q.w: If pressure fails and a point is seen, cauterise it. If not seen or it fails, pack the nose.
hq_q.f: Bleeding continues after packing → admit to ENT.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: pinching the soft part of his nose for 15 minutes
bleeding vessel on the anterior septum
tm.m: A visible anterior vessel can be sealed chemically
tm.g: Pressure failed and a bleeding point is seen: silver nitrate cautery
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Anterior nasal packing (Packing is for bleeding that cautery cannot control or where no bleeding point is seen; here a single vessel is visible)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Discharge with advice (He is still bleeding after 15 minutes of pressure, so he cannot go home)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ice pack to the neck (An ice pack has little effect; a visible bleeding point should be cauterised)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral tranexamic acid (Does not treat haemorrhoids and increases thromboembolic risk with a mechanical valve)
x: Packing is for bleeding that cautery cannot control or where no bleeding point is seen; here a single vessel is visible.
He is still bleeding after 15 minutes of pressure, so he cannot go home.
An ice pack has little effect; a visible bleeding point should be cauterised.
Does not treat haemorrhoids and increases thromboembolic risk with a mechanical valve

hq_q.s:
A 9 year old boy has had frequent small nosebleeds from his left nostril for 2 months. Each one stops within a few minutes with pressure. He picks his nose.
Anterior rhinoscopy shows crusting and prominent vessels on the left anterior septum in Little's area. There is no active bleeding. He has no allergies to peanut or soya.
hq_q.w: Naseptin, chlorhexidine with neomycin, for 10 days reduces crusting and recurrent bleeds. Key discriminator: Recurrent minor bleeds from Little's area in a child: Naseptin cream.
hq_q.f: Peanut or soya allergy → avoid Naseptin, try mupirocin.
hq_q.ql: Which treatment is most appropriate?

c: no allergies to peanut or soya
tm.m: Crusting from picking keeps Little's area bleeding; antiseptic cream lets it heal
tm.g: Recurrent minor bleeds from Little's area in a child: Naseptin cream
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Mupirocin nasal ointment (Mupirocin is the alternative when there is a peanut, soya or neomycin allergy; otherwise Naseptin is first choice)
brisk bleeding that pressure cannot stop and no visible point
both sides blocked with sneezing and itch
Major haemorrhage or life-threatening hyperfibrinolytic bleeding requiring antifibrinolytic therapy
x: Mupirocin is the alternative when there is a peanut, soya or neomycin allergy; otherwise Naseptin is first choice.
Ruled out here: requires brisk bleeding that pressure cannot stop and no visible point, whereas this patient has picks his nose, Little's area.
Ruled out here: requires both sides blocked with sneezing and itch, whereas this patient has picks his nose, Little's area.
Ruled out here: requires Major haemorrhage or life-threatening hyperfibrinolytic bleeding requiring antifibrinolytic therapy, whereas this patient has picks his nose, Little's area.

hq_q.s:
A 15 year old boy has had recurrent heavy nosebleeds from his left nostril for 3 months. He has a blocked nose on that side and his voice sounds nasal.
Anterior rhinoscopy shows a smooth, red mass at the back of the left nasal cavity. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy.
hq_q.w: A benign but vascular tumour of teenage boys. Refer to ENT and avoid biopsy because it can bleed heavily.
hq_q.f: A young child with one-sided smelly discharge → foreign body.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important diagnosis to exclude?

c: smooth, red mass at the back
tm.m: A benign but very vascular tumour of teenage boys bleeds heavily
tm.g: Recurrent heavy epistaxis with a nasal mass in a teenage boy is juvenile angiofibroma
f: seasonal sneezing with itchy eyes
the presentation instead showed features specific to Deviated nasal septum (A deviated septum causes blockage but not a red mass and heavy recurrent bleeding in a teenage boy)
a young child with one-sided smelly discharge
pale grey insensate masses in both nostrils
x: Ruled out here: requires seasonal sneezing with itchy eyes, whereas this patient has 15 year old boy, heavy nosebleeds.
A deviated septum causes blockage but not a red mass and heavy recurrent bleeding in a teenage boy.
Ruled out here: requires a young child with one-sided smelly discharge, whereas this patient has 15 year old boy, heavy nosebleeds.
Ruled out here: requires pale grey insensate masses in both nostrils, whereas this patient has 15 year old boy, heavy nosebleeds.

hq_q.s:
A 17 year old girl presents with a 10 day history of severe sore throat, fever, malaise, and profound fatigue that makes eating difficult.
Temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 88 bpm. Examination shows bilateral exudative tonsillitis, palatal petechiae, tender posterior triangle cervical lymphadenopathy, and a palpable spleen tip 2 cm below the left costal margin.
hq_q.w: Infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus infection) infects B lymphocytes and triggers a brisk proliferation of cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes, which appear on a peripheral blood film as large, pleomorphic atypical lymphocytes alongside a positive heterophile antibody test.
hq_q.f: Blast cells on the film → acute leukaemia.
hq_q.ql: Which blood film finding is most likely?

tm.m: EBV-infected B cells stimulate reactive cytotoxic CD8+ T cells that appear as atypical mononuclear cells on the film
tm.g: Exudative tonsillitis + posterior cervical nodes + splenomegaly -> atypical lymphocytes on blood film
f: progressive pallor, petechial bruising, neutropenic sepsis and thrombocytopenia from marrow failure
wheeze, urticaria and migrating pulmonary infiltrates after tropical travel
acute streptococcal tonsillitis with anterior jugulodigastric lymphadenopathy and no splenomegaly
chronic iron deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding or active inflammatory bowel disease
x: Circulating lymphoblasts or myeloblasts with Auer rods indicate acute leukaemia, which presents with pancytopenia, bone pain, and bruising.
Peripheral eosinophilia is characteristic of atopic disorders, drug reactions, or invasive helminthic parasitic infections.
Neutrophilia with toxic granulation and left shift is typical of acute streptococcal bacterial tonsillitis rather than EBV.
Infectious mononucleosis commonly causes mild autoimmune thrombocytopenia rather than reactive thrombocytosis.

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old university student was diagnosed with Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis 10 days ago. His fever and sore throat have now settled and his energy is returning. He plays flanker for his university rugby team and asks when he can resume full-contact training.
Abdominal examination reveals a palpable, mildly tender spleen tip.
hq_q.w: Splenomegaly in infectious mononucleosis renders the thinned splenic capsule vulnerable to life-threatening traumatic or spontaneous rupture. Patients must avoid contact sports and heavy lifting for at least 4 to 8 weeks until splenomegaly has fully resolved.
hq_q.f: Left upper quadrant pain and shock → splenic rupture.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate advice?

tm.m: Lymphoid infiltration stretches and thins the splenic capsule, creating a high risk of traumatic rupture during impact
tm.g: Infectious mononucleosis in a contact-sport athlete -> avoid contact sport for 8 weeks
f: returning to work or school after acute viral gastroenteritis once vomiting has stopped for 48 hours
stepping down isolation precautions after 72 hours of sensitivity-guided antibiotic treatment
never required for uncomplicated infectious mononucleosis once splenomegaly has resolved
resuming gentle non-contact desk study once fever and malaise have settled
x: Splenic enlargement persists for weeks after pyrexia resolves, so returning 48 hours after defervescence is dangerous.
Waiting only 72 hours leaves the enlarged spleen unprotected against blunt abdominal trauma on the rugby pitch.
Uncomplicated EBV splenomegaly resolves within 4 to 8 weeks, so a 12 month ban from sport is excessive.
Returning to rugby at 1 week carries peak risk of catastrophic splenic rupture, which is highest in weeks 2 to 3.

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old woman has had a sore throat for a week. Her GP started an antibiotic 3 days ago. She now has a widespread itchy rash.
There is a widespread maculopapular rash on the trunk and limbs, exudative tonsillitis and cervical lymphadenopathy. The monospot test is positive.
hq_q.w: Amoxicillin in glandular fever causes a widespread itchy rash in most patients. Key discriminator: Rash in glandular fever after an antibiotic: amoxicillin.
hq_q.f: Recurs with amoxicillin when well → consider true allergy testing.
hq_q.ql: Which antibiotic is most likely to have caused the rash?

tm.m: Aminopenicillins in EBV infection trigger a widespread rash
tm.g: Rash in glandular fever after an antibiotic: amoxicillin
f: INR rising after a new antibiotic
the presentation instead showed features specific to Doxycycline (Doxycycline is not a sore-throat antibiotic and does not cause this rash with glandular fever)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Erythromycin (A macrolide does not trigger the classic widespread rash seen when glandular fever meets amoxicillin)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Phenoxymethylpenicillin (Penicillin V can occasionally cause a rash, but amoxicillin causes it in most people with glandular fever)
x: Ruled out here: requires INR rising after a new antibiotic, whereas this patient has 3 days ago, widespread maculopapular rash.
Doxycycline is not a sore-throat antibiotic and does not cause this rash with glandular fever.
A macrolide does not trigger the classic widespread rash seen when glandular fever meets amoxicillin.
Penicillin V can occasionally cause a rash, but amoxicillin causes it in most people with glandular fever.

hq_q.s: A 48 year old woman has Ménière's disease confirmed by an ENT surgeon. She has attacks of vertigo every few weeks lasting several hours, with fluctuating hearing loss in her right ear. She asks for something to reduce how often the attacks happen.
hq_q.w: Betahistine can be tried to prevent attacks. Prochlorperazine treats the acute vertigo. Key discriminator: Ménière's prevention: betahistine.
hq_q.f: An acute attack → prochlorperazine or an antihistamine.
hq_q.ql: Which drug can be tried to reduce the frequency of attacks?

c: reduce how often the attacks happen
tm.m: Betahistine may improve inner ear blood flow and reduce attacks
tm.g: Ménière's prevention: betahistine
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amitriptyline (Amitriptyline is for neuropathic pain or migraine prevention, not reducing Ménière's attacks)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cinnarizine (Cinnarizine relieves an acute attack; betahistine is the drug tried to reduce how often they happen)
acute distress needing short-term calming alongside the antipsychotic
treating an acute attack
x: Amitriptyline is for neuropathic pain or migraine prevention, not reducing Ménière's attacks.
Cinnarizine relieves an acute attack; betahistine is the drug tried to reduce how often they happen.
Ruled out here: requires acute distress needing short-term calming alongside the antipsychotic, whereas this patient has reduce how often the attacks happen, A 48 year old woman has.
Ruled out here: requires treating an acute attack, whereas this patient has reduce how often the attacks happen, A 48 year old woman has.

hq_q.s:
A 40 year old man has had attacks of spinning vertigo lasting about 2 hours for 6 months. Each attack comes with ringing and a feeling of fullness in his left ear, and he feels a little deafer after each one. Between attacks he is well.
Otoscopy is normal. Audiometry shows low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss on the left.
hq_q.w: Meniere's disease is caused by endolymphatic hydrops of the membranous labyrinth, producing recurrent spontaneous attacks of rotational vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours accompanied by unilateral fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, roaring tinnitus, and aural fullness.
hq_q.f: Vertigo with migraine and no hearing loss → vestibular migraine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Endolymphatic distension of the cochlear duct and vestibular labyrinth causes episodic vertigo and low-tone loss
tm.g: Recurrent 2-hour vertigo spells with unilateral aural fullness, tinnitus and low-frequency sensorineural loss -> Meniere's disease
f: slowly progressive unilateral high-frequency deafness, continuous tinnitus and an absent corneal reflex
30 second bursts of spinning vertigo triggered by rolling over in bed with normal hearing
episodic vertigo accompanied by throbbing unilateral headache and photophobia with normal audiometry
a single continuous 4 day episode of severe vertigo after a viral coryza with normal hearing
x: An acoustic neuroma causes slowly progressive unilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss and mild disequilibrium rather than discrete 2 hour vertigo attacks.
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo causes brief vertigo lasting 10 to 30 seconds triggered by head movement without hearing loss or tinnitus.
Vestibular migraine causes episodic vertigo associated with photophobia, visual aura, or migrainous headaches without progressive sensorineural deafness.
Vestibular neuronitis causes a single prolonged episode of continuous vertigo lasting several days after a viral illness with completely normal hearing.

hq_q.s: A 52 year old sales representative has recently been diagnosed with Meniere's disease after experiencing three sudden, unheralded attacks of disabling rotational vertigo and vomiting over the past month. He receives no warning aura before an attack starts and asks about driving his car for work.
hq_q.w: Under DVLA fitness-to-drive regulations, any driver experiencing sudden, unprovoked or unheralded attacks of disabling dizziness or vertigo must cease driving immediately and notify the DVLA until attacks are satisfactorily controlled.
hq_q.f: Attacks fully controlled → can return once the DVLA agrees.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate advice?

c: unheralded attacks of disabling rotational vertigo
tm.m: Sudden unheralded rotational vertigo causes instantaneous loss of spatial orientation and vehicle control
tm.g: Unheralded disabling vertigo in a driver -> stop driving immediately and notify the DVLA
f: attacks that have been completely controlled on maintenance therapy with DVLA medical clearance
early nyctalopia with preserved daytime acuity meeting the legal number-plate standard
a provisional licence holder with no medical incapacity learning to drive under supervision
a minor medical condition that does not affect safe vehicle control or require DVLA notification
x: Simply starting prophylactic betahistine does not permit driving until satisfactory long-term control of unheralded attacks is demonstrated.
Sudden disabling vertigo without prodromal warning carries an unacceptable risk of collision during daylight hours just as at night.
Carrying a passenger cannot prevent a crash if the driver experiences acute unheralded rotational vertigo at speed.
Informing a motor insurer without ceasing driving and notifying the DVLA is unlawful when sudden disabling vertigo is present.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old man has snored loudly for years. His wife says he stops breathing at night. He falls asleep watching television and in meetings. He has a BMI of 34.
He completes the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, which gives a score of 15.
hq_q.w: An Epworth score over 10 suggests excessive sleepiness. OSA is a common cause. Key discriminator: Epworth over 10 means excessive daytime sleepiness.
hq_q.f: Epworth of 4 → normal.
hq_q.ql: What does this score suggest?

tm.m: The Epworth scale measures how likely you are to doze in daily situations
tm.g: Epworth over 10 means excessive daytime sleepiness
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Confirmed narcolepsy (An Epworth score cannot confirm narcolepsy; it measures sleepiness, and his history fits sleep apnoea)
a score of 4
2 weeks of low mood, anhedonia, early-morning waking
the presentation instead showed features specific to Severe chronic insomnia (Insomnia is difficulty sleeping; he falls asleep easily during the day)
x: An Epworth score cannot confirm narcolepsy; it measures sleepiness, and his history fits sleep apnoea.
Ruled out here: requires a score of 4, whereas this patient has falls asleep watching television, score of 15.
Ruled out here: requires 2 weeks of low mood, anhedonia, early-morning waking, whereas this patient has falls asleep watching television, score of 15.
Insomnia is difficulty sleeping; he falls asleep easily during the day.

hq_q.s: A 49 year old heavy goods vehicle (Group 2) lorry driver is reviewed following home sleep polygraphy, which confirmed moderate obstructive sleep apnoea with an apnoea-hypopnoea index of 22 events/hour. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 16/24, and he admits nodding off briefly at the wheel last week while awaiting CPAP.
hq_q.w: Drivers with confirmed moderate or severe obstructive sleep apnoea accompanied by excessive daytime sleepiness must stop driving immediately and notify the DVLA. Driving may only resume once CPAP therapy controls sleepiness and compliance is verified.
hq_q.f: Mild OSA without sleepiness → no driving restriction.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate driving advice?

c: nodding off briefly at the wheel
tm.m: Repetitive nocturnal arousal causes severe daytime microsleeps and high risk of catastrophic road traffic collisions
tm.g: Moderate or severe OSA with excessive daytime sleepiness -> stop driving immediately and inform the DVLA
f: never safe in untreated obstructive sleep apnoea with excessive daytime somnolence
never acceptable while a driver has uncontrolled excessive daytime sleepiness from sleep apnoea
routine fatigue management in a healthy driver without obstructive sleep apnoea or pathological sleepiness
mild situational tiredness in a healthy driver with no sleep disorder
x: Night shifts exacerbate circadian drowsiness, and all driving is prohibited until sleepiness is controlled on treatment.
Microsleeps and collisions occur on short local journeys as well as motorways when daytime somnolence is uncontrolled.
Scheduled rest breaks do not replace mandatory driving cessation and DVLA notification in obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome.
Caffeine does not treat nocturnal airway collapse or exempt a sleepy Group 2 driver from stopping driving and reporting to the DVLA.

hq_q.s:
A 55 year old man presents to the sleep clinic with loud disruptive snoring, witnessed nocturnal choking episodes, morning headaches, and falling asleep during afternoon meetings.
His BMI is 33 kg/m² and Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 15/24. Sleep polygraphy confirms moderate obstructive sleep apnoea (AHI 21/hour) despite 6 months of weight loss and alcohol reduction.
hq_q.w: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is NICE first-line therapy for symptomatic moderate or severe obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome. Pneumatic splinting keeps the collapsible pharyngeal airway open throughout inspiration and expiration, abolishing apnoeas and daytime somnolence.
hq_q.f: Mild OSA → lifestyle measures and a mandibular device.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Continuous positive airway pressure pneumatically splints the upper pharynx to prevent inspiratory collapse
tm.g: Symptomatic moderate or severe obstructive sleep apnoea -> continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
f: narcolepsy with cataplexy causing daytime sleep attacks despite normal nocturnal breathing
chronic hypoxaemia in severe COPD with daytime PaO2 below 7.3 kPa on two arterial blood gases
a 5 year old child with grade 4 kissing tonsils and obstructive sleep apnoea
short-term disabling acute insomnia after bereavement in a patient with normal nocturnal breathing
x: Modafinil is a central wakefulness-promoting agent and does not prevent nocturnal pharyngeal collapse or hypoxic desaturations.
Nocturnal low-flow oxygen does not stent the upper airway open and can prolong apnoeic episodes and hypercapnia.
Tonsillectomy is first-line for paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea caused by adenotonsillar hypertrophy rather than obesity-related adult OSA.
Zopiclone and other sedative-hypnotics reduce upper airway dilator muscle tone and worsen obstructive sleep apnoea.

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man with type 2 diabetes has had severe right ear pain and discharge for 4 weeks. It has not improved with antibiotic ear drops. The pain keeps him awake at night.
Temperature 37.8°C. There is granulation tissue on the floor of the right ear canal. There is weakness of the whole right side of his face.
hq_q.w: Necrotising otitis externa spreads to the skull base, usually Pseudomonas in diabetics. It needs IV antibiotics and imaging.
hq_q.f: Vesicles in the ear canal with facial weakness → Ramsay Hunt.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: pain keeps him awake at night
weakness of the whole right side of his face
tm.m: Pseudomonas spreads from the canal into the skull base and cranial nerves
tm.g: A diabetic with severe ear pain, granulation and a facial palsy has necrotising otitis externa
f: a tender boggy swelling behind the ear pushing it forward
a red bulging drum in a child
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cholesteatoma (Cholesteatoma is usually painless; severe night pain in an older diabetic points to necrotising otitis externa)
vesicles in the ear canal
x: Ruled out here: requires a tender boggy swelling behind the ear pushing it forward, whereas this patient has type 2 diabetes, pain keeps him awake at night.
Ruled out here: requires a red bulging drum in a child, whereas this patient has type 2 diabetes, pain keeps him awake at night.
Cholesteatoma is usually painless; severe night pain in an older diabetic points to necrotising otitis externa.
Ruled out here: requires vesicles in the ear canal, whereas this patient has type 2 diabetes, pain keeps him awake at night.

hq_q.s:
A 36 year old woman has had an itchy right ear for 3 weeks. She has used antibiotic and steroid ear drops for 2 weeks without improvement.
Otoscopy shows white, fluffy debris with black dots filling the external ear canal. The tympanic membrane is intact.
hq_q.w: Otomycosis from Aspergillus or Candida. Clean the ear and use antifungal drops such as clotrimazole.
hq_q.f: Green discharge with pain after swimming → Pseudomonas.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?

c: white, fluffy debris with black dots
tm.m: Antibiotic and steroid drops let fungi such as Aspergillus overgrow
tm.g: Fluffy debris with black dots after antibiotic drops is fungal otitis externa
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Contact eczema (Contact eczema from drops causes red itchy skin, not fluffy debris with black spores)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Herpes zoster (Zoster gives painful vesicles and may cause facial palsy, not fluffy debris)
green discharge and pain after swimming
the presentation instead showed features specific to Staph aureus (A bacterial infection would have responded to antibiotic drops; white debris after drops points to fungus)
x: Contact eczema from drops causes red itchy skin, not fluffy debris with black spores.
Zoster gives painful vesicles and may cause facial palsy, not fluffy debris.
Ruled out here: requires green discharge and pain after swimming, whereas this patient has for 2 weeks without improvement, white, fluffy debris with black dots.
A bacterial infection would have responded to antibiotic drops; white debris after drops points to fungus.

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old swimmer has had a painful, discharging left ear for 5 days. She is otherwise well.
Temperature 37.0°C. Moving the pinna is painful and the ear canal is swollen and red with debris. After microsuction, a small perforation of the tympanic membrane is seen.
hq_q.w: With a perforated drum, aminoglycoside drops can reach the inner ear and damage hearing and balance. A quinolone such as ciprofloxacin (here with a steroid) is not ototoxic and covers Pseudomonas, the usual cause in swimmers.
hq_q.f: Same otitis externa with an intact drum → acetic acid or an aminoglycoside with steroid is acceptable.
hq_q.ql: Which ear drops are most appropriate?

tm.m: Aminoglycosides are toxic to cochlear and vestibular hair cells if they pass through a perforation
tm.g: Perforated drum: quinolone drops, not aminoglycosides
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Acetic acid 2% (Acetic acid drops can be used for mild otitis externa, but they are not advised with a perforated drum)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Clotrimazole (Clotrimazole treats fungal otitis externa, with itch and fluffy white or black debris, not a painful bacterial infection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Gentamicin with hydrocortisone (Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside and is ototoxic through a perforated drum)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Neomycin with dexamethasone (Neomycin is also an aminoglycoside and is avoided when the drum is perforated)
x: Acetic acid drops can be used for mild otitis externa, but they are not advised with a perforated drum.
Clotrimazole treats fungal otitis externa, with itch and fluffy white or black debris, not a painful bacterial infection.
Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside and is ototoxic through a perforated drum.
Neomycin is also an aminoglycoside and is avoided when the drum is perforated.

hq_q.s:
A 2 year old boy has had right ear pain and fever for 2 days. He is drinking well.
Temperature 38.6°C. The right tympanic membrane is red and bulging, and there is purulent discharge in the right ear canal. The left ear is normal. There is no mastoid swelling. He has no drug allergies.
hq_q.w: Antibiotics are advised if there is discharge, or if under 2 with both ears affected. Amoxicillin is first line.
hq_q.f: Over 2 with mild symptoms and no discharge → no antibiotic or back-up.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: purulent discharge in the right ear canal
tm.m: A discharging ear means the drum has perforated with bacterial infection
tm.g: Otitis media with discharge: amoxicillin for 5 days
f: over 2 with mild symptoms and no discharge
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ciprofloxacin ear drops for 7 days (The discharge comes from otitis media through a perforated drum; NICE advises oral amoxicillin, not ear drops)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Delayed antibiotic (A delayed prescription is for uncomplicated otitis media; discharge from the ear means treat now)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Grommets (Grommets are for glue ear persisting over 3 months with hearing loss, not a first acute infection)
x: Ruled out here: requires over 2 with mild symptoms and no discharge, whereas this patient has 2 year old boy, purulent discharge in the right ear canal.
The discharge comes from otitis media through a perforated drum; NICE advises oral amoxicillin, not ear drops.
A delayed prescription is for uncomplicated otitis media; discharge from the ear means treat now.
Grommets are for glue ear persisting over 3 months with hearing loss, not a first acute infection.

hq_q.s:
A 4 year old girl has had reduced hearing for 3 months, with her nursery teacher reporting that she fails to respond when called and her speech clarity is lagging behind peers. She has no otalgia or fever.
Both tympanic membranes are dull and retracted with air-fluid levels, tympanometry shows flat type B traces bilaterally, and two pure-tone audiograms 3 months apart confirm a 30 dB bilateral conductive loss.
hq_q.w: Under NICE guideline NG233, bilateral otitis media with effusion (glue ear) persisting after 3 months of active observation with documented bilateral hearing loss impairing speech or educational development warrants ENT referral for ventilation tubes (grommets) or hearing aids.
hq_q.f: Glue ear for 1 month → watch and wait.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Persistent middle-ear serous effusion dampens ossicular conduction and impairs childhood speech acquisition
tm.g: Bilateral glue ear persisting >3 months with conductive hearing loss and speech delay -> refer for grommets
f: acute otitis media with a red bulging tympanic membrane, high fever and purulent otorrhoea
never recommended by NICE for the management of childhood otitis media with effusion
persistent seasonal allergic rhinitis with sneezing, nasal itch and pale boggy inferior turbinates
first presentation of asymptomatic unilateral middle-ear effusion with normal speech and development
x: Oral antibiotics have no sustained benefit in sterile chronic otitis media with effusion and are not recommended by NICE.
Oral decongestants and antihistamines are clinically ineffective in clearing middle-ear effusions and carry side-effect risks in young children.
Intranasal corticosteroid sprays do not hasten resolution of glue ear and are not recommended unless coexisting allergic rhinitis is present.
Waiting a further year when bilateral conductive deafness has already persisted for 3 months with speech delay risks permanent language impairment.

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old man has had a smelly discharge from his right ear for 6 months and his hearing on that side has worsened. Antibiotic drops have not helped.
Otoscopy shows foul-smelling discharge and a pearly white mass in the attic region of the right tympanic membrane. Rinne's test is negative on the right.
hq_q.w: Cholesteatoma is skin growing in the middle ear. It erodes bone and needs surgery. Key discriminator: Foul discharge with a pearly attic mass is cholesteatoma.
hq_q.f: Gradual conductive loss with normal drums in a young woman → otosclerosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: pearly white mass in the attic region
tm.m: Skin trapped in the middle ear grows and erodes bone
tm.g: Foul discharge with a pearly attic mass is cholesteatoma
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Acute otitis media (Acute otitis media is a painful red drum with fever over days, not 6 months of smelly discharge)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Impacted wax (Wax does not cause foul discharge or a pearly mass in the drum)
itchy canal with debris and pain on moving the pinna
gradual conductive loss with normal drums in a young woman
x: Acute otitis media is a painful red drum with fever over days, not 6 months of smelly discharge.
Wax does not cause foul discharge or a pearly mass in the drum.
Ruled out here: requires itchy canal with debris and pain on moving the pinna, whereas this patient has smelly discharge, pearly white mass in the attic region.
Ruled out here: requires gradual conductive loss with normal drums in a young woman, whereas this patient has smelly discharge, pearly white mass in the attic region.

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman has had a blocked nose, thick discharge and facial pain over her cheeks for 12 days after a cold. She started to feel better, then got worse again.
Temperature 37.9°C. There is tenderness over both maxillary sinuses. There is no periorbital swelling, visual disturbance or severe headache. She has no drug allergies.
hq_q.w: In acute rhinosinusitis lasting more than 10 days or showing 'double sickening' (secondary deterioration after initial viral improvement) without red-flag orbital or intracranial complications, NICE recommends considering a high-dose intranasal corticosteroid and a back-up (delayed) antibiotic prescription.
hq_q.f: Symptoms under 10 days → self-care.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Secondary bacterial superinfection of obstructed paranasal sinuses causes biphasic worsening after 10 days
tm.g: Uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis >10 days with double sickening -> nasal steroid and back-up antibiotic
f: periorbital cellulitis with proptosis, painful ophthalmoplegia and reduced visual acuity
severe chronic rhinosinusitis with obstructive bilateral nasal polyposis
eyelid swelling, diplopia and reduced visual acuity complicating frontal sinusitis
mild facial pressure and nasal congestion present for 4 days after a common cold
x: CT imaging of the paranasal sinuses is reserved for suspected orbital or intracranial complications or refractory chronic rhinosinusitis before surgery.
Systemic oral corticosteroids are not recommended for uncomplicated acute bacterial or viral rhinosinusitis.
Same-day ENT referral is indicated only when red-flag features such as periorbital oedema, diplopia, or frontal swelling are present.
Simple self-care alone is advised when acute viral rhinosinusitis has lasted fewer than 10 days without secondary worsening.

hq_q.s:
A 60 year old man has had a blocked right nostril for 6 weeks with blood-stained discharge. He has no symptoms on the left. He worked as a carpenter for 40 years.
Anterior rhinoscopy shows a friable mass in the right nasal cavity. There is a firm right cervical lymph node.
hq_q.w: One-sided symptoms with blood need ENT review to exclude a tumour. Key discriminator: One-sided blocked bleeding nose with a node in a woodworker: refer to ENT.
hq_q.f: Both sides blocked with sneezing → allergic rhinitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Wood dust causes sinonasal cancer, which blocks and bleeds on one side
tm.g: One-sided blocked bleeding nose with a node in a woodworker: refer to ENT
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Course of antibiotics (Delays diagnosis of sinonasal malignancy in a woodworker with unilateral symptoms)

the presentation instead showed features specific to Routine ENT referral (A one-sided bloody nasal mass with a neck node in a woodworker suggests sinonasal cancer, which needs the suspected cancer pathway, not a routine wait)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Saline rinse (Saline rinses ease symptoms but a friable mass in a woodworker needs urgent ENT review)
both sides blocked with sneezing and itch
x: Delays diagnosis of sinonasal malignancy in a woodworker with unilateral symptoms
A one-sided bloody nasal mass with a neck node in a woodworker suggests sinonasal cancer, which needs the suspected cancer pathway, not a routine wait.
Saline rinses ease symptoms but a friable mass in a woodworker needs urgent ENT review.
Ruled out here: requires both sides blocked with sneezing and itch, whereas this patient has blocked right nostril, blood-stained discharge.

hq_q.s:
A 60 year old man with asthma has had a blocked nose and loss of smell for a year. He had a severe attack of wheeze after taking aspirin for a headache last month.
Anterior rhinoscopy shows bilateral pale, grey, glistening masses that are insensate. There is mild expiratory wheeze.
hq_q.w: Samter's triad (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease) comprises adult-onset asthma, bilateral chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis, and acute bronchospasm or rhinorrhoea triggered by aspirin and other COX-1 inhibiting NSAIDs.
hq_q.f: A child with nasal polyps → test for cystic fibrosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: COX-1 inhibition shunts arachidonic acid metabolism into the lipoxygenase pathway, overproducing cysteinyl leukotrienes
tm.g: Asthma + bilateral insensate pale nasal polyps + aspirin-induced bronchospasm -> Samter's triad
f: unilateral nasal polyposis with thick dark brown fungal mucin and double-density sinus CT shadowing
seasonal sneezing, itchy eyes and tender swollen inferior turbinates triggered by grass pollen
a 7 year old child with bilateral nasal polyps, recurrent Pseudomonas chest infections and steatorrhoea
a unilateral friable bleeding nasal mass and cheek numbness in a retired cabinetmaker
x: Allergic fungal sinusitis causes thick inspissated 'peanut-butter' eosinophilic mucin and fungal hyphae without acute aspirin-induced bronchospasm.
Simple allergic rhinitis causes paroxysmal sneezing, watery rhinorrhoea, and swollen violaceous turbinates (which are tender to touch, unlike polyps).
Cystic fibrosis presents in childhood with bilateral nasal polyps, chronic productive bronchiectasis, and pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.
Sinonasal carcinoma presents with a unilateral friable, bleeding nasal mass, facial pain, or cranial nerve palsies, classically in hardwood workers.

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man has had a sore throat for 4 days. He has a cough and a runny nose. He has not had a fever.
Temperature 37.1°C. The tonsils are mildly inflamed without exudate. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. His FeverPAIN score is 1.
hq_q.w: Under NICE guideline NG84, a FeverPAIN score of 0 or 1 carries only a 13% to 18% likelihood of streptococcal infection. Neither immediate nor back-up antibiotics should be offered; recommend paracetamol or ibuprofen, oral fluids, and self-care.
hq_q.f: FeverPAIN 4 → consider an immediate antibiotic.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Coryza and cough with a FeverPAIN score of 1 strongly indicate self-limiting viral pharyngitis
tm.g: Acute sore throat with FeverPAIN score 0 or 1 -> no antibiotic and self-care advice
f: stridor, drooling and inability to swallow fluids with a unilateral peritonsillar swelling
acute tonsillitis with a FeverPAIN score of 3 in a systemically stable patient
purulent tonsillar exudate, fever within 24 hours, no cough and a FeverPAIN score of 5
persistent or recurrent pharyngitis failing empirical therapy or suspected scarlet fever outbreak investigation
x: Hospital admission is reserved for airway compromise, stridor, dehydration from inability to swallow, or peritonsillar abscess.
A back-up antibiotic prescription is considered only when the FeverPAIN score is 2 or 3.
Immediate phenoxymethylpenicillin is reserved for patients with a FeverPAIN score of 4 or 5 or severe systemic illness.
Routine throat swabs are not recommended in primary care management of uncomplicated acute viral sore throat.

hq_q.s:
A 25 year old man has had a worsening sore throat for 5 days, much worse on the left. He cannot open his mouth fully and his voice is muffled.
Temperature 38.7°C, pulse rate 108 bpm. There is trismus. The left soft palate is swollen and red and the uvula is pushed to the right. There is no stridor.
hq_q.w: Quinsy is a collection beside the tonsil. It is drained and treated with IV antibiotics.
hq_q.f: Both tonsils swollen with no deviation → tonsillitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: uvula is pushed to the right
tm.m: Pus collects beside one tonsil, pushing the palate and uvula across and irritating the jaw muscles
tm.g: One-sided palatal swelling with a deviated uvula and trismus is a peritonsillar abscess
f: drooling with a near-normal looking throat
the presentation instead showed features specific to Glandular fever (Glandular fever gives bilateral exudate and posterior nodes, not one-sided swelling with trismus)
a small child with neck stiffness and a bulge on the back of the pharynx
both tonsils swollen with no deviation
x: Ruled out here: requires drooling with a near-normal looking throat, whereas this patient has much worse on the left, trismus.
Glandular fever gives bilateral exudate and posterior nodes, not one-sided swelling with trismus.
Ruled out here: requires a small child with neck stiffness and a bulge on the back of the pharynx, whereas this patient has much worse on the left, trismus.
Ruled out here: requires both tonsils swollen with no deviation, whereas this patient has much worse on the left, trismus.

hq_q.s:
A 10 year old girl has had 8 episodes of tonsillitis in the last year. Each episode needed time off school and several needed antibiotics. Her parents ask what can be done.
Examination today shows mildly enlarged tonsils without exudate.
hq_q.w: SIGN criteria: 7 in 1 year, 5 a year for 2 years or 3 a year for 3 years.
hq_q.f: 2 episodes this year → watch and wait.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: 8 episodes of tonsillitis in the last year
tm.m: Frequent disabling episodes meet the criteria where surgery helps more than it harms
tm.g: 7 or more disabling episodes in a year: refer for tonsillectomy
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Antibiotics each time it recurs (She already meets the criteria for tonsillectomy (7 or more episodes in a year); treating each episode does not reduce how often they happen)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Long-term antibiotics (Antibiotics treat acute infection only; surgical excision prevents recurrent infections)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Throat swab (Throat swabs do not alter referral when Paradise criteria are met)
2 episodes this year
x: She already meets the criteria for tonsillectomy (7 or more episodes in a year); treating each episode does not reduce how often they happen.
Antibiotics treat acute infection only; surgical excision prevents recurrent infections
Throat swabs do not alter referral when Paradise criteria are met
Ruled out here: requires 2 episodes this year, whereas this patient has 8 episodes of tonsillitis in the last year, time off school.

hq_q.s:
A 3 year old girl has a small hole in front of her right ear that she was born with. It has discharged foul-smelling material and become swollen and red three times this year.
There is a 1 mm pit in front of the upper part of the right tragus with surrounding redness. The ear canal and tympanic membrane are normal.
hq_q.w: A preauricular sinus is a congenital epithelialised tract from incomplete fusion of the first and second branchial arch hillocks, presenting as a tiny pit just anterior to the helix or tragus. Recurrent infections warrant surgical excision.
hq_q.f: A lump in front of the upper sternomastoid in a young adult → branchial cyst.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: 1 mm pit in front of the upper part of the right tragus
tm.m: Incomplete embryological fusion of auricular hillocks leaves a squamous-lined pit prone to recurrent bacterial abscess
tm.g: Congenital pit immediately anterior to the tragus or helix with recurrent discharge -> preauricular sinus
f: a 4 cm fluctuant swelling at the anterior border of the upper sternocleidomastoid in a 22 year old
a painless submental midline neck swelling that does not elevate on tongue protrusion
an acquired firm intradermal nodule on the posterior earlobe with a central dark punctum
a midline neck swelling below the hyoid bone that moves upwards when the child sticks out her tongue
x: A branchial cyst presents in young adults as a smooth fluctuant mass along the upper anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
A midline neck dermoid cyst sits in the submental midline and does not move on tongue protrusion.
An epidermoid cyst is an acquired intradermal nodule with a central punctum rather than a congenital pit at the anterior helix.
A thyroglossal duct cyst is a midline anterior neck swelling near the hyoid bone that elevates on tongue protrusion.

hq_q.s:
A 20 year old man has noticed a painless lump in the left side of his neck for 2 months. It became larger and tender during a cold, then settled.
There is a 4 cm smooth, fluctuant lump at the anterior border of the left sternocleidomastoid muscle in the upper third of the neck. It does not move on swallowing or with tongue protrusion.
hq_q.w: A branchial cyst arises from incomplete obliteration of the second branchial cleft, presenting in young adults as a smooth, painless, fluctuant swelling at the upper third of the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle that swells during colds.
hq_q.f: A midline lump that moves with tongue protrusion → thyroglossal cyst.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: anterior border of the left sternocleidomastoid muscle in the upper third
does not move on swallowing or with tongue protrusion
tm.m: Persistent second branchial cleft epithelium forms a cholesterol-rich lymphoid-lined cyst that swells during viral pharyngitis
tm.g: Fluctuant mass at upper third of anterior border of sternocleidomastoid in a young adult -> branchial cyst
f: a soft compressible posterior triangle neck swelling present since infancy that transilluminates brightly
a soft lobulated subcutaneous swelling over the posterior neck that slips under the examining fingers
a 1 cm firm tender mobile jugulodigastric node during acute bacterial tonsillitis
a smooth midline anterior neck swelling that elevates visibly when the tongue is protruded
x: A cystic hygroma (lymphangioma) presents at birth or in infancy as a soft, compressible, brilliantly transilluminating mass in the posterior triangle.
A subcutaneous lipoma is a soft, lobulated fatty mass with slip sign that is not fluctuant and does not enlarge during viral colds.
A reactive cervical lymph node is firm, solid, and mobile rather than a 4 cm fluctuant cystic swelling.
A thyroglossal cyst lies in the anterior midline near the hyoid bone and rises upwards when the patient protrudes the tongue.

hq_q.s:
A baby girl born at term has a swelling in the left side of her neck. She is feeding well and breathing normally.
There is a 5 cm soft, compressible, painless swelling in the posterior triangle of the neck. It transilluminates brightly.
hq_q.w: A lymphatic malformation that transilluminates brightly, often in the posterior triangle. Key discriminator: A soft brightly transilluminating posterior triangle swelling in a baby is a cystic hygroma.
hq_q.f: A firm lump in the sternomastoid with a head tilt → sternomastoid tumour.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: A lymphatic malformation fills with clear lymph
tm.g: A soft brightly transilluminating posterior triangle swelling in a baby is a cystic hygroma
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Branchial cyst (A branchial cyst appears in young adults at the front of sternocleidomastoid, not as a large soft swelling at birth)
a red raised soft lump that grows then fades
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lymphadenopathy (Lymph nodes are firm, do not transilluminate and are not present as a soft cyst at birth)
a firm lump in the sternomastoid with a head tilt
x: A branchial cyst appears in young adults at the front of sternocleidomastoid, not as a large soft swelling at birth.
Ruled out here: requires a red raised soft lump that grows then fades, whereas this patient has born at term, posterior triangle.
Lymph nodes are firm, do not transilluminate and are not present as a soft cyst at birth.
Ruled out here: requires a firm lump in the sternomastoid with a head tilt, whereas this patient has born at term, posterior triangle.

hq_q.s:
A 2 year old boy has had a barking cough for 2 days that has worsened tonight. He has noisy breathing even when settled.
Temperature 38.0°C, pulse rate 168 bpm, respiratory rate 50 breaths per minute, SpO2 91% breathing air. He is drowsy, with stridor at rest and marked sternal recession.
hq_q.w: Life-threatening or severe viral croup (marked by stridor at rest, sternal recession, lethargy/drowsiness, or SpO2 <92%) requires immediate high-flow oxygen, nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine) to shrink subglottic mucosal oedema rapidly, and systemic corticosteroids alongside urgent senior anaesthetic support.
hq_q.f: Mild croup with no stridor at rest → single dose of oral dexamethasone.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction from nebulised adrenaline rapidly reduces subglottic mucosal oedema while steroids take effect
tm.g: Severe croup with stridor at rest, hypoxia and drowsiness -> nebulised adrenaline, oxygen and steroids
f: an acute wheeze exacerbation with prolonged expiration and widespread polyphonic wheeze
acute otitis media with bilateral bulging tympanic membranes and fever in an 18 month old
mild croup with an occasional barking cough, no stridor at rest, normal saturations and an alert child
never recommended in evidence-based paediatric guidelines due to lack of benefit and scald risk
x: Nebulised salbutamol is a beta-2 agonist bronchodilator for lower airway bronchospasm in asthma and does not relieve upper airway subglottic oedema.
Viral laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) is caused by parainfluenza virus, so oral amoxicillin provides no benefit.
Discharging a drowsy, hypoxic toddler with stridor at rest and SpO2 91% is unsafe; hospital admission and nebulised adrenaline are required.
Steam inhalation has no proven clinical efficacy in acute croup and risks severe thermal scald injuries in young children.

hq_q.s:
A 2 year old boy suddenly began coughing and choking while playing with his brother's small toys an hour ago. The coughing has settled but he now has noisy breathing. He was well before this.
Temperature 36.9°C, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, SpO2 95% breathing air. There is reduced air entry and a wheeze on the right side of the chest only.
hq_q.w: A sudden paroxysm of choking and coughing in an afebrile toddler playing with small toys, followed by persistent unilateral reduced air entry and a localized monophonic wheeze, is classic for bronchial foreign body aspiration requiring rigid bronchoscopy.
hq_q.f: A runny nose then a cough and wheeze in a baby → bronchiolitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: on the right side of the chest only
tm.m: An aspirated object lodges in the wider, more vertical right main bronchus, causing a unilateral ball-valve obstruction
tm.g: Sudden choking while playing with small toys + unilateral right-sided wheeze -> inhaled foreign body
f: bilateral widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze in a child with eczema and previous wheeze episodes
a 5 month old infant with 3 days of coryza followed by bilateral fine inspiratory crackles and wheeze
3 days of high fever, tachypnoea, dull percussion and focal bronchial breathing at the right base
a seal-like barking cough and harsh inspiratory stridor worse at night after a viral cold
x: Acute asthma causes bilateral widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze rather than sudden choking with strictly unilateral signs.
Viral bronchiolitis affects infants under 1 year, beginning with 2 to 3 days of coryza before bilateral fine crackles and wheeze develop.
Right lower lobe bacterial pneumonia presents with high fever, productive cough, bronchial breathing, and coarse crepitations rather than sudden choking.
Viral croup causes a prodromal coryza, barking cough, hoarse voice, and inspiratory stridor rather than unilateral bronchial wheeze.

hq_q.s: A 5 year old girl is eating grapes at a party when she suddenly starts choking. She is conscious but cannot cough, speak or cry, and she is becoming distressed.
hq_q.w: Give up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts in a child over 1. Infants get chest thrusts.
hq_q.f: The child becomes unconscious → start CPR.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first step?

c: conscious but cannot cough, speak or cry
tm.m: An ineffective cough means the airway is blocked; back blows try to dislodge it
tm.g: Choking, conscious, ineffective cough: 5 back blows first
f: back blows fail and she is still conscious
the presentation instead showed features specific to Blind finger sweep (Never perform blind finger sweeps as they push the foreign body deeper)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Encourage her to cough (Coughing is encouraged while the cough works; she cannot cough, speak or cry, so it is ineffective)
she becomes unconscious
x: Ruled out here: requires back blows fail and she is still conscious, whereas this patient has conscious but cannot cough, speak or cry, A 5 year old girl is.
Never perform blind finger sweeps as they push the foreign body deeper
Coughing is encouraged while the cough works; she cannot cough, speak or cry, so it is ineffective.
Ruled out here: requires she becomes unconscious, whereas this patient has conscious but cannot cough, speak or cry, A 5 year old girl is.

hq_q.s:
A 40 year old man woke this morning with a red patch in his right eye. He has had a bad cough for a week. The eye is not painful and his vision is normal.
Visual acuity 6/6 in both eyes. There is a well-defined, bright red area under the conjunctiva on the temporal side of the right eye. The cornea is clear and the pupil reacts normally.
hq_q.w: A painless, sharply demarcated bright-red patch after coughing or straining is a subconjunctival haemorrhage. It resolves spontaneously over 1 to 2 weeks without treatment, though blood pressure should be checked.
hq_q.f: Repeated haemorrhages on warfarin → check the INR.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Sudden venous pressure rise from coughing ruptures a fragile conjunctival capillary
tm.g: Painless bright-red patch after coughing with normal vision -> subconjunctival haemorrhage
f: severe eye pain with haloes around lights and a fixed mid-dilated pupil
deep boring ocular pain waking him at night with tender violaceous redness
gritty redness with mucopurulent discharge sticking the eyelids together on waking
a mildly sore sectoral leash of vessels that blanches with phenylephrine
x: Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes severe ocular pain, vomiting, reduced acuity, a hazy cornea and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.
Anterior scleritis causes severe deep boring pain that wakes the patient at night and violaceous injection.
Bacterial conjunctivitis causes diffuse conjunctival injection and mucopurulent discharge sticking the lashes rather than a confluent blood patch.
Sectoral episcleritis causes a localized leash of dilated superficial vessels rather than a uniform sheet of extravasated blood.

hq_q.s: A 45 year old man attends general practice with a 24 hour history of a red left eye. He does not wear contact lenses and reports no trauma. On examination, his visual acuity is 6/9 in the left eye and 6/6 in the right eye, and the GP assesses him for red-flag features requiring urgent ophthalmology review.
hq_q.w: Ocular pain accompanied by photophobia or reduced visual acuity indicates corneal, uveal, scleral, or acute intraocular pressure pathology, requiring same-day ophthalmology assessment rather than primary care management.
hq_q.f: Gritty and sticky with normal vision → conjunctivitis.
hq_q.ql: Which finding most suggests a serious cause?

tm.m: Ciliary spasm and corneal or intraocular inflammation cause pain on light exposure
tm.g: Red eye with pain and photophobia -> sight-threatening anterior segment pathology
f: asked which symptom is typical of uncomplicated viral conjunctivitis or dry eye
asked which feature points to seasonal allergic conjunctivitis
asked which feature is classic for uncomplicated acute bacterial conjunctivitis
asked which symptom is typical of simple nasolacrimal duct obstruction
x: A gritty foreign-body sensation is typical of superficial dry eye syndrome or simple infective conjunctivitis.
Bilateral itching is the hallmark of allergic conjunctivitis and does not indicate sight-threatening pathology.
Mucopurulent discharge coating the lashes with preserved vision and no photophobia points to simple bacterial conjunctivitis.
Epiphora alone is common in mild viral conjunctivitis, blepharitis, or nasolacrimal duct narrowing.

hq_q.s:
A 60 year old woman has had severe right eye pain, headache, and vomiting for 3 hours after watching television in a dark room. She sees haloes around lights and is hypermetropic.
Visual acuity is 6/36 on the right and 6/9 on the left. The right eye is congested with a hazy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, and a hard globe on palpation.
hq_q.w: Pupillary dilation in a dark room precipitates pupillary block in a shallow anterior chamber, causing an acute spike in intraocular pressure with corneal oedema, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, and a rock-hard globe.
hq_q.f: A small pupil with photophobia → anterior uveitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Iris-lens apposition blocks aqueous flow through the pupil in a hypermetropic eye
tm.g: Painful red eye with haloes, hazy cornea and fixed mid-dilated pupil -> acute angle-closure glaucoma
f: photophobia with a small irregular pupil and anterior chamber cells in ankylosing spondylitis
a focal white corneal opacity staining with fluorescein in an overnight contact lens wearer
fortification spectra spreading across both visual fields over 20 minutes with normal pupils
deep boring pain waking a patient with rheumatoid arthritis and bluish scleral thinning
x: Acute anterior uveitis causes a constricted, irregular pupil from posterior synechiae rather than a fixed mid-dilated pupil.
A bacterial corneal ulcer presents with a focal white stromal infiltrate and fluorescein-staining epithelial defect, usually in a contact lens wearer.
Migraine with aura causes transient binocular fortification spectra without corneal oedema or a fixed pupil.
Necrotising anterior scleritis causes severe pain and scleral thinning in rheumatoid arthritis but does not cause corneal oedema or acute angle closure.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman has had a lump in her left upper eyelid for 2 months. It has slowly grown but is not painful. She has blepharitis.
There is a 6 mm firm, non-tender, round swelling in the upper lid, away from the lid margin. The overlying skin is normal and not red. There is no lash loss.
hq_q.w: A chalazion is a blocked meibomian gland. Warm compresses help; it can be removed if it persists.
hq_q.f: A painful red lump at the lid margin → stye.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: A blocked meibomian gland forms a firm painless lump in the lid
tm.g: A painless firm lid lump away from the margin is a chalazion
f: a pearly nodule with lash loss
the presentation instead showed features specific to Dermoid cyst (A dermoid cyst is present from childhood at the outer edge of the eyebrow, not a new lid lump in blepharitis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Molluscum (Molluscum gives small pearly papules with a central dimple, often several, not a single firm lid lump)
a painful red lump at the lid margin
x: Ruled out here: requires a pearly nodule with lash loss, whereas this patient has blepharitis, non-tender.
A dermoid cyst is present from childhood at the outer edge of the eyebrow, not a new lid lump in blepharitis.
Molluscum gives small pearly papules with a central dimple, often several, not a single firm lid lump.
Ruled out here: requires a painful red lump at the lid margin, whereas this patient has blepharitis, non-tender.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old man has had gritty, itchy eyes for 6 months, worse in the mornings. His vision is normal.
The eyelid margins are red and thickened with crusting at the base of the lashes. The conjunctivae are mildly injected. The corneas are clear.
hq_q.w: Daily lid hygiene and warm compresses are key. It is long-term and recurs. Key discriminator: Blepharitis: lid hygiene first.
hq_q.f: It does not settle with hygiene → topical antibiotic ointment.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first treatment?

c: crusting at the base of the lashes
tm.m: Inflamed lid margins and blocked glands need daily cleaning and warmth
tm.g: Blepharitis: lid hygiene first
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Antibiotic drops (Antibiotic drops are not first line; lid hygiene treats blepharitis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lubricant drops (Lubricants ease the dry eye that comes with blepharitis, but they do not clear the crusts and blocked glands; lid hygiene does)
meibomian disease with rosacea not settling with hygiene
the presentation instead showed features specific to Steroid drops (Risks raised intraocular pressure, cataract and corneal thinning in primary care)
x: Antibiotic drops are not first line; lid hygiene treats blepharitis.
Lubricants ease the dry eye that comes with blepharitis, but they do not clear the crusts and blocked glands; lid hygiene does.
Ruled out here: requires meibomian disease with rosacea not settling with hygiene, whereas this patient has worse in the mornings, crusting at the base of the lashes.
Risks raised intraocular pressure, cataract and corneal thinning in primary care

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old woman has had a lump on her right lower eyelid for 8 months. It has slowly grown and occasionally bleeds. She has worked outdoors all her life.
There is a 5 mm pearly nodule on the lower lid margin with telangiectasia over its surface and loss of the eyelashes over it.
hq_q.w: Over 90% of malignant eyelid tumours are basal cell carcinomas on the lower lid. Slow growth, central ulceration or bleeding, pearly rolled margins, surface telangiectasia, and madarosis (eyelash loss) mandate urgent specialist excision.
hq_q.f: Yellow plaques near the inner corner → xanthelasma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Chronic ultraviolet exposure drives basal cell carcinoma that invades and destroys lash follicles
tm.g: Pearly lower-lid nodule with telangiectasia and eyelash loss -> basal cell carcinoma
f: a smooth firm painless pea-sized nodule within the tarsal plate sparing the lashes
an acutely tender erythematous lid swelling evolving over 3 days
a soft pedunculated skin-coloured frond on the lid margin with intact eyelashes
bilateral soft flat yellow plaques at the medial canthi in hypercholesterolaemia
x: A chalazion is a painless firm meibomian cyst deep within the tarsal plate that spares the eyelashes.
An internal hordeolum is an acute, tender, erythematous bacterial infection of a meibomian gland evolving over days.
A squamous cell papilloma is a benign pedunculated frond-like lesion that neither bleeds nor destroys eyelash follicles.
Xanthelasma presents as flat, soft, yellowish lipid plaques near the medial canthus rather than an ulcerating pearly nodule.

hq_q.s:
A 2 day old baby boy born via vaginal delivery has developed profuse sticky discharge from both eyes since this morning. His mother booked late in pregnancy and had no antenatal sexual health screening.
On examination, both eyelids are tensely oedematous and erythematous with copious purulent discharge pooling at the lid margins and marked conjunctival injection.
hq_q.w: Hyperacute bilateral purulent conjunctivitis presenting within the first 24 to 48 hours of life is classic for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, an ophthalmic emergency because untreated infection can rapidly penetrate intact corneal epithelium.
hq_q.f: Day 5 to 14 → chlamydia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?
