an initial bedside radiograph was performed for acute cough or suspected pneumothorax
she presented with episodic right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals requiring first-line imaging for gallstones

hq_q.s: A fit 58 year old woman has had chest pain after meals and episodes of vomiting for 6 months. A barium swallow shows a large paraoesophageal, rolling hiatus hernia with most of the stomach in the chest. She takes omeprazole.
hq_q.w: Symptomatic paraoesophageal hernias are repaired because they can volvulus or strangulate. Key discriminator: Symptomatic paraoesophageal hernia in a fit patient: laparoscopic repair.
hq_q.f: A small sliding hernia with reflux → PPI and lifestyle advice.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: most of the stomach in the chest
tm.m: A rolling hernia can twist and strangulate
tm.g: Symptomatic paraoesophageal hernia in a fit patient: laparoscopic repair
f: a small sliding hernia with reflux
the presentation instead showed features specific to Prokinetic drug (Prokinetics do not reduce a stomach that has moved into the chest)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Weight loss and review (A symptomatic paraoesophageal hernia risks volvulus and should be repaired in a fit patient)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Yearly barium swallow (Symptomatic paraoesophageal hernia in a fit patient requires surgical repair to prevent strangulation)
x: Ruled out here: requires a small sliding hernia with reflux, whereas this patient has fit 58 year old woman, paraoesophageal, rolling.
Prokinetics do not reduce a stomach that has moved into the chest.
A symptomatic paraoesophageal hernia risks volvulus and should be repaired in a fit patient.
Symptomatic paraoesophageal hernia in a fit patient requires surgical repair to prevent strangulation

hq_q.s:
A 46 year old man attends the surgical clinic 6 weeks after undergoing a laparoscopic 360-degree Nissen fundoplication for refractory gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. His heartburn and acid regurgitation have completely resolved, but he complains of postprandial upper abdominal fullness, inability to belch and increased rectal flatus. He has no dysphagia.
Abdominal examination shows mild tympanic epigastric distension. A water-soluble contrast swallow confirms an intact, well-positioned subdiaphragmatic wrap.
hq_q.w: Gas-bloat syndrome occurs after a 360-degree Nissen fundoplication because the competent one-way fundal wrap prevents normal venting of swallowed air from the stomach into the oesophagus (inability to belch or vomit). Swallowed gas accumulates, causing postprandial bloating and increased flatulence; it usually settles with dietary advice and avoiding carbonated drinks.
hq_q.f: Dysphagia to solids after the operation → wrap too tight.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?

tm.m: A 360-degree fundal wrap abolishes transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations, preventing retrograde venting of swallowed air and forcing gas distally through the bowel.
tm.g: Postprandial bloating, inability to belch and increased flatus with an intact Nissen wrap -> gas-bloat syndrome
x: A slipped or herniated wrap causes recurrent severe dysphagia, chest pain and contrast hold-up or supradiaphragmatic displacement on contrast swallow.
Achalasia causes progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids with a dilated oesophagus and 'bird-beak' tapering on contrast swallow.
Disruption of the wrap with recurrent hiatus hernia causes return of heartburn and acid regurgitation, whereas his reflux has completely resolved.
Accidental vagal nerve injury causes persistent nausea, early satiety and vomiting of undigested food rather than isolated inability to belch with increased flatus.
f: he developed severe dysphagia and chest pain after forceful retching, and contrast swallow showed the wrap herniated above the diaphragm
he had not had surgery and presented with dysphagia to both solids and liquids and a bird-beak lower oesophageal sphincter on barium swallow
his severe retrosternal heartburn and acid regurgitation recurred and contrast swallow showed wrap disruption with the cardia above the diaphragm
he had persistent vomiting of stale food eaten 12 hours earlier and a gastric emptying scintigraphy study showed severe retention at 4 hours

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man with asthma and hay fever came to the emergency department with food stuck in his gullet after eating steak. He has had difficulty swallowing solids for 2 years.
Endoscopy removes the food bolus and shows concentric rings and linear furrows along the oesophagus. Biopsies show more than 15 eosinophils per high-power field.
hq_q.w: EoE: an allergic disease of young atopic men with food bolus obstruction and a ringed oesophagus. Swallowed steroids treat it.
hq_q.f: White plaques in an immunosuppressed patient → candida oesophagitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: An allergic eosinophilic inflammation stiffens and narrows the oesophagus
tm.g: A young atopic man with a food bolus, rings and eosinophils has eosinophilic oesophagitis
f: dysphagia to solids and liquids with a bird's beak
white plaques in an immunosuppressed patient
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oesophageal web (A web is a thin membrane in the upper oesophagus, often with iron deficiency, not rings with eosinophils)
years of reflux with a smooth lower stricture
x: Ruled out here: requires dysphagia to solids and liquids with a bird's beak, whereas this patient has asthma and hay fever, food stuck.
Ruled out here: requires white plaques in an immunosuppressed patient, whereas this patient has asthma and hay fever, food stuck.
A web is a thin membrane in the upper oesophagus, often with iron deficiency, not rings with eosinophils.
Ruled out here: requires years of reflux with a smooth lower stricture, whereas this patient has asthma and hay fever, food stuck.

hq_q.s:
A 78 year old man presents to his GP with a 12-month history of high cervical dysphagia, severe halitosis, nocturnal coughing fits and effortless regurgitation of undigested food consumed several hours earlier. He has lost 3 kg in weight.
Examination of the neck reveals a soft, compressible swelling in the left anterior triangle that gurgles on palpation.
hq_q.w: A pharyngeal pouch (Zenker diverticulum) is a posterior pulsion diverticulum herniating through Killian's dehiscence (between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor). It causes regurgitation of stale undigested food, halitosis, aspiration cough and a gurgling left neck swelling; confirm with barium swallow (endoscopy risks perforation).
hq_q.f: A lump in the throat between meals that eating relieves → globus.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: regurgitation of undigested food consumed several hours earlier
tm.m: Uncoordinated cricopharyngeal relaxation raises hypopharyngeal intraluminal pressure, pushing mucosa posteriorly through Killian's triangle to form a food-trapping sac.
tm.g: Regurgitation of old undigested food + halitosis + gurgling neck swelling -> pharyngeal pouch (Zenker diverticulum)
x: Globus pharyngeus is a benign painless sensation of a lump in the throat between meals that improves during swallowing and never causes regurgitation, weight loss or halitosis.
Reflux oesophagitis causes retrosternal heartburn and acid regurgitation immediately after meals rather than hours-old undigested food and a gurgling neck mass.
Achalasia causes lower retrosternal dysphagia to solids and liquids with intrathoracic oesophageal dilatation rather than a gurgling cervical swelling.
Oesophageal carcinoma causes rapidly progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids) and hard cervical lymphadenopathy rather than a compressible gurgling sac.
f: a 30 year old anxious woman felt an intermittent lump in her throat when swallowing saliva that disappeared when eating food, with no weight loss
he had retrosternal burning pain and sour acid brash on lying flat after meals with normal swallowing
barium swallow showed a dilated thoracic oesophagus tapering smoothly to a 'bird-beak' at the lower oesophageal sphincter
a 70 year old heavy smoker and drinker had 8 weeks of rapidly progressive solid dysphagia, hoarseness and a hard fixed cervical lymph node

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man presents with a 3-month history of progressive dysphagia, initially to meat and bread and now to soft foods, accompanied by 7 kg unintentional weight loss. He has a 20-year history of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and a BMI of 34 kg/m². He has never smoked and drinks minimal alcohol.
Upper GI endoscopy reveals an ulcerated, stricturing tumour in the lower third of the oesophagus arising within a segment of Barrett's oesophagus.
hq_q.w: Oesophageal adenocarcinoma arises in the lower third of the oesophagus and gastro-oesophageal junction via the chronic GORD -> columnar metaplasia (Barrett's oesophagus) -> dysplasia -> adenocarcinoma sequence, strongly associated with central obesity. Squamous cell carcinoma arises in the upper/middle thirds and is linked to smoking and alcohol.
hq_q.f: Middle third tumour in a heavy smoker and drinker → squamous cell carcinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which histological subtype of oesophageal tumour is most likely?

tm.m: Chronic acid and bile reflux induces intestinal metaplasia (goblet-cell columnar epithelium, Barrett's oesophagus), which accumulates TP53 mutations and progresses to glandular adenocarcinoma.
tm.g: Lower-third oesophageal tumour arising in Barrett's oesophagus with chronic GORD/obesity -> oesophageal adenocarcinoma
x: Oesophageal leiomyoma is a benign, slow-growing submucosal smooth muscle tumour covered by intact normal mucosa, not an ulcerated malignant stricture in Barrett's.
GISTs arise from interstitial cells of Cajal (CD117/c-KIT positive), predominantly in the stomach, as submucosal masses rather than mucosal Barrett's carcinomas.
Squamous cell carcinoma typically affects the upper or middle third of the oesophagus and is driven by tobacco smoking, heavy alcohol intake, achalasia or caustic strictures.
Primary oesophageal neuroendocrine small cell carcinoma is exceedingly rare (<1% of oesophageal tumours) and unrelated to the Barrett's metaplasia-dysplasia pathway.
f: endoscopy showed a smooth, mobile submucosal mass with intact overlying mucosa in an asymptomatic 40 year old
endoscopy and CT showed a large submucosal gastric fundal mass with central ulceration positive for CD117 (c-KIT) on immunohistochemistry
a 68 year old who smoked 40 cigarettes daily and drank heavily presented with an ulcerated tumour in the middle third of the oesophagus
biopsy of a rapidly metastasising oesophageal mass showed small round blue cells staining positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin

hq_q.s:
A 41 year old man presents to his GP with a 2-month history of recurrent burning epigastric pain. The pain characteristically starts 2 to 3 hours after meals, frequently wakes him from sleep around 2 am, and is relieved within minutes by eating food or drinking milk. He takes no NSAIDs and has no dysphagia, vomiting, melaena or weight loss.
Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm. Examination shows mild localized epigastric tenderness only.
hq_q.w: Duodenal ulcers (90% associated with Helicobacter pylori or NSAIDs) cause epigastric 'hunger' pain occurring 2 to 3 hours after meals and at night when unbuffered gastric acid enters the duodenal bulb; eating triggers bicarbonate secretion and food buffers the acid, relieving the pain. Gastric ulcer pain is worsened by eating.
hq_q.f: Pain worse after eating with weight loss → gastric ulcer, which needs a check for cancer.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: relieved within minutes by eating food
tm.m: Food stimulates pyloric closure and buffers intragastric HCl; 2-3 hours later and overnight, unopposed basal acid secretion bathes the ulcerated duodenal bulb.
tm.g: Epigastric pain 2-3 hours postprandially and at night that is relieved by eating -> duodenal peptic ulcer
x: Chronic pancreatitis causes severe deep epigastric pain radiating straight through to the mid-back, worsened by food and accompanied by steatorrhoea and weight loss.
Gastric ulcers cause epigastric pain that comes on immediately or within 30 minutes of eating and is worsened rather than relieved by food, leading to food avoidance and weight loss.
GORD causes retrosternal burning rising towards the throat and sour acid regurgitation worse on lying flat or bending after large meals.
Biliary colic causes severe episodic right upper quadrant or epigastric pain triggered within an hour of fatty meals, lasting 1 to 5 hours, not relieved by eating.
f: he had a history of heavy alcohol intake, boring epigastric pain radiating to the back worse after eating, and pale floating stools
epigastric pain was triggered within 20 minutes of eating meals, causing him to avoid food and lose 4 kg in weight
he experienced retrosternal burning rising into the neck and an acid taste in his mouth when lying flat after dinner
he had severe attacks of right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right scapula 30 minutes after eating fried food

hq_q.s:
A 35 year old man attends the Emergency Department after passing a single episode of black, tarry stool this morning. He had taken oral ibuprofen for 4 days for a sprained ankle. He feels completely well, has no dizziness or abdominal pain, and has no medical history.
Pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg. Digital rectal examination shows normal brown stool with no fresh melaena. His calculated Glasgow-Blatchford score is 0.
o: Admit for inpatient endoscopy within 24 hours
Arrange an urgent CT mesenteric angiogram
Discharge home for outpatient upper GI endoscopy
Start an intravenous omeprazole infusion and admit
Transfuse 2 units of packed red blood cells
hq_q.w: The Glasgow-Blatchford score (GBS) is used at first assessment in acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. A score of 0 (normal haemoglobin, normal urea <6.5 mmol/L, normal pulse <100 bpm, normal BP, no melaena/syncope on exam, and no liver/heart disease) identifies very low-risk patients (<1% need for intervention) suitable for early discharge and outpatient endoscopy.
hq_q.f: Score of 8 → admit for endoscopy within 24 hours.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management plan?
hq_q.post: His Glasgow-Blatchford score is 0.

tm.m: Normal serum urea (5.8 mmol/L), normal haemoglobin (142 g/L) and normal haemodynamics exclude significant ongoing intraluminal blood loss.
tm.g: Suspected upper GI bleed with Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0 -> discharge home for outpatient endoscopy
x: Inpatient admission for endoscopy within 24 hours is required for haemodynamically stable patients with a Glasgow-Blatchford score of 1 or more.
CT angiography is reserved for active gastrointestinal bleeding where endoscopy fails to identify or control the bleeding source.
NICE guidelines explicitly advise against offering proton pump inhibitors before endoscopy in patients with suspected non-variceal upper GI bleeding.
His haemoglobin is completely normal at 142 g/L; restrictive red cell transfusion in upper GI bleeding is triggered only at Hb <=70 g/L.
f: his blood tests showed haemoglobin 108 g/L and serum urea 11.4 mmol/L, giving a Glasgow-Blatchford score of 6
he had ongoing brisk lower GI bleeding or persistent upper GI bleeding that could not be localised at urgent upper GI endoscopy
endoscopy had just been performed and demonstrated an ulcer with a visible non-bleeding vessel treated with adrenaline and clips
he presented with active haematemesis and a haemoglobin concentration of 64 g/L

hq_q.s: A 56 year old woman had dyspepsia and endoscopy showed a 1.5 cm gastric ulcer on the lesser curve that looked benign. Biopsies showed no cancer and H. pylori was found. She has completed H. pylori eradication and 8 weeks of a proton pump inhibitor and feels well.
o: Discharge to the GP with a PPI
hq_q.w: Gastric ulcers can hide cancer, so endoscopy is repeated to confirm healing and biopsy again.
hq_q.f: A duodenal ulcer → no routine repeat scope; confirm H. pylori eradication instead.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Gastric ulcers can hide cancer that early biopsies miss
tm.g: Gastric ulcer: repeat endoscopy in 6 to 8 weeks to confirm healing
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Barium meal in 3 months (Barium studies cannot take biopsies to exclude underlying gastric malignancy)
Visible haematuria with flank mass raises suspicion of renal carcinoma
the presentation instead showed features specific to Discharge to the GP with a PPI (A gastric ulcer needs a repeat scope to confirm healing, as some cancers look benign)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Serology for H. pylori (Serology stays positive after eradication, so it cannot confirm cure)
x: Barium studies cannot take biopsies to exclude underlying gastric malignancy
Ruled out here: requires Visible haematuria with flank mass raises suspicion of renal carcinoma, whereas this patient has gastric ulcer, lesser curve.
A gastric ulcer needs a repeat scope to confirm healing, as some cancers look benign.
Serology stays positive after eradication, so it cannot confirm cure.

hq_q.s: An 18 year old man is referred to the gastroenterology clinic because his father died of colorectal adenocarcinoma at 40. For 3 months he has had loose stools and intermittent bright red rectal bleeding. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium. Colonoscopy reveals hundreds of pedunculated polyps throughout the colon, confirmed on biopsy as tubular adenomas.
hq_q.w: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by germline APC tumour-suppressor mutations, characterised by >100 colorectal adenomatous polyps, congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) and a near-100% lifetime colorectal cancer risk requiring prophylactic colectomy.
hq_q.f: Non-polyposis proximal colon cancer with family history of endometrial and ovarian carcinoma -> Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: father died of colorectal adenocarcinoma at 40
congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
tm.m: Germline loss-of-function mutation in the APC gene on chromosome 5q21 prevents beta-catenin degradation in the Wnt signalling pathway, driving diffuse colonic epithelial neoplasia
tm.g: >100 colorectal adenomatous polyps + CHRPE + young family history of colon cancer = familial adenomatous polyposis (APC mutation)
x: Cowden syndrome causes mucocutaneous trichilemmomas, macrocephaly and gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps rather than hundreds of colorectal adenomas with CHRPE.
Juvenile polyposis produces 5 to 100 smooth hamartomatous retention polyps with dilated cystic glands rather than hundreds of dysplastic adenomas.
Lynch syndrome is caused by mismatch repair gene mutations and presents with proximal colon and endometrial cancers with only a few adenomas.
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome presents with mucocutaneous melanocytic macules on the lips and arborising smooth-muscle small-bowel hamartomas causing intussusception.
f: He presents with macrocephaly, facial trichilemmomas, thyroid follicular adenoma and colonic hamartomas due to a PTEN mutation.
Colonoscopy in a child with rectal bleeding shows 15 smooth cherry-red hamartomatous juvenile polyps with SMAD4 mutation.
A 42 year old woman with three relatives affected by colorectal and endometrial cancers has a solitary right-sided colonic tumour.
A teenager presents with dark pigmented freckling on the vermilion border of the lips and jejunal intussusception from hamartomatous polyps.

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man presents with a 2-month history of rectal bleeding mixed with stool and tenesmus. Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg. Colonoscopy identifies an ulcerated lesion 8 cm from the anal verge, and biopsy confirms rectal adenocarcinoma. Staging CT shows no distant metastases. The multidisciplinary team needs local staging to plan neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy.
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG151 guidelines, high-resolution pelvic MRI is the investigation of choice for local staging of rectal carcinoma, defining mural depth (T stage), nodal status (N stage) and proximity to the mesorectal fascia to guide neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy.
hq_q.f: Early T1 rectal lesion being evaluated for local transanal excision when MRI is equivocal -> endorectal ultrasound.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most appropriate for local staging of this tumour?

tm.m: T2-weighted high-resolution pelvic MRI differentiates muscularis propria from perirectal fat and visualises tumour extension within 1 mm of the mesorectal fascia
tm.g: Confirmed rectal adenocarcinoma local T/N and circumferential resection margin staging: high-resolution MRI pelvis
x: CT colonography evaluates the proximal colonic lumen when colonoscopy is incomplete, but lacks soft-tissue contrast to define the mesorectal fascia.
Barium contrast fluoroscopy only outlines the mucosal lumen and cannot assess mural invasion depth, mesorectal lymph nodes or the circumferential resection margin.
Endorectal ultrasound is reserved for very early T1 polyps considered for local excision and cannot reliably image the entire mesorectal fascia in mid-rectal tumours.
FDG PET-CT has poor spatial resolution for mesorectal fascia involvement and is used selectively to characterise equivocal distant metastases.
f: An stenosing rectal tumour prevents colonoscope passage and the proximal colon must be screened for synchronous lesions.
This obsolete luminal study has been superseded by colonoscopy and cross-sectional imaging.
A small 1.5 cm sessile rectal lesion is being assessed for T1 submucosa-limited local transanal endoscopic microsurgery.
Restaging is required prior to hepatic metastasectomy when liver MRI and CT findings are equivocal.

hq_q.s: A 68 year old man attends the colorectal oncology clinic 18 months after a curative right hemicolectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy for stage III caecal adenocarcinoma. He feels well with normal appetite, stable weight and unchanged bowel habit. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 70 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Surveillance blood tests show his serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) has risen from 2 ug/L to 18 ug/L.
o: Contrast CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis
Repeat serum CEA assay in 1 year
hq_q.w: In colorectal cancer surveillance (NICE NG151), a sustained rise in serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) strongly suggests local or distant recurrence (most commonly hepatic or pulmonary metastases) and mandates an urgent contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.
hq_q.f: Isolated resectable hepatic metastasis identified on restaging CT -> refer to hepatobiliary MDT for potentially curative liver resection.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

c: carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) has risen from 2 ug/L to 18 ug/L
tm.m: Proliferating colorectal adenocarcinoma cells shed cell-surface glycoprotein CEA into the portal and systemic circulation proportionally to occult metastatic tumour burden
tm.g: Rising serum CEA during post-resection colorectal cancer follow-up: urgent contrast CT chest, abdomen and pelvis
x: A progressive 9-fold elevation in serum CEA to 18 ug/L strongly indicates occult metastatic recurrence and must not be ignored for a year.
Systemic chemotherapy should not be commenced on a tumour marker rise alone before anatomical staging, as isolated hepatic or pulmonary metastases may be curatively resectable.
Colonoscopy only inspects the mucosal surface for intraluminal anastomotic recurrence or metachronous polyps and misses hepatic or pulmonary metastases.
Ultrasound has lower sensitivity than contrast-enhanced CT for hepatic deposits and provides no assessment of retroperitoneal nodal, peritoneal or pulmonary recurrence.
f: Surveillance serum CEA remains stable below 3 ug/L with normal scheduled CT imaging.
Biopsy-proven unresectable multifocal bilobar hepatic and pulmonary colorectal metastases are confirmed on CT.
Routine 1-year post-resection intraluminal mucosal clearance colonoscopy is due in a patient with normal CEA.
Biliary duct dilatation is suspected in a jaundiced patient with right upper quadrant pain.

hq_q.s: A 22 year old long-distance lorry driver presents with a 3-day history of throbbing pain and swelling at the top of his natal cleft. Temperature 37.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg. Examination reveals a hirsute lower back with a tender, fluctuant 3 cm swelling just left of the midline in the upper natal cleft, alongside midline skin pits containing protruding hair tufts.
hq_q.w: Pilonidal sinus disease arises when loose hairs penetrate skin in the sacrococcygeal natal cleft (typically in young hirsute men in sedentary jobs), forming midline pits and foreign-body cavities that frequently become infected to form an off-midline pilonidal abscess.
hq_q.f: Hot fluctuant swelling directly adjacent to the anal verge with no natal cleft pits -> cryptoglandular perianal abscess.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: midline skin pits containing protruding hair tufts
tm.m: Friction and negative pressure during sitting drive shed coarse hairs into midline natal cleft follicles, provoking a foreign-body reaction and polymicrobial subcutaneous abscess
tm.g: Young hirsute adult + fluctuant swelling at top of natal cleft + midline hair-filled pits = pilonidal sinus / abscess
x: A perianal abscess arises from an infected anal crypt gland immediately adjacent to the anal verge rather than superiorly in the sacrococcygeal natal cleft.
A sacrococcygeal dermoid or teratoma is a deep congenital developmental mass without acquired midline epidermal hair pits.
Fistula-in-ano presents as a chronic discharging external opening close to the anal verge rather than an acute abscess in the upper natal cleft with midline hair pits.
Hidradenitis suppurativa affects apocrine gland-bearing skin of the axillae, groins and perineum with multiple interconnecting sinus tracts and comedones.
f: Examination shows a hot, fluctuant swelling 1.5 cm from the anal margin at the 4 o'clock position with normal natal cleft skin.
An infant or young child presents with a deep midline presacral developmental mass without natal cleft hair sinuses.
He has a persistently discharging opening 2 cm from the anal margin 4 months after drainage of a perianal abscess.
He has recurrent bilateral inguinal and axillary nodules,rope-like scarring and discharging apocrine sinus tracts.

hq_q.s: A 38 year old man presents 4 months after incision and drainage of an acute perianal abscess. Since the operation, an opening beside his anus has intermittently discharged purulent and blood-stained fluid. He has normal bowel habit. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg. Inspection reveals an external opening 3 cm from the anal verge at 5 o'clock with granulation tissue.
hq_q.w: A persistent discharging perianal opening following drainage of a perianal abscess indicates a fistula-in-ano. High-resolution pelvic MRI is the gold-standard preoperative investigation to map the primary track, internal opening, secondary extensions and relationship to the anal sphincter complex.
hq_q.f: Suspected underlying Crohn's disease with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss -> add ileocolonoscopy alongside pelvic MRI.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most appropriate to delineate the anatomy before definitive surgery?

c: 4 months after incision and drainage of an acute perianal abscess
intermittently discharged purulent and blood-stained fluid
external opening 3 cm from the anal verge
tm.m: T2-weighted and STIR pelvic MRI sequences highlight fluid-filled fistula tracks against the striated external sphincter and smooth-muscle internal sphincter
tm.g: Preoperative anatomical mapping of fistula-in-ano: high-resolution MRI pelvis
x: Abdominal CT has poor soft-tissue contrast resolution in the pelvic floor compared with MRI and cannot distinguish the internal from the external anal sphincter.
Colonoscopy inspects the colonic mucosa when Crohn's disease is suspected, but cannot map the three-dimensional course of a fistula through the sphincter complex.
Barium enema evaluates the colonic lumen and fails to demonstrate perianal fistula tracks or their relationship to the internal and external anal sphincters.
Rigid sigmoidoscopy allows limited visual inspection of the distal rectum in clinic but cannot trace intersphincteric or trans-sphincteric extensions.
f: He presents with fever, left iliac fossa peritonism and suspected complicated sigmoid diverticulitis.
He has chronic bloody diarrhoea, weight loss and raised faecal calprotectin requiring mucosal biopsy for Crohn's colitis.
This test is not used to map perianal fistula anatomy or sphincter involvement.
Bedside inspection of the rectal mucosa is performed in clinic alongside proctoscopy.

hq_q.s: A 40 year old woman attends the colorectal clinic with a persistently discharging perianal fistula following two perianal abscesses. She has had three vaginal deliveries and reports mild faecal urgency. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 70 bpm, BP 120/74 mmHg. Pelvic MRI demonstrates a high trans-sphincteric fistula tract traversing the upper two-thirds of the external anal sphincter to enter the anal canal at the dentate line.
o: Laying-open fistulotomy of the entire tract
hq_q.w: For a high trans-sphincteric fistula-in-ano crossing most of the external anal sphincter, primary fistulotomy is contraindicated due to faecal incontinence risk. Insertion of a loose draining seton maintains drainage, prevents recurrent sepsis and preserves sphincter integrity.
hq_q.f: Simple low intersphincteric fistula involving minimal sphincter muscle -> laying-open fistulotomy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial surgical management?

c: upper two-thirds of the external anal sphincter
tm.m: A loose non-absorbable silastic or braided suture (seton) threaded through the fistula tract allows continuous purulent drainage and fibrosis without cutting the striated external sphincter
tm.g: High trans-sphincteric fistula-in-ano (crossing external anal sphincter): loose seton insertion to preserve continence
x: Botulinum toxin relaxes the internal anal sphincter to heal a chronic anal fissure and has no role in draining a trans-sphincteric fistula.
Dividing the upper two-thirds of the external anal sphincter (especially in a multiparous woman with prior obstetric trauma) carries a very high risk of permanent faecal incontinence.
Antibiotics alone treat surrounding cellulitis transiently but do not eradicate an epithelialised or granulating high trans-sphincteric fistula tract.
Topical calcium channel blockers reduce internal sphincter hypertonia in chronic anal fissure and do not treat a fistula-in-ano.
f: She has a chronic posterior midline anal fissure that has failed topical diltiazem and glyceryl trinitrate ointment.
Examination under anaesthetic reveals a simple low subcutaneous or superficial intersphincteric fistula involving minimal sphincter muscle.
She develops acute spreading perineal cellulitis awaiting definitive examination under anaesthetic.
She presents with severe post-defecatory tearing pain from a chronic anal fissure and suffers from migraines.

hq_q.s: A 38 year old woman presents with a 4-month history of painless bright red rectal bleeding on the toilet paper after defecation. Increasing fibre and fluid intake has softened her stools, but the bleeding persists. She has no change in bowel habit. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg. Proctoscopy shows internal haemorrhoids that prolapse on straining and reduce spontaneously.
hq_q.w: Internal haemorrhoids that prolapse during defecation and reduce spontaneously are second-degree (grade II) haemorrhoids. When bleeding persists despite high-fibre dietary advice and bulk-forming laxatives, outpatient clinic rubber band ligation (Barron's banding) above the dentate line is the first-line procedural treatment.
hq_q.f: Fourth-degree irreducible haemorrhoids or failure of banding -> surgical haemorrhoidectomy (or haemorrhoidal artery ligation).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?

c: prolapse on straining and reduce spontaneously
tm.m: Placing a tight elastic band at the base of the vascular anal cushion above the dentate line induces ischaemic necrosis, sloughing and submucosal fibrotic fixation to the underlying muscle
tm.g: Symptomatic grade I or II internal haemorrhoids refractory to fibre/fluids: outpatient rubber band ligation
x: Cryotherapy causes prolonged profuse foul-smelling discharge and sphincter irritation, and is not recommended over outpatient rubber band ligation.
Surgical haemorrhoidectomy is reserved for symptomatic grade III or IV haemorrhoids or when outpatient non-operative treatments have failed.
Phlebotonics provide only modest short-term symptom relief and are inferior to rubber band ligation for persistent second-degree haemorrhoidal bleeding.
Topical corticosteroids must not be used for longer than 7 days as they cause perianal cutaneous atrophy, contact dermatitis and fail to cure prolapsing cushions.
f: This outdated destructive modality is not first-line outpatient therapy for second-degree haemorrhoids.
She has large irreducible fourth-degree haemorrhoids with persistent prolapse and mucosal ulceration.
She declines procedural intervention during pregnancy and seeks temporary conservative symptom control.
She has a brief 4-day flare of acute perianal pruritus and mucosal inflammation.

hq_q.s: A 42 year old man attends clinic with a 2-month history of bright red blood dripping into the toilet pan after defecation. He reports no perianal pain or change in bowel habit. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg. Digital rectal examination is normal. Proctoscopy demonstrates internal haemorrhoidal cushions at the 3, 7 and 11 o'clock positions that bleed on contact without pain.
o: They are covered by stratified squamous epithelium
They are innervated by the somatic pudendal nerve
They originate superior to the dentate line
They prolapse outside the external anal sphincter
They receive an avascular venous blood supply
hq_q.w: Internal haemorrhoids arise above the dentate (pectinate) line, where hindgut endoderm receives autonomic visceral innervation (insensitive to cutting, banding or pinprick). Below the dentate line, ectodermal anoderm receives somatic pain fibres via the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve.
hq_q.f: Thrombosed external haemorrhoid or acute anal fissure inferior to the dentate line -> severe somatic pain transmitted via the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve.
hq_q.ql: Which anatomical feature explains why uncomplicated internal haemorrhoids are painless?

c: bright red blood dripping into the toilet pan
tm.m: Mucosa superior to the dentate line derives from embryological endoderm and is innervated solely by visceral autonomic pelvic splanchnic fibres lacking somatic nociceptors
tm.g: Internal haemorrhoids are painless (and can be banded without anaesthetic) because they lie above the dentate line (visceral autonomic innervation)
x: Internal haemorrhoids are lined by simple columnar rectal mucosa rather than keratinised stratified squamous skin.
The inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve supplies somatic pain fibres below the dentate line, whereas above the dentate line innervation is autonomic visceral.
Uncomplicated grade I internal haemorrhoids remain entirely within the upper anal canal above the dentate line.
Haemorrhoidal cushions are rich arteriovenous vascular plexuses supplied by terminal branches of the superior rectal artery.
f: External haemorrhoids below the dentate line are covered by somatically innervated anoderm skin.
A thrombosed external haemorrhoid or anal fissure below the dentate line causes severe sharp somatic pain via the pudendal nerve.
Fourth-degree haemorrhoids prolapse irreducible outside the anal margin and become strangulated and painful.
This statement is anatomically incorrect because anal cushions have a rich arterial blood supply.

hq_q.s: A 66 year old man presents to his GP with a 6-week history of bright red rectal bleeding mixed with his stool. Over the same period his bowel habit has changed to looser, more frequent motions three times daily. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 136/82 mmHg. Digital rectal examination is normal, and proctoscopy reveals second-degree internal haemorrhoids.
o: Advise high-fibre diet and review in 3 months
Prescribe topical hydrocortisone and cinchocaine ointment
Reassure that haemorrhoids explain his symptoms
Refer for routine outpatient rubber band ligation
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG12 guidelines, patients aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding and a persistent change in bowel habit to looser or more frequent stools require an urgent 2-week-wait suspected colorectal cancer referral, despite visible haemorrhoids.
hq_q.f: Patient aged 30 with outlet bright red bleeding on paper, normal bowel habit and grade II haemorrhoids -> conservative fibre advice or rubber band ligation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

tm.m: Visible haemorrhoids frequently coexist with a synchronous rectosigmoid or colonic adenocarcinoma, which causes intraluminal bleeding and altered colonic transit
tm.g: Age >= 50 with rectal bleeding + change to looser/more frequent stools: urgent suspected colorectal cancer referral despite visible haemorrhoids
x: Delaying colonic investigation for 3 months in an older adult meeting urgent cancer referral criteria is unsafe.
Topical haemorrhoidal preparations do not investigate red-flag symptoms of colorectal malignancy in a 66 year old.
Internal haemorrhoids are extremely common and never account for a persistent change in bowel habit to looser, more frequent stools.
Treating incidental haemorrhoids without investigating a 6-week change to looser stools and rectal bleeding in a 66 year old risks missing a proximal colorectal carcinoma.
f: A 25 year old with hard stools and occasional fresh outlet bleeding has normal digital rectal examination and grade I haemorrhoids.
He requires short-term symptomatic relief of acute haemorrhoidal perianal irritation after colorectal cancer has been excluded.
Incidental asymptomatic grade I haemorrhoids are noted during a normal completion colonoscopy.
A 32 year old with normal bowel habit, no weight loss and bright red bleeding on the paper has second-degree haemorrhoids.

hq_q.s: A 30 year old woman presents with a 4-day history of severe, razor-like tearing anal pain during defecation that throbs for an hour afterwards, with blood on the paper. She has passed hard stools for 2 weeks. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg. Gentle parting of the buttocks reveals a superficial linear tear in the posterior midline with no sentinel tag.
o: Oral laxatives and topical lidocaine gel
Oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily
hq_q.w: An acute anal fissure (<1-2 weeks duration) heals in most patients with conservative management: dietary fibre, oral fluids, stool-softening bulk-forming or osmotic laxatives, warm sitz baths and short-term topical local anaesthetic (lidocaine gel/ointment) applied before defecation.
hq_q.f: Chronic anal fissure persisting >6 weeks with sentinel skin tag -> add topical 0.4% glyceryl trinitrate ointment (or topical 2% diltiazem).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

c: 4-day history of severe, razor-like tearing anal pain
superficial linear tear in the posterior midline
tm.m: Softening the stool prevents recurrent mechanical tearing of the poorly perfused posterior midline anoderm while topical lidocaine blocks somatic pudendal nociception to break the pain-spasm cycle
tm.g: Acute anal fissure (<1-2 weeks duration): dietary fibre/fluids + stool-softening laxatives + short-term topical lidocaine
x: Botulinum toxin injection is a second- or third-line specialist treatment for chronic anal fissures (>6-8 weeks) that fail topical vasodilators.
Surgical division of the internal anal sphincter carries a risk of flatus or faecal incontinence and is reserved for refractory chronic fissures.
Antibiotics are not indicated for an uncomplicated primary acute posterior midline anal fissure without perianal sepsis or Crohn's disease.
Topical GTN ointment for 6-8 weeks is indicated when an anal fissure persists for more than 1-2 weeks or becomes chronic (>6 weeks).
f: Her posterior midline fissure persists after 8 weeks of topical glyceryl trinitrate and diltiazem therapy.
A chronic anal fissure with exposed internal sphincter fibres fails both topical vasodilators and botulinum toxin injection.
She has complex perianal Crohn's disease complicated by a purulent perianal fistula.
Her anal fissure symptoms have persisted for 7 weeks despite high-fibre intake, fluids and bulk-forming laxatives.

hq_q.s: A 28 year old man presents with a 1-week history of excruciating knife-like pain in his anus whenever he passes a stool, followed by an ache and streaks of bright red blood on the paper. He has hard stools and is visibly anxious about being examined. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg. Abdominal palpation is normal.
o: Arrange urgent examination under general anaesthetic
Gently part the buttocks for visual inspection
Perform an immediate digital rectal examination
hq_q.w: When the history indicates an acute anal fissure, examination is limited to gently parting the buttocks to inspect the distal anal verge for a midline tear. Digital rectal examination and proctoscopy are contraindicated acutely due to severe pain and spasm.
hq_q.f: Severe unremitting anal pain and fever with nothing visible on gentle parting of the buttocks -> urgent examination under anaesthetic to exclude an intersphincteric abscess.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial physical examination technique?

c: excruciating knife-like pain in his anus whenever he passes a stool
streaks of bright red blood on the paper
tm.m: Gentle lateral traction on the buttocks everts the distal anoderm below the dentate line, exposing the posterior midline tear without stretching the hypertonic internal anal sphincter
tm.g: Suspected acute anal fissure: examine by gently parting the buttocks only (defer DRE and proctoscopy due to pain/spasm)
x: Examination under anaesthetic is reserved for cases where visual inspection is non-diagnostic or a deep intersphincteric abscess is suspected despite a normal exterior.
Passing a rigid proctoscope across an acute anal fissure is intolerably painful and contraindicated in the acute phase.
Attempting a digital rectal examination in the presence of an acute anal fissure causes severe pain and internal sphincter spasm and should be avoided initially.
Rigid sigmoidoscopy requires instrumentation across the spastic anal canal and must be deferred until the acute fissure has healed.
f: He has severe throbbing deep rectal pain, fever of 38.8°C and normal external inspection, raising suspicion of an intersphincteric abscess.
Painless bright red bleeding without tearing defecatory pain is being evaluated for internal haemorrhoids.
His fissure has completely healed at 8-week follow-up and digital rectal examination can now be comfortably performed.
Rectal mucosal evaluation is performed weeks later once the acute anal fissure has resolved.

hq_q.s: A 42 year old woman had a botulinum toxin injection into the internal anal sphincter for a chronic anal fissure 3 weeks ago. Her pain has improved, but she has some leakage of wind that embarrasses her. She has no faecal incontinence.
o: Temporary, as the toxin wears off
hq_q.w: Botulinum toxin relaxes the sphincter for about 3 months, so minor incontinence is temporary. Key discriminator: Minor incontinence after botulinum toxin is usually temporary.
hq_q.f: Leakage after lateral sphincterotomy → can be permanent.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate advice?

tm.m: Botulinum toxin relaxes the sphincter for about 3 months
tm.g: Minor incontinence after botulinum toxin is usually temporary
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Biopsy the fissure base (A biopsy is not needed for a typical healing posterior fissure)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Repeat the injection sooner (Repeating botulinum toxin early would worsen internal sphincter weakness and flatus incontinence)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sphincter damage that needs repair (Botulinum toxin does not cut the sphincter; the weakness wears off)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Start loperamide long term (Long-term loperamide is not needed for temporary flatus leakage)
x: A biopsy is not needed for a typical healing posterior fissure.
Repeating botulinum toxin early would worsen internal sphincter weakness and flatus incontinence
Botulinum toxin does not cut the sphincter; the weakness wears off.
Long-term loperamide is not needed for temporary flatus leakage.

hq_q.s: An 82 year old woman with known sigmoid diverticulosis presents after passing two large volumes of fresh maroon-red blood and clots per rectum over 2 hours. She denies any abdominal pain or fever, and takes no anticoagulants. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg, SpO2 98% breathing air. Her abdomen is soft and completely non-tender. Digital rectal examination reveals dark red blood.
hq_q.w: Diverticular haemorrhage is the commonest cause of major acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding in older adults. Erosion of a vasa recta artery within a diverticulum produces sudden, painless, large-volume fresh or maroon rectal bleeding that ceases spontaneously in ~75-80% of cases.
hq_q.f: Sudden left-sided abdominal pain and tenderness followed by bloody diarrhoea in an arteriopath -> acute ischaemic colitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of her lower gastrointestinal bleeding?

c: large volumes of fresh maroon-red blood and clots
abdomen is soft and completely non-tender
tm.m: Asymmetrical intimal thickening and medial thinning of the vasa recta draped over the dome of a false colonic diverticulum leads to spontaneous arterial rupture into the colon lumen
tm.g: Sudden, painless, large-volume fresh/maroon rectal bleeding in an older adult with diverticulosis = diverticular bleed
x: Ischaemic colitis presents with sudden crampy left-sided abdominal pain and tenderness followed several hours later by bloody diarrhoea and raised lactate.
Colonic angiodysplasia typically causes chronic occult iron-deficiency anaemia or recurrent low-volume venous oozing rather than sudden massive arterial haematochezia in known diverticulosis.
Haemorrhoids produce small volumes of bright red outlet blood coating the stool or dripping into the pan rather than large-volume maroon blood and clots.
Colorectal carcinoma typically causes low-volume bleeding mixed with stool, altered bowel habit, tenesmus or weight loss rather than sudden massive painless clot passage.
f: She develops sudden severe left iliac fossa pain and tenderness after an episode of atrial fibrillation, followed by bloody diarrhoea and lactate 3.4 mmol/L.
An 86 year old with severe calcific aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome) presents with chronic iron-deficiency anaemia and right-sided submucosal vascular ectasias.
She notices small streaks of bright red blood on the toilet paper after straining with prolapsing anal cushions.
She reports a 3-month history of progressive constipation, 6 kg weight loss, tenesmus and dark blood mixed with stool.

hq_q.s: A 70 year old man is referred with a 4-month history of recurrent polymicrobial Escherichia coli and Enterococcus urinary tract infections. He reports passing gas bubbles at the end of micturition and noticing dark particulate debris in his urine. He has had two admissions for acute sigmoid diverticulitis. Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 134/80 mmHg. Abdominal palpation shows mild left iliac fossa fullness.
hq_q.w: Pneumaturia (passing gas bubbles in urine), faecaluria (faecal debris in urine) and recurrent polymicrobial enteric urinary tract infections are pathognomonic of a colovesical fistula, most commonly caused by complicated sigmoid diverticulitis (~65-70% of cases).
hq_q.f: Passage of flatus and faeces through the vagina in a woman with previous hysterectomy and diverticulitis -> colovaginal fistula.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: recurrent polymicrobial Escherichia coli and Enterococcus urinary tract infections
gas bubbles at the end of micturition
dark particulate debris in his urine
tm.m: Pericolic inflammation and localized abscess rupture from an inflamed sigmoid diverticulum erode directly through the adjacent dome of the urinary bladder, creating an epithelialised fistulous communication
tm.g: Pneumaturia + faecaluria + recurrent polymicrobial UTIs in a patient with diverticular disease = colovesical fistula
x: Emphysematous cystitis is an acute gas-forming bladder wall infection in poorly controlled diabetics and does not cause faecaluria (particulate stool debris in urine).
A colovaginal fistula occurs solely in women (typically following hysterectomy) and presents with passage of flatus and faeces per vaginam.

Uncomplicated ileocaecal Crohn's disease causes right iliac fossa pain and weight loss; sigmoid diverticulitis is far the commonest cause of colovesical fistula in older men with known diverticulitis.
Urothelial bladder cancer presents with painless visible haematuria rather than pneumaturia, faecaluria and polymicrobial enteric urinary tract infections.
f: A 72 year old with poorly controlled diabetes presents with acute sepsis, suprapubic pain and intramural bladder wall gas on CT without faecaluria.
A 74 year old woman with prior hysterectomy and diverticulitis presents with foul-smelling feculent vaginal discharge and vaginal flatus.
A 24 year old smoker presents with chronic diarrhoea, mouth ulcers, weight loss and a tender right iliac fossa mass.
A 68 year old smoker who worked in a dye factory presents with painless frank haematuria and a papillary mass on flexible cystoscopy.

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of worsening left iliac fossa pain and fevers. Temperature 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg, SpO2 98% breathing air. Examination reveals localised tenderness and fullness in the left iliac fossa with no generalised peritonism. Contrast CT demonstrates acute sigmoid diverticulitis complicated by a 6 cm walled-off pericolic abscess with no free gas.
o: Discharge on oral co-amoxiclav for 5 days
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG147 guidelines for acute complicated diverticulitis (Hinchey Ib/II), a walled-off pericolic or pelvic abscess measuring >3 cm (here 6 cm) without generalised peritonitis is managed with intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and CT-guided percutaneous drainage.
hq_q.f: Small pericolic abscess <3 cm in a haemodynamically stable patient -> trial of intravenous antibiotics alone with close clinical observation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

c: 6 cm walled-off pericolic abscess with no free gas
tm.m: Image-guided percutaneous catheter drainage evacuates the purulent collection under low pressure, allowing systemic beta-lactam/metronidazole therapy to sterilise the pericolic phlegmon without emergency stoma formation
tm.g: Acute diverticulitis with pericolic abscess >= 3-4 cm and no generalised peritonitis: IV antibiotics + CT-guided percutaneous drainage
x: Outpatient oral antibiotics cannot penetrate a 6 cm walled-off pericolic abscess in a febrile, tachycardic patient.
Laparoscopic lavage does not adequately drain a walled-off 6 cm mesocolic/pericolic abscess and carries higher re-intervention rates than image-guided drainage.
Immediate Hartmann's resection is indicated for generalised purulent or faecal peritonitis (Hinchey III/IV) or failure of percutaneous drainage, not a contained 6 cm pericolic abscess.
Colonoscopy is strictly contraindicated during acute complicated diverticulitis because gas insufflation risks converting a contained abscess into free perforation.
f: He has uncomplicated acute diverticulitis with no abscess on CT, mild malaise and is able to tolerate oral fluids at home.
Diagnostic laparoscopy finds Hinchey III purulent fluid without an overt faecal colonic defect.
CT shows perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with generalised free intraperitoneal gas, faecal peritonitis and septic shock.
Six weeks after complete resolution of acute complicated diverticulitis, luminal imaging is arranged to exclude an underlying carcinoma.

hq_q.s: A 78 year old man with peripheral arterial disease and atrial fibrillation presents after developing sudden cramping left-sided abdominal pain 6 hours ago, followed 3 hours later by urgent passage of dark bloody diarrhoea. Temperature 37.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm irregularly irregular, BP 138/76 mmHg. Examination shows focal tenderness over the left flank and left iliac fossa without guarding. Venous blood gas shows lactate 2.8 mmol/L (<2.0).
hq_q.w: Acute ischaemic colitis affects the colonic watershed zones (Griffiths' point at the splenic flexure and Sudeck's point at the rectosigmoid junction), presenting in older arteriopaths with sudden cramping left-sided abdominal pain followed within hours by bloody diarrhoea and raised lactate.
hq_q.f: Pain out of proportion to examination findings affecting the central abdomen in atrial fibrillation with severe metabolic acidosis -> acute superior mesenteric artery occlusion (small-bowel ischaemia).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: peripheral arterial disease and atrial fibrillation
followed 3 hours later by urgent passage of dark bloody diarrhoea
tm.m: Hypoperfusion at the splenic flexure watershed (Griffiths' point between the middle colic and left colic arterial territories) causes mucosal sloughing, submucosal haemorrhage and bloody diarrhoea
tm.g: Older vasculopath/AF patient + sudden left-sided abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhoea + raised lactate = acute ischaemic colitis
x: Diverticular bleeding is classically painless and presents with sudden large-volume arterial blood clots and a normal serum lactate.
Ulcerative colitis causes subacute bloody diarrhoea with urgency and tenesmus starting in the rectum rather than hyperacute left-sided pain with lactic acidosis in an elderly arteriopath.
Infective enterocolitis typically follows contaminated poultry ingestion with prodromal fever and watery diarrhoea over days rather than hyperacute watershed pain in a vasculopath.
Angiodysplasia causes painless intermittent venous bleeding or chronic iron-deficiency anaemia in the right colon rather than acute left-sided pain and elevated lactate.
f: He has sudden painless passage of large maroon blood clots with a completely non-tender abdomen and normal lactate.
A 28 year old non-smoker presents with a 4-week history of 8 bloody mucoid stools daily, tenesmus and continuous proctosigmoiditis.
A 24 year old develops fever, malaise and profuse watery then bloody diarrhoea 3 days after eating undercooked chicken.
He has painless recurrent dark red bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia with cherry-red vascular ectasias in the caecum.

hq_q.s: A 74 year old man presents to the Emergency Department after passing four large volumes of fresh red blood and clots per rectum over 3 hours. He feels faint on sitting up. Temperature 36.3°C, pulse rate 120 bpm, BP 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, SpO2 97% breathing air. He is pale with a capillary refill time of 3 seconds. His abdomen is soft and non-tender.
hq_q.w: The shock index is heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure ($120 \div 100 = 1.20$). Under BSG guidelines for acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding, a shock index $>1.0$ defines an unstable bleed requiring immediate resuscitation and urgent CT mesenteric angiography.
hq_q.f: Pulse rate 80 bpm and blood pressure 125/75 mmHg -> shock index 0.64 (haemodynamically stable bleed).
hq_q.ql: What is his calculated shock index?

c: four large volumes of fresh red blood
tm.m: Shock index (HR / systolic BP) integrates sympathetic baroreceptor tachycardia and falling stroke volume to detect occult hypovolaemic shock earlier than isolated vital signs
tm.g: Shock index = Heart Rate / Systolic BP (here 120 / 100 = 1.2); shock index > 1.0 defines an unstable GI bleed requiring urgent CT angiography
x: A shock index of 0.80 corresponds to a heart rate lower than the systolic blood pressure (e.g. pulse 96 bpm and systolic BP 120 mmHg), indicating haemodynamic stability.
A shock index of 1.00 occurs when heart rate numerically equals systolic blood pressure (e.g. pulse 100 bpm and systolic BP 100 mmHg).
A shock index of 1.50 would correspond to a pulse rate of 120 bpm with a systolic blood pressure of 80 mmHg.
1.94 is obtained by erroneously dividing heart rate (120 bpm) by diastolic blood pressure (62 mmHg) rather than systolic blood pressure (100 mmHg).
f: His observations on arrival are a pulse rate of 96 bpm and a blood pressure of 120/74 mmHg.
His observations on arrival are a pulse rate of 100 bpm and a blood pressure of 100/62 mmHg.
His pulse rate is 120 bpm and his blood pressure falls further to 80/48 mmHg.
This value results from mistakenly dividing heart rate by diastolic rather than systolic blood pressure.

hq_q.s: A 76 year old woman with atrial fibrillation presents with a 4-hour history of profuse fresh rectal bleeding. She took oral apixaban 5 mg 5 hours ago. Despite receiving 1 litre of crystalloid and 2 units of packed red cells, she continues to pass large clots. Temperature 36.2°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 96/54 mmHg (shock index 1.29), SpO2 96% breathing air.
o: Continue oral apixaban 5 mg twice daily
Reduce oral apixaban dose to 2.5 mg twice daily
Switch apixaban immediately to oral warfarin
Withhold apixaban and give andexanet alfa or PCC
hq_q.w: In haemodynamically unstable, life-threatening gastrointestinal bleeding (shock index >1.0) on a direct factor Xa inhibitor (apixaban or rivaroxaban), withhold the DOAC immediately and reverse with intravenous andexanet alfa or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) under BSG and NICE guidelines.
hq_q.f: Unstable gastrointestinal bleed on dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor) -> withhold dabigatran and reverse with intravenous idarucizumab.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulation management?

c: pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 96/54 mmHg (shock index 1.29)
tm.m: Andexanet alfa acts as a catalytically inactive recombinant factor Xa decoy that binds and sequesters circulating apixaban with high affinity, restoring endogenous factor Xa haemostasis
tm.g: Life-threatening GI bleed (shock index > 1) on apixaban/rivaroxaban: withhold DOAC and reverse with andexanet alfa (or 4-factor PCC)
x: Vitamin K restores hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors in warfarin therapy and has no effect on direct factor Xa inhibition by apixaban.
Continuing direct factor Xa inhibition during life-threatening haemorrhagic shock with a shock index >1.0 will cause exsanguination.
Dose reduction is used for stroke prevention in renal impairment, advanced age or low body weight, never during acute unstable gastrointestinal haemorrhage.
Initiating another anticoagulant during active haemodynamically unstable gastrointestinal bleeding is contraindicated.
f: She takes warfarin for a metallic heart valve with an INR of 8.5 and minor non-life-threatening bleeding.
She has a trivial self-limiting streak of haemorrhoidal outlet bleeding with normal haemoglobin and stable observations.
She is attending a routine outpatient clinic aged 82 with weight 56 kg and serum creatinine 138 umol/L.
She is stable in clinic and requires switching from a DOAC to warfarin following diagnosis of triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome.

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man presents to his GP with a 2-month history of a persistent change in bowel habit. Having previously opened his bowels once daily, he now passes stools only once every 3 days and has experienced 4 kg of unintentional weight loss. He denies abdominal pain or visible bleeding. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg. Abdominal and digital rectal examinations are normal.
o: FIT and suspected colorectal cancer referral
Prescribe macrogol laxatives and review in 3 months
Recommend increased dietary fibre and oral fluids
Repeat thyroid function and serum calcium tests
Request a plain supine abdominal radiograph
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG12 guidelines, an adult aged 60 or over with a persistent change in bowel habit, unintentional weight loss and microcytic anaemia (Hb 118 g/L, MCV 78 fL) requires quantitative FIT and an urgent suspected colorectal cancer referral.
hq_q.f: Young adult (<40 years) with chronic constipation, stable weight, normal Hb/MCV and no red flags -> dietary fibre, fluids and bulk-forming laxative.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
hq_q.post: TSH normal. Calcium normal.

tm.m: An annular stenosing left-sided colonic adenocarcinoma narrows the bowel lumen and oozes occult blood, presenting with new-onset constipation, weight loss and microcytic iron deficiency
tm.g: Age >= 60 with change in bowel habit + weight loss / microcytic anaemia: quantitative FIT and urgent 2-week-wait colorectal cancer referral
x: Empirical laxatives without urgent colonic investigation are unsafe in a patient over 60 with change in bowel habit, weight loss and mild microcytic anaemia.
Treating new-onset constipation, unintentional weight loss and microcytic anaemia in a 64 year old with dietary advice delays colorectal cancer diagnosis.
His serum TSH and corrected calcium are already confirmed normal, so repeating them will delay urgent exclusion of colorectal carcinoma.
Plain abdominal X-rays have no sensitivity for non-obstructing colorectal neoplasia and are not used in primary care investigation of chronic constipation.
f: Secondary causes and red flags have been excluded in a young adult with functional constipation.
A 26 year old woman with lifelong sluggish bowel habit, normal weight and normal full blood count seeks lifestyle advice.
A patient presents with constipation, lethargy, weight gain and cold intolerance without prior thyroid screening.
He presents acutely to the Emergency Department with absolute constipation, bilious vomiting and a distended tympanic abdomen.

hq_q.s: A 72 year old woman attends her GP with a 3-week history of new-onset constipation, passing hard stools twice weekly. She has permanent atrial fibrillation and severe asthma; 4 weeks ago her cardiologist started a new oral medication for ventricular rate control. She takes no opioids or iron. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 78 bpm irregularly irregular, BP 132/76 mmHg. Abdominal examination is normal.
hq_q.w: Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine L-type calcium channel blocker used for atrial fibrillation rate control when beta-blockers are contraindicated by asthma. By blocking L-type calcium influx in enteric smooth muscle, verapamil inhibits colonic peristalsis and commonly causes constipation.
hq_q.f: New-onset ankle swelling and facial flushing on a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker -> amlodipine.
hq_q.ql: Which newly started cardiac medication is the most likely cause of her constipation?

c: started a new oral medication for ventricular rate control
tm.m: Blockade of voltage-gated L-type calcium channels in colonic longitudinal and circular smooth muscle myocytes reduces enteric contractility and prolongs colonic transit time
tm.g: AF rate-control drug used in asthma that commonly causes constipation = verapamil
x: Amiodarone causes thyroid dysfunction, corneal microdeposits, pulmonary fibrosis and hepatotoxicity, and is not used as a routine rate-control switch for asthma.
Direct factor Xa inhibitors prevent thromboembolism in atrial fibrillation and do not inhibit gastrointestinal smooth muscle motility.
Beta-blockers are contraindicated in severe asthma and do not cause severe colonic smooth-muscle relaxation and constipation.
Cardiac glycosides cause nausea, anorexia, xanthopsia (yellow vision) and diarrhoea rather than constipation.
f: She develops photosensitivity, slate-grey skin discolouration and hypothyroidism on antiarrhythmic therapy.
She develops epistaxis and easy bruising after starting stroke prophylaxis for atrial fibrillation.
A patient without asthma develops sinus bradycardia and cold extremities on rate-control therapy.
An elderly patient with declining renal function develops nausea, blurred yellow vision and downsloping ST depression.

hq_q.s: A 45 year old man presents with a 3-day history of severe lower back pain radiating down both legs after lifting crates. Since this morning he has been unable to pass urine and has perianal numbness and faecal incontinence. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 86 bpm, BP 138/84 mmHg. Examination reveals absent ankle reflexes, reduced perianal pinprick sensation and lax anal sphincter tone. A bladder scan shows 700 mL residual urine.
o: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine
Insert a urinary catheter and discharge to urology clinic
Prescribe osmotic laxatives and review in 1 week
Request a plain anteroposterior lumbar spine X-ray
hq_q.w: Bilateral radicular leg pain accompanied by perianal ('saddle') anaesthesia, reduced anal sphincter tone, faecal incontinence and painless urinary retention (700 mL residual) is diagnostic of cauda equina syndrome, requiring an emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine and surgical decompression.
hq_q.f: Unilateral L5/S1 sciatica with preserved bladder function, normal anal tone and intact saddle sensation -> analgesia, mobilisation and non-emergency assessment.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management step?

tm.m: A large central lumbar intervertebral disc herniation (commonly L4/L5 or L5/S1) compresses the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris, interrupting S2-S4 somatic pudendal and parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic pathways
tm.g: Low back pain + saddle anaesthesia + lax anal tone + urinary retention (cauda equina syndrome): emergency MRI lumbosacral spine
x: Although bladder catheterisation relieves acute retention, discharging him without an emergency spine MRI misses time-critical neurosurgical decompression of the cauda equina.
Discharging a patient with saddle anaesthesia, lax anal tone and painless urinary retention will result in permanent paraparesis and double incontinence.
Outpatient physiotherapy is appropriate for uncomplicated mechanical low back pain without red-flag neurological deficits.
Plain radiographs cannot visualise a central intervertebral disc prolapse compressing the cauda equina nerve roots within the spinal canal.
f: An 78 year old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presents with painful acute urinary retention and completely normal lower-limb and perianal neurology.
He has simple opioid-induced constipation with normal perianal sensation, normal anal tone and normal post-void bladder volume.
He has localised lumbar muscular spasm with normal lower-limb reflexes, normal sphincter tone and no saddle numbness.
An elderly osteoporotic patient presents with localised thoracic point tenderness after a minor fall with intact neurology.

hq_q.s:
A 7-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of central abdominal pain. Three days ago he developed a sore throat and coryzal symptoms. He has not vomited and his bowels have opened normally.
Temperature is 39.0°C and heart rate is 118 bpm. Examination reveals bilateral tender cervical lymphadenopathy and mild periumbilical tenderness that shifts when he rolls onto his left side, without guarding.
hq_q.w: Mesenteric adenitis causes reactive enlargement of mesenteric lymph nodes following a viral upper respiratory tract infection in children. High fever, cervical lymphadenopathy, and tenderness that shifts with posture changes distinguish it from acute appendicitis.
hq_q.f: Pain migrating to the right iliac fossa with anorexia and localised guarding -> acute appendicitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: tenderness that shifts when he rolls onto his left side
tm.m: Viral pharyngitis triggers reactive hyperplasia of mobile mesenteric lymph nodes within the small bowel mesentery.
tm.g: Central abdominal pain following viral coryza with cervical lymphadenopathy and shifting tenderness -> Mesenteric adenitis
x: Acute appendicitis causes fixed right iliac fossa tenderness, guarding, and anorexia rather than shifting periumbilical tenderness after viral pharyngitis.
Ileo-colic intussusception presents in infants with paroxysmal colicky pain, drawing up of the legs, and redcurrant-jelly stool.
Meckel's diverticulitis causes fixed right lower quadrant peritonism or painless rectal bleeding rather than mobile nodal tenderness.
Urinary tract infection causes dysuria, frequency, and suprapubic or loin tenderness rather than shifting mesenteric tenderness after coryza.
f: Periumbilical pain migrating to McBurney's point with anorexia and localised right iliac fossa guarding
Episodic screaming attacks with pallor, a sausage-shaped right upper quadrant mass, and redcurrant-jelly stool
Painless dark rectal bleeding with fixed right lower quadrant tenderness and a positive technetium-99m pertechnetate scan
Dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic tenderness with leucocytes and nitrites on urine dipstick

hq_q.s:
A 66-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of constant right iliac fossa pain and nausea. Over the preceding 8 weeks he has noticed looser stools and unquantified weight loss.
Temperature is 37.9°C, heart rate is 96 bpm, and blood pressure is 134/82 mmHg. Examination reveals localised tenderness and voluntary guarding in the right iliac fossa without a discrete palpable mass.
o: Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis
hq_q.w: Older adults presenting with right iliac fossa pain and altered bowel habit require contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis to evaluate for acute appendicitis while excluding underlying caecal carcinoma or right-sided diverticulitis.
hq_q.f: A 19-year-old woman with right iliac fossa pain and suspected ovarian pathology -> pelvic ultrasonography.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation?

c: looser stools and unquantified weight loss
tm.m: In older adults, caecal adenocarcinoma can obstruct the appendiceal lumen or perforate locally, mimicking primary acute appendicitis.
tm.g: Right iliac fossa pain and altered bowel habit in an older adult -> Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis
x: Proceeding directly to laparoscopy without cross-sectional imaging risks missing an underlying caecal malignancy that requires formal oncological staging and resection.
Magnetic resonance enterography is used for outpatient small bowel Crohn's disease staging rather than acute surgical right iliac fossa pain.
Plain abdominal radiography has poor sensitivity for appendicitis, diverticulitis, and non-obstructing caecal tumours.
Transabdominal ultrasound is operator-dependent and obscured by bowel gas, offering inferior sensitivity to CT for caecal pathology in older men.
f: Young male with classic migrating pain, McBurney's point peritonism, and high clinical probability of uncomplicated appendicitis
Outpatient assessment of suspected small bowel Crohn's disease stricture in a young adult
Suspected acute sigmoid volvulus where rapid bedside confirmation of a coffee-bean sign is required
Young woman of reproductive age presenting with lower abdominal pain where adnexal pathology or appendicitis is suspected

hq_q.s:
A 26-year-old woman is reviewed on the surgical ward 5 days after a laparoscopic appendicectomy for a perforated gangrenous appendix. Over the past 24 hours she has developed a swinging pyrexia, loose mucous stools, and rectal tenesmus.
Temperature is 38.6°C and heart rate is 104 bpm. Her abdomen is soft centrally. Digital rectal examination reveals a warm, tender, boggy fullness anteriorly in the rectouterine pouch.
hq_q.w: A pelvic abscess in the rectouterine pouch of Douglas is a classic complication after perforated appendicitis. Purulent fluid irritates the adjacent rectum, causing mucous diarrhoea, tenesmus, swinging fever, and a boggy anterior rectal mass.
hq_q.f: Erythema, warmth, and purulent discharge at the umbilical port site -> superficial port-site wound infection.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely postoperative complication?

c: loose mucous stools, and rectal tenesmus
tender, boggy fullness anteriorly in the rectouterine pouch
tm.m: Infected peritoneal exudate gravitates into the dependent rectouterine pouch, forming a walled-off abscess that inflames the anterior rectal wall.
tm.g: Swinging fever, mucous diarrhoea, and boggy anterior rectal fullness after perforated appendicitis -> Pelvic intra-abdominal abscess
x: Adhesional small bowel obstruction causes colicky abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, and absolute constipation rather than mucous diarrhoea and rectal fullness.
Clostridioides difficile colitis causes profuse watery diarrhoea after antibiotics without a localized boggy mass in the pouch of Douglas.
Postoperative paralytic ileus presents with painless abdominal distension, absent bowel sounds, and nausea rather than swinging fever and tenesmus.
A superficial port-site wound infection causes localized incisional erythema and discharge rather than deep pelvic tenesmus and rectal boggy fullness.
f: Colicky central abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and dilated small bowel loops on CT
Profuse offensive watery diarrhoea after broad-spectrum antibiotics with positive stool toxin assay and diffuse pancolitis
Painless abdominal distension, absent bowel sounds, and high nasogastric aspirates without fever on day 3 postoperatively
Localised erythema, induration, and purulent discharge from the umbilical port incision with a soft non-tender pelvis

hq_q.s:
A 19-year-old man with homozygous sickle cell disease presents to the surgical clinic with a 2-month history of recurrent postprandial right upper quadrant pain. Each episode lasts 2 hours and resolves spontaneously.
Examination reveals mild scleral icterus and a soft, non-tender abdomen. Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrates multiple small radiopaque gallstones within a thin-walled gallbladder and a 4 mm common bile duct.
Total bilirubin is 48 µmol/L (<17), predominantly unconjugated.
hq_q.w: Chronic extravascular and intravascular haemolysis in sickle cell disease increases unconjugated bilirubin excretion into bile. Calcium bilirubinate precipitates as small, radiopaque black pigment gallstones within the gallbladder.
hq_q.f: An obese 44-year-old multiparous woman with radiolucent gallstones -> pure cholesterol or mixed cholesterol stones.
hq_q.ql: Which type of biliary calculus is most likely present?

c: recurrent postprandial right upper quadrant pain
Total bilirubin is 48 µmol/L (<17), predominantly unconjugated
tm.m: Chronic haemolysis saturates bile with unconjugated bilirubin, which polymerises with calcium to form radiopaque black pigment stones.
tm.g: Cholelithiasis in a young patient with chronic haemolytic anaemia -> Black bilirubin pigment stones
x: Calcium oxalate calculi form within the renal tract rather than the biliary tree.
Mixed cholesterol stones account for most adult gallstones associated with obesity and multiparity rather than chronic haemolysis.
Pure cholesterol stones are large, radiolucent calculi linked to metabolic syndrome and biliary cholesterol supersaturation.
Uric acid calculi precipitate in acidic urine within the urinary tract in gout or high cell turnover states.
f: Acute loin-to-groin colic with microscopic haematuria and a radiopaque calculus at the vesicoureteric junction
A 45-year-old woman with obesity and normal bilirubin presenting with radiolucent gallstones on ultrasound
A solitary large radiolucent gallbladder stone in a patient with metabolic syndrome and hyperlipidaemia
Renal colic with a radiolucent ureteric stone on plain film and persistent acidic urine pH of 5.0

hq_q.s:
A 64-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 2-week history of painless jaundice, generalized pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools. She drinks 4 units of alcohol weekly and takes no regular medications.
Examination confirms scleral icterus and scratch marks on her forearms. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender without palpable organomegaly or ascites.
hq_q.w: Marked elevation of ALP and GGT disproportionate to ALT with dark urine and pale stools indicates cholestatic jaundice. Transabdominal ultrasonography is the first-line investigation to assess biliary duct dilatation and identify gallstones or masses.
hq_q.f: ALT 1,450 IU/L with prodromal malaise and mild ALP rise -> viral hepatitis serology screen.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

tm.m: Biliary tract obstruction impairs conjugated bilirubin excretion and induces biliary epithelial synthesis of alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase.
tm.g: Painless cholestatic jaundice with disproportionate ALP and GGT elevation -> Transabdominal hepatobiliary ultrasonography
x: ERCP is an invasive therapeutic procedure carrying pancreatitis risk and is reserved until non-invasive imaging confirms ductal pathology requiring intervention.
Percutaneous liver biopsy is invasive and unsafe as an initial test before extrahepatic biliary obstruction has been excluded by ultrasound.
Serum paracetamol concentration is used in acute toxic hepatocellular injury rather than subacute painless cholestatic jaundice.
Viral hepatitis serology evaluates acute hepatocellular jaundice where transaminases are markedly elevated above alkaline phosphatase.
f: Confirmed distal common bile duct stone with ascending cholangitis requiring urgent biliary decompression
Unexplained parenchymal liver disease with non-dilated bile ducts on ultrasound and negative autoantibody and viral screens
Acute presentation 6 hours after a staggered paracetamol overdose with nausea and right upper quadrant tenderness
Prodromal fever and anorexia with ALT 1,600 IU/L and ALP 130 IU/L after travel abroad

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old man is on the intensive care unit 8 days after an emergency aortic aneurysm repair. He is ventilated and on parenteral nutrition. He has developed a new fever.
Temperature 38.8°C, pulse rate 112 bpm. There is tenderness in the right upper quadrant.
Ultrasound shows a distended gallbladder with a thickened wall and pericholecystic fluid. There are no gallstones and the bile ducts are not dilated.
hq_q.w: Critically ill patients get gallbladder stasis and ischaemia: cholecystitis without stones. A cholecystostomy may be needed.
hq_q.f: Stones with a positive Murphy's sign in a fit 40-year-old → calculous cholecystitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Critical illness and no eating cause bile stasis and gallbladder ischaemia
tm.g: An inflamed gallbladder with no stones in the critically ill is acalculous cholecystitis
f: fever, jaundice and a dilated duct
the presentation instead showed features specific to Biliary colic (Biliary colic needs gallstones and settles within hours; he has no stones and is septic)
