the presentation instead showed features specific to Gallbladder cancer (Gallbladder cancer develops over months, not fever in an ICU patient on parenteral nutrition)
Swinging high fevers, rigors, tender hepatomegaly, and fluid-filled hepatic lesion
x: Ruled out here: requires fever, jaundice and a dilated duct, whereas this patient has intensive care unit, parenteral nutrition.
Biliary colic needs gallstones and settles within hours; he has no stones and is septic.
Gallbladder cancer develops over months, not fever in an ICU patient on parenteral nutrition.
Ruled out here: requires Swinging high fevers, rigors, tender hepatomegaly, and fluid-filled hepatic lesion, whereas this patient has intensive care unit, parenteral nutrition.

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old woman has had right upper quadrant pain, fever and rigors for 1 day. Her family have noticed she is yellow.
Temperature 39.2°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 104/62 mmHg. She is jaundiced with right upper quadrant tenderness.
hq_q.w: Ultrasound shows duct dilatation and gallstones quickly at the bedside. Key discriminator: Charcot's triad: abdominal ultrasound first.
hq_q.f: Ultrasound duct is normal but suspicion stays high → MRCP.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first imaging?

tm.m: Ultrasound shows a dilated duct and stones quickly
tm.g: Charcot's triad: abdominal ultrasound first
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Contrast CT of abdomen (CT may follow, but ultrasound is first for suspected stones and duct dilatation)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Diagnostic ERCP (ERCP is for drainage once ducts are imaged, not the first diagnostic test)
the presentation instead showed features specific to HIDA scan (A HIDA scan is for cholecystitis, not cholangitis with jaundice)
a normal ultrasound but high suspicion
x: CT may follow, but ultrasound is first for suspected stones and duct dilatation.
ERCP is for drainage once ducts are imaged, not the first diagnostic test.
A HIDA scan is for cholecystitis, not cholangitis with jaundice.
Ruled out here: requires a normal ultrasound but high suspicion, whereas this patient has fever and rigors, jaundiced.

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man has fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with a stone. A diagnosis of ascending cholangitis is made and ERCP is being arranged. Blood cultures have been taken. He has no drug allergies.
Temperature 38.9°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 110/66 mmHg.
hq_q.w: Cholangitis needs cover for gut Gram-negatives and anaerobes. Follow local guidance and narrow once cultures return.
hq_q.f: Cultures grow a sensitive E. coli and he improves → switch to a narrower oral drug.
hq_q.ql: Which empirical antibiotic is most appropriate?

tm.m: Biliary infection is from gut Gram-negatives and anaerobes
tm.g: Cholangitis: piperacillin with tazobactam
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to IV benzylpenicillin (Benzylpenicillin covers streptococci, not the E. coli, Klebsiella and anaerobes that infect a blocked bile duct)
no prosthetic valve + meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV vancomycin (IV vancomycin does not cross into the gut lumen to treat C. difficile)

the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral ciprofloxacin and metronidazole (The spectrum is close, but he has cholangitis with sepsis and needs IV antibiotics; oral absorption cannot be relied on)
x: Benzylpenicillin covers streptococci, not the E. coli, Klebsiella and anaerobes that infect a blocked bile duct.
Ruled out here: requires no prosthetic valve + meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, whereas this patient has ascending cholangitis, no drug allergies.
IV vancomycin does not cross into the gut lumen to treat C. difficile
The spectrum is close, but he has cholangitis with sepsis and needs IV antibiotics; oral absorption cannot be relied on.

hq_q.s:
A 52-year-old man with ulcerative colitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis presents to the hepatology clinic with a 2-month history of worsening jaundice, generalized pruritus, and 6 kg unintentional weight loss. He has had no fevers or rigors.
Examination shows deep jaundice and cachexia with a soft, non-tender abdomen. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrates a dominant hilar stricture at the hepatic duct confluence with upstream intrahepatic duct dilatation, and serum CA 19-9 is markedly elevated.
hq_q.w: Primary sclerosing cholangitis carries a 10% to 15% lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma. Progressive painless jaundice, weight loss, raised CA 19-9, and a dominant stricture at the hepatic duct confluence (Klatskin tumour) are hallmark features.
hq_q.f: Fever, rigors, and right upper quadrant pain in a patient with a biliary stricture -> acute ascending cholangitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: ulcerative colitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis
dominant hilar stricture at the hepatic duct confluence
tm.m: Chronic biliary epithelial inflammation and periductal fibrosis in primary sclerosing cholangitis drive dysplasia and malignant transformation into cholangiocarcinoma.
tm.g: New dominant hilar stricture, weight loss, and raised CA 19-9 in primary sclerosing cholangitis -> Hilar cholangiocarcinoma
x: Acute ascending cholangitis presents acutely with fever, rigors, and right upper quadrant pain rather than afebrile weight loss over 2 months.
Gallbladder adenocarcinoma arises as a mass within the gallbladder fossa rather than a stricturing lesion at the hepatic duct confluence.
Hepatocellular carcinoma presents as an arterial-enhancing parenchymal liver mass with raised alpha-fetoprotein rather than a hilar bile duct stricture.
Mirizzi syndrome is extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct by an impacted stone in Hartmann's pouch or the cystic duct.
f: High fever, rigors, jaundice, and right upper quadrant tenderness with purulent bile above a biliary stricture
Irregular polypoid mass arising from a porcelain gallbladder wall invading segment IVb of the liver
Decompensated cirrhosis with a 4 cm arterial-enhancing liver nodule showing portal venous washout and AFP of 850 kU/L
Large gallstone impacted in the cystic duct externally compressing the common hepatic duct on MRCP

hq_q.s:
A 48-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of severe epigastric pain radiating straight to her back and persistent vomiting. She is teetotal and takes no regular medications.
Heart rate is 102 bpm and blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg. Examination reveals marked epigastric tenderness.
Serum amylase is 1,120 IU/L (<100), triglycerides are 1.4 mmol/L (<1.7), and adjusted calcium is 3.04 mmol/L (2.20-2.60). Ultrasound shows no gallstones.
hq_q.w: Hypercalcaemia (commonly secondary to primary hyperparathyroidism) causes acute pancreatitis by prematurely activating intra-acinar trypsinogen and promoting calcium deposition within pancreatic ducts.
hq_q.f: Fasting serum triglycerides of 22 mmol/L with eruptive xanthomas -> severe hypertriglyceridaemia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her acute pancreatitis?

c: teetotal and takes no regular medications
tm.m: Elevated cytosolic calcium within pancreatic acinar cells triggers premature zymogen activation and autodigestion of the gland.
tm.g: Acute pancreatitis with adjusted calcium of 3.04 mmol/L and normal biliary ultrasound -> Hypercalcaemia
x: She is completely teetotal, excluding alcohol-induced pancreatitis.
Transabdominal ultrasound shows no gallstones and a non-dilated common bile duct.
She takes no regular medications such as azathioprine, thiazides, or sodium valproate.
Hypertriglyceridaemia-induced pancreatitis requires triglyceride levels above 11.3 mmol/L, whereas her level is normal at 1.4 mmol/L.
f: Heavy daily alcohol intake of 80 units per week with macrocytosis and elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase
Multiple small gallstones on ultrasound with a dilated 9 mm common bile duct and ALT of 380 IU/L
Recent commencement of azathioprine for Crohn's disease 3 weeks before presentation
Lipaemic serum sample with fasting triglyceride concentration of 24 mmol/L and eruptive cutaneous xanthomas

hq_q.s:
A 46-year-old man is reviewed in clinic 5 weeks after an admission with alcohol-related acute pancreatitis. He reports early satiety and a dull epigastric ache, without fever.
Temperature is 36.7°C and heart rate is 76 bpm. Examination reveals a smooth, firm, non-tender epigastric fullness.
Contrast CT demonstrates a 7 cm round, homogeneous fluid collection in the lesser sac with a mature fibrous wall and no solid necrotic debris.
hq_q.w: According to the revised Atlanta classification, a homogeneous fluid collection persisting more than 4 weeks after acute pancreatitis with a well-defined fibrous or granulation wall and no solid necrosis is a pancreatic pseudocyst.
hq_q.f: Ill-defined fluid around the pancreas within the first 2 weeks of pancreatitis -> acute peripancreatic fluid collection.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: 5 weeks after an admission with alcohol-related acute pancreatitis
early satiety and a dull epigastric ache
mature fibrous wall and no solid necrotic debris
tm.m: Extravasated pancreatic juice rich in amylase becomes encapsulated by fibrous and granulation tissue lacking an epithelial lining over 4 weeks.
tm.g: Encapsulated homogeneous peripancreatic fluid collection >4 weeks after acute pancreatitis without solid debris -> Pancreatic pseudocyst
x: An acute peripancreatic fluid collection occurs within the first 4 weeks of pancreatitis and lacks a defined fibrous wall.
Infected walled-off necrosis contains heterogeneous solid necrotic debris and gas bubbles, accompanied by systemic sepsis and fever.
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma presents as a solid hypodense parenchymal mass causing painless jaundice and weight loss rather than a post-pancreatitis fluid cyst.
A splenic artery pseudoaneurysm demonstrates avid arterial-phase contrast enhancement continuous with the splenic artery on CT angiography.
f: Unencapsulated homogeneous fluid adjacent to the pancreas on CT performed 6 days after onset of acute pancreatitis
Swinging pyrexia and rising inflammatory markers at 5 weeks with gas locules and solid necrotic debris inside a walled collection
Painless obstructive jaundice, weight loss, and a 3 cm solid hypodense mass in the pancreatic head with double-duct dilatation
Sudden haematemesis or falling haemoglobin with a contrast-blushing vascular sac adjacent to the pancreas on arterial-phase CT

hq_q.s: A 44 year old woman has recovered from an episode of mild acute pancreatitis caused by gallstones. Her pain has settled, she is eating normally and her blood tests are improving. She is otherwise fit.
hq_q.w: Early cholecystectomy prevents recurrent attacks, which are common while waiting. Key discriminator: Mild gallstone pancreatitis: cholecystectomy in the same admission.
hq_q.f: Cholangitis or persistent bile duct obstruction → urgent ERCP.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?

c: mild acute pancreatitis caused by gallstones
tm.m: Stones left in place cause another attack within weeks
tm.g: Mild gallstone pancreatitis: cholecystectomy in the same admission
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Cholecystectomy after 6 months (Delaying surgery after mild gallstone pancreatitis carries a high risk of recurrent pancreatitis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Long-term ursodeoxycholic acid (Ursodeoxycholic acid does not prevent recurrent gallstone pancreatitis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Low-fat diet and discharge (Leaves the patient at high risk of life-threatening recurrent gallstone pancreatitis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Routine ERCP and sphincterotomy (ERCP is only for duct stones or cholangitis; her duct is clear)
x: Delaying surgery after mild gallstone pancreatitis carries a high risk of recurrent pancreatitis
Ursodeoxycholic acid does not prevent recurrent gallstone pancreatitis.
Leaves the patient at high risk of life-threatening recurrent gallstone pancreatitis
ERCP is only for duct stones or cholangitis; her duct is clear.

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old man attends for a routine review of his hypertension. He has no abdominal or back pain. He is an ex-smoker with 40 pack-years.
BP 142/84 mmHg, pulse rate 72 bpm. There is a pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus that is not tender. Femoral and foot pulses are present.
hq_q.w: Ultrasound measures the aortic diameter and is used for surveillance. Key discriminator: An asymptomatic pulsatile mass: abdominal ultrasound.
hq_q.f: Tender mass with hypotension → straight to theatre with the vascular team.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first investigation?

tm.m: Ultrasound measures the aortic diameter safely
tm.g: An asymptomatic pulsatile mass: abdominal ultrasound
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Abdominal X-ray (Insensitive for measuring aortic diameter and only occasionally shows mural calcification)
planning repair of a large aneurysm
the presentation instead showed features specific to Echocardiogram (Echo looks at the heart; an aneurysm is measured with abdominal ultrasound)
the presentation instead showed features specific to MRI abdomen (Ultrasound is the rapid, cost-effective, NICE-recommended first test for suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm)
x: Insensitive for measuring aortic diameter and only occasionally shows mural calcification
Ruled out here: requires planning repair of a large aneurysm, whereas this patient has 40 pack-years, pulsatile, expansile mass.
Echo looks at the heart; an aneurysm is measured with abdominal ultrasound.
Ultrasound is the rapid, cost-effective, NICE-recommended first test for suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man has a 4 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm found on screening and is on yearly ultrasound surveillance. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and takes amlodipine, atorvastatin and aspirin.
BP 134/80 mmHg. He asks what he can do to stop the aneurysm getting bigger.
hq_q.w: Smoking speeds up growth and rupture. Statins, antiplatelets and blood pressure control reduce cardiovascular events.
hq_q.f: He has hypertension too → treat it to cut cardiovascular risk.
hq_q.ql: Which measure most reduces aneurysm growth?

tm.m: Smoking speeds aneurysm growth and rupture
tm.g: Stopping smoking most slows aneurysm growth
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Beta-blocker (Trials show beta-blockers do not significantly slow abdominal aortic aneurysm expansion)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Doxycycline (Doxycycline was tested to slow aneurysm growth and did not work)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Low-salt diet (A low-salt diet helps blood pressure but does not slow aneurysm growth like stopping smoking)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Warfarin (Anticoagulation does not slow aneurysm growth and adds bleeding risk)
x: Trials show beta-blockers do not significantly slow abdominal aortic aneurysm expansion
Doxycycline was tested to slow aneurysm growth and did not work.
A low-salt diet helps blood pressure but does not slow aneurysm growth like stopping smoking.
Anticoagulation does not slow aneurysm growth and adds bleeding risk.

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old man had an open repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm with a Dacron graft 2 years ago. Last week he had a small episode of vomiting blood that stopped. Today he vomited a large amount of blood and passed black stools.
Pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 88/50 mmHg. There is a healed midline laparotomy scar. He takes no anti-inflammatory drugs and drinks little alcohol.
hq_q.w: The graft can erode into the third part of the duodenum. A small herald bleed often comes first.
hq_q.f: No previous surgery and taking NSAIDs → peptic ulcer.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: small episode of vomiting blood that stopped
tm.m: The graft erodes into the duodenum; a small herald bleed comes first
tm.g: A herald bleed then massive GI bleeding after an aortic graft is an aortoenteric fistula
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Angiodysplasia (Angiodysplasia bleeds slowly from the colon, not a herald haematemesis then massive bleeding after an aortic graft)
a small haematemesis after vomiting in a stable patient
cirrhosis with a large spleen
no previous surgery and taking NSAIDs
x: Angiodysplasia bleeds slowly from the colon, not a herald haematemesis then massive bleeding after an aortic graft.
Ruled out here: requires a small haematemesis after vomiting in a stable patient, whereas this patient has Dacron graft 2 years ago, small episode of vomiting blood that stopped.
Ruled out here: requires cirrhosis with a large spleen, whereas this patient has Dacron graft 2 years ago, small episode of vomiting blood that stopped.
Ruled out here: requires no previous surgery and taking NSAIDs, whereas this patient has Dacron graft 2 years ago, small episode of vomiting blood that stopped.

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old man vomited forcefully several times after a heavy night of drinking. He then developed severe central chest and upper abdominal pain that is worse on swallowing.
Temperature 38.0°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. There is crackling under the skin of the neck on palpation. ECG shows sinus tachycardia only.
hq_q.w: Full-thickness oesophageal rupture from vomiting: chest pain and surgical emphysema. CT with oral contrast confirms.
hq_q.f: Small haematemesis after vomiting in a stable patient → Mallory-Weiss tear.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: crackling under the skin of the neck
tm.m: Forceful vomiting ruptures the full oesophageal wall, leaking air into the mediastinum
tm.g: Chest pain with surgical emphysema after forceful vomiting is Boerhaave syndrome
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Acute pancreatitis (Pancreatitis does not cause surgical emphysema in the neck after forceful vomiting)
a small haematemesis after vomiting in a stable patient
Crushing central chest pain with regional ST-elevation on ECG
Epigastric pain better with food, on ibuprofen
x: Pancreatitis does not cause surgical emphysema in the neck after forceful vomiting.
Ruled out here: requires a small haematemesis after vomiting in a stable patient, whereas this patient has vomited forcefully, worse on swallowing.
Ruled out here: requires Crushing central chest pain with regional ST-elevation on ECG, whereas this patient has vomited forcefully, worse on swallowing.
Ruled out here: requires Epigastric pain better with food, on ibuprofen, whereas this patient has vomited forcefully, worse on swallowing.

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man has had sudden severe epigastric pain for 6 hours, now spreading across his whole abdomen. He takes naproxen for arthritis. He is otherwise fit.
Pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg. The abdomen is rigid with generalised tenderness and absent bowel sounds.
An erect chest X-ray shows free gas under the diaphragm, and CT confirms a perforated duodenal ulcer.
hq_q.w: Surgery closes the hole with an omental patch and washes out the abdomen. PPIs and H. pylori treatment follow.
hq_q.f: Frail patient with a sealed perforation on CT → conservative care with NG tube, PPI and antibiotics.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?

tm.m: The hole must be closed and the contaminated abdomen washed out
tm.g: Perforated duodenal ulcer in a fit patient: laparoscopic washout and omental patch
f: frail with a sealed perforation on CT
the presentation instead showed features specific to Distal partial gastrectomy (Gastrectomy is not needed for a perforated duodenal ulcer, which is patched)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Endoscopic clipping of the ulcer (Endoscopic clipping is for bleeding ulcers, not perforation with peritonitis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Truncal vagotomy and pyloroplasty (Vagotomy is rarely needed now that ulcers are healed with PPIs and H. pylori eradication)
x: Ruled out here: requires frail with a sealed perforation on CT, whereas this patient has naproxen, otherwise fit.
Gastrectomy is not needed for a perforated duodenal ulcer, which is patched.
Endoscopic clipping is for bleeding ulcers, not perforation with peritonitis.
Vagotomy is rarely needed now that ulcers are healed with PPIs and H. pylori eradication.

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old woman on peritoneal dialysis for diabetic kidney disease has had abdominal pain for 1 day. Her drained dialysis fluid has become cloudy.
Temperature 37.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 136/82 mmHg. There is mild generalised abdominal tenderness. The catheter exit site is clean.
The effluent white cell count is 300 per mm³, mostly neutrophils.
hq_q.w: PD peritonitis: cloudy fluid with over 100 white cells per mm3 and over 50% neutrophils. Treat with antibiotics in the dialysis fluid.
hq_q.f: Clear effluent with redness at the exit site → exit site infection.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Bacteria enter the peritoneum via the catheter; antibiotics in the dialysate reach it best
tm.g: Cloudy PD fluid with over 100 white cells: intraperitoneal antibiotics
f: peritonism, fever and a raised lactate suggesting strangulation
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral antibiotics at home (Oral antibiotics are less effective than intraperitoneal in PD peritonitis)
fungal or relapsing PD peritonitis
the presentation instead showed features specific to Switch to haemodialysis (Switching to haemodialysis is only needed if the infection fails to clear)
x: Ruled out here: requires peritonism, fever and a raised lactate suggesting strangulation, whereas this patient has peritoneal dialysis, cloudy.
Oral antibiotics are less effective than intraperitoneal in PD peritonitis.
Ruled out here: requires fungal or relapsing PD peritonitis, whereas this patient has peritoneal dialysis, cloudy.
Switching to haemodialysis is only needed if the infection fails to clear.

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old woman has had a productive cough and fever for 3 days. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. She has been given her first dose of intravenous antibiotics.
Temperature 38.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 94% breathing air. Her peripheries are cool.
Lactate 4.6 mmol/L (<2.0).
hq_q.w: Lactate of 4 or more or hypotension: give a crystalloid bolus over 15 minutes, reassess and call critical care if no response.
hq_q.f: Lactate 1.5 with a normal blood pressure → no bolus needed.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate step besides antibiotics?

tm.m: Sepsis with poor perfusion needs volume first
tm.g: Lactate 4 or more or hypotension: IV fluid bolus of 500 ml
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Await repeat lactate (Septic shock with hypotension or lactate ≥4 mmol/L requires immediate fluid resuscitation)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Dobutamine infusion (Inotropes come after fluid and only for persistent shock with poor cardiac output, usually in critical care)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Encourage oral fluids (Oral fluids are too slow for septic shock with a lactate of 4.6)
blood pressure stays low after adequate fluids
x: Septic shock with hypotension or lactate ≥4 mmol/L requires immediate fluid resuscitation
Inotropes come after fluid and only for persistent shock with poor cardiac output, usually in critical care.
Oral fluids are too slow for septic shock with a lactate of 4.6.
Ruled out here: requires blood pressure stays low after adequate fluids, whereas this patient has BP 96/60, cool.

hq_q.s:
A 19-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of high fever, watery diarrhoea, vomiting, and postural dizziness. She is on day 4 of her menstrual period and uses super-absorbent tampons.
Temperature is 39.6°C, heart rate is 132 bpm, and blood pressure is 84/48 mmHg. Examination reveals conjunctival suffusion, a strawberry tongue, and a diffuse blanching erythroderma resembling sunburn across her trunk, without neck stiffness.
hq_q.w: Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome is mediated by toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1), a superantigen that activates T cells polyclonally. It causes high fever, refractory hypotension, diffuse blanching erythroderma, mucosal hyperaemia, and multi-organ dysfunction.
hq_q.f: Non-blanching petechial and purpuric rash with neck stiffness and photophobia -> meningococcal septicaemia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: day 4 of her menstrual period and uses super-absorbent tampons
Temperature is 39.6°C, heart rate is 132 bpm, and blood pressure is 84/48 mmHg
tm.m: Staphylococcus aureus TSST-1 cross-links MHC class II and T-cell receptors non-specifically, triggering a massive cytokine storm and capillary leak.
tm.g: Menstruating tampon user with vasodilatory shock, conjunctival suffusion, and diffuse blanching erythroderma -> Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome
x: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis presenting in children under 5 years with 5 days of fever and cervical lymphadenopathy.
Meningococcal septicaemia produces a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash rather than diffuse blanching sunburn-like erythroderma.
Scarlet fever follows streptococcal pharyngitis with a rough sandpaper-like rash and circumoral pallor without tampon-associated shock.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome presents after a culprit medication with targetoid lesions, painful mucosal ulceration, and epidermal detachment.
f: A 3-year-old child with 6 days of high fever, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, cracked lips, and polymorphous rash
Rapidly spreading non-blanching purpuric rash with neck stiffness, photophobia, and haemodynamic instability
A 7-year-old child with exudative tonsillitis, tender anterior cervical nodes, and a fine rough sandpaper-like rash
Painful oral and conjunctival erosions with dusky targetoid macules and positive Nikolsky sign 10 days after starting lamotrigine

hq_q.s: A 28 year old man had a splenectomy after a motorcycle crash 2 weeks ago and is recovering well. He is due to go home and asks what he needs to do to stay well in the future.
hq_q.w: Without a spleen, encapsulated organisms can cause overwhelming infection. Vaccines, prophylactic antibiotics and an emergency supply are advised.
hq_q.f: Fever after splenectomy → urgent assessment and antibiotics.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate long-term measure?

tm.m: Without a spleen, encapsulated bacteria can cause overwhelming infection
tm.g: After splenectomy: vaccines and daily penicillin V
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Daily penicillin V (Penicillin is half the plan; without pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccines he stays exposed to strains it misses)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Long-term low-dose aspirin (Aspirin is for raised platelets after splenectomy, not the main protection against overwhelming infection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Meningococcal and Hib vaccines (These are needed too, but pneumococcal vaccine and daily penicillin are the core of his protection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pneumococcal vaccine (Pneumococcus is the main threat, but he also needs Hib and meningococcal vaccines and daily penicillin)
x: Penicillin is half the plan; without pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccines he stays exposed to strains it misses.
Aspirin is for raised platelets after splenectomy, not the main protection against overwhelming infection.
These are needed too, but pneumococcal vaccine and daily penicillin are the core of his protection.
Pneumococcus is the main threat, but he also needs Hib and meningococcal vaccines and daily penicillin.

hq_q.s:
A 24-year-old woman re-attends the emergency department 3 days after starting oral ofloxacin and metronidazole for pelvic inflammatory disease. Despite full adherence, her pain has worsened and she has developed rigors.
Temperature is 38.8°C, heart rate is 108 bpm, and blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg. There is rebound tenderness in the left iliac fossa. Urine beta-hCG is negative. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 5 cm complex thick-walled left adnexal mass.
hq_q.w: Failure of pelvic inflammatory disease to improve within 48 to 72 hours of outpatient antibiotics, accompanied by swinging fever and a complex thick-walled adnexal mass on ultrasound, indicates a tubo-ovarian abscess requiring inpatient intravenous therapy.
hq_q.f: Positive urine beta-hCG with an empty uterus and complex adnexal mass -> ruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: 3 days after starting oral ofloxacin and metronidazole for pelvic inflammatory disease
5 cm complex thick-walled left adnexal mass
tm.m: Ascending polymicrobial infection extends through the fallopian tube to the ovary, forming a walled-off purulent inflammatory mass.
tm.g: Worsening pelvic pain, persistent pyrexia, negative beta-hCG, and complex adnexal mass during PID treatment -> Tubo-ovarian abscess
x: Acute ovarian torsion causes sudden-onset severe unilateral pain and vomiting with an enlarged oedematous ovary showing reduced Doppler flow rather than high fever after PID.
A ruptured corpus luteum cyst causes sudden mid-cycle or luteal-phase pain and free pelvic fluid without persistent high fever of 38.8°C.
An ovarian endometrioma causes chronic cyclical dysmenorrhoea and a homogeneous ground-glass cyst rather than acute febrile sepsis.
A ruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy is excluded by the negative urine beta-hCG test.
f: Sudden-onset severe unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting and an enlarged 7 cm ovary with absent venous Doppler flow
Sudden sharp lower abdominal pain on day 21 of the menstrual cycle with apyrexia and free fluid in the pouch of Douglas
Chronic secondary dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia with a unilocular adnexal cyst showing diffuse low-level ground-glass echoes
Six weeks of amenorrhoea, vaginal spotting, positive urine beta-hCG, and free echogenic pelvic fluid with an empty uterine cavity

hq_q.s:
A 30-year-old woman presents to the sexual health clinic with a 4-day history of lower abdominal pain and deep dyspareunia. She has a copper intrauterine device and wishes to keep it.
Temperature is 37.3°C and heart rate is 78 bpm. Examination reveals cervical motion tenderness and mild bilateral adnexal tenderness without masses. Urine pregnancy test is negative. She starts outpatient oral antibiotics for mild pelvic inflammatory disease.
o: Exchange it immediately for a levonorgestrel intrauterine system
Leave the device in situ and review clinical response at 72 hours
Remove the device immediately and prescribe oral emergency contraception
Remove the device immediately without emergency contraception
Schedule routine removal once the 14-day antibiotic course is completed
hq_q.w: According to UK BASHH and FSRH guidelines, in mild-to-moderate pelvic inflammatory disease the intrauterine device may be left in situ while starting empirical antibiotics, with clinical review at 48 to 72 hours and removal only if symptoms fail to improve.
hq_q.f: Severe pelvic inflammatory disease or failure to improve after 72 hours of antibiotics -> remove the intrauterine device.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management regarding her copper intrauterine device?

c: lower abdominal pain and deep dyspareunia
copper intrauterine device and wishes to keep it
mild bilateral adnexal tenderness without masses
tm.m: Mild-to-moderate pelvic inflammatory disease responds to broad-spectrum antibiotics with the coil in situ; removal is only required if clinical improvement does not occur within 72 hours.
tm.g: Mild pelvic inflammatory disease in a patient wishing to keep her copper IUD -> Leave the device in situ and review clinical response at 72 hours
x: Inserting a new intrauterine system during active cervical and pelvic infection is contraindicated as it disseminates pathogens into the upper genital tract.
Immediate removal is unnecessary in mild disease when the patient wishes to keep the device, and should be deferred unless she fails to improve by 72 hours.
Immediate removal is not indicated for mild PID and removing a coil after recent intercourse without emergency contraception risks unintended pregnancy.
If symptoms resolve with the 14-day antibiotic course, the device does not need to be removed after treatment completion.
f: Request to switch from a copper coil to a hormonal coil for heavy menstrual bleeding after pelvic infection has fully resolved
Failure of fever and adnexal tenderness to improve after 72 hours of antibiotics in a patient who had intercourse 3 days ago
Severe sepsis from pelvic inflammatory disease requiring urgent coil removal in a patient who has been abstinent for 4 weeks
Patient who remains asymptomatic after completing PID treatment but requests elective discontinuation of intrauterine contraception

hq_q.s:
A 22 year old woman has had lower abdominal pain and deep dyspareunia for 1 week with an abnormal vaginal discharge. She has a new sexual partner.
Temperature 37.6°C. There is cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness. Pregnancy test is negative.
hq_q.w: Vulvovaginal or endocervical NAAT detects chlamydia and gonorrhoea. Treatment should not wait for the result.
hq_q.f: Positive gonorrhoea NAAT → culture before treatment for sensitivities.
hq_q.ql: Which test is most important to find the cause?

tm.m: Chlamydia and gonorrhoea ascend from the cervix to cause PID
tm.g: PID: NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Blood cultures (She is not septic; NAAT swabs identify chlamydia and gonorrhoea, the usual causes of PID)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Midstream urine culture (A urine culture finds bladder infection, not the cervical chlamydia or gonorrhoea that causes PID)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Serum CA-125 level (CA 125 rises in many pelvic conditions and does not identify the cause of PID)
a suspected adnexal mass or abscess
x: She is not septic; NAAT swabs identify chlamydia and gonorrhoea, the usual causes of PID.
A urine culture finds bladder infection, not the cervical chlamydia or gonorrhoea that causes PID.
CA 125 rises in many pelvic conditions and does not identify the cause of PID.
Ruled out here: requires a suspected adnexal mass or abscess, whereas this patient has new sexual partner, cervical motion tenderness.

hq_q.s:
A 76-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of progressive abdominal distension and failure to pass faeces or flatus. Over the preceding 3 months he has noticed looser stools and 6 kg weight loss. He has had no prior abdominal surgery.
Heart rate is 98 bpm. His abdomen is distended and tympanic without peritonism. Hernial orifices are normal and the rectum is empty.
hq_q.w: Colorectal adenocarcinoma is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction in the UK. Subacute change in bowel habit, weight loss, microcytic iron-deficiency anaemia, and colonic dilatation to the sigmoid colon confirm an obstructing left-sided tumour.
hq_q.f: Abrupt onset gross distension with a coffee-bean loop arising from the left iliac fossa -> sigmoid volvulus.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his bowel obstruction?
hq_q.post: Abdominal X-ray shows dilated colon down to the sigmoid.

c: looser stools and 6 kg weight loss
dilated colon down to the sigmoid
tm.m: An annular stenosing adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon progressively narrows the lumen while causing chronic occult mucosal blood loss.
tm.g: Large bowel obstruction with altered bowel habit, weight loss, and microcytic anaemia -> Colorectal adenocarcinoma
x: Peritoneal adhesions predominantly cause small bowel obstruction in patients with prior abdominal surgery, whereas he has an unoperated abdomen.
Severe faecal impaction reveals hard impacted stool filling the rectal ampulla on digital rectal examination rather than an empty rectum and microcytic anaemia.
Sigmoid volvulus causes acute gross distension with a classic coffee-bean sign on plain film rather than 3 months of weight loss and iron-deficiency anaemia.
A strangulated inguinal hernia presents with a tender, tense, irreducible groin swelling and predominantly small bowel obstruction.
f: Previous midline laparotomy with colicky central pain, early bilious vomiting, and dilated central bowel loops showing valvulae conniventes
Frail care-home resident on regular codeine with overflow diarrhoea and a rock-hard faecal mass filling the rectum on digital examination
Elderly nursing-home resident with chronic constipation and acute distension showing an inverted U-shaped coffee-bean loop pointing to the right upper quadrant
Painful, erythematous, irreducible lump above and medial to the pubic tubercle with absent cough impulse

hq_q.s:
A 64-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of colicky central abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, and failure to pass flatus. She had an open hysterectomy 10 years ago.
Temperature is 36.9°C, heart rate is 92 bpm, and blood pressure is 132/80 mmHg. Her abdomen is distended with a lower midline scar and mild tenderness without guarding. CT shows small bowel obstruction without ischaemia.
o: Discharge home with oral antiemetics and clinic review
Nasogastric tube decompression and intravenous fluids
Oral stimulant and osmotic laxative therapy
hq_q.w: Uncomplicated adhesional small bowel obstruction without peritonism, strangulation, or bowel ischaemia is initially managed conservatively ('drip and suck') with nil by mouth, nasogastric tube decompression, and intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement.
hq_q.f: Localised peritonism, rising lactate, or reduced bowel wall enhancement on CT -> emergency midline laparotomy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

tm.m: Gastric and proximal intestinal decompression reduces intraluminal wall tension and oedema, allowing up to 80% of simple adhesional obstructions to resolve non-operatively.
tm.g: Uncomplicated adhesional small bowel obstruction without ischaemia or peritonism -> Nasogastric tube decompression and intravenous fluids
x: Discharging a patient with acute mechanical small bowel obstruction and bilious vomiting risks severe dehydration, electrolyte derangement, and bowel strangulation.
Emergency laparotomy is reserved for patients with clinical peritonism, closed-loop obstruction, bowel ischaemia, or failure of conservative management after 72 hours.
Colonoscopy cannot reach a small bowel adhesional transition point and insufflation risks worsening abdominal distension.
Oral stimulant or osmotic laxatives are contraindicated in mechanical bowel obstruction as peristalsis against a fixed blockage risks perforation.
f: Mild self-limiting viral gastroenteritis in a patient tolerating oral fluids with a soft non-distended abdomen
Constant severe abdominal pain, generalised guarding, serum lactate of 4.6 mmol/L, and mesenteric haziness with poor mural enhancement on CT
Acute pseudo-obstruction of the colon refractory to electrolyte correction and intravenous neostigmine
Chronic functional constipation in an ambulatory patient with soft abdominal examination and no mechanical obstruction

hq_q.s:
An 84-year-old man is reviewed on the orthopaedic ward 3 days after a cemented hemiarthroplasty for a displaced intracapsular neck of femur fracture. His abdomen has become progressively distended without passage of flatus. He receives regular oral morphine sulfate and has a serum potassium of 3.0 mmol/L.
Heart rate is 92 bpm. His abdomen is grossly distended, tympanic, and non-tender. Contrast CT shows diffuse colonic dilatation with a 9 cm caecum and no mechanical transition point.
hq_q.w: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) causes massive non-mechanical dilatation of the colon in frail postoperative or medically unwell patients due to autonomic imbalance, opioids, and electrolyte derangements such as hypokalaemia.
hq_q.f: Inverted U-shaped coffee-bean loop twisting around its mesenteric axis -> sigmoid volvulus.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: regular oral morphine sulfate and has a serum potassium of 3.0 mmol/L
diffuse colonic dilatation with a 9 cm caecum and no mechanical transition point
tm.m: Impaired sacral parasympathetic outflow combined with sympathetic overactivity, opioid receptor activation, and hypokalaemia causes functional colonic atony.
tm.g: Massive postoperative colonic dilatation without a mechanical transition point on CT -> Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction
x: Toxic megacolon complicates severe acute colitis with high fever, tachycardia, bloody diarrhoea, and mucosal thumbprinting rather than painless postoperative distension.
An obstructing colonic carcinoma produces an abrupt mechanical transition point with a stenosing mural mass on contrast CT.
Postoperative small bowel ileus predominantly dilates small bowel loops rather than causing isolated massive colonic dilatation with a 9 cm caecum.
Sigmoid volvulus is a closed-loop mechanical obstruction demonstrating a mesenteric whirl sign and coffee-bean loop rather than patent non-obstructed colon.
f: Acute severe ulcerative colitis with temperature 39.1°C, heart rate 124 bpm, bloody diarrhoea, and transverse colon diameter of 7.5 cm
Annular soft-tissue mass in the descending colon with abrupt proximal colonic dilatation and collapsed distal rectosigmoid on CT
Uniformly dilated fluid-filled small bowel loops with collapsed colon and absent bowel sounds 48 hours after laparotomy
Abrupt-onset abdominal distension with a twisted sigmoid mesentery whirl sign and coffee-bean loop on imaging

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old woman has had sudden lower abdominal pain for 2 hours with pain at the tip of her left shoulder. She has light vaginal bleeding. Her last period was 7 weeks ago.
Pulse rate 120 bpm, BP 90/58 mmHg. She is pale. The abdomen is tender with guarding in both iliac fossae.
Urine pregnancy test is positive.
hq_q.w: Positive test, pain, shoulder tip pain from blood under the diaphragm and shock: ruptured ectopic, needing surgery.
hq_q.f: Negative test with sudden one-sided pain and vomiting → ovarian torsion.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: pain at the tip of her left shoulder
tm.m: Blood from a ruptured tube irritates the diaphragm and causes shock
tm.g: Positive test, pain, shoulder tip pain and shock is a ruptured ectopic pregnancy
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Acute appendicitis (Appendicitis does not cause shoulder tip pain, vaginal bleeding or a positive pregnancy test)
bleeding and cramps with an open cervix and stable observations
a negative test with sudden one-sided pain and vomiting
Purulent vaginal discharge, cervical motion tenderness, and bilateral adnexal pain
x: Appendicitis does not cause shoulder tip pain, vaginal bleeding or a positive pregnancy test.
Ruled out here: requires bleeding and cramps with an open cervix and stable observations, whereas this patient has pain at the tip of her left shoulder, 7 weeks ago.
Ruled out here: requires a negative test with sudden one-sided pain and vomiting, whereas this patient has pain at the tip of her left shoulder, 7 weeks ago.
Ruled out here: requires Purulent vaginal discharge, cervical motion tenderness, and bilateral adnexal pain, whereas this patient has pain at the tip of her left shoulder, 7 weeks ago.

hq_q.s:
A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department 2 hours after falling 3 metres from a ladder onto his left flank. He reports severe left upper quadrant abdominal pain and sharp pain radiating to the tip of his left shoulder when lying flat.
Heart rate is 112 bpm and blood pressure is 104/68 mmHg. Examination reveals bruising over the left 9th to 11th ribs and left upper quadrant guarding.
hq_q.w: Blunt trauma to the left lower ribs frequently lacerates the spleen. Subdiaphragmatic intraperitoneal blood irritates the left hemidiaphragm, referring pain via the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) to the supraclavicular dermatome at the left shoulder tip (Kehr's sign).
hq_q.f: Right lower rib trauma with right shoulder tip pain -> liver parenchyma laceration.
hq_q.ql: Which intra-abdominal organ is most likely injured?

c: falling 3 metres from a ladder onto his left flank
sharp pain radiating to the tip of his left shoulder when lying flat
bruising over the left 9th to 11th ribs
tm.m: Haemoperitoneum accumulating beneath the left hemidiaphragm stimulates phrenic nerve afferents (C3-C5), producing referred somatic pain in the ipsilateral supraclavicular nerves.
tm.g: Blunt left lower rib trauma with left upper quadrant peritonism and left shoulder tip pain -> Spleen
x: Blunt rupture of the gastric fundus is rare and presents with epigastric peritonism and pneumoperitoneum rather than isolated left rib trauma.
Renal laceration causes loin tenderness and visible haematuria; because the kidney is retroperitoneal, bleeding does not irritate the diaphragm to cause Kehr's sign.
Hepatic laceration follows right-sided thoracoabdominal trauma and causes right upper quadrant tenderness with right shoulder tip pain.
Pancreatic body transection typically follows midline handlebar compression against the vertebral column and presents with delayed epigastric and back pain.
f: Severe epigastric peritonitis with bloody nasogastric aspirate and subdiaphragmatic free gas on erect chest radiograph
Left loin contusion with frank visible haematuria and a retroperitoneal perinephric haematoma on contrast CT
Right lower rib fractures with right upper quadrant guarding and referred right shoulder tip pain
Direct bicycle handlebar blow to the epigastrium with boring back pain and serum amylase of 1,400 IU/L

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman has had abdominal pain and vomiting for 2 days and is now confused. She has been tired and has lost weight over 6 months. Her skin has become darker.
Temperature 37.8°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 82/50 mmHg. There is pigmentation of the palmar creases and buccal mucosa. The abdomen is diffusely tender without guarding.
hq_q.w: Abdominal pain with low sodium, high potassium, low glucose and shock suggests adrenal crisis. Give IV hydrocortisone straight away.
hq_q.f: Glucose of 28 with ketones → DKA.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Without cortisol and aldosterone, salt is lost, potassium rises and blood pressure falls
tm.g: Shock with low sodium, high potassium, low glucose and pigmentation is an adrenal crisis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Acute pancreatitis (Pancreatitis does not cause pigmentation, a high potassium and a low glucose)
glucose of 28 with ketones
the presentation instead showed features specific to Gastroenteritis (Gastroenteritis does not cause pigmentation, a high potassium and a low glucose)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Perforated ulcer (A perforation gives a rigid abdomen with guarding; she has none)
x: Pancreatitis does not cause pigmentation, a high potassium and a low glucose.
Ruled out here: requires glucose of 28 with ketones, whereas this patient has Her skin has become darker, palmar creases and buccal mucosa.
Gastroenteritis does not cause pigmentation, a high potassium and a low glucose.
A perforation gives a rigid abdomen with guarding; she has none.

hq_q.s: A pharmacist is checking ibuprofen prescriptions on a medical ward. Five patients have been prescribed it.
hq_q.w: NSAIDs reduce blood flow to the kidney and can tip chronic kidney disease into acute injury; they are avoided with an eGFR under 30, peptic ulcer, severe heart failure and aspirin-sensitive asthma.
hq_q.f: eGFR of 85 → NSAIDs can be used with care.
hq_q.ql: Which patient is at greatest risk of harm from ibuprofen?

c: Which patient is at greatest risk of harm from ibuprofen?
tm.m: NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that keep the kidney perfused
tm.g: Avoid NSAIDs with an eGFR under 30
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to A 25-year-old with a sprained ankle (A short course in a young adult with normal kidneys is appropriate)
the presentation instead showed features specific to A 30-year-old with migraine (Ibuprofen is a first-line acute migraine treatment in a healthy young adult)
the presentation instead showed features specific to A 40-year-old with dysmenorrhoea (NSAIDs are first-line for primary dysmenorrhoea when nothing else forbids them)
the presentation instead showed features specific to A 50-year-old with gout (An NSAID with PPI cover is a first-line gout treatment when kidney function is normal)
x: A short course in a young adult with normal kidneys is appropriate.
Ibuprofen is a first-line acute migraine treatment in a healthy young adult.
NSAIDs are first-line for primary dysmenorrhoea when nothing else forbids them.
An NSAID with PPI cover is a first-line gout treatment when kidney function is normal.

hq_q.s: A 31 year old woman had a caesarean section 2 days ago and is breastfeeding her baby. Regular paracetamol is not controlling her pain and she asks for something stronger. She has no asthma or kidney problems.
hq_q.w: Some mothers are ultra-rapid metabolisers of codeine to morphine, which passes into milk and can kill the baby.
hq_q.f: A 30-year-old who is not breastfeeding → codeine is an option.
hq_q.ql: Which drug carries the greatest risk to her baby?

tm.m: Ultra-rapid metabolisers turn codeine into lots of morphine, which passes into milk
tm.g: Breastfeeding: avoid codeine
f: rolling around + no drug allergies
normal kidney function
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral morphine short course (A short course of oral morphine at the lowest dose can be used while breastfeeding with monitoring of the baby)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Paracetamol regularly (Paracetamol is safe and first-line analgesia during breastfeeding)
x: Ruled out here: requires rolling around + no drug allergies, whereas this patient has breastfeeding, something stronger.
Ruled out here: requires normal kidney function, whereas this patient has breastfeeding, something stronger.
A short course of oral morphine at the lowest dose can be used while breastfeeding with monitoring of the baby.
Paracetamol is safe and first-line analgesia during breastfeeding

hq_q.s: A 68 year old man with advanced ovarian metastases from colon cancer has inoperable malignant bowel obstruction. He is receiving palliative care. He has colicky abdominal pain and is vomiting. His background pain is controlled with a subcutaneous morphine infusion.
hq_q.w: Hyoscine butylbromide relaxes gut smooth muscle and reduces secretions. Metoclopramide and stimulant laxatives can worsen colic.
hq_q.f: Pain from a bone metastasis → NSAID and radiotherapy.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most appropriate for the colicky pain?

tm.m: Antimuscarinics relax gut muscle and dry secretions
tm.g: Colic in malignant bowel obstruction: hyoscine butylbromide
f: Pinpoint pupils, coma, and profound respiratory depression responsive to naloxone
partial obstruction with nausea but no colic
first-line drugs fail
the presentation instead showed features specific to Senna (Stimulant laxatives worsen colicky pain and risk perforation in complete bowel obstruction)
x: Ruled out here: requires Pinpoint pupils, coma, and profound respiratory depression responsive to naloxone, whereas this patient has malignant bowel obstruction, colicky abdominal pain.
Ruled out here: requires partial obstruction with nausea but no colic, whereas this patient has malignant bowel obstruction, colicky abdominal pain.
Ruled out here: requires first-line drugs fail, whereas this patient has malignant bowel obstruction, colicky abdominal pain.
Stimulant laxatives worsen colicky pain and risk perforation in complete bowel obstruction

hq_q.s:
A 42-year-old man weighing 70 kg presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea, vomiting, and postural dizziness. He has no significant past medical history.
Heart rate is 116 bpm, blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg, and respiratory rate is 22 breaths/min. His oral mucosa is parched, capillary refill time is 4 seconds, and lung fields are clear to auscultation.
o: Balanced crystalloid 500 mL over less than 15 minutes
hq_q.w: According to NICE intravenous fluid therapy guidelines (CG174), adults with hypovolaemic shock and no cardiac impairment should receive an immediate intravenous fluid bolus of 500 mL of a crystalloid containing 130 to 154 mmol/L sodium over less than 15 minutes, followed by clinical reassessment.
hq_q.f: Hypovolaemic shock in a frail patient with severe congestive heart failure -> cautious 250 mL crystalloid bolus.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial intravenous fluid prescription?

c: Heart rate is 116 bpm, blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg
lung fields are clear to auscultation
tm.m: Rapid infusion of an isotonic crystalloid expands intravascular volume and restores preload, stroke volume, and tissue perfusion pressure.
tm.g: Hypovolaemic shock with systolic BP <90 mmHg and no heart failure -> Balanced crystalloid 500 mL over less than 15 minutes
x: 1,000 mL over 8 hours is a slow maintenance infusion rate that fails to restore intravascular volume in decompensated hypovolaemic shock.
NICE recommends titrated 500 mL boluses with formal haemodynamic reassessment after each bolus rather than an unmonitored 2,000 mL surge.
5% glucose distributes across total body water after glucose metabolism, leaving less than 10% within the intravascular compartment.
100 mL over 60 minutes is far too small and slow to correct hypotension and delayed capillary refill.
f: Routine maintenance fluid replacement in a haemodynamically stable euvolaemic postoperative patient
Massive obstetric or trauma haemorrhage protocol using rapid infuser blood products rather than unmonitored crystalloid
Immediate correction of severe hypoglycaemia when 10% or 20% glucose is unavailable
Slow background carrier infusion for an intravenous medication in a fluid-restricted patient

hq_q.s:
A 62 year old man is nil by mouth after bowel surgery. He has a peripheral cannula and is not on a cardiac monitor. He feels weak.
Pulse rate 84 bpm. ECG shows small T waves and U waves.
hq_q.w: Peripheral potassium should run at no more than 10 mmol per hour without cardiac monitoring.
hq_q.f: Potassium of 3.2 and eating → oral potassium.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate potassium replacement?

tm.m: Fast IV potassium can cause arrhythmias, so peripheral rates stay at 10 mmol an hour
tm.g: Peripheral potassium: 40 mmol in 1 litre over at least 4 hours
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to 20 mmol in 100 ml over 30 minutes (Exceeds maximum safe peripheral infusion rate (10 mmol/hour) and requires cardiac monitoring)
the presentation instead showed features specific to 20 mmol IV bolus over 5 minutes (Rapid IV potassium bolus causes fatal cardiac arrhythmias and cardiac arrest)
the presentation instead showed features specific to 80 mmol in 500 ml over 1 hour (Dangerously high concentration and rate for a peripheral line, risking phlebitis and arrest)
potassium of 3.2 and eating
x: Exceeds maximum safe peripheral infusion rate (10 mmol/hour) and requires cardiac monitoring
Rapid IV potassium bolus causes fatal cardiac arrhythmias and cardiac arrest
Dangerously high concentration and rate for a peripheral line, risking phlebitis and arrest
Ruled out here: requires potassium of 3.2 and eating, whereas this patient has nil by mouth, not on a cardiac monitor.

hq_q.s:
An 89-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being found on her kitchen floor, having fallen 48 hours earlier. She lives alone and has been unable to reach water. She is drowsy but opens her eyes to speech.
Heart rate is 102 bpm and blood pressure is 112/64 mmHg. Her tongue is dry and furrowed, and capillary refill time is 2 seconds.
o: 3% hypertonic sodium chloride 150 mL over 20 minutes
5% glucose infused slowly with serial sodium monitoring
Oral free water boluses with 12-hourly review
hq_q.w: Hypernatraemia (158 mmol/L) without haemodynamic shock following prolonged water deprivation reflects a pure free-water deficit. Slow intravenous 5% glucose replaces free water safely, keeping the serum sodium reduction below 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent cerebral oedema.
hq_q.f: Hypernatraemia with haemodynamic shock (BP 76/40 mmHg) -> resuscitate intravascular volume first with 0.9% sodium chloride.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate fluid management?

tm.m: Neurons accumulate idiogenic osmoles during chronic hypernatraemia; rapid extracellular hypotonicity drives water into brain cells and causes cerebral oedema.
tm.g: Haemodynamically stable severe hypernatraemia in a drowsy patient -> 5% glucose infused slowly with serial sodium monitoring
x: Rapid 0.9% sodium chloride is reserved for haemodynamic shock and provides a high solute load rather than correcting her pure water deficit.
3% hypertonic saline delivers 513 mmol/L of sodium and would dangerously worsen her severe hypernatraemia.
Rapid balanced crystalloid infusion over 30 minutes drops plasma osmolality too abruptly and risks precipitating cerebral oedema.
Oral water boluses are unsafe in a drowsy patient at high risk of pulmonary aspiration and provide unreliable water replacement.
f: Severe dehydration with systolic blood pressure 74/42 mmHg and cool mottled peripheries requiring initial intravascular resuscitation
Acute postoperative hyponatraemia (sodium 116 mmol/L) presenting with generalised tonic-clonic seizures
Acute normonatraemic hypovolaemia from gastroenteritis in a young adult with tachycardia and postural hypotension
Mild asymptomatic hypernatraemia (sodium 148 mmol/L) in an alert, oriented patient with an intact swallow

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old woman with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with a 3-hour history of sudden breathlessness, nausea and sweating. She denies any chest, jaw or arm pain.
Pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 148/88 mmHg, SpO2 96% breathing air. Heart and lung sounds are normal. A 12-lead ECG shows 1.5 mm horizontal ST-segment depression in leads V4 to V6.
hq_q.w: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) is diagnosed when ischaemic ECG changes (horizontal ST depression) accompany a dynamic rise in high-sensitivity cardiac troponin. Silent or painless myocardial infarction is common in older adults and patients with diabetic autonomic neuropathy.
hq_q.f: ST-segment elevation in contiguous leads V1 to V4 -> anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: denies any chest, jaw or arm pain
ST-segment depression in leads V4 to V6
tm.m: Subendocardial myocardial necrosis from a partially occlusive coronary thrombus releases cardiac troponin T while diabetic visceral neuropathy blunts nociceptive chest pain.
tm.g: Rising high-sensitivity troponin + horizontal ST depression in V4-V6 -> NSTEMI
x: Acute pericarditis causes sharp pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward and widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation rather than painless V4-V6 ST depression.
Pulmonary embolism causes pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia and sinus tachycardia or right heart strain (S1Q3T3, V1-V3 T-wave inversion) rather than lateral ST depression and a troponin rise to 410 ng/L.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is triggered by acute emotional or physical stress and typically produces anterior ST elevation and apical ballooning with unobstructed coronary arteries.
Unstable angina is myocardial ischaemia at rest without cardiomyocyte necrosis, so serial high-sensitivity troponin levels remain below the 99th centile.
f: sharp central chest pain eased by sitting forward with a pericardial friction rub and widespread concave ST elevation
acute pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia and tachycardia 1 week after knee arthroplasty with a filling defect on CTPA
acute chest pain immediately after bereavement with apical left ventricular ballooning and unobstructed coronaries
ischaemic rest symptoms and lateral ST depression where 0-hour and 3-hour high-sensitivity troponin levels remain normal

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man presents to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of crushing central chest pain radiating to his jaw and left arm, with dizziness and sweating.
Pulse rate 38 bpm, BP 92/56 mmHg, SpO2 97% breathing air. Cannon a waves are visible in the jugular venous pulse. ECG shows 3 mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF with complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block.
hq_q.w: ST-segment elevation in inferior leads (II, III and aVF) indicates an acute inferior STEMI, caused by right coronary artery occlusion in ~80% of people. Because it supplies the AV nodal branch, inferior STEMI is classically complicated by complete heart block.
hq_q.f: ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 -> left circumflex coronary artery.
hq_q.ql: Which coronary artery is most likely to be occluded?

tm.m: Thrombotic occlusion of the proximal right coronary artery causes transmural ischaemia of the inferior left ventricular wall and the AV nodal artery.
tm.g: Inferior STEMI (leads II, III, aVF) + complete heart block -> right coronary artery occlusion
x: The first diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery supplies the high anterolateral wall (leads I, aVL, V2), not the inferior wall or AV node.
The left anterior descending artery supplies the anterior wall and interventricular septum, producing ST elevation in leads V1 to V4.
The left circumflex artery supplies the lateral left ventricular wall (leads I, aVL, V5 and V6) and only supplies the AV node in the 10-15% of people with left-dominant circulation.
Left main stem occlusion causes massive anterior and lateral ischaemia, cardiogenic shock and widespread ST depression with ST elevation in aVR.
f: ST-segment elevation limited to leads I and aVL with reciprocal inferior ST depression
crushing chest pain with ST-segment elevation across precordial leads V1 to V4
acute lateral STEMI with ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6
cardiogenic shock with diffuse ST depression in eight leads and ST elevation in lead aVR

hq_q.s:
A 69 year old man on the coronary care unit was treated 4 days ago for a large myocardial infarction. Thirty minutes ago he became acutely breathless, coughing up frothy pink sputum.
Pulse rate 120 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths/min, SpO2 86% breathing air. Auscultation reveals a new loud apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the left axilla and bilateral inspiratory crackles.
o: Cardiac tamponade from free wall rupture
hq_q.w: Papillary muscle rupture occurs 2 to 7 days after myocardial infarction (most often the posteromedial muscle supplied by the posterior descending artery), causing acute severe mitral regurgitation with a new apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla and pulmonary oedema.
hq_q.f: Harsh pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge with a palpable parasternal thrill and step-up in RV oxygen saturation -> ventricular septal rupture.
hq_q.ql: Which mechanical complication is the most likely cause?

c: new loud apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the left axilla
tm.m: Coagulative necrosis of a papillary muscle head detaches the mitral chordae tendineae, causing acute systolic regurgitant jetting into a non-compliant left atrium and flash pulmonary oedema.
tm.g: Sudden pulmonary oedema 2-7 days post-MI + new apical pansystolic murmur radiating to axilla -> papillary muscle rupture
x: Left ventricular free wall rupture causes haemopericardium with Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds and raised JVP) and pulseless electrical activity rather than an apical pansystolic murmur.
Dressler syndrome develops 2 to 6 weeks after myocardial infarction and causes pleuritic pain, fever and a pericardial friction rub rather than flash pulmonary oedema on day 4.
A left ventricular aneurysm is a late complication (weeks to months) presenting with persistent ST elevation and mural thrombus rather than acute day-4 flash pulmonary oedema.
Interventricular septal rupture produces a harsh pansystolic murmur loudest at the lower left sternal edge with a palpable parasternal thrill rather than an apical murmur radiating to the axilla.
f: sudden collapse 5 days post-MI with muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins and electrical alternans
fever, pleuritic chest pain and a pericardial friction rub developing 4 weeks after myocardial infarction
persistent anterior ST-segment elevation and a dyskinetic apical bulge 8 weeks after an anterior MI
acute shock 4 days post-MI with a harsh pansystolic murmur and palpable thrill at the left sternal edge

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man with Marfan syndrome presents to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of sudden, tearing retrosternal chest pain radiating through to his interscapular back.
Pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 168/94 mmHg in the right arm and 138/80 mmHg in the left arm, SpO2 98% breathing air. He has arachnodactyly and an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge.
hq_q.w: Acute thoracic aortic dissection classically produces a widened superior mediastinum (>8 cm on an anteroposterior chest radiograph) or loss of the aortic knuckle contour, though CT aortic angiography is mandatory to confirm or exclude dissection.
hq_q.f: Definitive cross-sectional imaging in a haemodynamically stable patient -> CT angiogram of the aorta.
hq_q.ql: Which chest radiograph abnormality is most characteristic of this condition?

c: tearing retrosternal chest pain radiating through to his interscapular back
168/94 mmHg in the right arm and 138/80 mmHg in the left arm
tm.m: Fibrillin-1 connective tissue deficiency causes cystic medial necrosis of the ascending aorta; an intimal tear allows pulsatile blood to expand a false lumen within the tunica media, widening the mediastinal shadow.
tm.g: Suspected acute thoracic aortic dissection on chest X-ray -> widened mediastinum
x: Symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is characteristic of pulmonary sarcoidosis or lymphoma, not acute aortic dissection.
Kerley B lines represent interlobular septal oedema in chronic left ventricular failure or mitral stenosis.
When a leaking descending thoracic aortic dissection causes a haemothorax, it almost always effuses into the left pleural cavity rather than the right.

A visceral pleural line at the lung apex indicates a spontaneous pneumothorax (to which Marfan patients are also prone), which causes unilateral pleuritic pain and absent breath sounds rather than unequal arm BPs and an early diastolic murmur.
f: a 32 year old woman with erythema nodosum, arthralgia and non-caseating granulomas from sarcoidosis
cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with upper-lobe venous diversion and bilateral basal crackles
congestive cardiac failure or right lower-lobe parapneumonic effusion
sudden unilateral pleuritic chest pain and hyperresonance with absent breath sounds at the right apex

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man with hypertension presents to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of sudden tearing chest pain that radiates straight through to his back.
Pulse rate 96 bpm. BP is 172/98 mmHg in the left arm and 128/74 mmHg in the right arm, with a weak right radial pulse. A 12-lead ECG shows 2 mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF.
hq_q.w: A Stanford type A ascending aortic dissection can extend into the right coronary ostium (causing inferior ST elevation) and brachiocephalic trunk (causing a right-arm BP deficit). Urgent CT aortic angiography must precede any antiplatelets, heparin or thrombolysis.
hq_q.f: Crushing central chest pain with inferior ST elevation, equal arm BPs and no tearing back pain -> immediate primary PCI.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate next step?

c: tearing chest pain that radiates straight through to his back
172/98 mmHg in the left arm and 128/74 mmHg in the right arm
ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF
tm.m: Retrograde extension of an ascending aortic intimal flap occludes the right coronary ostium (producing inferior STEMI changes) and narrows the brachiocephalic artery.
tm.g: Inferior ST elevation WITH tearing interscapular pain and >20 mmHg inter-arm BP difference -> urgent CT aortic angiography before any antithrombotic therapy
x: Dual antiplatelet loading is contraindicated when acute type A aortic dissection is suspected because it causes uncontrollable surgical bleeding during emergency aortic root repair.
Fibrinolysis in an acute type A aortic dissection mimicking an inferior STEMI is rapidly fatal due to catastrophic haemopericardium and aortic rupture.
Anticoagulation with heparin in an acute ascending aortic dissection promotes false-lumen propagation and fatal pericardial tamponade.
Attempting coronary catheterisation through a dissected ascending aorta without prior CT aortic angiography risks aortic perforation and delays cardiothoracic repair.
f: uncomplicated inferior STEMI with equal arm blood pressures proceeding to primary PCI
acute STEMI when primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes and aortic dissection is not suspected
confirmed acute pulmonary embolism or non-ST-elevation ACS after aortic dissection has been excluded
typical crushing retrosternal chest pain with inferior ST elevation, equal radial pulses and no back pain

hq_q.s:
A 62 year old man with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden, tearing retrosternal pain radiating to his back. Urgent CT angiography confirms a Stanford type A aortic dissection involving the ascending aorta and aortic root.
Pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 156/52 mmHg (pulse pressure 104 mmHg). On praecordial auscultation, a new cardiac murmur is heard that was absent last month.
o: Continuous machinery murmur at the left clavicle
Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
Ejection systolic murmur at the right second space
Loud pansystolic murmur at the cardiac apex
Low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex
hq_q.w: Proximal extension of a Stanford type A aortic dissection into the aortic root unhinges the aortic valve commissures, causing acute aortic regurgitation with a wide pulse pressure and a high-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge.
hq_q.f: Harsh ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids with a narrow pulse pressure -> aortic stenosis.
hq_q.ql: Which cardiac murmur is most likely to be heard?

tm.m: Dissection of the ascending aortic media detaches the aortic valve annulus and commissural attachments, allowing diastolic regurgitant blood flow back into the left ventricle.
tm.g: Type A ascending aortic dissection + wide pulse pressure (156/52 mmHg) -> early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge (acute aortic regurgitation)
x: A continuous Gibson machinery murmur beneath the left clavicle is characteristic of a persistent patent ductus arteriosus, not acute aortic dissection.
A calcific aortic stenosis murmur is an ejection systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur associated with a slow-rising, narrow pulse pressure rather than 156/52 mmHg.
An apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla indicates mitral regurgitation (e.g. from papillary muscle rupture after MI) rather than aortic root dissection.
A low-pitched apical mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap indicates rheumatic mitral stenosis.
f: an infant or young adult with a persistent patent ductus arteriosus
exertional syncope, slow-rising carotid pulse and calcified aortic valve leaflets
acute pulmonary oedema 4 days after an inferior MI due to posteromedial papillary muscle rupture
a patient with rheumatic heart disease, malar flush, atrial fibrillation and an opening snap

hq_q.s:
A 59 year old man presents to his GP with a 2-month history of constricting central chest discomfort that radiates to his lower jaw. It comes on predictably when walking briskly uphill and resolves completely within 3 minutes of standing still or using sublingual glyceryl trinitrate.
BP 138/86 mmHg, pulse rate 72 bpm. Cardiovascular examination and resting 12-lead ECG are normal.
hq_q.w: Under NICE CG95 guidelines, typical angina requires all three features: (1) constricting discomfort in the front of the chest, neck, shoulders, jaw or arms; (2) precipitated by physical exertion; and (3) relieved by rest or sublingual GTN within 5 minutes.
hq_q.f: Patient has only 2 of the 3 NICE criteria -> atypical angina.
hq_q.ql: Which clinical classification best describes his chest pain?

c: constricting central chest discomfort that radiates to his lower jaw
resolves completely within 3 minutes of standing still or using sublingual glyceryl trinitrate
tm.m: Fixed atherosclerotic coronary artery stenosis (>70% luminal narrowing) prevents coronary blood flow from matching increased myocardial oxygen demand during exertion.
tm.g: All 3 NICE criteria (constricting chest/jaw pain + provoked by exertion + relieved within 5 min by rest/GTN) -> typical angina
x: Atypical angina is defined by NICE as the presence of exactly two of the three typical anginal features, whereas this patient has all three.
Non-anginal pain is defined as having one or none of the three NICE features.
Unstable angina occurs at rest or with minimal exertion in a rapidly worsening pattern, whereas his pain is reproducibly exertional and resolves within 3 minutes.
Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina occurs unprovoked at rest (typically between midnight and early morning) with transient ST-segment elevation caused by coronary artery spasm.
f: exertional chest discomfort that resolves within 3 minutes of rest but is described as sharp stabbing rather than constricting (2 of 3 features)
fleeting left submammary stabbing pain at rest that is tender to chest wall palpation (0 of 3 features)
constricting chest pain occurring unprovoked at rest for 25 minutes with horizontal ST depression and normal troponin
episodic rest chest pain at 04:00 in a young smoker with transient ST elevation that resolves with GTN

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old woman with stable angina and severe brittle asthma attends her GP practice because she still experiences exertional chest tightness three times a week. She has permanent atrial fibrillation with a resting ventricular rate of 78 bpm on modified-release diltiazem.
BP 134/78 mmHg. Beta-blockers are contraindicated by her asthma, and her GP reviews second-line anti-anginal options.
hq_q.w: Ivabradine selectively inhibits the sinoatrial node funny ($I_f$) pacemaker current, slowing heart rate solely when the sinoatrial node drives cardiac rhythm. It is only effective in sinus rhythm (resting HR >=70 bpm) and is ineffective in atrial fibrillation.
hq_q.f: Patient with asthma in sinus rhythm at 82 bpm -> ivabradine is an effective rate-lowering anti-anginal option.
hq_q.ql: Which anti-anginal drug requires the patient to be in sinus rhythm to be effective?

tm.m: Ivabradine blocks hyperpolarisation-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) f-channels exclusively in sinoatrial nodal pacemaker cells and has no action on AV nodal conduction in atrial fibrillation.
tm.g: Anti-anginal drug that acts on the SA node funny ($I_f$) channel and requires sinus rhythm -> ivabradine
x: Wait: diltiazem is already a calcium channel blocker so amlodipine is not added to diltiazem, and amlodipine acts on vascular L-type calcium channels regardless of cardiac rhythm.
Long-acting oral nitrates produce systemic venodilatation (reducing preload) and coronary vasodilatation independently of whether the patient is in sinus rhythm or atrial fibrillation.
Nicorandil is a potassium-channel activator and nitric oxide donor that dilates peripheral and coronary arterioles independently of sinoatrial node rhythm.
Ranolazine inhibits the late inward sodium current ($I_{Na}$) in ventricular myocytes to improve diastolic relaxation and remains effective in patients with atrial fibrillation.
f: adding a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker to a patient taking a beta-blocker
adding a preload-reducing venodilator with an asymmetrical dosing interval to prevent nitrate tolerance
anti-anginal therapy complicated by painful punched-out oral or anal mucosal ulceration
adjunctive anti-anginal therapy acting on the late inward sodium current in a patient with atrial fibrillation

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old man with severe stable angina presents to the colorectal clinic with a 3-month history of a painful, non-healing ulcer at his anal margin. His regular medications are aspirin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, isosorbide mononitrate and nicorandil.
Examination shows a deep 1.5 cm clean, punched-out ulcer at the anal verge. Biopsy shows non-specific ulceration with no dysplasia or malignancy.
hq_q.w: Nicorandil (a potassium-channel activator with a nitrate moiety) causes severe, painful, punched-out mucosal and cutaneous ulcers affecting the mouth, bowel, perianal skin and peristomal sites. These ulcers heal only when nicorandil is discontinued.
hq_q.f: Oral ulcers accompanied by bloody diarrhoea, perianal fistulae and skip lesions -> Crohn's disease.
hq_q.ql: Which of his regular medications is the most likely cause of the ulcer?

c: painful, non-healing ulcer at his anal margin
tm.m: Toxic accumulation of nicotinic acid and nitric oxide metabolites from nicorandil in terminal mucosal vascular beds causes focal chemical and ischaemic epithelial necrosis.
tm.g: Refractory punched-out oral, gastrointestinal or anal ulceration in an angina patient -> nicorandil
x: Low-dose aspirin causes gastric and duodenal mucosal erosions via COX-1 prostaglandin inhibition rather than isolated deep punched-out perianal ulcers.
Atorvastatin is associated with myalgia, transaminitis and rare rhabdomyolysis, not mucocutaneous or anal ulceration.
Beta-blockers cause bradycardia, fatigue, cold extremities and bronchospasm rather than gastrointestinal or anal ulceration.
Organic nitrates cause throbbing vasodilatory headaches, flushing and postural hypotension, not punched-out anal ulcers.
f: epigastric dyspepsia and a bleeding pre-pyloric gastric ulcer on gastroscopy
symmetrical proximal thigh aching and a serum creatine kinase >5 times the upper limit of normal
symptomatic sinus bradycardia of 44 bpm and cold fingers
throbbing bitemporal headaches and lightheadedness shortly after starting anti-anginal therapy

hq_q.s:
A 76 year old woman presents to her GP with a 5-day history of a fast, fluttering heartbeat. She has no chest pain, syncope or orthopnoea. She takes ramipril for hypertension and has no history of asthma.
Pulse rate 128 bpm, irregularly irregular, BP 138/82 mmHg, SpO2 98% breathing air. Her chest is clear. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation and thyroid function is normal.
hq_q.w: For haemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation lasting >48 hours, NICE recommends first-line rate control (plus CHA2DS2-VASc anticoagulation assessment) using either a standard beta-blocker (such as bisoprolol) or a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil).
hq_q.f: Haemodynamically unstable AF (shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia or acute pulmonary oedema) -> emergency synchronised DC cardioversion.
