hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug for rate control?

tm.m: Beta-1 adrenoceptor blockade slows AV nodal conduction and prolongs the AV nodal refractory period, controlling the ventricular response rate while atrial thrombi are excluded or anticoagulated.
tm.g: Haemodynamically stable AF >48 hours duration without asthma -> oral beta-blocker (bisoprolol) for first-line rate control
x: Cardioversion of atrial fibrillation lasting longer than 48 hours without 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation (or TOE exclusion of left atrial appendage thrombus) carries a high risk of thromboembolic stroke.
NICE recommends digoxin monotherapy only as a first-line option for non-paroxysmal AF in predominantly sedentary patients, as it relies on vagal tone and fails to control rate during exertion.
NICE specifically recommends against offering amiodarone for long-term rate control in stable atrial fibrillation due to its thyroid, pulmonary and hepatic toxicity.
Flecainide is a class IC rhythm-control agent (cardioversion), which is unsafe in unanticoagulated AF lasting >48 hours and contraindicated in structural or ischaemic heart disease.
f: new-onset atrial fibrillation with severe hypotension (BP 78/44 mmHg) and acute pulmonary oedema
rate control of permanent atrial fibrillation in a housebound, sedentary frail patient
pharmacological rhythm control in a patient with left ventricular systolic dysfunction after adequate anticoagulation
pharmacological ‘pill-in-the-pocket’ cardioversion of paroxysmal AF <48 hours onset in a young patient with no structural heart disease

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old woman is reviewed in the cardiology clinic after a brief episode of lightheadedness. She has no chest pain or breathlessness.
Pulse rate 58 bpm, irregularly irregular, BP 132/76 mmHg. Her 12-lead ECG rhythm strip demonstrates a PR interval that progressively lengthens over four beats until a P wave fails to conduct to a QRS complex, after which the cycle repeats.
hq_q.w: Mobitz type I second-degree AV block (Wenckebach phenomenon) is characterised by progressive PR interval prolongation from beat to beat until an atrial impulse fails to conduct (dropped QRS complex), followed by a shorter PR interval on the next beat.
hq_q.f: Constant PR interval with intermittent sudden non-conducted P waves (dropped QRS complexes) -> Mobitz type II AV block (His-Purkinje disease, requires permanent pacemaker).
hq_q.ql: Which conduction abnormality is shown on the ECG?

c: until a P wave fails to conduct to a QRS complex
tm.m: Incremental decremental conduction delay within fatigued AV nodal cells lengthens the PR interval until an impulse arrives during the absolute refractory period.
tm.g: Progressive PR lengthening culminating in a dropped QRS complex -> Mobitz type I second-degree AV block (Wenckebach)
x: In complete (third-degree) heart block there is complete AV dissociation: P waves march through at a constant rate and QRS complexes occur at a slow regular escape rate with no repeating cycle.
First-degree heart block produces a fixed prolonged PR interval (>200 ms) where every single P wave is followed by a QRS complex with no dropped beats.
In Mobitz type II block, the PR interval of conducted beats remains strictly constant before and after a sudden non-conducted P wave.
In sinus arrest, the sinoatrial node fails to fire so both the P wave and the QRS complex are absent during the pause, whereas here a non-conducted P wave is clearly visible.
f: complete AV dissociation with regular P waves at 85/min, regular escape QRS complexes at 36/min and cannon a waves
a fixed PR interval of 260 ms on every beat with 1:1 atrioventricular conduction and no dropped QRS complexes
a constant PR interval of 180 ms with intermittent sudden non-conducted P waves in a 3:2 or 4:3 ratio
a prolonged pause on the rhythm strip containing neither P waves nor QRS complexes

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old man attends the cardiology clinic with a 4-year history of recurrent episodes of rapid, regular palpitations that start and stop abruptly. He feels well between episodes.
Pulse rate 72 bpm, regular, BP 118/72 mmHg. Heart sounds are normal. His resting 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with a short PR interval of 100 ms (<120 ms) and a slurred initial upstroke of the QRS complex.
hq_q.w: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is caused by a congenital accessory atrioventricular pathway (bundle of Kent) that bypasses the AV node, producing a short PR interval (<120 ms), a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) and paroxysmal AV re-entrant tachycardia.
hq_q.f: Coved ST-segment elevation >=2 mm in V1-V2 with a pseudo-RBBB pattern and nocturnal syncope -> Brugada syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: slurred initial upstroke of the QRS complex
tm.m: Rapid anterograde conduction down the congenital muscular bundle of Kent depolarises ventricular myocardium early (forming the delta wave) before normal His-Purkinje activation arrives.
tm.g: Paroxysmal SVT + short PR interval (<120 ms) + slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) -> Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
x: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy causes fibrofatty replacement of the RV myocardium, producing T-wave inversion in V1-V3 and terminal QRS notch (epsilon waves) rather than a short PR and delta wave.
Brugada syndrome is an autosomal dominant SCN5A sodium channelopathy showing coved ST elevation and T-wave inversion in V1-V3 with a normal PR interval.
Long QT syndrome causes syncope or torsades de pointes triggered by exertion, swimming or sudden auditory stimuli, with a prolonged corrected QT interval (>450-470 ms).
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy produces tall left ventricular voltages, deep dagger-like lateral/inferior Q waves and giant T-wave inversion alongside an ejection systolic murmur.
f: exertional ventricular tachycardia with T-wave inversion in leads V1 to V3 and epsilon waves at the end of the QRS
syncope at rest with coved ST-segment elevation and T-wave inversion in leads V1 and V2
syncope triggered by diving into cold water or an alarm clock, with a QTc interval of 510 ms
exertional syncope, a jerky pulse, a murmur louder on Valsalva and deep dagger Q waves with LV hypertrophy

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old man presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of severe occipital headache and blurred vision.
BP is 232/134 mmHg in the right arm and 228/132 mmHg in the left, pulse rate 88 bpm. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral flame-shaped retinal haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and optic disc swelling (papilloedema). Serum creatinine is 186 µmol/L and urine dipstick shows protein 2+ and blood 1+.
o: Oral amlodipine and GP review in 1 week
Oral ramipril and outpatient clinic review
hq_q.w: Malignant hypertension complicated by acute target-organ damage (bilateral papilloedema/grade IV retinopathy and acute kidney injury) is a hypertensive emergency requiring immediate hospital admission for titrated intravenous labetalol, lowering mean arterial pressure by <=20-25% over the first few hours.
hq_q.f: Clinic BP >=180/120 mmHg WITHOUT papilloedema, retinal haemorrhage or acute target-organ damage -> start oral antihypertensive therapy and investigate.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

tm.m: Extreme systemic arterial pressure exceeds cerebral and renal autoregulatory limits, causing fibrinoid necrosis of small arterioles, retinal ischaemia, papilloedema and acute nephroangiosclerosis.
tm.g: BP >=180/120 mmHg WITH papilloedema and acute kidney injury -> admit for controlled IV labetalol
x: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is used to confirm stage 1 or 2 clinic hypertension, never when a patient has a hypertensive emergency with papilloedema and acute kidney injury.
Discharging a patient with bilateral papilloedema and acute kidney injury on oral therapy alone risks hypertensive encephalopathy, intracerebral haemorrhage or irreversible renal failure.
ACE inhibitors can cause a precipitous pressure drop in renin-driven malignant hypertension and worsen acute kidney injury; inpatient titrated therapy is required.
Sublingual or immediate-release nifedipine causes a rapid, uncontrollable plunge in blood pressure that precipitates watershed cerebral, retinal or myocardial infarction.
f: a clinic blood pressure reading of 148/94 mmHg in an asymptomatic patient with normal fundi
a clinic BP of 184/112 mmHg in an asymptomatic patient with normal fundoscopy, normal ECG and normal renal function
stage 2 hypertension in a 45 year old diabetic patient without acute target-organ damage
never recommended in hypertensive emergencies due to uncontrolled hypotension and watershed stroke risk

hq_q.s:
A 67 year old man attends clinic with poorly controlled hypertension despite amlodipine and indapamide. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history and intermittent claudication. Two weeks after starting oral ramipril 5 mg daily, his serum creatinine rose from 98 µmol/L to 164 µmol/L (60-120).
BP is 168/92 mmHg. Abdominal auscultation reveals a systolic-diastolic bruit 3 cm to the right of the epigastrium.
hq_q.w: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis should be suspected in older smokers with peripheral arterial disease and resistant hypertension who have a renal bruit or a >30% rise in serum creatinine within 2 weeks of starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
hq_q.f: Resistant hypertension in a 28-year-old woman with a 'string-of-beads' renal artery on CT angiography -> fibromuscular dysplasia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his secondary hypertension?

c: 40 pack-year smoking history and intermittent claudication
Two weeks after starting oral ramipril 5 mg daily, his serum creatinine rose from 98 µmol/L to 164 µmol/L
bruit 3 cm to the right of the epigastrium
tm.m: When renal perfusion pressure is reduced by proximal renal artery stenosis, glomerular filtration depends on angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction; blocking ACE dilates the efferent arteriole and drops GFR.
tm.g: Peripheral vascular disease + abdominal bruit + >30% creatinine rise after starting ACE inhibitor -> renal artery stenosis
x: Phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal episodes of severe headache, drenching diaphoresis, pallor and tachycardia with raised plasma metanephrines.
Coarctation of the aorta presents in children or young adults with upper-limb hypertension, radio-femoral arterial delay and rib notching on chest X-ray.
Conn's syndrome causes treatment-resistant hypertension with spontaneous hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis rather than a sharp creatinine jump on ramipril and an abdominal bruit.
Cushing's syndrome presents with centripetal obesity, moon facies, proximal myopathy and wide violaceous abdominal striae.
f: episodic paroxysms of pounding headache, sweating, anxiety and pallor with raised plasma free metanephrines
a 20 year old with hypertension in the arms, weak delayed femoral pulses and a systolic murmur over the left scapula
resistant hypertension with serum potassium 2.8 mmol/L, raised aldosterone and suppressed plasma renin
hypertension accompanied by central weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising and wide purple striae

hq_q.s:
A 79 year old man with resistant hypertension attends his GP after a fourth antihypertensive medication was added last week to amlodipine 10 mg, ramipril 10 mg and indapamide 2.5 mg daily. Since starting the new tablet he has felt lightheaded and nearly fainted when getting out of bed.
Supine BP is 142/80 mmHg, falling to 108/62 mmHg after standing. Serum potassium is 4.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.3).
hq_q.w: In step 4 resistant hypertension with serum potassium >4.5 mmol/L, NICE recommends adding an alpha-blocker (doxazosin) or beta-blocker. Alpha-1 blockers inhibit sympathetic vasoconstriction on standing, classically causing first-dose and postural hypotension in older adults.
hq_q.f: Painful gynaecomastia and hyperkalaemia (K+ 5.8 mmol/L) after starting a fourth-line antihypertensive -> spironolactone.
hq_q.ql: Which fourth-line antihypertensive drug is most likely to have been started?

c: lightheaded and nearly fainted when getting out of bed
Supine BP is 142/80 mmHg, falling to 108/62 mmHg after standing
tm.m: Peripheral alpha-1 adrenoceptor blockade prevents baroreceptor-mediated reflex arteriolar and venous constriction upon standing, causing venous pooling and a >20/10 mmHg postural blood pressure drop.
tm.g: Step 4 resistant hypertension (with K+ >4.5 mmol/L) causing marked first-dose/postural hypotension -> doxazosin
x: Low-dose aspirin is an antiplatelet agent that has no effect on blood pressure or orthostatic vascular tone.
Atorvastatin is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor for lipid lowering and does not cause postural hypotension.
Beta-blockers cause sinus bradycardia and fatigue rather than classic alpha-1-mediated first-dose orthostatic syncope with a normal heart rate.
Spironolactone is used at step 4 only when serum potassium is <=4.5 mmol/L, and its classic adverse effects are hyperkalaemia and tender gynaecomastia rather than acute first-dose postural syncope.
f: secondary prevention after a transient ischaemic attack causing dyspepsia
primary or secondary cardiovascular prevention causing proximal muscle aching
a step 4 antihypertensive causing a resting heart rate of 44 bpm and wheeze
a step 4 antihypertensive started when K+ was 4.1 mmol/L that subsequently caused tender gynaecomastia and K+ 5.7 mmol/L

hq_q.s:
A 62 year old woman attends her GP to discuss primary prevention of cardiovascular disease after her 10-year QRISK3 score is calculated at 18%. She previously trialled atorvastatin 20 mg and rosuvastatin 5 mg, developing severe reproducible bilateral thigh myalgia on each drug. She has no established cardiovascular disease.
Total cholesterol is 6.4 mmol/L (<5.0), creatine kinase is 110 IU/L and TSH is 1.9 mU/L.
hq_q.w: Under NICE lipid modification guidelines, when a patient has documented intolerance to multiple statins, oral ezetimibe 10 mg once daily (which blocks intestinal NPC1L1 cholesterol absorption) is recommended as alternative monotherapy for primary or secondary prevention.
hq_q.f: Secondary prevention with established CVD and persistent LDL >=2.6 mmol/L despite maximum tolerated lipid-lowering therapy -> injectable inclisiran or PCSK9 inhibitor (alirocumab/evolocumab).
hq_q.ql: Which lipid-lowering medication is most appropriate to offer?

c: severe reproducible bilateral thigh myalgia on each drug
tm.m: Ezetimibe selectively inhibits the Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) sterol transporter at the jejunal enterocyte brush border, reducing hepatic cholesterol delivery and upregulating LDL receptors without skeletal muscle toxicity.
tm.g: True statin intolerance in primary CVD prevention (QRISK3 >=10%) -> ezetimibe monotherapy
x: NICE specifically recommends against offering a bile acid sequestrant (anion-exchange resin) for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease.
NICE recommends against routinely offering fibrates for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease.
Inclisiran (a small interfering RNA targeting PCSK9 mRNA) is NICE-approved only for secondary prevention in patients with established cardiovascular disease and LDL >=2.6 mmol/L.
NICE explicitly states do not offer omega-3 fatty acid compounds for the primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.
f: symptomatic bile acid malabsorption diarrhoea following terminal ileal resection in Crohn's disease
severe hypertriglyceridaemia (>10-20 mmol/L) under specialist lipid clinic supervision to prevent pancreatitis
secondary prevention in a patient with a prior myocardial infarction and persistent LDL cholesterol of 3.1 mmol/L despite maximum tolerated therapy
icosapent ethyl in secondary prevention with statin-treated LDL and raised fasting triglycerides (>1.7 mmol/L)

hq_q.s:
A 51 year old woman attends her GP after a health check reveals a total cholesterol of 8.2 mmol/L (<5.0) and LDL cholesterol of 5.8 mmol/L (<3.0); her lipid profile 3 years ago was normal. Over 6 months she has gained 6 kg, felt constantly cold and lethargic, and developed constipation.
Pulse rate 54 bpm, BP 138/88 mmHg. Her ankle jerk reflexes show slow relaxation.
hq_q.w: Secondary causes of hypercholesterolaemia (especially hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome and cholestasis) must be excluded before starting a statin. Hypothyroidism reduces hepatic LDL receptor expression and predisposes to severe statin-induced rhabdomyolysis if untreated.
hq_q.f: New hypercholesterolaemia with frothy urine, hypoalbuminaemia and pitting ankle oedema -> urine albumin:creatinine ratio (nephrotic syndrome).
hq_q.ql: Which blood test is most appropriate before considering lipid-lowering therapy?

c: lipid profile 3 years ago was normal
gained 6 kg, felt constantly cold and lethargic
ankle jerk reflexes show slow relaxation
tm.m: Triiodothyronine (T3) normally stimulates transcription of hepatic LDL receptor genes; thyroid hormone deficiency reduces hepatic LDL clearance while increasing skeletal muscle vulnerability to statin myotoxicity.
tm.g: New hypercholesterolaemia + weight gain, cold intolerance, bradycardia and slow-relaxing reflexes -> thyroid function tests (TSH and free T4)
x: While CK is checked if muscle symptoms are present, identifying and treating the underlying primary hypothyroidism with thyroid function tests is the diagnostic priority that explains both her symptoms and her dyslipidaemia.
Diabetes mellitus causes hypertriglyceridaemia and low HDL rather than bradycardia, cold intolerance and slow-relaxing ankle reflexes.
Lipoprotein(a) is a genetically determined lifelong risk factor and would not cause an acute rise in total cholesterol over 3 years accompanied by hypothyroid signs.
Baseline liver transaminases are checked before starting a statin, but they do not diagnose primary hypothyroidism causing cold intolerance, bradycardia and delayed ankle jerks.
f: evaluating symmetrical proximal muscle aching before or during statin treatment
screening for type 2 diabetes mellitus in a patient with polyuria, polydipsia and raised triglycerides
specialist cardiovascular risk stratification in premature familial coronary disease
excluding cholestatic liver disease in a patient with pruritus, jaundice and xanthelasma

hq_q.s:
A 44 year old man attends his GP after a routine blood test shows a fasting serum triglyceride concentration of 22.4 mmol/L (<1.7) and total cholesterol of 7.8 mmol/L (<5.0). He drinks 4 units of alcohol per week and has no abdominal pain.
BMI is 25 kg/m². Examination shows yellowish-red papules (eruptive xanthomata) over his elbows and buttocks. HbA1c is 38 mmol/mol and TSH is 1.7 mU/L.
o: Reassure and give dietary advice alone
Repeat fasting lipid profile in 1 year
Urgent referral to a lipid clinic
hq_q.w: Under NICE lipid modification guidelines, a fasting triglyceride concentration above 20 mmol/L not caused by excess alcohol or poor glycaemic control requires urgent specialist referral to a lipid clinic due to the high immediate risk of acute pancreatitis.
hq_q.f: Triglyceride concentration between 10 and 20 mmol/L -> repeat a fasting lipid profile within 5 to 14 days and review for secondary causes.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: fasting serum triglyceride concentration of 22.4 mmol/L
drinks 4 units of alcohol per week
tm.m: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (>20 mmol/L, chylomicronaemia) leads to pancreatic capillary sludging and lipolysis by pancreatic lipase into cytotoxic free fatty acids, triggering acute necrotising pancreatitis.
tm.g: Fasting triglycerides >20 mmol/L not due to excess alcohol or poorly controlled diabetes -> urgent referral to a specialist lipid clinic
x: A triglyceride level above 20 mmol/L carries a high immediate risk of acute pancreatitis and requires urgent specialist lipid management alongside strict fat restriction.
Delaying follow-up for 12 months with triglycerides of 22.4 mmol/L leaves the patient exposed to life-threatening acute pancreatitis.
Statins primarily lower LDL cholesterol via hepatic HMG-CoA reductase inhibition and are insufficient for chylomicronaemic hypertriglyceridaemia >20 mmol/L.
Over-the-counter fish oil supplements are not recommended by NICE and cannot safely manage severe primary hypertriglyceridaemia >20 mmol/L without urgent specialist care.
f: mildly raised non-fasting triglycerides of 2.8 mmol/L in a patient with high refined carbohydrate intake
annual monitoring of a stable patient on established statin therapy
primary prevention of cardiovascular disease in a patient with QRISK3 >=10% and normal triglycerides
never recommended as primary care monotherapy for triglycerides >20 mmol/L

hq_q.s: A 78 year old man with a history of anterior myocardial infarction presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-hour history of severe resting breathlessness, orthopnoea and coughing up pink frothy sputum. On examination, he is sitting bolt upright and clammy, pulse is 110 bpm, blood pressure is 156/90 mmHg, respiratory rate is 30 breaths/min and SpO2 is 93% on 15 L/min oxygen. His JVP is elevated at 7 cm and there are widespread bilateral inspiratory crackles to the mid-zones.
hq_q.w: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema is managed immediately by sitting the patient upright, administering supplemental oxygen if hypoxic (or CPAP/NIPPV if respiratory distress persists) and giving an intravenous loop diuretic (furosemide 40 to 80 mg IV bolus). Furosemide produces rapid venodilation within 5 to 15 minutes (reducing left ventricular preload) followed by brisk natriuresis. NICE CG187 explicitly advises against the routine use of intravenous opioids (morphine) or routine intravenous nitrates unless there is concomitant myocardial ischaemia, severe hypertension or regurgitant valve disease.
hq_q.f: Still hypoxic and struggling despite this → CPAP.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line intravenous drug to administer?

tm.m: Acute left ventricular failure -> raised left atrial and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure -> alveolar flooding -> IV furosemide reduces preload and clears alveolar fluid
tm.g: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema first-line drug = IV loop diuretic (furosemide); avoid routine IV morphine or routine IV nitrates (NICE CG187)
x: NICE CG187 recommends against routine intravenous nitrates in acute heart failure, reserving them for concomitant myocardial ischaemia, severe hypertension or acute mitral/aortic regurgitation
Routine intravenous morphine is no longer recommended by NICE CG187 because it is associated with respiratory depression, higher ICU admission rates and increased mortality
Beta-blockers must not be initiated acutely during decompensated pulmonary oedema (though existing beta-blockers are continued unless heart rate is <50 bpm or shocked)
Oral spironolactone has a slow onset of action over days and is used for chronic HFrEF mortality reduction rather than acute pulmonary oedema rescue
f: acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema accompanied by refractory ischaemic chest pain or severe hypertension (BP 210/120 mmHg)
palliative symptom relief in end-stage terminal heart failure under specialist palliative care guidance
once acute pulmonary oedema has resolved and the patient is euvolaemic with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 32%
chronic symptomatic NYHA class III heart failure with ejection fraction 30% despite optimal ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker therapy

hq_q.s: A 70 year old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (FEV1 28% predicted) presents to the respiratory clinic with a 2-month history of progressive bilateral ankle and leg swelling and worsening exertional dyspnoea. She does not have orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. On examination, her SpO2 is 86% on room air, her JVP is elevated at 6 cm with a prominent a-wave, there is a left parasternal heave, a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound (P2), smooth tender hepatomegaly and pitting oedema to both knees; lung bases are clear of crackles.
hq_q.w: Cor pulmonale is right ventricular hypertrophy and failure secondary to chronic lung disease and alveolar hypoxia (most commonly severe COPD or interstitial lung disease). Chronic alveolar hypoxia (PaO2 <8 kPa) triggers diffuse hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular remodelling, raising pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure (producing a loud P2 and parasternal heave) and eventually causing systemic venous congestion (raised JVP, tender hepatomegaly and peripheral oedema) with clear lung bases.
hq_q.f: Orthopnoea and bibasal crackles → left ventricular failure.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound (P2)
tm.m: Chronic alveolar hypoxia in COPD -> hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction -> pulmonary hypertension (loud P2, RV heave) -> right ventricular failure (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ankle oedema)
tm.g: Severe COPD/hypoxia + raised JVP + loud P2 + hepatomegaly + ankle oedema with no orthopnoea/basal crackles = cor pulmonale
x: Presents with Kussmaul's sign (JVP rising on inspiration), an early diastolic pericardial knock and pericardial calcification on chest X-ray after tuberculosis or cardiac surgery
Causes orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, a displaced apex beat and fine bibasal inspiratory crackles from pulmonary venous congestion
Produces ascites, splenomegaly, spider naevi and a normal or low JVP without a loud P2 or left parasternal heave
Presents with periorbital and peripheral oedema, frothy urine (>3.5 g/day proteinuria), hypoalbuminaemia and a normal JVP
f: calcified pericardial rim on chest X-ray, pericardial knock and JVP that rises on inspiration 5 years after tuberculous pericarditis
three-pillow orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, S3 gallop and bibasal inspiratory crackles after an anterior MI
jaundice, spider naevi, shifting dullness, splenomegaly and a low JVP in a patient with chronic alcohol misuse
periorbital oedema, serum albumin 18 g/L, urine ACR 420 mg/mmol and a normal JVP

hq_q.s: A 74 year old man with heart failure has a chest X-ray during an admission with breathlessness. The X-ray shows fluid in the interstitium of the lungs.
hq_q.w: Kerley B lines are short horizontal lines at the lung edges from fluid in the interlobular septa. ABCDE: alveolar oedema, B lines, cardiomegaly, dilated upper vessels, effusions.
hq_q.f: Fluffy shadowing spreading out from both hila → alveolar oedema, the bat-wing sign.
hq_q.ql: Which sign on the X-ray shows interstitial oedema?

tm.m: Fluid in the interlobular septa shows as short horizontal lines at the lung edge
tm.g: Interstitial oedema: Kerley B lines
f: fluid filling the alveoli
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cardiothoracic ratio over 0.5 (A large heart shows cardiomegaly, not interstitial fluid)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pleural effusions (Effusions show fluid in the pleural space)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Upper lobe venous diversion (Upper lobe diversion is the earliest sign of raised venous pressure, before interstitial oedema)
x: Ruled out here: requires fluid filling the alveoli, whereas this patient has fluid in the interstitium, A 74 year old man with.
A large heart shows cardiomegaly, not interstitial fluid.
Effusions show fluid in the pleural space.
Upper lobe diversion is the earliest sign of raised venous pressure, before interstitial oedema.

hq_q.s: A 56 year old man with a history of ankylosing spondylitis presents to his GP with a 6-month history of progressive exertional breathlessness and awareness of a forceful heartbeat when lying on his left side at night. On examination, his pulse is 84 bpm with a rapid upstroke and precipitous descent ('water-hammer' collapsing character), blood pressure is 168/48 mmHg, the apex beat is hyperdynamic and displaced to the sixth intercostal space, and there is a high-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge, loudest sitting forward in end-expiration.
hq_q.w: Chronic aortic regurgitation (caused by aortic root dilatation from ankylosing spondylitis, Marfan syndrome, syphilis or aortic dissection, or leaflet disease from bicuspid aortic valve, infective endocarditis or rheumatic fever) allows diastolic reflux of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle. This produces a high-pitched blowing early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge (Erb's point) accented on sitting forward in expiration, left ventricular volume overload (thrusting displaced apex), high systolic stroke volume and low diastolic pressure (wide pulse pressure, 168/48 mmHg, and collapsing Corrigan's pulse).
hq_q.f: A mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with a loud S1 and AF → mitral stenosis.
hq_q.ql: Which heart valve lesion is most likely?

c: early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge, loudest sitting forward in end-expiration
tm.m: Incompetent aortic valve -> diastolic backflow from aorta into LV -> low diastolic BP (wide pulse pressure + collapsing pulse) + high-pitched early diastolic murmur at LSE
tm.g: Collapsing pulse + wide pulse pressure + early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge sitting forward in expiration = aortic regurgitation
x: Causes a narrow pulse pressure, slow-rising plateau pulse, quiet S2 and a harsh ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
Produces a blowing pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the left axilla with a soft S1
Produces a loud S1, opening snap and low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex (loudest in the left lateral position) with a malar flush
Produces a continuous 'machinery' murmur beneath the left clavicle throughout systole and diastole
f: exertional syncope, slow-rising carotid pulse, BP 112/88 mmHg and harsh ejection systolic murmur radiating to the neck
blowing pansystolic murmur loudest at the apex radiating to the left axilla heard best in expiration
tapping apex beat, loud first heart sound, opening snap and low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex in the left lateral position
continuous machinery-like murmur at the left infraclavicular area with a thrill in a young adult born prematurely

hq_q.s: A 26 year old woman presents to her GP with a 12-month history of occasional brief fluttering palpitations and atypical sharp left-sided chest twinges unrelated to exertion. She is tall and slender and feels otherwise well with normal exercise tolerance. On examination, her pulse is 76 bpm regular and blood pressure is 114/70 mmHg. Cardiac auscultation at the apex reveals a high-pitched mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur that moves earlier in systole when she stands up from a squatting position.
hq_q.w: Mitral valve prolapse (myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve leaflets and chordae, common in young women and connective tissue disorders such as Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) causes one or both mitral leaflets to billow back into the left atrium during ventricular contraction. Tensing of the elongated chordae tendineae produces a sharp mid-systolic click, followed by a late systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation. Standing or Valsalva reduces left ventricular end-diastolic volume, causing prolapse to occur earlier in systole (click moves closer to S1 and murmur lengthens).
hq_q.f: A murmur that gets louder on standing and Valsalva and softer on squatting → hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur
tm.m: Myxomatous redundancy of mitral leaflets/chordae -> leaflet billows into LA in mid-systole -> sudden chordal tensing creates a mid-systolic click followed by late systolic MR murmur
tm.g: Mid-systolic click + late systolic apical murmur = mitral valve prolapse
x: Causes a harsh crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotid arteries
Causes wide fixed splitting of the second heart sound (S2) and an ejection systolic flow murmur at the upper left sternal edge
Causes a jerky pulse, double apical impulse and a harsh ejection systolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that loudens on standing or Valsalva without a mid-systolic click
Produces a harsh pansystolic murmur and palpable thrill at the lower left sternal edge
f: slow-rising pulse, soft S2 and harsh ejection systolic murmur at the second right intercostal space radiating to the carotids
wide fixed splitting of S2 with a pulmonary ejection flow murmur at the upper left sternal edge
family history of sudden cardiac death, jerky carotid pulse and a harsh lower sternal ejection systolic murmur that intensifies during Valsalva strain
harsh pansystolic murmur and palpable thrill at the left lower sternal edge after an anterior myocardial infarction

hq_q.s: A 78 year old man is referred to the rapid-access cardiology clinic with a 4-month history of worsening exertional breathlessness and chest tightness when walking uphill. On examination, his pulse is 72 bpm and slow-rising, blood pressure is 118/84 mmHg, the apex beat is sustained and non-displaced, and there is a grade 3/6 ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to both carotid arteries with a quiet second heart sound. Transthoracic echocardiography is performed to grade his aortic stenosis.
o: Mean transvalvular pressure gradient over 40 mmHg
Peak aortic jet velocity of 2.6 m/s
hq_q.w: According to ESC and NICE heart valve disease guidelines, severe high-gradient aortic stenosis on transthoracic Doppler echocardiography is defined by three key haemodynamic criteria: a mean transvalvular pressure gradient >=40 mmHg, a peak aortic jet velocity (Vmax) >=4.0 m/s, and an effective aortic valve area (AVA) <1.0 cm2 (or indexed AVA <0.6 cm2/m2). Once severe aortic stenosis becomes symptomatic (angina, exertional syncope or heart failure dyspnoea) or LVEF drops below 50%, prompt valve intervention (SAVR or TAVI) is indicated.
hq_q.f: Severe AS with no symptoms and a normal exercise test → watchful waiting with surveillance.
hq_q.ql: Which transthoracic echocardiographic parameter defines severe high-gradient aortic stenosis?

c: ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to both carotid arteries
tm.m: Calcific narrowing of aortic valve orifice (<1.0 cm2) -> convective acceleration across valve -> peak jet velocity >=4.0 m/s and mean pressure gradient >=40 mmHg
tm.g: Severe aortic stenosis echo criteria: mean gradient >=40 mmHg, peak velocity >=4.0 m/s, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2
x: An aortic valve area >1.5 cm2 indicates mild aortic stenosis (1.0 to 1.5 cm2 is moderate; <1.0 cm2 is severe)
A left ventricular ejection fraction of 55% is within the normal range and does not grade the severity of valvular narrowing
A peak aortic jet velocity between 2.6 and 2.9 m/s indicates mild aortic stenosis (>=4.0 m/s defines severe)
A mean gradient <20 mmHg indicates mild aortic stenosis (20 to 39 mmHg is moderate; >=40 mmHg is severe)
f: echocardiographic valve area threshold confirming mild aortic stenosis (>1.5 cm2)
preserved left ventricular systolic function threshold above which asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis may be monitored closely
peak aortic jet velocity in a patient with mild aortic stenosis (2.6 to 2.9 m/s)
transvalvular pressure gradient seen in mild non-obstructive aortic valve disease

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man with a history of mitral valve prolapse presents to the Medical Assessment Unit with a 3-week history of drenching night sweats, anorexia, lethargy and a 3 kg weight loss. He underwent a dental extraction 6 weeks ago. On examination, he is alert and haemodynamically stable, temperature is 38.4°C, pulse is 96 bpm, blood pressure is 128/74 mmHg, there is a Grade 3/6 apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla, and three linear splinter haemorrhages are visible beneath his fingernails.
o: Obtain a single peripheral blood culture set and start antibiotics immediately
Obtain three sets of peripheral blood cultures from separate venepuncture sites spaced over 6 to 24 hours
Perform a chest radiograph, serum C-reactive protein and antistreptolysin O titre
Send a midstream urine culture and pharyngeal throat swab
hq_q.w: Demonstrating persistent bacteraemia is a Major Modified Duke Criterion for infective endocarditis and guides targeted bactericidal therapy for 4 to 6 weeks. In a haemodynamically stable patient with suspected subacute infective endocarditis, three separate sets of aerobic and anaerobic peripheral blood cultures must be drawn from distinct venepuncture sites (spaced at least 1 to 6 hours apart over up to 24 hours) BEFORE starting empirical antibiotics. If the patient has severe sepsis or septic shock, three sets are still taken from separate sites within 1 hour before immediate antibiotics.
hq_q.f: Septic and unstable → take 2 sets within an hour and start antibiotics.
hq_q.ql: Which microbiological step must be completed before empirical intravenous antibiotics are started?

tm.m: Subacute vegetative endocarditis sheds bacteria continuously into blood -> 3 separate peripheral blood culture sets spaced apart prove continuous bacteraemia (Major Duke criterion) and distinguish skin contaminants
tm.g: Suspected subacute infective endocarditis (haemodynamically stable) = take 3 sets of blood cultures from different sites at different times BEFORE starting antibiotics
x: Echocardiography (starting with transthoracic echo within 24 hours) is a Major imaging criterion but does not replace blood cultures before antibiotics

A single blood culture set cannot prove persistent bacteraemia and makes it impossible to distinguish true coagulase-negative staphylococcal or viridans streptococcal endocarditis from a skin contaminant
Inflammatory markers and ASO titres are non-specific (ASO is used for acute rheumatic fever, not bacterial endocarditis) and cannot guide antibiotic sensitivities
Throat and urine swabs do not sample endovascular vegetations and do not establish Duke blood culture criteria
f: patient with prosthetic mitral valve endocarditis or suspected aortic root abscess after transthoracic echocardiography is non-diagnostic
patient with meningococcal septicaemia and purpuric rash requiring immediate ceftriaxone after a rapid single blood culture draw
14 year old presenting 3 weeks after untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis with migratory polyarthritis, erythema marginatum and Sydenham's chorea
uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection or acute streptococcal tonsillitis in primary care

hq_q.s: A 44 year old woman with a history of intravenous drug use is admitted to the cardiology ward with a 2-week history of fevers, rigors and a new apical pansystolic murmur. Two sets of blood cultures have grown Staphylococcus aureus. On examination, her temperature is 38.2°C and she complains of throbbing pain in the tips of her right index and middle fingers, where there are pea-sized, exquisitely tender, violaceous subcutaneous nodules on the distal finger pads.
hq_q.w: Osler's nodes are painful, tender, erythematous or violaceous subcutaneous nodules located on the pads (pulps) of the fingers and toes in infective endocarditis (remember: 'Ouch = Osler's on the pads'). They result from immune-complex deposition (type III hypersensitivity) causing focal dermal vasculitis, making them an immunologici phenomenon in the Modified Duke Criteria (alongside Roth spots, glomerulonephritis and rheumatoid factor). By contrast, Janeway lesions are painless erythematous/haemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles caused by septic microemboli (vascular phenomenon).
hq_q.f: Painless flat red macules on the palms → Janeway lesions.
hq_q.ql: What is the eponymous name for these painful digital lesions?

c: exquisitely tender, violaceous subcutaneous nodules on the distal finger pads
tm.m: Circulating immune complexes in infective endocarditis deposit in digital arterioles -> focal dermal vasculitis -> painful tender nodules on finger/toe pulps (Osler's nodes)
tm.g: Endocarditis hand signs: Osler's nodes = PAINFUL tender nodules on finger/toe pulps (immunological); Janeway lesions = PAINLESS macules on palms/soles (septic emboli)
x: Hard bony osteophytic swellings over the dorsal aspect of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints in nodal osteoarthritis
Hard bony osteophytic swellings over the dorsal aspect of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints in nodal osteoarthritis
Painless erythematous or haemorrhagic macular lesions on the palms and soles caused by septic microemboli containing bacteria and neutrophils
Linear dark-red streaks beneath the nail plate caused by microemboli or trauma to the longitudinal nail-bed capillaries
f: chronic hard bony swellings at the proximal interphalangeal joints in a 68 year old woman with hand osteoarthritis
chronic hard bony swellings at the distal interphalangeal joints in nodal osteoarthritis
non-tender, painless flat haemorrhagic macules on the thenar and hypothenar eminences of the palms and soles in acute Staph aureus endocarditis
linear reddish-brown streaks in the distal third of the fingernail bed in infective endocarditis

hq_q.s: A 46 year old man is admitted to the cardiology ward with a 2-week history of fevers, drenching sweats and rigors. He has no prosthetic heart valves, no indwelling lines and no history of penicillin allergy. Examination reveals a temperature of 38.7°C, splinter haemorrhages and a new grade 3/6 apical pansystolic murmur. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates an 8 mm oscillating vegetation on the native mitral valve, and all three sets of blood cultures grow meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA).
hq_q.w: For native valve infective endocarditis caused by meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) in a patient without penicillin allergy, BSAC and ESC guidelines recommend high-dose intravenous flucloxacillin (2 g every 4 to 6 hours) for at least 4 weeks. Flucloxacillin is rapidly bactericidal against MSSA and achieves far faster vegetational clearance and lower relapse rates than glycopeptides (vancomycin), which have slower bactericidal kinetics and poorer tissue penetration and are reserved for MRSA or true severe penicillin allergy.
hq_q.f: MRSA → vancomycin or daptomycin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate targeted intravenous antibiotic regimen?

tm.m: MSSA produces penicillinase (resisting benzylpenicillin/amoxicillin) -> beta-lactamase-stable isoxazolyl penicillin (IV flucloxacillin) binds PBP2 with rapid bactericidal activity
tm.g: Native valve MSSA infective endocarditis (no penicillin allergy) = high-dose IV flucloxacillin for 4 weeks
x: Over 90% of Staphylococcus aureus strains produce beta-lactamase that hydrolyses amoxicillin; amoxicillin is used for Enterococcus faecalis or empirical subacute native valve therapy
Most Staphylococcus aureus strains produce penicillinase and are resistant to benzylpenicillin, which is used for penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci or Strep gallolyticus
Ceftriaxone has inferior antistaphylococcal activity compared with high-dose flucloxacillin and is used for HACEK organisms or streptococcal outpatient parenteral therapy
Vancomycin is less rapidly bactericidal than flucloxacillin against MSSA and is reserved for MRSA or patients with severe beta-lactam allergy
f: native valve infective endocarditis caused by amoxicillin-susceptible Enterococcus faecalis (combined with gentamicin or ceftriaxone)
native valve infective endocarditis caused by fully penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus sanguinis or Streptococcus gallolyticus
infective endocarditis caused by a HACEK group Gram-negative bacillus (such as Aggregatibacter or Cardiobacterium)
infective endocarditis caused by meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) or prosthetic valve Staphylococcus epidermidis

hq_q.s: A 36 year old man who moved to the UK from India 2 years ago presents to the Respiratory Clinic with a 2-month history of right-sided pleuritic chest ache, drenching night sweats, dry cough and a 5 kg unintentional weight loss. On examination, his temperature is 37.9°C, and there is stony dullness to percussion with absent breath sounds and reduced vocal fremitus over the right lower zone. Ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration yields straw-coloured fluid with protein 52 g/L, LDH 480 IU/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L, >85% lymphocytes and a negative Gram stain.
hq_q.w: A unilateral lymphocytic exudative pleural effusion (pleural protein >30 g/L) in a young adult from a tuberculosis-endemic region presenting with subacute fevers, night sweats and weight loss is tuberculous pleurisy until proven otherwise. Tuberculous pleurisy results from a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to rupture of a subpleural caseous focus into the pleural space. Because pleural fluid Ziehl-Neelsen microscopy is positive in <10% and fluid culture in ~30%, ultrasound-guided or thoracoscopic pleural biopsy (showing caseating granulomas and high tissue culture sensitivity) plus pleural fluid adenosine deaminase (ADA) provides the highest diagnostic yield.
hq_q.f: Asbestos exposure with irregular pleural thickening → mesothelioma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of his pleural effusion?

c: moved to the UK from India 2 years ago
tm.m: Subpleural Mycobacterium tuberculosis focus ruptures into pleural space -> T-cell delayed hypersensitivity -> high-protein lymphocytic exudate (+ raised pleural ADA)
tm.g: Young patient from endemic area + night sweats/weight loss + lymphocytic exudative pleural effusion = tuberculous pleurisy (confirm with pleural biopsy + ADA)
x: Acute bacterial parapneumonic effusions are predominantly neutrophilic (polymorphonuclear leukocytes) rather than >85% lymphocytic
Causes a bilateral (or right-greater-than-left) transudative effusion with pleural fluid protein <30 g/L and raised JVP/ankle oedema
Also causes a lymphocytic exudate, but typically presents in patients in their 60s to 80s with dull non-pleuritic chest wall pain and a 30 to 40 year lag after occupational asbestos exposure
Presents with acute dyspnoea, pleuritic pain and haemoptysis with a small blood-stained effusion rather than 2 months of drenching night sweats and a large lymphocytic effusion
f: 4 days of high fever, rusty sputum, lobar consolidation and a turbid neutrophilic pleural exudate
bilateral pleural effusions with pleural fluid protein 18 g/L, orthopnoea and raised JVP in a 76 year old with ischaemic cardiomyopathy
74 year old retired shipyard lagger presenting with dull progressive chest wall pain, pleural plaques and nodular circumferential pleural thickening on CT
sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea 10 days after knee arthroplasty with a small haemorrhagic effusion and filling defect on CTPA

hq_q.s: A 64 year old woman with a 20-year history of erosive, rheumatoid-factor-positive and anti-CCP-positive rheumatoid arthritis presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with a 4-week history of progressive exertional breathlessness. She is afebrile and has subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules over both olecranon processes and ulnar deviation at the metacarpophalangeal joints. Chest radiograph shows a moderate left pleural effusion. Ultrasound-guided diagnostic thoracentesis yields slightly turbid yellow fluid.
hq_q.w: Rheumatoid pleural effusions are exudates that classically occur in patients with longstanding seropositive, nodular rheumatoid arthritis. Their hallmark biochemical feature is a markedly low pleural fluid glucose (<1.6 mmol/L, or <3.3 mmol/L) caused by impaired glucose transport across the thickened, inflamed pleural membrane combined with high glucose consumption by pleural inflammatory cells. Rheumatoid effusions also typically show a low pH (~7.1 to 7.2), high LDH (>700 IU/L), low complement (C3/C4) and occasionally cholesterol crystals (pseudochylothorax) if chronic.
hq_q.f: A high amylase → pancreatitis or oesophageal rupture.
hq_q.ql: Which pleural fluid biochemical finding is most characteristic of a rheumatoid pleural effusion?

tm.m: Rheumatoid pleural serositis blocks glucose carrier transport across pleura + synovial-like inflammatory consumption -> characteristically very low pleural fluid glucose (<1.6 mmol/L)
tm.g: Exudative pleural effusion with VERY LOW glucose (<1.6 mmol/L) in an afebrile patient = rheumatoid arthritis effusion (other causes of low pleural glucose: empyema, TB, malignancy, oesophageal rupture)
x: Markedly raised pleural fluid amylase (salivary or pancreatic isozyme) is characteristic of oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave syndrome), acute pancreatitis or pancreatic pseudocyst
Rheumatoid pleural effusions are acidic (typically pH <7.20 due to lactate/CO2 accumulation), not alkaline
A pleural fluid protein of 18 g/L (<30 g/L) defines a transudate (such as heart failure or hypoalbuminaemia), whereas rheumatoid pleuritis is an exudate

Pleural fluid triglycerides >1.24 mmol/L (chylomicrons) define a true chylothorax from thoracic duct disruption; chronic rheumatoid effusions can cause a cholesterol-rich pseudochylothorax with low triglycerides
f: left-sided pleural effusion with hydropneumothorax after forceful vomiting (Boerhaave oesophageal rupture) or severe acute pancreatitis
normal physiological pleural fluid pH (7.60) or uncomplicated transudative effusion
bilateral pleural effusions secondary to decompensated congestive cardiac failure or hepatic cirrhosis
milky pleural effusion following thoracic surgery or mediastinal lymphoma caused by thoracic duct disruption (chylothorax)

hq_q.s: A 62 year old man who underwent a transthoracic Ivor-Lewis oesophagectomy for oesophageal adenocarcinoma 10 days ago becomes increasingly breathless on the surgical ward after starting enteral jejunostomy feeds. His right intercostal chest drain output has risen to 900 mL/day of milky-white, odourless fluid. On examination, he is afebrile, SpO2 is 94% on air and there is stony dullness at the right base. Analysis of the pleural fluid shows triglycerides of 4.5 mmol/L (>1.24 mmol/L), presence of chylomicrons, normal cholesterol and a negative Gram stain.
hq_q.w: Chylothorax is the accumulation of lymphatic chyle in the pleural space due to disruption or obstruction of the thoracic duct (most commonly iatrogenic trauma during oesophagectomy or cardiothoracic surgery, or non-traumatic mediastinal lymphoma). Notice that the thoracic duct crosses from right to left at T5, so damage below T5 causes a right-sided chylothorax. The fluid is milky-white, odourless, does not clear when centrifuged, and is biochemically confirmed by pleural fluid triglycerides >1.24 mmol/L (110 mg/dL) and chylomicrons on lipoprotein electrophoresis.
hq_q.f: Milky fluid with cholesterol crystals in a long-standing rheumatoid effusion → pseudochylothorax.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: oesophagectomy for oesophageal adenocarcinoma 10 days ago
tm.m: Intraoperative injury to the thoracic duct during oesophagectomy -> enteral fat absorption swells lymphatic chyle leak into pleural space -> milky fluid with triglycerides >1.24 mmol/L
tm.g: Milky pleural fluid after cardiothoracic/oesophageal surgery (or lymphoma) + pleural triglycerides >1.24 mmol/L = chylothorax
x: Also appears turbid or purulent, but is malodorous, neutrophilic with pH <7.2, and clears to a clear supernatant after centrifugation (as turbidity is from leukocytes, not lipids)
Presents with heavily blood-stained fluid where the pleural fluid haematocrit exceeds 50% of the peripheral blood haematocrit

Occurs in longstanding (>5 years) thick-walled effusions from rheumatoid arthritis or tuberculosis, showing high cholesterol (>5.18 mmol/L) with cholesterol crystals and LOW triglycerides (<0.56 mmol/L)
Produces clear or straw-coloured serous exudative fluid without elevated triglycerides
f: fever of 39°C, malodorous turbid pleural fluid with pH 7.04 that leaves a clear supernatant when centrifuged
bloody chest drain output after penetrating chest trauma with a pleural fluid haematocrit of 24% (serum haematocrit 40%)
chronic calcified pleural effusion present for 8 years in rheumatoid arthritis containing rhomboid cholesterol crystals and triglycerides of 0.3 mmol/L
straw-coloured pleural exudate with pH 7.34 and normal triglycerides overlying a lower lobe pneumonia

hq_q.s: A 62 year old woman with a history of vitiligo presents to her GP with a 3-month history of progressive fatigue, exertional breathlessness, a sore beefy-red tongue and symmetrical pins and needles in both feet. She eats a balanced diet including meat, fish and dairy daily and does not drink alcohol. On examination, she has conjunctival pallor, atrophic glossitis, absent ankle jerks with extensor plantar responses, and impaired vibration and joint position sense at both great toes. Blood tests show Hb 86 g/L and MCV 118 fL.
hq_q.w: Pernicious anaemia is the commonest cause of severe vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency in the UK and results from autoimmune gastritis with antibodies against gastric parietal cells (~90% sensitive) and intrinsic factor (~60% sensitive, >95% specific), abolishing terminal ileal B12 absorption despite normal dietary meat intake. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia (MCV >100 fL, hypersegmented neutrophils), glossitis, and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (dorsal column loss of vibration/proprioception plus lateral corticospinal tract upper motor neuron extensor plantars + peripheral neuropathy causing absent ankle jerks).
hq_q.f: No neurology, poor diet and on methotrexate → folate deficiency.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
hq_q.post: White cell count and platelets are low normal. Intrinsic factor antibodies are positive.

c: symmetrical pins and needles in both feet
absent ankle jerks with extensor plantar responses, and impaired vibration and joint position sense
tm.m: Autoimmune anti-intrinsic factor / anti-parietal cell antibodies -> failure of terminal ileal B12 absorption -> defective DNA synthesis (megaloblastic anaemia) + defective myelin methylation (subacute combined degeneration of the cord)
tm.g: Macrocytic anaemia + glossitis + dorsal column loss (vibration/proprioception) + absent ankle jerks with upgoing plantars = pernicious anaemia (B12 deficiency)
x: Alcohol causes a mild non-megaloblastic macrocytosis (typically MCV 100 to 110 fL without anaemia) and does not explain a normal-diet non-drinker with vitiligo and dorsal column/pyramidal signs

Folate deficiency causes an identical megaloblastic blood film and glossitis, but does NOT cause subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (and starting folic acid alone without B12 worsens cord demyelination)
Presents in elderly patients with refractory cytopenias, hypogranular Pelger-Huet neutrophils and ring sideroblasts without intrinsic-factor antibodies or cord demyelination
Causes mild non-megaloblastic macrocytosis with cold intolerance, weight gain and slow-relaxing reflexes rather than extensor plantars and dorsal column loss
f: asymptomatic 50 year old drinking 50 units of alcohol weekly with Hb 142 g/L, MCV 105 fL and raised gamma-GT
macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia in an elderly patient eating a strict tea-and-toast diet with normal serum B12 and no neurological deficit
78 year old with pancytopenia, macrocytosis, circulating blasts and dysplastic multilineage bone marrow changes
cold intolerance, constipation, bradycardia, slow-relaxing ankle reflexes, TSH 42 mU/L and MCV 103 fL

hq_q.s: A 32 year old man of Mediterranean heritage presents to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of severe fatigue, dizziness, scleral icterus and passing dark reddish-brown urine. Seven days ago he started taking primaquine after returning from rural malaria prophylaxis. On examination, he is pale and jaundiced with no hepatosplenomegaly. Blood tests show haemoglobin 84 g/L (130-175), MCV 96 fL, and a peripheral blood film shows numerous Heinz bodies and blister ('bite') cells.
hq_q.w: Primaquine is an oxidant antimalarial drug that triggers acute intravascular and extravascular haemolysis in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, denaturing haemoglobin into Heinz bodies that splenic macrophages bite out ('bite cells'). During haemolysis, free haemoglobin released from lysed erythrocytes binds tightly to plasma haptoglobin; the haptoglobin-haemoglobin complex is rapidly cleared by hepatic macrophages, causing serum haptoglobin to become very low or undetectable. The classic haemolysis panel shows: low haptoglobin, raised unconjugated bilirubin, raised LDH and reticulocytosis.
hq_q.f: A positive direct Coombs test → autoimmune haemolysis.
hq_q.ql: Which laboratory finding best confirms active intravascular and extravascular haemolysis?

c: scleral icterus and passing dark reddish-brown urine
tm.m: Oxidant stress (primaquine) in G6PD deficiency -> red cell lysis releases free Hb -> plasma haptoglobin binds free Hb and is cleared by the liver -> low/undetectable serum haptoglobin
tm.g: Haemolytic anaemia laboratory tetrad: LOW haptoglobin + HIGH unconjugated bilirubin + HIGH LDH + HIGH reticulocytes
x: Bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia in response to red cell destruction produces a marked reticulocytosis (elevated reticulocyte count), not reticulocytopenia

Haem catabolism produces water-insoluble unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin that exceeds hepatic glucuronidation capacity; conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia indicates biliary obstruction or hepatocellular cholestasis

Serum ferritin is normal or elevated in acute haemolysis from released red cell iron stores (only chronic intravascular haemolysis with prolonged haemoglobinuria such as paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria depletes iron)
Erythrocytes are rich in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), so red cell destruction causes a markedly elevated serum LDH
f: aplastic crisis caused by parvovirus B19 infection in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis or sickle cell disease
painless obstructive jaundice with pale stools, dark urine containing conjugated bilirubin and a dilated common bile duct
chronic gastrointestinal blood loss from a caecal carcinoma causing microcytic hypochromic anaemia
uncomplicated Gilbert's syndrome causing mild fasting unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with a completely normal blood count and no red cell lysis

hq_q.s: A 58 year old postmenopausal woman with poorly controlled seropositive rheumatoid arthritis attends the rheumatology clinic complaining of 3 months of fatigue. She has active synovitis in eight metacarpophalangeal and wrist joints despite oral methotrexate and folic acid. She eats meat regularly, has no indigestion, altered bowel habit or visible bleeding, and her menopause was 6 years ago. Blood tests show Hb 98 g/L (115-165), MCV 84 fL (80-96), serum iron 6 micromol/L (11-30), ferritin 240 micrograms/L (15-200), low total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) and ESR 64 mm/hour.
hq_q.w: Anaemia of chronic disease (anaemia of inflammation) is driven by chronic pro-inflammatory cytokines (particularly interleukin-6) in active rheumatoid arthritis, chronic infection or malignancy. IL-6 stimulates hepatic synthesis of hepcidin, which degrades ferroportin iron channels on macrophages and enterocytes. This locks iron inside reticuloendothelial macrophages (producing a normal or elevated serum ferritin) while starving bone marrow erythroblasts of circulating iron (low serum iron, low transferrin/TIBC, and normocytic or mildly microcytic anaemia).
hq_q.f: Ferritin 8 with a high TIBC → iron deficiency.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
hq_q.post: Total iron binding capacity is low.

c: active synovitis in eight metacarpophalangeal and wrist joints
ferritin 240 micrograms/L (15-200), low total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)
tm.m: Chronic IL-6 inflammation -> stimulates hepatic hepcidin release -> degrades ferroportin -> traps iron in macrophages (normal/high ferritin, low serum iron, low TIBC)
tm.g: Chronic inflammation (active RA) + normocytic/mildly microcytic anaemia + low serum iron + LOW TIBC + NORMAL/HIGH ferritin = anaemia of chronic disease
x: Causes lifelong marked microcytosis (MCV typically 60 to 70 fL) out of proportion to mild anaemia with a raised red cell count and normal serum iron
True iron deficiency produces a low serum ferritin (<15 to 30 micrograms/L) and a compensatorily HIGH total iron-binding capacity (high transferrin)
Characterised by ineffective erythropoiesis with HIGH serum iron, high transferrin saturation, high ferritin and ring sideroblasts on bone marrow Perls' Prussian blue stain
Produces a macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia (MCV >100 fL) rather than a normocytic anaemia with low serum iron
f: asymptomatic Cypriot adult with Hb 118 g/L, MCV 63 fL, red cell count 5.9 x 10^12/L, normal ferritin and HbA2 of 5.1%
postmenopausal woman taking daily ibuprofen for joint pain with Hb 92 g/L, MCV 71 fL, ferritin 8 micrograms/L and raised TIBC
patient treated with isoniazid without pyridoxine developing dimorphic anaemia, high serum iron and bone marrow ring sideroblasts
patient on methotrexate who omitted folic acid or has pernicious anaemia presenting with Hb 94 g/L and MCV 114 fL

hq_q.s: A 21 year old tall, thin male university student who smokes 10 cigarettes daily presents to the Emergency Department with a 4-hour history of sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild exertional breathlessness that began while sitting watching television. He has no history of asthma, trauma or venous thromboembolism. On examination, his pulse is 92 bpm, blood pressure is 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate is 20 breaths/min and SpO2 is 97% on room air. The trachea is central, expansion is reduced on the right, and there is a hyper-resonant percussion note with quiet breath sounds over the right upper and mid zones.
hq_q.w: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in patients without clinically apparent underlying lung disease, classically affecting tall, thin young men aged 15 to 30 years who smoke (smoking increases the risk ~20-fold). Rupture of subpleural apical emphysematous blebs or bullae allows air to enter the pleural space, abolishing the negative intrapleural pressure and causing ipsilateral lung collapse. Examination reveals reduced chest expansion, hyper-resonant percussion and diminished or absent breath sounds on the affected side.
hq_q.f: The same in a man with COPD → secondary pneumothorax.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: hyper-resonant percussion note with quiet breath sounds
tm.m: Rupture of congenital/smoking-related apical subpleural bleb -> air enters pleural space -> ipsilateral lung recoil -> hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds
tm.g: Tall thin young smoker + sudden pleuritic chest pain/dyspnoea + unilateral hyper-resonant percussion and reduced breath sounds = primary spontaneous pneumothorax
x: Causes central sharp chest pain relieved by sitting forward with a pericardial friction rub and widespread concave ST elevation, with normal resonant percussion and vesicular breath sounds
Presents with fever, productive cough, dullness to percussion, bronchial breathing and coarse crepitations over the consolidated lobe
Causes sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea with hypoxia and tachycardia, but chest percussion is normal (resonant) and breath sounds are preserved
Follows direct chest wall trauma or severe coughing and causes focal bony tenderness on rib springing with normal percussion
f: central pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward with a scratchy precordial friction rub and PR-segment depression on ECG
3 days of high fever, rusty sputum, dullness to percussion, bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance at the right base
sudden pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis and SpO2 90% with normal chest percussion and vesicular breath sounds 10 days after pelvic surgery
localized chest wall pain and exquisite point tenderness over the sixth rib following a rugby tackle

hq_q.s: A 23 year old woman with no prior respiratory disease presents to the Emergency Department with a 6-hour history of sudden-onset left-sided pleuritic chest pain. She reports no breathlessness at rest or when walking along the corridor. On examination, her pulse is 84 bpm, blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate is 16 breaths/min and SpO2 is 98% on room air. An erect PA chest radiograph shows a left-sided primary spontaneous pneumothorax measuring 3 cm from the lung edge to the chest wall at the level of the hilum, with no mediastinal shift.
o: Admit for inpatient high-flow oxygen therapy
Conservative management with analgesia, written safety-net advice and outpatient review in 2 to 4 days
Immediate intercostal Seldinger chest drain insertion
Immediate simple needle aspiration in the Emergency Department
hq_q.w: The updated 2023 British Thoracic Society (BTS) Pleural Disease Guideline shifted the management of primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) from radiographic size (the old 2 cm rule) to symptom-led care. Regardless of pneumothorax size on the chest radiograph, any adult with a primary spontaneous pneumothorax who has minimal or no breathlessness, is physiologically stable and can ambulate comfortably around the department should be offered conservative management (discharge with oral analgesia, written red-flag advice and outpatient chest clinic review in 2 to 4 days), which achieves similar resolution with fewer complications and hospital days than drainage.
hq_q.f: Breathless and in pain → needle aspiration or an ambulatory device.
hq_q.ql: Under British Thoracic Society (2023) guidelines, which is the most appropriate initial management?

c: no breathlessness at rest or when walking
3 cm from the lung edge to the chest wall
tm.m: BTS 2023 symptom-based PSP algorithm -> pleural air reabsorbs spontaneously without intervention when visceral pleural defect seals -> conservative care avoids drain complications regardless of X-ray size
tm.g: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax with minimal/no breathlessness and physiological stability (regardless of cm size on CXR, BTS 2023) = conservative management + outpatient review
x: Routine hospital admission for high-flow oxygen is no longer recommended in minimally symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax
Intercostal chest drain insertion is reserved for symptomatic/breathless patients (or secondary/tension/bilateral pneumothorax) or failed aspiration
Needle aspiration or ambulatory device insertion is indicated when the patient is significantly breathless and wants rapid symptom relief, not when asymptomatic
VATS pleurodesis/bullectomy is reserved for persistent air leak (>3 to 5 days), ipsilateral recurrence, contralateral pneumothorax, bilateral presentation or high-risk professions (pilots/divers)
f: 70 year old with severe COPD and a 1.5 cm secondary spontaneous pneumothorax requiring inpatient observation and controlled oxygen
patient with severe COPD, SpO2 88% and respiratory rate 28 breaths/min with a 2.5 cm secondary spontaneous pneumothorax
23 year old with a large primary spontaneous pneumothorax who is significantly breathless on minimal exertion and requests rapid symptom relief
commercial airline pilot or patient with a persistent air leak 5 days after intercostal chest drain insertion

hq_q.s: A 66 year old woman on the Intensive Care Unit undergoes right infraclavicular subclavian central venous catheter insertion under landmark guidance for vasopressor administration. Ten minutes after the procedure, she becomes acutely dyspnoeic, tachypnoeic and anxious. On examination, her pulse is 118 bpm, blood pressure is 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate is 28 breaths/min and SpO2 falls from 97% to 89% on 4 L/min oxygen. The trachea is central, neck veins are not distended, and the right hemithorax is hyper-resonant to percussion with markedly reduced breath sounds.
o: Catheter tip malposition in the right atrium
hq_q.w: Iatrogenic pneumothorax complicates 1% to 3% of subclavian central venous catheterisations (significantly higher than internal jugular ultrasound-guided access) because the dome of the apical parietal and visceral pleura lies directly beneath the posterior aspect of the medial third of the clavicle. Inadvertent needle puncture of the lung apex allows alveolar air to enter the pleural space, causing ipsilateral lung collapse with acute hypoxia, hyper-resonant percussion and reduced breath sounds. A post-procedure chest radiograph is mandatory after subclavian or internal jugular line placement.
hq_q.f: Sudden collapse with a churning heart sound while a line is removed sitting up → air embolism.
hq_q.ql: Which complication of central venous catheterisation is most likely?

c: right infraclavicular subclavian central venous catheter insertion
Ten minutes after the procedure, she becomes acutely dyspnoeic
right hemithorax is hyper-resonant to percussion with markedly reduced breath sounds
tm.m: Subclavian needle punctures apical visceral pleura beneath the clavicle -> alveolar air enters pleural space -> ipsilateral lung collapse with hyper-resonance and quiet breath sounds
tm.g: Acute dyspnoea/hypoxia minutes after subclavian CVC insertion + unilateral hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds = iatrogenic pneumothorax
x: Right atrial catheter tip placement provokes atrial or ventricular ectopics and arrhythmias on the cardiac monitor without unilateral hyper-resonance or loss of breath sounds
Subclavian artery or vein laceration bleeding into the pleural space causes stony dullness to percussion (not hyper-resonance) and haemorrhagic hypotension
Guidewire or catheter perforation of the right atrium/ventricle causes Beck's triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds) with normal bilateral breath sounds
Occurs if the hub is left open during inspiration, causing sudden cardiovascular collapse, a 'mill-wheel' churning precordial murmur and normal bilateral lung percussion
f: runs of supraventricular tachycardia and multifocal atrial ectopics appearing immediately as the guidewire is advanced, with normal bilateral breath sounds
falling haemoglobin, hypotension (BP 80/50 mmHg) and stony dullness to percussion over the right lower and mid zones after difficult subclavian cannulation
hypotension, markedly distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus with clear equal breath sounds after central line advancement
sudden hypoxia and circulatory collapse immediately after a disconnected central line hub is exposed to air during a deep inspiration, with a churning mill-wheel murmur

hq_q.s: A 64 year old woman with no previous history of respiratory disease presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever, rigors, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and a cough productive of rusty sputum. On examination, her temperature is 38.8°C, respiratory rate is 28 breaths/min, pulse is 106 bpm and SpO2 is 87% breathing room air. There is bronchial breathing and coarse crepitations over the right lower zone. Her arterial blood gas taken on room air is shown.
hq_q.w: Respiratory failure is defined by an arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) below 8.0 kPa (60 mmHg) breathing room air at sea level. It is subdivided by the arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2): Type 1 respiratory failure is hypoxaemia (PaO2 <8.0 kPa) with a normal or low PaCO2 (<6.0 kPa), caused by ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch or right-to-left intrapulmonary shunt (such as lobar pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, acute asthma or pulmonary oedema) where hyperventilation blows off CO2.
hq_q.f: PaCO2 of 7.5 kPa → type 2 respiratory failure.
hq_q.ql: Which acid-base and oxygenation pattern does this arterial blood gas demonstrate?
lab: Arterial blood gas breathing air: pH

c: right-sided pleuritic chest pain and a cough productive of rusty sputum
tm.m: Alveolar consolidation in lobar pneumonia -> V/Q mismatch and intrapulmonary shunt -> hypoxaemia (PaO2 <8.0 kPa) drives hypoxic hyperventilation -> normal/low PaCO2 (<6.0 kPa)
tm.g: PaO2 <8.0 kPa + normal or low PaCO2 (<6.0 kPa) = Type 1 respiratory failure (vs PaO2 <8.0 kPa + PaCO2 >6.0 kPa = Type 2 respiratory failure)
x: Shows PaO2 <8.0 kPa accompanied by hypercapnia (PaCO2 >6.0 kPa) and acidaemia (pH <7.35) with normal bicarbonate
Shows PaO2 <8.0 kPa with hypercapnia (PaCO2 >6.0 kPa), a normal pH (7.35 to 7.45) and a compensatorily elevated renal bicarbonate (>28 mmol/L)
Shows a low pH (<7.35) and low bicarbonate (<22 mmol/L) as the primary abnormality
A normal room-air arterial blood gas requires a PaO2 above 10.6 kPa and pH 7.35 to 7.45
f: exhausted patient with life-threatening asthma or acute COPD exacerbation showing pH 7.24, PaO2 6.8 kPa, PaCO2 8.2 kPa and HCO3- 25 mmol/L
stable outpatient with severe COPD showing pH 7.38, PaO2 7.4 kPa, PaCO2 7.6 kPa and HCO3- 34 mmol/L
patient with septic shock or diabetic ketoacidosis showing pH 7.18, PaO2 12.4 kPa, PaCO2 2.8 kPa and HCO3- 9 mmol/L
healthy resting adult breathing room air with pH 7.40, PaO2 12.8 kPa, PaCO2 5.1 kPa and HCO3- 24 mmol/L

hq_q.s: A 46 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department after 4 days of profuse, intractable non-bilious vomiting secondary to gastric outlet obstruction from chronic peptic ulcer disease. She has been unable to keep any fluids down. On examination, her mucous membranes are dry, pulse is 104 bpm, blood pressure is 108/68 mmHg and respiratory rate is 12 breaths/min. Her arterial blood gas on room air is shown.
hq_q.w: Prolonged vomiting of gastric contents causes direct loss of hydrochloric acid (H+ and Cl-) alongside volume depletion and secondary hyperaldosteronism (which drives renal H+ and K+ wasting in exchange for Na+ and HCO3- reabsorption). This produces a primary metabolic alkalosis (high pH >7.45 and high bicarbonate >26 mmol/L, accompanied by hypochloraemia and hypokalaemia). Peripheral chemoreceptors sense the alkalaemia and depress minute ventilation (respiratory rate 12/min), causing compensatory alveolar hypoventilation and a secondary rise in PaCO2 (>6.0 kPa).
hq_q.f: pH 7.30 with a low bicarbonate → metabolic acidosis.
hq_q.ql: Which acid-base disturbance is demonstrated by her arterial blood gas?
lab: Arterial blood gas breathing air: pH

c: 4 days of profuse, intractable non-bilious vomiting
unable to keep any fluids down
tm.m: Gastric HCl loss + hypovolaemic secondary hyperaldosteronism -> raised plasma HCO3- and pH >7.45 -> chemoreceptor hypoventilation retains CO2 (raised PaCO2) to partially compensate
tm.g: Persistent vomiting + pH >7.45 + high HCO3- + compensatorily raised PaCO2 = partially compensated hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
x: Produced by hyperventilation (such as anxiety or pain), showing pH >7.45 with a LOW PaCO2 (<4.7 kPa) and normal bicarbonate
Seen in chronic COPD CO2 retainers, where pH is on the acidic side of normal (7.35 to 7.39) with a primary high PaCO2 and secondary high bicarbonate
Shows a low pH (<7.35), low bicarbonate (<22 mmol/L) and compensatory hyperventilation (low PaCO2)
Shows a profoundly low pH (<7.35) with both an elevated PaCO2 and a reduced bicarbonate (such as in cardiac arrest)
f: anxious patient hyperventilating at 32 breaths/min with pH 7.52, PaCO2 3.1 kPa and HCO3- 24 mmol/L
patient with severe chronic bronchitis and emphysema with pH 7.36, PaCO2 7.8 kPa and HCO3- 33 mmol/L
patient with severe profuse secretory diarrhoea losing lower GI bicarbonate with pH 7.26, PaCO2 3.6 kPa and HCO3- 13 mmol/L
patient following out-of-hospital respiratory and cardiac arrest with pH 7.04, PaCO2 9.2 kPa and HCO3- 14 mmol/L

hq_q.s: A 72 year old man with severe COPD and known chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with an acute infective exacerbation. During the 25-minute ambulance transfer he was given 15 L/min oxygen via a non-rebreathe reservoir mask. On arrival, he is drowsy but rousable to voice (GCS 13/15), his respiratory rate is 12 breaths/min and his SpO2 is 99%. His arterial blood gas taken on 15 L/min oxygen is shown.
o: Continue 15 L/min oxygen via the non-rebreathe mask and start nebulisers
Give an intravenous bolus of naloxone 400 micrograms
Perform immediate rapid-sequence induction and endotracheal intubation
Remove the oxygen mask completely so he breathes room air and repeat the blood gas in 1 hour
Step down immediately to a controlled 24% or 28% Venturi mask titrated to target SpO2 88% to 92%
hq_q.w: Excessive uncontrolled oxygen therapy in COPD patients with chronic CO2 retention worsens hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis through three mechanisms: release of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (increasing dead-space V/Q mismatch), the Haldane effect (oxygenated haemoglobin binds less CO2, displacing CO2 into plasma), and blunting of carotid body hypoxic ventilatory drive. Crucially,BTS Oxygen Guidelines state you must NEVER stop oxygen abruptly (because alveolar CO2 displaces O2 and oxygen stores fall much faster than CO2 clears, causing fatal rebound hypoxaemia); instead, step down immediately to a controlled 24% or 28% Venturi mask targeting SpO2 88% to 92%.
hq_q.f: No risk of CO2 retention → target 94 to 98%.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate change to his oxygen therapy?

c: severe COPD and known chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure
15 L/min oxygen via a non-rebreathe reservoir mask
tm.m: Hyperoxia in COPD -> abolishes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (worsening V/Q mismatch) + Haldane effect + reduced hypoxic drive -> acute-on-chronic CO2 retention -> step down to 24-28% Venturi (target 88-92%), never stop O2 abruptly
tm.g: COPD CO2 retainer over-oxygenated on 15 L/min mask = step down immediately to 24% or 28% Venturi mask (target SpO2 88-92%); never remove oxygen abruptly
x: Continuing 15 L/min oxygen with SpO2 99% will worsen CO2 narcosis and precipitate respiratory arrest
His hypoventilation and drowsiness are caused by hyperoxic hypercapnia (CO2 narcosis), not opioid toxicity
Because he remains rousable (GCS 13/15), stepping down controlled oxygen to 88-92%, giving air-driven nebulisers and initiating BiPAP if acidosis persists avoids invasive intubation
Abruptly removing supplemental oxygen altogether causes PaO2 to plummet below baseline within minutes while PaCO2 remains high, risking life-threatening rebound hypoxaemia
f: patient with carbon monoxide poisoning, pneumothorax or cluster headache requiring high-concentration reservoir mask oxygen
postoperative patient on a morphine PCA with pinpoint pupils, respiratory rate 6 breaths/min and acute hypercapnia
patient in respiratory arrest or profound coma (GCS 5/15) failing non-invasive ventilation who is eligible for intensive care
stable ward patient without respiratory failure whose SpO2 is 98% on 2 L/min nasal cannulae after complete recovery from mild viral illness

hq_q.s: A 41 year old woman presents to the Ambulatory Care Unit with a 2-day history of progressive aching pain and swelling in her left calf. She returned from a 22-hour long-haul flight from Sydney 5 days ago and takes a combined oral contraceptive pill. She denies chest pain, haemoptysis or shortness of breath. On examination, her pulse is 84 bpm, blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg and SpO2 is 98% on air. Her left calf circumference is 4 cm larger than the right (measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity) with pitting oedema and tenderness along the deep venous system. Her two-level DVT Wells score is 3.
o: Arrange a CT venogram of the pelvis and lower limbs
Check a quantitative plasma D-dimer first and scan only if positive
Discharge with compression stockings and oral NSAID analgesia
Perform a proximal leg vein ultrasound scan within 4 hours
