Inflammatory DIP joint swelling accompanied by dactylitis, nail pitting, onycholysis, and scaly extensor plaques
Symmetrical boggy swelling of the MCP and PIP joints with morning stiffness lasting over 1 hour
An acutely hot, erythematous, swollen single joint with severely restricted movement and systemic fever

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old woman has had aching pain in both knees for 3 years, worse after walking and at the end of the day. Her morning stiffness lasts 15 minutes.
BMI 31 kg/m². Examination shows crepitus and bony enlargement across both tibiofemoral joints, with no joint effusion, erythema or warmth.
hq_q.w: NICE recommends therapeutic exercise (local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness) as a core treatment for all people with osteoarthritis, alongside weight loss if overweight. Acupuncture, hyaluronan, TENS, and lavage are not recommended.
hq_q.f: True mechanical knee locking from an intra-articular loose body -> arthroscopic removal.
hq_q.ql: Which core non-pharmacological treatment should be offered to her?

tm.m: Quadriceps strengthening offloads the tibiofemoral joint and reduces pain alongside weight reduction
tm.g: Osteoarthritis core management -> local muscle strengthening and aerobic exercise
x: NICE explicitly advises against offering acupuncture for the management of osteoarthritis because of insufficient clinical benefit.
Arthroscopic washout does not improve pain or function in uncomplicated knee osteoarthritis without mechanical locking.
NICE recommends against intra-articular hyaluronan injections for osteoarthritis due to poor cost-effectiveness and minimal benefit.
NICE advises against transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) as an adjunct for osteoarthritis pain.
f: Chronic primary pain such as fibromyalgia in an adult where NICE supports a trial of acupuncture
True mechanical locking of the knee caused by an X-ray-confirmed intra-articular loose body
A patient requesting advice on which intra-articular viscosity supplement NICE explicitly recommends against offering
Adjunctive patient-controlled analgesia during early labour in a woman requesting non-pharmacological pain relief

hq_q.s: A 52 year old woman has had pain, swelling and morning stiffness lasting 2 hours in the small joints of both hands for a year. Her rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are positive. Hand X-rays are taken.
hq_q.w: Rheumatoid arthritis causes periarticular osteopenia, symmetrical joint space loss and marginal (periarticular) erosions, starting at the MCP and PIP joints and the ulnar styloid. Osteophytes and sclerosis point to osteoarthritis.
hq_q.f: Joint space loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts in a painful knee → osteoarthritis.
hq_q.ql: Which X-ray finding is most likely?

tm.m: Inflamed synovium erodes bone at the joint margins where cartilage does not cover it
tm.g: RA on X-ray: periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Chondrocalcinosis (Chondrocalcinosis is calcium pyrophosphate deposition, usually in the knee or wrist cartilage)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Osteophytes at the DIP joints (Osteophytes at the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes) mean osteoarthritis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pencil-in-cup deformity (Pencil-in-cup is psoriatic arthritis, usually at the DIP joints with nail disease)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Subchondral sclerosis (Subchondral sclerosis is a feature of osteoarthritis)
x: Chondrocalcinosis is calcium pyrophosphate deposition, usually in the knee or wrist cartilage.
Osteophytes at the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes) mean osteoarthritis.
Pencil-in-cup is psoriatic arthritis, usually at the DIP joints with nail disease.
Subchondral sclerosis is a feature of osteoarthritis.

hq_q.s:
An 84 year old woman with moderate dementia fell in her care home and cannot bear weight. Before the fall she walked indoors with a frame only. She is otherwise medically stable.
Her right leg is shortened and externally rotated.
X-ray shows a displaced intracapsular fracture of the right neck of femur.
hq_q.w: Displaced intracapsular hip fractures disrupt the retinacular blood supply to the femoral head and require arthroplasty. NICE recommends hemiarthroplasty when cognitive impairment or limited outdoor mobility makes total hip replacement unsuitable.
hq_q.f: Independently mobile outdoors with a single stick and no cognitive impairment -> total hip replacement.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate operation?

c: walked indoors with a frame only
tm.m: Displaced intracapsular fractures sever the medial circumflex femoral vessels supplying the femoral head
tm.g: Displaced intracapsular fracture with limited mobility or cognitive impairment -> hemiarthroplasty
x: Internal fixation of a displaced intracapsular fracture in an elderly patient carries a high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union.
Used for extracapsular intertrochanteric fractures where the femoral head blood supply remains intact.
Reserved for subtrochanteric or reverse-obliquity extracapsular fractures rather than intracapsular neck fractures.
Offered only to patients who walk outdoors with no more than a stick, are cognitively intact, and are fit for anaesthesia.
f: An undisplaced valgus-impacted intracapsular neck of femur fracture where internal fixation preserves the native head
An extracapsular intertrochanteric neck of femur fracture distal to the capsular attachment
A subtrochanteric fracture extending below the lesser trochanter of the femur
A displaced intracapsular fracture in an alert patient who walks outdoors independently with at most one stick

hq_q.s:
A 76 year old woman had a left total hip replacement 12 years ago. For 6 months she has had left groin and thigh pain when she starts to walk, which eases after a few minutes. She has had no fever.
Temperature 36.8°C. The scar is healed and the hip is cool.
CRP 3 mg/L (<5). X-ray shows a lucent line around the femoral stem.
hq_q.w: Polyethylene wear debris triggers macrophage-mediated osteolysis around the implant over years, causing start-up pain and a periprosthetic radiolucent line with normal inflammatory markers. Symptomatic aseptic loosening is treated with revision arthroplasty.
hq_q.f: Constant pain, fever, sinus tract or raised CRP -> prosthetic joint infection.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: lucent line around the femoral stem
tm.m: Polyethylene wear particles stimulate macrophage-driven periprosthetic osteolysis over years
tm.g: Late start-up thigh pain, periprosthetic lucency, and normal CRP -> aseptic loosening
x: Causes painless progressive stiffness within months of surgery with ectopic bone in soft tissues on X-ray, not a periprosthetic lucency.
Presents with sudden severe pain and inability to bear weight after a fall, with a cortical fracture line on radiograph.
Presents acutely after deep hip flexion with sudden pain and a shortened, internally rotated limb.
Causes constant rest and night pain, systemic or local inflammation, and elevated CRP rather than isolated start-up pain with normal markers.
f: Progressive painless loss of hip range of motion 3 months after surgery with calcified soft-tissue bridging on X-ray
Sudden severe thigh pain after a fall with a cortical fracture line adjacent to the femoral stem
Sudden severe hip pain after bending down with a shortened, adducted, and internally rotated leg
Constant worsening hip pain with fever, wound sinus discharge, and a raised CRP

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man had a right total hip replacement 3 months ago. For 2 weeks he has had increasing pain in the hip and feels feverish. The wound healed slowly after surgery.
Temperature 38.2°C, pulse rate 96 bpm. The hip is warm and painful on movement. There is a small area of redness at the lower end of the scar.
CRP 96 mg/L (<5).
hq_q.w: Fever, progressive hip pain, delayed wound healing, and a markedly raised CRP within months of arthroplasty indicate prosthetic joint infection until proven otherwise. Urgent orthopaedic review and joint aspiration before antibiotics are essential.
hq_q.f: Start-up pain years after surgery with normal CRP and a radiolucent zone -> aseptic loosening.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important diagnosis to exclude?

tm.m: Bacteria introduced perioperatively form an adherent biofilm on the prosthesis and periprosthetic bone
tm.g: Fever, scar erythema, painful hip movement, and raised CRP post-arthroplasty -> prosthetic joint infection
x: Develops years after surgery with mechanical start-up pain and a normal CRP rather than fever and wound erythema at 3 months.
Causes painless progressive restriction of hip movement without fever, wound erythema, or elevated inflammatory markers.
Produces shooting pain down the leg with neurological signs and normal hip examination and CRP.
Follows acute trauma with sudden inability to weight-bear rather than a 2-week febrile illness with scar erythema.
f: Mechanical start-up thigh pain 10 years after surgery with a periprosthetic radiolucent line and normal CRP
Painless progressive stiffness 4 months postoperatively with normal CRP and ectopic bone visible around the joint capsule
Pain radiating from the lower back below the knee with a positive straight-leg raise and pain-free passive hip rotation
Sudden inability to bear weight after a fall with a fracture line around the femoral stem on X-ray

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old woman presents with a 12-hour history of a severe, throbbing left-sided headache accompanied by nausea and photophobia. Before the headache started, she saw shimmering zigzag lines spreading gradually across both visual fields over 20 minutes before resolving completely. She has had similar episodes since her teenage years.
BP 118/74 mmHg, pulse rate 72 bpm. Cranial nerve, limb and fundoscopic examinations are normal.
hq_q.w: Migraine with aura is characterised by fully reversible positive or negative cortical symptoms (such as fortification spectra or paraesthesiae) that spread gradually over 5 to 60 minutes, followed by a unilateral pulsating headache with nausea and photophobia.
hq_q.f: Sudden-onset negative visual loss (amaurosis fugax) lasting 5 minutes in an older arteriopath -> transient ischaemic attack.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Cortical spreading depression (a slow wave of neuronal depolarisation across the occipital cortex) produces the positive visual aura before trigeminovascular activation causes the headache.
tm.g: Gradually spreading positive visual aura (20 min) followed by unilateral throbbing headache and photophobia -> migraine with aura
x: Cluster headache causes excruciating strictly unilateral periorbital pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes with ipsilateral autonomic signs and restlessness, not a 12-hour headache with visual aura.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with a sudden thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity within 1 minute and meningism, not recurrent stereo-typed episodes since adolescence.
Tension-type headache produces a mild-to-moderate bilateral non-pulsating band-like tightness without nausea, photophobia or visual aura.
A transient ischaemic attack causes abrupt-onset negative focal neurological deficit (such as sudden monocular blindness) rather than positive shimmering zigzags marching over 20 minutes.
f: excruciating nightly periorbital pain lasting 45 minutes with ipsilateral lacrimation, ptosis and pacing restlessness
a sudden occipital thunderclap headache reaching maximal intensity within seconds with neck stiffness
a bilateral pressing band-like headache without nausea, vomiting, photophobia or visual aura
abrupt painless curtain-like loss of vision in one eye lasting 5 minutes in a 72 year old smoker with carotid stenosis

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman has migraine with aura. She is in a new relationship and asks about contraception.
She is a non-smoker with a BMI of 24 and BP 116/72 mmHg.
hq_q.w: Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of stroke risk. Key discriminator: Migraine with aura: avoid the combined pill.
hq_q.f: Migraine without aura under 35 → combined pill is UKMEC 2.
hq_q.ql: Which method is UKMEC category 4 for her?

tm.m: Oestrogen plus aura raises ischaemic stroke risk
tm.g: Migraine with aura: avoid the combined pill
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Copper IUD (A copper IUD contains no oestrogen and is safe with aura)
Daily oral tablet preferred when oestrogen is medically contraindicated
the presentation instead showed features specific to Implant (The implant is progestogen-only and safe with aura)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Levonorgestrel IUS (The IUS is progestogen-only and safe with aura)
x: A copper IUD contains no oestrogen and is safe with aura.
Ruled out here: requires Daily oral tablet preferred when oestrogen is medically contraindicated, whereas this patient has migraine with aura, A 30 year old woman has.
The implant is progestogen-only and safe with aura.
The IUS is progestogen-only and safe with aura.

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old woman presents to her GP with a 3-week history of a new persistent bitemporal headache, jaw pain when chewing tough food and scalp tenderness when brushing her hair. Her shoulders feel stiff each morning, and she has no visual disturbance.
Both superficial temporal arteries are thickened and tender with reduced pulsation. Visual acuity is 6/6 bilaterally and fundoscopy is normal.
o: Arrange an urgent non-contrast CT head
Temporal artery biopsy before starting steroids
Trial of oral sumatriptan 50 mg stat
hq_q.w: Suspected giant cell (temporal) arteritis without visual loss requires immediate high-dose oral prednisolone (40 to 60 mg daily) started the same day to prevent irreversible anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, followed by urgent temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy within 2 weeks.
hq_q.f: Giant cell arteritis presenting with visual loss or diplopia -> immediate high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management step?

c: superficial temporal arteries are thickened and tender
tm.m: Granulomatous inflammation of medium and large extracranial carotid branches narrows the posterior ciliary arteries, risking sudden optic nerve head infarction if steroids are delayed.
tm.g: Suspected giant cell arteritis without visual loss -> start high-dose oral prednisolone today before biopsy
x: Non-contrast CT of the head does not visualise extracranial temporal artery vasculitis and delays sight-saving corticosteroid therapy.
Lumbar puncture is used for meningitis or CT-negative subarachnoid haemorrhage and has no role in diagnosing giant cell arteritis.
Steroids must never be delayed while awaiting a temporal artery biopsy because skip lesions of granulomatous arteritis remain detectable for at least 1 to 2 weeks after starting prednisolone.
Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists that cause cranial vasoconstriction in migraine and could worsen ischaemia in active giant cell arteritis.
f: a sudden thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity within 1 minute to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage
suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage presenting more than 6 hours after symptom onset with a normal CT head
never appropriate; temporal artery biopsy is performed after starting immediate high-dose corticosteroids
acute moderate-to-severe migraine attack in a young adult without vascular disease

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman presents with a 2-month history of daily headaches that are worse on lying flat and waking, with transient visual obscurations lasting seconds. Her BMI is 38 kg/m² and she takes no medications.
Bilateral papilloedema is present with no focal deficit. Contrast CT head and CT venography are normal, and lumbar puncture opening pressure is 35 cm H2O with normal CSF constituents.
hq_q.w: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension typically affects women of childbearing age with obesity, presenting with pressure headaches, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus and bilateral papilloedema, confirmed by normal neuroimaging (including venography) and CSF opening pressure >25 cm H2O.
hq_q.f: Postpartum headache with seizures and filling defect in the superior sagittal sinus on CT venography -> cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Impaired arachnoid granulations CSF absorption and raised central venous pressure in obesity elevate intracranial pressure without hydrocephalus or mass lesion.
tm.g: Obese young woman + bilateral papilloedema + normal CT venogram + CSF opening pressure >25 cm H2O -> idiopathic intracranial hypertension
x: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is excluded here by the normal CT venography.
Chronic tension-type headache never causes bilateral papilloedema or an elevated CSF opening pressure of 35 cm H2O.
A pituitary macroadenoma causes bitemporal hemianopia and optic atrophy from chiasmal compression and would be visible on the CT head.
An intracranial tumour or abscess causing papilloedema would be demonstrated on the contrast CT head.
f: a prothrombotic postpartum patient with headache, focal seizures and an empty delta sign on CT venography
a bilateral pressing headache without papilloedema, visual obscurations or raised CSF opening pressure
progressive bitemporal hemianopia and hypopituitarism with a sellar mass compressing the optic chiasm on imaging
progressive morning headache with focal contralateral hemiparesis and a ring-enhancing mass on CT head

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man attends the emergency department after being struck on the right side of the head with a bottle. On arrival his GCS was 12 (E3 V4 M5) with equal reactive pupils.
One hour later his GCS falls to 9 (E2 V2 M5) and his right pupil becomes fixed and dilated at 7 mm. BP is 168/88 mmHg and pulse rate is 52 bpm.
hq_q.w: Expanding supratentorial mass effect forces the medial temporal lobe (uncus) to herniate transtentorially across the free edge of the tentorium cerebelli, compressing the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CN III) parasympathetic fibres and causing a fixed, dilated ipsilateral pupil.
hq_q.f: Bilateral pinpoint pupils with decerebrate posturing and respiratory arrest -> pontine haemorrhage.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of his pupil abnormality?

c: right pupil becomes fixed and dilated
BP is 168/88 mmHg and pulse rate is 52 bpm
tm.m: Superficial pupilloconstrictor parasympathetic Edinger-Westphal fibres on the dorsomedial aspect of the ipsilateral third cranial nerve are compressed against the tentorial notch by the herniating uncus.
tm.g: Falling GCS + ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil + Cushing reflex (hypertension and bradycardia) -> uncal herniation
x: Diffuse axonal injury causes immediate coma from rotational deceleration shearing of white-matter tracts rather than a delayed unilateral blown pupil with Cushing response.
An isolated optic nerve (CN II) injury causes a relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) with a preserved consensual constriction, not an absolute fixed dilated pupil and falling GCS.
Primary pontine haemorrhage disrupts descending sympathetic pathways, producing bilateral pinpoint (miotic) pupils rather than a unilateral dilated pupil.
A post-ictal state follows a witnessed convulsive seizure, improves over 30 to 60 minutes, and does not cause a persistently fixed unilateral dilated pupil with bradycardia.
f: immediate deep coma from the moment of a high-speed road traffic collision with petechial corpus callosum haemorrhages
monocular visual loss after direct orbital trauma with a relative afferent pupillary defect and GCS 15
sudden coma, tetraparesis and bilateral pinpoint reactive pupils
transient unilateral limb weakness recovering over 1 hour after a witnessed focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man who takes aspirin 75 mg daily tripped and struck his forehead 2 hours ago. He lost consciousness for approximately 1 minute and has vomited once since arrival.
His GCS was 15 on initial assessment at 30 minutes, but at 2 hours post-injury his GCS has dropped to 13 (E3 V4 M6). There are no signs of skull fracture.
hq_q.w: Under NICE head injury guidelines, a CT head scan is required within 1 hour if GCS is <13 initially, GCS is <15 at 2 hours post-injury, or there is a suspected skull fracture, seizure, focal deficit or >=2 vomits.
hq_q.f: Age >=65 years or dangerous mechanism or >30 minutes retrograde amnesia with some loss of consciousness -> CT head within 8 hours.
hq_q.ql: Which clinical feature in this patient mandates a CT head scan within 1 hour?

c: at 2 hours post-injury his GCS has dropped to 13
tm.m: Failure to maintain or recover a full GCS of 15 by 2 hours post-injury strongly predicts an expanding intracranial haematoma requiring urgent neurosurgical intervention.
tm.g: GCS <15 at 2 hours after head injury -> CT head within 1 hour
x: Age 65 years or over following loss of consciousness or amnesia is an indication for a CT head within 8 hours, not within 1 hour.
Brief loss of consciousness alone without a 1-hour red flag only triggers an 8-hour CT scan when paired with age >=65, coagulopathy or dangerous mechanism.
NICE head injury guidelines include anticoagulant therapy (warfarin, DOACs, heparin) as an indication for CT, whereas single antiplatelet aspirin alone does not mandate a 1-hour CT.
In adults, two or more episodes of post-traumatic vomiting are required to trigger a 1-hour CT head scan.
f: the question asked which factor alongside 1 minute of loss of consciousness requires a CT head within 8 hours
a 68 year old with 1 minute loss of consciousness whose GCS remained 15 at 2 hours, requiring CT within 8 hours
anticoagulant treatment with warfarin or apixaban in a patient with head injury and no other red flags (CT within 8 hours)
the patient had experienced 2 or more distinct episodes of vomiting after the head injury

hq_q.s:
A 44 year old woman had a sudden, severe occipital headache 3 days ago while lifting shopping. It peaked within a minute. She did not go to hospital. She now feels well apart from a mild headache.
Neurological examination is normal and there is no neck stiffness.
CT head is normal.
o: Repeat CT head with contrast in 1 week
hq_q.w: CT sensitivity falls after 6 hours. LP done at least 12 hours after onset looks for xanthochromia from broken-down blood.
hq_q.f: CT within 6 hours of onset is normal → SAH is very unlikely.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: sudden, severe occipital headache 3 days ago
tm.m: CT misses more bleeds after 6 hours; bilirubin in CSF shows a bleed
tm.g: Thunderclap headache with a normal CT days later: lumbar puncture for xanthochromia
f: CT within 6 hours of onset is normal with a normal examination
Tonic-clonic limb jerking, tongue biting, and prolonged post-ictal confusion
the presentation instead showed features specific to MRI of the cervical spine (A thunderclap headache points to the brain, not the cervical spine)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Repeat CT head with contrast in 1 week (CT sensitivity for subarachnoid blood falls rapidly after 6 hours)
x: Ruled out here: requires CT within 6 hours of onset is normal with a normal examination, whereas this patient has sudden, severe occipital headache 3 days ago, peaked within a minute.
Ruled out here: requires Tonic-clonic limb jerking, tongue biting, and prolonged post-ictal confusion, whereas this patient has sudden, severe occipital headache 3 days ago, peaked within a minute.
A thunderclap headache points to the brain, not the cervical spine.
CT sensitivity for subarachnoid blood falls rapidly after 6 hours

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman was admitted 5 days ago with an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage secured by coiling on day 1. She takes oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours.
Today (day 5) she becomes drowsy and develops new grade 3/5 weakness of her right arm and leg. Temperature is 37.1°C and BP is 138/84 mmHg.
hq_q.w: Delayed cerebral ischaemia secondary to cerebral arterial vasospasm is the leading cause of focal neurological deterioration between days 4 and 14 after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, once rebleeding, acute hydrocephalus and hyponatraemia have been excluded by CT and blood tests.
hq_q.f: Progressive drowsiness with dilated temporal horns and ventricles on repeat CT head -> acute communicating hydrocephalus.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
hq_q.post: CT head shows no new bleeding and no hydrocephalus.

c: new grade 3/5 weakness of her right arm
no new bleeding and no hydrocephalus
tm.m: Oxyhaemoglobin released from lysed erythrocytes in the basal cisterns scavenges nitric oxide and stimulates endothelin-1, inducing severe smooth muscle constriction in cerebral arteries.
tm.g: New focal neurological deficit on days 4-14 post-SAH with normal repeat CT and normal sodium -> cerebral vasospasm
x: Repeat non-contrast CT head explicitly shows no ventricular enlargement, ruling out obstructive or communicating hydrocephalus.
Her serum sodium is completely normal at 136 mmol/L (135-146), ruling out hyponatraemia as the cause of her confusion and hemiparesis.
Repeat non-contrast CT head shows no new subarachnoid or intracerebral blood, excluding aneurysmal rebleeding.
A persistent new focal hemiparesis emerging on day 5 after subarachnoid haemorrhage with normal electrolytes and CT is classic for delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm.
f: progressive drowsiness with upward gaze palsy and dilated ventricles on repeat CT head
generalised drowsiness, hypovolaemia and a serum sodium of 121 mmol/L with raised urinary sodium
a sudden second thunderclap headache, coma and fresh hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns on repeat CT
fluctuating gaze deviation and eyelid twitching with epileptiform discharges on urgent EEG

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old man with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease presents to the emergency department with a 2-hour history of a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds, accompanied by vomiting and photophobia.
Temperature 36.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 154/92 mmHg. He has marked neck stiffness. Non-contrast CT head demonstrates hyperdense blood filling the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures.
hq_q.w: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (PKD1/PKD2 mutations) causes defective polycystin expression in arterial smooth muscle and internal elastic lamina, predisposing ~10% of patients to saccular ('berry') aneurysms at arterial bifurcations in the circle of Willis.
hq_q.f: Cavernous sinus syndrome or pulsatile proptosis after skull base trauma -> carotid-cavernous fistula.
hq_q.ql: Which vascular abnormality explains his increased predisposition to this bleed?

c: hyperdense blood filling the basal cisterns
tm.m: Defective polycystin-1 or polycystin-2 weakens the tunica media and internal elastic lamina at circle of Willis branch points, forming thin-walled saccular berry aneurysms.
tm.g: Subarachnoid haemorrhage in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease -> rupture of circle of Willis berry aneurysm
x: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is linked to prothrombotic states or nephrotic syndrome rather than polycystic kidney disease, and does not fill the basal cisterns with arterial blood.
While hypertension increases wall shear stress, the specific structural cause of subarachnoid haemorrhage in ADPKD is saccular berry aneurysms in the circle of Willis.
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease causes renal and hepatic cysts, not hypersplenism or autoimmune thrombocytopenia.
Uraemic platelet dysfunction occurs in end-stage renal failure and causes mucosal oozing or pericarditis rather than aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.
f: nephrotic syndrome with urinary protein loss >3.5 g/day and a superior sagittal sinus clot on CT venography
a deep basal ganglia or thalamic intraparenchymal haemorrhage from Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms in chronic hypertension
mucocutaneous petechiae and epistaxis with a platelet count of 8 × 10⁹/L
epistaxis and prolonged skin bleeding time in a patient with end-stage renal failure and urea >40 mmol/L

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man was struck on the left temple by a cricket ball 2 hours ago. He lost consciousness for 1 minute, then walked off the pitch and conversed lucidly, before becoming drowsy.
His GCS is 11, his left pupil is dilated, and there is left temporal swelling. CT head shows a biconvex, lens-shaped hyperdense collection beneath the left temporal bone.
hq_q.w: An acute extradural haematoma typically follows a blow to the thin pterion that lacerates the middle meningeal artery. It presents with a lucid interval followed by rapid decline and a lens-shaped (biconvex) hyperdense clot bounded by cranial suture lines.
hq_q.f: Crescent-shaped (concave) hyperdense collection crossing suture lines after a fall -> acute subdural haematoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: High-pressure arterial bleeding from the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery strips the periosteal dura from the inner table of the skull up to the tight suture lines.
tm.g: Temporal blow + lucid interval + biconvex lens-shaped collection on CT -> extradural haematoma
x: Simple concussion has a completely normal CT head scan without any intracranial blood collection or pupillary dilatation.
A chronic subdural haematoma presents over weeks in older patients with a hypodense crescentic collection crossing suture lines rather than an acute lens-shaped arterial clot.
An intracerebral haemorrhage lies within the brain parenchyma itself rather than forming a lens-shaped extra-axial collection between skull and dura.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage tracks within the CSF spaces of the basal cisterns and sulci rather than forming a focal biconvex extradural mass.
f: brief loss of consciousness after a sports collision with a persistently normal GCS of 15 and normal CT head
fluctuating confusion over 4 weeks in an 82 year old with a crescent-shaped hypodense collection on CT
sudden right hemiplegia and hypertension in a 70 year old with a hyperdense haematoma inside the left putamen
sudden thunderclap headache with hyperdense blood filling the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man who takes clopidogrel 75 mg daily fell and struck his head 6 hours ago. Over the past 2 hours he has become progressively drowsy.
GCS is 12, pulse rate 64 bpm, BP 156/88 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows a crescent-shaped (concave) hyperdense collection over the right hemisphere that crosses the coronal suture line, confirming an acute subdural haematoma.
hq_q.w: Subdural haematomas result from tearing of the low-pressure cortical bridging veins as they cross the subdural space from the cerebral cortex to the dural venous sinuses. Age-related or alcohol-related cerebral atrophy stretches these veins, making them vulnerable to deceleration shearing.
hq_q.f: Biconvex extradural haematoma beneath a fractured pterion -> middle meningeal artery.
hq_q.ql: Which vessels are most commonly torn in this condition?

tm.m: Inertial movement of the brain relative to the fixed dural sinuses shears the taut cortical bridging veins, allowing venous blood to spread freely throughout the potential subdural space.
tm.g: Crescent-shaped subdural haematoma crossing suture lines -> torn cortical bridging veins
x: Rupture of an anterior cerebral or anterior communicating artery aneurysm causes subarachnoid and interhemispheric haemorrhage rather than a convexity subdural haematoma.
Laceration of the middle meningeal artery beneath the pterion causes a biconvex extradural haematoma that cannot cross cranial suture lines.
A posterior communicating artery aneurysm presents with a painful third nerve palsy and subarachnoid haemorrhage, not a traumatic crescentic subdural clot.
Vertebral artery dissection or rupture follows neck trauma and causes posterior circulation stroke or posterior fossa subarachnoid haemorrhage.
f: subarachnoid blood concentrated in the anterior interhemispheric fissure from a ruptured aneurysm
a biconvex lens-shaped extradural haematoma bounded by suture lines beneath a squamous temporal fracture
a painful oculomotor nerve palsy with ptosis and a dilated pupil followed by subarachnoid haemorrhage
lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) and neck pain following sudden cervical hyperextension

hq_q.s:
An 80 year old man taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation fell 2 days ago. Today he has a worsening headache and left-sided weakness. He took his morning dose of apixaban 4 hours ago.
GCS is 13 with grade 4/5 left hemiparesis. CT head shows a right subdural haematoma with 6 mm of midline shift. Neurosurgery has been contacted.
o: Continue apixaban at a reduced dose
Switch to an intravenous heparin infusion
hq_q.w: In life-threatening or intracranial haemorrhage on a direct factor Xa inhibitor (apixaban or rivaroxaban), immediately stop the anticoagulant and reverse factor Xa inhibition using intravenous andexanet alfa (or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate if andexanet alfa is unavailable) alongside neurosurgical referral.
hq_q.f: Intracranial haemorrhage on warfarin -> intravenous 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus intravenous phytomenadione (vitamin K).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological step?

c: morning dose of apixaban 4 hours ago
right subdural haematoma with 6 mm of midline shift
tm.m: Active factor Xa inhibition prevents thrombin generation and drives fatal haematoma expansion unless apixaban is stopped and reversed with a decoy Xa protein (andexanet alfa) or PCC.
tm.g: Intracranial haemorrhage on apixaban -> stop and reverse apixaban immediately
x: Continuing any dose of anticoagulation during an acute intracranial bleed with midline shift risks fatal haematoma expansion and coning.
Vitamin K restores synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors in warfarin anticoagulation and has no effect on direct factor Xa inhibitors like apixaban.
Unfractionated heparin is a potent anticoagulant and is strictly contraindicated in acute intracranial haemorrhage.
Apixaban inhibits factor Xa rather than platelet aggregation, and routine platelet transfusion does not reverse direct oral anticoagulants.
f: secondary stroke prevention several weeks later only if neurosurgery confirms complete resolution and very high thrombotic risk
asymptomatic supratherapeutic INR >8.0 in a patient taking warfarin without active bleeding
bridging a mechanical mitral valve in a patient without haemorrhage
intracranial haemorrhage in a patient with severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count <50 × 10⁹/L)

hq_q.s:
A 22 year old woman presents with a 12-hour history of severe headache, fever, photophobia and neck stiffness. She has no focal deficit or papilloedema.
Temperature 39.2°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg. Lumbar puncture yields turbid CSF with white cell count 1,500/mm³ (92% neutrophils), protein 1.8 g/L (0.15-0.45) and CSF glucose 1.2 mmol/L alongside a paired plasma glucose of 6.0 mmol/L.
hq_q.w: Acute bacterial meningitis produces turbid CSF with a marked neutrophilic pleocytosis (>1,000 cells/mm³), raised protein (>1.0 g/L) and low CSF glucose (<50% of paired plasma glucose). Viral meningitis gives lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose.
hq_q.f: Subacute meningitis with lymphocytic CSF, very high protein (>2 g/L) and low CSF:plasma glucose ratio -> tuberculous meningitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: CSF glucose 1.2 mmol/L alongside a paired plasma glucose of 6.0 mmol/L
tm.m: Proliferating pyogenic bacteria and recruited neutrophils consume CSF glucose via glycolysis and disrupt the blood-brain barrier, leaking plasma proteins into the subarachnoid space.
tm.g: Turbid CSF with neutrophil predominance + high protein + CSF glucose <50% plasma glucose -> bacterial meningitis
x: Cryptococcal meningitis occurs in severely immunocompromised (e.g. advanced HIV) patients and produces a lymphocytic CSF with positive India ink or cryptococcal antigen.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with a sudden afebrile thunderclap headache and uniformly blood-stained or xanthochromic CSF rather than 1,500 neutrophils/mm³ and glucose 1.2 mmol/L.
Tuberculous meningitis presents subacutely over weeks and produces a predominantly lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis rather than acute turbid 92% neutrophilic fluid.
Viral meningitis produces clear CSF with a lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal or mildly raised protein and a normal CSF:plasma glucose ratio.
f: subacute headache in a patient with HIV and CD4 count 30 cells/mm³ showing lymphocytic CSF and positive cryptococcal antigen
a thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity within seconds with xanthochromia on CSF spectrophotometry
a 3-week prodrome of fever, night sweats and sixth nerve palsy with lymphocytic CSF, high protein and low glucose
clear CSF showing 120 lymphocytes/mm³, protein 0.55 g/L and CSF glucose 3.8 mmol/L (plasma 5.8 mmol/L)

hq_q.s:
A 20 year old man attends the emergency department with a 6-hour history of fever, headache, photophobia and a spreading purple rash. Aged 10 he had severe anaphylaxis with stridor and hypotension after oral amoxicillin.
Temperature 39.5°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 92/56 mmHg. Examination reveals neck stiffness and a widespread non-blanching petechial and purpuric rash over his trunk and legs.
hq_q.w: Under NICE meningitis guidelines, patients with suspected meningococcal septicaemia or bacterial meningitis who have a documented history of severe penicillin or cephalosporin anaphylaxis should receive empirical intravenous chloramphenicol (which penetrates the blood-brain barrier well and is bactericidal against Neisseria meningitidis).
hq_q.f: No history of penicillin anaphylaxis -> empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily.
hq_q.ql: Which empirical intravenous antibiotic is most appropriate?

c: severe anaphylaxis with stridor and hypotension after oral amoxicillin
tm.m: Lipid-soluble chloramphenicol crosses the blood-brain barrier freely to inhibit bacterial 50S ribosomal peptidyl transferase without beta-lactam cross-reactivity.
tm.g: Suspected meningococcal meningitis/septicaemia + documented penicillin anaphylaxis -> IV chloramphenicol
x: Third-generation cephalosporins share a beta-lactam ring and are avoided in patients with a history of life-threatening penicillin anaphylaxis.
Macrolides such as clarithromycin do not cross the blood-brain barrier in sufficient concentrations to treat bacterial meningitis.
Aminoglycosides penetrate cerebrospinal fluid poorly when given intravenously and have inadequate activity against Neisseria meningitidis.
Vancomycin is a large glycopeptide with zero activity against Gram-negative diplococci such as Neisseria meningitidis.
f: first-line empirical hospital therapy for bacterial meningitis in a patient without severe beta-lactam allergy
atypical community-acquired pneumonia in a penicillin-allergic adult
severe Gram-negative urosepsis in a patient with normal renal function
adjunctive cover alongside ceftriaxone when penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae is suspected

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old man is admitted to the high-dependency unit with meningococcal meningitis confirmed on CSF PCR for Neisseria meningitidis. He lives in a shared flat with four flatmates where they cook and eat together daily. Three weeks ago he attended a birthday party, and 4 days ago he sat in a lecture theatre.
The hospital health protection team traces contacts to arrange single-dose oral ciprofloxacin chemoprophylaxis.
o: Everyone attending his lectures this week
Friends who attended the party 3 weeks ago
His household in the last 7 days
Lecturers who taught him this term
Ward staff who examined him on admission
hq_q.w: UKHSA guidance recommends single-dose oral ciprofloxacin chemoprophylaxis for close prolonged household contacts (such as flatmates) exposed during the 7 days before symptom onset, plus healthcare staff directly exposed to airway secretions without a mask.
hq_q.f: Doctor or paramedic who performed endotracheal intubation or suctioning without droplet protection -> also give single-dose ciprofloxacin.
hq_q.ql: Which group of contacts should receive antibiotic chemoprophylaxis?

c: lives in a shared flat with four flatmates
tm.m: Nasopharyngeal carriage of Neisseria meningitidis spreads via prolonged close household droplet exposure during the 7 days preceding index illness onset.
tm.g: Meningococcal meningitis chemoprophylaxis target -> close household contacts in the 7 days before onset
x: Casual classroom or lecture theatre attendance does not constitute prolonged household-type contact and does not warrant chemoprophylaxis unless an institutional outbreak occurs.
Contact tracing for meningococcal prophylaxis is strictly limited to the 7 days prior to symptom onset in the index case.
Brief non-intimate contact in a lecture hall carries negligible transmission risk and does not require antibiotic prophylaxis.
Healthcare workers only require chemoprophylaxis if their mouth or nose was directly exposed to large-droplet respiratory secretions (e.g. unprotected intubation).
f: mass vaccination and prophylaxis declared by public health during a multi-case university hall outbreak
never indicated; exposure 21 days before symptom onset falls outside the 7-day infectious window
never indicated for brief non-household classroom exposure
an anaesthetist who performed emergency endotracheal intubation and airway suctioning without a surgical mask

hq_q.s:
A 46 year old man presents with a 4-day history of fever and headache. Today he became confused, had a generalised seizure, and earlier complained of smelling burning rubber.
Temperature 38.6°C, pulse rate 98 bpm. He is disorientated with expressive dysphasia. CSF shows 80 lymphocytes/mm³, protein 0.85 g/L and normal glucose. Brain MRI shows hyperintense T2 signal in the left medial temporal lobe.
hq_q.w: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) is the commonest cause of sporadic fatal necrotising encephalitis in the UK, characteristically affecting the medial temporal lobes. CSF viral PCR for HSV-1/2 DNA is the diagnostic gold standard.
hq_q.f: Immunocompromised HIV patient with CD4 <100 cells/mm³ and subacute meningitis -> CSF cryptococcal antigen and India ink stain.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation confirms the most likely causative organism?

tm.m: Reactivated HSV-1 travels retrogradely along trigeminal or olfactory nerves to cause haemorrhagic necrosis of the uncus and medial temporal cortex, releasing viral DNA into CSF.
tm.g: Fever + olfactory hallucinations/seizures + temporal lobe MRI signal + lymphocytic CSF -> CSF herpes simplex PCR
x: Blood cultures are mandatory in febrile encephalopathy to exclude bacterial sepsis, but HSV-1 encephalitis is not viraemic on routine bacterial blood culture.
CSF Gram stain identifies bacteria in purulent neutrophilic meningitis but does not detect intracellular viruses like HSV-1.
India ink microscopy visualises encapsulated Cryptococcus neoformans yeasts in fungal meningitis rather than herpesviruses.
Unmatched IgG oligoclonal bands in CSF indicate chronic intrathecal B-cell synthesis in multiple sclerosis rather than acute viral encephalitis.
f: confirming bacteraemia in acute meningococcal or pneumococcal septicaemia
rapid identification of Gram-positive diplococci in turbid neutrophilic CSF from pneumococcal meningitis
suspected cryptococcal meningitis in a patient with advanced HIV and a CD4 count below 100 cells/mm³
confirming dissemination in time for a diagnosis of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old man was admitted 48 hours ago with fever, confusion and a tonic-clonic seizure. Intravenous aciclovir was started immediately.
A lumbar puncture performed 12 hours after symptom onset showed 45 lymphocytes/mm³, but the initial CSF herpes simplex PCR has returned negative. Brain MRI today shows bilateral asymmetrical temporal lobe oedema, and he remains febrile and confused.
o: Repeat the LP and continue aciclovir
Stop antivirals and give IV methylprednisolone
hq_q.w: CSF HSV PCR can be falsely negative during the first 24 to 72 hours of herpes simplex encephalitis. When clinical and MRI features strongly suggest HSV encephalitis, continue intravenous aciclovir and repeat the lumbar puncture after 48 to 72 hours.
hq_q.f: Repeat CSF HSV PCR on day 4 is negative AND brain MRI is normal -> consider stopping aciclovir and investigating alternatives.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next management step?

c: initial CSF herpes simplex PCR has returned negative
tm.m: Early parenchymal viral replication within temporal lobe neurones may precede detectable CSF viral shedding in the first 48 hours of illness.
tm.g: High clinical/MRI suspicion of HSV encephalitis + negative day-1 CSF PCR -> continue IV aciclovir and repeat LP
x: Adding corticosteroids without continuing antiviral therapy or repeating the LP does not address active viral replication.
Immunosuppressive therapy for autoimmune encephalitis should not replace aciclovir until a repeat LP at 48-72 hours has definitively excluded HSV-1.
Stopping intravenous aciclovir on the basis of a single day-1 PCR in a patient with bilateral temporal lobe MRI changes risks fatal necrotising encephalitis.
Intravenous ganciclovir is the treatment for cytomegalovirus (CMV) ventriculoencephalitis in severely immunocompromised hosts, not sporadic temporal lobe HSV-1 encephalitis.
f: adjunctive therapy before or with the first antibiotic dose in acute pneumococcal bacterial meningitis
confirmed anti-NMDA receptor or anti-LGI1 autoimmune encephalitis after repeat HSV PCR is negative
a repeat CSF HSV PCR taken >72 hours after onset is negative and brain MRI is completely normal
confirmed cytomegalovirus encephalitis or retinitis in a patient with advanced HIV or post-transplant immunosuppression

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old woman is admitted to the medical ward with fever, dysphasia and temporal lobe seizures and is started on high-dose intravenous aciclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours) for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis.
She has type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension treated with metformin and ramipril. Her admission blood tests show serum creatinine 104 µmol/L (60-120) and baseline eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m².
hq_q.w: High-dose intravenous aciclovir is excreted renally and is poorly soluble in urine. Dehydration or rapid infusion causes needle-shaped crystal precipitation in the distal renal tubules, requiring intravenous hydration and daily renal function monitoring.
hq_q.f: eGFR falls below 50 mL/min/1.73 m² -> reduce the intravenous aciclovir dosing frequency according to renal function.
hq_q.ql: Which blood test requires daily monitoring during intravenous aciclovir therapy?

tm.m: Intratubular supersaturation of poorly soluble aciclovir precipitates birefringent needle-shaped crystals in the collecting ducts, causing acute obstructive tubular injury.
tm.g: High-dose intravenous aciclovir therapy -> monitor kidney function (urea, creatinine and eGFR) and maintain hydration
x: Intravenous aciclovir does not disturb parathyroid function or calcium homeostasis; foscarnet causes hypocalcaemia.
Short-term intravenous aciclovir has no clinically significant effect on serum cholesterol or triglycerides.
Aciclovir causes obstructive crystal nephropathy in the renal tubules rather than acute drug-induced pancreatitis.
Intravenous aciclovir has no effect on thyroid hormone synthesis or pituitary TSH secretion.
f: intravenous foscarnet therapy for ganciclovir-resistant CMV infection, which chelates ionised calcium
monitoring systemic retinoid (isotretinoin) or protease inhibitor therapy
acute epigastric pain in a patient taking azathioprine or sodium valproate
6-monthly monitoring of a patient taking amiodarone or lithium carbonate

hq_q.s:
A 44 year old man presents with a 5-day history of worsening left-sided headache, fever and progressive right hemiparesis. Two weeks ago he had an upper molar dental abscess extracted.
Temperature 38.2°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg. He has grade 4/5 right hemiparesis and papilloedema, and is HIV negative. Contrast CT head shows a thin-walled ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontoparietal lobe with oedema.
hq_q.w: A cerebral abscess presents with headache, fever and focal neurological deficit following contiguous spread (dental, sinus or ear sepsis) or haematogenous seeding. Contrast CT/MRI shows a ring-enhancing lesion; lumbar puncture is contraindicated.
hq_q.f: Multiple ring-enhancing basal ganglia lesions in an HIV-positive patient with CD4 <100 cells/mm³ -> cerebral toxoplasmosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Haematogenous or venous spread of oral streptococci and anaerobes into the cerebral white matter triggers liquefactive necrosis encapsulated by a vascularised collagen capsule.
tm.g: Fever + focal deficit + recent dental abscess + ring-enhancing brain lesion in HIV-negative patient -> cerebral abscess
x: An acute ischaemic stroke presents with sudden-onset maximal deficit rather than a 5-day febrile progression and a ring-enhancing capsule.
Cerebral toxoplasmosis is an opportunistic reactivation in severely immunocompromised patients (HIV with CD4 <100 cells/mm³), and this patient is HIV negative.
Glioblastoma presents subacutely without fever or recent dental infection and typically shows an irregular thick shaggy rim crossing the corpus callosum.
Cerebral metastases occur at the grey-white matter junction in patients with a primary malignancy (such as lung or breast cancer) and do not cause acute high fever after dental extraction.
f: abrupt-onset right hemiplegia and aphasia in a patient with atrial fibrillation and a wedge-shaped hypodensity on CT
multiple basal ganglia ring-enhancing lesions in an untreated HIV patient with a CD4 count of 40 cells/mm³
an afebrile 64 year old with progressive personality change and an irregular butterfly mass crossing the corpus callosum
an afebrile 68 year old smoker with weight loss, haemoptysis and multiple grey-white junction lesions

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman presents with a 4-day history of severe frontal headache, high fever and new behavioural disinhibition. Three weeks ago she had untreated purulent acute frontal sinusitis.
Temperature 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg. There is right frontal sinus tenderness. Contrast MRI shows a 3 cm ring-enhancing abscess in the right frontal lobe contiguous with the sinus.
hq_q.w: Frontal lobe brain abscesses arising by contiguous spread from paranasal sinusitis or odontogenic infections are most commonly caused by microaerophilic streptococci of the Streptococcus anginosus (milleri) group, frequently mixed with oral obligate anaerobes such as Bacteroides or Fusobacterium.
hq_q.f: Brain abscess following penetrating cranial trauma or neurosurgical craniotomy -> Staphylococcus aureus.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely causative organism?

c: ring-enhancing abscess in the right frontal lobe
tm.m: Streptococcus anginosus group bacteria colonise the paranasal sinuses and spread via valveless diploic veins across the posterior wall of the frontal sinus, where they produce tissue-destroying hydrolytic enzymes.
tm.g: Frontal lobe brain abscess secondary to frontal sinusitis -> Streptococcus anginosus (milleri) group
x: Listeria monocytogenes is a food-borne intracellular bacillus that causes meningitis or rhombencephalitis (brainstem encephalitis) in elderly, pregnant or immunosuppressed patients, not sinogenic frontal abscesses.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is associated with malignant otitis externa in elderly diabetics or chronic suppurative otitis media rather than acute frontal sinusitis in a young adult.
Staphylococcus aureus is the predominant pathogen in brain abscesses following penetrating head trauma, compound skull fracture or neurosurgical procedures.
Toxoplasma gondii is an intracellular protozoan that causes multiple basal ganglia abscesses in severely immunocompromised patients (HIV CD4 <100 cells/mm³).
f: meningitis or brainstem encephalitis in a 74 year old or pregnant woman after eating soft unpasteurised cheese
a temporal lobe or cerebellar abscess secondary to necrotising otitis externa in an elderly diabetic patient
a cerebral abscess developing 2 weeks after a compound depressed skull fracture or neurosurgical craniotomy
multiple ring-enhancing basal ganglia lesions in a patient with advanced HIV and CD4 count 45 cells/mm³

hq_q.s:
A 36 year old woman is admitted with a 5-day history of fever, frontal headache and left facial weakness. She has chronic rhinosinusitis and has no drug allergies.
Temperature 38.5°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg. Contrast CT head shows a 3.5 cm ring-enhancing brain abscess in the right frontal lobe. Neurosurgery plans aspiration and requests empirical intravenous antibiotics.
hq_q.w: For a sinogenic or odontogenic brain abscess without penicillin allergy, UK empirical therapy is high-dose intravenous ceftriaxone plus metronidazole to cover Streptococcus anginosus group, Enterobacterales and obligate anaerobes.
hq_q.f: Brain abscess following neurosurgery or penetrating head trauma -> add vancomycin (or flucloxacillin) to cover staphylococci.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate empirical intravenous antibiotic combination?

c: ring-enhancing brain abscess in the right frontal lobe
tm.m: Third-generation cephalosporins and metronidazole both achieve high bactericidal concentrations inside cerebral abscess pus, covering microaerophilic streptococci and beta-lactamase-producing anaerobes.
tm.g: Sinogenic/odontogenic brain abscess without penicillin allergy -> IV ceftriaxone + IV metronidazole
x: Macrolides and tetracyclines are bacteriostatic, penetrate the blood-brain barrier poorly and do not reliably cover Streptococcus anginosus or anaerobes in brain abscess.
Flucloxacillin and rifampicin target staphylococcal infections and miss the anaerobic and Gram-negative flora of chronic rhinosinusitis.
Intravenous gentamicin crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly and neither gentamicin nor amoxicillin covers beta-lactamase-producing Bacteroides anaerobes.
Vancomycin and rifampicin target MRSA and coagulase-negative staphylococci and provide zero cover for Gram-negative bacilli or Bacteroides species.
f: ambulatory treatment of moderate community-acquired pneumonia with atypical cover
methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus prosthetic valve endocarditis or spinal implant infection
empirical synergistic therapy for Listeria monocytogenes meningitis or enterococcal endocarditis
a post-neurosurgical ventriculoperitoneal shunt infection caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis

hq_q.s:
A 7 year old girl is reviewed because her teacher has noticed 20 brief episodes each day where she stops speaking and stares blankly for 5 to 10 seconds before resuming her sentence as if nothing happened. She never falls.
Neurological examination is normal. Asking her to hyperventilate for 2 minutes in clinic reproduces a typical staring episode with eyelid flutter.
hq_q.w: Childhood absence epilepsy presents at ages 4 to 10 with frequent brief (5 to 15 second) staring spells with abrupt onset and offset, provocation by hyperventilation, and 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave discharges on EEG.
hq_q.f: Staring episodes lasting 1 to 2 minutes preceded by epigastric rising aura, lip-smacking automatisms and post-ictal confusion -> focal impaired awareness seizure.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: resuming her sentence as if nothing happened
tm.m: Synchronised oscillatory burst firing in thalamocortical relay loops (driven by T-type calcium channels) transiently suspends conscious awareness without loss of postural tone.
tm.g: Frequent 5-10s staring spells + immediate recovery + provoked by hyperventilation -> absence seizures
x: Normal childhood daydreaming occurs when bored rather than mid-sentence, can be interrupted immediately by calling the child's name, and is not triggered by hyperventilation.
Temporal lobe focal impaired awareness seizures last longer (1 to 2 minutes), are accompanied by oro-alimentary automatisms (lip-smacking) and are followed by post-ictal confusion.
Myoclonic seizures present in adolescence with sudden brief shock-like jerks of the upper limbs shortly after morning awakening rather than isolated childhood staring spells.
Night terrors are parasomnias arising from slow-wave sleep during the first third of the night, not daytime classroom staring episodes.
f: infrequent staring when bored in class that stops immediately on tactile or verbal prompting with a normal hyperventilation test
a 90-second episode preceded by a rising epigastric sensation, lip-smacking and 15 minutes of post-ictal confusion
a 15 year old dropping their breakfast cup due to sudden morning bilateral arm jerks after sleep deprivation
a child sitting bolt upright screaming inconsolably 90 minutes after falling asleep with complete morning amnesia

hq_q.s: A 15 year old girl has had jerks of her arms in the mornings, especially when tired, and had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure last month. EEG shows generalised polyspike and wave discharges. She is diagnosed with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
hq_q.w: Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen myoclonic and absence seizures. Levetiracetam is used in girls who may become pregnant.
hq_q.f: Focal seizures in an adult → carbamazepine is an option.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most likely to make her myoclonic jerks worse?

tm.m: Sodium channel blockers can worsen myoclonic and absence seizures
tm.g: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: avoid carbamazepine
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Clobazam (Clobazam is a benzodiazepine that can be used in myoclonic epilepsy)
Generalised tonic-clonic seizures recur with post-ictal confusion and tongue-biting
a 25 year old man
the presentation instead showed features specific to Topiramate (Contraindicated in pregnancy and without highly effective contraception due to teratogenicity)
x: Clobazam is a benzodiazepine that can be used in myoclonic epilepsy.
Ruled out here: requires Generalised tonic-clonic seizures recur with post-ictal confusion and tongue-biting, whereas this patient has juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, A 15 year old girl has.
Ruled out here: requires a 25 year old man, whereas this patient has juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, A 15 year old girl has.
Contraindicated in pregnancy and without highly effective contraception due to teratogenicity

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man with known epilepsy is having a continuous generalised tonic-clonic seizure on the floor of a supermarket. The convulsion has lasted 7 minutes without recovery of consciousness.
Paramedics have arrived, placed him in a safe lateral position and administered high-flow oxygen, but attempts at peripheral intravenous cannulation have failed. His airway is patent and capillary blood glucose is 5.4 mmol/L (4.0-7.8).
hq_q.w: Convulsive status epilepticus (a tonic-clonic seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer) requires immediate first-line benzodiazepine termination. When intravenous access is not immediately available in the community or pre-hospital setting, NICE recommends buccal midazolam (or rectal diazepam) as first-line treatment.
hq_q.f: Intravenous access is already established in hospital -> intravenous lorazepam 4 mg (up to two doses).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug and route?

c: attempts at peripheral intravenous cannulation have failed
tm.m: Transmucosal absorption of water-soluble midazolam across the vascular buccal mucosa rapidly potentiates central GABA-A chloride channels to terminate status epilepticus without IV access.
tm.g: Convulsive status epilepticus (>=5 min) without intravenous access -> buccal midazolam
x: Phenobarbital is a third-line hospital anticonvulsant with slow intramuscular absorption and severe respiratory depression risk, not pre-hospital first-line therapy.
Intravenous lorazepam is first-line when an IV cannula is in place, but here cannulation has failed and treatment must not be delayed by repeated IV attempts.
Phenytoin requires secure intravenous access, cardiac monitoring and a 20-minute infusion as second-line therapy after two benzodiazepine doses have failed.
Nothing should ever be placed for swallowing into the mouth of a patient having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure because of the high risk of airway obstruction and aspiration.
f: established status epilepticus in hospital refractory to benzodiazepines and first second-line intravenous agents
a patient in status epilepticus on the hospital ward with a patent intravenous cannula in situ
hospital second-line therapy when seizures persist after two doses of intravenous lorazepam
short-term oral anxiolysis in a fully conscious adult patient

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man presents with a 4-month history of slurred, nasal speech, choking on liquids and 5 kg weight loss. He has no diplopia or numbness.
Examination shows a wasted, fasciculating tongue, a brisk jaw jerk and hyperreflexia in all four limbs with extensor plantar responses. External ocular movements and pinprick/vibration sensation are normal.
hq_q.w: Bulbar-onset motor neurone disease produces mixed lower motor neurone signs (tongue wasting and fasciculations) and upper motor neurone signs (brisk jaw jerk, limb hyperreflexia and extensor plantars) while sparing sensation and eye movements.
hq_q.f: Fatigable ptosis, diplopia and bulbar weakness worsening through the day with normal reflexes -> myasthenia gravis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: External ocular movements and pinprick/vibration sensation are normal
tm.m: Selective degeneration of corticobulbar/corticospinal upper motor neurones and brainstem/anterior horn lower motor neurones causes mixed UMN and LMN weakness while sparing sensory neurones and oculomotor nuclei.
tm.g: Mixed LMN (tongue wasting/fasciculations) + UMN (brisk jaw jerk/limb hyperreflexia) + normal sensation/eye movements -> motor neurone disease
x: A brainstem stroke presents hyperacutely rather than progressing over 4 months with tongue fasciculations, and typically involves sensory tracts or cerebellar signs.
Multiple sclerosis causes central demyelination with sensory symptoms, optic neuritis and internuclear ophthalmoplegia, never lower motor neurone tongue wasting and fasciculations.
Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable ptosis, diplopia and dysarthria that worsen in the evening, without tongue fasciculations, brisk jaw jerk or extensor plantars.
Syringobulbia (brainstem syrinx) damages the spinal trigeminal nucleus and causes dissociated facial pain and temperature sensory loss alongside vertigo and nystagmus.
f: sudden-onset dysphagia, vertigo, ipsilateral Horner syndrome and contralateral spinothalamic sensory loss
a 28 year old woman with subacute internuclear ophthalmoplegia, sensory loss and periventricular plaques on MRI
fatigable bilateral ptosis, diplopia and nasal speech that worsen by evening with normal reflexes and no fasciculations
onion-skin loss of pain and temperature sensation over the face with rotary nystagmus and Arnold-Chiari malformation

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man has had progressive weakness of his hands and legs for 8 months. Motor neurone disease is being considered.
hq_q.w: MND is purely motor. Sensory loss, eye movement palsies or bladder problems suggest another cause.
hq_q.f: Fasciculations with brisk reflexes in the same limb → typical of MND.
hq_q.ql: Which finding most suggests a diagnosis other than motor neurone disease?

c: Motor neurone disease is being considered
tm.m: MND is purely motor
tm.g: Sensory loss argues against MND
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Brisk reflexes (Brisk reflexes are upper motor neurone signs that fit MND)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Emotional lability (Emotional lability is pseudobulbar affect and is common in MND)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fasciculations (Fasciculations are a lower motor neurone sign typical of MND)
Papilloedema and headache with normal MRI suggesting idiopathic intracranial hypertension
x: Brisk reflexes are upper motor neurone signs that fit MND.
Emotional lability is pseudobulbar affect and is common in MND.
Fasciculations are a lower motor neurone sign typical of MND.

Ruled out here: requires Papilloedema and headache with normal MRI suggesting idiopathic intracranial hypertension, whereas this patient has Motor neurone disease is being considered, A 58 year old man has.

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old woman with bulbar-onset motor neurone disease attends the multidisciplinary neurology clinic. She has severe dysphagia managed via a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube and is distressed by constant pooling and drooling of thin watery saliva (sialorrhoea). She has no history of glaucoma or urinary retention.
Pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg, SpO2 97% breathing air.
hq_q.w: In motor neurone disease, drooling (sialorrhoea) results from impaired bulbar swallowing. NICE recommends an antimuscarinic such as oral glycopyrronium bromide (which does not cross the blood-brain barrier) as first-line therapy.
hq_q.f: Painful muscle spasticity in motor neurone disease -> oral baclofen or tizanidine.
hq_q.ql: Which medication is most appropriate as first-line treatment for her drooling?

c: pooling and drooling of thin watery saliva
tm.m: Competitive blockade of M3 muscarinic receptors on the parotid and submandibular acinar glands reduces watery salivary secretion without crossing the blood-brain barrier.
tm.g: Troublesome sialorrhoea (drooling) in motor neurone disease -> antimuscarinic (glycopyrronium bromide)
x: Baclofen is a GABA-B receptor agonist used to treat upper motor neurone muscle spasticity rather than salivary gland secretion.
Pyridostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used in myasthenia gravis that increases muscarinic stimulation and actively worsens salivation and bronchial secretions.
Quinine reduces motor end-plate excitability to treat painful nocturnal muscle cramps in MND but has no effect on sialorrhoea.
Riluzole is a glutamate-release inhibitor that modestly prolongs tracheostomy-free survival in ALS by 2 to 3 months but does not relieve drooling.
f: painful lower-limb upper motor neurone spasticity and clonus interfering with transfers
symptomatic relief of fatigable muscle weakness in acetylcholine-receptor-positive myasthenia gravis
frequent painful nocturnal calf cramps in motor neurone disease
disease-modifying therapy to modestly prolong survival in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman presents with a 2-month history of drooping eyelids and double vision that are absent on waking but worsen progressively by the evening. Her voice becomes nasal during long phone calls.
Examination shows bilateral ptosis that worsens markedly during 60 seconds of sustained upgaze. Pupillary light reflexes, limb tendon reflexes and sensation are normal.
hq_q.w: Myasthenia gravis is caused by autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. It presents with fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness that worsens with sustained use and spares the pupils and tendon reflexes.
hq_q.f: Proximal leg weakness with areflexia and autonomic dry mouth that improves after brief exercise -> Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: worsens markedly during 60 seconds of sustained upgaze
Pupillary light reflexes, limb tendon reflexes and sensation are normal
tm.m: Autoantibodies block and internalise postsynaptic skeletal muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, so physiological rundown of acetylcholine release during sustained contraction causes fatigable weakness.
tm.g: Fatigable ptosis, diplopia and nasal speech worse in the evening with normal pupils and reflexes -> myasthenia gravis
x: Botulism causes an acute descending flaccid paralysis with prominent autonomic blockade (fixed dilated pupils, dry mouth and ileus) after contaminated food.
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome causes proximal lower-limb weakness, depressed reflexes that augment after exercise, and dry mouth, usually paraneoplastic to small-cell lung cancer.
Multiple sclerosis causes sustained demyelinating episodes (such as optic neuritis or internuclear ophthalmoplegia) lasting days to weeks with hyperreflexia, not diurnal fatigable ptosis.
A compressive oculomotor nerve palsy causes a constant unilateral 'down-and-out' eye with a fixed dilated pupil rather than fluctuating bilateral fatigable ptosis with normal pupils.
f: acute descending paralysis with fixed dilated pupils and constipation 24 hours after eating home-canned food
a 65 year old smoker with proximal leg weakness, dry mouth and absent knee jerks that return after 10 seconds of maximal quadriceps contraction
subacute unilateral painful visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect and brisk limb reflexes
acute unilateral complete ptosis, an eye deviated down and out, and a dilated sluggish pupil from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm

hq_q.s:
A 22 year old man presents to the emergency department with severe diffuse pain and swelling in his thighs and calves 24 hours after running his first marathon in warm weather. He has passed small volumes of dark reddish-brown urine today and took oral ibuprofen after the race.
Pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg. Both quadriceps and gastrocnemius compartments are swollen and tender.
hq_q.w: Exertional rhabdomyolysis releases creatine kinase, potassium and myoglobin from necrotic muscle. Filtered myoglobin causes dark brown urine and a positive dipstick for blood (3+) with no red cells on microscopy, risking acute tubular necrosis.
hq_q.f: Lifelong exercise-induced muscle cramps that improve after a 'second wind' -> McArdle disease (myophosphorylase deficiency).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
hq_q.post: Urine dipstick shows blood 3+ with no red cells on microscopy.

c: blood 3+ with no red cells on microscopy
tm.m: Sarcolemmal rupture releases haem-containing myoglobin that is freely filtered by the glomerulus, reacts with orthotolidine peroxidase on urine dipstick, and forms nephrotoxic casts in acidic renal tubules.
tm.g: Extreme exertion + dark brown urine + CK 50,000 IU/L + dipstick blood 3+ without RBCs on microscopy -> rhabdomyolysis
x: Dermatomyositis presents subacutely over weeks to months with proximal weakness, heliotrope eyelid rash and Gottron papules rather than acute myoglobinuria the day after a marathon.
McArdle disease (type V glycogenosis) causes lifelong exercise intolerance since childhood with a characteristic 'second wind' phenomenon after 10 minutes of gentle exercise.
Polymyalgia rheumatica affects adults aged over 50 years and causes morning shoulder and pelvic girdle stiffness with a raised ESR and a completely normal serum creatine kinase.
He is 22 years old, takes no lipid-lowering therapy and developed acute muscle necrosis immediately after a marathon.
f: a 2-month history of proximal shoulder and hip weakness with a violaceous eyelid rash and Gottron papules over the knuckles
lifelong cramping within minutes of starting exercise that resolves after resting briefly (the second wind phenomenon)
a 72 year old woman with bilateral shoulder and hip morning stiffness, ESR 78 mm/hr and a normal creatine kinase
a 66 year old man developing subacute thigh aching 4 weeks after starting atorvastatin 80 mg daily

hq_q.s:
A 25 year old man presents with a 12-month history of distal hand weakness and difficulty releasing his grip after shaking hands. His father developed bilateral cataracts aged 40 years and required a permanent pacemaker.
Examination reveals frontal balding, bilateral ptosis, temporalis wasting, weak ankle dorsiflexion, thenar percussion myotonia and bilateral lenticular opacities.
hq_q.w: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is an autosomal dominant CTG trinucleotide repeat disorder causing distal muscle weakness, delayed grip relaxation (myotonia), ptosis, temporalis wasting, frontal balding, early cataracts and cardiac conduction block.
hq_q.f: Young boy with proximal pelvic girdle weakness, Gowers' sign and calf pseudohypertrophy -> Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: difficulty releasing his grip after shaking hands
father developed bilateral cataracts aged 40 years and required a permanent pacemaker
tm.m: An expanded CTG repeat in the DMPK gene on chromosome 19q sequesters RNA-binding splicing proteins, impairing skeletal muscle chloride channels (causing myotonia) and cardiac conduction tissue.
tm.g: Grip myotonia + distal weakness + ptosis/frontal balding + early cataracts/cardiac conduction disease -> myotonic dystrophy
x: Becker muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive dystrophinopathy causing proximal lower-limb weakness and calf pseudohypertrophy without myotonia, ptosis or cataracts.
Duchenne muscular dystrophy presents in boys aged 3 to 5 years with severe proximal pelvic weakness, Gowers' sign and loss of ambulation by age 12.
Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy causes facial weakness (inability to whistle or close eyes tightly) and winged scapulae without grip myotonia, cataracts or heart block.
Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable ptosis and diplopia but never produces grip myotonia, distal muscle wasting, cataracts or cardiac conduction defects.
f: an adolescent boy with proximal hip weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy and raised CK without grip myotonia
a 4 year old boy with waddling gait, calf pseudohypertrophy and using his hands to climb up his thighs from the floor
inability to whistle, prominent scapular winging and biceps weakness without grip myotonia or cataracts
fluctuating ptosis and diplopia that worsen in the evening and resolve with rest, with normal hand grip release

hq_q.s:
A 44 year old office worker who leans on his elbows at his desk presents with a 3-month history of numbness in his right little finger and the medial half of his ring finger, and clumsiness fastening buttons.
Examination shows wasting of the first dorsal interosseous muscle, weak finger abduction, sensory loss over the medial one-and-a-half digits, and a positive Tinel's sign behind the medial epicondyle.
hq_q.w: Cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve entrapment at the medial epicondyle) causes sensory loss over the little finger and medial half of the ring finger alongside weakness and wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles (interossei and hypothenar).
hq_q.f: Numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers worse at night with thenar wasting -> median nerve (carpal tunnel syndrome).
hq_q.ql: Which peripheral nerve is affected?

c: little finger and the medial half of his ring finger
tm.m: Chronic compression of the ulnar nerve (C8-T1) within the cubital tunnel impairs conduction to the dorsal ulnar cutaneous nerve and deep motor branch supplying the interossei.
tm.g: Medial 1.5 finger sensory loss + weak finger abduction/first dorsal interosseous wasting + positive Tinel's at elbow -> ulnar nerve
x: The axillary nerve (C5-C6) supplies the deltoid muscle and regimental badge skin patch over the lateral shoulder, not the hand.
The median nerve supplies the lateral 3.5 digits (thumb, index, middle) and the LOAF muscles (thenar eminence), sparing the little finger and dorsal interossei.
The musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C7) supplies biceps brachii and sensation to the lateral forearm rather than the digits or intrinsic hand muscles.
The radial nerve supplies the wrist and finger extensors and dorsal first web space sensation, causing wrist drop rather than medial finger numbness.
f: inability to abduct the shoulder from 15 to 90 degrees and numbness over the lateral deltoid after anterior shoulder dislocation
nocturnal paraesthesiae in the thumb, index and middle fingers with wasting of abductor pollicis brevis
weak elbow flexion and supination with sensory loss over the radial aspect of the forearm
wrist drop and finger extension weakness with numbness over the dorsal first web space

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old cyclist presents after falling onto his right arm. Radiographs confirm a displaced fracture of the midshaft of the right humerus. He is unable to extend his right wrist or fingers.
Examination shows right wrist drop, preserved triceps reflex, and reduced pinprick sensation over the dorsal first web space between the thumb and index finger.
hq_q.w: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove of the midshaft humerus. Midshaft fractures commonly injure the radial nerve, causing paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors (wrist drop) and numbness over the dorsal first web space.
hq_q.f: Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus or anterior shoulder dislocation -> axillary nerve injury.
hq_q.ql: Which peripheral nerve has been injured?

c: fracture of the midshaft of the right humerus
unable to extend his right wrist
dorsal first web space between the thumb and index finger
tm.m: Displaced bone fragments in the spiral groove compress or contuse the radial nerve distal to the branches supplying the long and medial heads of triceps, paralysing the forearm extensor compartment.
tm.g: Midshaft humeral fracture + wrist drop + dorsal first web space numbness -> radial nerve
x: The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus and its injury causes deltoid paralysis and lateral shoulder numbness, not wrist drop.
The median nerve is injured in supracondylar humeral fractures or at the wrist, causing weak thumb opposition/abduction and palmar sensory loss over the lateral 3.5 digits.
The musculocutaneous nerve innervates the anterior arm flexors (biceps, brachialis) and lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle and its injury causes clawing of the ring and little fingers and interosseous weakness, not wrist drop.
f: a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus with weak shoulder abduction and regimental badge numbness
a supracondylar humeral fracture causing inability to flex the index DIP joint and thumb IP joint (anterior interosseous/median nerve)
weakness of elbow flexion and supination with numbness along the lateral border of the forearm
a medial epicondyle fracture causing numbness of the little finger and weakness of finger abduction

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old woman presents with a 2-year history of numbness and tingling in her right thumb, index and middle fingers. Nocturnal wrist splinting for 6 months and a local carpal tunnel corticosteroid injection have failed.
Examination reveals wasting of the right thenar eminence and weak thumb abduction. Nerve conduction studies show severe median nerve axonal loss across the wrist.
hq_q.w: Carpal tunnel syndrome accompanied by constant sensory deficit, motor weakness, thenar muscle wasting, or failure of conservative measures (nocturnal wrist splinting and local corticosteroid injection) requires surgical carpal tunnel decompression (division of the flexor retinaculum) to prevent permanent axonal loss.
hq_q.f: Mild intermittent nocturnal paraesthesiae without motor weakness or wasting -> nocturnal neutral-position wrist splint.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next management step?

c: right thumb, index and middle fingers
Nocturnal wrist splinting for 6 months and a local carpal tunnel corticosteroid injection have failed
wasting of the right thenar eminence
