tm.m: Chronic ischaemic compression of the median nerve beneath the transverse carpal ligament has progressed from demyelination to motor axonal degeneration of the recurrent motor branch.
tm.g: Carpal tunnel syndrome with thenar wasting / severe NCS changes / failed splint and steroid injection -> surgical decompression
x: Continuing conservative splinting in the presence of established thenar muscle wasting allows irreversible denervation of abductor pollicis brevis.
Oral corticosteroids are not recommended by NICE for carpal tunnel syndrome and cannot reverse severe mechanical axonal compression.
Tendon gliding exercises do not relieve severe mechanical compression when thenar wasting and axonal loss are already established.
She has already failed a steroid injection and now has objective thenar muscle wasting and severe axonal loss requiring surgical release.
f: new-onset mild nocturnal tingling in the lateral three digits with normal power and no thenar wasting
acute idiopathic facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy) presenting within 72 hours of onset
post-operative rehabilitation after flexor tendon repair
mild-to-moderate carpal tunnel syndrome without motor weakness or thenar wasting after splinting alone

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old man has believed for 5 months that a television news presenter is sending him private messages of love through the news. He has no hallucinations and his speech and behaviour are otherwise normal. He works full time and looks after himself.
Mental state examination shows a fixed false belief and no other abnormal findings.
hq_q.w: A persistent, circumscribed, non-bizarre delusion (such as erotomania) lasting over 3 months with preserved occupational functioning, normal affect, and absence of hallucinations or formal thought disorder is diagnostic of delusional disorder.
hq_q.f: Third-person voices and thought broadcasting → schizophrenia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: An encapsulated mono-delusional belief system persists without disorganized speech, negative symptoms, or functional decline
tm.g: Fixed delusion >3 months with normal occupational function and no hallucinations -> delusional disorder
f: pervasive lifelong suspiciousness and mistrust of others without a fixed encapsulated delusion
auditory hallucinations and delusions occurring concurrently with a full manic or depressive episode
third-person running commentary voices, thought broadcasting and marked occupational deterioration
lifelong eccentric behaviour, magical thinking and social anxiety without a fixed delusion
x: Paranoid personality disorder causes pervasive lifelong suspiciousness and grudge-holding without a fixed encapsulated erotomanic delusion.
Schizoaffective disorder requires prominent manic or depressive mood episodes occurring concurrently with first-rank psychotic symptoms.
Schizophrenia presents with auditory hallucinations, Schneiderian passivity phenomena, disorganized speech, or negative symptoms with marked functional decline.
Schizotypal disorder is characterized by lifelong eccentric behaviour, magical thinking, and odd speech rather than a single encapsulated delusion.

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man is brought to the psychiatric clinic by his parents after stopping work 6 weeks ago. He appears perplexed and distressed, explaining that his upstairs neighbour uses a device to suck thoughts directly out of his head, leaving his mind completely blank mid-sentence.
His urine drug screen is negative.
hq_q.w: Thought withdrawal is a Schneiderian first-rank symptom of schizophrenia in which the patient experiences their thoughts being actively removed from their mind by an external agency, often explaining a sudden arrest in the train of thought.
hq_q.f: He believes others can hear his thoughts → thought broadcast.
hq_q.ql: What is this symptom called?

c: suck thoughts directly out of his head
tm.m: Loss of the ego boundary leads to attributing subjective thought arrest to external extraction
tm.g: Delusional belief that an external force is taking thoughts out of the patient's head -> thought withdrawal
f: feeling that his emotions of anger or sadness are being forced on him by an external agency
an objective sudden stop in his train of speech with no delusional belief about an external force
believing that his unspoken thoughts are diffusing out of his head so passers-by can hear them
believing that his neighbour is placing foreign thoughts into his head against his will
x: Passivity of affect is the experience that one's emotions or feelings are being externally imposed and controlled by an outside agent.
Thought block is the objective sudden arrest in the flow of speech without the delusional belief that an external agent extracted the thought.
Thought broadcast is the delusion that one's private thoughts are escaping silently so that others around can hear or share them.
Thought insertion is the first-rank delusion that alien thoughts belonging to an outside person are being placed into one's mind.

hq_q.s:
A 20 year old university student was admitted to the psychiatric ward after developing abrupt-onset persecutory delusions and second-person auditory hallucinations over 48 hours following his final examinations. He does not use cannabis or illicit substances.
After 3 weeks of low-dose antipsychotic therapy, his psychotic symptoms resolved completely and he has returned to full-time study.
hq_q.w: Under ICD-11, acute and transient psychotic disorder is characterised by an abrupt onset of delusions, hallucinations, or perplexity (within 2 weeks) often precipitated by acute stress, with complete resolution back to premorbid functioning within 1 to 3 months.
hq_q.f: Psychotic symptoms with depression in the same episode → schizoaffective disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Acute stress triggers a brief, self-limiting dopaminergic psychotic episode that remits fully within 3 months
tm.g: Abrupt onset of non-organic psychosis resolving completely within 3 weeks -> acute and transient psychotic disorder
f: grandiose delusions with elated mood, pressured speech and no need for sleep lasting 10 days
acute paranoia and hallucinations beginning immediately after smoking high-potency cannabis
a single fixed non-bizarre delusion persisting for 6 months without hallucinations
persistent third-person hallucinations and negative symptoms continuing despite two antipsychotic trials
x: Bipolar affective disorder presents with sustained episodes of mania (elevated mood, grandiosity, and decreased need for sleep) or depression.
Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder requires evidence of recent heavy cannabis intoxication or withdrawal, which is excluded here.
Delusional disorder requires a single persistent non-bizarre delusion lasting at least 3 months without prominent hallucinations.
Schizophrenia requires persistent psychotic symptoms for at least 1 month (or 6 months under DSM-5) without rapid complete return to baseline within 3 weeks.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man with schizophrenia started haloperidol 5 days ago. He is now confused and stiff.
Temperature 39.8°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 168/102 mmHg, then 104/62 mmHg an hour later. He is sweating with lead-pipe rigidity in all limbs. Reflexes are normal and there is no clonus.
hq_q.w: NMS develops over days with lead-pipe rigidity, fever, autonomic instability and high CK. Stop the antipsychotic and cool.
hq_q.f: Clonus and brisk reflexes after adding tramadol to sertraline → serotonin syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Dopamine blockade disturbs temperature control and muscle tone
tm.g: Fever, lead-pipe rigidity and high CK days after an antipsychotic is NMS
f: rigidity and fever during a general anaesthetic
Give 3, take 3, within 1 hour.
clonus and brisk reflexes after adding tramadol to sertraline
poorly controlled Graves' disease + emergency appendicectomy
x: Ruled out here: requires rigidity and fever during a general anaesthetic, whereas this patient has started haloperidol 5 days ago, lead-pipe rigidity.
Ruled out here: requires Give 3, take 3, within 1 hour, whereas this patient has started haloperidol 5 days ago, lead-pipe rigidity.
Ruled out here: requires clonus and brisk reflexes after adding tramadol to sertraline, whereas this patient has started haloperidol 5 days ago, lead-pipe rigidity.
Ruled out here: requires poorly controlled Graves' disease + emergency appendicectomy, whereas this patient has started haloperidol 5 days ago, lead-pipe rigidity.

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old man with a 4 year history of paranoid schizophrenia continues to experience distressing command auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions. He has completed two sequential trials of oral risperidone (6 mg daily for 10 weeks) and oral olanzapine (20 mg daily for 10 weeks), with confirmed adherence.
Baseline neutrophil count and ECG are normal.
hq_q.w: Under NICE CG178, clozapine must be offered for treatment-resistant schizophrenia that has not responded adequately to sequential 6 to 8 week trials of at least two different antipsychotics (including one second-generation drug).
hq_q.f: He does not take tablets reliably → consider a depot.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate drug?

tm.m: Clozapine's weak D2 and potent 5-HT2A/D4 receptor antagonism provides unique efficacy in treatment-resistant schizophrenia
tm.g: Schizophrenia refractory to two adequate antipsychotic trials -> offer clozapine with mandatory FBC monitoring
f: marked hyperprolactinaemia and galactorrhoea on risperidone with good symptom control
relapse driven by poor adherence to oral tablets in a patient who prefers monthly injections
good remission of positive symptoms already achieved on his current olanzapine regimen
visual hallucinations and delusions in Parkinson's disease where D2 potency must be minimised
x: Switching to a third standard oral antipsychotic such as aripiprazole delays initiating clozapine, the only agent proven in treatment resistance.
A long-acting depot injection such as haloperidol decanoate addresses covert non-adherence, whereas his adherence to oral therapy is confirmed.
Continuing olanzapine after 10 weeks at maximal therapeutic dose without response leaves his psychosis untreated.
Quetiapine is a standard second-generation antipsychotic that is inferior to clozapine once two adequate trials have failed.

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has taken clozapine for 4 months. She has had a sore throat and fever for 1 day.
Temperature 38.4°C, pulse rate 104 bpm. Her pharynx is red.
hq_q.w: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis. A low neutrophil count means stopping it at once under specialist advice.
hq_q.f: Chest pain and tachycardia in the first weeks → check troponin for myocarditis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important test?

tm.m: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis
tm.g: Infection on clozapine: urgent full blood count
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Blood cultures (Cultures matter, but agranulocytosis must be excluded first with a full blood count)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Liver function (Liver tests do not detect clozapine agranulocytosis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Throat swab (Urgent full blood count is mandatory first to exclude life-threatening agranulocytosis)
chest pain and a fast pulse in the first weeks
x: Cultures matter, but agranulocytosis must be excluded first with a full blood count.
Liver tests do not detect clozapine agranulocytosis.
Urgent full blood count is mandatory first to exclude life-threatening agranulocytosis
Ruled out here: requires chest pain and a fast pulse in the first weeks, whereas this patient has clozapine for 4 months, sore throat and fever.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman attends general practice reporting 6 weeks of low mood and tearfulness since being made redundant from her office job. She still enjoys reading to her children in the evenings, maintains her appetite, and sleeps 6 hours a night. She has no thoughts of self-harm.
She completes a Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and scores 8 out of 27.
hq_q.w: On the 9-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), scores are banded as 0 to 4 minimal, 5 to 9 mild, 10 to 14 moderate, 15 to 19 moderately severe, and 20 to 27 severe depression.
hq_q.f: PHQ-9 of 22 → severe depression.
hq_q.ql: Which is the severity of her depression?

tm.m: PHQ-9 quantifies depressive symptom frequency over 2 weeks across nine DSM core criteria
tm.g: PHQ-9 score of 5 to 9 -> mild depression
f: a PHQ-9 score of 3 out of 27 with transient sadness and full daily enjoyment
a PHQ-9 score of 12 out of 27 with persistent anhedonia and poor concentration
a PHQ-9 score of 17 out of 27 with marked daily functional impairment
a PHQ-9 score of 23 out of 27 with psychomotor retardation and pervasive hopelessness
x: A minimal or subclinical PHQ-9 score is between 0 and 4 out of 27.
Moderate depression on the PHQ-9 corresponds to a score between 10 and 14 out of 27.
Moderately severe depression on the PHQ-9 corresponds to a score between 15 and 19 out of 27.
Severe depression on the PHQ-9 corresponds to a score of 20 to 27 out of 27.

hq_q.s: A 74 year old woman with ischaemic heart disease takes aspirin 75 mg daily. She has moderate depression and is starting sertraline. She has never had a peptic ulcer.
hq_q.w: SSRIs with aspirin or NSAIDs raise the risk of GI bleeding, so consider gastroprotection with a PPI.
hq_q.f: She is 80 and on sertraline with confusion → check sodium for hyponatraemia.
hq_q.ql: Which additional drug should be considered?

tm.m: SSRIs reduce platelet serotonin, adding to aspirin's bleeding risk
tm.g: SSRI with aspirin in an older person: add omeprazole
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Famotidine (An H2 blocker gives weaker protection than a PPI and is not the recommended choice)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Misoprostol (Misoprostol protects against NSAID ulcers but causes diarrhoea and is not used for SSRI with aspirin)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sodium alginate (An alginate eases reflux symptoms; it does not protect against GI bleeding)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sucralfate (Sucralfate coats ulcers but is not used to prevent bleeding with an SSRI and aspirin; a PPI is)
x: An H2 blocker gives weaker protection than a PPI and is not the recommended choice.
Misoprostol protects against NSAID ulcers but causes diarrhoea and is not used for SSRI with aspirin.
An alginate eases reflux symptoms; it does not protect against GI bleeding.
Sucralfate coats ulcers but is not used to prevent bleeding with an SSRI and aspirin; a PPI is.

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old man has had depression for 6 months. His marriage has ended and he has lost his job. He says he has a plan to hang himself at the weekend and has given away his possessions and written letters to his children.
He has poor eye contact and appears hopeless. He has no psychotic symptoms.
hq_q.w: A depressed patient disclosing a specific, lethal suicide plan accompanied by preparatory final acts (giving away possessions and writing farewell letters) is at imminent suicide risk and requires same-day crisis team assessment.
hq_q.f: Passive thoughts with strong protective factors → safety plan and close follow-up.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: plan to hang himself at the weekend
tm.m: Final preparatory acts combined with a specific lethal method and timeframe indicate imminent suicidal intent
tm.g: Active suicide plan with preparatory acts -> same-day crisis resolution team assessment
f: starting sertraline in a low-risk adult aged 32 with moderate depression and no suicidal ideation
mild-to-moderate depression with intact protective factors and no thoughts of self-harm
mild situational distress after bereavement with strong family support and no suicidal intent
more severe depression in a patient with strong social support and no active suicidal plans
x: Reviewing in 2 weeks is dangerous when the patient has a concrete plan to end his life this weekend.
A routine outpatient psychological therapy waiting list leaves an acutely suicidal patient unsupported during an imminent crisis.
Providing a leaflet and helpline number alone is inadequate when final preparatory acts and a lethal plan are present.
Dispensing an SSRI and sending him home is unsafe because antidepressants take weeks to work and provide a means of overdose.

hq_q.s:
A 31 year old woman has had elevated mood, less need for sleep and more energy for 5 days. She has started several new projects at work and talks quickly. She is still working and managing her finances, and her family are not worried about her safety.
There are no delusions or hallucinations. Thyroid function is normal and urine drug screen is negative.
hq_q.w: Hypomania is characterised by persistently elevated or irritable mood, increased energy, pressured speech, and reduced need for sleep lasting at least 4 consecutive days, without psychotic symptoms (delusions or hallucinations) and without severe occupational impairment requiring hospitalisation.
hq_q.f: Symptoms for 10 days and she cannot work → mania.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: still working and managing her finances
tm.m: Mild-to-moderate dopaminergic and noradrenergic elevation increases energy and speech without loss of reality testing
tm.g: Elevated mood >=4 days with preserved occupational functioning and no psychosis -> hypomania
f: two years of fluctuating mild mood swings that never meet full criteria for hypomania or depression
10 days of elated mood with grandiose delusions, reckless spending of life savings and total insomnia
racing thoughts and psychomotor agitation combined with profound tearful hopelessness and suicidal ideation
third-person auditory hallucinations and thought insertion occurring alongside a manic episode
x: Cyclothymia is a chronic 2 year pattern of subthreshold mood fluctuations rather than a discrete 5 day affective episode.
Mania lasts at least 7 days (or requires hospital admission) and causes severe functional impairment or grandiose psychotic symptoms.
A mixed affective state involves concurrent or rapidly alternating manic and depressive symptoms such as tearful agitation and suicidal ideation.
Schizoaffective disorder requires first-rank psychotic symptoms alongside prominent mood episodes, whereas she has no delusions or hallucinations.

hq_q.s: A 44 year old man with bipolar disorder has taken lithium for 2 years. He is well. His lithium level taken 12 hours after his last dose is 0.6 mmol/L, and his levels have been stable for over a year. His kidney and thyroid function are normal.
hq_q.w: Once a patient on lithium has been stable for over 1 year with normal renal and thyroid function and levels below 0.8 mmol/L, NICE recommends checking 12-hour serum lithium every 6 months.
hq_q.f: Last level 0.9 or a new ACE inhibitor → keep checking every 3 months.
hq_q.ql: How often should his lithium level be checked?

c: kidney and thyroid function are normal
tm.m: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index (0.4-1.0 mmol/L) requiring scheduled maintenance monitoring even when stable
tm.g: Stable lithium therapy after the first year with no risk factors -> check plasma lithium level every 6 months
f: annual lipid and glucose metabolic monitoring in a stable patient taking aripiprazole
a patient in their first year of lithium therapy or newly started on an ACE inhibitor
monthly white cell and neutrophil monitoring during maintenance clozapine treatment
5 to 7 days after initiating lithium or adjusting the daily dose
x: Waiting 12 months between lithium levels is too infrequent for a drug with a narrow therapeutic window.
Three-monthly lithium monitoring is required during the first year of treatment or in older adults, renal impairment, interacting drugs, or levels >=0.8 mmol/L.
Monthly plasma lithium levels are unnecessary in a stable patient with normal renal function after 2 years.
Weekly lithium checks (5 to 7 days after each adjustment) are performed during initial titration or after a dose change until stable.

hq_q.s: A 29 year old woman with bipolar I disorder attends her preconception psychiatry review. Her mood has been stable for 3 years on oral sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, following two severe manic admissions in her twenties. She and her partner plan to stop contraception in 3 months to conceive. A pregnancy test today is negative.
o: Continue sodium valproate with folic acid
Halve the daily dose of sodium valproate
hq_q.w: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential due to a 10% risk of congenital malformations and 30% to 40% risk of neurodevelopmental impairment. Switch gradually to a safer prophylactic antipsychotic.
hq_q.f: Lithium in pregnancy → avoid in the first trimester if possible, high monitoring.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Valproate inhibits histone deacetylase and folate metabolism, causing neural tube defects and cognitive impairment in utero
tm.g: Woman with bipolar disorder on valproate planning pregnancy -> switch to an antipsychotic under specialist care
f: never appropriate in bipolar disorder because valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy
never safe in pregnancy because no dose of sodium valproate is free from teratogenic risk
never recommended because abrupt withdrawal precipitates acute bipolar relapse
trigeminal neuralgia in a non-pregnant patient where carbamazepine is first-line therapy
x: High-dose folic acid does not eliminate the 10% teratogenic malformation risk or 40% neurodevelopmental toxicity of valproate.
Neurodevelopmental harm and congenital anomalies occur even at lower valproate doses, and subtherapeutic dosing risks manic relapse.
Abruptly stopping prophylaxis without cross-tapering to an alternative carries a very high risk of severe manic relapse.
Carbamazepine is also a human teratogen causing neural tube and craniofacial defects and is avoided in pregnancy.

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old woman has had sudden episodes of palpitations, sweating, shaking and a fear that she is dying, about twice a week for 3 months. They come out of the blue and peak within 10 minutes. She now avoids going out alone in case one happens.
Pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg. Examination is normal. Thyroid function and ECG are normal.
hq_q.w: Panic disorder is defined by recurrent, unexpected surges of severe autonomic anxiety peaking within 10 minutes, accompanied by persistent anticipatory fear of further attacks or phobic avoidance of situations where escape is difficult.
hq_q.f: Constant worry about many things for 6 months → GAD.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: Thyroid function and ECG are normal
tm.m: Paroxysmal sympathetic surges trigger catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations and secondary agoraphobic avoidance
tm.g: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks peaking within 10 minutes with anticipatory avoidance -> panic disorder
f: persistent daily worry about finances, health and work for 8 months with muscle tension and insomnia
weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, fine tremor and a suppressed serum TSH
paroxysmal severe hypertension (BP 220/120 mmHg), pounding headaches and raised plasma metanephrines
marked autonomic anxiety occurring exclusively when speaking in meetings or eating in front of others
x: Generalised anxiety disorder causes chronic, free-floating worry across multiple everyday domains for at least 6 months rather than discrete 10-minute autonomic peaks.
Hyperthyroidism causes persistent sinus tachycardia, tremor, weight loss, and heat intolerance with a suppressed TSH, whereas her thyroid tests are normal.
Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension, drenching sweats, and pounding headaches from catecholamine secretion, whereas her blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg.
Social anxiety disorder is triggered specifically by scrutiny or performance in social interactions rather than occurring unexpectedly out of the blue.

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old accountant presents to his GP with an 8 month history of uncontrollable daily worry about his job security, mortgage payments, and children's health. He describes constant neck and shoulder tension, restlessness, irritable poor concentration at work, and difficulty falling asleep.
His thyroid function is normal and his GAD-7 questionnaire score is 17 out of 21.
hq_q.w: The 7-item Generalised Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7) scores symptom frequency over 2 weeks out of 21: 0 to 4 indicates minimal, 5 to 9 mild, 10 to 14 moderate, and 15 to 21 severe anxiety.
hq_q.f: GAD-7 of 7 → mild anxiety.
hq_q.ql: Which is the severity of his anxiety?

tm.m: The GAD-7 stratifies generalised anxiety severity using standard cut-offs of 5, 10, and 15 points
tm.g: GAD-7 score >=15 -> severe generalised anxiety
f: a GAD-7 score of 7 out of 21 with mild intermittent restlessness
a GAD-7 score of 2 out of 21 in an asymptomatic patient
a GAD-7 score of 12 out of 21 with moderate worry
fleeting situational worry before an examination lasting 3 days with a GAD-7 score of 4
x: Mild anxiety on the GAD-7 scale corresponds to a total score between 5 and 9 out of 21.
Minimal anxiety on the GAD-7 scale corresponds to a total score between 0 and 4 out of 21.
Moderate anxiety on the GAD-7 scale corresponds to a total score between 10 and 14 out of 21.
Subthreshold anxiety is not a valid band for a score of 17/21, which exceeds the severe threshold of 15.

hq_q.s: A 46 year old woman has generalised anxiety disorder. She has had high-intensity CBT and adequate trials of sertraline and then venlafaxine, without improvement. She has no history of substance misuse.
hq_q.w: NICE: sertraline first, then another SSRI or SNRI, then pregabalin if those are not tolerated or effective.
hq_q.f: Short-term crisis → benzodiazepines for 2 to 4 weeks.
hq_q.ql: Which drug can be offered next?

tm.m: Pregabalin is the next step after an SSRI and an SNRI
tm.g: GAD after an SSRI and an SNRI: pregabalin
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam long term (Benzodiazepines must not be used beyond 2 to 4 weeks due to dependence)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Haloperidol (Antipsychotics are not used for GAD in primary care)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lithium (Lithium is for bipolar disorder, not GAD)
inner restlessness weeks after starting
x: Benzodiazepines must not be used beyond 2 to 4 weeks due to dependence
Antipsychotics are not used for GAD in primary care.
Lithium is for bipolar disorder, not GAD.
Ruled out here: requires inner restlessness weeks after starting, whereas this patient has sertraline and then venlafaxine, A 46 year old woman has.

hq_q.s:
A 29 year old woman was assaulted on her way home 2 days ago. She has not been physically injured. Since then she has felt numb and detached, cannot sleep and keeps replaying the event in her mind. She has no previous mental health problems.
She is tearful but coherent, with no thoughts of self-harm.
hq_q.w: Symptoms within hours to days of a stressor are an acute stress reaction. PTSD needs symptoms for over a month.
hq_q.f: The same symptoms 6 weeks later → PTSD.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Stress symptoms in the first days after trauma usually settle
tm.g: Symptoms within days of a trauma is an acute stress reaction
f: low mood and worry after a break-up with no re-experiencing
the presentation instead showed features specific to Depression (Depression needs 2 weeks of symptoms; this started 2 days ago after a trauma)
Anxiety is a smoke alarm that rings for toast. CBT recalibrates the alarm.
the same symptoms 6 weeks later
x: Ruled out here: requires low mood and worry after a break-up with no re-experiencing, whereas this patient has 2 days ago, numb and detached.
Depression needs 2 weeks of symptoms; this started 2 days ago after a trauma.
Ruled out here: requires Anxiety is a smoke alarm that rings for toast. CBT recalibrates the alarm, whereas this patient has 2 days ago, numb and detached.
Ruled out here: requires the same symptoms 6 weeks later, whereas this patient has 2 days ago, numb and detached.

hq_q.s: A 38 year old man was in a serious car crash 6 months ago. He has had nightmares and flashbacks since, avoids driving and is constantly on edge. His sleep and work have suffered. He has no thoughts of self-harm.
hq_q.w: Trauma-focused CBT or EMDR are first line. Debriefing is not recommended and can make things worse.
hq_q.f: Therapy not acceptable → venlafaxine or an SSRI.
hq_q.ql: Which treatment is most appropriate first?

tm.m: Trauma-focused therapy helps process the memory
tm.g: PTSD: trauma-focused CBT first
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Benzodiazepine (Benzodiazepines are ineffective in PTSD and risk dependence)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Propranolol (Propranolol does not treat PTSD)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Psychodynamic therapy (NICE recommends trauma-focused CBT or EMDR first-line for PTSD)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Single-session debriefing (NICE explicitly advises against single-session psychological debriefing after trauma)
x: Benzodiazepines are ineffective in PTSD and risk dependence
Propranolol does not treat PTSD.
NICE recommends trauma-focused CBT or EMDR first-line for PTSD
NICE explicitly advises against single-session psychological debriefing after trauma

hq_q.s: A 41 year old delivery driver was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder 8 months after a high-speed motorway collision in which his van overturned. Since the crash he has refused to drive or sit in any motor vehicle and walks 3 miles out of his way each morning so he does not see the junction where the accident occurred.
hq_q.w: Post-traumatic stress disorder comprises three core ICD-11 symptom clusters: re-experiencing the trauma in the present (flashbacks and nightmares), deliberate avoidance of internal or external trauma reminders, and persistent perception of heightened current threat (hypervigilance and exaggerated startle).
hq_q.f: Flashbacks and nightmares → re-experiencing.
hq_q.ql: Which symptom cluster is this?

c: walks 3 miles out of his way
tm.m: Conditioned fear responses drive active behavioural avoidance of situations and places linked to the index trauma
tm.g: Refusing to enter cars and detouring away from the crash site in PTSD -> avoidance symptom cluster
f: feeling detached from his own body as though watching himself from outside during stress
jumping violently at sudden noises and constantly scanning mirrors for danger
persistent survivor guilt, emotional numbness and feeling alienated from his family
vivid daytime flashbacks in which he feels he is back inside the overturning van
x: Dissociation involves depersonalisation or derealisation (feeling detached from one's body or that the surroundings are unreal), not detouring around a road.
Hyperarousal involves constant hypervigilance, scanning for danger, irritability, insomnia, and an exaggerated startle response to loud noises.
Negative alterations in mood and cognition involve persistent self-blame, emotional numbing, and inability to feel positive emotions.
Re-experiencing involves vivid intrusive flashbacks, distressing recurrent trauma nightmares, and physiological distress on exposure to cues.

hq_q.s: A 32 year old man washes his hands about 50 times a day because he fears catching germs. The washing makes his skin crack and bleed and takes up hours of his day. He knows the fear is excessive and tries to resist, but his anxiety rises until he washes.
hq_q.w: In obsessive-compulsive disorder, obsessions are recurrent, unwanted, ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts, images, or urges that generate intense anxiety, whereas compulsions are repetitive overt behaviours (such as handwashing or checking) or mental rituals performed to neutralise that anxiety.
hq_q.f: The intrusive fear of germs itself → obsession.
hq_q.ql: What is the hand washing called?

c: washes his hands about 50 times a day
tm.m: Repetitive ritualistic behaviours temporarily reduce obsessional anxiety, negatively reinforcing the cycle
tm.g: Repetitive ritualistic act performed to relieve anxiety from an intrusive thought -> compulsion
f: involuntary repetitive shoulder shrugging and throat clearing preceded by a physical premonitory urge
asked to name the recurrent intrusive thought of catching germs rather than the washing act
an unshakeable conviction held without insight that secret agents have poisoned his tap water
marked fear and avoidance of needles or spiders without repetitive neutralising washing rituals
x: A motor tic is a sudden, rapid, non-rhythmic movement preceded by a premonitory somatic urge rather than a goal-directed ritual driven by germ fear.
An obsession is the intrusive, unwanted fear of contamination entering his mind, whereas the physical act of washing is the compulsion.
A delusion is an unshakeable false belief held without insight, whereas he recognises that his contamination fear is excessive and irrational.
A specific phobia causes avoidance of a circumscribed external stimulus (such as spiders or heights) rather than hours of ritualistic handwashing.

hq_q.s: A 29 year old woman has moderate obsessive-compulsive disorder with checking rituals that take 2 hours a day. She has completed a course of CBT including exposure and response prevention, but still struggles. She is not pregnant.
hq_q.w: An SSRI is first choice for OCD, often at higher doses. Clomipramine is used if SSRIs fail.
hq_q.f: She has tried two SSRIs → clomipramine.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most appropriate?

tm.m: SSRIs reduce obsessions, often at higher doses
tm.g: OCD still troublesome after CBT: sertraline
f: two SSRIs have failed
the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam (Benzodiazepines do not treat OCD and risk dependence)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lithium (Lithium is not used for OCD)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Olanzapine (An antipsychotic is an add-on only when SSRIs and clomipramine fail)
x: Ruled out here: requires two SSRIs have failed, whereas this patient has moderate obsessive-compulsive disorder, completed a course of CBT.
Benzodiazepines do not treat OCD and risk dependence.
Lithium is not used for OCD.
An antipsychotic is an add-on only when SSRIs and clomipramine fail.

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old man spends several hours each day checking his nose in mirrors and asking his partner for reassurance. He is convinced his nose is deformed and has stopped going out. He has asked about cosmetic surgery.
On examination his nose looks normal. He accepts that others may not see a problem.
hq_q.w: Body dysmorphic disorder (part of the obsessive-compulsive spectrum) is characterised by distressing preoccupation with a perceived defect or ugliness in physical appearance that is unobservable or appears slight to others, accompanied by repetitive mirror checking, camouflaging, or reassurance seeking.
hq_q.f: Fear of having a serious illness → hypochondriasis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: accepts that others may not see
tm.m: Distorted body-image processing drives obsessive appearance preoccupation and compulsive mirror-checking rituals
tm.g: Preoccupation with an imagined facial flaw + mirror checking + preserved insight -> body dysmorphic disorder
f: an unshakeable psychotic conviction that his nose is rotting away despite zero objective abnormality
persistent fear that minor headaches indicate an undiagnosed brain tumour despite normal MRI scans
intrusive fears of house fires driving 3 hours of repetitive stove and lock checking
blushing and tremor when speaking to strangers without any belief that a body part is deformed
x: Somatic delusional disorder involves a fixed, unshakeable conviction held with zero insight, whereas he accepts others may not see a flaw.
Hypochondriasis (health anxiety disorder) is a preoccupation with having a serious undiagnosed medical disease rather than an aesthetic flaw in appearance.
Classic obsessive-compulsive disorder centres on contamination, harm, or symmetry obsessions rather than perceived ugliness of a facial feature.
Social anxiety disorder is a fear of embarrassment or scrutiny in social interactions without preoccupation with a specific bodily deformity.

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman has had many years of pain in different places, bloating, nausea, dizziness and tiredness. Extensive investigations have found no cause and she has seen many specialists. The symptoms cause her great distress and she is unable to work.
Physical examination is normal. Blood tests are normal.
hq_q.w: Somatisation disorder (bodily distress disorder in ICD-11) is characterised by multiple, recurrent, and frequently changing physical symptoms across several organ systems persisting for at least 2 years, resulting in repeated negative medical investigations and significant occupational and social impairment.
hq_q.f: Focus on fear of a specific disease → hypochondriasis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: pain in different places, bloating, nausea, dizziness
Extensive investigations have found no cause
tm.m: Psychological distress is experienced and communicated through chronic, multi-system somatic symptoms
tm.g: Multiple unexplained physical symptoms across several systems over years causing distress -> somatisation disorder
f: surreptitiously injecting exogenous insulin to induce hypoglycaemia with low C-peptide in order to be admitted
sudden left leg paralysis with a positive Hoover's sign and normal spinal MRI after an acute stressor
persistent conviction of having colon cancer despite normal colonoscopy and minimal physical symptoms
deliberately fabricating back pain solely to obtain a financial insurance payout or avoid court
x: Factitious disorder involves intentional fabrication or induction of clinical signs (such as injecting exogenous insulin) to assume the sick role.

Conversion (functional neurological) disorder presents with a specific motor or sensory neurological deficit (such as functional weakness or non-epileptic attacks) rather than years of multi-system pain and gastrointestinal symptoms.
Hypochondriasis centres on the fearful conviction of having one specific serious progressive disease (such as cancer) rather than distress from multiple symptoms.
Malingering is the conscious feigning of symptoms for an external material incentive (such as financial compensation or evading prosecution).

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old nurse has had three episodes of hypoglycaemia at work, one with a seizure. She does not have diabetes.
During an episode, her glucose is 1.8 mmol/L (4.0–7.8). Plasma insulin is high and C-peptide is low. A sulfonylurea screen is negative.
hq_q.w: Injected insulin has no C-peptide. Self-induced illness to take the sick role is factitious disorder.
hq_q.f: High insulin and high C-peptide → insulinoma or sulfonylurea.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely explanation?

c: insulin is high and C-peptide is low
tm.m: Injected insulin has no C-peptide; the pancreas would release both
tm.g: High insulin with low C-peptide in a health worker is factitious hypoglycaemia
f: high insulin and C-peptide with a negative sulfonylurea screen
the presentation instead showed features specific to Malingering (Malingering is faking for a clear external gain; she gains nothing but the sick role)
Multiple chronic unexplained physical symptoms persist for years with doctor-shopping
high C-peptide with a positive sulfonylurea screen
x: Ruled out here: requires high insulin and C-peptide with a negative sulfonylurea screen, whereas this patient has nurse, does not have diabetes.
Malingering is faking for a clear external gain; she gains nothing but the sick role.
Ruled out here: requires Multiple chronic unexplained physical symptoms persist for years with doctor-shopping, whereas this patient has nurse, does not have diabetes.
Ruled out here: requires high C-peptide with a positive sulfonylurea screen, whereas this patient has nurse, does not have diabetes.

hq_q.s:
A 46 year old woman has been unable to move her right leg since she heard of her mother's sudden death this morning. She has no headache or other symptoms.
Tone and reflexes are normal and plantars are flexor. She cannot lift her right leg from the bed, but when she lifts her left leg against resistance, her right hip extends strongly. Hoover's sign is positive.
hq_q.w: Functional symptoms show inconsistency on examination, such as Hoover's sign, and are not consciously produced.
hq_q.f: A man fakes back pain for compensation → malingering.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Functional weakness disappears when attention is drawn elsewhere
tm.g: Weakness with inconsistent signs and a positive Hoover's sign is functional
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Factitious disorder imposed on self (In factitious disorder symptoms are faked to take on the sick role; nothing here suggests deliberate faking)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lacunar stroke (A lacunar stroke gives consistent weakness and later brisk reflexes; Hoover's sign is positive)
faking symptoms for compensation
the presentation instead showed features specific to Multiple sclerosis relapse (An MS relapse gives consistent upper motor neurone signs, not a positive Hoover's sign)
x: In factitious disorder symptoms are faked to take on the sick role; nothing here suggests deliberate faking.
A lacunar stroke gives consistent weakness and later brisk reflexes; Hoover's sign is positive.
Ruled out here: requires faking symptoms for compensation, whereas this patient has mother's sudden death this morning, plantars are flexor.
An MS relapse gives consistent upper motor neurone signs, not a positive Hoover's sign.

hq_q.s:
A 17 year old girl has been eating large amounts of food in secret several times a week for 6 months, then making herself vomit. She feels out of control during the binges and ashamed afterwards. She worries a lot about her weight.
Her BMI is 22. She has calluses on the backs of her fingers and swollen parotid glands.
hq_q.w: Bulimia nervosa is characterised by recurrent episodes of uncontrolled binge eating accompanied by inappropriate compensatory weight-control behaviours (self-induced vomiting, laxative misuse, or fasting), morbid preoccupation with body shape and weight, and a normal or overweight BMI (>=18.5 kg/m²).
hq_q.f: Binges with no compensation → binge eating disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: eating large amounts of food in secret
calluses on the backs of her fingers
tm.m: Cycle of dietary restriction, loss-of-control bingeing, and compensatory purging maintains a normal BMI while causing Russell's sign and parotid sialadenitis
tm.g: Recurrent binge eating + compensatory self-induced vomiting + normal BMI (22 kg/m²) -> bulimia nervosa
f: severe dietary restriction, fear of weight gain, secondary amenorrhoea and a BMI of 15.2 kg/m²
avoiding solid foods after a choking episode with weight loss but no concern about body shape
recurrent distressing secret binges twice weekly with no self-induced vomiting or laxative use
subthreshold purging once a month that does not meet the frequency criteria for bulimia nervosa
x: Anorexia nervosa (binge-purge subtype) requires significantly low body weight (typically BMI <18.5 kg/m² in adults), whereas her BMI is 22 kg/m².
Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) involves restricted eating due to sensory aversion or fear of choking without body-shape distortion or purging.
Binge eating disorder involves recurrent distressing binges without regular compensatory purging behaviours such as vomiting or laxative abuse.
Other specified feeding or eating disorder (OSFED) is reserved for presentations that fail to meet full diagnostic thresholds, whereas she fulfils all criteria for bulimia nervosa.

hq_q.s:
A 22 year old woman with bulimia nervosa has been vomiting several times a day for a month. She feels weak.
Pulse rate 96 bpm. Her parotid glands are swollen.
hq_q.w: Vomiting loses stomach acid, causing a hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Key discriminator: Vomiting causes a hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.
hq_q.f: Laxative misuse → metabolic acidosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely acid-base disorder?

tm.m: Vomiting loses stomach acid and chloride; the kidney swaps potassium to hold sodium
tm.g: Vomiting causes a hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis
f: laxative misuse
the presentation instead showed features specific to Mixed acidosis (The bicarbonate is high, so this is an alkalosis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Respiratory acidosis (Vomiting causes a metabolic, not a respiratory, disorder)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Respiratory alkalosis (The raised bicarbonate shows a metabolic process; respiratory alkalosis lowers bicarbonate)
x: Ruled out here: requires laxative misuse, whereas this patient has vomiting several times a day, year old woman with.
The bicarbonate is high, so this is an alkalosis.
Vomiting causes a metabolic, not a respiratory, disorder.
The raised bicarbonate shows a metabolic process; respiratory alkalosis lowers bicarbonate.

hq_q.s:
A 16 year old girl with severe restricting anorexia nervosa and a BMI of 13.0 kg/m² was admitted to the paediatric ward and started on nasogastric feeding. On day 3 of refeeding she becomes acutely weak, confused, and breathless with bilateral ankle swelling.
Pulse rate is 112 bpm and pitting oedema is present to both ankles. Serum phosphate is 0.31 mmol/L (0.80-1.50), potassium is 2.7 mmol/L, and magnesium is 0.48 mmol/L.
hq_q.w: Refeeding syndrome occurs within 2 to 5 days of reintroducing carbohydrate to a starved patient. The resulting insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, causing severe hypophosphataemia, oedema, and cardiac failure.
hq_q.f: Before feeding high-risk patients → give thiamine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Carbohydrate refeeding triggers an insulin surge that shifts phosphate, potassium, and magnesium intracellularly and depletes ATP
tm.g: Hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and oedema days after starting nutrition in starvation -> refeeding syndrome
f: severe hypocalcaemia with carpopedal spasm and perioral tingling 2 days after parathyroidectomy
low serum calcium and raised serum phosphate following total thyroidectomy
hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and hypocalcaemia 48 hours after starting lymphoma chemotherapy
chronic proximal muscle weakness, bone pain and raised alkaline phosphatase with low 25-hydroxyvitamin D
x: Hungry bone syndrome occurs after parathyroidectomy for severe hyperparathyroidism, causing profound hypocalcaemia alongside hypophosphataemia.
Hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcaemia with hyperphosphataemia (raised serum phosphate), the opposite of her phosphate of 0.31 mmol/L.
Tumour lysis syndrome follows cytotoxic chemotherapy for high-grade lymphoma or leukaemia, causing hyperkalaemia and hyperphosphataemia.
Chronic vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia and mild hypocalcaemia over months rather than acute day-3 refeeding oedema and profound hypophosphataemia.

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old man lives alone and works night shifts in a warehouse, where he speaks to no one. His sister says he has always preferred to be alone, shows little emotion and is indifferent to praise or criticism. He has no friends and is content with this.
Mental state examination shows a flat but appropriate affect. He has no odd beliefs, magical thinking or hallucinations.
hq_q.w: Schizoid personality disorder is characterised by lifelong detachment from social relationships, contented preference for solitary activities, emotional coldness, flat affect, and indifference to praise or criticism, in the absence of cognitive-perceptual distortions or delusions.
hq_q.f: Wants friends but avoids them for fear of rejection → avoidant personality.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Enduring constitutional lack of desire for social affiliation and restricted emotional expression without psychosis
tm.g: Contented lifelong preference for solitude, emotional coldness and indifference to praise/criticism -> schizoid personality disorder
f: early childhood speech delay, sensory overload, rigid routines and lining up objects
craving close friendships and affection while avoiding social events out of intense fear of rejection
pervasive mistrust, bearing unforgiving grudges and suspecting colleagues of plotting against him
bizarre dress, magical belief in clairvoyance, circumstantial speech and suspiciousness
x: Autism spectrum disorder presents from early childhood with developmental language delay, sensory sensitivities, and distressed resistance to routine changes.
Avoidant personality disorder patients strongly desire close relationships and companionship but avoid social contact out of intense fear of rejection and criticism.
Paranoid personality disorder is dominated by pervasive mistrust, hypervigilance, and reading hidden threats into benign remarks rather than calm indifference.
Schizotypal disorder includes eccentric behaviour, magical thinking, odd speech, and transient quasi-psychotic perceptual experiences.

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old woman with emotionally unstable (borderline) personality disorder is reviewed in the community mental health clinic. She describes turbulent interpersonal relationships, an intense fear of abandonment, chronic feelings of emptiness, rapid affective instability, and recurrent superficial cutting of her forearms when distressed.
She has no comorbid depression or psychosis.
o: Regular oral diazepam three times daily
hq_q.w: Under NICE CG78, dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) is the psychological treatment of choice for women with emotionally unstable (borderline) personality disorder to reduce recurrent self-harm; drug therapy is not recommended for core symptoms.
hq_q.f: Short crisis period → a sedative antihistamine for a week.
hq_q.ql: Which treatment is most appropriate?

tm.m: Dialectical behaviour therapy combines mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, and interpersonal effectiveness training
tm.g: Emotionally unstable (borderline) personality disorder with recurrent self-harm -> dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT)
f: long-term prophylaxis of bipolar I disorder after recovery from an episode of acute mania
moderate-to-severe comorbid major depressive disorder or bulimia nervosa
maintenance treatment of relapsing paranoid schizophrenia in a patient with poor tablet adherence
inpatient alcohol withdrawal detoxification using a reducing chlordiazepoxide or diazepam regimen
x: Lithium is used for prophylaxis of bipolar I disorder and is dangerous in overdose in patients who self-harm.
NICE CG78 states that antidepressants must not be used specifically for borderline personality disorder in the absence of a comorbid depressive illness.
NICE CG78 explicitly advises against medium- or long-term antipsychotic treatment for emotionally unstable personality disorder.
Benzodiazepines cause dependence, tolerance, and paradoxical behavioural disinhibition that increases impulsive self-harm.

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old man is assessed by the prison forensic psychiatry team. He has a history since adolescence of repeated fraud, burglary, and unprovoked physical assaults on strangers, expressing complete indifference toward his victims. School records confirm he was expelled at age 13 for arson, truancy, and cruelty to animals.
Mental state examination shows no delusions or hallucinations.
hq_q.w: Dissocial (antisocial) personality disorder is characterised by a pervasive disregard for social obligations, callous lack of empathy or remorse, impulsivity, and low frustration tolerance in an adult (>=18 years) with documented conduct disorder before age 15.
hq_q.f: Grandiosity and a need for admiration → narcissistic personality.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Childhood-onset conduct disorder persists into adulthood as callous-unemotional disregard for others' rights and safety
tm.g: Adult pattern of violence, deceit and lack of remorse + childhood conduct disorder -> dissocial personality disorder
f: frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, unstable relationships, chronic emptiness and self-harm
grandiose sense of self-importance, entitlement and constant need for admiration
pervasive mistrust, bearing grudges and suspecting others of exploitation without criminal violence
lifelong contented preference for solitude and emotional detachment without aggression
x: Emotionally unstable (borderline) personality disorder is driven by fear of abandonment, affective instability, and self-harm rather than callous predation.
Narcissistic personality disorder centres on grandiose self-importance, fantasies of unlimited success, and need for admiration rather than violent criminality.
Paranoid personality disorder features pervasive suspiciousness and reading hidden threats into benign actions rather than remorseless criminality.
Schizoid personality disorder is characterised by quiet solitary detachment and emotional coldness without aggression or law-breaking.

hq_q.s: A 46 year old man attends general practice for a routine NHS cardiovascular health check. He works in marketing and reports drinking 3 standard bottles of red wine over the course of each week with evening meals. Each bottle contains 750 mL of wine at 12% alcohol by volume (ABV), and he consumes no beer or spirits.
hq_q.w: UK alcohol units equal volume in litres multiplied by percentage ABV: 0.75 L multiplied by 12% equals 9 units per bottle, giving 27 units per week for 3 bottles.
hq_q.f: The UK guideline → no more than 14 units a week.
hq_q.ql: How many units of alcohol does he drink each week?

tm.m: One UK unit equals 10 mL (8 g) of pure ethanol: (volume in mL x % ABV) / 1000
tm.g: 3 bottles x 0.75 L x 12% ABV -> 27 units per week
f: drinking 2 bottles (750 mL each) of 12% ABV wine per week
drinking 4 bottles (750 mL each) of 12% ABV wine per week
drinking 5 bottles (750 mL each) of 12% ABV wine per week
drinking 1 bottle (750 mL) of 12% ABV wine in a week
x: Eighteen units corresponds to drinking 2 bottles (1500 mL) of 12% wine per week.
Thirty-six units corresponds to drinking 4 bottles of 12% wine per week.
Forty-five units corresponds to drinking 5 bottles of 12% wine per week.
Nine units represents the alcohol content of a single 750 mL bottle of 12% wine rather than 3 bottles.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old man who drinks a litre of vodka a day was admitted with a fractured wrist 18 hours ago. His last drink was yesterday afternoon.
Pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 162/96 mmHg. He is sweating, agitated and has a coarse tremor. He is orientated and has no hallucinations. His CIWA score is 22.
hq_q.w: A long-acting benzodiazepine on a reducing course prevents withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens. Key discriminator: Moderate to severe withdrawal: reducing chlordiazepoxide.
hq_q.f: Liver failure → use a short-acting benzodiazepine like lorazepam.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate drug?

tm.m: A long-acting benzodiazepine replaces alcohol's GABA effect and prevents seizures
tm.g: Moderate to severe withdrawal: reducing chlordiazepoxide
f: preventing relapse after withdrawal
the presentation instead showed features specific to Disulfiram (Disulfiram is for keeping off alcohol after withdrawal, not for treating withdrawal)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Haloperidol (Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold and does not treat withdrawal)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Phenobarbital (Benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide or lorazepam) are first-line for acute alcohol withdrawal)
x: Ruled out here: requires preventing relapse after withdrawal, whereas this patient has 18 hours ago, coarse tremor.
Disulfiram is for keeping off alcohol after withdrawal, not for treating withdrawal.
Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold and does not treat withdrawal.
Benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide or lorazepam) are first-line for acute alcohol withdrawal

hq_q.s: A 48 year old man has completed an assisted alcohol withdrawal and wants to stay abstinent. He has no liver disease and his kidney function is normal. He is attending a psychosocial support group.
hq_q.w: Acamprosate reduces cravings. Naltrexone and disulfiram are other options. Key discriminator: Relapse prevention: acamprosate.
hq_q.f: He wants a deterrent and has no heart disease → disulfiram.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most appropriate?

tm.m: Acamprosate reduces craving by calming glutamate activity
tm.g: Relapse prevention: acamprosate
f: treating withdrawal symptoms
the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam (Diazepam is for withdrawal, not for staying abstinent)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Methadone (Methadone is for opioid dependence, not alcohol)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Thiamine (Thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy but does not reduce craving)
x: Ruled out here: requires treating withdrawal symptoms, whereas this patient has wants to stay abstinent, no liver disease.
Diazepam is for withdrawal, not for staying abstinent.
Methadone is for opioid dependence, not alcohol.
Thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy but does not reduce craving.

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old woman took 30 paracetamol 500 mg tablets 4 hours ago after an argument. She has no symptoms. She weighs 60 kg.
Her paracetamol level taken at 4 hours is above the treatment line on the nomogram. Liver function and INR are normal.
hq_q.w: After an acute single-timepoint paracetamol overdose, plasma paracetamol concentration is measured at 4 hours post-ingestion (or on arrival if >4 hours). If the level lies on or above the nomogram treatment line, intravenous acetylcysteine is started immediately.
hq_q.f: Took the tablets 30 minutes ago → activated charcoal can be given.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: Liver function and INR are normal
tm.m: Acetylcysteine replenishes hepatic glutathione stores required to conjugate the hepatotoxic metabolite NAPQI
tm.g: 4-hour plasma paracetamol concentration on or above the treatment line -> intravenous acetylcysteine
f: presenting within 45 minutes of ingesting a potentially toxic paracetamol overdose
a 4-hour plasma paracetamol level well below the treatment line with normal liver blood tests
respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils following an opioid overdose
a blood sample mistakenly drawn only 2 hours after ingestion before peak absorption
x: Oral activated charcoal reduces gastrointestinal absorption only when given within 1 hour of ingestion, not at 4 hours.
Normal baseline transaminases and INR at 4 hours do not exclude impending hepatic necrosis when the paracetamol level exceeds the treatment line.
Intravenous naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist used for opioid toxicity (co-codamol codeine component), not paracetamol hepatotoxicity.
A plasma paracetamol level taken at 4 hours is fully reliable after a single acute ingestion and must be treated without waiting a further 4 hours.

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old man has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for 10 years with stable levels. A new drug was started for his blood pressure 2 weeks ago. He now has a coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea and confusion.
He is ataxic with a coarse tremor and brisk reflexes.
hq_q.w: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics such as indapamide cut lithium excretion. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and NSAIDs also raise lithium levels.
hq_q.f: Fine tremor at a level of 0.8 → normal side effect.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most likely to have been started?

c: new drug was started for his blood pressure
tm.m: Thiazides make the kidney hold on to lithium
tm.g: Lithium toxicity after a new antihypertensive: a thiazide-like diuretic such as indapamide
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amlodipine (Amlodipine does not raise lithium levels)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Doxazosin (Doxazosin does not raise lithium levels)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Labetalol (Labetalol does not change how the kidney handles lithium)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Moxonidine (Moxonidine does not raise lithium levels)
x: Amlodipine does not raise lithium levels.
Doxazosin does not raise lithium levels.
Labetalol does not change how the kidney handles lithium.
Moxonidine does not raise lithium levels.

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old woman took an overdose of amitriptyline 3 hours ago. She is drowsy.
Pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg. Her pupils are dilated and her skin is dry.
ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 140 ms. Venous pH 7.34 (7.35–7.45).
hq_q.w: Tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline block fast cardiac voltage-gated sodium channels, widening the QRS complex and risking fatal ventricular arrhythmias. Intravenous 8.4% sodium bicarbonate increases extracellular sodium and alkalinises plasma (target pH 7.45 to 7.55) to uncouple drug binding.
hq_q.f: Benzodiazepine overdose → supportive care, avoid flumazenil.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Hypertonic sodium load and systemic alkalinisation overcome fast cardiac sodium-channel blockade by tricyclics
tm.g: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS widening (>100-120 ms) or arrhythmia -> intravenous sodium bicarbonate
f: haemodynamically stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia unrelated to sodium-channel blocker toxicity
iatrogenic respiratory depression caused solely by midazolam during conscious endoscopy
polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (torsades de pointes) with marked QT prolongation
coma, respiratory rate of 6 breaths/min and pinpoint pupils from heroin toxicity
x: Amiodarone prolongs the QT interval and worsens cardiac conduction delay in tricyclic antidepressant cardiotoxicity.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine sedation and is strictly contraindicated in tricyclic overdose because it precipitates refractory status epilepticus.
Magnesium sulfate is first-line for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (torsades de pointes), whereas sodium bicarbonate is first-line for tricyclic QRS widening.
Naloxone reverses opioid receptor toxicity (miosis and bradypnoea) rather than anticholinergic tricyclic cardiotoxicity.

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old man takes sertraline for depression. He started tramadol for back pain 2 days ago. Since this morning he has been agitated and sweaty with a tremor and diarrhoea.
Temperature 38.4°C, pulse rate 122 bpm, BP 156/92 mmHg. His pupils are dilated. Reflexes are brisk with sustained clonus at both ankles.
hq_q.w: Rapid onset with clonus and hyperreflexia. Stop the drugs and consider cyproheptadine. Key discriminator: Clonus, hyperreflexia and agitation within a day of a serotonergic drug is serotonin syndrome.
hq_q.f: Days of rigidity on an antipsychotic → NMS.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Two serotonergic drugs together overload serotonin
tm.g: Clonus, hyperreflexia and agitation within a day of a serotonergic drug is serotonin syndrome
f: tremor, sweating and agitation a day after stopping drinking
days of lead-pipe rigidity on an antipsychotic
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sepsis (Sepsis does not cause clonus and dilated pupils after starting tramadol)
Graves' is the only cause with eyes and shins.
x: Ruled out here: requires tremor, sweating and agitation a day after stopping drinking, whereas this patient has sertraline, started tramadol.
Ruled out here: requires days of lead-pipe rigidity on an antipsychotic, whereas this patient has sertraline, started tramadol.
Sepsis does not cause clonus and dilated pupils after starting tramadol.
Ruled out here: requires Graves' is the only cause with eyes and shins, whereas this patient has sertraline, started tramadol.

hq_q.s: A 34 year old woman was admitted to a medical ward as a voluntary patient after an overdose. She is now trying to leave, saying she will kill herself when she gets home. The duty psychiatrist is 2 hours away. You are the doctor in charge of her care on the ward.
hq_q.w: Section 5(2) of the Mental Health Act 1983 empowers the doctor in charge of a voluntary inpatient's treatment (or nominated deputy) to detain the patient for up to 72 hours pending formal assessment.
hq_q.f: A nurse holds the patient → Section 5.4, up to 6 hours.
hq_q.ql: Which section of the Mental Health Act can be used to hold her?

c: kill herself when she gets home
doctor in charge of her care
tm.m: Section 5(2) provides an emergency 72-hour holding power over an already admitted informal hospital inpatient
tm.g: Voluntary hospital inpatient attempting to leave at acute psychiatric risk -> Section 5(2) holding power (up to 72 hours)
f: police requiring a magistrate's warrant to enter a locked private flat to remove a patient to safety
police finding an acutely distressed person in a public shopping centre or on a motorway bridge
formal detention for psychiatric assessment for up to 28 days completed by an AMHP and two doctors
formal detention for treatment for up to 6 months in a patient with a known diagnosis
x: Section 135 is a magistrate's warrant allowing police to enter private premises and remove a person to a place of safety.
Section 136 allows a police officer to remove a person appearing mentally disordered in a public place to a place of safety for up to 24 hours.
Section 2 authorises formal detention for assessment for up to 28 days, requiring an Approved Mental Health Professional and two medical recommendations.
Section 3 authorises formal detention for psychiatric treatment for up to 6 months where the disorder and treatment are already established.

hq_q.s: Police find a 28 year old man shouting at passers-by in a shopping centre. He is distressed and says strangers are trying to poison him. He appears to be mentally unwell.
hq_q.w: Section 136 lets the police take someone from a public place to a place of safety for up to 24 hours.
hq_q.f: Police need a warrant to enter a home → Section 135.
hq_q.ql: Which section of the Mental Health Act can the police use?

tm.m: Police can take someone from a public place to a place of safety
tm.g: Police removing someone from a public place: Section 136
f: police need a warrant to enter a home
the presentation instead showed features specific to Section 2 (Section 2 needs two doctors and an AMHP, not a police officer in a public place)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Section 4 (Section 4 is an emergency admission by one doctor and an AMHP)
the doctor in charge is present
x: Ruled out here: requires police need a warrant to enter a home, whereas this patient has Police, shopping centre.
Section 2 needs two doctors and an AMHP, not a police officer in a public place.
Section 4 is an emergency admission by one doctor and an AMHP.
Ruled out here: requires the doctor in charge is present, whereas this patient has Police, shopping centre.

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old woman with severe depression has stopped eating and drinking over 3 days. She barely speaks and stays in one position for hours.
When the examiner lifts her arm, she holds it in the air for several minutes. She resists being moved. She is afebrile with normal reflexes. Creatine kinase is normal.
hq_q.w: Catatonia is a severe psychomotor syndrome occurring in mood disorders, schizophrenia, or medical encephalitis, characterised by stupor, mutism, negativism, posturing, and waxy flexibility (maintaining limbs in positions placed by the examiner). First-line treatment is lorazepam or electroconvulsive therapy.
hq_q.f: Fluctuating attention and confusion with an infection → delirium.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: holds it in the air for several minutes
tm.m: GABAergic and dopaminergic striato-cortical dysregulation produces mutism, stupor, negativism, and waxy flexibility
tm.g: Severe depression with mutism, stupor, posturing and waxy flexibility (normal CK/afebrile) -> catatonia
f: acute fluctuating disorientation and inattention precipitated by urosepsis or hyponatraemia
quadriplegia and anarthria after a basilar artery stroke with preserved vertical eye blinking
high fever, labile blood pressure, lead-pipe rigidity and creatine kinase of 18,000 U/L on haloperidol
gradual cognitive and functional decline over 5 years without acute waxy posturing
x: Hypoactive delirium causes fluctuating clouding of consciousness and disorientation secondary to an acute medical illness rather than waxy flexibility.
Locked-in syndrome from ventral pontine infarction causes quadriplegia and aphonia with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements, not waxy flexibility.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows dopamine antagonist exposure and causes high fever, autonomic instability, lead-pipe rigidity, and markedly elevated creatine kinase.
Severe neurodegenerative dementia progresses insidiously over years rather than presenting over 3 days with waxy flexibility.

hq_q.s: A 34 year old man with schizophrenia has catatonia. He has not eaten or drunk for 3 days and is mute and immobile. He is afebrile and his creatine kinase is normal.
hq_q.w: Benzodiazepines are first line, often with fast improvement. Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia or trigger NMS.
hq_q.f: No response to lorazepam within days → ECT.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first treatment?

tm.m: Benzodiazepines often reverse catatonia quickly
tm.g: Catatonia: lorazepam first
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Haloperidol (Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and risk NMS)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Olanzapine (Antipsychotics are avoided until catatonia is treated)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sertraline (An SSRI takes weeks and does not treat catatonia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Zopiclone (Zopiclone is a hypnotic and is not used for catatonia)
x: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and risk NMS.
Antipsychotics are avoided until catatonia is treated.
An SSRI takes weeks and does not treat catatonia.
Zopiclone is a hypnotic and is not used for catatonia.

hq_q.s: A 64 year old woman with severe psychotic depression has stopped eating and drinking and has not responded to two antidepressant trials plus an antipsychotic. Her psychiatrist recommends a course of bilateral electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), and she and her family ask about the most frequent adverse effect.
hq_q.w: The commonest cognitive side effect of electroconvulsive therapy is short-term retrograde and anterograde amnesia for events occurring around the treatment course, alongside transient post-ictal headache and myalgia; memory typically recovers within weeks to months.
hq_q.f: Before ECT → check for raised intracranial pressure and recent MI.
hq_q.ql: Which side effect is most common?

tm.m: Brief generalized seizure activity transiently disrupts hippocampal memory consolidation for periprocedural events
tm.g: Commonest characteristic adverse effect of electroconvulsive therapy -> memory loss around the treatment course
f: historical unmodified convulsive therapy performed without a muscle relaxant
anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture or severe orbitofrontal traumatic brain injury
hippocampal sclerosis or a cortical scar following a penetrating head injury
untreated atrial fibrillation with a high CHA2DS2-VASc score and left atrial appendage thrombus
x: Vertebral fractures were a historical complication of unmodified ECT and are now prevented by short-acting neuromuscular blockade (suxamethonium).
Electroconvulsive therapy does not alter underlying personality structure or cause frontal lobe personality syndromes.
Induced therapeutic seizures during ECT do not kindle chronic spontaneous epilepsy.
Cerebrovascular accidents during modified ECT are exceptionally rare.

hq_q.s:
A 3 year old girl has been referred because she is not talking like other children. She has only a few words. Her parents say she rarely responds to her name, does not point to show them things and spends hours lining up her toys. She becomes very upset if her routine changes.
Her hearing test is normal. She makes little eye contact during the consultation.
hq_q.w: Autism spectrum disorder presents in early childhood with persistent deficits in social communication and joint attention (poor eye contact, absent pointing) alongside restricted, repetitive behaviour (lining up toys and distress at routine changes).
hq_q.f: Good eye contact and pointing but few words → speech and language delay.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Neurodevelopmental differences in social-communicative networks impair joint attention and drive repetitive, routine-bound behaviour
tm.g: Impaired joint attention and eye contact + repetitive lining up of toys + normal hearing -> autism spectrum disorder
f: significant delay across gross motor sitting/walking, fine motor grip and language milestones
speech delay in a child who makes warm eye contact, gestures eagerly and has flat tympanometry
inhibited emotionally withdrawn behaviour toward adult caregivers following severe early neglect
speaking fluently in full sentences at home while remaining completely silent at nursery
x: Global developmental delay involves significant delay (>=2 standard deviations) across two or more domains including gross and fine motor milestones.
Isolated sensorineural or conductive hearing impairment causes speech delay with keen non-verbal pointing and eye contact, and her audiogram is normal.
Reactive attachment disorder occurs in the context of severe early institutional neglect or abuse and does not explain repetitive lining up of toys.
In selective mutism, the child speaks fluently and interacts normally at home with parents but becomes mute in specific social settings such as nursery.

hq_q.s: A 26 year old autistic man needs a blood test. He is in a busy, noisy outpatient waiting area and is becoming distressed, covering his ears and rocking.
o: Carer to hold his arm still
Proceed quickly in the waiting area
hq_q.w: Predictable routine, less sensory input and clear explanation reduce distress. Ask about a hospital passport.
hq_q.f: He is upset by change → explain each step in advance.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most helpful adjustment?

tm.m: Sensory overload and uncertainty drive distress in autism
tm.g: Reduce sensory load and explain steps: quiet room and clear steps
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Carer to hold his arm still (Holding him still without consent is restrictive and escalates distress; adjust the setting first)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral lorazepam before the test (Sedation is a last resort; most autistic adults manage with simple adjustments to the setting)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Proceed quickly in the waiting area (Speed does not remove the noise that is overwhelming him; take away the trigger first)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Rebook under general anaesthetic (An anaesthetic is far out of proportion to a blood test)
x: Holding him still without consent is restrictive and escalates distress; adjust the setting first.
Sedation is a last resort; most autistic adults manage with simple adjustments to the setting.
Speed does not remove the noise that is overwhelming him; take away the trigger first.
An anaesthetic is far out of proportion to a blood test.

hq_q.s: An 11 year old boy with autism spectrum disorder and moderate intellectual disability is reviewed in the specialist CAMHS clinic because of 6 months of severe, daily physical aggression and self-injurious head-banging that recently fractured his mother's wrist. Medical, dental, and environmental triggers have been excluded, and intensive functional behavioural and parent-training programmes have failed.
hq_q.w: Under NICE guideline CG170, short-term low-dose antipsychotic medication (most commonly risperidone, which is licensed for severe aggression in autism) may be considered by a specialist when behaviour that challenges is severe and psychosocial or environmental interventions alone have been unsuccessful.
hq_q.f: Coexisting ADHD → methylphenidate can help.
hq_q.ql: Which drug may be considered?

tm.m: D2 and 5-HT2A antagonism with low-dose risperidone reduces severe irritability and impulsive aggression when behavioural strategies fail
tm.g: Severe physical aggression in autism refractory to psychosocial and behavioural interventions -> specialist trial of risperidone
f: acute pre-hospital termination of a prolonged generalized tonic-clonic seizure
moderate-to-severe comorbid major depressive disorder failing psychological therapy
confirmed comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder causing pervasive inattention and hyperactivity
generalized tonic-clonic epilepsy in a male child requiring anticonvulsant prophylaxis
x: Benzodiazepines such as diazepam are avoided for chronic challenging behaviour in autism as they cause sedation and paradoxical disinhibition.
Fluoxetine is not effective for severe physical aggression in autism and is used only for comorbid depression or OCD.
Methylphenidate is a CNS stimulant used when comorbid ADHD (hyperactivity and inattention) is the primary diagnosis.
Sodium valproate is an anticonvulsant mood stabiliser and is not recommended for challenging behaviour in autism without epilepsy.

hq_q.s: A 28 year old woman gave birth to her first baby 4 days ago. She is tearful and anxious and feels overwhelmed. She is feeding and caring for her baby well and sleeps when the baby sleeps. She has no thoughts of harming herself or the baby.
hq_q.w: Baby blues affect many mothers between days 3 and 10 and settle without treatment. Key discriminator: Tearfulness on days 3 to 10 with normal functioning is baby blues.
hq_q.f: Low mood that lasts beyond 2 weeks → postnatal depression.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Hormonal shifts after birth cause brief tearfulness that settles by 2 weeks
tm.g: Tearfulness on days 3 to 10 with normal functioning is baby blues
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Adjustment disorder (Tearfulness in the first days after birth that settles within 2 weeks is the baby blues)
low mood lasting beyond 2 weeks
confusion, mania or delusions in the first weeks
gave birth 4 months ago + neck is not painful
x: Tearfulness in the first days after birth that settles within 2 weeks is the baby blues.
Ruled out here: requires low mood lasting beyond 2 weeks, whereas this patient has 4 days ago, caring for her baby well.
Ruled out here: requires confusion, mania or delusions in the first weeks, whereas this patient has 4 days ago, caring for her baby well.
Ruled out here: requires gave birth 4 months ago + neck is not painful, whereas this patient has 4 days ago, caring for her baby well.

hq_q.s: A 32 year old woman gave birth 8 weeks ago and is breastfeeding. She has had low mood, poor concentration and loss of interest for 5 weeks. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 17. She has no thoughts of self-harm and wants medication alongside therapy.
