hq_q.w: Sertraline (or paroxetine) is the preferred SSRI antidepressant in women who are breastfeeding because it has high plasma protein binding and very low transfer into breast milk, resulting in undetectable or minimal infant serum levels.
hq_q.f: She was well on another SSRI before pregnancy → discuss continuing that drug.
hq_q.ql: Which antidepressant is most appropriate?

c: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 17
tm.m: Sertraline has extensive maternal protein binding and a short-to-intermediate half-life, minimising infant exposure via breast milk
tm.g: First-line SSRI for postnatal depression in a breastfeeding mother -> sertraline
f: an adult who is not breastfeeding and has previously responded well to citalopram
adolescent major depressive disorder in a non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding patient
major depression with severe insomnia and weight loss in a non-breastfeeding adult
severe treatment-resistant depression in a non-breastfeeding patient after two SSRIs have failed
x: Citalopram achieves higher relative infant doses in breast milk than sertraline and can occasionally cause infant drowsiness or colic.
Fluoxetine and its active metabolite norfluoxetine have very long half-lives and high transfer into breast milk, risking accumulation in the infant.
Mirtazapine causes marked maternal sedation that can impair safe night-time infant care and is not first-line in lactation.
Venlafaxine is a second-line SNRI with higher breast-milk transfer and neonatal discontinuation symptoms.

hq_q.s: A 30 year old woman attends her routine 6 week postnatal check with the health visitor. She reports tearfulness, feeling overwhelmed, guilt about her parenting, and inability to sleep even when her baby settles. She completes a validated 10-item self-report questionnaire that deliberately omits somatic pregnancy symptoms and scores 16 out of 30.
hq_q.w: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is a validated 10-item screening questionnaire scored out of 30 that omits normal postpartum somatic symptoms. A score of 13 or more indicates probable postnatal depression.
hq_q.f: Brief screen at booking → the Whooley questions.
hq_q.ql: Which tool was most likely used?

tm.m: The 10-item EPDS screens cognitive and affective depressive symptoms without confounding normal postpartum somatic changes
tm.g: 10-item postnatal mood screening tool (cut-off >=13/30) -> Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)
f: a 7-item questionnaire scored out of 21 assessing chronic worry and restlessness
a 14-item combined anxiety and depression questionnaire used in general medical outpatients
a 30-point bedside cognitive test of orientation, recall and pentagon copying
a 9-item depression scale scored out of 27 used in general adult primary care
x: The GAD-7 is a 7-item questionnaire scored out of 21 used to screen and grade generalised anxiety disorder.
The Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) is a 14-item scale (7 anxiety, 7 depression) designed for general medical outpatients.
The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) is a 30-point bedside test of cognitive orientation, registration, recall, and language in dementia.
The PHQ-9 is a 9-item depression questionnaire scored out of 27 that includes somatic items such as sleep and appetite.

hq_q.s:
An 85 year old man is admitted to the geriatric medical ward with fever, dysuria, and Escherichia coli urinary tract infection. On day 2 of admission, nursing staff report that he has become acutely muddled, drowsy during the afternoon, and unable to recite the months of the year backwards.
He scores 6 on the 4AT rapid clinical test.
hq_q.w: The 4AT is a rapid 4-item bedside delirium screen assessing alertness, AMT4 orientation, attention (months backwards), and acute fluctuation: 0 indicates delirium unlikely, 1 to 3 possible cognitive impairment, and 4 or more possible delirium.
hq_q.f: 4AT of 2 → possible cognitive impairment.
hq_q.ql: What does this score most likely show?

tm.m: Acute systemic infection triggers fluctuating attentional and arousal failure captured by a 4AT score >=4
tm.g: 4AT score >=4 -> possible delirium (+/- underlying cognitive impairment)
f: a fully alert, oriented patient who recites the months backwards with a 4AT score of 0
a stable alert patient with mild memory errors and no acute change scoring 2 on the 4AT
auditory hallucinations and thought insertion in a clear sensorium with a 4AT score of 0
chronic stable cognitive decline over 4 years with no acute change or fluctuation
x: A 4AT score of 0 suggests that delirium or severe cognitive impairment is unlikely.
A 4AT score of 1 to 3 indicates possible chronic cognitive impairment without acute delirium.
The 4AT evaluates acute attentional and arousal disturbance (delirium) rather than primary functional psychotic disorders.
Although dementia predisposes to delirium, acute onset over 24 hours with a 4AT score of 6 specifically flags acute delirium.

hq_q.s:
An 82 year old woman had a hemiarthroplasty for a hip fracture 2 days ago. Today she is confused and agitated. She is on regular morphine and has not opened her bowels since admission.
Temperature 37.3°C. There is a tender, dull suprapubic mass.
hq_q.w: Pain, constipation, retention, infection, drugs and low sodium are common reversible causes of delirium after surgery.
hq_q.f: Confusion after starting tramadol → review the drug chart.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of her confusion?

tm.m: Opioids, constipation and retention are common reversible causes of delirium
tm.g: New confusion with a tender dull suprapubic mass: urinary retention
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Hyponatraemia (Low sodium is common after surgery, but it does not explain a tender, dull mass above the pubis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Opioid toxicity (Opioid excess makes patients drowsy with small pupils and slow breathing; she is agitated, with a palpable bladder)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pneumonia (She has no cough, hypoxia or fever above 37.3°C; the examination finding is the bladder)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Stroke (A stroke gives focal weakness or speech change, not agitation with a tender bladder)
x: Low sodium is common after surgery, but it does not explain a tender, dull mass above the pubis.
Opioid excess makes patients drowsy with small pupils and slow breathing; she is agitated, with a palpable bladder.
She has no cough, hypoxia or fever above 37.3°C; the examination finding is the bladder.
A stroke gives focal weakness or speech change, not agitation with a tender bladder.

hq_q.s: A 78 year old man with idiopathic Parkinson's disease admitted with community-acquired pneumonia develops acute hyperactive delirium on the ward. He is terrified by visual hallucinations, repeatedly tries to climb over the bedrails, and strikes a healthcare assistant. Verbal de-escalation, lighting adjustments, spectacles, and his daughter's presence have failed to keep him safe.
hq_q.w: In patients with Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies who require emergency pharmacological sedation for severe distressed delirium posing an immediate safety risk, dopamine-blocking antipsychotics (especially haloperidol) are contraindicated; cautious low-dose oral or intramuscular lorazepam is used.
hq_q.f: No Parkinson's → low-dose haloperidol short term.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most appropriate?

tm.m: Dopamine D2 antagonists precipitate severe akinetic-rigid crises in Parkinson's disease, whereas GABA-A potentiation by lorazepam spares nigrostriatal dopamine
tm.g: Emergency pharmacological management of distressed delirium in Parkinson's disease -> cautious low-dose lorazepam
f: never appropriate in frail older adults with Parkinson's disease and delirium
short-term distress in hyperactive delirium in a patient without Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia
never used for geriatric delirium because central anticholinergic blockade worsens confusion
persistent severe aggression in Alzheimer's dementia without parkinsonism when non-drug measures fail
x: Chlorpromazine is a phenothiazine dopamine antagonist with strong alpha-adrenergic and anticholinergic effects that worsens parkinsonism, hypotension, and confusion.
Haloperidol is a potent nigrostriatal D2 antagonist that is strictly contraindicated in Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia.
Promethazine is a sedating H1 antihistamine with potent central anticholinergic activity that severely exacerbates delirium in older adults.
Risperidone has high D2 receptor occupancy and precipitates severe extrapyramidal motor deterioration in Parkinson's disease.

hq_q.s:
A 40 year old woman has felt low and worried for 6 weeks since her husband left. She cries at times and worries about money. She is sleeping and eating normally, still enjoys time with her children and is still working. She has no thoughts of self-harm.
Her PHQ-9 score is 7.
hq_q.w: Distress within a month of a stressor that does not meet depression criteria, settling within 6 months.
hq_q.f: Low mood, poor sleep, poor appetite and loss of interest for 6 weeks → depression.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: still enjoys time with her children
tm.m: Distress after a life event without meeting depression criteria is an adjustment reaction
tm.g: Low mood and worry after a stressor, short of depression, is adjustment disorder
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Dysthymia (Dysthymia needs 2 years of low mood; hers is 6 weeks after a stressor)
constant worry about many things for 6 months
low mood with poor sleep, appetite and loss of interest for weeks
8 months ago + flashbacks and nightmares
x: Dysthymia needs 2 years of low mood; hers is 6 weeks after a stressor.
Ruled out here: requires constant worry about many things for 6 months, whereas this patient has since her husband left, still enjoys time with her children.
Ruled out here: requires low mood with poor sleep, appetite and loss of interest for weeks, whereas this patient has since her husband left, still enjoys time with her children.
Ruled out here: requires 8 months ago + flashbacks and nightmares, whereas this patient has since her husband left, still enjoys time with her children.

hq_q.s: A 52 year old man was made redundant 4 weeks ago. Since then he has felt low and irritable and has trouble sleeping. He does not meet the criteria for depression and has no thoughts of self-harm.
o: Refer to community mental health team
hq_q.w: Support, counselling and practical problem-solving help. Most settle without medication. Key discriminator: Adjustment disorder: support and problem-solving.
hq_q.f: It turns into depression → treat as depression.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: does not meet the criteria for depression
tm.m: Adjustment disorder usually settles with support as the person adapts
tm.g: Adjustment disorder: support and problem-solving
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Daily diazepam for a month (Benzodiazepines are not recommended; they risk dependence and do not treat the reaction)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Refer to community mental health team (He has no risk and no severe illness; secondary care is not needed for an adjustment disorder)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Start sertraline (Antidepressants are not first-line for adjustment disorder; they are kept for depression)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Trauma-focused CBT (Trauma-focused CBT is for PTSD after a life-threatening event, not redundancy)
x: Benzodiazepines are not recommended; they risk dependence and do not treat the reaction.
He has no risk and no severe illness; secondary care is not needed for an adjustment disorder.
Antidepressants are not first-line for adjustment disorder; they are kept for depression.
Trauma-focused CBT is for PTSD after a life-threatening event, not redundancy.

hq_q.s: A 38 year old woman was diagnosed with adjustment disorder after a car crash. The legal case and her injuries were settled 9 months ago, but her symptoms persist. She has low mood most days and has lost interest in her hobbies.
hq_q.w: Adjustment disorder usually resolves within 6 months of the stressor ending, so persistent symptoms suggest another diagnosis.
hq_q.f: Symptoms began 1 week after the stressor → fits adjustment disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Adjustment disorder should settle within 6 months of the stressor ending
tm.g: Symptoms lasting beyond 6 months after the stressor: reassess the diagnosis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Continue problem-solving support (Support suits adjustment disorder; persisting symptoms 9 months after the stressor ended suggest depression)

the presentation instead showed features specific to Reassure that it will settle (Adjustment disorder settles within 6 months of the stressor ending; persisting low mood and loss of interest mean another diagnosis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Refer for trauma-focused CBT (She has no flashbacks or avoidance; the question is depression, not PTSD)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Start diazepam (Benzodiazepines risk dependence and do not treat persistent post-trauma symptoms)
x: Support suits adjustment disorder; persisting symptoms 9 months after the stressor ended suggest depression.
Adjustment disorder settles within 6 months of the stressor ending; persisting low mood and loss of interest mean another diagnosis.
She has no flashbacks or avoidance; the question is depression, not PTSD.
Benzodiazepines risk dependence and do not treat persistent post-trauma symptoms

hq_q.s: A 30 year old man has an intense fear of being judged when eating or speaking in public. He avoids work parties and meetings and has turned down a promotion. He has no panic attacks in other situations and is comfortable with close friends.
hq_q.w: Social anxiety: fear of scrutiny and embarrassment in social settings. Individual CBT is first line.
hq_q.f: Fear of crowds and places where escape is hard → agoraphobia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Fear of scrutiny drives avoidance of social and performance situations
tm.g: Fear of being judged in social situations is social anxiety disorder
f: fear of crowds and places where escape is hard
the presentation instead showed features specific to Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD is worry about many things; his fear is specific to being judged)
normal blood pressure during attacks with normal metanephrines
fear of one object such as needles
x: Ruled out here: requires fear of crowds and places where escape is hard, whereas this patient has fear of being judged, comfortable with close friends.
GAD is worry about many things; his fear is specific to being judged.
Ruled out here: requires normal blood pressure during attacks with normal metanephrines, whereas this patient has fear of being judged, comfortable with close friends.
Ruled out here: requires fear of one object such as needles, whereas this patient has fear of being judged, comfortable with close friends.

hq_q.s: A 34 year old woman with hypothyroidism attends general practice because she has avoided all blood tests and vaccinations for 8 years due to an intense fear of needles. Whenever she sees a syringe she experiences dizziness, pallor, and vasovagal syncope. She has no generalised anxiety or depression and wants to overcome her fear.
hq_q.w: Cognitive behavioural therapy incorporating graded exposure in vivo (combined with applied muscle tension for blood-injection-injury phobia with vasovagal syncope) is the first-line treatment of choice for specific phobias; routine pharmacological treatment is not recommended.
hq_q.f: Faints at the sight of blood → applied tension technique.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first treatment?

tm.m: Systematic hierarchical exposure extinguishes conditioned phobic fear through habituation and inhibitory learning
tm.g: Specific phobia (such as needle phobia) -> graded exposure therapy (CBT)
f: emergency seizure termination rather than long-term cure of a specific phobia
situational autonomic tremor before a one-off musical performance in a normotensive adult
severe generalised anxiety disorder or panic disorder failing psychological therapy
never first-line over graded exposure therapy for a circumscribed specific phobia
x: Pre-procedural benzodiazepines impair fear extinction learning during exposure and carry risks of sedation and dependence.
Beta-blockers such as propranolol blunt sympathetic tachycardia but worsen hypotension and bradycardia in vasovagal blood-injury-injection syncope.
Daily SSRI antidepressants are used for generalised anxiety disorder, panic disorder, or social anxiety rather than isolated specific phobias.
Unstructured psychodynamic psychotherapy does not provide behavioural fear habituation and is inferior to CBT with graded exposure.

hq_q.s: A 28 year old man has social anxiety disorder. He has completed a course of individual CBT for social anxiety but still struggles to go to work meetings. He has no other medical problems.
hq_q.w: NICE: an SSRI such as escitalopram or sertraline if CBT is declined or does not work.
hq_q.f: SSRI not effective → venlafaxine or another SSRI.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most appropriate first?

c: completed a course of individual CBT
tm.m: SSRIs reduce social anxiety when CBT alone is not enough
tm.g: Social anxiety after CBT: escitalopram
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam (Benzodiazepines are contraindicated for routine management of social anxiety disorder)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Mirtazapine (Mirtazapine is not a first-line drug for social anxiety)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Propranolol (Propranolol helps performance tremor but does not treat social anxiety disorder)
an SSRI has not helped
x: Benzodiazepines are contraindicated for routine management of social anxiety disorder
Mirtazapine is not a first-line drug for social anxiety.
Propranolol helps performance tremor but does not treat social anxiety disorder.
Ruled out here: requires an SSRI has not helped, whereas this patient has completed a course of individual CBT, A 28 year old man has.

hq_q.s: A 9 year old boy has been diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder by the community paediatric service after impairing hyperactivity and inattention at both home and school persisted despite a parent-training programme. He is starting modified-release oral methylphenidate. His baseline ECG, heart examination, and family cardiac history are normal.
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG87, stimulants such as methylphenidate suppress appetite and raise heart rate and blood pressure. Height and weight must be plotted on centile charts every 3 to 6 months alongside pulse and blood pressure.
hq_q.f: Family history of sudden cardiac death → ECG before starting.
hq_q.ql: Which monitoring is most important?

c: baseline ECG, heart examination, and family cardiac history are normal
tm.m: Catecholamine reuptake inhibition suppresses appetite (slowing growth) and elevates heart rate and blood pressure
tm.g: Routine physical monitoring on methylphenidate -> height, weight (centile charts), pulse rate and blood pressure
f: maintenance lithium carbonate therapy in bipolar affective disorder
monitoring hepatotoxicity during antituberculous therapy with isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide
monitoring narrow-therapeutic-index drugs such as lithium or phenytoin
six-monthly monitoring of a patient taking lithium or amiodarone
x: Methylphenidate is not nephrotoxic and does not require routine renal function or electrolyte blood tests.
Routine monthly liver function blood tests are not required for children taking methylphenidate.
Methylphenidate dosing is titrated against clinical symptom response and side effects rather than serum drug concentrations.
Methylphenidate does not cause hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism and requires no routine thyroid blood monitoring.

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old woman was diagnosed with ADHD after a specialist assessment. Her inattention and impulsivity are affecting her work. She has no history of heart disease, substance misuse or psychosis.
Her BP is 118/74 mmHg.
hq_q.w: NICE: lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate first for adults. Key discriminator: Adult ADHD: lisdexamfetamine first.
hq_q.f: Stimulants not tolerated → atomoxetine.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is first line?

c: no history of heart disease, substance misuse or psychosis
tm.m: Stimulants work best and are first line in adult ADHD
tm.g: Adult ADHD: lisdexamfetamine first
f: stimulants are not tolerated
the presentation instead showed features specific to Dexamfetamine (Dexamfetamine is offered when lisdexamfetamine helps but its longer action is not tolerated, not first)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Guanfacine (Guanfacine is for children and young people, not adults first line)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Modafinil (Modafinil is not licensed for ADHD)
x: Ruled out here: requires stimulants are not tolerated, whereas this patient has no history of heart disease, substance misuse or psychosis, A 24 year old woman was.
Dexamfetamine is offered when lisdexamfetamine helps but its longer action is not tolerated, not first.
Guanfacine is for children and young people, not adults first line.
Modafinil is not licensed for ADHD.

hq_q.s: A 7 year old boy is brought to his GP because his year 3 class teacher reports that he stares out of the window, fails to finish worksheets, and fidgets in class. However, his parents report that he concentrates for hours on Lego and reading at home, follows instructions calmly at Beavers and football coaching, and had no issues in nursery.
hq_q.w: Diagnosing ADHD requires core symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity causing impairment across two or more independent settings (such as home and school). Symptoms confined to school warrant investigating learning difficulties, hearing, or bullying.
hq_q.f: Symptoms at home and school for over 6 months → refer for ADHD assessment.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: concentrates for hours on Lego and reading at home
follows instructions calmly at Beavers and football
tm.m: Neurodevelopmental ADHD is pervasive across environments, whereas single-setting school inattention points to educational, sensory, or social factors
tm.g: Inattention and restlessness confined to a single setting (school only) -> look for other causes (hearing, vision, dyslexia, bullying)
f: pervasive inattention and hyperactivity causing impairment at school, at home and at sports clubs
poor eye contact, lack of peer relationships, rigid routines and sensory overload
specialist-confirmed severe ADHD persisting across home and school after environmental modifications
oppositional and defiant behaviour occurring predominantly at home with his parents
x: ADHD cannot be diagnosed when symptoms are absent at home and in recreational clubs, as pervasiveness across at least two settings is mandatory.
He interacts well at Beavers and football and has no social communication deficits or restricted repetitive behaviours suggesting autism.
Methylphenidate must never be initiated in primary care or without a confirmed multi-setting specialist diagnosis of ADHD.
Parent-training programmes address behavioural difficulties at home, whereas his parents report calm, focused behaviour outside school.

hq_q.s:
A 9 year old boy is referred by his school SENCO because for the past 12 months he has argued daily with teachers and his parents, actively refused to follow classroom rules, blamed others for his mistakes, and deliberately annoyed his younger sister.
He has never been physically cruel to people or animals, has never destroyed property or set fires, and has never stolen.
hq_q.w: Oppositional defiant disorder is characterised by a persistent pattern (at least 6 months) of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behaviour toward authority figures, and vindictiveness, without the severe physical aggression, cruelty to animals, property destruction, or theft that define conduct disorder.
hq_q.f: Cruelty to animals and fire setting → conduct disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: argued daily with teachers and his parents
tm.m: Persistent defiance and temper outbursts toward authority figures without violation of others' basic rights or societal laws
tm.g: Persistent defiance, arguing and temper loss without violence, cruelty or property destruction -> oppositional defiant disorder
f: pervasive distractibility, losing belongings and inability to sit still without deliberate spitefulness
impaired eye contact, literal language, sensory hypersensitivity and distress when routines change
repeated physical fights with weapons, cruelty to animals, arson and shoplifting
generalized delay in academic learning and daily living skills with an IQ of 62
x: ADHD is defined by pervasive inattention, forgetfulness, and hyperactive impulsivity rather than deliberate defiance and vindictiveness.
Autism spectrum disorder is characterised by impaired reciprocal social communication and distress at routine changes rather than calculated annoyance of others.
Conduct disorder requires repetitive violation of the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms (violence, cruelty to animals, fire-setting, or theft).
Intellectual disability involves generalized deficits in intellectual and adaptive functioning across conceptual, social, and practical domains.

hq_q.s: An 8 year old boy has conduct disorder with aggression and stealing. His parents are struggling to manage his behaviour. There are no concerns about ADHD or learning difficulties.
hq_q.w: Group parent training programmes are first line for children aged 3 to 11. Key discriminator: Conduct disorder under 12: group parent training.
hq_q.f: A 14-year-old → individual social and cognitive programmes.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

tm.m: Parenting programmes change the patterns that maintain the behaviour
tm.g: Conduct disorder under 12: group parent training
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Lithium (Lithium is not used for conduct disorder)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Methylphenidate (Methylphenidate treats coexisting ADHD, which he does not have)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Residential care placement (Residential care is a last resort, not first line)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Risperidone (Risperidone is only for severe aggression after psychosocial help has failed)
x: Lithium is not used for conduct disorder.
Methylphenidate treats coexisting ADHD, which he does not have.
Residential care is a last resort, not first line.
Risperidone is only for severe aggression after psychosocial help has failed.

hq_q.s: A 13 year old boy has conduct disorder that started at age 8. He has been excluded from school for violence and has been cautioned by police for theft. His mother asks about the long-term outlook.
hq_q.w: Conduct disorder before 15 is a requirement for, and a strong predictor of, antisocial personality disorder.
hq_q.f: Early parent training → lowers the risk.
hq_q.ql: Which adult outcome is he at highest risk of?

tm.m: Early-onset conduct disorder often continues into adult antisocial behaviour
tm.g: Early conduct disorder leads most often to antisocial personality disorder
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Anorexia nervosa (Anorexia is not linked to conduct disorder)
discrete episodes of high mood lasting a week or more
the presentation instead showed features specific to Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD is not linked to conduct disorder)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Schizophrenia (Conduct disorder does not strongly predict schizophrenia)
x: Anorexia is not linked to conduct disorder.
Ruled out here: requires discrete episodes of high mood lasting a week or more, whereas this patient has started at age 8, cautioned by police.
OCD is not linked to conduct disorder.
Conduct disorder does not strongly predict schizophrenia.

hq_q.s:
A 25 year old woman attends her annual primary care learning disability health check accompanied by her support worker. She completed mainstream schooling with learning support, lives in a supported flat, travels on familiar bus routes, cooks simple meals, and works part-time in a supermarket.
Formal psychometric assessment records a full-scale IQ of 60.
hq_q.w: Under ICD-10/ICD-11 and DSM-5, intellectual disability is stratified by adaptive functioning and approximate IQ bands: mild (IQ 50 to 69, ~85% of cases), moderate (IQ 35 to 49), severe (IQ 20 to 34), and profound (IQ under 20).
hq_q.f: IQ of 25 → severe.
hq_q.ql: How is her intellectual disability classified?

tm.m: An IQ between 50 and 69 (2 to 3 standard deviations below the mean) with semi-independent living skills defines mild intellectual disability
tm.g: Intellectual disability with IQ 50 to 69 and semi-independent daily living skills -> mild intellectual disability
f: an IQ of 76 with mild academic difficulty and full independent living
an IQ of 42 with basic self-care skills requiring daily supervised support
an IQ of 16 with non-verbal communication and 24-hour dependence for all personal care
an IQ of 28 with single-word speech and need for daily assistance with dressing and washing
x: Borderline intellectual functioning corresponds to an IQ of 70 to 84 and does not meet the threshold (<70) for intellectual disability.
Moderate intellectual disability corresponds to an IQ of 35 to 49, typically requiring substantial daily supervision.
Profound intellectual disability corresponds to an IQ below 20, with minimal verbal communication and full dependence for all personal care.
Severe intellectual disability corresponds to an IQ of 20 to 34, with very limited language and need for continuous personal support.

hq_q.s: A 34 year old man with a severe learning disability and no speech has started hitting his head and refusing food over a week. His carers say this is new. He has had no change in his routine or carers.
hq_q.w: Change in behaviour often reflects pain, constipation, dental problems, reflux or infection. He may not be able to say.
hq_q.f: No physical cause found → look at changes in his environment and routine.
hq_q.ql: Which should be excluded first?

c: hitting his head and refusing food
tm.m: People who cannot speak show pain or illness through behaviour
tm.g: New behaviour change in someone who cannot communicate: exclude pain or physical illness
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Autism (Autism does not start suddenly in adulthood)

the presentation instead showed features specific to Depression (Depression can cause withdrawal, but new head banging and food refusal in someone who cannot speak is pain or illness until proven otherwise)
the presentation instead showed features specific to New-onset psychotic illness (Psychosis is considered only after physical causes)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Personality disorder (Enduring maladaptive traits since adolescence, not an acute 1-week behaviour change)
x: Autism does not start suddenly in adulthood.
Depression can cause withdrawal, but new head banging and food refusal in someone who cannot speak is pain or illness until proven otherwise.
Psychosis is considered only after physical causes.
Enduring maladaptive traits since adolescence, not an acute 1-week behaviour change

hq_q.s:
A 20 year old man with a moderate learning disability attends a review with his mother. He has poor eye contact and is anxious in social situations. His maternal uncle also has a learning disability.
He has a long face, prominent jaw, large ears and enlarged testes. There is joint hypermobility.
hq_q.w: Fragile X is the commonest inherited cause of learning disability: a CGG repeat in FMR1 on the X chromosome.
hq_q.f: Learning disability with a high risk of early Alzheimer's → Down syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: long face, prominent jaw, large ears and enlarged testes
tm.m: A CGG repeat on the X chromosome silences FMR1, passed through the mother
tm.g: Learning disability with a long face, large ears and large testes is fragile X
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Down syndrome (Down syndrome has upslanting eyes and a flat face, not a long face, large ears and large testes)
tall with small testes and gynaecomastia
overeating and obesity after a floppy infancy
an elfin face, over-friendliness and high calcium
x: Down syndrome has upslanting eyes and a flat face, not a long face, large ears and large testes.
Ruled out here: requires tall with small testes and gynaecomastia, whereas this patient has maternal uncle, long face, prominent jaw, large ears and enlarged testes.
Ruled out here: requires overeating and obesity after a floppy infancy, whereas this patient has maternal uncle, long face, prominent jaw, large ears and enlarged testes.
Ruled out here: requires an elfin face, over-friendliness and high calcium, whereas this patient has maternal uncle, long face, prominent jaw, large ears and enlarged testes.

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man presents to his GP with a 6-week history of passing looser, more frequent stools three times daily. He has no visible rectal bleeding, pain or weight loss. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 130/78 mmHg. Abdominal and rectal examinations are normal. Haemoglobin is 132 g/L. A quantitative faecal immunochemical test (FIT) returns at 64 ug Hb/g faeces (<10).
o: Reassure that no visible rectal bleeding is present
Refer for routine non-urgent CT colonography
Repeat the faecal immunochemical test in 3 months
Urgent suspected lower GI cancer pathway referral
hq_q.w: Under NICE DG56 and NG12 guidelines, a quantitative faecal immunochemical test (FIT) result of >=10 ug haemoglobin per gram of faeces in a patient with lower gastrointestinal symptoms mandates an urgent 2-week-wait suspected colorectal cancer referral for colonoscopy.
hq_q.f: Quantitative FIT <10 ug Hb/g faeces with no iron-deficiency anaemia or palpable abdominal/rectal mass -> manage in primary care with safety-netting.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

tm.m: Quantitative FIT uses antibodies specific to intact human globin, detecting occult lower gastrointestinal mucosal bleeding from colorectal neoplasia undisturbed by dietary peroxidase
tm.g: Symptomatic patient with quantitative FIT >= 10 ug Hb/g faeces: urgent 2-week-wait suspected lower GI cancer referral
x: Serum CEA has poor sensitivity and specificity for primary diagnosis of colorectal cancer and is used only for post-resection surveillance.
Occult neoplastic bleeding frequently occurs without visible haematochezia; a positive FIT (>=10 ug Hb/g) carries a high positive predictive value for colorectal cancer.
A symptomatic adult with a FIT >=10 ug Hb/g requires an urgent 2-week-wait suspected cancer referral rather than a routine non-urgent scan.
Repeating a positive FIT delays definitive colonoscopy and is explicitly advised against by NICE DG56 guidelines.
f: He has completed curative resection of a stage III colon carcinoma and requires postoperative recurrence monitoring.
A 28 year old with 3 days of self-limiting viral gastroenteritis has resolved symptoms and no red flags.
A frail patient with severe cardiopulmonary comorbidity is evaluated via the urgent cancer pathway when unfit for colonoscopy.
An initial stool sample was rejected by the laboratory due to a technical collection error.

hq_q.s: A 73 year old woman presents to her GP with a 3-month history of progressive exertional breathlessness, fatigue and 4 kg of unintentional weight loss. She opens her bowels once daily with normal-calibre brown stools and has never seen rectal bleeding. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 124/72 mmHg. Her conjunctivae are pale. Abdominal palpation reveals a firm, non-tender 5 cm mass in the right iliac fossa.
hq_q.w: Right-sided (caecal and ascending colon) adenocarcinomas bleed occultly into liquid faecal effluent within a wide-calibre lumen, rarely causing obstruction or visible bleeding. They classically present with severe microcytic iron-deficiency anaemia, weight loss and a palpable right iliac fossa mass.
hq_q.f: Alternating constipation and looser stools with visible blood mixed in the stool and tenesmus -> left-sided (sigmoid or rectal) carcinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: firm, non-tender 5 cm mass in the right iliac fossa
tm.m: Exophytic ulcerated caecal tumours bleed occultly into liquid ileocaecal contents without obstructing luminal transit, depleting iron stores before altering bowel habit
tm.g: Older adult with unexplained microcytic iron-deficiency anaemia + weight loss + painless right iliac fossa mass = caecal carcinoma
x: An appendix abscess presents acutely with fever, right iliac fossa tenderness, localised guarding and neutrophilia rather than a 3-month painless mass with severe microcytic anaemia.
Crohn's disease typically presents in younger adults with crampy abdominal pain, chronic diarrhoea and raised inflammatory markers rather than painless profound iron deficiency at age 73.
Diverticular abscesses occur predominantly in the left iliac fossa (sigmoid colon) and present with acute pain, fever and tenderness.
Left-sided sigmoid tumours grow annularly around a narrower lumen containing solid stool, presenting with altered bowel habit, obstruction or visible bleeding rather than a right iliac fossa mass.
f: She presents with a 5-day history of migratory right iliac fossa pain, pyrexia of 38.5°C, tender right iliac fossa mass and leucocytosis.
A 22 year old smoker presents with a 4-month history of crampy right iliac fossa pain, watery diarrhoea, aphthous mouth ulcers and weight loss.
She presents with acute left iliac fossa pain, fever of 38.4°C and a tender left-sided mass.
She presents with progressive constipation, tenesmus, dark red blood mixed with stool and a left iliac fossa mass.

hq_q.s: A 69 year old man has had rectal bleeding and tenesmus. MRI pelvis shows a rectal cancer 3 cm from the anal verge that invades the anal sphincter complex. CT shows no distant spread. He has completed chemoradiotherapy and is fit for surgery.
hq_q.w: A very low tumour that involves the sphincters cannot be joined back up, so the rectum and anus are removed with a permanent end colostomy.
hq_q.f: Tumour in the upper rectum 12 cm from the verge → anterior resection with a join.
hq_q.ql: Which operation is most appropriate?

tm.m: A tumour in the sphincters cannot be removed with a join
tm.g: Low rectal cancer involving the sphincters: abdominoperineal resection
f: cancer of the descending colon
emergency obstruction in a frail patient
an upper rectal tumour 12 cm from the verge
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sigmoid colectomy (A sigmoid colectomy removes the sigmoid, not a low rectal cancer)
x: Ruled out here: requires cancer of the descending colon, whereas this patient has 3 cm from the anal verge, invades the anal sphincter.
Ruled out here: requires emergency obstruction in a frail patient, whereas this patient has 3 cm from the anal verge, invades the anal sphincter.
Ruled out here: requires an upper rectal tumour 12 cm from the verge, whereas this patient has 3 cm from the anal verge, invades the anal sphincter.
A sigmoid colectomy removes the sigmoid, not a low rectal cancer.

hq_q.s: A 34 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of severe throbbing perianal pain that prevents him from sitting down. He has no history of inflammatory bowel disease. Temperature 38.0°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg. Inspection of the perineum reveals a 3 cm erythematous, hot, exquisitely tender, fluctuant swelling situated 2 cm from the anal verge at the 4 o'clock position.
hq_q.w: An acute perianal abscess arises from infection of a cryptoglandular anal gland at the dentate line. Definitive immediate treatment is prompt surgical incision and drainage (usually under general anaesthetic); oral antibiotics alone do not clear a collection of pus.
hq_q.f: Recurrent perianal abscess or persistent discharging sinus opening -> arrange pelvic MRI and examination under anaesthetic for fistula-in-ano.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

c: 3 cm erythematous, hot, exquisitely tender, fluctuant swelling
tm.m: Obstruction of an anal crypt gland duct in the intersphincteric plane leads to bacterial proliferation and tracking of pus caudally to the perianal skin, requiring surgical decompression
tm.g: Acute perianal abscess (hot, tender, fluctuant perianal swelling + fever): surgical incision and drainage (do not treat with antibiotics alone)
x: Oral antibiotics alone cannot penetrate a walled-off cavity of pus and leaving a perianal abscess undrained risks fistula formation or Fournier's gangrene.
Rubber band ligation treats internal haemorrhoids above the dentate line and is strictly contraindicated in acute anorectal sepsis.
Waiting for an outpatient or inpatient MRI in an uncomplicated primary acute perianal abscess delays urgent source control and risks spreading perineal sepsis.
Topical GTN relaxes the internal anal sphincter in chronic anal fissure and has no role in draining a purulent perianal abscess.
f: He has minor perianal cellulitis following abscess incision and drainage in a patient with diabetes mellitus.
He presents with painless bright red rectal bleeding from prolapsing second-degree internal haemorrhoids.
He has a complex recurrent horseshoe fistula-in-ano requiring preoperative anatomical sphincter mapping.
He has a chronic posterior midline anal fissure causing tearing pain strictly during and after defecation without a fluctuant mass or fever.

hq_q.s: A 42 year old man attends clinic with a discharging perianal fistula 5 months after drainage of a perianal abscess. He has no bowel symptoms. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg. Examination in the lithotomy position identifies an external fistula opening located 3 cm from the anal verge at the 7 o'clock position, posterior to an imaginary transverse line across the anus.
o: Internal opening at 12 o'clock via a curved tract
Internal opening at 1 o'clock via a curved tract
Internal opening at 3 o'clock via a straight radial tract
Internal opening at 6 o'clock via a curved tract
Internal opening at 7 o'clock via a straight radial tract
hq_q.w: Goodsall's rule states that an imaginary transverse line between 3 and 9 o'clock divides the anus in the lithotomy position: posterior external fistula openings (like 7 o'clock) follow a curved track to open in the posterior midline at 6 o'clock.
hq_q.f: External fistula opening at 2 o'clock (anterior to the transverse anal line) -> straight radial track to an internal opening at 2 o'clock.
hq_q.ql: According to Goodsall's rule, where is the internal opening and what is the expected course of the fistula tract?

c: external fistula opening located 3 cm from the anal verge at the 7 o'clock position
posterior to an imaginary transverse line
tm.m: Posterior perianal abscesses originate predominantly from the deep post-anal space and posterior midline crypt gland at 6 o'clock, tracking circumferentially around the sphincter
tm.g: Goodsall's rule: posterior external opening (behind 3-9 o'clock line) -> curved track to internal opening at 6 o'clock; anterior opening -> straight radial track
x: Posterior external openings drain into the posterior midline crypt at 6 o'clock rather than the anterior midline at 12 o'clock.
A posterior external opening does not curve anteriorly to the 1 o'clock position.
Straight radial tracts are characteristic of external openings situated anterior to the transverse anal line, not at 7 o'clock.
External openings situated posterior to the transverse anal line follow a curved horseshoe path to the posterior midline (6 o'clock) rather than running radially to 7 o'clock.
f: An anterior midline crypt infection drains directly anteriorly at the 12 o'clock position.
An anterior external opening at 1 o'clock within 3 cm of the anal verge runs directly radially to 1 o'clock.
The external fistula opening is identified at the 3 o'clock position, 2 cm from the anal verge.
The external fistula opening lies anterior to the transverse line at 10 o'clock and tracks radially to 10 o'clock.

hq_q.s: A 26 year old woman presents with a 4-month history of loose stools four times daily, colicky right lower quadrant abdominal pain and 6 kg weight loss. Over 6 weeks she has developed two painful discharging openings around her anus. Temperature 37.3°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg. Examination reveals aphthous oral ulcers, multiple perianal fistula openings and oedematous skin tags. Serum CRP is 48 mg/L and faecal calprotectin is 920 ug/g.
hq_q.w: Transmural granulomatous inflammation in Crohn's disease penetrates the full thickness of the bowel wall, causing deep fissures, complex or multiple perianal fistulae, large oedematous anal skin tags and aphthous oral ulceration alongside chronic diarrhoea and raised faecal calprotectin.
hq_q.f: Continuous superficial mucosal inflammation limited to the colon and rectum with bloody diarrhoea and no fistulae -> ulcerative colitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

c: colicky right lower quadrant abdominal pain and 6 kg weight loss
tm.m: Full-thickness transmural Th1/Th17-mediated inflammation extending from the anal crypts through the sphincter planes creates branching perianal fistulous tracts
tm.g: Multiple/complex perianal fistulae + oedematous skin tags + aphthous ulcers + chronic diarrhoea = Crohn's disease
x: Ileocaecal tuberculosis rarely causes multiple perianal fistulae with aphthous mouth ulcers in a patient without tuberculosis exposure or constitutional night sweats.
Hidradenitis suppurativa affects apocrine skin folds with comedones and scarring and does not cause aphthous stomatitis, weight loss or raised faecal calprotectin.
Pilonidal disease is confined to midline hair-bearing pits in the upper natal cleft and does not cause chronic diarrhoea, oral ulcers or elevated faecal calprotectin.
Ulcerative colitis is restricted to the colonic mucosa and submucosa (sparing the small bowel and mouth) and does not cause transmural perianal fistulae.
f: A recent migrant from an endemic region presents with drenching night sweats, pulmonary cavitation and caseating granulomas on ileal biopsy.
She has normal bowel habit and normal faecal calprotectin with recurrent abscesses and sinus tracts in both axillae and groins.
A hirsute man with normal bowel habit has a discharging sinus in the upper natal cleft containing hair tufts.
She presents with bloody mucoid diarrhoea, tenesmus and continuous superficial mucosal inflammation extending proximally from the rectum without fistulae.

hq_q.s: A 42 year old man presents with a 3-week history of bright red blood noticed on the toilet paper and dripping into the pan after defecation. The bleeding is completely painless and never mixed in with the stool. His bowel habit is unchanged and he strains with hard stools. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg. Abdominal and digital rectal examinations are normal.
hq_q.w: Painless bright red rectal bleeding seen on the toilet paper or dripping into the pan at the end of defecation (separate from the stool) in a patient who strains is the classic presentation of internal haemorrhoids above the dentate line.
hq_q.f: Severe tearing pain during defecation with a linear split at 6 o'clock -> acute anal fissure.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: bright red blood noticed on the toilet paper and dripping into the pan
never mixed in with the stool
tm.m: Shearing forces during straining engorge and disrupt the submucosal arteriovenous vascular cushions above the dentate line, causing painless arterial-bright outlet bleeding
tm.g: Painless bright red blood on paper / dripping in pan after defecation (not mixed with stool) = internal haemorrhoids
x: An anal fissure causes severe, razor-like tearing pain during and for an hour after defecation rather than painless bright red dripping blood.
A fistula-in-ano presents with chronic purulent and serosanguinous discharge onto the underwear from a perianal external opening rather than painless outlet bleeding.
Rectosigmoid carcinoma typically presents in older adults with dark blood mixed with the stool, tenesmus or a change in bowel habit.
A thrombosed external haemorrhoid (perianal haematoma) presents with an acutely painful, tense, purple subcutaneous swelling at the anal verge.
f: He experiences severe tearing anal pain on passing stool that throbs for an hour afterwards with a visible posterior midline split.
He has persistent purulent discharge onto his underwear from a granulating papule 2 cm from the anal margin following a previous abscess.
A 66 year old man presents with dark red blood mixed throughout the stool, tenesmus and a 6-week change to looser motions.
He develops a sudden, exquisitely painful 1.5 cm tense purple lump at the anal margin 24 hours after straining.

hq_q.s: A 48 year old woman attends clinic with a 12-month history of painless bright red outlet bleeding and a mucosal lump that prolapses through her anus when she opens her bowels. The prolapsed tissue stays outside until she pushes it back inside manually with her finger. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg. Proctoscopy confirms internal haemorrhoids that prolapse on straining and require digital reduction.
hq_q.w: Goligher's classification grades internal haemorrhoids from I to IV: grade I bleed without prolapse; grade II prolapse on straining and reduce spontaneously; grade III prolapse on straining and require manual digital reduction; and grade IV are irreducibly prolapsed.
hq_q.f: Haemorrhoids prolapse on straining and reduce spontaneously -> second-degree (grade II) internal haemorrhoids.
hq_q.ql: According to Goligher's classification, which degree of internal haemorrhoids does she have?

c: prolapses through her anus when she opens her bowels
pushes it back inside manually with her finger
tm.m: Progressive attenuation and fragmentation of Treitz's suspensory fibromuscular ligament allows the superior haemorrhoidal cushion to descend below the anal sphincter until digitally replaced
tm.g: Haemorrhoid grading: I = no prolapse; II = spontaneous reduction; III = manual digital reduction required; IV = irreducible
x: First-degree haemorrhoids project into the lumen and bleed on defecation but never prolapse beyond the anal verge.
Fourth-degree haemorrhoids are permanently prolapsed outside the anal canal and cannot be reduced manually.
Second-degree haemorrhoids prolapse through the anal verge during straining but retract spontaneously once straining ceases.
External haemorrhoids originate below the dentate line, are covered by somatic anoderm skin and do not reduce into the upper anal canal.
f: Proctoscopy shows vascular cushions that bleed on contact but remain entirely within the anal canal on straining.
The prolapsed haemorrhoidal cushions lie permanently outside the anal margin and cannot be pushed back inside digitally.
The haemorrhoidal cushions prolapse on straining at stool and return spontaneously into the anal canal without digital assistance.
She has an acutely painful, tense blueberry-coloured subcutaneous swelling at the anal verge below the dentate line.

hq_q.s: A 30 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 24-hour history of an exquisitely painful swelling at the edge of his anus that appeared suddenly after straining to pass a hard stool. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg. Inspection of the anal verge reveals a tense, tender, 1.5 cm bluish-purple subcutaneous nodule at the anal margin covered by intact anoderm skin.
o: Conservative care with ice and stool softeners
Excision of the clot under local anaesthetic
hq_q.w: An acute thrombosed external haemorrhoid (perianal haematoma) presenting within 72 hours of onset causes severe somatic pain below the dentate line. Excision of the thrombosed varix under local anaesthetic provides rapid pain relief; presentations after 72 hours are managed conservatively.
hq_q.f: Presentation more than 72 hours after onset with improving pain -> conservative management with analgesia, ice packs and stool softeners.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management to provide rapid symptom relief?

c: 24-hour history of an exquisitely painful swelling
after straining to pass a hard stool
1.5 cm bluish-purple subcutaneous nodule at the anal margin
tm.m: Acute high venous pressure during straining ruptures or thromboses the inferior haemorrhoidal venous plexus beneath the somatically innervated anoderm
tm.g: Acute thrombosed external haemorrhoid (<72 hours onset): excision under local anaesthetic (>72 hours: conservative management)
x: Conservative management is preferred when presentation is delayed beyond 72 hours, as spontaneous clot resolution is already underway.
Inpatient three-column internal/external haemorrhoidectomy under general anaesthetic is excessive for a solitary acute thrombosed external haemorrhoidal varix.
A thrombosed external haemorrhoid is an acute intravascular venous clot rather than a bacterial abscess, so antibiotics are ineffective.
Applying a rubber band below the dentate line on somatic skin-covered external haemorrhoids causes excruciating pain and is strictly contraindicated.
f: He presents 5 days after symptom onset when the pain and swelling are already beginning to subside.
He has circumferential grade IV internal and external haemorrhoids failing outpatient therapies.
He has a hot, erythematous fluctuant perianal abscess with cellulitis and systemic pyrexia.
He has painless bleeding from second-degree internal haemorrhoids situated above the dentate line.

hq_q.s: A 28 year old woman presents with a 2-week history of severe, knife-like tearing anal pain during defecation that persists as a throbbing ache for an hour afterwards. She has noticed bright red blood streaks on the toilet paper and has been constipated. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg. Gentle parting of the buttocks reveals a longitudinal mucosal split in the posterior midline.
hq_q.w: An anal fissure is a longitudinal linear tear in the squamous anoderm below the dentate line. Around 90% occur in the posterior midline (6 o'clock), presenting with severe tearing pain during defecation, reflex sphincter spasm and bright red blood on the paper.
hq_q.f: Multiple, painless or lateral/off-midline anal fissures with chronic diarrhoea -> investigate for underlying Crohn's disease, HIV, syphilis or anal carcinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: knife-like tearing anal pain during defecation
throbbing ache for an hour afterwards
bright red blood streaks on the toilet paper
longitudinal mucosal split in the posterior midline
tm.m: Passage of a hard faecal bolus tears the relatively avascular posterior midline anoderm, exposing the internal anal sphincter and triggering ischaemic hypertonic spasm
tm.g: Severe tearing pain on defecation lasting ~1 hour + bright red blood on paper + posterior midline (6 o'clock) mucosal tear = anal fissure
x: A perianal abscess causes continuous worsening throbbing pain, fever and a hot fluctuant perianal swelling rather than pain triggered strictly by defecation.
A fistula-in-ano causes chronic purulent perianal discharge from a granulating external opening rather than acute tearing defecatory pain at 6 o'clock.
Internal haemorrhoids originate above the dentate line and cause painless bright red bleeding rather than severe knife-like post-defecatory pain.
Ulcerative proctitis causes bloody mucoid discharge, rectal tenesmus and urgency rather than a discrete posterior midline linear tear after passing hard stool.
f: She has a 3-day history of fever (38.3°C) and a hot, fluctuant, erythematous 3 cm swelling beside the anal verge.
She has persistent purulent discharge onto her underwear 3 months after surgical drainage of a perianal abscess.
She has painless bright red blood dripping into the toilet pan with no tear visible on parting the buttocks.
She passes bloody mucus six times daily with tenesmus and proctoscopy shows diffuse friable rectal mucosal inflammation.

hq_q.s:
A 36 year old man has had pain and bleeding on opening his bowels for 8 weeks. He has taken laxatives and his stools are now soft, but the pain continues.
There is a posterior midline anal fissure with a sentinel skin tag.
hq_q.w: A chronic fissure, over 6 weeks, is treated first with topical GTN for 6 to 8 weeks to relax the sphincter and let it heal.
hq_q.f: Still not healed after 8 weeks of GTN → refer for botulinum toxin or sphincterotomy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: GTN relaxes the internal sphincter and improves blood flow to the fissure
tm.g: Chronic fissure over 6 weeks: topical GTN 0.4%
f: still not healed after 8 weeks of GTN
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lateral internal sphincterotomy (Sphincterotomy is for fissures that fail medical treatment, as it risks incontinence)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral metronidazole (Metronidazole is not used for fissures)
a dry, scaly, itchy rash that lasts for weeks
x: Ruled out here: requires still not healed after 8 weeks of GTN, whereas this patient has 8 weeks, stools are now soft.
Sphincterotomy is for fissures that fail medical treatment, as it risks incontinence.
Metronidazole is not used for fissures.
Ruled out here: requires a dry, scaly, itchy rash that lasts for weeks, whereas this patient has 8 weeks, stools are now soft.

hq_q.s: A 40 year old woman has a chronic posterior anal fissure for 3 months. She started topical glyceryl trinitrate 0.4% ointment but stopped after 3 days because of severe headaches.
hq_q.w: Topical diltiazem relaxes the internal sphincter like GTN but with fewer headaches. Headache is the main reason people stop GTN.
hq_q.f: Both topical treatments fail → surgical referral.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate alternative?

tm.m: Diltiazem relaxes the sphincter without the GTN headache
tm.g: Fissure with GTN headaches: topical diltiazem 2%
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Lidocaine gel (Lidocaine eases pain but does not relax the sphincter)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral nifedipine (Topical diltiazem has fewer systemic cardiovascular side effects than oral nifedipine)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Topical clotrimazole (Clotrimazole is an antifungal)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Topical hydrocortisone (Hydrocortisone does not relax the sphincter or heal fissures)
x: Lidocaine eases pain but does not relax the sphincter.
Topical diltiazem has fewer systemic cardiovascular side effects than oral nifedipine
Clotrimazole is an antifungal.
Hydrocortisone does not relax the sphincter or heal fissures.

hq_q.s: A 63 year old woman presents to her GP with a 2-day history of mild aching pain in the left iliac fossa. She is tolerating food and fluids and is immunocompetent. Previous colonoscopy confirmed sigmoid diverticulosis. Temperature 37.6°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg, SpO2 98% breathing air. Abdominal palpation reveals mild tenderness in the left iliac fossa with no guarding, rebound or palpable mass.
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG147 guidelines, patients with suspected uncomplicated acute diverticulitis who are systemically well and immunocompetent should be offered a no-antibiotic strategy, simple analgesia with paracetamol (avoiding NSAIDs and opioids), oral fluids and review within 48 hours if symptoms worsen.
hq_q.f: Systemically unwell, immunosuppressed or significant comorbidity -> offer oral co-amoxiclav for 5 days (or admit for IV antibiotics if severe/complicated).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management strategy?

c: mild tenderness in the left iliac fossa with no guarding
tm.m: Mild localized pericolic inflammation around an obstructed diverticulum is predominantly inflammatory rather than invasive bacterial sepsis and resolves with bowel rest and paracetamol
tm.g: Systemically well, immunocompetent adult with mild uncomplicated acute diverticulitis (NICE NG147): paracetamol and no antibiotics (avoid NSAIDs/opioids)
x: Inpatient intravenous antibiotics are reserved for patients with suspected complicated diverticulitis, systemic sepsis, inability to tolerate oral fluids or severe comorbidity.
Routine oral antibiotics are not offered to systemically well, immunocompetent patients with uncomplicated mild acute diverticulitis.
NICE NG147 explicitly advises against NSAIDs and opioid analgesics in diverticular disease because they increase the risk of diverticular perforation.
Cross-sectional imaging is not required in primary care for mild uncomplicated acute diverticulitis without systemic sepsis or peritonism.
f: She is febrile at 38.9°C, tachycardic at 112 bpm, vomiting and has localised guarding in the left iliac fossa.
She is systemically unwell or immunosuppressed on methotrexate with uncomplicated acute diverticulitis.
These analgesics are contraindicated in acute diverticulitis as they increase colonic intraluminal pressure and mucosal perforation risk.
She fails to improve after 48 hours or develops severe pain, fever and a palpable left iliac fossa mass.

hq_q.s: A 70 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of worsening left iliac fossa pain, anorexia and rigors. Temperature 38.6°C, pulse rate 106 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, SpO2 97% breathing air. Abdominal examination reveals a tender, ill-defined mass in the left iliac fossa with localised guarding. Blood tests show a white cell count of 18 x 10^9/L and CRP of 210 mg/L.
o: Contrast CT of abdomen and pelvis
Erect chest and supine abdominal X-rays
hq_q.w: In patients admitted with suspected acute complicated diverticulitis (fever, leucocytosis, CRP >200 mg/L, tender left iliac fossa mass or guarding), NICE NG147 recommends a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis to identify abscess, fistula or perforation.
hq_q.f: Six weeks after resolution of complicated acute diverticulitis -> outpatient colonoscopy or CT colonography to exclude underlying sigmoid malignancy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

c: tender, ill-defined mass in the left iliac fossa with localised guarding
tm.m: Intravenous contrast-enhanced CT delineates colonic wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding, extraluminal gas and walled-off pericolic or pelvic abscesses according to the Hinchey classification
tm.g: Suspected acute complicated diverticulitis (fever + LIF mass/guarding + raised WCC/CRP): contrast CT abdomen and pelvis (avoid acute colonoscopy)
x: Barium enema is strictly contraindicated in acute diverticulitis because high-pressure barium extravasation through a perforation causes fatal barium peritonitis.
Plain radiographs have low sensitivity for pericolic abscesses, colovesical fistulae or contained diverticular perforations compared with contrast CT.
Endoscopic luminal instrumentation and gas insufflation during acute diverticulitis carry a high risk of iatrogenic colonic perforation.
Colonoscopy is contraindicated during acute diverticulitis and must be deferred for 6 weeks after resolution if luminal exclusion of malignancy is required.
f: This study is contraindicated in acute diverticulitis due to the risk of barium peritonitis.
An initial rapid screen for large-volume pneumoperitoneum is performed when CT is unavailable.
Symptomatic outlet bleeding in an afebrile patient without peritonism or diverticulitis is being investigated.
Six weeks after recovery from complicated diverticulitis, colonoscopy is performed to exclude a coexisting sigmoid carcinoma.

hq_q.s: A 76 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of severe generalised abdominal pain. Temperature 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 92/54 mmHg, SpO2 94% breathing air. His abdomen is board-like and rigid with diffuse rebound tenderness. Contrast CT demonstrates perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with widespread pneumoperitoneum and free faecal contamination across all four quadrants.
o: Conservative management with intravenous antibiotics alone
Emergency right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis
hq_q.w: Perforated sigmoid diverticulitis causing generalised faecal peritonitis (Hinchey stage IV) and septic shock requires emergency laparotomy and Hartmann's procedure: resection of the perforated sigmoid colon, formation of an end colostomy and closure of the distal rectal stump.
hq_q.f: Contained 5 cm pericolic diverticular abscess (Hinchey stage II) without generalised peritonitis -> intravenous antibiotics and CT-guided percutaneous drainage.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate definitive surgical procedure?

c: Temperature 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 92/54 mmHg
free faecal contamination across all four quadrants
tm.m: Excising the perforated sigmoid segment eliminates ongoing faecal contamination while exteriorising the proximal colon as an end colostomy avoids anastomotic dehiscence in septic shock
tm.g: Perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with generalised faecal peritonitis (Hinchey IV) and shock: emergency Hartmann's procedure
x: Free faecal peritonitis (Hinchey stage IV) with septic shock is rapidly fatal without emergency surgical source control and resection of the perforated colon.
Percutaneous drainage treats a contained pericolic abscess (Hinchey II) and cannot clear free four-quadrant faecal peritonitis (Hinchey IV).
The perforation is in the sigmoid colon (left colon), and performing a primary anastomosis in a shocked patient with faecal peritonitis carries an unacceptably high anastomotic leak rate.
Colonic stenting relieves malignant large-bowel obstruction and is strictly contraindicated when free colonic perforation and faecal peritonitis are present.
f: He has uncomplicated Hinchey Ia acute sigmoid diverticulitis with mild localised pericolic fat stranding only.
He is haemodynamically stable with a walled-off 5 cm pericolic diverticular abscess and no free intraperitoneal gas.
He has an obstructing caecal carcinoma in the right colon without faecal peritonitis.
He presents with acute closed-loop malignant sigmoid obstruction without perforation as a bridge to elective surgery.

hq_q.s: A 71 year old woman presents after passing bright red blood mixed with stool twice this morning. She has had no further rectal bleeding over 6 hours, feels well and takes no anticoagulants. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 136/80 mmHg, SpO2 99% breathing air. Abdominal palpation is normal and rectal examination shows a trace of red blood. Haemoglobin is 138 g/L and her Oakland score is 6.
o: Request an immediate CT mesenteric angiogram
Transfuse 2 units of packed red blood cells
hq_q.w: Under BSG guidelines for acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding, patients are risk-stratified using the Oakland score. An Oakland score <=8 (with no other indication for admission) identifies a minor bleed suitable for safe immediate discharge and urgent outpatient colonic investigation.
hq_q.f: Oakland score >8 (haemodynamically stable) -> admit to hospital for inpatient colonoscopy on the next available list.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: An Oakland score <=8 predicts a >=95% probability of safe discharge without rebleeding, transfusion requirement or therapeutic intervention
tm.g: Acute lower GI bleed with Oakland score <= 8 and Shock Index <= 1: safe discharge for urgent outpatient colonoscopy
x: Inpatient admission and urgent colonoscopy are indicated for major lower gastrointestinal bleeds with an Oakland score >8.
Laparotomy is a last-resort salvage procedure for exsanguinating lower GI bleeding when radiological embolisation and endoscopy have failed.
CT angiography is reserved for haemodynamically unstable lower GI bleeds with a shock index >1.0.
Red cell transfusion is restricted to haemoglobin <70 g/L (<80 g/L in cardiovascular disease), whereas her haemoglobin is normal at 138 g/L.
f: She has ongoing rectal bleeding with a haemoglobin of 98 g/L, pulse rate 102 bpm and an Oakland score of 14.
She is in refractory haemorrhagic shock despite massive transfusion and failed mesenteric angiographic embolisation.
She is tachycardic at 124 bpm with BP 92/56 mmHg (shock index 1.35) and active brisk haematochezia.
She has acute symptomatic anaemia with haemoglobin 64 g/L and ischaemic chest pain.

hq_q.s: A 76 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-hour history of profuse, continuous fresh maroon rectal bleeding. Despite resuscitation with 2 litres of intravenous crystalloid, he remains clammy and hypotensive. Temperature 36.2°C, pulse rate 120 bpm, BP 95/60 mmHg (shock index 1.26), SpO2 96% breathing air. His abdomen is soft. Blood tests show haemoglobin 84 g/L and a normal serum urea of 5.2 mmol/L.
hq_q.w: Under BSG guidelines for acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding, a patient who is haemodynamically unstable or has a shock index (HR / systolic BP) >1.0 after resuscitation must undergo immediate CT mesenteric angiography to localise bleeding for interventional radiology embolisation.
hq_q.f: Haemodynamically unstable haematochezia with raised serum urea and history of peptic ulcer disease -> urgent upper GI endoscopy to exclude a brisk upper GI source.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate diagnostic investigation?

c: profuse, continuous fresh maroon rectal bleeding
pulse rate 120 bpm, BP 95/60 mmHg (shock index 1.26)
tm.m: Arterial- and portal-phase multidetector CT angiography detects intraluminal contrast extravasation at bleeding rates as low as 0.3 mL/min, guiding superselective transcatheter coil embolisation
tm.g: Unstable acute lower GI bleed (shock index > 1.0): urgent CT mesenteric angiography first-line
x: An erect chest X-ray screens for pneumoperitoneum in suspected visceral perforation and does not localise lower gastrointestinal haemorrhage.
Blind laparotomy without preoperative localisation of the bleeding site carries very high mortality compared with CT angiography and superselective embolisation.
In an actively bleeding unstable patient with a shock index >1.0, unprepped colonoscopy is poorly visualised and inferior to CT angiography.
Capsule endoscopy is an elective investigation for obscure small-bowel bleeding after negative upper and lower endoscopy, not for acute unstable shock.
f: He presents with sudden severe epigastric pain and a rigid abdomen from a perforated duodenal ulcer.
Catheter embolisation and endoscopic haemostasis have both failed to control life-threatening haemorrhage.
He is haemodynamically stable (shock index 0.7) with an Oakland score of 12 and has completed oral polyethylene glycol bowel preparation.
He has chronic occult iron-deficiency anaemia with normal gastroscopy and normal colonoscopy.

hq_q.s: An 88 year old man is referred to the gastroenterology clinic with a 6-month history of recurrent episodes of painless dark red rectal bleeding and progressive exertional breathlessness. He has known severe calcific aortic stenosis awaiting transcatheter aortic valve implantation. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 118/78 mmHg. Auscultation reveals a harsh ejection systolic murmur radiating to both carotid arteries, and abdominal palpation is normal.
hq_q.w: Angiodysplasia consists of fragile dilated submucosal vessels in the right colon of older adults. Its association with calcific aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome) occurs because shear stress across the stenotic valve induces acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency via ADAMTS13 proteolysis.
hq_q.f: Definitive cardiac treatment that resolves both the aortic valve gradient and the acquired von Willebrand bleeding tendency -> aortic valve replacement (TAVI or surgical AVR).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his gastrointestinal bleeding?
hq_q.post: Colonoscopy shows no tumour or diverticula.

c: Colonoscopy shows no tumour or diverticula
tm.m: High shear stress across a calcified stenotic aortic valve unfolds high-molecular-weight vWF multimers, exposing them to cleavage by ADAMTS13 and causing bleeding from caecal angiodysplasia
tm.g: Older patient with aortic stenosis + recurrent painless GI bleeding / iron-deficiency anaemia = colonic angiodysplasia (Heyde syndrome)
x: Ischaemic colitis presents acutely with cramping left-sided abdominal pain, tenderness and bloody diarrhoea rather than chronic painless bleeding over 6 months.
Internal haemorrhoids cause bright red outlet bleeding on the paper or dripping into the pan rather than dark red bleeding with severe microcytic anaemia.
Colonoscopy confirmed no colonic diverticula are present, and diverticular bleeds typically present as acute large-volume haematochezia.
Colonoscopy has already excluded a mucosal tumour, whereas small flat vascular ectasias in the right colon are easily missed or require argon plasma coagulation.
f: He develops sudden left-sided abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea with mucosal thumbprinting at the splenic flexure.
He has bright red blood dripping into the pan after defecation with prolapsing anal cushions on proctoscopy.
Colonoscopy demonstrates multiple sigmoid diverticula with an adherent clot at the neck of a diverticulum.
Colonoscopy identifies a friable, ulcerated exophytic mass in the caecum confirmed on biopsy as adenocarcinoma.

hq_q.s: A 45 year old woman presents to her GP with a 2-year history of chronic idiopathic constipation, passing hard stools twice a week. She has increased her dietary fibre, oral water intake and exercise for 3 months without benefit. She takes no medications and has no red flags. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg. Abdominal and rectal examinations, blood count, TSH and calcium are normal.
hq_q.w: Under NICE CKS guidelines for chronic idiopathic constipation in adults when lifestyle measures fail, first-line treatment is a bulk-forming laxative (such as ispaghula husk) with adequate fluid. If stools remain hard, add or switch to an osmotic laxative (macrogol).
hq_q.f: Opioid-induced constipation -> prescribe an osmotic laxative (macrogol) and/or a stimulant laxative (senna), and strictly avoid bulk-forming laxatives.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?

c: increased her dietary fibre, oral water intake and exercise
tm.m: Hydrophilic mucilage polysaccharides in ispaghula husk absorb intraluminal water to increase faecal mass, distending the colonic wall and stimulating physiological peristalsis
tm.g: First-line laxative in chronic idiopathic constipation (non-opioid): bulk-forming laxative (ispaghula husk) with adequate fluid
x: Docusate is a surface-wetting stool softener with weak evidence of efficacy and is not first-line ahead of a bulk-forming laxative.
Osmotic laxatives (macrogol first, then lactulose) are second-line in chronic idiopathic constipation if bulk-forming laxatives are ineffective or stools remain hard.
Prucalopride (a selective 5-HT4 receptor agonist) is a specialist third-line agent used only when at least two different classes of laxatives at maximum doses for 6 months have failed.
Stimulant laxatives are added only if stools are soft but difficult to pass or if bulk-forming plus osmotic laxatives fail to produce adequate defecation.
f: A frail patient with anal fissure requires a gentle adjuvant stool-softening agent alongside an osmotic laxative.
Her stools remain hard despite adequate doses of a bulk-forming laxative and macrogol is not tolerated.
She has severe chronic constipation that has failed 6 months of full-dose bulk-forming, osmotic and stimulant laxatives.
She is taking regular morphine for cancer pain and requires an osmotic plus stimulant laxative regimen.

hq_q.s: An 88 year old woman in a nursing home is reviewed for a 1-week history of liquid stool leaking onto her pads. She started regular codeine phosphate 3 weeks ago after a fracture and is bedbound. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 128/74 mmHg. Palpation reveals mild distension and an indentable mass in the left iliac fossa. Digital rectal examination reveals a dilated rectum packed with rock-hard faeces.
hq_q.w: Faecal impaction with overflow diarrhoea occurs commonly in frail, immobile older adults prescribed opioids (codeine). Bacterial liquefaction of proximal stool allows liquid faeces to seep past the rock-hard rectal faecaloma. Avoid loperamide and disimpact with high-dose oral macrogol or enemas.
hq_q.f: Profuse watery diarrhoea with fever and raised WCC after cephalosporin/co-amoxiclav therapy -> send stool for Clostridioides difficile toxin and start oral vancomycin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of her loose stools?

c: liquid stool leaking onto her pads
indentable mass in the left iliac fossa
dilated rectum packed with rock-hard faeces
tm.m: Chronic rectal distension by an opioid-induced faecaloma blunts rectoanal sensation and chronically relaxes the internal anal sphincter via the rectoanal inhibitory reflex, allowing liquid proximal stool to leak around the bolus
tm.g: Loose/leaking stool in a frail or opioid-treated patient + rock-hard stool in rectum on DRE = faecal impaction with overflow diarrhoea
x: Viral gastroenteritis causes acute self-limiting vomiting and watery diarrhoea over 48-72 hours without hard indentable colonic and rectal faecal loading.
In complete malignant large-bowel obstruction, the rectal vault below the tumour is typically empty and collapsed rather than distended with rock-hard impacted stool.
Clostridioides difficile infection follows broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy with fever and profuse watery diarrhoea rather than rock-hard rectal stool on codeine.
Irritable bowel syndrome is a chronic relapsing functional disorder of young adults and never presents de novo at age 88 with a rock-hard rectal faecaloma.
f: Several residents and staff on her floor develop sudden projectile vomiting and watery diarrhoea resolving within 48 hours.
She has progressive weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, colicky pain and an empty collapsed rectum on digital rectal examination.
She completed a 10-day course of clindamycin and developed fever, abdominal cramps, leucocytosis and profuse watery green diarrhoea.
A 26 year old woman has a 1-year history of abdominal pain relieved by defecation with normal examination and normal faecal calprotectin.

hq_q.s: A 66 year old woman with breast cancer and skeletal metastases presents with a 1-week history of worsening constipation, nausea, lethargy and confusion. Her husband reports that she has been drinking constantly and passing large volumes of urine day and night. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg. She has dry mucous membranes and focal tenderness over the L3 vertebra.
hq_q.w: Malignant hypercalcaemia (corrected calcium 3.15 mmol/L) from osteolytic bone metastases reduces smooth-muscle excitability (constipation, nausea), induces nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration) and causes confusion.
