hq_q.f: Prolonged hypotension with muddy brown granular casts on urine microscopy -> acute tubular necrosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of her acute kidney injury?

c: started oral omeprazole 20 mg daily 10 days ago
fever, arthralgia and an itchy rash
tm.m: Idiosyncratic drug-specific T-cell hypersensitivity triggers inflammatory infiltrate and oedema in the renal tubulointerstitium.
tm.g: Fever, rash, eosinophilia and sterile pyuria 10 days after starting a PPI -> Acute interstitial nephritis
f: prolonged septic shock with hypotension and muddy brown granular casts on urine microscopy
livedo reticularis and blue toes with AKI 1 week after coronary angiography
creatinine rising 48 hours after a contrast-enhanced CT scan without rash or fever
cola-coloured urine, red cell casts, hypertension and low C3 complement 2 weeks after pharyngitis
x: Acute tubular necrosis follows prolonged renal ischaemia or direct nephrotoxins and shows muddy brown granular casts rather than fever, rash and eosinophiluria.
Cholesterol embolisation occurs after endovascular aortic procedures, causing livedo reticularis, purple toes and hypocomplementaemia.
Contrast nephropathy occurs 24–72 hours after iodinated contrast exposure without systemic hypersensitivity features like fever, rash or sterile pyuria.
Glomerulonephritis presents with haematuria, red cell casts and proteinuria rather than a drug-induced hypersensitivity rash with sterile pyuria.

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old man returned from visiting family in Pakistan 2 weeks ago. He did not have pre-travel vaccines. He has had a fever that has risen each day for a week, with a headache, abdominal discomfort and constipation.
Temperature 39.4°C, pulse rate 64 bpm. There are a few faint pink macules on his abdomen and the spleen tip is palpable.
Malaria films are negative.
hq_q.w: Enteric fever: stepwise rising fever, relative bradycardia, rose spots and constipation early. Blood cultures confirm it.
hq_q.f: Watery diarrhoea and bloating weeks after drinking stream water → Giardia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: fever that has risen each day
tm.m: Salmonella Typhi invades the gut lymphatics and blood, with a slow pulse for the fever
tm.g: Stepwise fever with relative bradycardia, rose spots and a spleen tip is typhoid
f: fever with rash and low platelets after South-East Asia
the presentation instead showed features specific to Giardiasis (Giardiasis causes diarrhoea and bloating, not a high fever with a slow pulse)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hepatitis A (Hepatitis A gives jaundice, not stepwise fever with a slow pulse and rose spots)
parasites on the blood films
x: Ruled out here: requires fever with rash and low platelets after South-East Asia, whereas this patient has Pakistan, fever that has risen each day.
Giardiasis causes diarrhoea and bloating, not a high fever with a slow pulse.
Hepatitis A gives jaundice, not stepwise fever with a slow pulse and rose spots.
Ruled out here: requires parasites on the blood films, whereas this patient has Pakistan, fever that has risen each day.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman returned from Nigeria 10 days ago. She did not take malaria prophylaxis. She has had fever, rigors, headache and muscle aches for 2 days.
Temperature 39.2°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg. She is alert. There is no rash or neck stiffness.
hq_q.w: Malaria must be excluded in any febrile traveller from an endemic area. One negative film does not rule it out.
hq_q.f: Films negative but fever with rash and low platelets after Thailand → dengue.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first test?

tm.m: Falciparum malaria can kill within days, so it is excluded first
tm.g: Febrile traveller from Africa: thick and thin blood films
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Blood cultures (Cultures are taken too, but malaria must be excluded first with films)
films negative with a rash and low platelets after Thailand
the presentation instead showed features specific to Malaria antibody serology (Serology detects past exposure and is useless for diagnosing acute malaria)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Stool culture (She has no diarrhoea, and malaria must be excluded first)
x: Cultures are taken too, but malaria must be excluded first with films.
Ruled out here: requires films negative with a rash and low platelets after Thailand, whereas this patient has Nigeria, did not take malaria prophylaxis.
Serology detects past exposure and is useless for diagnosing acute malaria
She has no diarrhoea, and malaria must be excluded first.

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old man is admitted to hospital with typhoid fever confirmed by blood culture after a trip to Bangladesh. He has vomited four times today and cannot keep oral fluids down. Sensitivity results are not yet available.
Temperature 39.6°C, pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg. His abdomen is mildly tender without peritonism.
hq_q.w: Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone is first-line for patients admitted to hospital with enteric (typhoid) fever imported from South Asia, especially when vomiting precludes oral therapy, because fluoroquinolone resistance exceeds 80% in the region. Oral azithromycin is an option for uncomplicated outpatient cases.
hq_q.f: Strain shown to be quinolone sensitive → ciprofloxacin is an option.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial antibiotic treatment?

c: Sensitivity results are not yet available
tm.m: Many South Asian typhoid strains resist quinolones
tm.g: Typhoid from South Asia before sensitivities: ceftriaxone
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amoxicillin (Widespread multidrug resistance in South Asia makes empirical amoxicillin ineffective)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Chloramphenicol (High resistance rates and bone marrow toxicity preclude empirical use)
the strain is shown to be quinolone sensitive
the presentation instead showed features specific to Doxycycline (Doxycycline is not used for typhoid)
x: Widespread multidrug resistance in South Asia makes empirical amoxicillin ineffective
High resistance rates and bone marrow toxicity preclude empirical use
Ruled out here: requires the strain is shown to be quinolone sensitive, whereas this patient has Bangladesh, Sensitivity results are not yet available.
Doxycycline is not used for typhoid.

hq_q.s:
A 27 year old man has noticed pale patches on his upper back after a sunny holiday in Spain. They are slightly itchy.
There are multiple pale, oval, finely scaling patches on the upper back and chest that have not tanned like the surrounding skin. Skin scrapings show short hyphae and round yeasts.
hq_q.w: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia, a yeast that normally lives on the skin and overgrows in heat and humidity. It makes azelaic acid, which stops melanocytes making pigment, so the patches stay pale after sun.
hq_q.f: Red scaly ring with central clearing and hyphae without yeasts on scraping → tinea corporis (Trichophyton).
hq_q.ql: Which organism is most likely?

tm.m: Malassezia makes azelaic acid, which blocks tyrosinase in melanocytes
tm.g: Hyphae and yeasts together ("spaghetti and meatballs"): Malassezia
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Candida albicans (Candida causes moist red rashes in skin folds with satellite spots, not pale scaly patches on the trunk)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Microsporum canis (Microsporum canis causes ringworm caught from cats, with hyphae but no yeasts)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Staphylococcus aureus (Staphylococcus aureus causes impetigo and folliculitis, not pale scaly patches)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Trichophyton rubrum (Trichophyton causes tinea of the body, feet and nails, with red rings and hyphae only)
x: Candida causes moist red rashes in skin folds with satellite spots, not pale scaly patches on the trunk.
Microsporum canis causes ringworm caught from cats, with hyphae but no yeasts.
Staphylococcus aureus causes impetigo and folliculitis, not pale scaly patches.
Trichophyton causes tinea of the body, feet and nails, with red rings and hyphae only.

hq_q.s: A 24 year old man presents with a 2-month history of coalescing, finely scaling hypopigmented and light-brown macules covering his upper chest, shoulders and entire back, noticed after a summer holiday. He is otherwise healthy with normal liver function tests. Potassium hydroxide microscopy of skin scrapings shows clusters of round yeasts and short septate hyphae in a 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern.
hq_q.w: For widespread truncal pityriasis versicolor where topical creams are impractical, NICE CKS recommends ketoconazole 2% shampoo applied once daily for 5 days before rinsing. Oral itraconazole is reserved for refractory cases; oral terbinafine is ineffective against Malassezia.
hq_q.f: Refractory or recurrent widespread pityriasis versicolor failing topical ketoconazole -> oral itraconazole.
hq_q.ql: Given the extensive body surface area involved, which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

c: finely scaling hypopigmented and light-brown macules
tm.m: Topical ketoconazole shampoo inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis across large truncal surface areas where creams are impractical.
tm.g: Widespread truncal pityriasis versicolor -> Ketoconazole 2% shampoo
f: localized non-bullous impetigo with golden crusted lesions around the nose
mild flexural atopic eczema flare without fungal infection
extensive coral-pink fluorescent erythrasma in the intertriginous groins
dermatophyte onychomycosis or extensive tinea corporis confirmed on fungal culture
x: Fusidic acid is an antistaphylococcal antibacterial agent used for localized impetigo and has no activity against Malassezia yeasts.
Topical corticosteroids suppress cutaneous inflammation but do not eradicate Malassezia furfur and may worsen superficial fungal proliferation.
Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic ineffective against Malassezia yeasts; erythrasma responds to antibacterials, not pityriasis versicolor.
Unlike dermatophyte infections, Malassezia species in pityriasis versicolor do not respond to oral terbinafine; oral itraconazole or fluconazole is used if systemic therapy is needed.

hq_q.s: A 26 year old man returns for review 3 weeks after completing a 5-day course of ketoconazole 2% shampoo for confirmed pityriasis versicolor across his upper back and shoulders. He reports that the mild itch and fine branny scaling have completely resolved, but several pale hypopigmented macules remain visible against his tanned skin. Examination confirms flat, non-erythematous pale macules with no residual surface scale on gentle scraping.
o: Arrange an urgent diagnostic punch biopsy
Reassure that pigment returns over months
Switch to oral itraconazole 200 mg daily
hq_q.w: Malassezia yeasts produce dicarboxylic acids (such as azelaic acid) that inhibit tyrosinase and melanosome transfer. Even after successful fungal eradication (confirmed by absence of scale), hypopigmented macules typically take several months to repigment fully.
hq_q.f: Persistent fine scale on scraping after topical treatment -> re-treat or switch to oral itraconazole.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: ketoconazole 2% shampoo for confirmed pityriasis versicolor
itch and fine branny scaling have completely resolved
tm.m: Malassezia azelaic acid reversibly inhibits melanocyte tyrosinase; once the yeast is cleared, melanosome regeneration takes months.
tm.g: Pale macules with no residual scale after treating pityriasis versicolor -> Reassure that pigment returns over months
f: atypical hypopigmented plaques with induration and epidermal atrophy raising suspicion of hypopigmented mycosis fungoides
post-inflammatory hypopigmentation secondary to an active flare of atopic dermatitis
progressive symmetrical depigmented macules of non-segmental vitiligo refractory to topical therapy
persistent fine branny scaling and positive KOH microscopy despite completed topical ketoconazole therapy
x: Punch biopsy is unnecessary when pityriasis versicolor has already been confirmed and scaling has resolved completely.
Topical corticosteroids do not accelerate melanocyte repigmentation after pityriasis versicolor and risk promoting fungal recurrence.
Narrowband UVB phototherapy is used for extensive vitiligo or psoriasis, not transient post-fungal hypopigmentation.
Absence of surface scale on scraping indicates mycological cure; repeating or escalating antifungal therapy does not speed repigmentation.

hq_q.s: A 22 year old man presents with painless visible haematuria that began yesterday, 24 hours after developing a viral sore throat. He recalls a similar episode of red urine 10 months ago during a cold. Temperature is 37.2°C, pulse 72 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. There is no oedema. Urine dipstick shows blood 3+ and protein 1+, and serum creatinine is 84 µmol/L (60–120).
hq_q.w: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) is the commonest primary glomerulonephritis, presenting in young adults with episodic visible haematuria 24 to 72 hours after a mucosal respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis has a 1 to 3 week latency.
hq_q.f: Haematuria, oedema, hypertension and low C3 occurring 2 weeks after tonsillitis -> post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: 24 hours after developing a viral sore throat
similar episode of red urine 10 months ago
tm.m: Mucosal infection triggers overproduction of galactose-deficient IgA1, which deposits in the glomerular mesangium and activates complement.
tm.g: Recurrent visible haematuria within 1–2 days of a sore throat -> IgA nephropathy
f: persistent haematuria accompanied by bilateral high-frequency sensorineural deafness and a maternal family history of renal failure
generalized periorbital and leg oedema with urine protein:creatinine ratio >350 mg/mmol and serum albumin 18 g/L
smoky brown urine, hypertension and periorbital oedema 14 days after streptococcal tonsillitis with low C3
incidental lifelong isolated microscopic haematuria with normal renal function and an autosomal dominant family history
x: Alport syndrome causes persistent microscopic haematuria with progressive sensorineural deafness and anterior lenticonus rather than synpharyngitic flares.
Minimal change disease presents with nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria >3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia and generalized oedema) without visible haematuria.
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis develops after a latent period of 1 to 3 weeks following streptococcal pharyngitis, with low C3 complement.
Thin basement membrane disease causes lifelong benign microscopic haematuria without recurrent macroscopic synpharyngitic episodes or proteinuria.

hq_q.s:
A 9 year old boy has had dark brown urine and puffy eyes for 2 days. He had a sore throat 2 weeks ago that settled without treatment.
BP 138/90 mmHg. There is periorbital oedema.
Urine dipstick shows blood 3+ and protein 2+. Creatinine is mildly raised.
o: Low C3 and raised ASO titre
Raised serum IgA with normal C3
hq_q.w: Immune complex disease consumes complement, so C3 is low, and ASO titres show recent strep infection.
hq_q.f: Positive anti-GBM antibodies with haemoptysis → Goodpasture disease.
hq_q.ql: Which result supports post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

tm.m: Immune complexes after Strep infection consume complement
tm.g: Nephritis 2 weeks after a sore throat: low C3 and a raised ASO titre
f: coughing up blood with nephritis
the presentation instead showed features specific to Low C4 and positive ANA (A low C4 and positive ANA suggest lupus)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Positive c-ANCA (c-ANCA suggests GPA)
haematuria within days of a sore throat with normal complement
x: Ruled out here: requires coughing up blood with nephritis, whereas this patient has 2 weeks ago, 138/90.
A low C4 and positive ANA suggest lupus.
c-ANCA suggests GPA.
Ruled out here: requires haematuria within days of a sore throat with normal complement, whereas this patient has 2 weeks ago, 138/90.

hq_q.s: A 20 year old man is referred after persistent microscopic haematuria and proteinuria were detected at a pre-employment medical check. He reports increasing difficulty following conversations in noisy rooms over the past 3 years. His maternal uncle required haemodialysis at age 34. BP is 142/88 mmHg. Pure tone audiometry shows bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, and slit-lamp examination reveals bilateral anterior lenticonus.
hq_q.w: Alport syndrome is a hereditary disorder of type IV collagen (most commonly X-linked COL4A5 mutation), affecting the glomerular basement membrane, cochlear stria vascularis and lens capsule. It presents with progressive haematuric nephritis, bilateral high-frequency sensorineural deafness and anterior lenticonus.
hq_q.f: Isolated familial microscopic haematuria with normal hearing and preserved GFR -> thin basement membrane disease.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: difficulty following conversations in noisy rooms
tm.m: Defective type IV collagen alpha-3/4/5 chains cause splitting of the glomerular basement membrane, cochlear stria vascularis and lens capsule.
tm.g: Haematuric nephritis + sensorineural deafness + anterior lenticonus -> Alport syndrome
f: bilateral ballotable flank masses, multiple renal and hepatic cysts on ultrasound and family history of berry aneurysm
visible haematuria 24 hours after an upper respiratory infection with normal hearing and slit-lamp exam
isolated asymptomatic microscopic haematuria with normal audiometry, normal BP and no family history of ESKD
a painless unilateral abdominal mass and haematuria in a 3 year old child
x: ADPKD presents with bilateral flank masses, hepatic cysts and hypertension without sensorineural deafness or anterior lenticonus.
IgA nephropathy causes recurrent synpharyngitic macroscopic haematuria without sensorineural hearing loss, lenticonus or X-linked renal failure.
Thin basement membrane disease causes benign familial microscopic haematuria with preserved renal function, normal hearing and no ocular anomalies.
Wilms tumour is an embryonal renal malignancy presenting as an abdominal mass in children under 5 years of age.

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents with a 2-day history of sudden-onset double vision. He describes two images side by side that separate maximally when he looks to the right and disappear when either eye is covered. On examination, his right eye fails to abduct beyond the midline on rightward gaze. Vertical eye movements, adduction, pupil reactions and upper eyelids are normal.
hq_q.w: The sixth cranial (abducens) nerve innervates the ipsilateral lateral rectus muscle, which abducts the eye. A right sixth nerve palsy causes failure of right eye abduction past the midline and horizontal diplopia maximal on rightward gaze.
hq_q.f: Vertical diplopia worse descending stairs with a head tilt -> fourth (trochlear) nerve palsy.
hq_q.ql: Which cranial nerve palsy is present?

c: separate maximally when he looks to the right
right eye fails to abduct beyond the midline
tm.m: Denervation of the right lateral rectus muscle prevents abduction of the right eye, causing uncrossed horizontal diplopia on right gaze.
tm.g: Failure of right eye abduction with horizontal diplopia worst on right gaze -> Right sixth nerve palsy
f: vertical diplopia when walking downstairs with a compensatory head tilt away from the affected left side
horizontal diplopia worst on looking to the left with failure of left eye abduction past the midline
vertical diplopia on reading or descending stairs with the right eye hypertropic in adduction
right upper lid ptosis with the right eye deviated down and out and impaired adduction
x: A fourth (trochlear) nerve palsy impairs superior oblique, causing vertical and torsional diplopia worse on looking down and inwards.
A left sixth nerve palsy impairs abduction of the left eye, causing horizontal diplopia that is worst on leftward gaze.
A right fourth nerve palsy causes vertical diplopia worse on downward and inward gaze rather than pure horizontal failure of abduction.
A right third (oculomotor) nerve palsy causes complete ptosis and a 'down and out' eye with impaired adduction and vertical gaze.

hq_q.s: A 32 year old woman with a BMI of 36 kg/m² presents with a 6-week history of daily morning headaches, transient visual obscurations on bending and recent horizontal double vision. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral grade 3 papilloedema. Cranial nerve examination demonstrates impaired abduction of the left eye, with normal pupils and no ptosis. MRI brain and MR venography show no mass lesion or venous thrombosis.
o: It ascends a long vertical path over the petrous temporal ridge
It emerges from the dorsal aspect of the midbrain
It passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries
It runs through the narrow optic canal within the sphenoid bone
It shares the facial canal within the petrous temporal bone
hq_q.w: The sixth cranial (abducens) nerve has a long vertical subarachnoid trajectory ascending the clivus and bending sharply over the petrous apex into Dorello's canal. Downward brainstem traction in raised intracranial pressure stretches it, producing a false localising sign.
hq_q.f: Painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil -> compression by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
hq_q.ql: Which anatomical feature explains why this cranial nerve is vulnerable to raised intracranial pressure?

c: impaired abduction of the left eye
no mass lesion or venous thrombosis
tm.m: Downward traction from raised intracranial pressure stretches the abducens nerve along its vertical clival course over the petrous apex.
tm.g: False localising sixth nerve palsy in raised ICP -> It ascends a long vertical path over the petrous temporal ridge
f: vulnerability of the trochlear nerve to shearing injury against the tentorium in closed head trauma
painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy caused by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm
compressive optic neuropathy from fibrous dysplasia or fracture of the optic canal
lower motor neuron facial weakness caused by inflammatory swelling within the bony facial canal
x: Emerging dorsally from the midbrain and decussating in the superior medullary velum describes the fourth (trochlear) nerve, not the sixth.
Passing between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries adjacent to the posterior communicating artery describes the third (oculomotor) nerve.
The optic nerve (CN II) and ophthalmic artery traverse the optic canal, whereas the sixth nerve enters the orbit via the superior orbital fissure.
The seventh (facial) nerve traverses the fallopian facial canal in the temporal bone, whereas the sixth nerve crosses the petrous apex into Dorello's canal.

hq_q.s: A 48 year old woman presents with a 5-day history of severe pain behind her right eye, fever and double vision. Two weeks ago she squeezed a furuncle on her right upper lip. Temperature is 38.4°C, pulse 108 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. Examination reveals right proptosis, conjunctival chemosis, complete palsies of the right third, fourth and sixth cranial nerves, and numbness over the right forehead.
hq_q.w: The cavernous sinus transmits the internal carotid artery, sixth nerve, and in its lateral wall the third, fourth, V1 and V2 nerves, while draining the ophthalmic veins. Midfacial infections can spread via valveless veins to cause septic cavernous sinus thrombosis.
hq_q.f: Unilateral sensorineural deafness, absent corneal reflex and facial weakness -> cerebellopontine angle cistern.
hq_q.ql: Where is the anatomical site of the lesion?

c: furuncle on her right upper lip
right third, fourth and sixth cranial nerves
tm.m: Septic thrombosis spreading from facial veins into the cavernous sinus obstructs ophthalmic venous drainage and compresses CN III, IV, VI, V1 and V2.
tm.g: Proptosis + chemosis + CN III, IV, VI palsies + V1 sensory loss after facial infection -> Cavernous sinus
f: unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, absent corneal reflex and facial weakness from a vestibular schwannoma
ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis and no orbital congestion
progressive bitemporal hemianopia and hypopituitarism from a pituitary macroadenoma
isolated cheek and upper dental numbness without ophthalmoplegia or proptosis
x: Cerebellopontine angle lesions affect CN V, VII and VIII, causing sensorineural deafness, tinnitus and facial weakness rather than proptosis and ophthalmoplegia.
Midbrain lesions cause Parinaud's syndrome or Weber's syndrome (ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiplegia), without proptosis, chemosis or CN VI palsy.
Compression of the optic chiasm causes bitemporal hemianopia without painful proptosis, chemosis or multiple ocular motor palsies.
The pterygopalatine fossa contains the maxillary nerve (V2) and sphenopalatine ganglion, not the ocular motor nerves (CN III, IV, VI) or ophthalmic veins.

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old woman has had a hot, swollen, painful right knee for 2 days. She can barely bend it. She has type 2 diabetes.
Temperature 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm. The right knee is warm with a large effusion and painful restriction of all movement.
hq_q.w: A hot swollen joint is septic until proven otherwise. Aspirate first, then give antibiotics. Key discriminator: Hot swollen joint: aspiration of the knee first.
hq_q.f: Known gout but fever and very high CRP → still aspirate, as septic and gout can coexist.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first investigation?

tm.m: A septic joint destroys cartilage within days
tm.g: Hot swollen joint: aspiration of the knee first
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Blood cultures (Cultures are taken, but joint aspiration is the key diagnostic test)
the presentation instead showed features specific to MRI of the knee (MRI delays the diagnosis of septic arthritis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Plain X-ray of the knee (X-ray does not exclude infection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Serum urate (Serum urate can be normal during an acute flare and cannot exclude sepsis)
x: Cultures are taken, but joint aspiration is the key diagnostic test.
MRI delays the diagnosis of septic arthritis.
X-ray does not exclude infection.
Serum urate can be normal during an acute flare and cannot exclude sepsis

hq_q.s: A 76 year old woman presents with a 2-day history of an acutely painful, swollen left knee preventing weight-bearing. She has no trauma or recent diarrhoea. Temperature is 37.6°C, pulse 82 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. The left knee is warm with a tense effusion. Joint aspirate shows negative Gram stain and rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals under polarised light. Knee X-ray shows meniscal chondrocalcinosis.
hq_q.w: Acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (pseudogout) commonly affects the knee or wrist in older adults. Synovial fluid polarised light microscopy demonstrates rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals, often accompanied by articular cartilage calcification (chondrocalcinosis) on plain radiographs.
hq_q.f: Needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals in synovial fluid -> acute monosodium urate gout.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Shedding of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals from calcified articular fibrocartilage into the joint space triggers inflammasome-mediated synovitis.
tm.g: Rhomboid positively birefringent crystals + chondrocalcinosis -> Calcium pyrophosphate arthritis
f: acute first metatarsophalangeal joint podagra with needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals on joint aspiration
asymmetrical lower limb oligoarthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis 2 weeks after Campylobacter enteritis
symmetrical swelling of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints with positive anti-CCP antibodies
high fever, rigors and purulent synovial fluid showing Gram-positive cocci in clusters
x: Acute gout shows needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals rather than rhomboid positively birefringent crystals.
Reactive arthritis is a sterile seronegative oligoarthritis following enteric or chlamydial infection, with no crystals or chondrocalcinosis.
Rheumatoid arthritis causes symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis without synovial calcium pyrophosphate crystals on polarised microscopy.
Septic arthritis shows purulent synovial fluid with organisms on Gram stain or culture; crystals with negative Gram stain and chondrocalcinosis indicate pseudogout.

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old man who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation has had a swollen, painful right knee for 1 day. He has had no injury. He recently finished a course of clarithromycin for a chest infection.
Temperature 36.9°C. The right knee is swollen and tense with a large effusion. There is bruising on his forearms.
White cell count normal. CRP 8 mg/L (<5). INR 6.4.
hq_q.w: A high INR can cause spontaneous bleeding into a joint. Reverse anticoagulation and consider aspiration.
hq_q.f: INR in range with fever 38.5 and a white count of 18 → septic arthritis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Clarithromycin raises warfarin levels, so the joint bleeds spontaneously
tm.g: A tense knee with a very high INR and normal inflammation is haemarthrosis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Cellulitis (Cellulitis is spreading redness of the skin, not a swollen knee effusion on warfarin)
a hot big toe after a heavy meal
OA is better in the morning, worse by evening. Inflammatory is worse in the morning, better with use.
INR in range with fever and a high white count
x: Cellulitis is spreading redness of the skin, not a swollen knee effusion on warfarin.
Ruled out here: requires a hot big toe after a heavy meal, whereas this patient has warfarin, clarithromycin.
Ruled out here: requires OA is better in the morning, worse by evening. Inflammatory is worse in the morning, better with use, whereas this patient has warfarin, clarithromycin.
Ruled out here: requires INR in range with fever and a high white count, whereas this patient has warfarin, clarithromycin.

hq_q.s:
A 22 year old woman noticed a lump in her left breast 2 weeks ago while showering. It is painless and she has no nipple discharge or family history of breast cancer.
Examination reveals a 2 cm smooth, rubbery, well-circumscribed lump in the upper outer quadrant that slips easily beneath the examining fingers. There is no skin tethering or axillary lymphadenopathy.
hq_q.w: A fibroadenoma ('breast mouse') is a benign proliferation of terminal duct lobular stroma and epithelium, presenting in women under 30 as a smooth, firm, rubbery, highly mobile lump with no skin tethering.
hq_q.f: Rapidly growing 6 cm breast mass in a 45-year-old woman -> phyllodes tumour.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: slips easily beneath the examining fingers
tm.m: Hormone-sensitive hyperplasia of a single terminal duct-lobular unit creates an encapsulated, mobile fibroepithelial nodule
tm.g: Smooth, rubbery, highly mobile breast lump in a woman under 30 -> fibroadenoma
x: Typically presents in older women as a hard, irregular, fixed mass with skin dimpling or nipple retraction.
Most common between ages 35 and 50 as a tender, fluctuant fluid-filled sac during lobular involution.
Presents in women aged 40 to 50 as a large (>4 to 5 cm), rapidly enlarging mass.
Follows breast trauma or surgery, producing a hard, irregular mass with skin tethering.
f: A 60-year-old woman with a hard, irregular, fixed breast lump, skin dimpling, and an enlarged axillary node
A 46-year-old woman with a tender fluctuant lump that is anechoic on ultrasound
A 45-year-old woman with a 6 cm mobile breast lump that has grown rapidly over 8 weeks
A hard, irregular lump with skin tethering developing 6 weeks after a seatbelt injury

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old woman attends her GP after noticing a painless lump in her right breast 4 weeks ago. It has persisted unchanged through her menstrual period. She has no nipple discharge, no skin changes, and no family history of breast cancer.
Examination shows a 2 cm discrete, smooth, mobile lump in the upper outer quadrant with no axillary lymphadenopathy.
o: Non-urgent referral to the breast clinic
Reassurance in primary care without referral
Review in primary care after 6 months
Suspected cancer pathway referral within 2 weeks
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG12 guidelines, women aged 30 and over with an unexplained breast lump require a 2-week-wait suspected cancer referral, whereas women under 30 with an unexplained lump and no red flags should receive a non-urgent breast clinic referral.
hq_q.f: Unexplained discrete breast lump in a woman aged 30 or over -> suspected cancer pathway referral within 2 weeks.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate referral pathway?

c: persisted unchanged through her menstrual period
tm.m: Breast cancer incidence under age 30 is very low, so NICE stratifies unexplained benign-feeling lumps under 30 to non-urgent triple assessment
tm.g: Unexplained breast lump in a woman aged under 30 -> non-urgent referral to the breast clinic
x: Reserved for acute surgical emergencies such as breast abscess with systemic sepsis, not a painless mobile lump.
Every persistent discrete breast lump requires triple assessment in a breast clinic regardless of age.
Observing a persistent discrete lump for 6 months without imaging or biopsy is unsafe.
NICE sets the age threshold for a 2-week-wait suspected cancer referral for an unexplained breast lump at 30 years and over.
f: A lactating woman with a pointing breast abscess, high fever, tachycardia, and hypotension
Diffuse bilateral premenstrual breast tenderness that resolves completely after menstruation with no discrete lump
Routine blood pressure and lipid check in a woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill
An unexplained breast lump in a woman aged 32 years

hq_q.s:
A 23 year old woman attends the one-stop breast clinic with a painless lump in her left breast. Clinical examination reveals a 1.5 cm smooth, mobile mass in the upper outer quadrant. Breast ultrasound shows a benign oval hypoechoic mass, and ultrasound-guided core biopsy confirms a simple fibroadenoma.
She is reassured by the benign result and does not wish to undergo surgery.
o: Open surgical excision of the lump
Repeat breast ultrasound scan in 6 months
hq_q.w: Once triple assessment (clinical examination, ultrasound, and core biopsy) confirms a simple fibroadenoma under 3 cm with concordant benign features, no excision or routine imaging follow-up is required; the patient is reassured and discharged.
hq_q.f: Fibroadenoma >3 to 4 cm, rapidly enlarging, or causing persistent anxiety -> vacuum-assisted or surgical excision.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: core biopsy confirms a simple fibroadenoma
does not wish to undergo surgery
tm.m: Concordant benign triple assessment of a small fibroadenoma carries no excess malignancy risk and most remain stable or regress
tm.g: Biopsy-confirmed simple fibroadenoma <3 cm -> reassurance and discharge from clinic
x: Contraindicated in a 23-year-old due to dense breast tissue and unnecessary radiation for a benign lesion.
Reserved for giant (>4 cm) or rapidly enlarging fibroadenomas, cellular fibroepithelial lesions, or patient request.
Not required when core biopsy has already histologically confirmed a concordant simple fibroadenoma.
Used for B3 lesions of uncertain malignant potential or symptomatic fibroadenomas the patient wishes removed.
f: A 43-year-old woman with a strong family history of breast cancer under annual mammographic surveillance
A 5 cm rapidly enlarging fibroepithelial mass where phyllodes tumour cannot be excluded
A 19-year-old woman with a <2 cm typical ultrasound fibroadenoma managed without initial core biopsy
A radial scar or flat epithelial atypia (B3 lesion) on core biopsy requiring wider tissue sampling

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old woman has noticed a tender lump in her right breast that appeared suddenly over a week. Her menstrual periods have become irregular over the past 8 months.
There is a 2 cm smooth, well-defined, fluctuant lump in the upper outer quadrant.
Breast ultrasound shows a round, thin-walled, completely anechoic lesion with posterior acoustic enhancement.
hq_q.w: Simple breast cysts arise from distended, involuting terminal duct lobular units in perimenopausal women (aged 35 to 50). On ultrasound they appear as round, thin-walled, completely anechoic lesions with posterior acoustic enhancement.
hq_q.f: Solid oval hypoechoic mobile mass in a 21-year-old woman -> fibroadenoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: anechoic lesion with posterior acoustic enhancement
tm.m: Perimenopausal hormonal fluctuations cause unbalanced lobular involution and fluid distension of acini
tm.g: Perimenopausal fluctuant lump that is thin-walled and anechoic on ultrasound -> simple breast cyst
x: Appears on ultrasound as a solid, uniform hypoechoic oval mass rather than a fluid-filled anechoic sac.
Presents with fever, overlying erythema, and a thick-walled collection containing echogenic purulent debris.
Occurs during or shortly after breastfeeding and contains echogenic fat-fluid levels on ultrasound.
Presents as a soft, doughy solid fatty mass isoechoic or mildly hyperechoic to adjacent fat.
f: A solid, well-circumscribed hypoechoic mass wider than tall in a 22-year-old woman
A febrile breastfeeding woman with a thick-walled echogenic collection and surrounding hyperaemia on ultrasound
A painless subareolar cyst yielding milky fluid 6 weeks after stopping breastfeeding
A soft, doughy, non-tender mass composed of compressible mature adipose tissue

hq_q.s: A 48 year old woman attends the one-stop breast clinic with a 3 cm lump in her left breast. Breast ultrasound demonstrates a complex cystic lesion containing internal echoes and a thickened wall. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration yields heavily blood-stained fluid, and a firm 1.5 cm mass remains palpable immediately after aspiration.
o: Immediate open excision of the cyst wall
Oral flucloxacillin for 7 days and review
Reassurance and discharge to routine screening
hq_q.w: Whereas clear fluid and complete resolution of a simple cyst require no further action, a blood-stained aspirate, internal mural echoes, or a residual palpable mass suggests intracystic papillary or necrotic carcinoma, mandating fluid cytology and core needle biopsy.
hq_q.f: Clear straw-coloured fluid with complete disappearance of the mass -> discard the fluid and reassure.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

c: complex cystic lesion containing internal echoes
firm 1.5 cm mass remains palpable immediately after aspiration
tm.m: Intracystic carcinoma or necrotic ductal carcinoma bleeds into the cyst cavity and leaves a persistent solid mural component after aspiration
tm.g: Blood-stained cyst aspirate or residual post-aspiration mass -> fluid cytology and core needle biopsy
x: Preoperative histological diagnosis by core needle biopsy is mandatory before planning definitive breast surgery.
Bloody fluid with a residual solid mass indicates suspected malignancy, not bacterial mastitis.
Only safe when cyst fluid is non-bloody and the palpable mass disappears completely.
Delays urgent histological diagnosis of an underlying intracystic malignancy.
f: A lesion that remains diagnostically equivocal (B3/B4) despite repeat vacuum-assisted core biopsy
Purulent pus aspirated from an acutely inflamed, febrile lactational breast abscess
Aspiration of clear yellow fluid from a simple cyst with complete resolution of the palpable lump
A recurrent painful simple cyst that previously resolved completely with clear straw-coloured fluid

hq_q.s:
A 35 year old woman has had tender, heavy, lumpy breasts during the week before each menstrual period for the past year. The discomfort affects both breasts symmetrically and resolves once her period starts. She has no nipple discharge.
Clinical examination shows diffuse bilateral nodularity with no discrete mass, and breast ultrasound is normal.
hq_q.w: First-line management of benign cyclical mastalgia is reassurance, wearing a well-fitted supportive bra (including at night), and simple oral or topical NSAID analgesia. Evening primrose oil is not recommended by NICE due to lack of benefit.
hq_q.f: Severe intractable cyclical mastalgia refractory to 6 months of conservative care -> specialist breast clinic consideration of low-dose tamoxifen or danazol.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

c: tender, heavy, lumpy breasts during the week before each menstrual period
no discrete mass, and breast ultrasound is normal
tm.m: Mechanical breast support and topical/oral NSAIDs relieve luteal-phase stromal oedema without endocrine adverse effects
tm.g: First-line management of cyclical mastalgia -> reassurance, supportive bra, and simple analgesia
x: Randomized trials show no benefit over placebo, and NICE CKS advises against prescribing evening primrose oil (gamolenic acid).
Dopamine agonist rarely used for mastalgia because of severe nausea, postural hypotension, and headache.
Synthetic androgen reserved for severe refractory mastalgia in secondary care due to androgenic side effects (acne, hirsutism, voice deepening).
Specialist third-line endocrine option for severe refractory mastalgia due to thromboembolic and menopausal side effects.
f: An over-the-counter supplement that NICE explicitly advises has no evidence of benefit in cyclical breast pain
Hyperprolactinaemic galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea caused by a pituitary microprolactinoma
Severe disabling cyclical mastalgia in secondary care unresponsive to 6 months of conservative therapy and topical NSAIDs
Adjuvant endocrine therapy for premenopausal oestrogen receptor-positive invasive breast cancer

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman is breastfeeding her 3-week-old baby. She has had a painful red wedge-shaped area in her right breast for 2 days accompanied by myalgia and chills. Symptoms have not improved after 24 hours of frequent breastfeeding and manual expression. She has no drug allergies.
Temperature 38.4°C, pulse rate 98 bpm. There is a tender, erythematous wedge in the upper outer quadrant without fluctuance.
o: Rest the right breast completely for 48 hours
hq_q.w: Lactational mastitis with systemic symptoms or no improvement after 12 to 24 hours of effective milk removal is treated with oral flucloxacillin for 10 to 14 days while continuing frequent breastfeeding or expression to prevent milk stasis and abscess formation.
hq_q.f: Development of a tender fluctuant swelling despite antibiotics -> ultrasound-guided needle aspiration.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: not improved after 24 hours of frequent breastfeeding
tm.m: Flucloxacillin targets beta-lactamase-producing Staphylococcus aureus while continued milk drainage prevents intraductal stasis and abscess formation
tm.g: Lactational mastitis with fever not settling after 24 hours -> oral flucloxacillin and continue breastfeeding
x: Abruptly stopping lactation worsens milk engorgement and stasis, increasing the risk of a breast abscess.
Flucloxacillin is first line when there is no penicillin allergy, and breastfeeding must be continued.
Stopping milk drainage from the affected breast causes milk stasis and promotes progression to an abscess.
There is no fluctuant collection to aspirate; aspiration is indicated only if a breast abscess forms.
f: Pharmacological suppression of lactation immediately following a late intrauterine fetal death
Non-lactational periductal infection in a penicillin-allergic patient where macrolide therapy is indicated
Never appropriate in mastitis, as milk stasis precipitates abscess formation
A tender, fluctuant 3 cm breast swelling with persistent fever after 5 days of flucloxacillin

hq_q.s:
A 35 year old woman has had a red, tender swelling beside her left areola for 5 days. This is her third similar episode in a year. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day. She is not breastfeeding and has never been pregnant.
Temperature 37.5°C. There is a tender, red swelling at the areolar edge with slight nipple retraction. Periductal mastitis is diagnosed.
hq_q.w: Periductal mastitis is strongly linked to smoking, which damages the ducts behind the nipple. Stopping smoking is the main way to prevent recurrence; acute episodes need antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav, and abscesses need drainage.
hq_q.f: Same swelling in a breastfeeding woman with a fever → lactational mastitis; keep feeding and give flucloxacillin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important advice to prevent further episodes?

tm.m: Smoking toxins damage the subareolar ducts, which become inflamed and infected
tm.g: Recurrent periareolar infection in a smoker: stop smoking
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Avoid caffeine (Caffeine is often blamed for breast pain but has no link to periductal mastitis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Long-term antibiotics (Long-term antibiotics do not remove the cause and drive resistance)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lose weight (Weight is not the key risk here; smoking is)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Stop wearing underwired bras (Underwired bras do not cause periductal mastitis)
x: Caffeine is often blamed for breast pain but has no link to periductal mastitis.
Long-term antibiotics do not remove the cause and drive resistance.
Weight is not the key risk here; smoking is.
Underwired bras do not cause periductal mastitis.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman has had a red, swollen left breast for 4 weeks. She is not breastfeeding and has no fever. Two courses of antibiotics have not helped.
Temperature 36.8°C. The left breast is diffusely red, warm and swollen with skin like orange peel. There is a firm left axillary lymph node.
hq_q.w: A red, swollen breast with peau d'orange and an axillary node that has not responded to antibiotics, in a woman who is not breastfeeding, is inflammatory breast cancer until proven otherwise. Refer on the suspected cancer pathway for triple assessment with core and skin biopsy.
hq_q.f: Fever, a tender fluctuant lump and breastfeeding → breast abscess; ultrasound-guided aspiration.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: Two courses of antibiotics have not helped
tm.m: Tumour cells block the dermal lymphatics, so the skin swells and pits
tm.g: Red breast not settling on antibiotics + node: suspected cancer referral
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to A third course of antibiotics (Two courses have failed; more antibiotics delay the diagnosis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Mammogram in 3 months (Imaging is part of triple assessment, but it must happen within 2 weeks, not 3 months)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Review in 6 weeks (Inflammatory breast cancer progresses within weeks; waiting is unsafe)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ultrasound and aspiration (Aspiration treats an abscess, but there is no fever or fluctuant lump)
x: Two courses have failed; more antibiotics delay the diagnosis.
Imaging is part of triple assessment, but it must happen within 2 weeks, not 3 months.
Inflammatory breast cancer progresses within weeks; waiting is unsafe.
Aspiration treats an abscess, but there is no fever or fluctuant lump.

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old woman with schizophrenia has noticed milky discharge from both nipples for 2 months and her menstrual periods have stopped. She was started on oral risperidone 4 months ago. She has no headaches or visual disturbance.
Urine pregnancy test is negative, serum TSH is 1.9 mU/L (0.4–4.5), and serum prolactin is 1,850 mU/L (100–500).
hq_q.w: Antipsychotics such as risperidone, haloperidol, and amisulpride antagonise dopamine D2 receptors on pituitary lactotrophs, removing tonic inhibition of prolactin secretion and causing galactorrhoea and hypogonadotrophic amenorrhoea.
hq_q.f: Headache and bitemporal hemianopia with prolactin >5,000 mU/L in a patient on no medication -> pituitary macroprolactinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of her presentation?

c: started on oral risperidone 4 months ago
tm.m: Tuberoinfundibular dopamine normally inhibits prolactin release via D2 receptors; risperidone D2 blockade elevates prolactin and suppresses GnRH
tm.g: Galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea after starting risperidone -> drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia
x: Causes spontaneous unilateral single-duct bloody or serous discharge with normal prolactin and regular menses.
Causes thick greenish multi-duct discharge in perimenopausal women without amenorrhoea or hyperprolactinaemia.
Can cause mild stalk-compression hyperprolactinaemia alongside headache and bitemporal visual field loss, but she has no neurological symptoms and recently started risperidone.
Elevated TRH can stimulate prolactin, but her serum TSH is normal (1.9 mU/L).
f: Unilateral spontaneous blood-stained discharge from a single duct with normal menstrual cycles
Thick green nipple discharge and slit-like nipple inversion in a 56-year-old woman
Bitemporal superior quadrantanopia, headache, and a 2.5 cm sellar mass with mild prolactin elevation of 1,100 mU/L
Galactorrhoea, weight gain, cold intolerance, and a serum TSH of 68 mU/L

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old postmenopausal woman has had spontaneous clear serous discharge from her right nipple for 3 weeks, staining her nightdress. She has no breast pain or skin rash.
Examination shows expressible clear fluid arising from a single duct of the right nipple, with no palpable breast lump, skin tethering or axillary lymphadenopathy.
o: Non-urgent referral to the breast clinic
Reassurance in primary care without referral
Review in primary care after 6 weeks
Routine NHS Breast Screening Programme mammogram
hq_q.w: NICE NG12 guidelines recommend a 2-week-wait suspected cancer pathway referral for anyone aged 50 and over who presents with unilateral nipple discharge (particularly spontaneous or single-duct), nipple retraction, or other changes of concern in one nipple.
hq_q.f: Unexplained breast lump in a woman under 30 -> consider non-urgent referral to the breast clinic.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate referral pathway?

c: spontaneous clear serous discharge from her right nipple
single duct of the right nipple
tm.m: Spontaneous unilateral single-duct discharge in a woman aged >=50 carries a significant risk of underlying ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive carcinoma
tm.g: Unilateral nipple discharge aged 50 or over -> suspected cancer pathway referral within 2 weeks
x: Insufficient urgency for unilateral single-duct discharge in a woman over 50, which meets NICE 2-week-wait criteria.
Spontaneous single-duct discharge in a postmenopausal woman requires triple assessment even when clear rather than bloody.
Delays exclusion of intraductal carcinoma in a woman over 50.
Screening mammography is for asymptomatic women; symptomatic single-duct discharge requires full one-stop triple assessment.
f: A 24-year-old woman with a discrete mobile breast lump and no red-flag nipple changes
Physiological trace bilateral milky fluid expressed only on firm squeezing in a parous 30-year-old woman with normal prolactin
Mild cyclical premenstrual breast tenderness in a 28-year-old woman trialling a supportive bra
An asymptomatic 53-year-old woman attending her triennial population screening invitation

hq_q.s:
A 61 year old woman has had a red, scaly, crusting rash on her left nipple for 3 months. It has slowly spread onto the areola and is eroding the nipple. It has not settled with a steroid cream. The right nipple is normal.
There is no palpable breast lump and no axillary lymphadenopathy.
o: Reassure as there is no lump
hq_q.w: Paget's disease of the nipple is an eczema-like change that starts on the nipple and does not respond to steroids. Most women have an underlying breast cancer (DCIS or invasive), so it needs a suspected cancer referral for mammography and a punch biopsy, even without a lump.
hq_q.f: Itchy rash that starts on the areola, affects both sides and settles with a steroid → eczema.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: not settled with a steroid cream
tm.m: Cancer cells spread up the ducts into the nipple skin
tm.g: One-sided nipple rash not settling on steroids: biopsy for Paget's
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Patch testing (Patch testing is for suspected contact dermatitis, which is usually on both sides and responds to steroids)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Potent steroid cream for 4 weeks (Steroid cream has already failed; more of it delays the diagnosis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Reassure as there is no lump (Most women with Paget's have an underlying cancer even without a palpable lump)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Topical antifungal cream (There is no sign of candida, and a one-sided eroding nipple needs a biopsy)
x: Patch testing is for suspected contact dermatitis, which is usually on both sides and responds to steroids.
Steroid cream has already failed; more of it delays the diagnosis.
Most women with Paget's have an underlying cancer even without a palpable lump.
There is no sign of candida, and a one-sided eroding nipple needs a biopsy.

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old woman was involved in a motor vehicle collision 2 months ago in which the seatbelt heavily bruised her anterior chest wall. She has now noticed a painless lump in her left breast.
Examination reveals a 2 cm firm, irregular mass in the upper inner quadrant directly beneath the fading bruise, with slight overlying skin tethering and no axillary lymphadenopathy.
hq_q.w: Traumatic fat necrosis follows blunt injury (such as a seatbelt contusion), breast surgery, or radiotherapy. Saponification and fibrosis of necrotic adipocytes produce a firm, irregular mass with skin tethering that clinically and radiologically mimics carcinoma, requiring triple assessment.
hq_q.f: Progressive hard irregular mass with no history of trauma and malignant ductal cells on biopsy -> invasive ductal carcinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: seatbelt heavily bruised her anterior chest wall
tm.m: Adipocyte rupture releases neutral lipids that undergo saponification, lipid-laden macrophage phagocytosis, and stellate scar fibrosis
tm.g: Firm irregular tethered breast mass at the site of recent seatbelt trauma -> traumatic fat necrosis
x: Presents within hours to days of trauma as a painful, fluctuant ecchymotic swelling rather than a firm tethered mass 2 months later.
Presents in young women under 30 as a smooth, rubbery, mobile lump without skin tethering.
Must be excluded by core biopsy, but the exact correspondence with recent seatbelt bruising makes fat necrosis most likely.
Forms a soft, doughy, mobile fatty lump with no skin tethering.
f: A painful, tense, bruised swelling developing 12 hours after a fall in a patient taking warfarin
A smooth, rubbery, mobile 2 cm lump in a 22-year-old woman with no skin tethering
A hard, irregular, tethered lump with enlarged axillary nodes and malignant invasive cords on core biopsy
A soft, doughy, mobile lump with no skin tethering and benign encapsulated fat on ultrasound

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old woman has had a creamy, green-tinged discharge from both nipples for 3 months. It comes from several ducts. She smokes.
Both nipples have a slit-like inversion. There is no palpable lump and no axillary lymphadenopathy. Mammogram shows benign calcification behind the nipples.
hq_q.w: Duct ectasia is dilatation and shortening of the subareolar ducts around and after the menopause. It causes a thick, coloured discharge from several ducts on both sides and a slit-like nipple inversion, with benign calcification on mammography.
hq_q.f: Blood-stained discharge from a single duct on one side → intraductal papilloma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: creamy, green-tinged discharge from both nipples
tm.m: Ducts behind the nipple widen, fill with secretions and shorten, pulling the nipple in
tm.g: Thick coloured discharge, several ducts, slit nipple: duct ectasia
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS is usually found as clustered microcalcification on screening, or bloody discharge from one duct)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Intraductal papilloma (A papilloma causes bloody or clear discharge from a single duct on one side)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Paget's disease of the nipple (Paget's causes a red, scaly, eroding nipple on one side, not discharge from both)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Periductal mastitis (Periductal mastitis causes painful inflammation and abscesses beside the areola in younger smokers)
x: DCIS is usually found as clustered microcalcification on screening, or bloody discharge from one duct.
A papilloma causes bloody or clear discharge from a single duct on one side.
Paget's causes a red, scaly, eroding nipple on one side, not discharge from both.
Periductal mastitis causes painful inflammation and abscesses beside the areola in younger smokers.

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man with heart failure has had tender enlargement of both breasts for 2 months. He takes ramipril, bisoprolol, furosemide and spironolactone, which was started 6 months ago. He drinks little alcohol.
There is tender, rubbery tissue beneath both nipples. Testes are normal. Liver function is normal.
hq_q.w: Spironolactone blocks androgen receptors and causes gynaecomastia. Eplerenone is a more selective swap. Key discriminator: Tender gynaecomastia on a new diuretic: spironolactone.
hq_q.f: A 24-year-old man with gynaecomastia and a painless testicular lump → a germ cell tumour making hCG.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most likely to be the cause?

c: spironolactone, which was started 6 months ago
tm.m: Spironolactone blocks androgen receptors
tm.g: Tender gynaecomastia on a new diuretic: spironolactone
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Aspirin (Used for: ACS, TIA or ischaemic stroke: 300 mg now)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Bisoprolol (Bisoprolol does not cause gynaecomastia)
not responding to spironolactone alone
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ramipril (Ramipril does not cause gynaecomastia)
x: Used for: ACS, TIA or ischaemic stroke: 300 mg now
Bisoprolol does not cause gynaecomastia.
Ruled out here: requires not responding to spironolactone alone, whereas this patient has both breasts, spironolactone, which was started 6 months ago.
Ramipril does not cause gynaecomastia.

hq_q.s:
A 47 year old woman attends her GP for a routine blood pressure check and asks when she will start receiving routine invitations for the NHS Breast Screening Programme. She has no breast symptoms and no family history of breast or ovarian cancer.
Pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg. Clinical breast examination is normal.
o: All women aged over 40 every year
Women with a first-degree family history only
hq_q.w: The UK NHS Breast Screening Programme invites all registered women aged 50 up to their 71st birthday for two-view digital mammography every 3 years. Women aged 71 and over are not automatically invited but can self-refer every 3 years.
hq_q.f: Women aged 40 to 49 at moderate or high familial breast cancer risk -> annual mammography via specialist genetics/family history surveillance.
hq_q.ql: Which group is routinely invited to the UK NHS Breast Screening Programme?

c: routine invitations for the NHS Breast Screening Programme
no breast symptoms and no family history
tm.m: Population mammographic screening every 3 years between ages 50 and 70 optimises breast cancer mortality reduction relative to overdiagnosis
tm.g: Routine UK NHS Breast Screening Programme schedule -> women aged 50 to 71 every 3 years
x: Annual mammography from age 40 is reserved for women at moderate or high familial risk, not the general population.
Population screening in the UK does not begin at age 40 or use a 2-year interval.
Matches cervical screening intervals in older women rather than the 3-yearly 50 to 71 breast screening programme.
The NHS Breast Screening Programme is a universal population screening programme for all women aged 50 to 71 regardless of family history.
f: High-risk surveillance protocol for women aged 40 to 49 with a strong familial breast cancer history
Biannual mammographic follow-up schedule used in some non-UK screening programmes
Five-yearly cervical screening interval for women aged 25 to 64 in the NHS Cervical Screening Programme
Referral criteria for a specialist familial breast cancer risk assessment clinic

hq_q.s: A 41 year old woman has undergone wide local excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy for a 1.8 cm grade 2 invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast. She continues to have regular monthly menstrual periods. Histopathology shows the tumour is oestrogen receptor positive (Allred 8/8) and HER2 negative, with negative sentinel nodes.
hq_q.w: Tamoxifen is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that competitively blocks oestrogen receptors in breast tissue and is the standard first-line adjuvant endocrine therapy for premenopausal women with ER-positive breast cancer.
hq_q.f: Postmenopausal woman with ER-positive invasive breast cancer -> oral aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole or letrozole).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line adjuvant endocrine therapy?

tm.m: In premenopausal women, aromatase inhibitors alone fail to block ovarian oestrogen synthesis and trigger reflex gonadotrophin surges, whereas tamoxifen directly blocks breast ER
tm.g: Premenopausal ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer -> oral tamoxifen
x: Non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor ineffective as monotherapy in premenopausal women with functioning ovaries.
Steroidal irreversible aromatase inactivator used in postmenopausal women (or premenopausal women only alongside ovarian suppression).
Non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor used for postmenopausal ER-positive breast cancer.
Anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody indicated only when the tumour overexpresses HER2.
f: First-line adjuvant endocrine therapy in a 62-year-old postmenopausal woman with ER-positive breast cancer
Adjuvant steroidal aromatase inhibitor switch after 2 to 3 years of tamoxifen in a postmenopausal woman
Extended adjuvant endocrine therapy in a postmenopausal woman with node-positive ER-positive breast cancer
Adjuvant targeted therapy in a woman with a HER2-positive (IHC 3+) invasive ductal carcinoma

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old woman is reviewed in the oncology clinic before starting adjuvant oral anastrozole for 5 years following wide local excision of an oestrogen receptor-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma. She went through the menopause at age 50.
Pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg. Her full blood count, renal profile, and liver function tests are normal.
hq_q.w: Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane) profoundly deplete circulating postmenopausal oestrogen, accelerating bone mineral density loss and osteoporotic fracture risk. NICE recommends a baseline DEXA bone density scan when starting an aromatase inhibitor.
hq_q.f: Starting adjuvant trastuzumab (Herceptin) -> baseline and 3-monthly transthoracic echocardiogram to monitor left ventricular ejection fraction.
hq_q.ql: Which baseline investigation is most important before starting anastrozole?

c: went through the menopause at age 50
tm.m: Inhibition of peripheral aromatase lowers oestradiol levels, increasing osteoclast activity and trabecular bone resorption
tm.g: Starting an aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole/letrozole) -> baseline DEXA bone mineral density scan
x: Used for patients on long-term hydroxychloroquine (retinopathy), not aromatase inhibitors.
Routine monthly liver function tests are not required for anastrozole therapy.
Required before starting cardiotoxic HER2-targeted therapy (trastuzumab) or anthracyclines, not anastrozole.
Indicated for postmenopausal vaginal bleeding on tamoxifen (which has partial endometrial agonist activity), whereas anastrozole causes endometrial atrophy.
f: Long-term hydroxychloroquine therapy for systemic lupus erythematosus
Initiation of hepatotoxic disease-modifying therapy such as methotrexate or leflunomide
Baseline cardiac assessment before starting adjuvant trastuzumab for HER2-positive breast cancer
Postmenopausal vaginal bleeding in a woman taking adjuvant tamoxifen

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old woman attends the emergency department with a 12-hour history of a painful lump in her right groin and repeated bilious vomiting. She has not passed flatus since yesterday.
Temperature 37.4°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg. Examination reveals a 3 cm tender, firm, irreducible swelling located below and lateral to the right pubic tubercle with no cough impulse.
hq_q.w: A femoral hernia protrudes through the rigid femoral ring inferior to the inguinal ligament, lying below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. It is commonest in older women and carries a high strangulation risk, requiring emergency surgical repair.
hq_q.f: Groin lump located above and medial to the pubic tubercle -> inguinal hernia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: below and lateral to the right pubic tubercle
tm.m: The rigid borders of the femoral ring (inguinal ligament anteriorly, lacunar ligament medially, pectineal ligament posteriorly) rapidly strangulate herniated bowel
tm.g: Tender irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle with vomiting -> strangulated femoral hernia
x: Emerges above and medial to the pubic tubercle through Hesselbach's triangle and rarely strangulates.
Emerges through the superficial inguinal ring above and medial to the pubic tubercle.
Does not cause mechanical small bowel obstruction and repeated bilious vomiting.
Forms a soft, compressible, bluish venous swelling that empties on lying flat and has a fluid thrill on coughing.
f: A wide-necked reducible swelling above and medial to the pubic tubercle that bulges despite deep ring pressure
A groin swelling above and medial to the pubic tubercle controlled by pressure over the deep inguinal ring
A firm, mobile groin nodule with no vomiting and an infected skin wound on the ipsilateral leg
A soft, bluish groin lump that disappears when supine and has a palpable cough thrill

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man attends the surgical clinic with a painless reducible right groin swelling.
On examination, the lump lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle. After reducing the hernia with the patient supine, the examiner presses firmly over the midpoint of the inguinal ligament; when the patient coughs, the lump does not reappear until pressure is released.
hq_q.w: The deep inguinal ring lies 1.5 cm above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament (midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle). Controlling a reduced inguinal hernia by pressure over the deep ring indicates an indirect inguinal hernia.
hq_q.f: Hernia still bulges medially on coughing despite deep ring occlusion -> direct inguinal hernia.
hq_q.ql: Which type of hernia does this examination finding demonstrate?

c: above and medial to the pubic tubercle
presses firmly over the midpoint of the inguinal ligament
does not reappear until pressure is released
tm.m: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the inguinal canal through the deep ring at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels
tm.g: Inguinal hernia prevented from protruding by pressure over the deep ring -> indirect inguinal hernia
x: Herniates directly through the weakened transversalis fascia of Hesselbach's triangle medial to the deep ring, so it still protrudes during the test.
Emerges below the inguinal ligament, inferior and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
Deep pelvic hernia presenting with bowel obstruction and medial thigh pain without a palpable groin swelling.
Herniates through the semilunar line at the lateral edge of the rectus sheath above the groin.
f: A reducible inguinal swelling that bulges medial to the examining finger despite occlusion of the deep inguinal ring
A groin swelling located below and lateral to the pubic tubercle
Small bowel obstruction and pain radiating down the medial thigh in a frail elderly woman with no groin lump
A swelling along the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle midway between the umbilicus and anterior superior iliac spine

hq_q.s:
A thin 84 year old woman has had colicky abdominal pain and bilious vomiting for 2 days. She has lancinating pain down the inner side of her right thigh to the knee that worsens when her hip is extended and internally rotated.
Pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 114/68 mmHg. The abdomen is distended with high-pitched bowel sounds, and there is no palpable swelling in either groin.
hq_q.w: An obturator hernia protrudes through the obturator canal in thin elderly women. Compression of the obturator nerve within the canal causes referred pain and paraesthesia along the medial thigh exacerbated by hip extension or rotation (Howship-Romberg sign).
hq_q.f: Tender irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle -> femoral hernia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of her bowel obstruction?

c: lancinating pain down the inner side of her right thigh
worsens when her hip is extended and internally rotated
no palpable swelling in either groin
tm.m: Loss of preperitoneal fat in the obturator canal allows small bowel to incarcerate alongside the obturator nerve
tm.g: Small bowel obstruction with medial thigh pain on hip rotation (Howship-Romberg sign) and no groin lump -> obturator hernia
x: Produces a palpable, tender lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle rather than an occult deep pelvic hernia.
Presents as a palpable defect and bulge through a previous abdominal surgical scar.
Produces a palpable groin lump above and medial to the pubic tubercle.
Forms an interparietal bulge at the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis without obturator nerve compression.
f: Small bowel obstruction with a tender, irreducible 3 cm lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle
Small bowel obstruction with a tender irreducible bulge within an old midline laparotomy scar
Small bowel obstruction with a tense irreducible swelling above and medial to the pubic tubercle
A tender lump at the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis below the umbilicus

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old man presents to the emergency department with a 50-minute history of severe, crushing retrosternal chest pain radiating to his left arm.
Pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 138/84 mmHg, SpO2 97% breathing air. A 12-lead ECG demonstrates 3 mm ST-segment elevation in leads V1 to V4. He has received aspirin 300 mg. The regional heart attack centre can perform PCI within 90 minutes.
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG185 guidelines, patients presenting with an acute STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset should receive immediate primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) if it can be delivered within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could be given.
hq_q.f: Primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes -> give immediate systemic fibrinolysis (e.g. tenecteplase/alteplase) and antithrombin, then repeat ECG at 60-90 minutes.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

c: 3 mm ST-segment elevation in leads V1 to V4
tm.m: Mechanical guidewire recanalisation, thrombus aspiration and drug-eluting stent deployment in the occluded left anterior descending artery restores TIMI-3 flow with higher patency and lower intracranial haemorrhage risk than fibrinolysis.
tm.g: Acute STEMI presenting within 12 hours + primary PCI deliverable within 120 minutes -> primary percutaneous coronary intervention
x: Primary percutaneous coronary intervention is much faster than emergency sternotomy and bypass grafting for acute STEMI reperfusion.
Conservative medical therapy with fondaparinux without immediate mechanical or pharmacological reperfusion is the management for low-risk NSTEMI, not an acute anterior STEMI.
An acute STEMI is a clinical and ECG diagnosis requiring immediate coronary reperfusion; waiting 3 hours for troponin results causes irreversible transmural myocardial necrosis.
Intravenous fibrinolysis is used only when primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes; here the heart attack centre can open the artery within 90 minutes.
f: severe three-vessel or left main stem coronary disease unsuitable for PCI after initial stabilisation
non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction with a low GRACE 6-month mortality risk score
suspected NSTEMI in a patient with a normal or non-diagnostic initial 12-lead ECG
acute STEMI in a remote hospital where transfer to a PCI centre would take longer than 120 minutes

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents to the emergency department after experiencing 30 minutes of heavy central chest tightness at rest this morning that has now resolved.
Pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 142/86 mmHg, SpO2 98% breathing air. Cardiovascular examination is normal. Her 12-lead ECG shows 1 mm horizontal ST-segment depression in leads V4 to V6.
hq_q.w: Unstable angina is an acute coronary syndrome characterised by resting or crescendo myocardial ischaemia and ischaemic ECG changes (horizontal ST depression) without cardiomyocyte necrosis, so serial 0-hour and 3-hour high-sensitivity troponin concentrations remain normal (<14 ng/L).
hq_q.f: Same clinical presentation and ECG with a dynamic rise in high-sensitivity troponin above the 99th centile -> NSTEMI.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: 30 minutes of heavy central chest tightness at rest
ST-segment depression in leads V4 to V6
tm.m: Subocclusive platelet-rich thrombus over a ruptured coronary plaque causes transient resting subendocardial ischaemia (ST depression) that resolves before irreversible myocyte necrosis and troponin release occur.
tm.g: Ischaemic rest chest pain + ST depression + normal serial 0h and 3h high-sensitivity troponin -> unstable angina
x: Stable angina is brought on predictably by physical exertion and relieved within 5 minutes of rest, whereas she had unprovoked chest tightness at rest lasting 30 minutes.
NSTEMI requires a dynamic rise and/or fall in cardiac troponin with at least one value above the 99th centile (>14 ng/L), whereas her 0-hour (8 ng/L) and 3-hour (9 ng/L) troponins are normal.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy follows an acute emotional or physical stressor and produces a modest troponin rise and apical left ventricular ballooning.
Vasospastic angina typically occurs in younger smokers in the early hours of the morning with transient ST-segment elevation that resolves completely when pain subsides.
f: chest tightness occurring only when walking uphill and resolving within 3 minutes of rest
the 3-hour high-sensitivity troponin T had risen from 8 ng/L to 185 ng/L
acute chest pain after severe emotional shock with elevated troponin and apical left ventricular akinesia
recurrent nocturnal rest chest pain with transient ST-segment elevation that resolves with nitrates

hq_q.s:
A 61 year old man presents to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of severe, crushing central chest pain radiating to his back and left arm.
Pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg, SpO2 97% breathing air. His standard 12-lead ECG shows 2 mm horizontal ST-segment depression, tall broad R waves and upright T waves in leads V1 to V3, without ST elevation elsewhere.
o: Perform a treadmill exercise tolerance test
Record posterior leads V7 to V9
Wait and repeat troponin at 3 hours
hq_q.w: Horizontal ST depression with tall broad dominant R waves and upright T waves in leads V1 to V3 during acute ischaemic chest pain represents reciprocal changes of a true posterior STEMI. Recording posterior leads V7 to V9 confirms ST elevation.
hq_q.f: Inferior STEMI (ST elevation in II, III, aVF) -> record right-sided chest leads (V3R, V4R) to detect right ventricular infarction.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate next step to confirm the diagnosis?

c: 1-hour history of severe, crushing central chest pain
horizontal ST-segment depression, tall broad R waves
tm.m: Because none of the standard 12 ECG leads face the posterior left ventricular wall directly, transmural posterior ST elevation and Q waves appear reciprocally in V1-V3 as ST depression and tall R waves.
tm.g: Ongoing chest pain + horizontal ST depression and tall dominant R waves in V1-V3 -> record posterior leads V7 to V9 (posterior STEMI)
x: CT coronary angiography is an elective investigation for stable chest pain, whereas this patient has an acute coronary occlusion requiring immediate emergency confirmation.
Exercise stress testing is strictly contraindicated in any patient with acute ongoing chest pain and resting ST-segment depression.
Recording posterior ECG leads V7 to V9 at the bedside takes 2 minutes and directly demonstrates posterior ST elevation to activate the primary PCI pathway.
Waiting 3 hours for a repeat troponin delays time-critical primary PCI in an acute posterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
f: first-line investigation of stable exertional angina in an outpatient with a normal resting ECG
functional assessment of exercise capacity in a stable cardiac rehabilitation patient
assessing left ventricular ejection fraction and valve function after primary PCI has been completed
suspected NSTEMI with non-specific T-wave flattening and resolved chest pain

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man with hypertension presents to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of sudden, severe tearing chest pain radiating straight through to his interscapular back.
Pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 168/92 mmHg in the right arm and 128/80 mmHg in the left arm, SpO2 97% breathing air. Auscultation reveals a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy.
hq_q.w: Sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the interscapular back, a systolic blood pressure differential >20 mmHg between the arms and a new early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation are the classic triad of acute thoracic aortic dissection.
hq_q.f: Severe retrosternal chest pain after forceful vomiting with subcutaneous neck emphysema -> Boerhaave oesophageal rupture.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: tearing chest pain radiating straight through to his interscapular back
168/92 mmHg in the right arm and 128/80 mmHg in the left arm
tm.m: An intimal tear in the ascending aorta propagates along the media to compromise the left subclavian ostium (reducing left arm BP) and prolapse an aortic valve cusp (causing aortic regurgitation).
tm.g: Tearing interscapular pain + >20 mmHg inter-arm BP difference + new early diastolic murmur -> aortic dissection
x: An uncomplicated myocardial infarction does not produce a 40 mmHg inter-arm systolic blood pressure difference or an early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation, and the ECG shows no ST elevation.
Acute pericarditis causes sharp pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward with a pericardial friction rub and widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation.
