Boerhaave syndrome follows forceful retching or vomiting and causes odynophagia, left pleural effusion and palpable cervical surgical emphysema rather than unequal arm BPs and aortic regurgitation.
Pulmonary embolism causes pleuritic pain, severe hypoxia, raised JVP and right ventricular strain rather than a 40 mmHg inter-arm BP difference and an early diastolic murmur.
f: crushing central chest pain radiating to the left jaw with equal arm blood pressures and anterior ST elevation
sharp central chest pain relieved by sitting forward with a pericardial rub and widespread concave ST elevation
severe retrosternal pain immediately after violent vomiting with subcutaneous emphysema in the neck and pneumomediastinum
sudden breathlessness, hypoxia (SpO2 84%) and pleuritic pain 10 days after pelvic cancer surgery

hq_q.s:
A 59 year old woman with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department with a 2-hour history of sudden, severe tearing interscapular back pain. Acute thoracic aortic dissection is suspected.
Pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 150/88 mmHg in both arms, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, SpO2 98% breathing air. She is alert and haemodynamically stable, and her baseline eGFR is 82 mL/min/1.73 m².
hq_q.w: ECG-gated CT angiography of the aorta is the gold-standard first-line investigation for suspected acute aortic dissection in haemodynamically stable patients, with >98% sensitivity for visualising the intimal flap, true and false lumens, and branch vessel involvement.
hq_q.f: Patient is too haemodynamically unstable to transfer to the CT scanner -> bedside transoesophageal echocardiography.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

c: sudden, severe tearing interscapular back pain
Acute thoracic aortic dissection is suspected
tm.m: Arterial-phase iodinated contrast CT delineates the intimal dissection flap separating the true and false lumens throughout the entire thoracoabdominal aorta within seconds.
tm.g: Definitive first-line imaging for suspected aortic dissection in a stable patient -> CT angiogram of the aorta
x: While a portable chest X-ray may show a widened mediastinum, up to 20% of patients with acute aortic dissection have a normal chest radiograph, so it cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis.
MR angiography is too slow and poorly accessible in the emergency department for an acute life-threatening aortic syndrome.
Plasma D-dimer is a non-specific fibrin degradation product that cannot anatomically confirm an intimal flap or distinguish aortic dissection from pulmonary embolism.
Transthoracic echocardiography has limited views of the distal ascending aorta, aortic arch and descending thoracic aorta, so it cannot exclude type B or arch dissection.
f: initial bedside screening for pneumothorax, although a normal chest X-ray never rules out aortic dissection
elective serial surveillance of stable aortic root dilatation in a young patient with Marfan syndrome to avoid radiation
ruling out deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism in a patient with a low Wells clinical probability score
rapid bedside screening for pericardial tamponade or aortic regurgitation while awaiting CT aortic angiography

hq_q.s: A 66 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-hour history of sudden, severe interscapular back pain. Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 182/104 mmHg, SpO2 98% breathing air. Bilateral femoral and pedal pulses are symmetrical and his abdomen is soft. Urine output and renal function are normal. CT aortogram demonstrates a descending thoracic aortic dissection distal to the left subclavian artery without malperfusion.
hq_q.w: Uncomplicated Stanford type B aortic dissection (distal to the left subclavian artery without organ or limb malperfusion) is managed medically first-line with intravenous labetalol to reduce heart rate below 60 bpm and systolic blood pressure to 100-120 mmHg.
hq_q.f: Dissection involving the ascending thoracic aorta (Stanford type A) -> emergency open cardiothoracic surgical repair.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

c: distal to the left subclavian artery
tm.m: Combined alpha- and beta-blockade reduces left ventricular ejection velocity (dP/dt) and systolic pressure, halting propagation of the descending false lumen
tm.g: Uncomplicated Stanford type B aortic dissection: first-line intravenous labetalol to control heart rate and blood pressure
x: Uncomplicated Stanford type B dissection distal to the left subclavian artery without malperfusion is managed medically rather than by open surgery.
Systemic thrombolysis is strictly contraindicated in aortic dissection as it causes fatal extension of the false lumen and haemothorax.
Vasodilators given without prior beta-blockade induce reflex tachycardia and increased left ventricular contractility, increasing aortic wall shear stress.
Antiplatelet therapy is contraindicated in acute aortic dissection because it impairs platelet function and worsens catastrophic haemorrhage if rupture occurs.
f: The CT aortogram demonstrates a Stanford type A dissection involving the ascending thoracic aorta.
He presents with massive pulmonary embolism causing obstructive cardiogenic shock without aortic pathology.
Blood pressure remains persistently elevated after heart rate has already been lowered below 60 bpm with intravenous beta-blockade.
An acute coronary syndrome has been confirmed on ECG after excluding aortic dissection.

hq_q.s: A 61 year old man presents to the cardiology clinic with a 2-month history of retrosternal chest tightness triggered by walking uphill that resolves within 4 minutes of resting. He uses a sublingual glyceryl trinitrate spray as required and has no history of asthma, peripheral vascular disease or heart failure. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 136/84 mmHg. CT coronary angiography confirms obstructive coronary artery disease.
hq_q.w: Under NICE CG126 guidelines for stable angina, first-line regular preventative anti-anginal therapy is either a beta-blocker (such as bisoprolol) or a calcium channel blocker, alongside sublingual glyceryl trinitrate, low-dose aspirin and statin secondary prevention.
hq_q.f: Coexisting brittle asthma contraindicating beta-blockade -> a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker such as verapamil or diltiazem.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line regular anti-anginal drug?

tm.m: Cardioselective beta-1 blockade reduces exercise heart rate and myocardial contractility, lowering myocardial oxygen demand during exertion
tm.g: First-line regular anti-anginal prophylaxis in stable angina without asthma: oral beta-blocker (bisoprolol) or calcium channel blocker
x: Long-acting nitrates are second-line add-on or alternative agents rather than first-line monotherapy when beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are tolerated.
Ivabradine is a second-line sinus node inhibitor used only when beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are contraindicated or insufficient.
Potassium-channel activators are second-line anti-anginal options due to inferior outcome evidence and the risk of mucocutaneous and gastrointestinal ulceration.
Late sodium current inhibition with ranolazine is reserved as a second-line adjunct when first-line rate-limiting therapy fails.
f: Both beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated for his stable angina.
He remains symptomatic despite maximum tolerated beta-blocker or cannot tolerate beta-blockers while in sinus rhythm with heart rate above 70 bpm.
First-line beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers fail to control angina symptoms or are contraindicated.
Exertional angina persists despite dual therapy with a beta-blocker and a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.

hq_q.s: A 57 year old woman presents to the rapid access chest pain clinic with a 6-week history of central constricting chest pain provoked by brisk walking and relieved within 3 minutes of rest. She smokes and takes amlodipine for hypertension. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 142/86 mmHg, SpO2 98% breathing air. Heart sounds are normal and her resting 12-lead ECG shows normal sinus rhythm.
hq_q.w: Under NICE CG95 guidelines, 64-slice (or above) CT coronary angiography is the first-line diagnostic investigation for patients with typical or atypical stable anginal chest pain and no prior history of coronary artery disease.
hq_q.f: CT coronary angiography shows coronary stenosis of uncertain functional significance -> non-invasive functional imaging (myocardial perfusion scan or stress echocardiography).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line diagnostic investigation?

c: resting 12-lead ECG shows normal sinus rhythm
tm.m: Contrast-enhanced CT coronary angiography directly visualises coronary lumen stenosis and atherosclerotic plaque with very high negative predictive value
tm.g: New-onset typical or atypical stable angina with normal resting ECG: first-line CT coronary angiography (NICE CG95)
x: Stress echocardiography is a second-line functional test used only if CT coronary angiography is non-diagnostic or shows indeterminate stenosis.
NICE CG95 explicitly advises against using an exercise ECG to diagnose or exclude stable angina in patients without known coronary artery disease.
Invasive catheter angiography is reserved as a third-line test when non-invasive functional imaging is inconclusive or revascularisation is planned.
Non-invasive functional imaging is second-line when CT coronary angiography shows coronary disease of uncertain functional significance or is non-diagnostic.
f: Extensive coronary calcification renders CT coronary angiography non-diagnostic and functional ischaemia testing is required.
She already has established coronary artery disease and functional exercise capacity is being evaluated.
Non-invasive functional imaging results are inconclusive or she presents with a high-risk acute coronary syndrome.
CT coronary angiography has demonstrated coronary artery stenosis of uncertain haemodynamic significance.

hq_q.s: A 68 year old man attends his GP with persistent exertional angina occurring most days when climbing stairs. His current medications are bisoprolol 10 mg daily, aspirin 75 mg daily, atorvastatin 80 mg daily and sublingual glyceryl trinitrate spray. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 58 bpm regular, BP 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min. Heart sounds are normal and there is no ankle oedema.
hq_q.w: When stable angina is not controlled by a beta-blocker alone, NICE CG126 recommends adding a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (such as amlodipine). Rate-limiting calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) must not be combined with beta-blockers.
hq_q.f: Both a beta-blocker and a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker are contraindicated -> add a long-acting nitrate, ivabradine, nicorandil or ranolazine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate regular anti-anginal drug to add?

tm.m: Long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockade dilates peripheral and coronary arteries, reducing afterload without depressing the sinoatrial or atrioventricular nodes
tm.g: Dual therapy for stable angina already on a beta-blocker: add a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (amlodipine)
x: Short-acting dihydropyridines cause abrupt peripheral vasodilation and reflex sympathetic tachycardia, worsening myocardial ischaemia and angina.
Cardiac glycosides have no anti-anginal role in sinus rhythm and increase myocardial oxygen consumption by raising intracellular calcium.
Combining a rate-limiting benzothiazepine calcium channel blocker with full-dose bisoprolol at 58 bpm risks profound bradycardia and heart block.
Co-prescribing verapamil with a beta-blocker is contraindicated because dual AV nodal depression precipitates complete heart block and asystole.
f: Modified-release long-acting dihydropyridine therapy is prescribed rather than an immediate-release formulation.
He develops atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate alongside sedentary lifestyle or heart failure.
Bisoprolol is stopped due to severe bronchospasm and single-agent rate-limiting therapy is needed instead.
He has asthma preventing beta-blocker use and requires a first-line rate-limiting calcium channel blocker monotherapy.

hq_q.s: A 24 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 30-minute history of sudden-onset rapid regular palpitations. She reports two previous brief episodes that terminated spontaneously. She has no chest pain, syncope or breathlessness. Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 186 bpm regular, BP 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, SpO2 99% breathing air. A 12-lead ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia without visible P waves.
hq_q.w: According to Resuscitation Council UK ALS guidelines, a haemodynamically stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia (supraventricular tachycardia) is managed first-line with vagal manoeuvres (such as the modified Valsalva manoeuvre), followed by rapid intravenous adenosine (6 mg, 12 mg, 18 mg) if unsuccessful.
hq_q.f: Adverse signs present (shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia or acute heart failure) -> immediate synchronised DC cardioversion.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial management step?

tm.m: Increased efferent vagal tone transiently prolongs atrioventricular nodal refractoriness, interrupting the AV nodal re-entry circuit
tm.g: Haemodynamically stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: perform vagal manoeuvres first, then intravenous adenosine
x: Adenosine is given only if vagal manoeuvres fail to terminate a haemodynamically stable regular narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia.
Amiodarone has slow onset and significant toxicity, and is not indicated before vagal manoeuvres and adenosine in stable SVT.
Oral beta-blockers act too slowly for acute termination of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia in the Emergency Department.
Immediate electrical cardioversion is reserved for tachyarrhythmias accompanied by life-threatening adverse features (shock, syncope, ischaemia or heart failure).
f: Modified Valsalva and carotid sinus massage fail to terminate her regular narrow-complex tachycardia.
She presents with haemodynamically stable monomorphic broad-complex ventricular tachycardia.
Acute SVT has been terminated and oral prophylaxis against recurrent paroxysms is being initiated.
She is hypotensive with BP 76/44 mmHg, pale, clammy and experiencing ongoing ischaemic chest pain.

hq_q.s: A 70 year old man presents to the acute medical unit with a 2-day history of persistent palpitations and mild exertional breathlessness. He has a history of hypertension and mild COPD. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 150 bpm regular, BP 132/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, SpO2 96% breathing air. His 12-lead ECG demonstrates a saw-tooth baseline in leads II, III and aVF with regular narrow QRS complexes.
hq_q.w: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at a ventricular rate close to 150 bpm with a saw-tooth baseline in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF) is diagnostic of atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular block (atrial rate 300 bpm).
hq_q.f: Irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no discernible P waves -> atrial fibrillation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: saw-tooth baseline in leads II, III and aVF
tm.m: A cavotricuspid isthmus macro-re-entrant circuit discharges in the right atrium at 300 bpm, with physiological 2:1 AV nodal refractoriness conducting 150 bpm
tm.g: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 bpm with inferior saw-tooth F waves = atrial flutter with 2:1 block
x: Atrial fibrillation produces an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm with absent P waves rather than a regular rate of 150 bpm with saw-tooth waves.
AVNRT typically presents at rates of 160-220 bpm with buried or retrograde P waves, not a classic 300 bpm saw-tooth atrial baseline.
Ventricular tachycardia produces broad QRS complexes (>120 ms) with atrioventricular dissociation rather than narrow QRS complexes driven by flutter waves.
Sinus tachycardia exhibits discrete upright P waves in leads I and II preceding each QRS complex and varies with physiological demand.
f: The pulse is irregularly irregular and the ECG shows a chaotic fibrillatory baseline with variable RR intervals.
A 26 year old woman has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 bpm with no saw-tooth flutter waves.
The ECG shows regular broad QRS complexes of 160 ms with fusion beats, capture beats and chest lead concordance.
He is febrile and hypovolaemic with discrete upright P waves preceding every QRS complex at 128 bpm.

hq_q.s: A 72 year old woman admitted with pneumonia is receiving intravenous clarithromycin and takes oral haloperidol for delirium. She experiences a brief witnessed syncopal episode on the ward and regains consciousness rapidly. Temperature 37.3°C, pulse rate 160 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg, SpO2 96% breathing air. Continuous cardiac telemetry shows a polymorphic broad-complex tachycardia with QRS complexes twisting around the isoelectric baseline. Serum potassium is 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.3).
hq_q.w: Torsades de pointes (polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with drug-induced QT prolongation from clarithromycin and haloperidol) is treated immediately with intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 10 minutes regardless of baseline serum magnesium, alongside stopping all QT-prolonging drugs.
hq_q.f: Pulseless polymorphic ventricular tachycardia -> immediate unsynchronised defibrillation following the ALS shockable cardiac arrest algorithm.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate intravenous pharmacological treatment?

c: QRS complexes twisting around the isoelectric baseline
tm.m: Magnesium suppresses early afterdepolarisations across the ventricular myocardium by inhibiting L-type calcium influx during prolonged phase 2/3 repolarisation
tm.g: Haemodynamically stable torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT with long QT): intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g first-line
x: Adenosine blocks the AV node in narrow-complex SVT and is ineffective in polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.
Class III antiarrhythmics further prolong myocardial repolarisation and the QT interval, exacerbating torsades de pointes.
Rapid bolus intravenous potassium is hazardous and her serum potassium is already within the normal reference range at 4.2 mmol/L.
Verapamil is contraindicated in broad-complex tachycardias as it causes severe hypotension and degenerates VT into ventricular fibrillation.
f: Telemetry shows a regular narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia at 185 bpm refractory to vagal manoeuvres.
Telemetry shows sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia without baseline QT prolongation.
She is in sinus rhythm with flat T waves, prominent U waves and severe hypokalaemia of 2.4 mmol/L requiring controlled infusion.
A patient with asthma and stable regular narrow-complex SVT fails vagal manoeuvres and cannot receive adenosine.

hq_q.s:
A 49 year old man attends for an NHS Health Check. He feels well.
Clinic BP is 156/96 mmHg on two readings, 10 minutes apart. Fundoscopy is normal. Urine dipstick is normal.
hq_q.w: Clinic BP from 140/90 to 179/119 is confirmed with ABPM, or home monitoring if ABPM is not tolerated, before diagnosing hypertension.
hq_q.f: BP 180/120 or more with papilloedema or retinal haemorrhage → same-day specialist referral.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Clinic readings overestimate blood pressure in many people
tm.g: Clinic BP of 140/90 to 179/119: confirm with ambulatory monitoring
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Repeat clinic reading in 1 year (A year is too long to confirm hypertension)
180/120 or more with papilloedema
the presentation instead showed features specific to Start amlodipine today (Amlodipine is not started on clinic readings alone; ABPM confirms the diagnosis first)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Start ramipril today (Ramipril is not started on clinic readings alone; at 49 it would also only follow a confirmed diagnosis)
x: A year is too long to confirm hypertension.
Ruled out here: requires 180/120 or more with papilloedema, whereas this patient has 156/96 mmHg on two readings, Fundoscopy is normal.
Amlodipine is not started on clinic readings alone; ABPM confirms the diagnosis first.
Ramipril is not started on clinic readings alone; at 49 it would also only follow a confirmed diagnosis.

hq_q.s: A 54 year old man of Black African family origin attends his GP after ambulatory blood pressure monitoring confirms stage 2 hypertension with an average daytime reading of 152/94 mmHg. He is asymptomatic, does not smoke and has no history of diabetes mellitus or cardiovascular disease. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm, clinic BP 158/98 mmHg. Serum electrolytes, eGFR, HbA1c and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio are all normal.
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG136 hypertension guidelines, adults of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin of any age who do not have type 2 diabetes should be offered a calcium channel blocker (such as amlodipine) as step 1 antihypertensive therapy.
hq_q.f: Coexisting type 2 diabetes mellitus -> start an ACE inhibitor (ramipril) or ARB first-line regardless of age or family origin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive drug?

c: 54 year old man of Black African family origin
tm.m: Patients of Black African origin predominantly exhibit low-renin, volume-dependent hypertension that responds far more effectively to calcium channel blockade than RAS inhibition
tm.g: Step 1 hypertension treatment in Black African/African-Caribbean origin without diabetes (any age): calcium channel blocker (amlodipine)
x: Beta-blockers are not first-line step 1 therapy for primary hypertension unless there is a compelling cardiac indication such as angina or heart failure.
Alpha-blockers are fourth-line agents reserved for step 4 resistant hypertension when potassium exceeds 4.5 mmol/L.
Thiazide-like diuretics are step 2 add-on agents under NICE NG136 unless a calcium channel blocker is not tolerated because of oedema.
People of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin typically have low-renin hypertension and respond poorly to ACE inhibitor monotherapy without diabetes.
f: He has symptomatic ischaemic heart disease or heart failure with reduced ejection fraction alongside hypertension.
His hypertension remains uncontrolled on triple therapy (ACE inhibitor, calcium channel blocker and thiazide-like diuretic) with serum potassium 4.9 mmol/L.
He develops severe ankle oedema on amlodipine and requires an alternative step 1 agent.
He has coexisting type 2 diabetes mellitus or chronic kidney disease with a urine ACR of 30 mg/mmol or more.

hq_q.s: A 66 year old woman attends her GP for review of poorly controlled primary hypertension. She adheres strictly to ramipril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily and indapamide 2.5 mg daily. She is asymptomatic. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 68 bpm, clinic BP 158/96 mmHg with no postural blood pressure drop. Repeat ambulatory blood pressure monitoring confirms an average daytime reading of 150/92 mmHg.
hq_q.w: In NICE NG136 step 4 resistant hypertension, treatment depends on serum potassium: if <=4.5 mmol/L add low-dose spironolactone; if >4.5 mmol/L (here 4.9 mmol/L) add an alpha-blocker (doxazosin) or beta-blocker. Never combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB.
hq_q.f: Serum potassium 4.5 mmol/L or lower -> low-dose oral spironolactone 25 mg once daily.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate drug to add at step 4?

c: ramipril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily and indapamide 2.5 mg daily
tm.m: Selective alpha-1 adrenoceptor blockade reduces peripheral vascular resistance without further impairing renal potassium excretion when baseline potassium exceeds 4.5 mmol/L
tm.g: Step 4 resistant hypertension: K+ <= 4.5 mmol/L -> low-dose spironolactone; K+ > 4.5 mmol/L -> alpha-blocker (doxazosin) or beta-blocker
x: Loop diuretics are indicated for fluid overload or severe renal impairment rather than routine step 4 resistant hypertension with normal creatinine.
Combining an angiotensin receptor blocker with an ACE inhibitor (ramipril) is contraindicated due to high risks of hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury.
Low-dose spironolactone at step 4 is restricted to patients whose serum potassium is 4.5 mmol/L or lower because of hyperkalaemia risk.
Adding a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker to maximum-dose amlodipine is inappropriate; NICE step 4 specifies an alpha-blocker or beta-blocker when potassium >4.5 mmol/L.
f: She develops decompensated heart failure with bibasal pulmonary crackles, raised JVP and peripheral oedema.
She develops a persistent dry cough on ramipril requiring replacement of the ACE inhibitor rather than step 4 addition.
Her repeat serum blood tests show a serum potassium concentration of 4.1 mmol/L.
Amlodipine is discontinued and she requires rate control for supraventricular arrhythmias.

hq_q.s: A 55 year old man attends his GP for an annual cardiovascular risk assessment. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily and his brother had a myocardial infarction aged 58, though he has no personal history of cardiovascular disease or diabetes. Following lifestyle changes, he wishes to start lipid modification. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 134/84 mmHg. Baseline liver and renal function are normal.
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG238 guidelines, atorvastatin 20 mg once daily is offered for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease to adults with a 10-year QRISK3 score of 10% or greater (or chronic kidney disease or type 1 diabetes) after lifestyle modification.
hq_q.f: Secondary prevention of established cardiovascular disease (prior MI, angina, stroke, TIA or PAD) -> oral atorvastatin 80 mg once daily.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate lipid-lowering regimen to initiate?
hq_q.post: His QRISK3 score is 14%.

tm.m: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition upregulates hepatic LDL receptors, lowering circulating atherogenic non-HDL cholesterol and halving primary cardiovascular events
tm.g: Primary CVD prevention with 10-year QRISK3 >= 10%: start oral atorvastatin 20 mg once daily
x: Atorvastatin 80 mg is the high-intensity dose used for secondary prevention of established cardiovascular disease rather than primary prevention.
Ezetimibe monotherapy is reserved for patients who have documented contraindications or intolerance to statin therapy.
NICE NG238 advises against routinely offering fibrates for the primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.
NICE NG238 explicitly states that omega-3 fatty acid compounds must not be offered for primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.
f: He is being discharged after an acute non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction or ischaemic stroke.
He developed severe myalgia and a 10-fold elevation in serum creatine kinase on three different statins.
Specialist lipid clinic advice recommends fibrate therapy for persistent severe hypertriglyceridaemia above 10 mmol/L despite statin therapy.
This option is not recommended by NICE for primary cardiovascular disease risk reduction.

hq_q.s: A 63 year old woman attends her GP for a 3-month lipid review following an acute ischaemic stroke. She has taken atorvastatin 80 mg once daily consistently since hospital discharge without muscle symptoms, alongside clopidogrel 75 mg daily. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg. Baseline total cholesterol was 6.4 mmol/L and non-HDL cholesterol was 5.1 mmol/L; repeat non-HDL cholesterol today is 3.7 mmol/L.
o: Add oral omega-3 fatty acid capsules
Continue current therapy with no changes
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG238 guidelines for secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease, the target is an LDL cholesterol <=2.0 mmol/L (or non-HDL <=2.6 mmol/L). When LDL remains above target despite adherent atorvastatin 80 mg, add oral ezetimibe 10 mg daily.
hq_q.f: LDL cholesterol already <= 2.0 mmol/L on atorvastatin 80 mg daily -> continue current therapy with annual review.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management step?
hq_q.post: Liver function is normal.

tm.m: Inhibiting the intestinal NPC1L1 sterol transporter with ezetimibe blocks biliary and dietary cholesterol absorption, providing an additive 20% reduction in LDL cholesterol
tm.g: Secondary CVD prevention with LDL > 2.0 mmol/L despite adherent atorvastatin 80 mg: add oral ezetimibe 10 mg daily
x: NICE guidelines advise against routinely combining a fibrate with a statin for secondary cardiovascular prevention due to myopathy risk and lack of benefit.
Omega-3 fatty acid compounds have no role in secondary stroke prevention under NICE NG238 guidelines.
Her LDL cholesterol of 2.9 mmol/L remains above the NICE NG238 secondary prevention target of 2.0 mmol/L or less (and <40% non-HDL reduction).
Discontinuing high-intensity statin therapy after an ischaemic stroke markedly increases the risk of recurrent stroke and myocardial infarction.
f: She has severe refractory hypertriglyceridaemia at risk of acute pancreatitis managed in a specialist lipid clinic.
She requires icosapent ethyl specifically for elevated fasting triglycerides (>=1.7 mmol/L) with LDL cholesterol between 1.04 and 2.60 mmol/L.
Repeat lipid profile shows LDL cholesterol is 1.7 mmol/L with a 48% reduction in non-HDL cholesterol.
She develops rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury and a creatine kinase greater than 10 times the upper limit of normal.

hq_q.s: A 31 year old man attends his GP after a routine screen found a total cholesterol of 9.4 mmol/L (<5.0). His father died of an acute myocardial infarction at 46. He does not smoke and has a BMI of 23 kg/m2. Examination reveals nodular thickening of both Achilles tendons and corneal arcus. Fasting LDL cholesterol is 7.2 mmol/L (<3.0), triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L and TSH 1.8 mU/L.
hq_q.w: Under the Simon Broome criteria (NICE CG71), a total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L or LDL cholesterol >4.9 mmol/L in an adult plus tendon xanthomata in the patient or a first/second-degree relative confirms definite familial hypercholesterolaemia.
hq_q.f: Eruptive yellow papules with creamy serum and fasting triglycerides >20 mmol/L -> familial hypertriglyceridaemia / chylomicronaemia syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: father died of an acute myocardial infarction at 46
nodular thickening of both Achilles tendons
tm.m: Autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutations in LDLR (or APOB/PCSK9) impair hepatic LDL clearance from birth, causing cholesterol deposition in tendons and coronary arteries
tm.g: Total cholesterol > 7.5 mmol/L (or LDL > 4.9 mmol/L) + tendon xanthomata + premature family CHD = familial hypercholesterolaemia
x: Familial combined hyperlipidaemia presents with moderate elevations of both cholesterol and triglycerides and lacks tendon xanthomata.
His fasting triglycerides are normal at 1.4 mmol/L, whereas familial hypertriglyceridaemia causes marked triglyceride elevation and eruptive xanthomata.
Nephrotic hyperlipidaemia is accompanied by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and peripheral oedema rather than isolated lifelong LDL elevation with tendon xanthomata.
Secondary hypercholesterolaemia from hypothyroidism is excluded by his normal thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 1.8 mU/L.
f: He has no tendon xanthomata and blood tests show total cholesterol 6.8 mmol/L with fasting triglycerides 4.2 mmol/L.
He presents with eruptive yellow cutaneous papules over his buttocks, lipaemia retinalis and fasting triglycerides of 22 mmol/L.
He presents with bilateral pitting leg oedema, periorbital puffiness, serum albumin 19 g/L and 4+ proteinuria.
He reports cold intolerance, weight gain and constipation with a serum TSH of 48 mU/L and low free T4.

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old woman is newly diagnosed with asthma after presenting with a 4-month history of episodic wheeze and cough occurring twice a week during exercise. She is not woken at night and has no daily symptoms between episodes.
Pulse rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99% breathing air. Chest auscultation is clear. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide is 58 ppb.
hq_q.w: The 2024 BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma guideline recommends starting newly diagnosed adults on an anti-inflammatory reliever (AIR) regimen: low-dose inhaled corticosteroid with formoterol (budesonide/formoterol) taken as needed. SABA monotherapy is no longer recommended.
hq_q.f: Still uncontrolled on as-needed ICS with formoterol → low-dose maintenance and reliever therapy, MART.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial inhaler regimen under UK asthma guidelines?

tm.m: Formoterol provides rapid onset bronchodilation (~1-3 minutes) while the co-administered inhaled corticosteroid treats underlying eosinophilic inflammation with every reliever actuation.
tm.g: Newly diagnosed adult asthma with infrequent symptoms -> as-needed low-dose budesonide with formoterol (AIR)
x: SABA-only treatment leaves airway inflammation untreated and is associated with preventable severe exacerbations and asthma deaths; NICE/BTS/SIGN 2024 prohibits SABA monotherapy.
High-dose maintenance ICS is a much later step for severe uncontrolled asthma; new mild asthma starts on as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol.
Leukotriene receptor antagonists are third-line add-on controllers after ICS/formoterol MART therapy, never first-line monotherapy in adults.
Long-acting beta-2 agonist monotherapy without an inhaled corticosteroid masks airway inflammation and increases asthma-related mortality.
f: salbutamol via a spacer was being used strictly for immediate emergency bronchodilation during an acute hospital admission alongside systemic steroids
a patient already on moderate-dose MART therapy had persistent daily symptoms and exacerbations requiring step-up to high-dose ICS
an add-on oral controller was needed for a patient whose asthma remained uncontrolled despite moderate-dose ICS/formoterol MART therapy
a long-acting bronchodilator was being initiated for a patient with stable COPD and no asthmatic features

hq_q.s:
A 31 year old man with asthma attends the Emergency Department with 24 hours of worsening wheeze.
Temperature 36.8°C, pulse rate 115 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute, SpO2 95% breathing air. He cannot complete sentences in one breath. Auscultation reveals widespread wheeze. Peak expiratory flow is 40% of his personal best.
hq_q.w: Under BTS/SIGN and NICE criteria, acute severe asthma is defined by any of: peak flow 33-50% of best/predicted, respiratory rate >=25/min, heart rate >=110 bpm, or inability to complete sentences, with preserved SpO2 >=92%.
hq_q.f: Peak flow under 33%, saturations under 92%, a silent chest or a normal PaCO2 → life-threatening.
hq_q.ql: Which severity grade best classifies this acute asthma exacerbation?

tm.m: Severe bronchospasm and mucosal oedema reduce peak flow to 33-50% and trigger tachypnoea and tachycardia while oxygenation remains preserved above 92%.
tm.g: PEF 33-50% + RR >=25 + HR >=110 + unable to complete sentences with SpO2 >=92% -> acute severe asthma
x: Life-threatening asthma requires features such as SpO2 <92%, peak flow <33%, silent chest, cyanosis, hypotension, exhaustion or normal/high PaCO2.
Mild asthma does not cause inability to complete sentences, tachycardia of 115 bpm, tachypnoea of 27/min or a peak flow of 40%.
Moderate asthma exacerbation has a peak flow >50% to 75% of best/predicted, normal speech, RR <25/min and pulse <110 bpm.
Near-fatal asthma is defined by a raised arterial carbon dioxide tension (PaCO2 >6.0 kPa) and/or requirement for mechanical ventilation with raised inflation pressures.
f: his oxygen saturation on room air was 89%, his peak flow was 28% of best, or auscultation revealed a silent chest
he was attending a routine GP review speaking in full sentences with normal vital signs and a peak flow of 85% of personal best
he could speak in complete sentences, had a respiratory rate of 20/min, pulse 96 bpm, SpO2 97% and a peak flow of 60% of best
arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated a rising PaCO2 of 6.8 kPa with respiratory acidosis requiring endotracheal intubation

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old woman is in the Emergency Department with acute severe asthma. She has received oxygen, back-to-back nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, and oral prednisolone 40 mg.
At reassessment 30 minutes later, her respiratory rate is 28 breaths per minute, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg and SpO2 94% on oxygen. Peak expiratory flow remains 38% of best.
hq_q.w: In acute severe or life-threatening asthma that responds poorly to initial inhaled beta-2 agonists, nebulised ipratropium and systemic corticosteroids, BTS/SIGN and NICE recommend a single intravenous infusion of magnesium sulfate (1.2 to 2 g over 20 minutes) after senior review.
hq_q.f: Rising PaCO2, exhaustion or confusion → call critical care for intubation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next pharmacological intervention?

tm.m: Magnesium ions competitively inhibit calcium influx into bronchial smooth muscle cells and reduce presynaptic acetylcholine release, producing additive bronchodilation.
tm.g: Acute severe asthma with incomplete response to nebulised SABA, ipratropium and steroids -> IV magnesium sulfate
x: Intravenous aminophylline has a narrow therapeutic index (arrhythmias, seizures) and is considered only by critical care seniors after IV magnesium fails.
Intravenous salbutamol carries high risks of lactic acidosis, hypokalaemia and tachyarrhythmia and is reserved for ICU-level refractory disease after IV magnesium.
Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema in acute severe croup or anaphylactic stridor rather than lower airway bronchospasm in asthma.
Oral leukotriene receptor antagonists are slow-acting maintenance controllers and have no evidence-based role in acute severe asthma resuscitation.
f: she was in the intensive care unit with life-threatening asthma refractory to nebulisers and IV magnesium sulfate, after checking serum theophylline levels
ventilator pressures remained critically high in a ventilated patient despite nebulised bronchodilators and IV magnesium sulfate, with close lactate/potassium monitoring
a 2 year old child presented with barking cough, inspiratory stridor at rest and sternal recession due to severe viral croup
an outpatient with chronic exercise-induced and allergic asthma needed step-up controller therapy added to inhaled ICS/LABA

hq_q.s:
A 63 year old man presents with 3 years of progressive exertional breathlessness and a daily morning cough productive of white sputum. He has a 40 pack-year cigarette smoking history and no history of atopy.
SpO2 94% breathing air. Auscultation reveals scattered expiratory wheeze.
Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.61 with a 3% change in FEV1.
hq_q.w: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is diagnosed in adults aged over 35 with a smoking history and progressive exertional breathlessness or chronic cough when post-bronchodilator spirometry demonstrates fixed airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70) without marked reversibility.
hq_q.f: FEV1/FVC 0.78 with daily cupfuls of purulent sputum → bronchiectasis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Cigarette smoke triggers neutrophilic small-airway remodelling (chronic bronchitis) and elastolytic alveolar destruction (emphysema), causing poorly reversible airflow limitation.
tm.g: Smoker >35 years with progressive dyspnoea and post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 -> chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
x: Asthma is characterised by marked diurnal symptom variation, atopic history, raised FeNO and significant bronchodilator reversibility (>12% and >200 mL).
Bronchiectasis causes large volumes of daily purulent sputum, coarse basal crackles and bronchial dilatation on HRCT rather than mucoid smoker's cough.
Heart failure causes orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, elevated JVP, bibasal fine crackles, ankle oedema and raised NT-proBNP.
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis causes dry cough, finger clubbing, bibasal velcro crackles and restrictive spirometry (FEV1/FVC >0.70).
f: spirometry showed an increase in FEV1 of 420 mL (18%) after salbutamol alongside a FeNO of 62 ppb and nocturnal wheeze
he coughed up cups of thick green sputum daily with coarse basal crackles, finger clubbing and signet-ring airway dilatation on HRCT
he had orthopnoea, pitting ankle oedema, bibasal fine crackles and an NT-proBNP of 2,400 ng/L
he had a dry cough, digital clubbing, bibasal fine end-inspiratory crackles and a restrictive FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.84

hq_q.s:
A 67 year old woman with confirmed COPD attends her GP with persistent exertional breathlessness that limits her daily activities despite using an as-needed salbutamol inhaler. She stopped smoking 2 years ago, has never had asthma or atopy, and has had one non-severe exacerbation in the past year.
SpO2 95% breathing air. Blood eosinophil count is 0.12 x 10^9/L (0.04-0.40) and spirometry shows no bronchodilator reversibility.
o: Triple therapy with ICS, LABA and LAMA
hq_q.w: Under NICE COPD guidance, patients remaining breathless despite a short-acting bronchodilator who have no asthmatic features or steroid-responsive traits (no asthma/atopy, normal eosinophils) should step up to a combined LABA plus LAMA inhaler.
hq_q.f: Previous asthma diagnosis, raised eosinophils or variable FEV1 → LABA with an inhaled steroid.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in maintenance inhaler therapy?

tm.m: Dual beta-2 agonist and muscarinic antagonist therapy maximises airway smooth muscle relaxation without exposing non-eosinophilic COPD patients to inhaled steroid pneumonia risk.
tm.g: Symptomatic COPD without asthmatic features or eosinophilia -> combined LABA with LAMA inhaler
x: ICS with LABA is offered when COPD is accompanied by asthmatic features, atopy, higher blood eosinophil count or substantial diurnal FEV1/PEF variation.
Oral theophylline has a narrow therapeutic window and is reserved for patients who remain symptomatic after trials of short- and long-acting inhaled bronchodilators.
Leukotriene receptor antagonists are licensed for asthma and allergic rhinitis and have no efficacy in non-asthmatic COPD.
Triple therapy (ICS/LABA/LAMA) is reserved for patients on LABA/LAMA who have frequent (>=2 moderate or 1 hospitalised) exacerbations or severe day-to-day symptoms.
f: she had a history of adult-onset asthma, marked day-to-day peak flow variability and a blood eosinophil count of 0.45 x 10^9/L
she was unable to use inhaled therapy effectively or remained breathless despite optimal triple inhaled therapy
a patient with atopic asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis required an oral add-on controller after ICS/LABA
she was already taking a combined LABA/LAMA inhaler and had suffered two moderate exacerbations or one hospital admission this year

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man with severe COPD attends a stability review. He stopped smoking 14 months ago and remains breathless at rest despite triple inhaler therapy.
Pulse rate 84 bpm, SpO2 87% breathing air. Examination reveals bilateral pitting ankle oedema and a raised JVP.
Arterial blood gases breathing air on two occasions 3 weeks apart show PaO2 7.6 kPa.
o: Ambulatory oxygen for 2 hours during exercise
Continue medical therapy without home oxygen
Long-term oxygen therapy for 15 hours daily
Short-burst oxygen for 15 minutes after exertion
hq_q.w: Long-term oxygen therapy (>=15 hours daily) is indicated in stable non-smoking COPD patients when resting PaO2 is <7.3 kPa, or 7.3 to 8.0 kPa accompanied by peripheral oedema (cor pulmonale), polycythaemia or pulmonary hypertension.
hq_q.f: He still smokes → no LTOT, because of the fire risk.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate oxygen management?

tm.m: Continuous domiciliary oxygen (>=15 hours/day) reverses chronic hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, reducing right ventricular afterload and mortality in cor pulmonale.
tm.g: Stable non-smoker with COPD + PaO2 7.3-8.0 kPa + peripheral oedema -> long-term oxygen therapy
x: Portable ambulatory oxygen is used for mobile patients who desaturate on exertion or are already on LTOT, whereas resting cor pulmonale requires >=15 hours/day LTOT.
Withholding LTOT in a non-smoker with PaO2 7.6 kPa and cor pulmonale denies a proven mortality-reducing intervention.
Home NIV is indicated for persistent hypercapnic ventilatory failure after an acute acidotic exacerbation rather than chronic hypoxaemic cor pulmonale.
Intermittent short-burst oxygen has no survival or symptomatic benefit in COPD and is not recommended by NICE.
f: his resting PaO2 was 8.8 kPa with no oedema, but he desaturated to 84% on a 6-minute walk test with improved exercise capacity on oxygen
he was still actively smoking cigarettes (contraindicating home oxygen due to severe fire and facial burn risk) or had no oedema/polycythaemia at PaO2 7.6 kPa
he had persistent daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 7.5 kPa) and nocturnal hypoventilation following an admission for acute acidotic respiratory failure
high-flow 100% oxygen via a non-rebreather mask for 15 minutes was being prescribed for an acute cluster headache attack

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old woman who has never smoked presents with a 2-year history of a daily cough productive of large volumes of mucopurulent sputum and four lower respiratory tract infections in the past 12 months. She had severe pertussis requiring hospital admission at age 5.
Temperature 36.7°C, SpO2 96% breathing air. Examination reveals bilateral finger clubbing and coarse inspiratory  and expiratory crackles at both lung bases.
hq_q.w: High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the thorax is the gold standard for confirming bronchiectasis, showing bronchial internal diameter exceeding the adjacent pulmonary artery (signet-ring sign), lack of normal tapering, and peripheral airway visibility.
hq_q.f: A young adult with malabsorption, diabetes or infertility as well → sweat test or genetic test for cystic fibrosis.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is the gold standard to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

tm.m: Thin-section non-contrast HRCT directly visualises irreversible transmural bronchial wall destruction and abnormal airway-to-artery diameter ratios.
tm.g: Chronic daily purulent sputum and coarse basal crackles -> high-resolution CT thorax confirms bronchiectasis
x: Sweat chloride testing investigates cystic fibrosis as a specific underlying cause in younger patients, rather than anatomically confirming bronchiectasis.
A plain chest X-ray is frequently normal or shows only non-specific tramline/ring shadows and cannot reliably confirm or exclude bronchiectasis.
Spirometry quantifies obstructive functional impairment but cannot demonstrate structural bronchial dilatation.
Sputum culture identifies colonising pathogens (such as Haemophilus or Pseudomonas) to guide antibiotic choice but does not establish the structural diagnosis.
f: bronchiectasis had already been confirmed on HRCT in a 19 year old with steatorrhoea and upper-lobe disease requiring exclusion of cystic fibrosis
an initial first-line radiograph was being requested in primary care before specialist referral
she presented with episodic wheeze and nocturnal cough with a normal chest examination to evaluate suspected asthma
she already had HRCT-confirmed bronchiectasis and presented with an acute infective exacerbation requiring targeted antibiotic selection

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old man with severe bilateral bronchiectasis presents with hisfourth infective exacerbation this year, reporting increased breathlessness and copious green-blue purulent sputum.
Temperature 37.9°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 92% breathing air. Coarse crackles and wheezes are audible bilaterally.
Sputum culture grows oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli that produce a blue-green pigment and a sweet grape-like odour on agar.
hq_q.w: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an aerobic, non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod that produces pyocyanin and pyoverdine (blue-green pigment) and a characteristic grape-like odour. Chronic colonisation in bronchiectasis accelerates FEV1 decline; ciprofloxacin is the only oral antipseudomonal antibiotic.
hq_q.f: Gram-negative coccobacilli that need factor X and V → Haemophilus influenzae, the commonest organism overall.
hq_q.ql: Which pathogen has been isolated from his sputum?

c: blue-green pigment and a sweet grape-like odour
tm.m: Pseudomonas aeruginosa secretes phenazine pigments (pyocyanin) and 2-aminoacetophenone (grape odour) and forms alginate biofilms in structurally damaged bronchi.
tm.g: Oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod with blue-green pigment and grape odour -> Pseudomonas aeruginosa
x: Haemophilus influenzae is a small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacillus requiring X (haemin) and V (NAD) factors on chocolate agar without green pigment.
Klebsiella pneumoniae is an oxidase-negative, lactose-fermenting encapsulated Gram-negative rod forming mucoid pink colonies on MacConkey agar.
Moraxella catarrhalis is an aerobic Gram-negative diplococcus ('hockey-puck' colonies) rather than a pigment-producing Gram-negative bacillus.
Staphylococcus aureus is a catalase-positive, coagulase-positive Gram-positive coccus in clusters forming golden-yellow colonies.
f: sputum culture grew small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli on chocolate agar requiring both factor X (haemin) and factor V (NAD)
sputum from an alcohol-dependent patient with upper-lobe cavitation grew large mucoid lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rods on MacConkey agar
culture grew oxidase-positive, tributyrin-hydrolysing Gram-negative diplococci whose colonies slid intact across the agar plate
culture from a patient with post-influenza cavitating pneumonia grew catalase- and coagulase-positive Gram-positive cocci in clusters

hq_q.s:
A 37 year old woman with lifelong asthma presents with 12 months of worsening wheeze and a cough productive of firm brownish-green mucus casts.
SpO2 95% breathing air. Auscultation reveals widespread polyphonic wheeze.
Blood tests show eosinophils 1.8 x 10^9/L (0.04-0.40), total IgE 1,450 kU/L (<100) and positive Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE. CT thorax shows central bronchiectasis.
hq_q.w: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus in asthma or cystic fibrosis, causing brown mucus plugs, peripheral eosinophilia, elevated total and Aspergillus-specific IgE, and proximal central bronchiectasis.
hq_q.f: A fungal ball in an old TB cavity with an air crescent → aspergilloma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: IgE- and IgG-mediated hypersensitivity to noninvasive endobronchial Aspergillus hyphae triggers intense eosinophilic inflammation, mucoid impaction and proximal bronchial wall destruction.
tm.g: Asthma + brown mucus plugs + peripheral eosinophilia + high total/Aspergillus IgE + central bronchiectasis -> ABPA
x: Cystic fibrosis can be complicated by ABPA, but alone does not explain high Aspergillus-specific IgE and total IgE >1,000 kU/L in lifelong asthma without steatorrhoea.
Invasive aspergillosis occurs in profound neutropenia or haematological malignancy, presenting with high fever, pleuritic pain and the CT 'halo' sign.
EGPA (Churg-Strauss) causes asthma, eosinophilia, paranasal sinusitis, mononeuritis multiplex and p-ANCA vasculitis rather than Aspergillus IgE positivity and brown plugs.
An aspergilloma is a saprophytic fungal ball inside a pre-existing lung cavity (such as healed tuberculosis) presenting with haemoptysis and an air-crescent sign.
f: a young adult had upper-lobe bronchiectasis, pancreatic steatorrhoea, azoospermia and a sweat chloride of 82 mmol/L with normal Aspergillus serology
a profoundly neutropenic acute leukaemia patient developed persistent febrile neutropenia, haemoptysis and a nodule with a ground-glass halo on CT
an asthmatic with eosinophilia developed foot drop (mononeuritis multiplex), purpuric skin lesions, glomerulonephritis and positive anti-MPO ANCA
a patient with an old healed upper-lobe tuberculosis cavity presented with haemoptysis and CT showed a mobile intracavitary mass with a crescent of air

hq_q.s:
A previously healthy 34 year old woman presents to her GP with a 10-day history of a cough productive of small amounts of clear-to-yellowish sputum following a self-limiting coryzal illness. She has no haemoptysis, chest pain or breathlessness, and does not smoke.
Temperature 36.9°C, pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 98% breathing air. Chest percussion and auscultation are completely normal.
o: Immediate oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days
Immediate oral doxycycline 200 mg stat then 100 mg daily
Oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days
Reassurance and self-care advice without antibiotics
hq_q.w: Acute bronchitis in a systemically well adult with normal vital signs and a clear chest is usually viral and self-limiting over 3 to 4 weeks. NICE recommends reassurance, self-care advice and no routine antibiotics.
hq_q.f: Focal crackles, fever and a fast breathing rate → assess for pneumonia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Transient viral tracheobronchial epithelial inflammation causes cough receptor hypersensitivity for up to 3 weeks without alveolar bacterial consolidation.
tm.g: Uncomplicated acute cough <3 weeks in a systemically well adult with a clear chest -> reassurance and self-care advice
x: Amoxicillin is first line for low-severity community-acquired pneumonia, not uncomplicated viral bronchitis with normal observations.
Doxycycline is first line only when an antibiotic is clinically indicated for acute cough (such as systemic sepsis, severe comorbidity or CRP >100 mg/L).
Oral corticosteroids have no benefit in acute bronchitis in adults without underlying asthma or COPD.
A chest X-ray is not indicated in acute cough under 3 weeks when vital signs are normal and there are no focal chest signs or haemoptysis.
f: she had fever, pleuritic pain, bronchial breathing at the right base and radiographic consolidation confirming low-severity CAP
point-of-care CRP testing in a systemically unwell patient was 118 mg/L or the patient had severe frailty and heart failure
she had known asthma and presented with widespread expiratory wheeze and a peak flow drop to 55% of her personal best
her cough had persisted for over 3 weeks in a smoker aged over 40, or she had focal dullness and bronchial breathing

hq_q.s:
A 71 year old man with type 2 diabetes presents with an 8-day history of a productive cough and mild malaise.
Temperature 37.6°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 134/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 96% breathing air. Coarse crackles clear completely after coughing.
A point-of-care C-reactive protein (CRP) test in the surgery is 46 mg/L (<5).
o: Arrange a same-day chest X-ray before any decision
Immediate hospital admission for intravenous antibiotics
Issue a delayed (back-up) oral antibiotic prescription
Start an immediate 5-day course of oral antibiotics
Withhold antibiotics completely without a back-up script
hq_q.w: When point-of-care CRP guides prescribing in adults with acute lower respiratory tract symptoms without clinical pneumonia, NICE advises: <20 mg/L no antibiotic; 20 to 100 mg/L consider a delayed (back-up) antibiotic; >100 mg/L immediate antibiotic.
hq_q.f: CRP 130 mg/L → immediate antibiotic.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic prescribing strategy?

c: CRP) test in the surgery is 46 mg/L
tm.m: An intermediate CRP of 20-100 mg/L indicates moderate airway inflammation where most cases resolve spontaneously, so a back-up prescription safely limits unnecessary antibiotic use.
tm.g: Acute LRTI without focal consolidation and point-of-care CRP 20-100 mg/L -> delayed (back-up) antibiotic prescription
x: Transmitted sounds that clear with coughing and normal respiratory rate/oxygenation argue against lobar pneumonia, so immediate radiography is unnecessary.
He is haemodynamically stable, alert and normoxic (SpO2 96%), so hospital admission is not indicated.
Immediate antibiotics on CRP criteria require a reading above 100 mg/L (or focal pneumonic consolidation/systemic sepsis).
Complete withholding without a delayed script is the threshold for a point-of-care CRP below 20 mg/L in low-risk patients.
f: auscultation revealed persistent focal bronchial breathing and dullness to percussion that did not clear with coughing
he was confused with a respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute, blood pressure 86/54 mmHg and SpO2 88%
his point-of-care CRP concentration measured 125 mg/L or he had focal signs of community-acquired pneumonia
he was a healthy 35 year old with a clear chest and a point-of-care CRP concentration of 12 mg/L

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old man presents with a 10-day history of a productive cough and fevers. He has no past medical history and no drug allergies.
Temperature 38.0°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97% breathing air. There are transmitted rhonchi with no focal bronchial breathing.
Point-of-care CRP is 120 mg/L (<5), so an antibiotic is prescribed.
hq_q.w: Under NICE acute cough guidance (NG120), when an oral antibiotic is indicated for an adult without suspected pneumonia, oral doxycycline (200 mg on day 1, then 100 mg daily for 4 days) is first choice.
hq_q.f: She is pregnant or the patient is a child → amoxicillin; tetracyclines stain developing teeth and bone.
hq_q.ql: Which is the first-choice oral antibiotic recommended by NICE for acute cough?

tm.m: Doxycycline inhibits bacterial 30S ribosomal protein synthesis, covering both typical respiratory bacteria and intracellular atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila).
tm.g: Adult acute cough (acute bronchitis) requiring an antibiotic -> oral doxycycline first line
x: Ciprofloxacin has poor activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae, carries tendonitis/aortic aneurysm warnings, and is not used for routine acute bronchitis.
Co-amoxiclav is broad-spectrum, increases Clostridioides difficile risk, and is reserved for hospital-acquired or aspiration pneumonia rather than community acute cough.
Flucloxacillin is a narrow-spectrum antistaphylococcal penicillin for skin and soft-tissue infections and lacks cover against Haemophilus influenzae.
Nitrofurantoin concentrates only in the lower urinary tract and achieves negligible lung parenchymal or bronchial concentrations.
f: the patient had known structural bronchiectasis chronically colonised with Pseudomonas aeruginosa
the patient developed non-severe hospital-acquired pneumonia 4 days after abdominal surgery
the patient presented with spreading erythema, warmth and tenderness of the lower leg consistent with acute bacterial cellulitis
the patient presented with dysuria and frequency due to an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection with normal renal function

hq_q.s:
A 78 year old woman attends the Emergency Department with 3 days of productive cough and fever. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.
She is alert and orientated (AMTS 10/10). Temperature 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 104/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, SpO2 92% breathing air.
Serum urea is 9.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.8).
hq_q.w: CURB-65 awards 1 point each for Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate >=30/min, Blood pressure <90 systolic or <=60 mmHg diastolic, and age >=65. She scores 4 points (urea, respiratory rate, diastolic BP, age).
hq_q.f: Diastolic 64 mmHg → 3, still high severity.
hq_q.ql: What is this patient's CURB-65 pneumonia severity score?

tm.m: CURB-65 integrates age and four physiological/biochemical markers of organ hypoperfusion and respiratory compromise to stratify 30-day pneumonia mortality.
tm.g: Age >=65 + Urea >7 + RR >=30 + Diastolic BP <=60 with normal cognition -> CURB-65 score of 4
x: A score of 1 would count only her age (78 years), overlooking her raised urea (9.2 mmol/L), tachypnoea (32/min) and diastolic hypotension (58 mmHg).
A score of 2 misses two of her four positive markers; remember that a diastolic blood pressure of 60 mmHg or less scores 1 point even when systolic BP is >90 mmHg.
A score of 3 typically occurs when a candidate forgets that diastolic BP <=60 mmHg (here 58 mmHg) scores a point despite the systolic BP being 104 mmHg.
A maximum score of 5 requires all five criteria including new-onset confusion (AMTS <=8), whereas she is fully alert and orientated (AMTS 10/10).
f: her urea was 5.4 mmol/L, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min and blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, leaving age 78 as her only criterion
her blood pressure was 124/72 mmHg and respiratory rate was 24 breaths/min, so she scored only for age 78 and urea 9.2 mmol/L
her blood pressure was 124/72 mmHg while her age (78), urea (9.2 mmol/L) and respiratory rate (32/min) remained unchanged
she also had new-onset disorientation in time and place with an abbreviated mental test score of 6/10

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old man presents with 3 days of fever, pleuritic chest pain and rusty sputum. Chest X-ray confirms left lower lobe consolidation. He has a history of immediate anaphylaxis with laryngeal oedema following oral amoxicillin.
Temperature 38.1°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 96% breathing air. His CURB-65 score is 0.
hq_q.w: For low-severity community-acquired pneumonia (CURB-65 0 or 1), oral amoxicillin is first line, but in penicillin allergy NICE recommends oral doxycycline or clarithromycin for 5 days. Beta-lactams are avoided after penicillin anaphylaxis.
hq_q.f: No allergy → amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate empirical oral antibiotic?

c: immediate anaphylaxis with laryngeal oedema following oral amoxicillin
tm.m: Doxycycline provides non-beta-lactam bactericidal/bacteriostatic cover against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and atypical pathogens without cross-reacting with anti-penicillin IgE.
tm.g: Low-severity CAP (CURB-65 0-1) + penicillin anaphylaxis -> oral doxycycline (or clarithromycin)
x: Amoxicillin is a penicillin and is strictly contraindicated in a patient with a history of immediate penicillin anaphylaxis.
First-generation cephalosporins share beta-lactam side-chain similarity with aminopenicillins and must be avoided in patients with immediate penicillin anaphylaxis.
Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin (a penicillin) and will trigger life-threatening IgE-mediated anaphylaxis in this patient.
Flucloxacillin is an isoxazolyl penicillin, so it is strictly contraindicated in penicillin anaphylaxis and lacks cover for routine CAP.
f: he had no history of drug allergy and required standard first-line empirical therapy for low-severity community-acquired pneumonia
a pregnant woman without beta-lactam allergy required empirical treatment for an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection
he had no penicillin allergy and presented with high-severity pneumonia (CURB-65 score 3) requiring co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin
he had no penicillin allergy and presented with acute weeping crusted impetigo or lower-limb erysipelas

hq_q.s:
A 61 year old man presents 5 days after returning from a hotel holiday in Spain with high fevers, a dry cough, watery diarrhoea and acute confusion.
Temperature 39.6°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 92% breathing air. Coarse crackles are audible at the right base, and chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.
hq_q.w: Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumophila) is acquired by inhaling aerosolised water droplets from colonised hotel plumbing, spa pools or cooling towers. It causes severe pneumonia with relative bradycardia, neurological features (confusion), gastrointestinal upset (diarrhoea), hyponatraemia (SIADH) and deranged liver transaminases.
hq_q.f: Young adult with erythema multiforme and cold agglutinins → Mycoplasma.
hq_q.ql: Which causative organism is most likely responsible?
hq_q.post: Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.

tm.m: Inhaled Legionella pneumophila multiplies inside alveolar macrophages, triggering severe systemic cytokine release, SIADH-driven hyponatraemia and hepatic transaminitis.
tm.g: Pneumonia after hotel spa/water exposure + diarrhoea + confusion + hyponatraemia + raised ALT -> Legionella pneumophila
x: Psittacosis follows exposure to infected psittacine birds (parrots, cockatiels) and causes dry cough, splenomegaly and headache rather than hotel water outbreaks.
Q fever follows inhalation of aerosols from birthing sheep, goats or cattle (abattoir/farm workers) rather than hotel spa water systems.
Mycoplasma affects younger cohorts in close quarters with headache, bullous myringitis, erythema multiforme and cold agglutinin haemolysis.
Pneumococcal pneumonia typically causes acute lobar consolidation with rust-coloured sputum and herpes labialis without watery diarrhoea and profound hyponatraemia.
f: he had recently bought a sick pet parrot and developed dry cough, high fever, severe headache and splenomegaly
a livestock farmer assisted with sheep lambing 2 weeks ago and developed fever, retro-orbital headache, hepatitis and culture-negative endocarditis
a 19 year old university student developed dry cough, targetoid skin lesions on the palms and autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
he presented with sudden-onset rigors, rust-coloured sputum, cold sores on the lip and Gram-positive diplococci in sputum

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man who moved to the UK from a high-incidence country 3 years ago presents with 2 months of drenching night sweats, 6 kg weight loss and blood-streaked sputum.
Temperature 37.8°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, SpO2 96% breathing air. Crackles are audible at the right apex.
Chest X-ray shows a 3 cm cavity in the right upper lobe.
o: High-resolution CT scan of the thorax
Sputum samples for AFB smear, culture and NAAT
hq_q.w: When active pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected, NICE recommends sending three sputum samples (including an early-morning sample) for acid-fast bacilli microscopy, mycobacterial culture and rapid nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT).
hq_q.f: A well household contact with no symptoms → IGRA or Mantoux to screen for latent TB.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

c: drenching night sweats, 6 kg weight loss
cavity in the right upper lobe
tm.m: Cavitating apical lesions erode into bronchi and discharge high numbers of Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacilli, allowing direct microbiological identification and rpoB rifampicin-resistance detection.
tm.g: Suspected active pulmonary TB with productive cough and apical cavity -> three sputum samples for AFB smear, culture and NAAT
x: IGRA measures T-cell memory to tuberculosis antigens and cannot distinguish latent infection from active cavitating pulmonary tuberculosis.
Bronchoscopy generates infectious aerosols and is reserved for patients who cannot expectorate sputum spontaneously or after hypertonic saline induction.
Chest X-ray already shows a classic upper-lobe cavity; microbiological confirmation and drug-susceptibility testing on sputum are the urgent priorities.
The Mantoux skin test is used for latent TB screening and cannot differentiate latent infection, prior BCG vaccination and active pulmonary disease.
f: an asymptomatic household contact with a completely normal chest X-ray was being screened for latent tuberculosis
the patient had a dry cough and could not produce sputum even after nebulised hypertonic saline induction
sputum smears were repeatedly negative and cross-sectional imaging was needed to evaluate an indeterminate pulmonary mass
a healthy 4 year old child who was a close contact of pulmonary tuberculosis required initial screening for latent infection

hq_q.s:
A 46 year old woman attends clinic 6 weeks after starting rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for pulmonary tuberculosis. She complains of burning numbness and pins and needles in both feet. She drinks heavily and forgot to take the vitamin tablet prescribed with her therapy.
Examination shows reduced pinprick and vibration sensation in both feet and absent ankle jerks.
hq_q.w: Isoniazid causes a symmetrical distal sensory peripheral neuropathy by depleting active vitamin B6 (pyridoxal 5'-phosphate). Prophylactic oral pyridoxine is co-prescribed in patients with alcohol dependence, malnutrition, HIV, diabetes or pregnancy.
hq_q.f: Blurred vision and red-green colour loss → ethambutol, optic neuritis.
hq_q.ql: Which anti-tuberculosis drug is responsible for this adverse effect?

c: burning numbness and pins and needles in both feet
forgot to take the vitamin tablet
tm.m: Isoniazid depletes active vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate), a required cofactor for glutamic acid decarboxylase and sphingomyelin synthesis in peripheral axons.
tm.g: Stocking peripheral neuropathy on TB therapy without pyridoxine -> isoniazid
x: Ethambutol causes dose-related retrobulbar optic neuritis presenting with reduced visual acuity and loss of red-green colour vision, not stocking neuropathy.
Moxifloxacin is a second-line fluoroquinolone (not part of standard RIPE therapy) associated with QT prolongation and tendonitis.
Pyrazinamide inhibits renal tubular urate secretion, causing hyperuricaemia, arthralgia, acute gout and hepatotoxicity rather than peripheral neuropathy.
Rifampicin causes orange-red discolouration of urine and tears, potent hepatic P450 enzyme induction and hepatitis, not pyridoxine-deficiency neuropathy.
f: she complained of blurred central vision and difficulty distinguishing red from green traffic lights on Ishihara testing
a patient on a multidrug-resistant TB regimen developed Achilles tendon pain and QTc prolongation to 510 ms on ECG
she developed an acutely painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint with a serum urate concentration of 620 µmol/L
she noticed harmless orange-red discolouration of her urine and contact lenses and experienced breakthrough bleeding on the oral contraceptive pill

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman is newly diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis and is due to commence standard 6-month treatment with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol today. She currently takes the combined oral contraceptive pill (ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel) and wishes to avoid pregnancy during her treatment.
Pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 114/70 mmHg. Her urinary pregnancy test today is negative.
o: Continue standard combined oral contraceptive pill
hq_q.w: Rifampicin is a potent hepatic CYP450 enzyme inducer that accelerates the breakdown of oral, patch, ring and implant hormonal contraceptives. FSRH/BNF advise switching to a copper IUD, levonorgestrel-IUS or depot medroxyprogesterone injection.
hq_q.f: Isoniazid alone for latent TB → no interaction with hormonal contraception.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate contraceptive method to recommend during her treatment?

tm.m: Rifampicin activates nuclear pregnane X receptors, markedly upregulating hepatic CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein and clearing circulating steroid hormones.
tm.g: Contraception while taking rifampicin -> copper IUD (or LNG-IUS / depot medroxyprogesterone)
x: Systemic oestrogen and progestogen absorbed from a transdermal patch still undergo rapid hepatic CYP3A4 breakdown induced by rifampicin.
Rifampicin accelerates first-pass and systemic clearance of ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel, causing high rates of contraceptive failure.
Oral progestogen-only pills rely on systemic hormone levels that are rapidly metabolised by rifampicin-induced hepatic enzymes.
Subdermal etonogestrel concentrations are significantly reduced by potent CYP3A4 inducers like rifampicin, leading to unintended pregnancy.
f: she was taking non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics such as amoxicillin or doxycycline and preferred a weekly transdermal patch
she was starting a 6-month course of isoniazid monotherapy for latent tuberculosis without rifampicin or rifapentine
she was not taking enzyme-inducing drugs but had migraine with aura contraindicating oestrogen-containing contraception
she was taking standard non-interacting antihypertensives and wanted a 3-year subdermal long-acting reversible contraceptive

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history presents with 2 months of cough, 6 kg weight loss and worsening confusion.
BP 128/78 mmHg. He is clinically euvolaemic with no oedema.
Blood tests show sodium 121 mmol/L (135-146) and serum osmolality 250 mOsm/kg. Urine osmolality is 510 mOsm/kg and urine sodium is 52 mmol/L. CT thorax shows a central hilar mass.
hq_q.w: Small cell lung carcinoma is a central neuroendocrine tumour in heavy smokers that frequently secretes ectopic ADH (causing euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with raised urinary sodium, SIADH) or ectopic ACTH.
hq_q.f: Calcium 3.1 mmol/L with a low PTH → squamous cell, which makes PTH-related peptide.
hq_q.ql: Which histological subtype of thoracic malignancy is most likely?

tm.m: Neuroendocrine Kulchitsky-type tumour cells synthesise and autonomously secrete arginine vasopressin (ADH), causing water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia.
tm.g: Central hilar mass in a heavy smoker + euvolaemic hyponatraemia (SIADH) -> small cell lung carcinoma
x: Bronchial carcinoid is a slow-growing neuroendocrine tumour in younger patients causing endobronchial obstruction, haemoptysis or carcinoid syndrome rather than bulky central SCLC with SIADH.
Adenocarcinoma typically presents as a peripheral lung mass and is the commonest lung cancer in non-smokers, rarely causing paraneoplastic SIADH.
Mesothelioma encases the pleura with a unilateral bloody effusion and chest wall pain decades after asbestos exposure rather than forming a central hilar mass with SIADH.
Squamous cell carcinoma forms a central cavitating mass in smokers but characteristically causes hypercalcaemia via PTH-related peptide (PTHrP) rather than SIADH.
f: a 32 year old non-smoker presented with recurrent right middle lobe pneumonia, episodic facial flushing and a smooth vascular endobronchial mass
a 50 year old never-smoker presented with a peripheral right upper lobe spiculated nodule harbouring an EGFR mutation
a 74 year old retired pipe lagger presented with dull chest pain, unilateral pleural effusion and nodular pleural rind encasing the lung
he presented with a central cavitating lung mass, thirst, constipation, an adjusted calcium of 3.25 mmol/L and suppressed PTH

hq_q.s:
A 61 year old man who smokes has had pain in his left shoulder going down the inner arm for 3 months. He has lost 5 kg.
There is wasting of the small muscles of the left hand. There is a left ptosis and a small left pupil, and the left side of his face does not sweat.
hq_q.w: Horner's syndrome with shoulder pain, T1 wasting and weight loss in a smoker suggests an apical lung tumour (Pancoast) invading the sympathetic chain and brachial plexus. An urgent chest X-ray comes first; CT chest and a suspected cancer referral follow.
hq_q.f: Painful Horner's with neck pain after neck manipulation → carotid dissection; CT or MR angiography.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most appropriate first?

tm.m: A tumour at the lung apex invades the T1 root and the sympathetic chain
tm.g: Smoker with Horner's and T1 wasting: chest X-ray for a Pancoast tumour
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Carotid Doppler (Carotid dissection causes a painful Horner's after neck strain, not weight loss and hand wasting)
the presentation instead showed features specific to CT head (The lesion is at the lung apex, not in the brain)
the presentation instead showed features specific to MRI cervical spine (Cervical root disease causes pain and weakness but not Horner's syndrome with weight loss)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Nerve conduction studies (Nerve studies show plexus damage but not the cause)
x: Carotid dissection causes a painful Horner's after neck strain, not weight loss and hand wasting.
The lesion is at the lung apex, not in the brain.
Cervical root disease causes pain and weakness but not Horner's syndrome with weight loss.
Nerve studies show plexus damage but not the cause.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old ex-smoker (30 pack-year history) presents to his GP after coughing up teaspoonful amounts of fresh red blood twice over the past 3 weeks. He has no fever, chest pain or breathlessness.
Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, SpO2 98% breathing air. Chest examination, full blood count and a plain chest X-ray are all completely normal.
o: Arrange a repeat plain chest X-ray in 6 weeks
Empirical oral amoxicillin and clinical review in 2 weeks
Reassure and discharge as the chest X-ray is normal
Request a routine outpatient CT thorax in 6 months
hq_q.w: Under NICE suspected cancer guidelines (NG12), any adult aged 40 or over with unexplained haemoptysis requires an urgent 2-week-wait suspected lung cancer referral for CT thorax and bronchoscopy, even when the chest X-ray is normal.
hq_q.f: A 32-year-old non-smoker coughing blood during a chest infection → treat the infection and review.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next management step?

c: coughing up teaspoonful amounts of fresh red blood
plain chest X-ray are all completely normal
tm.m: Up to 10-20% of endobronchial lung carcinomas (especially central hilar tumours) are invisible on a plain posteroanterior chest radiograph despite causing mucosal bleeding.
tm.g: Unexplained haemoptysis in an adult aged 40 or over -> urgent 2-week-wait suspected cancer referral
x: A 6-week repeat chest X-ray is used after treated pneumonia, whereas unexplained haemoptysis at age >=40 mandates immediate 2-week-wait referral.
He has no fever, purulent sputum or infective signs, so empirical antibiotics delay urgent investigation for an endobronchial malignancy.
A normal plain chest radiograph does not exclude central endobronchial carcinoma in a 52 year old ex-smoker with recurrent haemoptysis.
A 6-month delay for CT thorax is unsafe when NICE NG12 mandates assessment within 2 weeks on a suspected lung cancer pathway.
f: he had just completed treatment for radiologically confirmed community-acquired pneumonia with full resolution of infective symptoms
a 24 year old non-smoker had a single streak of blood in purulent sputum during an acute febrile lower respiratory tract infection
a 22 year old never-smoker had a resolved viral cough of 2 weeks' duration with no haemoptysis or red flag features
an incidental 5 mm smooth subsolid pulmonary nodule was being followed up according to BTS nodule surveillance guidelines

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old retired naval dockyard electrician undergoes pre-operative assessment before hernia surgery. He worked alongside pipe laggers for 25 years. He has no cough, chest pain, weight loss or exertional breathlessness, and never smoked.
SpO2 98% breathing air. Chest auscultation is clear.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral calcified plaques along the parietal pleura and diaphragms. Spirometry is normal.
hq_q.w: Benign pleural plaques are circumscribed areas of hyaline fibrosis and calcification on the parietal and diaphragmatic pleura after asbestos exposure. They are asymptomatic, preserve lung function, are not premalignant and require reassurance only.
hq_q.f: Chest pain, weight loss and a unilateral bloody effusion → mesothelioma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: no cough, chest pain, weight loss or exertional breathlessness
calcified plaques along the parietal pleura
