tm.m: Inhaled asbestos fibres reach the parietal pleura via subpleural lymphatics, inducing acellular collagenous plaques that calcify over decades without invading lung parenchyma.
tm.g: Asymptomatic calcified parietal/diaphragmatic pleural lesions with normal spirometry after asbestos exposure -> benign pleural plaques
x: Asbestosis is parenchymal interstitial lung fibrosis causing exertional dyspnoea, clubbing, basal velcro crackles and restrictive spirometry.
Diffuse pleural thickening affects the visceral pleura, obliterates the costophrenic angles and causes restrictive breathlessness and reduced FVC.
Mesothelioma causes progressive chest wall pain, weight loss, a unilateral bloody pleural effusion and nodular pleural rind encasing the lung.
Sarcoidosis causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and perilymphatic upper/mid-zone parenchymal infiltrates rather than calcified diaphragmatic plaques.
f: he had progressive breathlessness, digital clubbing, bibasal end-inspiratory crackles and subpleural lower-zone honeycombing on HRCT
he had exertional dyspnoea, restrictive spirometry and continuous smooth pleural thickening blunting the costophrenic angle
he had dull unilateral chest wall pain, 8 kg weight loss and a large pleural effusion with nodular mediastinal pleural thickening
a 32 year old presented with erythema nodosum, anterior uveitis, hypercalcaemia and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old stonemason presents with a 2-year history of progressive exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. He has cut sandstone and granite for 35 years and never smoked.
Respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 95% breathing air. Fine crackles are audible over both upper zones.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral upper-zone fibrotic nodules and 'eggshell' calcification of the hilar lymph nodes.
hq_q.w: Chronic silicosis results from prolonged inhalation of crystalline silica dust (stone cutting, sandblasting, quarrying, foundry work). It causes bilateral upper-zone nodular fibrosis and characteristic peripheral 'eggshell' calcification of hilar lymph nodes, and markedly increases susceptibility to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
hq_q.f: Lower zone fibrosis with clubbing in a pipe lagger → asbestosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: 'eggshell' calcification of the hilar lymph nodes
tm.m: Ingested crystalline quartz particles lyse alveolar macrophage phagolysosomes, triggering fibrogenic cytokine release, concentrically laminated hyalinised upper-zone nodules and rim calcification of hilar nodes.
tm.g: Stonemason/quarry worker + upper-zone nodules + eggshell hilar calcification -> silicosis
x: Asbestosis follows insulation or shipyard exposure and causes lower-zone reticular fibrosis, pleural plaques and finger clubbing rather than upper-zone nodules and eggshell hilar nodes.
Chronic berylliosis occurs in aerospace, nuclear and electronics workers, causing non-caseating granulomas rather than eggshell calcification in a stonemason.
Coal worker's pneumoconiosis occurs in underground coal miners with black sputum and coal macules, rarely causing classic eggshell hilar calcification.
Sarcoidosis is an idiopathic multisystem granulomatous disease presenting with uveitis, skin lesions and hypercalcaemia rather than occupational silica exposure in a stonemason.
f: a retired pipe lagger presented with bibasal velcro crackles, digital clubbing and lower-lobe subpleural fibrosis
an aerospace alloy machinist developed dyspnoea, hilar lymphadenopathy and a positive beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test
a retired underground coal miner presented with melanoptysis (black sputum) and fine upper-zone coal macules without eggshell hilar nodes
a 30 year old office worker presented with erythema nodosum, anterior uveitis, raised serum ACE and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy

hq_q.s: A 79 year old retired heating engineer who installed asbestos-lined industrial boilers for 30 years was diagnosed with biopsy-proven malignant pleural mesothelioma 14 months ago. He has died peacefully at home under specialist palliative care, as anticipated. His GP reviewed him at home 5 days ago and is now contacted by the family regarding the medical certificate of cause of death.
o: Advise the family to register the death without a medical certificate
Complete cremation forms and release the body to the funeral director
Issue the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death immediately
Refer the death to the coroner before issuing a certificate
Request family consent for a hospital post-mortem examination
hq_q.w: Under the Notification of Deaths Regulations, any death caused by an occupational or industrial disease (such as malignant mesothelioma, asbestosis or pneumoconiosis) must be referred to the coroner, regardless of whether death was expected.
hq_q.f: Expected death from lung cancer in a lifelong smoker with no work exposure → medical examiner review and an MCCD.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate statutory action regarding death certification?

tm.m: Deaths resulting from industrial exposure (asbestos) are classified in law as unnatural deaths requiring coronial investigation and recording for industrial injuries compensation.
tm.g: Death from an industrial/occupational disease (mesothelioma) -> mandatory referral to the coroner
x: A death cannot be legally registered in the UK without either a Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (agreed with the Medical Examiner) or Coroner's authorisation.
Cremation cannot proceed until the coroner has investigated an industrial disease death and issued the appropriate coronial cremation certificate.
Even when the patient was seen within 28 days and the death was expected, industrial disease is a mandatory statutory trigger for coroner referral.
A hospital (consented) post-mortem is unlawful when a death is reportable to the coroner; any post-mortem is ordered under the coroner's statutory authority.
f: the coroner had already completed an inquest and issued Form 99 directly to the registrar, allowing the family to attend registration
the patient died of non-industrial metastatic prostate cancer, the Medical Examiner had scrutinised the MCCD, and no coronial criteria applied
the patient died expectedly at home from non-occupational colon cancer after being seen by the GP 5 days ago, following Medical Examiner scrutiny
the coroner had formally declined jurisdiction on a natural non-industrial death, and clinicians wished to clarify an academic question with family consent

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old retired accountant presents with 18 months of progressive exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. He has never kept birds, has no occupational dust exposure and takes no regular medications.
SpO2 93% breathing air. Examination reveals digital clubbing and fine end-inspiratory ('velcro') crackles at both lung bases.
Spirometry shows a restrictive ventilatory defect with a reduced transfer factor (TLCO).
hq_q.w: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis affects older adults, presenting with progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, digital clubbing, bibasal end-inspiratory velcro crackles, restrictive spirometry with low TLCO, and basal subpleural honeycombing on HRCT.
hq_q.f: Fever and breathlessness 4 to 6 hours after handling mouldy hay → extrinsic allergic alveolitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Aberrant alveolar epithelial repair and myofibroblast proliferation deposit dense collagen in the lower-zone interstitium without an identifiable exogenous antigen or drug trigger.
tm.g: Older adult + dry cough + clubbing + bibasal velcro crackles + restriction with no drug/antigen exposure -> idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
x: Bronchiectasis causes a chronic cough productive of copious purulent sputum, coarse leathery crackles and obstructive/mixed spirometry rather than dry cough and velcro crackles.
COPD causes hyperinflation, wheeze and an obstructive FEV1/FVC ratio (<0.70) without digital clubbing or bibasal velcro crackles.
Extrinsic allergic alveolitis follows bird or mould antigen exposure, shows upper/mid-zone ground-glass/centrilobular nodules and rarely causes finger clubbing.
Sarcoidosis typically presents in younger adults with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, upper/mid-zone perilymphatic nodules, uveitis and erythema nodosum without clubbing.
f: he coughed up large volumes of purulent green sputum every morning and HRCT showed dilated non-tapering bronchi
he had a 45 pack-year smoking history, quiet breath sounds, scattered wheeze, no clubbing and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.56
he kept racing pigeons and developed fevers and breathlessness 6 hours after loft cleaning with positive avian precipitins
a 32 year old presented with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, anterior uveitis, erythema nodosum and hypercalcaemia

hq_q.s:
A 76 year old woman presents with 3 months of progressive exertional breathlessness and a persistent dry cough. For 2 years she has taken a nightly oral prophylactic medication for recurrent urinary tract infections.
Respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 93% breathing air. Fine end-inspiratory crackles are audible at both bases. HRCT thorax shows interstitial pulmonary fibrosis, and blood tests show ALT 118 IU/L (10-45).
hq_q.w: Long-term prophylactic oral nitrofurantoin can cause chronic interstitial pulmonary fibrosis and autoimmune-like hepatitis (raised ALT). MHRA/BNF guidance requires monitoring lung and liver function during long-term therapy and stopping immediately if toxicity occurs.
hq_q.f: A dry tickly cough with a clear chest on ramipril → ACE inhibitor cough, switch to an ARB.
hq_q.ql: Which regular medication is the most likely cause of her pulmonary and hepatic findings?

tm.m: Nitrofurantoin redox cycling generates reactive oxygen species and immune-mediated alveolitis/fibrosis alongside hepatocyte injury during prolonged therapy.
tm.g: Pulmonary fibrosis + raised ALT on long-term nightly UTI prophylaxis -> oral nitrofurantoin
x: Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker that causes ankle oedema, flushing and gingival hyperplasia, not pulmonary fibrosis or UTI prophylaxis.
Bisoprolol is a cardioselective beta-blocker that can trigger bronchospasm in asthma but does not cause interstitial lung fibrosis or prevent UTIs.
Ramipril inhibits ACE and bradykinin breakdown, causing a common dry tickly cough with a normal chest CT and normal liver enzymes rather than pulmonary fibrosis.
Trimethoprim is used for UTI prophylaxis and causes folate-antagonist myelosuppression and hyperkalaemia (via ENaC blockade), not chronic pulmonary fibrosis.
f: she developed bilateral pitting ankle oedema and facial flushing after starting a first-line antihypertensive
an asthmatic patient developed acute expiratory wheeze and bradycardia (pulse 46 bpm) after starting a medication for angina
she developed a persistent dry tickly cough with a completely normal chest X-ray, normal CT thorax and normal ALT after starting an antihypertensive
she developed hyperkalaemia (potassium 5.9 mmol/L) and macrocytic pancytopenia on UTI prophylaxis with normal lung fields

hq_q.s:
A 27 year old woman presents with 2 weeks of painful red lumps on both shins, bilateral ankle swelling and a mild dry cough.
Temperature 37.6°C, SpO2 99% breathing air. Examination confirms tender pretibial erythema nodosum and symmetrical ankle synovitis. Slit-lamp eye examination is normal.
Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Adjusted serum calcium is 2.38 mmol/L (2.20-2.60).
o: Endobronchial ultrasound and transbronchial node biopsy
Oral NSAIDs and outpatient clinical review
Weekly oral methotrexate with folic acid cover
hq_q.w: Erythema nodosum, bilateral ankle arthritis and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy form Lofgren syndrome, an acute self-limiting presentation of sarcoidosis. When calcium, eyes and heart are normal, management is supportive with oral NSAIDs and clinical review.
hq_q.f: Hypercalcaemia, eye, heart or nerve involvement, or falling lung function → oral steroids.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

tm.m: Lofgren syndrome is an acute self-limiting Th1 immune reaction (strongly linked to HLA-DRB1*03) that resolves spontaneously without progressive parenchymal fibrosis.
tm.g: Classic Lofgren triad (erythema nodosum + bilateral ankle arthritis + BHL) with normal calcium and no organ threat -> NSAIDs and clinical review
x: Classic Lofgren syndrome has such high clinical specificity and spontaneous resolution rate that invasive mediastinal biopsy is unnecessary unless atypical features arise.
Long-term systemic corticosteroids are reserved for progressive parenchymal lung disease, hypercalcaemia, posterior uveitis, cardiac or neurological sarcoidosis.
Symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with acute ankle periarthritis and erythema nodosum in a low-risk patient is Lofgren syndrome, not active tuberculosis.
Methotrexate is a second-line steroid-sparing immunosuppressant for chronic refractory extrapulmonary or progressive pulmonary sarcoidosis.
f: mediastinal lymphadenopathy was asymmetrical with B symptoms and no erythema nodosum, requiring exclusion of lymphoma
she had hypercalcaemia (calcium 2.95 mmol/L), sight-threatening posterior uveitis, cardiac arrhythmias or progressive pulmonary infiltration
sputum nucleic acid amplification and Ziehl-Neelsen smear confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis from an upper-lobe cavity
she had chronic progressive stage III pulmonary sarcoidosis that relapsed repeatedly upon tapering oral prednisolone

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man is admitted to the coronary care unit with central chest pain at rest and dynamic lateral ST-segment depression. Troponin T rises from 42 ng/L to 310 ng/L (<14). Diagnostic angiography shows diffuse distal vessel disease suitable for medical management without percutaneous coronary intervention. He has received aspirin 300 mg, has no bleeding history and takes no anticoagulants.
hq_q.w: For acute coronary syndromes managed medically without percutaneous coronary intervention, NICE recommends dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus ticagrelor for 12 months unless bleeding risk is high. Prasugrel is only used when proceeding to PCI.
hq_q.f: High bleeding risk → aspirin plus clopidogrel.
hq_q.ql: Which second antiplatelet drug is most appropriate?

c: medical management without percutaneous coronary intervention
tm.m: Reversible P2Y12 receptor blockade with ticagrelor alongside aspirin reduces recurrent ischaemic events after medically managed NSTEMI.
tm.g: Medically managed ACS with low bleeding risk -> add ticagrelor to aspirin
x: Reserved for patients with a high bleeding risk or those requiring concurrent oral anticoagulation.
Used for secondary prevention after ischaemic stroke when clopidogrel and aspirin are contraindicated, not acute coronary syndrome.
Only recommended by NICE for acute coronary syndrome when the patient is proceeding directly to percutaneous coronary intervention.
An oral vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant rather than an antiplatelet agent, and not indicated for uncomplicated NSTEMI in sinus rhythm.
f: the patient had a high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or was taking an oral anticoagulant
secondary prevention was needed after an ischaemic stroke in a patient intolerant of aspirin and clopidogrel
coronary angiography showed a culprit lesion proceeding immediately to percutaneous coronary intervention
the patient required anticoagulation for a mechanical mitral valve or valvular atrial fibrillation

hq_q.s: A 58 year old woman attends cardiology follow-up 2 weeks after an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with primary percutaneous coronary intervention and a drug-eluting stent to the left anterior descending artery. She takes aspirin 75 mg daily and ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, has no history of gastrointestinal bleeding or anaemia, and has normal renal function.
hq_q.w: Following acute coronary syndrome treated with percutaneous coronary intervention and drug-eluting stent insertion, NICE recommends continuing dual antiplatelet therapy for 12 months in patients without excessive bleeding risk, after which lifelong aspirin monotherapy is continued.
hq_q.f: The question asks about aspirin → lifelong.
hq_q.ql: For how long should the second antiplatelet drug usually be continued?

tm.m: Twelve months of dual antiplatelet therapy prevents stent thrombosis while the drug-eluting stent struts endothelialise.
tm.g: Uncomplicated drug-eluting stent after ACS -> continue second antiplatelet for 12 months
x: Stopping the P2Y12 inhibitor at 1 month carries a high risk of subacute stent thrombosis in low-bleeding-risk patients.
Three months is shortened dual antiplatelet duration reserved for patients with very high bleeding risk.
Six months is used after elective stable angina stenting or high bleeding risk, whereas ACS requires 12 months.
Aspirin continues lifelong after acute coronary syndrome, whereas the second antiplatelet is stopped at 12 months.
f: triple antithrombotic therapy was being stepped down early due to life-threatening bleeding risk
a shortened dual antiplatelet course was required because of recurrent major gastrointestinal bleeding
the stent had been placed electively for stable angina in a patient with elevated bleeding risk
the question asked how long low-dose aspirin monotherapy should be continued after ACS

hq_q.s: A 66 year old man attends general practice with 3 weeks of retrosternal burning pain worse on lying flat after meals. Two months ago he underwent percutaneous coronary intervention with a drug-eluting stent and takes aspirin 75 mg daily and clopidogrel 75 mg daily. Pulse rate is 68 bpm, BP 126/76 mmHg, and haemoglobin is 144 g/L (130-175).
hq_q.w: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by hepatic CYP2C19. Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19 and reduce the antiplatelet efficacy of clopidogrel, risking stent thrombosis, so lansoprazole or pantoprazole are preferred when gastroprotection is required.
hq_q.f: He takes aspirin alone → any PPI is fine.
hq_q.ql: Which proton pump inhibitor is the most appropriate choice?

c: takes aspirin 75 mg daily and clopidogrel
tm.m: Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19 conversion of clopidogrel to its active thiol metabolite; lansoprazole avoids this clinically significant interaction.
tm.g: PPI needed in a patient taking clopidogrel -> choose lansoprazole
x: A histamine H2-receptor antagonist that strongly inhibits multiple hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes including CYP2C19, impairing clopidogrel activation.
Inhibits hepatic CYP2C19 and reduces conversion of clopidogrel into its active antiplatelet metabolite.
Blocks CYP2C19-mediated bioactivation of clopidogrel and is specifically advised against by the MHRA during clopidogrel therapy.
Combining a PPI with cimetidine adds CYP2C19 inhibition that impairs clopidogrel bioactivation.
f: identifying a classic H2-receptor antagonist that inhibits cytochrome P450 enzymes and causes gynaecomastia
high-dose intravenous acid suppression was needed after endoscopic haemostasis in a patient not on clopidogrel
gastroprotection was required for a patient taking low-dose aspirin monotherapy without clopidogrel
dual acid suppression was never indicated and would block clopidogrel metabolism via cimetidine

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man with exertional angina is reviewed in cardiology clinic after starting sublingual glyceryl trinitrate spray alongside bisoprolol 5 mg daily, aspirin 75 mg daily and atorvastatin 80 mg daily. His pulse rate is 62 bpm and BP is 128/78 mmHg. He is counselled on managing acute chest pain episodes at home.
o: After taking a third dose at 15 minutes
Only if sweating or nausea develops
Straight after the first spray dose
hq_q.w: BNF and NICE guidance for sublingual glyceryl trinitrate in angina advises taking one dose at symptom onset, repeating a second dose after 5 minutes if pain persists, and calling 999 if pain remains 5 minutes after the second dose.
hq_q.f: Pain settles within 2 minutes of the first dose → rest and carry on.
hq_q.ql: When should he dial 999 for an emergency ambulance if chest pain persists?

c: managing acute chest pain episodes at home
tm.m: Chest pain refractory to two sublingual GTN doses spaced 5 minutes apart indicates likely acute coronary syndrome requiring urgent hospital assessment.
tm.g: Unrelieved angina pain -> repeat GTN at 5 minutes, call 999 if pain persists 5 minutes after the second dose
x: Waiting 30 minutes with ongoing ischaemic chest pain delays emergency reperfusion in acute myocardial infarction.
Current UK NICE/BNF patient advice removes the historic third GTN dose and triggers a 999 call 5 minutes after the second dose.
Autonomic features may be absent in myocardial infarction; persistent pain 5 minutes after a second GTN dose mandates calling 999.
A second sublingual GTN dose should be taken after 5 minutes before calling 999 unless pain is immediately crushing and severe.
f: the patient was resting after a mild sprain rather than experiencing unrelieved ischaemic chest pain
following outdated historical protocols rather than current BNF guidance to call 999 after two doses
identifying autonomic symptoms that often accompany myocardial infarction rather than the timing rule for calling 999
the question asked when the patient should stop exercising and sit down to take the first spray

hq_q.s: A 62 year old man has stable angina and takes isosorbide mononitrate. He asks about a medicine for erectile dysfunction that a friend recommended.
hq_q.w: Nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors both raise cyclic GMP and together cause profound hypotension. Key discriminator: Nitrates must not be taken with sildenafil.
hq_q.f: Tamsulosin → use with caution for postural drop, but it is not contraindicated.
hq_q.ql: Which drug carries the greatest risk with isosorbide mononitrate?

tm.m: Nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors together cause dangerous hypotension
tm.g: Nitrates must not be taken with sildenafil
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Aspirin (Used for: ACS, TIA or ischaemic stroke: 300 mg now)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Atorvastatin (Atorvastatin is safe with nitrates)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Bisoprolol (Bisoprolol is safe with nitrates)
asked which drug needs caution for a postural drop but is allowed
x: Used for: ACS, TIA or ischaemic stroke: 300 mg now
Atorvastatin is safe with nitrates.
Bisoprolol is safe with nitrates.
Ruled out here: requires asked which drug needs caution for a postural drop but is allowed, whereas this patient has isosorbide mononitrate, erectile dysfunction.

hq_q.s: A 70 year old woman with chronic stable angina attends her GP because her exertional chest tightness has become more frequent over the past 2 months despite full adherence. She takes bisoprolol 10 mg once daily and standard-release isosorbide mononitrate 20 mg twice daily at 8 am and 8 pm. Pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP is 124/74 mmHg.
o: Add a third nitrate dose at bedtime
Add nicorandil 10 mg twice daily now
Double both the 8 am and 8 pm doses
Move the second dose to 2 pm
Switch to a continuous 24-hour GTN patch
hq_q.w: Continuous 24-hour exposure to organic nitrates depletes vascular sulfhydryl groups and induces rapid tachyphylaxis. Standard-release twice-daily isosorbide mononitrate must be prescribed asymmetrically (for example at 8 am and 2 pm) to provide an overnight nitrate-free interval.
hq_q.f: She takes a once-daily modified-release tablet → already has a gap; no change needed.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate adjustment to her nitrate regimen?

c: standard-release isosorbide mononitrate 20 mg twice daily at 8 am and 8 pm
more frequent over the past 2 months
tm.m: Symmetric 12-hourly dosing eliminates the nitrate-free period, causing nitrate tolerance; asymmetric dosing (8 am and 2 pm) restores vascular responsiveness.
tm.g: Twice-daily standard-release ISMN at 8 am and 8 pm losing effect -> move the second dose to 2 pm
x: Adding a bedtime dose increases continuous 24-hour nitrate exposure and worsens nitrate tolerance.
Her loss of angina control is caused by nitrate tolerance from symmetric 12-hourly dosing, which should be corrected first.
Increasing the dose on a symmetric 12-hourly schedule fails to provide a nitrate-free window and perpetuates tolerance.
Wearing a transdermal GTN patch continuously for 24 hours without removing it overnight also causes nitrate tolerance.
f: three-times-daily dosing of an non-nitrate antianginal drug without tachyphylaxis was required
angina remained uncontrolled despite optimal asymmetric nitrate dosing and beta-blockade
titrating a drug that does not exhibit tachyphylaxis, such as a beta-blocker when heart rate is high
transdermal nitrate therapy was needed in a patient unable to swallow, removed for 8-12 hours each night

hq_q.s: A 66 year old man has been prescribed bisoprolol for angina. His notes list several long-term conditions.
o: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
hq_q.w: Beta-blockers can cause severe bronchospasm in asthma. Cardioselective ones are safe in COPD and help in heart failure.
hq_q.f: COPD → a cardioselective beta-blocker such as bisoprolol can be used.
hq_q.ql: In which condition does a beta-blocker carry the greatest risk?

tm.m: Beta-blockers can cause severe bronchospasm in asthma
tm.g: Beta-blockers are contraindicated in asthma
f: a fixed low ratio in a smoker with little variation
proliferative retinopathy causing a tractional detachment
the presentation instead showed features specific to Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (Bisoprolol is a cornerstone life-prolonging drug in stable HFrEF)
calf pain on walking eased by standing still, with absent pulses
x: Ruled out here: requires a fixed low ratio in a smoker with little variation, whereas this patient has prescribed bisoprolol, several long-term conditions.
Ruled out here: requires proliferative retinopathy causing a tractional detachment, whereas this patient has prescribed bisoprolol, several long-term conditions.
Bisoprolol is a cornerstone life-prolonging drug in stable HFrEF
Ruled out here: requires calf pain on walking eased by standing still, with absent pulses, whereas this patient has prescribed bisoprolol, several long-term conditions.

hq_q.s: A 76 year old man with permanent atrial fibrillation and hypertension attends the medical assessment unit with fast palpitations and mild breathlessness. He takes bisoprolol 10 mg daily and apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Pulse rate is 118 bpm irregularly irregular and BP is 146/88 mmHg. A rate-limiting agent or antihypertensive addition is being considered.
hq_q.w: Combining a beta-blocker such as bisoprolol with the non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker verapamil causes profound additive depression of atrioventricular nodal conduction and myocardial contractility, risking severe bradycardia, complete heart block, heart failure and asystole.
hq_q.f: Bisoprolol with amlodipine → safe, as amlodipine does not slow the AV node.
hq_q.ql: Which drug combination carries the greatest risk of complete heart block and asystole?

tm.m: Both beta-blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) suppress SA and AV nodal conduction and negative inotropy.
tm.g: Beta-blocker + verapamil -> severe bradycardia, complete heart block and asystole
x: Amlodipine is a vascular-selective dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that does not suppress AV nodal conduction.
Digoxin is safely combined with a beta-blocker for dual-agent rate control in atrial fibrillation when monotherapy is insufficient.
Angiotensin receptor blockers do not slow atrioventricular conduction and are safely co-prescribed with beta-blockers.
ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers are standard cornerstone co-therapy in heart failure and ischaemic heart disease without AV block interaction.
f: a safe vasodilator calcium channel blocker was needed alongside bisoprolol to control hypertension
second-line pharmacological rate control was being added to bisoprolol in sedentary atrial fibrillation
an ARB was being added to bisoprolol for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or hypertension
prognostic neurohormonal blockade was required for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

hq_q.s: A 34 year old woman is brought to the resuscitation bay 2 hours after an intentional overdose of 40 propranolol 40 mg tablets. She is drowsy with cool peripheries. Pulse rate is 38 bpm and BP is 70/40 mmHg despite 1 L intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride and 3 mg intravenous atropine. Capillary blood glucose is 3.6 mmol/L (4.0-7.8).
hq_q.w: In severe beta-blocker overdose with bradycardia and hypotension refractory to intravenous fluids and atropine, intravenous glucagon is the specific antidote. Glucagon activates myocardial adenylate cyclase via glucagon receptors, increasing intracellular cAMP independently of blocked beta-adrenoceptors.
hq_q.f: Calcium channel blocker overdose → IV calcium and high-dose insulin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next intravenous drug treatment?

c: Pulse rate is 38 bpm and BP is 70/40 mmHg
despite 1 L intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride and 3 mg intravenous atropine
tm.m: Glucagon stimulatesGs-coupled myocardial glucagon receptors to raise intracellular cyclic AMP and contractility, bypassing blockaded beta-1 receptors.
tm.g: Refractory bradycardia and shock in beta-blocker overdose -> intravenous glucagon
x: A benzodiazepine antagonist that does not reverse beta-blocker cardiotoxicity and lowers the seizure threshold in propranolol overdose.
An opioid receptor antagonist indicated for respiratory depression with pinpoint pupils, not beta-blocker cardiogenic shock.
A cholinesterase inhibitor that increases vagal tone and can precipitate fatal asystole in bradycardic beta-blocker poisoning.
First-line for QRS broadening and ventricular arrhythmias in tricyclic antidepressant overdose, though propranolol shock requires glucagon first.
f: iatrogenic oversedation with midazolam had occurred during an endoscopic procedure in a patient without epilepsy
the patient had respiratory depression with a respiratory rate of 6 breaths/min and pinpoint pupils
pure central anticholinergic delirium was being treated by toxicology specialists in the absence of QRS or AV conduction delay
the ECG showed a broadened QRS complex (>120 ms) and metabolic acidosis after an amitriptyline overdose

hq_q.s: A 64 year old woman attends general practice for a blood pressure review 8 weeks after starting amlodipine 10 mg once daily for stage 2 hypertension. Her clinic BP is now 132/78 mmHg and pulse rate is 72 bpm. Examination shows normal heart sounds, clear lung fields and no elevated jugular venous pressure, but she reports a new daily symptom.
hq_q.w: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine preferentially dilate pre-capillary arterioles without matching post-capillary venular dilation. The resulting rise in capillary hydrostatic pressure causes dose-dependent bilateral peripheral ankle oedema.
hq_q.f: Verapamil → constipation and bradycardia.
hq_q.ql: Which adverse effect is most characteristic of amlodipine?

c: clear lung fields and no elevated jugular venous pressure
tm.m: Selective pre-capillary arteriolar vasodilation increases intracapillary hydrostatic pressure, driving fluid transudation into the ankle interstitium.
tm.g: Amlodipine therapy -> peripheral ankle swelling
x: Non-dihydropyridines such as verapamil and diltiazem slow the AV node, whereas amlodipine is vascular-selective and can cause mild reflex tachycardia.
Accumulation of bradykinin and substance P causing a persistent dry cough is characteristic of ACE inhibitors such as ramipril.
Impaired renal tubular urate excretion precipitating acute gout is a classic adverse effect of thiazide-like diuretics such as indapamide.
Reduced aldosterone-mediated potassium excretion causing hyperkalaemia is caused by ACE inhibitors, ARBs and spironolactone, not amlodipine.
f: the patient had been prescribed verapamil or diltiazem rather than a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
the patient had been started on ramipril and developed a persistent non-productive cough with a clear chest
the patient had started indapamide or bendroflumethiazide and presented with a painful red first metatarsophalangeal joint
the patient had started ramipril or spironolactone and routine blood tests showed a potassium of 6.1 mmol/L

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome has had palpitations for 1 hour.
Pulse rate 220 bpm, irregular. BP 124/76 mmHg. He is alert and has no chest pain.
ECG shows a fast, irregular broad complex tachycardia with varying QRS morphology.
hq_q.w: AV node blockers such as verapamil, digoxin and adenosine in AF with an accessory pathway can push conduction down the pathway and cause VF.
hq_q.f: AF with no accessory pathway → verapamil or diltiazem are fine for rate control.
hq_q.ql: Which treatment carries the greatest risk?

tm.m: Blocking the AV node pushes impulses down the accessory pathway, risking VF
tm.g: Pre-excited AF: avoid verapamil
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Electrophysiology referral (Referral is right, so it is not the drug to avoid)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Flecainide (Used for: Pill in the pocket for paroxysmal AF with a normal heart)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Procainamide (Used for: US books for stable VT)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Synchronised DC cardioversion (Used for: Tachycardia with shock, syncope, ischaemia or heart failure: up to 3 shocks)
x: Referral is right, so it is not the drug to avoid.
Used for: Pill in the pocket for paroxysmal AF with a normal heart
Used for: US books for stable VT
Used for: Tachycardia with shock, syncope, ischaemia or heart failure: up to 3 shocks

hq_q.s: A 66 year old man with ischaemic heart disease attends his GP for review. He has taken simvastatin 80 mg nightly for 6 years with a total cholesterol of 3.8 mmol/L. Following ambulatory blood pressure monitoring showing an average of 154/94 mmHg, he is started on amlodipine 5 mg once daily. Renal and liver function tests are normal and he has no myalgia.
hq_q.w: Amlodipine weakly inhibits intestinal and hepatic CYP3A4, increasing plasma simvastatin concentrations and the risk of dose-related myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. MHRA and BNF guidance caps the maximum daily dose of simvastatin at 20 mg when co-prescribed with amlodipine or diltiazem.
hq_q.f: He takes atorvastatin → no dose cap with amlodipine.
hq_q.ql: Which adjustment to his lipid-lowering regimen is required?

c: started on amlodipine 5 mg once daily
tm.m: Amlodipine inhibits CYP3A4 metabolism of simvastatin, markedly increasing systemic statin exposure and skeletal muscle toxicity above 20 mg daily.
tm.g: Simvastatin co-prescribed with amlodipine -> cap simvastatin at 20 mg daily (or switch to atorvastatin)
x: Adding ezetimibe while leaving simvastatin at 80 mg with amlodipine fails to address the dangerous CYP3A4 myopathy interaction.
Continuing simvastatin 80 mg alongside amlodipine carries a high risk of severe myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
He has established ischaemic heart disease requiring ongoing secondary prevention statin therapy rather than cessation.
Verapamil is an even stronger CYP3A4 inhibitor than amlodipine and also caps simvastatin at 20 mg daily.
f: LDL cholesterol remained above target despite maximum tolerated atorvastatin 80 mg daily
the patient was taking atorvastatin 20 mg daily, which does not require a mandatory 20 mg dose cap with amlodipine
he developed severe generalized myalgia with a serum creatine kinase more than 5 times the upper limit of normal
rate control for supraventricular tachycardia was needed in an asthmatic patient not taking a beta-blocker

hq_q.s: A 58 year old woman attends general practice with a 2-month history of a persistent dry, tickly cough that disturbs her sleep. She started ramipril 5 mg once daily for essential hypertension 3 months ago. She has never smoked and has no weight loss, haemoptysis or acid reflux. BP is 128/78 mmHg, respiratory examination is normal, and a chest X-ray is clear.
o: Halve the ramipril to 2.5 mg daily
hq_q.w: ACE inhibitors inhibit angiotensin-converting enzyme (kininase II), preventing the breakdown of bradykinin and substance P in the bronchial tree and causing a dry cough in up to 15% of patients. Switching to an angiotensin II receptor blocker such as losartan resolves the cough while maintaining RAAS blockade.
hq_q.f: Lip and tongue swelling → stop and avoid ACE inhibitors for life.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate change to her antihypertensive treatment?

tm.m: ACE inhibition impairs degradation of bradykinin and substance P in airway C-fibres; angiotensin receptor blockers selectively block AT1 receptors without affecting bradykinin.
tm.g: Troublesome dry cough on an ACE inhibitor -> switch to an ARB (losartan)
x: Symptomatic cough suppressants do not prevent bradykinin accumulation and are inappropriate when switching to an ARB cures the cause.
An ACE inhibitor cough does not resolve while the drug is continued and impairs sleep and adherence.
Bradykinin-mediated cough is not dose-dependent and persists even at low doses of any ACE inhibitor.
Beta-blockers are not first-line antihypertensives in uncomplicated essential hypertension under NICE guidance.
f: palliative symptomatic relief of an intractable dry cough in terminal lung cancer was required
a transient mild dizziness on standing had occurred during the first 2 days of starting ramipril and had already resolved
asymptomatic postural hypotension had occurred on high-dose ramipril without any cough
she had developed new symptomatic angina or heart failure with reduced ejection fraction requiring beta-blockade

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man with type 2 diabetes and hypertension attends for routine renal function monitoring 2 weeks after starting ramipril 2.5 mg once daily. He feels well and has no urinary symptoms. Clinic BP is 134/82 mmHg. Before starting ramipril, serum creatinine was 100 micromol/L (eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m2) and potassium was 4.4 mmol/L. Today creatinine is 118 micromol/L (eGFR 56 mL/min/1.73 m2) and potassium is 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.3).
o: Halve the dose to 1.25 mg daily
hq_q.w: After initiating or uptitrating an ACE inhibitor or ARB, a rise in serum creatinine of up to 30% from baseline (or a fall in eGFR of up to 25%) with serum potassium below 5.5 mmol/L reflects expected efferent arteriolar vasodilation and is acceptable; continue the drug and recheck.
hq_q.f: Creatinine up by more than 30% → stop or reduce and consider renal artery stenosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: ACE inhibition dilates the glomerular efferent arteriole, beneficially lowering intraglomerular filtration pressure and causing a modest (<30%) rise in serum creatinine.
tm.g: Creatinine rise <30% (18% here) and eGFR fall <25% (18% here) with K+ <5.5 on ACEi -> continue and recheck
x: Dose reduction is unnecessary when the creatinine rise is under 30%, eGFR fall is under 25%, and potassium remains below 5.5 mmol/L.
Renal artery stenosis investigation is only triggered if creatinine rises by more than 30% or eGFR falls by more than 25%.
Stopping renoprotective ACE inhibitor therapy for a physiological 18% creatinine rise deprives a diabetic patient of nephroprotection.
Angiotensin receptor blockers cause the exact same efferent arteriolar vasodilation and haemodynamic GFR change as ACE inhibitors.
f: his blood pressure had fallen excessively with symptomatic postural dizziness despite acceptable renal indices
serum creatinine had risen by 45% to 145 micromol/L within 2 weeks in a smoker with peripheral arterial disease
serum creatinine had risen above 130 micromol/L (>30% increase) or potassium had reached 6.0 mmol/L
he had developed a persistent dry tickly cough on ramipril with stable renal function

hq_q.s: A 34 year old woman attends her GP for preconception counselling. She has essential hypertension diagnosed 2 years ago and takes ramipril 5 mg once daily. She plans to stop her barrier contraception next month to try for her first pregnancy. Clinic BP is 126/78 mmHg, urine dipstick is negative for protein, and serum creatinine is 64 micromol/L (45-90).
o: Continue ramipril until a positive pregnancy test
hq_q.w: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers are fetotoxic and teratogenic, causing fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia and skull ossification defects. Women planning pregnancy should switch to a pregnancy-safe antihypertensive such as labetalol or modified-release nifedipine before conception.
hq_q.f: Switching ramipril to sacubitril-valsartan → stop ramipril 36 hours first to avoid angioedema.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate change to her antihypertensive medication?

tm.m: Fetal RAAS blockade impairs renal perfusion and skull ossification; labetalol controls maternal BP safely without teratogenicity.
tm.g: Woman on ACE inhibitor planning pregnancy -> switch to labetalol (or nifedipine)
x: ACE inhibitors carry first-trimester teratogenic and second/third-trimester fetotoxic risks and should be switched before conception in planned pregnancy.
Stopping treatment entirely risks uncontrolled maternal hypertension, pre-eclampsia and placental abruption during pregnancy.
Angiotensin II receptor blockers share the exact same fetal renal and cranial teratogenicity as ACE inhibitors and are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Spironolactone is contraindicated in pregnancy because its potent anti-androgenic activity risks feminisation of a male fetus.
f: the drug was levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, which must be continued and increased upon confirmation of pregnancy
blood pressure had been normal off medication and white-coat hypertension had been confirmed on ambulatory monitoring
she was not planning pregnancy and had developed a troublesome bradykinin-mediated dry cough on ramipril
she was a 60 year old with resistant hypertension and a serum potassium of 3.9 mmol/L requiring a fourth-line agent

hq_q.s: A 70 year old man attends general practice with a 24-hour history of severe throbbing pain, redness and swelling in his right first metatarsophalangeal joint that woke him from sleep. Three months ago he started indapamide 2.5 mg once daily for isolated systolic hypertension. Temperature is 37.3°C, BP is 136/78 mmHg, and the right big toe base is exquisitely tender and erythematous.
hq_q.w: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics such as indapamide compete with uric acid for organic anion transporters in the proximal renal tubule, reducing urate excretion, raising serum urate, and precipitating acute gout flares.
hq_q.f: A loop diuretic instead → low calcium, low potassium and ototoxicity at high doses.
hq_q.ql: Which metabolic complication is indapamide most likely to precipitate?

tm.m: Thiazide-like diuretics increase proximal tubular urate reabsorption and compete for tubular secretion, causing hyperuricaemia and monosodium urate crystal arthritis.
tm.g: Indapamide (thiazide-like diuretic) + acute monoarthritis of first MTPJ -> gout
x: Thiazide-like diuretics increase distal sodium delivery and aldosterone-driven potassium wasting, causing hypokalaemia rather than hyperkalaemia.
Thiazide-like diuretics impair urinary dilution in the distal convoluted tubule and commonly cause hyponatraemia, not hypernatraemia.
Thiazides enhance distal tubular calcium reabsorption and cause mild hypercalcaemia, whereas loop diuretics such as furosemide cause hypocalcaemia.
Thiazide-like diuretics impair pancreatic insulin release via hypokalaemia and cause hyperglycaemia rather than hypoglycaemia.
f: he had been started on spironolactone or amiloride, which block distal potassium secretion
he had developed lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with restricted access to free water
he was receiving high-dose intravenous furosemide, which inhibits paracellular calcium reabsorption in the loop of Henle
he had been started on gliclazide for type 2 diabetes and missed his midday meal

hq_q.s: An 81 year old woman is brought to the acute medical unit after becoming increasingly unsteady and confused over 7 days, culminating in an indoor fall yesterday. She started indapamide 2.5 mg daily for hypertension 6 weeks ago and eats and drinks normally. She is clinically euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes and BP 132/78 mmHg. Serum sodium is 122 mmol/L (135-146), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.3), and glucose 5.4 mmol/L.
o: Continue indapamide and recheck sodium in 1 month
Infuse 3% hypertonic sodium chloride bolus immediately
Prescribe oral slow sodium tablets alongside indapamide
Restrict oral fluids to 500 mL daily and continue indapamide
Stop indapamide and monitor serum sodium
hq_q.w: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics such as indapamide are a leading cause of symptomatic euvolaemic or mildly hypovolaemic hyponatraemia in older women. The essential management step is to stop the causative thiazide diuretic and monitor serum sodium closely to avoid overly rapid correction.
hq_q.f: Sodium 133 mmol/L with no symptoms → continue and monitor.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial management step?

tm.m: Thiazides block the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, impairing maximal urinary dilution while leaving ADH-mediated water reabsorption intact.
tm.g: Symptomatic hyponatraemia on indapamide without seizures/coma -> stop indapamide and monitor sodium
x: A serum sodium of 122 mmol/L with confusion and falls requires immediate drug cessation and close inpatient monitoring.
Hypertonic 3% saline is reserved for life-threatening neurological features of acute hyponatraemia such as seizures, coma or impending herniation.
Oral salt tablets without stopping the offending thiazide fail to correct thiazide-induced impaired free water excretion.
Continuing the causative thiazide diuretic perpetuates impaired urinary dilution and prevents sodium recovery.
f: she was completely asymptomatic with a borderline serum sodium of 133 mmol/L
she presented with generalised tonic-clonic seizures or coma (GCS <8) from severe acute hyponatraemia
mild salt-wasting nephropathy was being managed by a renal specialist in a patient not taking thiazides
she had chronic SIADH secondary to small-cell lung cancer and was not taking a diuretic

hq_q.s: A 78 year old man admitted with acute decompensated heart failure is receiving high-dose intravenous furosemide 160 mg daily for pulmonary oedema. On day 3 of admission he develops rigors, left loin pain and catheter-associated urosepsis. Temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 98/62 mmHg, and serum creatinine is 154 micromol/L (60-120).
hq_q.w: Both loop diuretics (especially high-dose intravenous furosemide) and aminoglycosides (such as gentamicin) damage cochlear hair cells and the stria vascularis. Co-administration markedly increases the risk of permanent sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular toxicity.
hq_q.f: Vancomycin → adds to kidney damage risk with gentamicin.
hq_q.ql: Which empirical antibiotic carries the highest risk of synergistic ototoxicity if co-prescribed with high-dose furosemide?

tm.m: Loop diuretics alter endolymphatic ion gradients in the stria vascularis and increase inner-ear penetration of aminoglycosides, causing synergistic cochlear hair cell apoptosis.
tm.g: High-dose IV furosemide + aminoglycoside -> synergistic ototoxicity -> gentamicin
x: Beta-lactam penicillins are not ototoxic and do not interact with loop diuretics at the inner ear.
High-dose intravenous macrolides can rarely cause reversible hearing loss and QTc prolongation, but aminoglycosides carry the classic severe permanent ototoxicity interaction with loop diuretics.
Tetracyclines cause photosensitivity and oesophagitis rather than inner ear cochleotoxicity.
Metronidazole can cause peripheral neuropathy on prolonged use and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, not synergistic cochlear toxicity with furosemide.
f: asking which antibiotic commonly causes a non-allergic maculopapular rash when prescribed during acute Epstein-Barr virus infection
the patient was taking simvastatin and amiodarone and we needed to identify a CYP3A4 inhibitor that prolongs QTc
asking which antibiotic causes severe sun-exposed photosensitivity and chelates with calcium or iron
asking which antibiotic causes severe flushing and vomiting if the patient drinks alcohol

hq_q.s: A 72 year old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 32%) attends for a routine blood test 3 weeks after starting spironolactone 25 mg once daily alongside ramipril 5 mg twice daily and bisoprolol 5 mg once daily. He feels well with no chest pain or palpitations. Pulse rate is 64 bpm, BP is 118/72 mmHg, and a 12-lead ECG is normal. Serum potassium is 6.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.3) and creatinine is 116 micromol/L (60-120).
o: Continue spironolactone and recheck in 1 month
Give intravenous 10% calcium gluconate in the GP surgery
Halve spironolactone to 12.5 mg alternate days
Switch ramipril to losartan and continue spironolactone
hq_q.w: Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) inhibit distal renal potassium secretion and carry a high risk of hyperkalaemia when combined with ACE inhibitors. Under NICE and BNF heart failure guidance, if serum potassium rises to 6.0 mmol/L or above, spironolactone must be stopped immediately and electrolytes rechecked.
hq_q.f: Potassium 5.4 mmol/L → continue at a lower dose with monitoring.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate adjustment to his medication?
hq_q.post: ECG shows no changes of hyperkalaemia.

tm.m: Mineralocorticoid receptor blockade in the cortical collecting tubule downregulates ENaC and ROMK channels, impairing renal potassium excretion.
tm.g: Potassium >= 6.0 mmol/L on spironolactone with normal ECG -> stop spironolactone and recheck U&Es
x: Continuing spironolactone with a potassium of 6.2 mmol/L risks life-threatening hyperkalaemic ventricular arrhythmias.
Intravenous calcium gluconate is an emergency hospital treatment for hyperkalaemia with ECG changes or potassium >= 6.5 mmol/L.
Halving the spironolactone dose is the BNF rule for moderate hyperkalaemia of 5.5 to 5.9 mmol/L, whereas >= 6.0 mmol/L requires cessation.
Replacing an ACE inhibitor with an ARB maintains RAAS blockade and potassium retention without resolving the hyperkalaemia.
f: serum potassium was 4.9 mmol/L and renal function was stable at routine monitoring
the 12-lead ECG showed tall tented T waves, flattened P waves and QRS widening
serum potassium was between 5.5 and 5.9 mmol/L with stable renal function
he had a persistent ACE-inhibitor dry cough with a normal serum potassium of 4.4 mmol/L

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old woman has hypertension that needed three drugs to control. She feels tired and has occasional muscle cramps. She takes no diuretics or laxatives.
BP 162/98 mmHg.
hq_q.w: Hypertension with unexplained low potassium suggests primary hyperaldosteronism, Conn's. Screen with the aldosterone to renin ratio.
hq_q.f: Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations → plasma metanephrines.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

tm.m: Excess aldosterone retains sodium and wastes potassium
tm.g: Resistant hypertension with unexplained low potassium: aldosterone to renin ratio
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Overnight dexamethasone suppression test (Cushing's can raise BP and lower potassium, but she has no cushingoid features; primary aldosteronism is far commoner)
episodic headache, sweating and palpitations
the presentation instead showed features specific to Renal artery Doppler (Renal artery stenosis raises renin; this is first excluded with the ratio)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Thyroid function tests (Thyroid disease does not cause low potassium with alkalosis)
x: Cushing's can raise BP and lower potassium, but she has no cushingoid features; primary aldosteronism is far commoner.
Ruled out here: requires episodic headache, sweating and palpitations, whereas this patient has three drugs, no diuretics or laxatives.
Renal artery stenosis raises renin; this is first excluded with the ratio.
Thyroid disease does not cause low potassium with alkalosis.

hq_q.s: A 56 year old man with Child-Pugh B alcohol-related cirrhosis attends hepatology clinic with a 3-week history of progressive abdominal distension and ankle swelling. He has been abstinent from alcohol for 6 months. Temperature is 36.7°C, BP is 116/70 mmHg, and examination shows shifting dullness with a non-tender abdomen. Diagnostic ascitic tap shows a serum-ascites albumin gradient >11 g/L and neutrophil count 80 cells/mm3 (<250). Serum sodium is 136 mmol/L and potassium is 4.1 mmol/L.
hq_q.w: Portal hypertension in cirrhosis triggers splanchnic vasodilation and secondary hyperaldosteronism, driving avid distal renal sodium and water retention. An aldosterone antagonist such as spironolactone (starting at 100 mg daily) is therefore first-line diuretic therapy for cirrhotic ascites, combined with a low-sodium diet.
hq_q.f: Not responding to spironolactone → add furosemide.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line diuretic to initiate?
hq_q.post: Ascitic neutrophil count is normal.

tm.m: Cirrhotic ascites is driven by intense secondary hyperaldosteronism; competitive mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism with spironolactone directly blocks aldosterone-mediated sodium retention.
tm.g: Uncomplicated cirrhotic ascites -> spironolactone first-line
x: Acts directly on ENaC channels rather than blocking aldosterone receptors and is less effective than spironolactone, reserved for patients with severe gynaecomastia.
Thiazide diuretics act in the distal convoluted tubule and do not overcome the intense secondary hyperaldosteronism of cirrhosis.
Loop diuretics alone are less effective than spironolactone in cirrhotic ascites and cause severe hypokalaemia unless paired with spironolactone.
An osmotic diuretic used acutely for raised intracranial pressure with impending cerebral herniation, not cirrhotic ascites.
f: the patient developed painful gynaecomastia on spironolactone and eplerenone was unavailable
first-line diuretic therapy was needed for essential hypertension where a thiazide-like diuretic was indicated
ascites failed to mobilise adequately on spironolactone monotherapy and a second diuretic was being added in a 100:40 mg ratio
the patient had an acute subdural haematoma with a fixed dilated pupil awaiting neurosurgical decompression

hq_q.s: An 82 year old woman with permanent atrial fibrillation is brought to the emergency department with a 3-day history of anorexia, nausea, confusion and seeing yellowish-green halos around household lights. She takes digoxin 125 micrograms daily, apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily and bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg daily started 4 weeks ago. Pulse rate is 46 bpm irregular and BP is 126/70 mmHg. Serum potassium is 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.3) and creatinine is 142 micromol/L (45-90).
hq_q.w: Digoxin toxicity presents classically with gastrointestinal upset (anorexia, nausea, vomiting), neurological disturbance (confusion, lethargy), chromatopsia (yellow-green halos, xanthopsia) and bradyarrhythmias or heart block, precipitated by renal impairment and thiazide-induced hypokalaemia.
hq_q.f: The ECG shows reverse tick ST depression with no symptoms → digoxin effect, not toxicity.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Hypokalaemia increases digoxin binding to the alpha-subunit of myocardial, neural and retinal Na+/K+-ATPase pumps, causing bradyarrhythmias, encephalopathy and cone dysfunction (xanthopsia).
tm.g: Nausea, confusion, xanthopsia and bradycardia in a patient on digoxin with hypokalaemia -> digoxin toxicity
x: Cataracts cause gradual painless visual blurring and glare over months to years, without acute nausea, confusion or bradycardia.
Hypercalcaemia causes polyuria, polydipsia, constipation and confusion, not yellow-green visual halos or marked bradycardia with hypokalaemia.
Migraine visual aura consists of transient shimmering fortificaton spectra lasting 15 to 60 minutes, not persistent 3-day xanthopsia and bradycardia.
Vertebrobasilar stroke causes sudden-onset homonymous hemianopia, diplopia, vertigo and ataxia rather than bilateral yellow-green colour distortion and bradycardia.
f: she presented with a 2-year history of gradual painless visual blurring and dazzle from oncoming car headlights at night
she had metastatic breast cancer with bone pain, polyuria, constipation and an adjusted serum calcium of 3.4 mmol/L
she had recurrent episodes of 20-minute zig-zag visual fortification spectra followed by unilateral throbbing headache
she developed sudden-onset left homonymous hemianopia, vertigo, dysarthria and ipsilateral limb ataxia

hq_q.s: A 76 year old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and permanent atrial fibrillation attends the heart failure clinic after starting oral furosemide 80 mg daily alongside digoxin 125 micrograms daily, ramipril 5 mg daily and apixaban 5 mg twice daily. His pulse rate is 62 bpm irregular, BP is 118/72 mmHg, and he has mild bilateral ankle oedema. Repeat blood tests are requested to prevent cardiotoxicity.
hq_q.w: Digoxin binds to the extracellular potassium-binding site on the myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase pump. Hypokalaemia (commonly precipitated by loop or thiazide diuretics) reduces competition at this binding site, markedly increasing digoxin binding and precipitating toxicity even at normal serum digoxin concentrations.
hq_q.f: Hypercalcaemia → also raises toxicity.
hq_q.ql: Which electrolyte abnormality most strongly predisposes to digoxin toxicity?

tm.m: Potassium and digoxin compete for the same binding site on cardiac Na+/K+-ATPase; low extracellular K+ enhances digoxin binding and pump inhibition.
tm.g: Diuretic added to digoxin -> hypokalaemia strongly increases digoxin toxicity
x: Acute digoxin overdose causes hyperkalaemia by shutting down Na+/K+-ATPase, whereas low potassium is the electrolyte disturbance that sensitises the heart to digoxin.
Serum sodium fluctuations do not directly compete at the extracellular potassium-binding site of the cardiac Na+/K+-ATPase pump.
Hypercalcaemia (not hypocalcaemia) increases intracellular calcium overload and potentiates digoxin-induced arrhythmias.
Low phosphate is seen in refeeding syndrome and hyperparathyroidism and does not sensitise cardiac Na+/K+-ATPase to digoxin.
f: the question asked which electrolyte abnormality is caused by massive acute digoxin poisoning
identifying an electrolyte disturbance that increases lithium reabsorption in the proximal tubule
the patient had post-parathyroidectomy perioral paraesthesia, carpopedal spasm and a prolonged QTc interval
a malnourished patient developed muscle weakness and arrhythmias 3 days after starting high-calorie parenteral nutrition

hq_q.s:
A 78 year old woman with digoxin toxicity has runs of ventricular tachycardia on the monitor. She is drowsy.
Pulse rate 140 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg.
Potassium 6.2 mmol/L (3.5–5.3). Digoxin level is high.
hq_q.w: Life-threatening digoxin toxicity is reversed with digoxin-specific antibody fragments. High potassium here is a marker of severe poisoning.
hq_q.f: Mild nausea with a stable rhythm → withhold digoxin and correct potassium.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Antibody fragments bind digoxin and remove it from the pump
tm.g: Life-threatening digoxin toxicity: digoxin-specific antibody
f: symptomatic bradycardia alone while the antibody is awaited
tingling lips and a positive Chvostek sign on day 1
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV lidocaine (Lidocaine is not the first treatment for digoxin toxicity)
clarithromycin + haloperidol
x: Ruled out here: requires symptomatic bradycardia alone while the antibody is awaited, whereas this patient has runs of ventricular tachycardia, Potassium 6.2.
Ruled out here: requires tingling lips and a positive Chvostek sign on day 1, whereas this patient has runs of ventricular tachycardia, Potassium 6.2.
Lidocaine is not the first treatment for digoxin toxicity.
Ruled out here: requires clarithromycin + haloperidol, whereas this patient has runs of ventricular tachycardia, Potassium 6.2.

hq_q.s: A 68 year old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (left ventricular ejection fraction 34%) and recurrent symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is reviewed in cardiology clinic to initiate long-term oral amiodarone 200 mg daily after loading. He has no history of respiratory, hepatic or thyroid disease. Pulse rate is 76 bpm in sinus rhythm and BP is 122/74 mmHg.
o: Bone mineral density DEXA scan and serum calcium
Full blood count and reticulocyte count weekly
hq_q.w: Amiodarone contains iodine and accumulates in tissues with a half-life of several weeks, causing hypo- or hyperthyroidism, hepatotoxicity, and pulmonary fibrosis. BNF guidance mandates baseline thyroid function tests, liver function tests, urea and electrolytes (potassium), an ECG, and a chest X-ray before starting treatment, with TFTs and LFTs repeated every 6 months.
hq_q.f: Breathless with fine crackles on amiodarone → pulmonary fibrosis.
hq_q.ql: Which set of baseline investigations is required before starting long-term amiodarone?

c: no history of respiratory, hepatic or thyroid disease
tm.m: Amiodarone has a high iodine content (affecting thyroid synthesis) and forms tissue-toxic phospholipid complexes in hepatocytes and alveolar pneumocytes.
tm.g: Starting long-term amiodarone -> baseline TFTs, LFTs, U&Es, ECG and chest X-ray
x: Corneal microdeposits occur in almost all patients on amiodarone without impairing vision, so routine baseline slit-lamp and hearing tests are not required.
Amiodarone does not cause bone demineralisation or require baseline DEXA scanning.
Amiodarone does not cause metabolic syndrome or diabetes, unlike atypical antipsychotics such as olanzapine or clozapine.
Amiodarone does not require weekly haematological monitoring for agranulocytosis, unlike clozapine.
f: the patient was starting long-term hydroxychloroquine (>5 years) requiring retinal screening or high-dose cisplatin requiring audiometry
the patient was starting long-term oral prednisolone or aromatase inhibitor therapy for breast cancer
the patient was starting olanzapine or clozapine for schizophrenia and needed baseline metabolic monitoring
the patient was initiating clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia

hq_q.s: A 30 year old woman with brittle asthma (previous ICU admission) presents to the emergency department with a 40-minute history of sudden-onset regular palpitations. She has no chest pain, syncope or breathlessness. Pulse rate is 184 bpm regular, BP is 122/78 mmHg, and SpO2 is 98% on air. A 12-lead ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia without visible P waves. Carotid sinus massage and a modified Valsalva manoeuvre fail to restore sinus rhythm.
hq_q.w: In haemodynamically stable supraventricular tachycardia unresponsive to vagal manoeuvres, intravenous adenosine is usually first-line. However, adenosine causes mast cell degranulation and A2B-mediated bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma; intravenous verapamil (2.5-5 mg over 2 minutes) is the recommended choice.
hq_q.f: No asthma → adenosine 6 mg rapid IV bolus.
hq_q.ql: Which intravenous drug is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Adenosine triggers severe bronchospasm in asthmatics via bronchial adenosine receptors; verapamil safely slows AV nodal reentry via L-type calcium channel blockade.
tm.g: Haemodynamically stable SVT refractory to vagal manoeuvres in a patient with asthma -> IV verapamil
x: Contraindicated in patients with asthma because it triggers severe, potentially fatal bronchospasm.
Reserved for broad-complex tachycardia or refractory arrhythmias, with slower onset and significant systemic toxicity.
Has a slow onset over several hours and is used for rate control in atrial fibrillation, not acute termination of AVNRT/AVRT.
A class Ic sodium channel blocker used for rhythm control or pill-in-the-pocket paroxysmal AF, not first-line AV nodal blockade in SVT.
f: the patient had no history of asthma or COPD and failed vagal manoeuvres
the ECG showed a haemodynamically stable regular broad-complex tachycardia of uncertain origin
rate control was required for fast atrial fibrillation in a patient with decompensated heart failure
cardioversion of recent-onset paroxysmal atrial fibrillation was planned in a patient with a structurally normal heart

hq_q.s: A 62 year old man attends cardiology clinic with episodes of symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation occurring every 6 to 8 weeks. He is in sinus rhythm today with a pulse rate of 68 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg, and takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily and amlodipine 5 mg once daily. Self-administered 'pill-in-the-pocket' oral flecainide is being evaluated.
o: Well-controlled hypertension without left ventricular hypertrophy
hq_q.w: Flecainide is a Vaughan Williams class Ic sodium channel blocker that slows phase 0 depolarisation in ventricular myocardium. As demonstrated in the CAST trial, flecainide increases mortality from fatal ventricular arrhythmias in patients with previous myocardial infarction, ischaemic heart disease or structural heart disease.
hq_q.f: A structurally normal heart → flecainide as a pill in the pocket.
hq_q.ql: Which feature in a patient's medical history is a contraindication to flecainide?

tm.m: Class Ic Na+ channel blockade slows conduction across scarred or ischaemic ventricular myocardium, promoting lethal re-entrant ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation.
tm.g: Flecainide contraindication -> previous myocardial infarction or structural heart disease
x: Age alone is not a contraindication to flecainide provided structural and ischaemic heart disease have been excluded.
Oral anticoagulation does not interact with flecainide and is appropriate when stroke risk factors are present.
Infrequent symptomatic episodes are the ideal indication for a pill-in-the-pocket strategy rather than daily prophylaxis.
Uncomplicated controlled hypertension with a structurally normal heart on echocardiography does not contraindicate flecainide.
f: assessing a CHA2DS2-VASc stroke risk threshold rather than a contraindication to class Ic antiarrhythmics
intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase was being considered in a patient who took apixaban 2 hours ago
defining the exact frequency pattern that makes a patient suitable for pill-in-the-pocket cardioversion
identifying a clinical feature compatible with safe pill-in-the-pocket flecainide use

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man with hypertension and a 10-year QRISK3 score of 16% attends his GP to start lipid-lowering therapy for primary cardiovascular prevention. Because of a previous mild intolerance to atorvastatin, he is prescribed simvastatin 40 mg once daily. Total cholesterol is 6.1 mmol/L, HDL cholesterol 1.1 mmol/L, and ALT 26 IU/L (10-50).
o: First thing in the morning on an empty stomach
With a glass of grapefruit juice
hq_q.w: Endogenous hepatic cholesterol biosynthesis via HMG-CoA reductase peaks overnight during fasting. Because simvastatin has a short plasma half-life of around 2 to 3 hours, it must be taken in the evening or at night to achieve maximal LDL-cholesterol reduction.
hq_q.f: He takes atorvastatin → any time of day.
hq_q.ql: When during the day should he be advised to take simvastatin?

tm.m: Simvastatin has a short elimination half-life, so nocturnal dosing aligns peak hepatic HMG-CoA reductase inhibition with the circadian midnight peak in cholesterol synthesis.
tm.g: Short-acting statin (simvastatin) -> take at night
x: Morning dosing of short-acting simvastatin misses the nocturnal peak in hepatic cholesterol synthesis and is used for levothyroxine or bisphosphonates.
Simvastatin is licensed for once-daily nocturnal dosing rather than alternate-day lunchtime administration.
Grapefruit juice potently inhibits intestinal CYP3A4, markedly increasing plasma simvastatin concentrations and risking rhabdomyolysis.
Unlike long-acting atorvastatin or rosuvastatin, short-acting simvastatin is less effective when taken in the morning.
f: he was being counselled on how to take oral alendronic acid or levothyroxine
a lipid clinic specialist was trialling ultra-low-dose rosuvastatin in a patient with recurrent statin myalgia
identifying the dietary drink that must be strictly avoided by patients taking simvastatin
he had been prescribed prednisolone 30 mg daily for an acute flare of polymyalgia rheumatica to avoid nocturnal insomnia

hq_q.s: A 66 year old woman takes simvastatin 40 mg daily. She has a chest infection and is allergic to penicillin. Her GP plans a 7-day course of clarithromycin.
hq_q.w: Clarithromycin blocks CYP3A4 and raises simvastatin levels, risking rhabdomyolysis. Pause the statin. Key discriminator: Short clarithromycin course on simvastatin: stop simvastatin during the course.
hq_q.f: The antibiotic is amoxicillin → no interaction.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate advice about her statin?

tm.m: Clarithromycin blocks CYP3A4, raising simvastatin and myopathy risk
tm.g: Short clarithromycin course on simvastatin: stop simvastatin during the course
f: the antibiotic is amoxicillin
the presentation instead showed features specific to Halve the statin dose (Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4 - simvastatin must be paused completely)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Swap to fluvastatin long term (A short course does not need a permanent switch)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Take them 12 hours apart (CYP3A4 inhibition persists 24 hours a day regardless of dosing gap)
x: Ruled out here: requires the antibiotic is amoxicillin, whereas this patient has simvastatin 40 mg, clarithromycin.
Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4 - simvastatin must be paused completely
A short course does not need a permanent switch.
CYP3A4 inhibition persists 24 hours a day regardless of dosing gap

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man attends general practice for routine blood monitoring 3 months after starting atorvastatin 20 mg once daily for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease. He feels well and reports no muscle aches, weakness, dark urine or abdominal pain. Total cholesterol has fallen from 6.4 mmol/L to 4.1 mmol/L. Serum ALT is 92 IU/L (normal range 10-50 IU/L) and bilirubin is 12 micromol/L (<17).
hq_q.w: Mild asymptomatic elevations in serum transaminases (ALT or AST less than 3 times the upper limit of normal) are common after starting statin therapy and usually resolve spontaneously. NICE guidance advises continuing the statin at the current dose and repeating liver function tests in 4 to 6 weeks.
hq_q.f: ALT 4 times the upper limit → stop the statin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Transient hepatocellular membrane adaptation during hepatic HMG-CoA reductase inhibition commonly causes benign transaminase rises below 3x ULN without true hepatotoxicity.
tm.g: Asymptomatic ALT < 3x ULN on a statin -> continue statin and recheck LFTs
x: Dose reduction is not required when serum ALT remains less than 3 times the upper limit of normal (150 IU/L here).
An asymptomatic ALT under twice the upper limit of normal with normal bilirubin does not warrant specialist hepatology referral.
Statins should only be discontinued for liver enzyme elevation if transaminases rise above 3 times the upper limit of normal.
Ezetimibe is less effective for cardiovascular risk reduction and switching is unnecessary when ALT is below 3 times the upper limit of normal.
f: the patient had mild muscle aches with a normal creatine kinase and requested a trial of a lower statin dose
he developed clinical jaundice with a serum bilirubin of 95 micromol/L and ALT of 650 IU/L
his repeat serum ALT had risen to 180 IU/L (more than 3 times the upper limit of normal)
statins were contraindicated due to persistent ALT >3x ULN or recurrent rhabdomyolysis

hq_q.s: A 72 year old woman with permanent non-valvular atrial fibrillation, hypertension and stage 5 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 12 mL/min/1.73 m2) attends the anticoagulation clinic to start warfarin therapy. Her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 4. Echocardiography shows normal mitral and aortic valve function. Baseline INR is 1.0 and platelet count is 240 x 10^9/L (150-400).
hq_q.w: For stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (as well as treatment of a first deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism), the standard UK target INR for warfarin is 2.5, with an acceptable therapeutic range of 2.0 to 3.0.
hq_q.f: Recurrent VTE while in range → target 3.5.
hq_q.ql: What is the standard target INR for this patient?

c: normal mitral and aortic valve function
tm.m: Maintaining an INR of 2.5 (range 2.0-3.0) balances vitamin K-dependent clotting factor (II, VII, IX, X) suppression against the risk of major intracranial haemorrhage.
tm.g: Warfarin in atrial fibrillation -> target INR 2.5 (range 2.0-3.0)
x: An INR of 1.5 is subtherapeutic and leaves the patient unprotected against left atrial appendage thromboembolism and ischaemic stroke.
A target INR of 3.0 is used for certain mechanical aortic valves with risk factors, whereas atrial fibrillation targets 2.5.
A target INR of 3.5 (range 3.0-4.0) is reserved for patients with recurrent venous thromboembolism while anticoagulated within the 2.0-3.0 range or mechanical mitral valves.
An INR target of 4.5 is supratherapeutic for all clinical indications and carries an unacceptably high risk of fatal haemorrhage.
f: explaining why low-intensity warfarin below 2.0 fails to prevent cardioembolic stroke in atrial fibrillation
anticoagulating a patient with a bileaflet mechanical aortic valve who also had additional prothrombotic risk factors
she had suffered a recurrent pulmonary embolism while therapeutically anticoagulated with an INR of 2.6, or had a mechanical mitral valve
identifying a supratherapeutic INR level that increases bleeding risk without additional antithrombotic benefit

hq_q.s: A 76 year old man taking warfarin for permanent atrial fibrillation attends the anticoagulation clinic for a routine blood test after finishing a course of metronidazole for a dental infection. He feels well and reports no epistaxis, gum bleeding, bruising, haematuria or melaena. Pulse rate is 72 bpm, BP is 134/78 mmHg, haemoglobin is 142 g/L, and today's INR is 9.2.
o: Give 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and IV vitamin K
Give intravenous vitamin K 5 mg slowly
Omit 1 or 2 doses of warfarin and recheck
Reduce the maintenance warfarin dose and continue
Stop warfarin and give oral vitamin K
hq_q.w: Under BNF and British Society for Haematology guidelines, a patient on warfarin with an INR above 8.0 and no bleeding (or only minor bleeding) should have warfarin stopped, receive low-dose oral phytomenadione (vitamin K 1-5 mg), have the INR rechecked at 24 hours, and restart warfarin once INR is below 5.0.
hq_q.f: INR 6.5 with no bleeding → withhold 1 or 2 doses and reduce the maintenance dose.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

c: no epistaxis, gum bleeding, bruising, haematuria or melaena
tm.m: Low-dose oral vitamin K1 restores hepatic gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X within 24 hours without rendering the patient refractory to subsequent warfarin.
tm.g: INR > 8.0 on warfarin with no bleeding -> stop warfarin and give oral vitamin K
x: Prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K is reserved for major or life-threatening bleeding (such as intracranial or severe GI haemorrhage) on warfarin.
Intravenous vitamin K is reserved for active major or minor bleeding at INR >8.0, whereas asymptomatic patients receive oral vitamin K.
Withholding 1 or 2 doses without vitamin K is the management for an asymptomatic INR between 5.0 and 8.0, not above 8.0.
Dose reduction alone is only appropriate for mild INR elevations (such as 3.5-4.9); an INR of 9.2 carries a high spontaneous bleed risk.
f: he presented with severe haematemesis and melaena or an acute subdural haematoma while on warfarin
he had minor mucosal bleeding with an INR above 8.0 or required reversal alongside PCC for major bleeding
his routine INR check had returned at 6.4 with no signs of bleeding
his INR was mildly elevated at 3.8 on a routine check with no bleeding

hq_q.s: A 58 year old woman with a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin 6 mg daily and has maintained a stable INR between 3.0 and 3.8 for the past year. Two weeks after starting a new medication prescribed in neurology clinic for trigeminal neuralgia, her routine INR falls to 1.4 despite full adherence and unchanged diet. She is asymptomatic with a crisp metallic first heart sound.
hq_q.w: Carbamazepine is a potent hepatic cytochrome P450 enzyme inducer (including CYP2C9 and CYP3A4). Over 1 to 3 weeks of initiation, it accelerates the hepatic clearance of warfarin, causing a marked fall in INR and risking prosthetic valve thrombosis.
hq_q.f: She started clarithromycin → INR rises.
hq_q.ql: Which newly started medication is most likely to have caused the fall in INR?

tm.m: Carbamazepine activates nuclear pregnane X receptors to upregulate hepatic CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 transcription, accelerating S- and R-warfarin metabolism.
tm.g: Neurology drug causing a fall in warfarin INR -> carbamazepine (P450 enzyme inducer)
x: Amiodarone inhibits hepatic CYP2C9, reducing warfarin clearance and causing the INR to rise rather than fall.
Fluoroquinolones inhibit warfarin metabolism and displace vitamin K-producing gut flora, raising the INR rather than lowering it.
Macrolide antibiotics are potent cytochrome P450 inhibitors that increase warfarin concentrations and elevate the INR.
Sodium valproate is a cytochrome P450 enzyme inhibitor and plasma protein displacer, rather than an enzyme inducer that lowers INR.
f: her INR had risen from 3.2 to 5.8 two weeks after starting an antiarrhythmic drug
her INR had risen sharply after starting treatment for pyelonephritis

hq_q.s: An 82 year old woman with newly diagnosed persistent non-valvular atrial fibrillation and hypertension is reviewed in clinic to initiate oral anticoagulation with apixaban. Her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 4. She weighs 58 kg, her pulse rate is 78 bpm irregular, and her BP is 136/80 mmHg. Serum creatinine is 90 micromol/L (45-90), haemoglobin is 128 g/L, and liver function tests are normal.
hq_q.w: For stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation, the standard apixaban dose of 5 mg twice daily is reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily if the patient meets at least two of the ABC criteria: Age 80 years or over, Body weight 60 kg or less, or serum Creatinine 133 micromol/L (1.5 mg/dL) or above.
