hq_q.s: A 64 year old woman presents to cardiology clinic with a 4-week history of exertional breathlessness and palpitations. She grew up in rural Pakistan and had rheumatic fever as a child. Pulse rate is 102 bpm irregularly irregular, BP is 124/76 mmHg, and auscultation reveals a loud first heart sound with a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation and echocardiography shows moderate rheumatic mitral stenosis (valve area 1.3 cm2).
hq_q.w: Atrial fibrillation accompanied by moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve is classified as valvular atrial fibrillation. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are excluded in these patients due to high thromboembolic risk, so anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin, target INR 2.5) is required.

hq_q.w: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is an immune-mediated prothrombotic disorder caused by IgG antibodies against heparin-platelet factor 4 (PF4) complexes. It typically presents 5 to 10 days after starting heparin with a >50% fall in platelet count and paradoxical venous or arterial thrombosis; all heparins must be stopped and switched to a non-heparin anticoagulant (e.g. argatroban or fondaparinux).

hq_q.s: A 74 year old woman presents to the acute medical unit with sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. CT pulmonary angiography confirms bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli without right ventricular strain. She has stage 4 chronic kidney disease secondary to diabetic nephropathy with a stable eGFR of 18 mL/min/1.73 m2 (creatinineclearance 16 mL/min). Pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP is 128/76 mmHg, and SpO2 is 95% on air.
hq_q.w: Low-molecular-weight heparins (such as standard-dose enoxaparin) and fondaparinux are cleared primarily by the kidneys and bioaccumulate in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2), risking major haemorrhage. An intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion (or specialist anti-Xa-monitored reduced-dose LMWH) is preferred because its clearance is largely hepatic/reticuloendothelial, it has a short half-life, and it is fully reversible with protamine.

hq_q.w: A high level means slow clearance. The dose interval is lengthened to allow the level to fall, protecting the kidneys and ears.
hq_q.f: Level in the 24-hour zone → give the next dose at 24 hours.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate change?

tm.m: A high level means slow clearance and risk of toxicity
tm.g: Gentamicin level above the line: extend the dosing interval

hq_q.w: Restoration of circulating volume is always the top priority in diabetic ketoacidosis. hq_q.s: A 26 year old man with type 1 diabetes has been treated for diabetic ketoacidosis for the past 6 hours with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride containing 40 mmol/L potassium chloride and a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour. He is alert and sipping water. His pulse is 92 bpm and blood pressure is 120/76 mmHg. Repeat bedside capillary glucose is 11.8 mmol/L, capillary ketones are 2.4 mmol/L, venous pH is 7.24 and bicarbonate is 13 mmol/L.
o: Add intravenous 10% glucose at 125 mL/hour alongside the 0.9% saline and continue the fixed-rate insulin
Give his usual subcutaneous basal insulin and stop the intravenous insulin infusion now
Reduce the intravenous insulin infusion to 0.05 units/kg/hour without adding glucose
Stop the intravenous insulin infusion until capillary blood glucose rises above 15 mmol/L
Switch from fixed-rate intravenous insulin to a variable-rate sliding scale
hq_q.w: In DKA, blood glucose falls much faster than blood ketones clear. The primary purpose of the fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/hour) is to suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis until ketonaemia resolves (ketones <0.6 mmol/L and venous pH >7.30). Under JBDS guidelines, as soon as capillary glucose falls below 14.0 mmol/L, intravenous 10% glucose at 125 mL/hour must be started alongside the 0.9% sodium chloride infusion to prevent hypoglycaemia while continuing the insulin infusion.
hq_q.f: Ketones under 0.6, pH normal and eating → switch to subcutaneous insulin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in his management?

tm.m: Glycaemia corrects before ketonaemia -> stopping insulin restarts ketogenesis -> add 10% glucose at 125 mL/h when glucose <14 mmol/L to sustain fixed-rate insulin until ketones <0.6
tm.g: DKA glucose falls <14.0 mmol/L with persistent ketonaemia (>0.6 mmol/L) = add IV 10% glucose at 125 mL/hour alongside 0.9% saline and continue fixed-rate insulin
x: Transition to subcutaneous insulin requires resolution of DKA (ketones <0.6 mmol/L, venous pH >7.30) and a patient who is eating and drinking normally
Reducing the insulin rate without adding substrate glucose when glucose is <14 mmol/L risks hypoglycaemia and slows ketone clearance
Interrupting intravenous insulin while ketones are 2.4 mmol/L and pH is 7.24 triggers immediate rebound ketoacidosis
Variable-rate insulin infusions (sliding scales) titrate insulin down as glucose falls, failing to clear ketonaemia in DKA
f: capillary ketones of 0.3 mmol/L, venous pH 7.36, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L and the patient eating lunch comfortably
patient whose glucose is <14 mmol/L and who is already receiving 10% glucose alongside 0.9% saline, where JBDS allows considering a reduction to 0.05 units/kg/h to avoid hypoglycaemia
serum potassium dropping to 3.1 mmol/L during DKA resuscitation, requiring temporary insulin suspension while K+ is replaced
fasting patient with insulin-treated diabetes undergoing major elective bowel surgery who is NOT in DKA

hq_q.s: An 82 year old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and linagliptin is brought to the Emergency Department after a week of dysuria, reduced fluid intake and progressive drowsiness. On examination, her mucous membranes are parched, skin turgor is reduced, pulse is 112 bpm, blood pressure is 102/60 mmHg and GCS is 13/15. Admission venous blood tests are shown.
hq_q.w: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) develops over several days in older patients with type 2 diabetes, often triggered by intercurrent infection (such as urosepsis or pneumonia) and poor fluid intake. Residual endogenous insulin secretion is sufficient to prevent lipolysis and ketogenesis (ketones <3.0 mmol/L, venous pH >7.30), but insufficient to prevent severe hyperglycaemia (>=30 mmol/L) and osmotic diuresis, leading to hyperosmolality (>=320 mOsm/kg) and profound dehydration.
hq_q.f: Ketones of 5 mmol/L and pH 7.1 → DKA.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: 82 year old woman with type 2 diabetes
week of dysuria, reduced fluid intake
tm.m: Residual beta-cell insulin suppresses ketogenesis but cannot prevent hyperglycaemia -> days of osmotic diuresis -> glucose >=30 mmol/L and osmolality >=320 mOsm/kg without acidosis
tm.g: Elderly type 2 diabetes + days of dehydration + glucose >=30 mmol/L + osmolality >=320 mOsm/kg + pH >7.30 and ketones <3.0 mmol/L = HHS
x: Causes dilute polyuria and hypernatraemia with a normal plasma glucose rather than severe hyperglycaemia
Requires significant ketonaemia (>=3.0 mmol/L) and metabolic acidosis (venous pH <7.30 or bicarbonate <15.0 mmol/L)
Presents on an SGLT2 inhibitor with raised blood ketones (>3.0 mmol/L) and metabolic acidosis despite a near-normal glucose (<14 mmol/L)
Produces a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (pH <7.30) with plasma lactate >5.0 mmol/L and normal blood ketones
f: polyuria of 7 L/day with urine osmolality 95 mOsm/kg, serum sodium 154 mmol/L and plasma glucose 4.9 mmol/L after head injury
capillary blood ketones of 5.2 mmol/L, venous pH of 7.12 and venous bicarbonate of 8 mmol/L
patient taking dapagliflozin with capillary glucose 10.8 mmol/L, blood ketones 4.4 mmol/L and venous pH 7.19
acute kidney injury (eGFR 11 mL/min/1.73 m2) on high-dose metformin with venous pH 7.14, lactate 9.2 mmol/L and ketones 0.4 mmol/L

hq_q.s: A 78 year old man with type 2 diabetes is admitted drowsy and dehydrated.
hq_q.w: Osmolality is 2 times sodium plus glucose plus urea: 300 plus 40 plus 20. Key discriminator: 300 plus 40 plus 20 is 360.
hq_q.f: Sodium 140 with the same glucose and urea → 340, still over the HHS threshold of 320.
hq_q.ql: Which is his calculated serum osmolality?

tm.m: Osmolality is twice the sodium plus glucose plus urea
tm.g: 300 plus 40 plus 20 is 360
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to 300 mOsm/kg (Equals 2 × Na alone, forgetting to add glucose (40) and urea (20))
the presentation instead showed features specific to 320 mOsm/kg (Forgets to include the blood glucose of 40 mmol/L in the formula)
a sodium of 140 with the same glucose and urea
the presentation instead showed features specific to 380 mOsm/kg (Arithmetic error or doubling urea in 2 × Na + glucose + urea)
x: Equals 2 × Na alone, forgetting to add glucose (40) and urea (20)
Forgets to include the blood glucose of 40 mmol/L in the formula
Ruled out here: requires a sodium of 140 with the same glucose and urea, whereas this patient has year old man with, 2 diabetes is admitted.
Arithmetic error or doubling urea in 2 × Na + glucose + urea

hq_q.s: A 74 year old man admitted with hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (admission plasma glucose 46 mmol/L, calculated osmolality 358 mOsm/kg, capillary ketones 0.5 mmol/L, venous pH 7.37) has received 2 litres of intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride over the first 2 hours. He is now more alert and passing 65 mL/hour of urine. Repeat plasma glucose is falling steadily by 5 mmol/L per hour and osmolality by 5 mOsm/kg per hour.
o: Continue intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride without starting insulin
Start a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour
Stop intravenous fluids and switch to oral water
hq_q.w: In hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state without significant ketonaemia (ketones <=1.0 mmol/L), intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride alone expands intravascular volume and increases renal glucose excretion, lowering plasma glucose and osmolality safely. Under JBDS guidelines, low-dose intravenous insulin (0.05 units/kg/hour) is introduced only once plasma glucose stops falling despite adequate fluid replacement. Starting insulin while glucose is already falling by 5 mmol/L/hour risks a dangerous drop in osmolality (>8 mOsm/kg/hour), circulatory collapse and cerebral oedema.
hq_q.f: Glucose not falling with fluids, or ketones over 1 → low-dose fixed-rate insulin at 0.05 units per kg per hour.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in his metabolic management?

c: falling steadily by 5 mmol/L per hour
tm.m: Volume expansion with 0.9% saline restores GFR and glycosuria -> glucose and osmolality fall steadily without insulin -> withhold insulin until glucose fall plateaus
tm.g: HHS with ketones <=1.0 mmol/L and glucose falling on IV 0.9% saline = continue IV 0.9% saline without insulin (start 0.05 units/kg/h insulin only when glucose plateaus)
x: Intravenous 10% glucose is added only once plasma glucose falls below 14.0 mmol/L
Venous pH is normal (7.37) and bicarbonate is not indicated in hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state
DKA-dose insulin (0.1 units/kg/hour) drops osmolality precipitously in HHS; even low-dose insulin (0.05 units/kg/hour) is withheld while glucose is falling with fluids
Total fluid deficit in HHS is 100 to 220 mL/kg (8 to 15 litres) and must be replaced gradually over 24 to 72 hours with intravenous fluids
f: later stage of HHS recovery when plasma glucose falls to 12.8 mmol/L while intravenous saline is still required
hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis (pH 7.11, bicarbonate 9 mmol/L) in acute renal tubular necrosis
admission blood ketones of 3.6 mmol/L with venous pH 7.18 indicating mixed DKA and hyperosmolar state
full clinical and biochemical resolution 48 hours later once osmolality is 292 mOsm/kg and the patient is eating normally

hq_q.s: A 34 year old woman with type 1 diabetes attends an outpatient clinic appointment and begins to feel sweaty, tremulous and light-headed 60 minutes after injecting her lunchtime rapid-acting insulin aspart, having eaten only half of her sandwich. On examination, she is fully alert (GCS 15/15), orientated and able to swallow safely. Her pulse is 102 bpm, blood pressure is 124/76 mmHg and capillary blood glucose is 2.8 mmol/L.
o: Give 150 to 200 mL of pure fruit juice orally
Give a glass of milk and two digestive biscuits first
Give intramuscular glucagon 1 mg into the deltoid
Give intravenous 20% glucose 75 mL over 10 minutes
Recheck capillary blood glucose in 30 minutes before treating
hq_q.w: In a conscious, cooperative patient with hypoglycaemia (blood glucose <4.0 mmol/L) who can swallow safely, immediate treatment is 15 to 20 g of oral fast-acting simple carbohydrate (such as 150 to 200 mL of pure fruit juice, 4 to 5 glucotabs, or 50 to 60 mL of Lift glucose liquid). Capillary blood glucose is rechecked after 10 to 15 minutes (repeating up to 3 cycles if still <4.0 mmol/L), followed by a long-acting complex carbohydrate snack (biscuits, toast or milk) once glucose exceeds 4.0 mmol/L.
hq_q.f: Unconscious or cannot swallow → IM glucagon or IV glucose.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

tm.m: Conscious hypoglycaemia with intact swallow -> 15 to 20 g oral fast-acting carbohydrate rapidly raises plasma glucose within 10 to 15 minutes
tm.g: Conscious hypoglycaemia (<4.0 mmol/L) able to swallow = 15 to 20 g fast-acting oral carbohydrate (150-200 mL fruit juice / glucose tablets), recheck in 10-15 min, then long-acting snack
x: Fat and protein in milk and biscuits delay gastric emptying and slow glucose absorption; they are given as the follow-up snack once glucose is >4.0 mmol/L
Intramuscular glucagon is reserved for drowsy, uncooperative or unconscious patients who cannot swallow safely and lack intravenous access
Intravenous 10% or 20% glucose is reserved for patients with impaired consciousness or an unsafe swallow
Symptomatic hypoglycaemia (2.8 mmol/L) must be treated immediately and rechecked after 10 to 15 minutes, not left untreated for 30 minutes
f: repeat capillary blood glucose of 4.6 mmol/L 15 minutes after fruit juice in a patient whose next meal is 2 hours away
patient found drowsy (GCS 9/15) and unable to swallow at home with no intravenous cannula in situ
unconscious inpatient (GCS 6/15) on a medical ward with a patent forearm intravenous cannula and capillary glucose 1.8 mmol/L
asymptomatic non-diabetic patient with a normal postprandial capillary glucose of 5.6 mmol/L

hq_q.s: An 80 year old man with type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide 80 mg twice daily is brought to the Emergency Department at 10 am after his wife found him slumped and confused in his armchair. He had eaten very little for 2 days because of a dental abscess. On arrival, his capillary glucose was 2.1 mmol/L and his eGFR is 38 mL/min/1.73 m2. After oral glucose gel and a sandwich, he is alert with a capillary glucose of 6.8 mmol/L.
o: Admit to hospital for prolonged blood glucose monitoring
Discharge home with an intramuscular glucagon kit
Discharge home with his wife and advise regular meals
Halve the gliclazide dose to 40 mg twice daily and discharge
Stop gliclazide, start basal insulin and discharge home
hq_q.w: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia (particularly with gliclazide or glimepiride in older patients or those with renal impairment) carries a high risk of prolonged, recurrent neuroglycopenia lasting 24 to 48 hours as active metabolites continue to stimulate pancreatic beta-cell insulin release after the initial glucose load wears off. Even if the patient recovers fully in the Emergency Department, hospital admission for close blood glucose monitoring (and intravenous 10% glucose infusion if recurrent) is mandatory while withholding the sulfonylurea.
hq_q.f: Insulin hypo with a clear cause and full recovery → long-acting carbohydrate and home with a responsible adult.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in his management?

c: capillary glucose was 2.1 mmol/L and his eGFR is 38 mL/min/1.73 m2
tm.m: Accumulated renally cleared sulfonylurea metabolites -> sustained beta-cell insulin release for 24 to 48 hours -> high risk of recurrent hypoglycaemia after initial recovery
tm.g: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia (especially in older patients or CKD) = admit to hospital for prolonged glucose monitoring even after full initial recovery
x: Glucagon stimulates endogenous insulin release as well as glycogenolysis and does not prevent protracted sulfonylurea-induced recurrent hypoglycaemia
Discharging a frail older patient after sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia risks fatal nocturnal recurrence once the initial meal is absorbed
Gliclazide must be stopped completely and the patient admitted for monitoring rather than discharged on a reduced dose
Initiating insulin in an 80 year old with poor oral intake and CKD who just had severe hypoglycaemia is dangerous and inappropriate
f: newly diagnosed 19 year old with type 1 diabetes being educated on emergency home rescue for severe insulin-induced hypoglycaemia
26 year old man with type 1 diabetes who had a mild daytime hypo (3.4 mmol/L) after jogging, recovered fully with juice and toast, and has a responsible adult at home
outpatient diabetes review in a 58 year old with eGFR 75 mL/min/1.73 m2 and occasional mild pre-lunch readings of 4.1 mmol/L without severe hypoglycaemia
symptomatic inpatient with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes and ketonaemia once acute DKA has resolved

hq_q.s: A 45 year old man with type 1 diabetes treated with a basal-bolus regimen of insulin glargine and pre-meal insulin lispro attends his annual diabetes clinic review. He holds a Group 1 car driving licence and commutes 35 minutes by car each morning. He has intact hypoglycaemia awareness and has never experienced severe hypoglycaemia. He asks what minimum capillary blood glucose reading is required before starting a journey without needing extra carbohydrate.
hq_q.w: The DVLA Group 1 ('5 to drive') guidance for insulin-treated drivers states that blood glucose must be above 5.0 mmol/L to set off without eating extra carbohydrate. If blood glucose is between 4.0 and 5.0 mmol/L, the driver must eat a carbohydrate snack before driving. If blood glucose is below 4.0 mmol/L (or if they feel hypoglycaemic), they must not drive, must take fast-acting and long-acting carbohydrate, and must wait 45 minutes after blood glucose has returned above 5.0 mmol/L before driving.
hq_q.f: The level is 4.5 → eat and wait 45 minutes after it rises above 5 before driving.
hq_q.ql: Under DVLA Group 1 guidance, above what minimum capillary blood glucose threshold may he drive without first taking extra carbohydrate?

tm.m: Cognitive reaction times deteriorate as glucose approaches 4.0 mmol/L -> DVLA mandates >5.0 mmol/L to drive without a snack ('5 to drive')
tm.g: DVLA '5 to drive': >5.0 mmol/L = safe to drive; 4.0 to 5.0 mmol/L = eat carbohydrate snack before driving; <4.0 mmol/L = do not drive, treat and wait 45 min after >5.0 mmol/L
x: 10.0 mmol/L is well into the hyperglycaemic range and is not the DVLA pre-driving threshold
At 3.0 mmol/L the patient is frankly hypoglycaemic and must stop driving, move out of the driver's seat, treat and wait 45 minutes after recovery
4.0 mmol/L is the floor below which driving is prohibited; between 4.0 and 5.0 mmol/L a carbohydrate snack is required before driving
7.0 mmol/L exceeds the statutory DVLA minimum pre-driving threshold of 5.0 mmol/L
f: renal threshold for glycosuria (in mmol/L) in a patient with normal renal tubular function
biochemical threshold below which Level 2 clinically significant hypoglycaemia is defined in clinical trials
threshold below which a driver must not drive at all and must wait 45 minutes after recovery (>5.0 mmol/L) before resuming
upper target limit for pre-meal capillary blood glucose (4.0 to 7.0 mmol/L) in adults with type 1 diabetes under NICE NG17

hq_q.s: A 58 year old woman with type 2 diabetes attends her GP surgery for her annual review. She feels well and takes modified-release metformin 1 g twice daily. Her clinic blood pressure is 132/80 mmHg and her BMI is 27 kg/m2. Early-morning spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 8.4 mg/mmol (<3.0), confirming a previous reading of 7.9 mg/mmol taken 3 months ago; urinalysis shows no haematuria or nitrites. Her eGFR is 72 mL/min/1.73 m2 and potassium is 4.4 mmol/L.
o: Keep current medication unchanged as blood pressure is <140/90 mmHg
Repeat the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio in 12 months
Start an ACE inhibitor such as ramipril and titrate to maximum tolerated dose
Start oral furosemide 40 mg once daily
Start oral spironolactone 25 mg once daily
hq_q.w: In any patient with type 1 or type 2 diabetes and confirmed persistent albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio >=3 mg/mmol on at least two early-morning samples), NICE NG28 and NG203 recommend starting an ACE inhibitor (or ARB if intolerant) and titrating to the maximum tolerated licensed dose, even when clinic blood pressure is normal (<140/90 mmHg). Blocking angiotensin II dilates the efferent glomerular arteriole, lowering intraglomerular hypertension and slowing progression of diabetic nephropathy.
hq_q.f: ACR under 3 and blood pressure at target → no ACE inhibitor just for the kidneys.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in her management?

c: albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 8.4 mg/mmol (<3.0), confirming a previous reading of 7.9 mg/mmol
tm.m: Persistent microalbuminuria (ACR >=3 mg/mmol) in diabetes -> efferent arteriolar constriction drives glomerular hyperfiltration -> start ACEi/ARB regardless of normal blood pressure
tm.g: Diabetes + confirmed urine ACR >=3 mg/mmol (even if normotensive) = start ACE inhibitor or ARB and titrate to maximum tolerated dose
x: An ACE inhibitor or ARB is indicated for renoprotection whenever ACR is >=3 mg/mmol in diabetes, regardless of whether blood pressure is already at target
Microalbuminuria has already been confirmed on two separate samples 3 months apart, so treatment should begin now rather than waiting another year
Loop diuretics control volume overload in heart failure or advanced CKD but do not reduce intraglomerular pressure or albuminuria
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists carry a hyperkalaemia risk and are not first-line ahead of an ACE inhibitor or ARB
f: 58 year old woman with type 2 diabetes on metformin with clinic BP 128/76 mmHg and urine ACR of 1.2 mg/mmol
single isolated urine ACR of 4.2 mg/mmol during a urinary tract infection that normalises to 1.1 mg/mmol after antibiotic treatment
patient with nephrotic syndrome, bilateral pitting leg oedema to the knees and pulmonary congestion requiring diuresis
resistant hypertension on maximum ramipril, amlodipine and indapamide with serum potassium of 4.1 mmol/L

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man with type 2 diabetes presents to his GP with a 6-month history of distressing burning and tingling pain in both feet and lower legs that is worse at night and disturbs his sleep. Regular paracetamol has provided no relief. He has no history of ischaemic heart disease, urinary retention or glaucoma. Examination shows reduced 10 g monofilament and 128 Hz vibration sensation in a stocking distribution to the mid-shins, with palpable pedal pulses.
hq_q.w: NICE CG173 (Neuropathic pain in adults) recommends offering a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin as initial pharmacological treatment for all neuropathic pain EXCEPT trigeminal neuralgia. If the initial choice is ineffective or not tolerated, switch to one of the remaining three first-line agents. Carbamazepine is first-line specifically for trigeminal neuralgia, while tramadol is restricted to short-term acute rescue therapy only and strong opioids (morphine) should not be initiated in primary care.
hq_q.f: Electric-shock pains in one side of the face → trigeminal neuralgia, carbamazepine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment for his painful diabetic neuropathy?

c: burning and tingling pain in both feet
tm.m: Serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibition in the dorsal horn (duloxetine) -> augments descending inhibitory pain pathways -> relieves diabetic neuropathic pain
tm.g: First-line painful diabetic neuropathy (NICE CG173) = one of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin (carbamazepine is for trigeminal neuralgia only)
x: Carbamazepine is the specific first-line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia, not peripheral diabetic neuropathy
Strong opioids such as morphine are poorly effective for neuropathic pain and carry high risks of dependence, hyperalgesia and falls
Simple analgesics (paracetamol and NSAIDs) do not modulate central neuropathic pain pathways and NSAIDs risk nephrotoxicity in diabetes
Under NICE CG173, tramadol is reserved solely for short-term acute rescue therapy while titrating a first-line neuropathic agent
f: paroxysmal unilateral electric-shock-like pain in the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve triggered by brushing teeth
severe background cancer pain from metastatic prostatic bone disease unresponsive to weak opioids
nociceptive mechanical knee pain from mild osteoarthritis in a patient without diabetes or renal impairment
short-term acute rescue analgesia during a severe flare of neuropathic pain while awaiting titration of a first-line agent

hq_q.s:
A 61 year old man has type 2 diabetes with peripheral neuropathy. His right foot has been hot, red and swollen for 2 weeks. It is not very painful and he has no fever.
The right foot is 3°C warmer than the left. The foot pulses are present. There is no ulcer or break in the skin.
X-ray of the foot is normal.
hq_q.w: Charcot foot: a numb foot that breaks down its own bones and joints. Early X-rays can be normal. It needs urgent offloading in a cast to prevent collapse.
hq_q.f: An ulcer that can be probed down to bone → osteomyelitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: X-ray of the foot is normal
tm.m: A numb foot breaks down its own bones and joints; early X-rays can be normal
tm.g: A hot swollen neuropathic foot with no ulcer and normal inflammation is Charcot neuroarthropathy
f: an ulcer that can be probed down to bone
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cellulitis (Classic picture: Spreading red, hot skin with no clear edge)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Deep vein thrombosis (A DVT affects the calf, not a hot foot)
a hot red big toe joint
x: Ruled out here: requires an ulcer that can be probed down to bone, whereas this patient has 3°C warmer, no ulcer.
Classic picture: Spreading red, hot skin with no clear edge
A DVT affects the calf, not a hot foot.
Ruled out here: requires a hot red big toe joint, whereas this patient has 3°C warmer, no ulcer.

hq_q.s: A 32 year old woman presents to her GP with a 3-month history of 6 kg unintentional weight loss despite an increased appetite, palpitations, heat intolerance and gritty, watering eyes. On examination, her pulse is 112 bpm, she has a fine tremor, bilateral proptosis with lid lag, a smooth diffusely enlarged thyroid with an audible systolic bruit, and raised, non-pitting violaceous plaques over both shins. TSH is <0.01 mU/L and free T4 is 48 pmol/L (12-22).
hq_q.w: Graves' disease is an autoimmune thyroid disorder driven by IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSH-receptor antibodies, TRAB) that bind and activate the TSH receptor on thyroid follicular cells, increasing hormone synthesis and vascularity (producing a smooth diffuse goitre with a bruit). Because orbital fibroblasts and dermal fibroblasts also express TSH-receptor antigens, Graves' disease uniquely causes thyroid eye disease (exophthalmos, chemosis, ophthalmoplegia) and pretibial myxoedema.
hq_q.f: A tender neck after a viral illness with low uptake on scan → de Quervain's thyroiditis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: smooth diffusely enlarged thyroid with an audible systolic bruit
tm.m: Agonist TSH-receptor autoantibodies (TRAB) -> stimulate follicular cells (diffuse goitre + bruit) and cross-react with orbital/pretibial fibroblasts -> exophthalmos + pretibial myxoedema
tm.g: Thyrotoxicosis + thyroid bruit + exophthalmos (thyroid eye disease) + pretibial myxoedema = Graves' disease (pathognomonic extrathyroidal triad)
x: Causes an acutely painful, tender thyroid after a viral illness with raised ESR and absent radionuclide uptake, without eye signs or pretibial myxoedema
Causes transient painless thyrotoxicosis within 12 months of childbirth with negative TRAB and no orbitopathy or pretibial myxoedema
Presents with a single palpable hyperfunctioning nodule without extrathyroidal features such as proptosis or pretibial myxoedema
Presents in older patients as an irregular nodular goitre without autoimmune orbitopathy or pretibial myxoedema
f: fever, jaw pain, exquisitely tender goitre and ESR 85 mm/hour 2 weeks after an influenza-like illness
painless thyrotoxicosis 4 months after childbirth with negative TRAB and diffusely absent uptake on technetium scan
palpable 3 cm nodule in the left lobe showing isolated hot uptake with complete suppression of the contralateral lobe
74 year old woman with a longstanding lumpy goitre developing new atrial fibrillation and patchy hot and cold areas on uptake scan

hq_q.s: A 38 year old woman who was started on carbimazole 30 mg once daily 6 weeks ago for Graves' disease contacts her GP surgery for an urgent appointment because she has had a painful sore throat, odynophagia and fever for 48 hours. On examination, her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse is 104 bpm, blood pressure is 122/76 mmHg and her pharynx is diffusely erythematous without tonsillar exudate or cervical lymphadenopathy.
o: Continue carbimazole and start oral amoxicillin
Halve the dose of carbimazole to 15 mg daily
Stop carbimazole immediately and check an urgent same-day full blood count
Switch carbimazole immediately to oral propylthiouracil
Take a throat swab for culture and review in 72 hours
hq_q.w: Any patient taking carbimazole or propylthiouracil who develops a sore throat, mouth ulcers or fever must have the thionamide stopped immediately and undergo an urgent same-day full blood count to exclude drug-induced agranulocytosis (neutrophil count <0.5 x 10^9/L). If agranulocytosis is confirmed, the patient requires urgent hospital admission for protective isolation and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and must never receive carbimazole or propylthiouracil again due to ~50% cross-reactivity.
hq_q.f: Planning pregnancy in the first trimester → propylthiouracil is used.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management step?

c: started on carbimazole 30 mg once daily 6 weeks ago
painful sore throat, odynophagia and fever
tm.m: Idiosyncratic immune-mediated destruction of myeloid precursors by carbimazole -> severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis -> oropharyngeal infection
tm.g: Sore throat/fever/mouth ulcers on carbimazole = stop carbimazole immediately + urgent same-day FBC (do not switch to PTU if agranulocytosis confirmed)
x: Continuing carbimazole while giving oral amoxicillin fails to arrest marrow suppression and risks fatal neutropenic sepsis
Agranulocytosis is an idiosyncratic reaction rather than a predictable dose-dependent side effect, so the drug must be stopped completely
Propylthiouracil shares up to 50% cross-reactivity for agranulocytosis with carbimazole and must not be substituted before checking the neutrophil count
Waiting 72 hours for a throat swab without checking a same-day neutrophil count can allow rapid progression to septic shock
f: immunocompetent patient not on thionamides presenting with acute bacterial sinusitis and purulent nasal discharge
biochemically euthyroid patient on titration carbimazole after 8 weeks whose free T4 is now 14 pmol/L with no sore throat
woman on carbimazole with a normal neutrophil count who is planning pregnancy and switching prior to conception
afebrile schoolchild with mild sore throat, cough and coryza not taking any regular medication

hq_q.s: A 34 year old woman with poorly controlled Graves' disease (who had missed her carbimazole for 3 weeks) underwent an emergency laparoscopic appendicectomy for acute non-perforated appendicitis this afternoon. Six hours postoperatively on the surgical ward, she becomes acutely agitated, delirious and tremulous, with profuse sweating and vomiting. Her temperature is 40.1°C, pulse is 162 bpm in fast atrial fibrillation and blood pressure is 154/62 mmHg. Her abdominal incisions are clean and she has received no antipsychotics or serotonergic drugs.
hq_q.w: Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis) is an acute life-threatening exacerbation of untreated or poorly controlled hyperthyroidism, classically precipitated by emergency surgery, trauma, sepsis, childbirth or acute iodine load. It presents with hyperpyrexia (>39.5°C), disproportionate tachycardia or fast atrial fibrillation, widened pulse pressure, high-output cardiac failure, agitation/delirium and gastrointestinal upset (vomiting/diarrhoea). Emergency management comprises intravenous beta-blockade (propranolol/esmolol), propylthiouracil, hydrocortisone/dexamethasone (blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion) and Lugol's iodine given at least 1 hour AFTER the thionamide.
hq_q.f: Rigidity and rising CO2 during anaesthesia with a volatile agent → malignant hyperthermia, dantrolene.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: temperature is 40.1°C, pulse is 162 bpm in fast atrial fibrillation
tm.m: Surgical stress in untreated Graves' disease -> acute surge in free thyroid hormone and catecholamine receptor sensitivity -> hyperpyrexia, fast AF and delirium
tm.g: Emergency surgery/infection in poorly controlled Graves' + hyperpyrexia (40°C) + fast AF + agitation/vomiting = thyroid storm (treat with propranolol + PTU + steroid + delayed iodine)
x: Triggered intraoperatively or immediately on induction by volatile inhalational anaesthetics or suxamethonium, causing masseter spasm, generalized rigidity and rising end-tidal CO2
Develops over days after starting or increasing a dopamine antagonist (antipsychotic), presenting with lead-pipe muscular rigidity, hyporeflexia and elevated creatine kinase
Surgical site infection rarely presents within 6 hours of a clean-contaminated appendicectomy and does not explain a pulse of 162 bpm in AF with widened pulse pressure in untreated Graves'
Occurs after combining serotonergic agents (such as an SSRI and tramadol/linezolid) and features hyperreflexia, inducible ankle clonus and ocular clonus
f: intraoperative masseter muscle spasm, generalized rigidity and rapidly rising end-tidal CO2 minutes after sevoflurane and suxamethonium induction
lead-pipe muscular rigidity, mutism, fever of 39.6°C and creatine kinase of 18,000 U/L 5 days after starting intramuscular haloperidol
erythematous fluctuant umbilical port site discharging pus on postoperative day 5 with normal thyroid function
agitation, dilated pupils, hyperreflexia and sustained bilateral ankle clonus 6 hours after adding tramadol to high-dose sertraline

hq_q.s: A 78 year old man with a history of three-vessel ischaemic heart disease and stable exertional angina presents to his GP with 6 months of progressive fatigue, cold intolerance, dry skin and a 4 kg weight gain. On examination, his pulse is 58 bpm regular, blood pressure is 134/78 mmHg and ankle reflexes show delayed relaxation. Blood tests show TSH 32 mU/L (0.3-4.2) and free T4 6.1 pmol/L (12-22).
o: Watchful waiting without thyroid hormone replacement
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG145 and BNF guidance, adults aged over 65 years or those with ischaemic heart disease, heart failure or severe prolonged hypothyroidism must start levothyroxine at a low cautious dose of 25 micrograms once daily (or 25 to 50 micrograms), titrated upwards in 25 microgram increments every 4 weeks according to symptoms and TSH. Starting full weight-based replacement (1.6 micrograms/kg/day, ~100 to 150 micrograms) acutely increases myocardial oxygen demand and can precipitate unstable angina, myocardial infarction or arrhythmias.
hq_q.f: A fit 35-year-old → about 1.6 micrograms per kg, around 100 micrograms.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate starting regimen for his thyroid replacement?

c: ischaemic heart disease and stable exertional angina
TSH 32 mU/L (0.3-4.2) and free T4 6.1 pmol/L
tm.m: Thyroid hormone upregulates myocardial beta-1 receptors and heart work -> rapid full-dose replacement triggers acute coronary ischaemia -> start low at 25 micrograms daily and titrate slowly
tm.g: Primary hypothyroidism in a patient >65 years OR with ischaemic heart disease = start levothyroxine at 25 micrograms once daily and uptitrate every 4 weeks
x: Starting at 100 micrograms daily is appropriate for fit adults under 65 without cardiac disease, but risks precipitating acute myocardial infarction in stable angina
150 micrograms daily is an excessive starting dose in an elderly patient with coronary artery disease
Liothyronine (T3) causes sharp peaks in serum T3 that provoke angina and arrhythmias and is contraindicated here
With overt primary hypothyroidism (TSH 32 mU/L, low free T4 of 6.1 pmol/L) and classic symptoms, treatment is required rather than watchful waiting
f: fit 34 year old woman weighing 62 kg with no cardiovascular history and newly diagnosed overt primary hypothyroidism
fit 40 year old man weighing 95 kg (1.6 micrograms/kg/day) with no comorbidities and overt primary hypothyroidism
critical care patient in myxoedema coma receiving cautious low-dose intravenous thyroid hormone alongside intravenous hydrocortisone
asymptomatic 78 year old man with subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 6.8 mU/L and normal free T4 of 15 pmol/L)

hq_q.s: A 70 year old woman attends her GP surgery to review routine blood tests taken during an annual hypertension check. She feels well and denies tiredness, cold intolerance, constipation, hair loss or weight gain. She has no history of thyroid disease or neck irradiation. Physical examination is normal with no palpable goitre. Blood tests show TSH 6.4 mU/L (0.3-4.2) and free T4 14.8 pmol/L (12-22) on a first sample.
o: Repeat serum TSH and free T4 in 3 months
Start oral carbimazole 20 mg once daily
Start oral levothyroxine 50 micrograms once daily today
Test anti-TPO antibodies and start levothyroxine if positive
hq_q.w: When a routine blood test reveals an isolated mild elevation of TSH (<10 mU/L) with a normal free T4 (biochemical subclinical hypothyroidism) for the first time, thyroid function normalises spontaneously in up to 50% of patients (for example after transient viral illness or biological variation). NICE NG145 recommends repeating serum TSH and free T4 (along with anti-TPO antibodies if not yet checked) after 3 months to confirm persistence before considering any long-term diagnostic label or therapy.
hq_q.f: TSH 12 mU/L on two readings 3 months apart → offer levothyroxine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: TSH 6.4 mU/L (0.3-4.2) and free T4 14.8 pmol/L (12-22) on a first sample
tm.m: Single mild TSH rise (<10 mU/L) with normal fT4 often reflects transient non-thyroidal fluctuation -> repeat TSH and free T4 in 3 months before confirming subclinical hypothyroidism
tm.g: First finding of TSH 4.5 to 10 mU/L with normal free T4 = repeat TSH and free T4 in 3 months
x: Radioactive iodine treats hyperthyroidism (such as toxic multinodular goitre or Graves' disease), not elevated TSH
Carbimazole is an antithyroid drug used for hyperthyroidism and would worsen an elevated TSH
Immediate levothyroxine is not indicated on a single unconfirmed TSH of 6.4 mU/L with normal free T4 in an asymptomatic 70 year old
In an asymptomatic 70 year old with TSH <10 mU/L, positive anti-TPO antibodies predict higher risk of progression (requiring annual monitoring) but are not an indication to start levothyroxine
f: 70 year old woman with toxic multinodular goitre, TSH <0.01 mU/L, free T4 34 pmol/L and recurrent atrial fibrillation
first-presentation Graves' disease with TSH <0.01 mU/L, free T4 42 pmol/L and positive TSH-receptor antibodies
persistent TSH of 14.2 mU/L with normal free T4 confirmed on two samples 3 months apart
28 year old woman actively trying to conceive who has persistent subclinical hypothyroidism and positive anti-TPO antibodies

hq_q.s: A 30 year old woman with autoimmune primary hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine 100 micrograms once daily contacts her GP surgery after a positive home urinary pregnancy test at 5 weeks' gestation. She feels well and her most recent serum TSH checked 2 months ago was 1.4 mU/L (0.3-4.2). She asks what adjustment, if any, she should make to her levothyroxine while awaiting her antenatal booking bloods.
o: Halve the levothyroxine dose during the first trimester
Increase the levothyroxine dose immediately (typically by 25 to 50 micrograms daily) and check thyroid function
Keep the same dose until the 12-week dating ultrasound scan
Stop levothyroxine until the second trimester to avoid teratogenicity
Switch levothyroxine to oral liothyronine throughout pregnancy
hq_q.w: During the first trimester, rising oestrogen increases hepatic thyroxine-binding globulin synthesis and placental deiodinase degrades maternal T4, raising levothyroxine requirements by 25% to 50%. Because the fetal thyroid is inactive until 12 to 14 weeks, early fetal neurodevelopment relies entirely on maternal free T4; increase levothyroxine by 25 to 50 micrograms daily immediately and check TFTs.
hq_q.f: After delivery → return to the pre-pregnancy dose.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate advice regarding her levothyroxine dose?

c: positive home urinary pregnancy test at 5 weeks' gestation
tm.m: Oestrogen-driven rise in TBG + placental deiodination -> 30 to 50% higher T4 demand in 1st trimester while fetal brain relies entirely on maternal T4 -> increase levothyroxine immediately
tm.g: Known hypothyroidism on levothyroxine + positive pregnancy test = increase levothyroxine dose immediately by 25 to 50 micrograms daily (30-50%) and check TFTs
x: Halving the dose precipitates maternal hypothyroidism during first-trimester neurogenesis, increasing the risk of miscarriage and lower offspring IQ
Waiting until 12 weeks misses the critical first-trimester window when the fetus has no functioning thyroid gland of its own
Levothyroxine is identical to endogenous T4 and is completely safe and essential in pregnancy; stopping it harms the fetus
Maternal T3 (liothyronine) does not cross the placenta effectively and leaves the fetal brain hypothyroid because fetal neurons require maternal free T4 for local deiodination
f: postpartum day 1 after delivery, when levothyroxine is reduced back down toward the pre-pregnancy dose
routine first-trimester nuchal translucency and crown-rump length ultrasound timing in an uncomplicated pregnancy
woman taking atorvastatin and ramipril who discovers she is 5 weeks pregnant and must stop teratogenic cardiovascular medications
never appropriate in pregnancy because fetal cerebral cortex requires maternal free T4 rather than T3

hq_q.s: A 29 year old woman presents to the Head and Neck Clinic with a 3-month history of a painless right neck swelling. She feels well with no voice change or dysphagia. Examination reveals a firm 2 cm right thyroid nodule and two mobile ipsilateral lower deep cervical lymph nodes. TSH is 1.8 mU/L. Fine-needle aspiration shows branching papillae, optically clear ('Orphan Annie eye') nuclei with longitudinal nuclear grooves and concentric calcified psammoma bodies.
hq_q.w: Papillary thyroid carcinoma accounts for ~80% of all thyroid malignancies and characteristically affects young women (peak age 20 to 40 years) or those with prior childhood neck radiation. It spreads predominantly via lymphatics to regional cervical lymph nodes (which does not abolish its >95% 10-year survival). Pathognomonic cytological features on fine-needle aspiration are optically clear chromatin-poor nuclei ('Orphan Annie eye' nuclei), intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions, longitudinal nuclear grooves and laminated calcified spheres (psammoma bodies).
hq_q.f: A rapidly growing hard mass with stridor in an 80-year-old → anaplastic carcinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: ipsilateral lower deep cervical lymph nodes
optically clear ('Orphan Annie eye') nuclei with longitudinal nuclear grooves and concentric calcified psammoma bodies
tm.m: BRAF V600E / RET-PTC rearrangement in follicular epithelium -> papillary proliferation with lymphatic spread to cervical nodes, Orphan Annie nuclei and psammoma bodies
tm.g: Young woman + thyroid nodule with cervical lymph node spread + Orphan Annie eye nuclei / nuclear grooves / psammoma bodies on FNA = papillary thyroid carcinoma
x: Presents in elderly patients (>70 years) with rapid local invasion, stridor and pleomorphic giant cells on biopsy
Spreads haematogenously to bone and lungs rather than lymphatics, lacks nuclear grooves/psammoma bodies, and cannot be distinguished from a follicular adenoma on FNA alone
Shows nests of spindle/polygonal C-cells in an amyloid-rich stroma (Congo red positive) with raised serum calcitonin
Shows a monomorphic sheet of malignant B-lymphocytes arising in longstanding Hashimoto's thyroiditis
f: 81 year old woman with a rapidly growing fixed neck mass, hoarseness, stridor and pleomorphic spindle/giant cells
Thy3f follicular neoplasm on FNA requiring diagnostic hemithyroidectomy to demonstrate capsular and vascular invasion
thyroid tumour with apple-green birefringent amyloid stroma on Congo red staining and elevated serum calcitonin
rapidly enlarging diffuse goitre in a 66 year old with Hashimoto's thyroiditis showing diffuse large B-cell lymphoma on core biopsy

hq_q.s: A 40 year old man attends the oncology outpatient clinic 6 weeks after undergoing a total thyroidectomy and central compartment neck dissection for a 2.8 cm medullary thyroid carcinoma. Preoperative urinary metanephrines and serum calcium were normal, and germline RET gene testing is pending. He has started oral levothyroxine replacement to maintain a normal serum TSH. The multidisciplinary team plans his biochemical surveillance for residual or recurrent tumour.
hq_q.w: Medullary thyroid carcinoma originates from neuroendocrine parafollicular C-cells (neural crest origin), not from follicular epithelial cells. Consequently, medullary thyroid carcinoma secretes calcitonin (along with carcinoembryonic antigen, CEA), and serial serum calcitonin + CEA measurements are used to detect residual disease or recurrence after total thyroidectomy. Because C-cells do not synthesise thyroglobulin or respond to TSH, serum thyroglobulin monitoring and TSH suppression are used only for differentiated follicular-derived cancers (papillary and follicular).
hq_q.f: Follow-up after total thyroidectomy for papillary cancer → thyroglobulin.
hq_q.ql: Which serum tumour marker is most useful for postoperative surveillance of his malignancy?

c: biochemical surveillance for residual or recurrent tumour
tm.m: Medullary thyroid cancer arises from parafollicular C-cells -> secretes calcitonin (and CEA), whereas thyroglobulin is only made by follicular cells
tm.g: Postoperative tumour marker follow-up: medullary thyroid cancer = calcitonin (+ CEA); papillary/follicular thyroid cancer = thyroglobulin
x: Alpha-fetoprotein is a tumour marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and non-seminomatous testicular/ovarian yolk sac germ cell tumours
CA 19-9 is a sialylated Lewis antigen marker used to monitor pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma
Parathyroid hormone is measured post-thyroidectomy to diagnose iatrogenic hypoparathyroidism if hypocalcaemia develops, not as a thyroid cancer marker
Thyroglobulin is produced exclusively by thyroid follicular cells and is the surveillance marker for papillary and follicular thyroid carcinomas after total thyroidectomy
f: surveillance after curative resection of hepatocellular carcinoma or a non-seminomatous testicular germ cell tumour
monitoring treatment response in locally advanced pancreatic head adenocarcinoma
investigating perioral paraesthesia, carpopedal spasm and a corrected serum calcium of 1.78 mmol/L 24 hours after total thyroidectomy
detecting recurrence after total thyroidectomy and radioiodine remnant ablation for papillary or follicular thyroid carcinoma

hq_q.s: A 46 year old woman underwent an uncomplicated total thyroidectomy 4 hours ago for a multinodular goitre and is recovering on the surgical ward. She rings the call bell complaining of sudden severe neck tightness, restlessness and difficulty breathing. On examination, her respiratory rate is 28 breaths/min, SpO2 is 92% on 15 L/min oxygen, and there is a tense, rapidly expanding swelling beneath the transverse collar incision with audible inspiratory stridor.
o: Arrange an urgent portable chest radiograph and CT angiogram of the neck
Await arrival of the consultant anaesthetist before touching the wound
Give 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate intravenously over 10 minutes
Give 5 mg nebulised adrenaline and intravenous hydrocortisone
Open the skin and deep cervical fascia sutures at the bedside using a clip remover
hq_q.w: Post-thyroidectomy haemorrhage into the closed deep cervical space beneath the strap muscles causes venous and lymphatic congestion, rapidly leading to laryngeal oedema, tracheal compression and asphyxiation within minutes. This is an immediate clinical surgical emergency: the bedside clinician must open BOTH the skin clips/sutures AND the deep layer (strap muscle/platysma sutures) immediately at the bedside using the stitch cutter/clip remover kept taped to the bedhead (the SCOOP protocol), before transferring the patient back to theatre for definitive haemostasis.
hq_q.f: Tingling lips and a positive Chvostek sign on day 1 → hypocalcaemia from parathyroid damage, IV calcium gluconate.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate bedside action?

c: tense, rapidly expanding swelling beneath the transverse collar incision
tm.m: Arterial bleeding beneath closed strap muscles -> compartment hypertension compresses tracheal venous/lymphatic drainage -> acute laryngeal oedema and airway obstruction -> immediate bedside suture release
tm.g: Post-thyroidectomy tense neck swelling + stridor/dyspnoea = open wound clips AND deep strap-muscle sutures immediately at the bedside, then return to theatre
x: Transferring a stridulous patient with an expanding neck haematoma to radiology causes fatal respiratory arrest
Waiting for the anaesthetist before releasing the haematoma allows worsening laryngeal venous oedema that makes endotracheal intubation impossible
Intravenous calcium gluconate treats hypocalcaemic laryngospasm (typically 24 to 72 hours postoperatively without a tense neck swelling), not an acute compressive haematoma
Nebulised adrenaline does not decompress a tense sub-platysmal and deep cervical haematoma
f: haemodynamically stable patient 2 weeks after neck surgery with mild superficial wound induration and no stridor
elective fibreoptic awake intubation in theatre for a stable outpatient with a longstanding retrosternal goitre
perioral tingling, positive Chvostek sign, QT prolongation and carpopedal spasm 36 hours after total thyroidectomy with a flat, soft neck wound
2 year old child with barking cough, hoarse voice and stridor from severe viral croup

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman has had hearing loss and ringing in her right ear only for 6 months. She has no ear pain or discharge.
Both ear drums are normal. Rinne's test is positive on both sides, and Weber's test lateralises to the left.
Audiometry shows a right-sided sensorineural loss.
o: Contrast CT of the brain and sinuses
MRI of the internal acoustic meatus
hq_q.w: Unilateral or asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss accompanied by unilateral tinnitus requires gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal acoustic meatus (IAM) to exclude a cerebellopontine angle vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma).
hq_q.f: Bilateral schwannomas in a young adult → neurofibromatosis type 2.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

c: Weber's test lateralises to the left
tm.m: Asymmetric eighth cranial nerve dysfunction requires high-resolution MRI of the cerebellopontine angle and internal auditory canal
tm.g: Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus -> MRI of the internal acoustic meatus
f: assessing bilateral peripheral vestibular hypofunction in chronic unexplained oscillopsia
evaluating bony erosion of the scutum and ossicular chain in chronic middle-ear cholesteatoma
monitoring mild symmetrical age-related high-frequency presbycusis in an older adult
suspected bilateral otitis media with effusion causing conductive hearing loss in a child
x: Caloric testing evaluates horizontal semicircular canal function in vertigo and cannot image a cerebellopontine angle tumour.
CT has poor soft-tissue resolution in the posterior fossa due to petrous bone artefact and misses small intracanalicular schwannomas.
Delaying investigation for a year risks progressive growth of a vestibular schwannoma with brainstem and cranial nerve compression.
Tympanometry assesses middle-ear pressure and tympanic membrane compliance in conductive deafness rather than retrocochlear pathology.

hq_q.s: A 58 year old woman under ENT clinic surveillance has a left-sided vestibular schwannoma causing progressive left sensorineural hearing loss and high-pitched tinnitus over the past year. Serial gadolinium-enhanced MRI now shows the tumour has expanded out of the internal acoustic meatus into the cerebellopontine angle cistern.
hq_q.w: As a vestibular schwannoma expands into the cerebellopontine angle, the trigeminal sensory root (CN V) is compressed early, making ipsilateral loss of the corneal reflex the earliest extra-auditory sign; facial motor fibres tolerate slow stretching.
hq_q.f: The tumour grows larger with ataxia and headache → cerebellar compression and hydrocephalus.
hq_q.ql: Which cranial nerve sign, besides hearing loss, tends to appear first?

tm.m: Superior extension in the cerebellopontine angle compresses the trigeminal sensory root before motor facial fibres fail
tm.g: Earliest cranial nerve sign of an expanding vestibular schwannoma after CN VIII -> reduced corneal reflex (CN V)
f: a glomus jugulare or hypoglossal canal tumour eroding the lower skull base
raised intracranial pressure with papilloedema causing a false-localising sixth nerve palsy
a malignant parotid gland carcinoma invading the facial nerve trunk early
a jugular foramen schwannoma or glomus jugulare tumour compressing cranial nerves IX, X and XI
x: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) palsy causing tongue deviation occurs only with massive inferior extension to the hypoglossal canal.
Abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy causing horizontal diplopia is a late feature of raised intracranial pressure or medial pontine compression.
Despite running through the internal acoustic meatus, motor fibres of the facial nerve (CN VII) tolerate slow stretching and develop weakness late.
Vagal nerve (CN X) compression causing vocal cord palsy and hoarseness occurs only with large tumours reaching the jugular foramen.

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man has had hearing loss in both ears for a year. He had cataracts removed in his teens. His father had brain tumours.
MRI shows bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
hq_q.w: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define NF2, an autosomal dominant condition on chromosome 22 with meningiomas and early cataracts.
hq_q.f: Café-au-lait spots, axillary freckles and skin neurofibromas → neurofibromatosis type 1.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: A chromosome 22 gene loss causes schwannomas, meningiomas and early cataracts
tm.g: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define neurofibromatosis type 2
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1 causes parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumours)
café-au-lait spots with axillary freckles
the presentation instead showed features specific to Tuberous sclerosis (Tuberous sclerosis gives skin lesions and seizures, not bilateral vestibular schwannomas)
haemangioblastomas with renal cysts
x: MEN1 causes parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumours.
Ruled out here: requires café-au-lait spots with axillary freckles, whereas this patient has both ears, cataracts removed in his teens.
Tuberous sclerosis gives skin lesions and seizures, not bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
Ruled out here: requires haemangioblastomas with renal cysts, whereas this patient has both ears, cataracts removed in his teens.

hq_q.s:
A 35 year old woman woke this morning with weakness of the left side of her face. Sounds are too loud in her left ear. She has no ear pain or rash.
There is weakness of the whole left side of the face, including the forehead. She cannot close her left eye. There are no vesicles in the ear. Limb examination is normal.
hq_q.w: Bell's palsy is an acute idiopathic lower motor neurone paralysis of the facial nerve (CN VII). Because the lesion is infranuclear, both forehead wrinkling and lower facial muscles are paralysed, often with hyperacusis (stapedius palsy) and altered taste.
hq_q.f: The forehead is spared and the arm is weak → stroke, an upper motor neurone lesion.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Inflammatory oedema of CN VII within the narrow fallopian canal paralyses all ipsilateral facial muscles and stapedius
tm.g: Sudden complete unilateral facial weakness including the forehead without ear vesicles -> Bell's palsy
f: bilateral lower motor neurone facial palsy 3 weeks after a bull's-eye rash from a forest tick bite
gradually progressive facial nerve weakness over 3 months with a rock-hard fixed parotid lump
severe ear pain with clustered vesicles in the external auditory canal and conchal bowl
sudden lower facial droop with preserved bilateral forehead wrinkling and ipsilateral arm weakness
x: Lyme neuroborreliosis typically presents weeks after an Ixodes tick bite and erythema migrans rash, often with bilateral facial palsy or radiculoneuritis.
A malignant parotid gland tumour causes gradually progressive facial weakness over weeks or months accompanied by a firm preauricular mass.
Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) causes severe otalgia and painful vesicular lesions in the external auditory canal or soft palate.
An upper motor neurone hemispheric stroke spares the forehead muscles due to bilateral corticonuclear innervation of the upper facial nucleus.

hq_q.s:
A 40 year old man noticed weakness of the right side of his face 36 hours ago. He has no rash or ear pain.
There is weakness of the whole right side of the face, including the forehead. He cannot close his right eye fully. The ear canal is normal.
hq_q.w: Steroids within 72 hours improve recovery. Protect the eye with lubricants and taping at night, as it cannot close.
hq_q.f: Presenting after 72 hours → steroids are less helpful; focus on eye protection.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

c: cannot close his right eye fully
tm.m: Steroids within 72 hours reduce nerve swelling and improve recovery
tm.g: Bell's palsy within 72 hours: prednisolone, plus eye care
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Aciclovir (Antivirals add nothing on their own in Bell's palsy without a rash; prednisolone within 72 hours is the treatment)
the presentation instead showed features specific to No treatment (Within 72 hours prednisolone improves recovery, and the eye needs protecting now)

the presentation instead showed features specific to Prednisolone and aciclovir (Adding an antiviral gives little extra benefit in Bell's palsy and is not routine; it is used when Ramsay Hunt syndrome is suspected)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Surgical decompression (Not recommended for Bell's palsy as oral prednisolone is effective)
x: Antivirals add nothing on their own in Bell's palsy without a rash; prednisolone within 72 hours is the treatment.
Within 72 hours prednisolone improves recovery, and the eye needs protecting now.
Adding an antiviral gives little extra benefit in Bell's palsy and is not routine; it is used when Ramsay Hunt syndrome is suspected.
Not recommended for Bell's palsy as oral prednisolone is effective

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man has had a painful left ear for 3 days. Today his face is drooping on the left.
There are vesicles in the left ear canal and on the pinna. There is weakness of the whole left side of the face, including the forehead. There are no other neurological signs.
hq_q.w: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is varicella zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion. Oral aciclovir (or valaciclovir) with prednisolone, started within 72 hours, gives the best chance of facial recovery; protect the eye if it cannot close.
hq_q.f: Same facial weakness with no vesicles or ear pain → Bell's palsy; prednisolone without an antiviral.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

c: vesicles in the left ear canal
weakness of the whole left side of the face
tm.m: Zoster in the geniculate ganglion inflames the facial nerve inside its bony canal
tm.g: Ramsay Hunt: antiviral plus steroid
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amoxicillin and ear drops (There is no otitis media; the vesicles show a viral cause)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ciprofloxacin ear drops (Ear drops treat otitis externa, not zoster of the facial nerve)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Topical aciclovir cream (Cream on the skin does not reach the infected nerve ganglion)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Watch and wait (Ramsay Hunt has a worse outlook than Bell's palsy, so treatment should start now)
x: There is no otitis media; the vesicles show a viral cause.
Ear drops treat otitis externa, not zoster of the facial nerve.
Cream on the skin does not reach the infected nerve ganglion.
Ramsay Hunt has a worse outlook than Bell's palsy, so treatment should start now.

hq_q.s:
A 60 year old woman has had brief spells of spinning lasting under a minute for 2 weeks. They happen when she turns over in bed or looks up. She has no hearing loss or tinnitus.
The Dix-Hallpike test is positive on the right, with rotational nystagmus towards the right ear that fades within 30 seconds. Neurological examination is otherwise normal.
hq_q.w: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is caused by free-floating calcium carbonate otoconia in the posterior semicircular canal. A canalith repositioning procedure (Epley manoeuvre) guides the debris back into the utricle and resolves symptoms in over 80% of patients.
hq_q.f: Nystagmus that is vertical or does not fade → central cause, MRI.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Canalithiasis in the posterior semicircular canal deflects the cupula transiently upon head rotation
tm.g: Brief positional vertigo with fatiguing torsional nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike -> Epley manoeuvre
f: recurrent 3 hour bouts of spontaneous vertigo with unilateral low-frequency deafness and tinnitus
purely vertical non-fatiguing positional nystagmus with no latency on Dix-Hallpike testing
short-term symptomatic relief for 48 hours during severe vomiting from acute vestibular neuritis
intractable disabling positional vertigo refractory to multiple particle repositioning manoeuvres over a year
x: Betahistine is used for prophylaxis of endolymphatic hydrops in Meniere's disease and has no role in mechanical canalithiasis.
Neuroimaging with MRI head is unnecessary when Dix-Hallpike testing shows typical latent, fatiguing torsional nystagmus and normal neurology.
Long-term vestibular sedatives such as prochlorperazine do not reposition otoconia and impair central vestibular compensation.
Surgical posterior canal occlusion is a last-resort procedure reserved for intractable cases failing repeated repositioning manoeuvres.

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old man had a cold a week ago. For 3 days he has had constant severe vertigo with nausea and vomiting. His hearing is normal and he has no tinnitus.
There is horizontal nystagmus in one direction. The head impulse test is abnormal. There is no skew deviation. He can walk with help.
hq_q.w: Vestibular neuritis inflames the vestibular nerve only, so vertigo lasts days with no hearing loss.
hq_q.f: The same story with sudden hearing loss → labyrinthitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve spares the cochlea
tm.g: Viral onset with normal hearing and an abnormal head impulse is vestibular neuritis
f: brief spells on turning in bed
the same story with sudden hearing loss
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ménière's disease (Ménière's attacks last hours with hearing loss and tinnitus; his vertigo is constant and his hearing normal)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Posterior circulation stroke (A stroke gives a normal head impulse test)
x: Ruled out here: requires brief spells on turning in bed, whereas this patient has cold a week ago, hearing is normal.
Ruled out here: requires the same story with sudden hearing loss, whereas this patient has cold a week ago, hearing is normal.
Ménière's attacks last hours with hearing loss and tinnitus; his vertigo is constant and his hearing normal.
A stroke gives a normal head impulse test.

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man with hypertension has had continuous vertigo for 6 hours. He is vomiting and cannot walk unaided.
The head impulse test is normal. The nystagmus changes direction with gaze. There is a vertical skew deviation on cover testing.
hq_q.w: HINTS: in acute vertigo, a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation suggests a central cause such as cerebellar stroke.
hq_q.f: An abnormal head impulse with one-direction nystagmus and no skew → vestibular neuritis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?

tm.m: A normal head impulse in acute vertigo means the inner ear is working
tm.g: Normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus and skew is a posterior circulation stroke
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV causes brief episodes, not continuous vertigo)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Labyrinthitis (Labyrinthitis gives an abnormal head impulse test and hearing loss; his normal head impulse is a central sign)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ménière's disease (Ménière's attacks come with tinnitus and hearing loss; skew and direction-changing nystagmus are central signs)
an abnormal head impulse, one-direction nystagmus and no skew
x: BPPV causes brief episodes, not continuous vertigo.
Labyrinthitis gives an abnormal head impulse test and hearing loss; his normal head impulse is a central sign.
Ménière's attacks come with tinnitus and hearing loss; skew and direction-changing nystagmus are central signs.
Ruled out here: requires an abnormal head impulse, one-direction nystagmus and no skew, whereas this patient has hypertension, head impulse test is normal.

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old man presents to the emergency department with a 12 hour history of worsening severe sore throat, odynophagia, a muffled voice, and inability to swallow his own saliva.
Temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and SpO2 95% on air. He is sitting upright leaning forward and has soft inspiratory stridor.
o: Lie him flat for a chest X-ray
hq_q.w: Acute epiglottitis or supraglottitis with stridor and drooling is an immediate life-threatening airway emergency. Summon the senior anaesthetic and ENT airway team at once to secure the airway under controlled conditions before attempting examination or radiography.
hq_q.f: A 2-year-old with a barking cough and a cold → croup, oral dexamethasone.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first step?

c: inability to swallow his own saliva
tm.m: Rapidly progressive inflammatory oedema of the supraglottis can precipitate sudden complete airway occlusion
tm.g: Suspected acute epiglottitis with drooling and stridor -> call senior airway team immediately
f: a systemically well young adult with sore throat, no stridor and normal swallowing
a stable patient without stridor or drooling where airway specialists are already at the bedside
never appropriate in acute upper airway obstruction where the patient splints the airway upright
uncomplicated acute streptococcal tonsillitis with a FeverPAIN score of 4 and no airway signs
x: Inspecting the pharynx with a tongue depressor can trigger vagal laryngospasm and immediate complete airway obstruction.
Transferring an unstable stridulous patient to radiology for a lateral neck radiograph risks fatal airway arrest outside resus.
Laying a patient with acute supraglottic oedema flat allows the swollen epiglottis to fall posteriorly and occlude the glottis.
Discharging or giving oral antibiotics is dangerous because the patient cannot swallow and requires emergency airway protection and IV ceftriaxone.

hq_q.s:
A 3 year old boy whose parents declined all routine childhood vaccinations is brought to the emergency department with a 6 hour history of high fever, severe odynophagia, drooling, and soft inspiratory stridor.
Temperature is 39.7°C and pulse rate is 162 bpm. He is sitting upright in the tripod position looking toxic and refusing to lie down.
hq_q.w: Before routine conjugate Hib vaccination, Haemophilus influenzae type b was the classic cause of acute childhood epiglottitis. Conjugate vaccination has markedly reduced paediatric cases, though unvaccinated children remain at high risk.
hq_q.f: Barking cough after a cold in a toddler → parainfluenza virus croup.
hq_q.ql: Which organism classically caused epiglottitis in children before routine vaccination?

tm.m: Capsulated Haemophilus influenzae type b invades the supraglottic mucosa, causing rapid cellulitic oedema
tm.g: Classic bacterial cause of acute childhood epiglottitis in unvaccinated children -> Haemophilus influenzae type b
f: a toddler with a seal-like barking cough, hoarse voice and coryzal prodrome without drooling
a 4 month old infant with coryza, tachypnoea, chest recession and widespread fine crackles
secondary bacterial tracheitis with thick purulent tracheal membranes in a child worsening after croup
acute purulent otitis media and lobar pneumonia in a child
x: Parainfluenza virus causes subglottic viral laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) with a barking cough rather than toxic bacterial epiglottitis.
Respiratory syncytial virus causes lower respiratory tract bronchiolitis in infants with fine crackles and wheeze.
Staphylococcus aureus is associated with bacterial tracheitis following viral croup rather than classic primary epiglottitis.
Streptococcus pneumoniae can cause adult supraglottitis or acute otitis media, whereas Haemophilus influenzae type b was the classic childhood pathogen.

hq_q.s:
A 4 year old boy has had a high fever and stridor for 6 hours. He is drooling. His airway is stable and has been secured by the anaesthetist.
A lateral neck X-ray shows a swollen epiglottis that looks like a thumb.
hq_q.w: The thumb sign is a swollen epiglottis on a lateral film. Imaging is only done if the airway is safe.
hq_q.f: A tapered narrowing below the cords on the front view → steeple sign, croup.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: A swollen epiglottis looks like a thumb on a lateral X-ray
tm.g: The thumb sign is epiglottitis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Bacterial tracheitis (Tracheitis follows a croup-like illness with a brassy cough; a swollen thumb-shaped epiglottis is epiglottitis)
a tapered narrowing below the cords on the front view
suddenly began coughing and choking + small toys
the presentation instead showed features specific to Retropharyngeal abscess (A retropharyngeal abscess widens the space behind the pharynx)
x: Tracheitis follows a croup-like illness with a brassy cough; a swollen thumb-shaped epiglottis is epiglottitis.
Ruled out here: requires a tapered narrowing below the cords on the front view, whereas this patient has drooling, thumb.
Ruled out here: requires suddenly began coughing and choking + small toys, whereas this patient has drooling, thumb.
A retropharyngeal abscess widens the space behind the pharynx.

hq_q.s:
A 15 year old boy attends the walk-in centre with brisk fresh bleeding from his right nostril that started spontaneously 5 minutes ago after blowing his nose. He is otherwise healthy, has no bleeding disorder, and takes no regular medications.
On examination, he is alert with pulse rate 78 bpm and blood pressure 118/72 mmHg.
o: Apply an ice pack to the back of the neck
Lean forward, pinch the soft nose
Lie him flat with his legs elevated
Pack the nostril tightly with dry tissue paper
Tilt his head backwards and pinch the bridge
hq_q.w: First-aid management of acute anterior epistaxis is to sit upright leaning slightly forward (to prevent swallowing or aspirating blood) and pinch the soft cartilaginous lower part of the nose firmly for 10 to 15 minutes.
hq_q.f: Still bleeding after 15 minutes → cautery if a bleeding point is seen, otherwise nasal packing.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first aid?

c: fresh bleeding from his right nostril
tm.m: Direct digital compression of the cartilaginous alae tamponades bleeding vessels on the anterior septum (Little's area)
tm.g: First aid for acute anterior epistaxis -> sit upright, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose
f: used only as an optional adjunct alongside continuous firm pinching of the soft lower nose
hypovolaemic syncope once the airway is protected and active nasal bleeding is controlled
formal anterior nasal tamponade with a lubricated Rapid Rhino or Merocel pack if pinching fails
never appropriate because pinching the nasal bones does not compress Kiesselbach's plexus
x: Applying ice to the neck does not tamponade bleeding vessels in Little's area without direct compression of the soft nose.
Lying supine in a normotensive patient causes blood to pool in the posterior pharynx, provoking vomiting and airway aspiration.
Stuffing dry tissue into the nose abrades the fragile septal mucosa and avulses any forming clot when pulled out.
Tilting the head back directs blood into the pharynx and pinching the bony nasal bridge fails to compress the anterior septum.

hq_q.s: A 14 year old girl has frequent nosebleeds from one side. They stop with pressure.
o: Ethmoidal arteries in the nasal roof
Little's area on the anterior septum
hq_q.w: About 90% come from Little's area, where several arteries join on the front of the septum.
hq_q.f: An older person on anticoagulants bleeding down the back of the throat despite an anterior pack → posterior bleed from the sphenopalatine artery.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely source of the bleeding?

tm.m: Several arteries join at the front of the septum
tm.g: Most nosebleeds come from Little's area on the anterior septum
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Ethmoidal arteries in the nasal roof (Ethmoidal arteries are a rare source)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Inferior turbinate (The turbinate is not the main source)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Posterior nasopharynx (Posterior bleeds are rarer and occur in older people)
an older patient bleeding down the throat despite an anterior pack
x: Ethmoidal arteries are a rare source.
The turbinate is not the main source.
Posterior bleeds are rarer and occur in older people.
Ruled out here: requires an older patient bleeding down the throat despite an anterior pack, whereas this patient has one side, stop with pressure.

hq_q.s: A 10 year old boy has recurrent nosebleeds from his left nostril. He has had silver nitrate cautery today. He has a peanut allergy.
hq_q.w: Naseptin, chlorhexidine with neomycin, contains arachis oil from peanuts, so it is avoided in peanut or soya allergy.
hq_q.f: No allergy → Naseptin for 10 days.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate antiseptic cream?

tm.m: Naseptin contains arachis oil
tm.g: Peanut allergy: use mupirocin instead of Naseptin
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Clotrimazole (Clotrimazole is an antifungal)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fusidic acid (Fusidic acid is not the recommended alternative)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hydrocortisone (A steroid cream has no antiseptic action; mupirocin replaces Naseptin when there is a peanut allergy)
no allergy
x: Clotrimazole is an antifungal.
Fusidic acid is not the recommended alternative.
A steroid cream has no antiseptic action; mupirocin replaces Naseptin when there is a peanut allergy.
Ruled out here: requires no allergy, whereas this patient has peanut allergy, A 10 year old boy has.

hq_q.s:
A 17 year old girl presents to her GP with a 7 day history of severe sore throat, fevers, aching muscles, and profound lethargy. Five days of amoxicillin prescribed at an urgent care clinic caused a widespread maculopapular rash.
Temperature is 38.2°C. Examination shows enlarged tonsils with grey-white exudate, tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and a palpable spleen tip.
hq_q.w: Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis presents in teenagers and young adults with the triad of fever, exudative pharyngitis, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, accompanied by profound fatigue, splenomegaly, and a classic maculopapular rash if exposed to amoxicillin.
hq_q.f: High fever, exudate and tender front neck nodes with no cough or tiredness → bacterial tonsillitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Epstein-Barr virus infects oropharyngeal B lymphocytes, causing generalized reticuloendothelial hyperplasia and splenomegaly
tm.g: Exudative tonsillitis + posterior cervical lymphadenopathy + splenomegaly + amoxicillin rash -> infectious mononucleosis
f: painless posterior cervical lymphadenopathy without exudative tonsillitis after eating undercooked lamb
fever, oral and genital mucocutaneous ulcers and diarrhoea 3 weeks after condomless sex
acute purulent tonsillitis with tender anterior jugulodigastric nodes, no splenomegaly and rapid response to penicillin
prolonged fever, mild transaminitis and atypical lymphocytosis with a normal non-exudative pharynx
x: Immunocompetent toxoplasmosis typically presents with painless isolated cervical lymphadenopathy after eating undercooked meat rather than exudative tonsillitis.
Primary HIV seroconversion causes fever, mucocutaneous ulceration, and a truncal maculopapular rash rather than thick grey-white tonsillar exudates.
Streptococcal tonsillitis causes anterior jugulodigastric lymphadenopathy without splenomegaly, posterior cervical nodes, or an amoxicillin rash.
Cytomegalovirus causes prolonged fever and mild hepatitis with minimal pharyngitis and rarely produces severe exudative tonsillitis.

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old man had a sore throat and was given amoxicillin 2 days ago. He now has a widespread itchy red rash. He has also been very tired for a week.
Temperature 37.9°C. There is a widespread maculopapular rash. There are tender posterior neck lymph nodes. There is no lip swelling or mucosal involvement.
o: Scarlet fever from group A strep
hq_q.w: Most people with glandular fever get a rash with amoxicillin. It is not true allergy, which is why amoxicillin is avoided for sore throats.
hq_q.f: Rash after penicillin V without glandular fever features → possible true allergy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely explanation?

c: no lip swelling or mucosal involvement
