tm.m: Amoxicillin in EBV infection triggers a widespread rash that is not true allergy
tm.g: Rash after amoxicillin with glandular fever features is glandular fever with amoxicillin
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Measles (Measles brings cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with a rash spreading from behind the ears, not a rash after amoxicillin)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Scarlet fever from group A strep (Scarlet fever causes a sandpaper rash)
mucosal erosions with skin detachment after a new drug
a rash after penicillin V with no glandular fever features
x: Measles brings cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with a rash spreading from behind the ears, not a rash after amoxicillin.
Scarlet fever causes a sandpaper rash.
Ruled out here: requires mucosal erosions with skin detachment after a new drug, whereas this patient has given amoxicillin 2 days ago, very tired for a week.
Ruled out here: requires a rash after penicillin V with no glandular fever features, whereas this patient has given amoxicillin 2 days ago, very tired for a week.

hq_q.s:
A 16 year old girl presents with a 3 day history of severe sore throat, fever, malaise, and tender lumps down the back of her neck.
Temperature is 38.0°C. Examination reveals bilateral tonsillar hypertrophy with palatal petechiae and tender posterior triangle cervical lymphadenopathy. Full blood count shows lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, but a heterophile antibody (Monospot) test is negative.
o: Bone marrow aspirate and blood film
Throat swab for routine bacterial culture
hq_q.w: Heterophile antibody (Monospot) tests have a 25% false-negative rate during the first week of infectious mononucleosis because IgM heterophile antibodies take time to rise. EBV-specific viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM and IgG serology confirms acute infection.
hq_q.f: Monospot positive in the second week → confirms the diagnosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Heterophile antibodies often remain undetectable during week 1, whereas EBV viral capsid antigen IgM rises early
tm.g: Suspected infectious mononucleosis in week 1 with negative Monospot -> EBV-specific antibody testing
f: unexplained pancytopenia, circulating blasts and suspected acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
negative EBV viral capsid antigen IgM and positive EBNA IgG confirming past immunity rather than acute infection
never appropriate when infectious mononucleosis is suspected because amoxicillin triggers a widespread drug rash
suspected scarlet fever or persistent bacterial tonsillitis without posterior cervical nodes or atypical lymphocytosis
x: Atypical lymphocytes are already demonstrated on the blood count, and invasive marrow sampling is unnecessary in typical early EBV.
Up to 25% of patients with true EBV infectious mononucleosis have a false-negative Monospot test during the first week of illness.
Antibiotics do not treat viral EBV pharyngitis, and amoxicillin precipitates a florid generalized maculopapular rash in infectious mononucleosis.
A throat swab does not detect Epstein-Barr virus and may merely grow commensal or carriage flora.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman has had episodes of vertigo lasting from minutes to several hours for a year. Some come with a throbbing headache and sensitivity to light. She has had migraines since her teens. Her hearing is normal during and between attacks.
Ear examination, audiometry and neurological examination are normal.
hq_q.w: Recurrent vertigo with migraine features (headache, light sensitivity, aura) in someone with a migraine history and normal hearing fits vestibular migraine, a common cause of recurrent vertigo.
hq_q.f: Attacks of 2 to 3 hours with fluctuating one-sided hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness → Ménière's disease.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: throbbing headache and sensitivity to light
tm.m: Migraine mechanisms disturb the vestibular nuclei and inner ear
tm.g: Recurrent vertigo + migraine features + normal hearing: vestibular migraine
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to BPPV (BPPV causes seconds-long vertigo triggered by head position, not attacks lasting hours with headache)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ménière's disease (Ménière's needs fluctuating hearing loss with tinnitus or fullness; her hearing is normal)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Vestibular neuritis (Vestibular neuritis is a single episode of constant vertigo lasting days, often after a viral illness)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Vestibular schwannoma (A vestibular schwannoma causes slowly progressive one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus, rarely episodic vertigo)
x: BPPV causes seconds-long vertigo triggered by head position, not attacks lasting hours with headache.
Ménière's needs fluctuating hearing loss with tinnitus or fullness; her hearing is normal.
Vestibular neuritis is a single episode of constant vertigo lasting days, often after a viral illness.
A vestibular schwannoma causes slowly progressive one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus, rarely episodic vertigo.

hq_q.s: A 52 year old man has Ménière's disease with attacks every few weeks. He wants to reduce the number of attacks.
hq_q.w: Betahistine is used to try to prevent attacks. Prochlorperazine or cyclizine are for the acute attack only.
hq_q.f: An attack is happening now → buccal prochlorperazine.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most commonly used?

tm.m: Betahistine may improve inner ear blood flow
tm.g: Preventing Ménière's attacks: betahistine
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amitriptyline (Amitriptyline is for neuropathic pain or migraine prevention, not Ménière's attacks)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam (Diazepam is for acute attacks)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Gentamicin injection (Gentamicin is for refractory disease)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Prochlorperazine long-term (Vestibular sedatives are ineffective in BPPV and delay central vestibular compensation)
x: Amitriptyline is for neuropathic pain or migraine prevention, not Ménière's attacks.
Diazepam is for acute attacks.
Gentamicin is for refractory disease.
Vestibular sedatives are ineffective in BPPV and delay central vestibular compensation

hq_q.s: A 48 year old teacher with established left-sided Meniere's disease attends general practice after suffering two sudden, unheralded episodes of disabling rotational vertigo and falls over the past 3 weeks. She gets no warning aura before an attack and drives a car 20 miles to school each day.
o: Continue driving during daylight hours only
Drive only on short local familiar roads
No driving restriction is required for Group 1
Notify her motor insurer and continue driving
Stop driving and tell the DVLA
hq_q.w: Under DVLA fitness-to-drive regulations, Group 1 and Group 2 drivers who experience sudden, unprovoked or unheralded attacks of disabling dizziness or vertigo must stop driving immediately and inform the DVLA until attacks are satisfactorily controlled.
hq_q.f: Attacks are controlled with warning symptoms → driving can restart once the DVLA agrees.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate advice about driving?

c: unheralded episodes of disabling rotational vertigo
tm.m: Unheralded labyrinthine crises cause sudden loss of postural and visual stability at the wheel
tm.g: Unheralded disabling vertigo in a car driver -> stop driving immediately and notify the DVLA
f: mild night-time glare with preserved daytime visual acuity and no vestibular symptoms
never permissible when a driver suffers unheralded disabling vertigo attacks
brief positional vertigo occurring only when rolling over in bed that never occurs while seated upright driving
a stable medical condition that does not impair driving safety or require DVLA notification
x: Sudden unheralded disabling vertigo can occur at any hour and prohibits all driving regardless of daylight.
Loss of control during an acute rotational vertigo attack is hazardous on local streets just as on motorways.
Uncontrolled sudden disabling dizziness disqualifies both Group 1 (car) and Group 2 (lorry/bus) licence holders.
Notifying an insurer does not override the statutory requirement to cease driving and report disabling vertigo to the DVLA.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old man is referred to the sleep clinic because of loud nocturnal snoring, witnessed apnoeic pauses reported by his wife, unrefreshing sleep, and nodding off in daytime meetings.
His BMI is 34 kg/m², collar size is 44 cm, and Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 15/24. Overnight sleep polygraphy records an apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) of 34 events per hour.
hq_q.w: In adults, obstructive sleep apnoea severity on sleep polygraphy is graded by the apnoea-hypopnoea index (events per hour): normal is under 5, mild is 5 to 14, moderate is 15 to 30, and severe is over 30.
hq_q.f: AHI of 8 → mild.
hq_q.ql: How is his obstructive sleep apnoea classed?

tm.m: More than 30 obstructive apnoeas or hypopnoeas per hour defines severe obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome
tm.g: Apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) >30 events/hour -> severe obstructive sleep apnoea
f: Cheyne-Stokes periodic breathing with absent thoracoabdominal effort in severe left ventricular failure
overnight sleep polygraphy showing an apnoea-hypopnoea index of 9 events per hour
overnight sleep polygraphy showing an apnoea-hypopnoea index of 22 events per hour
primary simple snoring with an apnoea-hypopnoea index of 2 events per hour
x: Central sleep apnoea is characterised by cessation of respiratory effort without snoring or thoracoabdominal paradox, typically in heart failure or brainstem lesions.
Mild obstructive sleep apnoea is defined by an apnoea-hypopnoea index between 5 and 14 events per hour.
Moderate obstructive sleep apnoea is defined by an apnoea-hypopnoea index between 15 and 30 events per hour.
A normal adult sleep study has an apnoea-hypopnoea index of fewer than 5 events per hour.

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old man snores loudly and his partner has seen him stop breathing at night. He falls asleep in meetings. He has hypertension.
BMI 36 kg/m². Neck circumference 45 cm. Epworth sleepiness score 16.
hq_q.w: NICE advises home respiratory polygraphy (a home sleep study recording airflow, breathing effort and oxygen saturation) to confirm obstructive sleep apnoea and give an apnoea-hypopnoea index.
hq_q.f: Sleepiness with cataplexy and normal breathing at night → multiple sleep latency test for narcolepsy.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?

tm.m: The upper airway collapses repeatedly in sleep, causing apnoeas and oxygen dips
tm.g: Suspected OSA: home sleep study
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Arterial blood gas (A blood gas may show hypercapnia in obesity hypoventilation, but it does not diagnose OSA)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Echocardiogram (An echocardiogram looks for complications such as pulmonary hypertension, not OSA itself)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Multiple sleep latency test (The multiple sleep latency test is used for narcolepsy, not to count apnoeas)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Spirometry (Spirometry measures airflow obstruction in the lungs while awake, not airway collapse in sleep)
x: A blood gas may show hypercapnia in obesity hypoventilation, but it does not diagnose OSA.
An echocardiogram looks for complications such as pulmonary hypertension, not OSA itself.
The multiple sleep latency test is used for narcolepsy, not to count apnoeas.
Spirometry measures airflow obstruction in the lungs while awake, not airway collapse in sleep.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old municipal bus driver (Group 2 licence) attends his GP reporting 4 months of loud snoring, morning headaches, and severe daytime drowsiness. Last week he briefly nodded off while stopped at traffic lights.
His BMI is 35 kg/m² and Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 17/24. Urgent sleep clinic polygraphy has been requested for suspected obstructive sleep apnoea.
o: Continue driving on morning shifts only
No notification needed until sleep study results
Stop driving and tell the DVLA
Take strong caffeine before each bus shift
Tell his employer but continue driving
hq_q.w: Any driver – and especially a Group 2 bus or lorry driver – with suspected or confirmed obstructive sleep apnoea causing excessive daytime sleepiness must stop driving immediately and notify the DVLA until the condition is investigated and satisfactorily controlled.
hq_q.f: OSA without excessive sleepiness → no need to stop driving.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate advice?

c: nodded off while stopped at traffic lights
tm.m: Untreated sleepiness in a Group 2 public service vehicle driver carries an immediate risk of high-fatality road accidents
tm.g: Excessive daytime sleepiness with suspected OSA in a bus driver -> stop driving and notify the DVLA
f: never permissible when a professional driver has excessive daytime somnolence
asymptomatic snoring without daytime sleepiness or nodding off at the wheel
never an acceptable substitute for driving cessation in sleepy obstructive sleep apnoea
a musculoskeletal back strain requiring seat adjustment that does not affect alertness
x: Uncontrolled sleepiness from sleep apnoea impairs vigilance at all times of day, including morning shifts.
Waiting for formal sleep study confirmation before stopping driving is unsafe when excessive sleepiness is already present.
Stimulants do not prevent microsleeps in untreated sleep apnoea and cannot substitute for stopping driving.
While he should inform his employer for occupational adjustments, he must cease driving immediately and notify the DVLA.

hq_q.s:
A 25 year old woman is a keen swimmer. She has had an itchy, painful right ear with discharge for 4 days. She is otherwise well.
Temperature 36.9°C. Pulling the pinna hurts. The ear canal is red and swollen with debris. The drum is intact. There is no spreading redness.
hq_q.w: Uncomplicated acute diffuse otitis externa (commonly seen in swimmers) is treated first line with a topical antibiotic-corticosteroid combination drop (such as ciprofloxacin-dexamethasone or acetic acid/neomycin-steroid when the tympanic membrane is intact) for 7 days alongside water precautions.
hq_q.f: The drum is perforated → avoid aminoglycoside drops; use ciprofloxacin drops.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Maceration of canal skin allows Pseudomonas or Staphylococcus infection; topical antibiotic-steroid drops eradicate bacteria and reduce canal oedema
tm.g: Uncomplicated acute otitis externa with intact drum and no cellulitis -> topical antibiotic and steroid drops
f: persistent ear itch after prolonged antibacterial drops with fluffy white debris and black fungal spores
simple impacted cerumen causing conductive hearing loss with normal uninflamed canal skin
acute otitis media in a toddler with bilateral bulging tympanic membranes and high fever
severe unrelenting night otalgia and granulation tissue at the bone-cartilage junction in an elderly diabetic
x: Topical clotrimazole drops are reserved for fungal otomycosis, which shows fluffy white hyphae or black Aspergillus spores on otoscopy.
Aural toilet alone without topical antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory drops fails to eradicate active bacterial canal wall infection.
Oral amoxicillin does not cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa and systemic antibiotics are unnecessary without spreading pinna cellulitis.
Oral ciprofloxacin is reserved for spreading cellulitis beyond the ear canal or suspected malignant (necrotising) otitis externa in diabetes.

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old woman used antibiotic ear drops for a week for otitis externa. Her ear is now very itchy, but less painful.
The ear canal contains white, fluffy debris with black dots. The drum is intact.
hq_q.w: Antibiotic drops can lead to fungal infection, often Aspergillus or Candida. Treat with clotrimazole drops and clean the ear.
hq_q.f: Painful canal with green pus → bacterial, often Pseudomonas.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: antibiotic ear drops for a week
white, fluffy debris with black dots
tm.m: Antibiotic drops let fungi such as Aspergillus overgrow
tm.g: Fluffy debris with black dots after antibiotic drops is fungal otitis externa
f: a painful canal with green pus
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cholesteatoma (Cholesteatoma is a painless smelly discharge with attic debris, not fluffy white debris after antibiotic drops)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Malignant otitis externa (Malignant otitis externa causes severe pain in diabetes)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Wax impaction (Wax is brown, not fluffy with black dots)
x: Ruled out here: requires a painful canal with green pus, whereas this patient has antibiotic ear drops for a week, white, fluffy debris with black dots.
Cholesteatoma is a painless smelly discharge with attic debris, not fluffy white debris after antibiotic drops.
Malignant otitis externa causes severe pain in diabetes.
Wax is brown, not fluffy with black dots.

hq_q.s:
A 78 year old man with type 2 diabetes has had severe pain in his right ear for 6 weeks, worse at night. Antibiotic drops have not helped. His face has started to droop on the right.
There is granulation tissue in the floor of the ear canal. There is right lower motor neurone facial weakness.
CRP 64 mg/L (<5).
hq_q.w: Malignant otitis externa is Pseudomonas spreading into the skull base in older diabetic people. Pain at night, granulation tissue and nerve palsies. It needs IV antibiotics and imaging.
hq_q.f: A young swimmer with pain on moving the pinna → ordinary otitis externa.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Pseudomonas spreads from the canal into the skull base in diabetics
tm.g: A diabetic with night ear pain, granulation and a facial palsy has malignant otitis externa
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Acute mastoiditis (Mastoiditis pushes the pinna forward with swelling behind the ear, usually in a child after otitis media)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cholesteatoma (Cholesteatoma is painless; severe night pain with facial weakness in a diabetic is malignant otitis externa)
vesicles in the ear canal
a young swimmer with pain on moving the pinna
x: Mastoiditis pushes the pinna forward with swelling behind the ear, usually in a child after otitis media.
Cholesteatoma is painless; severe night pain with facial weakness in a diabetic is malignant otitis externa.
Ruled out here: requires vesicles in the ear canal, whereas this patient has type 2 diabetes, worse at night.
Ruled out here: requires a young swimmer with pain on moving the pinna, whereas this patient has type 2 diabetes, worse at night.

hq_q.s:
A 3 year old girl is brought to general practice with a 2 day history of left earache after a viral cold. She is eating and drinking well, has not vomited, and has no ear discharge.
Temperature is 38.0°C. She is alert and playing in the consulting room. Otoscopy shows a red, bulging, intact left tympanic membrane with a normal right ear and no mastoid tenderness.
hq_q.w: Under NICE guideline NG91, most systemically well children over 2 years with unilateral acute otitis media without otorrhoea recover within 3 days without antibiotics. Regular analgesia with no immediate antibiotic avoids unnecessary side effects.
hq_q.f: Under 2 with infection in both ears, or with discharge → amoxicillin for 5 days.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Most uncomplicated acute otitis media in immunocompetent children resolves spontaneously within 72 hours
tm.g: Systemically well child >=2 years with unilateral AOM and no discharge -> regular analgesia and no immediate antibiotic
f: bilateral glue ear persisting for over 3 months with a 30 dB conductive hearing loss
purulent discharge in the ear canal from a perforated tympanic membrane or bilateral AOM in a 14 month old
acute viral croup presenting with a seal-like barking cough and inspiratory stridor
tender boggy swelling over the mastoid process pushing the pinna forwards and downwards
x: Grommets are surgical ventilation tubes for chronic otitis media with effusion persisting over 3 months, not acute otitis media.
Immediate oral amoxicillin is indicated for children under 2 years with bilateral acute otitis media, any child with otorrhoea, or systemic toxicity.
Systemic corticosteroids provide no clinical benefit in acute otitis media and are not recommended.
Same-day hospital referral is reserved for systemic sepsis or suspected acute mastoiditis with post-auricular swelling and pinna protrusion.

hq_q.s:
A 4 year old boy is brought to his GP because his nursery staff noticed over the past month that he sits very close to the television and frequently asks for instructions to be repeated. He has had no earache, fever, or discharge.
Both tympanic membranes are dull grey and retracted with absent light reflexes, and tympanometry shows flat type B traces bilaterally.
hq_q.w: Newly identified otitis media with effusion (glue ear) resolves spontaneously within 3 months in over 50% of children. NICE recommends a 3 month period of active observation with repeat audiometry and tympanometry before considering referral for grommets.
hq_q.f: Persists over 3 months with hearing loss in both ears → grommets.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Eustachian tube maturation allows most middle-ear serous effusions to clear spontaneously within 12 weeks
tm.g: Newly diagnosed bilateral glue ear without severe developmental disability -> active observation and review in 3 months
f: persistent glue ear requiring repeat grommet surgery accompanied by chronic nasal obstruction
acute suppurative otitis media with high fever and purulent discharge from the ear canal
bilateral conductive hearing loss still present at the 3 month follow-up audiogram
acute severe asthma exacerbation with hypoxia and widespread expiratory wheeze
x: Adenoidectomy is only considered alongside grommet insertion when chronic glue ear persists and causes recurrent upper respiratory symptoms.
Oral antibiotics are ineffective in sterile non-suppurative otitis media with effusion and are not recommended by NICE.
Immediate grommet surgery skips the mandatory 3 month active observation period during which most effusions resolve naturally.
Oral corticosteroids have no lasting benefit in otitis media with effusion and expose children to systemic side effects.

hq_q.s:
A 50 year old man of southern Chinese family origin has had a blocked feeling in his left ear for 2 months. He has noticed a lump in his neck. He has not had a cold.
There is a dull left ear drum with fluid behind it. There is a hard, non-tender lymph node in the upper left neck.
o: Eustachian tube dysfunction after a cold
hq_q.w: A new one-sided middle ear effusion in an adult can be a tumour blocking the Eustachian tube. The postnasal space must be examined.
hq_q.f: A child with glue ear in both ears after colds → otitis media with effusion.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important cause to exclude?

c: blocked feeling in his left ear
tm.m: A nasopharyngeal tumour blocks the Eustachian tube and spreads to neck nodes
tm.g: A one-sided adult middle ear effusion with a neck node: exclude nasopharyngeal carcinoma
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Acoustic neuroma (An acoustic neuroma causes sensorineural loss, not a middle ear effusion with a neck node)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cholesteatoma (Cholesteatoma gives a smelly discharge, not an effusion with a hard neck node)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Eustachian tube dysfunction after a cold (He has had no cold)
a child with glue ear in both ears after colds
x: An acoustic neuroma causes sensorineural loss, not a middle ear effusion with a neck node.
Cholesteatoma gives a smelly discharge, not an effusion with a hard neck node.
He has had no cold.
Ruled out here: requires a child with glue ear in both ears after colds, whereas this patient has southern Chinese, blocked feeling in his left ear.

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman has had a blocked nose and facial pain for 5 days after a cold. She is otherwise well.
Temperature 37.4°C. There is mild tenderness over the cheeks. There is no swelling around the eyes.
hq_q.w: Acute sinusitis is usually viral and gets better within 2 to 3 weeks. Antibiotics are not needed in the first 10 days.
hq_q.f: Symptoms beyond 10 days → a high-dose nasal steroid for 14 days, with a back-up antibiotic.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Acute sinusitis is usually viral and settles within 2 to 3 weeks
tm.g: Sinusitis for under 10 days: self-care with analgesia
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amoxicillin (Sinusitis for under 10 days is usually viral; antibiotics are not needed)
the presentation instead showed features specific to CT sinuses (CT is not needed for acute sinusitis)
symptoms beyond 10 days
the presentation instead showed features specific to Phenoxymethylpenicillin (Antibiotics are for symptoms over 10 days)
x: Sinusitis for under 10 days is usually viral; antibiotics are not needed.
CT is not needed for acute sinusitis.
Ruled out here: requires symptoms beyond 10 days, whereas this patient has 5 days, no swelling around the eyes.
Antibiotics are for symptoms over 10 days.

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old man has had sinusitis for 12 days. It is getting worse rather than better. He is systemically well and not at high risk of complications. He has no drug allergies.
Temperature 37.8°C. There is facial tenderness and purulent nasal discharge. There are no eye or neurological signs.
hq_q.w: NICE first choice for acute sinusitis needing an antibiotic is phenoxymethylpenicillin for 5 days. Key discriminator: Sinusitis needing an antibiotic: phenoxymethylpenicillin.
hq_q.f: Penicillin allergy → doxycycline or clarithromycin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-choice antibiotic?

tm.m: Phenoxymethylpenicillin covers the usual sinus pathogens narrowly
tm.g: Sinusitis needing an antibiotic: phenoxymethylpenicillin
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amoxicillin (Amoxicillin works, but NICE names phenoxymethylpenicillin first for sinusitis)
penicillin allergy
systemically very unwell or at high risk
the presentation instead showed features specific to Doxycycline 200 mg then 100 mg (Doxycycline is the choice for penicillin allergy; he has none)
x: Amoxicillin works, but NICE names phenoxymethylpenicillin first for sinusitis.
Ruled out here: requires penicillin allergy, whereas this patient has 12 days, getting worse rather than better.
Ruled out here: requires systemically very unwell or at high risk, whereas this patient has 12 days, getting worse rather than better.
Doxycycline is the choice for penicillin allergy; he has none.

hq_q.s:
A 63 year old man worked in a furniture factory sanding hardwood for 30 years. He has had a blocked left nostril for 3 months with bloody discharge, and his left cheek is numb.
There is a friable mass in the left nasal cavity and reduced sensation over the left cheek.
hq_q.w: Hardwood dust raises the risk of sinonasal adenocarcinoma (intestinal type, usually in the ethmoid) many times over. Squamous cell carcinoma is commoner overall, but the occupational link points to adenocarcinoma. He needs a suspected cancer referral.
hq_q.f: Nickel refinery worker or heavy smoker with a maxillary sinus mass → squamous cell carcinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which type of cancer is most likely?

tm.m: Wood dust settles in the upper nose and drives metaplasia of the ethmoid lining
tm.g: Hardwood dust + one-sided nasal mass: adenocarcinoma
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Mucosal melanoma (Mucosal melanoma is rare, often pigmented, and has no link to wood dust)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is linked to EBV and southern Chinese origin and often presents with a neck lump or glue ear)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Olfactory neuroblastoma (Olfactory neuroblastoma arises high in the nasal roof, causes loss of smell and has no occupational link)

the presentation instead showed features specific to Squamous cell carcinoma (Squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest sinonasal cancer overall, linked to smoking and nickel, but hardwood dust points to adenocarcinoma)
x: Mucosal melanoma is rare, often pigmented, and has no link to wood dust.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is linked to EBV and southern Chinese origin and often presents with a neck lump or glue ear.
Olfactory neuroblastoma arises high in the nasal roof, causes loss of smell and has no occupational link.
Squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest sinonasal cancer overall, linked to smoking and nickel, but hardwood dust points to adenocarcinoma.

hq_q.s:
A 22 year old woman attends general practice with a 2 day history of severe sore throat and painful swallowing that started rapidly over 24 hours. She has no cough or coryzal symptoms.
Temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 84 bpm. She is able to swallow fluids, has no stridor or trismus, and examination reveals markedly inflamed tonsils coated in purulent exudate, giving a FeverPAIN score of 4.
hq_q.w: Under NICE guideline NG84, a FeverPAIN score of 4 or 5 indicates a high likelihood of streptococcal tonsillitis, warranting an immediate antibiotic prescription (first-line oral phenoxymethylpenicillin for 5 to 10 days) or a back-up prescription.
hq_q.f: FeverPAIN of 1 → no antibiotic.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: markedly inflamed tonsils coated in purulent exudate
tm.m: High FeverPAIN score (fever, purulence, rapid attendance, severe inflammation, no cough) predicts Streptococcus pyogenes infection
tm.g: Uncomplicated acute tonsillitis with FeverPAIN score 4 or 5 -> oral phenoxymethylpenicillin
f: inability to swallow fluids with trismus, a muffled voice and unilateral peritonsillar swelling
a mild sore throat accompanied by cough and runny nose with a FeverPAIN score of 1
persistent tonsillitis failing empirical penicillin therapy or an institutional scarlet fever outbreak
seven documented episodes of disabling acute tonsillitis over the past 12 months
x: Hospital admission for intravenous antibiotics is unnecessary because she can swallow oral fluids and has no airway compromise or quinsy.
Withholding antibiotics completely is recommended for a FeverPAIN score of 0 or 1 rather than a score of 4.
Routine throat swab culture delays symptom relief and is not required before treating a clinical FeverPAIN score of 4.
Elective tonsillectomy referral is reserved for recurrent disabling tonsillitis meeting Paradise criteria (such as 7 episodes in 1 year).

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old man has bacterial tonsillitis and needs an antibiotic. He has no drug allergies. Glandular fever has not been excluded.
Temperature 38.4°C. There is tonsillar exudate and tender anterior neck nodes. He has no cough.
hq_q.w: Phenoxymethylpenicillin for 5 to 10 days. Amoxicillin is avoided because of the rash in glandular fever.
hq_q.f: Penicillin allergy → clarithromycin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?

c: Glandular fever has not been excluded
tm.m: Amoxicillin causes a rash in glandular fever
tm.g: Tonsillitis needing an antibiotic: phenoxymethylpenicillin
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amoxicillin (Causes a widespread maculopapular rash if the patient has underlying glandular fever)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Clarithromycin for 5 days (Clarithromycin is for penicillin allergy; he has none)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Co-amoxiclav (Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin, which causes a rash if this is glandular fever)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Flucloxacillin (Flucloxacillin targets staphylococci; tonsillitis is streptococcal)
x: Causes a widespread maculopapular rash if the patient has underlying glandular fever
Clarithromycin is for penicillin allergy; he has none.
Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin, which causes a rash if this is glandular fever.
Flucloxacillin targets staphylococci; tonsillitis is streptococcal.

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old man has had a sore throat for 5 days that is worse on the right. He cannot open his mouth fully and is struggling to swallow his saliva.
Temperature 38.6°C, SpO2 98% breathing air. His voice is muffled. The right soft palate bulges and the uvula is pushed to the left. There is no stridor.
o: Oral penicillin and review in 48 hours
hq_q.w: A peritonsillar abscess needs the pus drained (needle aspiration or incision under local anaesthetic) with IV antibiotics such as benzylpenicillin and metronidazole, plus fluids and analgesia.
hq_q.f: Both tonsils swollen with exudate, a central uvula and no trismus → tonsillitis; antibiotics by FeverPAIN score.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: uvula is pushed to the left
tm.m: Pus collects between the tonsil capsule and the superior constrictor and does not clear with antibiotics without drainage
tm.g: Quinsy: drain it and give IV antibiotics
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Emergency tracheostomy (His airway is not obstructed; a tracheostomy is not needed)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Immediate tonsillectomy (Hot tonsillectomy is rarely done; drain first, with interval tonsillectomy for recurrent quinsy)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV dexamethasone and discharge (Steroids may ease swelling, but he needs the pus drained and admission because he cannot swallow)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral penicillin and review in 48 hours (Oral antibiotics do not clear a collection, and he cannot swallow)
x: His airway is not obstructed; a tracheostomy is not needed.
Hot tonsillectomy is rarely done; drain first, with interval tonsillectomy for recurrent quinsy.
Steroids may ease swelling, but he needs the pus drained and admission because he cannot swallow.
Oral antibiotics do not clear a collection, and he cannot swallow.

hq_q.s:
A 6 year old boy has had a painless lump in the middle of his neck for 3 months. It has slowly grown. He is otherwise well.
There is a 1.5 cm smooth, round, midline swelling just below the hyoid bone. It moves up when he sticks his tongue out. It is not tender.
hq_q.w: The thyroglossal duct runs from the tongue base to the thyroid, so the cyst is midline and rises with the tongue.
hq_q.f: A lump at the front border of sternocleidomastoid in a young adult → branchial cyst.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: moves up when he sticks his tongue out
tm.m: The thyroglossal duct remnant is attached to the tongue base
tm.g: A midline lump that rises on tongue protrusion is a thyroglossal cyst
f: a lump at the front border of sternomastoid in a young adult
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cystic hygroma (A cystic hygroma is a soft, transilluminating lump in the posterior triangle of a baby, not midline)
a midline lump that does not move with the tongue
the presentation instead showed features specific to Thyroid nodule (A thyroid nodule moves on swallowing, not on tongue protrusion)
x: Ruled out here: requires a lump at the front border of sternomastoid in a young adult, whereas this patient has middle of his neck, moves up when he sticks his tongue out.
A cystic hygroma is a soft, transilluminating lump in the posterior triangle of a baby, not midline.
Ruled out here: requires a midline lump that does not move with the tongue, whereas this patient has middle of his neck, moves up when he sticks his tongue out.
A thyroid nodule moves on swallowing, not on tongue protrusion.

hq_q.s:
A 3 week old baby boy has a firm lump on the right side of his neck, first noticed a week ago. He was born by a difficult forceps delivery. He holds his head tilted to the right with his chin turned to the left.
There is a 2 cm hard, non-tender mass within the lower right sternocleidomastoid muscle. It does not transilluminate.
hq_q.w: A sternomastoid tumour (fibromatosis colli) is a firm fibrous swelling within the muscle, often after a difficult birth, that appears in the first weeks and causes torticollis. Most settle with stretching physiotherapy.
hq_q.f: Soft, compressible swelling in the posterior triangle that transilluminates brightly → cystic hygroma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Birth injury or fetal position causes fibrosis within the muscle, which shortens it
tm.g: Newborn, hard lump in sternomastoid, torticollis: sternomastoid tumour
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Branchial cyst (A branchial cyst lies at the front border of sternocleidomastoid, usually appears in young adults and is fluctuant)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cystic hygroma (A cystic hygroma is soft, compressible and transilluminates brightly)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Reactive lymph node (A reactive node is not within the muscle and would not cause torticollis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Thyroglossal cyst (A thyroglossal cyst is midline and moves with tongue protrusion)
x: A branchial cyst lies at the front border of sternocleidomastoid, usually appears in young adults and is fluctuant.
A cystic hygroma is soft, compressible and transilluminates brightly.
A reactive node is not within the muscle and would not cause torticollis.
A thyroglossal cyst is midline and moves with tongue protrusion.

hq_q.s:
A 9 year old girl is seen in the paediatric ENT clinic with a painless 2 cm midline anterior neck swelling just below the hyoid bone that rises visibly when she swallows or protrudes her tongue. It became red and infected once last winter.
Neck ultrasound confirms a midline thyroglossal duct cyst and a normal bilobed thyroid gland in the lower neck.
hq_q.w: A thyroglossal duct cyst is excised using the Sistrunk procedure, which removes the cyst, the entire thyroglossal tract up to the foramen caecum, and the central body of the hyoid bone, reducing recurrence below 5%.
hq_q.f: The cyst is infected → antibiotics first, then surgery once settled.
hq_q.ql: Which operation is most appropriate?

tm.m: The embryological thyroglossal duct passes intimately through the central hyoid bone, which must be resected to prevent recurrence
tm.g: Definitive surgical excision of a thyroglossal duct cyst -> Sistrunk procedure
f: diagnostic fine-needle aspiration cytology of a suspicious solid solitary thyroid nodule
treating an acute erythematous cellulitic flare of the cyst prior to scheduling elective surgery
relapsed Graves' thyrotoxicosis in an adult after a course of carbimazole
excising a superficial cutaneous epidermoid cyst that has no deep embryological tract
x: Needle aspiration leaves the secretory epithelial lining and tract behind, resulting in rapid recurrence and risk of fistulation.
Prophylactic long-term antibiotics do not obliterate the congenital epithelial tract; acute antibiotics are used only before elective excision.
Radioactive iodine ablates hyperfunctioning thyroid tissue in Graves' disease or thyroid cancer and has no role in a benign thyroglossal cyst.
Simple cyst enucleation without removing the central hyoid bone leaves microscopic duct remnants and carries a recurrence rate above 40%.

hq_q.s:
A 2 year old boy has had a barking cough and a hoarse voice for a day after a cold.
Temperature 37.8°C, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, SpO2 97% breathing air. He has stridor only when upset. There is no recession and he is alert and drinking.
hq_q.w: Croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg reduces swelling. Mild croup can go home with advice.
hq_q.f: Stridor at rest with recession → nebulised adrenaline and oxygen, and admit.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Steroids reduce subglottic swelling
tm.g: Mild croup: a single dose of oral dexamethasone
f: stridor at rest with recession
the presentation instead showed features specific to Inhaled salbutamol (Salbutamol does not treat croup)
the presentation instead showed features specific to No treatment (All children with croup require a single dose of oral dexamethasone)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral amoxicillin (Croup is viral (parainfluenza virus), so antibiotics are ineffective)
x: Ruled out here: requires stridor at rest with recession, whereas this patient has barking cough, stridor only when upset.
Salbutamol does not treat croup.
All children with croup require a single dose of oral dexamethasone
Croup is viral (parainfluenza virus), so antibiotics are ineffective

hq_q.s: A 2 year old girl choked on a grape at a party. Five back blows and five abdominal thrusts have not cleared it. She has now become unresponsive and is not breathing normally.
hq_q.w: When a choking child becomes unresponsive, shout for help, open the airway, remove an object if one can be seen, give 5 rescue breaths and start CPR. Chest compressions can dislodge the object.
hq_q.f: Still conscious with an ineffective cough → back blows, then abdominal thrusts.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Chest compressions raise the pressure in the chest, acting like a stronger cough
tm.g: Unresponsive choking child: rescue breaths and CPR
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Blind finger sweep (Blind finger sweeps can push the object further in; remove it only if you can see it)
the presentation instead showed features specific to More abdominal thrusts (Abdominal thrusts are for a conscious child; once she is unresponsive, CPR replaces them)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Turn her into recovery position (She is not breathing normally, so she needs CPR, not the recovery position)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Wait for the ambulance (Waiting wastes minutes of hypoxia; CPR must start now while help comes)
x: Blind finger sweeps can push the object further in; remove it only if you can see it.
Abdominal thrusts are for a conscious child; once she is unresponsive, CPR replaces them.
She is not breathing normally, so she needs CPR, not the recovery position.
Waiting wastes minutes of hypoxia; CPR must start now while help comes.

hq_q.s:
A 5 year old boy had a sudden paroxysm of coughing and choking while eating roasted peanuts 2 days ago. Since then he has had a persistent dry cough and noisy breathing, though he is afebrile.
Respiratory rate is 28 breaths/min and SpO2 is 95% on air. Auscultation reveals diminished breath sounds and a localized monophonic wheeze over one hemithorax.
hq_q.w: Because the right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and diverges from the trachea at a more vertical angle than the left main bronchus, inhaled foreign bodies preferentially enter and lodge in the right main bronchus.
hq_q.f: An expiratory film shows one lung staying blown up → air trapping behind a ball-valve foreign body.
hq_q.ql: Where is the peanut most likely to be?

tm.m: The right main bronchus has a wider lumen and a more vertical anatomical trajectory from the carina
tm.g: Anatomical site where an inhaled foreign body most commonly lodges -> right main bronchus
f: sudden complete aphonia, severe inspiratory stridor and cyanosis immediately after choking
asked which main bronchus branches at a more acute horizontal angle above the left atrium
biphasic stridor and a palpable thud over the windpipe with symmetrical vesicular breath sounds
swallowing a coin followed by drooling, refusal of food and normal symmetrical breath sounds
x: Impact at the laryngeal inlet causes acute life-threatening inspiratory stridor, aphonia, and cyanosis rather than a unilateral chest wheeze 2 days later.
The left main bronchus branches at a sharper, more horizontal angle from the carina, making left-sided impaction less frequent.
A tracheal foreign body causes biphasic central stridor and symmetrical chest signs rather than unilateral reduced air entry.
An oesophageal foreign body causes drooling, dysphagia, and retrosternal discomfort rather than unilateral reduced air entry and bronchial wheeze.

hq_q.s: A 42 year old woman has had a red left eye for 2 days. She is deciding whether she needs to be seen today.
hq_q.w: Red flags in a red eye: reduced vision, real pain, photophobia, an abnormal pupil, a corneal opacity or contact lens wear.
hq_q.f: Normal vision, sticky discharge and no pain → conjunctivitis, managed in primary care.
hq_q.ql: Which feature most clearly means she needs same-day ophthalmology review?

tm.m: Reduced vision means the cornea, iris or pressure is involved
tm.g: A red eye with reduced visual acuity needs same-day review
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Bilateral redness (Bilateral redness suggests conjunctivitis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Gritty, sandy feeling (Grittiness suggests dry eye)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Itch (Itch suggests allergy)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Watery discharge (A watery discharge suggests a virus)
x: Bilateral redness suggests conjunctivitis.
Grittiness suggests dry eye.
Itch suggests allergy.
A watery discharge suggests a virus.

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. He noticed a bright red patch over the white of his left eye this morning. It does not hurt, his vision is normal and he has had no injury.
BP 148/88 mmHg. There is a flat, sharply edged red area over the sclera. The cornea is clear and the pupil reacts normally. Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes.
o: CT head to exclude a bleed
hq_q.w: A subconjunctival haemorrhage is harmless and clears in 2 to 3 weeks. In someone on warfarin it is a prompt to check the INR (and blood pressure), because a high INR raises the risk of serious bleeding elsewhere.
hq_q.f: Same red patch after a hammering injury → exclude a penetrating injury or foreign body.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: A fragile conjunctival vessel bleeds under the conjunctiva; anticoagulation makes this more likely
tm.g: Subconjunctival haemorrhage on warfarin: check the INR
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Chloramphenicol eye drops (There is no infection or discharge; antibiotic drops do nothing for blood under the conjunctiva)
the presentation instead showed features specific to CT head to exclude a bleed (He has no headache or neurological signs; a bleed on the eye surface does not suggest a brain bleed)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Same-day eye casualty review (A painless red patch with normal vision and a clear cornea does not need eye casualty unless there was trauma)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Stop warfarin for a week (Stopping warfarin raises his stroke risk; the dose is adjusted if the INR is high, not stopped for a harmless bleed)
x: There is no infection or discharge; antibiotic drops do nothing for blood under the conjunctiva.
He has no headache or neurological signs; a bleed on the eye surface does not suggest a brain bleed.
A painless red patch with normal vision and a clear cornea does not need eye casualty unless there was trauma.
Stopping warfarin raises his stroke risk; the dose is adjusted if the INR is high, not stopped for a harmless bleed.

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old woman sleeps in her monthly soft contact lenses. She has had a painful red right eye with thick discharge for a day. Bright light hurts.
Visual acuity is 6/24 in the right eye. There is a white corneal infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect and a small layer of pus in the anterior chamber.
hq_q.w: Pseudomonas is the commonest cause of bacterial keratitis in soft contact lens wearers, especially with overnight wear. It progresses within hours to a hypopyon and can perforate the cornea, so she needs same-day eye casualty.
hq_q.f: Lenses rinsed in tap water, pain far worse than the signs and a ring infiltrate → Acanthamoeba.
hq_q.ql: Which organism is most likely?

c: sleeps in her monthly soft contact lenses
tm.m: Lens wear injures the corneal surface and Pseudomonas from the lens case invades it
tm.g: Contact lens keratitis with fast hypopyon: Pseudomonas
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Acanthamoeba (Acanthamoeba follows tap water or swimming exposure, progresses over days to weeks and gives a ring infiltrate with pain out of proportion)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Adenovirus (Adenovirus causes a watery follicular conjunctivitis, not a corneal ulcer with pus)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Herpes simplex virus (Herpes simplex gives a dendritic ulcer, often after a cold sore, not a fast suppurative ulcer in a lens wearer)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pneumococcus can cause keratitis after corneal injury, but in soft lens wearers Pseudomonas is far more common)
x: Acanthamoeba follows tap water or swimming exposure, progresses over days to weeks and gives a ring infiltrate with pain out of proportion.
Adenovirus causes a watery follicular conjunctivitis, not a corneal ulcer with pus.
Herpes simplex gives a dendritic ulcer, often after a cold sore, not a fast suppurative ulcer in a lens wearer.
Pneumococcus can cause keratitis after corneal injury, but in soft lens wearers Pseudomonas is far more common.

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old woman has had gritty, burning eyes for 6 months. Her eyelids are crusty every morning. Her vision is normal.
The lid margins are red, with crusting at the base of the lashes. The conjunctiva is mildly red. The cornea is clear.
hq_q.w: Blepharitis is chronic: lid hygiene with warm compresses and cleaning is the mainstay, plus lubricating drops.
hq_q.f: Posterior blepharitis with rosacea not settling with lid hygiene → oral doxycycline or lymecycline.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first treatment?

c: crusting at the base of the lashes
tm.m: Chronic lid margin inflammation needs daily cleaning
tm.g: Blepharitis: warm compresses and lid hygiene
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Chloramphenicol drops (Chloramphenicol is for infection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hypromellose drops (Lubricants ease the dry-eye symptoms but do not clear the crusts and blocked glands)
posterior blepharitis with rosacea not settling with hygiene
the presentation instead showed features specific to Steroid eye drops (Specialist-only due to risks of raised intraocular pressure, cataract and infection)
x: Chloramphenicol is for infection.
Lubricants ease the dry-eye symptoms but do not clear the crusts and blocked glands.
Ruled out here: requires posterior blepharitis with rosacea not settling with hygiene, whereas this patient has crusty every morning, crusting at the base of the lashes.
Specialist-only due to risks of raised intraocular pressure, cataract and infection

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old man has had a lump in his upper eyelid for 3 weeks. It was slightly sore at first but is now painless. It is not affecting his vision.
There is a 5 mm firm, round, non-tender swelling in the upper lid away from the lash line. The skin over it is not red and moves freely.
hq_q.w: This is a chalazion. Most settle within weeks with warm compresses and gentle massage towards the lid margin, which soften and drain the blocked meibomian gland.
hq_q.f: Same lump still there after 6 months and bothering him → refer for incision and curettage.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first management?

tm.m: A blocked meibomian gland forms a sterile lipogranuloma that usually drains with heat
tm.g: Chalazion: warm compresses first
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Chloramphenicol ointment (A chalazion is sterile; topical antibiotics do not help it)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Incision and curettage (Incision and curettage is for a chalazion that persists for months or keeps bothering him, after conservative treatment)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral flucloxacillin (Antibiotics are for spreading cellulitis around the lid, not a sterile lump)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Steroid injection into the lump (Steroid injection is a specialist option for a persistent chalazion and can depigment the skin)
x: A chalazion is sterile; topical antibiotics do not help it.
Incision and curettage is for a chalazion that persists for months or keeps bothering him, after conservative treatment.
Antibiotics are for spreading cellulitis around the lid, not a sterile lump.
Steroid injection is a specialist option for a persistent chalazion and can depigment the skin.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman with facial papulopustular rosacea has had bilateral burning, gritty eyes and intermittent blurring that clears on blinking for 6 months.
Slit-lamp examination reveals a frothy tear film along the lower lid margins and inspissated, capped meibomian gland orifices along the posterior lid margin, while the anterior eyelash bases are clean.
hq_q.w: Posterior blepharitis is caused by meibomian gland dysfunction and is strongly associated with ocular rosacea. Inspissated lipid secretions cap the gland orifices, destabilising the tear film and causing rapid evaporative dry eye.
hq_q.f: Crusts and collarettes around the base of the lashes → anterior blepharitis, from staph or seborrhoea.
hq_q.ql: Which type of blepharitis is this?

tm.m: Meibomian gland obstruction impairs the lipid tear layer, accelerating tear evaporation
tm.g: Capped meibomian orifices and frothy tear film in rosacea -> posterior blepharitis
f: acute itchy erythematous scaly eyelid skin after starting a new eye drop
waxy cylindrical sleeves around the base of the eyelashes with microscopic mites
greasy scales clinging to the anterior eyelash bases in a patient with scalp dandruff
hard brittle crusts at the eyelash bases that leave bleeding micro-ulcers when removed
x: Allergic contact blepharitis presents with acute eczematous erythema, swelling, and pruritus of the eyelid skin after new cosmetics or drops.
Demodex blepharitis produces characteristic pathognomonic cylindrical dandruff cuffs around the base of the upper eyelashes.
Anterior blepharitis affects the anterior lid margin around the eyelashes with greasy scales or collarettes, which are absent here.
Staphylococcal anterior blepharitis causes hard brittle fibrinous crusts and micro-ulceration at the anterior lash follicles.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man has had a sticky red right eye for 5 days. It has not settled. He does not wear contact lenses. He has no pain or photophobia.
Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes. There is purulent discharge. The cornea is clear and does not stain with fluorescein.
hq_q.w: Most bacterial conjunctivitis settles alone. If treatment is needed, chloramphenicol drops or ointment. Key discriminator: Bacterial conjunctivitis needing treatment: chloramphenicol eye drops.
hq_q.f: Pregnant → fusidic acid drops.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Bacterial conjunctivitis is mild; a broad topical antibiotic speeds recovery
tm.g: Bacterial conjunctivitis needing treatment: chloramphenicol eye drops
f: a branching dendritic ulcer
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral amoxicillin (Oral antibiotics are not used)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Steroid eye drops (Contraindicated in infective conjunctivitis as steroids worsen bacterial and herpetic infection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Topical ciprofloxacin (Ciprofloxacin is for contact lens wearers)
x: Ruled out here: requires a branching dendritic ulcer, whereas this patient has sticky, does not wear contact lenses.
Oral antibiotics are not used.
Contraindicated in infective conjunctivitis as steroids worsen bacterial and herpetic infection
Ciprofloxacin is for contact lens wearers.

hq_q.s:
A 10 day old baby girl has had watery, then sticky discharge from both eyes for 3 days. She was born by vaginal delivery. She is feeding well and has no fever.
Both eyelids are mildly swollen with mucopurulent discharge. The corneas are clear. A conjunctival swab is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis on nucleic acid testing.
hq_q.w: Chlamydial conjunctivitis in a newborn needs a systemic macrolide such as oral erythromycin, because it can also cause pneumonia. The mother and her partner need testing and treatment too.
hq_q.f: Day 2 with profuse pus and marked lid swelling → Neisseria gonorrhoeae, needing IV ceftriaxone.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Chlamydia is passed on during vaginal birth and can spread from the eye to the lungs
tm.g: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis: oral erythromycin
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Chloramphenicol eye drops (Topical drops do not clear chlamydia or prevent chlamydial pneumonia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV ceftriaxone (IV ceftriaxone treats gonococcal ophthalmia, which starts in the first days of life with profuse pus)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Saline cleaning and review (Cleaning helps the discharge, but untreated chlamydia can cause pneumonia and corneal scarring)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Topical fusidic acid (Fusidic acid covers staphylococci, not chlamydia)
x: Topical drops do not clear chlamydia or prevent chlamydial pneumonia.
IV ceftriaxone treats gonococcal ophthalmia, which starts in the first days of life with profuse pus.
Cleaning helps the discharge, but untreated chlamydia can cause pneumonia and corneal scarring.
Fusidic acid covers staphylococci, not chlamydia.

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old teacher had a cold last week. Her right eye became red and watery 4 days ago, and now the left eye is too. Several children in her class have red eyes.
There is watery discharge with follicles on the inside of the lower lids. There is a tender lymph node in front of the right ear. Visual acuity is normal.
hq_q.w: Adenovirus conjunctivitis: watery, follicles, a preauricular node and a recent cold. It is very contagious; good hand hygiene matters.
hq_q.f: Itch, stringy discharge and hay fever → allergic conjunctivitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: lymph node in front of the right ear
tm.m: Adenovirus spreads easily and causes follicles and a preauricular node
tm.g: Watery follicular conjunctivitis with a preauricular node after a cold is viral
f: itch with stringy discharge and hay fever
the presentation instead showed features specific to Anterior uveitis (Uveitis gives pain, photophobia and a small pupil in one eye, not watery bilateral redness after a cold)
purulent discharge with lids stuck together
the presentation instead showed features specific to Herpes simplex keratitis (HSV keratitis causes a dendritic ulcer)
x: Ruled out here: requires itch with stringy discharge and hay fever, whereas this patient has had a cold last week, watery discharge with follicles.
Uveitis gives pain, photophobia and a small pupil in one eye, not watery bilateral redness after a cold.
Ruled out here: requires purulent discharge with lids stuck together, whereas this patient has had a cold last week, watery discharge with follicles.
HSV keratitis causes a dendritic ulcer.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man presents with a 2 day history of a painful, watery, photophobic right eye and mildly blurred vision. He does not wear contact lenses and had a cold sore on his upper lip last week.
Visual acuity is 6/9 on the right. Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining reveals a branching dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs on the central cornea.
hq_q.w: A branching dendritic corneal ulcer on fluorescein staining is pathognomonic for herpes simplex epithelial keratitis. First-line treatment is topical aciclovir 3% eye ointment five times daily; topical corticosteroids are strictly contraindicated as they cause geographic ulceration and perforation.
hq_q.f: The ulcer is round with pus in a contact lens wearer → bacterial keratitis, intensive antibiotic drops.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

c: cold sore on his upper lip
tm.m: Herpes simplex virus replicates in corneal epithelial cells, creating a branching linear defect
tm.g: Branching dendritic corneal ulcer on fluorescein -> topical aciclovir eye ointment
f: a simple superficial corneal abrasion with no dendritic branching after a fingernail scratch
a round suppurative stromal corneal infiltrate with hypopyon in a soft contact lens wearer
an indolent corneal ulcer with feathery margins and satellite lesions after a tree branch injury
non-infectious acute anterior uveitis with an intact fluorescein-negative corneal epithelium
x: Chloramphenicol is a broad-spectrum antibacterial agent with no activity against herpes simplex virus replication.
Intensive topical fluoroquinolones treat Pseudomonas bacterial keratitis in contact lens wearers, not viral dendritic ulcers.
Natamycin is a polyene antifungal reserved for filamentous fungal keratitis following agricultural plant trauma.
Unopposed topical corticosteroids in epithelial herpes simplex keratitis suppress local immunity and convert a dendritic ulcer into a sight-threatening ameboid geographic ulcer.

hq_q.s: A 28 year old woman has just finished treatment for Acanthamoeba keratitis in her left eye. She wears monthly soft contact lenses and wants to know how to stop it happening again.
o: Keep lenses away from tap water
hq_q.w: Acanthamoeba lives in tap water, swimming pools and hot tubs. Rinsing lenses or the case in tap water, or swimming and showering in lenses, is the main risk, so lenses and cases must not touch water.
hq_q.f: Pseudomonas keratitis in a lens wearer who sleeps in lenses → advise removing lenses overnight.
hq_q.ql: Which advice is most important?

tm.m: The amoeba lives in water, sticks to the lens surface and then invades a damaged cornea
tm.g: Acanthamoeba prevention: no water near contact lenses
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Change lenses every 2 weeks (Replacing lenses more often helps hygiene, but water contact is the risk that drives Acanthamoeba)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Remove lenses before bed (Overnight wear is the main risk for bacterial (Pseudomonas) keratitis; for Acanthamoeba the risk is water)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Use chloramphenicol after swimming (Antibiotic drops do not kill Acanthamoeba cysts and are not used as routine prevention)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Use lubricant drops daily (Lubricants ease dryness but do nothing to keep amoebae off the lens)
x: Replacing lenses more often helps hygiene, but water contact is the risk that drives Acanthamoeba.
Overnight wear is the main risk for bacterial (Pseudomonas) keratitis; for Acanthamoeba the risk is water.
Antibiotic drops do not kill Acanthamoeba cysts and are not used as routine prevention.
Lubricants ease dryness but do nothing to keep amoebae off the lens.

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man presents with a 2 day history of burning pain and a blistering rash over the right side of his forehead. He is immunocompetent and has no past medical history.
On examination, there are clustered vesicles on an erythematous base across the right forehead, scalp, and the tip of his nose. His right eye is currently white with visual acuity of 6/6.
hq_q.w: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose in herpes zoster ophthalmicus constitute a positive Hutchinson's sign, indicating nasociliary nerve involvement and a high risk of ocular complications such as keratitis, iritis, and scleritis.
hq_q.f: Vesicles only on the forehead with a normal eye → oral antiviral within 72 hours, eye review if symptoms start.
hq_q.ql: What does the rash on the tip of the nose mean?

tm.m: The nasociliary branch of V1 supplies both the skin of the nasal tip and the cornea and anterior uvea
tm.g: Nasal tip vesicles in forehead shingles (Hutchinson's sign) -> likely eye involvement
f: spreading periocular erythema, warmth and golden crusting over burst vesicles
widespread vesicles scattered across the trunk and limbs in a patient on chemotherapy
sparing of the nasal tip and eyelids with vesicles confined to the upper scalp
vesicles distributed over the malar cheek, upper lip and lateral ala of the nose
x: Secondary bacterial superinfection presents with golden honey-coloured crusting, spreading cellulitis, and purulent exudate rather than clean dermatomal vesicles.
Disseminated herpes zoster is defined by more than 20 vesicles outside the primary and adjacent dermatomes in an immunocompromised patient.
A positive Hutchinson's sign indicates high ocular risk rather than low risk, mandating oral antivirals and urgent ophthalmic assessment.
The tip of the nose is innervated by the external nasal branch of the nasociliary nerve (V1), not the maxillary division (V2).

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman has had painful red eyes with photophobia for a week. She has had painful red lumps on both shins for 3 weeks and a dry cough.
Visual acuity is 6/9 in both eyes. Ophthalmology confirm bilateral anterior uveitis. A chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
hq_q.w: Erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and bilateral uveitis together point to sarcoidosis. Uveitis is one of its most common eye features.
hq_q.f: One-sided recurrent uveitis with back stiffness that eases with exercise → ankylosing spondylitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying condition?

c: painful red lumps on both shins
tm.m: Non-caseating granulomas form in the lungs, skin and uveal tract
tm.g: Uveitis + erythema nodosum + hilar nodes: sarcoidosis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Ankylosing spondylitis (Ankylosing spondylitis causes recurrent one-sided anterior uveitis with inflammatory back pain, not hilar nodes)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Behçet's disease (Behçet's causes uveitis with mouth and genital ulcers, not hilar lymphadenopathy)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD can cause uveitis and erythema nodosum, but she has no bowel symptoms and IBD does not cause hilar nodes)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Tuberculosis (TB can cause uveitis and hilar nodes, but the nodes are usually one-sided, with fever, sweats and weight loss)
x: Ankylosing spondylitis causes recurrent one-sided anterior uveitis with inflammatory back pain, not hilar nodes.
Behçet's causes uveitis with mouth and genital ulcers, not hilar lymphadenopathy.
IBD can cause uveitis and erythema nodosum, but she has no bowel symptoms and IBD does not cause hilar nodes.
TB can cause uveitis and hilar nodes, but the nodes are usually one-sided, with fever, sweats and weight loss.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman with HLA-B27 positive ankylosing spondylitis attends the emergency eye clinic with a 3 day history of aching pain, redness, and severe photophobia in her right eye.
Visual acuity is 6/12 on the right. Slit-lamp examination confirms acute anterior uveitis with circumcorneal injection, a small irregular pupil, anterior chamber cells and flare, and an intact fluorescein-negative cornea.
hq_q.w: Acute non-infectious anterior uveitis is treated with frequent topical corticosteroid drops (such as dexamethasone or prednisolone) to suppress anterior chamber inflammation alongside a cycloplegic agent (such as cyclopentolate) to relieve ciliary spasm and prevent posterior synechiae.
hq_q.f: Seen in primary care without a slit lamp → do not start steroid drops; refer the same day.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Topical steroids suppress uveal leukocytic exudation while cycloplegics dilate the pupil and paralyse ciliary spasm
tm.g: Confirmed acute anterior uveitis -> topical steroid and cycloplegic drops
f: acute purulent conjunctivitis with normal pupils and no anterior chamber reaction
a vesicular rash in the ophthalmic trigeminal dermatome affecting the forehead and nasal tip
acute angle-closure glaucoma to pull the peripheral iris away from the trabecular meshwork
primary open-angle glaucoma with cupped optic discs and raised intraocular pressure
x: Chloramphenicol is a topical antibacterial for infective conjunctivitis and has no anti-inflammatory effect in sterile iritis.
Oral aciclovir treats herpes zoster ophthalmicus or herpetic keratitis, whereas HLA-B27 anterior uveitis is an autoimmune inflammation.
Pilocarpine constricts the pupil and exacerbates ciliary spasm and posterior synechiae formation in acute anterior uveitis.
Timolol and latanoprost are intraocular pressure-lowering drops used in chronic open-angle glaucoma rather than acute uveitis.

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old man attends eye casualty after his third episode in 2 years of a painful, photophobic red eye confirmed on slit-lamp examination as acute anterior uveitis. He also reports a 3 year history of lower back and buttock stiffness that lasts over an hour each morning and improves with exercise.
Examination shows reduced lumbar forward flexion on modified Schober's test.
hq_q.w: Recurrent acute unilateral anterior uveitis is the commonest extra-articular manifestation of HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, occurring in up to 40% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis alongside inflammatory morning back stiffness and sacroiliitis.
hq_q.f: Mouth and genital ulcers as well → Behçet's disease.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying condition?

tm.m: HLA-B27 antigen presentation drives enthesitis in the axial skeleton and autoimmune iridocyclitis
tm.g: Recurrent acute anterior uveitis + morning back stiffness relieved by exercise -> ankylosing spondylitis
f: recurrent painful oral and scrotal ulcers with pathergy and bilateral retinal vasculitis
symmetrical swelling of the metacarpophalangeal joints with necrotising anterior scleritis
bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum and mutton-fat keratic precipitates
a photosensitive malar rash, pleuritic chest pain and retinal vasculitis with cotton-wool spots
x: Behcet's disease causes panuveitis with retinal vasculitis and hypopyon alongside recurrent painful oral and genital ulceration.
Rheumatoid arthritis causes symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis and is classically associated with scleritis and keratoconjunctivitis sicca rather than HLA-B27 iritis.
Sarcoidosis typically causes bilateral granulomatous uveitis with mutton-fat keratic precipitates, erythema nodosum, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
Systemic lupus erythematosus causes photosensitive malar rash, serositis, and retinal cotton-wool spots rather than HLA-B27 axial spondyloarthritis.

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has had severe, boring pain in her right eye for 3 days. It wakes her at night.
The eye is tender, deep red and has a purple tinge. The redness does not blanch with phenylephrine drops. Visual acuity is 6/9.
hq_q.w: Scleritis is deep, painful and tender, does not blanch with phenylephrine and threatens sight. Key discriminator: A deep tender red eye with a purple tinge that does not blanch is scleritis.
hq_q.f: A mild ache with sectoral redness that blanches with phenylephrine → episcleritis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Inflammation of the deep sclera causes boring pain; deep vessels do not blanch
tm.g: A deep tender red eye with a purple tinge that does not blanch is scleritis
f: photophobia with a small irregular pupil
the presentation instead showed features specific to Conjunctivitis (Conjunctivitis is sticky and gritty, not severe boring pain that wakes her)
a mild ache with sectoral redness that blanches with phenylephrine
the presentation instead showed features specific to Subconjunctival haemorrhage (A subconjunctival bleed is a painless flat red patch)
x: Ruled out here: requires photophobia with a small irregular pupil, whereas this patient has rheumatoid arthritis, wakes her at night.
Conjunctivitis is sticky and gritty, not severe boring pain that wakes her.
Ruled out here: requires a mild ache with sectoral redness that blanches with phenylephrine, whereas this patient has rheumatoid arthritis, wakes her at night.
A subconjunctival bleed is a painless flat red patch.

hq_q.s: A 52 year old woman has a painful, deep red eye that is tender to touch. Scleritis is diagnosed. The team looks for an underlying cause.
hq_q.w: About half of scleritis is linked to systemic disease, rheumatoid arthritis most often, then vasculitis such as GPA.
hq_q.f: Nasal crusting and blood in the urine as well → granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
hq_q.ql: Which condition is most commonly associated with scleritis?

tm.m: About half of scleritis is linked with systemic autoimmune disease
tm.g: Scleritis is most often linked with rheumatoid arthritis
f: three episodes + low back stiffness
the presentation instead showed features specific to Diabetes mellitus (Diabetes is not a recognised cause of scleritis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hypertension (Hypertension is not linked to scleritis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ulcerative colitis (IBD can cause episcleritis or uveitis more often than scleritis; rheumatoid arthritis is the commonest association)
x: Ruled out here: requires three episodes + low back stiffness, whereas this patient has Scleritis is diagnosed, A 52 year old woman has.
Diabetes is not a recognised cause of scleritis.
Hypertension is not linked to scleritis.
IBD can cause episcleritis or uveitis more often than scleritis; rheumatoid arthritis is the commonest association.

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis presents to her GP with a 3 day history of severe, deep boring pain in her left eye that radiates to her temple and wakes her from sleep.
Visual acuity is 6/12 on the left. The globe shows diffuse violaceous redness that does not blanch with topical phenylephrine, and gentle palpation through the closed eyelid is exquisitely tender.
o: Topical steroid drops from the GP
hq_q.w: Scleritis is a severe, sight-threatening full-thickness inflammation of the scleral wall strongly linked to rheumatoid arthritis and systemic vasculitis. Same-day ophthalmology referral is mandatory for systemic NSAIDs, corticosteroids, or immunosuppression to prevent globe perforation.
hq_q.f: Episcleritis → reassure, lubricants, and an oral NSAID if sore.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Immune-complex vasculitis of the deep episcleral and scleral plexus causes necrotising scleral thinning
tm.g: Severe boring eye pain with violaceous redness and globe tenderness -> same-day ophthalmology referral
f: gritty redness with mucopurulent discharge and no globe tenderness or visual loss
mild painless sectoral redness whose vessels move freely and blanch with phenylephrine
gradual painless bilateral glare and reduced night driving vision from age-related cataracts
postoperative anterior chamber inflammation managed in the hospital ophthalmology clinic
x: Topical antibiotic drops treat superficial bacterial conjunctivitis and have no effect on deep autoimmune scleral inflammation.
Lubricating artificial tears are used for mild self-limiting episcleritis or dry eye syndrome, not sight-threatening scleritis.
Routine outpatient referral risks progressive scleral necrosis, uveitis, and globe perforation before specialist treatment starts.
Topical steroid drops neither penetrate deeply enough to control scleritis nor should they ever be initiated in primary care without slit-lamp assessment.

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old hypermetropic woman presented yesterday with acute angle-closure glaucoma of her right eye, with an initial intraocular pressure of 56 mmHg. After intravenous acetazolamide and topical timolol, apraclonidine, prednisolone, and pilocarpine, her cornea has cleared and intraocular pressure is now 14 mmHg in both eyes.
Gonioscopy confirms narrow occludable drainage angles bilaterally.
hq_q.w: Once acute angle-closure glaucoma is medically broken and corneal oedema clears, bilateral Nd:YAG laser peripheral iridotomy is the definitive treatment. Creating a full-thickness iris opening equalises anterior and posterior chamber pressures and prevents attacks in the fellow eye.
hq_q.f: Pressure still high → medical treatment first: acetazolamide, pilocarpine and a beta-blocker drop.
hq_q.ql: Which is the definitive treatment?

tm.m: A laser opening in the peripheral iris bypasses pupillary block in both the affected and fellow eye
tm.g: Resolved acute angle-closure glaucoma -> bilateral laser peripheral iridotomy
f: visually significant nuclear sclerotic lens opacity causing disabling glare in an open-angle eye
short-term bridge therapy while awaiting laser iridotomy after intraocular pressure is lowered
newly diagnosed primary open-angle glaucoma with an open angle on gonioscopy
progressive primary open-angle glaucoma despite maximal tolerated topical drops and laser trabeculoplasty
x: Elective cataract surgery deepens the anterior chamber long term, but laser peripheral iridotomy is the immediate definitive procedure to protect both eyes.
Long-term pilocarpine causes chronic miosis, brow ache, and synechiae and does not replace definitive anatomical relief of pupil block.
Selective laser trabeculoplasty targets the trabecular meshwork in primary open-angle glaucoma and cannot access a closed drainage angle.
Trabeculectomy creates a surgical drainage bleb for refractory open-angle glaucoma when medical and laser trabeculoplasty fail.

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man has newly diagnosed primary open-angle glaucoma. He has no symptoms.
Intraocular pressure 28 mmHg in both eyes. There is cupping of both optic discs. Visual field testing shows early loss.
hq_q.w: NICE 2022: SLT is first-line for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension of 24 mmHg or more.
hq_q.f: SLT is unsuitable or declined → a prostaglandin analogue such as latanoprost.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

tm.m: Laser to the trabecular meshwork improves outflow without daily drops
tm.g: New open-angle glaucoma: selective laser trabeculoplasty first
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Acetazolamide tablets (Acetazolamide is for short-term use)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Laser peripheral iridotomy (Iridotomy is for angle closure)
laser is unsuitable or declined
the presentation instead showed features specific to Timolol drops (Drops are used if laser is unsuitable; NICE now offers selective laser trabeculoplasty first)
x: Acetazolamide is for short-term use.
Iridotomy is for angle closure.
Ruled out here: requires laser is unsuitable or declined, whereas this patient has no symptoms, 28 mmHg.
Drops are used if laser is unsuitable; NICE now offers selective laser trabeculoplasty first.

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man has glaucoma and asthma. He started a new eye drop 2 weeks ago. He now has wheeze and needs his salbutamol more often.
Pulse rate 56 bpm.
hq_q.w: Beta-blocker drops are absorbed through the tear duct and nasal lining and can cause bronchospasm and bradycardia.
hq_q.f: His iris darkens and his eyelashes grow longer → latanoprost.
