hq_q.ql: Which drop is most likely responsible?

tm.m: Beta-blocker drops are absorbed through the nose into the blood
tm.g: Wheeze and a slow pulse after a new glaucoma drop: timolol
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Brimonidine (Brimonidine does not cause bronchospasm)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Dorzolamide (Dorzolamide does not cause bronchospasm)
a darker iris and longer eyelashes
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pilocarpine (Pilocarpine can blur vision and cause brow ache, but beta-blocker drops cause the wheeze and slow pulse)
x: Brimonidine does not cause bronchospasm.
Dorzolamide does not cause bronchospasm.
Ruled out here: requires a darker iris and longer eyelashes, whereas this patient has asthma, new eye drop.
Pilocarpine can blur vision and cause brow ache, but beta-blocker drops cause the wheeze and slow pulse.

hq_q.s:
A 9 year old boy had sinusitis last week. His left eyelid has become swollen and red over a day.
Temperature 38.7°C. The left eye bulges forward. It hurts to move the eye, and eye movements are reduced. Visual acuity is reduced in the left eye.
hq_q.w: Orbital cellulitis lies behind the orbital septum: painful eye movements, proptosis, reduced vision or an RAPD. It is an emergency.
hq_q.f: Swollen lids but painless full eye movements and normal vision → preseptal cellulitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Infection behind the orbital septum affects the eye muscles and optic nerve
tm.g: Proptosis, painful limited movement and reduced vision after sinusitis is orbital cellulitis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Allergic reaction (An allergy does not cause fever or reduced vision)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Chalazion (A chalazion is a painless lid lump; it does not cause fever, proptosis or reduced eye movement)
a tender swelling over the tear sac at the inner corner
swollen lids with painless full movements and normal vision
x: An allergy does not cause fever or reduced vision.
A chalazion is a painless lid lump; it does not cause fever, proptosis or reduced eye movement.
Ruled out here: requires a tender swelling over the tear sac at the inner corner, whereas this patient has sinusitis last week, bulges forward.
Ruled out here: requires swollen lids with painless full movements and normal vision, whereas this patient has sinusitis last week, bulges forward.

hq_q.s: A 12 year old girl has a swollen, red left eye with pain on eye movement and proptosis. She has been admitted for IV antibiotics. Orbital cellulitis is suspected.
o: Plain X-ray of the orbits and sinuses
hq_q.w: CT shows the extent and any abscess needing drainage, alongside admission and IV antibiotics. Key discriminator: Suspected orbital cellulitis: contrast CT orbits and sinuses.
hq_q.f: Preseptal cellulitis in a well adult → oral co-amoxiclav.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most appropriate?

c: pain on eye movement and proptosis
tm.m: CT shows the extent of spread and any abscess needing drainage
tm.g: Suspected orbital cellulitis: contrast CT orbits and sinuses
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Blood cultures (Cultures are taken, but they do not show the extent of orbital spread or an abscess)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Conjunctival swab (A swab does not show orbital spread)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Plain X-ray of the orbits and sinuses (X-rays do not show soft tissue)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ultrasound of the globe (Ultrasound does not show the sinuses)
x: Cultures are taken, but they do not show the extent of orbital spread or an abscess.
A swab does not show orbital spread.
X-rays do not show soft tissue.
Ultrasound does not show the sinuses.

hq_q.s: A 10 year old boy has orbital cellulitis after a sinus infection.
hq_q.w: The ethmoid sinus is separated from the orbit by the thin lamina papyracea, which infection crosses easily.
hq_q.f: Both eyes affected with cranial nerve palsies → cavernous sinus thrombosis.
hq_q.ql: Which sinus is the most likely source?

tm.m: Only the thin lamina papyracea separates the ethmoid sinus from the orbit
tm.g: Orbital spread most often comes from the ethmoid sinus
f: pain over the forehead worse on lying flat
the presentation instead showed features specific to Mastoid air cells (Mastoid air cells are in the temporal bone)
chronic sinusitis + When he bends forward, purulent fluid pours from his nose
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sphenoid sinus (The sphenoid is a rarer source)
x: Ruled out here: requires pain over the forehead worse on lying flat, whereas this patient has sinus infection, A 10 year old boy has.
Mastoid air cells are in the temporal bone.
Ruled out here: requires chronic sinusitis + When he bends forward, purulent fluid pours from his nose, whereas this patient has sinus infection, A 10 year old boy has.
The sphenoid is a rarer source.

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old man with proliferative diabetic retinopathy has had gradual loss of vision in his right eye over a month, like a shadow spreading. He has had no flashes or new floaters.
Visual acuity is 6/36 in the right eye. Fundoscopy shows fibrovascular bands over the retina, which is raised and concave in the upper half. No retinal tear is seen.
hq_q.w: In proliferative diabetic retinopathy, fibrovascular membranes contract and pull the retina off. Tractional detachments are concave, progress slowly and have no tear or flashes.
hq_q.f: Flashes, floaters, then a curtain in a short-sighted man, with a tear seen → rhegmatogenous detachment.
hq_q.ql: Which type of detachment is this?

tm.m: Contracting scar tissue on the retinal surface pulls it away
tm.g: Diabetes, fibrous bands, no tear: tractional detachment
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Exudative retinal detachment (Exudative detachments come from fluid leaking under the retina (tumour, inflammation, severe hypertension) and shift with posture; there is no traction)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Posterior vitreous detachment (A posterior vitreous detachment causes flashes and floaters but does not lift the retina or cause a shadow)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Retinoschisis (Retinoschisis is a split within the retina, usually symmetrical and inferotemporal, with no fibrous bands)

the presentation instead showed features specific to Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (Rhegmatogenous detachments start with a tear, usually with flashes and floaters, and the retina is convex and mobile)
x: Exudative detachments come from fluid leaking under the retina (tumour, inflammation, severe hypertension) and shift with posture; there is no traction.
A posterior vitreous detachment causes flashes and floaters but does not lift the retina or cause a shadow.
Retinoschisis is a split within the retina, usually symmetrical and inferotemporal, with no fibrous bands.
Rhegmatogenous detachments start with a tear, usually with flashes and floaters, and the retina is convex and mobile.

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man is referred to the vitreoretinal unit after developing flashing lights, a shower of dark floaters, and a peripheral shadow in his left eye. Dilated fundoscopy confirms a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment with an upper temporal retinal break, and the surgical team prioritises the theatre list.
o: Her central vision is still intact
Vision already reduced to counting fingers
hq_q.w: Retinal detachment repair is most urgent when the macula remains attached and central visual acuity is still intact (macula-on detachment). Once the fovea detaches (macula-off), photoreceptor damage occurs rapidly and visual prognosis is poorer even with surgery.
hq_q.f: The macula has already detached → surgery within days, with a poorer outlook.
hq_q.ql: Which feature makes surgery most urgent?

tm.m: Preserving foveal attachment prevents permanent macular photoreceptor separation and central visual loss
tm.g: Retinal detachment surgical urgency is highest while central vision and macular attachment remain intact
f: asked which feature indicates a chronic detachment with a poorer visual prognosis
asked which symptom reflects syneresis and mobile condensations in the vitreous gel
asked which baseline refractive error predisposes the fellow eye to future retinal tears
asked which finding confirms that subretinal fluid has already detached the fovea
x: A detachment present for over a week with established macular involvement is repaired semi-urgently rather than as an immediate emergency.
Vitreous floaters occur in both uncomplicated posterior vitreous detachment and retinal tears and do not determine macular surgical urgency.
Myopia in the fellow eye is a predisposing risk factor for detachment but does not dictate the immediate timing of surgery on the affected eye.
Acuity reduced to counting fingers indicates the macula has already detached, making same-day emergency repair less time-critical than macula-on detachment.

hq_q.s: A 44 year old woman has had a retinal tear repaired. She asks why it happened.
hq_q.w: Long, short-sighted eyes have thin peripheral retina that tears easily. Cataract surgery and trauma are other risks.
hq_q.f: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy → tractional detachment, from scar tissue pulling.
hq_q.ql: Which is the strongest risk factor for a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?

tm.m: Long myopic eyes have thin peripheral retina that tears easily
tm.g: The strongest risk factor is high myopia
f: proliferative retinopathy causing a tractional detachment
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hypertension (Hypertension does not cause retinal tears)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Long-sightedness (Long-sightedness is a risk for angle closure)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Smoking (Smoking is a risk for vascular eye disease, not rhegmatogenous detachment)
x: Ruled out here: requires proliferative retinopathy causing a tractional detachment, whereas this patient has retinal tear, A 44 year old woman has.
Hypertension does not cause retinal tears.
Long-sightedness is a risk for angle closure.
Smoking is a risk for vascular eye disease, not rhegmatogenous detachment.

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old man has had sudden painless loss of vision in his right eye for an hour. He has hypertension and atrial fibrillation.
Visual acuity is counting fingers in the right eye. There is a right relative afferent pupillary defect. The retina is pale with a cherry-red spot at the macula.
hq_q.w: In CRAO the inner retina is pale and swollen while the thin fovea lets the choroid show through as a cherry-red spot.
hq_q.f: Widespread haemorrhages like a stormy sky → central retinal vein occlusion.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: An embolus blocks the central retinal artery; the thin fovea shows the choroid as a red spot
tm.g: Sudden painless loss with a pale retina and a cherry-red spot is central retinal artery occlusion
f: a pale swollen disc with jaw claudication
widespread haemorrhages like a stormy sky
the presentation instead showed features specific to Retinal detachment (A detachment comes with flashes and floaters; his AF points to an embolus)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Vitreous haemorrhage (A vitreous bleed hides the retina; here a pale retina with a cherry-red spot is seen)
x: Ruled out here: requires a pale swollen disc with jaw claudication, whereas this patient has atrial fibrillation, pale.
Ruled out here: requires widespread haemorrhages like a stormy sky, whereas this patient has atrial fibrillation, pale.
A detachment comes with flashes and floaters; his AF points to an embolus.
A vitreous bleed hides the retina; here a pale retina with a cherry-red spot is seen.

hq_q.s:
A 76 year old woman presents to eye casualty 3 hours after sudden, complete, painless loss of vision in her left eye. Over the past 2 weeks she has had a right-sided temporal headache, scalp tenderness when combing her hair, and aching in her jaw when chewing.
Visual acuity is perception of light on the left with a relative afferent pupillary defect, a pale retina, and a macular cherry-red spot.
hq_q.w: In patients over 50 with central retinal artery occlusion accompanied by temporal headache or jaw claudication, giant cell arteritis must be excluded immediately with urgent ESR and CRP alongside immediate high-dose systemic corticosteroids to protect the fellow eye.
hq_q.f: A 45-year-old with AF → urgent stroke work-up for an embolic source.
hq_q.ql: Which test is most urgent?

tm.m: Granulomatous arteritis of the ophthalmic and central retinal arteries causes bilateral blindness within days if untreated
tm.g: CRAO with jaw claudication and scalp tenderness -> urgent ESR and CRP (and immediate high-dose steroids)
f: non-arteritic amaurosis fugax with a carotid bruit requiring urgent carotid imaging within 24 hours
routine vascular risk assessment after giant cell arteritis has been excluded
monitoring chronic progression of arcuate scotomas in primary open-angle glaucoma
embolic branch retinal artery occlusion in a young patient with a cardiac murmur
x: Outpatient carotid imaging in a month fails to exclude giant cell arteritis, which can blind the fellow eye within 24 to 48 hours.
Cardiovascular risk profiling is part of secondary stroke prevention but does not address the immediate threat of arteritic bilateral blindness.
Formal perimetry has no role in acute complete monocular blindness and delays emergency management of giant cell arteritis.
Echocardiography assesses cardioembolic sources in non-arteritic retinal occlusion but is not the immediate priority when jaw claudication points to GCA.

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man had a painless dark curtain descend vertically over the vision of his left eye this morning, which resolved completely after 5 minutes. He has hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and smokes 20 cigarettes daily.
Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes, fundoscopy is normal, and auscultation of the neck reveals a left carotid bruit.
hq_q.w: Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular blindness) represents a retinal transient ischaemic attack, typically caused by platelet-fibrin emboli from an ipsilateral internal carotid artery stenosis. Immediate aspirin 300 mg daily and urgent specialist TIA clinic assessment within 24 hours are required.
hq_q.f: Zigzag lines spreading over 20 minutes, followed by a headache → migraine aura.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Cholesterol or platelet-fibrin microemboli from an internal carotid plaque transiently occlude the retinal artery
tm.g: Amaurosis fugax with carotid bruit -> immediate aspirin 300 mg and urgent TIA clinic referral
f: gradual unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus requiring MRI of the internal acoustic meatus
a single long-standing stable floater with normal dilated fundoscopy and no flashes
gradual bilateral difficulty reading small print in a 50 year old with presbyopia
recurrent throbbing unilateral headache preceded by 20 minutes of binocular visual aura
x: Waiting 6 weeks for an outpatient MRI misses the high early stroke risk window when carotid endarterectomy is most protective.
Reassuring the patient despite complete symptom resolution ignores a high immediate risk of hemispheric ischaemic stroke.
Routine optometry assessment cannot provide carotid duplex imaging, antiplatelet initiation, or secondary stroke prevention.
Triptans treat acute migraine headaches and are contraindicated in patients with cerebrovascular ischaemia or carotid stenosis.

hq_q.s:
An 80 year old woman has noticed her vision becoming gradually blurred over a year. Car headlights cause glare at night. She has no eye pain.
Visual acuity is 6/18 in both eyes, improving little with a pinhole. The red reflex is reduced in both eyes.
hq_q.w: Cataract: slow, painless blur with glare and halos, and a dimmed red reflex. Key discriminator: Slow painless blur with glare and a dim red reflex is cataract.
hq_q.f: Straight lines look wavy and the centre is distorted → macular degeneration.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: The lens clouds slowly and scatters light
tm.g: Slow painless blur with glare and a dim red reflex is cataract
f: straight lines look wavy with central distortion
the presentation instead showed features specific to Chronic open-angle glaucoma (Glaucoma takes peripheral vision first and does not cause glare or a dim red reflex)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Diabetic retinopathy (Retinopathy causes patchy loss, not glare with a dim red reflex)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Retinal detachment (A detachment is sudden, with flashes, floaters and a curtain)
x: Ruled out here: requires straight lines look wavy with central distortion, whereas this patient has gradually blurred over a year, glare.
Glaucoma takes peripheral vision first and does not cause glare or a dim red reflex.
Retinopathy causes patchy loss, not glare with a dim red reflex.
A detachment is sudden, with flashes, floaters and a curtain.

hq_q.s: A 72 year old delivery driver attends his GP after his optometrist noted bilateral nuclear sclerotic cataracts. His best-corrected Snellen visual acuity is 6/9 in both eyes, and his ocular pressures and maculae are normal. However, severe dazzle and glare from oncoming headlights now prevent him from driving at dusk, threatening his job.
hq_q.w: Under NICE guideline NG77, referral for cataract surgery must be based on whether visual impairment – including glare, contrast loss, or night-driving difficulty – affects the patient's quality of life and occupation, not on arbitrary Snellen visual acuity thresholds.
hq_q.f: No effect on his daily life → no referral yet.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Lenticular opacities scatter incoming light, causing disabling disability glare despite preserved high-contrast Snellen acuity
tm.g: Symptomatic cataract impairing work or night driving -> refer for cataract surgery regardless of 6/9 acuity
f: mild evaporative dry eye symptoms causing intermittent blurring that clears on blinking
simple uncorrected myopic refractive error with clear crystalline lenses on slit-lamp examination
incidental mild lens opacity in an asymptomatic patient who does not wish to have surgery
never appropriate under UK NICE guidelines, which forbid fixed Snellen acuity thresholds
x: No pharmacological eye drops can dissolve or reverse age-related crystalline lens protein opacification.
Updating spectacle refraction cannot eliminate intraocular light scatter and glare caused by nuclear lens opacities.
Withholding referral when cataract glare threatens his employment breaches NICE guidance against acuity-only gatekeeping.
NICE NG77 explicitly prohibits restricting cataract surgery access by waiting for visual acuity to drop to 6/18.

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old woman has taken oral prednisolone for severe asthma for years. She has glare from bright lights and has trouble reading.
Visual acuity is 6/12 in both eyes. There is a reduced red reflex.
hq_q.w: Steroids cause posterior subcapsular cataract, which affects reading and glare early as it sits in the visual axis.
hq_q.f: The same complaint in an 80-year-old on no drugs → age-related nuclear cataract.
hq_q.ql: Which type of cataract is she most likely to have?

tm.m: Steroids cause opacity at the back of the lens, worst in bright light and for reading
tm.g: Long-term steroids cause posterior subcapsular cataract
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Congenital lamellar cataract (Congenital cataract is present from birth)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cortical cataract (Cortical cataract is age-related)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Mature white cataract (A mature cataract causes severe loss)
an 80 year old on no drugs
x: Congenital cataract is present from birth.
Cortical cataract is age-related.
A mature cataract causes severe loss.
Ruled out here: requires an 80 year old on no drugs, whereas this patient has oral prednisolone, trouble reading.

hq_q.s:
A 78 year old woman has noticed over a week that door frames look bent and there is a blurred patch in the middle of her vision in her right eye.
Visual acuity is 6/24 in the right eye. The Amsler grid shows distortion. Fundoscopy shows a haemorrhage at the macula.
hq_q.w: Wet AMD: new vessels under the macula leak, causing rapid central distortion. NICE: refer to a macular service within 1 working day.
hq_q.f: Gradual central loss over years with drusen → dry AMD.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: New vessels under the macula leak and bleed
tm.g: Rapid distortion with a macular haemorrhage is wet macular degeneration
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Cataract (Cataract blurs vision slowly over months without straight lines looking bent)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Central retinal vein occlusion (A vein occlusion causes widespread haemorrhages)
gradual central loss over years with drusen
the presentation instead showed features specific to Retinal detachment (A detachment gives flashes, floaters and a curtain, not central distortion)
x: Cataract blurs vision slowly over months without straight lines looking bent.
A vein occlusion causes widespread haemorrhages.
Ruled out here: requires gradual central loss over years with drusen, whereas this patient has over a week, door frames look bent.
A detachment gives flashes, floaters and a curtain, not central distortion.

hq_q.s:
A 76 year old man presents with a 2 week history of straight doorframes appearing wavy and a smudged dark patch in the centre of his left visual field. His peripheral vision is normal.
Visual acuity is 6/24 on the left. Optical coherence tomography confirms neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration with subretinal fluid and choroidal neovascularisation.
o: Laser photocoagulation of the whole retina
hq_q.w: Neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration is driven by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) stimulating fragile, leaky choroidal new vessels beneath the macula. First-line treatment is urgent intravitreal anti-VEGF injections (such as aflibercept, ranibizumab, or faricimab).
hq_q.f: Dry AMD → no anti-VEGF; vitamin supplements in some, and low-vision support.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

c: centre of his left visual field
tm.m: VEGF drives fragile choroidal neovascular membranes that leak fluid and blood under the fovea
tm.g: Confirmed wet age-related macular degeneration -> intravitreal anti-VEGF injections
f: proliferative diabetic retinopathy with new vessels on the optic disc
sight-threatening giant cell arteritis presenting with acute anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
intermediate dry age-related macular degeneration with extensive macular drusen and no neovascularisation
a non-clearing dense vitreous haemorrhage secondary to proliferative diabetic retinopathy
x: Panretinal laser photocoagulation ablates ischaemic peripheral retina in proliferative diabetic retinopathy and does not treat macular choroidal neovascularisation.
Oral corticosteroids do not halt choroidal neovascular angiogenesis in wet age-related macular degeneration.
Antioxidant vitamin supplements (AREDS2 formula) may slow progression of intermediate dry AMD but cannot treat active wet neovascular exudation.
Pars plana vitrectomy is used for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment, not subretinal choroidal neovascularisation.

hq_q.s:
An 84 year old woman has severe macular degeneration in both eyes. For a month she has seen vivid people and patterns. She knows they are not real and is not distressed. She has no memory problems.
She is alert and orientated. Cognitive testing is normal. There are no features of parkinsonism.
hq_q.w: Charles Bonnet syndrome: visual hallucinations from visual loss, with insight and no other mental illness. Reassurance helps.
hq_q.f: Hallucinations with fluctuating confusion and parkinsonism → dementia with Lewy bodies.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: The visual cortex makes its own images when input is lost
tm.g: Vivid hallucinations with insight in severe visual loss is Charles Bonnet syndrome
f: fluctuating attention with an infection
fluctuating confusion with parkinsonism
the presentation instead showed features specific to Late-onset psychosis (In psychosis the person lacks insight)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Migraine (Migraine aura lasts under an hour with headache, not a month of complex images)
x: Ruled out here: requires fluctuating attention with an infection, whereas this patient has knows they are not real, Cognitive testing is normal.
Ruled out here: requires fluctuating confusion with parkinsonism, whereas this patient has knows they are not real, Cognitive testing is normal.
In psychosis the person lacks insight.
Migraine aura lasts under an hour with headache, not a month of complex images.

hq_q.s:
A 55 year old woman presents to the emergency department with a sudden, severe right-sided retro-orbital headache that started 3 hours ago, accompanied by double vision and a drooping left eyelid.
On examination, she has complete left ptosis, the left eye rests down and out, and the left pupil is dilated at 7 mm and sluggishly reactive to light.
hq_q.w: Parasympathetic pupillomotor fibres travel in the superficial perimeter of the oculomotor nerve. A painful third nerve palsy with a dilated unreactive pupil indicates extrinsic compression by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm requiring urgent CT angiography.
hq_q.f: The pupil is spared in a person with diabetes → microvascular, ischaemic third nerve palsy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?

tm.m: An aneurysm at the junction of the internal carotid and posterior communicating arteries compresses outer CN III pupil fibres
tm.g: Painful third nerve palsy with a dilated unreactive pupil -> posterior communicating artery aneurysm
f: a painless or mildly aching third nerve palsy with a normal-sized briskly reactive pupil in diabetes
impaired adduction of one eye with contralateral abducting nystagmus in a 28 year old woman
fatigable bilateral ptosis and diplopia worse in the evening with completely normal pupil reactions
excluded intracranial aneurysm on angiography in a child with recurrent migraine-associated cranial neuropathy
x: Diabetic microvascular ischaemia affects the central core of the nerve and spares the superficial pupillomotor fibres, leaving the pupil normal.
Multiple sclerosis typically causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia or optic neuritis rather than a compressive pupil-involving third nerve palsy.
Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable ptosis and variable diplopia but strictly spares the pupils.
Ophthalmoplegic migraine is an extremely rare diagnosis of exclusion in children and must never be assumed before excluding an aneurysm.

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old man with a 16 year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and hypertension attends his annual digital diabetic retinal screening appointment. He reports no visual symptoms.
Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes. Fundus photography of the right eye reveals fine, fragile neovascular fronds growing on the optic disc alongside scattered blot haemorrhages.
hq_q.w: New vessels on the optic disc or elsewhere on the retina define proliferative diabetic retinopathy, driven by retinal ischaemia and VEGF release. Urgent ophthalmology referral for panretinal laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF therapy prevents vitreous haemorrhage and detachment.
hq_q.f: Hard exudates near the macula → diabetic maculopathy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: neovascular fronds growing on the optic disc
tm.m: Chronic retinal capillary non-perfusion induces VEGF-mediated growth of fragile preretinal neovascular fronds
tm.g: New vessels on the optic disc or retina -> proliferative diabetic retinopathy
f: isolated microaneurysms and a few dot haemorrhages with no ischaemic signs or new vessels
circinate rings of hard exudates and macular oedema threatening the central fovea
arteriovenous nipping, silver wiring and flame haemorrhages in severe uncontrolled hypertension
venous beading, multiple cotton-wool spots and deep blot haemorrhages without new vessels
x: Background diabetic retinopathy consists only of microaneurysms, dot-and-blot haemorrhages, and occasional hard exudates without neovascularisation.
Diabetic maculopathy is defined by hard exudates, retinal thickening, or oedema within one disc diameter of the central fovea.
Hypertensive retinopathy produces arteriovenous nipping, silver wiring, flame haemorrhages, and optic disc swelling rather than disc neovascularisation.
Pre-proliferative retinopathy shows severe retinal ischaemia (venous beading, multiple cotton-wool spots, and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities) before new vessels form.

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old woman had a chiropractic neck manipulation yesterday. Since then she has had pain on the left side of her neck and a headache. She has noticed her left eyelid drooping.
There is mild left ptosis and a small left pupil. Eye movements are normal. Limb examination is normal.
hq_q.w: Painful Horner syndrome after neck trauma suggests carotid dissection, which damages the sympathetic fibres around the artery. It can cause stroke.
hq_q.f: Horner syndrome with wasting of the hand muscles in a smoker → Pancoast tumour.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: pain on the left side of her neck
tm.m: A tear in the carotid wall damages the sympathetic fibres around it
tm.g: Painful Horner syndrome after neck manipulation is carotid artery dissection
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Cluster headache (Cluster headache causes attacks of eye pain with tearing, not constant neck pain after manipulation)
Horner syndrome with vertigo and crossed sensory loss
Horner syndrome with hand wasting in a smoker
the presentation instead showed features specific to Third nerve palsy (A third nerve palsy causes a dilated pupil)
x: Cluster headache causes attacks of eye pain with tearing, not constant neck pain after manipulation.
Ruled out here: requires Horner syndrome with vertigo and crossed sensory loss, whereas this patient has chiropractic neck manipulation, pain on the left side of her neck.
Ruled out here: requires Horner syndrome with hand wasting in a smoker, whereas this patient has chiropractic neck manipulation, pain on the left side of her neck.
A third nerve palsy causes a dilated pupil.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old construction worker arrives at the emergency department 10 minutes after wet alkaline cement splashed directly into his right eye on a building site. He has severe burning ocular pain, blepharospasm, and epiphora.
Inspection shows cement particulate debris in the lower conjunctival fornix and diffuse conjunctival hyperaemia.
hq_q.w: Alkali burns saponify cell membranes and rapidly penetrate the corneal stroma. Chemical eye injury is the one ophthalmic emergency where immediate, copious saline irrigation takes priority over measuring visual acuity until conjunctival pH is neutral.
hq_q.f: Blunt injury with blood in the anterior chamber → hyphaema, same-day ophthalmology.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first step?

tm.m: Alkali hydroxyl ions saponify cell membranes and liquefy corneal collagen until washed out and neutralised
tm.g: Acute chemical splash to the eye -> immediate copious irrigation before visual acuity testing
f: prophylactic topical cover after irrigation is complete and conjunctival pH has been neutralised
assessing corneal epithelial defect size once conjunctival pH has stabilised at 7.4
specialist assessment after immediate on-site irrigation has restored a neutral conjunctival pH
blunt orbital trauma or a non-chemical red eye where baseline visual acuity is always recorded first
x: Applying topical antibiotic drops before washing out the alkali leaves corrosive cement burning the cornea and limbal stem cells.
Fluorescein staining assesses the extent of epithelial loss only after all chemical particulate matter has been irrigated and pH is neutral.
Waiting for specialist ophthalmology review before starting irrigation allows irreversible corneal opacification and limbal ischaemia.
Measuring Snellen visual acuity first delays time-critical alkali removal; irrigation must start at once.

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old man presents to the emergency department 45 minutes after being struck sharply in the left eye by a springing hawthorn branch while trimming hedges.
Visual acuity is 6/36 in the left eye and 6/6 in the right. Inspection reveals a small full-thickness paracentral corneal laceration, a shallow anterior chamber, and a peaked teardrop-shaped pupil pointing toward the wound.
hq_q.w: A peaked teardrop-shaped pupil with a shallow anterior chamber after sharp trauma indicates a penetrating globe injury with iris prolapse. Apply a rigid protective shield without pressure, keep nil by mouth, and arrange emergency ophthalmic surgical repair.
hq_q.f: A superficial corneal abrasion with an intact globe → chloramphenicol ointment.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Aqueous humour escape draws the iris into the full-thickness corneal defect, peaking the pupil
tm.g: Teardrop pupil after sharp eye injury -> rigid shield (no pressure pad) and emergency ophthalmology referral
f: an uncomplicated superficial corneal abrasion with a round reactive pupil and deep anterior chamber
an acute alkaline plaster or cement splash into the eye with an intact globe
suspected acute angle-closure glaucoma with an intact cornea and a fixed mid-dilated pupil
a superficial metallic speck sitting on the tarsal conjunctiva after subtarsal lid eversion
x: Applying ointment and a compressive eye pad exerts pressure on an open globe and can extrude intraocular contents.
Forceful saline irrigation is reserved for chemical burns and can introduce fluid or disrupt the iris plug in an open globe.
Applanation tonometry presses directly on the cornea and is strictly contraindicated when globe perforation is suspected.
Attempting to extract embedded intraocular material or iris tissue outside theatre risks vitreous loss and expulsive haemorrhage.

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man was punched in the right eye last night. He has double vision on looking up.
There is bruising around the right eye. Upward gaze is limited on the right. There is numbness of the right cheek and upper lip. Visual acuity is normal.
hq_q.w: A blow-out fracture traps the inferior rectus, limiting upward gaze, and damages the infraorbital nerve, numbing the cheek.
hq_q.f: A tense, bulging, rock-hard eye with falling vision after trauma → retrobulbar haemorrhage, lateral canthotomy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: The orbital floor breaks, trapping inferior rectus and the infraorbital nerve
tm.g: Limited upgaze with cheek numbness after a punch is an orbital floor blow-out fracture
f: Vertical diplopia on downgaze with contralateral head tilt
the presentation instead showed features specific to Isolated zygomatic arch fracture (A zygomatic arch fracture limits mouth opening, not upward gaze)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Orbital cellulitis (Orbital cellulitis follows sinusitis with fever, not a punch with cheek numbness)
a tense bulging hard eye with falling vision
x: Ruled out here: requires Vertical diplopia on downgaze with contralateral head tilt, whereas this patient has double vision on looking up, numbness of the right cheek.
A zygomatic arch fracture limits mouth opening, not upward gaze.
Orbital cellulitis follows sinusitis with fever, not a punch with cheek numbness.
Ruled out here: requires a tense bulging hard eye with falling vision, whereas this patient has double vision on looking up, numbness of the right cheek.

hq_q.s:
A 23 year old student presents to his GP with a 3-day history of severe crampy central and lower abdominal pain, fever and frequent bloody diarrhoea. Four days before symptom onset, he attended a summer barbecue where he ate undercooked chicken drumsticks.
Temperature 38.2°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg. Examination shows dry mucous membranes and mild generalized abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound.
hq_q.w: Campylobacter jejuni is the commonest bacterial cause of acute gastroenteritis in the UK, typically transmitted via undercooked poultry, unpasteurised milk or untreated water with an incubation period of 2 to 5 days. It causes fever, severe abdominal cramps (often mimicking appendicitis) and bloody diarrhoea, and is the leading antecedent of Guillain-Barre syndrome.
hq_q.f: Vomiting within 1 to 6 hours of reheated fried rice → Bacillus cereus.
hq_q.ql: Which causative organism is most likely responsible?

tm.m: Curved, comma-shaped, microaerophilic, oxidase-positive Gram-negative rods invade jejunal, ileal and colonic epithelium and secrete cytolethal distending toxin.
tm.g: Fever, severe cramps and bloody diarrhoea 2-5 days after undercooked poultry -> Campylobacter jejuni
x: Bacillus cereus causes acute vomiting within 1 to 6 hours of eating reheated fried rice (emetic toxin) or watery diarrhoea 8 to 16 hours after meat/stews, without bloody stools.
Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli O157 follows undercooked beef burgers or petting farm contact and causes painful bloody diarrhoea typically without high fever.
Non-typhoidal Salmonella typically follows raw/undercooked eggs or poultry after a shorter 12 to 36 hour incubation and causes watery (less commonly bloody) diarrhoea.
Shigella sonnei is transmitted person-to-person via the faecal-oral route (nurseries, men who have sex with men) rather than undercooked barbecue chicken.
f: he developed profuse vomiting 2 hours after eating reheated egg fried rice from a buffet with no fever or bloody diarrhoea
a child visited a petting farm 3 days ago and developed bloody diarrhoea, afebrile abdominal cramps, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
several guests developed fever and profuse watery diarrhoea 18 hours after eating homemade raw-egg mayonnaise
a nursery worker developed acute tenesmus and mucoid bloody dysentery during a person-to-person classroom outbreak

hq_q.s:
Twelve guests who attended a summer wedding reception attend the Emergency Department with sudden-onset nausea, violent retching, profuse vomiting and abdominal cramps starting 2 hours after eating from an unrefrigerated buffet. All affected guests had eaten sliced ham sandwiches and custard cream cakes. Very few have loose stools and all are afebrile.
Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg.
hq_q.w: Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning is caused by ingestion of preformed, heat-stable staphylococcal enterotoxins produced when food handlers contaminate salty or creamy foods (sliced ham, poultry, custard, cream cakes, potato salad) left at room temperature. It causes abrupt vomiting within 1 to 6 hours without fever, resolving within 24 hours.
hq_q.f: Watery diarrhoea and vomiting starting 1 to 2 days later on a cruise ship → norovirus.
hq_q.ql: Which organism is the most likely cause of this foodborne outbreak?

c: sliced ham sandwiches and custard cream cakes
tm.m: Preformed staphylococcal enterotoxin acts as a superantigen on gut vagal afferents, directly stimulating the medullary vomiting centre within 1 to 6 hours.
tm.g: Abrupt afebrile vomiting 1-6 hours after eating unrefrigerated ham, dairy or cream cakes -> Staphylococcus aureus
x: Campylobacter jejuni requires 2 to 5 days to multiply and invade the mucosa, causing febrile bloody diarrhoea rather than vomiting after 2 hours.
Clostridium perfringens spores germinate in large meat stews or gravies, causing watery diarrhoea and cramps 8 to 16 hours after ingestion with little vomiting.
Norovirus has a 12 to 48 hour incubation period and spreads person-to-person or via raw oysters/leafy greens.
Salmonella has a 12 to 36 hour incubation period and causes fever and inflammatory diarrhoea rather than afebrile toxin-mediated vomiting at 2 hours.
f: patients developed fever, severe abdominal cramps and bloody diarrhoea 3 days after eating undercooked poultry
guests developed abdominal cramps and watery diarrhoea without vomiting 12 hours after eating a large reheated beef gravy casserole
passengers on a cruise ship developed projectile vomiting and watery diarrhoea 24 to 36 hours after index cases on board
guests developed fever, headache and watery diarrhoea 24 hours after eating lightly cooked eggs and tiramisu

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old woman presents with a 2-day history of severe crampy abdominal pain and frequent bloody diarrhoea. Three days before symptom onset she visited a country petting farm where she handled calves and lambs.
Temperature 37.3°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 116/74 mmHg. There is mild lower abdominal tenderness without guarding.
Stool culture isolates Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli O157. Haemoglobin, platelets and creatinine are currently normal.
o: Oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 5 days
Oral loperamide 4 mg stat then 2 mg after each loose stool
Oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 7 days
Supportive fluid therapy and close monitoring
hq_q.w: Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC O157:H7) causes haemorrhagic colitis and carries a 5 to 15% risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome (MAHA, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury). Both antibiotics and antimotility agents (loperamide) are strictly contraindicated because bacterial lysis and gut stasis increase Shiga toxin release and absorption; give supportive fluids and monitor FBC/renal function.
hq_q.f: Severe Campylobacter in an immunosuppressed patient → clarithromycin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate clinical management?

c: Haemoglobin, platelets and creatinine are currently normal
tm.m: Antibiotics induce bacteriophage lysis and release preformed Shiga toxin (verocytotoxin), while antimotility drugs prolong mucosal contact, precipitating glomerular endothelial damage and HUS.
tm.g: Confirmed E. coli O157 gastroenteritis -> supportive fluid therapy and close monitoring (avoid antibiotics and loperamide)
x: Antibiotics are contraindicated in STEC O157 infection because they increase bacteriophage-mediated Shiga toxin release and precipitate haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
Fluoroquinolones strongly induce Shiga-toxin prophages in E. coli O157, substantially increasing the risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
Antimotility drugs slow intestinal clearance of Shiga toxin, increasing systemic toxin absorption and the risk of HUS and toxic megacolon.
Metronidazole has no activity against aerobic E. coli and antibiotics are contraindicated in STEC O157 colitis.
f: an immunosuppressed patient had severe invasive Campylobacter or dysenteric traveller's diarrhoea from South Asia with negative STEC testing
a frail inpatient had invasive bacteraemic non-typhoidal Salmonella infection confirmed sensitive to fluoroquinolones
an adult had chronic non-infective diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome with normal stool cultures
stool microscopy or antigen testing confirmed Giardia lamblia or Entamoeba histolytica colitis

hq_q.s:
A 27 year old woman presents with a 3-week history of passing small amounts of fresh bright-red blood and mucus per rectum, accompanied by rectal urgency and tenesmus. She opens her bowels 3 times daily, feels systemically well and has no abdominal pain or weight loss.
Temperature 36.8°C, pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg. Flexible sigmoidoscopy and biopsy confirm mild active ulcerative colitis confined entirely to the rectum (proctitis).
hq_q.w: Under NICE guidelines (NG130) for mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis confined to the rectum (ulcerative proctitis), a topical (rectal) aminosalicylate (mesalazine suppository) alone is first-line therapy to induce remission. If remission is not achieved within 4 weeks, add an oral aminosalicylate before considering topical or oral corticosteroids.
hq_q.f: Extensive colitis that is mild to moderate → rectal plus high-dose oral aminosalicylate.
hq_q.ql: Which is the first-line treatment recommended by NICE to induce remission?
hq_q.post: Sigmoidoscopy and biopsy show mild ulcerative colitis confined to the rectum.

c: ulcerative colitis confined entirely to the rectum
tm.m: Mesalazine suppositories deliver high local 5-aminosalicylic acid concentrations directly to the inflamed rectal mucosa, inhibiting prostaglandin, leukotriene and NF-kappaB signalling with minimal systemic absorption.
tm.g: Mild-to-moderate ulcerative proctitis -> topical (rectal) aminosalicylate (mesalazine suppository) first line
x: Oral corticosteroids are reserved for flares that fail to respond to combined topical and oral aminosalicylates and a topical corticosteroid.
Intravenous infliximab is a rescue biological therapy for acute severe colitis refractory to intravenous corticosteroids or moderate-to-severe refractory disease.
Ileal-release oral budesonide targets the terminal ileum and ascending colon in mild-to-moderate ileocaecal Crohn's disease, not distal ulcerative proctitis.
Thiopurines take 8 to 12 weeks to become effective, so they cannot induce acute remission and are used for steroid-sparing maintenance.
f: her proctitis failed to respond after 4 weeks of combined topical and oral mesalazine plus a topical corticosteroid foam
she was admitted with acute severe pan-colitis that failed to respond after 72 hours of intravenous hydrocortisone
she presented with a mild flare of isolated ileocaecal Crohn's disease and wished to avoid systemic prednisolone side effects
she had suffered two severe colitis flares requiring systemic corticosteroids in a 12-month period and needed steroid-sparing maintenance

hq_q.s:
A 31 year old man with known left-sided ulcerative colitis presents with a 4-day history of passing 8 bloody stools daily despite adherence to maintenance oral and topical mesalazine.
Temperature 38.1°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. His abdomen is soft with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no distension. Plain abdominal X-ray shows no colonic dilatation.
o: Double the dose of oral mesalazine at home
Prescribe oral loperamide to reduce stool frequency
Proceed directly to emergency subtotal colectomy
Start oral prednisolone 40 mg daily as an outpatient
hq_q.w: By Truelove and Witts criteria, passing >=6 bloody stools daily PLUS at least one marker of systemic toxicity (temperature >37.8°C, pulse >90 bpm, haemoglobin <105 g/L or ESR/CRP >30) defines acute severe ulcerative colitis. This medical emergency requires immediate hospital admission for intravenous hydrocortisone (100 mg four times daily), LMWH thromboprophylaxis, stool cultures/C. diff exclusion and surgical review.
hq_q.f: No better after 72 hours of IV steroids → add ciclosporin or infliximab, or consider colectomy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
hq_q.post: Abdominal X-ray shows no colonic dilatation.

tm.m: Acute severe colitis carries a high risk of venous thromboembolism, toxic megacolon and perforation, requiring parenteral corticosteroids as gut mucosal oedema impairs oral absorption.
tm.g: >=6 bloody stools/day + systemic toxicity (fever >37.8°C, HR >90, Hb <105 or CRP >30) -> admit for IV hydrocortisone
x: Escalating oral mesalazine is appropriate only for mild flares (<4 stools/day without systemic upset) and is unsafe in Truelove and Witts acute severe colitis.
Antimotility agents are strictly contraindicated during an acute ulcerative colitis flare because paralysing colonic motility precipitates toxic megacolon.
He has no perforation or toxic megacolon on abdominal X-ray; first-line therapy is 72 hours of IV corticosteroids with daily reassessment before rescue therapy or colectomy.
Outpatient oral prednisolone is used for moderate flares (4-5 stools/day with no systemic toxicity); systemic fever, tachycardia and Hb 101 g/L mandate admission for IV steroids.
f: he was passing 3 stools daily with a trace of blood, felt systemically well, and had normal observations, haemoglobin and CRP
he had diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome with normal faecal calprotectin and no mucosal inflammation
he developed free colonic perforation or toxic megacolon (transverse colon >6 cm) refractory to medical rescue therapy
he was passing 5 stools daily with no fever, pulse 74 bpm, haemoglobin 138 g/L and had not responded to optimised mesalazine

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man with ileocolonic Crohn's disease has experienced two acute flares over the past 10 months, each requiring an 8-week tapering course of oral prednisolone. He is currently in clinical remission, and the gastroenterology team plans to initiate oral azathioprine as steroid-sparing maintenance therapy.
Pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 120/76 mmHg. Baseline full blood count, renal function and liver enzymes are normal.
hq_q.w: Azathioprine is a prodrug cleaved to 6-mercaptopurine and inactivated by thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT). Patients with homozygous or compound heterozygous TPMT deficiency (~1 in 300) shunt drug metabolism into cytotoxic 6-thioguanine nucleotides, causing life-threatening bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia/agranulocytosis); TPMT activity (and NUDT15 where available) must be measured before initiation.
hq_q.f: About to start fluorouracil chemotherapy → DPYD testing.
hq_q.ql: Which enzyme or genetic test must be checked before starting azathioprine?

tm.m: Deficient TPMT enzyme activity prevents methylation of 6-mercaptopurine, causing accumulation of myelotoxic 6-thioguanine nucleotides in haematopoietic stem cells.
tm.g: Before starting azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine -> check thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity
x: DPYD genotyping is performed prior to starting fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy (5-fluorouracil or capecitabine) for colorectal or breast cancer, not azathioprine.
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity is checked before prescribing oxidant drugs such as dapsone, primaquine or rasburicase to prevent haemolysis.
HLA-B*58:01 screening is used before starting allopurinol in Han Chinese, Thai or Korean patients to prevent Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Vitamin D is monitored in IBD bone health (especially with steroid exposure) but does not govern azathioprine metabolism or marrow toxicity.
f: a patient with stage III colon adenocarcinoma was about to start adjuvant capecitabine and oxaliplatin chemotherapy
a patient with dermatitis herpetiformis or Plasmodium vivax malaria was about to start oral dapsone or primaquine
a patient of Han Chinese descent with chronic tophaceous gout was being assessed for allopurinol urate-lowering therapy
bone protection and calcium/cholecalciferol supplementation were being assessed during prolonged systemic corticosteroid therapy

hq_q.s:
A 46 year old man with severe alcohol dependence and self-neglect is admitted to the medical ward after being found weak at home. He reports having eaten almost no solid food for the past 10 days.
Pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg. His BMI is 15.5 kg/m². Intravenous Pabrinex (high-potency thiamine) is administered and nasogastric enteral nutrition is commenced.
hq_q.w: In refeeding syndrome, reintroduction of carbohydrate after prolonged starvation (>5-10 days) triggers a rapid insulin surge. Insulin drives glucose, phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and accelerates intracellular ATP and 2,3-DPG synthesis. Severe hypophosphataemia is the hallmark abnormality, causing respiratory muscle failure, rhabdomyolysis, arrhythmias, seizures and cardiac arrest.
hq_q.f: The question asks what to give before feeding to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy → thiamine.
hq_q.ql: Which intracellular shift-related serum electrolyte abnormality is the hallmark biochemical feature of refeeding syndrome?

c: eaten almost no solid food for the past 10 days
tm.m: Carbohydrate refeeding switches metabolism from fat catabolism to glycolysis, triggering an insulin surge that drives extracellular phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells for ATP synthesis.
tm.g: Reintroducing nutrition after starvation (BMI 15.5, 10 days nil by mouth) -> severe hypophosphataemia (plus hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia)
x: Refeeding syndrome does not cause hypercalcaemia; if anything, hypomagnesaemia and phosphate therapy can lower ionized calcium.
Insulin promotes renal tubular sodium and water retention (causing fluid overload and oedema) rather than hypernatraemia.
Hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis results from prolonged gastric acid vomiting (such as pyloric stenosis) rather than carbohydrate refeeding.
Refeeding drives intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium and magnesium rather than causing a primary metabolic acidosis (unless thiamine is omitted, causing lactic acidosis).
f: a patient with squamous cell lung cancer or primary hyperparathyroidism presented with polyuria, polydipsia and constipation
an elderly patient with dementia had no access to water for 4 days, resulting in severe free-water dehydration
a patient with peptic gastric outlet obstruction had profuse non-bilious vomiting of gastric HCl for a week
he had ingested ethylene glycol or methanol, or developed diabetic ketoacidosis with a high anion gap

hq_q.s:
A 23 year old woman with severe restricting anorexia nervosa is admitted to the medical ward with profound weakness and postural dizziness. She has eaten almost nothing for the past 14 days.
Temperature 35.9°C, pulse rate 52 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg. Her BMI is 15.0 kg/m². Oral and intravenous thiamine and vitamin B co strong are given prior to commencing enteral nutrition.
hq_q.w: Under NICE nutrition support guidelines (CG32), patients at high risk of refeeding syndrome (BMI <16 kg/m², unintentional weight loss >15%, little/no intake for >10 days, or low baseline potassium, phosphate or magnesium) must start nutrition at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day, increasing slowly to full requirements over 4 to 7 days.
hq_q.f: BMI under 14 or no intake for over 15 days → start at 5 kcal per kg per day.
hq_q.ql: What is the maximum recommended starting caloric intake for this high-risk patient?

c: eaten almost nothing for the past 14 days
tm.m: Limiting initial carbohydrate load to <=10 kcal/kg/day blunts the postprandial insulin surge and prevents precipitous intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium and magnesium.
tm.g: High refeeding risk (BMI <16 kg/m² or >10 days little/no intake) -> start at maximum 10 kcal/kg/day
x: 5 kcal/kg/day with cardiac rhythm monitoring is reserved for extreme refeeding risk (BMI <14 kg/m² or negligible intake for >15 days).
25 to 30 kcal/kg/day is the full maintenance energy target for non-malnourished adults and will precipitate fatal refeeding syndrome here.
35 kcal/kg/day is an excessive hypercaloric rate at initiation that will trigger a massive insulin surge and life-threatening hypophosphataemia.
50 kcal/kg/day at initiation in a patient with a BMI of 15 kg/m² causes catastrophic refeeding syndrome, cardiac failure and arrhythmias.
f: her BMI was below 14 kg/m² (such as 12.2 kg/m²) or she had had negligible nutritional intake for more than 15 consecutive days
a well-nourished inpatient with a normal BMI of 23 kg/m² and normal electrolytes required standard maintenance enteral feeding
the patient had safely completed 7 to 10 days of gradual refeeding and was now in the supervised weight-restoration phase
a hypermetabolic major burns patient with no prior starvation required peak catabolic energy replacement

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old widower who lives alone and subsists almost entirely on white toast, sweet tea and plain biscuits presents to his GP with a 6-week history of fatigue, poor wound healing, bleeding gums and painful leg bruising.
Examination reveals swollen, spongy, friable gingivae, sheet-like ecchymoses over both thighs, coiled 'corkscrew' body hairs and perifolicular hyperkeratotic petechiae.
Platelet count, prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are all normal.
hq_q.w: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency causes scurvy in patients eating a 'tea and toast' diet devoid of fresh fruit and vegetables. Ascorbate is an obligate cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in collagen triple-helix cross-linking; defective vascular collagen causes gingival bleeding, perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew hairs and normal clotting studies.
hq_q.f: Bruising with a prolonged PT and normal gums → vitamin K deficiency.
hq_q.ql: Which vitamin deficiency is the most likely cause of his presentation?

c: white toast, sweet tea and plain biscuits
tm.m: Ascorbic acid keeps iron in the reduced ferrous (Fe2+) state required by prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases; its absence produces fragile basement membrane collagen and capillary fragility.
tm.g: Tea-and-toast diet + spongy bleeding gums + corkscrew hairs + perifollicular petechiae + normal clotting -> vitamin C deficiency (scurvy)
x: Folate deficiency also occurs in 'tea and toast' diets and causes megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia and glossitis, not corkscrew hairs or perifollicular haemorrhage.
Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and wet/dry beriberi rather than defective collagen synthesis and capillary bleeding.
Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia with bone pain and proximal myopathy rather than gingival bleeding and perifollicular petechiae.
Vitamin K deficiency impairs gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X, causing a prolonged prothrombin time/INR rather than a normal clotting screen.
f: he presented with pallor, breathlessness, a smooth beefy-red tongue and a macrocytic anaemia (MCV 112 fL) without skin bleeding
he presented with acute confusion, bilateral abducens nerve palsies, horizontal nystagmus and a wide-based ataxic gait
he presented with diffuse rib and pelvic bone tenderness, waddling proximal leg weakness, low calcium and raised alkaline phosphatase
a patient with obstructive jaundice or malabsorption presented with easy bruising and a prolonged prothrombin time (INR 3.8)

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old man who drinks 60 units of alcohol per week presents with a 3-month history of pale, bulky, greasy stools that float and are difficult to flush, alongside 6 kg weight loss. He has a 5-year history of recurrent boring epigastric pain radiating to his back.
His BMI is 19.0 kg/m². Blood tests show a newly elevated HbA1c of 54 mmol/mol (20-42) and negative IgA tissue transglutaminase.
hq_q.w: Chronic calcific pancreatitis from heavy alcohol excess destroys both pancreatic acinar tissue (causing lipase deficiency and steatorrhoea) and islet beta cells (causing pancreatogenic type 3c diabetes). Low faecal elastase-1 (<200 µg/g, severe <100 µg/g) is the non-invasive gold standard for confirming exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
hq_q.f: Watery diarrhoea after a terminal ileal resection → SeHCAT for bile acid malabsorption.
hq_q.ql: Which non-invasive investigation best confirms the suspected cause of his steatorrhoea?

c: epigastric pain radiating to his back
tm.m: Human pancreatic elastase-1 is secreted by acinar cells and transits the gut undegraded; a low stool concentration directly reflects acinar destruction.
tm.g: Recurrent epigastric-to-back pain + steatorrhoea + new diabetes in heavy drinker -> faecal elastase-1
x: A SeHCAT scan measures ileal bile acid reabsorption in chronic watery (non-greasy) diarrhoea after ileal resection or cholecystectomy.
Faecal calprotectin measures neutrophil-derived mucosal inflammation to differentiate inflammatory bowel disease from irritable bowel syndrome.
A glucose or lactulose hydrogen breath test detects small intestinal bacterial overgrowth or carbohydrate malabsorption rather than pancreatic exocrine failure.
Coeliac serology is already negative and coeliac disease does not cause boring epigastric-to-back pain with pancreatogenic diabetes.
f: he had chronic watery non-fatty diarrhoea following a terminal ileal resection for Crohn's disease or cholecystectomy
a 26 year old presented with bloody mucoid diarrhoea and crampy lower abdominal pain to evaluate suspected inflammatory bowel disease
a patient with systemic sclerosis had postprandial bloating, high serum folate and low serum vitamin B12
a patient who had been on a gluten-free diet completed a 6-week gluten challenge to evaluate suspected coeliac disease

hq_q.s:
A 39 year old woman who underwent a 40 cm terminal ileal resection for stricturing Crohn's disease 6 months ago presents with persistent urgency and 6 watery, non-bloody stools daily. She has no abdominal pain, fever or weight loss.
Pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 120/74 mmHg. Blood tests show CRP 3 mg/L (<5), faecal calprotectin is 40 µg/g (<50), and a 7-day SeHCAT scan demonstrates 5% bile acid retention (normal >15%).
hq_q.w: The terminal ileum reabsorbs 95% of conjugated bile acids via the apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter. After ileal resection (Type 1 bile acid malabsorption, confirmed by 7-day SeHCAT retention <15%), unabsorbed bile acids spill into the colon and stimulate chloride/water secretion; bile acid sequestrants (colestyramine or colesevelam) are first-line treatment.
hq_q.f: Low faecal elastase → pancreatic enzyme replacement with meals.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?

tm.m: Colestyramine is an anion-exchange resin that binds unabsorbed bile acids in the intestinal lumen into insoluble complexes, preventing colonic secretory diarrhoea.
tm.g: Watery diarrhoea after terminal ileal resection with low SeHCAT retention (<15%) -> oral colestyramine
x: Loperamide slows transit in non-specific diarrhoea, whereas proven bile acid malabsorption responds specifically and dramatically to a bile acid sequestrant.
Metronidazole treats anaerobic bacterial overgrowth or Giardia; her SeHCAT scan of 5% proves bile acid malabsorption rather than infection.
Pancreatic enzyme replacement treats exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (low faecal elastase and greasy steatorrhoea), not watery bile acid diarrhoea.
Her CRP (3 mg/L) and faecal calprotectin (40 µg/g) confirm her Crohn's disease is in remission, and mesalazine has minimal efficacy in Crohn's or bile acid diarrhoea.
f: she had diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome with a normal SeHCAT scan (>15% retention) and normal calprotectin
she had developed foul-smelling steatorrhoea and bloating from bacterial overgrowth across a surgical blind loop
she had chronic pancreatitis with pale, greasy floating stools and a faecal elastase of 45 µg/g
a patient presented with a mild-to-moderate flare of left-sided ulcerative colitis with raised faecal calprotectin

hq_q.s:
A 51 year old man presents with a 6-month history of pale, bulky steatorrhoea, 9 kg unintentional weight loss and migratory non-deforming polyarthralgia of the knees and wrists. His wife reports progressive forgetfulness, confusion and vertical gaze difficulty.
Examination reveals generalized lymphadenopathy, bronze skin hyperpigmentation and rhythmic convergence-retraction eye movements. Serum albumin is 26 g/L (35-50). Duodenal biopsy reveals lamina propria macrophages strongly positive on periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining.
hq_q.w: Whipple's disease is a rare multisystem infection caused by the Gram-positive actinomycete Tropheryma whipplei, classically affecting middle-aged men. It causes malabsorption/steatorrhoea, migratory seronegative arthralgia, skin hyperpigmentation, lymphadenopathy and CNS involvement (dementia, ophthalmoplegia, oculomasticatory myorhythmia). Duodenal biopsy shows foamy PAS-positive macrophages; treat with IV ceftriaxone then 12 months of co-trimoxazole.
hq_q.f: Villous atrophy with a positive tTG → coeliac disease.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Tropheryma whipplei bacilli replicate inside intestinal lamina propria macrophages, obstructing lymphatic lacteals (causing protein-losing enteropathy and steatorrhoea) and seeding the CNS and synovium.
tm.g: Steatorrhoea + arthralgia + hyperpigmentation + CNS signs + PAS-positive duodenal macrophages -> Whipple's disease
x: Giardiasis causes small-bowel steatorrhoea and bloating after contaminated water exposure without arthralgia, dementia, lymphadenopathy or PAS-positive macrophages.
Crohn's disease shows transmural inflammation and non-caseating epithelioid granulomas rather than foamy PAS-positive bacillary macrophages and dementia.
Tropical sprue causes malabsorption and megaloblastic folate deficiency after prolonged tropical residence without CNS disease or PAS-positive macrophages.
Coeliac disease shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis with positive tTG serology, not PAS-positive macrophages.
f: stool antigen and duodenal aspirate identified pear-shaped binucleate flagellated trophozoites after a camping trip
endoscopy showed skip lesions, perianal fistulae and non-caseating granulomas without PAS-positive intracellular bacilli
he developed chronic steatorrhoea and severe megaloblastic folate deficiency after living in rural India for 2 years
duodenal biopsy showed subtotal villous atrophy and raised intraepithelial lymphocytes with positive IgA tissue transglutaminase

hq_q.s:
A 29 year old woman presents to her GP with a 12-month history of fatigue, postprandial abdominal bloating and passing 3 loose, pale stools daily. She eats a standard diet containing wheat bread, cereals and pasta every day.
Pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 114/70 mmHg. Abdominal examination is normal. Blood tests show microcytic anaemia.
o: Immediate upper GI endoscopy and duodenal biopsy
Serum IgA tissue transglutaminase and total IgA
hq_q.w: Under NICE coeliac disease guidelines (NG20), the first-choice serological test in adults eating a gluten-containing diet is serum IgA tissue transglutaminase (tTG) measured alongside total serum IgA (to detect selective IgA deficiency, which affects 2-3% of coeliac patients and causes false-negative IgA tTG results).
hq_q.f: Total IgA is low → use IgG-based tests such as IgG deamidated gliadin or IgG endomysial antibody.
hq_q.ql: Which is the recommended first-line serological test to investigate suspected coeliac disease?

tm.m: IgA autoantibodies against tissue transglutaminase-2 have >95% sensitivity and specificity in IgA-competent patients actively consuming gluten.
tm.g: First-line screening test for suspected coeliac disease on gluten -> serum IgA tTG plus total IgA
x: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 is positive in 30-40% of the healthy general population, so it is reserved for specialist rule-out testing rather than primary-care diagnosis.
Endoscopic duodenal biopsy is the confirmatory step performed after a positive serological test (or high clinical suspicion despite negative serology), not before serology.
IgG-based coeliac tests (IgG EMA, IgG DGP or IgG tTG) are used only when concurrent total IgA testing reveals selective IgA deficiency.
Faecal calprotectin detects colonic/ileal neutrophilic inflammation in suspected inflammatory bowel disease, not coeliac villous atrophy.
f: a specialist needed to rule out coeliac disease in a patient already on a long-term gluten-free diet who was unable to tolerate a gluten challenge
her serum IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody had just returned strongly positive and histological confirmation was required
initial testing had demonstrated selective IgA deficiency with a total serum IgA concentration below 0.05 g/L
she had normal haemoglobin and ferritin and presented with bloody mucoid diarrhoea to differentiate IBD from IBS

hq_q.s:
A 33 year old man presents to his GP requesting a formal diagnosis of coeliac disease. Three months ago he eliminated all bread, pasta and barley from his diet after reading online advice for bloating and loose stools, and his symptoms improved.
Abdominal examination is normal. A serum IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody test sent last week is negative with a normal total serum IgA.
o: Maintain the gluten-free diet and repeat tTG in 12 months
Reassure him that coeliac disease is definitively excluded
Refer immediately for upper GI endoscopy and duodenal biopsy
Reintroduce gluten in >1 meal daily for 6 weeks then retest
Request HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 typing to confirm diagnosis
hq_q.w: Both coeliac serology (IgA tTG) and duodenal histology normalise after weeks to months on a gluten-free diet, rendering tests taken off gluten unreliable. NICE guidelines advise instructing the patient to reintroduce gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before repeating IgA tTG serology (and biopsy).
hq_q.f: Positive tTG while still eating gluten → refer for duodenal biopsy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step to accurately assess him for coeliac disease?

c: eliminated all bread, pasta and barley from his diet
IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody test sent last week is negative
tm.m: Without ongoing dietary gliadin antigen presentation, mucosal plasma cells cease anti-tTG IgA production and duodenal villi regenerate, causing false-negative tests.
tm.g: Suspected coeliac disease already on a gluten-free diet -> reintroduce gluten in >1 meal daily for at least 6 weeks then retest
x: Repeating IgA tTG while remaining on a gluten-free diet will simply yield another false-negative result.
A negative IgA tTG taken 3 months after stopping gluten is a false-negative screen and cannot exclude coeliac disease.
Duodenal villous architecture also recovers on a 3-month gluten-free diet, so immediate biopsy without a 6-week gluten challenge risks a false-negative biopsy.
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 is present in ~35% of the normal population; a positive result cannot confirm coeliac disease (it only has negative predictive value).
f: he already had biopsy-proven coeliac disease and was having annual serology to monitor dietary adherence
he had been eating gluten in multiple meals every day for the past 6 months and had a negative IgA tTG with normal total IgA
he had been eating gluten daily and his serum IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody returned positive
he refused or was medically unable to undertake a 6-week gluten challenge and a negative HLA test was sought to rule out coeliac disease

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old woman with coeliac disease has had an intensely itchy rash for a month. She has not been sticking to her gluten-free diet.
There are grouped, small blisters and excoriations on her elbows, knees and buttocks.
hq_q.w: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin form of coeliac disease: IgA deposits in the dermal papillae on biopsy. A gluten-free diet and dapsone treat it.
hq_q.f: Tense blisters on the flexures of an 80-year-old → bullous pemphigoid.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: IgA deposits in the skin cause itchy blisters on extensor surfaces in coeliac disease
tm.g: Itchy grouped blisters on extensor surfaces in coeliac disease is dermatitis herpetiformis
f: tense blisters on the flexures in an 80 year old
the presentation instead showed features specific to Eczema herpeticum (Classic picture: Eczema suddenly turns into punched-out painful erosions, unwell)
Treat the whole household on the same day, or it comes back.
extensor surface of his elbows, scalp and back + well demarcated
x: Ruled out here: requires tense blisters on the flexures in an 80 year old, whereas this patient has not been sticking, grouped, small blisters.
Classic picture: Eczema suddenly turns into punched-out painful erosions, unwell
Ruled out here: requires Treat the whole household on the same day, or it comes back, whereas this patient has not been sticking, grouped, small blisters.
Ruled out here: requires extensor surface of his elbows, scalp and back + well demarcated, whereas this patient has not been sticking, grouped, small blisters.

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old woman presents to her GP with an 8-month history of recurrent crampy lower abdominal pain that is relieved by opening her bowels, accompanied by abdominal bloating and stools alternating between hard pellets and loose motions. She has no rectal bleeding, nocturnal diarrhoea, fever or weight loss, and no family history of bowel or ovarian cancer.
Abdominal and rectal examinations are normal.
o: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen
Three stool samples for ova, cysts and parasites
hq_q.w: Under NICE guidelines (CG61), patients meeting the clinical diagnostic criteria for irritable bowel syndrome (abdominal pain relieved by defaecation or associated with altered stool frequency/form for >=6 months, with no red flags) must have four baseline tests to exclude mimics: full blood count, ESR/CRP, coeliac serology (IgA tTG) and (in young adults with diarrhoea) faecal calprotectin.
hq_q.f: Age 60 or over with a change in bowel habit → suspected cancer pathway.
hq_q.ql: Which baseline blood investigation is recommended by NICE before confirming a diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome?

c: alternating between hard pellets and loose motions
no rectal bleeding, nocturnal diarrhoea, fever or weight loss
tm.m: Coeliac disease frequently mimics diarrhoea- or mixed-pattern irritable bowel syndrome in young adults and must be serologically excluded before making a functional diagnosis.
tm.g: Baseline primary-care blood screen before diagnosing IBS -> FBC, ESR/CRP and coeliac serology (IgA tTG)
x: NICE explicitly states that abdominal ultrasound, CT and barium enema are not required to confirm IBS in the absence of red flag symptoms.
Colonoscopy is not indicated in a 26 year old with typical IBS symptoms, no red flags and normal inflammatory markers.
Upper GI endoscopy investigates dysphagia, upper GI bleeding or dyspepsia with alarm features, not functional lower bowel symptoms.
Routine stool microscopy/culture or ova and parasite testing is not recommended by NICE before diagnosing IBS unless there is a history of foreign travel or water exposure.
f: a 65 year old patient presented with unexplained weight loss, abdominal pain and a palpable abdominal mass
her baseline faecal calprotectin returned markedly elevated at 450 µg/g, raising suspicion of inflammatory bowel disease
her IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody returned positive and duodenal biopsy was needed to confirm coeliac disease
she had developed persistent greasy diarrhoea and foul-smelling wind after drinking untreated stream water on a trekking holiday

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man with confirmed irritable bowel syndrome attends his GP for review. Despite 3 months of dietary modifications, regular antispasmodic therapy (oral mebeverine) and laxative titration, he continues to experience frequent, distressing crampy abdominal pain that interferes with his sleep and work. His mood is normal (PHQ-9 score 2).
Abdominal examination is normal.
hq_q.w: Under NICE guidelines (CG61), if abdominal pain or global symptoms in irritable bowel syndrome do not respond to first-line antispasmodics, laxatives or loperamide, a low-dose tricyclic antidepressant (such as amitriptyline 5 to 10 mg taken at night, titrated up to 30 mg) is the preferred second-line visceral analgesic. SSRIs are considered only if tricyclics are ineffective or contraindicated.
hq_q.f: Constipation-predominant IBS starting a laxative → ispaghula, and avoid lactulose because it causes bloating.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate second-line pharmacological treatment for his abdominal pain?

c: Despite 3 months of dietary modifications, regular antispasmodic therapy
tm.m: Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants modulate central descending noradrenergic/serotonergic pain pathways and peripheral gut visceral hypersensitivity at doses well below antidepressant thresholds.
tm.g: Refractory IBS pain despite first-line antispasmodics/laxatives -> low-dose oral amitriptyline at night
x: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are third-line options in IBS, considered only if low-dose tricyclic antidepressants fail or are not tolerated.
Linaclotide is reserved for chronic (>12 months) refractory constipation-predominant IBS that has failed multiple classes of laxatives, rather than general second-line visceral analgesia.
NICE explicitly advises against using lactulose in patients with IBS because colonic bacterial fermentation worsens gas and abdominal pain.
Opioid analgesics cause opioid-induced bowel dysfunction, narcotic bowel syndrome and dependence, and are contraindicated for chronic IBS pain.
f: he had already trialled low-dose amitriptyline without benefit (or had a prolonged QTc interval contraindicating tricyclics)
he had severe constipation-predominant IBS for over 12 months that had failed optimal trials of both macrogol and senna
a patient with decompensated liver cirrhosis required bowel acidification to prevent recurrent hepatic encephalopathy
short-term step-2 analgesia was needed for an acute traumatic fracture in a patient without functional bowel disease

hq_q.s:
A 29 year old man presents to his GP with a 3-month history of passing 4 loose, non-bloody stools daily and mild lower abdominal cramps. He has no nocturnal diarrhoea, fever, mouth ulcers or weight loss.
Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm. Abdominal and rectal examinations are normal.
Blood tests show haemoglobin 138 g/L, negative IgA tissue transglutaminase and negative stool culture, but faecal calprotectin is 320 µg/g (<50).
o: Diagnose irritable bowel syndrome and reassure
Refer to a dietitian for a low-FODMAP diet
Repeat the faecal calprotectin test in 12 months
Start regular oral loperamide and review in 3 months
hq_q.w: Faecal calprotectin is a calcium- and zinc-binding protein released by neutrophils into the bowel lumen during mucosal inflammation. A markedly elevated level (>250 µg/g, here 320 µg/g) in a young adult with chronic diarrhoea strongly suggests inflammatory bowel disease rather than irritable bowel syndrome and warrants urgent gastroenterology referral for ileocolonoscopy.
hq_q.f: Calprotectin under 50 µg/g → IBD is unlikely; manage as IBS.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next management step?

c: 3-month history of passing 4 loose, non-bloody stools daily
tm.m: Transmigration of neutrophils across inflamed intestinal epithelium releases cytosolic calprotectin into the faeces, distinguishing organic IBD from functional IBS.
tm.g: Chronic diarrhoea in a young adult + markedly raised faecal calprotectin (>250 µg/g) -> refer to gastroenterology for colonoscopy
x: A diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome requires a normal faecal calprotectin (<50 µg/g); a value of 320 µg/g indicates active intestinal inflammation.
A low-FODMAP diet is a second-line intervention for confirmed IBS and must not delay endoscopic investigation of suspected inflammatory bowel disease.
Waiting 12 months to repeat a markedly elevated calprotectin (>250 µg/g) risks progressive bowel damage from untreated Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.
Symptomatically masking inflammatory diarrhoea with loperamide leaves underlying inflammatory bowel disease undiagnosed and untreated.
f: his faecal calprotectin concentration was 24 µg/g (<50) alongside a normal full blood count, CRP and coeliac serology
he had confirmed IBS with a faecal calprotectin of 18 µg/g and persistent bloating despite 3 months of first-line dietary advice
a patient with known Crohn's disease in clinical remission was having routine annual non-invasive biomarker surveillance
