he had confirmed diarrhoea-predominant IBS with a normal faecal calprotectin and wanted symptomatic control of urgency

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old woman presents to the surgical clinic with a 12-month history of postprandial retrosternal pressure, early satiety and shortness of breath after large meals. She has minimal acid regurgitation.
Pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 134/78 mmHg. A barium swallow contrast study demonstrates the gastric fundus herniating through the diaphragmatic hiatus alongside the distal oesophagus, while the gastro-oesophageal junction remains fixed below the diaphragm.
hq_q.w: In a rolling (Type II paraoesophageal) hiatus hernia (5-10% of hiatus hernias), the gastro-oesophageal junction remains anchored below the diaphragm while the gastric fundus rolls up through the hiatus alongside the oesophagus. Unlike sliding hernias, rolling hernias carry a high risk of gastric volvulus, strangulation and perforation, so symptomatic cases warrant surgical repair.
hq_q.f: The junction itself slides up into the chest → sliding hiatus hernia, about 80% of cases.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: gastro-oesophageal junction remains fixed below the diaphragm
tm.m: A focal defect in the phrenoesophageal membrane allows the anterior gastric fundus to herniate into the thorax alongside a normally positioned gastro-oesophageal junction.
tm.g: Gastric fundus in chest alongside oesophagus + GOJ remains below diaphragm -> rolling (paraoesophageal) hiatus hernia
x: A peptic stricture causes concentric luminal narrowing of the lower oesophagus and progressive solid dysphagia rather than fundal herniation beside the oesophagus.
A pharyngeal pouch (Zenker diverticulum) arises in the neck above the cricopharyngeus muscle and causes halitosis and regurgitation of hours-old food.
Achalasia causes a dilated oesophagus with smooth 'bird-beak' tapering at the lower oesophageal sphincter rather than intrathoracic gastric fundus herniation.
In a sliding hiatus hernia (90% of cases), the gastro-oesophageal junction and proximal gastric cardia slide upwards above the diaphragm together.
f: barium swallow showed a smooth concentric narrowing in the distal oesophagus above the gastro-oesophageal junction in a patient with solid dysphagia
barium swallow showed a contrast-filled posterior outpouching in the neck at the level of C5/C6 above the cricopharyngeus
barium swallow showed a dilated, aperistaltic oesophagus terminating in a tight 'bird-beak' narrowing at the gastro-oesophageal junction
barium swallow showed the gastro-oesophageal junction itself displaced 4 cm above the diaphragmatic hiatus into the posterior mediastinum

hq_q.s:
A 79 year old woman with a 15-year history of postprandial heartburn and regurgitation undergoes a plain posteroanterior chest X-ray during an outpatient assessment for a mild chronic cough. She has no fever, night sweats, haemoptysis or weight loss.
Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm, SpO2 97% breathing air. Chest auscultation is clear.
The chest X-ray shows clear lung fields and a well-defined retrocardiac gas shadow containing a horizontal air-fluid level.
hq_q.w: A well-circumscribed retrocardiac soft-tissue mass containing a gas bubble and horizontal air-fluid level behind the cardiac silhouette on a plain posteroanterior chest radiograph is the classic radiographic appearance of an intrathoracic hiatus hernia (containing gastric air and fluid).
hq_q.f: A round cavity with an air-fluid level in the lung field after aspiration → lung abscess.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of this radiographic finding?

c: retrocardiac gas shadow containing a horizontal air-fluid level
tm.m: Herniation of the proximal stomach through the oesophageal hiatus into the posterior mediastinum traps swallowed air above gastric secretions behind the heart.
tm.g: Well patient with chronic reflux + retrocardiac gas shadow with air-fluid level on CXR -> hiatus hernia
x: A lung abscess presents with high swinging fever, foul purulent sputum and a thick-walled parenchymal cavity surrounded by pneumonic consolidation.
A Bochdalek hernia is a congenital posterolateral diaphragmatic defect presenting in neonates with severe respiratory distress and pulmonary hypoplasia.
Achalasia produces a widened superior/middle mediastinal shadow with an air-fluid level in the upper thorax and an absent normal gastric air bubble, accompanied by severe dysphagia.
Pneumomediastinum produces linear streaks of free gas outlining the mediastinal pleura and aortic knuckle rather than a contained retrocardiac air-fluid level.
f: she was febrile (39.0°C) expectorating foul-smelling pus after an aspiration episode with a thick-walled cavity in the lung parenchyma
a newborn infant presented immediately after birth with cyanosis, a scaphoid abdomen and bowel loops in the left hemithorax
a 35 year old had dysphagia to solids and liquids, an absent gastric fundus gas bubble and a dilated tubular oesophagus along the right heart border
a 22 year old asthmatic developed central chest pain and neck crunching (Hamman sign) with linear gas streaks along the left heart border

hq_q.s:
An 81 year old woman with a known large rolling paraoesophageal hiatus hernia is brought to the Emergency Department with a 2-hour history of sudden-onset, agonising epigastric and retrosternal pain. She has been retching violently every few minutes but is unable to bring up any vomit.
Pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg, SpO2 94% breathing air. There is tense epigastric distension and tenderness. Repeated attempts to pass a nasogastric tube arrest at the distal oesophagus. ECG shows sinus tachycardia.
hq_q.w: Acute gastric volvulus is a life-threatening complication of a large rolling (paraoesophageal) hiatus hernia in which the stomach rotates >180 degrees around its organoaxial or mesenteroaxial axis, obstructing both the cardia and pylorus. It presents with Borchardt's classic triad: severe epigastric/chest pain, violent unproductive retching, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube. Urgent surgical decompression and gastropexy/repair are required.
hq_q.f: Pain after forceful vomiting with surgical emphysema → Boerhaave syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which surgical emergency has developed?

c: unable to bring up any vomit
nasogastric tube arrest at the distal oesophagus
tm.m: Torsion of the intrathoracic stomach twists the gastro-oesophageal junction closed (preventing emesis and NG tube passage) and compromises gastric blood supply, risking strangulation and necrosis.
tm.g: Borchardt triad (severe epigastric pain + unproductive retching + failure to pass NG tube) in hiatus hernia -> acute gastric volvulus
x: Acute pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with profuse bilious vomiting and allows easy passage of a nasogastric tube.
Boerhaave syndrome follows forceful vomiting of gastric contents and causes subcutaneous neck emphysema, pleural effusion and pneumomediastinum.
Her 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia only without ST-segment elevation, and myocardial infarction does not mechanically obstruct nasogastric tube passage.
Perforated peptic ulcer causes generalized board-like abdominal rigidity and subdiaphragmatic free gas without mechanical obstruction to a nasogastric tube.
f: she had profuse bilious vomiting, epigastric pain radiating to the back and a serum lipase more than three times the upper limit of normal
chest pain developed immediately after forceful vomiting of food and examination revealed palpable surgical emphysema in the supraclavicular fossa
her 12-lead ECG demonstrated ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in leads I and aVL
she had a rigid board-like abdomen with absent bowel sounds and free gas under both hemidiaphragms on erect chest radiograph

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old man presents to his GP with a 2-month history of retrosternal burning pain and sour acid regurgitation occurring after large evening meals and when lying flat in bed. He has no dysphagia, odynophagia, unintentional weight loss, vomiting or melaena.
Pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, BMI 29 kg/m². Abdominal examination is normal and his full blood count is normal.
o: Barium swallow contrast study within 2 weeks
Full-dose proton pump inhibitor for 4 weeks
hq_q.w: Under NICE guidelines (CG184) for adults with uninvestigated classical gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms (heartburn and acid regurgitation) and no alarm features (no dysphagia, weight loss or aged >=55 with red flags), first-line management is lifestyle modification plus an empirical 4-week (or 4-8 week) trial of a full-dose proton pump inhibitor (such as omeprazole 20 mg or lansoprazole 30 mg daily).
hq_q.f: Age 55 or over with weight loss and reflux → suspected cancer referral for endoscopy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial medical management alongside lifestyle advice?

c: retrosternal burning pain and sour acid regurgitation
no dysphagia, odynophagia, unintentional weight loss
tm.m: Irreversible covalent inhibition of gastric parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase proton pumps suppresses basal and stimulated acid secretion, healing mucosal acid injury.
tm.g: Uninvestigated classical GORD without alarm features -> full-dose PPI for 4 weeks alongside lifestyle advice
x: Barium swallow is used to delineate hiatus hernia anatomy or suspected pharyngeal pouch/achalasia, not uncomplicated primary-care reflux.
H2-receptor antagonists (such as famotidine) are less effective than proton pump inhibitors at healing reflux oesophagitis and are second-line options.
Anti-reflux surgery is reserved for patients with objectively confirmed GORD who respond to but wish to discontinue long-term PPI therapy.
Urgent 2-week-wait endoscopy is indicated for dysphagia at any age, or age >=55 with weight loss and reflux/dyspepsia; he is 38 with no alarm features.
f: a 78 year old presented with high dysphagia, halitosis and a gurgling left neck swelling suggestive of a pharyngeal pouch
he had completed a trial of a full-dose proton pump inhibitor and experienced an inadequate response or intolerance
he was a young patient with pH-manometry-proven severe volume reflux who responded to PPIs but declined lifelong tablet therapy
he had progressive difficulty swallowing solid food or was aged 58 with 6 kg unintentional weight loss

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man has had reflux for many years. Endoscopy shows a 2 cm segment of Barrett's oesophagus. Biopsies show no dysplasia.
hq_q.w: Barrett's without dysplasia is watched with interval endoscopy, sooner for longer segments, and a PPI for symptoms.
hq_q.f: High-grade dysplasia → endoscopic resection and ablation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Barrett's can progress slowly to cancer; surveillance catches dysplasia
tm.g: Barrett's without dysplasia: PPI and interval surveillance
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Discharge from follow-up (Non-dysplastic Barrett's oesophagus requires endoscopic surveillance every 3 to 5 years)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Endoscopy every 3 months (Non-dysplastic short-segment (<3 cm) Barrett's is surveyed every 3 to 5 years)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oesophagectomy (Oesophagectomy is for cancer)
high-grade dysplasia
x: Non-dysplastic Barrett's oesophagus requires endoscopic surveillance every 3 to 5 years
Non-dysplastic short-segment (<3 cm) Barrett's is surveyed every 3 to 5 years
Oesophagectomy is for cancer.
Ruled out here: requires high-grade dysplasia, whereas this patient has Barrett's, no dysplasia.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman presents with a 12-month history of progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the onset of her symptoms, accompanied by nocturnal regurgitation of undigested food, retrosternal cramps and 4 kg weight loss.
Barium swallow demonstrates a dilated, aperistaltic thoracic oesophagus tapering smoothly to a 'bird's beak' at the gastro-oesophageal junction, and upper GI endoscopy excludes a gastro-oesophageal junction tumour.
o: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax
Repeat upper GI endoscopy with biopsies
hq_q.w: Achalasia is caused by degeneration of inhibitory nitric oxide/VIP myenteric plexus ganglion cells (Auerbach's plexus) in the distal oesophagus. After upper GI endoscopy excludes pseudoachalasia (malignancy), high-resolution oesophageal manometry is the diagnostic gold standard, showing incomplete lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation (raised integrated relaxation pressure) and absent normal peristalsis.
hq_q.f: Solids then liquids with weight loss in an older smoker → endoscopy for cancer.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is the gold standard to definitively confirm this diagnosis?

c: dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the onset
tm.m: Loss of inhibitory nitrergic myenteric neurones prevents lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation on swallowing and abolishes coordinated oesophageal body peristalsis.
tm.g: Suspected achalasia (dysphagia to solids and liquids + bird's beak on barium) -> high-resolution oesophageal manometry confirms
x: Ambulatory pH monitoring quantifies acid reflux prior to anti-reflux surgery, whereas achalasia is a primary motility disorder diagnosed by manometry.
CT thorax assesses extrinsic mediastinal compression or staging of cancer, which has already been excluded endoscopically.
Barium swallow has already demonstrated the classic bird's beak appearance; manometry is required to measure sphincter pressures and classify the achalasia subtype.
Endoscopy has already been performed to exclude a gastro-oesophageal junction tumour (pseudoachalasia) and cannot measure sphincter relaxation pressure.
f: she had refractory heartburn with a normal endoscopy and normal manometry prior to planned Nissen fundoplication
endoscopy had confirmed an infiltrating adenocarcinoma at the gastro-oesophageal junction requiring TNM staging
she had already undergone pneumatic dilatation or Heller myotomy and objective post-treatment emptying was being assessed
she had long-segment Barrett's oesophagus requiring scheduled endoscopic surveillance with Seattle protocol biopsies

hq_q.s:
A 44 year old woman presents to her GP with a 2-month history of epigastric discomfort, postprandial fullness and nausea. She has no dysphagia, unintentional weight loss, vomiting or melaena. She takes no NSAIDs and has no known drug allergies.
Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm. Abdominal examination is normal.
A Helicobacter pylori monoclonal stool antigen test is positive.
o: Bismuth subsalicylate, PPI, metronidazole and tetracycline
Dual therapy with a PPI and oral amoxicillin for 7 days
Full-dose proton pump inhibitor monotherapy for 8 weeks
Triple therapy with a PPI, metronidazole and doxycycline
hq_q.w: Under NICE guidelines (CG184) for Helicobacter pylori eradication in adults without penicillin allergy or recent macrolide/metronidazole exposure, first-line treatment is a 7-day twice-daily triple regimen comprising a proton pump inhibitor plus amoxicillin and either clarithromycin or metronidazole.
hq_q.f: Penicillin allergy → PPI with clarithromycin and metronidazole.
hq_q.ql: Which is the recommended first-line 7-day eradication regimen?

c: Helicobacter pylori monoclonal stool antigen test is positive
tm.m: Proton pump inhibition raises intragastric pH, driving Helicobacter pylori into active replication where amoxicillin (cell wall) and clarithromycin (50S ribosome) act synergistically.
tm.g: First-line H. pylori eradication without penicillin allergy -> 7 days of PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin (or metronidazole)
x: Bismuth-based quadruple therapy is reserved for second-line rescue eradication when patients have had previous clarithromycin and metronidazole exposure.
Dual therapy with a PPI and amoxicillin alone achieves unacceptably low eradication rates (<60%) compared with standard triple therapy.
A PPI alone suppresses acid and heals symptoms temporarily but never eradicates Helicobacter pylori infection.
In penicillin-allergic patients, first-line therapy is a PPI plus clarithromycin and metronidazole; doxycycline is not used in first-line triple regimens.
f: she had penicillin allergy and had previously received both clarithromycin and metronidazole for other infections
high-dose, high-frequency vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy was being used in a specialist refractory trial protocol
her Helicobacter pylori stool antigen test was negative and she had functional or NSAID-related dyspepsia
a tetracycline-containing quadruple regimen (using tetracycline hydrochloride rather than doxycycline) was required for second-line relapse

hq_q.s:
A 50 year old man attends his GP with recurrent epigastric pain and postprandial fullness. He has been buying over-the-counter omeprazole 20 mg daily for the past 4 weeks, which partially relieves his pain. He has no dysphagia, weight loss or anaemia, and has not taken any antibiotics in the past year.
The GP arranges a carbon-13 urea breath test to test for Helicobacter pylori.
o: Cancel the breath test and rely on serum IgG serology
Continue omeprazole as no washout period is needed
Stop all oral antibiotics 1 week before the test
Stop the proton pump inhibitor 48 hours before the test
Stop the proton pump inhibitor at least 2 weeks before the test
hq_q.w: Proton pump inhibitors suppress Helicobacter pylori bacterial load and urease activity in the gastric antrum, causing false-negative carbon-13 urea breath tests and stool antigen tests. NICE guidance requires stopping any PPI at least 2 weeks before testing (and stopping systemic antibiotics at least 4 weeks before testing).
hq_q.f: Recent antibiotics for a chest infection → wait 4 weeks after the course.
hq_q.ql: Which preparation instruction is required before performing the urea breath test?

tm.m: PPI-induced hypochlorhydria inhibits H. pylori urease activity and reduces bacterial density in the gastric mucosa, preventing cleavage of labelled 13C-urea into exhaled 13CO2.
tm.g: Before a H. pylori urea breath test or stool antigen test -> stop PPIs for at least 2 weeks (and antibiotics for 4 weeks)
x: Laboratory IgG serology has lower accuracy than the urea breath test or stool antigen test and cannot distinguish active infection from past eradicated infection.
Continuing omeprazole up to the day of the urea breath test produces up to a 40% false-negative rate.
When antibiotics have been taken, a 4-week washout (not 1 week) is required before performing a urea breath test or stool antigen test.
A 48-hour washout is sufficient for H2-receptor antagonists or antacids, whereas irreversible proton pump inhibitors require a full 2-week washout.
f: an epidemiological population seroprevalence survey was being conducted where active vs past infection distinction was unnecessary
he was taking simple alginate/antacid tablets up until the day before the test rather than a proton pump inhibitor
never; antibiotics require a 4-week washout before H. pylori breath or stool testing
he was taking an H2-receptor antagonist (such as famotidine) rather than a proton pump inhibitor

hq_q.s:
A 59 year old man with Child-Pugh B alcohol-related liver cirrhosis is brought to the Emergency Department having vomited 500 mL of fresh bright-red blood twice in the past hour.
Pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 92/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Examination reveals spider naevi, palmar erythema, splenomegaly and shifting dullness. Two large-bore intravenous cannulae are inserted and resuscitation has begun.
o: Immediate oral propranolol 40 mg twice daily
hq_q.w: Under NICE guidelines (CG141) for suspected acute variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding in cirrhosis, immediately commence a vasoactive splanchnic vasoconstrictor (intravenous terlipressin, or octreotide) to lower portal venous pressure PLUS prophylactic broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (which significantly reduce bacterial translocation, rebleeding and mortality), followed by urgent endoscopic variceal band ligation.
hq_q.f: Non-variceal bleed → no PPI before endoscopy; give it after endoscopic treatment.
hq_q.ql: Which specific pharmacological regimen must be started immediately before urgent endoscopy?
hq_q.post: Two large-bore cannulas are in and fluids have started.

c: vomited 500 mL of fresh bright-red blood
tm.m: Terlipressin activates splanchnic V1 vasopressin receptors to constrict mesenteric arterioles and lower portal hypertension, while prophylactic antibiotics prevent sepsis-driven portal pressure surges.
tm.g: Suspected acute variceal haemorrhage in cirrhosis -> IV terlipressin + prophylactic IV antibiotics before endoscopy
x: High-dose intravenous PPI infusion is given after endoscopic haemostasis of high-risk non-variceal peptic ulcers, not before endoscopy for variceal bleeding.
The HALT-IT trial demonstrated that high-dose tranexamic acid does not reduce mortality in acute GI bleeding and increases venous thromboembolism risk in cirrhosis.
Non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol or carvedilol) are used for primary and secondary variceal prophylaxis when stable, but cause dangerous hypotension in acute haemorrhagic shock.
Prothrombin complex concentrate is for warfarin reversal; platelets are transfused in active bleeding when the count is <50 x 10^9/L (his is 64 x 10^9/L).
f: endoscopy had confirmed a bleeding duodenal ulcer with an adherent clot treated by adrenaline injection and thermal coagulation
he presented within 3 hours of major blunt polytrauma with haemorrhagic shock (CRASH-2 criteria)
he had recovered from his acute bleed 5 days later, was haemodynamically stable off terlipressin, and required secondary variceal prophylaxis
he was taking warfarin for a mechanical heart valve and presented with life-threatening bleeding and an INR of 6.2

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man presents with a 12-month history of urinary hesitancy, a weak stream, terminal dribbling and nocturia twice nightly that significantly disturb his sleep. He has no visible haematuria or dysuria.
BP 138/82 mmHg. His abdomen is soft with no palpable bladder. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate (~25 g). Urine dipstick is normal and serum PSA is 1.2 ng/mL (<4.5).
hq_q.w: For men with moderate-to-severe bothersome voiding lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic enlargement, NICE recommends an oral selective alpha-1A adrenoceptor blocker such as tamsulosin 400 micrograms once daily, which relaxes prostatic and bladder neck smooth muscle within days.
hq_q.f: Prostate >30 g or PSA >1.4 ng/mL with high risk of progression -> add or combine with finasteride.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug?

c: urinary hesitancy, a weak stream, terminal dribbling
tm.m: Alpha-1A adrenoceptor blockade relaxes smooth muscle in the prostatic stroma and bladder neck, reducing dynamic bladder outlet resistance within 48 to 72 hours.
tm.g: Bothersome voiding LUTS from benign prostatic hyperplasia -> first-line tamsulosin
x: Desmopressin is an antidiuretic hormone analogue that causes severe hyponatraemia in older men and does not relieve prostatic bladder outlet obstruction.
Finasteride takes 6 months to shrink the prostate and is reserved for men with significantly enlarged glands (>30 g or PSA >1.4 ng/mL), usually in combination.
Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic for storage urgency and overactive bladder; in predominant voiding obstruction it can precipitate acute urinary retention.
Sildenafil is a first-line phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor for erectile dysfunction rather than first-line monotherapy for obstructive voiding LUTS.
f: primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a child aged over 7 years after alarm therapy
a prostate volume of 55 mL and PSA of 3.2 ng/mL requiring long-term gland size reduction
predominant urinary urgency, frequency and urge incontinence with normal voiding flow
a man requesting treatment for erectile dysfunction rather than voiding hesitancy

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old man attends his GP practice for an annual medication review. He has taken oral finasteride 5 mg daily plus tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily for the past 14 months for benign prostatic hyperplasia, with good relief of his lower urinary tract symptoms.
Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, benign-feeling prostate. A routine serum PSA test returns at 2.5 ng/mL (age-specific reference <5.0).
o: Double it, treating it as about 5 ng/mL
Halve it, treating it as about 1.25 ng/mL
It cannot be interpreted on finasteride
Read it directly as the measured 2.5 ng/mL
Stop finasteride for 1 month and repeat
hq_q.w: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride and dutasteride reduce prostatic glandular epithelial volume and halve serum PSA concentrations after 6 months of continuous therapy. To assess prostate cancer risk against age-specific reference ranges, the measured PSA value must be doubled.
hq_q.f: Patient taking an alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) alone -> interpret the measured PSA without adjustment.
hq_q.ql: How should this serum PSA result be interpreted?

c: serum PSA test returns at 2.5 ng/mL
tm.m: Inhibition of type II 5-alpha-reductase depletes intraprostatic dihydrotestosterone, reducing PSA transcription and halving circulating PSA levels by 6 months.
tm.g: Interpreting serum PSA after >=6 months on finasteride -> double the measured PSA value
x: Finasteride has already halved the patient's true baseline PSA; halving it again would mask an elevated age-specific PSA of 5.0 ng/mL.
Serum PSA remains a valid screening and monitoring marker on finasteride provided the clinician doubles the measured value.
Reading the unadjusted value on finasteride underestimates the true PSA by 50% and risks missing clinically significant prostate cancer.
Stopping finasteride is unnecessary and would worsen his voiding symptoms; doubling the on-treatment PSA accurately adjusts for the drug effect.
f: estimating what a baseline pre-treatment PSA of 2.5 ng/mL is expected to fall to after 6 months of finasteride
a PSA sample taken within 48 hours of an acute bacterial urinary tract infection or bladder catheterisation
the patient was taking tamsulosin monotherapy without a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor
repeating a PSA test 6 weeks after treating a documented acute urinary tract infection

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old man has had a slow, spraying stream for 6 months. He was treated for gonorrhoea a year ago.
Rectal examination shows a normal prostate.
A urine flow test shows a flat, box-shaped curve with a low maximum flow.
hq_q.w: A retrograde urethrogram outlines the urethra with contrast and shows the site and length of a stricture, which guides treatment (urethrotomy, dilatation or urethroplasty). Flexible cystoscopy can also show it.
hq_q.f: Older man with frequency, nocturia and a smooth, enlarged prostate → benign prostatic hyperplasia.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation will best show the cause?

tm.m: Scarring from infection or catheters narrows the urethra
tm.g: Box-shaped flow + past urethritis: urethrogram
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to CT KUB (CT KUB looks for stones; it does not outline the urethra)
the presentation instead showed features specific to PSA (PSA relates to the prostate, which is normal; the problem is the urethra)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Transrectal ultrasound (Transrectal ultrasound images the prostate, not the urethral lumen)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Urine cytology (Cytology screens for bladder cancer in painless haematuria, not a narrowed stream)
x: CT KUB looks for stones; it does not outline the urethra.
PSA relates to the prostate, which is normal; the problem is the urethra.
Transrectal ultrasound images the prostate, not the urethral lumen.
Cytology screens for bladder cancer in painless haematuria, not a narrowed stream.

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man presents to his GP with a 4-month history of nocturia twice nightly and mild hesitancy. He has no dysuria, visible haematuria, weight loss or back pain.
BP 134/78 mmHg. Abdomen is soft with no palpable bladder. Digital rectal examination reveals an asymmetrical, hard, craggy nodule in the left lobe of the prostate. Urine dipstick is negative and serum PSA is 3.0 ng/mL (<4.5).
o: Reassure him as the serum PSA is normal
Repeat the serum PSA test in 6 months
hq_q.w: Any man whose prostate feels malignant (hard, craggy, nodular or asymmetrical) on digital rectal examination must be referred urgently via the 2-week-wait suspected cancer pathway regardless of whether the serum PSA is within the age-specific reference range.
hq_q.f: Smooth, benign-feeling prostate with normal age-specific PSA -> manage LUTS in primary care without 2-week-wait referral.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Poorly differentiated high-grade prostate adenocarcinomas or neuroendocrine variants may lose PSA expression while producing a palpable hard cortical nodule.
tm.g: Hard, irregular or nodular prostate on DRE -> suspected cancer pathway referral regardless of PSA level
x: Up to 15% of men with clinically significant prostate cancer (including poorly differentiated tumours) have a serum PSA within the normal reference range.
Waiting 6 months to repeat a blood test when the prostate already feels malignant on rectal examination delays diagnosis of locally advanced cancer.
A hard, craggy prostate meets the NICE NG12 criterion for a 2-week-wait suspected cancer referral rather than a routine urology wait.
Prescribing tamsulosin without urgent oncological investigation ignores the malignant digital rectal examination finding.
f: an asymptomatic man with a smooth, normal-feeling prostate and a normal age-specific PSA
a borderline PSA rise after recent vigorous cycling with a completely smooth, normal-feeling prostate
bothersome voiding symptoms from a smooth, benign-feeling prostate that have not responded to primary care medical therapy
moderate voiding LUTS with a smooth, symmetrically enlarged benign prostate and normal PSA

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man attends the rapid-access urology clinic via a 2-week-wait referral after two consecutive serum PSA measurements of 7.8 ng/mL and 8.2 ng/mL (age-specific reference <4.5). He has mild urinary frequency but no bone pain or haematuria.
Digital rectal examination shows a smoothly enlarged prostate. Midstream urine culture is negative and his eGFR is 84 mL/min/1.73 m².
o: Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis
hq_q.w: NICE recommends multiparametric MRI of the prostate as the first-line investigation in secondary care for men with suspected localised prostate cancer. The Likert or PI-RADS score (1 to 5) determines whether a targeted transperineal prostate biopsy is required.
hq_q.f: Multiparametric MRI Likert score >=3 -> proceed to targeted transperineal prostate biopsy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first investigation in secondary care?

tm.m: Multiparametric MRI combines T2-weighted, diffusion-weighted and dynamic contrast sequences to localise high-grade lesions and avoid unnecessary biopsies in Likert 1-2 glands.
tm.g: Suspected prostate cancer referred to secondary care -> multiparametric MRI of the prostate before biopsy
x: CT has poor soft-tissue contrast resolution within the prostate gland and is used for nodal staging after biopsy confirmation rather than primary diagnosis.
An isotope bone scan assesses osteoblastic skeletal metastases in confirmed high-risk disease rather than diagnosing a primary prostatic lesion.
PSMA PET-CT is reserved for staging high-risk prostate cancer or detecting biochemical recurrence after radical treatment, not initial diagnostic work-up.
Performing an upfront blind TRUS biopsy before MRI misses anterior tumours, overdiagnoses insignificant cancers and causes rectal bleeding or sepsis that obscures MRI.
f: distant nodal and visceral staging after biopsy confirms high-risk prostate adenocarcinoma
staging for skeletal metastases in biopsy-proven Gleason 4+5=9 prostate cancer with bone pain
localising occult recurrence when serum PSA rises after radical prostatectomy
multiparametric MRI is contraindicated due to a non-MRI-compatible metallic implant

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man has newly diagnosed metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma with multiple osteoblastic metastases in his lumbar spine on isotope bone scan. He reports mild lower back ache controlled with paracetamol and has normal lower-limb power, tone, reflexes and sensation.
His serum PSA is 110 ng/mL (<4.5). He is scheduled to begin subcutaneous goserelin therapy next week.
hq_q.w: Before starting a GnRH agonist such as goserelin in metastatic prostate cancer, oral bicalutamide is started 1 week prior and continued for 2 to 3 weeks to prevent the initial testosterone surge from flaring bone metastases.
hq_q.f: Starting a GnRH antagonist (degarelix) -> immediate LH/testosterone suppression without flare.
hq_q.ql: Which drug should be started first?

c: osteoblastic metastases in his lumbar spine
tm.m: Initial GnRH receptor stimulation transiently increases pituitary LH and testicular testosterone before receptor downregulation occurs at 2 to 3 weeks.
tm.g: Preventing testosterone flare when starting goserelin in spinal metastatic prostate cancer -> bicalutamide first
x: High-dose dexamethasone is indicated for acute malignant spinal cord compression with neurological deficit, not routine anti-androgen flare prophylaxis.
Docetaxel is a taxane chemotherapy added after androgen deprivation is established, and it does not block the acute testosterone surge from goserelin.
Tamsulosin is an alpha-1A blocker for bladder outflow symptoms and has no effect on androgen receptors or vertebral metastases.
Zoledronic acid is a bisphosphonate used in hormone-relapsed bone metastases to reduce skeletal events, not to block acute goserelin-induced testosterone flare.
f: he developed acute bilateral leg weakness, brisk reflexes and a sensory level from spinal cord compression
systemic taxane chemotherapy started alongside established androgen deprivation therapy
symptomatic urinary hesitancy and poor stream from benign prostatic enlargement
preventing skeletal-related events in castration-resistant prostate cancer with bone metastases

hq_q.s:
A 67 year old man presents to his GP after passing frank blood with small clots in his urine on three occasions over the past week. He has no dysuria, loin pain or fever. He smoked 20 cigarettes daily for 40 years and worked for 25 years in an industrial textile dye factory.
BP 136/80 mmHg. Abdominal and rectal examinations are normal, and midstream urine culture is negative.
o: Adenocarcinoma of the urachal bladder dome
Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder
Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder
hq_q.w: Transitional cell (urothelial) carcinoma accounts for over 90% of UK bladder cancers and presents with painless visible haematuria. Major risk factors are smoking and occupational exposure to aromatic amines in dyes and rubber.
hq_q.f: Chronic urinary schistosomiasis (Schistosoma haematobium) or long-term indwelling catheter -> squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: no dysuria, loin pain or fever
tm.m: Renally excreted aromatic amine carcinogens and tobacco metabolites are concentrated in bladder urine, causing DNA adducts in transitional urothelium.
tm.g: Painless visible haematuria in a smoker and dye worker -> transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder
x: Primary bladder adenocarcinoma is rare (<2% of bladder tumours) and arises from a urachal remnant at the bladder dome or bladder exstrophy.
His rectal examination is normal and aromatic amine dye exposure is a specific carcinogen for urothelial transitional cell carcinoma rather than prostate cancer.
Renal cell carcinoma presents with a flank mass and loin pain and is not specifically linked to industrial aniline dye exposure.
Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder arises from chronic squamous metaplasia due to Schistosoma haematobium infection or long-term catheter stones, not dye exposure.
f: a mucin-secreting tumour arising at the dome of the bladder from a persistent urachal remnant
progressive nocturia, back pain, a hard nodular prostate on rectal examination and a PSA of 45 ng/mL
left loin pain, a palpable ballotable flank mass and paraneoplastic polycythaemia
a patient who grew up in rural Egypt with childhood terminal haematuria and calcified bladder wall ova from Schistosoma haematobium

hq_q.s:
A 62 year old woman attends her GP practice after routine blood and urine checks. She has no visible haematuria,  dysuria, frequency, flank pain or fever.
Temperature 36.7°C, BP 132/76 mmHg. Abdominal examination is normal. Two consecutive urine dipstick tests taken 2 weeks apart show blood 2+ with negative nitrites. Urine culture is sterile and white cell count is 13.2 × 10⁹/L (3.8-10.0).
o: Empirical antibiotics and repeat urine dipstick
Reassure her and discharge without follow-up
Repeat urine dipstick and blood tests in 1 year
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG12 suspected cancer guidelines, patients aged 60 years and over with unexplained non-visible haematuria PLUS either dysuria or a raised white cell count on a blood test must be referred urgently via the 2-week-wait suspected bladder cancer pathway.
hq_q.f: Aged 45 years and over with unexplained visible haematuria without UTI -> 2-week-wait suspected bladder cancer referral.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate referral or management step?

tm.m: Persistent unexplained non-visible haematuria accompanied by systemic leukocytosis in a patient aged >=60 years carries a significant positive predictive value for urothelial malignancy.
tm.g: Aged >=60 with unexplained non-visible haematuria + raised blood white cell count -> suspected cancer pathway referral
x: Her midstream urine culture is sterile and she has no urinary tract infection symptoms, so empirical antibiotics will only delay cancer investigation.
Because she is over 60 with persistent non-visible haematuria and a raised blood white cell count, she meets the NICE threshold for a 2-week-wait cancer referral.
Persistent non-visible haematuria in a 62 year old woman with leucocytosis requires endoscopic exclusion of urothelial malignancy.
Deferring investigation for 12 months risks progression of an underlying high-grade urothelial carcinoma.
f: acute dysuria and frequency with a positive urine culture for Escherichia coli
persistent unexplained non-visible haematuria in a 52 year old without dysuria, proteinuria or raised white cell count
transient dipstick haematuria during menstruation that resolves completely on repeat testing
annual primary care monitoring of isolated microscopic haematuria after urology has already excluded malignancy

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man attends the urology clinic after transurethral resection of a 3 cm bladder tumour. Histopathology confirms high-grade non-muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma invading the subepithelial lamina propria (pT1G3) with uninvolved detrusor muscle in the specimen.
Staging CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no nodal or distant metastases. He is fit with an eGFR of 76 mL/min/1.73 m².
hq_q.w: High-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (pT1 or high-grade/G3 or carcinoma in situ) is treated with adjuvant intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) immunotherapy instillations, which provoke a local cell-mediated immune response that significantly reduces tumour recurrence and progression.
hq_q.f: Muscle-invasive bladder tumour (pT2+) -> radical cystectomy or radical radiotherapy with neoadjuvant cisplatin chemotherapy.
hq_q.ql: Which further treatment is most appropriate?

tm.m: Live attenuated intravesical BCG stimulates urothelial cytokine release and cytotoxic T-cell infiltration that eradicates residual microscopic high-grade carcinoma.
tm.g: High-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (pT1G3) -> intravesical BCG
x: External-beam pelvic radiotherapy is used for muscle-invasive (pT2+) bladder cancer rather than lamina-propria-confined non-muscle-invasive disease.
Primary radical cystectomy is first-line for muscle-invasive (pT2+) bladder cancer, whereas intravesical BCG is standard first-line adjuvant therapy for pT1 disease.
High-grade pT1 bladder cancer has a high progression rate to muscle invasion if managed with cystoscopic surveillance alone without intravesical BCG.
Systemic intravenous cisplatin chemotherapy is reserved for muscle-invasive or metastatic urothelial cancer, not non-muscle-invasive disease.
f: muscle-invasive pT2 urothelial carcinoma in a patient choosing bladder-sparing radical chemoradiotherapy
histopathology showing tumour invasion into the detrusor muscularis propria (pT2)
solitary low-risk, low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma (pTaG1) after complete resection and single mitomycin instillation
neoadjuvant chemotherapy prior to radical cystectomy for T2-T4a muscle-invasive bladder cancer

hq_q.s:
A 62 year old man presents with a 1-week history of painless visible haematuria and a 1-month history of swelling in his left hemiscrotum. He has lost 4 kg unintentionally over 2 months.
BP 146/88 mmHg. There is a firm, ballotable mass in the left flank and a left-sided scrotal varicocele feeling like a bag of worms that fails to empty when he lies supine.
hq_q.w: Left renal cell carcinoma can invade the left renal vein, into which the left testicular vein drains directly. This obstructs testicular venous outflow and produces a left varicocele that fails to collapse when lying supine.
hq_q.f: Child under 5 years with a painless unilateral flank mass -> Wilms' tumour (nephroblastoma).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: fails to empty when he lies supine
tm.m: Tumour thrombus extending into the left renal vein blocks venous outflow from the left internal spermatic vein, preventing the pampiniform plexus from draining when supine.
tm.g: Visible haematuria + left flank mass + fixed non-emptying left varicocele -> renal cell carcinoma
x: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease causes bilateral bosselated flank masses and hypertension but does not invade the left renal vein to cause an acute fixed varicocele.
Bladder cancer causes painless visible haematuria but does not produce a ballotable left flank mass or obstruct the left renal vein.
Testicular cancer presents as a solid intratesticular lump rather than a compressible pampiniform varicocele accompanied by a flank mass and haematuria.
Wilms' tumour is an embryonal kidney cancer of early childhood (under 6 years) rather than a 62 year old man.
f: bilateral palpable knobbly kidneys, hepatic cysts and a family history of intracranial berry aneurysms
isolated painless visible haematuria in a dye worker with a normal abdominal and scrotal examination
a hard, painless intratesticular mass in a 28 year old man with raised serum AFP and no haematuria
a 3 year old child presenting with a smooth unilateral abdominal mass that does not cross the midline

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man presents with a 2-month history of right loin ache and mild lethargy. He never smoked, has no lung disease and takes no medications.
Pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 148/86 mmHg, SpO2 98% breathing air. There is a firm, ballotable right flank mass. Haemoglobin is 195 g/L (130-175), white cell count 6.8 × 10⁹/L (3.8-10.0) and platelets 240 × 10⁹/L (150-400).
hq_q.w: Renal cell carcinoma is associated with several paraneoplastic syndromes, including ectopic erythropoietin secretion causing secondary polycythaemia, PTHrP secretion causing humoral hypercalcaemia, renin-mediated hypertension and non-metastatic hepatic dysfunction (Stauffer syndrome).
hq_q.f: JAK2 V617F positive with splenomegaly, aquagenic pruritus and suppressed erythropoietin -> polycythaemia rubra vera.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely explanation for his raised haemoglobin?

tm.m: Constitutive hypoxia-inducible factor activation in clear cell renal carcinoma drives autonomous paraneoplastic erythropoietin secretion despite normal arterial oxygenation.
tm.g: Ballotable flank mass with isolated erythrocytosis and normal SpO2 -> tumour erythropoietin secretion
x: His oxygen saturation is 98% breathing room air and he has never smoked or had lung disease, excluding hypoxic secondary polycythaemia.
Mild dehydration causes only a modest relative rise in haematocrit and does not produce a haemoglobin of 195 g/L with a ballotable renal mass.
Polycythaemia rubra vera causes panmyelosis (raised red cells, white cells and platelets) with splenomegaly and low erythropoietin rather than a unilateral renal mass.
He takes no exogenous medications, and the presence of a ballotable right flank mass points directly to paraneoplastic erythropoietin from a renal tumour.
f: severe COPD with chronic resting SpO2 of 86% breathing air and cor pulmonale
profuse vomiting and diarrhoea with hypotension, tachycardia and acute prerenal kidney injury
splenomegaly, post-bath itching, platelets of 680 × 10⁹/L and a JAK2 V617F mutation
an athlete injecting exogenous androgenic steroids with suppressed LH and FSH and normal kidney imaging

hq_q.s: A 28 year old man has von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, confirmed on genetic testing after a cerebellar haemangioblastoma. His father died of kidney cancer at 40. He is about to have surgery for a renal tumour.
hq_q.w: VHL causes phaeochromocytoma as well as haemangioblastomas, retinal angiomas and clear cell renal cancer. An unrecognised phaeochromocytoma can cause a fatal hypertensive crisis under anaesthesia, so plasma metanephrines are checked first.
hq_q.f: Medullary thyroid cancer and phaeochromocytoma in a family with a RET mutation → MEN 2.
hq_q.ql: Which other tumour must be excluded before his operation?

tm.m: Loss of the VHL protein switches on hypoxia signalling, driving vascular tumours
tm.g: VHL before surgery: exclude phaeochromocytoma
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Cardiac rhabdomyoma (Cardiac rhabdomyomas occur in tuberous sclerosis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Medullary thyroid cancer (Medullary thyroid cancer belongs to MEN 2, not VHL)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Neurofibroma (Neurofibromas are the hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 1)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Parathyroid adenoma (Parathyroid adenomas are part of MEN 1 and MEN 2A)
x: Cardiac rhabdomyomas occur in tuberous sclerosis.
Medullary thyroid cancer belongs to MEN 2, not VHL.
Neurofibromas are the hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 1.
Parathyroid adenomas are part of MEN 1 and MEN 2A.

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old man presents with a 2-hour history of excruciating colicky pain radiating from his left loin to his left groin. He is restless and pacing the room. He has no asthma, peptic ulcer disease or drug allergies.
Temperature 36.9°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 142/88 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows blood 3+ and serum creatinine is 78 µmol/L (60-120).
hq_q.w: NICE guidelines on renal and ureteric stones recommend a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) such as diclofenac (by any route) as first-line analgesia for suspected acute renal colic, as NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin-mediated ureteric spasm and afferent arteriolar vasodilatation.
hq_q.f: NSAIDs contraindicated (e.g. CKD, active peptic ulcer or NSAID-sensitive asthma) -> intravenous paracetamol second-line.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line analgesia?

c: left loin to his left groin
no asthma, peptic ulcer disease or drug allergies
tm.m: Prostaglandin inhibition reduces glomerular filtration pressure behind the stone and directly decreases ureteric smooth muscle contractility and mucosal oedema.
tm.g: First-line acute analgesia for renal colic with normal renal function -> NSAID (diclofenac)
x: NICE specifically recommends against antispasmodics such as hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan) for acute renal colic because they provide no analgesic benefit.
Opioids are reserved as third-line analgesia in acute renal colic only when both NSAIDs and intravenous paracetamol are contraindicated or ineffective.
NSAIDs are superior to paracetamol for first-line relief of renal colic; intravenous paracetamol is used second-line when NSAIDs are contraindicated.
Tamsulosin is an alpha-blocker used as medical expulsive therapy for distal ureteric stones <10 mm, not for immediate acute pain relief in the emergency department.
f: symptomatic smooth muscle cramping in irritable bowel syndrome
severe renal colic refractory to both an NSAID and intravenous paracetamol
intravenous paracetamol when NSAIDs are contraindicated due to stage 4 chronic kidney disease
facilitating spontaneous passage of a confirmed 6 mm distal ureteric stone once acute pain is controlled

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old man is reviewed 4 hours after presenting with acute left renal colic. His pain has settled completely after diclofenac and he is passing clear urine.
Temperature 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg. Non-contrast CT KUB shows a 7 mm stone in the distal left ureter with mild hydronephrosis. White cell count is 7.5 × 10⁹/L (3.8-10.0) and creatinine is 84 µmol/L (60-120).
hq_q.w: For an uncomplicated distal ureteric stone measuring 5 to 10 mm without infection, acute kidney injury or refractory pain, NICE recommends considering medical expulsive therapy with an oral alpha-blocker alongside watchful waiting, as alpha-1A blockade relaxes distal ureteric smooth muscle.
hq_q.f: Renal pelvic stone >20 mm (or staghorn calculus) -> percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: 7 mm stone in the distal left ureter
tm.m: Alpha-1A adrenoceptors predominate in the distal third of the ureter; tamsulosin reduces intramural ureteric tone and peristaltic spasm to aid stone expulsion.
tm.g: Uncomplicated 5-10 mm distal ureteric stone with controlled pain and no sepsis -> tamsulosin and watchful waiting
x: Immediate shockwave lithotripsy is not required when a 7 mm distal ureteric stone is pain-free and likely to pass with medical expulsive therapy.
Percutaneous nephrolithotomy is an invasive keyhole procedure into the renal pelvis reserved for large renal stones (>20 mm) or staghorn calculi.
Emergency percutaneous nephrostomy is reserved for an obstructed infected kidney with urosepsis or severe acute kidney injury.
Immediate ureteroscopy is reserved for stones over 10 mm, uncontrolled pain or failure of conservative passage after 4 weeks.
f: a 9 mm proximal ureteric or renal calyceal stone that fails conservative passage
a 2.5 cm staghorn calculus filling the renal pelvis and calyces
an obstructing ureteric stone accompanied by high fever, rigors and hypotension
a 12 mm distal ureteric stone or persistent obstruction after 4 weeks of conservative therapy

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old woman presents with right loin pain, rigors and confusion 6 hours after developing colicky flank pain.
Temperature 39.2°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 94/56 mmHg. CT KUB shows a 6 mm calculus obstructing the mid-right ureter with moderate right hydronephrosis. White cell count is 18.4 × 10⁹/L (3.8-10.0). Intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics have been started.
hq_q.w: An infected, obstructed kidney (pyonephrosis) is a life-threatening urological emergency that rapidly progresses to septic shock and renal loss. Alongside intravenous antibiotics and fluid resuscitation, immediate decompression by percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stenting is mandatory.
hq_q.f: Afebrile patient with a 6 mm ureteric stone and normal white cell count -> conservative management with analgesia and tamsulosin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next management step?

c: Temperature 39.2°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 94/56 mmHg
6 mm calculus obstructing the mid-right ureter
tm.m: Complete ureteric obstruction prevents antibiotic excretion into the renal pelvis and traps purulent urine under high pressure, driving Gram-negative bacteraemia.
tm.g: Obstructed hydronephrotic kidney with fever/sepsis -> urgent decompression via percutaneous nephrostomy (or retrograde stent)
x: She has septic shock (BP 94/56 mmHg, HR 124 bpm, T 39.2°C) from an obstructed infected kidney and requires immediate inpatient drainage.
Shockwave lithotripsy is strictly contraindicated in acute infection and obstruction because shockwaves force bacteria into the bloodstream and worsen urosepsis.
Intravenous antibiotics cannot sterilise pus trapped behind an obstructing stone without immediate mechanical drainage of the collecting system.
High-pressure ureteroscopic irrigation and stone manipulation during active urosepsis force bacteria into the renal veins; decompress first and clear the stone electively.
f: uncomplicated afebrile lower urinary tract infection in a haemodynamically stable outpatient
an elective, sterile 8 mm renal pelvic stone with no urinary tract infection
never sufficient in an obstructed infected kidney; urgent drainage is mandatory alongside IV antibiotics
elective definitive stone clearance 4 weeks after urosepsis has resolved and the kidney has been decompressed

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman presents with a 2-day history of burning dysuria, urinary urgency and hourly frequency. She has no fever, rigors, loin pain or vaginal discharge, and she is not pregnant.
Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic tenderness. Urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leucocytes, and eGFR is >90 mL/min/1.73 m².
hq_q.w: For an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection in a non-pregnant woman under 65 years with normal renal function (eGFR >=45 mL/min/1.73 m²), NICE recommends a 3-day course of oral nitrofurantoin (or trimethoprim if there is a low risk of resistance).
hq_q.f: Renal impairment with eGFR <45 mL/min/1.73 m² -> avoid nitrofurantoin; use trimethoprim or pivmecillinam.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line antibiotic regimen?

tm.m: Nitrofurantoin is rapidly filtered and concentrated in the lower urinary tract, achieving bactericidal levels against Escherichia coli in the bladder lumen with minimal systemic resistance.
tm.g: Uncomplicated lower UTI in a non-pregnant woman with normal eGFR -> nitrofurantoin for 3 days
x: Over 50% of community uropathogenic Escherichia coli strains produce beta-lactamases, so amoxicillin is never used empirically without confirmed culture sensitivity.
A 7-day course of broad-spectrum cefalexin is reserved for acute pyelonephritis or complicated UTI in pregnancy, not uncomplicated cystitis.
Fluoroquinolones are restricted to acute pyelonephritis or acute prostatitis due to tendon, aortic and neurological toxicity and antimicrobial stewardship.
Broad-spectrum co-amoxiclav carries a high risk of Clostridioides difficile and is reserved for upper urinary tract infections rather than simple cystitis.
f: a lower UTI in pregnancy where midstream urine culture has specifically confirmed amoxicillin-sensitive Enterococcus
acute pyelonephritis or a second-line UTI in pregnancy requiring a 7-day course
acute bacterial prostatitis or complicated upper UTI where culture confirms fluoroquinolone sensitivity
acute upper urinary tract infection (pyelonephritis) where culture confirms susceptibility

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman at 12 weeks gestation presents to her GP with a 24-hour history of burning dysuria and urinary frequency. She has no fever, nausea, vomiting or loin pain.
Temperature 36.8°C, pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft. Urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes, a midstream urine specimen has been sent, and eGFR is >90 mL/min/1.73 m².
hq_q.w: Symptomatic lower UTI in pregnancy requires a midstream urine culture and a 7-day antibiotic course. Nitrofurantoin for 7 days is first-line in early pregnancy, whereas trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester due to folate antagonism.
hq_q.f: UTI at term (38 weeks gestation) -> avoid nitrofurantoin due to neonatal haemolysis risk; use cefalexin or amoxicillin (if sensitive).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?

c: no fever, nausea, vomiting or loin pain
midstream urine specimen has been sent
tm.m: Progesterone-mediated ureteric smooth muscle relaxation in pregnancy predisposes to ascending pyelonephritis and preterm labour, requiring a full 7-day course of a non-teratogenic antibiotic.
tm.g: Lower UTI at 12 weeks pregnancy (first trimester) -> nitrofurantoin for 7 days
x: Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin are avoided throughout pregnancy because of arthropathy and cartilage damage in animal fetal studies.
Tetracyclines such as doxycycline are contraindicated in pregnancy because they chelate calcium in fetal bones and cause permanent dental staining.
Waiting 48 to 72 hours for culture results in a symptomatic pregnant woman carries a high risk of ascending acute pyelonephritis and miscarriage.
Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and is teratogenic (neural tube defects) in the first trimester, and 3 days is too short in pregnancy.
f: acute pyelonephritis in a non-pregnant adult woman with confirmed ciprofloxacin sensitivity
uncomplicated urogenital Chlamydia trachomatis infection in a non-pregnant woman
screening midstream urine culture in an asymptomatic pregnant woman before bacteriuria is confirmed
uncomplicated lower UTI in a non-pregnant woman with a low risk of trimethoprim resistance

hq_q.s:
A 35 year old woman has had fever, right loin pain and rigors for a day. She is not pregnant and she is well enough to go home. She has no drug allergies.
Temperature 38.4°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg. There is right renal angle tenderness.
Urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes. A sample has been sent for culture.
hq_q.w: For acute pyelonephritis in a non-pregnant adult who can go home, NICE first choices are oral cefalexin, co-amoxiclav or trimethoprim (if the organism is sensitive) or ciprofloxacin. Drugs that work only in the bladder will fail.
hq_q.f: Dysuria and frequency without fever or loin pain → lower UTI; nitrofurantoin or pivmecillinam.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?

tm.m: Pyelonephritis needs a drug that reaches kidney tissue, not just the urine
tm.g: Pyelonephritis: a drug that reaches the kidney (cefalexin)
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amoxicillin (Amoxicillin resistance in E. coli is common, so it is used when culture shows sensitivity)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fosfomycin single dose (Single-dose fosfomycin treats lower UTI; it does not reach kidney tissue reliably)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Nitrofurantoin (Nitrofurantoin concentrates in urine but does not reach kidney tissue)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pivmecillinam (Pivmecillinam is a lower UTI drug and does not treat pyelonephritis)
x: Amoxicillin resistance in E. coli is common, so it is used when culture shows sensitivity.
Single-dose fosfomycin treats lower UTI; it does not reach kidney tissue reliably.
Nitrofurantoin concentrates in urine but does not reach kidney tissue.
Pivmecillinam is a lower UTI drug and does not treat pyelonephritis.

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old man presents with a 3-month history of a painless swelling in his right scrotum that has gradually enlarged. He has no urinary or bowel symptoms.
Examination reveals a smooth, fluctuant swelling in the right hemiscrotum. It transilluminates brightly with a pen torch, the examiner can get above its upper pole, and the right testis cannot be palpated separately.
hq_q.w: A hydrocele is a collection of serous fluid within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. Because it envelops the testis, the testis cannot be felt separately, the examiner can get above it, and it transilluminates brightly.
hq_q.f: Transilluminating swelling separate from and posterior/superior to a palpable normal testis -> epididymal cyst.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: fluctuant swelling in the right hemiscrotum
tm.m: Imbalance between serous secretion and lymphatic absorption within the parietal and visceral layers of the tunica vaginalis surrounds the testis in a fluid jacket.
tm.g: Brightly transilluminating scrotal swelling that you can get above and where the testis cannot be felt separately -> hydrocele
x: An epididymal cyst lies superior and posterior to the testis, so the body of the testis can always be palpated separately from the cyst.
An inguinoscrotal hernia extends down from the deep inguinal ring so the examiner cannot get above it, and it does not transilluminate brightly.
A primary testicular tumour is a firm, solid mass that does not transilluminate, although a secondary reactive hydrocele should be excluded by ultrasound if in doubt.
A varicocele is a non-transilluminating venous plexus superior to the testis that feels like a bag of worms on standing and collapses when supine.
f: a transilluminating globular swelling in the upper scrotum where the normal testis is felt separately below it
a reducible inguinoscrotal mass with a cough impulse where the examiner cannot get above its neck
a hard, craggy, non-transilluminating mass within the testis with raised serum beta-hCG
a left-sided dragging scrotal swelling feeling like a bag of worms that disappears when lying down

hq_q.s:
A 76 year old uncircumcised man had an indwelling urethral catheter placed 6 hours ago. His foreskin was left retracted behind the glans after the procedure, and he now has severe pain and swelling at the tip of his penis.
Examination reveals a tight constricting ring of oedematous foreskin trapped behind the coronal sulcus. The glans is swollen and congested but remains pink with brisk capillary refill.
hq_q.w: Paraphimosis with a viable pink glans is an emergency managed by immediate manual reduction under analgesia, using steady compression (often with osmotic gauze) to reduce glans oedema before drawing the foreskin forward.
hq_q.f: Manual reduction fails despite compression or glans is necrotic -> urgent dorsal slit or emergency circumcision.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

c: tight constricting ring of oedematous foreskin
glans is swollen and congested but remains pink
tm.m: Circumferential compression expels interstitial oedema fluid from the glans and prepuce across the constricting ring, allowing the foreskin to be reduced over the corona.
tm.g: Acute paraphimosis with a viable pink glans -> immediate manual reduction
x: Immediate surgical dorsal slit or circumcision is reserved for paraphimosis that fails manual reduction or when glans necrosis has developed.
Paraphimosis is a mechanical venous and lymphatic tourniquet rather than a bacterial cellulitis; oral antibiotics will not relieve the constriction.
Removing the urethral catheter alone does not reduce the retracted preputial ring over the coronal sulcus.
Topical potent steroid ointment over weeks is used for non-acute pathological phimosis, not an acute urological emergency like paraphimosis.
f: manual reduction failed despite analgesia and osmotic compression
superficial infective bacterial balanoposthitis with a normally positioned foreskin
catheter-related bladder spasms without preputial retraction
chronic non-retractile phimosis in a boy with ballooning of the foreskin on micturition

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man with homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS) presents to the emergency department with a painful, persistent erection that began spontaneously 5 hours ago without sexual stimulation.
Temperature 36.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg. Examination reveals rock-hard, tender bilateral corpora cavernosa while the glans penis and corpus spongiosum remain soft. Oral analgesia and intravenous fluids have been given.
hq_q.w: Low-flow (ischaemic) priapism lasting over 4 hours is a compartment syndrome of the corpora cavernosa that risks irreversible erectile dysfunction. Immediate decompression by corporal aspiration (with intracavernosal phenylephrine if needed) is mandatory.
hq_q.f: Painless partial erection following blunt perineal straddle trauma -> high-flow (non-ischaemic) arterial priapism, managed conservatively or by selective embolisation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate urological intervention?

c: rock-hard, tender bilateral corpora cavernosa while the glans penis and corpus spongiosum remain soft
tm.m: Sickled erythrocytes occlude subtunical venules draining the corpora cavernosa, trapping hypoxic, acidotic blood while sparing the separately drained corpus spongiosum and glans.
tm.g: Ischaemic priapism lasting >4 hours (rigid tender corpora cavernosa, soft glans) -> immediate corporal aspiration (+/- intracavernosal phenylephrine)
x: Ischaemic priapism lasting over 4 hours is an immediate surgical emergency; delaying for an outpatient scan guarantees permanent erectile dysfunction.
Exchange transfusion takes hours to arrange, does not rapidly decompress trapped intracavernosal blood and has been linked to neurological events in sickle priapism.
Cold packs can precipitate further erythrocyte sickling in HbSS disease and delay mandatory corporal decompression beyond the 4-hour ischaemic threshold.
Oral beta-2 agonists such as terbutaline are ineffective for established ischaemic priapism lasting longer than 4 hours.
f: follow-up assessment of painless high-flow arterial priapism after perineal trauma
acute chest syndrome or acute ischaemic stroke in a patient with sickle cell disease
minor self-limiting stuttering priapism episodes lasting less than 1 hour that resolve with exercise and hydration
never recommended as monotherapy for ischaemic priapism exceeding 4 hours

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man presents with a 3-day history of progressive pain and swelling in his left hemiscrotum accompanied by dysuria and a mucopurulent urethral discharge. He has had three new sexual partners over the past 2 months.
Temperature 37.8°C, pulse rate 86 bpm. The left epididymis is swollen and tender, the testis has a normal vertical lie, and elevating the scrotum eases the pain.
hq_q.w: In sexually active men under 35 years with urethral discharge, acute epididymo-orchitis is usually caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae and treated with intramuscular ceftriaxone 1 g stat plus oral doxycycline for 10 to 14 days.
hq_q.f: Older man with BPH, nitrituria and no STI risk factors -> enteric coliforms, treated with oral ofloxacin or levofloxacin for 14 days.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

c: left epididymis is swollen and tender
tm.m: Intramuscular ceftriaxone provides single-dose bactericidal cover for Neisseria gonorrhoeae while a 2-week course of doxycycline eradicates intracellular Chlamydia trachomatis.
tm.g: Sexually acquired epididymo-orchitis (age <35, urethral discharge, multiple partners) -> IM ceftriaxone + oral doxycycline
x: Neither amoxicillin nor metronidazole is active against Chlamydia trachomatis or beta-lactamase-producing Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Nitrofurantoin only achieves therapeutic concentrations in bladder urine, does not penetrate the epididymis and has no activity against Chlamydia or gonorrhoea.
Fluoroquinolone monotherapy is used for enteric coliform epididymo-orchitis in older men without STI risk factors, as gonococcal quinolone resistance is widespread.
Trimethoprim has no activity against Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
f: acute dental pericoronitis or anaerobic odontogenic infection
uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) in a non-pregnant woman
a 72 year old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia, nitrituria and no sexual risk factors
uncomplicated coliform cystitis where culture confirms trimethoprim sensitivity

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old man presents with a 2-day history of painful right testicular swelling and fever. Seven days ago he had fever and painful bilateral swelling in front of his ears. He never received his childhood MMR vaccinations.
Temperature 38.2°C, pulse rate 94 bpm. The right testis is diffusely swollen and tender, and the left parotid gland remains mildly enlarged.
hq_q.w: Mumps orchitis develops 4 to 8 days after parotitis in 20% to 30% of unvaccinated post-pubertal men. Management is supportive with rest, scrotal support and NSAID analgesia; subfertility is uncommon unless bilateral.
hq_q.f: Sudden-onset severe scrotal pain without prodromal parotitis and with a high horizontal testis -> testicular torsion.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: painful bilateral swelling in front of his ears
never received his childhood MMR vaccinations
right testis is diffusely swollen and tender
tm.m: Viraemic dissemination of the single-stranded RNA paramyxovirus from the parotid glands to the seminiferous tubules causes acute interstitial testicular oedema and lymphocytic infiltration.
tm.g: Acute painful orchitis 1 week after parotitis in an unvaccinated young man -> mumps orchitis
x: Bacterial epididymo-orchitis follows either a sexually transmitted urethritis or a coliform UTI and is not preceded by bilateral parotitis.
IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) can cause scrotal pain in young boys but is accompanied by palpable purpura over the buttocks and legs, arthralgia and abdominal pain.
Testicular torsion causes hyperacute pain with a high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex, not fever 1 week after parotitis.
Testicular germ cell tumours typically present as a painless, firm intratesticular nodule without acute fever or preceding parotitis.
f: unilateral epididymal swelling with mucopurulent urethral discharge after unprotected sexual intercourse
a 7 year old boy with palpable purpura on his buttocks and legs, colicky abdominal pain and arthralgia
abrupt-onset severe scrotal pain with vomiting, a high horizontal testis and an absent cremasteric reflex
a painless, hard, non-transilluminating intratesticular lump noticed over several weeks

hq_q.s:
A 16 year old boy has had pain in his left testicle for 4 hours. It came on during the night. Lifting the testis eases the pain.
The left testis is tender and swollen. The cremasteric reflex is present.
o: Analgesia and review in the morning
hq_q.w: Prehn's sign is unreliable. A teenager with acute testicular pain has torsion until proven otherwise, and only surgery proves it.
hq_q.f: A 35-year-old with 3 days of gradual pain, dysuria and positive chlamydia → treat epididymo-orchitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Prehn's sign and the reflex are unreliable; torsion cannot be excluded clinically
tm.g: Acute testicular pain in a teenager: urgent scrotal exploration
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Analgesia and review in the morning (Delays surgery past the 6-hour testicular salvage window)
a 35 year old with 3 days of gradual pain and positive chlamydia
the presentation instead showed features specific to Urgent scrotal ultrasound first (Imaging must never delay surgical exploration when torsion is suspected)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Urinalysis and discharge (Missing testicular torsion leads to irreversible testicular infarction)
x: Delays surgery past the 6-hour testicular salvage window
Ruled out here: requires a 35 year old with 3 days of gradual pain and positive chlamydia, whereas this patient has 16 year old boy, 4 hours.
Imaging must never delay surgical exploration when torsion is suspected
Missing testicular torsion leads to irreversible testicular infarction

hq_q.s:
A 14 year old boy woke with sudden severe pain in his right testicle 2 hours ago. He has vomited twice.
The right testis lies high with a horizontal lie and is very tender. The right cremasteric reflex is absent.
hq_q.w: Clinical torsion goes straight to theatre. Ultrasound delays surgery and can miss it. Key discriminator: Clinical testicular torsion: urgent scrotal exploration.
hq_q.f: A tender blue dot at the top of the testis with a normal lie → torsion of the appendix testis, managed conservatively.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: A twisted cord cuts the blood supply within hours
tm.g: Clinical testicular torsion: urgent scrotal exploration
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Antibiotics and analgesia (Antibiotics treat epididymitis, not torsion)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Manual detorsion and discharge (Even if detorsion succeeds, bilateral orchidopexy is still mandatory)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Urgent Doppler ultrasound first (Ultrasound delays surgery)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Urinalysis (Normal urinalysis does not exclude torsion and must not delay theatre)
x: Antibiotics treat epididymitis, not torsion.
Even if detorsion succeeds, bilateral orchidopexy is still mandatory
Ultrasound delays surgery.
Normal urinalysis does not exclude torsion and must not delay theatre

hq_q.s:
A 15 year old boy attends the emergency department with sudden-onset severe left testicular pain that woke him from sleep 2 hours ago, with nausea and vomiting.
Temperature 37.1°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg. The left hemiscrotum is erythematous and swollen, the left testis lies high and horizontally, and the left cremasteric reflex is absent. He is booked for immediate emergency scrotal exploration.
hq_q.w: In acute spermatic cord torsion, testicular viability depends directly on warm ischaemia time: surgical detorsion within 6 hours of symptom onset achieves a salvage rate above 90%, falling to ~50% at 12 hours and <10% after 24 hours.
hq_q.f: Ischaemia duration exceeding 24 hours -> testicular salvage rate falls below 10%.
hq_q.ql: Within what maximum time window from symptom onset does surgical detorsion achieve a testicular salvage rate above 90%?

tm.m: Haemorrhagic venous infarction progresses to irreversible arterial ischaemic necrosis of Leydig and Sertoli cells once warm ischaemia exceeds 6 hours.
tm.g: Golden window for >90% testicular salvage in acute testicular torsion -> within 6 hours
x: While immediate theatre is always required, the >90% salvage window extends up to 6 hours from pain onset rather than ending at 2 hours.
By 12 hours of warm ischaemia, progressive haemorrhagic infarction reduces the testicular salvage rate to approximately 50%.
After 24 hours of spermatic cord torsion, irreversible coagulative necrosis reduces testicular salvage below 10%.
At 48 hours of untreated torsion, the testis is almost universally necrotic and requires orchidectomy with contralateral orchidopexy.
f: never the cut-off threshold; >90% salvage is maintained throughout the first 6 hours
the time point at which testicular salvage drops to approximately 50%
the time point beyond which testicular salvage falls below 10%
delayed presentation with a non-viable infarcted testis requiring orchidectomy

hq_q.s:
A 13 year old boy is undergoing emergency scrotal exploration 4 hours after the sudden onset of severe right testicular pain and vomiting. On opening the right tunica vaginalis, the spermatic cord is found twisted 540 degrees in a bell-clapper deformity.
Following manual detorsion and application of warm saline-soaked swabs the right testis regains a healthy pink colour and brisk arterial bleeding is seen on nicking the tunica.
o: Close the scrotum and review in clinic
Fix the other testis at a later operation
hq_q.w: Intravaginal testicular torsion results from the congenital bell-clapper deformity, which is bilateral in over 80% of cases. Both the salvaged ipsilateral testis and the contralateral testis must be fixed during the same operation.
hq_q.f: Testis remains black and necrotic after detorsion and warming -> perform right orchidectomy and left orchidopexy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next operative step?

c: twisted 540 degrees in a bell-clapper deformity
tm.m: Three-point non-absorbable suture fixation of both testes to the dartos pouch prevents recurrent ipsilateral torsion and asynchronous contralateral torsion.
tm.g: Viable testis after surgical detorsion -> fix both testes at the same operation
x: Closing the scrotum without suture fixation leaves the bell-clapper deformity uncorrected and carries a high risk of repeat torsion.
Delaying contralateral orchidopexy exposes the patient to a second general anaesthetic and the risk of contralateral torsion in the interim.
Because the bell-clapper anomaly is bilateral in >80% of boys, unilateral fixation leaves the contralateral testis unprotected against torsion.
The right testis has turned pink with brisk capsular bleeding within 4 hours of onset, so it is viable and must be preserved.
f: exploration had revealed torsion of the appendix testis with a normal anatomical attachment of the testis
staged bilateral procedures for complex high intra-abdominal undescended testes
elective unilateral orchidopexy for an isolated congenital undescended testis
the right testis remained black, dusky and non-viable after detorsion and warming

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old man presents to his GP after noticing a painless lump in his right testicle 2 weeks ago. He has no weight loss, back pain or dysuria.
BP 124/76 mmHg, pulse rate 68 bpm. There is a 1.5 cm hard, irregular, non-tender nodule within the body of the right testis that does not transilluminate. The left testis and inguinal nodes are normal.
o: Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
hq_q.w: Any patient with a non-transilluminating intratesticular mass requires an urgent 2-week-wait referral and scrotal ultrasound scan, which has >95% sensitivity for distinguishing solid intratesticular malignancy from benign extratesticular lesions. Trans-scrotal biopsy is strictly contraindicated.
hq_q.f: Solid intratesticular mass confirmed on ultrasound -> measure serum AFP, beta-hCG and LDH, arrange staging CT CAP and perform radical inguinal orchidectomy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line diagnostic investigation?

c: painless lump in his right testicle
hard, irregular, non-tender nodule within the body of the right testis
tm.m: High-frequency grey-scale and colour Doppler scrotal ultrasonography differentiates vascular intratesticular neoplasms from benign extratesticular cysts without breaching scrotal lymphatics.
tm.g: Painless hard non-transilluminating intratesticular lump -> urgent scrotal ultrasound first
x: Staging CT chest, abdomen and pelvis is performed after scrotal ultrasound confirms a solid intratesticular mass, not as the initial diagnostic test for a scrotal lump.
Pelvic MRI is not the first-line imaging modality for a scrotal mass; high-resolution scrotal ultrasound is rapid, inexpensive and highly sensitive.
Serum tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG and LDH) are measured alongside investigation, but normal AFP never excludes testicular cancer (e.g. pure seminoma) and cannot replace ultrasound.
Trans-scrotal needle biopsy is strictly contraindicated because breaching the scrotal skin Violates lymphatic planes and seeds tumour to superficial inguinal nodes.
f: staging for retroperitoneal para-aortic nodal and pulmonary metastases after ultrasound confirms a testicular tumour
local staging of biopsy-proven prostate cancer or an equivocal scrotal ultrasound
monitoring for biochemical relapse after orchidectomy for a known AFP-secreting yolk sac tumour
never performed for a suspected testicular tumour; histological diagnosis is made via radical inguinal orchidectomy

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old man presents with a 4-week history of a painless, heavy swelling in his left hemiscrotum. He has no past medical history of cryptorchidism.
