Examination reveals a 3 cm hard, irregular, non-tender mass within the left testis. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrates a heterogeneous solid intratesticular tumour with cystic areas. Serum AFP is 480 kU/L (<10), beta-hCG is 45 IU/L (<5) and LDH is 220 IU/L (140-280).
hq_q.w: Pure classical seminoma never secretes alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), although 10% to 15% mildly raise beta-hCG. Any testicular germ cell tumour with a raised serum AFP is classified and treated as a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour.
hq_q.f: Solid homogeneous testicular mass with normal AFP and mildly raised or normal beta-hCG -> classical seminoma.
hq_q.ql: Which histological tumour type is most likely?

tm.m: Yolk sac and embryonal carcinoma components within a mixed non-seminomatous germ cell tumour transcribe alpha-fetoprotein, which is absent in pure seminoma.
tm.g: Solid testicular tumour with raised serum AFP (480 kU/L) -> non-seminomatous germ cell tumour
x: Pure classical seminoma is strictly AFP-negative; an AFP of 480 kU/L proves the presence of non-seminomatous yolk sac or embryonal elements.
Primary testicular lymphoma occurs in men over 60 years and does not secrete alpha-fetoprotein or beta-hCG.
Leydig cell tumours are sex-cord stromal neoplasms that secrete testosterone or oestradiol (causing gynaecomastia) rather than alpha-fetoprotein.
Spermatocytic tumours are rare indolent neoplasms of older men (mean age >55 years) that never secrete AFP or beta-hCG.
f: a 36 year old man with a homogeneous hypoechoic testicular tumour, normal serum AFP (<10 kU/L) and beta-hCG of 30 IU/L
a 74 year old man with a diffuse testicular mass, B symptoms and normal serum AFP and beta-hCG
a small solid testicular mass presenting with tender bilateral gynaecomastia and normal AFP and beta-hCG
an indolent testicular mass in a 65 year old man with normal serum AFP and beta-hCG and low metastatic potential

hq_q.s:
A 71 year old man presents with a 1-month history of painless progressive enlargement of his right testis, drenching night sweats and 6 kg of unintentional weight loss. He has no dysuria or visible haematuria.
Temperature 37.3°C, pulse rate 80 bpm. Examination reveals a firm, diffusely enlarged, non-tender right testis that does not transilluminate. Serum AFP and beta-hCG are normal, while serum LDH is 640 IU/L (140-280).
hq_q.w: While germ cell tumours (seminoma and non-seminoma) account for 95% of testicular tumours in men aged 20 to 45 years, primary non-Hodgkin testicular lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) is the commonest testicular malignancy in men aged over 60 years.
hq_q.f: Painless solid testicular mass in a 32-year-old man -> germ cell tumour (seminoma or NSGCT).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: painless progressive enlargement of his right testis
drenching night sweats and 6 kg of unintentional weight loss
tm.m: Clonal B-cell proliferation within the testicular interstitium presents in older men with diffuse testicular enlargement, elevated LDH and systemic B symptoms.
tm.g: Painless non-transilluminating testicular mass in a man >60 years with B symptoms -> lymphoma
x: An epididymal cyst is a benign, fluctuant, brightly transilluminating swelling separate from the testis that does not cause weight loss or night sweats.
Leydig cell tumours cause androgen or oestrogen excess (gynaecomastia) rather than systemic B symptoms and high LDH in a 71 year old man.
Classical seminoma peaks between 30 and 45 years of age and is rare in men over 70 years compared with testicular lymphoma.
Testicular teratoma is a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour occurring in young men aged 20 to 35 years.
f: a smooth, fluctuant, brightly transilluminating swelling palpable separate from and posterior to the testis
a small intratesticular nodule associated with bilateral gynaecomastia and suppressed gonadotrophins
a 34 year old man with a painless solid testicular mass, no B symptoms and normal serum AFP
a 25 year old man with a heterogeneous cystic and calcified intratesticular tumour

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presents to the emergency department with painful acute urinary retention and a palpable bladder containing 750 mL on bladder scan.
Using aseptic technique and urethral anaesthetic lubricating gel, a 14 Fr Foley catheter is passed smoothly along the urethra until two-thirds of its length is inside, but no urine has drained into the receiver yet.
o: Swap to a smaller 10 Fr catheter
hq_q.w: During male urethral catheterisation, advance the catheter fully to the bifurcation hub and wait for urine to flow before inflating the balloon with 10 mL of sterile water, preventing intra-urethral balloon inflation.
hq_q.f: Urine flows freely after advancing to the hub -> inflate the balloon with 10 mL of sterile water and withdraw gently until resistance is felt at the bladder neck.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: two-thirds of its length is inside
no urine has drained into the receiver yet
tm.m: Advancing the catheter fully to the bifurcation hub ensures the balloon lies safely within the bladder lumen above the prostatic urethra, while gentle suprapubic pressure clears gel from the eyelets.
tm.g: Catheter passed partway with no urine flow yet -> advance fully to the hub and wait for urine before inflating
x: Inflating the retention balloon when only two-thirds of the catheter is inserted and no urine has flowed risks rupturing the prostatic or bulbar urethra.
Foley catheter balloons must never be inflated with air because air is compressible, leaks across the valve and causes the balloon to float away from the bladder neck.
A very thin 10 Fr catheter bends easily in an enlarged prostatic urethra; in male BPH, a 14 to 16 Fr catheter advanced fully to the hub is standard.
Withdrawing the catheter 5 cm pulls the balloon directly into the bulbar urethra, where inflation will cause a severe urethral tear.
f: the catheter is at the bifurcation hub and urine is flowing freely into the receiver
never appropriate; catheter balloons are always inflated with 10 mL of sterile water once urine flows
paediatric catheterisation rather than adult male prostatic outflow obstruction
gently drawing the catheter back until the inflated balloon rests against the bladder neck AFTER urine has flowed and the balloon is inflated

hq_q.s:
A 78 year old man had a urethral catheter inserted 4 hours ago after hip replacement. Over the past 3 hours the catheter drainage bag has remained completely empty and he has developed worsening suprapubic discomfort.
Pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 142/86 mmHg, temperature 36.7°C. His lower abdomen is dull and tender, and a bladder ultrasound scan shows 600 mL of urine.
hq_q.w: An empty catheter bag accompanied by suprapubic pain and 600 mL on bladder scan indicates catheter lumen blockage or kinking rather than true oliguria. Check the tubing and flush or replace the catheter.
hq_q.f: Low urine output with an empty bladder (<50 mL) on bladder scan -> true oliguria; assess fluid status and treat prerenal/intrinsic AKI.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: catheter drainage bag has remained completely empty
tm.m: Normal renal urine production is trapped inside the bladder behind an occluded catheter lumen, causing painful secondary retention.
tm.g: Empty catheter bag + palpable bladder / 600 mL on bladder scan -> blocked catheter: flush or replace it
x: His kidneys have already produced 600 mL of urine that is trapped in the bladder; an intravenous fluid bolus will worsen painful bladder distension.
Loop diuretics are contraindicated when bladder outflow is mechanically blocked because forcing diuresis against a blocked catheter worsens retention.
Leaving a 600 mL obstructed bladder unaddressed for another 4 hours causes severe pain, detrusor overdistension injury and autonomic hypertension.
Simply removing the catheter in a post-operative patient with 600 mL retention without ensuring bladder emptying leaves him in acute urinary retention.
f: post-operative oliguria where the bedside bladder scan shows an empty bladder (<50 mL) and the patient is hypovolaemic
fluid overload with pulmonary oedema and a patent catheter confirming true oliguria
a comfortable patient with a patent catheter draining >0.5 mL/kg/hour and an empty bladder scan
planned trial without catheter (TWOC) on the morning after surgery once the bladder is empty and the patient is mobile

hq_q.s:
An 82 year old woman with a long-term indwelling urethral catheter (last changed 10 weeks ago) is admitted from her care home with a 6-hour history of fever, rigors and right loin pain.
Temperature 38.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Examination reveals marked right renal angle tenderness and cloudy urine in the catheter tubing.
o: Antibiotics and keep the old catheter
Await urine culture, then start antibiotics
Collect sample from the drainage bag, then antibiotics
Remove the catheter with no replacement
hq_q.w: In catheter-associated pyelonephritis where the catheter has been in place over 7 days, NICE recommends changing the catheter, taking a urine culture from the new catheter's sampling port, and starting empirical antibiotics.
hq_q.f: Asymptomatic cloudy urine in a well patient with a long-term catheter -> no culture and no antibiotics.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate sequence of actions?

c: long-term indwelling urethral catheter (last changed 10 weeks ago)
fever, rigors and right loin pain
tm.m: Long-term catheters harbour a mature polymicrobial biofilm that shields bacteria from antibiotics and yields unrepresentative culture results if sampled directly.
tm.g: Catheter-associated pyelonephritis with catheter in situ >7 days -> insert new catheter, take sample from new catheter, start antibiotics
x: Leaving a 10-week-old biofilm-coated catheter in situ during acute pyelonephritis leads to persistent bacteraemia and treatment failure.
She has systemic sepsis (T 38.6°C, HR 108 bpm, rigors) from acute pyelonephritis; delaying empirical antibiotics for 48-hour culture results is unsafe.
Urine must never be sampled from the drainage bag because stagnant bag urine is heavily overgrown with environmental contaminants.
She requires a long-term catheter for chronic urinary retention and needs accurate hourly urine output monitoring during acute urosepsis.
f: a catheter inserted less than 48 hours ago where removal would risk urethral trauma after recent urological surgery
asymptomatic bacteriuria screening in pregnancy before starting targeted treatment
never appropriate; catheter urine samples are always taken aseptically from the needleless sampling port
a short-term catheter that is no longer clinically needed in a patient who can void spontaneously

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old woman has had aching pain in her right knee for a year. It is worse when climbing stairs and walking, and eases with rest. Her morning stiffness lasts about 15 minutes.
BMI 30 kg/m². Examination shows tibiofemoral crepitus on movement, with no joint effusion, warmth or redness.
o: Magnetic resonance imaging of the knee
hq_q.w: NICE states that osteoarthritis should be diagnosed clinically without imaging in adults aged 45 or over who have activity-related joint pain and either no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting under 30 minutes.
hq_q.f: Atypically rapid progression, hot swollen joint, or red-flag features -> investigate with imaging or aspiration.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate way to make the diagnosis?

c: worse when climbing stairs and walking
no joint effusion, warmth or redness
tm.m: Typical osteoarthritis over age 45 with mechanical pain and brief stiffness is diagnosed clinically because radiographic changes correlate poorly with symptoms
tm.g: Age >=45, activity-related pain, stiffness <30 minutes, and no atypical features -> clinical diagnosis without imaging
x: Indicated for an acutely hot, swollen knee to exclude septic or crystal arthritis, not dry crepitus without effusion.
Reserved for suspected internal derangement such as true mechanical locking or ligamentous injury, not typical osteoarthritis.
Used when inflammatory polyarthritis with prolonged morning stiffness and soft-tissue synovitis is suspected.
Not required to diagnose typical osteoarthritis in primary care and are reserved for atypical features or preoperative planning.
f: An acutely hot, swollen, erythematous knee with fever or suspected crystal synovitis
A younger patient after a twisting knee injury with true mechanical locking and joint-line tenderness
Symmetrical boggy swelling of the small hand and knee joints with morning stiffness lasting over 1 hour
Severe refractory knee osteoarthritis being referred to orthopaedics for preoperative assessment of joint replacement

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man with bilateral knee osteoarthritis attends his GP for review. He is doing regular quadriceps strengthening exercises and losing weight, but still has daily knee pain when walking to work. He has no history of asthma, kidney disease or peptic ulceration.
BP 126/78 mmHg. There is bony enlargement and crepitus in both knees without effusion.
hq_q.w: NICE recommends a topical NSAID as first-line pharmacological analgesia for knee osteoarthritis alongside core exercise and weight loss. Oral NSAIDs with gastroprotection are considered if topical NSAIDs are ineffective; routine paracetamol and opioids are avoided.
hq_q.f: Persistent knee pain despite a trial of topical NSAID -> oral NSAID with a proton pump inhibitor.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological analgesic?

c: still has daily knee pain when walking
no history of asthma, kidney disease or peptic ulceration
tm.m: Topical NSAIDs penetrate superficial joints such as the knee to inhibit local cyclo-oxygenase with minimal systemic exposure
tm.g: First-line pharmacological analgesia in knee osteoarthritis -> topical NSAID
x: Used only for short-term relief of moderate-to-severe flares when other pharmacological treatments are ineffective or unsuitable.
NICE recommends against weak or strong opioids for osteoarthritis because their limited benefit is outweighed by harm.
Considered second line when topical NSAIDs provide insufficient pain relief, or first line in deep joints such as the hip.
NICE advises against routinely offering paracetamol for osteoarthritis due to minimal clinical effectiveness.
f: An acute debilitating flare of knee osteoarthritis needing short-term pain relief after topical and oral NSAIDs fail
Acute nociceptive pain after limb trauma where NSAIDs are contraindicated and short-term step-two analgesia is needed
Hip osteoarthritis where deep joint anatomy makes topical NSAIDs ineffective, or knee osteoarthritis unresponsive to topical NSAIDs
Short-term infrequent analgesia when both topical and oral NSAIDs are contraindicated or not tolerated

hq_q.s:
A 67 year old woman has severe osteoarthritis of the right hip. She can no longer walk to the shops and is woken by pain at night, despite physiotherapy exercises, weight-loss support and oral naproxen with omeprazole.
BMI 38 kg/m². Examination shows fixed flexion and painful, restricted internal rotation of the right hip.
X-ray shows joint-space loss, osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis.
o: Arthroscopic washout of the right hip
Delay surgical referral until her BMI is under 30
Refer for consideration of joint replacement
hq_q.w: NICE states that patients should be referred for consideration of joint replacement when joint symptoms substantially impact quality of life and are refractory to non-surgical treatments. Age, smoking, and BMI must not be barriers to referral.
hq_q.f: Mild hip pain well controlled with exercise and oral NSAIDs -> continue primary care management.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

c: severe osteoarthritis of the right hip
despite physiotherapy exercises, weight-loss support and oral naproxen
tm.m: Total hip replacement restores function in end-stage osteoarthritis, and NICE prohibits arbitrary BMI thresholds from blocking referral
tm.g: Refractory hip osteoarthritis impacting sleep and mobility despite core and drug therapy -> refer for joint replacement regardless of BMI
x: Arthroscopic lavage is ineffective for osteoarthritis and is only used in native hip septic arthritis.
NICE explicitly states that patient-specific factors including BMI, age, and smoking must not exclude referral for joint replacement.
Strong opioids are recommended against in osteoarthritis because of dependence, falls, and lack of long-term efficacy.
Paracetamol has minimal efficacy in osteoarthritis and stepping down from an NSAID in severe disease will worsen pain.
f: Acute native hip septic arthritis with fever, inability to weight-bear, and purulent joint aspirate
A patient asking which commissioning restriction NICE explicitly prohibits when considering arthroplasty referral
Severe cancer-related bone pain in palliative care unresponsive to non-opioid analgesia
Mild episodic joint pain in a patient who develops peptic ulceration or renal impairment on oral NSAIDs

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old woman had a right total hip replacement through a posterior approach 2 weeks ago. This morning she bent down to pick up her shoe and felt a sudden clunk and severe pain in her right hip. She cannot bear weight.
Pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 136/82 mmHg. Her right leg is shortened, adducted and internally rotated.
hq_q.w: Following a posterior-approach total hip replacement, excessive hip flexion, adduction, and internal rotation dislocate the prosthetic femoral head posteriorly, producing sudden severe pain and a shortened, internally rotated limb.
hq_q.f: Shortened and externally rotated leg after a fall -> periprosthetic or native neck of femur fracture.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: bent down to pick up her shoe
tm.m: Deep flexion and internal rotation lever the prosthetic head out through the posterior capsular repair
tm.g: Sudden hip pain on bending after posterior THR with a short, internally rotated leg -> posterior hip dislocation
x: Occurs years after surgery with gradual start-up pain and normal leg alignment rather than acute deformity at 2 weeks.
Causes unilateral pitting calf swelling and tenderness without acute leg shortening or internal rotation.
Follows a fall or trauma and typically leaves the leg shortened and externally rotated.
Presents over days with fever, wound erythema or discharge, and raised inflammatory markers rather than a sudden mechanical clunk.
f: Gradual start-up groin pain 10 years after hip replacement with a radiolucent line around the stem
Unilateral warm, pitting calf swelling 2 weeks after hip surgery with normal hip position and range of movement
Sudden thigh pain after a fall onto the side with a shortened, externally rotated leg and a cortical fracture near the stem
Increasing hip pain, fever of 38.5°C, and purulent wound discharge 2 weeks after surgery

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man had a right total knee replacement 6 weeks ago. For 4 days the knee has been red, swollen and increasingly painful, and he has had rigors.
Temperature 38.4°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg. The right knee is warm with a tense effusion. The surgical wound has healed.
o: Oral flucloxacillin for 14 days in primary care
hq_q.w: In a haemodynamically stable patient with suspected prosthetic joint infection, synovial fluid aspiration and blood cultures must be obtained under aseptic orthopaedic conditions before starting antibiotics so the causative organism is identified.
hq_q.f: Haemodynamic instability and septic shock -> immediate intravenous antibiotics after blood cultures.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Administering antibiotics before synovial sampling sterilises the aspirate and prevents targeted biofilm therapy
tm.g: Haemodynamically stable suspected prosthetic joint infection -> joint aspiration before antibiotics
x: Starting antibiotics before synovial sampling in a normotensive patient obscures the organism and compromises biofilm eradication.
Investigates deep vein thrombosis, which causes calf swelling rather than a febrile knee effusion with a CRP of 140 mg/L.
Inadequate for deep prosthetic joint infection, which requires specialist orthopaedic sampling, washout/debridement, and prolonged targeted therapy.
Missing an acute prosthetic joint infection leads to biofilm maturation, implant loosening, and systemic sepsis.
f: Frank septic shock with a blood pressure of 76/42 mmHg and lactate of 5.1 mmol/L where antibiotics cannot be delayed
Unilateral pitting calf oedema and calf tenderness postoperatively with a cool, non-tender knee and normal temperature
Localized superficial stitch erythema in an afebrile patient with a pain-free knee, no effusion, and normal CRP
Mild post-exercise knee stiffness 6 weeks after replacement with no effusion, normal temperature, and normal CRP

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old woman has undergone an uncomplicated elective left total hip replacement for severe osteoarthritis. By postoperative day 2 she is mobilising along the ward with crutches and is medically ready for discharge. She has been receiving prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin since surgery.
Pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg.
hq_q.w: NICE recommends extended pharmacological VTE prophylaxis for 28 days (up to 35 days) after elective total hip replacement, using low-molecular-weight heparin, rivaroxaban, apixaban, or 10 days of LMWH followed by 28 days of aspirin.
hq_q.f: Elective total knee replacement -> 14 days of pharmacological VTE prophylaxis.
hq_q.ql: How long should venous thromboembolism prophylaxis continue after her operation?

tm.m: Prothrombotic endothelial and venous stasis risk persists for 4 to 5 weeks after hip arthroplasty
tm.g: Elective total hip replacement VTE prophylaxis duration -> 28 days
x: 14 days is the NICE duration for elective total knee replacement, which is too short after total hip replacement.
3 months is the therapeutic anticoagulation duration for a confirmed provoked DVT or PE, not routine prophylaxis.
6 months is used for therapeutic anticoagulation after an unprovoked venous thromboembolism.
7 days is far too short for hip arthroplasty, where most postoperative venous thromboembolism occurs after hospital discharge.
f: An uncomplicated elective total knee replacement being discharged home
A confirmed symptomatic deep vein thrombosis provoked by the hip replacement surgery
An unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis with no transient surgical or medical risk factor
An acute medical inpatient admission with reduced mobility requiring prophylaxis for at least 7 days

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man has noticed a swelling behind his right knee for a month. It does not hurt. He smokes.
There is a 3 cm pulsatile, expansile swelling in the right popliteal fossa. Foot pulses are present.
hq_q.w: Popliteal aneurysms are the commonest peripheral aneurysm: a pulsatile and expansile mass in the popliteal fossa. They thrombose or throw emboli rather than burst.
hq_q.f: Non-pulsatile fluctuant swelling in a person with knee osteoarthritis → Baker's cyst.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Popliteal aneurysms are the commonest peripheral aneurysm
tm.g: A pulsatile expansile swelling behind the knee is a popliteal artery aneurysm
f: a non-pulsatile fluctuant swelling with knee osteoarthritis
the presentation instead showed features specific to Deep vein thrombosis (A DVT is not pulsatile)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ganglion of the knee joint (A ganglion is not pulsatile)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lipoma (A lipoma is not pulsatile)
x: Ruled out here: requires a non-pulsatile fluctuant swelling with knee osteoarthritis, whereas this patient has smokes, pulsatile, expansile.
A DVT is not pulsatile.
A ganglion is not pulsatile.
A lipoma is not pulsatile.

hq_q.s: A 70 year old man has a right popliteal artery aneurysm confirmed on duplex scan. He has no symptoms.
hq_q.w: Half of popliteal aneurysms are bilateral and many people also have an aortic aneurysm, so both are scanned.
hq_q.f: Pulsatile groin lump after a femoral angiogram → false aneurysm, treated with ultrasound-guided thrombin injection.
hq_q.ql: Which further investigation is most important?

tm.m: Popliteal aneurysms are often bilateral and linked with AAA
tm.g: Popliteal aneurysm: ultrasound of the aorta and the other leg
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI is less important)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Coronary angiogram (Coronary angiography is not routine)
the presentation instead showed features specific to CT head (CT head is not needed)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Echocardiogram (Used for: Murmur, heart failure, new AF)
x: ABPI is less important.
Coronary angiography is not routine.
CT head is not needed.
Used for: Murmur, heart failure, new AF

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man underwent diagnostic coronary angiography via the right common femoral artery yesterday. Today he complains of a painful, throbbing swelling in his right groin.
Pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 134/78 mmHg. Examination reveals a 4 cm tender, expansile, pulsatile mass in the right groin with a harsh systolic bruit. Distal pedal pulses are palpable.
hq_q.w: An arterial puncture that fails to seal leaks blood into surrounding perivascular tissues, forming a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) connected to the femoral artery lumen by a neck. It produces a painful, expansile pulsatile mass with a systolic bruit.
hq_q.f: Continuous machinery bruit and thrill over the femoral puncture site -> arteriovenous fistula.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: coronary angiography via the right common femoral artery yesterday
expansile, pulsatile mass in the right groin
tm.m: Persistent blood flow through an unsealed arterial puncture wall forms a perfused cavity bounded only by adventitia and perivascular haematoma
tm.g: Pulsatile groin mass with a systolic bruit after femoral arterial catheterisation -> femoral false aneurysm
x: Produces a continuous systolic-diastolic machinery bruit and palpable thrill rather than a discrete expansile mass with a systolic bruit.
Forms a non-pulsatile irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle unrelated to arterial puncture.
Causes bruising and a firm non-pulsatile swelling without expansile pulsation or a systolic bruit.
Presents as a firm, discrete, non-pulsatile rubbery nodule in the groin.
f: A continuous machinery bruit and palpable thrill in the right groin after simultaneous femoral artery and vein puncture
A tender, non-pulsatile, irreducible groin lump below the inguinal ligament with vomiting and bowel obstruction
A tender, bruised, non-pulsatile groin swelling after angiography with no bruit and no flow within the mass on duplex
A firm, discrete, non-pulsatile groin lump in a patient with an infected toe ulcer

hq_q.s:
A 76 year old woman with atrial fibrillation has had a cold, pale, painful right leg for 3 hours. She stopped taking her oral anticoagulant 2 weeks ago. She has never had leg pain on walking.
The right leg is cold and pale. The right femoral pulse is palpable, but the popliteal and pedal pulses are absent. All left leg pulses are normal.
o: Acute Stanford type B aortic dissection
hq_q.w: Sudden severe limb ischaemia in a patient with unanticoagulated atrial fibrillation, no history of intermittent claudication, and normal contralateral pulses is characteristic of acute arterial embolisation, typically lodging at the femoral or popliteal bifurcation.
hq_q.f: Prior history of intermittent claudication and absent contralateral pedal pulses -> acute thrombosis in situ on plaque.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?

c: never had leg pain on walking
All left leg pulses are normal
tm.m: Left atrial appendage thrombus embolises into a previously normal peripheral arterial tree lacking collateral vessels
tm.g: Sudden white leg in AF with no prior claudication and normal contralateral pulses -> embolic arterial occlusion
x: Presents with sudden tearing interscapular back pain and loss of the femoral pulse rather than an isolated popliteal occlusion with a normal femoral pulse.
Occurs in young heavy smokers under 45 with distal digital ulceration and superficial migratory thrombophlebitis.
Causes a congested, warm, swollen cyanotic leg rather than a cold, white, pulseless limb.
Develops on a background of chronic intermittent claudication, trophic skin changes, and reduced contralateral pulses.
f: Sudden tearing interscapular back pain with severe hypertension and an absent right femoral pulse
Distal toe ulcers, rest pain, and migratory superficial thrombophlebitis in a 32-year-old heavy cigarette smoker
Acute painful, tense, pitting swelling of the entire right leg with distended superficial veins
Subacute worsening of leg pain on a 3-year background of 100-metre calf claudication and absent contralateral pedal pulses

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man has had a cold, painful left leg for 4 hours. Acute limb ischaemia is diagnosed.
The left leg is pale. The foot pulses cannot be felt. Sensation and movement are intact.
hq_q.w: Heparin stops the clot spreading while the vascular team plans embolectomy, bypass or thrombolysis. Every hour of ischaemia counts.
hq_q.f: Fixed mottling, a rigid calf and paralysis → irreversible: amputation or palliation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

tm.m: Heparin stops the clot spreading while revascularisation is planned
tm.g: Acute limb ischaemia with a viable leg: IV heparin and urgent vascular review
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Aspirin and outpatient review (This is an emergency)
the presentation instead showed features specific to CT angiogram then discharge home (Acute limb ischaemia is a surgical emergency threatening limb loss)
fixed mottling, a rigid calf and paralysis
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ward thrombolysis (Thrombolysis is done by specialists)
x: This is an emergency.
Acute limb ischaemia is a surgical emergency threatening limb loss
Ruled out here: requires fixed mottling, a rigid calf and paralysis, whereas this patient has 4 hours, Sensation and movement are intact.
Thrombolysis is done by specialists.

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old woman had a femoral embolectomy 6 hours ago for a leg ischaemic for 10 hours. She now has severe calf pain.
The calf is tense and tender. Passive movement of the foot causes severe pain. The foot pulses are present.
hq_q.w: Reperfusion swells the muscle inside tight fascia: compartment syndrome. Pain on passive stretch is the earliest sign; pulses are often still present. Fasciotomy is needed.
hq_q.f: The foot goes white and pulseless again → re-occlusion, back to theatre.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: Passive movement of the foot causes severe pain
tm.m: Reperfused muscle swells inside tight fascia
tm.g: Reperfusion compartment syndrome: four-compartment fasciotomy
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Analgesia and elevation (Elevating the limb above heart level reduces perfusion pressure further)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Compression bandage (External compression worsens compartment pressure and causes muscle necrosis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Heparin infusion (Contraindicated within 24 hours of thrombolysis due to haemorrhagic transformation risk)
the foot goes white and pulseless again
x: Elevating the limb above heart level reduces perfusion pressure further
External compression worsens compartment pressure and causes muscle necrosis
Contraindicated within 24 hours of thrombolysis due to haemorrhagic transformation risk
Ruled out here: requires the foot goes white and pulseless again, whereas this patient has embolectomy 6 hours ago, ischaemic for 10 hours.

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man smokes 20 cigarettes a day. He gets pain in his right calf after walking 200 m, which goes with rest. He has no pain at rest.
The foot pulses are weak on the right. There are no ulcers.
Ankle-brachial pressure index 0.7 on the right.
hq_q.w: Intermittent claudication: supervised exercise, stopping smoking and cardiovascular risk reduction first. Most people improve. Key discriminator: Intermittent claudication: supervised exercise programme first.
hq_q.f: Still limited after the exercise programme → imaging to consider angioplasty.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

tm.m: Exercise builds collateral flow and walking distance
tm.g: Intermittent claudication: supervised exercise programme first
f: still limited after exercise, wanting revascularisation
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cilostazol (NICE does not recommend cilostazol for intermittent claudication)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Femoropopliteal bypass (Bypass is for critical ischaemia)
exercise has not helped and revascularisation is not wanted
x: Ruled out here: requires still limited after exercise, wanting revascularisation, whereas this patient has smokes 20, 200 m.
NICE does not recommend cilostazol for intermittent claudication
Bypass is for critical ischaemia.
Ruled out here: requires exercise has not helped and revascularisation is not wanted, whereas this patient has smokes 20, 200 m.

hq_q.s:
A 71 year old man with a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes and stage 3 chronic kidney disease attends the vascular clinic with cramping pain in both calves after walking 150 metres.
Pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 142/82 mmHg. His feet are cool and pedal pulses cannot be felt bilaterally.
Resting ankle-brachial pressure index is 1.45 in both legs.
o: Repeat ankle-brachial pressure index in 1 year
hq_q.w: In long-standing diabetes and chronic kidney disease, Monckeberg's medial arterial calcification renders crural arteries incompressible, producing a falsely elevated ABPI (>1.3). Digital arteries are spared calcification, so toe-brachial pressure index or duplex ultrasound is used.
hq_q.f: Resting ABPI 0.65 with compressible vessels -> confirms moderate peripheral arterial disease.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to assess his arterial perfusion?

c: cramping pain in both calves after walking 150 metres
tm.m: Medial calcinosis stiffens the tibial arteries against cuff compression while sparing digital arterioles
tm.g: ABPI >1.3 in a diabetic patient with absent pulses -> measure toe-brachial pressure index
x: Images the pulmonary arterial tree for pulmonary embolism rather than lower-limb peripheral arterial disease.
An ABPI above 1.3 indicates artefactual arterial incompressibility rather than normal perfusion, so discharging misses significant ischaemia.
Assesses saphenous venous reflux rather than arterial inflow in a patient with absent pedal pulses and claudication.
Repeating cuff compression on calcified tibial vessels will again yield an uninterpretable reading above 1.3.
f: Acute pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, and hypoxia with a high Wells score for pulmonary embolism
A resting ABPI of 1.08 with strong pedal pulses and pain explained by benign nocturnal leg cramps
Aching tortuous varicose veins with medial ankle haemosiderin staining and strong pedal pulses
Stable mild peripheral arterial disease under routine vascular nurse surveillance with compressible arteries

hq_q.s:
A 57 year old man who smokes 25 cigarettes a day has had cramping pain in both buttocks and thighs for 8 months. The pain starts after walking 100 metres and resolves within 5 minutes of standing still. He also reports erectile dysfunction.
Both femoral pulses and all distal lower-limb pulses are absent. Straight-leg raise is normal.
hq_q.w: Leriche syndrome is atherosclerotic occlusion of the distal abdominal aorta and common iliac bifurcation, producing the classic triad of bilateral buttock and thigh claudication, erectile dysfunction (internal iliac hypoperfusion), and absent femoral pulses.
hq_q.f: Bilateral leg pain worse walking downhill and eased by leaning forward with normal femoral pulses -> lumbar spinal canal stenosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: cramping pain in both buttocks and thighs
Both femoral pulses and all distal lower-limb pulses are absent
tm.m: Aortoiliac bifurcation occlusion impairs blood flow to the external iliacs (thighs) and internal iliacs (gluteal muscles and corpora cavernosa)
tm.g: Buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, and absent femoral pulses -> Leriche aortoiliac syndrome
x: Causes groin pain and restricted internal hip rotation with preserved femoral and pedal pulses.
Causes neurogenic claudication relieved by lumbar flexion (sitting or leaning forward) with intact lower-limb pulses.
Presents in young muscular athletes with unilateral calf claudication and preserved femoral pulses.
Produces shooting pain down the back of one leg with a positive straight-leg raise and intact femoral pulses.
f: Groin pain on weight-bearing with painful restriction of internal hip rotation and strong femoral pulses
Bilateral thigh and calf pain on walking downhill that eases only on sitting or leaning forward, with normal pulses
Exertional calf pain in a 22-year-old runner where pedal pulses disappear on active plantarflexion
Shooting pain from the lower back to the lateral foot with an absent ankle jerk and positive straight-leg raise

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man with type 2 diabetes has an ulcer under his foot. It does not hurt.
There is a deep, painless ulcer under the first metatarsal head with surrounding callus. He cannot feel a 10 g monofilament on either foot. The foot is warm and the pulses are present. There is no redness, swelling or discharge.
o: Foot care team within 1 working day
hq_q.w: NICE advises referring any diabetic foot ulcer to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 1 working day, and immediately if there is ischaemia, spreading infection or gangrene. Offloading, debridement and checks for infection and ischaemia start there.
hq_q.f: Same ulcer with spreading cellulitis, fever or a cold, pulseless foot → immediate admission.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Loss of protective sensation lets repeated pressure break the skin unnoticed
tm.g: Diabetic foot ulcer: foot care team within 1 working day
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Compression bandaging (Compression is for venous ulcers and can harm a diabetic foot)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral flucloxacillin and GP review (There is no sign of infection; antibiotics are for infected ulcers)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Routine podiatry in 6 weeks (A diabetic foot ulcer cannot wait 6 weeks; it can progress to infection and amputation)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Vascular surgery referral (His pulses are present and the foot is warm, so this is not an ischaemic ulcer)
x: Compression is for venous ulcers and can harm a diabetic foot.
There is no sign of infection; antibiotics are for infected ulcers.
A diabetic foot ulcer cannot wait 6 weeks; it can progress to infection and amputation.
His pulses are present and the foot is warm, so this is not an ischaemic ulcer.

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old woman has had an ulcer above her left medial malleolus for 3 months. She has varicose veins.
There is a shallow ulcer with a sloughy base and surrounding haemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis. The foot pulses are present.
Ankle-brachial pressure index 0.9.
hq_q.w: Compression is the treatment for venous ulcers once arterial disease is excluded with an ABPI of 0.8 or more.
hq_q.f: ABPI 0.5 → no compression; refer to vascular surgery.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Compression reverses venous hypertension once arterial disease is excluded
tm.g: Venous ulcer with ABPI over 0.8: multilayer compression
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral antibiotics (There is no infection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Split-skin graft to the ulcer (Grafting is for failure to heal)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Topical steroid (Worsens bacterial skin infection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Vascular bypass (Bypass is for arterial disease)
x: There is no infection.
Grafting is for failure to heal.
Worsens bacterial skin infection
Bypass is for arterial disease.

hq_q.s:
A 77 year old man has had a venous ulcer on his right leg for 15 years. Over 3 months it has grown and bleeds easily.
There is a 5 cm ulcer with a raised, rolled, everted edge. There is an enlarged inguinal lymph node on the right.
hq_q.w: A long-standing ulcer that changes, with a raised rolled edge, bleeding and a regional node, may have turned into a squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin ulcer). Biopsies from several places on the edge confirm it, and the node is assessed too.
hq_q.f: Painful ulcer with a purple, undermined edge in a man with ulcerative colitis → pyoderma gangrenosum.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most appropriate?

tm.m: Chronic inflammation in a scar or ulcer drives malignant change in the squamous epithelium
tm.g: Old ulcer with a new rolled edge: biopsy for SCC
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI checks the arterial supply before compression; it does not show cancer)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Compression and review (Compression delays the diagnosis of a likely cancer)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Swab for culture (Chronic ulcers are always colonised; a swab does not explain a rolled, bleeding edge)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Venous duplex ultrasound (Venous duplex shows the reflux that caused the original ulcer, not the new change)
x: ABPI checks the arterial supply before compression; it does not show cancer.
Compression delays the diagnosis of a likely cancer.
Chronic ulcers are always colonised; a swab does not explain a rolled, bleeding edge.
Venous duplex shows the reflux that caused the original ulcer, not the new change.

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old woman attends her GP requesting removal of varicose veins on both lower legs because she dislikes their appearance when wearing skirts. She has no leg aching, heaviness, itching, eczema, ulceration or superficial thrombophlebitis.
Examination shows mild tortuous tributary veins over both calves with normal overlying skin and strong pedal pulses.
o: Refer to the vascular surgery service
hq_q.w: Under NICE guidelines, vascular referral is indicated for varicose veins only when accompanied by lower-limb symptoms (pain, aching, heaviness), venous skin changes, superficial vein thrombosis, venous ulceration, or bleeding. Purely cosmetic varicosities are managed with reassurance.
hq_q.f: Varicose veins causing aching or venous skin changes -> refer to a vascular service for duplex ultrasound.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management in NHS primary care?

c: no leg aching, heaviness, itching, eczema, ulceration
tm.m: Asymptomatic uncomplicated varicose veins carry a low risk of ulceration and do not meet NICE criteria for NHS vascular referral
tm.g: Purely cosmetic asymptomatic varicose veins with normal skin -> reassurance and self-care advice
x: First-line interventional treatment in secondary care for symptomatic truncal reflux, not asymptomatic cosmetic veins.
NICE advises against compression stockings for asymptomatic varicose veins or when interventional treatment is appropriate.
NICE referral criteria require symptoms (ache, heaviness, itch), skin changes, thrombophlebitis, bleeding, or ulceration.
Second-line intervention for symptomatic varicose veins unsuitable for endothermal ablation.
f: Symptomatic great saphenous vein reflux confirmed on duplex ultrasound in a vascular clinic
Symptomatic varicose veins during pregnancy or when interventional ablation is clinically unsuitable
Varicose veins accompanied by daily leg aching, ankle haemosiderin staining, or a bleeding varix
Symptomatic recurrent varicose veins where endothermal catheter ablation is anatomically unsuitable

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old man has varicose veins in his right leg. Over a year the skin above his ankle has become brown and itchy. He has no ulcer.
There is brown pigmentation and venous eczema above the medial malleolus. Foot pulses are present.
hq_q.w: NICE advises referral to a vascular service for varicose veins with skin changes (pigmentation, eczema, lipodermatosclerosis), bleeding, thrombophlebitis or ulceration. Compression is not offered instead of treatment unless intervention is unsuitable.
hq_q.f: Varicose veins with no symptoms or skin changes, wanted removed for appearance → reassure.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Failed valves cause venous hypertension that leaks red cells and fluid into the skin
tm.g: Varicose veins with skin changes: refer
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Compression stockings and review (NICE does not offer compression as treatment for symptomatic varicose veins unless intervention is unsuitable)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral antibiotics (The skin is itchy and pigmented, not infected)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Reassure (Skin changes show venous hypertension that leads to ulcers; he needs assessment)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Topical steroid and discharge (A steroid can ease the eczema, but he still needs referral for the cause)
x: NICE does not offer compression as treatment for symptomatic varicose veins unless intervention is unsuitable.
The skin is itchy and pigmented, not infected.
Skin changes show venous hypertension that leads to ulcers; he needs assessment.
A steroid can ease the eczema, but he still needs referral for the cause.

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old woman attends the vascular clinic with a 2-year history of aching varicose veins over the back of her right calf that worsen after standing all day.
Examination shows prominent tortuous varicosities tracking behind the right lateral malleolus and up the posterior calf. Venous duplex ultrasound confirms isolated junctional valve incompetence.
hq_q.w: The small (short) saphenous vein originates behind the lateral malleolus, ascends the posterior aspect of the calf, and perforates the deep fascia in the popliteal fossa to join the popliteal vein at the saphenopopliteal junction.
hq_q.f: Varicosities along the medial malleolus, medial calf, and medial thigh -> saphenofemoral junction incompetence.
hq_q.ql: Which venous junction is most likely to be incompetent?

c: aching varicose veins over the back of her right calf
behind the right lateral malleolus and up the posterior calf
tm.m: The small saphenous vein drains the lateral foot and posterior calf into the popliteal vein at the saphenopopliteal junction
tm.g: Posterior calf varicosities extending from behind the lateral malleolus -> saphenopopliteal venous junction
x: Part of the deep iliofemoral venous conduit above the inguinal ligament rather than a superficial saphenous junction.
Connect the posterior arch tributaties to the posterior tibial veins above the medial malleolus rather than draining the posterior-lateral calf.
An arterial branching point rather than a venous valve junction.
Drains the great saphenous vein, which ascends anterior to the medial malleolus along the medial calf and thigh.
f: Deep venous reflux or post-thrombotic obstruction at the inguinal ligament on duplex scanning
Localised medial supramalleolar venous eczema and blow-out varicosities with competent saphenous junctions
A saddle arterial embolus lodging at the division of the popliteal artery into tibial vessels
Varicosities running anterior to the medial malleolus and up the medial aspect of the calf and thigh

hq_q.s:
A 62 year old woman underwent a left mastectomy with axillary lymph node clearance and adjuvant radiotherapy 12 months ago. Over the past 4 months her left arm has slowly become heavy and swollen. She feels well and has no fever.
The left arm shows firm, non-pitting swelling extending to the hand, and the skin at the base of her fingers cannot be pinched.
hq_q.w: Axillary lymph node dissection combined with radiotherapy disrupts lymphatic drainage from the upper limb, causing secondary lymphoedema characterised by firm, non-pitting swelling and a positive Stemmer's sign (inability to pinch dorsal digital skin).
hq_q.f: Acute painful dusky swelling of the arm with prominent chest wall veins -> axillary-subclavian vein thrombosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: axillary lymph node clearance and adjuvant radiotherapy
firm, non-pitting swelling extending to the hand
skin at the base of her fingers cannot be pinched
tm.m: Surgical excision and radiation fibrosis of axillary lymphatics cause interstitial accumulation of protein-rich lymph and dermal fibrosis
tm.g: Gradual non-pitting arm swelling with positive Stemmer's sign after axillary clearance -> secondary post-surgical lymphoedema
x: Presents acutely over days with painful, pitting, cyanotic swelling and distended superficial collateral veins.
Causes symmetrical dependent pitting oedema of the ankles and sacrum with elevated jugular venous pressure.
Affects the lower limbs symmetrically in women and spares the hands and feet (negative Stemmer's sign).
Presents acutely with hot, erythematous, tender skin and systemic fever rather than a 4-month painless swelling.
f: Sudden painful, dusky, pitting swelling of the arm with engorged superficial veins in a patient with a PICC line
Bilateral pitting ankle oedema, orthopnoea, raised JVP, and bibasal lung crackles
Symmetrical tender, easily bruised fatty enlargement of both legs from hips to ankles sparing the feet
Acute onset of spreading erythema, warmth, tenderness, and fever of 38.5°C in the arm

hq_q.s:
A 35 year old woman has had progressively enlarged legs since her early twenties despite maintaining a normal upper-body weight. Her legs ache by evening, feel tender when knocked, and bruise easily.
Examination shows symmetrical, soft, non-pitting enlargement of both legs from the iliac crests to the ankles, with a sharp step-off at the malleoli and completely normal feet.
hq_q.w: Lipoedema is a chronic disorder of symmetrical subcutaneous adipose tissue deposition almost exclusively affecting women. It causes tender, easily bruised legs with a characteristic ankle cuff that spares the feet (negative Stemmer's sign).
hq_q.f: Non-pitting swelling extending onto the dorsum of the feet with a positive Stemmer's sign -> primary lymphoedema.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: tender when knocked, and bruise easily
sharp step-off at the malleoli and completely normal feet
tm.m: Oestrogen-influenced pathological adipocyte hypertrophy and capillary fragility affect the hips, thighs, and calves while sparing the feet
tm.g: Symmetrical tender, easily bruised non-pitting legs sparing the feet -> lipoedema
x: Extends onto the dorsum of the feet and toes with thickened skin and a positive Stemmer's sign.
Produces pitting ankle oedema, varicose veins, and gaiter haemosiderin pigmentation rather than symmetrical hip-to-ankle fat deposition.
Causes dependent pitting oedema involving the feet and ankles alongside dyspnoea and raised jugular venous pressure.
Produces generalized soft pitting oedema including the feet and periorbital tissues with heavy proteinuria.
f: Non-pitting swelling involving the dorsum of both feet and toes with an inability to pinch the skin at the second toe base
Aching lower legs with tortuous varicose veins, pitting ankle oedema, and brown gaiter pigmentation
Bilateral pitting foot and ankle oedema with orthopnoea, raised JVP, and elevated NT-proBNP
Pitting oedema of the feet and face with frothy urine, 4+ proteinuria, and serum albumin of 19 g/L

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man has chronic secondary lymphoedema of his right leg following inguinal node dissection for melanoma 4 years ago. He wears a flat-knit compression garment daily and uses emollients, and his interdigital web spaces are intact with no tinea pedis. Over the past 10 months he has had 3 episodes of acute right leg cellulitis requiring antibiotics.
o: Continue compression hosiery without drug prophylaxis
Radical surgical debulking of subcutaneous tissue
hq_q.w: In patients with lymphoedema who experience 2 or more episodes of cellulitis per year despite optimal skin care and compression, UK British Lymphology Society and NICE guidance recommend long-term low-dose oral phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) prophylaxis.
hq_q.f: Interdigital maceration and scaling from tinea pedis -> treat with topical terbinafine to close the portal of bacterial entry.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate long-term measure to prevent further episodes?

c: chronic secondary lymphoedema of his right leg
wears a flat-knit compression garment daily
3 episodes of acute right leg cellulitis
tm.m: Impaired lymphatic trafficking compromises local immune surveillance against beta-haemolytic streptococci, warranting suppressive penicillin prophylaxis
tm.g: Two or more episodes of cellulitis per year in lymphoedema -> low-dose oral phenoxymethylpenicillin prophylaxis
x: He has already had 3 episodes in 10 months despite daily compression and skin care, meeting the threshold for antibiotic prophylaxis.
Loop diuretics do not Mobilise protein-rich interstitial lymphoedema and do not prevent streptococcal cellulitis.
His interdigital web spaces are intact with no fungal infection, so antifungal therapy alone will not prevent recurrences.
Charles-type excisional debulking is a last-resort procedure for extreme elephantiasis, not standard prevention of recurrent cellulitis.
f: A single isolated episode of cellulitis that resolved completely with no previous attacks
Bilateral pitting lower-limb oedema secondary to congestive heart failure with fluid overload
Macerated, fissured interdigital tinea pedis acting as the entry portal for bacteria
End-stage disabling elephantiasis refractory to all conservative decompression measures

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman has painful fingers in the cold. They turn white, then blue, then red when they warm up. She has no other symptoms. Gloves and stopping smoking have not been enough.
The hands are normal between attacks with no ulcers or skin thickening.
Antinuclear antibodies are negative.
o: Sildenafil 20 mg three times a day
hq_q.w: Primary Raynaud's: keep warm and stop smoking, then modified-release nifedipine. IV prostacyclins are for severe secondary disease.
hq_q.f: Digital ulcers or onset after 30 → look for secondary causes such as connective tissue disease.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate drug?

tm.m: Calcium channel blockers relax spasm in the digital arteries
tm.g: Primary Raynaud's despite lifestyle measures: modified-release nifedipine
f: cold hands and slow pulse
the presentation instead showed features specific to Iloprost infusion (Iloprost is for severe secondary Raynaud's)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Low-dose aspirin (Not enough after a venous clot)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sildenafil 20 mg three times a day (Sildenafil is second line)
x: Ruled out here: requires cold hands and slow pulse, whereas this patient has white, then blue, then red, no ulcers.
Iloprost is for severe secondary Raynaud's.
Not enough after a venous clot
Sildenafil is second line.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman has had Raynaud's for 5 years. She has trouble swallowing.
There is tight, shiny skin on her fingers only. There is telangiectasia on her face and calcium deposits in her fingertips.
Anti-centromere antibodies are positive.
hq_q.w: CREST: calcinosis, Raynaud's, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly and telangiectasia, with anti-centromere antibodies. Key discriminator: CREST features with anti-centromere antibodies is limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.
hq_q.f: Anti-Scl-70 with skin thickening up to the trunk → diffuse systemic sclerosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Anti-centromere antibodies mark the limited form with CREST features
tm.g: CREST features with anti-centromere antibodies is limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis
f: a heliotrope rash with proximal weakness
anti-Scl-70 with skin thickening up to the trunk
the presentation instead showed features specific to Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD has anti-U1 RNP)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE does not cause calcinosis)
x: Ruled out here: requires a heliotrope rash with proximal weakness, whereas this patient has trouble swallowing, fingers only.
Ruled out here: requires anti-Scl-70 with skin thickening up to the trunk, whereas this patient has trouble swallowing, fingers only.
MCTD has anti-U1 RNP.
SLE does not cause calcinosis.

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old orchestral violinist has had mild primary Raynaud's phenomenon since his teens. Over the past 6 weeks his fingers have become painfully white and numb whenever he walks outdoors. Two months ago his GP prescribed an as-needed tablet to control hand tremor and palpitations before concert performances.
Pulse rate 56 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg. Radial pulses are normal.
hq_q.w: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker commonly prescribed for situational performance anxiety and tremor. Blocking peripheral beta-2 vasodilatory receptors leaves alpha-mediated digital vasoconstriction unopposed, precipitating or worsening Raynaud's phenomenon.
hq_q.f: First-line oral vasodilator to treat troublesome Raynaud's attacks -> nifedipine.
hq_q.ql: Which drug prescribed by his GP is most likely to be responsible?

c: control hand tremor and palpitations before concert performances
tm.m: Non-selective beta-1 and beta-2 blockade reduces cardiac output and blocks peripheral beta-2 vasodilation in digital arterioles
tm.g: Worsening Raynaud's after starting medication for performance anxiety tremor -> propranolol
x: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor used for generalised anxiety that does not cause peripheral beta-blockade or bradycardia.
Benzodiazepine anxiolytic that causes sedation rather than peripheral digital vasoconstriction.
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that dilates digital arterioles and is the first-line treatment for Raynaud's phenomenon.
Simple central analgesic with no effect on peripheral vascular tone or sympathetic tremor.
f: First-line pharmacological treatment for generalised anxiety disorder with hyponatraemia as a recognised side effect
Short-term crisis relief of severe acute agitation causing drowsiness and ataxia
First-line vasodilator therapy prescribed to reduce the frequency and severity of Raynaud's attacks
First-line step-one oral analgesia for mild musculoskeletal pain

hq_q.s:
A 23 year old man has heard two voices talking about him in the third person for 2 months. He says his neighbours are taking his thoughts out of his head. He has stopped going to work. He does not use drugs and his mood is not low or elevated.
He is guarded and distracted.
Urine drug screen is negative.
hq_q.w: Third-person auditory hallucinations (voices discussing or commenting on the patient) and thought withdrawal are Schneiderian first-rank symptoms. Persistence for over 1 month with occupational decline and negative urine toxicology in a euthymic patient confirms schizophrenia.
hq_q.f: A single fixed belief for months with otherwise normal behaviour and no hallucinations → delusional disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: mood is not low or elevated
tm.m: Mesolimbic dopaminergic hyperactivity and aberrant salience produce first-rank hallucinations and passivity phenomena
tm.g: Third-person auditory hallucinations + thought withdrawal for >1 month without mood symptoms or drug use -> schizophrenia
f: a single fixed non-bizarre belief for 6 months with preserved work function and no hallucinations
acute paranoia and hallucinations after smoking high-potency cannabis with a positive urine screen
profound depressed mood, psychomotor retardation and nihilistic delusions that his organs have rotted
third-person voices and thought withdrawal occurring alongside a full manic or severe depressive episode
x: Delusional disorder features a circumscribed non-bizarre delusion with preserved occupational function and no prominent third-person hallucinations or thought withdrawal.
Drug-induced psychosis requires recent intoxication or withdrawal from a psychotogenic substance, whereas he denies drug use and his urine screen is negative.
Psychotic depression presents with profound low mood, anhedonia, and mood-congruent delusions of guilt, poverty, or nihilism.
Schizoaffective disorder requires a major depressive or manic episode occurring concurrently with first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia.

hq_q.s: A 25 year old man saw a red car parked outside his flat this morning. He says he knew at once that it meant he had been chosen to save the world. He is otherwise calm and orientated.
hq_q.w: A normal perception (a red car) is given a sudden, unrelated delusional meaning. Delusional perception is a first-rank symptom of schizophrenia.
hq_q.f: Believing a TV presenter is talking about him → delusion of reference.
hq_q.ql: Which term best describes this?

c: saw a red car parked outside
knew at once that it meant
tm.m: A real perception is followed by an instant delusional meaning that has no logical link to it
tm.g: Normal perception, then sudden delusional meaning: delusional perception
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Delusion of reference (A delusion of reference is believing that events or people refer to you, such as TV messages; here a real perception triggers a new meaning)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Grandiose delusion (The content is grandiose, but the term that describes how it arose from a perception is delusional perception)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Overvalued idea (An overvalued idea is an understandable belief held too strongly, not a sudden unshakeable revelation)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Thought insertion (Thought insertion is believing thoughts are put into your mind by an outside force)
x: A delusion of reference is believing that events or people refer to you, such as TV messages; here a real perception triggers a new meaning.
The content is grandiose, but the term that describes how it arose from a perception is delusional perception.
An overvalued idea is an understandable belief held too strongly, not a sudden unshakeable revelation.
Thought insertion is believing thoughts are put into your mind by an outside force.

hq_q.s: A 68 year old woman is admitted to the older adult psychiatric ward with severe melancholic depression, psychomotor retardation, and weight loss of 9 kg over 6 weeks. She refuses food and water, telling nurses that there is no point eating because she is already dead and her bowels have completely rotted away.
hq_q.w: Cotard syndrome is a rare nihilistic delusion classically seen in severe psychotic depression, in which the patient holds the fixed conviction that they are dead, do not exist, or that their internal organs have rotted.
hq_q.f: Believes a famous person is secretly in love with her → de Clérambault syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which term describes this?

tm.m: Profound psychotic depressive mood-congruent distortion produces nihilistic somatic delusions of non-existence or putrefaction
tm.g: Nihilistic delusion that one is dead or that internal organs have rotted away -> Cotard syndrome
f: believing that her husband has been replaced by an identical-looking double or impostor
believing that a famous television newsreader is secretly in love with her
insisting that microscopic insects are crawling beneath her skin and bringing lint samples in matchboxes
believing that different passers-by on the street are the same persecutor wearing disguises
x: Capgras syndrome is a delusional misidentification in which the patient believes a close relative or spouse has been replaced by an identical-looking impostor.
De Clerambault syndrome (erotomania) is the delusional belief that a high-status person or celebrity is secretly in love with the patient.
Ekbom syndrome (delusional parasitosis) is the fixed false belief that one's skin is infested with insects, mites, or parasites.
Fregoli syndrome is the delusional belief that various different strangers are actually a single familiar persecutor in changing disguises.

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old man had his first dose of haloperidol 6 hours ago for acute psychosis. He is distressed.
His neck is twisted to one side and his eyes are fixed looking upwards. He is alert. Temperature 36.9°C.
hq_q.w: Acute dystonia appears within hours to days of starting an antipsychotic. An anticholinergic such as procyclidine reverses it quickly.
hq_q.f: Inner restlessness and unable to sit still after a few weeks → akathisia, reduce the dose or try propranolol.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Sudden dopamine blockade causes sustained muscle spasm
tm.g: Acute dystonia after haloperidol: procyclidine
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Dantrolene (Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia or NMS, not acute dystonia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lorazepam (Lorazepam is not first line for dystonia)
inner restlessness weeks after starting
the presentation instead showed features specific to Tetrabenazine (Tetrabenazine treats tardive dyskinesia)
x: Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia or NMS, not acute dystonia.
Lorazepam is not first line for dystonia.
Ruled out here: requires inner restlessness weeks after starting, whereas this patient has 6 hours ago, neck is twisted.
Tetrabenazine treats tardive dyskinesia.

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old woman has taken haloperidol for schizophrenia for 6 years. Her family has noticed odd movements of her mouth.
There is lip smacking, tongue thrusting and chewing movements. There is no rigidity.
hq_q.w: Tardive dyskinesia comes after months to years of dopamine blockade. Anticholinergics make it worse. Key discriminator: Late lip smacking and tongue thrusting on haloperidol is tardive dyskinesia.
hq_q.f: Within hours of the first dose with eyes rolled upwards → acute dystonia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Years of dopamine blockade cause receptor supersensitivity
tm.g: Late lip smacking and tongue thrusting on haloperidol is tardive dyskinesia
f: within hours of the first dose with eyes rolled up
inner restlessness and pacing
the presentation instead showed features specific to Drug-induced parkinsonism (Parkinsonism causes rigidity and tremor)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS is acute with fever and rigidity, not years of mouth movements)
x: Ruled out here: requires within hours of the first dose with eyes rolled up, whereas this patient has 6 years, lip smacking, tongue thrusting.
Ruled out here: requires inner restlessness and pacing, whereas this patient has 6 years, lip smacking, tongue thrusting.
Parkinsonism causes rigidity and tremor.
NMS is acute with fever and rigidity, not years of mouth movements.

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old man with acute mania was started on oral haloperidol 5 days ago. Over the past 24 hours he has become increasingly confused, mute, and diaphoretic.
Temperature is 39.5°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, and blood pressure fluctuates between 110/70 and 180/100 mmHg. He has generalized lead-pipe muscle rigidity, hyporeflexia, and no clonus. Serum creatine kinase is 12,000 U/L.
hq_q.w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction to dopamine D2 receptor antagonists characterised by hyperthermia, autonomic instability, generalized lead-pipe rigidity, and rhabdomyolysis (markedly raised CK). Immediately stop the antipsychotic, give aggressive intravenous crystalloids, and cool the patient.
hq_q.f: Clonus and hyperreflexia within 24 hours of adding tramadol to sertraline → serotonin syndrome, cyproheptadine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: started on oral haloperidol 5 days ago
tm.m: Sudden central hypothalamic and nigrostriatal D2 blockade causes hyperthermia, autonomic lability, lead-pipe rigidity, and rhabdomyolysis
tm.g: Fever + autonomic lability + lead-pipe rigidity + high CK on haloperidol -> stop haloperidol and give IV fluids
f: acute painful torticollis and upward deviation of the eyes 4 hours after a dose of haloperidol
hyperreflexia, inducible ankle clonus and agitation within hours of combining tramadol with sertraline
persistent manic psychosis in a patient with normal temperature, normal muscle tone and normal creatine kinase
never appropriate because the offending dopamine antagonist must be stopped immediately in NMS
x: Antimuscarinic procyclidine treats acute focal dystonia (such as oculogyric crisis or torticollis) but impairs sweating and worsens hyperthermia in NMS.
Cyproheptadine is a 5-HT2A antagonist used for serotonin syndrome, which presents with hyperreflexia and ankle clonus rather than lead-pipe rigidity.
Increasing the dose of haloperidol deepens striatal and hypothalamic dopamine blockade and can prove rapidly fatal in NMS.
Continuing the causative antipsychotic in neuroleptic malignant syndrome perpetuates rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, and mortality.

hq_q.s: A 34 year old man has had low mood, poor sleep and loss of interest for 3 months. His depression is more severe. He would like medication alongside talking therapy. He has no other illnesses and takes no other medicines.
hq_q.w: An SSRI such as sertraline is first-line: effective, safer in overdose and well tolerated. Combine it with CBT for more severe depression.
hq_q.f: Under 18 → fluoxetine, alongside psychological therapy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first drug?

tm.m: SSRIs are effective and safer in overdose
tm.g: Depression needing medication: sertraline
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amitriptyline (Tricyclics are dangerous in overdose and are not first line)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam (Diazepam does not treat depression)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lithium (Lithium is an augmenting agent, not a first drug for depression)
the presentation instead showed features specific to St John's wort (Not prescribed due to variable potency and cytochrome P450 drug interactions)
x: Tricyclics are dangerous in overdose and are not first line.
Diazepam does not treat depression.
Lithium is an augmenting agent, not a first drug for depression.
Not prescribed due to variable potency and cytochrome P450 drug interactions

hq_q.s: A 22 year old university student attends general practice with a 2 month history of persistent low mood, anhedonia, early morning wakening, and impaired concentration (PHQ-9 score 16). Following shared decision-making, she starts oral sertraline 50 mg daily today alongside a cognitive behavioural therapy referral. She denies current suicidal ideation.
hq_q.w: Under NICE guideline NG222, patients aged 18 to 25 years (or anyone deemed at increased risk of suicide) starting antidepressant medication must be reviewed after 1 week because SSRIs can transiently increase agitation and suicidal ideation early in treatment.
hq_q.f: A 45-year-old with no raised risk → review at 2 weeks.
hq_q.ql: When should she next be reviewed?

c: starts oral sertraline 50 mg daily today
tm.m: Early serotonergic activation before mood improvement can transiently increase suicidal ideation in adults under 25
tm.g: Patient aged under 25 (or high risk) starting an antidepressant -> clinical review after 1 week
f: reviewing stable maintenance antidepressant therapy during remission
a 42 year old patient starting sertraline with no suicidal ideation or risk factors
routine follow-up after an adult over 25 has already been reviewed safely at 2 weeks
assessing initial treatment response to fluoxetine in adult obsessive-compulsive disorder after early safety checks
x: Twelve weeks is far too late for initial safety monitoring after starting an antidepressant.
Two weeks is the standard initial review interval for adults aged over 25 who do not have an elevated baseline suicide risk.
Waiting 4 weeks misses the peak early window (days 7 to 14) for antidepressant-associated emergent suicidal thoughts in a 22 year old.
A 6 week gap before first review is unsafe when initiating an SSRI in a young adult under 25.

hq_q.s: A 56 year old man attends general practice with a 3 month history of low mood, early morning wakening, and weight loss since his divorce last year. He lives alone, works full-time as an engineer, drinks 10 units of alcohol per week, and sees his daughter every Sunday. He took a paracetamol overdose at age 35.
hq_q.w: Final preparatory acts – such as unexpectedly making or updating a will, giving away prized possessions, or writing farewell notes – indicate active suicidal planning and settled intent, representing the strongest immediate clinical warning sign of imminent suicide.
hq_q.f: No plan, future-focused and close to family → lower immediate risk, but still make a safety plan.
hq_q.ql: Which feature most raises his immediate risk of suicide?

tm.m: Final preparatory arrangements demonstrate transition from passive suicidal ideation to settled imminent intent
tm.g: Feature indicating highest immediate suicide risk -> final preparatory acts such as recently making a will
f: asked which historical background factor increases lifetime statistical risk compared with the general population
heavy daily alcohol binges of 20 units causing acute disinhibition during a suicidal crisis
asked which social factor in his history acts as a protective buffer against suicide
asked which interpersonal factor reduces isolation and protects against suicide
x: A self-harm episode 20 years ago is a static historical risk factor, whereas recent final acts signal acute imminent intent today.
Drinking 10 units of alcohol per week lies within the UK Chief Medical Officers' low-risk guideline (<14 units/week).
Continuing in full-time employment provides routine, social connectedness, and serves as a protective factor against suicide.
Regular supportive contact with his daughter is a key protective factor rather than a risk factor.

hq_q.s:
A 27 year old man has slept 2 hours a night for 6 days. He has spent £8,000 on a car he cannot afford. His family say he is not himself.
He speaks rapidly and cannot be interrupted. He says he has been chosen by God to lead the country.
Urine drug screen and thyroid function are normal.
hq_q.w: Mania: elevated mood, reduced need for sleep, pressured speech and reckless spending, with grandiose delusions here. It marks bipolar type I.
hq_q.f: The same mood change for 4 days, still working and no psychosis → hypomania.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Mania raises mood and energy, impairs judgement and can bring grandiose delusions
tm.g: Elevated mood with no sleep, reckless spending and grandiose delusions is mania with psychotic symptoms
f: inattentive, impulsive and hyperactive with normal social skills
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cyclothymia (Cyclothymia is mild and lasting)
4 days of mood change, still working, with no psychosis
the presentation instead showed features specific to Schizophrenia (His grandiosity comes with elevated mood, no sleep and reckless spending, which is mania)
x: Ruled out here: requires inattentive, impulsive and hyperactive with normal social skills, whereas this patient has 2 hours a night for 6 days, £8,000.
Cyclothymia is mild and lasting.
Ruled out here: requires 4 days of mood change, still working, with no psychosis, whereas this patient has 2 hours a night for 6 days, £8,000.
His grandiosity comes with elevated mood, no sleep and reckless spending, which is mania.

hq_q.s:
A 31 year old woman has her first manic episode. She takes no psychiatric drugs. She is not pregnant.
She is elated, with pressured speech and grandiose ideas.
hq_q.w: NICE: acute mania is treated with an antipsychotic such as haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone. Stop any antidepressant.
hq_q.f: Not responding to two antipsychotics → add lithium.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

tm.m: Antipsychotics control acute mania quickly
tm.g: Acute mania: olanzapine
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Carbamazepine (Carbamazepine is not a first-line treatment for acute mania)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Clonazepam (Clonazepam is used only for short-term sedation)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lamotrigine (Lamotrigine helps bipolar depression, not acute mania)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sertraline (An antidepressant can worsen mania)
x: Carbamazepine is not a first-line treatment for acute mania.
Clonazepam is used only for short-term sedation.
Lamotrigine helps bipolar depression, not acute mania.
An antidepressant can worsen mania.

hq_q.s: A 36 year old man with bipolar I disorder was initiated on modified-release oral lithium carbonate 400 mg once daily at 22:00 five days ago following normal baseline renal function, thyroid function, calcium, and ECG. He attends the phlebotomy clinic to arrange his first therapeutic drug monitoring blood test.
hq_q.w: Serum lithium concentrations must be sampled 12 hours after the last dose (just before a morning dose if twice daily, or at 10:00 following a 22:00 night-time dose), checked 1 week after initiation or any dose change until stable.
hq_q.f: Level 1.6 mmol/L with a coarse tremor → toxic: stop lithium, check kidney function and look for a cause.
hq_q.ql: When should the blood sample for his lithium level be taken?

c: initiated on modified-release oral lithium carbonate
tm.m: Lithium undergoes biphasic tissue distribution over 6 to 10 hours, so therapeutic ranges (0.4-1.0 mmol/L) are standardised at 12 hours post-dose
tm.g: Standardised timing for a therapeutic serum lithium blood sample -> 12 hours after the last dose
f: trough level sampling immediately before the next dose of once-daily gentamicin or vancomycin
measuring peak serum levels in acute overdose assessment rather than routine therapeutic monitoring
serial monitoring every 6 hours during inpatient management of severe acute lithium overdose
checking serum thyroid-stimulating hormone or HbA1c where timing relative to tablet ingestion does not matter
x: Sampling 24 hours after a once-daily dose yields a sub-trough reading that underestimates the true 12-hour therapeutic exposure.
Sampling 2 hours after ingestion measures the unabsorbed/distributing peak concentration and yields a falsely toxic reading.
At 6 hours post-dose, tissue distribution is still incomplete, producing a falsely elevated serum lithium concentration.
Random untimed samples cannot be interpreted against the 12-hour BNF therapeutic reference range of 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L.

hq_q.s: A 41 year old woman has worried excessively about everything on most days for a year. She has trouble sleeping and feels tense. Guided self-help has not worked and she would like medication.
