hq_q.w: NICE: sertraline is the first drug for GAD. Benzodiazepines are only for short crises. Key discriminator: GAD needing medication: sertraline.
hq_q.f: SSRIs and SNRIs not tolerated → pregabalin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first drug?

tm.m: SSRIs reduce anxiety and are first line for GAD
tm.g: GAD needing medication: sertraline
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Buspirone (Buspirone is not first line)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam long-term (Benzodiazepines must not be used beyond 2-4 weeks due to dependence)
SSRIs and SNRIs not tolerated
the presentation instead showed features specific to Propranolol (Propranolol eases tremor but does not treat GAD)
x: Buspirone is not first line.
Benzodiazepines must not be used beyond 2-4 weeks due to dependence
Ruled out here: requires SSRIs and SNRIs not tolerated, whereas this patient has Guided self-help has not worked, A 41 year old woman has.
Propranolol eases tremor but does not treat GAD.

hq_q.s: A 26 year old man has panic disorder. He has had sudden attacks of palpitations and fear of dying about twice a week for 4 months. He has read about the options and does not want to take medication.
hq_q.w: NICE offers psychological therapy (CBT) for panic disorder as the treatment with the longest-lasting effect. An SSRI is the drug option if he wanted one.
hq_q.f: Panic disorder and he would prefer a tablet → an SSRI such as sertraline.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

c: does not want to take medication
tm.m: CBT teaches that the body sensations are not dangerous, which breaks the fear-of-fear cycle
tm.g: Panic disorder without medication: CBT
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam when attacks start (Benzodiazepines are not used for panic disorder; they are linked to a worse long-term outcome)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Propranolol as needed (Propranolol blunts tremor and palpitations but does not treat panic disorder)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Psychodynamic psychotherapy (Psychodynamic therapy is not recommended for panic disorder)
he would prefer medication
x: Benzodiazepines are not used for panic disorder; they are linked to a worse long-term outcome.
Propranolol blunts tremor and palpitations but does not treat panic disorder.
Psychodynamic therapy is not recommended for panic disorder.
An SSRI is the drug option, but he does not want medication.

hq_q.s:
A 44 year old woman has had sudden attacks of pounding headache, sweating and palpitations for 3 months. They last about 20 minutes.
During an attack her pulse rate is 128 bpm and BP 210/110 mmHg. Between attacks, BP is 146/92 mmHg.
hq_q.w: Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with severe hypertension points to a catecholamine-secreting tumour. Test plasma metanephrines.
hq_q.f: Normal blood pressure during attacks and normal metanephrines → panic disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: A catecholamine-secreting tumour releases adrenaline in bursts
tm.g: Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with severe hypertension is phaeochromocytoma
f: flushing and diarrhoea with liver metastases
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hypoglycaemia (Hypoglycaemia does not cause a BP of 210/110)
normal blood pressure during attacks with normal metanephrines
the presentation instead showed features specific to Thyrotoxicosis (Thyrotoxicosis is constant, not paroxysmal attacks with severe hypertension)
x: Ruled out here: requires flushing and diarrhoea with liver metastases, whereas this patient has pounding headache, sweating and palpitations, 210/110.
Hypoglycaemia does not cause a BP of 210/110.
Ruled out here: requires normal blood pressure during attacks with normal metanephrines, whereas this patient has pounding headache, sweating and palpitations, 210/110.
Thyrotoxicosis is constant, not paroxysmal attacks with severe hypertension.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man was in a car crash 8 months ago. He has flashbacks and nightmares about it. He avoids driving and jumps at loud noises. He is sleeping badly and his work is suffering.
He is tense and startles easily during the consultation.
hq_q.w: PTSD: re-experiencing, avoidance and a sense of current threat such as hypervigilance, lasting weeks or more after a trauma.
hq_q.f: Low mood and worry after a break-up with no re-experiencing → adjustment disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Trauma memories stay unprocessed, causing re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal
tm.g: Re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal months after trauma is PTSD
f: symptoms only in the first days after the trauma
low mood and worry after a break-up with no re-experiencing
the presentation instead showed features specific to Depressive episode (Depression does not cause flashbacks)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD is widespread worry, not flashbacks of a specific trauma)
x: Ruled out here: requires symptoms only in the first days after the trauma, whereas this patient has 8 months ago, flashbacks and nightmares.
Ruled out here: requires low mood and worry after a break-up with no re-experiencing, whereas this patient has 8 months ago, flashbacks and nightmares.
Depression does not cause flashbacks.
GAD is widespread worry, not flashbacks of a specific trauma.

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman presents to her GP 6 months after surviving a violent street robbery. She experiences vivid daytime flashbacks of the attacker, recurrent nightmares, avoidance of walking outdoors after dusk, and constant hypervigilance with an exaggerated startle response.
A diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder is made, and she prefers psychological therapy.
hq_q.w: Under NICE guideline NG116, trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (TF-CBT) or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) are first-line treatments for adults presenting with post-traumatic stress disorder more than 1 month after a traumatic event.
hq_q.f: She prefers medication → venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

c: 6 months after surviving a violent street robbery
tm.m: Trauma-focused CBT facilitates elaboration and contextual integration of fragmented sensory trauma memories into autobiographical memory
tm.g: First-line psychological treatment for adult PTSD -> trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (or EMDR)
f: acute inpatient alcohol withdrawal syndrome managed with a reducing chlordiazepoxide regimen
never recommended ahead of trauma-focused CBT or EMDR for established post-traumatic stress disorder
an adult with PTSD who declines psychological therapy or has severe comorbid depression
never recommended by NICE NG116 for either prevention or treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder
x: Benzodiazepines impair fear extinction learning, worsen dissociation, and carry high risks of dependence in PTSD.
Non-directive supportive counselling is significantly less effective than trauma-focused CBT and is not recommended by NICE.
Antidepressants (venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline) are second-line options reserved for patients who decline or cannot engage in trauma-focused therapy.
Single-session psychological debriefing is ineffective and contraindicated by NICE because it can impede natural recovery.

hq_q.s: Two days after an explosion and fire at a manufacturing plant in which several workers were hospitalised, the company's human resources director contacts the occupational health physician asking to arrange a mandatory single-session psychological debriefing for all 80 employees tomorrow to prevent post-traumatic stress disorder.
o: Advise that all staff attend debriefing
Restrict compulsory debriefing to injured staff
Start prophylactic SSRIs to prevent PTSD
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG116, mandatory single-session psychological debriefing must not be offered after a traumatic event because it does not prevent PTSD and may worsen symptoms. Offer practical support and active monitoring over the first month.
hq_q.f: Clear PTSD symptoms still present after a month → trauma-focused CBT.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate advice?

tm.m: Forced early emotional recounting within days of trauma disrupts natural cognitive recovery and increases PTSD incidence
tm.g: Management of asymptomatic or mildly distressed survivors 2 days after a major incident -> practical support and active monitoring
f: never recommended because mandatory psychological debriefing increases long-term trauma symptoms
never appropriate for preventing post-traumatic stress disorder after a traumatic incident
individual trauma-focused CBT offered to symptomatic individuals who develop acute stress disorder or PTSD
established PTSD persisting beyond 1 month in a patient who declines trauma-focused therapy
x: Randomised trials show compulsory group debriefing increases the risk of developing PTSD and is explicitly prohibited by NICE.
Prophylactic benzodiazepines interfere with normal memory consolidation after trauma and cause dependence.
Single-session psychological debriefing is harmful and contraindicated even when restricted to physically injured survivors.
Routine prophylactic antidepressants immediately after trauma do not prevent PTSD.

hq_q.s:
A 29 year old woman gave birth 6 weeks ago. She has intrusive thoughts that she might harm her baby, which horrify her. She checks the baby's breathing many times a night to calm the fear. She has no low mood, hallucinations or delusions.
She is anxious but caring towards her baby. She has full insight.
hq_q.w: OCD: unwanted intrusive thoughts that the person resists, followed by compulsions that relieve the anxiety. She has insight and no intent.
hq_q.f: Rigid perfectionism and rules she sees as right, with no intrusive thoughts → anankastic personality disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Unwanted thoughts cause anxiety that rituals briefly relieve
tm.g: Horrifying intrusive thoughts with checking rituals and insight is OCD
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD is worry about many things; she has specific intrusive thoughts with checking rituals)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD is about rules and perfectionism, not intrusive thoughts)
persistent low mood and loss of interest
confusion, hallucinations and delusions in the first weeks after birth
x: GAD is worry about many things; she has specific intrusive thoughts with checking rituals.
OCPD is about rules and perfectionism, not intrusive thoughts.
Ruled out here: requires persistent low mood and loss of interest, whereas this patient has intrusive thoughts, horrify her.
Ruled out here: requires confusion, hallucinations and delusions in the first weeks after birth, whereas this patient has intrusive thoughts, horrify her.

hq_q.s: A 36 year old man has obsessive-compulsive disorder. He has had CBT with exposure and response prevention and two SSRIs at full dose for 12 weeks each. He still spends 4 hours a day on checking rituals.
hq_q.w: Clomipramine, a strongly serotonergic tricyclic, is next for OCD that has not responded to SSRIs.
hq_q.f: No treatment yet → SSRI with CBT including exposure and response prevention.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next drug?

c: two SSRIs at full dose for 12 weeks each
tm.m: Clomipramine is strongly serotonergic
tm.g: OCD after two adequate SSRIs: clomipramine
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amitriptyline (Of the tricyclics only clomipramine is effective in OCD)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam (Diazepam does not treat OCD)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lithium (Lithium is not used for OCD)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Propranolol (Propranolol does not treat OCD)
x: Of the tricyclics only clomipramine is effective in OCD.
Diazepam does not treat OCD.
Lithium is not used for OCD.
Propranolol does not treat OCD.

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old woman with severe contamination obsessions and handwashing compulsions (spending 3 hours daily washing) was started on oral fluoxetine 40 mg daily alongside cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention 6 weeks ago.
At review today she reports a modest 25% reduction in ritual time and has no adverse drug effects.
hq_q.w: Obsessive-compulsive disorder responds more slowly to SSRIs than major depression and typically requires higher doses (such as fluoxetine 60 mg) and an adequate trial duration of at least 12 weeks before judging efficacy or switching agents.
hq_q.f: No response at 12 weeks on the maximum dose → switch SSRI or try clomipramine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Downregulation of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical serotonergic autoreceptors in OCD takes 10 to 12 weeks for maximal benefit
tm.g: Partial improvement of OCD after 6 weeks of an SSRI with good tolerability -> continue trial to 12 weeks (optimising dose)
f: refractory OCD showing incomplete response after 12 weeks of maximal-dose SSRI and CBT
acute manic switch in a patient with undiagnosed bipolar disorder
no clinical improvement after 12 weeks of maximal-dose SSRI therapy plus exposure and response prevention
severe intolerable adverse effects early in fluoxetine treatment requiring a class switch
x: Augmentation with low-dose risperidone or aripiprazole is a specialist step reserved for cases refractory after full 12-week trials of SSRIs/clomipramine and CBT.
Stopping an SSRI that is well tolerated and already producing partial benefit at 6 weeks causes relapse.
Clomipramine is reserved until at least one full 12-week trial of an SSRI at maximum tolerated dose has failed.
Switching to another SSRI at 6 weeks is premature when partial improvement is already occurring.

hq_q.s:
A 35 year old woman is convinced she has bowel cancer. A colonoscopy, scans and blood tests are all normal, but reassurance does not last. She has few physical symptoms. She accepts it may be anxiety when calm.
Examination is normal.
hq_q.w: Hypochondriasis, or health anxiety, is fear of one serious disease that persists despite reassurance. The fear matters more than the symptoms.
hq_q.f: Many physical symptoms across different systems over years → somatisation disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Health anxiety focuses on one feared disease despite normal tests
tm.g: Fear of one serious disease despite normal tests is hypochondriasis
f: a fixed false belief with no insight
the presentation instead showed features specific to Factitious disorder (In factitious disorder symptoms are invented)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Malingering (She gains nothing by her fear; malingering is deliberate faking for gain)
many physical symptoms across systems over years
x: Ruled out here: requires a fixed false belief with no insight, whereas this patient has convinced she has bowel cancer, reassurance does not last.
In factitious disorder symptoms are invented.
She gains nothing by her fear; malingering is deliberate faking for gain.
Ruled out here: requires many physical symptoms across systems over years, whereas this patient has convinced she has bowel cancer, reassurance does not last.

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old warehouse worker is pursuing a high-value personal injury compensation claim against his employer after a minor low-speed forklift bump 4 months ago. In clinic he arrives in a wheelchair stating that his legs are completely paralysed.
Neurological examination shows normal tone, intact reflexes, and flexor plantars, and nursing staff observe him walking briskly to the hospital cafe when he believes he is unobserved.
hq_q.w: Malingering is the intentional production of false or exaggerated physical or psychological symptoms motivated by an external incentive (such as financial compensation or avoiding court); it is not a psychiatric disorder.
hq_q.f: Secretly injects insulin to be admitted with nothing to gain but the sick role → factitious disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely explanation?

c: walking briskly to the hospital cafe
tm.m: Conscious, volitional simulation of disability is maintained only during observation to secure external financial gain
tm.g: Conscious simulation of paralysis for financial compensation that disappears when unobserved -> malingering
f: involuntary leg weakness with a positive Hoover's sign that persists when unobserved and has no financial motive
deliberately contaminating a wound with faeces solely to remain a hospital inpatient with no financial claim
genuine distressing fear that minor muscle twitches represent motor neurone disease
years of genuine distress from unexplained pain, bloating and fatigue without conscious deception
x: In conversion (functional neurological) disorder, weakness is genuinely experienced without conscious deception and persists when the patient is alone.
Factitious disorder (Munchausen's syndrome) involves conscious fabrication of illness solely for the internal psychological gain of adopting the sick role, without financial incentive.
Hypochondriasis (health anxiety) is a genuine fearful preoccupation with having a serious progressive disease despite normal tests.
Somatisation disorder involves chronic, genuine distress from multiple unexplained physical symptoms across several organ systems without conscious deception.

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old woman has a 5 year history of multiple medically unexplained symptoms – including migratory joint pains, abdominal bloating, non-cardiac chest tightness, and chronic fatigue – with extensive normal investigations across rheumatology, gastroenterology, and cardiology.
She attends urgent walk-in GP appointments twice a week requesting new specialist referrals and repeat scans.
hq_q.w: Management of persistent medically unexplained symptoms (somatisation/bodily distress disorder) centres on continuity of care with a single named GP through regular, pre-scheduled appointments (independent of new symptoms), validating her distress, avoiding unnecessary repeat investigations or referrals, and offering CBT.
hq_q.f: A new red flag symptom → investigate it properly.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: attends urgent walk-in GP appointments twice a week
tm.m: Scheduled proactive reviews by a single trusted clinician decouple healthcare contact from crisis symptom presentation
tm.g: Persistent medically unexplained symptoms with frequent attendance -> regular planned reviews with one named GP
f: monosymptomatic somatic delusional disorder where the patient holds a fixed psychotic delusion
a single transient tension headache in a non-anxious patient with normal neurology
new objective red-flag signs such as unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia or a palpable mass
monitoring a known chronic disease such as checking HbA1c every 6 months in diabetes
x: Antipsychotic drugs have no role in non-psychotic somatisation disorder and expose the patient to metabolic and extrapyramidal harm.
Abruptly discharging her with simple reassurance leaves her feeling dismissed and drives further emergency department attendances.
Referring to a new hospital specialist for every symptom fragments care and increases iatrogenic harm from invasive procedures.
Repeating normal diagnostic blood tests and scans at every consultation provides only fleeting reassurance and reinforces health anxiety.

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old woman with anorexia nervosa is seen in clinic. She feels dizzy and faint.
BMI 12.8 kg/m². Pulse rate 38 bpm, BP 78/46 mmHg. Temperature 35.2°C.
Potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.3). ECG shows sinus bradycardia.
hq_q.w: Very low BMI, bradycardia and hypotension are high-risk markers. She needs admission for safe refeeding with cardiac monitoring.
hq_q.f: BMI 16.5 with stable observations → outpatient eating disorder-focused therapy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Severe starvation causes bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia and electrolyte loss
tm.g: Anorexia with very low BMI and unstable observations: urgent medical admission
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Increase outpatient sessions (She is medically unstable)
BMI 16.5 with stable observations
the presentation instead showed features specific to Start fluoxetine (Drugs do not treat anorexia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Urgent dietitian referral (Dietetics alone without medical admission risks fatal arrhythmia or refeeding syndrome)
x: She is medically unstable.
Ruled out here: requires BMI 16.5 with stable observations, whereas this patient has BMI 12.8, Pulse rate 38.
Drugs do not treat anorexia.
Dietetics alone without medical admission risks fatal arrhythmia or refeeding syndrome

hq_q.s:
A 22 year old woman has bulimia nervosa. She binges and makes herself vomit 3 times a week. She has had no treatment before.
BMI 22 kg/m². Pulse rate 76 bpm.
Potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5–5.3).
hq_q.w: NICE starts adults with bulimia on bulimia-focused guided self-help. If it is not enough after 4 weeks, individual eating-disorder CBT follows.
hq_q.f: Bulimia under 18 → bulimia-focused family therapy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first treatment?

tm.m: Guided self-help regularises eating and breaks the binge-purge cycle
tm.g: Adult bulimia, first treatment: bulimia-focused guided self-help
f: she was 16 and living with her parents
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fluoxetine 60 mg daily (Medication is not offered as the sole treatment for bulimia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Inpatient refeeding (Her BMI and potassium are normal; she is medically stable)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT is not a first-line bulimia treatment in current NICE guidance)
x: Family therapy is first-line for children and young people, not a 22 year old.
Medication is not offered as the sole treatment for bulimia.
Her BMI and potassium are normal; she is medically stable.
IPT is not a first-line bulimia treatment in current NICE guidance.

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old woman with bulimia nervosa presents to general practice with a 3 week history of muscle cramps, generalised weakness, and occasional palpitations. She admits to binge eating and inducing vomiting four times daily.
Her BMI is 21.5 kg/m², pulse rate is 88 bpm, blood pressure is 104/66 mmHg, and she has dorsal knuckle calluses and dental enamel erosion.
hq_q.w: Recurrent self-induced vomiting causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and volume depletion. Secondary hyperaldosteronism conserves sodium in the distal nephron at the expense of renal potassium and hydrogen ion excretion, producing a classic hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.
hq_q.f: Laxative misuse → low potassium with a metabolic acidosis.
hq_q.ql: Which result is most likely?

tm.m: Gastric HCl loss and hypovolaemia-driven hyperaldosteronism cause renal potassium wasting and bicarbonate retention
tm.g: Frequent self-induced vomiting in bulimia nervosa -> hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (low K+, raised HCO3-)
f: primary hyperparathyroidism presenting with kidney stones, bone pain and constipation
omitting insulin doses to lose weight (diabulimia) in a patient with type 1 diabetes
primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) or spironolactone toxicity
lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with polyuria and water deprivation
x: Self-induced vomiting does not cause hypercalcaemia (calcium 3.0 mmol/L), which is seen in primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy.
Purging by vomiting does not cause hyperglycaemia (glucose 15 mmol/L); blood glucose is normal or mildly low.
Hyperkalaemia with low bicarbonate (metabolic acidosis) occurs in acute kidney injury or Addison's disease, the opposite of vomiting.
Severe hypernatraemia (sodium 150 mmol/L) is characteristic of cranial or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus rather than bulimic vomiting.

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old woman is assessed by the community mental health team. Since late adolescence she has had intense, stormy relationships, a frantic fear of abandonment, rapid mood shifts lasting a few hours, chronic feelings of emptiness, and recurrent impulsive self-harm by cutting.
She has no delusions, hallucinations, or sustained multi-day manic episodes.
hq_q.w: Borderline (emotionally unstable) personality disorder is characterised by pervasive instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affect (shifting over hours), accompanied by frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, chronic feelings of emptiness, and recurrent impulsive self-harm.
hq_q.f: Shallow emotions with dramatic attention-seeking → histrionic personality disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Affective hyper-reactivity and attachment insecurity drive rapid hour-to-hour emotional shifts and impulsive self-injury
tm.g: Unstable relationships + fear of abandonment + chronic emptiness + hour-to-hour mood shifts + self-harm -> borderline personality disorder
f: childhood fire-setting and cruelty to animals followed by adult violence and lack of remorse
sustained 10-day episodes of elated mood, grandiosity, pressured speech and no need for sleep
passive submissive reliance on others to make all everyday decisions without anger or self-harm
theatrical self-dramatisation, seductive behaviour and discomfort whenever not the centre of attention
x: Antisocial (dissocial) personality disorder is defined by callous disregard for others' rights, deceit, violence, and lack of remorse since childhood conduct disorder.
Bipolar affective disorder causes sustained affective episodes of mania or hypomania lasting at least 4 to 7 days rather than reactive shifts over a few hours.
Dependent personality disorder features submissive clinging and need to be taken care of without rage, stormy devaluation, or self-harm.
Histrionic personality disorder is characterised by theatricality, shallow labile affect, and constant desire to be the centre of attention without emptiness or self-mutilation.

hq_q.s: A 26 year old woman with borderline personality disorder is in a crisis after a row with her partner. She has not slept for 3 nights. She has no psychotic symptoms. Her crisis plan is being reviewed.
hq_q.w: In a crisis, NICE allows a short course (up to a week) of a sedative antihistamine such as promethazine. Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs are avoided because of dependence and overdose risk.
hq_q.f: BPD with recurrent self-harm, long-term treatment → dialectical behaviour therapy.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most appropriate for a few nights?

tm.m: A sedating antihistamine helps sleep for a few nights without the dependence of a benzodiazepine
tm.g: BPD crisis, short-term sleep: a sedative antihistamine such as promethazine
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam (Benzodiazepines are avoided in BPD because of dependence, disinhibition and overdose risk)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fluoxetine (An SSRI takes weeks to work and does not treat the core features of BPD)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Quetiapine (Antipsychotics are not used for BPD crises without psychotic symptoms)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Zopiclone (Z-drugs carry dependence and overdose risk, so a sedative antihistamine is preferred)
x: Benzodiazepines are avoided in BPD because of dependence, disinhibition and overdose risk.
An SSRI takes weeks to work and does not treat the core features of BPD.
Antipsychotics are not used for BPD crises without psychotic symptoms.
Z-drugs carry dependence and overdose risk, so a sedative antihistamine is preferred.

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old man has always been seen as odd. He dresses unusually, believes he can sense what others are thinking and says strangers on the bus are talking about him, though he can be talked out of it. He has few friends and feels anxious with people.
His speech is vague and digressive. There are no hallucinations or fixed delusions.
hq_q.w: Eccentric behaviour, magical thinking, ideas of reference that can be challenged and odd speech, without fixed delusions, is schizotypal disorder.
hq_q.f: Contented solitude with no odd beliefs → schizoid personality disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: can be talked out of it
tm.m: Schizotypal disorder sits on the schizophrenia spectrum: odd beliefs and perceptions without full psychosis
tm.g: Odd beliefs, magical thinking and eccentricity without fixed delusions: schizotypal disorder
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Autism spectrum disorder (Autism is present from early childhood with social communication difficulty and rigid interests, not magical thinking)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Paranoid personality disorder (Paranoid personality is pervasive suspicion and grudges, without magical thinking or eccentric dress)
he were emotionally cold and content alone with no odd beliefs
the beliefs were fixed and he heard voices
x: Autism is present from early childhood with social communication difficulty and rigid interests, not magical thinking.
Paranoid personality is pervasive suspicion and grudges, without magical thinking or eccentric dress.
Schizoid personality is emotional coldness and contented solitude, without odd beliefs.
Schizophrenia needs fixed delusions or hallucinations; his ideas can be challenged.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old man who drinks heavily has been brought in by his wife because he has become confused over 2 days and is unsteady on his feet. He has eaten little for weeks.
He is disorientated. There is horizontal nystagmus and an ataxic gait.
Glucose 5.4 mmol/L (4.0–7.8).
hq_q.w: Confusion, ataxia and nystagmus in a heavy drinker is Wernicke encephalopathy. Give high-dose IV thiamine (Pabrinex) straight away, before or with any glucose.
hq_q.f: Permanent memory loss with confabulation → Korsakoff's syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

tm.m: Thiamine deficiency damages the mamillary bodies and brainstem
tm.g: Wernicke's encephalopathy: IV high-dose thiamine
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Chlordiazepoxide (A benzodiazepine treats withdrawal, but confusion, ataxia and nystagmus need thiamine first)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Haloperidol (Haloperidol does nothing for Wernicke encephalopathy and lowers the seizure threshold)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV glucose first (Giving glucose before thiamine exhausts remaining B1 and precipitates Korsakoff psychosis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral thiamine (Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in alcohol misuse)
x: A benzodiazepine treats withdrawal, but confusion, ataxia and nystagmus need thiamine first.
Haloperidol does nothing for Wernicke encephalopathy and lowers the seizure threshold.
Giving glucose before thiamine exhausts remaining B1 and precipitates Korsakoff psychosis
Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in alcohol misuse.

hq_q.s:
A 54 year old man who drinks heavily was admitted 3 days ago with a broken ankle. He has become confused and agitated and says he can see insects on the walls.
Temperature 38.1°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 162/96 mmHg. He is sweating and has a coarse tremor.
Glucose 5.8 mmol/L (4.0–7.8).
hq_q.w: Withdrawal timeline: tremor at 6 to 12 hours, hallucinosis at 12 to 24, seizures at 24 to 48 and delirium tremens at 48 to 72 hours.
hq_q.f: Hallucinations at 12 to 24 hours with a clear mind → alcoholic hallucinosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Sudden loss of alcohol's GABA effect causes autonomic overdrive and delirium at 2 to 3 days
tm.g: Confusion, hallucinations and fever days after stopping alcohol is delirium tremens
f: hallucinations at 12 to 24 hours with a clear mind
confusion with a flapping tremor, jaundice and ascites
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sepsis (Sepsis can cause delirium, but visual hallucinations with tremor 3 days after his last drink are DTs)
confusion with ataxia and nystagmus
x: Ruled out here: requires hallucinations at 12 to 24 hours with a clear mind, whereas this patient has 3 days ago, insects on the walls.
Ruled out here: requires confusion with a flapping tremor, jaundice and ascites, whereas this patient has 3 days ago, insects on the walls.
Sepsis can cause delirium, but visual hallucinations with tremor 3 days after his last drink are DTs.
Ruled out here: requires confusion with ataxia and nystagmus, whereas this patient has 3 days ago, insects on the walls.

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old man with decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis was admitted with ascites. He last drank yesterday and now has a tremor and sweating. His CIWA score is rising.
He is jaundiced with ascites. There is no flap.
hq_q.w: Long-acting benzodiazepines build up when the liver fails. A shorter-acting one such as lorazepam or oxazepam is safer.
hq_q.f: Normal liver function → chlordiazepoxide reducing regimen.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate drug?
hq_q.post: INR 1.9.

tm.m: Long-acting benzodiazepines build up when the liver fails
tm.g: Alcohol withdrawal with liver failure: lorazepam
f: normal liver function
the presentation instead showed features specific to Clomethiazole (High risk of fatal respiratory depression in severe hepatic impairment)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam (Diazepam builds up in liver failure)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Haloperidol (Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold and does not treat withdrawal)
x: Ruled out here: requires normal liver function, whereas this patient has decompensated, year old man with.
High risk of fatal respiratory depression in severe hepatic impairment
Diazepam builds up in liver failure.
Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold and does not treat withdrawal.

hq_q.s:
A 22 year old woman attends the emergency department reporting that she swallowed approximately 24 paracetamol 500 mg tablets in divided doses over the past 24 hours after an argument with her partner. She is unsure of the exact times and currently has mild nausea.
She weighs 58 kg, pulse rate is 92 bpm, and blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg.
hq_q.w: A paracetamol overdose ingested over more than 1 hour is a staggered overdose. Because the treatment nomogram applies only to single acute ingestions, intravenous acetylcysteine must be started immediately without waiting for levels.
hq_q.f: A single overdose 2 hours ago → take a level at 4 hours and plot it.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: divided doses over the past 24 hours
tm.m: Staggered paracetamol ingestion invalidates the single-timepoint nomogram while depleting hepatic glutathione stores
tm.g: Staggered paracetamol overdose (>1 hour) -> start intravenous acetylcysteine immediately
f: presenting within 45 minutes of a single acute ingestion of 24 paracetamol tablets
never safe in a staggered supratherapeutic paracetamol overdose
a single acute overdose taken at one known timepoint 2 hours ago
never preferred over intravenous acetylcysteine in UK hospital practice
x: Activated charcoal only reduces paracetamol absorption when administered within 1 hour of a single acute overdose.
Patients with severe paracetamol hepatotoxicity are often asymptomatic for the first 24 hours; discharging without treatment risks fatal liver failure.
The 4-hour paracetamol treatment nomogram cannot be used when tablets were taken over a staggered 24-hour period.
Oral methionine is obsolete in UK practice; intravenous acetylcysteine is the standard antidote.

hq_q.s:
A 44 year old woman with bipolar I disorder stably maintained on lithium carbonate for 5 years presents to her GP with a 3 day history of coarse hand tremor, slurred dysarthric speech, nausea, watery diarrhoea, and ataxia. Ten days ago she started buying over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for low back pain.
She is alert with a serum lithium of 2.1 mmol/L and creatinine of 128 µmol/L.
hq_q.w: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (such as ibuprofen), ACE inhibitors, and thiazide diuretics reduce renal clearance of lithium and precipitate acute-on-chronic lithium toxicity (coarse tremor, dysarthria, ataxia, and diarrhoea). Immediately stop both lithium and ibuprofen and administer intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride rehydration.
hq_q.f: Level over 4 mmol/L, or severe neurological features or kidney failure → haemodialysis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: NSAID inhibition of renal prostaglandins reduces glomerular filtration and increases proximal tubular reabsorption of lithium
tm.g: Mild-to-moderate lithium toxicity precipitated by an NSAID -> stop lithium and NSAID and give IV 0.9% saline fluids
f: acute carbamazepine or tricyclic antidepressant overdose presenting within 1 hour
acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with bibasal crackles and fluid overload
an asymptomatic patient with a 12-hour lithium level of 0.95 mmol/L and no toxic signs
coma, status epilepticus and a serum lithium concentration of 4.2 mmol/L
x: Oral activated charcoal does not bind small charged metal ions such as lithium or iron.
Intravenous loop diuretics such as furosemide cause volume depletion, stimulating compensatory proximal tubular sodium and lithium reabsorption.
Simply reducing the dose while continuing lithium during clinical toxicity (coarse tremor and ataxia) allows neurotoxicity to progress.
Emergency haemodialysis is reserved for severe lithium toxicity (coma, seizures, arrhythmias, renal failure, or levels >4.0 mmol/L, or >2.5 mmol/L with severe symptoms).

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old man is brought to resuscitation by ambulance 2 hours after taking a large impulsive overdose of his prescribed amitriptyline tablets.
He is drowsy (GCS 10/15) with dilated pupils, dry skin, pulse rate 128 bpm, and blood pressure 85/50 mmHg. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a broadened QRS duration of 140 ms, and venous blood gas shows pH 7.30.
hq_q.w: Amitriptyline blocks fast cardiac sodium channels, widening the QRS complex (>120 ms) and causing arrhythmias. Immediate intravenous 8.4% sodium bicarbonate provides sodium loading and plasma alkalinisation (target pH 7.45-7.55), narrowing the QRS.
hq_q.f: Pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6 → naloxone.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Sodium loading and plasma alkalinisation reduce protonation of tricyclic molecules and unblock cardiac fast Na+ channels
tm.g: Tricyclic overdose with hypotension, metabolic acidosis and QRS >120 ms -> intravenous sodium bicarbonate
f: isolated iatrogenic midazolam over-sedation after an endoscopic procedure
local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (bupivacaine cardiac arrest) or tricyclic arrest refractory to bicarbonate
respiratory depression (rate 5 breaths/min) and pinpoint pupils after intravenous heroin
never used in tricyclic antidepressant cardiotoxicity due to risk of fatal asystole
x: Flumazenil antagonises benzodiazepine GABA-A sites and precipitates refractory status epilepticus in tricyclic antidepressant overdose.
Intravenous lipid emulsion (Intralipid) is a rescue therapy reserved for refractory cardiac arrest or shock unresponsive to sodium bicarbonate.
Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity (pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression), not anticholinergic tricyclic cardiotoxicity.
Physostigmine is contraindicated in tricyclic antidepressant overdose because cholinesterase inhibition precipitates bradycardia and asystole.

hq_q.s: A 34 year old man with known schizophrenia has relapsed after stopping his medication. He believes his family are poisoning him and has not eaten for days. He refuses admission. His diagnosis and the treatment that works for him are known.
hq_q.w: Section 3 is for treatment, up to 6 months, when the diagnosis is known. Section 2 is for assessment, up to 28 days.
hq_q.f: First presentation where the diagnosis is not known → section 2.
hq_q.ql: Which section of the Mental Health Act is most appropriate?

c: treatment that works for him are known
tm.m: Section 3 allows treatment when the diagnosis and treatment are established
tm.g: Relapse of known schizophrenia needing treatment: Section 3
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Section 136 (Section 136 is a police power in a public place)
a first presentation with an unknown diagnosis
the presentation instead showed features specific to Section 4 (Section 4 is for an emergency when a second doctor cannot come in time)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Section 5.2 (Section 5(2) is a doctor's holding power for inpatients)
x: Section 136 is a police power in a public place.
Ruled out here: requires a first presentation with an unknown diagnosis, whereas this patient has known schizophrenia, refuses admission.
Section 4 is for an emergency when a second doctor cannot come in time.
Section 5(2) is a doctor's holding power for inpatients.

hq_q.s: Police find a distressed man in a public place threatening to jump from a bridge. He appears to be mentally unwell.
hq_q.w: Section 136 lets the police take someone from a public place to a place of safety for up to 24 hours for assessment.
hq_q.f: The person is inside their own home → section 135, a magistrate's warrant to enter.
hq_q.ql: Which power allows them to take him to a place of safety?

c: Police find a distressed man in
tm.m: Police can remove someone from a public place to a place of safety
tm.g: Police in a public place: Section 136
f: the person is inside their own home
the presentation instead showed features specific to Section 2 (Section 2 is an assessment order by two doctors and an AMHP)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Section 4 (Section 4 is an emergency admission by one doctor and an AMHP)
informal patient + tries to leave at night
x: Ruled out here: requires the person is inside their own home, whereas this patient has public place, Police find a distressed man in.
Section 2 is an assessment order by two doctors and an AMHP.
Section 4 is an emergency admission by one doctor and an AMHP.
Ruled out here: requires informal patient + tries to leave at night, whereas this patient has public place, Police find a distressed man in.

hq_q.s: A 30 year old woman admitted voluntarily to an acute psychiatric ward with severe depression becomes acutely distressed at 02:00, states she is leaving the hospital immediately to jump from a bridge, and heads for the ward exit. The on-call duty doctor is attending a medical emergency on another site, and a registered mental health nurse is on duty.
hq_q.w: Section 5(4) of the Mental Health Act 1983 is the nurse's holding power, allowing a registered mental health or learning disability nurse to detain an informal inpatient for up to 6 hours until a doctor arrives.
hq_q.f: The doctor in charge or their deputy is available → section 5.2, up to 72 hours.
hq_q.ql: For how long can the nurse hold her?

c: leaving the hospital immediately to jump
duty doctor is attending a medical emergency
tm.m: Section 5(4) grants a registered mental health nurse an emergency 6-hour holding power over an informal inpatient until a doctor attends
tm.g: Maximum duration of the nurse's holding power under Section 5(4) MHA -> 6 hours
f: never a statutory detention duration under the Mental Health Act 1983
police detaining a person from a public place to a place of safety under Section 136
formal detention for psychiatric assessment under Section 2 signed by two doctors and an AMHP
the doctor in charge of her inpatient care detaining her under Section 5(2)
x: Section 5(4) expires after a maximum of 6 hours and cannot be extended or renewed to 12 hours.
Twenty-four hours is the maximum detention period for police powers in a public place under Section 136, not Section 5(4).
Twenty-eight days is the maximum duration of formal admission for assessment under Section 2 of the Mental Health Act.
Seventy-two hours is the maximum duration of the doctor's holding power under Section 5(2) or emergency admission under Section 4.

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old woman with severe depression has stopped talking and moving over 2 days. She stares and holds odd postures. Catatonia is suspected.
Temperature 36.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm. Creatine kinase is normal. She takes no antipsychotics.
hq_q.w: A rapid improvement after IV or oral lorazepam supports catatonia and starts treatment at the same time.
hq_q.f: Catatonia not responding to lorazepam after several days → ECT.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most useful test to support the diagnosis?

tm.m: GABA-A stimulation by a benzodiazepine reverses catatonia quickly
tm.g: Suspected catatonia: a lorazepam challenge is diagnostic and therapeutic
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to CT head (Imaging looks for a structural cause but does not confirm catatonia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Haloperidol test dose (Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and trigger NMS)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lumbar puncture (LP is for suspected encephalitis; nothing here points to infection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Serum prolactin (Prolactin does not help diagnose catatonia)
x: Imaging looks for a structural cause but does not confirm catatonia.
Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and trigger NMS.
LP is for suspected encephalitis; nothing here points to infection.
Prolactin does not help diagnose catatonia.

hq_q.s: A 40 year old man is mute and still. When the doctor raises his arm, it stays in the raised position for several minutes, and he can be moulded into new postures with slight resistance.
hq_q.w: Waxy flexibility is slight, even resistance to being moved, after which the limb stays where it is placed. It is a sign of catatonia.
hq_q.f: He copies the examiner's movements → echopraxia.
hq_q.ql: Which sign is this?

c: moulded into new postures with slight resistance
tm.m: In catatonia posture is held passively against gravity, like a candle being moulded
tm.g: Limbs moulded and held where placed: waxy flexibility
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Cogwheel rigidity (Cogwheel rigidity is a ratcheting resistance in parkinsonism; the limb does not stay where placed)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Echopraxia (Echopraxia is copying the examiner's movements)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Mitgehen (Mitgehen is moving the limb in response to the lightest touch, like an anglepoise lamp, not holding a moulded posture)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Negativism (Negativism is resisting or doing the opposite of every instruction)
x: Cogwheel rigidity is a ratcheting resistance in parkinsonism; the limb does not stay where placed.
Echopraxia is copying the examiner's movements.
Mitgehen is moving the limb in response to the lightest touch, like an anglepoise lamp, not holding a moulded posture.
Negativism is resisting or doing the opposite of every instruction.

hq_q.s: A psychiatrist is consenting a 68 year old woman with severe depression for ECT. The team reviews her medical history for contraindications.
hq_q.w: ECT briefly raises intracranial pressure, so raised pressure is the absolute contraindication. Pregnancy and old age are not.
hq_q.f: Myocardial infarction within the last 3 months → a relative contraindication needing cardiology input.
hq_q.ql: Which condition carries the greatest risk with ECT?

tm.m: ECT briefly raises intracranial pressure
tm.g: The only absolute contraindication to ECT is raised intracranial pressure
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Age over 80 (ECT is safe and effective in older adults)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pacemaker (A pacemaker is not a contraindication; it is checked before and after ECT)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pregnancy (ECT is safe in pregnancy for severe psychosis or depression)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Previous myocardial infarction 2 years ago (A past MI is a relative risk)
x: ECT is safe and effective in older adults
A pacemaker is not a contraindication; it is checked before and after ECT.
ECT is safe in pregnancy for severe psychosis or depression
A past MI is a relative risk.

hq_q.s:
A 7 year old boy is brought by his parents. His teachers say he has poor eye contact and does not join in group play. At home he lines up his toys and becomes very upset at any change to his routine. He takes jokes literally.
His speech is fluent and his hearing is normal.
hq_q.w: Autism: differences in social communication plus restricted, repetitive behaviour and interests, present from early childhood.
hq_q.f: Inattentive, impulsive and hyperactive at home and school with normal social skills → ADHD.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Autism is social communication difference with restricted, repetitive behaviour
tm.g: Social communication difficulties with rigid routines is autism spectrum disorder
f: inattentive, impulsive and hyperactive with normal social skills
the presentation instead showed features specific to Intellectual disability (His speech is fluent and the problem is social communication with rigid routines)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD involves obsessions)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Selective mutism (Selective mutism is not speaking in certain settings)
x: Ruled out here: requires inattentive, impulsive and hyperactive with normal social skills, whereas this patient has poor eye contact, lines up his toys.
His speech is fluent and the problem is social communication with rigid routines.
OCD involves obsessions.
Selective mutism is not speaking in certain settings.

hq_q.s: A 5 year old girl rarely makes eye contact, does not point to share interest and has repetitive hand flapping. Her parents are worried. Her GP suspects autism.
hq_q.w: Autism is diagnosed by a specialist multidisciplinary team using history and observation. There is no blood test or scan for it.
hq_q.f: A girl who loses her speech and develops hand-wringing → Rett syndrome, test for MECP2.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Autism is diagnosed by a specialist multidisciplinary team
tm.g: Suspected autism: refer to the autism assessment team
f: a girl who loses her speech and develops hand-wringing
the presentation instead showed features specific to MRI brain (Imaging is not part of a routine autism assessment)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Review in 2 years (Delays crucial early developmental and educational support)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Trial of risperidone (Medication does not treat core features of autism)
x: Ruled out here: requires a girl who loses her speech and develops hand-wringing, whereas this patient has does not point, hand flapping.
Imaging is not part of a routine autism assessment.
Delays crucial early developmental and educational support
Medication does not treat core features of autism

hq_q.s: A 24 year old autistic woman has had anxiety for a year that stops her using public transport and going to the shops. She has no learning disability and wants help.
hq_q.w: Anxiety in autistic adults is treated as in anyone else, with psychological therapy adapted to the person: more concrete, structured and visual CBT.
hq_q.f: Severe aggression in an autistic child after behaviour support fails → risperidone may be considered.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first treatment?

tm.m: The same evidence-based therapy works when delivery is adjusted to how autistic people process information
tm.g: Anxiety in an autistic adult: CBT adapted for autism
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Lorazepam as needed (Benzodiazepines are not a treatment for anxiety disorders and risk dependence)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Psychodynamic psychotherapy (Psychodynamic therapy is not recommended for anxiety in autism)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Risperidone (Antipsychotics are not used for anxiety; they are kept for severe aggression)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sertraline (An SSRI may come later, but adapted psychological therapy is first)
x: Benzodiazepines are not a treatment for anxiety disorders and risk dependence.
Psychodynamic therapy is not recommended for anxiety in autism.
Antipsychotics are not used for anxiety; they are kept for severe aggression.
An SSRI may come later, but adapted psychological therapy is first.

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old woman with bipolar disorder gave birth 10 days ago. Over 2 days she has become confused and sleepless. She says her baby is evil.
She is agitated, distractible and responding to voices.
hq_q.w: Postpartum psychosis starts suddenly within 2 weeks of birth, often with mania and confusion. Bipolar disorder is the main risk. It is an emergency: admit to a mother and baby unit.
hq_q.f: Tearful and emotional on day 4 and fine by 2 weeks → baby blues.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Hormonal shifts after birth can trigger sudden psychosis, especially with bipolar disorder
tm.g: Sudden psychosis with confusion within 2 weeks of birth is postpartum psychosis
f: tearful on day 4 and fine by 2 weeks
the presentation instead showed features specific to Postnatal depression (Postnatal depression develops over weeks without confusion or hallucinations)
unwanted intrusive thoughts with insight
fever with offensive lochia
x: Ruled out here: requires tearful on day 4 and fine by 2 weeks, whereas this patient has 10 days ago, confused and sleepless.
Postnatal depression develops over weeks without confusion or hallucinations.
Ruled out here: requires unwanted intrusive thoughts with insight, whereas this patient has 10 days ago, confused and sleepless.
Ruled out here: requires fever with offensive lochia, whereas this patient has 10 days ago, confused and sleepless.

hq_q.s: A 29 year old woman gave birth 2 months ago and is breastfeeding. She has moderate postnatal depression and wants medication alongside therapy.
hq_q.w: Sertraline passes into breast milk in very small amounts and is the usual choice. Fluoxetine's long half-life can build up in the baby.
hq_q.f: She takes lithium for bipolar disorder → breastfeeding is not recommended.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate choice?

tm.m: Sertraline passes into breast milk in very small amounts
tm.g: Postnatal depression while breastfeeding: sertraline
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Doxepin (Contraindicated in breastfeeding due to infant sedation and respiratory depression)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fluoxetine (Long half-life leads to accumulation in breast milk and infant irritability)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lithium (Lithium passes into breast milk and is not used for postnatal depression)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Mirtazapine high dose (High-dose mirtazapine is not preferred while breastfeeding)
x: Contraindicated in breastfeeding due to infant sedation and respiratory depression
Long half-life leads to accumulation in breast milk and infant irritability
Lithium passes into breast milk and is not used for postnatal depression.
High-dose mirtazapine is not preferred while breastfeeding.

hq_q.s: A 33 year old woman with bipolar disorder stopped lithium for her pregnancy. She is 30 weeks pregnant and well. Her care team is planning her perinatal care.
hq_q.w: The days after birth carry the highest risk of relapse and postpartum psychosis. Plan close monitoring for then.
hq_q.f: No history of mental illness and tearful on day 4 → baby blues, reassure.
hq_q.ql: When is her risk of relapse highest?

tm.m: The days after birth carry the highest risk of relapse and psychosis
tm.g: Highest relapse risk: the first 2 weeks after delivery
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Around 6 months after delivery (Peak incidence of postpartum psychosis and bipolar relapse is within 2 weeks)
the presentation instead showed features specific to First trimester (Relapse risk is highest immediately postpartum after abrupt hormone drop)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Second trimester (Postpartum period carries a much higher relapse risk than mid-pregnancy)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Third trimester (Delivery and the first 14 days postpartum carry the peak risk)
x: Peak incidence of postpartum psychosis and bipolar relapse is within 2 weeks
Relapse risk is highest immediately postpartum after abrupt hormone drop
Postpartum period carries a much higher relapse risk than mid-pregnancy
Delivery and the first 14 days postpartum carry the peak risk

hq_q.s:
An 84 year old woman with a urinary infection has been confused for 2 days. Her family say she was sharp last week. She is drowsy in the morning and agitated at night.
Temperature 37.9°C. She cannot keep her attention on a conversation and cannot say the months backwards.
hq_q.w: Delirium: acute, fluctuating confusion with poor attention and altered alertness, usually from a physical cause such as infection or drugs.
hq_q.f: Gradual decline over 2 years with normal alertness → dementia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: drowsy in the morning and agitated at night
tm.m: Acute illness disrupts brain function, causing fluctuating inattention
tm.g: Acute fluctuating confusion with poor attention during an infection is delirium
f: gradual decline over 2 years with normal alertness
months of visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and fluctuations
the presentation instead showed features specific to Depression (Depression does not fluctuate through the day with inattention during an infection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Stroke (Stroke causes focal signs)
x: Ruled out here: requires gradual decline over 2 years with normal alertness, whereas this patient has sharp last week, drowsy in the morning and agitated at night.
Ruled out here: requires months of visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and fluctuations, whereas this patient has sharp last week, drowsy in the morning and agitated at night.
Depression does not fluctuate through the day with inattention during an infection.
Stroke causes focal signs.

hq_q.s: An 84 year old woman with mild dementia is admitted for a hip fracture repair. She is at high risk of delirium. The ward team is planning her care.
o: Bed rails and wrist restraint at night
Move to a quieter ward at night
hq_q.w: NICE prevents delirium with a multicomponent plan: orientation, hearing and vision aids, hydration, nutrition, mobility, pain control, avoiding unneeded moves and good sleep.
hq_q.f: Delirium already present with dangerous agitation after non-drug measures → short-term low-dose haloperidol.
hq_q.ql: Which measure most reduces her risk of delirium?

tm.m: Delirium is triggered by many small insults; removing each one prevents it
tm.g: Delirium prevention: a multicomponent non-drug plan
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Bed rails and wrist restraint at night (Restraint increases agitation, falls and injury)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Move to a quieter ward at night (Moving wards disorientates and raises delirium risk; NICE advises avoiding moves)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Night-time haloperidol (Antipsychotics do not prevent delirium and add risk in dementia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Night-time lorazepam (Benzodiazepines can cause delirium in older people)
x: Restraint increases agitation, falls and injury.
Moving wards disorientates and raises delirium risk; NICE advises avoiding moves.
Antipsychotics do not prevent delirium and add risk in dementia.
Benzodiazepines can cause delirium in older people.

hq_q.s:
An 80 year old man was admitted with pneumonia 2 days ago. He has become quiet, sleepy and withdrawn and is not eating. His family say this is not like him.
Temperature 37.8°C. He is drowsy but rousable and cannot name the months backwards.
His 4AT score is 6.
hq_q.w: Hypoactive delirium is the commonest subtype of delirium in older hospitalised adults, presenting with acute quietness, psychomotor retardation, drowsiness, anorexia, and inattention (unable to recite months backwards, 4AT >=4). It is frequently misdiagnosed as depression and carries a high mortality.
hq_q.f: 4AT score of 0 with low mood for months → depression.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Systemic inflammatory cytokines and cholinergic deficiency acutely disrupt ascending reticular arousal and frontoparietal attention networks
tm.g: Acute withdrawal, drowsiness and inattention (4AT >=4) over 48 hours in pneumonia -> hypoactive delirium
f: progressive cognitive decline over 18 months with recurrent vivid visual hallucinations and spontaneous parkinsonism
waxy flexibility, posturing and mutism with normal alertness in severe psychiatric illness
6 weeks of persistent low mood, anhedonia and guilt with normal alertness and a 4AT score of 0
preserved alertness, orientation and ability to recite the months backwards with a 4AT score of 0
x: Dementia with Lewy bodies develops over months to years with well-formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and REM sleep behaviour disorder.
Catatonia presents with waxy flexibility, mutism, posturing, and negativism rather than acute infection-driven fluctuating drowsiness.
Major depression evolves over weeks with persistent low mood and anhedonia in a clear sensorium (normal attention and 4AT <4).
Acute onset of drowsiness, withdrawal, and attentional failure over 48 hours is never a feature of normal ageing.

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old man lost his job 3 months ago. For 6 weeks he has felt low every day, wakes at 4 am and cannot get back to sleep, has lost 5 kg and no longer enjoys seeing his children. He feels worthless. He has no thoughts of self-harm.
PHQ-9 score 18.
hq_q.w: A stressor does not rule out depression. Two weeks of low mood with loss of pleasure, early waking, weight loss and worthlessness meets criteria for a depressive episode, here moderately severe by PHQ-9.
hq_q.f: Low and worried after redundancy but still enjoying things, PHQ-9 of 7 → adjustment disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: no longer enjoys seeing his children
tm.m: Once biological symptoms and loss of pleasure appear, the reaction has become a depressive illness
tm.g: Stressor plus full depressive features: depressive episode, not adjustment disorder
f: he were low and worried but still enjoying things, sleeping and eating normally
the presentation instead showed features specific to Dysthymia (Dysthymia is milder low mood lasting at least 2 years)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Generalised anxiety disorder (His main features are low mood and loss of pleasure, not widespread worry)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Normal grief (Grief follows a bereavement; he lost a job, and his symptoms meet depression criteria)
x: Adjustment disorder is diagnosed only when criteria for depression are not met; his are.
Dysthymia is milder low mood lasting at least 2 years.
His main features are low mood and loss of pleasure, not widespread worry.
Grief follows a bereavement; he lost a job, and his symptoms meet depression criteria.

hq_q.s: A 38 year old woman attends general practice reporting tearfulness, preoccupation, difficulty sleeping, and feeling overwhelmed since her home was repossessed following mortgage arrears. She has no anhedonia, no psychotic features, and no thoughts of self-harm, and her GP considers a diagnosis of adjustment disorder.
hq_q.w: Under ICD-11, adjustment disorder is a maladaptive emotional and cognitive reaction (preoccupation and failure to adapt) to an identifiable psychosocial stressor, with symptoms beginning within 1 month of the stressor and typically resolving within 6 months once the stressor ends.
hq_q.f: Symptoms still present long after the stressor has ended → reconsider the diagnosis.
hq_q.ql: Within what time after a stressor do the symptoms of adjustment disorder usually begin?

tm.m: Impaired psychological adaptation to an identifiable life event emerges within 1 month of the stressor
tm.g: ICD-11 onset window for adjustment disorder after an identifiable stressor -> within 1 month
f: acute stress reaction beginning immediately within hours to days of a terrifying trauma
never consistent with adjustment disorder, which begins within 1 month of the stressor
chronic symptoms persisting beyond 6 months that warrant reassessment for major depression or GAD
asked within what timeframe adjustment disorder symptoms typically resolve once the stressor ceases
x: Restricting onset to 1 week is too narrow; ICD-11 specifies onset within 1 month of the stressful life event.
An onset delayed by 1 year after a stressor does not meet diagnostic criteria for adjustment disorder.
Three months is the DSM-5 onset threshold, whereas UK/ICD-11 criteria specify onset within 1 month of the stressor.
Six months is the expected time within which adjustment disorder resolves after the stressor ends, not the onset window.

hq_q.s: A 42 year old woman has an adjustment disorder after her divorce was finalised 2 months ago. She asks how long it is likely to last.
hq_q.w: Adjustment disorder starts within a month of a stressor and usually resolves within 6 months once the stressor and its consequences have ended.
hq_q.f: Low mood persisting 9 months after the stressor ended → reassess for depression.
hq_q.ql: Within what time do symptoms usually resolve after the stressor has ended?

c: how long it is likely to last
tm.m: An adjustment reaction fades as the person adapts to the change
tm.g: Adjustment disorder usually resolves within 6 months of the stressor ending
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to After at least 2 years (Two years of low mood suggests dysthymia, not adjustment disorder)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Within 1 week (One week is the time course of an acute stress reaction, not adjustment disorder)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Within 2 weeks (It typically lasts longer than this; the outer limit is about 6 months)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Within 3 days (Settling within days is an acute stress reaction)
x: Two years of low mood suggests dysthymia, not adjustment disorder.
One week is the time course of an acute stress reaction, not adjustment disorder.
It typically lasts longer than this; the outer limit is about 6 months.
Settling within days is an acute stress reaction.

hq_q.s: A 32 year old woman avoids buses, supermarkets and crowds because she fears she could not escape or get help if she panicked. She now rarely leaves home.
hq_q.w: Agoraphobia is fear of places where escape or help would be difficult, leading to avoidance.
hq_q.f: Fear only of being judged when eating or speaking in front of others → social anxiety disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: could not escape or get help
tm.m: Fear of being trapped during panic leads to avoiding public places
tm.g: Avoiding places where escape is hard is agoraphobia
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Claustrophobia (Claustrophobia is fear of enclosed spaces)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD is worry about many things, not avoidance of places where escape is hard)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Panic disorder (Panic disorder is unexpected attacks)
fear only of being judged when eating or speaking
x: Claustrophobia is fear of enclosed spaces.
GAD is worry about many things, not avoidance of places where escape is hard.
Panic disorder is unexpected attacks.
Ruled out here: requires fear only of being judged when eating or speaking, whereas this patient has could not escape or get help, rarely leaves home.

hq_q.s: A 34 year old man has a specific phobia of dogs. It stops him walking to work. He has no other anxiety symptoms.
hq_q.w: Specific phobias respond to graded exposure: facing the feared thing step by step until the fear fades.
hq_q.f: Social anxiety disorder → individual CBT designed for social anxiety.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Gradual exposure lets fear fade
tm.g: Specific phobia: graded exposure therapy
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam before walks (Prevents habituation during exposure and risks benzodiazepine dependence)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hypnosis (Not recommended by NICE due to lack of robust evidence)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Propranolol (Propranolol does not treat a phobia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sertraline (An SSRI does not treat a specific phobia)
x: Prevents habituation during exposure and risks benzodiazepine dependence
Not recommended by NICE due to lack of robust evidence
Propranolol does not treat a phobia.
An SSRI does not treat a specific phobia.

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old woman with a lifelong blood-injection-injury phobia needs routine antenatal venepuncture. On previous occasions, seeing a needle caused an initial surge of palpitations followed within seconds by bradycardia, sweating, pallor, and a vasovagal syncopal faint.
She attends CBT to learn a physical counter-manoeuvre.
hq_q.w: Blood-injection-injury phobia triggers an initial sympathetic surge followed by a sudden vagal drop in blood pressure and syncope. Applied muscle tension (repeatedly tensing skeletal muscles) raises venous return and prevents fainting.
hq_q.f: Panic around spiders with no fainting → graded exposure with relaxation.
hq_q.ql: Which technique is most appropriate?

tm.m: Isometric skeletal muscle contraction increases peripheral vascular resistance and venous return, counteracting reflex vagal hypotension
tm.g: Blood-injection-injury phobia with vasovagal syncope -> applied muscle tension
f: never appropriate because avoidance maintains the phobia and compromises clinical care
never recommended for vasovagal needle syncope
situational sympathetic performance tremor in a musician without vasovagal syncope
hyperventilation during a non-syncopal panic attack where blood pressure remains elevated
x: Avoiding all venepuncture reinforces phobic avoidance and prevents essential antenatal blood screening and anti-D prophylaxis.
Pre-procedural oral diazepam causes sedation, does not prevent the reflex vasovagal blood pressure drop, and blocks exposure learning.
Beta-blockers such as propranolol lower heart rate and blood pressure further, worsening vasovagal syncope during venepuncture.
Slow relaxation breathing lowers sympathetic tone and systemic blood pressure further, accelerating vasovagal fainting in blood-injury phobia.

hq_q.s: An 8 year old boy has ADHD that still severely affects his schooling. Changes to his classroom and a parent training programme have been tried. He has no heart disease.
hq_q.w: NICE: methylphenidate is first-line for children aged 5 and over. Lisdexamfetamine is next if a 6-week trial does not work.
hq_q.f: An adult → lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate first.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first drug?

c: parent training programme have been tried
tm.m: Methylphenidate improves attention and impulse control in children
tm.g: Child ADHD after environmental measures: methylphenidate
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Atomoxetine (Atomoxetine is used when stimulants are not tolerated or do not work)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Guanfacine (Guanfacine is third line)
an adult
the presentation instead showed features specific to Melatonin (Melatonin is for sleep)
x: Atomoxetine is used when stimulants are not tolerated or do not work.
Guanfacine is third line.
Ruled out here: requires an adult, whereas this patient has 8 year old boy, parent training programme have been tried.
Melatonin is for sleep.

hq_q.s: A 9 year old boy with ADHD is about to start methylphenidate.
o: MRI brain and urine drug screen
hq_q.w: Stimulants reduce appetite and can slow growth and raise pulse and blood pressure. Plot growth and monitor every 6 months.
hq_q.f: A family history of sudden cardiac death or fainting on exercise → ECG and cardiology advice first.
hq_q.ql: Which baseline measures are needed?

tm.m: Stimulants reduce appetite and growth and raise pulse and BP
tm.g: Before methylphenidate: growth, pulse and blood pressure
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Echocardiogram (Echo is only for a cardiac history or examination finding)
the presentation instead showed features specific to EEG (EEG is only if seizures are suspected)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Liver and kidney function (Methylphenidate does not require routine baseline renal or liver blood tests)
the presentation instead showed features specific to MRI brain and urine drug screen (Neither neuroimaging nor routine toxicology is required before starting methylphenidate)
x: Echo is only for a cardiac history or examination finding.
EEG is only if seizures are suspected.
Methylphenidate does not require routine baseline renal or liver blood tests
Neither neuroimaging nor routine toxicology is required before starting methylphenidate

hq_q.s: A 10 year old boy has taken modified-release oral methylphenidate for 18 months for severe attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, with marked improvement in his classroom focus and home behaviour. However, his lunchtime appetite is suppressed and serial centile charting shows his height has crossed down from the 50th to the 25th centile.
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG87, if a child on methylphenidate has faltering growth across centiles despite taking tablets after meals, a planned treatment break ('drug holiday') during school holidays is recommended to allow catch-up growth.
hq_q.f: Growth and weight on track → continue with checks every 6 months.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate step?

tm.m: Central dopaminergic and noradrenergic stimulation suppresses hypothalamic appetite centres and transiently slows linear growth
tm.g: Height faltering across centiles on well-controlled methylphenidate -> planned treatment break during school holidays
f: acute serotonin syndrome where cyproheptadine acts as a 5-HT2A antagonist
biochemically confirmed pituitary growth hormone deficiency on provocation testing
severe cardiovascular toxicity or psychosis precipitated by stimulant therapy
inadequate ADHD symptom control after an adequate trial of maximum tolerated methylphenidate
x: Appetite stimulants such as cyproheptadine are not recommended by NICE for stimulant-induced growth suppression.
Recombinant growth hormone is reserved for proven pituitary growth hormone deficiency or Turner syndrome, not stimulant appetite suppression.
Permanently stopping methylphenidate when his ADHD was previously severe risks educational and social breakdown when holiday breaks suffice.
Dexamfetamine is an amphetamine stimulant that causes equal or greater appetite and linear growth suppression than methylphenidate.

hq_q.s: A 13 year old boy has repeatedly hurt the family dog and set fire to a shed. He steals from shops and often stays out all night.
hq_q.w: Conduct disorder breaks the rights of others: cruelty, fire-setting, theft and serious rule-breaking. Key discriminator: Cruelty to animals, fire-setting and theft in a teenager is conduct disorder.
hq_q.f: Angry, argumentative and defiant but no cruelty, theft or violence → oppositional defiant disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Conduct disorder violates the rights of others
tm.g: Cruelty to animals, fire-setting and theft in a teenager is conduct disorder
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Antisocial personality disorder (He is under 18)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD does not cause cruelty)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Autism spectrum disorder (Autism does not cause cruelty and fire-setting)
angry and defiant with no cruelty, theft or violence
x: He is under 18.
ADHD does not cause cruelty.
Autism does not cause cruelty and fire-setting.
Ruled out here: requires angry and defiant with no cruelty, theft or violence, whereas this patient has hurt the family dog, set fire.

hq_q.s: A 6 year old boy is often angry and argumentative. He refuses to follow rules at home and deliberately annoys others. There is no violence or cruelty. He is diagnosed with oppositional defiant disorder.
hq_q.w: NICE: parent-training programmes are first-line for children under 12 with conduct problems. Drugs are not used for the behaviour itself.
hq_q.f: He also has ADHD → treat the ADHD as well.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first intervention?

tm.m: Parenting programmes change the patterns that keep defiance going
tm.g: Oppositional defiant disorder: group parent-training programme
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Foster care placement (Foster care is not first line)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Individual psychotherapy for the child (Parent training is first line)
he also has ADHD
the presentation instead showed features specific to Risperidone (Risperidone is not used for ODD)
x: Foster care is not first line.
Parent training is first line.
Ruled out here: requires he also has ADHD, whereas this patient has 6 year old, no violence or cruelty.
Risperidone is not used for ODD.

hq_q.s: A 19 year old man has stolen, lied and been violent since the age of 12. He shows no remorse. He has been excluded from school and has lost several jobs.
hq_q.w: Antisocial personality disorder is diagnosed from 18 when there was conduct disorder before 15. Key discriminator: Lifelong antisocial behaviour without remorse in an adult is antisocial personality disorder.
hq_q.f: He is 16 → conduct disorder; personality disorder is not diagnosed under 18.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Antisocial personality disorder is diagnosed from 18 with conduct problems before 15
tm.g: Lifelong antisocial behaviour without remorse in an adult is antisocial personality disorder
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Bipolar disorder (Bipolar disorder causes mood episodes, not a lifelong pattern of remorseless antisocial behaviour)
he is 16
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD is defiance in younger children without serious violence)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Schizophrenia (There are no psychotic symptoms)
x: Bipolar disorder causes mood episodes, not a lifelong pattern of remorseless antisocial behaviour.
Ruled out here: requires he is 16, whereas this patient has 19 year old, since the age of 12.
ODD is defiance in younger children without serious violence.
There are no psychotic symptoms.

hq_q.s:
