A 15 year old girl attends a transition review with the community learning disability team. She speaks in simple phrases, reads familiar signs, dresses and washes with daily prompting from her parents, and attends a specialist school.
Formal cognitive testing using the Wechsler Intelligence Scale records an IQ of 45.
hq_q.w: Under ICD-10/ICD-11 and DSM-5, intellectual disability is classified into mild (IQ 50 to 69), moderate (IQ 35 to 49), severe (IQ 20 to 34), and profound (IQ under 20), alongside assessment of conceptual, social, and practical adaptive functioning.
hq_q.f: IQ of 62 → mild.
hq_q.ql: How is her intellectual disability classed?

c: dresses and washes with daily prompting
tm.m: An IQ of 35 to 49 (3 to 4 standard deviations below the population mean) with need for daily support defines moderate intellectual disability
tm.g: Intellectual disability with IQ 35 to 49 -> moderate intellectual disability
f: an IQ of 78 with mild academic delay and full independence in personal care
an IQ of 62 with ability to live semi-independently and hold supported employment
an IQ of 15 with absence of speech and 24-hour dependence for all personal care
an IQ of 26 with single-word communication and need for continuous supervision
x: Borderline intellectual functioning corresponds to an IQ of 70 to 84 and is not classified as an intellectual disability.
Mild intellectual disability corresponds to an IQ between 50 and 69.
Profound intellectual disability corresponds to an IQ below 20 with complete dependence for all physical care.
Severe intellectual disability corresponds to an IQ between 20 and 34.

hq_q.s:
A 14 year old boy with a mild learning disability is always hungry and takes food from bins. He was floppy as a baby and fed poorly. He has small hands and feet and short stature.
BMI 34 kg/m². His testes are small.
hq_q.w: Neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding, then insatiable hunger with obesity, small hands and feet, short stature, hypogonadism and learning disability is Prader-Willi syndrome (paternal 15q11-13).
hq_q.f: Long face, large ears and large testes in a boy with learning disability → fragile X syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: always hungry and takes food from bins
tm.m: Loss of paternal genes on chromosome 15 disrupts the hypothalamus, so satiety and sex hormones fail
tm.g: Hypotonic baby who becomes hyperphagic and obese: Prader-Willi syndrome
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Angelman syndrome (Angelman gives severe disability, seizures, little speech and a happy, excitable manner, not hyperphagia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Down syndrome (Down syndrome has a recognisable face, single palmar crease and heart defects; hyperphagia is not its hallmark)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fragile X syndrome (Fragile X gives a long face, large ears and large testes, not small testes with hyperphagia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Williams syndrome (Williams gives an elfin face, overfriendliness, supravalvular aortic stenosis and high calcium)
x: Angelman gives severe disability, seizures, little speech and a happy, excitable manner, not hyperphagia.
Down syndrome has a recognisable face, single palmar crease and heart defects; hyperphagia is not its hallmark.
Fragile X gives a long face, large ears and large testes, not small testes with hyperphagia.
Williams gives an elfin face, overfriendliness, supravalvular aortic stenosis and high calcium.

hq_q.s:
A 40 year old man has a severe learning disability and no speech. He lives in a supported home. Over a week he has started banging his head and refusing food. Staff say this is new.
He is distressed. Temperature 37.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm. A full examination has not been possible.
hq_q.w: In a non-verbal adult with severe learning disability, acute self-injurious behaviour and food refusal often express unrecognised physical pain (dental abscess, infection, or constipation). Avoid diagnostic overshadowing and examine for physical causes first.
hq_q.f: Physical causes excluded and the behaviour continues → a positive behaviour support plan.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first step?

c: banging his head and refusing food
tm.m: Non-verbal patients express nociceptive pain (dental, gastrointestinal, or urinary) through acute behavioural distress
tm.g: Acute onset of head-banging and food refusal in a non-verbal adult with learning disability -> look for an underlying physical cause
f: never appropriate before excluding acute physical pain or infection
severe acute psychotic or manic illness after physical causes have been ruled out
chronic environmentally reinforced behaviour after all physical and medical causes have been excluded
persistent severe aggression causing injury after physical causes and behavioural interventions have been addressed
x: Sedating a distressed non-verbal patient masks the clinical signs of an underlying painful medical or surgical condition.
Admitting to a psychiatric ward is inappropriate when tachycardia, low-grade fever, and food refusal point to an acute physical cause.
Formulating a chronic behavioural plan before excluding an acute dental abscess, ear infection, or constipation misses treatable pain.
NICE NG11 states antipsychotics must never be started for challenging behaviour without first excluding and treating physical health causes.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man presents with a 3-week history of excruciating, boring pain strictly behind his right eye. Attacks wake him nightly, last 45 minutes and cause him to pace the bedroom floor.
During attacks his right eye becomes bloodshot and waters profusely, his right eyelid droops and his right nostril blocks. Between attacks his neurological examination is normal.
hq_q.w: Cluster headache causes bouts of excruciating strictly unilateral orbital pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes with ipsilateral autonomic signs (lacrimation, ptosis, nasal congestion) and pacing restlessness. Treat acutely with 100% oxygen and a subcutaneous/nasal triptan.
hq_q.f: Brief 10-second electric-shock stabbing pains in the cheek triggered by light touch or chewing -> trigeminal neuralgia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: excruciating, boring pain strictly behind his right eye
right eye becomes bloodshot and waters profusely, his right eyelid droops
tm.m: Posterior hypothalamic circadian pacemakers activate the trigeminal-autonomic reflex arc, causing ipsilateral cranial parasympathetic outflow and sympathetic Horner features.
tm.g: Strictly unilateral 15-180 min orbital pain + ipsilateral lacrimation/ptosis + pacing restlessness -> cluster headache
x: Acute sinusitis causes continuous dull facial pressure worse on bending forward with purulent nasal discharge after an upper respiratory viral infection, not 45-minute nightly bouts.
Migraine attacks last 4 to 72 hours, cause patients to lie still in a dark quiet room rather than pace in agitation, and lack prominent unilateral autonomic tearing and ptosis.
Tension-type headache causes mild-to-moderate bilateral pressing tightness without restlessness or cranial autonomic features.
Trigeminal neuralgia causes paroxysms of shooting electric-shock pain in the V2/V3 distribution lasting seconds (not 45 minutes) triggered by washing, shaving or chewing.
f: continuous maxillary facial pain worse on bending forward with purulent rhinorrhoea and fever following a coryzal illness
a 12-hour throbbing unilateral headache preceded by 20 minutes of zigzag visual aura where the patient lies still in a dark room
a mild bilateral band-like pressing headache at the end of the working day without autonomic signs
brief 5-second paroxysms of lancinating electric-shock pain in the right jaw triggered by brushing teeth or cold wind

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman with moderate persistent asthma (treated with a beclometasone/formoterol inhaler) presents to her GP requesting prophylactic medication for episodic migraine without aura. She currently experiences six debilitating migraine days per month that cause her to miss work. She is sexually active, does not use contraception and hopes to conceive within the next year.
BP 118/74 mmHg, pulse rate 70 bpm. Neurological examination is normal.
hq_q.w: For migraine prophylaxis, propranolol is contraindicated in asthma, and both topiramate and sodium valproate are teratogenic and contraindicated in women who may become pregnant, making amitriptyline the safest effective choice.
hq_q.f: Woman without asthma or heart block -> oral propranolol is a safe first-line migraine preventative.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate prophylactic medication?

c: six debilitating migraine days per month
does not use contraception and hopes to conceive
tm.m: Tricyclic inhibition of central serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake modulates descending pain pathways without causing beta-2 bronchoconstriction or topiramate/valproate teratogenicity.
tm.g: Migraine prophylaxis in a patient with asthma who may become pregnant -> amitriptyline
x: Non-selective beta-blockers such as propranolol block bronchial beta-2 adrenoceptors and are contraindicated in patients with asthma.

Sodium valproate is strictly contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless under the Pregnancy Prevention Programme because of a 10% risk of major congenital malformations and 30-40% risk of neurodevelopmental delay.
Sumatriptan is an acute 5-HT1B/1D agonist taken at the onset of a migraine headache and is not used daily for migraine prophylaxis (daily use causes medication-overuse headache).

Topiramate is teratogenic (causing cleft lip/palate and fetal growth restriction) and is contraindicated under MHRA rules in women of childbearing potential unless using highly effective contraception.
f: migraine prophylaxis in a woman planning pregnancy who has no history of asthma or bradycardia
generalised epilepsy in an adult male patient
abortive treatment taken at the onset of an individual moderate-to-severe migraine headache
migraine prophylaxis in a patient with asthma who has a subdermal contraceptive implant and has signed the pregnancy prevention form

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old woman presents with a 2-week history of right temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw ache when chewing. Two hours ago the vision in her left eye suddenly became severely blurred.
The right temporal artery is tender. Visual acuity is 6/36 in the left eye with a relative afferent pupillary defect and pale, swollen disc. ESR is 88 mm/hour and CRP 96 mg/L (<5).
o: Arrange temporal artery biopsy before treatment
Check repeat ESR and review tomorrow
Urgent non-contrast CT head scan first
hq_q.w: Giant cell arteritis complicated by acute visual loss (anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy) threatens bilateral blindness within hours. Give immediate high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (500 mg to 1 g daily) before arranging temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy.
hq_q.f: Giant cell arteritis WITHOUT visual loss or jaw claudication -> start oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily immediately.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management step?

c: vision in her left eye suddenly became severely blurred
Visual acuity is 6/36 in the left eye
tm.m: Granulomatous occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries causes optic nerve head infarction; immediate intravenous pulse corticosteroid therapy suppresses vasculitis to save the fellow eye.
tm.g: Giant cell arteritis WITH acute visual loss -> immediate high-dose IV methylprednisolone
x: Delaying corticosteroid therapy for a surgical biopsy when one eye already has ischaemic optic neuropathy risks irreversible blindness in the contralateral eye.
Visual loss in giant cell arteritis is a same-hour emergency; waiting until tomorrow risks permanent bilateral blindness.
Oral prednisolone 15 to 20 mg daily is the dose for uncomplicated polymyalgia rheumatica and is completely inadequate for giant cell arteritis with visual loss.
CT head does not diagnose giant cell arteritis or anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy and must not delay intravenous methylprednisolone.
f: never appropriate; temporal artery biopsy is performed within 1 to 2 weeks AFTER starting immediate steroid therapy
never appropriate in suspected giant cell arteritis
isolated polymyalgia rheumatica (shoulder and hip girdle morning stiffness) without headache, jaw claudication or visual symptoms
acute stroke or subarachnoid haemorrhage presenting with focal limb weakness or thunderclap headache

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old man was admitted after a head injury. He was alert on arrival, but his GCS has now fallen to 8.
BP has risen to 190/100 mmHg and his pulse rate has fallen to 46 bpm. His breathing has become irregular.
hq_q.w: Cushing's triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing is a late sign of brain herniation. Call the neurosurgeons and protect the airway.
hq_q.f: Low blood pressure with a fast pulse → bleeding elsewhere; the head injury alone rarely causes shock.
hq_q.ql: What do these signs show?

tm.m: Rising pressure compresses the brainstem, triggering Cushing's response
tm.g: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing after head injury is raised intracranial pressure
f: a spinal injury above T6 with a full bladder
low blood pressure with a fast pulse
low blood pressure with a slow pulse after spinal injury
the presentation instead showed features specific to Vasovagal response (A vasovagal response causes low BP)
x: Ruled out here: requires a spinal injury above T6 with a full bladder, whereas this patient has GCS has now fallen to 8, 190/100.
Ruled out here: requires low blood pressure with a fast pulse, whereas this patient has GCS has now fallen to 8, 190/100.
Ruled out here: requires low blood pressure with a slow pulse after spinal injury, whereas this patient has GCS has now fallen to 8, 190/100.
A vasovagal response causes low BP.

hq_q.s:
A 27 year old woman presents with a 3-month history of daily headaches that are worse on lying flat and coughing, with brief visual blackouts on standing.
Her BMI is 36 kg/m². Fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilloedema with enlarged blind spots. Brain MRI and MR venography are normal, and lumbar puncture opening pressure is 34 cm CSF with normal constituents.
hq_q.w: First-line management of idiopathic intracranial hypertension combines structured weight loss (the only disease-modifying intervention) with oral acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces choroid plexus cerebrospinal fluid secretion by ~50% to protect optic nerve function.
hq_q.f: Rapidly declining visual acuity or visual fields despite maximal medical therapy -> urgent optic nerve sheath fenestration or ventriculoperitoneal/lumboperitoneal shunt.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line medication alongside weight loss?

c: worse on lying flat and coughing
tm.m: Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in the choroid plexus epithelium decreases bicarbonate and sodium transport into the ventricles, lowering CSF production and intracranial pressure.
tm.g: First-line medical therapy for idiopathic intracranial hypertension alongside weight loss -> acetazolamide
x: Loop diuretics have a weaker effect on choroid plexus CSF production than carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and are used only as an adjunct or second-line option.
Long-term corticosteroids promote weight gain and fluid retention, and withdrawal of steroids can trigger rebound intracranial hypertension.
Sumatriptan is an abortive 5-HT1B/1D agonist for migraine attacks and does not lower cerebrospinal fluid pressure or protect against papilloedema-induced visual loss.
Topiramate has weak carbonic anhydrase activity and is used second-line if acetazolamide is not tolerated, but it is teratogenic in women of childbearing age without contraception.
f: acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with fluid overload
acute giant cell arteritis presenting with temporal headache and jaw claudication
acute symptomatic relief of an episodic migraine attack
second-line therapy when acetazolamide is not tolerated in a woman using highly effective contraception

hq_q.s:
A 40 year old man attends the emergency department with a 24-hour history of severe headache, fever and progressive drowsiness.
Temperature 39.2°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 132/76 mmHg. His GCS is 10 (E3 V2 M5) and examination reveals neck stiffness and bilateral papilloedema. Venous access has been secured and blood cultures have been taken.
hq_q.w: In suspected bacterial meningitis with signs of raised intracranial pressure (papilloedema or GCS <13), lumbar puncture risks fatal cerebral herniation. Give empirical intravenous antibiotics immediately after blood cultures, then perform a CT head scan.
hq_q.f: Suspected bacterial meningitis with GCS 15, no papilloedema, no focal neurology and no seizures -> perform lumbar puncture within 1 hour without prior CT.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate sequence of management?

tm.m: Withdrawing lumbar CSF below an obstructed or oedematous supratentorial compartment creates a rostrocaudal pressure gradient that precipitates uncal or tonsillar herniation.
tm.g: Suspected bacterial meningitis WITH papilloedema or GCS <13 -> immediate IV antibiotics first, then CT head (never delay antibiotics for CT, never LP before CT)
x: Performing a lumbar puncture in a patient with a GCS of 10 and bilateral papilloedema without prior neuroimaging risks fatal brainstem coning.
Neuroimaging must never delay the administration of life-saving empirical intravenous antibiotics once blood cultures have been drawn in acute bacterial meningitis.
Lumbar puncture is strictly contraindicated here because of bilateral papilloedema and a GCS of 10.
Arranging an MRI scan takes far too long in an acutely deteriorating patient with GCS 10 and dangerously delays empirical antibiotics.
f: suspected bacterial meningitis in a patient with GCS 15, normal fundoscopy and no focal neurological signs where LP is delayed
never appropriate; empirical IV antibiotics must always be given before sending the patient to the CT scanner
haemodynamically stable patient with suspected meningitis, GCS 15, no papilloedema and no focal signs where LP can be done immediately
never appropriate in acute bacterial meningitis with reduced consciousness

hq_q.s:
A 49 year old woman was lifting weights at the gym 2 hours ago when she developed an explosive occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within 30 seconds. She describes it as the worst headache of her life and has vomited twice.
Temperature 37.1°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 168/94 mmHg. GCS is 15 with photophobia and neck stiffness.
hq_q.w: A thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity within 1 minute accompanied by vomiting, photophobia and neck stiffness is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. Non-contrast CT head within 6 hours has >98% sensitivity.
hq_q.f: Recurrent thunderclap headaches over 1 to 2 weeks triggered by SSRIs or vasoconstrictors with 'string-of-beads' cerebral arteries -> reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Sudden surge in transmural arterial pressure during Valsalva ruptures a saccular berry aneurysm in the circle of Willis, ejecting arterial blood into the subarachnoid cisterns and irritating the meninges.
tm.g: Exertional thunderclap headache peaking within seconds + vomiting + neck stiffness -> subarachnoid haemorrhage
x: Bacterial meningitis develops over hours to days with high fever and systemic sepsis rather than an instantaneous headache peaking within 30 seconds during exercise.
Cluster headache causes recurrent 15 to 180 minute bouts of strictly unilateral orbital pain with ipsilateral tearing and ptosis, not a single occipital thunderclap with neck stiffness.
Migraine builds up gradually over 30 minutes to hours and does not peak within 30 seconds or cause objective neck stiffness.

Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome typically causes multiple recurrent short thunderclap headaches over 1 to 3 weeks (often postpartum or on vasoactive drugs) without subarachnoid meningism, and SAH must always be excluded first.
f: a 12-hour history of fever 39.4°C, rigors, neck stiffness and a non-blanching petechial rash
nightly 45-minute attacks of right orbital pain with ipsilateral lacrimation, ptosis and pacing
a unilateral throbbing headache building up over 2 hours with nausea and no neck stiffness
recurrent short thunderclap headaches over 10 days after starting sertraline or nasal decongestants, with normal CT/LP and segmental arterial beading on CTA

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman is admitted to the neurosurgical unit after presenting with a sudden thunderclap headache, photophobia and vomiting. Non-contrast CT head confirms diffuse basal subarachnoid haemorrhage, and CT angiography demonstrates a 6 mm anterior communicating artery saccular aneurysm scheduled for endovascular coiling.
Her GCS is 15, pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP is 144/84 mmHg.
hq_q.w: Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days is given routinely to all patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. As a lipophilic dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, it reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm and significantly improves neurological outcome.
hq_q.f: Definitive prevention of aneurysmal rebleeding -> urgent endovascular coiling (or surgical clipping) within 24 to 48 hours.
hq_q.ql: Which medication should be started to prevent delayed cerebral ischaemia?

c: 6 mm anterior communicating artery saccular aneurysm
tm.m: Lipid-soluble nimodipine crosses the blood-brain barrier and blocks L-type voltage-gated calcium channels on cerebral vascular smooth muscle and neurones, reducing vasospasm-induced infarction.
tm.g: Preventing delayed cerebral ischaemia (vasospasm) in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage -> oral nimodipine
x: Routine corticosteroids do not reduce cerebral vasospasm or improve outcomes in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Aggressive blood pressure lowering with labetalol in aneurysmal SAH reduces cerebral perfusion pressure and worsens delayed cerebral ischaemia once vasospasm develops.
Intravenous mannitol is an osmotic diuretic used as a temporary bridge for impending cerebral herniation, not for 21-day prophylaxis of arterial vasospasm.
NICE recommends against routine antifibrinolytic therapy (tranexamic acid) in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage because it increases cerebral ischaemia without improving functional outcome.
f: vasogenic cerebral oedema surrounding a high-grade glioma or brain metastasis
hypertensive encephalopathy or acute aortic dissection with systolic BP >180 mmHg
acute transtentorial uncal herniation with a fixed dilated pupil awaiting emergency craniotomy
major extracranial trauma haemorrhage within 3 hours of injury

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old man was admitted 5 days ago with an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Over the past 24 hours he has become drowsy and has passed 3.8 litres of urine.
Examination shows dry mucous membranes, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg lying (86/50 mmHg sitting). Serum sodium is 126 mmol/L (135-146) and urinary sodium is 92 mmol/L (>20).
hq_q.w: Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia with high urinary sodium and polyuria after subarachnoid haemorrhage indicates cerebral salt wasting rather than SIADH. Treat with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride; fluid restriction is contraindicated as it precipitates vasospasm.
hq_q.f: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with low urine volume and high urine osmolality outside SAH -> SIADH, managed with fluid restriction.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: 5 days ago with an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage
Serum sodium is 126 mmol/L (135-146) and urinary sodium is 92 mmol/L
tm.m: Sympathetic surge and natriuretic peptide release after subarachnoid haemorrhage inhibit renal tubular sodium and water reabsorption, causing true intravascular volume depletion.
tm.g: Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia + high urine sodium + polyuria after SAH = cerebral salt wasting -> IV 0.9% sodium chloride
x: Desmopressin promotes free water retention in cranial diabetes insipidus (hypernatraemia) and would dangerously worsen hyponatraemia of 126 mmol/L.
Fluid restriction is strictly contraindicated in post-SAH hypovolaemic cerebral salt wasting because volume depletion triggers cerebral vasospasm and cortical infarction.
Loop diuretics increase renal sodium and water loss, worsening both his hypovolaemia and his cerebral salt-wasting hyponatraemia.
Vasopressin V2-receptor antagonists (vaptans) cause aquaresis and worsen intravascular volume depletion in hypovolaemic cerebral salt wasting.
f: cranial diabetes insipidus after pituitary surgery with serum sodium 156 mmol/L and dilute polyuria
chronic euvolaemic SIADH secondary to small-cell lung cancer without subarachnoid haemorrhage
hypervolaemic hyponatraemia in decompensated congestive heart failure with pulmonary oedema
refractory euvolaemic SIADH under specialist endocrinology supervision

hq_q.s:
An 81 year old man who drinks 50 units of alcohol per week and has had several minor falls presents with a 3-week history of confusion and drowsiness, fluctuating markedly from day to day.
Examination shows GCS 13 and mild grade 4/5 right hemiparesis. Non-contrast CT head demonstrates a crescent-shaped hypodense collection over the left cerebral hemisphere.
hq_q.w: Chronic subdural haematoma occurs weeks after minor head trauma in elderly patients or heavy drinkers due to tearing of stretched cortical bridging veins. It causes fluctuating confusion and hemiparesis with a crescent-shaped hypodense collection on CT.
hq_q.f: Temporal skull fracture with a lucid interval and a biconvex hyperdense clot -> acute extradural haematoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: drinks 50 units of alcohol per week
fluctuating markedly from day to day
tm.m: Age- and alcohol-related cerebral atrophy increases tension on cortical bridging veins; slow venous oozing forms an encapsulated subdural collection that liquefies into hypodense fluid over 2 to 3 weeks.
tm.g: Subacute fluctuating confusion + falls/alcohol + crescent-shaped hypodense collection on CT -> chronic subdural haematoma
x: An acute ischaemic stroke presents with sudden-onset maximal deficit and a wedge-shaped parenchymal infarct rather than a 3-week fluctuating extra-axial crescent.
Alzheimer's disease causes gradual progressive memory decline over years without day-to-day drowsiness fluctuations, right hemiparesis or a crescentic subdural collection.
An extradural haematoma is an acute arterial bleed beneath a skull fracture that forms a biconvex lens-shaped hyperdense mass bounded by suture lines.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with a hyperacute thunderclap headache and blood in the basal cisterns rather than a 3-week hypodense convexity crescent.
f: abrupt-onset right hemiplegia and global aphasia with a wedge-shaped parenchymal hypodensity in the left MCA territory
gradual 2-year decline in short-term episodic memory with medial temporal atrophy and no subdural collection
acute deterioration 2 hours after a blow to the temple with a biconvex hyperdense collection on CT
an explosive thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity in seconds with hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns

hq_q.s:
A 20 year old man was struck on the right side of his head by a cricket ball 90 minutes ago. He lost consciousness briefly, recovered and chatted normally, then collapsed 15 minutes ago.
His GCS is 7 and his right pupil is fixed and dilated. CT head shows a biconvex hyperdense collection beneath the right temporal bone that does not cross the coronal or lambdoid suture lines.
o: Berry aneurysm in the circle of Willis
hq_q.w: The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery runs deep to the thin pterion in the temporal fossa. Pterion fractures lacerate this artery, producing a biconvex extradural haematoma bounded by cranial suture lines.
hq_q.f: Crescent-shaped subdural haematoma crossing cranial suture lines -> cortical bridging veins.
hq_q.ql: Which blood vessel is most likely to be the source of bleeding?

c: struck on the right side of his head by a cricket ball
does not cross the coronal or lambdoid suture lines
tm.m: Arterial bleeding from the middle meningeal artery dissects the periosteal layer of dura away from the inner table of the skull up to the cranial sutures where dura is tightly fused.
tm.g: Temporal blow + lucid interval + biconvex collection bounded by suture lines -> middle meningeal artery
x: Rupture of a circle of Willis berry aneurysm causes subarachnoid haemorrhage within the basal cisterns rather than a lens-shaped extradural clot.
Tearing of cortical bridging veins produces a crescent-shaped subdural haematoma that spreads freely across cranial suture lines.
The middle cerebral artery runs within the Sylvian fissure to supply the lateral cerebral cortex; its occlusion or rupture causes parenchymal stroke or intracerebral haemorrhage.
Superior sagittal sinus injury occurs with depressed vertex skull fractures rather than lateral temporal pterion blows.
f: spontaneous thunderclap headache with hyperdense blood filling the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures
a crescent-shaped hyperdense collection crossing suture lines over the cerebral hemisphere after a fall
acute contralateral face-and-arm hemiplegia and aphasia from a dense MCA sign on CT
a depressed midline vertex skull fracture overlying the superior sagittal sinus

hq_q.s:
A 79 year old woman who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation fell 3 hours ago and struck her head. Over the past hour she has developed a headache and become drowsy.
Her GCS is 13, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 152/86 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head demonstrates an acute right subdural haematoma with 5 mm midline shift. Her urgent INR is 3.4.
hq_q.w: For intracranial haemorrhage on warfarin, British Society for Haematology and NICE guidelines recommend immediate 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (which reverses INR within 15 minutes) plus intravenous vitamin K 5 mg to sustain factor synthesis.
hq_q.f: Life-threatening intracranial haemorrhage on dabigatran -> intravenous idarucizumab.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate anticoagulation reversal regimen?

tm.m: Four-factor PCC provides immediate preformed vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors II, VII, IX and X, while intravenous vitamin K1 restores hepatic gamma-carboxylation within 6 hours as PCC factors decay.
tm.g: Intracranial haemorrhage on warfarin -> 4-factor PCC + intravenous vitamin K immediately
x: Fresh frozen plasma requires ABO matching, thawing and large infusion volumes, reverses INR slowly and incompletely, and is used only if prothrombin complex concentrate is unavailable.
Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase rather than platelet function; platelet transfusion does not lower the INR or reverse warfarin.
Protamine sulfate is a strongly basic peptide that binds and neutralises unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin, not warfarin.
Tranexamic acid inhibits plasminogen activation but does not replace the missing vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX and X in warfarin-associated intracranial haemorrhage.
f: four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is completely unavailable in a resource-limited setting
intracranial haemorrhage in a patient with severe bone marrow thrombocytopenia (platelets <50 × 10⁹/L)
life-threatening bleeding during an intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion
major obstetric postpartum haemorrhage or extracranial trauma bleeding within 3 hours

hq_q.s:
An 18 year old man is brought to a rural GP surgery with a 6-hour history of fever, headache and drowsiness. An ambulance has been called and will arrive in 15 minutes. He has no drug allergies.
Temperature 39.2°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 96/58 mmHg. Examination reveals neck stiffness and a spreading non-blanching purpuric rash over both legs.
hq_q.w: When meningococcal septicaemia (meningitis with a non-blanching purpuric rash) is suspected in primary care or the community, NICE recommends giving immediate parenteral (intramuscular or intravenous) benzylpenicillin at the earliest opportunity, provided it does not delay urgent ambulance transfer to hospital.
hq_q.f: Patient has already arrived in the hospital emergency department -> give intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily after blood cultures.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate antibiotic management in primary care?

c: neck stiffness and a spreading non-blanching purpuric rash
tm.m: Early parenteral bactericidal beta-lactam administration in the community rapidly reduces circulating Neisseria meningitidis endotoxin load and mortality before hospital arrival.
tm.g: Suspected meningococcal disease with non-blanching rash in primary care -> immediate IM/IV benzylpenicillin (without delaying transfer)
x: Pre-hospital corticosteroid monotherapy without parenteral antibiotics is dangerous in meningococcal septicaemia.
When meningococcal septicaemia with a non-blanching rash is identified in primary care and benzylpenicillin is on hand while awaiting the ambulance, withholding it delays bactericidal therapy.
Oral antibiotics have slow, erratic gut absorption in a shocked febrile patient and cannot achieve the rapid bactericidal CSF and plasma levels required in meningococcal sepsis.
Single-dose oral ciprofloxacin is used for asymptomatic close household contact chemoprophylaxis, not for treating active invasive meningococcal septicaemia.
f: pre-hospital treatment of severe viral croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) with stridor at rest
suspected bacterial meningitis WITHOUT a non-blanching rash where urgent hospital transfer takes priority
uncomplicated acute otitis media or streptococcal pharyngitis in a stable outpatient
chemoprophylaxis for his asymptomatic flatmates who shared the flat in the 7 days before symptom onset

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old man presents with a 3-week history of progressive headache, fever, night sweats and double vision. He moved to the UK from Somalia 6 months ago.
Temperature 38.0°C, pulse rate 92 bpm. He has neck stiffness and a left abducens (sixth cranial nerve) palsy. Lumbar puncture shows 300/mm³ (88% lymphocytes), CSF protein 2.5 g/L (0.15-0.45) and a CSF:plasma glucose ratio of 0.28.
hq_q.w: Tuberculous meningitis presents subacutely over weeks with fever, night sweats, basal cranial nerve palsies (CN VI) and a CSF showing lymphocytic pleocytosis, markedly raised protein (>1.5 g/L) and low glucose (<50% of plasma).
hq_q.f: Acute 12-hour history with turbid CSF showing 1,500 neutrophils/mm³ and low glucose -> acute pyogenic bacterial meningitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Rupture of a subependymal Rich focus releases Mycobacterium tuberculosis into the basal cisterns, forming a thick gelatinous basal exudate that entraps cranial nerves and consumes CSF glucose.
tm.g: Subacute meningitis + cranial nerve VI palsy + lymphocytic CSF + very high protein (2.5 g/L) + low glucose ratio -> tuberculous meningitis
x: Untreated pyogenic bacterial meningitis presents fulminantly over hours to a couple of days with predominantly neutrophilic CSF (>80-90% neutrophils), not a 3-week lymphocytic illness.
Cryptococcal meningitis occurs primarily in advanced HIV (CD4 <100 cells/mm³) with subacute headache and raised opening pressure rather than a thick proteinaceous basal exudate of 2.5 g/L.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with a hyperacute thunderclap headache and blood-stained/xanthochromic CSF rather than 3 weeks of night sweats and 300 lymphocytes/mm³.
Viral meningitis is a self-limiting illness with mildly raised CSF protein (<1.0 g/L), a normal CSF:plasma glucose ratio (>0.6) and no basal cranial nerve palsies.
f: a 12-hour history of fever and meningism with turbid CSF showing 2,000 neutrophils/mm³ and low glucose
an HIV-positive patient with CD4 count 35 cells/mm³ and a positive CSF cryptococcal antigen and India ink stain
a sudden occipital thunderclap headache peaking within seconds with xanthochromia on CSF spectrophotometry
a 3-day headache and photophobia with 100 lymphocytes/mm³, protein 0.5 g/L and a normal CSF:plasma glucose ratio

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man is brought to the emergency department with an 18-hour history of fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and acute confusion. He has no drug allergies.
Temperature 39.0°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 136/78 mmHg. Blood cultures have been drawn and empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily plus intravenous dexamethasone have been prescribed for suspected acute bacterial meningitis.
hq_q.w: In patients aged 60 years and over (or pregnant or immunocompromised) with suspected bacterial meningitis, NICE recommends adding intravenous amoxicillin to ceftriaxone because Listeria monocytogenes is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins.
hq_q.f: Recent travel to an area with high prevalence of penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae -> add intravenous vancomycin (or rifampicin).
hq_q.ql: Which additional intravenous antibiotic must be added to cover his age group?

tm.m: Listeria monocytogenes expresses altered penicillin-binding proteins that have very low affinity for third-generation cephalosporins, requiring aminopenicillin (amoxicillin/ampicillin) binding for bactericidal activity.
tm.g: Empirical bacterial meningitis treatment in an adult aged >=60 years -> add IV amoxicillin to ceftriaxone for Listeria cover
x: Intravenous aciclovir treats herpes simplex viral encephalitis and has no antibacterial activity against Listeria monocytogenes.
Intravenous gentamicin penetrates the blood-brain barrier poorly and is not added routinely to ceftriaxone for empirical community adult meningitis.
Metronidazole covers obligate anaerobes in brain abscess rather than aerobic Gram-positive Listeria monocytogenes in acute meningitis.
Vancomycin is added to ceftriaxone when cephalosporin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae is suspected (e.g. recent travel), not for routine Listeria cover in UK patients over 60.
f: suspected herpes simplex encephalitis presenting with temporal lobe seizures, dysphasia and behavioural change
synergistic therapy alongside amoxicillin once Listeria monocytogenes is confirmed on culture in a neonate
empirical treatment alongside ceftriaxone for a ring-enhancing frontal lobe brain abscess
suspected pneumococcal meningitis after recent prolonged travel to a region with high beta-lactam resistance

hq_q.s:
A 54 year old woman attends the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever, severe headache and uncharacteristic bizarre behaviour. Thirty minutes ago she had a tonic-clonic seizure.
Temperature 38.6°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg. She is disorientated, with no rash and no neck stiffness. CT head is normal and a lumbar puncture is being performed.
hq_q.w: Fever with altered behaviour, confusion and seizures indicates acute viral encephalitis (most commonly HSV-1). Untreated mortality exceeds 70%, so empirical intravenous aciclovir must be started immediately before CSF PCR results return.
hq_q.f: Immunocompromised patient with confirmed cytomegalovirus (CMV) encephalitis -> intravenous ganciclovir.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate empirical treatment?

c: no rash and no neck stiffness
tm.m: Aciclovir is phosphorylated selectively by herpes simplex viral thymidine kinase into aciclovir triphosphate, terminating viral DNA polymerase chain elongation in infected temporal lobe neurones.
tm.g: Suspected acute viral encephalitis (fever + behavioural change + seizures) -> immediate IV aciclovir
x: Antibiotics alone do not treat herpes simplex virus, which is the leading cause of sporadic necrotising encephalitis presenting with behavioural change and seizures.
Corticosteroid monotherapy without antiviral cover promotes unchecked viral replication in acute herpes simplex encephalitis.
Ganciclovir causes severe bone marrow myelosuppression and is reserved for cytomegalovirus (CMV) or HHV-6 encephalitis in immunocompromised patients.
Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor for influenza A and B respiratory infection and has no activity against herpes simplex virus.
f: acute purulent bacterial meningitis with neck stiffness, photophobia and neutrophilic CSF
cerebral vasogenic oedema surrounding a metastatic brain tumour
cytomegalovirus ventriculoencephalitis in a patient with advanced HIV and CD4 <50 cells/mm³
influenza A pneumonia within 48 hours of symptom onset in an at-risk adult

hq_q.s:
A 46 year old man is admitted to the acute medical unit with a 3-day history of fever, headache, acute confusion, olfactory hallucinations of burning toast and two focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
Temperature 38.7°C, pulse rate 96 bpm. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows 110 lymphocytes/mm³, protein 0.92 g/L and normal glucose, and CSF PCR is positive for herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1).
hq_q.w: Herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis characteristically causes asymmetrical, necrotising, haemorrhagic inflammation of the medial temporal lobes, insula and inferior frontal (orbitofrontal) cortex, seen as T2/FLAIR hyperintensity on brain MRI. Spread occurs via the olfactory tract or trigeminal nerve reactivation.
hq_q.f: Symmetrical T2 hyperintensity in the pulvinar or dorsomedial thalami and basal ganglia -> Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease or Japanese/arboviral encephalitis.
hq_q.ql: Which anatomical region is most characteristically affected on brain MRI in this condition?

c: CSF PCR is positive for herpes simplex virus type 1
tm.m: HSV-1 travels retrogradely along olfactory and trigeminal pathways to infect limbic cortex neurones in the medial temporal lobes and insula.
tm.g: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) encephalitis -> medial temporal (and inferior frontal) lobes on MRI
x: Symmetrical basal ganglia and thalamic involvement is typical of carbon monoxide poisoning, Wilson disease or flavivirus (Japanese) encephalitis rather than HSV-1.
Isolated cerebellar inflammation (acute cerebellitis) is classically associated with varicella-zoster virus in children or Listeria rhombencephalitis rather than adult HSV-1.
Multiple discrete ring-enhancing lesions at the corticomedullary junction suggest haematogenous brain metastases or septic emboli, not HSV-1 encephalitis.
Ovoid T2 hyperintense plaques perpendicular to the lateral ventricles (Dawson fingers) are characteristic of multiple sclerosis demyelination.
f: acute carbon monoxide poisoning or Japanese encephalitis affecting the globus pallidus and thalamus
acute post-infectious varicella cerebellitis presenting with gait ataxia, dysmetria and nystagmus
haematogenous cerebral metastases from primary bronchial carcinoma
relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis showing periventricular Dawson fingers on FLAIR MRI

hq_q.s:
A 23 year old woman was admitted 2 weeks ago with acute paranoia and hallucinations. Over the past 48 hours she has developed seizures, repetitive involuntary grimacing and chewing movements, and labile blood pressure.
Temperature 37.9°C. CSF shows 35 lymphocytes/mm³ with negative HSV PCR. Brain MRI is normal, and pelvic ultrasound shows a 5 cm complex right ovarian mass.
hq_q.w: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is an autoimmune encephalitis in young women, often paraneoplastic to an ovarian teratoma. It progresses from acute psychosis to seizures, orofacial dyskinesias and autonomic instability; treat with immunotherapy and teratoma resection.
hq_q.f: Fever, temporal lobe T2 hyperintensity on MRI and positive CSF HSV-1 PCR -> herpes simplex encephalitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: repetitive involuntary grimacing and chewing movements
tm.m: IgG autoantibodies generated against neural tissue within an ovarian teratoma cross-react with and internalise synaptic GluN1 subunits of central NMDA glutamate receptors.
tm.g: Young woman + psychiatric onset + seizures + orofacial dyskinesias + autonomic instability + ovarian teratoma -> anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
x: Primary schizophrenia does not cause generalised seizures, orofacial dyskinesias in a neuroleptic-naive patient, autonomic instability or CSF lymphocytosis.
Herpes simplex encephalitis is excluded here by the negative CSF HSV PCR, normal temporal lobes on MRI and the presence of an ovarian teratoma with orofacial dyskinesia.

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows dopamine antagonist exposure and causes lead-pipe muscle rigidity, hyperpyrexia and markedly raised creatine kinase rather than CSF lymphocytosis and an ovarian mass.
Wernicke's encephalopathy results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency and presents with the triad of acute confusion, cerebellar ataxia and ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus.
f: a 6-month history of auditory hallucinations and thought insertion with normal vital signs, normal CSF and no seizures
acute febrile confusion with medial temporal lobe T2 hyperintensity and a positive CSF HSV-1 PCR
lead-pipe muscular rigidity, temperature 40.2°C and creatine kinase 18,000 IU/L 5 days after starting haloperidol
acute confusion, sixth nerve palsies, nystagmus and broad-based gait ataxia in a patient with chronic alcohol dependency

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man presents with a 7-day history of worsening left frontal headache, fever and progressive right arm weakness. Three weeks ago he had root canal treatment for an infected upper left premolar.
Temperature 38.2°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg. He has grade 4/5 right upper-limb weakness. Contrast CT head shows a 3 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe.
hq_q.w: A smooth, thin-walled ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding vasogenic oedema in a febrile patient with focal neurological signs following a recent odontogenic or sinus infection is characteristic of a bacterial brain abscess. Neurosurgical aspiration and intravenous ceftriaxone plus metronidazole are required.
hq_q.f: Afebrile older smoker with weight loss and multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the grey-white matter junction -> cerebral metastases.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: 7-day history of worsening left frontal headache, fever
tm.m: Haematogenous or venous spread of oral flora from the dental apex into the frontal white matter forms a central core of purulent necrosis surrounded by a contrast-enhancing capsule.
tm.g: Fever + focal weakness + recent dental infection + smooth ring-enhancing frontal lesion -> brain abscess
x: Cerebral metastases typically occur as multiple lesions at the grey-white matter junction in an afebrile patient with a known systemic primary cancer.
Cerebral toxoplasmosis presents as multiple basal ganglia ring-enhancing lesions in severely immunocompromised patients (HIV with CD4 <100 cells/mm³).
Glioblastoma presents in older adults without fever or dental sepsis and shows a thick, irregular, shaggy enhancing rim crossing the corpus callosum.
Multiple sclerosis causes periventricular open-ring or ovoid demyelinating plaques without high fever or recent odontogenic sepsis.
f: multiple grey-white junction lesions in an afebrile 68 year old with a spiculated lung mass
multiple ring-enhancing basal ganglia lesions in a patient with untreated HIV and CD4 count 30 cells/mm³
an afebrile 65 year old with a thick irregular butterfly lesion crossing the splenium of the corpus callosum
subacute optic neuritis and sensory loss in a 26 year old afebrile woman with periventricular Dawson fingers

hq_q.s: A 42 year old woman has fever, headache and left-sided weakness. CT head shows a brain abscess with surrounding swelling.
hq_q.w: A mass with oedema makes LP dangerous because of herniation. Diagnose with imaging, cultures and aspiration of the abscess.
hq_q.f: No mass on imaging and no raised pressure → LP is safe.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation carries the greatest risk?

tm.m: A mass with oedema makes lumbar puncture risk herniation
tm.g: Brain abscess with mass effect: avoid lumbar puncture
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Blood cultures (Used for: Fever with a source unknown, sepsis, endocarditis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Dental review (Essential source-control assessment rather than a contraindicated investigation)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Echocardiogram (Used for: Murmur, heart failure, new AF)
the presentation instead showed features specific to MRI head (MRI is useful)
x: Used for: Fever with a source unknown, sepsis, endocarditis
Essential source-control assessment rather than a contraindicated investigation
Used for: Murmur, heart failure, new AF
MRI is useful.

hq_q.s:
A 36 year old man presents with a 5-day history of fever, left-sided headache and receptive dysphasia. For 8 months he has had a foul-smelling purulent discharge from his left ear.
Temperature 38.4°C, pulse rate 98 bpm. Otoscopy shows a perforation in the attic of the left tympanic membrane. Contrast CT head shows a 3.5 cm ring-enhancing abscess in the left temporal lobe.
hq_q.w: Contiguous brain abscesses localise next to their source: chronic suppurative otitis media and mastoiditis spread through the tegmen tympani into the ipsilateral temporal lobe or cerebellum, whereas sinus and dental infections seed the frontal lobe.
hq_q.f: Solitary frontal lobe brain abscess -> contiguous spread from frontal/ethmoidal sinusitis or odontogenic infection.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely primary source of infection?

c: foul-smelling purulent discharge from his left ear
attic of the left tympanic membrane
tm.m: Chronic middle ear and mastoid infection erodes upward through the thin bony roof of the middle ear (tegmen tympani) or spreads via emissary veins directly into the overlying temporal lobe.
tm.g: Temporal lobe (or cerebellar) brain abscess + chronic discharging ear -> otitis media / mastoiditis
x: Frontal sinusitis spreads through the posterior wall of the frontal sinus to produce an anterior frontal lobe abscess rather than a temporal lobe abscess.
Haematogenous seeding from infective endocarditis produces multiple small abscesses distributed across the middle cerebral artery grey-white matter junction in both hemispheres.
Odontogenic infections spread anteriorly into the frontal lobe rather than the posterior temporal lobe, and he has chronic purulent ear discharge.
Haematogenous spread from bronchiectasis or a lung abscess causes multiple bilateral abscesses rather than a single temporal lobe abscess above a discharging ear.
f: a right anterior frontal lobe abscess following purulent right frontal sinusitis
multiple bilateral grey-white junction abscesses in an intravenous drug user with a new regurgitant heart murmur
a solitary anterior frontal lobe abscess 2 weeks after extraction of an abscessed upper molar tooth
multiple cerebral abscesses in a patient with chronic bronchiectasis and clubbing

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old woman is reviewed in the first-seizure neurology clinic after experiencing two unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizures over the past 3 months, each followed by tongue biting and 20 minutes of post-ictal confusion. She is sexually active and not currently planning pregnancy, but uses barrier contraception only.
Neurological examination and brain MRI are normal. Interictal EEG demonstrates generalised polyspike-and-wave discharges.
hq_q.w: In women and girls of childbearing potential with idiopathic generalised epilepsy (generalised tonic-clonic seizures), NICE recommends lamotrigine or levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy. Sodium valproate is contraindicated due to its high risk of major congenital malformations (10%) and neurodevelopmental impairment (30-40%).
hq_q.f: Childhood absence seizures alone without tonic-clonic seizures -> oral ethosuximide first-line.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line antiseizure medication?

tm.m: Lamotrigine stabilises presynaptic voltage-gated sodium channels to suppress generalised spike-wave discharges without carrying the severe teratogenic risk of sodium valproate.
tm.g: Generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy in a woman of childbearing potential -> lamotrigine (or levetiracetam)
x: Carbamazepine is a narrow-spectrum sodium channel blocker used for focal seizures and trigeminal neuralgia; it can exacerbate generalised spike-wave, myoclonic and absence seizures.
Ethosuximide only blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels to control absence seizures and provides zero protection against generalised tonic-clonic convulsions.
Phenytoin has zero-order saturable pharmacokinetics, causes gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism and fetal hydantoin syndrome, and can worsen generalised epilepsies.

MHRA and NICE regulations prohibit starting sodium valproate in women of childbearing potential unless all other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated and the Pregnancy Prevention Programme is in place.
f: first-line treatment of trigeminal neuralgia or focal-onset seizures in a male patient
isolated childhood absence epilepsy (3 Hz spike-and-wave) without generalised tonic-clonic seizures
second-line intravenous infusion for established convulsive status epilepticus in hospital
generalised tonic-clonic or juvenile myoclonic epilepsy when all other antiseizure medications have failed and the Pregnancy Prevention Programme is fulfilled

hq_q.s:
An 8 year old girl is reviewed with a 3-month history of brief staring episodes occurring up to 30 times a day. She pauses mid-sentence for 8 seconds with eyelid flutter and then continues talking. She has never had a tonic-clonic convulsion.
Hyperventilation triggers a typical episode, and EEG shows bilateral 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges.
hq_q.w: NICE recommends oral ethosuximide as first-line monotherapy for childhood absence epilepsy (3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG), as it selectively blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels without valproate's teratogenic and metabolic risks.
hq_q.f: Absence seizures accompanied by generalised tonic-clonic seizures -> lamotrigine or levetiracetam (or valproate if eligible).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug?

c: brief staring episodes occurring up to 30 times a day
tm.m: Ethosuximide inhibits low-threshold T-type voltage-gated calcium currents in thalamic relay neurones, abolishing the 3 Hz oscillatory burst firing that generates absence seizures.
tm.g: Isolated childhood absence epilepsy (3 Hz spike-and-wave) -> ethosuximide first-line
x: Carbamazepine is contraindicated in absence epilepsy because it synchronises thalamocortical loops and precipitates absence status epilepticus.
Gabapentin is ineffective in generalised spike-and-wave epilepsies and can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures.
Phenytoin exacerbates typical absence seizures and causes cosmetic and metabolic toxicity in children.
Vigabatrin inhibits GABA transaminase, causes irreversible concentric visual field constriction, and worsens typical absence seizures.
f: focal-onset aware or impaired awareness seizures arising from a temporal lobe focus
peripheral diabetic neuropathic pain or post-herpetic neuralgia in an adult
second-line intravenous therapy for benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive status epilepticus
infantile spasms (West syndrome) with hypsarrhythmia associated with tuberous sclerosis

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old man with epilepsy has been having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure for 5 minutes in the emergency department. He has IV access.
Capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L (4.0–7.8). SpO2 92% on high-flow oxygen.
hq_q.w: Convulsive status: a benzodiazepine at 5 minutes, repeated once after 5 to 10 minutes if needed. Buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam if there is no IV access.
hq_q.f: Two benzodiazepine doses given and still fitting → IV levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first drug?

tm.m: Benzodiazepines are the fastest way to stop a prolonged seizure
tm.g: Convulsive status with IV access: IV lorazepam 4 mg
f: still fitting after two benzodiazepine doses
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV phenytoin (Phenytoin is second line)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV thiopental (Thiopental is for refractory status)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral clobazam (Oral drugs cannot be given in a seizure)
x: Ruled out here: requires still fitting after two benzodiazepine doses, whereas this patient has 5 minutes, IV access.
Phenytoin is second line.
Thiopental is for refractory status.
Oral drugs cannot be given in a seizure.

hq_q.s: A 61 year old man with motor neurone disease has lost 8% of his body weight in 3 months. Meals take over an hour and he coughs when he drinks. His forced vital capacity is 70% of predicted. He wants to stay at home.
hq_q.w: NICE advises discussing gastrostomy early in MND, when weight is falling and swallowing is unsafe, and placing it before breathing declines further, because the procedure becomes riskier as vital capacity falls.
hq_q.f: Same man with morning headaches, daytime sleepiness and a falling vital capacity → non-invasive ventilation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate nutritional plan?

tm.m: Bulbar weakness makes swallowing slow and unsafe, so intake falls and aspiration risk rises
tm.g: MND with weight loss and unsafe swallow: gastrostomy, early
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to High-calorie oral supplements (Supplements help early on, but he is coughing on fluids and losing weight, so oral intake is unsafe and not enough)

the presentation instead showed features specific to Long-term nasogastric feeding (Nasogastric tubes are uncomfortable and easily displaced; they are a short-term bridge, not a long-term plan at home)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Parenteral nutrition (His gut works; parenteral feeding carries line infection and metabolic risks and is not used here)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Thickened fluids and review (Thickened fluids can ease coughing, but they will not reverse ongoing weight loss)
x: Supplements help early on, but he is coughing on fluids and losing weight, so oral intake is unsafe and not enough.
Nasogastric tubes are uncomfortable and easily displaced; they are a short-term bridge, not a long-term plan at home.
His gut works; parenteral feeding carries line infection and metabolic risks and is not used here.
Thickened fluids can ease coughing, but they will not reverse ongoing weight loss.

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old man attends the neurology clinic after electromyography and nerve conduction studies confirm amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the commonest form of motor neurone disease. He has mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs in his right arm and both legs, with preserved forced vital capacity (84% predicted).
He is keen to start disease-modifying pharmacotherapy to slow disease progression.
hq_q.w: Riluzole (50 mg twice daily) is the only NICE-recommended disease-modifying drug for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, inhibiting presynaptic glutamate release to reduce excitotoxicity and extend survival by 2 to 3 months.
hq_q.f: Nocturnal hypoventilation with morning headaches and FVC <50% predicted -> non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP), which confers a larger survival benefit.
hq_q.ql: Which medication is recommended by NICE to modestly prolong survival in this condition?

c: mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs
tm.m: Riluzole blocks tetrodotoxin-sensitive sodium channels on glutamatergic nerve terminals and enhances astrocytic glutamate uptake, attenuating NMDA/AMPA excitotoxicity on anterior horn cells.
tm.g: Disease-modifying drug that prolongs survival in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis -> riluzole
x: Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist that provides symptomatic relief of muscle spasticity in MND but has no effect on motor neurone degeneration or survival.
Intravenous immunoglobulin is effective in multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block and Guillain-Barre syndrome, but has no benefit in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
Corticosteroids have no neuroprotective effect in motor neurone disease and accelerate muscle wasting via steroid myopathy.
Pyridostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used for myasthenia gravis; it does not prolong survival in MND and worsens bulbar sialorrhoea.
f: symptomatic relief of painful upper motor neurone lower-limb spasticity
multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block on nerve conduction studies and anti-GM1 antibodies
autoimmune inflammatory myopathy (polymyositis or dermatomyositis) with raised creatine kinase
symptomatic treatment of fatigable weakness in acetylcholine-receptor-positive myasthenia gravis

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old woman with motor neurone disease attends the respiratory clinic with a 4-week history of unrefreshing sleep, vivid nightmares, early-morning throbbing headaches and daytime somnolence.
Respiratory rate is 22 breaths/min and SpO2 is 94% breathing air. She uses her sternocleidomastoid accessory muscles and has orthopnoea. Forced vital capacity is 48% of predicted, and morning venous bicarbonate is 32 mmol/L (22-30).
hq_q.w: Diaphragmatic weakness in motor neurone disease causes nocturnal hypoventilation (morning headaches, somnolence, FVC <50% predicted and raised bicarbonate). Nocturnal non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) improves both quality of life and survival.
hq_q.f: Troublesome pooling and drooling of saliva (sialorrhoea) -> oral glycopyrronium bromide or transdermal hyoscine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate intervention?

c: early-morning throbbing headaches and daytime somnolence
Forced vital capacity is 48% of predicted
tm.m: Loss of phrenic lower motor neurones weakens the diaphragm, causing supine REM-sleep alveolar hypoventilation, hypercapnic cerebral vasodilatation (morning headache) and renal bicarbonate retention.
tm.g: Motor neurone disease with nocturnal hypoventilation (morning headache, FVC <50%, raised bicarbonate) -> non-invasive ventilation
x: Riluzole has a fixed dose of 50 mg twice daily, does not improve diaphragmatic mechanics, and dose escalation causes hepatotoxicity.
Non-invasive positive-pressure mask ventilation (BiPAP) is the first-line standard of care for neuromuscular hypoventilation rather than invasive tracheostomy.
Benzodiazepines depress central medullary respiratory drive and upper airway tone, which can precipitate fatal hypercapnic respiratory arrest in neuromuscular weakness.
Giving supplemental oxygen alone without ventilatory pressure support blunts hypoxic respiratory drive and worsens hypercapnic carbon dioxide narcosis.
f: never recommended; riluzole dosing is fixed at 50 mg twice daily
acute upper airway obstruction or prolonged intensive care mechanical ventilation weaning
never appropriate for sleep disturbance caused by neuromuscular nocturnal hypoventilation
long-term oxygen therapy in severe hypoxic COPD without hypercapnia

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old woman presents with a 2-month history of difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a low chair and brushing her hair, with 4 kg weight loss.
Examination shows grade 3/5 proximal shoulder and hip weakness, a violaceous (purple) oedematous rash over her upper eyelids, and erythematous scaly papules over her metacarpophalangeal knuckles. Serum creatine kinase is 2,400 IU/L (25-200).
hq_q.w: Dermatomyositis presents with symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, raised creatine kinase, a violaceous heliotrope eyelid rash and Gottron papules over the knuckles. Because ~25% of adult cases are paraneoplastic, screen thoroughly for underlying malignancy.
hq_q.f: Pain and morning stiffness in shoulders and hips in a 72-year-old with raised ESR and normal creatine kinase -> polymyalgia rheumatica.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a low chair
violaceous (purple) oedematous rash over her upper eyelids
erythematous scaly papules over her metacarpophalangeal
tm.m: Complement-mediated microangiopathy (C5b-9 membrane attack complex deposition) in perimysial capillaries causes perifascicular muscle fibre atrophy and cutaneous interface dermatitis.
tm.g: Symmetrical proximal weakness + raised CK + heliotrope eyelid rash + Gottron papules -> dermatomyositis
x: Inclusion body myositis affects older men (>60 years) with asymmetrical weakness of the deep finger flexors and quadriceps, mildly raised CK and no skin rash.
Polymyalgia rheumatica causes proximal aching and morning stiffness without true muscle fibre necrosis, so serum creatine kinase is strictly normal and there is no heliotrope rash.
Statin myopathy causes muscle aching and weakness in patients taking HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, without a heliotrope eyelid rash or Gottron papules.
Systemic lupus erythematosus causes a malar butterfly rash sparing the nasolabial folds and arthralgia rather than Gottron papules over the knuckles and a CK of 2,400 IU/L.
f: a 70 year old man with slowly progressive asymmetrical weakness of grip (finger flexion) and knee extension without a rash
aching morning stiffness of the shoulders and pelvic girdle with ESR 85 mm/hr and a normal creatine kinase of 90 IU/L
symmetrical thigh aching and raised CK starting 6 weeks after initiating atorvastatin 80 mg daily, with no rash
photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, oral ulcers, pleuritis and positive anti-dsDNA antibodies

hq_q.s:
A 65 year old man presents with a 3-week history of bilateral aching and cramping in his thighs and shoulders. Two months ago he started atorvastatin 80 mg nightly after a myocardial infarction.
Examination shows mild thigh tenderness with 5/5 power. Serum creatine kinase is 2,100 IU/L (10.5 times the upper limit of normal, 25-200), creatinine is 86 µmol/L and TSH is 1.8 mU/L.
o: Continue atorvastatin and recheck in 3 months
hq_q.w: If a patient on a statin develops muscle pain with a serum creatine kinase exceeding 5 times the upper limit of normal, stop the statin immediately and recheck CK; a lower dose or alternative statin can be tried once resolved.
hq_q.f: Tolerable muscle aches with a serum creatine kinase <5 times the upper limit of normal -> reassure or trial a short statin holiday / lower dose.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

c: bilateral aching and cramping in his thighs
creatine kinase is 2,100 IU/L (10.5 times the upper limit of normal
tm.m: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition depletes intramuscular ubiquinone and prenylated proteins, causing dose-dependent myocyte toxicity that progresses to rhabdomyolysis if continued when CK >5x ULN.
tm.g: Muscle symptoms on a statin with CK >5x upper limit of normal -> stop the statin immediately
x: NICE explicitly recommends against prescribing coenzyme Q10 or vitamin D for statin-related myopathy, and continuing atorvastatin with a CK >10x ULN risks rhabdomyolysis.
Continuing high-intensity atorvastatin when serum CK is >10 times the upper limit of normal risks progression to acute rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuric kidney injury.
When CK exceeds 5 times the upper limit of normal, the statin must be stopped completely rather than merely reduced in dose until CK returns to baseline.
An alternative statin must not be started on the same day while active myonecrosis (CK 2,100 IU/L) is present; wait until symptoms and CK have fully normalised.
f: never recommended by NICE for the management of statin-associated muscle symptoms
an asymptomatic patient with a normal baseline CK attending for routine 3-month lipid review
reintroducing lipid-lowering therapy at a lower dose AFTER stopping the statin and confirming CK has returned to normal
switching to a water-soluble statin 4 weeks later once muscle symptoms have resolved and serum CK is normal

hq_q.s:
A 46 year old woman with myasthenia gravis is admitted with worsening weakness and difficulty swallowing over 2 days.
Respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97% breathing air. Her voice is weak.
hq_q.w: In neuromuscular weakness, saturations stay normal until late. FVC falls first. Under 15 to 20 ml per kg means intensive care.
hq_q.f: Weakness that improves with repeated effort in a smoker → Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which measure is most important to monitor her breathing?

tm.m: Saturations stay normal until breathing muscles fail late
tm.g: Neuromuscular weakness: monitor forced vital capacity
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Arterial gas (Hypercapnia is a late sign when respiratory failure is already imminent)
the presentation instead showed features specific to ECG (An ECG does not measure respiratory muscle weakness)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oxygen saturation on air (Falls only late in neuromuscular hypoventilation once atelectasis or hypoxia develops)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Peak flow (Peak flow is for airway obstruction)
x: Hypercapnia is a late sign when respiratory failure is already imminent
An ECG does not measure respiratory muscle weakness.
Falls only late in neuromuscular hypoventilation once atelectasis or hypoxia develops
Peak flow is for airway obstruction.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man who sits with his legs crossed presents with a 2-week history of his right foot slapping the ground when walking. He has no back pain.
Examination of the right leg shows grade 2/5 weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, extensor hallucis longus and ankle eversion, while ankle inversion and plantarflexion are 5/5. Dorsal foot sensation is reduced and the ankle jerk is normal.
hq_q.w: Compression of the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck causes foot drop with weak ankle dorsiflexion (deep peroneal) and weak ankle eversion (superficial peroneal), while sparing tibial-innervated ankle inversion and the ankle reflex.
hq_q.f: Foot drop accompanied by weak ankle inversion, radiating sciatica and reduced sensation on the medial foot -> L5 radiculopathy.
hq_q.ql: Which nerve or nerve root is affected?

c: weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, extensor hallucis longus and ankle eversion
tm.m: Compression of the common peroneal nerve against the fibular neck impairs both the anterior compartment (dorsiflexors) and lateral compartment (peroneus longus/brevis evertors) while sparing the tibial nerve (tibialis posterior invertor).
tm.g: Foot drop + weak dorsiflexion AND weak eversion + spared ankle inversion + normal ankle reflex -> common peroneal nerve palsy
x: The femoral nerve (L2-L4) supplies quadriceps femoris (knee extension), iliacus and the saphenous nerve over the medial shin, not ankle dorsiflexion or eversion.
An isolated deep peroneal nerve lesion weakens ankle dorsiflexion and numbs only the first dorsal web space, sparing ankle eversion (superficial peroneal nerve).
An L5 radiculopathy weakens tibialis posterior (ankle inversion) as well as dorsiflexion and causes radicular low back-to-leg pain, whereas ankle inversion is 5/5 here.
A complete sciatic nerve lesion paralyses both the tibial division (plantarflexion, ankle inversion and absent ankle jerk) and the common peroneal division.
f: weak knee extension, absent patellar reflex and numbness over the anterior thigh and medial calf after pelvic surgery
anterior tarsal tunnel entrapment causing numbness restricted to the first dorsal web space with normal ankle eversion
low back pain radiating down the lateral leg with foot drop AND weak ankle inversion (tibialis posterior)
flail foot with absent plantarflexion, absent dorsiflexion, weak knee flexion and an absent ankle reflex after posterior hip dislocation

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman presents with a 5-day history of symmetrical weakness that began in her feet and has ascended to her thighs, with distal tingling. She had bloody diarrhoea 2 weeks ago.
Examination reveals grade 3/5 lower-limb weakness, generalized areflexia at the ankles and knees, and reduced distal vibration sense. Forced vital capacity is 3.1 litres.
hq_q.w: Guillain-Barre syndrome follows 1 to 3 weeks after Campylobacter jejuni enteritis, presenting with ascending symmetrical flaccid weakness and areflexia. Monitor forced vital capacity (FVC) closely and treat with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange.
hq_q.f: Progressive or relapsing demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy evolving for >8 weeks -> chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: began in her feet and has ascended to her thighs
tm.m: Molecular mimicry between Campylobacter jejuni lipooligosaccharides and peripheral nerve gangliosides triggers macrophage- and antibody-mediated demyelination of spinal roots and peripheral nerves.
tm.g: Acute ascending symmetrical weakness + areflexia 2 weeks after diarrhoea -> Guillain-Barre syndrome
x: Transverse myelitis is a spinal cord lesion causing a distinct truncal sensory level, early urinary retention and upper motor neurone hyperreflexia/upgoing plantars.
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) by definition progresses steadily or relapses over more than 8 weeks rather than presenting 5 days after gastroenteritis.
Motor neurone disease evolves over months without sensory paraesthesiae and produces mixed upper motor neurone hyperreflexia and fasciculations rather than acute post-diarrhoeal areflexia.
Myasthenia gravis causes diurnal fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness with normal tendon reflexes and no sensory tingling.
f: paraparesis with a sharp T8 pinprick sensory level, urinary retention and extensor plantar responses
symmetrical proximal and distal weakness with areflexia progressing steadily over 4 months
a 64 year old with a 6-month history of fasciculations, brisk reflexes, extensor plantars and normal sensation
fatigable bilateral ptosis and diplopia worsening in the evening with completely normal deep tendon reflexes

hq_q.s: A 28 year old man cut his wrist on glass. He now has marked clawing of the ring and little fingers.
o: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
hq_q.w: The ulnar paradox: at the wrist, the long finger flexors still work and pull the fingers into a claw. Higher up, those flexors are weak too, so there is less clawing.
hq_q.f: The ulnar nerve is damaged at the elbow → less clawing despite a more serious lesion.
hq_q.ql: Which nerve lesion is most likely?

tm.m: A low lesion spares flexor digitorum profundus, so the fingers curl more
tm.g: The ulnar paradox: an ulnar lesion at the wrist gives the most clawing
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Brachial plexus T1 root lesion (A T1 lesion causes global hand wasting)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Median nerve at the wrist (A median lesion causes thenar wasting)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Radial nerve in the spiral groove (A radial lesion causes wrist drop)
asked which higher lesion gives less clawing
x: A T1 lesion causes global hand wasting.
A median lesion causes thenar wasting.
A radial lesion causes wrist drop.
Ruled out here: requires asked which higher lesion gives less clawing, whereas this patient has cut his wrist on glass, A 28 year old man cut.

hq_q.s: A 74 year old woman with a history of hypertension presents to her GP with a 2-month history of progressive exertional breathlessness, two-pillow orthopnoea and bilateral ankle swelling that worsens by evening. On examination, her pulse is 92 bpm regular, blood pressure is 148/88 mmHg, her JVP is elevated at 5 cm, and she has fine bibasal inspiratory crackles and pitting oedema to both mid-shins. A 12-lead ECG shows voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy.
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG106 (Chronic heart failure in adults), N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is the mandatory first-line gatekeeper blood test in patients with suspected chronic heart failure. Ventricular wall stretch and volume overload trigger cardiomyocyte release of proBNP, which is cleaved into biologically active BNP and stable NT-proBNP. The NT-proBNP concentration determines referral urgency: >2,000 ng/L mandates specialist assessment and transthoracic echocardiography within 2 weeks; 400 to 2,000 ng/L mandates assessment within 6 weeks; <400 ng/L makes heart failure unlikely.
hq_q.f: Sudden breathlessness with pink frothy sputum and hypoxia → acute pulmonary oedema: sit up, oxygen, IV furosemide, no waiting for blood tests.
hq_q.ql: Under NICE guidelines, which initial blood test determines the urgency of her specialist heart failure referral and transthoracic echocardiogram?

c: exertional breathlessness, two-pillow orthopnoea and bilateral ankle swelling
tm.m: Left ventricular wall stretch and diastolic/systolic wall stress -> ventricular myocytes secrete proBNP -> serum NT-proBNP level stratifies 2-week (>2,000 ng/L) vs 6-week (400-2,000 ng/L) echo referral
tm.g: Suspected chronic heart failure gatekeeper test (NICE NG106) = serum NT-proBNP (>2,000 ng/L = 2-week echo; 400-2,000 ng/L = 6-week echo; <400 ng/L = HF unlikely)
x: A chest radiograph is performed to look for cardiomegaly, upper-lobe venous diversion or pulmonary pathology, but does not set the NICE 2-week vs 6-week echocardiogram referral window
Cardiac troponin T detects acute myocardial necrosis in suspected acute coronary syndrome or myocarditis rather than triaging chronic heart failure
D-dimer is used to exclude acute venous thromboembolism when the Wells score is low, not to triage chronic heart failure
Thyroid function tests are part of the baseline metabolic workup for breathlessness and oedema, but do not determine echocardiogram urgency
f: demonstrating alveolar bats-wing shadowing, Kerley B lines and cardiomegaly during an acute breathless presentation
excluding non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction in a patient presenting with 30 minutes of crushing central chest pain
ruling out acute pulmonary embolism in a patient with pleuritic chest pain and a two-level PE Wells score of 2
identifying reversible high-output or bradycardic endocrine precipitant in newly diagnosed heart failure or atrial fibrillation

hq_q.s: A 79 year old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents to his GP with a 6-week history of progressive breathlessness on walking 50 metres, three-pillow orthopnoea and bilateral ankle oedema. On examination, his pulse is 88 bpm, blood pressure is 138/82 mmHg, JVP is raised at 6 cm, and there are fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles and pitting ankle oedema. His serum NT-proBNP returns at 2,600 ng/L.
o: No referral is required as the level is below the diagnostic threshold
hq_q.w: NICE NG106 stratifies outpatient specialist heart failure assessment and transthoracic Doppler echocardiography according to serum NT-proBNP levels: an NT-proBNP level above 2,000 ng/L (>236 pmol/L) is associated with high short-term mortality and hospitalisation risk, mandating urgent specialist heart failure review and echocardiography within a maximum of 2 weeks. An NT-proBNP between 400 and 2,000 ng/L (47 to 236 pmol/L) requires specialist assessment and echocardiography within 6 weeks, whereas a level <400 ng/L makes heart failure unlikely.
hq_q.f: NT-proBNP 900 ng/L → within 6 weeks.
hq_q.ql: Under NICE guidelines, within what maximum timeframe must he undergo specialist heart failure assessment and transthoracic echocardiography?

c: breathlessness on walking 50 metres, three-pillow orthopnoea
tm.m: Markedly elevated NT-proBNP (>2,000 ng/L) reflects severe ventricular wall stress and high near-term decompensation risk -> NICE NG106 mandates echo + specialist review within 2 weeks
tm.g: NICE NG106 NT-proBNP referral timeframes: >2,000 ng/L = within 2 weeks; 400 to 2,000 ng/L = within 6 weeks; <400 ng/L = HF unlikely
