A score of 2 misses one of her three 1-point risk factors: age 65–74 (1 point), female sex (1 point) and hypertension (1 point).
A score of 4 would require an additional 1-point risk factor (such as diabetes) or age >=75 years (which scores 2 points).
A score of 5 would require prior stroke/TIA (2 points) or multiple additional comorbidities not present in this patient.
f: a 68 year old man with lone atrial fibrillation and no hypertension, diabetes or vascular disease
a 70 year old woman with atrial fibrillation and no hypertension, diabetes, heart failure or vascular disease
a 76 year old woman with hypertension and atrial fibrillation
a 70 year old woman with hypertension and a previous transient ischaemic attack

hq_q.s: A 74 year old man is diagnosed with persistent atrial fibrillation after presenting with mild exertional breathlessness. He has hypertension, stage 3a chronic kidney disease (eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m²) and a haemoglobin of 138 g/L. His CHA2DS2-VASc score is 2, and direct oral anticoagulation with apixaban is recommended. In accordance with NICE guidance, a formal bleeding risk score is calculated to identify modifiable risk factors.
hq_q.w: NICE NG196 recommends the ORBIT bleeding risk score (evaluating older age >=75, reduced haemoglobin/haematocrit, bleeding history, insufficient kidney function and antiplatelet treatment) when starting anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, as it predicts absolute bleeding risk more accurately than HAS-BLED.
hq_q.f: Estimating thromboembolic stroke risk in atrial fibrillation -> CHA2DS2-VASc score.
hq_q.ql: Which bleeding risk tool does NICE recommend before starting anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation?

tm.m: ORBIT weights five clinical variables (anaemia, prior bleed, age >=75, eGFR <60, antiplatelet therapy) to quantify major bleeding risk on anticoagulants.
tm.g: NICE-recommended bleeding risk score in atrial fibrillation -> ORBIT
x: CURB-65 stratifies mortality risk in community-acquired pneumonia, not major bleeding risk on anticoagulation.
The GRACE score estimates 6-month mortality in non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndromes to guide angiography timing.
QRISK3 estimates 10-year primary cardiovascular disease risk to guide statin initiation, not anticoagulant bleeding risk.
The Wells score estimates pre-test clinical probability of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.
f: assessing severity and inpatient admission need in community-acquired pneumonia
estimating 6-month mortality risk in a patient admitted with an NSTEMI
estimating 10-year cardiovascular risk in primary care before starting atorvastatin 20 mg
estimating pre-test probability of deep vein thrombosis in a patient with unilateral calf swelling

hq_q.s: A GP is calculating 10-year cardiovascular risk for several patients to decide on statin treatment.
hq_q.w: QRISK3 is for primary prevention. People with established cardiovascular disease, type 1 diabetes or familial hypercholesterolaemia are already high risk.
hq_q.f: A 60-year-old with no heart disease → QRISK3, treating at 10% or more.
hq_q.ql: Which patient should be offered a statin without a QRISK3 score?

tm.m: QRISK3 estimates first events, not risk after an event
tm.g: QRISK3 is not for someone who has already had an MI
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to A 38-year-old with a family history (QRISK3 is valid from age 25 to 84 and includes family history)
the presentation instead showed features specific to A 45-year-old smoker (Smoking status is an included primary prevention variable in QRISK3)
the presentation instead showed features specific to A 50-year-old with migraine (Migraine is specifically incorporated as a risk factor in QRISK3)
the presentation instead showed features specific to A 55-year-old with SLE (Systemic lupus erythematosus is specifically included inside the QRISK3 calculator)
x: QRISK3 is valid from age 25 to 84 and includes family history
Smoking status is an included primary prevention variable in QRISK3
Migraine is specifically incorporated as a risk factor in QRISK3
Systemic lupus erythematosus is specifically included inside the QRISK3 calculator

hq_q.s: A 42 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance 40 minutes after falling down a flight of concrete stairs. His airway is patent with a cervical collar in place, respiratory rate is 18 breaths/min, pulse 86 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. On neurological assessment, he opens his eyes only to supraorbital pressure, utters incomprehensible groans and withdraws his right arm from nailbed pressure.
hq_q.w: The Glasgow Coma Scale sums eye, verbal and motor responses: eye opening to pain scores 2 (E2), incomprehensible sounds score 2 (V2), and flexion withdrawal from pain scores 4 (M4), giving a total GCS of 8/15.
hq_q.f: Localising to supraorbital pressure instead of withdrawing -> motor score 5 (M5), giving a total GCS of 9.
hq_q.ql: What is his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?

c: opens his eyes only to supraorbital pressure
withdraws his right arm from nailbed pressure
tm.m: Summing Eye (E2) + Verbal (V2) + Motor (M4) components quantifies impaired consciousness at the critical airway threshold of 8.
tm.g: E2 (pain) + V2 (sounds) + M4 (withdrawal) -> GCS 8
x: A GCS of 10 would require either eye opening to speech (E3) with localising (M5) or confused speech (V4) with withdrawal (M4).
A GCS of 6 would require abnormal flexion (M3) or extension (M2) to pain rather than withdrawal from pain (M4).
A GCS of 7 would occur if his motor response were abnormal decorticate flexion to pain (M3) alongside E2 and V2.
A GCS of 9 would require him to localise to a painful stimulus (M5) or use inappropriate words (V3) alongside E2.
f: eyes opening to speech (E3), inappropriate words (V3) and withdrawal from pain (M4)
eyes opening to pain (E2), incomprehensible sounds (V2) and decerebrate extension to pain (M2)
eyes opening to pain (E2), incomprehensible sounds (V2) and abnormal flexion to pain (M3)
eyes opening to pain (E2), incomprehensible sounds (V2) and localising to supraorbital pain (M5)

hq_q.s: A 66 year old man on the surgical ward is 3 days post-laparoscopic anterior resection and becomes acutely breathless and sweaty. He is alert and oriented, breathing room air (SpO2 scale 1). Nursing staff record a full set of physiological observations on his National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) chart, and an urgent clinical review is triggered because a single parameter scores 3 points (red score).
hq_q.w: On the RCP NEWS2 chart, a single parameter scores 3 points ('red score') when respiratory rate is >=25 or <=8/min, SpO2 <=91% (scale 1), systolic BP <=90 or >=220 mmHg, pulse >=131 or <=40 bpm, temperature <=35.0°C, or new confusion.
hq_q.f: Respiratory rate of 21 to 24 breaths/min -> scores 2 points on NEWS2.
hq_q.ql: Which of the following individual observations scores 3 points by itself on NEWS2?

tm.m: Tachypnoea >=25 breaths/min is a sensitive early physiological marker of critical illness and scores the maximum 3 points on NEWS2.
tm.g: Respiratory rate >=25 breaths/min -> Scores 3 points on NEWS2
x: A heart rate of 91–110 bpm scores 1 point on NEWS2; a heart rate must reach >=131 bpm (or <=40 bpm) to score 3 points.
On NEWS2 SpO2 scale 1, an oxygen saturation of 94–95% scores 1 point; 3 points requires a saturation of <=91%.
A systolic blood pressure of 101–110 mmHg scores 1 point on NEWS2; 3 points requires <=90 mmHg or >=220 mmHg.
A temperature of 38.1–39.0°C scores 1 point on NEWS2 (and >=39.1°C scores 2 points); only hypothermia <=35.0°C scores 3 points.
f: a sinus tachycardia of 136 beats/min scoring 3 points on the heart rate parameter
an oxygen saturation of 90% on room air in a patient without hypercapnic respiratory failure
hypotension with a systolic blood pressure of 86 mmHg scoring 3 points
hypothermia with a core temperature of 34.8°C scoring 3 points

hq_q.s: A 72 year old man with severe COPD and previous admissions for decompensated hypercapnic (type 2) respiratory failure is admitted with an infective exacerbation. Arterial blood gas on room air shows pH 7.38, PaCO2 6.8 kPa and PaO2 7.9 kPa, and his prescribed target oxygen saturation is 88–92%. On routine ward observations, his SpO2 is 89% breathing room air.
o: Add 2 extra points for chronic COPD
Leave the SpO2 row blank on the chart
hq_q.w: NEWS2 includes a dedicated oxygen saturation scale (SpO2 scale 2) for patients with confirmed hypercapnic (type 2) respiratory failure and a prescribed target range of 88–92%. On scale 2, an SpO2 of 88–92% (or >=93% on air) scores 0 points.
hq_q.f: SpO2 of 95% while receiving supplemental oxygen on SpO2 scale 2 -> scores 2 points for hyperoxia risk (plus 2 points for supplemental O2).
hq_q.ql: How should his oxygen saturation be recorded on the NEWS2 chart?

tm.m: SpO2 scale 2 calibrates scoring to the 88–92% target range, preventing inappropriate oxygen escalation and CO2 retention.
tm.g: Confirmed type 2 respiratory failure (target 88–92%) with SpO2 89% on air -> Score 0 points using SpO2 scale 2
x: NEWS2 adds 2 points for supplemental oxygen therapy, not for the diagnosis of COPD itself.
Omitting any of the six core physiological parameters invalidates the aggregate NEWS2 score and compromises patient safety monitoring.
Scale 1 is for patients without hypercapnic respiratory failure (target 94–98%), where 94–95% scores 1 point and 89% would score 3 points.
Using scale 1 in a patient with confirmed hypercapnic respiratory failure falsely scores 89% as 3 points and risks inappropriate high-flow oxygen administration.
f: a patient requiring supplemental oxygen via a 24% Venturi mask to maintain target saturations
incomplete observation charting that fails RCP NEWS2 compliance standards
an SpO2 of 94% on room air in a patient with normal baseline carbon dioxide levels
an SpO2 of 89% on room air in an asthma or pneumonia patient without chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man with hypertension and a 30 pack-year smoking history presents with a 1-hour history of severe, crushing central chest pain radiating to his jaw and left arm, associated with sweating and nausea. Pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. A 12-lead ECG demonstrates 4 mm convex ST-segment elevation in leads V1, V2, V3 and V4.
hq_q.w: ST-segment elevation in precordial leads V1 to V4 localises to the anteroseptal and anterior left ventricular wall (left anterior descending artery). Leads II, III and aVF reflect the inferior wall; I, aVL, V5 and V6 reflect the lateral wall.
hq_q.f: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF -> inferior left ventricular wall (usually right coronary artery).
hq_q.ql: Which myocardial territory is affected?

c: ST-segment elevation in leads V1, V2, V3 and V4
tm.m: Precordial leads V1–V4 directly overlie the interventricular septum and anterior wall supplied by the left anterior descending artery.
tm.g: ST elevation in V1–V4 -> Anterior left ventricular wall
x: Inferior STEMI produces ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF, usually from right coronary artery occlusion.
Lateral STEMI produces ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6, typically from left circumflex artery occlusion.
Posterior myocardial infarction causes horizontal ST depression, tall broad R waves and upright T waves in leads V1 to V3, confirmed by ST elevation in V7–V9.
Right ventricular infarction accompanies inferior STEMI and is confirmed by ST-segment elevation in right-sided precordial lead V4R.
f: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL
ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 due to left circumflex artery occlusion
horizontal ST depression and tall R waves in leads V1 to V3 with ST elevation in posterior leads V7 to V9
hypotension, raised JVP, clear lung fields and ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF and V4R

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 is admitted with a chest infection. He has no chest pain.
Pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 136/82 mmHg. The ECG shows no ischaemic changes.
hq_q.w: A raised troponin that stays flat (no significant rise or fall between samples) without ischaemic symptoms or ECG change is chronic myocardial injury, common in chronic kidney disease. An MI needs a rise or fall with evidence of ischaemia.
hq_q.f: Troponin rising from 52 to 410 ng/L with ST depression → NSTEMI.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely explanation for the troponin?

tm.m: Reduced clearance and ongoing low-grade myocyte damage keep troponin steadily raised
tm.g: Raised but flat troponin, no ischaemia: chronic injury
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Acute myocarditis (Myocarditis causes chest pain or heart failure with a dynamic troponin, often after a viral illness)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Laboratory error (Two consistent results make error unlikely; this pattern is common in CKD)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Type 1 myocardial infarction (An MI needs a significant rise or fall in troponin plus symptoms or ECG signs of ischaemia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Unstable angina (Unstable angina causes ischaemic chest pain with a normal troponin)
x: Myocarditis causes chest pain or heart failure with a dynamic troponin, often after a viral illness.
Two consistent results make error unlikely; this pattern is common in CKD.
An MI needs a significant rise or fall in troponin plus symptoms or ECG signs of ischaemia.
Unstable angina causes ischaemic chest pain with a normal troponin.

hq_q.s: A 28 year old man had a viral upper respiratory infection 1 week ago. For 2 days he has had sharp central chest pain that worsens when lying flat and improves sitting forward. Temperature is 37.8°C, pulse 96 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. Auscultation reveals a scratchy triphasic sound at the left lower sternal edge. ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation and PR-segment depression.
hq_q.w: Acute pericarditis presents with sharp positional chest pain relieved by sitting forward, a pericardial friction rub, and widespread concave ('saddle-shaped') ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression across non-anatomical territories. First-line treatment is an NSAID plus colchicine.
hq_q.f: Localized convex ST elevation with reciprocal ST depression -> acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: worsens when lying flat and improves sitting forward
widespread concave ST elevation and PR-segment depression
tm.m: Diffuse epicardial and atrial subepicardial inflammation produces widespread concave ST elevation and atrial PR-segment depression.
tm.g: Positional chest pain relieved sitting forward + friction rub + widespread concave ST elevation and PR depression -> Acute pericarditis
x: Anterior STEMI causes convex ST elevation restricted to a coronary arterial territory (V1–V4) with reciprocal ST depression, not widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression.
Brugada syndrome causes coved ST-segment elevation (>=2 mm) followed by a negative T wave confined to right precordial leads V1–V2 without chest pain or friction rub.
A ventricular aneurysm causes persistent ST elevation weeks after a transmural myocardial infarction with deep Q waves, not acute positional pain with PR depression.
Hyperkalaemia causes tall tented T waves, flattened P waves and QRS widening rather than saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression and a pericardial rub.
f: crushing exertional chest pain with convex ST elevation in leads V1 to V4 and reciprocal inferior ST depression
syncope in a young man with coved ST elevation and T-wave inversion in leads V1 and V2
persistent anterior ST elevation and deep Q waves 8 weeks after an anterior myocardial infarction
tall tented T waves, broadened QRS complexes and serum potassium 7.1 mmol/L in acute kidney injury

hq_q.s: A 55 year old postmenopausal woman presents to her GP with an 8-week history of persistent abdominal bloating, early satiety and lower abdominal discomfort occurring most days of the week. She reports increased urinary urgency but no dysuria, haematuria, rectal bleeding or change in bowel habit. Abdominal palpation, bimanual pelvic examination and urine dipstick are normal.
hq_q.w: NICE NG12 recommends measuring serum CA-125 in primary care for women (especially >=50 years) with persistent or frequent (>=12 times/month) bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain or urinary urgency. If CA-125 is >=35 IU/mL, arrange an urgent pelvic ultrasound.
hq_q.f: Palpable pelvic mass or ascites on examination -> urgent 2-week-wait gynaecological oncology referral directly.
hq_q.ql: According to NICE suspected cancer guidelines, which initial investigation should be arranged in primary care?

c: occurring most days of the week
tm.m: Coelomic epithelium-derived serous ovarian carcinomas shed mucin glycoprotein CA-125 into the circulation.
tm.g: Persistent bloating/early satiety in a woman >=50 with normal exam -> Serum CA-125 first
x: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a tumour marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumours, not epithelial ovarian cancer.
CA 19-9 is associated with pancreatic and biliary tract adenocarcinoma, not primary care investigation of persistent bloating in women over 50.
Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is used for postoperative surveillance of colorectal cancer, not primary diagnosis of ovarian malignancy.
Inhibin B is a specialist marker for rare granulosa cell ovarian tumours and is not the first-line NICE test for suspected ovarian cancer.
f: surveillance or investigation of a liver mass in a patient with cirrhosis or a young patient with a germ cell tumour
monitoring response to treatment in confirmed pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
postoperative surveillance for recurrence following curative resection of colorectal adenocarcinoma
specialist endocrine follow-up of a confirmed granulosa cell tumour of the ovary

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man attends colorectal follow-up clinic 12 months after undergoing an uncomplicated laparoscopic right hemicolectomy for a stage II (T3 N0 M0) caecal adenocarcinoma. He feels well with stable weight and normal bowel habit. Alongside his scheduled surveillance CT scan of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis, a serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) blood test is arranged.
o: Confirming primary diagnosis in symptomatic patients
Screening asymptomatic adults in the general population
hq_q.w: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) lacks the sensitivity and specificity required for population screening or primary diagnosis of colorectal cancer. Under NICE guidance, its principal role is regular postoperative surveillance after curative resection to detect hepatic or local recurrence early.
hq_q.f: Primary care triage of unexplained change in bowel habit -> quantitative faecal immunochemical test (FIT).
hq_q.ql: What is the primary clinical role of measuring serum CEA in colorectal cancer?

c: 12 months after undergoing an uncomplicated laparoscopic right hemicolectomy
tm.m: Serial postoperative CEA rises above baseline indicate recurrent or metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma shedding oncofetal glycoprotein.
tm.g: Clinical role of serum CEA in colorectal cancer -> Monitoring for postoperative disease recurrence
x: CEA has poor sensitivity and specificity in early colorectal cancer and can be raised in smoking, IBD, pancreatitis and cirrhosis.
Preoperative staging of colorectal cancer relies on contrast CT of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis (plus pelvic MRI for rectal cancer) and histology.
Population bowel cancer screening in the UK uses the home faecal immunochemical test (FIT), as serum CEA is neither sensitive nor specific enough.
Surveillance colonoscopy is scheduled routinely at 1 year and 3–5 years post-resection regardless of normal CEA levels to detect metachronous polyps.
f: investigating iron deficiency anaemia or rectal bleeding, where colonoscopy or CT colonography is required
preoperative staging of newly diagnosed colon cancer using contrast CT thorax, abdomen and pelvis
asymptomatic population bowel cancer screening using a home faecal immunochemical test
routine 1-year postoperative endoscopic clearance check for metachronous colonic adenomas

hq_q.s:
A 62 year old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis is having surveillance. He feels well.
His AFP has risen from 8 to 240 kU/L over 6 months.
hq_q.w: Cirrhosis carries a risk of HCC, so patients have 6-monthly ultrasound with or without AFP.
hq_q.f: A young man with a testicular lump and a raised AFP → non-seminomatous germ cell tumour.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?

tm.m: Hepatocellular carcinoma secretes AFP
tm.g: A rising AFP in cirrhosis suggests hepatocellular carcinoma
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Gallstones (Gallstones do not raise AFP)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hilar cholangiocarcinoma (Cholangiocarcinoma raises CA 19-9)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pancreatic cancer (Pancreatic cancer raises CA 19-9)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Testicular seminoma (Seminoma does not raise AFP)
x: Gallstones do not raise AFP.
Cholangiocarcinoma raises CA 19-9.
Pancreatic cancer raises CA 19-9.
Seminoma does not raise AFP.

hq_q.s: A 46 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds while lifting weights 7 hours ago. She has mild photophobia and nausea. Temperature is 36.7°C, BP 142/86 mmHg and GCS 15/15, with no focal neurological deficit. An urgent non-contrast CT head performed at 7 hours after symptom onset shows no intracranial haemorrhage.
o: At least 12 hours after headache onset
At least 1 week after headache onset
At least 2 hours after headache onset
At least 48 hours after headache onset
Immediately at 7 hours after headache onset
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG228, if a non-contrast CT head performed >6 hours after thunderclap headache onset is normal, lumbar puncture should be done at least 12 hours after symptom onset so erythrocytes lyse into bilirubin (xanthochromia) detectable on CSF spectrophotometry.
hq_q.f: Normal high-resolution non-contrast CT head performed within 6 hours of thunderclap headache onset -> SAH excluded without routine LP.
hq_q.ql: To allow reliable spectrophotometric detection of xanthochromia, when should the lumbar puncture be performed?

c: CT head performed at 7 hours after symptom onset shows no intracranial haemorrhage
tm.m: In vivo enzymatic conversion of subarachnoid oxyhaemoglobin to bilirubin by arachnoid macrophages takes up to 12 hours.
tm.g: Negative CT head performed >6 hours after thunderclap headache -> Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after headache onset
x: Deferring lumbar puncture for a week leaves a potentially ruptured intracranial aneurysm unsecured during the peak window for fatal rebleeding.
At 2 hours after onset, haemoglobin breakdown to bilirubin has not yet occurred in the subarachnoid space, making spectrophotometry unreliable.
Waiting 48 hours unnecessarily delays the diagnosis of aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage and exposes the patient to catastrophic rebleeding risk.
Performing a lumbar puncture before 12 hours have elapsed risks a false-negative xanthochromia result because red cell lysis into bilirubin is incomplete.
f: late presentation of thunderclap headache where CT angiogram or MR angiogram is required
early non-contrast CT head performed within 6 hours of thunderclap headache onset
delayed presentation where xanthochromia remains detectable for up to 2 weeks
suspected acute bacterial meningitis with fever and meningism requiring immediate CSF sampling before or shortly after antibiotics

hq_q.s: A 27 year old woman with a BMI of 35 kg/m² presents with a 2-month history of daily morning headaches, pulsatile tinnitus and brief dimming of vision on bending forward. Visual acuity is 6/6 bilaterally, and fundoscopy shows bilateral optic disc swelling. MRI brain and MR venography are normal. Lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position shows normal CSF white cells, protein and glucose.
o: Total CSF protein concentration of 3.0 g/L
hq_q.w: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension affects young women with obesity, causing raised intracranial pressure headaches, pulsatile tinnitus, visual obscurations and papilloedema. Diagnosis requires normal neuroimaging and venography, normal CSF constituents, and a raised CSF opening pressure (>25 cmCSF in adults).
hq_q.f: Unmatched IgG oligoclonal bands in CSF with periventricular white matter lesions -> multiple sclerosis.
hq_q.ql: Which lumbar puncture finding confirms the diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension?

c: normal CSF white cells, protein and glucose
tm.m: Impaired arachnoid villi CSF resorption or venous sinus hypertension elevates CSF opening pressure (>25 cmCSF) without cellular inflammation.
tm.g: Papilloedema + normal MRI/MRV + normal CSF composition -> Opening pressure >25 cmCSF (34 cmCSF) confirms IIH
x: A low CSF-to-serum glucose ratio (<0.5) indicates bacterial, tuberculous or fungal meningitis, whereas CSF biochemistry is normal in IIH.
An elevated CSF lymphocyte count indicates viral or tuberculous meningitis; IIH requires normal CSF cellularity.
Markedly elevated CSF protein occurs in Guillain-Barre syndrome, spinal block or tuberculous meningitis, whereas CSF protein is normal in IIH.
Unmatched oligoclonal bands in the CSF indicate intrathecal IgG synthesis in demyelinating disorders such as multiple sclerosis, not IIH.
f: subacute headache, cranial nerve palsies and basilar meningeal enhancement in tuberculous meningitis
acute headache, photophobia and neck stiffness due to enteroviral meningitis
ascending areflexic weakness with albuminocytological dissociation in Guillain-Barre syndrome
painful unilateral optic neuritis and periventricular white matter plaques in multiple sclerosis

hq_q.s: A 38 year old man presents with a 7-day history of progressive symmetrical weakness and tingling ascending from his feet to his thighs, 2 weeks after an episode of acute Campylobacter jejuni enteritis. Examination reveals grade 3/5 distal lower limb weakness and absent knee and ankle reflexes bilaterally. Lumbar puncture demonstrates a CSF protein of 1.8 g/L (0.15–0.45) and a white cell count of 2 lymphocytes/mm³ (<5).
hq_q.w: Albuminocytological dissociation-an elevated cerebrospinal fluid protein concentration alongside a normal CSF white blood cell count-is the classic hallmark of Guillain-Barré syndrome, reflecting inflammatory breakdown of the blood-nerve barrier at the spinal nerve roots.
hq_q.f: High CSF protein with marked lymphocytic pleocytosis and very low CSF glucose -> tuberculous meningitis.
hq_q.ql: Which term describes this characteristic cerebrospinal fluid pattern?

c: weakness and tingling ascending from his feet
CSF protein of 1.8 g/L (0.15–0.45) and a white cell count of 2
tm.m: Autoimmune demyelination of proximal spinal nerve roots increases blood-nerve barrier permeability, leaking albumin into CSF without cellular pleocytosis.
tm.g: High CSF protein + normal CSF white cell count in Guillain-Barré syndrome -> Albuminocytological dissociation
x: Polymorphonuclear pleocytosis with low glucose and high protein characterises acute bacterial meningitis, whereas CSF white cells are normal here.
Unmatched CSF oligoclonal IgG bands indicate central nervous system demyelination such as multiple sclerosis rather than acute inflammatory polyradiculoneuropathy.
Xanthochromia refers to bilirubin pigmentation of CSF following red blood cell lysis after subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Lymphocytic pleocytosis describes an elevated CSF lymphocyte count with normal or mildly raised protein in viral meningitis.
f: fever, neck stiffness, petechial rash and turbid CSF with 1500 neutrophils/mm³ in meningococcal meningitis
relapsing-remitting sensory and visual episodes with periventricular Dawson's fingers on brain MRI
sudden thunderclap headache with elevated CSF bilirubin on spectrophotometry 14 hours after onset
headache, photophobia and fever with 180 lymphocytes/mm³ and normal CSF glucose

hq_q.s: An 80 year old woman in a residential care home has been mildly confused and eating less for 2 days. She has no dysuria, frequency, incontinence, loin pain or fever. Temperature is 36.9°C, pulse 84 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Abdominal examination shows no suprapubic tenderness, though hard stool is palpable in the left iliac fossa. A urine dipstick is positive for leucocytes and nitrites.
o: Assess for non-urinary causes of delirium
Issue a back-up prescription for nitrofurantoin
Obtain an in-out catheter urine specimen
Repeat the urine dipstick every 24 hours
hq_q.w: Under NICE and UKHSA guidance, urine dipsticks should not be used to diagnose UTI in adults over 65 because asymptomatic bacteriuria is very common. Without focal urinary symptoms or sepsis, investigate other causes of delirium (such as constipation or dehydration).
hq_q.f: Non-pregnant woman aged 30 with acute dysuria, frequency and positive nitrites -> treat for lower urinary tract infection.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management step?

c: 80 year old woman in a residential care home
no dysuria, frequency, incontinence, loin pain or fever
tm.m: High prevalence of harmless bladder colonisation (asymptomatic bacteriuria) in older adults makes dipstick nitrites/leucocytes non-predictive of acute infection.
tm.g: Positive urine dipstick in an afebrile care home resident >65 with no urinary symptoms -> Assess for non-urinary causes of delirium
x: Prescribing antibiotics for asymptomatic bacteriuria in older care home residents does not improve delirium and increases C. difficile and resistance risk.
Invasive urethral catheterisation is inappropriate when there are no clinical symptoms or signs of urinary tract infection.
NICE and UKHSA state that urine dipsticks should not be used to diagnose UTI in patients over 65 years because asymptomatic bacteriuria is very common.
A positive dipstick in an afebrile older patient without localising urinary symptoms represents asymptomatic bacteriuria and should not be treated with antibiotics.
f: mild lower urinary tract symptoms in a younger non-pregnant woman where delayed prescribing is agreed
acute urinary retention with a painful palpable bladder dull to the umbilicus
monitoring proteinuria resolution in a young patient recovering from glomerulonephritis
new-onset dysuria, frequency and suprapubic tenderness in an older patient with a positive urine culture

hq_q.s: A 24 year old woman has had dysuria and frequency for 2 days. She is not pregnant. A urine dipstick is done.
hq_q.w: Nitrites come from bacteria converting nitrate, so they are more specific than leucocytes. Key discriminator: Nitrites most strongly suggest a UTI.
hq_q.f: Leucocytes alone with no nitrites → less certain; send a culture.
hq_q.ql: Which dipstick result most strongly suggests a UTI?

tm.m: Gram-negative bacteria convert nitrate to nitrite
tm.g: Nitrites most strongly suggest a UTI
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Blood (Blood is non-specific)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Glucose (Glucose suggests diabetes)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ketones (Ketones suggest fasting)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Protein (Protein is non-specific)
x: Blood is non-specific.
Glucose suggests diabetes.
Ketones suggest fasting.
Protein is non-specific.

hq_q.s: A 22 year old woman presents with a 3-week history of dysuria, urinary frequency and mild mucopurulent vaginal discharge that began 2 weeks after starting a relationship with a new male partner. She is afebrile with no loin pain. Two separate midstream urine samples sent by her GP show >50 white blood cells per high-power field on microscopy, but standard aerobic urine cultures report no bacterial growth.
hq_q.w: Sterile pyuria (elevated urinary white cells with negative routine bacterial culture) in a sexually active young adult is classically caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, an obligate intracellular bacterium that requires nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) rather than standard agar culture.
hq_q.f: Sterile pyuria with chronic weight loss, night sweats and haematuria in a patient from an endemic region -> renal tuberculosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of her sterile pyuria?

c: standard aerobic urine cultures report no bacterial growth
tm.m: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular organism that triggers urethral neutrophil exudation without growing on standard cell-free agar.
tm.g: Sterile pyuria + dysuria + new sexual partner -> Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis
x: Bacterial pyelonephritis presents with high fever, rigors, loin pain and positive urine and blood cultures for uropathogens.
Uncomplicated E. coli cystitis grows readily (>=10⁵ CFU/mL) on standard routine Cysteine Lactose Electrolyte Deficient (CLED) agar culture.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria by definition has no dysuria or frequency and yields a heavy pure growth of bacteria on standard urine culture.
Renal cell carcinoma is a tumour of older adults presenting with painless haematuria, flank mass and loin pain rather than dysuria after a new sexual partner.
f: high fever, rigors, renal angle tenderness and E. coli bacteraemia
acute dysuria and frequency with >10⁵ CFU/mL coliforms isolated on midstream urine culture
incidental bacterial growth >10⁵ CFU/mL on routine antenatal screening in an asymptomatic pregnant woman
painless visible haematuria, left flank pain and a palpable renal mass in a 68 year old smoker

hq_q.s: A 72 year old woman with metastatic breast carcinoma presents with a 3-week history of progressive exertional breathlessness and a dull right chest ache. Respiratory rate is 22 breaths/min and SpO2 93% on air. Examination reveals reduced expansion, a stony dull percussion note and absent breath sounds over the right lower zone. Chest X-ray shows dense basal opacification with a concave upper meniscus.
hq_q.w: Pleural fluid accumulates in the dependent costophrenic recess, producing reduced chest expansion, stony dullness to percussion, diminished vocal resonance and breath sounds, and homogeneous basal opacification on erect chest X-ray bounded superiorly by a concave meniscus rising toward the axilla.
hq_q.f: Dense lobar opacification containing air bronchograms with bronchial breathing -> right lower lobe consolidation.
hq_q.ql: Which radiological abnormality is shown on the chest radiograph?

c: absent breath sounds over the right lower zone
dense basal opacification with a concave upper meniscus
tm.m: Capillary and pleural surface tension draws free fluid slightly higher along the lateral chest wall, creating a concave radiological meniscus.
tm.g: Stony dull base + basal opacity with concave lateral meniscus -> Right-sided pleural effusion
x: A raised hemidiaphragm (from phrenic nerve palsy or hepatomegaly) retains a smooth dome-shaped convexity rather than a laterally rising concave meniscus.
Lobar consolidation produces airspace shadowing with air bronchograms and preserved lung volume rather than a stony dull base with a concave fluid meniscus.
Lobar collapse causes volume loss, tracheal or mediastinal shift toward the lesion and crowding of ribs rather than a basal meniscus.
A pneumothorax produces hyperresonance to percussion and a visible visceral pleural line with absent peripheral lung markings, not stony dull basal opacification.
f: a smooth dome-shaped elevation of the right diaphragm following phrenic nerve injury
fever, rusty sputum, bronchial breathing and lobar opacification containing air bronchograms
right lower zone triangular opacity with depression of the horizontal fissure and mediastinal shift to the right
sudden pleuritic pain, hyperresonant percussion and a visible pleural edge with dark avascular peripheral hemithorax

hq_q.s: A 66 year old man with a 45 pack-year smoking history presents with a 4-week history of worsening breathlessness, weight loss and intermittent haemoptysis. Respiratory rate is 20 breaths/min and SpO2 94% on air. Examination shows reduced expansion and diminished breath sounds at the left lung base. An erect PA chest X-ray demonstrates a sharply marginated triangular retrocardiac opacity and loss of the medial left hemidiaphragm outline.
hq_q.w: Left lower lobe collapse retracts posteromedially behind the heart, producing the classic 'sail sign'-a triangular retrocardiac density with a sharp oblique lateral border formed by the displaced oblique fissure-alongside silhouette loss of the medial left hemidiaphragm and descending aorta.
hq_q.f: Retrocardiac shadow containing a horizontal air-fluid level -> hiatus hernia.
hq_q.ql: Which radiological diagnosis best accounts for these chest X-ray findings?

c: loss of the medial left hemidiaphragm outline
tm.m: Endobronchial obstruction of the left lower lobe bronchus causes resorption atelectasis, pulling the lobe medially behind the left atrium and ventricle.
tm.g: Triangular retrocardiac density ('sail sign') + loss of medial left hemidiaphragm -> Left lower lobe collapse
x: A hiatus hernia produces a retrocardiac mass that typically contains an air-fluid level and leaves the left hemidiaphragm and lung volume intact.
Left lower lobe consolidation obscures the left hemidiaphragm with ill-defined airspace shadowing and air bronchograms, without collapsing into a sharp retrocardiac triangle.
A pleural effusion blunts the lateral costophrenic angle with a concave meniscus rising toward the axilla rather than forming a medial retrocardiac triangle.
A large pericardial effusion causes symmetrical globular ('water-bottle') enlargement of the cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields.
f: a retrocardiac soft-tissue shadow containing a distinct horizontal air-fluid level in a patient with reflux
high fever, productive cough and ill-defined left basal airspace shadowing with air bronchograms
basal opacification blunting the left costophrenic angle with a concave lateral meniscus
globular enlargement of the cardiac silhouette with low-voltage QRS complexes and muffled heart sounds

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man presents with a 3-hour history of sudden, severe epigastric pain. He has taken ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for 6 weeks for knee osteoarthritis and has had no recent abdominal surgery. Pulse is 112 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg and temperature 37.5°C. His abdomen is board-like and rigid. Erect chest X-ray shows a thin radiolucent crescent under the right hemidiaphragm.
hq_q.w: Free intraperitoneal gas beneath the right hemidiaphragm (pneumoperitoneum) on an erect chest radiograph in a patient with sudden epigastric pain, NSAID use and peritonitic rigidity indicates hollow viscus perforation, most commonly an anterior duodenal or gastric ulcer.
hq_q.f: Haustrated bowel gas interposed between liver and right hemidiaphragm in an asymptomatic patient -> Chilaiditi sign.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: radiolucent crescent under the right hemidiaphragm
tm.m: NSAID-induced prostaglandin inhibition causes full-thickness gastroduodenal ulceration, releasing intraluminal gas into the peritoneal cavity that rises beneath the diaphragm.
tm.g: Sudden rigid abdomen + NSAID use + free subdiaphragmatic gas -> Perforated peptic ulcer
x: Chilaiditi sign is asymptomatic interposition of haustrated colon between the liver and right diaphragm in a patient without peritonism.
The physiological gastric air bubble lies beneath the left hemidiaphragm below a thicker stomach wall, not as a thin crescent above the liver on the right.
Pneumothorax lies above the diaphragm within the pleural cavity, causing unilateral hyperresonance and absent breath sounds rather than abdominal rigidity and subdiaphragmatic air.
A subphrenic abscess typically develops 1–3 weeks after abdominal surgery with swinging pyrexia and a localized air-fluid level, not sudden peritonism within 3 hours.
f: incidental subdiaphragmatic gas containing colonic haustral folds in an asymptomatic patient with a soft abdomen
rounded gas collection with a fluid level beneath the left hemidiaphragm in a patient with a soft abdomen
acute pleuritic chest pain, tracheal deviation and hyperresonance with air above the diaphragm
swinging fever, right shoulder-tip pain and a subdiaphragmatic air-fluid level 10 days after laparotomy

hq_q.s: An 82 year old man from a nursing home with Parkinson's disease and chronic constipation presents with 4 days of progressive abdominal distension, colicky pain and absolute constipation. Pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 126/76 mmHg. The abdomen is grossly distended and tympanic. Abdominal X-ray shows a massively dilated, ahaustral loop of colon shaped like a coffee bean rising from the left iliac fossa.
hq_q.w: Sigmoid volvulus occurs when a redundant sigmoid colon twists on its mesentery, causing closed-loop obstruction. Abdominal X-ray shows an ahaustral 'coffee-bean' loop rising from the left iliac fossa; first-line decompression is sigmoidoscopy with flatus tube insertion.
hq_q.f: Transverse colon dilated >6 cm with fever and bloody diarrhoea in ulcerative colitis -> toxic megacolon.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: shaped like a coffee bean rising from the left iliac fossa
tm.m: Torsion of a redundant sigmoid loop around its mesenteric pedicle creates a closed-loop obstruction whose apposed medial walls form the cleft of a coffee bean.
tm.g: Tympanic distension + coffee-bean loop arising from the left iliac fossa -> Sigmoid volvulus
x: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome) causes diffuse gaseous dilatation throughout the colon without a twisted closed-loop coffee-bean configuration.
Small bowel obstruction produces central dilated loops (>3 cm) with valvulae conniventes crossing the full width of the bowel lumen.
Caecal volvulus arises in the right iliac fossa and points toward the left upper quadrant, often retaining haustral markings and associated with small bowel obstruction.
Toxic megacolon presents with bloody diarrhoea, fever, tachycardia and transverse colonic dilatation >6 cm in acute severe colitis.
f: diffuse pan-colonic dilatation without a transition point on CT in a frail patient 3 days after hip arthroplasty
central ladder-like dilated bowel loops with valvulae conniventes in a patient with previous laparotomy scars
a dilated comma-shaped viscus extending from the right iliac fossa toward the left upper quadrant with collapsed distal colon
bloody diarrhoea, high fever, tachycardia and transverse colon diameter of 8 cm in acute ulcerative colitis

hq_q.s: A 76 year old woman presents with 3 days of lower abdominal pain, distension and absolute constipation following 4 months of worsening constipation and weight loss. Pulse is 102 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. There is mild right iliac fossa tenderness. Supine abdominal X-ray shows closed-loop large bowel obstruction from a distal colonic lesion with a competent ileocaecal valve and marked caecal distension.
hq_q.w: By the radiological '3-6-9 rule', upper normal diameters are 3 cm for small bowel, 6 cm for colon and 9 cm for the caecum. Caecal dilatation above 9 cm indicates a high risk of imminent ischaemic perforation.
hq_q.f: Small bowel loops exceeding 3 cm with valvulae conniventes -> small bowel obstruction.
hq_q.ql: Above which radiographic diameter is the caecum considered at high risk of imminent ischaemic perforation?

tm.m: By Laplace's law (wall tension = pressure x radius), the thin-walled wide-radius caecum experiences the highest mural tension and perforates when dilated >9 cm.
tm.g: 3-6-9 rule threshold for caecal perforation risk -> 9 cm
x: Perforation risk becomes critical once caecal diameter exceeds 9–12 cm; waiting until 15 cm carries a high rate of fatal faecal peritonitis.
3 cm is the upper limit of normal radiographic diameter for the small bowel in the 3-6-9 rule, not the caecum.
5 cm is within the normal radiographic calibre for both the transverse colon (<6 cm) and the caecum (<9 cm).
6 cm is the upper limit of normal diameter for the transverse colon (above which toxic megacolon is diagnosed), not the caecum.
f: late neglected megacolon well beyond the critical threshold for emergency surgical decompression
the upper normal luminal diameter threshold used to diagnose small bowel dilatation
normal colonic calibre on a supine abdominal radiograph without risk of perforation
the transverse colon diameter threshold used to define toxic megacolon in acute severe colitis

hq_q.s: A 54 year old man with a 20-year history of extensive pancolonic ulcerative colitis attends gastroenterology clinic with mildly increased stool frequency of three loose, non-bloody motions daily. He is afebrile with pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg and a soft, non-tender abdomen. A plain abdominal radiograph shows a shortened, tubular, featureless colon with complete loss of haustral folds and no luminal dilatation.
hq_q.w: Chronic mucosal inflammation and submucosal fibrosis in long-standing ulcerative colitis cause muscularis mucosae atrophy, colonic shortening and complete loss of normal haustral markings, producing a smooth, featureless 'lead-pipe' colon on abdominal radiography.
hq_q.f: Rounded soft-tissue indentations ('thumbprints') along the colonic wall in acute colitis -> mucosal thumbprinting from submucosal oedema.
hq_q.ql: Which radiological sign is demonstrated on this abdominal X-ray?

c: 20-year history of extensive pancolonic ulcerative colitis
tm.m: Chronic mucosal ulceration, regeneration and submucosal fibrosis obliterate haustral folds and shorten the colonic tube.
tm.g: Featureless, ahaustral, narrowed colon in long-standing ulcerative colitis -> Lead-pipe colon
x: The coffee-bean sign represents a massively dilated, twisted loop of sigmoid colon in acute sigmoid volvulus.
Rigler's sign is visualisation of both the luminal and serosal surfaces of the bowel wall due to free intraperitoneal gas (pneumoperitoneum).
Thumbprinting represents smooth, rounded soft-tissue indentations into the bowel lumen caused by severe submucosal oedema in acute ischaemic or infective colitis.
Toxic megacolon is defined by acute colonic dilatation (>6 cm in the transverse colon) with systemic toxicity, whereas this colon is narrowed and non-dilated.
f: gross tympanic abdominal distension and a dilated loop arising from the left pelvis
free intraperitoneal gas outlining both sides of the bowel wall on a supine radiograph after viscus perforation
acute bloody diarrhoea and severe left-sided pain with rounded submucosal wall indentations
acute severe colitis with fever, tachycardia and transverse colon dilatation exceeding 6 cm

hq_q.s: A 45 year old man fell 2 metres from a ladder onto a paved driveway and struck his occiput. He had a witnessed 1-minute loss of consciousness, has a headache and has not vomited. He takes no anticoagulants. On reassessment in the Emergency Department 2 hours after the injury, his GCS is 13/15 (E3 V4 M6) with equal reactive pupils.
o: No CT head scan is required
On the next routine daytime list
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG232, an immediate CT head scan within 1 hour is required for adults with GCS <13 initially, GCS <15 at 2 hours post-injury, suspected open/depressed or basal skull fracture, post-traumatic seizure, focal neurological deficit, or >1 episode of vomiting.
hq_q.f: Patient aged >=65 with brief loss of consciousness who is now GCS 15 with no 1-hour red flags -> CT head within 8 hours.
hq_q.ql: According to NICE head injury guidelines, within what timeframe should a non-contrast CT head scan be performed?

c: 2 hours after the injury, his GCS is 13/15
tm.m: Failure of GCS to return to 15 within 2 hours of head trauma carries a high probability of neurosurgically significant intracranial haemorrhage.
tm.g: GCS <15 at 2 hours post-head injury -> CT head within 1 hour of assessment
x: Withholding CT in a patient whose GCS remains below 15 at 2 hours post-injury risks missing an expanding intracranial haematoma.
Deferring imaging to the next day is dangerous when an acute traumatic intracranial haematoma is suspected from a persistent GCS deficit.
Waiting up to 24 hours is unsafe when GCS has failed to recover to 15 at 2 hours after head trauma.
The 8-hour CT window applies to patients with loss of consciousness or amnesia plus risk factors (such as age >=65 or anticoagulation) whose GCS is 15.
f: a patient with a minor head injury, GCS 15 throughout, no loss of consciousness and no risk factors
outpatient neuroimaging for chronic tension-type headache without red flags
non-urgent inpatient neuroimaging for subacute cognitive decline without acute trauma
a 70 year old patient with brief loss of consciousness after a fall who has recovered to GCS 15

hq_q.s: A 79 year old woman taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation tripped at home 2 hours ago and struck her forehead against a table. She did not lose consciousness, has no amnesia, has not vomited and had no seizure. Examination shows GCS 15/15, equal reactive pupils, normal neurology and a 2 cm forehead contusion.
o: CT head within 1 hour of assessment
CT head within 8 hours of injury
MRI head within 24 hours of admission
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG232, adults on anticoagulant therapy (including DOACs or warfarin) or non-aspirin antiplatelets who sustain a head injury without any 1-hour red flags should have a non-contrast CT head scan within 8 hours of injury.
hq_q.f: Anticoagulated patient with head injury who has vomited twice or has GCS 14 -> CT head within 1 hour.
hq_q.ql: According to NICE head injury guidelines, which is the most appropriate neuroimaging plan?

tm.m: Systemic anticoagulation impairs haemostasis after minor bridging vein shearing, requiring CT exclusion of subdural or intracranial bleeding within 8 hours.
tm.g: Head injury on anticoagulant with GCS 15 and no 1-hour red flags -> CT head within 8 hours of injury
x: Under NICE NG232, anticoagulated patients without any 1-hour red flags (such as GCS <15 at 2 hours, focal neurology, seizure or >1 vomit) require CT within 8 hours rather than 1 hour.
Anticoagulant therapy (including DOACs and warfarin) significantly increases the risk of traumatic intracranial haemorrhage even without loss of consciousness.
Non-contrast CT head is the rapid, sensitive first-line modality for acute traumatic intracranial haemorrhage, not MRI.
Plain skull X-rays have poor sensitivity for intracranial haemorrhage and are not used in modern NICE head injury pathways.
f: the same anticoagulated patient who has also vomited twice or developed a focal neurological deficit
a 40 year old patient not on anticoagulants or antiplatelets with GCS 15 and no loss of consciousness
subacute assessment of suspected diffuse axonal injury days after a normal initial CT head
skeletal survey investigation in suspected non-accidental injury in an infant

hq_q.s: A 30 year old man presents to the Emergency Department 18 hours after being struck on the side of the head during an assault. He complains of a persistent headache and salty-tasting clear fluid dripping continuously from his right nostril when leaning forward. GCS is 15/15. Examination reveals bruising over the right mastoid process, bilateral periorbital ecchymoses sparing the tarsal plates, and right haemotympanum on otoscopy.
hq_q.w: Signs of a basal skull fracture include CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea, bilateral periorbital ecchymoses ('panda eyes'), mastoid ecchymosis (Battle's sign) and haemotympanum. Any sign of a basal skull fracture requires an urgent CT head within 1 hour.
hq_q.f: Temporal blow followed by lucid interval, falling GCS and biconvex hyperdense collection -> acute extradural haematoma.
hq_q.ql: Which diagnosis do these clinical signs indicate?

c: clear fluid dripping continuously from his right nostril
bruising over the right mastoid process
tm.m: Fracture propagation through the anterior cranial fossa (cribriform plate) and petrous temporal bone tears the adherent dura, leaking CSF and tracking blood to the orbits and mastoid.
tm.g: CSF rhinorrhoea + panda eyes + Battle's sign + haemotympanum -> Basal skull fracture
x: Acute rhinosinusitis causes purulent nasal discharge and facial pain after a viral URTI, not post-traumatic Battle's sign, panda eyes and haemotympanum.
An extradural haematoma arises from middle meningeal artery laceration at the squamous temporal bone (pterion), causing a lucid interval and coma rather than CSF rhinorrhoea and mastoid bruising.
An isolated nasal fracture causes epistaxis, nasal bridge swelling and septal deviation, but does not cause haemotympanum or mastoid bruising (Battle's sign).
Concussion is a functional brain injury without structural fracture and never causes CSF rhinorrhoea, periorbital ecchymoses or haemotympanum.
f: purulent nasal discharge, fever and facial pain worse on bending forward after a viral cold
head strike at the temple followed by a lucid interval, rapid drop in GCS and a fixed dilated ipsilateral pupil
nasal bridge deformity, crepitus and anterior epistaxis without mastoid bruising or CSF leak
mild headache, dizziness and poor concentration for 2 weeks after a sports head injury with normal examination

hq_q.s: A 66 year old woman with hypertension presents with 90 minutes of sudden, tearing central chest pain radiating to her interscapular back. Pulse is 102 bpm, and BP is 168/92 mmHg in the right arm and 134/78 mmHg in the left. Acute aortic dissection is suspected and urgent CT aortography is needed, but her notes record generalised urticaria after iodinated contrast 4 years ago.
o: Cancel CT and rely on plain chest X-ray
Order a routine outpatient cardiac MRI
hq_q.w: When urgent CT angiography is required in a patient with prior iodinated contrast hypersensitivity, discuss immediately with radiology so they can either proceed using low-osmolar contrast with steroid/antihistamine cover and resuscitation readiness, or perform emergency transoesophageal echocardiography.
hq_q.f: Patient reports seafood/shellfish allergy only -> not a contraindication to iodinated contrast; proceed as normal.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step regarding imaging?

c: tearing central chest pain radiating to her interscapular back
168/92 mmHg in the right arm and 134/78 mmHg in the left
tm.m: In a life-threatening emergency, specialist radiology liaison balances immediate diagnostic necessity against hypersensitivity mitigation or alternative imaging (TOE).
tm.g: Urgent contrast CT needed + prior contrast reaction -> Discuss urgent protocol with radiology
x: A normal chest radiograph does not exclude acute aortic dissection, and cancelling definitive imaging in a surgical emergency can be fatal.
Proceeding without informing radiology or preparing resuscitation/premedication or alternative imaging (such as TOE) ignores a documented hypersensitivity reaction.
Outpatient MRI is far too slow for suspected acute aortic dissection, which carries a 1–2% per hour mortality if untreated.
Transabdominal ultrasound cannot visualise the thoracic aorta and cannot diagnose or exclude a Stanford type A or B thoracic aortic dissection.
f: initial bedside screening in low-risk chest pain where dissection is not clinically suspected
a patient reporting a minor shellfish intolerance with no prior reaction to iodinated contrast media
elective follow-up surveillance of a stable, chronic, medically managed aortic root dilatation
population screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm in a 65 year old man

hq_q.s: A 74 year old man with atrial fibrillation who stopped taking his oral anticoagulant 2 weeks ago presents with 6 hours of sudden, severe central abdominal pain out of proportion to examination findings. Pulse is 118 bpm irregular and BP 104/62 mmHg. His abdomen is soft with mild periumbilical tenderness and no guarding. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.26 and lactate 6.0 mmol/L (<2.0).
hq_q.w: Acute mesenteric ischaemia (classically from superior mesenteric artery embolism in atrial fibrillation) causes severe abdominal pain out of proportion to examination findings and lactic acidosis. Biphasic CT mesenteric angiography is the rapid diagnostic gold standard.
hq_q.f: Subacute left iliac fossa pain and bloody diarrhoea after hypotensive episode -> ischaemic colitis (CT abdomen/pelvis then cautious flexible sigmoidoscopy).
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis rapidly?

c: out of proportion to examination findings
tm.m: Arterial-phase CT angiography directly visualises thromboembolic occlusion within the superior mesenteric artery and assesses bowel wall enhancement and pneumatosis.
tm.g: Pain out of proportion to exam + AF + high lactate -> CT mesenteric angiography
x: Barium enema is contraindicated in an acute surgical abdomen and cannot visualise arterial thromboembolism in the superior mesenteric artery.
Colonoscopy only inspects the colonic mucosa, misses small bowel superior mesenteric artery ischaemia, and risks perforation in gangrenous bowel.
Duplex ultrasound is limited by overlying bowel gas in acute abdominal distension and cannot assess distal mesenteric branches or bowel viability.
Plain abdominal X-ray is frequently normal or shows only non-specific ileus in early acute mesenteric ischaemia, delaying revascularisation.
f: elective evaluation of a colonic stricture when colonoscopy is incomplete
subacute bloody diarrhoea and left iliac fossa tenderness in stable non-occlusive ischaemic colitis
outpatient investigation of chronic postprandial abdominal angina (chronic mesenteric ischaemia)
initial bedside assessment of suspected mechanical small bowel obstruction

hq_q.s: A 72 year old man with hypertensive nephrosclerosis and stable stage 4 chronic kidney disease (baseline eGFR 25 mL/min/1.73 m², serum creatinine 230 µmol/L) requires an urgent contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis to stage a newly biopsied caecal adenocarcinoma. He is clinically euvolaemic with BP 134/78 mmHg, pulse rate 76 bpm, clear lung fields and no peripheral oedema.
o: Halve the iodinated contrast volume by 50%
Proceed with 0 mL peri-scan fluid prophylaxis
hq_q.w: In high-risk patients (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²) undergoing iodinated contrast imaging, NICE NG148 recommends volume expansion with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride or isotonic sodium bicarbonate before and after scanning, while temporarily withholding nephrotoxic drugs.
hq_q.f: Patient with normal renal function (eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m²) -> no intravenous fluid prophylaxis required.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate measure to reduce the risk of contrast-induced acute kidney injury?

tm.m: Isotonic intravascular volume expansion increases renal tubular flow, diluting contrast concentration in the renal medulla and blunting medullary vasoconstriction.
tm.g: Contrast CT in CKD with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² -> Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride hydration
x: Loop diuretics induce intravascular volume depletion and renal vasoconstriction, increasing the risk of contrast-induced acute kidney injury.
Arbitrarily halving contrast below the diagnostic threshold risks an uninterpretable staging scan requiring repeat contrast administration.
Large randomised trials (such as ACT and PRESERVE) showed oral N-acetylcysteine provides no protection against contrast nephropathy, and NICE advises against it.
An eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² is a major risk factor for contrast-induced nephropathy, requiring peri-procedural volume expansion and withholding nephrotoxins.
f: treating acute decompensated pulmonary oedema in a patient with fluid overload
using the minimum diagnostic volume of iso-osmolar or low-osmolar contrast alongside IV hydration
administering intravenous N-acetylcysteine for acute paracetamol overdose
a patient with normal renal function (eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73 m²) undergoing routine contrast CT

hq_q.s: A 70 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer presents with a 2-week history of worsening mid-thoracic back pain and a 24-hour history of bilateral leg weakness and inability to pass urine. Examination shows grade 3/5 power in both lower limbs, brisk knee and ankle reflexes, extensor plantar responses, a sensory level at T8 and a palpable bladder. Oral dexamethasone 16 mg is given immediately.
o: Plain radiographs of the whole spine
Whole-spine MRI within 7 days of admission
hq_q.w: In suspected metastatic spinal cord compression with neurological signs, NICE recommends immediate high-dose dexamethasone and urgent MRI of the whole spine within 24 hours to identify all sites of epidural cord compression and guide decompression or radiotherapy.
hq_q.f: Known cancer with new spinal pain suggestive of bone metastases but no neurological deficit -> MRI within 1 week.
hq_q.ql: According to NICE guidelines, which imaging investigation must be performed next?

c: bilateral leg weakness and inability to pass urine
tm.m: Vertebral metastases frequently involve multiple non-contiguous spinal levels, so whole-spine MRI within 24 hours is essential to plan decompression or radiotherapy.
tm.g: Suspected metastatic spinal cord compression with neurological signs -> Whole-spine MRI within 24 hours
x: Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy detects osteoblastic bone turnover but cannot visualise the spinal cord, epidural space or thecal sac compression.
Imaging only the lumbar spine misses thoracic and cervical epidural metastases; synchronous multi-level cord compression occurs in up to 30% of patients.
Plain spinal X-rays cannot visualise the spinal cord or epidural soft-tissue tumour and miss up to 20% of vertebral metastases.
A 1-week timeframe applies only to spinal pain suspicious of bone metastases without neurological symptoms or signs of cord compression.
f: staging asymptomatic skeletal metastases in newly diagnosed high-risk prostate cancer without neurological signs
cauda equina syndrome from a known benign L4/L5 disc prolapse without malignancy
initial assessment of suspected osteoporotic vertebral wedge fracture without neurological deficit
known cancer with new localised thoracic spinal pain but normal power, reflexes, sensation and bladder function

hq_q.s: A 54 year old man is referred by ENT for an outpatient MRI of the internal auditory meatuses to investigate a 6-month history of progressive unilateral right-sided sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus. During completion of the MRI safety questionnaire, he reports working for 25 years as a structural steel welder and metal grinder and recalls several occasions when sparks struck his face.
o: Check serum creatinine and eGFR first
Order a high-dose CT head scan instead
Plain orbital X-ray to exclude metal
Proceed directly into the MRI scanner
Remove all dental amalgam fillings first
hq_q.w: Sheet-metal workers, welders and grinders may harbour asymptomatic ferromagnetic intraorbital foreign bodies. Because the strong magnetic field of an MRI scanner can torque metal fragments and lacerate the globe or optic nerve, screening orbital radiographs must be performed beforehand.
hq_q.f: Patient with an older non-MR-conditional cardiac pacemaker -> MRI is contraindicated; use alternative imaging or specialist cardiology protocol.
hq_q.ql: Which safety step must be completed before he enters the MRI scanner room?

c: MRI of the internal auditory meatuses
structural steel welder and metal grinder
tm.m: Strong static magnetic fields exert translational and rotational torque on ferromagnetic intraocular splinters, risking vitreous haemorrhage and blindness.
tm.g: History of metalworking/grinding before MRI -> Plain orbital X-ray to exclude metal
x: Renal function affects gadolinium contrast administration in severe CKD, not ferromagnetic foreign body hazard in a metal worker.
Screening orbital radiographs (or low-dose orbital CT) quickly exclude intraorbital metal so the patient can still undergo the superior soft-tissue MRI scan.
Entering a high-field magnet with an occult ferromagnetic intraorbital foreign body can cause fragment movement and irreversible blindness.
Standard dental amalgam and gold fillings are non-ferromagnetic and safe in an MRI scanner, causing only minor local image artefact.
f: assessing nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk before giving gadolinium in a patient with stage 5 CKD
emergency assessment of acute head trauma where non-contrast CT head is the primary modality
a patient with no history of metalworking, shrapnel injury or implanted electronic devices
evaluating local susceptibility artefact over the maxilla on facial MRI sequences

hq_q.s: A 32 year old woman has had blurred vision with pain in her right eye on movement, and tingling in her legs a year ago. Multiple sclerosis is suspected.
hq_q.w: MRI shows white matter lesions in time and space. Gadolinium enhancing lesions are active. Key discriminator: Suspected MS: MRI brain and spine with gadolinium.
hq_q.f: Oligoclonal bands only in CSF → supports MS, but MRI is the key test.
hq_q.ql: Which test is most sensitive for multiple sclerosis lesions?

c: pain in her right eye on movement
tingling in her legs a year ago
tm.m: MRI shows demyelinating lesions separated in time and space
tm.g: Suspected MS: MRI brain and spine with gadolinium
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to CT head with contrast (Poor soft-tissue resolution for demyelinating white matter plaques)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lumbar puncture (LP is supportive)
Persistent distal glove-and-stocking numbness at rest without positional claudication
the presentation instead showed features specific to Visual evoked potentials (VEPs are less sensitive)
x: Poor soft-tissue resolution for demyelinating white matter plaques
LP is supportive.

Ruled out here: requires Persistent distal glove-and-stocking numbness at rest without positional claudication, whereas this patient has pain in her right eye on movement, tingling in her legs a year ago.
VEPs are less sensitive.

hq_q.s: A 34 year old man is brought to the resuscitation bay after a high-speed head-on motor vehicle collision. He has a transverse seatbelt contusion across his lower abdomen and complains of diffuse abdominal pain. Airway and breathing are intact. Pulse rate is 128 bpm, BP 82/50 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths/min. His abdomen is distended and diffusely tender on palpation.
o: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma
hq_q.w: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) is a rapid, non-invasive bedside ultrasound examination of four windows (hepatorenal space, splenorenal space, pelvis and pericardium) to detect free fluid (blood) in haemodynamically unstable trauma patients.
hq_q.f: Haemodynamically stable blunt abdominal trauma patient -> contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis.
hq_q.ql: Which rapid bedside investigation should be performed immediately to detect haemoperitoneum?

c: Pulse rate is 128 bpm, BP 82/50 mmHg
tm.m: Bedside ultrasonography identifies anechoic free blood in dependent peritoneal recesses (Morison's pouch, splenorenal recess, pouch of Douglas) without moving an unstable patient.
tm.g: Haemodynamically unstable blunt abdominal trauma -> Focused assessment with sonography for trauma
x: Transferring a haemodynamically unstable trauma patient (BP 82/50 mmHg) to the CT scanner is unsafe before resuscitation or laparotomy.
Diagnostic peritoneal lavage is an invasive procedure that has been superseded by bedside FAST ultrasound in modern trauma resuscitation.
Laparoscopy requires general anaesthesia and pneumoperitoneum, which worsens hypotension in unstable trauma; bedside FAST or laparotomy is used.
Plain radiographs cannot detect free intraperitoneal blood and have no role in assessing haemoperitoneum in unstable trauma.
f: a haemodynamically stable blunt abdominal trauma patient with seatbelt bruising
resource-limited trauma setting where neither ultrasound nor CT is available
stable penetrating left thoracoabdominal stab wound to exclude diaphragmatic injury
suspected radiopaque ingested or retained foreign body in a stable patient

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old woman has had pain in the right upper abdomen after fatty meals for 3 months.
Temperature 36.9°C. There is mild right upper quadrant tenderness. Murphy's sign is negative.
hq_q.w: Ultrasound is cheap, quick, radiation free and very sensitive for gallbladder stones and wall thickening.
hq_q.f: Ultrasound shows a dilated duct but no stone is seen → MRCP.
hq_q.ql: Which is the first-line imaging for suspected gallstones?

tm.m: Ultrasound is quick, radiation free and very sensitive for stones
tm.g: Suspected gallstones: abdominal ultrasound first
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to CT abdomen with contrast (CT misses many stones)
the presentation instead showed features specific to ERCP (Used for: Cholangitis, common bile duct stones: therapeutic)
the presentation instead showed features specific to HIDA scan (HIDA is for cholecystitis)
a dilated duct with no stone seen
x: CT misses many stones.
Used for: Cholangitis, common bile duct stones: therapeutic
HIDA is for cholecystitis.
Ruled out here: requires a dilated duct with no stone seen, whereas this patient has after fatty meals, Murphy's sign is negative.

hq_q.s: A 15 year old boy is brought to the Emergency Department with a 2-hour history of sudden, severe left-sided scrotal pain that woke him from sleep, accompanied by nausea and two episodes of vomiting. He has no dysuria or urethral discharge. Temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 98 bpm. The left hemiscrotum is erythematous and swollen, with a high-riding horizontal left testis and an absent left cremasteric reflex.
o: Arrange an urgent colour Doppler ultrasound
Perform bedside manual detorsion and discharge
Request a radionuclide testicular perfusion scan
hq_q.w: Acute testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis requiring emergency surgical scrotal exploration, detorsion and bilateral three-point orchidopexy within 6 hours of symptom onset. Scrotal Doppler ultrasound must not be arranged when torsion is clinically suspected, as it delays theatre.
hq_q.f: Painless firm intratesticular lump noticed over several weeks -> urgent 2-week-wait scrotal ultrasound.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

c: 2-hour history of sudden, severe left-sided scrotal pain
tm.m: Rotation of the testis on the spermatic cord occludes venous and arterial flow, causing irreversible ischaemic necrosis after 6 hours unless surgically detorted.
tm.g: Acute scrotal pain + high-riding testis + absent cremasteric reflex -> Immediate surgical scrotal exploration
x: Ordering scrotal Doppler ultrasound when testicular torsion is clinically clear delays surgical detorsion beyond the 6-hour testicular salvage window.
Empirical STI antibiotic therapy treats epididymo-orchitis, whereas sudden pain, high-riding testis and absent cremasteric reflex in a 15 year old indicate torsion.
Even if manual detorsion relieves pain temporarily, immediate bilateral surgical orchidopexy in theatre remains mandatory to prevent recurrence.
Radionuclide scintigraphy is time-consuming and must never delay urgent surgical exploration when acute spermatic cord torsion is suspected.
f: equivocal mild scrotal ache in an adult where torsion is clinically unlikely
gradual-onset unilateral scrotal pain with urethral discharge, dysuria and positive Prehn's sign
temporary bedside pain relief only while awaiting immediate transfer to the operating theatre
obsolete testicular perfusion imaging superseded by immediate exploration

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old man has had upper abdominal pain and indigestion for 6 weeks and has lost 5 kg without trying. He has no difficulty swallowing.
The abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness. There is no mass.
hq_q.w: NICE NG12: offer urgent direct-access upper GI endoscopy (within 2 weeks) to people aged 55 or over with weight loss and upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia, to look for oesophageal or stomach cancer.
hq_q.f: Same symptoms at 40 with no weight loss → test and treat for H. pylori or a month of full-dose PPI.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Weight loss with dyspepsia after 55 raises the chance of upper GI cancer enough to warrant urgent endoscopy
tm.g: 55 or over + weight loss + dyspepsia: urgent endoscopy
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Abdominal ultrasound (Ultrasound can be used for upper abdominal masses, but it does not see the stomach lining)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Full-dose PPI for 4 weeks (A PPI trial is for uncomplicated dyspepsia without alarm features)
the presentation instead showed features specific to H. pylori test and treat (Test and treat is for younger people without alarm features)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Routine endoscopy referral (With weight loss at 58 he meets the urgent 2-week criteria)
x: Ultrasound can be used for upper abdominal masses, but it does not see the stomach lining.
A PPI trial is for uncomplicated dyspepsia without alarm features.
Test and treat is for younger people without alarm features.
With weight loss at 58 he meets the urgent 2-week criteria.

hq_q.s: A 56 year old woman with a 3-month history of epigastric discomfort, postprandial fullness and acid regurgitation is scheduled for an elective diagnostic upper gastrointestinal endoscopy in 4 weeks' time. She has no dysphagia, haematemesis or melaena, and her haemoglobin is 134 g/L. She currently takes oral omeprazole 20 mg once daily and is advised to stop it 2 weeks before the procedure.
o: They can heal mucosal lesions and mask H. pylori
They delay the onset of intravenous midazolam sedation
They increase the risk of endoscopic biopsy bleeding
They increase the risk of pulmonary acid aspiration
They stain the gastric mucosa and obscure visualization
hq_q.w: NICE recommends stopping proton pump inhibitors at least 2 weeks before an elective diagnostic upper GI endoscopy (and before H. pylori breath or stool antigen testing) because acid suppression can partially heal peptic ulcers or early gastric malignancies and cause false-negative H. pylori urease biopsy results.
hq_q.f: Patient presenting with acute upper GI bleeding (haematemesis/melaena) -> do not delay endoscopy; give IV PPI after endoscopy.
hq_q.ql: What is the primary clinical reason for withholding proton pump inhibitors for 2 weeks before diagnostic gastroscopy?

c: stop it 2 weeks before the procedure
tm.m: Gastric acid suppression suppresses H. pylori bacterial density and re-epithelialises malignant or peptic ulcers, causing false-negative biopsies and missed pathology.
tm.g: Withholding PPI for 2 weeks before diagnostic OGD -> They can heal mucosal lesions and mask H. pylori
x: Proton pump inhibitors do not prevent benzodiazepine sedation from acting during upper gastrointestinal endoscopy.
Acid suppression promotes platelet aggregation and clot stability in the stomach, reducing rather than increasing upper gastrointestinal bleeding risk.
By raising gastric pH and reducing gastric acid volume, proton pump inhibitors reduce rather than increase chemical pneumonitis risk.
Oral iron tablets and particulate antacids stain or coat the mucosa, whereas omeprazole capsules leave the mucosal surface clear.
f: hepatic enzyme interactions that do not prevent procedural conscious sedation
stopping clopidogrel or direct oral anticoagulants prior to high-risk endoscopic polypectomy
fasting from solid food for 6 hours before endoscopy to prevent aspiration
stopping oral ferrous sulfate 5 days before colonoscopy to prevent dark stool staining

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man has had difficulty swallowing solids for 2 months and has lost 4 kg. He has had reflux for years.
Upper GI endoscopy shows a stricture in the lower oesophagus.
hq_q.w: All strictures and suspicious lesions are biopsied, as cancers can look like benign strictures. Key discriminator: Every oesophageal stricture is biopsied to exclude cancer.
hq_q.f: Biopsies show only peptic stricture → PPI and dilation.
hq_q.ql: Which step is essential?

tm.m: A malignant stricture can look just like a peptic one
tm.g: Every oesophageal stricture is biopsied to exclude cancer
f: biopsies show only a peptic stricture
the presentation instead showed features specific to Immediate surgery (Surgery comes after diagnosis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to PPI and discharge (Misses underlying oesophageal adenocarcinoma mimicking a benign peptic stricture)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Repeat scope in a year (Biopsy is needed now)
x: Ruled out here: requires biopsies show only a peptic stricture, whereas this patient has difficulty swallowing solids, lost 4 kg.
Surgery comes after diagnosis.
Misses underlying oesophageal adenocarcinoma mimicking a benign peptic stricture
Biopsy is needed now.

hq_q.s: A 52 year old woman asks whether she will be invited for bowel cancer screening. She lives in England and has no bowel symptoms or family history.
hq_q.w: England has lowered the start age to 50. A home FIT kit is sent every 2 years until 74. Over 75 can ask for a kit.
hq_q.f: A positive screening FIT → colonoscopy.
hq_q.ql: Who is invited for NHS bowel cancer screening in England?

c: no bowel symptoms or family history
tm.m: A home FIT kit is posted to people in the screening age range
tm.g: NHS bowel screening in England: aged 50 to 74, every 2 years
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Aged 55, a single scope (The former Bowel Scope flexible sigmoidoscopy programme at 55 was discontinued)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Aged 60 to 70, once (Screening is every 2 years, not once)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Everyone over 40, every year (NHS screening starts from age 50 every 2 years, not 40 yearly)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Family history (It is for everyone in the age range)
x: The former Bowel Scope flexible sigmoidoscopy programme at 55 was discontinued
Screening is every 2 years, not once.
NHS screening starts from age 50 every 2 years, not 40 yearly
It is for everyone in the age range.

hq_q.s: An 88 year old woman living in a nursing home with moderate vascular dementia and frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 6) presents with a 3-month history of 6 kg unintentional weight loss and fatigue. Blood tests show haemoglobin 88 g/L (115–150), MCV 71 fL (80–100) and ferritin 7 µg/L (15–300). She is unable to tolerate oral polyethylene glycol bowel preparation for a full optical colonoscopy.
o: CT colonography or contrast CT abdomen
hq_q.w: In frail older patients with suspected colorectal cancer (such as iron deficiency anaemia and weight loss) who cannot tolerate full cathartic bowel preparation for optical colonoscopy, CT colonography (with minimal faecal tagging) or a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the investigation of choice.
hq_q.f: Fit patient able to tolerate bowel preparation -> optical colonoscopy and biopsy (the diagnostic gold standard).
hq_q.ql: Which colonic investigation is most appropriate for this patient?

c: unable to tolerate oral polyethylene glycol bowel preparation
tm.m: CT colonography with oral contrast faecal tagging detects clinically significant colorectal masses (>1 cm) and extracolonic disease without dehydrating bowel preparation.
tm.g: Suspected colorectal cancer in a frail patient unfit for colonoscopy prep -> CT colonography or contrast CT abdomen
