x: Barium enema requires full cathartic bowel preparation and physically demanding patient turning on the table, making it unsuitable for frail older adults.
Flexible sigmoidoscopy only visualises the rectum and left colon up to the splenic flexure, missing right-sided caecal tumours that cause iron deficiency anaemia.
She already has proven iron deficiency anaemia and weight loss (2-week-wait criteria), so FIT is not needed to decide whether to image the colon.
Plain abdominal X-ray cannot detect non-obstructing mucosal or mural colonic carcinomas causing chronic occult blood loss.
f: historical colonic imaging now superseded by CT colonography
fresh bright red rectal bleeding in a younger patient to inspect the rectum and sigmoid
primary care triage of low-risk abdominal pain or change in bowel habit without iron deficiency anaemia
emergency assessment of acute abdominal distension and suspected bowel obstruction

hq_q.s:
A 76 year old man with peripheral vascular disease has had sudden left-sided abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea for a day.
Pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg. There is left-sided abdominal tenderness without peritonism. Lactate is normal.
Colonoscopy shows a 6 cm segment of inflamed colon near the splenic flexure, with a sharp line between it and normal mucosa. The rectum is normal.
hq_q.w: Most ischaemic colitis is non-gangrenous and settles with supportive care: IV fluids, bowel rest, and often antibiotics, with treatment of the cardiovascular risk factors. Surgery is for peritonitis, gangrene or perforation.
hq_q.f: Same picture with peritonism, a rising lactate and gas in the bowel wall → gangrenous colitis; emergency resection.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: The watershed area at the splenic flexure loses blood flow first when perfusion drops
tm.g: Ischaemic colitis without peritonism: supportive care
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Emergency left hemicolectomy (Surgery is for gangrene, perforation or peritonitis, which he does not have)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV hydrocortisone for colitis (Steroids treat severe ulcerative colitis; this is ischaemic, with a normal rectum)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Mesalazine enemas nightly (Mesalazine treats ulcerative colitis, which starts in the rectum)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral vancomycin for 10 days (Vancomycin treats C. difficile, which gives diffuse pseudomembranes, not a segment with a sharp edge)
x: Surgery is for gangrene, perforation or peritonitis, which he does not have.
Steroids treat severe ulcerative colitis; this is ischaemic, with a normal rectum.
Mesalazine treats ulcerative colitis, which starts in the rectum.
Vancomycin treats C. difficile, which gives diffuse pseudomembranes, not a segment with a sharp edge.

hq_q.s: A 54 year old woman presents after a 4-hour episode of colicky right upper quadrant pain radiating to her right scapula that settled with analgesia. She is afebrile with pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and no abdominal guarding. Blood tests show bilirubin 28 µmol/L (<17) and alkaline phosphatase 240 IU/L (25–115). Transabdominal ultrasound shows multiple gallstones and a dilated common bile duct of 9 mm, with no ductal stone visualised.
hq_q.w: When transabdominal ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct (>6 mm) and cholestatic liver biochemistry but does not visualise a ductal stone, NICE recommends magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) or endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) to confirm choledocholithiasis non-invasively before undertaking therapeutic ERCP.
hq_q.f: Confirmed CBD stone with fever, rigors and jaundice (Charcot's triad) -> urgent therapeutic ERCP with sphincterotomy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

c: dilated common bile duct of 9 mm
tm.m: Heavy T2-weighted MRI sequences render static bile bright and intraluminal calculi as dark filling defects without ionising radiation or papillary instrumentation.
tm.g: Dilated CBD on ultrasound + cholestatic LFTs with no stone seen -> Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography
x: ERCP carries a 3–5% risk of acute pancreatitis, bleeding and perforation and is reserved for therapeutic stone extraction or stenting, not pure diagnosis.
Cholescintigraphy (HIDA scan) assesses cystic duct patency in suspected acute acalculous cholecystitis or biliary dyskinesia, not choledocholithiasis.
PTC is an invasive transhepatic biliary puncture reserved for proximal biliary drainage when ERCP fails or anatomy is altered.
Delaying investigation of a dilated 9 mm common bile duct with cholestatic liver tests risks acute ascending cholangitis or gallstone pancreatitis.
f: confirmed common bile duct stone on MRCP or ascending cholangitis requiring therapeutic biliary decompression
suspected acute cholecystitis when ultrasound is equivocal
hilar cholangiocarcinoma or Roux-en-Y anatomy where endoscopic biliary cannulation has failed
incidental asymptomatic gallbladder polyps <5 mm requiring routine sonographic surveillance

hq_q.s: A 62 year old man with obstructive jaundice and a 7 mm distal common bile duct calculus confirmed on MRCP is scheduled for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with biliary sphincterotomy and stone extraction. His serum bilirubin is 64 µmol/L (<17), alkaline phosphatase 380 IU/L (25–115) and INR 1.0. Rectal indometacin 100 mg is prescribed periprocedurally to reduce his risk of the commonest serious complication.
hq_q.w: Post-ERCP acute pancreatitis is the commonest serious complication of ERCP, occurring in 3% to 5% of patients due to mechanical, hydrostatic or thermal injury to the pancreatic duct orifice at the ampulla of Vater. NICE and ESGE recommend routine prophylactic rectal NSAIDs (indometacin or diclofenac).
hq_q.f: Retroperitoneal air and bilious peritonitis after sphincterotomy -> duodenal perforation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the commonest serious complication of ERCP?

tm.m: Cannulation oedema and contrast injection at the ampulla of Vater transiently obstruct pancreatic duct outflow, triggering premature intra-acinar trypsinogen activation.
tm.g: Commonest serious complication of ERCP (prevented by rectal NSAIDs) -> Acute pancreatitis
x: Colonic pseudo-obstruction is not a recognised complication of upper gastrointestinal duodenoscopy and biliary cannulation.
Urinary retention follows spinal anaesthesia, pelvic surgery or anticholinergic drugs rather than endoscopic biliary sphincterotomy.
Pneumothorax complicates subclavian central venous cannulation or transbronchial lung biopsy, not endoscopic biliary stone extraction.
Bile acid malabsorption follows terminal ileal resection or cholecystectomy rather than acute endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography.
f: postoperative adynamic colonic dilatation following major orthopaedic or pelvic surgery
inability to void following inguinal hernia repair under spinal anaesthesia
pleuritic chest pain and hypoxia following subclavian central line insertion
chronic watery diarrhoea following right hemicolectomy and terminal ileal resection for Crohn's disease

hq_q.s: A 66 year old man presents with a 4-week history of progressive painless jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and 7 kg weight loss. Serum bilirubin is 142 µmol/L (<17) and CA 19-9 is elevated. Triple-phase pancreas-protocol CT of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis demonstrates a borderline-resectable 3 cm mass in the head of the pancreas encasing the superior mesenteric vein, with no distant metastases. Histological confirmation is required before neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
o: Diagnostic staging laparotomy and wedge biopsy
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG85, endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) with EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration or core biopsy through the duodenal or gastric wall is the preferred method for obtaining a tissue diagnosis in pancreatic head masses, offering high sensitivity while avoiding peritoneal tumour seeding along a percutaneous needle tract.
hq_q.f: Unresectable pancreatic cancer with multiple liver metastases -> percutaneous ultrasound-guided biopsy of a liver metastasis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate technique to obtain a tissue diagnosis?

c: 3 cm mass in the head of the pancreas
tm.m: Transduodenal EUS places the ultrasound transducer directly adjacent to the pancreatic head, allowing short-path needle biopsy within future resection margins.
tm.g: Tissue diagnosis of a pancreatic head mass -> Endoscopic ultrasound-guided biopsy
x: Open laparotomy for tissue biopsy is unnecessarily invasive and delays systemic neoadjuvant chemotherapy compared with endoscopic ultrasound.
Biliary brush cytology at ERCP has low diagnostic sensitivity (30–50%) compared with EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy (>85–90%).
MRCP is a non-invasive imaging modality that cannot obtain tissue or cytology for histological diagnosis.
Percutaneous biopsy of a potentially resectable pancreatic mass carries a significant risk of needle-tract peritoneal tumour seeding.
f: emergency surgical exploration for perforated viscus or acute abdomen
decompressing malignant biliary obstruction with a metal stent when a mass is not directly targetable
non-invasive imaging of suspected choledocholithiasis when ultrasound is inconclusive
percutaneous biopsy of a liver metastasis in already confirmed stage IV metastatic disease

hq_q.s: A 70 year old man who is an ex-smoker presents to his GP after passing dark red urine containing small clots on two occasions this week. He has no dysuria, urinary frequency, loin pain or fever. Blood pressure is 136/80 mmHg, abdominal and digital rectal examinations are normal, serum creatinine is 88 µmol/L (60–120), and a midstream urine culture shows no bacterial growth.
o: Midstream urine culture and sensitivity only
Serum PSA and transrectal prostate biopsy
Urine cytology and repeat dipstick in 1 month
hq_q.w: Aged 45 and over with unexplained visible haematuria without urinary tract infection warrants an urgent 2-week-wait urological referral. Investigation requires flexible cystoscopy (to inspect the urethra and bladder mucosa directly) combined with upper urinary tract imaging, typically a CT urogram.
hq_q.f: Painful visible haematuria with proven E. coli UTI in a 25 year old woman that resolves after antibiotics -> no further investigation needed.
hq_q.ql: When referred on the 2-week-wait urology pathway, which combination of investigations is required?

c: midstream urine culture shows no bacterial growth
tm.m: Flexible cystoscopy directly visualises bladder urothelium (where >90% of urothelial cancers arise), while CT urography images the renal pelvises and ureters.
tm.g: Unexplained painless visible haematuria -> Flexible cystoscopy and CT urogram
x: Urine culture has already excluded infection; painless visible haematuria in a 70 year old mandates endoscopic bladder and upper tract imaging.
Ultrasound alone misses flat urothelial carcinoma in situ and small papillary bladder tumours that require direct cystoscopic inspection.
Painless visible haematuria is the classic presentation of urothelial bladder or upper tract transitional cell carcinoma rather than prostate cancer.
Urine cytology has poor sensitivity for low-grade urothelial tumours and can never replace flexible cystoscopy and upper tract imaging.
f: dysuria and frequency in a young woman where urinary tract infection is suspected
initial imaging of non-visible microscopic haematuria alongside flexible cystoscopy
an elevated age-specific PSA and hard nodular prostate on digital rectal examination
adjunctive high-grade urothelial surveillance alongside cystoscopy

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old man with chronic urinary retention had a catheter inserted 2 hours ago, draining 1.8 litres. Since then he has passed about 400 ml of urine an hour.
Pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 108/64 mmHg. He feels light-headed when he sits up.
o: Clamp the catheter for an hour
Hourly urine output and IV fluids
hq_q.w: After relief of chronic obstruction the kidneys can pour out salt and water (post-obstructive diuresis). He is becoming fluid depleted, so measure urine output hourly, replace losses with IV fluids and check electrolytes.
hq_q.f: Steady urine output of about 60 ml an hour with normal blood pressure → routine catheter care and kidney function checks.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Obstructed tubules lose concentrating ability, and retained urea drives an osmotic diuresis
tm.g: Big diuresis after a catheter: measure and replace
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Clamp the catheter for an hour (Clamping does not prevent the diuresis and is no longer advised)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV furosemide (He is already losing too much fluid; a diuretic would make him more depleted)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Remove the catheter (He still needs drainage of a chronically obstructed bladder)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Restrict oral fluids (Restricting fluid during a diuresis causes dehydration and kidney injury)
x: Clamping does not prevent the diuresis and is no longer advised.
He is already losing too much fluid; a diuretic would make him more depleted.
He still needs drainage of a chronically obstructed bladder.
Restricting fluid during a diuresis causes dehydration and kidney injury.

hq_q.s: A 66 year old man presents to the lower urinary tract symptoms clinic with a 12-month history of urinary hesitancy, a weak intermittent stream, terminal dribbling and nocturia three times nightly. Digital rectal examination reveals a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate gland with a palpable median sulcus. PSA is 2.1 ng/mL (<4.0). He voids into a uroflowmeter followed by a bladder ultrasound scan.
o: Total voided urine volume of 400 mL
hq_q.w: On uroflowmetry (valid when voided volume exceeds 150 mL), a normal curve is bell-shaped with a peak flow rate (Qmax) above 15 mL/second. A Qmax below 10 mL/second with a prolonged, flattened curve indicates bladder outlet obstruction (such as benign prostatic hyperplasia) or detrusor underactivity.
hq_q.f: Flat, plateau 'box-shaped' uroflowmetry curve in a young man after urethral trauma -> urethral stricture.
hq_q.ql: Which uroflowmetry finding indicates bladder outlet obstruction?

c: urinary hesitancy, a weak intermittent stream
tm.m: Prostatic compression of the prostatic urethra increases urethral resistance, reducing maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax <10 mL/s) and prolonging voiding time.
tm.g: Uroflowmetry hallmark of bladder outlet obstruction -> Peak flow rate (Qmax) <10 mL/second (8 mL/second)
x: A rapid rise to peak flow with a smooth symmetrical bell-shaped curve is the normal unobstructed uroflowmetry pattern.
A peak urinary flow rate above 15–20 mL/second excludes significant bladder outlet obstruction.
A post-void residual bladder volume under 50 mL indicates complete bladder emptying rather than chronic retention from outflow obstruction.
A voided volume between 150 mL and 400 mL is the normal functional bladder capacity required for a valid uroflowmetry reading.
f: unobstructed voiding in a healthy young adult
normal peak urinary flow rate on uroflowmetry
normal bladder emptying on post-void ultrasound scan
an adequate voided volume ensuring a technically valid uroflowmetry test

hq_q.s: A 62 year old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive exertional breathlessness and a persistent dry cough. He has never smoked and keeps no birds. Respiratory rate is 20 breaths/min and SpO2 94% on air. Examination reveals finger clubbing and fine end-inspiratory 'Velcro-like' crackles at both lung bases. Spirometry shows FEV1 2.0 L (72% predicted), FVC 2.4 L (64% predicted) and FEV1/FVC ratio 0.83.
hq_q.w: A restrictive spirometry pattern is defined by a reduced forced vital capacity (FVC <80% predicted) with a preserved or elevated FEV1/FVC ratio (>=0.70, here 0.83). In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, increased lung elastic recoil maintains early expiratory flow relative to the shrunken lung volume.
hq_q.f: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio <0.70 in a smoker with chronic cough -> obstructive ventilatory defect (COPD).
hq_q.ql: Which ventilatory pattern is demonstrated on his spirometry?

c: FVC 2.4 L (64% predicted) and FEV1/FVC ratio 0.83
tm.m: Interstitial fibrosis reduces total lung compliance and forced vital capacity while increased radial traction preserves or increases the FEV1/FVC ratio.
tm.g: Reduced FVC (<80% predicted) + FEV1/FVC ratio >=0.70 -> Restrictive ventilatory defect
x: A mixed obstructive-restrictive defect requires both a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (<0.70) and a reduced FVC, whereas his FEV1/FVC ratio is elevated at 0.83.
Although the FEV1/FVC ratio is above 0.70, his forced vital capacity (FVC) is significantly reduced at 64% predicted, excluding normal lung function.
Obstructive lung diseases (asthma, COPD) reduce FEV1 disproportionately to FVC, producing an FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70.
Upper airway obstruction flattens the inspiratory or expiratory limb of the flow-volume loop rather than causing basal crackles, clubbing and high FEV1/FVC.
f: coexistent severe emphysema and pulmonary fibrosis with FEV1/FVC 0.58 and reduced FVC
FEV1 95% predicted, FVC 98% predicted and FEV1/FVC ratio 0.80
a 40 pack-year smoker with breathlessness and post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.56
stridor and a flattened inspiratory limb on the flow-volume loop from vocal cord palsy

hq_q.s: A 30 year old woman presents with a 3-month history of episodic dry cough, chest tightness and wheeze that is worse at night and after jogging in cold air. She has a childhood history of atopic eczema, has never smoked and takes no inhaled corticosteroids. Chest auscultation in clinic today is clear. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) testing is performed and measures 52 parts per billion (ppb).
hq_q.w: Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) is produced by airway epithelial inducible nitric oxide synthase driven by IL-4 and IL-13 in eosinophilic airway inflammation. Under joint BTS/NICE/SIGN guidance, a FeNO >=50 ppb (or >=40 ppb with typical symptoms) in a steroid-naive adult supports a diagnosis of asthma.
hq_q.f: Smoker with suspected asthma and FeNO 22 ppb -> cigarette smoke suppresses FeNO, so a low reading does not exclude asthma.
hq_q.ql: According to joint BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma guidelines, which diagnosis does this FeNO result support?

c: worse at night and after jogging in cold air
tm.m: Type 2 helper T-cell cytokines (IL-4, IL-13) upregulate bronchial epithelial inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), increasing exhaled nitric oxide.
tm.g: Nocturnal/exercise wheeze + FeNO >=50 ppb in steroid-naive adult -> Eosinophilic asthma
x: COPD occurs in smokers typically over 35 years with neutrophil-predominant airway inflammation and low or normal FeNO levels.
Pulmonary congestion in heart failure causes orthopnoea, bibasal crackles and elevated NT-proBNP rather than elevated exhaled nitric oxide.
In steroid-naive adults, a FeNO concentration of 50 ppb or above is significantly elevated and indicates active type 2 eosinophilic airway inflammation.
Bronchiectasis is driven by neutrophilic airway infection and mucus hypersecretion (often with low FeNO), presenting with daily purulent sputum.
f: progressive breathlessness and fixed airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC <0.7) in a 60 year old heavy smoker
orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, displaced apex beat and NT-proBNP 2400 ng/L
a FeNO reading of 15 ppb in a healthy asymptomatic adult
chronic daily production of copious purulent sputum and tram-track bronchial dilatation on high-resolution CT

hq_q.s:
A 62 year old man has smoked for 40 pack-years. He has had breathlessness on exertion and a morning cough for 2 years.
Post-bronchodilator spirometry: FEV1/FVC ratio 0.58, FEV1 62% of predicted. FEV1 improves by 5% after salbutamol.
hq_q.w: A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 means airflow obstruction, and a change of under 12% after salbutamol means it is largely fixed. In a long-term smoker with these symptoms this supports COPD; an FEV1 of 50 to 79% is moderate.
hq_q.f: FEV1 rises by more than 12% and 200 ml after salbutamol → reversible obstruction, which suggests asthma.
hq_q.ql: Which pattern does this show?

tm.m: Destroyed alveolar walls and narrowed small airways limit airflow in a way bronchodilators barely change
tm.g: Ratio under 0.7, little reversibility: fixed obstruction (COPD)
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Mixed obstruction and restriction (A mixed defect needs a low ratio and a reduced total lung capacity on full lung function tests)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Normal spirometry (A ratio of 0.58 is well below the 0.7 cut-off)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Restrictive defect (Restriction gives a normal or high ratio with a low FVC)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Reversible obstruction (Reversibility needs an FEV1 rise of 12% and 200 ml or more; his rose 5%)
x: A mixed defect needs a low ratio and a reduced total lung capacity on full lung function tests.
A ratio of 0.58 is well below the 0.7 cut-off.
Restriction gives a normal or high ratio with a low FVC.
Reversibility needs an FEV1 rise of 12% and 200 ml or more; his rose 5%.

hq_q.s: A 55 year old woman presents with a 4-week history of sudden-onset, rapid fluttering palpitations that occur once or twice a week and last 15 to 20 minutes before stopping abruptly. She has no chest pain, breathlessness or syncope. Pulse rate is 72 bpm regular, BP 128/76 mmHg and heart sounds are normal. Thyroid function, full blood count and a resting 12-lead ECG are normal.
hq_q.w: Ambulatory ECG duration must match symptom frequency: daily palpitations warrant a 24- to 48-hour Holter monitor; episodes occurring every few days or weekly warrant a 7- to 14-day external patch or patient-activated event recorder; rare episodes (<1/month) warrant an implantable loop recorder.
hq_q.f: Palpitations occurring multiple times every day -> 24-hour Holter monitor.
hq_q.ql: Which ambulatory ECG monitoring modality is most appropriate to capture her arrhythmia?

c: occur once or twice a week
no chest pain, breathlessness or syncope
tm.m: Extending continuous or patient-triggered ECG recording across 1 to 2 weeks matches the inter-episode interval of weekly paroxysmal arrhythmias.
tm.g: Palpitations occurring every few days / weekly -> 7 to 14 day external event recorder
x: A 24-hour Holter monitor is appropriate only when palpitations occur daily; it will likely miss episodes occurring once or twice a week.
Exercise stress testing is indicated when arrhythmia or angina is specifically provoked by physical exertion rather than spontaneous weekly episodes at rest.
An implantable loop recorder requires minor surgical insertion and is reserved for infrequent episodes (less than once a month) or unexplained syncope.
Echocardiography assesses structural heart disease and valve function but cannot record transient electrical arrhythmias causing weekly palpitations.
f: frequent palpitations occurring several times every day
palpitations or chest tightness reproducibly triggered only during vigorous exercise
unexplained recurrent syncope occurring once every 4 to 6 months after negative external monitoring
an ejection systolic murmur or suspected structural cardiomyopathy

hq_q.s: A 52 year old man has a clinic blood pressure of 148/92 mmHg measured on two separate occasions during a routine health check. He is asymptomatic, does not smoke, has no diabetes or renal disease, and has normal fundoscopy and 12-lead ECG. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) is arranged and demonstrates a daytime average blood pressure of 137/86 mmHg.
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG136, when clinic blood pressure is >=140/90 mmHg, ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) is offered to confirm the diagnosis. An ABPM daytime average of 135/85 mmHg to 149/94 mmHg (clinic 140/90 to 159/99 mmHg) defines stage 1 hypertension; >=150/95 mmHg defines stage 2 hypertension.
hq_q.f: Clinic BP 150/94 mmHg with ABPM daytime average 128/78 mmHg -> white-coat hypertension.
hq_q.ql: According to NICE hypertension guidelines, what is the correct diagnosis?

c: daytime average blood pressure of 137/86 mmHg
tm.m: Out-of-office ABPM eliminates white-coat alerting responses; a daytime average >=135/85 mmHg (and <150/95 mmHg) confirms stage 1 hypertension.
tm.g: Clinic BP >=140/90 + ABPM daytime average 135/85 to 149/94 mmHg -> Stage 1 hypertension
x: Normal daytime average ABPM is below 135/85 mmHg; a daytime average of 137/86 mmHg exceeds both systolic and diastolic thresholds for hypertension.
Severe hypertension is defined by a clinic blood pressure of >=180/120 mmHg, often accompanied by retinal haemorrhages, exudates or papilloedema.
Stage 2 hypertension requires a clinic BP >=160/100 mmHg with a subsequent ABPM/HBPM daytime average of >=150/95 mmHg.
White-coat hypertension is defined by an elevated clinic BP (>=140/90 mmHg) with a normal daytime average ABPM (<135/85 mmHg).
f: clinic BP 128/78 mmHg and daytime average ABPM 124/76 mmHg
clinic blood pressure of 188/124 mmHg with bilateral retinal flame haemorrhages and papilloedema
clinic BP 166/104 mmHg and daytime average ABPM 154/96 mmHg
clinic BP 152/94 mmHg with a subsequent daytime average ABPM of 128/78 mmHg

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man fainted suddenly without warning while playing football. He recovered within a minute. His uncle died suddenly at 35.
Pulse rate 68 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg. There is an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge.
hq_q.w: Exertional syncope suggests a heart cause such as aortic stenosis, HCM or arrhythmia. It needs urgent cardiology review and no driving.
hq_q.f: Fainting after standing in a hot queue with warning signs → vasovagal.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important initial step?

tm.m: Exertional syncope with a murmur and a family sudden death suggests HCM or a channelopathy
tm.g: Exertional syncope with red flags: urgent cardiology review
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Advise more salt (He has red flags for a cardiac cause)
fainting in a hot queue with warning symptoms

the presentation instead showed features specific to Routine cardiology clinic (A routine wait is unsafe: exertional syncope with a murmur and a family history of sudden death suggests HCM, which needs urgent assessment)
Recurrent unexplained postural syncope in young patient with normal ECG
x: He has red flags for a cardiac cause.
Ruled out here: requires fainting in a hot queue with warning symptoms, whereas this patient has without warning, playing football.
A routine wait is unsafe: exertional syncope with a murmur and a family history of sudden death suggests HCM, which needs urgent assessment.
Ruled out here: requires Recurrent unexplained postural syncope in young patient with normal ECG, whereas this patient has without warning, playing football.

hq_q.s: A 48 year old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents with a 3-week history of fever, night sweats and weight loss. Temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. Auscultation reveals a new grade 3/6 pansystolic murmur at the apex, and two sets of blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) shows no vegetations, but clinical suspicion of infective endocarditis remains high.
hq_q.w: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is the first-line imaging test in suspected infective endocarditis (sensitivity ~60–75%). If TTE is negative or equivocal despite high clinical suspicion (such as Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia and a new murmur), or in prosthetic valves or suspected aortic root abscess, transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE, sensitivity >90%) is indicated.
hq_q.f: Prolonged PR interval on ECG in aortic valve endocarditis -> aortic root abscess; urgent TOE.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation should be performed next?

c: suspicion of infective endocarditis remains high
tm.m: Positioning the high-frequency ultrasound transducer in the oesophagus directly behind the left atrium eliminates chest wall attenuation, resolving vegetations <2 mm and paravalvular abscesses.
tm.g: Negative TTE with high clinical suspicion of endocarditis (or prosthetic valve / root abscess) -> Transoesophageal echocardiography
x: Standard thoracic CT does not have the temporal resolution to detect small mobile valvular vegetations or leaflet perforations.
Cardiac MRI is used to evaluate myocardial inflammation (myocarditis) or infiltrative cardiomyopathy rather than small mobile valve vegetations.
Chest X-ray assesses pulmonary oedema or septic emboli but cannot visualise cardiac valve leaflets or intracardiac vegetations.
Waiting 6 months in untreated or uncharacterised Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis risks fatal valve destruction, aortic root abscess and systemic embolisation.
f: detecting septic pulmonary emboli in confirmed right-sided tricuspid valve endocarditis
suspected acute viral myocarditis with troponin rise and normal coronary arteries
assessing acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from severe valvular regurgitation
routine surveillance of asymptomatic mild native mitral valve prolapse without infection

hq_q.s: A 66 year old man with a previous anterior myocardial infarction presents with a 3-month history of progressive exertional breathlessness, orthopnoea requiring three pillows and bilateral ankle swelling. Pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg, JVP is elevated 5 cm and there are bibasal pulmonary crackles. Serum NT-proBNP is 2,650 ng/L (<400). Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 35%.
o: Heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
hq_q.w: ESC and NICE guidelines classify heart failure by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF): heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is LVEF <=40%; mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) is LVEF 41–49%; and preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is LVEF >=50% with objective evidence of diastolic dysfunction and raised natriuretic peptides.
hq_q.f: Breathlessness, raised NT-proBNP, concentric LV hypertrophy and LVEF 56% -> heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF).
hq_q.ql: How is his heart failure classified according to left ventricular ejection fraction?

tm.m: Post-infarction left ventricular remodelling impairs myocardial contractility, reducing stroke volume as a fraction of end-diastolic volume to <=40%.
tm.g: Heart failure symptoms + LVEF <=40% (35%) -> Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
x: Cor pulmonale is right ventricular hypertrophy and failure secondary to chronic lung disease and pulmonary hypertension with preserved LVEF.
Heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) is defined by an LVEF between 41% and 49%, whereas his LVEF is 35%.
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) requires an LVEF >=50% alongside structural/diastolic dysfunction and raised natriuretic peptides.
A normal left ventricular ejection fraction is >=50–55%; an LVEF of 35% represents moderate-to-severe systolic dysfunction.
f: elevated JVP, parasternal heave and ankle oedema in severe COPD with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction
clinical heart failure with elevated NT-proBNP and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45%
clinical heart failure, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, raised NT-proBNP and an LVEF of 58%
an asymptomatic individual with normal NT-proBNP and an LVEF of 60%

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old athlete fainted while running. He has had chest pain on exertion.
There is an ejection systolic murmur that gets louder on standing and quieter on squatting.
ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T wave inversion. Echo shows an interventricular septum of 25 mm.
hq_q.w: HCM: asymmetric septal hypertrophy and outflow obstruction. It is a cause of sudden death in young athletes.
hq_q.f: Mild symmetrical thickening that regresses with rest from training → athlete's heart.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: louder on standing and quieter on squatting
tm.m: A thick septum obstructs outflow, which worsens when preload falls
tm.g: A murmur louder on standing with a 25 mm septum is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
f: a slow-rising pulse and a murmur to the carotids in an older person
mild symmetrical thickening that regresses with rest from training
the presentation instead showed features specific to Dilated cardiomyopathy (Classic picture: Doxorubicin toxicity)
started treatment with clozapine 3 weeks ago + Troponin I
x: Ruled out here: requires a slow-rising pulse and a murmur to the carotids in an older person, whereas this patient has fainted while running, louder on standing and quieter on squatting.
Ruled out here: requires mild symmetrical thickening that regresses with rest from training, whereas this patient has fainted while running, louder on standing and quieter on squatting.
Classic picture: Doxorubicin toxicity
Ruled out here: requires started treatment with clozapine 3 weeks ago + Troponin I, whereas this patient has fainted while running, louder on standing and quieter on squatting.

hq_q.s: A 66 year old postmenopausal woman sustained a displaced distal radius (Colles') fracture after tripping on a flat pavement from standing height. Her serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels are normal. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scanning of the lumbar spine and femoral neck is performed and reports a femoral neck T-score of -2.8.
hq_q.w: World Health Organization criteria classify dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) T-scores (standard deviations compared with a young adult reference population): >= -1.0 is normal, between -1.0 and -2.5 is osteopenia, and <= -2.5 is osteoporosis. With a fragility fracture plus T-score <= -2.5, oral bisphosphonate therapy (alendronic acid) is indicated.
hq_q.f: DEXA T-score of -1.8 SD -> osteopenia.
hq_q.ql: What diagnosis is established by this DEXA T-score?

c: tripping on a flat pavement from standing height
tm.m: Postmenopausal oestrogen deficiency accelerates osteoclast-mediated trabecular and cortical bone resorption, reducing bone mineral density >=2.5 SD below the young adult mean.
tm.g: DEXA T-score <= -2.5 (-2.8) -> Osteoporosis
x: Normal bone mineral density on DEXA is defined by a T-score of -1.0 or higher (above -1.0 SD of the young adult mean).
Osteomalacia is defective osteoid mineralisation caused by vitamin D deficiency (presenting with low calcium/phosphate and high ALP/PTH), whereas her bone profile is normal.
Osteopenia is defined by a DEXA T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 (exclusive of -2.5), whereas her T-score is -2.8.
Paget's disease causes focal disorganised bone remodelling with cortical thickening, bone expansion and markedly raised ALP rather than a generalised low DEXA T-score.
f: a femoral neck and lumbar spine T-score of -0.6 SD
proximal myopathy, bone pain, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D, hypocalcaemia and raised alkaline phosphatase
a femoral neck DEXA T-score of -1.8 SD
pelvic bone pain, focal cortical thickening and bone expansion on X-ray, and isolated high alkaline phosphatase

hq_q.s: A 74 year old man with high-grade prostatic adenocarcinoma presents with a 2-month history of progressive aching pain across his lower back, pelvis and ribs that disturbs his sleep. Blood tests show PSA 86 ng/mL (<4.0), alkaline phosphatase 420 IU/L (25–115) and adjusted calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). A technetium-99m MDP isotope bone scan shows multiple asymmetrical foci of intense tracer uptake across the thoracolumbar spine, ribs and pelvis.
hq_q.w: Technetium-99m bisphosphonate bone scintigraphy binds to hydroxyapatite at sites of active osteoblastic bone formation. Prostate cancer metastases are characteristically osteoblastic (sclerotic), producing raised alkaline phosphatase and multiple asymmetric 'hot spots' across the axial skeleton.
hq_q.f: Multiple punched-out lytic lesions that are 'cold' on isotope bone scan -> multiple myeloma (investigate with whole-body MRI or low-dose CT).
hq_q.ql: What is the most likely diagnosis?

c: multiple asymmetrical foci of intense tracer uptake
tm.m: Prostate cancer cells secrete endothelin-1 and bone morphogenetic proteins that stimulate local osteoblast activity, concentrating technetium-99m MDP tracer.
tm.g: Prostate cancer + raised ALP + multiple hot spots on isotope bone scan -> Osteoblastic bone metastases
x: Uncomplicated osteoporosis causes diffuse osteopenia without focal osteoblastic 'hot spots' on bone scintigraphy or an ALP of 420 IU/L.
Multiple myeloma causes purely osteolytic lesions due to osteoclast activation and osteoblast inhibition, which typically appear 'cold' (negative) on isotope bone scans.
Normal bone scintigraphy shows symmetric uptake with renal and bladder excretion; multiple asymmetrical spinal and rib hot spots are abnormal.
While Paget's disease increases ALP and uptake in single bones, multiple asymmetric axial hot spots with PSA 86 ng/mL in prostate cancer indicate metastases.
f: uniformly reduced bone mineral density on DEXA with normal alkaline phosphatase and PSA
punched-out lytic skull and pelvic lesions on whole-body MRI/CT with a paraprotein spike and negative bone scan
symmetrical skeletal tracer distribution with normal urinary bladder excretion
isolated expansion and cortical thickening of the hemipelvis with a normal PSA of 1.2 ng/mL

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history undergoes a contrast CT scan of the thorax after presenting with a 3-week cough. The CT demonstrates an solitary 12 mm pulmonary nodule in the periphery of the right upper lobe with irregular spiculated margins, and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion. His Brock score indicates a >10% risk of malignancy.
o: Repeat plain chest X-ray in 12 months
hq_q.w: Under BTS pulmonary nodule guidelines, solid nodules >=8 mm (or >=300 mm³) with a Brock malignancy risk >10% are investigated with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET-CT, with post-test probability refined using the Herder model to guide CT-guided biopsy or surgical resection.
hq_q.f: Smooth, well-circumscribed solid pulmonary nodule measuring 4 mm -> discharge with no CT follow-up required.
hq_q.ql: According to British Thoracic Society guidelines, which investigation should be arranged next to assess malignancy risk and guide biopsy?

tm.m: Malignant pulmonary nodules overexpress GLUT-1 glucose transporters and hexokinase, trapping radiolabelled 18F-FDG proportional to metabolic proliferation.
tm.g: Pulmonary nodule >=8 mm with Brock risk >10% -> FDG PET-CT scan
x: Standard flexible bronchoscopy visualises only the central lobar and segmental airways and has very low yield for peripheral 12 mm nodules.
A 12 mm spiculated nodule in a heavy smoker carries high malignancy risk and requires immediate PET-CT assessment rather than 1-year plain X-ray delay.
Sputum cytology has extremely low sensitivity for small peripheral pulmonary nodules and has no role in the BTS pulmonary nodule pathway.
V/Q scanning assesses pulmonary arterial perfusion in suspected thromboembolism, not metabolic glucose uptake in a pulmonary nodule.
f: a central endobronchial mass visible within the right main bronchus causing haemoptysis
no follow-up needed for a <5 mm smooth benign-appearing nodule
historical investigation of large central squamous carcinomas in patients unfit for bronchoscopy
suspected chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension or acute pulmonary embolism

hq_q.s: A 46 year old man presents with a 4-month history of progressive frontal headaches, reduced libido, erectile dysfunction and repeatedly bumping into door frames and parked cars on either side. Visual acuity is 6/9 in both eyes. Formal automated perimetry and confrontation visual field testing demonstrate complete loss of the temporal (outer) half of the visual field in both eyes.
hq_q.w: Unmyelinated nasal retinal ganglion axons from both eyes-which carry the temporal (lateral) visual fields-decussate at the optic chiasm. Compression of the optic chiasm from below by a pituitary macroadenoma or above by a craniopharyngioma produces a bitemporal hemianopia.
hq_q.f: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing -> occipital visual cortex lesion (posterior cerebral artery infarction).
hq_q.ql: Where is the anatomical site of the lesion?

c: loss of the temporal (outer) half of the visual field in both eyes
tm.m: Decussating nasal retinal fibres carrying both temporal hemifields are compressed in the midline at the optic chiasm by a sellar mass.
tm.g: Bitemporal hemianopia -> Optic chiasm
x: A lesion of the left optic nerve causes ipsilateral monocular visual loss and a left relative afferent pupillary defect, sparing the right eye.
A lesion of the left optic tract interrupts left temporal and right nasal fibres, causing a right homonymous hemianopia rather than bitemporal hemianopia.
A unilateral occipital cortex lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing due to dual middle and posterior cerebral artery supply.
Damage to Meyer's loop of the right temporal optic radiation causes a contralateral (left) superior homonymous quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky').
f: complete loss of vision in the left eye only with a normal right visual field
loss of the right half of the visual field in both eyes (right homonymous hemianopia)
right homonymous hemianopia with sparing of central macular vision following a left PCA stroke
left upper quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky') in both eyes from a right temporal lobe lesion

hq_q.s: A 32 year old woman presents with a 4-week history of progressive bilateral frontal headaches that are worst on waking in the morning and aggravated by coughing or straining. She also reports brief episodes of visual greying when standing up. Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes, and pupils are equal and reactive. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral hyperaemic, elevated optic discs with blurred margins and absent spontaneous venous pulsation.
hq_q.w: Papilloedema refers specifically to bilateral optic disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure transmitted along the subarachnoid sheath of the optic nerves. Early signs include loss of spontaneous venous pulsation and blurring of the disc margins; urgent neuroimaging (MRI/CT head and venography) is mandatory.
hq_q.f: Unilateral swollen disc with painful eye movements, reduced colour vision (dyschromatopsia) and RAPD -> optic neuritis.
hq_q.ql: Which fundoscopic sign is described?

c: worst on waking in the morning and aggravated by coughing
bilateral hyperaemic, elevated optic discs with blurred margins
tm.m: Elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure within the subarachnoid optic nerve sheath arrests axoplasmic transport at the lamina cribrosa, swelling the optic nerve head bilaterally.
tm.g: Bilateral swollen optic discs + morning headache worse on Valsalva -> Papilloedema
x: Central retinal vein occlusion is almost always unilateral, causing sudden painless visual loss with a 'stormy sunset' fundus of widespread flame haemorrhages and tortuous veins.
Chronic glaucoma causes progressive pale cupping of the optic disc (increased cup-to-disc ratio >0.6) rather than bilateral hyperaemic disc swelling.
Diabetic retinopathy causes microaneurysms, blot haemorrhages, hard exudates and neovascularisation rather than isolated bilateral optic disc swelling with morning headaches.
Optic atrophy presents as flat, chalky-white pale optic discs with sharp margins and reduced visual acuity, representing end-stage axonal loss.
f: sudden painless unilateral visual loss with widespread retinal haemorrhages and dilated tortuous veins in one eye
asymptomatic peripheral visual field loss with pale, deeply cupped optic discs and cup-to-disc ratio 0.8
microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots and fragile new vessels on the disc in long-standing diabetes
pale, flat, sharply marginated optic discs with reduced visual acuity after previous optic neuropathy

hq_q.s: A 34 year old man presents with a 3-day history of a painful, gritty, watering right eye and photophobia. He has a history of recurrent cold sores on his upper lip. Visual acuity is 6/12 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left. Topical fluorescein 1% drops are instilled and examined under a cobalt-blue slit-lamp light, revealing a bright green, branching dendritic lesion with terminal bulbs.
hq_q.w: Topical fluorescein is a water-soluble dye that is excluded by intact, hydrophobic corneal epithelium but adheres to the exposed hydrophilic corneal stroma (Bowman's layer) wherever corneal epithelial cells are lost, glowing bright green under cobalt-blue light. A branching dendritic ulcer indicates herpes simplex keratitis.
hq_q.f: Well-demarcated linear green corneal staining after being poked in the eye by a fingernail -> simple traumatic corneal abrasion.
hq_q.ql: Which anatomical layer of the eye is disrupted to produce this fluorescein staining?

tm.m: Loss of intact hydrophobic corneal epithelial tight junctions exposes the hydrophilic basement membrane and stroma, which absorb water-soluble fluorescein.
tm.g: Bright green uptake of topical fluorescein under cobalt-blue light -> Corneal epithelium defect
x: The crystalline lens lies deep behind the iris and aqueous humour and cannot be contacted by topical fluorescein drops instilled into the tear film.
Dendritic ulceration with terminal bulbs is pathognomonic of herpes simplex keratitis of the cornea rather than diffuse bulbar conjunctivitis.
The retina lines the posterior segment of the globe and is visualised by fundoscopy or fluorescein angiography, not topical tear-film staining.
The vitreous humour fills the posterior cavity behind the lens and is completely isolated from topical ocular surface dye.
f: anterior subcapsular cataract or lenticonus seen on retroillumination slit-lamp examination
diffuse conjunctival injection and chemosis without corneal epithelial loss
intravenous fundus fluorescein angiography demonstrating retinal capillary leakage in diabetic maculopathy
floaters and flashes caused by posterior vitreous detachment on dilated fundoscopy

hq_q.s: A 46 year old man presents with a 2-month history of muffled hearing in his right ear with no pain or vertigo. Left-sided hearing is normal. On tuning fork examination with a 512 Hz fork, Weber's test placed on the forehead lateralises to the right ear. Rinne's test shows bone conduction is louder than air conduction on the right, and air conduction is louder than bone conduction on the left.
hq_q.w: In unilateral conductive hearing loss, Rinne's test is negative on the affected side (bone conduction louder than air conduction) and Weber's test lateralises to the affected ear (because reduced ambient room noise masks the affected cochlea less).
hq_q.f: Right-sided hearing loss where Weber lateralises to the left and Rinne is positive bilaterally -> right sensorineural hearing loss.
hq_q.ql: Which type of hearing loss do these tuning fork results demonstrate?

c: Weber's test placed on the forehead lateralises to the right ear
bone conduction is louder than air conduction on the right
tm.m: External or middle ear obstruction attenuates air conduction below bone conduction (negative Rinne) and eliminates ambient masking noise, making Weber louder in the affected ear.
tm.g: Weber lateralises to right + Rinne negative (BC > AC) on right -> Right conductive hearing loss
x: Normal hearing produces a midline Weber test and positive Rinne tests (air conduction louder than bone conduction) in both ears.
In left conductive hearing loss, Weber's test would lateralise to the left ear and Rinne's test would be negative on the left.
In left sensorineural hearing loss, Weber lateralises to the right (good) ear, but Rinne remains positive (air > bone) in both ears.
In right sensorineural hearing loss, Weber's test lateralises away from the affected ear to the left, and Rinne's test is positive on the right.
f: Weber central in the midline and Rinne positive (AC > BC) bilaterally
Weber lateralising to the left ear with bone conduction louder than air conduction on the left
left-sided deafness where Weber lateralises to the right and Rinne is positive (AC > BC) bilaterally
right-sided deafness where Weber lateralises to the left ear and Rinne is positive bilaterally

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old man has worked in a noisy factory for 30 years without ear protection. He has difficulty hearing in noisy places.
Both ear drums are normal.
Audiometry shows a dip at 4 kHz in both ears with recovery at 8 kHz.
hq_q.w: Noise damage typically causes a notch at around 4 kHz, often with recovery at 8 kHz.
hq_q.f: Sloping high-frequency loss in an older person → presbycusis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?

tm.m: Noise damages the hair cells tuned to about 4 kHz
tm.g: A 4 kHz notch with recovery at 8 kHz is noise-induced hearing loss
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Ménière's disease (Classic picture: Hours of vertigo + roaring tinnitus + fullness + fluctuating low-tone hearing loss. Ménière's disease)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Otosclerosis of both ears (Otosclerosis is conductive)
a sloping high-frequency loss in an older person
one-sided loss with tinnitus and imbalance
x: Classic picture: Hours of vertigo + roaring tinnitus + fullness + fluctuating low-tone hearing loss. Ménière's disease
Otosclerosis is conductive.
Ruled out here: requires a sloping high-frequency loss in an older person, whereas this patient has noisy factory, dip at 4 kHz.
Ruled out here: requires one-sided loss with tinnitus and imbalance, whereas this patient has noisy factory, dip at 4 kHz.

hq_q.s: A 44 year old woman presents to her GP after waking yesterday morning with sudden, severe hearing loss and high-pitched tinnitus in her left ear. She has no otalgia, otorrhoea or vertigo. Otoscopy reveals clear external auditory canals and normal pearly-grey tympanic membranes bilaterally. Using a 512 Hz tuning fork, Weber's test lateralises to the right ear, and Rinne's test is positive on both sides.
o: Prescribe a 5-day course of oral amoxicillin
Reassure and review in 4 weeks if persistent
Syringe both ears after olive oil drops
hq_q.w: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (>=30 dB loss over <72 hours, confirmed here by normal otoscopy, Weber lateralising to the contralateral right ear and bilateral positive Rinne) is an otological emergency. NICE NG98 mandates immediate (same-day/within 24 hours) ENT referral for urgent audiometry, high-dose oral or intratympanic corticosteroids, and MRI to exclude vestibular schwannoma.
hq_q.f: Conductive hearing loss with impacted cerumen occluding the external canal -> olive oil drops and ear irrigation/microsuction.
hq_q.ql: According to NICE guidelines, which is the most appropriate immediate management?

c: waking yesterday morning with sudden, severe hearing loss
Weber's test lateralises to the right ear
Rinne's test is positive on both sides
tm.m: Acute cochlear hair cell or spiral ganglion inflammation/ischaemia requires prompt corticosteroid therapy within days of onset to prevent permanent deafness.
tm.g: Sudden unilateral sensorineural hearing loss -> Same-day emergency ENT referral
x: Antibiotics treat acute bacterial otitis media, whereas normal tympanic membranes and tuning forks here indicate sudden sensorineural hearing loss.
Delaying treatment for 4 weeks in idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss misses the critical window for high-dose steroid cochlear salvage.
Routine audiometry referral is for gradual age-related presbycusis; sudden sensorineural hearing loss within 30 days requires emergency ENT assessment within 24 hours.
Ear irrigation treats impacted cerumen (which causes conductive loss and is visible on otoscopy), whereas her ear canals are clear and loss is sensorineural.
f: acute otalgia, fever and a bulging erythematous tympanic membrane in acute otitis media
mild transient Eustachian tube dysfunction with conductive muffled hearing after a cold
gradual bilateral high-frequency hearing loss developing over 3 years in a 75 year old
occlusive impacted earwax visible on otoscopy causing conductive hearing loss

hq_q.s: A 25 year old man is reviewed in the Emergency Department 4 hours after a witnessed 2-minute generalised tonic-clonic seizure with tongue biting and post-ictal drowsiness. He has now returned to his baseline GCS of 15/15 with normal neurological examination, normal capillary glucose, normal serum electrolytes and a normal 12-lead ECG. He is discharged with safety advice and referred to the first-seizure clinic.
o: Arrange soon after specialist review to support classification
Defer EEG until he has a second unprovoked seizure
Discharge if the interictal EEG recording is normal
Perform an immediate EEG in the Emergency Department
Repeat the EEG annually to monitor drug levels
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG217, after a first unprovoked seizure an urgent specialist review (within 2 weeks) is arranged, and an EEG is performed soon after if requested by the specialist to help determine seizure type, epilepsy syndrome and recurrence risk. A normal interictal EEG never excludes epilepsy.
hq_q.f: Persistently reduced consciousness after convulsive status epilepticus -> urgent inpatient EEG to exclude non-convulsive status epilepticus.
hq_q.ql: How should an electroencephalogram (EEG) be used in his assessment?

c: returned to his baseline GCS of 15/15
tm.m: Interictal epileptiform discharges (such as 3 Hz spike-and-wave or focal spikes) help classify generalised versus focal epilepsy syndromes and predict recurrence risk.
tm.g: Role of EEG after a first unprovoked seizure -> Arrange soon after specialist review to support classification
x: NICE NG217 recommends offering an EEG after a first unprovoked seizure if requested by the specialist to stratify recurrence risk and classify syndrome.
A routine interictal EEG is normal in up to 50% of people with epilepsy, so a normal EEG can never be used alone to exclude epilepsy.
Immediate ED EEG is reserved for suspected non-convulsive status epilepticus in a persistently comatose patient, not a recovered first seizure.
Routine serial EEGs are not used to monitor anti-seizure medication adherence or efficacy in well-controlled epilepsy.
f: older guidance before modern first-seizure risk stratification
misinterpreting a normal interictal EEG as ruling out a clinical seizure disorder
persistent unexplained coma after convulsive status epilepticus to exclude non-convulsive status
monitoring clinical seizure freedom rather than repeating routine EEGs

hq_q.s: A 48 year old woman who works as a data-entry clerk presents with a 4-month history of numbness, tingling and burning pain in the thumb, index and middle fingers of her right hand that wakes her from sleep and improves when she shakes her wrist. Examination shows mild right thenar wasting, a positive Phalen's test, and preserved sensation over the thenar palm. Nerve conduction studies show median nerve slowing across the wrist.
hq_q.w: Carpal tunnel syndrome is entrapment of the median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) at the wrist, causing nocturnal paraesthesia in the palmar thumb, index, middle and lateral ring fingers. Sensation over the thenar eminence is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel.
hq_q.f: Numbness of the little and ring fingers with weak finger abduction and Froment's sign -> ulnar nerve palsy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: improves when she shakes her wrist
positive Phalen's test, and preserved sensation over the thenar palm
median nerve slowing across the wrist
tm.m: Compression of the median nerve under the flexor retinaculum causes focal demyelinating conduction slowing while sparing the superficial palmar cutaneous branch.
tm.g: Nocturnal thumb/index/middle paraesthesia relieved by shaking + spared thenar sensation -> Carpal tunnel syndrome
x: C6 radiculopathy causes neck pain radiating down the lateral forearm with reduced biceps/supinator reflexes and does not spare the palmar cutaneous branch or slow conduction at the wrist.
Cubital tunnel syndrome compresses the ulnar nerve at the medial epicondyle of the elbow, causing paraesthesia in the little and ring fingers and interosseous wasting.
Diabetic polyneuropathy causes symmetrical length-dependent 'glove and stocking' sensory loss starting in both feet rather than isolated nocturnal median nerve symptoms.
Guyon's canal compression at the wrist affects the ulnar nerve, causing hypothenar and interosseous weakness and fifth-finger sensory loss.
f: shooting neck pain into the thumb with a diminished biceps reflex and normal wrist nerve conduction
numbness in the little and medial ring fingers with weak finger abduction and conduction block at the elbow
bilateral burning foot pain and absent ankle reflexes in a stocking distribution
numbness of the palmar little finger and weakness of intrinsic hand muscles in a long-distance cyclist

hq_q.s: A 42 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 24-hour history of continuous, severe spinning vertigo, nausea, vomiting and unsteadiness on walking. She has no hearing loss, tinnitus, diplopia, dysarthria or limb ataxia, and unidirectional horizontal nystagmus is present at rest. A bedside three-step HINTS (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) examination is performed to differentiate vestibular neuritis from a posterior circulation stroke.
o: Abnormal head impulse test with catch-up saccade
Absent spontaneous nystagmus in all positions
Vertical ocular misalignment on cover-uncover testing
hq_q.w: In acute vestibular syndrome (continuous vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus), the HINTS exam is reassuring for a peripheral cause (vestibular neuritis) ONLY when all three are peripheral: an ABNORMAL head impulse test (unilateral catch-up saccade), unidirectional nystagmus, and no vertical skew deviation. Any central feature ('INFARCT': Impulse Normal, Fast-phase Alternating, Refixation on Cover Test) indicates possible posterior circulation stroke.
hq_q.f: Normal head impulse test or direction-changing nystagmus or vertical skew deviation ('INFARCT') -> central posterior circulation stroke.
hq_q.ql: Which finding on the HINTS examination supports a benign peripheral vestibular cause?

c: HINTS (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) examination
tm.m: Peripheral eighth nerve inflammation impairs the ipsilateral vestibulo-ocular reflex, causing the eyes to drift with a rapid head turn and require a corrective catch-up saccade.
tm.g: HINTS finding reassuring for peripheral vestibular neuritis -> Abnormal head impulse test with catch-up saccade
x: The HINTS examination is only validated in acute vestibular syndrome when continuous spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus is present.
Nystagmus that reverses direction when looking left versus right is a central brainstem/cerebellar sign ('INFARCT').
In a patient with continuous acute vertigo and nystagmus, a normal head impulse test indicates intact peripheral vestibulo-ocular reflexes and strongly suggests a central brainstem/cerebellar stroke.
Vertical skew deviation on alternate cover testing reflects central graviceptive pathway disruption in the brainstem or cerebellum.
f: episodic positional vertigo lasting 30 seconds triggered only on the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre in BPPV
horizontal nystagmus beating to the right on rightward gaze and reversing to beat left on leftward gaze
acute continuous vertigo and nystagmus with an intact vestibulo-ocular reflex on rapid head thrust
vertical refixation movement of the uncovered eye on alternate cover testing

hq_q.s: A 36 year old woman who works full-time as a salon hairdresser presents with a 4-month history of erythematous, fissured, vesicular plaques over the dorsum of both hands and fingers. She reports that the rash improves significantly during 2-week holidays away from the salon and flares within 48 hours of returning to using permanent hair dyes containing paraphenylenediamine (PPD). Allergic contact dermatitis is suspected.
hq_q.w: Allergic contact dermatitis is a T-cell-mediated delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction to haptens such as nickel, fragrances, rubber accelerators or hair dye (paraphenylenediamine). Cutaneous patch testing-applying standardised allergen chambers to the upper back for 48 hours and reading at 48 and 96 hours-is the diagnostic gold standard.
hq_q.f: Immediate wheal-and-flare urticaria within 15 minutes of exposure -> skin prick testing or serum specific IgE (type I hypersensitivity).
hq_q.ql: Which diagnostic investigation confirms the specific causative allergen?

tm.m: Epidermal Langerhans cells present hapten-protein complexes to sensitised Th1 memory T cells, reproducing a localized eczematous plaque at 48–96 hours under the patch chamber.
tm.g: Confirming type IV allergic contact dermatitis -> Cutaneous patch testing
x: Skin prick testing evaluates immediate IgE-mediated (type I) hypersensitivity reactions within 15 minutes (such as peanut or pollen allergy), not delayed contact eczema.
Dermoscopy magnifies epidermal and dermal pigment patterns to evaluate melanocytic lesions and skin cancers, not contact allergens.
Serum specific IgE measures circulating type I antibodies, whereas allergic contact dermatitis is a cell-mediated type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction.
Wood's lamp (365 nm ultraviolet light) detects porphyrin or pteridine fluorescence in erythrasma and Microsporum infections, not contact allergy.
f: immediate urticaria, angioedema and wheeze within 10 minutes of peanut ingestion
evaluating atypical pigment network and blue-white veil in a changing melanocytic naevus
investigating suspected IgE-mediated venom or food allergy in a patient taking antihistamines
coral-pink fluorescence of intertriginous Corynebacterium erythrasma

hq_q.s: A 48 year old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and a BMI of 33 kg/m² presents with a 3-month history of persistent, well-demarcated reddish-brown macular patches in both inguinal folds. The rash is minimally pruritic, has fine superficial scaling without an active raised vesicular border or satellite pustules. Examination of the groin under an ultraviolet Wood's lamp (365 nm) demonstrates striking coral-pink fluorescence.
hq_q.w: Erythrasma is a superficial bacterial skin infection of intertriginous folds (groin, axillae, toe webs) caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum, predisposed by diabetes, obesity and warm climates. Bacterial production of water-soluble coproporphyrin III produces pathognomonic coral-red/pink fluorescence under Wood's lamp illumination.
hq_q.f: Intensely itchy groin rash with an active raised scaly edge and central clearing -> tinea cruris.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: well-demarcated reddish-brown macular patches in both inguinal folds
tm.m: Corynebacterium minutissimum synthesises coproporphyrin III in the stratum corneum, which absorbs 365 nm UV light and emits coral-pink fluorescence.
tm.g: Reddish-brown groin macules + coral-pink fluorescence under Wood's lamp -> Erythrasma
x: Cutaneous candidiasis produces beefy-red moist macerated plaques with peripheral satellite papules and pustules, and does not fluoresce coral-pink under Wood's lamp.
Flexural psoriasis produces smooth, glazed, well-demarcated salmon-red plaques in skin folds without scale or coral-pink Wood's lamp fluorescence.
Pityriasis versicolor affects the upper trunk with hypo- or hyperpigmented macules that show pale yellow-gold fluorescence under Wood's light, not coral-pink.
Tinea cruris is intensely itchy with an active, raised, scaly annular border and central clearing, and dermatophytes do not fluoresce coral-pink.
f: beefy-red moist groin erythema surrounded by satellite pustules in a patient after broad-spectrum antibiotics
smooth glazed erythematous plaques in the natal cleft and groin with nail pitting and extensor plaques
coalescing hypopigmented scaly macules on the upper back showing yellow-gold fluorescence
intensely itchy annular groin plaques with a raised scaly edge, central clearing and hyphae on KOH scraping

hq_q.s: A 34 year old woman presents with a 4-week history of an itchy, slowly expanding erythematous ring on her right forearm. She recently adopted a stray kitten that has scaly patches of alopecia on its ears. Examination reveals a single 3 cm annular plaque with a raised, scaly, slightly pustular advancing border and central clearing. Before prescribing antifungal therapy, her GP wishes to confirm the mycological diagnosis.
o: Skin scrapings for microscopy and culture
hq_q.w: To confirm tinea corporis before or alongside treatment (and distinguish it from annular psoriasis, discoid eczema or pityriasis rosea), blunt scalpel skin scrapings should be taken from the active, leading scaly edge for potassium hydroxide (KOH) microscopy and fungal culture.
hq_q.f: Single oval salmon-pink herald patch followed 1 week later by a fir-tree truncal eruption with collarette scale -> pityriasis rosea (clinical diagnosis).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

c: stray kitten that has scaly patches of alopecia
3 cm annular plaque with a raised, scaly, slightly pustular advancing border and central clearing
tm.m: Blunt scraping of the active advancing scaly border harvests keratinised stratum corneum containing branching septate dermatophyte hyphae for KOH microscopy.
tm.g: Confirming suspected tinea corporis (ringworm) -> Skin scrapings for microscopy and culture
x: Patch testing investigates delayed type IV allergic contact dermatitis on the back over 96 hours, not superficial dermatophyte infection.
An invasive punch biopsy requiring local anaesthetic and suturing is unnecessary when superficial epidermal scale scrapings readily demonstrate fungal hyphae.
Superficial dermatophyte infections are confined to the keratinised stratum corneum and are not diagnosed by serum antibody testing.
Most dermatophytes causing tinea corporis (such as Trichophyton rubrum) do not fluoresce under Wood's light, so a negative Wood's lamp does not exclude ringworm.
f: recurrent vesicular hand dermatitis in a hairdresser suspected of paraphenylenediamine allergy
suspected cutaneous lupus erythematosus or bullous pemphigoid requiring histopathology and immunofluorescence
suspected chronic pulmonary aspergillosis or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis using Aspergillus IgG/IgE
coral-pink fluorescence in intertriginous erythrasma

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old man drinks most days. He completes an AUDIT questionnaire.
His AUDIT score is 22.
hq_q.w: AUDIT 0 to 7 low risk, 8 to 15 hazardous, 16 to 19 harmful, 20 or more possible dependence.
hq_q.f: AUDIT 10 → hazardous drinking, brief intervention.
hq_q.ql: What does this suggest?

tm.m: AUDIT bands rise from low risk to possible dependence
tm.g: AUDIT 20 or more suggests possible alcohol dependence
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Binge drinking pattern (Binge drinking is a pattern, not an AUDIT band)
an AUDIT score of 17
an AUDIT score of 10
the presentation instead showed features specific to Low-risk drinking (Low risk is 0 to 7)
x: Binge drinking is a pattern, not an AUDIT band.
Ruled out here: requires an AUDIT score of 17, whereas this patient has drinks most days, AUDIT score is 22.
Ruled out here: requires an AUDIT score of 10, whereas this patient has drinks most days, AUDIT score is 22.
Low risk is 0 to 7.

hq_q.s: A 34 year old woman presents to her GP with a 2-month history of pervasive low mood, marked anhedonia, early morning wakening at 4 am, poor appetite with 4 kg weight loss, feelings of worthlessness and impaired concentration at work. She has passive thoughts that life is not worth living but no active suicidal intent or plan. She completes a Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and scores 21 out of 27.
hq_q.w: The Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores each of the nine DSM/ICD depressive criteria from 0 ('not at all') to 3 ('nearly every day'), giving a total from 0 to 27: 0–4 none/minimal, 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 moderately severe, and 20–27 severe depression (NICE NG222 classifies >=16 as more severe depression).
hq_q.f: PHQ-9 score of 12 out of 27 -> moderate depression.
hq_q.ql: How is a PHQ-9 score of 21 classified?

tm.m: Summing frequency scores (0–3) across all nine core and biological depressive symptoms quantifies symptom burden and functional severity.
tm.g: PHQ-9 score of 20–27 (21) -> Severe depression
x: A PHQ-9 score of 5 to 9 corresponds to mild depressive symptoms, far below her score of 21.
A PHQ-9 score of 0 to 4 indicates minimal or absent depressive symptoms.
A PHQ-9 score of 10 to 14 corresponds to moderate depression.
A PHQ-9 score of 15 to 19 corresponds to moderately severe depression, whereas scores of 20 to 27 indicate severe depression.
f: a PHQ-9 score of 7 out of 27 in a patient with mild subthreshold low mood
a PHQ-9 score of 2 out of 27 on routine screening
a PHQ-9 score of 12 out of 27
a PHQ-9 score of 17 out of 27

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman gave birth 6 weeks ago. At her review she completes the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale.
She scores 15, including a positive answer to the self-harm question.
hq_q.w: A positive answer to item 10, thoughts of self-harm, needs urgent assessment whatever the total.
hq_q.f: Score 8 with no self-harm thoughts → watchful waiting and support.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate step?

c: positive answer to the self-harm question
tm.m: Any self-harm thoughts on item 10 need urgent assessment, whatever the total
tm.g: Positive self-harm item on the EPDS: same-day risk assessment
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Reassure as baby blues (Baby blues settle within 2 weeks)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Repeat in 6 weeks (Unsafe delay when active self-harm thoughts are reported on the EPDS)
thoughts of self-harm are absent and symptoms are mild
the presentation instead showed features specific to Start an SSRI by phone (Requires urgent face-to-face suicide and safeguarding risk assessment first)
x: Baby blues settle within 2 weeks.

hq_q.s:

A 64 year old man has sudden severe chest pain that tears through to his back between the shoulder blades. He has long-standing hypertension.

hq_q.w: Suspected aortic dissection is confirmed with CT angiography of the whole aorta (transoesophageal echo if too unstable to move). Type A (ascending) needs emergency surgery; type B is usually managed by controlling blood pressure.
hq_q.f: Crushing central chest pain with ST elevation in II, III and aVF and equal arm pressures → inferior STEMI; primary PCI.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most appropriate?

tm.m: A tear in the intima lets blood split the aortic wall

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 90-minute history of sudden, tearing retrosternal chest pain radiating through to his interscapular back. He has a history of hypertension. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 182/96 mmHg in the right arm and 148/80 mmHg in the left arm, SpO2 97% breathing air. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ST-segment shift.
o: CT angiography of the whole aorta
Repeat high-sensitivity troponin T at 3 hours
hq_q.w: ECG-gated CT angiography of the whole aorta (aortogram) is the first-line gold-standard diagnostic investigation for suspected acute thoracic aortic dissection in a haemodynamically stable patient, delineating the intimal flap, false lumen and branch vessel involvement.
hq_q.f: Haemodynamically unstable patient too unwell for transfer to the CT scanner -> bedside transoesophageal echocardiography.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

c: 182/96 mmHg in the right arm and 148/80 mmHg in the left arm
tm.m: High-resolution contrast CT aortography identifies the intimal tear, true and false lumens, pericardial effusion and visceral branch perfusion with >98% sensitivity
tm.g: Suspected acute aortic dissection (tearing back pain + >20 mmHg inter-arm BP difference): immediate CT angiography of the aorta
x: A plain chest radiograph is insensitive (normal in up to 20% of cases) and cannot definitively visualise an aortic intimal flap or branch involvement.
Transthoracic echocardiography has low sensitivity for the distal ascending arch and descending thoracic aorta compared with ECG-gated CT aortography.
Although D-dimer is elevated in both conditions, tearing interscapular pain with a 34 mmHg inter-arm blood pressure discrepancy indicates aortic dissection, requiring aortography.
Serial troponin assays evaluate acute myocardial infarction and will delay surgical diagnosis of a life-threatening thoracic aortic dissection.
f: An initial bedside screen is performed before definitive imaging, showing a widened mediastinum but not confirming the dissection extent.

hq_q.s: A 70 year old woman is diagnosed on CT aortography with an acute uncomplicated Stanford type B aortic dissection confined to the descending thoracic aorta. She is alert with warm legs, normal urine output and no abdominal pain. She has brittle asthma that required intensive care admission last year. Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 176/94 mmHg, SpO2 97% breathing air.
hq_q.w: Uncomplicated Stanford type B aortic dissection requires immediate anti-impulse therapy (target HR <60 bpm, systolic BP 100-120 mmHg). When beta-blockers (labetalol) are contraindicated by severe asthma, an intravenous rate-limiting calcium channel blocker (verapamil or diltiazem) is used first-line.
hq_q.f: No history of asthma -> intravenous labetalol (or esmolol) infusion first-line.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial drug to control her heart rate and blood pressure?

c: brittle asthma that required intensive care admission
tm.m: Non-dihydropyridine L-type calcium channel blockade slows sinoatrial discharge and decreases left ventricular contractility (dP/dt) without triggering beta-2 mediated bronchospasm
tm.g: Acute aortic dissection requiring anti-impulse rate control when beta-blockers are contraindicated (severe asthma): IV verapamil or diltiazem
x: Starting a vasodilator before achieving rate control causes reflex sympathetic tachycardia, increasing aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt) and false lumen propagation.
Non-selective beta-blockade with labetalol is strictly contraindicated in patients with severe life-threatening asthma due to fatal bronchospasm.
Oral dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers have slow onset, cannot be rapidly titrated and cause reflex tachycardia rather than rate control.
Oral ACE inhibitors have a slow, unpredictable onset in acute aortic dissection and provide no negative chronotropic reduction in shear stress.
f: Her heart rate is already controlled below 60 bpm with verapamil, but her systolic blood pressure remains above 120 mmHg.
She has no history of asthma or reactive airways disease and requires first-line anti-impulse therapy.
She is being transitioned to long-term outpatient oral antihypertensive therapy prior to hospital discharge.
She requires long-term outpatient remodeling and blood pressure control weeks after acute aortic stabilisation.

hq_q.s: A 46 year old unvaccinated man presents to the Emergency Department with a 6-day history of persistent fever, dry hacking cough, diffuse myalgia and sudden complete loss of his sense of smell and taste. Over the past 24 hours he has become breathless walking across a room. On examination, his temperature is 38.3°C, pulse is 98 bpm, respiratory rate is 24 breaths/min and SpO2 is 91% breathing room air, with fine bibasal crackles. Chest radiograph shows bilateral peripheral and basal patchy ground-glass airspace shadowing.
hq_q.w: The combination of a viral prodrome (fever, dry cough, myalgia and characteristic olfactory/gustatory dysfunction with anosmia and ageusia) progressing around day 6 to 10 into hypoxic type 1 respiratory failure (SpO2 91% on air) with bilateral peripheral and basal ground-glass opacities on chest radiograph is the classic presentation of acute SARS-CoV-2 (Covid-19) pneumonitis. Because he requires supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 >=94%, inpatient treatment includes controlled oxygen, oral or intravenous dexamethasone 6 mg once daily for up to 10 days (plus tocilizumab or baricitinib if CRP >=75 mg/L or worsening) and LMWH thromboprophylaxis.
hq_q.f: High fever, rusty sputum and one lobe consolidated → bacterial lobar pneumonia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: dry hacking cough, diffuse myalgia and sudden complete loss of his sense of smell and taste
bilateral peripheral and basal patchy ground-glass airspace shadowing
tm.m: SARS-CoV-2 binds ACE2 receptors on olfactory sustentacular cells (anosmia) and type II pneumocytes -> alveolar-capillary inflammation in week 2 -> bilateral peripheral ground-glass pneumonitis and hypoxia
tm.g: Fever + dry cough + anosmia + week-2 hypoxia (SpO2 <92%) + bilateral peripheral ground-glass shadowing on CXR = Covid-19 pneumonitis
x: Uncomplicated acute viral bronchitis does not cause hypoxia (SpO2 91%) or bilateral peripheral alveolar shadowing on chest radiograph
Tracheobronchitis alone has a normal chest radiograph and preserved oxygen saturation

Typically presents with acute rigors, rusty purulent sputum, pleuritic pain and dense unilateral lobar consolidation with air bronchograms rather than anosmia and bilateral peripheral ground-glass change
Can complicate Covid-19, but does not explain a 6-day febrile prodrome with anosmia, myalgia and bilateral peripheral ground-glass consolidation
f: 3 days of cough and coryza with SpO2 98%, normal respiratory rate and a completely clear chest radiograph
abrupt-onset fever, headache and retrosternal tracheal soreness during a winter Influenza A outbreak with SpO2 97% and normal CXR
acute rigors, rusty sputum, right lower lobe bronchial breathing and dense homogeneous right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms
sudden pleuritic chest pain and collapse 10 days after knee surgery with a normal chest radiograph and filling defect on CTPA
