hq_q.s:
A 32 year old man presents with a 10-day history of a cough productive of clear sputum after a viral upper respiratory tract infection. He has no chest pain or asthma and never smoked.
Temperature 37.4°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98% breathing air. Auscultation reveals scattered wheezes that shift with coughing, and no focal crackles or bronchial breathing.
hq_q.w: Acute bronchitis is a self-limiting viral inflammation of the large and medium airways following a cold, presenting with cough lasting up to 3 weeks, normal vital signs and no focal alveolar consolidation.
hq_q.f: Paroxysms of cough ending in a whoop or vomiting → pertussis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: no focal crackles or bronchial breathing
tm.m: Viral infection of large and medium bronchi causes transient mucosal oedema, mucus hypersecretion and bronchial hyper-reactivity without alveolar exudate.
tm.g: Sub-3-week cough after a cold + normal vital signs + scattered wheeze without focal consolidation -> acute bronchitis
x: Asthma is a chronic relapsing condition (>6 weeks/months) with diurnal and exercise-induced wheeze rather than a single 10-day post-coryzal episode.
Community-acquired pneumonia causes high fever, tachypnoea, tachycardia, hypoxia and focal chest signs (dullness, bronchial breathing, coarse crepitations).
Pertussis causes prolonged paroxysmal coughing bouts lasting weeks that end in an inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting.
Post-nasal drip causes throat clearing and a sensation of liquid dripping down the posterior pharynx without lower airway expiratory wheeze.
f: he had a 6-month history of recurrent nocturnal cough and wheeze triggered by cold air and exercise with a FeNO of 54 ppb
he had a temperature of 39.1°C, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 91% and focal bronchial breathing at the right lung base
he had violent paroxysms of coughing for 3 weeks ending in a high-pitched inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting
he had chronic nasal congestion, cobblestoning of the posterior pharyngeal wall, frequent throat clearing and a completely clear chest

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old man presents with a 10-day history of a cough productive of yellowish sputum after a cold. He feels well, has no comorbidities and does not smoke.
Temperature 37.4°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 120/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98% breathing air. Chest auscultation shows no focal signs.
Point-of-care C-reactive protein (CRP) test performed in the surgery is 18 mg/L (<5).
o: Arrange an urgent chest X-ray within 48 hours
Issue a delayed (back-up) oral antibiotic prescription
Prescribe immediate oral doxycycline for 5 days
Prescribe oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days
Withhold antibiotics and give safety-netting advice
hq_q.w: When point-of-care CRP testing is used in adults with acute lower respiratory tract symptoms and no signs of pneumonia, NICE advises withholding antibiotics and giving safety-netting advice when the CRP is below 20 mg/L.
hq_q.f: CRP 72 → consider a back-up prescription.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management under NICE guidelines?

c: CRP) test performed in the surgery is 18 mg/L
tm.m: A C-reactive protein level below 20 mg/L has a high negative predictive value for bacterial pneumonia, confirming self-limiting viral bronchitis.
tm.g: Acute LRTI without focal signs + point-of-care CRP <20 mg/L -> withhold antibiotics and give safety-netting advice
x: Chest radiography is unnecessary in an otherwise healthy young adult with a 10-day cough, normal observations, clear chest and CRP of 18 mg/L.
A delayed (back-up) antibiotic prescription is the NICE recommendation when point-of-care CRP lies between 20 and 100 mg/L, not below 20 mg/L.
Immediate antibiotics are reserved for point-of-care CRP above 100 mg/L, clinical pneumonia, systemic sepsis or severe comorbidity.
Systemic corticosteroids are not indicated for acute bronchitis in patients without underlying asthma or COPD.
f: he had unexplained haemoptysis or a persistent cough lasting over 3 weeks in a smoker aged over 40
his point-of-care CRP reading in the surgery measured 54 mg/L (within the 20 to 100 mg/L intermediate range)
his point-of-care CRP reading measured 135 mg/L (>100 mg/L) or he was systemically unwell

hq_q.s:
A 79 year old woman with severe NYHA class III heart failure presents to her GP with a 6-day history of a cough productive of purulent green sputum, fever and breathlessness. She has a history of generalized urticaria and angioedema to penicillin.
Temperature 37.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg, SpO2 95% breathing air. Auscultation reveals scattered rhonchi without focal bronchial breathing.
hq_q.w: Under NICE acute cough guidance, adults at high risk of complications due to significant comorbidity (such as severe heart failure) should be offered an immediate antibiotic. Oral doxycycline is first choice and safe in penicillin allergy.
hq_q.f: Pregnant and allergic to penicillin → clarithromycin or erythromycin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate oral treatment?

tm.m: Frail older adults with severe cardiac comorbidity are at high risk of acute decompensation from lower respiratory infection; doxycycline covers typical and atypical pathogens safely.
tm.g: Acute cough in frail older adult with heart failure + penicillin allergy -> immediate oral doxycycline
x: Amoxicillin is a penicillin and is strictly contraindicated in a patient with prior penicillin-induced urticaria and angioedema.
Ciprofloxacin has poor activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae and is not recommended for community lower respiratory tract infections unless Pseudomonas is suspected.
Oral prednisolone causes fluid retention that can precipitate acute pulmonary oedema in heart failure and has no role in non-asthmatic/non-COPD bronchitis.
Withholding antibiotics is unsafe in a 79 year old woman with severe heart failure and febrile purulent lower respiratory tract infection.
f: she had no penicillin allergy and amoxicillin was selected as the alternative first-line beta-lactam agent
she had known bronchiectasis with sputum cultures growing Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to beta-lactams
she had an acute non-infective exacerbation of asthma with widespread wheeze and normal cardiac function
the patient was a fit 30 year old with no comorbidities, normal vital signs and a mild post-coryzal cough

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old man with a 25-year history of heavy alcohol excess presents with a 4-month history of pale, bulky, greasy stools that float and are difficult to flush, accompanied by 6 kg weight loss. He has had several hospital admissions over the past decade for severe epigastric pain radiating to his back.
His BMI is 18.2 kg/m². Abdominal examination is soft and non-tender.
Blood tests show HbA1c 54 mmol/mol (20-42).
hq_q.w: Chronic pancreatitis (most commonly caused by chronic alcohol excess in adults) causes progressive fibrotic destruction of both exocrine acinar cells (presenting with steatorrhoea once >90% of lipase output is lost) and endocrine islets of Langerhans (causing pancreatogenic type 3c diabetes mellitus with raised HbA1c).
hq_q.f: Same stools in a young woman with iron deficiency and blistering itchy elbows → coeliac disease.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: epigastric pain radiating to his back
tm.m: Recurrent alcohol-induced pancreatic stellate cell activation replaces acinar and islet parenchyma with fibrous tissue and intraductal calcium carbonate stones.
tm.g: Heavy alcohol intake + recurrent epigastric-to-back pain + steatorrhoea + new diabetes (HbA1c >=48) -> chronic pancreatitis
x: Coeliac disease is associated with type 1 autoimmune diabetes in youth, but does not cause recurrent alcoholic epigastric-to-back pain.
Crohn's disease causes right iliac fossa pain, diarrhoea, perianal disease and raised faecal calprotectin rather than steatorrhoea with new diabetes in a heavy drinker.
Small bowel bacterial overgrowth occurs in anatomical stasis or systemic sclerosis, causing bloating and low B12/high folate without pancreatogenic diabetes.
Whipple's disease causes malabsorption with migratory arthralgia, skin hyperpigmentation, lymphadenopathy and CNS symptoms.
f: he had microcytic iron deficiency anaemia, an itchy vesicular rash on his elbows and positive IgA tissue transglutaminase antibodies
he had colicky right iliac fossa pain, mouth ulcers, perianal fistulae and a faecal calprotectin of 650 µg/g
he had systemic sclerosis with postprandial bloating, low serum vitamin B12, raised serum folate and a positive hydrogen breath test
he had migratory polyarthralgia, cognitive decline, hyperpigmentation and PAS-positive macrophages on duodenal biopsy

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old man with a history of heavy alcohol intake presents to the gastroenterology clinic with a 4-month history of pale, greasy, offensive stools that float in the pan and 5 kg unintentional weight loss.
Pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, BMI 18.5 kg/m². Abdominal examination is soft.
Investigations show faecal elastase 62 µg/g (>200), serum IgA tissue transglutaminase 2 U/mL (<15) and faecal calprotectin 38 µg/g (<50).
hq_q.w: Faecal elastase-1 is a pancreas-specific protease that is not degraded during intestinal transit. A concentration below 200 µg/g confirms exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and a value below 100 µg/g (here 62 µg/g) indicates severe exocrine failure requiring oral pancreatin (Creon) supplementation with meals. Serum amylase is usually normal in chronic pancreatitis.
hq_q.f: Faecal calprotectin of 600 → inflammation, colonoscopy for IBD.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation result confirms exocrine pancreatic insufficiency?

tm.m: Acinar atrophy in chronic pancreatitis reduces synthesis and duodenal secretion of pancreatic elastase-1, resulting in low stool concentrations (<100 µg/g).
tm.g: Steatorrhoea + faecal elastase <100 µg/g -> confirms severe exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
x: His IgA tissue transglutaminase is normal (2 U/mL), which excludes coeliac disease rather than confirming pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.
Serum amylase and lipase rise during acute pancreatic acinar necrosis, but are typically normal or low-normal in burnt-out chronic pancreatitis.
His faecal calprotectin is normal (38 µg/g), which excludes active luminal inflammatory bowel disease rather than measuring pancreatic enzyme output.
Stool culture identifies acute bacterial enteropathogens (Campylobacter, Salmonella) and does not assess exocrine pancreatic function.
f: his serum IgA tissue transglutaminase was elevated at 140 U/mL, indicating coeliac enteropathy as the cause of malabsorption
he presented to the Emergency Department with 6 hours of acute severe epigastric pain and vomiting due to acute gallstone pancreatitis
his faecal calprotectin was elevated at 580 µg/g, pointing to inflammatory bowel disease as the cause of chronic diarrhoea
he presented with 4 days of acute febrile bloody diarrhoea after eating undercooked poultry

hq_q.s: A 56 year old man has chronic pancreatitis with steatorrhoea and weight loss. He has stopped drinking.
hq_q.w: Pancreatin taken with meals and snacks replaces the missing enzymes. A PPI can be added if the response is poor, as acid inactivates them.
hq_q.f: Diarrhoea after a terminal ileal resection → cholestyramine for bile acid diarrhoea.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment for his steatorrhoea?

tm.m: Enzymes taken with food replace missing lipase
tm.g: Pancreatic steatorrhoea: pancreatic enzymes with meals
f: diarrhoea after a terminal ileal resection
the presentation instead showed features specific to Loperamide (Used for: Diarrhoea in IBS-D)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Low-fat diet (Restricting dietary fat worsens malnutrition and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Proton pump inhibitor (A PPI is an add-on)
x: Ruled out here: requires diarrhoea after a terminal ileal resection, whereas this patient has chronic pancreatitis with steatorrhoea, stopped drinking.
Used for: Diarrhoea in IBS-D
Restricting dietary fat worsens malnutrition and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
A PPI is an add-on.

hq_q.s:
A 27 year old woman has had abdominal pain for 9 months. It is relieved by opening her bowels. She has bloating and her stools alternate between loose and hard. She has not lost weight and has no rectal bleeding.
Examination is normal.
hq_q.w: Pain linked to defaecation, bloating and change in stool form for over 6 months with no red flags fits IBS.
hq_q.f: Same pain with weight loss, mouth ulcers and a high calprotectin → Crohn's disease.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Gut-brain hypersensitivity causes pain tied to defaecation without structural disease
tm.g: Pain eased by defaecation with bloating and altered stool, no red flags, is IBS
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Coeliac disease (Classic picture: Bloating, iron deficiency, itchy blisters on elbows. Coeliac disease: tTG IgA while eating gluten)
weight loss, mouth ulcers and a high calprotectin
the presentation instead showed features specific to Endometriosis (Endometriosis is cyclical)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ovarian cancer (She is young with no red flags)
x: Classic picture: Bloating, iron deficiency, itchy blisters on elbows. Coeliac disease: tTG IgA while eating gluten
Ruled out here: requires weight loss, mouth ulcers and a high calprotectin, whereas this patient has relieved by opening her bowels, bloating.
Endometriosis is cyclical.
She is young with no red flags.

hq_q.s:
A 27 year old woman presents to her GP with a 9-month history of crampy lower abdominal pain relieved by opening her bowels, abdominal bloating and loose stools 3 times daily. She has no rectal bleeding, nocturnal diarrhoea, fever or weight loss.
Abdominal examination is normal. Her GP arranges baseline investigations, which show serum IgA tissue transglutaminase 1 U/mL (<15) and faecal calprotectin 32 µg/g (<50).
o: Arrange an abdominal and pelvic ultrasound scan
Repeat the stool faecal calprotectin test in 6 weeks
Results support a positive clinical diagnosis of IBS
Send three stool samples for bacterial culture first
Urgent referral for diagnostic colonoscopy is required
hq_q.w: Under NICE guidelines (CG61), irritable bowel syndrome is a positive clinical diagnosis in patients with typical symptoms (abdominal pain relieved by defaecation with altered bowel habit for >=6 months and no red flags) once baseline blood tests (FBC, CRP/ESR, IgA tTG) and faecal calprotectin (<50 µg/g) are normal. No endoscopy or ultrasound is needed.
hq_q.f: Calprotectin 260 → refer for colonoscopy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate clinical interpretation of these results?
hq_q.post: Tissue transglutaminase IgA 1 U/mL. Faecal calprotectin 32 µg/g.

tm.m: Normal haemoglobin, CRP, IgA tissue transglutaminase and faecal calprotectin (<50 µg/g) reliably exclude coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease in a young adult without alarm features.
tm.g: Typical IBS symptoms + no red flags + normal FBC, CRP, tTG and faecal calprotectin (<50 µg/g) -> positive diagnosis of IBS
x: NICE explicitly states that abdominal ultrasound is unnecessary to confirm IBS in a 27 year old with typical symptoms and normal baseline tests.
Repeating calprotectin after 4-6 weeks is done for borderline indeterminate results (50-100 or 50-250 µg/g), whereas 32 µg/g is completely normal.
Stool bacterial cultures are for acute infectious diarrhoea (<2 weeks) and are not indicated in a 9-month history of typical IBS.
Colonoscopy is reserved for patients with red flag features or an elevated faecal calprotectin suggesting inflammatory bowel disease.
f: a 56 year old woman presented with new daily bloating and early satiety and had a serum CA-125 of 68 IU/mL
her initial faecal calprotectin was mildly borderline at 85 µg/g after taking ibuprofen for a headache
she presented with a 5-day history of acute febrile bloody diarrhoea after returning from abroad
her faecal calprotectin returned markedly elevated at 380 µg/g or she had dark rectal bleeding and weight loss

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old woman presents to her GP with a 2-month history of persistent daily abdominal bloating, early satiety when eating meals, mild lower abdominal discomfort and slightly looser stools. She has never previously suffered from irritable bowel syndrome or gastrointestinal complaints.
Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg. Abdominal and bimanual pelvic examinations reveal mild distension without a discrete mass.
o: Serum IgA tTG and IgA1 serology
hq_q.w: New-onset irritable bowel syndrome is uncommon in women aged over 50 years. Under NICE guidelines (NG12), any woman aged 50 or over presenting with new IBS-like symptoms (persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain or altered bowel habit within the past 12 months) must undergo serum CA-125 testing to exclude ovarian cancer; if CA-125 is >=35 IU/mL, arrange an urgent ultrasound.
hq_q.f: Same symptoms at 27 for years → IBS work-up.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line investigation in primary care?

c: persistent daily abdominal bloating, early satiety
never previously suffered from irritable bowel syndrome
tm.m: Ovarian carcinoma frequently seeds the peritoneal cavity before forming a palpable pelvic mass, presenting with subacute bloating, early satiety and altered bowel habit mimicking IBS.
tm.g: New IBS-like symptoms (bloating, early satiety) in a woman aged 50 or over -> measure serum CA-125 first
x: While colorectal pathology is also considered in older adults with altered bowel habit (via FIT testing), NICE specifically mandates serum CA-125 first when persistent bloating and early satiety predominate in a woman >=50.
Treating empirically as IBS with antispasmodics in a 58 year old woman with new-onset bloating and early satiety risks missing ovarian malignancy.
Coeliac serology does not exclude ovarian carcinoma, which is the critical time-sensitive diagnosis to rule out in a 58 year old woman with new bloating and early satiety.
Faecal calprotectin is validated in primary care for younger adults (<40-45 years) to distinguish IBD from IBS, not in a 58 year old woman with bloating and early satiety.
f: she presented with unexplained iron deficiency anaemia and a positive faecal immunochemical test (FIT 45 µg Hb/g)
a 24 year old woman with confirmed IBS and normal baseline bloods/calprotectin requested symptomatic relief for abdominal cramps
a 26 year old woman presented with chronic loose stools, fatigue and microcytic iron deficiency anaemia
a 25 year old presented with a 3-month history of loose stools and abdominal cramps to differentiate IBD from IBS

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man vomited repeatedly after drinking heavily last night. The last vomit contained a small amount of fresh blood. He has no abdominal or chest pain.
Pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg. The abdomen is soft and non-tender. There is no crackling under the skin of the neck.
hq_q.w: A small amount of fresh blood after repeated retching or vomiting, in a stable patient with normal blood tests, is a Mallory-Weiss tear of the mucosa at the gastro-oesophageal junction. Most heal without treatment; his Glasgow-Blatchford score is 0.
hq_q.f: Forceful vomiting then severe chest pain, surgical emphysema and air in the mediastinum → Boerhaave syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Retching tears the mucosa where the oesophagus meets the stomach
tm.g: Small bleed after retching, stable: Mallory-Weiss
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Boerhaave syndrome (Boerhaave is a full-thickness rupture with severe chest pain and surgical emphysema; he has neither)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oesophageal varices (Variceal bleeds are large and occur with portal hypertension and signs of liver disease)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Peptic ulcer bleed (A peptic ulcer bleed usually follows dyspepsia or NSAID use, often with melaena and a raised urea)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Reflux oesophagitis (Oesophagitis causes heartburn and occasional slow blood loss, not fresh blood after vomiting)
x: Boerhaave is a full-thickness rupture with severe chest pain and surgical emphysema; he has neither.
Variceal bleeds are large and occur with portal hypertension and signs of liver disease.
A peptic ulcer bleed usually follows dyspepsia or NSAID use, often with melaena and a raised urea.
Oesophagitis causes heartburn and occasional slow blood loss, not fresh blood after vomiting.

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old woman has a large rolling hiatus hernia with acute gastric volvulus. She is in pain and retching.
Pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 102/66 mmHg.
hq_q.w: CT shows the twist and any ischaemia quickly. A rising lactate suggests the stomach is compromised and needs urgent surgery.
hq_q.f: Stable woman with reflux and a small sliding hernia → no imaging; PPI and lifestyle.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

tm.m: CT shows the twist and any ischaemia quickly
tm.g: Suspected gastric volvulus with a raised lactate: CT chest and abdomen with contrast
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Barium swallow (Barium is unsafe with possible strangulation)
solids and liquids + from the start
the presentation instead showed features specific to Plain abdominal X-ray (CT with contrast is required to assess gastric rotation and wall ischaemia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Upper GI endoscopy first (Endoscopy follows imaging)
x: Barium is unsafe with possible strangulation.
Ruled out here: requires solids and liquids + from the start, whereas this patient has acute gastric volvulus, year old woman has.
CT with contrast is required to assess gastric rotation and wall ischaemia
Endoscopy follows imaging.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old man presents to his GP with a 6-week history of troublesome retrosternal heartburn and acid regurgitation caused by a small sliding hiatus hernia. Three months ago he suffered an acute non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting coronary artery stent, and he takes dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin 75 mg daily and clopidogrel 75 mg daily.
Pulse rate 64 bpm, BP 126/76 mmHg.
hq_q.w: Clopidogrel is an inactive prodrug that requires hepatic bioactivation by cytochrome P450 2C19 (CYP2C19) to inhibit platelet P2Y12 receptors. Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19, reducing clopidogrel's antiplatelet efficacy and increasing stent thrombosis risk; MHRA/BNF advise using lansoprazole or pantoprazole instead.
hq_q.f: No clopidogrel → any PPI, omeprazole is fine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate proton pump inhibitor to prescribe?

tm.m: Omeprazole and esomeprazole competitively inhibit hepatic CYP2C19, blocking conversion of clopidogrel to its active thiol metabolite; lansoprazole and pantoprazole avoid significant CYP2C19 inhibition.
tm.g: Proton pump inhibitor required in a patient taking clopidogrel -> oral lansoprazole (or pantoprazole)
x: Cimetidine is a histamine H2-receptor antagonist (not a PPI) and is itself a potent CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 inhibitor that blocks clopidogrel activation.
Esomeprazole is the S-isomer of omeprazole and inhibits CYP2C19, so the MHRA advises against co-prescribing it with clopidogrel.
Omeprazole inhibits hepatic CYP2C19 and reduces conversion of clopidogrel to its active metabolite, increasing the risk of coronary stent thrombosis.
Sucralfate is a topical aluminium hydroxide mucosal protectant rather than a proton pump inhibitor and is far less effective for reflux oesophagitis.
f: never in a patient on clopidogrel; cimetidine inhibits CYP2C19 and causes gynaecomastia
he was taking ticagrelor or prasugrel (which do not depend on CYP2C19 bioactivation) or aspirin monotherapy
he had completed his 12 months of clopidogrel and remained on lifelong aspirin 75 mg monotherapy alone
a pregnant woman with mild reflux wanted a non-absorbed mucosal protectant after lifestyle and alginate measures

hq_q.s: A 34 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of severe, worsening throbbing perianal pain that prevents him from sleeping or sitting down. He has no history of constipation or inflammatory bowel disease. Temperature 38.1°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg. Examination of the perineum reveals a 2.5 cm erythematous, hot, fluctuant, exquisitely tender swelling located 2 cm from the anal margin.
hq_q.w: A continuous, worsening throbbing pain beside the anus accompanied by pyrexia and a hot, erythematous, tender, fluctuant swelling adjacent to the anal verge is diagnostic of an acute perianal abscess (arising from cryptoglandular anal gland infection in the intersphincteric space).
hq_q.f: Afebrile patient with sudden painful tense bluish-purple nodule at the anal margin after straining -> thrombosed external haemorrhoid.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: erythematous, hot, fluctuant, exquisitely tender swelling located 2 cm from the anal margin
tm.m: Bacterial infection of an obstructed anal gland at the dentate line suppurates within the intersphincteric plane and tracks inferiorly to point at the perianal skin
tm.g: Throbbing perianal pain + fever + hot, red, fluctuant swelling beside the anal margin = perianal abscess
x: An anal fissure causes sharp tearing pain strictly during and for an hour after defecation with no fever or fluctuant perianal swelling.
A pilonidal abscess arises superiorly in the midline natal cleft over the sacrum/coccyx with hair-filled pits rather than 2 cm from the anal margin.
Anal carcinoma presents insidiously with a chronic indurated ulcerated mass, bleeding and inguinal lymphadenopathy rather than an acute 3-day febrile fluctuant swelling.
A thrombosed external haemorrhoid presents as an afebrile, firm, bluish-purple subcutaneous clot at the anal verge rather than a febrile fluctuant abscess.
f: He has severe razor-like tearing pain during defecation with a linear posterior midline split and normal temperature.
He has a hot fluctuant swelling at the top of the natal cleft with midline skin pits containing protruding hairs.
A 62 year old man with HIV presents with a 4-month history of an indurated, ulcerating mass at the anal verge and palpable inguinal nodes.
He is afebrile with a tense 1 cm purple-blue subcutaneous nodule at the anal margin after straining.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man had a perianal abscess drained 3 months ago. Since then a small opening beside his anus keeps discharging pus. He has no diarrhoea or weight loss.
There is a small opening 3 cm from the anal verge at the 5 o'clock position. Digital rectal examination is normal.
hq_q.w: A persistent discharging opening after a perianal abscess is a fistula-in-ano. MRI of the pelvis maps the track and how it relates to the sphincters before surgery (laying open or a seton).
hq_q.f: Several fistulas with weight loss and diarrhoea → Crohn's disease; colonoscopy as well.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most appropriate?

tm.m: An infected anal gland leaves a track to the skin
tm.g: Discharging opening after an abscess: fistula, MRI pelvis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Barium enema (A barium enema shows the colon, not the anal sphincters)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Colonoscopy (Colonoscopy is for suspected Crohn's or cancer; he has no bowel symptoms)
the presentation instead showed features specific to CT abdomen (CT shows collections but maps the sphincters poorly)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Swab for culture (A swab grows gut organisms and does not show the track)
x: A barium enema shows the colon, not the anal sphincters.
Colonoscopy is for suspected Crohn's or cancer; he has no bowel symptoms.
CT shows collections but maps the sphincters poorly.
A swab grows gut organisms and does not show the track.

hq_q.s: A 22 year old woman presents to the surgical clinic after incision and drainage of her third perianal abscess in 12 months. Over 4 months she has experienced loose non-bloody stools four times daily, crampy abdominal pain and 5 kg of unintentional weight loss. Temperature 36.8°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 114/70 mmHg. Perineal inspection reveals two indurated discharging fistula openings beside the anus and oedematous skin tags.
hq_q.w: Recurrent perianal abscesses and multiple or complex fistulae-in-ano in a young adult accompanied by chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain and weight loss strongly suggest underlying Crohn's disease. Investigation requires faecal calprotectin, pelvic MRI and ileocolonoscopy with biopsy.
hq_q.f: Recurrent abscesses and sinus tracts in the axillae, groins and perineum with normal bowel habit -> hidradenitis suppurativa.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important underlying diagnosis to investigate?

c: loose non-bloody stools four times daily
tm.m: Transmural granulomatous inflammation of the anorectum breaches the muscularis propria and anal sphincter planes, creating recurrent abscesses and branching fistulous tracts
tm.g: Recurrent perianal abscesses / multiple fistulae + chronic diarrhoea and weight loss in a young adult = Crohn's disease
x: Hidradenitis suppurativa affects apocrine sweat glands in the axillae and groins and does not explain a 4-month history of loose stools, abdominal cramps and weight loss.
HIV infection does not directly cause chronic diarrhoea with multiple perianal fistulae and oedematous anal skin tags in the absence of opportunistic enterocolitis or Crohn's disease.
Although poorly controlled diabetes predisposes to cutaneous staphylococcal abscesses, it does not cause chronic diarrhoea with multiple complex anal fistulae and oedematous skin tags.
Ulcerative colitis is confined to the mucosa and submucosa of the colon and rectum and rarely causes recurrent transmural perianal abscesses or multiple fistulae.
f: She has normal bowel habit and stable weight with recurrent discharging nodules and sinus tracts in both axillae and groins.
She presents with an acute febrile mononucleosis-like illness with sore throat, generalised lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash.
She presents with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, ketonuria and a random plasma glucose of 24 mmol/L.
She presents with bloody mucoid diarrhoea and continuous superficial rectal inflammation without perianal fistulae.

hq_q.s: A 41 year old man presents to his GP with a 3-week history of painless bright red blood noticed on the toilet paper after defecation. He has no anal pain, weight loss or change in bowel habit. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg. Digital rectal examination is normal; proctoscopy shows vascular cushions above the dentate line that prolapse on straining and reduce spontaneously.
hq_q.w: Internal haemorrhoids originate from the vascular anal cushions above the dentate line and cause painless bright red outlet bleeding. When they prolapse during straining and reduce spontaneously once straining stops, they are classified as second-degree (grade II) internal haemorrhoids.
hq_q.f: Haemorrhoids prolapse on straining and require manual digital replacement -> third-degree (grade III) internal haemorrhoids.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: painless bright red blood noticed on the toilet paper
prolapse on straining and reduce spontaneously
tm.m: Laxity of the submucosal connective tissue cushion above the dentate line permits transient downward prolapse during straining that retracts via elastic recoil
tm.g: Painless bright red bleeding + cushions above dentate line that prolapse on straining and reduce spontaneously = second-degree haemorrhoids
x: An anal fissure presents with severe tearing pain during defecation and a visible linear tear in the distal anoderm rather than painless prolapsing vascular cushions.
Fourth-degree haemorrhoids remain permanently prolapsed outside the anal verge and cannot be reduced even with digital pressure.
Complete rectal prolapse involves concentric full-thickness folds of the entire rectal wall protruding several centimetres, most commonly in elderly multiparous women.
A rectal polyp is a single discrete neoplastic mucosal lesion palpable on digital rectal examination rather than circumferential vascular cushions above the dentate line.
f: He has severe post-defecatory tearing pain with a posterior midline tear and a sentinel pile.
Examination reveals permanently prolapsed, irreducible congested haemorrhoidal cushions outside the anal margin.
An 82 year old woman has a 6 cm protruding mass with concentric mucosal rings on straining and faecal incontinence.
Digital rectal examination and flexible sigmoidoscopy identify a solitary 2 cm pedunculated fleshy polyp on a stalk in the mid-rectum.

hq_q.s: A 63 year old woman presents to her GP with a 1-month history of bright red rectal bleeding and a 2-month history of looser, more frequent stools three times daily. She also reports increasing fatigue on climbing stairs. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg. Abdominal and digital rectal examinations are normal, and clinic proctoscopy demonstrates second-degree internal haemorrhoids.
o: Advise high-fibre diet, fluids and review in 3 months
FIT and urgent suspected cancer referral
Prescribe oral ferrous sulfate and reassure
Prescribe topical lidocaine and hydrocortisone cream
Refer for routine haemorrhoid rubber band ligation
hq_q.w: Under NICE NG12 guidelines, an adult aged 60 or over with iron-deficiency anaemia, rectal bleeding and a persistent change in bowel habit to looser stools requires quantitative FIT and an urgent suspected colorectal cancer referral, despite visible haemorrhoids.
hq_q.f: Patient aged 30 with normal haemoglobin/ferritin, normal bowel habit and bleeding grade II haemorrhoids -> dietary fibre and outpatient rubber band ligation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

tm.m: Incidental internal haemorrhoids are present in a large proportion of older adults and do not exclude a synchronous bleeding colorectal adenocarcinoma causing iron deficiency and altered transit
tm.g: Age >= 60 with iron-deficiency anaemia + change in bowel habit + rectal bleeding: urgent 2-week-wait suspected colorectal cancer referral despite haemorrhoids
x: Delaying urgent colorectal investigation in a patient aged over 60 with iron-deficiency anaemia, rectal bleeding and altered bowel habit is unsafe.
Oral iron replacement without investigating the underlying gastrointestinal source of iron-deficiency anaemia and altered bowel habit in a 63 year old is inappropriate.
Topical haemorrhoidal preparations provide only local symptom relief and fail to exclude a proximal colonic or rectal malignancy.
Attributing microcytic iron-deficiency anaemia and a 2-month change to looser stools in a 63 year old solely to visible haemorrhoids risks missing a colorectal carcinoma.
f: A 28 year old with hard stools, normal blood count and occasional outlet blood on the paper is managed conservatively.
A 22 year old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding, normal bowel habit and negative coeliac serology is treated for menorrhagia-related iron deficiency.
She requires short-term symptom relief for perianal irritation after colonoscopy has excluded colorectal neoplasia.
A 34 year old woman with normal haemoglobin, normal ferritin and unchanged bowel habit has persistent bleeding from grade II haemorrhoids.

hq_q.s: A 45 year old man attends his GP with persistent painless bright red rectal bleeding from known second-degree internal haemorrhoids despite 3 months of a high-fibre diet and bulk-forming laxatives. He has a mechanical bileaflet mitral valve prosthesis and takes lifelong oral warfarin. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg. His latest INR is 3.1 (target range 2.5-3.5) and haemoglobin is 138 g/L.
o: Prescribe regular oral tranexamic acid tablets
Stop warfarin for 7 days in primary care, then band
Switch warfarin to oral apixaban 5 mg twice daily
hq_q.w: Rubber band ligation on anticoagulation carries a risk of delayed secondary haemorrhage (at days 7-14), while stopping warfarin with a mechanical mitral valve risks fatal valve thrombosis. Specialist review is required to plan bridging or alternative treatment.
hq_q.f: Patient not taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy with persistent grade II haemorrhoidal bleeding -> outpatient rubber band ligation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

tm.m: Mucosal sloughing 7-14 days after rubber band ligation exposes submucosal branches of the superior rectal artery, while mechanical mitral valves require continuous anticoagulation (bridging with LMWH/UFH if warfarin is interrupted)
tm.g: Second-degree haemorrhoids needing procedural treatment in a patient on warfarin for a mechanical heart valve: specialist referral (never stop warfarin unilaterally or switch to DOAC)
x: Antifibrinolytic therapy in a patient with a mechanical mitral valve risks catastrophic prosthetic valve thrombosis and thromboembolism.
Emergency excisional haemorrhoidectomy on therapeutic warfarin with INR 3.1 carries a high risk of severe haemorrhage and is not indicated for stable grade II haemorrhoids.
Stopping warfarin for 7 days without specialist heparin bridging in a patient with a mechanical mitral valve carries a high risk of fatal valve thrombosis and stroke.
Direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) are strictly contraindicated in patients with mechanical prosthetic heart valves.
f: A patient without prosthetic heart valves or thromboembolic risk has heavy menstrual bleeding.
He has strangulated, gangrenous fourth-degree haemorrhoids after specialist perioperative bridging anticoagulation has been arranged.
A low-risk patient taking prophylactic anticoagulation that can be safely paused under protocol undergoes an elective procedure.
He has non-valvular atrial fibrillation with no mechanical heart valve and unstable INR control on warfarin.

hq_q.s:
A 29 year old woman has had severe tearing pain on opening her bowels for 8 weeks, with streaks of bright blood on the paper. Fibre, fluids, laxatives and simple analgesia have not helped.
Gently parting the buttocks shows a split in the posterior midline with a skin tag at its lower end.
hq_q.w: A chronic anal fissure (over 6 weeks) that has not healed with stool softeners is treated with topical GTN 0.4% for 6 to 8 weeks, which relaxes the internal sphincter and improves blood flow. Headache is the common side effect.
hq_q.f: GTN and diltiazem have both failed after 8 weeks → refer for botulinum toxin or lateral sphincterotomy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Internal sphincter spasm cuts the blood flow to the posterior midline
tm.g: Chronic fissure: GTN ointment
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Hydrocortisone cream (Steroid creams do not heal a fissure)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lateral sphincterotomy (Sphincterotomy risks incontinence and is kept for fissures that fail medical treatment)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral metronidazole (There is no infection; the problem is sphincter spasm)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Rubber band ligation (Banding treats internal haemorrhoids, not a fissure)
x: Steroid creams do not heal a fissure.
Sphincterotomy risks incontinence and is kept for fissures that fail medical treatment.
There is no infection; the problem is sphincter spasm.
Banding treats internal haemorrhoids, not a fissure.

hq_q.s: A 31 year old man presents with a 3-month history of a persistent, painless fissure on the left lateral wall of his anal canal. Over the same period he has passed four loose stools daily, lost 4 kg in weight and suffered recurrent mouth ulcers. Temperature 37.1°C, pulse rate 80 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg. Examination reveals a deep lateral anal fissure at 3 o'clock and an oedematous purplish anal skin tag.
hq_q.w: Primary benign anal fissures occur in the posterior midline (90%) or anterior midline (10%). Fissures that are lateral (off-midline), multiple, painless or refractory-especially alongside oedematous skin tags, oral aphthous ulcers and chronic diarrhoea-strongly indicate perianal Crohn's disease.
hq_q.f: Acutely painful linear tear in the posterior midline (6 o'clock) following constipation -> primary benign anal fissure.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

c: left lateral wall of his anal canal
four loose stools daily, lost 4 kg in weight
tm.m: Transmural non-caseating granulomatous inflammation in Crohn's disease causes indolent, full-thickness ulceration at atypical lateral sites around the anal canal alongside lymphatic-oedema skin tags
tm.g: Atypical anal fissure (lateral/off-midline, multiple or painless) + oedematous skin tags + diarrhoea/mouth ulcers = Crohn's disease
x: Primary syphilis causes a solitary indurated painless genital or anal chancre with rubbery inguinal lymphadenopathy, not chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and oedematous Crohn's skin tags.
Internal haemorrhoids are mucosal vascular cushions above the dentate line and do not cause lateral anal fissures, chronic diarrhoea, weight loss or oral ulcers.
Anal carcinoma typically presents in older adults with a painful indurated ulcerating mass and inguinal lymphadenopathy rather than a young adult with diarrhoea and aphthous ulcers.
Ulcerative colitis causes continuous superficial colonic inflammation with bloody diarrhoea and rarely produces deep, indolent lateral fissures or large oedematous perianal skin tags.
f: He presents 3 weeks after unprotected receptive anal intercourse with a solitary indurated painless anal ulcer and positive Treponema pallidum PCR.
He has painless bright red outlet bleeding with vascular cushions prolapsing at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock and normal bowel habit.
A 65 year old with HPV-16 infection presents with a hard, bleeding, fungating mass at the anal margin and enlarged inguinal lymph nodes.
He presents with bloody mucoid diarrhoea, tenesmus and continuous superficial proctocolitis without perianal skin tags or mouth ulcers.

hq_q.s: A 34 year old woman presents with an 8-week history of severe tearing pain during defecation and blood on the paper that has failed to resolve with a high-fibre diet, fluids and ispaghula husk. She suffers from frequent migraines with aura. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg. Gentle parting of the buttocks reveals a chronic posterior midline anal fissure with a sentinel skin tag.
o: Oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily
hq_q.w: Chronic anal fissures (>6-8 weeks) are treated by relaxing the internal anal sphincter. Because topical 0.4% glyceryl trinitrate ointment commonly triggers severe vasodilatory headaches, topical 2% diltiazem cream (which has equivalent healing and minimal headache risk) is preferred in migraineurs.
hq_q.f: No history of migraine or headaches -> topical 0.4% glyceryl trinitrate rectal ointment twice daily for 6-8 weeks.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate topical pharmacological treatment?

c: chronic posterior midline anal fissure with a sentinel skin tag
tm.m: Topical L-type calcium channel blockade relaxes internal anal sphincter smooth-muscle spasm, reducing resting anal canal pressure and restoring anodermal arteriolar blood flow without systemic nitrate-induced meningeal vasodilation
tm.g: Chronic anal fissure (>6-8 weeks) in a patient with severe migraines (or GTN headache intolerance): topical 2% diltiazem
x: Botulinum toxin injection requires hospital referral and is reserved for chronic anal fissures that fail an 8-week course of topical vasodilator therapy.
Surgical sphincterotomy carries a risk of permanent incontinence to flatus or liquid stool and is reserved for fissures refractory to both topical vasodilators and botulinum toxin.
Oral antibiotics have no effect on internal anal sphincter hypertonia in a primary chronic posterior midline anal fissure.
Systemic absorption of topical glyceryl trinitrate causes dose-limiting vasodilatory headaches in over 30-50% of patients and exacerbates severe migraine.
f: Her chronic posterior midline fissure fails to heal after an 8-week course of topical diltiazem cream.
Her fissure persists despite both an 8-week course of topical diltiazem and intrasphincteric botulinum toxin injection.
She has a purulent perianal fistula secondary to anorectal Crohn's disease.
She has no history of headaches or migraines and requires first-line licensed topical therapy for a chronic anal fissure.

hq_q.s:
A 79 year old woman with known diverticular disease has passed a large volume of maroon and fresh red blood with clots. She has no abdominal pain and takes no NSAIDs or anticoagulants.
Pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 88/54 mmHg after 2 units of blood. The abdomen is soft and non-tender.
hq_q.w: An unstable lower GI bleed (shock index over 1) needs CT angiography to find the bleeding point, then catheter embolisation by interventional radiology. Most diverticular bleeds stop on their own, but this one has not.
hq_q.f: Stable after one bleed with a shock index under 1 → admit and arrange colonoscopy on the next available list.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: A vessel stretched over a diverticulum ruptures into the bowel
tm.g: Unstable lower GI bleed: CT angiography then embolisation
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Barium enema (Barium has no place in active bleeding and blocks later imaging)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Capsule endoscopy (Capsule endoscopy looks for small bowel bleeding in a stable patient)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Colonoscopy tomorrow (Colonoscopy suits a stable patient; she is shocked despite transfusion)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Emergency laparotomy (Surgery without knowing the bleeding point risks the wrong resection; it is a last resort)
x: Barium has no place in active bleeding and blocks later imaging.
Capsule endoscopy looks for small bowel bleeding in a stable patient.
Colonoscopy suits a stable patient; she is shocked despite transfusion.
Surgery without knowing the bleeding point risks the wrong resection; it is a last resort.

hq_q.s: A 79 year old woman presents after passing three large volumes of fresh red blood and clots per rectum over 2 hours. She feels dizzy and clammy. Temperature 36.2°C, pulse rate 120 bpm, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 96% breathing air. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and rectal examination shows fresh red blood. Blood tests show haemoglobin 92 g/L and serum urea 6.1 mmol/L.
hq_q.w: The shock index is heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure ($120 \div 96 = 1.25$). Under BSG lower gastrointestinal bleeding guidelines, a shock index $>1.0$ defines an unstable bleed requiring immediate resuscitation and urgent CT mesenteric angiography.
hq_q.f: Pulse rate 80 bpm and blood pressure 128/76 mmHg -> shock index 0.625 (haemodynamically stable bleed).
hq_q.ql: What is her calculated shock index?

c: fresh red blood and clots per rectum
tm.m: Shock index (HR / systolic BP) quantifies the ratio of sympathetic chronotropic compensation to arterial pulse pressure, identifying unstable haemorrhage when >1.0
tm.g: Shock index = Heart Rate / Systolic BP (here 120 / 96 = 1.25); >1.0 indicates an unstable lower GI bleed
x: A shock index of 0.80 indicates a heart rate lower than systolic blood pressure (e.g. pulse 96 bpm and systolic BP 120 mmHg), representing haemodynamic stability.
A shock index of 1.00 occurs when heart rate equals systolic blood pressure (e.g. pulse 96 bpm and systolic BP 96 mmHg).
A shock index of 1.50 would correspond to a pulse rate of 120 bpm with a systolic blood pressure of 80 mmHg.
2.07 is obtained by erroneously dividing heart rate (120 bpm) by diastolic blood pressure (58 mmHg) rather than systolic blood pressure (96 mmHg).
f: Her observations on arrival are a pulse rate of 96 bpm and a blood pressure of 120/70 mmHg.
Her observations on arrival are a pulse rate of 96 bpm and a blood pressure of 96/58 mmHg.
Her pulse rate is 120 bpm and her blood pressure falls to 80/48 mmHg.
This number results from mistakenly dividing heart rate by diastolic rather than systolic blood pressure.

hq_q.s: A 79 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-hour history of profuse, ongoing fresh rectal bleeding and clots. She takes oral apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation and took her last tablet 6 hours ago. Temperature 36.1°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 88/52 mmHg (shock index 1.41), SpO2 95% breathing air. Intravenous resuscitation is underway and apixaban has been withheld.
o: Continue oral apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily
hq_q.w: For life-threatening, haemodynamically unstable gastrointestinal bleeding (shock index >1.0) on a direct factor Xa inhibitor (apixaban or rivaroxaban), BSG and NICE guidelines recommend stopping the DOAC and giving intravenous andexanet alfa or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC).
hq_q.f: Life-threatening gastrointestinal haemorrhage in a patient taking warfarin -> intravenous phytomenadione (vitamin K) plus 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate targeted haemostatic reversal agent to administer?

c: pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 88/52 mmHg (shock index 1.41)
tm.m: Andexanet alfa is a recombinant modified human factor Xa decoy protein that binds circulating apixaban with high affinity, restoring endogenous factor Xa activity and thrombin generation
tm.g: Life-threatening GI bleed on apixaban/rivaroxaban: withhold DOAC and reverse with IV andexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC
x: Continuing any dose of direct factor Xa inhibitor during life-threatening haemorrhagic shock (shock index 1.41) will worsen fatal exsanguination.
Fresh frozen plasma does not reverse direct factor Xa inhibition by apixaban and requires large fluid volumes that delay targeted haemostasis.
Vitamin K promotes hepatic gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X in warfarin reversal and has zero effect on direct factor Xa inhibitors.
Protamine sulfate is a strongly basic peptide that binds and neutralises unfractionated heparin (and partially LMWH), with no effect on apixaban.
f: She has no active bleeding and is attending a routine outpatient clinic for renal dose adjustment.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation with fibrinogen depletion and prolonged PT/APTT is being managed alongside cryoprecipitate.
She takes warfarin with an INR of 6.8 and requires sustained reversal alongside 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate.
She develops life-threatening haemorrhage while receiving an unfractionated intravenous heparin infusion.

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old woman has had colicky pain in the right upper abdomen for 2 days, and her family say her eyes have turned yellow. Her urine is dark. She had gallstones on a scan last year. She has no fever or rigors.
Temperature 36.9°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 136/82 mmHg. She is jaundiced, with mild right upper quadrant tenderness. Murphy's sign is negative.
hq_q.w: Colicky pain with obstructive jaundice in someone with gallstones, but no fever and a normal white count, is a stone in the common bile duct without infection. Ultrasound, then MRCP, then ERCP to clear it.
hq_q.f: Fever, rigors and jaundice with RUQ pain → ascending cholangitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: colicky pain in the right upper abdomen
She has no fever or rigors
tm.m: A stone blocking the common bile duct backs bile into the blood; without infection there is no fever
tm.g: Gallstone colic with obstructive jaundice but no fever is a common bile duct stone
f: constant pain with fever and a positive Murphy sign but no jaundice
the same picture with fever, rigors and a white count of 18
the presentation instead showed features specific to Mirizzi syndrome (Mirizzi is a stone in the gallbladder neck pressing on the duct; it is rare, and a duct stone is far more likely)
painless jaundice with weight loss and a palpable gallbladder
x: Cholecystitis gives constant pain, fever and a positive Murphy sign, and does not usually cause jaundice.
Cholangitis needs infection: fever, rigors and a high white count; she is afebrile with a white count of 8.4.
Mirizzi is a stone in the gallbladder neck pressing on the duct; it is rare, and a duct stone is far more likely.
Pancreatic cancer causes painless jaundice with weight loss; hers comes with colicky pain and known gallstones.

hq_q.s: A 74 year old woman has ascending cholangitis. She has fever, rigors and jaundice.
hq_q.w: An ALP far higher than ALT, with jaundice, is the cholestatic pattern of a blocked duct. The amylase is a decoy, under 3 times the limit.
hq_q.f: ALT 1,500 with ALP 140 → hepatitic pattern, think viral or drug cause.
hq_q.ql: Which result best shows the obstruction?

tm.m: A blocked duct backs bile up, raising ALP far more than ALT
tm.g: ALP far above ALT with jaundice is the obstructive pattern
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to ALT 140 (ALT shows hepatocyte injury)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Amylase 240 (Amylase is non-specific)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Normal albumin (Albumin does not show obstruction)
the presentation instead showed features specific to White cell count 17.6 (The white count shows infection)
x: ALT shows hepatocyte injury.
Amylase is non-specific.
Albumin does not show obstruction.
The white count shows infection.

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old woman has ascending cholangitis from a stone in a dilated common bile duct. She had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 8 years ago. An ERCP this morning could not reach the bile duct. She has had IV antibiotics and fluids for 12 hours and is becoming more confused.
Temperature 39.2°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 88/50 mmHg.
o: Continue antibiotics and repeat ERCP next week
hq_q.w: Septic cholangitis needs the duct drained. When ERCP cannot reach the papilla, as after a Roux-en-Y bypass, the duct is drained through the liver percutaneously.
hq_q.f: Cholangitis with normal anatomy not settling on antibiotics → urgent ERCP.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: could not reach the bile duct
tm.m: An infected, blocked duct must be drained; if the endoscope cannot reach it, it is drained through the liver
tm.g: Cholangitis when ERCP is not possible: percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Continue antibiotics and repeat ERCP next week (She is septic and worsening after 12 hours; the duct must be drained today, not next week)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Emergency open cholecystectomy (Removing the gallbladder does not clear the duct stone, and open surgery in septic shock is high risk)
the presentation instead showed features specific to MRCP to confirm the stone (The stone and dilated duct are already shown; more imaging only delays drainage)
normal anatomy, with the first attempt failing only on a difficult cannulation
x: She is septic and worsening after 12 hours; the duct must be drained today, not next week.
Removing the gallbladder does not clear the duct stone, and open surgery in septic shock is high risk.
The stone and dilated duct are already shown; more imaging only delays drainage.
After a Roux-en-Y bypass the scope cannot reach the papilla, so a repeat attempt fails the same way.

hq_q.s: A 24 year old woman is diagnosed with pelvic inflammatory disease and starts outpatient antibiotics. Her swab results are not back yet. She has one regular male partner, who has no symptoms.
o: Partner tested and treated if her swabs are positive
Partner tested and treated; no sex until both finish
Partner tested at his next routine check
Partner tested if he develops symptoms
hq_q.w: PID is usually sexually transmitted and often silent in men. BASHH advises contacting, testing and treating current partners whatever her swabs show, and avoiding sex until both have finished treatment.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate advice about her partner?

c: Her swab results are not back yet
tm.m: Chlamydia and gonorrhoea are often silent in men, so treating her alone invites reinfection
tm.g: PID: test and treat current partners, and no sex until both have finished treatment
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to No partner action is needed (An untreated partner reinfects her; current partners are always contacted and treated)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Partner tested and treated if her swabs are positive (Swabs are often negative in PID; partners are treated whatever her results)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Partner tested at his next routine check (Waiting lets reinfection happen; he should be seen now)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Partner tested if he develops symptoms (Chlamydia and gonorrhoea are often silent in men; he needs testing and treatment without symptoms)
x: An untreated partner reinfects her; current partners are always contacted and treated.
Swabs are often negative in PID; partners are treated whatever her results.
Waiting lets reinfection happen; he should be seen now.
Chlamydia and gonorrhoea are often silent in men; he needs testing and treatment without symptoms.

hq_q.s:
A 22-year-old woman presents to her GP surgery with a 3-day history of bilateral lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, and abnormal vaginal discharge. She has a new male sexual partner and uses barrier contraception inconsistently.
Temperature is 37.9°C, heart rate is 88 bpm, and blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg. Bimanual examination reveals cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness without a palpable mass. Urine pregnancy test is negative.
o: Arrange diagnostic laparoscopy before prescribing antibiotics
Arrange transvaginal pelvic ultrasound before prescribing antibiotics
Await endocervical NAAT results before prescribing antibiotics
Obtain endocervical swabs and start empirical antibiotics the same day
Prescribe empirical antibiotics for her sexual partner only
hq_q.w: Pelvic inflammatory disease is a clinical diagnosis; delaying antibiotic treatment while awaiting nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) results increases the risk of tubal scarring, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy. Swabs are taken and empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics started immediately.
hq_q.f: High fever (39.0°C), peritonism, or suspected tubo-ovarian abscess -> admit for intravenous antibiotics and urgent pelvic ultrasound.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

c: bilateral lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, and abnormal vaginal discharge
cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness without a palpable mass
tm.m: Prompt empirical eradication of Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and anaerobes arrests fallopian tubal epithelial destruction and fibrinous adhesion formation.
tm.g: Clinically suspected uncomplicated PID -> Obtain endocervical swabs and start empirical antibiotics the same day
x: Diagnostic laparoscopy is an invasive surgical procedure reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or failure to respond to therapy.
Delaying empirical antibiotics to await outpatient pelvic ultrasonography increases the risk of irreversible tubal damage.
NAAT results take several days and negative swabs do not exclude upper genital tract PID; treatment must not wait.
The index patient requires immediate empirical triple-therapy antibiotics alongside partner notification and treatment.
f: Acute right iliac fossa peritonism where appendicitis and ovarian torsion cannot be distinguished clinically or radiologically
Severe inpatient PID with a palpable adnexal mass where a tubo-ovarian abscess is suspected alongside IV antibiotics
Asymptomatic routine sexual health screening in an individual with no pelvic pain or examination signs
Management of an asymptomatic male contact who attends clinic after the index patient has already started therapy

hq_q.s:
A 22-year-old woman presents to the sexual health clinic with a 4-day history of lower abdominal pain, intermenstrual bleeding, and deep dyspareunia. She is systemically well and suitable for outpatient therapy. Her medical records confirm a previous anaphylactic reaction to cefalexin.
Temperature is 37.6°C and heart rate is 84 bpm. Bimanual examination demonstrates cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness. Urine pregnancy test is negative.
o: Intramuscular ceftriaxone, oral doxycycline, and oral metronidazole
Oral nitrofurantoin and oral doxycycline for 14 days
Oral ofloxacin and oral metronidazole for 14 days
hq_q.w: According to UK BASHH guidelines, when intramuscular ceftriaxone is contraindicated due to severe cephalosporin or beta-lactam allergy in low-risk outpatient pelvic inflammatory disease, a 14-day oral regimen of ofloxacin 400 mg twice daily plus metronidazole 400 mg twice daily (or oral moxifloxacin) is recommended.
hq_q.f: Outpatient PID with no drug allergies -> intramuscular ceftriaxone 1 g stat plus oral doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate outpatient antibiotic regimen?

c: lower abdominal pain, intermenstrual bleeding, and deep dyspareunia
cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness
tm.m: Ofloxacin provides intracellular activity against Chlamydia trachomatis and susceptible Gram-negative pathogens while metronidazole covers pelvic anaerobes in patients with cephalosporin anaphylaxis.
tm.g: Outpatient pelvic inflammatory disease with cephalosporin anaphylaxis -> Oral ofloxacin and oral metronidazole for 14 days
x: Intramuscular ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin and is contraindicated given her history of anaphylaxis to cefalexin.
Oral co-amoxiclav lacks activity against intracellular Chlamydia trachomatis and carries cross-reactivity risk in severe beta-lactam allergy.
Nitrofurantoin concentrates exclusively in the lower urinary tract and has no tissue penetration in the fallopian tubes.
Single-dose azithromycin monotherapy is inadequate for upper genital tract pelvic inflammatory disease and lacks anaerobic cover.
f: First-line outpatient pelvic inflammatory disease treatment in a patient with no history of beta-lactam allergy
Infected dog bite wound in a patient with no beta-lactam allergy
Uncomplicated lower urinary tract cystitis in a woman with normal renal function
Historical single-dose regimen for uncomplicated lower genital tract urethritis when doxycycline is contraindicated

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman is breastfeeding her 4-week-old baby. For the past 24 hours she has had a painful, hot red area on her left breast accompanied by aching muscles and shivers.
Temperature 38.4°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg. Examination shows a tender, erythematous, wedge-shaped area in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast with no fluctuant mass.
hq_q.w: Lactational mastitis presents in breastfeeding women with a painful, erythematous, wedge-shaped segment of breast inflammation and flu-like pyrexia, caused by milk stasis and secondary Staphylococcus aureus infection via a nipple fissure.
hq_q.f: Localised fluctuant breast swelling persisting despite oral flucloxacillin -> lactational breast abscess.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Intraductal milk stasis within a breast lobe complicated by Staphylococcus aureus entry through the nipple inflames a wedge-shaped anatomical segment
tm.g: Febrile breastfeeding woman with a tender erythematous breast wedge and no fluctuance -> lactational mastitis
x: Occurs in non-lactating women with afebrile diffuse peau d'orange skin oedema and axillary lymphadenopathy.
Presents with a discrete, tender, fluctuant pus collection that fails to settle with antibiotics.
Forms a painless, non-erythematous, afebrile subareolar milk cyst.
Occurs in non-lactating cigarette smokers as recurrent periareolar inflammation and nipple inversion.
f: An afebrile 54-year-old woman with diffuse peau d'orange skin pitting and a hard axillary lymph node
A 3 cm tender, fluctuant swelling in a lactating woman whose fever persists after 5 days of flucloxacillin
An afebrile woman with a painless, fluctuant subareolar lump yielding milky fluid on aspiration
Recurrent painful periareolar swelling and subareolar fistula in a non-lactating smoker

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old breastfeeding woman has been taking oral flucloxacillin for 4 days for left lactational mastitis. Despite completing her doses and expressing milk, she still has a swinging fever and her left breast has become more painful.
Temperature 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg. There is a 3.5 cm tender, fluctuant swelling in the upper outer left breast.
o: Core needle biopsy of the breast swelling
Immediate cease of breastfeeding from the left side
Switch to oral co-amoxiclav and review in 7 days
hq_q.w: A tender, fluctuant breast swelling with persistent fever despite flucloxacillin indicates a lactational breast abscess. First-line management is ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (repeated if necessary) with pus sent for culture, while continuing breastfeeding and antibiotics.
hq_q.f: Overlying skin necrosis or multiloculated abscess failing repeated needle aspirations -> surgical incision and drainage.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

tm.m: Once mastitis liquefies into a walled-off purulent abscess cavity, antibiotics alone cannot penetrate without mechanical drainage
tm.g: Fluctuant swelling and persistent fever in lactational mastitis -> ultrasound-guided needle aspiration
x: Solid-tissue core biopsy is not indicated for an acute fluctuant lactational abscess.
Stopping milk removal causes severe engorgement and stasis; mothers should continue feeding or expressing.
Changing oral antibiotics without draining the pus collection will fail to resolve a formed abscess.
Painful compression mammography is inappropriate and obscured by dense lactating breast tissue in a 28-year-old.
f: A persistent solid irregular mass in a non-lactating woman suspected of inflammatory breast carcinoma
Active maternal treatment with cytotoxic chemotherapy where breast milk is contraindicated for the infant
Non-lactational periductal mastitis with mixed anaerobes and aerobes and no abscess on ultrasound
A 55-year-old woman presenting with a new painless solid breast lump

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old woman who is breastfeeding her 3-week-old son attends her GP with a 2-day history of severe pain and redness in her right breast that has not improved with frequent feeding. She developed an itchy maculopapular rash after taking phenoxymethylpenicillin 3 years ago.
Temperature 38.2°C, pulse rate 96 bpm. There is a red, tender wedge-shaped area on the right breast without fluctuance.
hq_q.w: In penicillin-allergic women with lactational mastitis, NICE recommends oral clarithromycin or erythromycin for 10 to 14 days to cover Staphylococcus aureus, as macrolides are effective and safe during breastfeeding. Tetracyclines and quinolones are avoided.
hq_q.f: Lactational mastitis with no history of penicillin allergy -> oral flucloxacillin for 10 to 14 days.
hq_q.ql: Which oral antibiotic is most appropriate?

c: red, tender wedge-shaped area on the right breast without fluctuance
tm.m: Clarithromycin inhibits bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit synthesis, covering beta-lactamase-producing Staphylococcus aureus safely in penicillin allergy and lactation
tm.g: Lactational mastitis with penicillin allergy -> clarithromycin (or erythromycin)
x: Contraindicated in penicillin allergy and inactivated by staphylococcal penicillinase.
Avoided in breastfeeding mothers and has poor activity against Gram-positive staphylococci and streptococci.
First-line antibiotic for lactational mastitis, but contraindicated due to her history of penicillin allergy.
Contraindicated during breastfeeding because tetracyclines chelate calcium in developing infant teeth and bone.
f: Acute streptococcal pharyngitis or otitis media in a patient with no penicillin allergy
Complicated Gram-negative pyelonephritis in a non-pregnant, non-lactating adult
Lactational mastitis in a mother with no history of penicillin allergy
Chlamydial urethritis or acne vulgaris in a non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding adult

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman was involved in a road traffic collision 6 weeks ago in which the diagonal seatbelt caused heavy bruising across her right chest. She has now found a painless lump in her right breast.
Examination reveals a 2.5 cm firm, irregular lump in the upper inner right breast with mild overlying skin tethering and no palpable axillary lymph nodes.
hq_q.w: Traumatic fat necrosis occurs after blunt breast trauma (classically a seatbelt injury), breast surgery, or radiotherapy. Saponification and scarring of necrotic adipose tissue create a firm, irregular mass with skin tethering that mimics breast carcinoma.
hq_q.f: Soft, doughy, mobile lump with benign fatty appearance on imaging and no trauma history -> subcutaneous breast lipoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Traumatic disruption of adipocytes releases triglycerides that saponify with calcium and induce dense fibrous scarring
tm.g: Firm irregular tethered breast lump at the site of seatbelt bruising -> traumatic fat necrosis
x: Presents in young women under 30 as a smooth, rubbery, mobile lump without skin tethering.
Presents in breastfeeding women with acute pain, fever, erythema, and a fluctuant collection.
Forms a smooth, discrete, fluctuant lump without skin tethering.
Forms a soft, doughy, mobile mass with no skin tethering.
f: A smooth, rubbery, highly mobile 2 cm lump in a 21-year-old woman
A painful, hot, fluctuant breast swelling with fever in a breastfeeding mother
A smooth, fluctuant lump in a 46-year-old woman that is anechoic on ultrasound
A soft, doughy, mobile lump composed of mature adipocytes with no skin tethering

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman attends the breast clinic with a 2 cm hard, irregular lump in the upper inner quadrant of her right breast, 6 weeks after sustaining seatbelt bruising in a car collision. Clinical examination shows a firm mass with mild overlying skin tethering and no axillary lymphadenopathy.
Traumatic fat necrosis is suspected clinically.
o: Open surgical excision without prior imaging
Review in the breast clinic in 3 months
hq_q.w: Because traumatic fat necrosis produces a hard, irregular mass with skin tethering and spiculated calcification that closely mimics invasive breast carcinoma, a history of trauma never removes the requirement for full triple assessment (mammography/ultrasound and core needle biopsy).
hq_q.f: Concordant benign fat necrosis confirmed on mammography and core needle biopsy -> reassure and discharge without excision.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

c: Traumatic fat necrosis is suspected clinically
tm.m: Fat necrosis is indistinguishable from invasive carcinoma on clinical palpation and requires histological confirmation via core biopsy
tm.g: Hard irregular tethered breast lump even after trauma -> full triple assessment including core needle biopsy
x: Cannot reliably distinguish invasive carcinoma from reactive atypia or fat necrosis and lacks architectural histology.
Operating without preoperative imaging and core biopsy violates standard breast triple-assessment practice.
Coincidental trauma often draws attention to a preexisting breast carcinoma, so discharging without biopsy is unsafe.
Deferring biopsy of a hard tethered lump in a 52-year-old woman delays potential cancer diagnosis by 3 months.
f: Therapeutic aspiration of a simple anechoic breast cyst confirmed on ultrasound
Never appropriate for a solid breast mass before triple assessment
After mammography, ultrasound, and core biopsy have all confirmed concordant benign fat necrosis
Follow-up after drainage of a complex non-lactational breast abscess once malignancy has been excluded

hq_q.s:
A 55 year old woman has a breast lump that has grown quickly over 2 months.
There is a smooth, mobile, 7 cm mass in the left breast. The skin is stretched but not tethered.
Core biopsy shows leaf-like stroma with high cellularity.
hq_q.w: A phyllodes tumour needs wide local excision because it recurs if margins are close. Malignant ones can spread by blood.
hq_q.f: A 2 cm fibroadenoma in a 20-year-old → reassure, no routine excision.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Phyllodes tumours recur locally unless removed with a clear margin
tm.g: Phyllodes tumour: wide local excision with clear margins
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Adjuvant breast radiotherapy (Radiotherapy is not routine)
a small fibroadenoma that the patient wants removed
the presentation instead showed features specific to Tamoxifen for 5 years (Tamoxifen is for ER-positive cancer)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Watch and rescan in 6 months (Waiting is unsafe)
x: Radiotherapy is not routine.
Ruled out here: requires a small fibroadenoma that the patient wants removed, whereas this patient has grown quickly over 2 months, 7 cm.
Tamoxifen is for ER-positive cancer.
Waiting is unsafe.

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old woman has had a tender lump in her right groin for 12 hours. She has vomited several times.
Pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg. There is a tender, irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. The abdomen is distended.
hq_q.w: A tender irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle in an older woman with obstruction is a femoral hernia, which often strangulates.
hq_q.f: Soft lump that disappears on lying down with a fluid thrill on coughing → saphena varix.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: tender lump in her right groin for 12 hours
below and lateral to the pubic tubercle
tm.m: The narrow rigid femoral canal traps and strangles bowel
tm.g: A tender irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle with obstruction is a strangulated femoral hernia
f: a lump above and medial to the pubic tubercle
the presentation instead showed features specific to Inguinal lymph node (A node does not cause obstruction)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Psoas abscess (A psoas abscess causes fever)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Thrombosed saphena varix (A thrombosed varix is tender, but it does not cause vomiting and a distended abdomen)
x: Ruled out here: requires a lump above and medial to the pubic tubercle, whereas this patient has tender lump in her right groin for 12 hours, vomited several times.
A node does not cause obstruction.
A psoas abscess causes fever.
A thrombosed varix is tender, but it does not cause vomiting and a distended abdomen.

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old woman presents to the emergency department with an 18-hour history of severe right groin pain and repeated bilious vomiting. She has not passed wind today.
Temperature 37.8°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 106/68 mmHg. Examination shows a 3 cm tense, exquisitely tender, irreducible femoral hernia with overlying skin erythema.
hq_q.w: An elevated blood lactate (4.1 mmol/L) in a patient with an irreducible hernia indicates anaerobic glycolysis from mesenteric venous congestion and arterial strangulation (ischaemic bowel), mandating emergency surgical exploration and potential bowel resection.
hq_q.f: Serum amylase >1,000 U/L (>3 times upper limit of normal) with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back -> acute pancreatitis.
hq_q.ql: Which finding most strongly indicates that the incarcerated bowel is ischaemic?

tm.m: Strangulation occludes mesenteric perfusion to the trapped bowel loop, shifting enterocytes to anaerobic metabolism and releasing lactic acid
tm.g: Irreducible hernia with lactate 4.1 mmol/L -> strangulated ischaemic bowel
x: Reflects mechanical proximal small bowel obstruction, which occurs in both viable incarcerated and strangulated hernias.
Mild amylase elevation (<3 times upper limit) is a non-specific finding in uncomplicated mechanical small bowel obstruction.
Mild CRP elevation is a non-specific acute-phase response that does not specifically distinguish strangulation from simple incarceration.
Occurs in any acutely incarcerated tense hernia even before transmural bowel ischaemia develops.
f: A clinical feature confirming mechanical small bowel obstruction rather than transmural necrosis
A serum amylase of 1,800 U/L confirming acute gallstone pancreatitis
A non-specific inflammatory marker used to track resolution of diverticulitis
An acutely incarcerated hernia with normal blood lactate (0.9 mmol/L) and viable bowel at surgery

hq_q.s:
A 35 year old man has a lump in his left groin. It causes him only minimal discomfort. He wants to know what happens next.
There is a reducible left inguinal hernia that is not tender.
hq_q.w: Minimally symptomatic inguinal hernias in men can be watched or repaired electively. Many go on to need repair.
hq_q.f: Femoral hernia of the same size → offer repair soon because of strangulation risk.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: reducible left inguinal hernia that is not tender
tm.m: Inguinal hernias in men have a low strangulation risk
tm.g: Minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia: watchful waiting or elective repair
f: tender, irreducible and vomiting
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fit a truss and discharge (A truss is not standard)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ultrasound every 6 months (Clinical diagnosis does not require serial ultrasound surveillance)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Urgent CT abdomen (CT is not needed)
x: Ruled out here: requires tender, irreducible and vomiting, whereas this patient has minimal discomfort, reducible left inguinal hernia that is not tender.
A truss is not standard.
Clinical diagnosis does not require serial ultrasound surveillance
CT is not needed.

hq_q.s: A 69 year old man smokes. Duplex ultrasound shows a 3 cm popliteal artery aneurysm behind his left knee with some thrombus lining it. He has no symptoms and the foot pulses are present. An abdominal aortic ultrasound is normal.
hq_q.w: Popliteal aneurysms rarely rupture; the danger is thrombosis or emboli that cut off blood to the foot. An aneurysm of 2 cm or more, especially with thrombus inside, is repaired electively (bypass and exclusion, or a stent graft) before that happens.
hq_q.f: Sudden cold, painful foot in a man with a known popliteal aneurysm → acute thrombosis; emergency revascularisation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management of the aneurysm?

tm.m: Thrombus in the aneurysm can block it or throw emboli down the leg
tm.g: Popliteal aneurysm 2 cm or more: repair electively
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Annual duplex surveillance (Surveillance suits aneurysms under 2 cm without thrombus; at 3 cm with thrombus the risk of losing the limb is too high)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Compression stockings (Stockings are for venous disease and do nothing for an arterial aneurysm)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Emergency bypass today (He has no symptoms and a healthy foot, so this is elective, not an emergency)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Thrombolysis (Thrombolysis is for an acutely blocked artery; it does not treat an aneurysm)
