x: Surveillance suits aneurysms under 2 cm without thrombus; at 3 cm with thrombus the risk of losing the limb is too high.
Stockings are for venous disease and do nothing for an arterial aneurysm.
He has no symptoms and a healthy foot, so this is elective, not an emergency.
Thrombolysis is for an acutely blocked artery; it does not treat an aneurysm.

hq_q.s: A 69 year old man has a 2.6 cm popliteal artery aneurysm on duplex scan. He has no symptoms.
hq_q.w: Up to half have an abdominal aortic aneurysm and many have one in the other leg, so both are scanned.
hq_q.f: AAA found first → scan both popliteal arteries.
hq_q.ql: Which other investigation is most important?

tm.m: Aneurysmal disease affects several sites; up to half also have an AAA
tm.g: Popliteal aneurysm: ultrasound of the abdominal aorta
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Carotid artery duplex (Carotid duplex is less important)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lower limb venous duplex (This is an arterial problem)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Renal tract ultrasound (Used for: Hydronephrosis, AKI with retention, recurrent UTI in men)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Transthoracic echocardiogram (Echo is less important)
x: Carotid duplex is less important.
This is an arterial problem.
Used for: Hydronephrosis, AKI with retention, recurrent UTI in men
Echo is less important.

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man attends the vascular surveillance clinic for a routine ultrasound of his known infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm. He is completely asymptomatic with no abdominal or back pain.
Pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg. Twelve months ago his maximum aortic diameter was 4.6 cm; today's ultrasound measures 5.3 cm.
o: Refer for surgical repair within 2 weeks
hq_q.w: Under NHS AAA screening and NICE guidelines, medium aneurysms measuring 4.5 to 5.4 cm undergo 3-monthly ultrasound surveillance. Urgent 2-week vascular referral for repair is triggered at >=5.5 cm, growth >1.0 cm/year (here 0.7 cm/year), or symptoms.
hq_q.f: Aortic diameter reaches 5.5 cm or grows >1.0 cm in 12 months -> refer to vascular surgery within 2 weeks.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

c: Twelve months ago his maximum aortic diameter was 4.6 cm
tm.m: Aneurysms between 4.5 and 5.4 cm growing <=1.0 cm/year remain below the elective repair threshold and require 3-monthly ultrasound
tm.g: Asymptomatic AAA 5.3 cm with 0.7 cm/year growth -> repeat abdominal ultrasound in 3 months
x: An infrarenal aortic diameter of 5.3 cm carries a significant risk of progression to rupture and requires close 3-monthly monitoring.
Triggered only when the diameter reaches 5.5 cm, growth exceeds 1.0 cm/year, or the aneurysm becomes symptomatic.
Annual surveillance is used for small aneurysms measuring 3.0 to 4.4 cm, not medium aneurysms of 4.5 to 5.4 cm.
Beta-blockers do not slow abdominal aortic aneurysm expansion and are not indicated solely for aneurysm size.
f: A screening ultrasound at age 65 showing a normal infrarenal aortic diameter of 1.9 cm
An aortic diameter reaching 5.6 cm today, or expanding from 4.5 cm to 5.6 cm over 12 months
An asymptomatic small abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 3.8 cm on ultrasound
Concomitant heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or angina pectoris requiring rate control

hq_q.s:
A 78 year old woman with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is not taking anticoagulation. Her right leg has been suddenly painful, cold and white for 3 hours. She has never had cramping pain in her legs on walking.
Pulse rate 110 bpm, irregularly irregular. Right popliteal and pedal pulses are absent, while all left leg pulses are strong.
hq_q.w: Abrupt onset of a cold, white, pulseless leg in a patient with unanticoagulated atrial fibrillation, no history of claudication, and normal contralateral pulses indicates acute cardiogenic arterial embolism rather than thrombosis in situ.
hq_q.f: Previous intermittent claudication with absent contralateral pulses and trophic skin changes -> in-situ atherosclerotic thrombosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?

c: all left leg pulses are strong
tm.m: Left atrial thrombus detaches and occludes an uncollateralised peripheral arterial bifurcation, producing profound acute ischaemia
tm.g: Abrupt white pulseless leg with AF, no claudication, and normal contralateral pulses -> cardiogenic arterial embolus
x: Produces a warm, swollen, congested leg rather than a cold, white, pulseless extremity.
Occurs on preexisting peripheral arterial disease with prior claudication and diminished contralateral pulses.
Causes exertional neurogenic leg pain relieved by sitting forward with preserved pedal pulses.
Causes a tense, bruised, expanding swelling behind the knee rather than isolated distal pallor.
f: Acute painful pitting oedema and cyanotic congestion of the entire right leg after pelvic surgery
Worsening rest pain on a 5-year background of 100-metre calf claudication and absent contralateral foot pulses
Bilateral leg pain on walking downhill relieved by sitting, with normal pedal pulses
Sudden severe pain and a rapidly expanding, pulsatile haematoma in the popliteal fossa

hq_q.s:
A 78 year old woman with atrial fibrillation attends the emergency department with a 4-hour history of severe constant pain in her right lower leg.
Pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 138/82 mmHg. Her right foot and lower calf are cold and pale with absent pedal pulses. There is sensory loss extending proximal to the toes and mild weakness of ankle dorsiflexion.
hq_q.w: In the Rutherford classification of acute limb ischaemia, sensory loss extending beyond the toes accompanied by mild-to-moderate muscle weakness defines a Category IIb (immediately threatened) limb, requiring emergency revascularisation.
hq_q.f: Complete anaesthesia, paralysis with muscle rigor, and fixed skin mottling -> Category III irreversible ischaemia.
hq_q.ql: Which Rutherford category of acute limb ischaemia is this?

c: cold and pale with absent pedal pulses
sensory loss extending proximal to the toes
tm.m: Ischaemic dysfunction of both sensory and motor peripheral nerve fibres indicates imminent muscle necrosis without immediate revascularisation
tm.g: Sensory loss beyond the toes plus mild motor weakness -> Category IIb immediately threatened
x: Has no motor weakness and sensory loss is absent or restricted strictly to the toes.
Shows complete limb paralysis, profound anaesthesia, fixed mottling, and absent venous and arterial Doppler signals.
Has intact sensation and normal motor power with audible arterial and venous Doppler signals.
Stages chronic peripheral arterial disease over weeks rather than a 4-hour acute ischaemic emergency with motor deficit.
f: Numbness confined strictly to the toes with normal ankle dorsiflexion power and audible venous Doppler
A cold leg with fixed non-blanching mottling, rigid calf muscles, complete paralysis, and absent Doppler signals
An acutely cold, pale foot with normal toe sensation, full ankle power, and audible arterial Doppler signals
A 6-week history of burning forefoot pain at night relieved by hanging the foot out of bed, with normal motor power

hq_q.s:
A 78 year old woman with atrial fibrillation presents with a 3-hour history of a cold, white, painful right leg caused by an acute femoral artery embolus. Three weeks ago she was admitted with a large intracerebral haemorrhagic stroke.
Pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 144/84 mmHg. Her right foot is cold with reduced toe sensation and mild weakness of dorsiflexion.
o: Oral apixaban 5 mg twice daily and discharge
hq_q.w: A recent intracerebral haemorrhage is an absolute contraindication to both systemic and catheter-directed thrombolysis. Moreover, a Rutherford IIb limb with motor weakness requires immediate surgical Fogarty balloon embolectomy, which can be performed under local anaesthesia.
hq_q.f: Category IIa limb with distal tibial thrombosis and no bleeding contraindications -> catheter-directed intra-arterial thrombolysis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment to salvage her limb?

c: reduced toe sensation and mild weakness of dorsiflexion
tm.m: Recent intracranial haemorrhage precludes fibrinolytic therapy, and motor deficit demands immediate mechanical clot extraction via Fogarty catheter
tm.g: Threatened embolic limb ischaemia after recent haemorrhagic stroke -> surgical femoral embolectomy
x: Absolutely contraindicated within 3 months of an intracranial haemorrhage and too slow for a limb with motor weakness.
An immediately threatened (Category IIb) limb will progress rapidly to irreversible gangrene without revascularisation.
Oral anticoagulation neither lyses the occluding embolus nor restores arterial flow, and is unsafe 3 weeks after a large brain bleed.
Carries a catastrophic risk of fatal recurrent intracranial haemorrhage.
f: A Category IIa marginally threatened limb with no motor deficit and no history of stroke or bleeding risk
Mild intermittent claudication at 300 metres in a patient with a viable limb and no rest pain
Long-term outpatient stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation with no history of intracranial bleed
Acute ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours of onset after CT head excludes intracranial haemorrhage

hq_q.s:
A 61 year old woman had a right mastectomy with axillary clearance and radiotherapy 2 years ago. Her right arm has become swollen. Lymphoedema is diagnosed.
The skin is thickened. She cannot pinch the skin on the back of her fingers. There is no redness or warmth.
hq_q.w: Lymphoedema is managed by a lymphoedema service with compression garments or bandaging, skin care to prevent cellulitis, exercise and manual lymphatic drainage. Diuretics do not work because the fluid is protein-rich.
hq_q.f: Sudden red, hot, painful swelling of the arm with fever → cellulitis; antibiotics.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Removed or scarred lymphatics cannot drain protein-rich fluid from the arm
tm.g: Lymphoedema: compression and skin care
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Anticoagulation (There is no DVT; the swelling is from damaged lymphatics)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Furosemide 40 mg daily (Diuretics do not shift protein-rich lymph and can cause dehydration)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral flucloxacillin (There is no redness or warmth to suggest infection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Surgical debulking of the arm (Surgery is a rare last resort when compression fails)
x: There is no DVT; the swelling is from damaged lymphatics.
Diuretics do not shift protein-rich lymph and can cause dehydration.
There is no redness or warmth to suggest infection.
Surgery is a rare last resort when compression fails.

hq_q.s:
A 61 year old woman has developed progressive swelling of her right arm over the past 6 weeks. She underwent wide local excision and sentinel node biopsy for right breast cancer 2 years ago, and her arm had been completely normal until 6 weeks ago.
Examination shows firm non-pitting swelling of the right arm and a 2.5 cm hard, fixed mass in the right axilla.
o: Empirical trial of oral furosemide 40 mg daily
Reassurance that post-surgical swelling is expected
Urgent breast clinic review for nodal recurrence
hq_q.w: New-onset or rapidly worsening upper-limb lymphoedema developing years after breast cancer surgery, particularly with a palpable axillary mass, suggests malignant nodal recurrence compressing the axillary lymphatics and veins, requiring urgent oncology/breast clinic assessment.
hq_q.f: Chronic stable post-clearance lymphoedema with a normal axilla -> specialist lymphoedema clinic for compression hosiery and skin care.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

c: progressive swelling of her right arm over the past 6 weeks
2.5 cm hard, fixed mass in the right axilla
tm.m: Metastatic tumour recurrence in axillary lymph nodes obstructs lymphatic and venous outflow from the upper limb
tm.g: Delayed-onset arm lymphoedema with a hard axillary node after breast cancer -> urgent breast clinic review for recurrence
x: Applying compression without investigating the new hard axillary mass delays diagnosis of locoregional breast cancer recurrence.
Diuretics are ineffective for lymphatic obstruction and fail to address the suspicious axillary mass.
Functional lymphatic mapping is unnecessary when a palpable axillary mass requires urgent ultrasound and core biopsy.
Subacute swelling with a hard fixed axillary node 2 years after sentinel node biopsy is a red flag for recurrence.
f: Stable mild arm lymphoedema after axillary clearance with a normal axillary examination and no new lumps
Bilateral pitting ankle oedema and pulmonary congestion caused by decompensated heart failure
Unexplained primary lower-limb swelling in a young adult where congenital lymphatic hypoplasia requires confirmation
Mild transient breast bruise and seroma fullness 5 days after wide local excision with no axillary mass

hq_q.s:
A 61 year old woman with chronic right arm lymphoedema following breast cancer surgery presents with a 2-day history of a hot, red, tender right forearm and rigors. She developed a widespread urticarial rash after taking amoxicillin 5 years ago.
Temperature 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg. The right forearm is diffusely erythematous and warm.
hq_q.w: Acute cellulitis in a lymphoedematous limb is caused predominantly by beta-haemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus. In penicillin-allergic patients, NICE and British Lymphology Society guidelines recommend clarithromycin (or erythromycin), while pausing compression garments.
hq_q.f: No penicillin allergy -> oral flucloxacillin (or amoxicillin plus flucloxacillin per BLS guidance).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate oral antibiotic treatment?

c: widespread urticarial rash after taking amoxicillin
tm.m: Macrolide antibiotics inhibit bacterial 50S ribosomal protein synthesis, covering Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus safely in penicillin allergy
tm.g: Acute cellulitis in lymphoedema with penicillin allergy -> clarithromycin
x: Fluoroquinolones have poor activity against beta-haemolytic streptococci and are not first line for skin cellulitis.
Compression garments must be temporarily removed during acute cellulitis and do not treat bacterial infection.
Contraindicated because she has a history of an immediate-type urticarial hypersensitivity reaction to penicillins.
Loop diuretics neither mobilize protein-rich lymphoedema nor treat acute bacterial cellulitis.
f: Complicated Pseudomonas aeruginosa urinary tract or external ear infection in a penicillin-allergic adult
Long-term decongestive maintenance of stable lymphoedema once acute cellulitis has completely resolved
Acute limb cellulitis in a patient with no history of penicillin hypersensitivity
Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with bilateral basal crackles and fluid overload

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old woman attends her GP with a 2-year history of her fingers turning white and then blue in cold weather, alongside worsening retrosternal dysphagia for solid food and heartburn.
Examination shows tight, shiny, thickened skin confined to her fingers (sclerodactyly), two fingertip pitting scars, and facial telangiectasia.
hq_q.w: Raynaud's phenomenon accompanied by sclerodactyly, digital pitting scars, oesophageal dysmotility, and telangiectasia is characteristic of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome), which is strongly associated with anti-centromere antibodies.
hq_q.f: Raynaud's phenomenon with photosensitive malar rash, oral ulcers, and anti-dsDNA antibodies -> systemic lupus erythematosus.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

c: fingers turning white and then blue
tight, shiny, thickened skin confined to her fingers (sclerodactyly)
tm.m: Autoimmune endothelial injury and fibroblast activation cause digital microangiopathy, dermal collagen deposition, and smooth muscle atrophy of the lower oesophagus
tm.g: Raynaud's phenomenon plus sclerodactyly, telangiectasia, and dysphagia -> limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis
x: Causes benign vasospasm without sclerodactyly, digital pitting ulcers, telangiectasia, or oesophageal dysmotility.
Causes symmetrical boggy synovitis of the MCP and PIP joints rather than tight shiny skin and oesophageal dysmotility.
Can cause secondary Raynaud's alongside malar rash, serositis, and cytopenias, but does not cause sclerodactyly.
Causes unilateral positional arm paraesthesia or subclavian steal rather than bilateral sclerodactyly and dysphagia.
f: Symmetrical cold-induced colour change in an 18-year-old woman with normal skin, no ulcers, and negative ANA
Symmetrical boggy swelling of the MCP and PIP joints with morning stiffness over 1 hour and positive anti-CCP
Raynaud's phenomenon with a photosensitive butterfly facial rash, painless oral ulcers, and positive anti-dsDNA
Unilateral ulnar border numbness, intrinsic hand wasting, and loss of the radial pulse on arm abduction

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old woman is referred to the rheumatology clinic with a 3-year history of severe Raynaud's phenomenon, heartburn, and tight, shiny skin over her fingers distal to the metacarpophalangeal joints, with small subcutaneous calcium deposits on her fingertips.
Antinuclear antibody is positive at 1:640 with a discrete speckled pattern.
hq_q.w: Anti-centromere antibodies are present in 70 to 80% of patients with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (calcinosis, Raynaud's, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia) and confer an increased risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension.
hq_q.f: Diffuse skin thickening proximal to the elbows and early interstitial lung fibrosis -> anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibody.
hq_q.ql: Which specific autoantibody is most likely to be positive?

c: tight, shiny skin over her fingers distal to the metacarpophalangeal joints
subcutaneous calcium deposits on her fingertips
tm.m: Autoantibodies against kinetochore centromere proteins (CENP-B) are specific markers of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis
tm.g: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST features) -> anti-centromere antibody
x: Highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus and correlates with lupus nephritis disease activity.
Associated with antisynthetase syndrome (inflammatory myositis, mechanic's hands, and interstitial lung disease).
Associated with primary Sjogren's syndrome, subacute cutaneous lupus, and neonatal congenital heart block.
Found in rheumatoid arthritis and cryoglobulinaemia rather than limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.
f: Photosensitive malar rash, pleuritic chest pain, and glomerulonephritis with haematuria and low complement
Proximal muscle weakness, raised creatine kinase, fissured mechanic's hands, and interstitial lung disease
Persistent dry eyes and dry mouth (keratoconjunctivitis sicca and xerostomia) with parotid enlargement
Symmetrical deforming erosive polyarthritis of the wrists and metacarpophalangeal joints

hq_q.s:
A 56 year old man with a history of primary Raynaud's phenomenon and hypertension attends his GP. Over the past 4 weeks his fingers have turned painfully white and blue several times a day. A new antihypertensive tablet was added to his regimen 1 month ago.
Pulse rate 54 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg. Radial pulses are symmetrical.
hq_q.w: Beta-blockers (including cardioselective agents such as bisoprolol) reduce cardiac output and promote peripheral vasoconstriction, exacerbating Raynaud's phenomenon. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine or nifedipine are used to treat it.
hq_q.f: Antihypertensive that also relieves Raynaud's vasospasm -> amlodipine or nifedipine.
hq_q.ql: Which antihypertensive drug added 1 month ago is most likely responsible?

c: painfully white and blue several times a day
tm.m: Beta-adrenoreceptor blockade reduces digital perfusion pressure and leaves alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction unopposed
tm.g: Worsening Raynaud's phenomenon with bradycardia after starting an antihypertensive -> beta-blocker (bisoprolol)
x: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that dilates peripheral arterioles and improves Raynaud's symptoms.
Angiotensin receptor blocker that causes systemic vasodilation without inducing bradycardia or digital vasospasm.
Alpha-1 adrenoceptor antagonist that blocks peripheral alpha vasoconstriction and dilates cutaneous vessels.
ACE inhibitor that reduces angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction without worsening Raynaud's phenomenon.
f: An antihypertensive chosen to treat both high blood pressure and Raynaud's phenomenon
An antihypertensive substituted when an ACE inhibitor causes an intolerable dry cough
An antihypertensive causing postural hypotension in a man with benign prostatic hyperplasia
First-line antihypertensive in a patient with type 2 diabetes and proteinuria

hq_q.s: A 46 year old woman presents to her GP with a 4-month history of progressive tiredness, 5 kg weight gain despite a reduced appetite, constipation, menorrhagia and feeling cold when others are comfortable. Her mother has pernicious anaemia. On examination, her pulse is 56 bpm, her skin and hair are coarse and dry, there is a small firm painless diffuse goitre, and her ankle jerk reflexes show slow relaxation. Blood test results are shown.
hq_q.w: Primary hypothyroidism (most commonly autoimmune Hashimoto's thyroiditis in iodine-replete countries, strongly associated with anti-TPO antibodies and other autoimmune conditions such as pernicious anaemia) results from failure of the thyroid gland itself. Low circulating free T4 removes negative feedback on the anterior pituitary, driving a markedly elevated serum TSH (>10 mU/L). Hyponatraemia frequently accompanies severe primary hypothyroidism due to reduced cardiac output and non-osmotic ADH release impairing free water excretion.
hq_q.f: Low TSH with a low free T4 → secondary, pituitary hypothyroidism.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: ankle jerk reflexes show slow relaxation
tm.m: Autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicles -> low free T4 -> loss of negative feedback on pituitary thyrotrophs -> markedly raised TSH
tm.g: Cold intolerance + weight gain + slow-relaxing reflexes + low free T4 + high TSH = primary hypothyroidism
x: Depression does not cause bradycardia, slow-relaxing ankle reflexes, a low free T4 of 6 pmol/L and a TSH of 24 mU/L
Sick euthyroid syndrome occurs in acutely unwell hospitalised patients and typically shows low free T3 with low-normal TSH and T4
Secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism presents with a low free T4 accompanied by a low or inappropriately normal TSH
Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined by an elevated TSH alongside a normal free T4 within the reference range
f: 4 months of pervasive low mood, anhedonia, early-morning wakening and guilt with a normal TSH of 1.6 mU/L and free T4 of 15 pmol/L
intensive care patient with severe pneumococcal sepsis found to have free T3 2.1 pmol/L, free T4 11 pmol/L and TSH 0.4 mU/L
lethargy, headache and bitemporal hemianopia with free T4 6 pmol/L and an inappropriately normal TSH of 0.9 mU/L
asymptomatic 46 year old woman with TSH 7.8 mU/L and a normal free T4 of 15.2 pmol/L

hq_q.s: A 78 year old man with a history of previous inferior myocardial infarction and stable exertional angina controlled on bisoprolol, aspirin, atorvastatin and sublingual glyceryl trinitrate spray is diagnosed with overt primary hypothyroidism after presenting with lethargy and cold intolerance. On examination, he weighs 75 kg, his pulse is 58 bpm regular and blood pressure is 136/80 mmHg. His serum TSH is 28 mU/L (0.3-4.2) and free T4 is 6.8 pmol/L (12-22).
o: 1.6 micrograms per kg (120 micrograms) once daily
hq_q.w: In patients aged 65 years or over, or in any patient with ischaemic heart disease (angina, previous myocardial infarction) or heart failure, NICE NG145 recommends initiating oral levothyroxine at 25 micrograms once daily and increasing gradually by 25 micrograms every 4 weeks based on symptom tolerance and repeat TSH. Starting full weight-based dosing (1.6 micrograms/kg/day) in a patient with coronary artery stenosis rapidly increases heart rate, contractility and myocardial oxygen consumption, risking acute coronary syndrome.
hq_q.f: Fit 40-year-old → full replacement of about 1.6 micrograms per kg.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial dose of oral levothyroxine?

c: previous inferior myocardial infarction and stable exertional angina
TSH is 28 mU/L (0.3-4.2) and free T4 is 6.8 pmol/L
tm.m: Rapid restoration of T4 increases myocardial oxygen demand across fixed coronary stenoses -> precipitates angina/MI -> start at 25 micrograms daily and uptitrate every 4 weeks
tm.g: Starting levothyroxine in ischaemic heart disease or age >=65 years = 25 micrograms once daily (vs 1.6 micrograms/kg/day in fit adults <65 years)
x: 100 micrograms once daily risks precipitating unstable angina or myocardial infarction in a 78 year old with ischaemic heart disease
1.6 micrograms/kg/day (rounded to the nearest 25 micrograms) is the NICE starting dose for adults under 65 WITHOUT cardiovascular disease
200 micrograms once weekly is an under-replacement dose and not standard initial titration for cardiac patients
50 micrograms twice daily equals 100 micrograms/day, which is too high for a patient with angina and is given twice daily rather than once daily
f: fit 32 year old woman weighing 62 kg without heart disease starting full weight-based replacement
fit 38 year old man weighing 75 kg with no cardiovascular history and newly diagnosed overt primary hypothyroidism
supervised directly observed weekly dosing regimen only ever used by specialists in rare cases of severe refractory non-adherence
patient requiring maintenance 100 micrograms/day once fully titrated (taken as a single morning dose on an empty stomach)

hq_q.s: A 52 year old woman takes a stable dose of levothyroxine with breakfast. She recently started two new tablets.
hq_q.w: Calcium and iron bind levothyroxine in the gut. Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach, 4 hours apart from them.
hq_q.f: She also started the combined pill → oestrogen raises binding globulin and the dose may need raising.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?

c: stable dose of levothyroxine with breakfast
tm.m: Calcium and iron bind levothyroxine in the gut and stop absorption
tm.g: Raised TSH on a stable dose after starting new tablets: calcium carbonate
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amlodipine (Amlodipine does not affect absorption)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Atorvastatin (Atorvastatin does not affect absorption)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Paracetamol (Used for: Step 1 for all pain: 1 g four times a day, less if under 50 kg)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sertraline 50 mg (Classic picture: Depression after an MI)
x: Amlodipine does not affect absorption.
Atorvastatin does not affect absorption.
Used for: Step 1 for all pain: 1 g four times a day, less if under 50 kg
Classic picture: Depression after an MI

hq_q.s:
A 69 year old man presents to his GP with a 6-month history of mild urinary hesitancy, a slightly reduced stream and nocturia once nightly. He has no fever, perineal pain or visible haematuria.
Temperature 36.6°C, BP 136/82 mmHg. Digital rectal examination reveals a hard, irregular, asymmetric nodular prostate with loss of the median sulcus. Serum PSA is 22 ng/mL (<4.5) and creatinine is 92 µmol/L (60-120).
hq_q.w: A hard, irregular, asymmetric or craggy nodular prostate with obliteration of the median sulcus on digital rectal examination alongside a markedly elevated serum PSA (22 ng/mL) is characteristic of prostate adenocarcinoma, requiring an urgent 2-week-wait referral for multiparametric MRI.
hq_q.f: Smooth, rubbery, symmetrically enlarged prostate with preserved median sulcus and PSA 2.8 ng/mL -> benign prostatic hyperplasia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Malignant acinar proliferation in the peripheral zone of the prostate induces desmoplastic stromal fibrosis (producing a rock-hard nodule) and disrupts basement membranes, leaking PSA into the circulation.
tm.g: Hard, irregular, nodular prostate on DRE + raised PSA (22 ng/mL) -> prostate cancer
x: Benign prostatic hyperplasia produces a smooth, firm, rubbery, symmetrical enlargement of the transition zone with a preserved median sulcus rather than a hard craggy gland.
Chronic bacterial prostatitis presents with recurrent urinary tract infections and dull perineal or ejaculatory pain with a normal or mildly boggy prostate.
A prostatic abscess presents acutely in febrile, septic or diabetic men with severe perineal pain and a exquisitely tender, fluctuant boggy prostate.
A urethral stricture causes a spraying, plateau-shaped slow stream after urethral trauma or urethritis with a normal small prostate and normal PSA.
f: a smooth, rubbery, symmetrically enlarged prostate with a preserved median sulcus and a PSA of 2.8 ng/mL
recurrent coliform UTIs with dull perineal ache, painful ejaculation and a mildly tender prostate
spiking fever, rigors, acute urinary retention and an exquisitely tender fluctuant boggy prostate in a diabetic man
a 40 year old man with a slow spraying stream after previous catheterisation, a normal prostate and normal PSA

hq_q.s:
A 69 year old man is reviewed in the secondary care urology clinic via a 2-week-wait referral after presenting with mild urinary hesitancy. Digital rectal examination confirms a hard, irregular right prostatic lobe.
BP 134/78 mmHg, eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73 m². Repeat serum PSA is 22 ng/mL (<4.5) and midstream urine culture is negative. He has no metallic implants or claustrophobia.
o: Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Repeat serum PSA test in 3 months
hq_q.w: multiparametric MRI of the prostate is the first-line diagnostic investigation in secondary care for men with suspected localised or locally advanced prostate cancer, used to score lesions (Likert 1 to 5) and guide targeted transperineal biopsy.
hq_q.f: High-risk prostate cancer confirmed on MRI and biopsy -> arrange isotope bone scan and staging CT chest, abdomen and pelvis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first investigation in secondary care?

tm.m: Pre-biopsy multiparametric MRI identifies high-grade lesions for targeted biopsy cores and avoids post-biopsy haemorrhage artefact that would otherwise degrade local T-staging.
tm.g: First secondary-care investigation for suspected prostate cancer -> multiparametric MRI of the prostate
x: Abdominopelvic CT cannot distinguish intraprostatic tumour foci from benign hyperplasia and is reserved for distant nodal staging once high-risk cancer is confirmed.
An isotope bone scan assesses skeletal metastases after histological confirmation of high-risk disease rather than serving as the primary diagnostic test before MRI and biopsy.
With a hard irregular prostate and a PSA of 22 ng/mL, delaying investigation for 3 months to repeat PSA is inappropriate.
Performing prostate biopsy before multiparametric MRI misses anterior tumours and causes intraprostatic haemorrhage that obscures subsequent MRI local staging.
f: distant nodal and visceral staging after biopsy confirms high-grade Gleason 9 prostate cancer
evaluating for osteoblastic bone metastases after biopsy confirms high-risk prostate cancer
a mildly raised PSA of 4.8 ng/mL with a normal smooth prostate 2 weeks after a treated UTI
multiparametric MRI is contraindicated due to a non-compatible implanted cardiac device

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man takes goserelin for metastatic prostate cancer. For 3 days he has had back pain, leg weakness and difficulty passing urine.
There is weakness of both legs with a sensory level at T12. The bladder is palpable.
hq_q.w: Suspected spinal cord compression: dexamethasone straight away, then MRI of the whole spine within 24 hours and radiotherapy or surgery.
hq_q.f: Back pain with no neurology → MRI within a week, analgesia, and review.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

tm.m: Steroids reduce oedema around the compressed cord
tm.g: Suspected metastatic cord compression: dexamethasone 16 mg straight away
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Bicalutamide (Used for: Anti-androgen for flare cover or alone)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Intravenous zoledronic acid (Zoledronic acid is not urgent)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Morphine sulfate (Morphine treats pain but not the cord)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Tamsulosin (Used for: BPH symptoms now; helps ureteric stones under 10 mm pass)
x: Used for: Anti-androgen for flare cover or alone
Zoledronic acid is not urgent.
Morphine treats pain but not the cord.
Used for: BPH symptoms now; helps ureteric stones under 10 mm pass

hq_q.s:
A 15 year old boy attends the emergency department after waking from sleep 2 hours ago with sudden, severe left testicular pain and has vomited twice, with no dysuria.
Temperature 37.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 120/74 mmHg. The left hemiscrotum is swollen and erythematous, the left testis lies high and horizontally, and the left cremasteric reflex is absent.
hq_q.w: Acute testicular torsion typically presents in adolescents with sudden-onset severe unilateral testicular and lower abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, a high-riding horizontally lying testis (bell-clapper deformity) and an absent ipsilateral cremasteric reflex. Immediate surgical exploration within 6 hours is mandatory.
hq_q.f: Localised upper-pole pain with a visible paratesticular 'blue dot' and preserved cremasteric reflex -> torsion of the appendix testis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: waking from sleep 2 hours ago with sudden, severe left testicular pain
tm.m: Rotation of the testis on its spermatic cord shortens the cord (pulling the testis high and horizontal), interrupts the cremasteric reflex arc and occludes testicular blood flow.
tm.g: Sudden severe testicular pain + vomiting + high horizontal lie + absent cremasteric reflex -> testicular torsion
x: Epididymo-orchitis presents more gradually over days with dysuria, fever, a normal vertical testicular lie and pain relief on scrotal elevation.
An incarcerated inguinal hernia produces a tender irreducible lump extending from the inguinal canal into the scrotum that the examiner cannot get above.
Torsion of the appendix testis causes milder, gradual pain localised to the upper pole with a visible blue dot sign and an intact cremasteric reflex.
A varicocele causes a chronic dull dragging ache worse on standing with a compressible bag-of-worms venous plexus, not hyperacute pain and vomiting.
f: gradual onset of scrotal pain over 3 days with fever, dysuria, positive urinary nitrites and a normal vertical lie
a tense irreducible inguinoscrotal mass extending through the superficial inguinal ring that you cannot get above
gradual pain localised to the upper pole of a vertically lying testis with a visible blue dot and intact cremasteric reflex
a 3-month dull left scrotal ache on standing with a compressible bag-of-worms swelling above a normal testis

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old man has noticed a soft swelling above his left testis for a month. It feels like a bag of worms. He has had one episode of blood in his urine.
The swelling stays the same size when he lies down. Both testes feel normal.
hq_q.w: A new varicocele in an older man, especially one that does not empty when he lies down or comes with haematuria, can be caused by a renal tumour compressing or invading the left renal vein. The kidneys are imaged first.
hq_q.f: Varicocele in a 17 year old that empties when he lies down → benign; reassure, or refer if painful or affecting fertility.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most important?

c: stays the same size when he lies down
tm.m: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, which a renal tumour can block
tm.g: New varicocele in an older man: image the kidney
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Scrotal support and reassure (Reassurance is right for a typical teenage varicocele, not a new one with haematuria in a 58 year old)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Testicular tumour markers (Both testes are normal; the concern is the kidney, not the testis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Urine culture (There are no infection symptoms; visible haematuria at his age needs imaging and cancer pathway referral)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Varicocele embolisation (Treating the varicocele before finding its cause misses a possible renal cancer)
x: Reassurance is right for a typical teenage varicocele, not a new one with haematuria in a 58 year old.
Both testes are normal; the concern is the kidney, not the testis.
There are no infection symptoms; visible haematuria at his age needs imaging and cancer pathway referral.
Treating the varicocele before finding its cause misses a possible renal cancer.

hq_q.s:
A 15 year old boy is undergoing emergency scrotal exploration 3 hours after presenting with acute left testicular pain and vomiting. On opening the left tunica vaginalis, the left testis is found twisted 360 degrees within a high-attaching tunica vaginalis.
Following detorsion and warm saline packs, the left testis rapidly recovers a normal pink colour with brisk arterial bleeding from the tunica.
hq_q.w: Because the predisposing congenital bell-clapper deformity of the tunica vaginalis is bilateral in over 80% of affected males, both the salvaged left testis and the contralateral right testis must be fixed (bilateral orchidopexy).
hq_q.f: Left testis remains black and non-viable after detorsion -> perform left orchidectomy and right prophylactic orchidopexy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate additional operative step?

tm.m: Three-point non-absorbable suture orchidopexy of both testes to the dartos fascia prevents both ipsilateral re-torsion and future contralateral torsion.
tm.g: Viable testis at exploration for testicular torsion -> fix both testes (bilateral orchidopexy)
x: Fixing only the left testis leaves the right testis with an uncorrected bell-clapper deformity and a high risk of future torsion.
Without suture fixation to the dartos pouch, the freely mobile testis will twist again within the capacious tunica vaginalis.
The left testis was explored within 3 hours and has recovered normal pink perfusion, so it is viable and must be salvaged.
The contralateral right testis is completely healthy and requires prophylactic three-point fixation, never orchidectomy.
f: elective unilateral orchidopexy for an isolated congenital undescended left testis
never appropriate in spermatic cord torsion; bilateral three-point fixation is mandatory
delayed presentation at 36 hours where the left testis remained black and necrotic after detorsion
never indicated; the healthy contralateral testis is always preserved and fixed

hq_q.s:
A 47 year old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband with a 2-day history of fever, severe temporal headache, uncharacteristic confusion and difficulty naming everyday objects. One hour ago she had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure.
Temperature 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 130/78 mmHg. Her GCS is 13 (E3 V4 M6) with receptive and expressive dysphasia, no rash and no neck stiffness.
o: Delirium secondary to a urinary tract infection
hq_q.w: Fever accompanied by altered behaviour, dysphasia and seizures in an adult indicates herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) encephalitis affecting the medial temporal lobes. Start empirical intravenous aciclovir immediately.
hq_q.f: Fever, severe neck stiffness, photophobia and a non-blanching petechial rash with preserved cortical language function -> meningococcal meningitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: 2-day history of fever, severe temporal headache
no rash and no neck stiffness
tm.m: HSV-1 replication within the dominant temporal lobe cortex causes acute haemorrhagic necrotising inflammation, producing dysphasia, behavioural change and focal-to-bilateral seizures.
tm.g: Fever + acute confusion/dysphasia + seizure without meningism -> herpes simplex encephalitis
x: Bacterial meningitis primarily inflames the leptomeninges (causing prominent neck stiffness and photophobia) rather than presenting with early cortical dysphasia and seizures without meningism.
A bacterial brain abscess typically follows chronic otitis media, sinusitis or dental sepsis over 1 to 2 weeks and presents with progressive hemiparesis or raised ICP.
Uncomplicated urinary tract infection causes delirium in frail elderly patients with cognitive impairment, not high fever, dysphasia and a convulsive seizure in a previously well 47 year old.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with an instantaneous afebrile thunderclap headache and neck stiffness rather than a 2-day febrile illness with dysphasia.
f: a 12-hour history of high fever, severe neck stiffness, photophobia and a non-blanching purpuric rash
a 2-week history of headache, low-grade fever and right hemiparesis following chronic suppurative otitis media
acute confusion and dysuria in a frail 86 year old woman with dementia, normal temperature and no seizures
an abrupt afebrile thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity in seconds with neck stiffness

hq_q.s:
A 47 year old woman is admitted with a 2-day history of fever, confusion, dysphasia and a focal seizure. Intravenous aciclovir has been started for suspected viral encephalitis. CT head is normal and a lumbar puncture is performed.
CSF shows white cell count 140/mm³ (90% lymphocytes), protein 0.90 g/L (0.15-0.45) and CSF glucose 3.4 mmol/L alongside a paired plasma glucose of 5.6 mmol/L (4.0-7.8).
hq_q.w: Viral encephalitis produces a lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis, mildly raised protein and a normal CSF:plasma glucose ratio (>50%), whereas bacterial meningitis produces neutrophilic CSF with low glucose. Confirm HSV-1 by CSF PCR.
hq_q.f: Turbid CSF with neutrophil predominance and CSF glucose <40% of paired plasma glucose -> acute bacterial meningitis.
hq_q.ql: Which cerebrospinal fluid interpretation best matches these findings?

c: CSF glucose 3.4 mmol/L alongside a paired plasma glucose of 5.6 mmol/L
tm.m: Intracellular viral replication in temporal lobe neurones recruits T-lymphocytes into the subarachnoid space without bacterial glucose consumption.
tm.g: Viral encephalitis CSF pattern -> lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal CSF:plasma glucose ratio (>50%)
x: Xanthochromia (yellow bilirubin pigment from red cell lysis) confirms subarachnoid haemorrhage at >12 hours, whereas her CSF has <5 red cells/mm³ and 140 lymphocytes/mm³.
Normal adult CSF contains <=5 white cells/mm³ and protein 0.15-0.45 g/L; her CSF white cell count of 140/mm³ and protein of 0.90 g/L are clearly abnormal.
Unmatched CSF oligoclonal IgG bands with <5 cells/mm³ characterise chronic demyelination in multiple sclerosis rather than acute febrile viral encephalitis with 140 lymphocytes/mm³.
A neutrophilic pleocytosis with low CSF glucose (<40-50% of plasma) is the hallmark of acute pyogenic bacterial meningitis, whereas her CSF is 90% lymphocytic with a glucose ratio of 0.61.
f: CT-negative subarachnoid haemorrhage sampled 14 hours after a thunderclap headache
CSF showing 2 lymphocytes/mm³, protein 0.28 g/L and CSF glucose 3.6 mmol/L
relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis with normal CSF cell count and unmatched IgG oligoclonal bands
acute pneumococcal meningitis with turbid CSF showing 1,800 neutrophils/mm³ and CSF glucose 1.1 mmol/L

hq_q.s:
A 47 year old woman with herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis is on day 4 of high-dose intravenous aciclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours). She has had poor oral fluid intake and no maintenance fluids.
Today her urine output has fallen and her eGFR has dropped from 85 to 28 mL/min/1.73 m², with serum creatinine rising to 198 µmol/L (60-120).
o: Continue aciclovir at the same dose
Reduce the aciclovir dose and give fluids
Stop IV aciclovir and switch to oral valaciclovir
hq_q.w: Intravenous aciclovir is poorly soluble in urine and precipitates as crystals in the renal tubules when patients are dehydrated. Manage aciclovir nephrotoxicity by giving intravenous fluids and reducing the aciclovir dose to match the eGFR.
hq_q.f: Normal baseline renal function (eGFR >50 mL/min/1.73 m²) -> maintain standard 10 mg/kg every 8 hours with slow 1-hour infusions and adequate IV hydration.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate adjustment to her management?

c: eGFR has dropped from 85 to 28 mL/min/1.73 m²
tm.m: Volume depletion concentrates filtered aciclovir in collecting duct urine beyond its solubility limit, causing intratubular crystal obstruction that resolves with crystalloid hydration and renal dose reduction.
tm.g: Acute kidney injury on IV aciclovir for HSV encephalitis -> give IV fluids and reduce the IV aciclovir dose to match eGFR
x: Corticosteroids do not dissolve intratubular aciclovir crystals or treat aciclovir crystal nephropathy.
Continuing unadjusted 8-hourly high-dose aciclovir at an eGFR of 28 mL/min/1.73 m² worsens renal tubular obstruction and causes neurotoxicity (myoclonus, agitation and coma).

Herpes simplex encephalitis requires a full 14 to 21 day intravenous course to prevent fatal relapse, and valaciclovir is a prodrug of aciclovir with the exact same renal clearance and crystal toxicity.
Ganciclovir is ALSO renally excreted, causes severe neutropenia and is used for CMV rather than routine HSV-1 encephalitis.
f: acute bacterial pneumococcal meningitis prior to the first antibiotic dose
her eGFR had remained above 50 mL/min/1.73 m² with good urine output
stepping down treatment of uncomplicated cutaneous herpes zoster in a patient with normal renal function
confirmed cytomegalovirus encephalitis or retinitis

hq_q.s:
A 36 year old man with HIV, who stopped his antiretroviral treatment a year ago, has had a headache and fever for 10 days. Today his right arm became weak.
Temperature 38.0°C. There is weakness of the right arm.
CT head with contrast shows several ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia and at the grey-white junction.
hq_q.w: Several ring-enhancing lesions with oedema in someone with a CD4 count below 100 is cerebral toxoplasmosis until proven otherwise. Treatment is pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine with folinic acid, and a response on repeat imaging confirms it.
hq_q.f: A single lesion beside the ventricles in advanced HIV with EBV in the CSF → primary CNS lymphoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Dormant Toxoplasma cysts in the brain reactivate when CD4 cells fall
tm.g: HIV, low CD4, several ring lesions: toxoplasmosis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Cerebral abscess (A bacterial abscess is usually single, with a source such as teeth or sinuses)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Cryptococcal meningitis (Cryptococcal meningitis causes headache and raised pressure without ring-enhancing lesions)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Glioblastoma (Glioblastoma is usually a single irregular mass, not several small lesions with fever)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Primary CNS lymphoma (Primary CNS lymphoma is usually a single lesion near the ventricles; it is considered if toxoplasmosis treatment fails)
x: A bacterial abscess is usually single, with a source such as teeth or sinuses.
Cryptococcal meningitis causes headache and raised pressure without ring-enhancing lesions.
Glioblastoma is usually a single irregular mass, not several small lesions with fever.
Primary CNS lymphoma is usually a single lesion near the ventricles; it is considered if toxoplasmosis treatment fails.

hq_q.s:
A 36 year old man has a frontal cerebral abscess after a dental abscess. He has a headache and is drowsy. Neurosurgery plan to aspirate it.
GCS 13.
hq_q.w: A brain abscess from a dental or sinus source is usually mixed streptococci and anaerobes. IV ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) with metronidazole crosses into the brain and covers both, alongside neurosurgical aspiration; treatment lasts several weeks.
hq_q.f: Ring-enhancing lesions in someone with advanced HIV → toxoplasmosis; pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine.
hq_q.ql: Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

tm.m: Mouth bacteria spread to the frontal lobe and wall off as an abscess
tm.g: Brain abscess from the teeth: ceftriaxone + metronidazole and drainage
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to High-dose IV benzylpenicillin (Benzylpenicillin on its own misses the anaerobes in a dental-source abscess)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV aciclovir (Aciclovir treats herpes simplex encephalitis, not a bacterial abscess)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral amoxicillin (Oral treatment does not reach adequate brain levels at the start)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Vancomycin and gentamicin (Gentamicin gets into the brain poorly, and this misses anaerobes)
x: Benzylpenicillin on its own misses the anaerobes in a dental-source abscess.
Aciclovir treats herpes simplex encephalitis, not a bacterial abscess.
Oral treatment does not reach adequate brain levels at the start.
Gentamicin gets into the brain poorly, and this misses anaerobes.

hq_q.s:
A 36 year old man presents to the emergency department with a 6-day history of fever, severe headache and left arm weakness 2 weeks after an infected molar tooth extraction. At age 18 he suffered life-threatening anaphylaxis with laryngeal oedema and shock after taking oral phenoxymethylpenicillin.
Temperature 38.5°C, pulse rate 100 bpm. Contrast CT head shows a 3 cm right frontal ring-enhancing brain abscess.
hq_q.w: Odontogenic brain abscesses are usually treated with ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, but after life-threatening penicillin anaphylaxis beta-lactams are avoided and intravenous chloramphenicol plus metronidazole is used.
hq_q.f: No history of penicillin allergy -> intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily plus intravenous metronidazole.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate empirical intravenous antibiotic regimen?

tm.m: Chloramphenicol is highly lipid-soluble, achieves cerebral abscess pus concentrations exceeding 50% of serum levels, and covers Streptococcus anginosus and Gram-negative bacilli without beta-lactam cross-reactivity, while metronidazole covers anaerobes.
tm.g: Odontogenic brain abscess + life-threatening penicillin anaphylaxis -> IV chloramphenicol and metronidazole
x: Benzylpenicillin is strictly contraindicated in a patient with documented life-threatening penicillin anaphylaxis.
Ceftriaxone is first-line in patients without severe allergy, but third-generation cephalosporins are avoided after life-threatening penicillin anaphylaxis with laryngeal oedema.
Flucloxacillin is a penicillin (contraindicated in penicillin anaphylaxis), gentamicin penetrates the blood-brain barrier poorly, and neither covers oral anaerobes.
Amoxicillin is a penicillin (strictly contraindicated in anaphylaxis) and oral monotherapy is completely inadequate for a brain abscess.
f: historical penicillin-based regimen in a patient with confirmed penicillin sensitivity and no beta-lactam allergy
first-line empirical therapy for an odontogenic or sinogenic brain abscess in a patient without penicillin anaphylaxis
methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus native valve endocarditis in a patient with no penicillin allergy
uncomplicated dental abscess drainage in an outpatient with no penicillin allergy

hq_q.s: A 32 year old woman has worried constantly about her job, health and family for 7 months. She sleeps poorly, her muscles are tense and she cannot concentrate. She has no panic attacks.
hq_q.w: Excessive, hard-to-control worry about many things on most days for at least 6 months, with physical tension, is GAD.
hq_q.f: Sudden surges of fear peaking within 10 minutes, with fear of the next one → panic disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: worried constantly about her job, health and family
tm.m: Excessive, uncontrollable worry about many things for 6 months defines GAD
tm.g: Widespread worry for over 6 months with tension and poor sleep is generalised anxiety disorder
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Depression (Her picture is worry, tension and poor concentration rather than low mood and loss of pleasure)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hypochondriasis (Hypochondriasis is about one illness)
sudden surges of fear peaking within minutes
fear only of being judged in social settings
x: Her picture is worry, tension and poor concentration rather than low mood and loss of pleasure.
Hypochondriasis is about one illness.
Ruled out here: requires sudden surges of fear peaking within minutes, whereas this patient has worried constantly about her job, health and family, 7 months.
Ruled out here: requires fear only of being judged in social settings, whereas this patient has worried constantly about her job, health and family, 7 months.

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old woman has symptoms of anxiety with palpitations and weight loss.
Pulse rate 108 bpm. There is a fine tremor.
hq_q.w: Thyrotoxicosis mimics anxiety. Thyroid function is checked before diagnosing an anxiety disorder. Key discriminator: Anxiety with tremor and weight loss: suppressed TSH with a high free T4 explains it.
hq_q.f: Normal thyroid function and a GAD-7 of 14 → moderate GAD.
hq_q.ql: Which result best explains her symptoms?

tm.m: Thyrotoxicosis mimics anxiety with adrenergic symptoms
tm.g: Anxiety with tremor and weight loss: suppressed TSH with a high free T4 explains it
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to GAD-7 score of 14 out of 21 (A GAD-7 score measures anxiety but does not explain the tremor and weight loss)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Glucose of 5.4 mmol/L (Normal blood glucose that excludes hypoglycaemia as the cause of tremor)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Haemoglobin of 128 g/L (Normal haemoglobin level in a woman that does not explain tachycardia)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sinus rhythm on ECG (Confirms sinus tachycardia rather than identifying the underlying endocrine cause)
x: A GAD-7 score measures anxiety but does not explain the tremor and weight loss.
Normal blood glucose that excludes hypoglycaemia as the cause of tremor
Normal haemoglobin level in a woman that does not explain tachycardia
Confirms sinus tachycardia rather than identifying the underlying endocrine cause

hq_q.s: A 32 year old woman has a 10 month history of generalised anxiety disorder characterised by constant worry, muscle tension, restlessness, and poor sleep (GAD-7 score 16). She has completed step 1 education and a full course of high-intensity individual cognitive behavioural therapy, but her symptoms remain functionally impairing and she requests pharmacological treatment.
hq_q.w: Under NICE guideline CG113, when a patient with generalised anxiety disorder chooses drug treatment or has not improved after stepped psychological interventions, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (specifically sertraline first line) should be offered before considering an SNRI or pregabalin.
hq_q.f: Sertraline and an SNRI not tolerated → pregabalin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate drug?

tm.m: Chronic SSRI administration downregulates postsynaptic 5-HT receptors and dampens amygdala fear-circuit hyper-reactivity
tm.g: First-line pharmacological treatment for generalised anxiety disorder -> sertraline
f: short-term crisis management for no longer than 2 weeks during an acute disabling crisis
generalised anxiety disorder where both SSRIs (sertraline) and SNRIs (venlafaxine/duloxetine) are not tolerated
symptomatic relief of situational autonomic tremor and palpitations before public speaking
inadequate response to an adequate trial of sertraline and a second SSRI
x: NICE CG113 states that benzodiazepines such as diazepam must not be offered for the routine treatment of generalised anxiety disorder except as a short-term crisis measure (<2 to 4 weeks).
Pregabalin is reserved for patients with generalised anxiety disorder who cannot tolerate SSRIs and SNRIs.
Beta-blockers such as propranolol reduce peripheral autonomic tremor and tachycardia but do not treat the core cognitive psychic worry of GAD.
Venlafaxine or duloxetine (SNRIs) are second-line options used when sertraline and an alternative SSRI are ineffective.

hq_q.s: A 28 year old paramedic has post-traumatic stress disorder after attending a fatal crash. He has been offered trauma-focused CBT and EMDR but does not want a psychological treatment. He would like medication.
hq_q.w: NICE offers venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline for PTSD in adults who prefer medication. Benzodiazepines are not used.
hq_q.f: PTSD and willing to try a talking therapy → trauma-focused CBT or EMDR.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most appropriate?

c: does not want a psychological treatment
tm.m: An SSRI damps the hyperarousal and intrusive memories over weeks
tm.g: PTSD in an adult who wants medication: an SSRI such as sertraline or venlafaxine
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam (Benzodiazepines do not treat PTSD and may hinder recovery)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Propranolol (Propranolol is not recommended for treating or preventing PTSD)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Risperidone (Antipsychotics are only an add-on for disabling symptoms that persist despite other treatment)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Zopiclone (A hypnotic may help sleep for a short time but does not treat PTSD)
x: Benzodiazepines do not treat PTSD and may hinder recovery.
Propranolol is not recommended for treating or preventing PTSD.
Antipsychotics are only an add-on for disabling symptoms that persist despite other treatment.
A hypnotic may help sleep for a short time but does not treat PTSD.

hq_q.s: A 28 year old paramedic is assessed in the occupational mental health clinic 3 months after attending a fatal multi-vehicle motorway collision involving young children. He has been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder and describes several distressing daily symptoms across the three core ICD-11 diagnostic symptom clusters.
hq_q.w: In post-traumatic stress disorder, the re-experiencing symptom cluster comprises vivid intrusive daytime flashbacks (acting or feeling as if the traumatic event is recurring in the present), repetitive distressing trauma nightmares, and intense physiological reactivity to trauma cues.
hq_q.f: Jumpy and always on guard → hyperarousal, a sense of current threat.
hq_q.ql: Which symptom belongs to the re-experiencing cluster?

tm.m: Unprocessed sensory-perceptual trauma memories intrude involuntarily into consciousness as present-tense flashbacks
tm.g: Core symptom belonging to the PTSD re-experiencing cluster -> intrusive flashbacks (and nightmares)
f: asked which symptom belongs to the deliberate avoidance cluster of PTSD
asked which symptom belongs to the hyperarousal and heightened threat cluster
asked which symptom represents negative alterations in mood and cognition
asked which behavioural feature belongs to the autonomic hyperarousal cluster
x: Deliberately detouring away from the collision site belongs to the avoidance cluster rather than re-experiencing.
Insomnia, hypervigilance, and an exaggerated startle response belong to the hyperarousal (heightened current threat) cluster.
Emotional numbing and detachment from others belong to negative alterations in mood and cognition.
Irritability and angry outbursts are manifestations of autonomic hyperarousal rather than re-experiencing.

hq_q.s: A 28 year old paramedic with post-traumatic stress disorder asks for treatment. He has asthma.
hq_q.w: Trauma-focused CBT or EMDR is first line. Debriefing is not recommended. Propranolol is not used, and asthma would block it anyway.
hq_q.f: Declines psychological therapy → sertraline or venlafaxine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first treatment?

tm.m: Trauma-focused therapy processes the memory so it stops intruding
tm.g: PTSD first line: trauma-focused CBT or EMDR
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Diazepam (Benzodiazepines are ineffective in PTSD and carry a high risk of dependence)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Propranolol (Propranolol does not treat PTSD and is unsafe with asthma)
he declines psychological therapy
the presentation instead showed features specific to Single debriefing session (NICE explicitly recommends against single-session psychological debriefing after trauma)
x: Benzodiazepines are ineffective in PTSD and carry a high risk of dependence
Propranolol does not treat PTSD and is unsafe with asthma.
Ruled out here: requires he declines psychological therapy, whereas this patient has post-traumatic stress disorder, asks for treatment.
NICE explicitly recommends against single-session psychological debriefing after trauma

hq_q.s: A 40 year old accountant works 70 hours a week. He makes detailed lists for everything, insists that his team follow his procedures exactly and redoes their work if it is not perfect. He has few close friends. He sees no problem with how he works and has no intrusive thoughts or rituals.
hq_q.w: Lifelong perfectionism, rigidity and preoccupation with rules and order, which the person sees as right (ego-syntonic), without obsessions or compulsions, is obsessive-compulsive (anankastic) personality disorder.
hq_q.f: Intrusive unwanted thoughts with rituals he tries to resist → OCD.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: sees no problem with how he works
tm.m: In the personality disorder the rigidity feels right to the person; in OCD the thoughts feel alien and distressing
tm.g: Perfectionism and rules he is happy with, no obsessions: obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Autism spectrum disorder (Autism starts in early childhood with social communication difficulty, not perfectionism at work)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Emotionally unstable personality disorder (EUPD is emotional instability, impulsivity and fear of abandonment, not rigid perfectionism)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD is distressing worry about many things; he is not worried, he is rigid)
he had distressing intrusive thoughts that he tried to resist with rituals
x: Autism starts in early childhood with social communication difficulty, not perfectionism at work.
EUPD is emotional instability, impulsivity and fear of abandonment, not rigid perfectionism.
GAD is distressing worry about many things; he is not worried, he is rigid.
OCD needs obsessions or compulsions that feel unwanted; he has none.

hq_q.s: A 24 year old man has obsessive-compulsive disorder with checking rituals. He is offered psychological therapy.
hq_q.w: CBT with ERP exposes him to the trigger while he resists the compulsion, so the anxiety fades without it.
hq_q.f: Severe impairment from the start → ERP plus an SSRI.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate approach?

tm.m: Exposure without performing the ritual lets anxiety fall by itself
tm.g: OCD therapy: exposure and response prevention
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Counselling (Non-directive supportive counselling is not effective for obsessive-compulsive rituals)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hypnotherapy (Lacks evidence in OCD and is not recommended by NICE)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Progressive muscle relaxation training (Used as a control condition in trials and does not treat compulsions)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Psychodynamic therapy (Not recommended by NICE for treating obsessive-compulsive disorder)
x: Non-directive supportive counselling is not effective for obsessive-compulsive rituals
Lacks evidence in OCD and is not recommended by NICE
Used as a control condition in trials and does not treat compulsions
Not recommended by NICE for treating obsessive-compulsive disorder

hq_q.s: A 24 year old man with obsessive-compulsive disorder has taken sertraline at a moderate dose for 12 weeks with no benefit. He takes it every day and has no side effects. He is also having CBT with exposure and response prevention.
hq_q.w: OCD often needs higher SSRI doses for longer. Increase the dose, then try another SSRI or clomipramine if it still fails.
hq_q.f: Two SSRIs fail → clomipramine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: moderate dose for 12 weeks with no benefit
tm.m: OCD often needs higher SSRI doses for longer than depression
tm.g: Partial OCD response with good adherence and tolerance: increase the sertraline dose
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Add diazepam to the sertraline (Benzodiazepines do not treat OCD and should not be used long term)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Stop all treatment (OCD typically requires higher SSRI doses and longer trials before switching)
two SSRIs have failed
the presentation instead showed features specific to Switch to haloperidol (Haloperidol is not first line in OCD)
x: Benzodiazepines do not treat OCD and should not be used long term
OCD typically requires higher SSRI doses and longer trials before switching
Ruled out here: requires two SSRIs have failed, whereas this patient has moderate dose for 12 weeks with no benefit, takes it every day.
Haloperidol is not first line in OCD.

hq_q.s: A 35 year old woman has been convinced for 2 years that she has bowel cancer. A colonoscopy and CT scan were normal, but the relief lasts only days. She checks her stools daily and searches online for hours. She accepts that the fear may be excessive.
hq_q.w: Hypochondriasis (health anxiety) is treated with CBT that targets checking, reassurance seeking and catastrophic beliefs. More tests feed the cycle.
hq_q.f: Many unexplained symptoms across body systems for years → somatisation disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

c: accepts that the fear may be excessive
tm.m: Each test gives brief relief that rewards checking, so the worry returns stronger
tm.g: Health anxiety with insight: CBT, not more tests
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Low-dose antipsychotic (She has insight, so this is not a delusion; antipsychotics are not used)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Regular benzodiazepine (Benzodiazepines do not treat health anxiety and risk dependence)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Repeat colonoscopy to reassure her (Repeat tests give short relief and reinforce the cycle)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Yearly CT scans (Surveillance scans add radiation and reinforce checking)
x: She has insight, so this is not a delusion; antipsychotics are not used.
Benzodiazepines do not treat health anxiety and risk dependence.
Repeat tests give short relief and reinforce the cycle.
Surveillance scans add radiation and reinforce checking.

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old surgical ward nurse has had three episodes of acute confusion, drenching sweats, and tremor while on duty over the past month, resolving rapidly with intravenous dextrose. She has no history of diabetes.
During a witnessed hypoglycaemic episode, laboratory venous blood shows plasma glucose 1.8 mmol/L, serum insulin 410 pmol/L (high), and C-peptide <50 pmol/L (suppressed).
hq_q.w: Endogenous pancreatic proinsulin is cleaved into equimolar amounts of insulin and C-peptide, whereas commercial pharmaceutical insulin preparations contain no C-peptide. Hypoglycaemia with high serum insulin and suppressed C-peptide is diagnostic of exogenous insulin injection (factitious disorder).
hq_q.f: High insulin and high C-peptide → insulinoma or a sulfonylurea; check a drug screen.
hq_q.ql: Which result best explains these episodes?

tm.m: Exogenous pharmaceutical insulin lacks C-peptide and suppresses endogenous pancreatic beta-cell proinsulin cleavage
tm.g: Hypoglycaemia + high serum insulin + suppressed C-peptide -> exogenous injected insulin
f: hypoglycaemia with suppressed plasma insulin, suppressed C-peptide, hyponatraemia and hyperpigmentation
postprandial hypoglycaemia 2 hours after a high-carbohydrate meal following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
fasting hypoglycaemia with high serum insulin, elevated C-peptide and a negative sulfonylurea screen
hypoglycaemia with elevated serum insulin, elevated C-peptide and a positive urine sulfonylurea assay
x: Primary adrenal insufficiency causes fasting hypoglycaemia with appropriately suppressed endogenous insulin and low C-peptide alongside hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia.
Late dumping syndrome occurs 1 to 3 hours after gastric bypass surgery and causes endogenous hyperinsulinaemia with raised C-peptide.
An endogenous pancreatic beta-cell insulinoma secretes proinsulin cleavage products, elevating both serum insulin and C-peptide simultaneously.
Sulfonylureas (such as gliclazide) stimulate endogenous pancreatic beta-cell secretion, raising both serum insulin and C-peptide.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman with a 4 year history of somatisation disorder has undergone normal upper and lower GI endoscopies, pelvic laparoscopy, and three abdominal CT scans across four hospitals. Today she attends an urgent GP slot requesting a fourth CT scan for recurrent migratory abdominal pain.
Abdominal examination is soft and non-tender, with normal observations.
o: Arrange the scan to reassure her
Tell her the tests are all normal
hq_q.w: Patients with somatisation disorder benefit from regular, pre-booked appointments with a single consistent GP (not contingent on developing new symptoms), empathetic validation of their distress, avoidance of unnecessary repeat imaging that carries radiation and iatrogenic harm, and cognitive behavioural therapy.
hq_q.f: A new red flag such as weight loss → investigate that sign.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate approach?

tm.m: Consistent scheduled follow-up with one clinician contains health anxiety and breaks the cycle of crisis attendance and iatrogenic testing
tm.g: Long-term primary care management of somatisation disorder -> regular planned appointments with one named GP
f: new peritonism, high fever and raised inflammatory markers suggesting an acute surgical abdomen
acute severe nociceptive pain immediately following a displaced long-bone fracture
new unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia or rectal bleeding meeting 2-week-wait criteria
never effective without empathetic explanation and structured ongoing primary care support
x: Ordering a fourth CT scan without red-flag signs exposes her to cumulative ionising radiation and reinforces illness conviction.
Prescribing opioid analgesia for chronic functional pain causes dependence, tolerance, and narcotic bowel hyperalgesia.
Referring to another hospital clinic fragments care and leads to further unnecessary invasive investigations.
Bluntly stating that all tests are normal without offering structured follow-up leaves her feeling dismissed and triggers emergency attendances.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man takes sertraline. He started tramadol 2 days ago. He is agitated and sweating with a tremor.
Temperature 38.2°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 150/90 mmHg. His pupils are dilated. There is inducible clonus at both ankles. He is alert.
hq_q.w: Serotonin syndrome is treated by stopping every serotonergic drug, with supportive care, fluids and a benzodiazepine for agitation. Cyproheptadine is added if it is moderate or severe.
hq_q.f: Rigidity, a very high CK and reduced reflexes on an antipsychotic → stop the antipsychotic for NMS.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first step?

tm.m: Two serotonergic drugs together flood the synapse; removing them lets it settle
tm.g: Serotonin syndrome: stop all serotonergic drugs first
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Bromocriptine (Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used in NMS and can worsen serotonin syndrome)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Dantrolene (Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia; it does not help serotonin syndrome)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Haloperidol for agitation (Antipsychotics can worsen the picture and mask NMS; a benzodiazepine is used for agitation)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Paracetamol for the fever (The heat comes from muscle activity, so antipyretics do not work)
x: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used in NMS and can worsen serotonin syndrome.
Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia; it does not help serotonin syndrome.
Antipsychotics can worsen the picture and mask NMS; a benzodiazepine is used for agitation.
The heat comes from muscle activity, so antipyretics do not work.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man takes sertraline and started tramadol for back pain 2 days ago. He is agitated, sweating and feverish.
Temperature 38.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm. His reflexes are brisk with inducible clonus at both ankles.
Creatine kinase 640 IU/L (25–200).
hq_q.w: Clonus and hyperreflexia are the signature of serotonin syndrome (Hunter criteria). NMS gives slow-onset lead-pipe rigidity with reduced reflexes.
hq_q.f: Lead-pipe rigidity and a CK of 18,000 days after haloperidol → NMS.
hq_q.ql: Which finding most specifically points to serotonin syndrome rather than neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

tm.m: Excess serotonin overstimulates the spinal reflexes, so clonus appears; NMS blocks dopamine and stiffens muscle instead
tm.g: Clonus is the sign that separates serotonin syndrome from NMS
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Creatine kinase of 640 IU/L (A raised CK occurs in both, and is usually far higher in NMS)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fever of 38.4°C (Fever occurs in both syndromes)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pulse rate of 118 bpm (Tachycardia occurs in both syndromes)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sweating (Sweating is an autonomic feature of both)
x: A raised CK occurs in both, and is usually far higher in NMS.
Fever occurs in both syndromes.
Tachycardia occurs in both syndromes.
Sweating is an autonomic feature of both.

hq_q.s: A 30 year old woman is an informal patient on a psychiatric ward. Her psychosis is getting worse. She tries to leave at night. Only a nurse with the right qualification is present.
hq_q.w: Section 5.4 lets a qualified nurse hold an informal inpatient for up to 6 hours until a doctor arrives.
hq_q.f: The doctor in charge is there → section 5.2, up to 72 hours.
hq_q.ql: Which power can be used?

c: Only a nurse with the right qualification is present
tm.m: A qualified nurse can hold an informal inpatient until a doctor arrives
tm.g: Informal inpatient leaving with only a qualified nurse present: section 5.4, up to 6 hours
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Section 136 (Section 136 is a police power in a public place)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Section 2 (Section 2 needs two doctors and an AMHP)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Section 3 (Section 3 needs two doctors and an AMHP)
the doctor in charge is present
x: Section 136 is a police power in a public place.
Section 2 needs two doctors and an AMHP.
Section 3 needs two doctors and an AMHP.
Ruled out here: requires the doctor in charge is present, whereas this patient has informal patient, tries to leave at night.

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old woman with severe depression has stopped eating and drinking for 5 days and barely speaks. She believes her bowels have rotted. She has not responded to two antidepressants.
Pulse rate 108 bpm. Her mucous membranes are dry.
Creatinine has risen from 70 to 140 µmol/L.
hq_q.w: Life-threatening depression with refusal of food and fluids, psychotic features and no response to drugs is an indication for ECT, which works fastest.
hq_q.f: Moderate depression that has not responded to one SSRI → switch or increase the antidepressant.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

c: stopped eating and drinking for 5 days
tm.m: ECT works in days, which matters when dehydration is already damaging the kidneys
tm.g: Life-threatening or psychotic depression not responding to drugs: ECT
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Add mirtazapine (Drug changes take weeks; she is already in acute kidney injury from not drinking)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Increase the sertraline dose (A dose rise works too slowly for life-threatening depression)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Inpatient CBT (She cannot engage in therapy while mute and psychotic)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lithium augmentation (Lithium is dangerous with rising creatinine and dehydration, and it is slow)
x: Drug changes take weeks; she is already in acute kidney injury from not drinking.
A dose rise works too slowly for life-threatening depression.
She cannot engage in therapy while mute and psychotic.
Lithium is dangerous with rising creatinine and dehydration, and it is slow.

hq_q.s:
A 41 year old woman admitted with acute psychosis was started on intramuscular haloperidol 4 days ago and has become mute, rigid, and stuporous. The ward team considers catatonia versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
On examination, her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate is 130 bpm, blood pressure is labile, and serum creatine kinase is 18,400 U/L.
o: Holding abnormal limb postures for hours
Refusing all oral food and fluids
hq_q.w: Although both catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) can feature mutism, stupor, and motor rigidity, high fever, marked autonomic instability (tachycardia and labile blood pressure), and severe rhabdomyolysis (creatine kinase >1000 U/L, here 18,400 U/L) after antipsychotic exposure distinguish NMS.
hq_q.f: Normal temperature and CK → catatonia, lorazepam challenge.
hq_q.ql: Which finding most suggests neuroleptic malignant syndrome rather than catatonia?

tm.m: Hypothalamic D2 blockade and severe sustained skeletal muscle contraction cause hyperthermia and massive creatine kinase release
tm.g: Feature distinguishing neuroleptic malignant syndrome from simple catatonia -> high fever with markedly raised creatine kinase
f: asked which speech abnormality is shared by both catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome
asked which motor sign is classic for catatonia with normal temperature and normal creatine kinase
asked which behavioural sign is typical of afebrile catatonic stupor
asked which feature of depressive catatonia necessitates urgent electroconvulsive therapy
x: Mutism occurs in both primary affective/psychotic catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Sustained posturing and catalepsy are classic motor features of uncomplicated catatonia and do not by themselves establish NMS.
Psychomotor stupor and fixed staring are core diagnostic features of catatonia even when temperature and CK are normal.
Negativistic refusal of food and drink is common in severe depressive catatonia and does not specifically point to NMS.

hq_q.s:
