Stopping potassium replacement while serum potassium is 3.0 mmol/L and magnesium is 0.38 mmol/L risks life-threatening torsades de pointes.
Peripheral infusions exceeding 40 mmol/L cause severe chemical phlebitis and tissue necrosis, and potassium will still be wasted in urine until magnesium is repleted.
f: Chronic metabolic acidosis with serum bicarbonate of 16 mmol/L in stage 4 chronic kidney disease
Confirmed primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) with hypertension, normal magnesium, and suppressed plasma renin
Resolved hypokalaemia where repeat serum potassium has risen to 5.4 mmol/L
Never permissible via a peripheral venous cannula due to severe vein necrosis and cardiac toxicity risk

hq_q.s: A 26 year old woman of Greek Cypriot family origin attends her GP surgery after routine blood tests taken before trying to conceive. She feels completely well, eats a balanced diet including red meat, has regular light menstrual periods and is not pregnant. Physical examination is normal with no pallor or hepatosplenomegaly. Full blood count and haematinics show: haemoglobin 114 g/L (115-165), MCV 63 fL (80-96), red blood cell count 5.9 x 10^12/L (3.8-5.2) and serum ferritin 92 micrograms/L (15-200).
o: Diagnostic bone marrow aspirate and trephine
Three-month therapeutic trial of oral ferrous sulfate
hq_q.w: Profound microcytosis (MCV 63 fL) accompanied by a normal or only minimally reduced haemoglobin (114 g/L), an elevated red blood cell count (erythrocytosis, 5.9 x 10^12/L, giving a Mentzer index MCV/RBC of 63/5.9 = 10.7, which is <13) and a completely normal serum ferritin (92 micrograms/L) in a patient of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern or South Asian heritage is the classic hallmark of beta-thalassaemia trait (minor). Diagnosis is confirmed by haemoglobin electrophoresis or high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), which demonstrates an elevated HbA2 (alpha2-delta2 >3.5%) and mildly raised HbF.
hq_q.f: Ferritin of 5 with heavy periods → iron deficiency, oral iron.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate confirmatory diagnostic investigation?

c: MCV 63 fL (80-96), red blood cell count 5.9 x 10^12/L (3.8-5.2) and serum ferritin 92 micrograms/L
tm.m: Heterozygous beta-globin gene mutation -> reduced beta-chain synthesis -> compensatory marrow erythrocytosis (high RBC count) with very small red cells (MCV <70 fL, Mentzer <13) and raised HbA2 (>3.5%)
tm.g: Marked microcytosis (MCV ~60-68 fL) + mild/no anaemia + HIGH RBC count + NORMAL ferritin in Mediterranean/Asian patient = thalassaemia trait -> confirm with haemoglobin electrophoresis / HPLC (raised HbA2)
x: Coeliac disease causes malabsorptive iron-deficiency anaemia with a LOW serum ferritin (<15 micrograms/L), whereas her ferritin is 92 micrograms/L
Invasive bone marrow biopsy is not required when peripheral blood haemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC diagnoses thalassaemia trait non-invasively
Bidirectional GI endoscopy is indicated for unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia (low ferritin) in men or postmenopausal women, not thalassaemia trait with normal ferritin
Giving oral iron to a patient with thalassaemia trait and normal ferritin (92 micrograms/L) will not raise the MCV and risks iron overload
f: 26 year old woman with bloating, weight loss, Hb 96 g/L, MCV 72 fL and serum ferritin of 6 micrograms/L
unexplained pancytopenia with circulating blasts and dysplastic neutrophils on peripheral blood film
66 year old man presenting with Hb 94 g/L, MCV 73 fL and a serum ferritin of 8 micrograms/L
26 year old woman with heavy periods, Hb 98 g/L, MCV 74 fL, RBC 3.7 x 10^12/L and serum ferritin of 9 micrograms/L

hq_q.s: A 62 year old woman with active seropositive rheumatoid arthritis presents to her GP with 2 months of lethargy. She has morning stiffness lasting 90 minutes and symmetrical swelling of her wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints. She denies indigestion, weight loss or rectal bleeding. Blood tests show: haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-165), MCV 82 fL (80-96), serum iron 5 micromol/L (11-30), total iron-binding capacity 38 micromol/L (45-72, low), transferrin saturation 13%, serum ferritin 310 micrograms/L (15-200) and CRP 58 mg/L.
hq_q.w: This iron profile is diagnostic of anaemia of chronic disease (anaemia of inflammation): low serum iron, low transferrin saturation, LOW total iron-binding capacity (because transferrin is a negative acute-phase protein downregulated by inflammation), and an ELEVATED serum ferritin (310 micrograms/L, because IL-6 induces hepatic hepcidin, which blocks macrophage ferroportin and traps iron inside reticuloendothelial stores, and because ferritin is a positive acute-phase reactant). Treating the underlying rheumatoid inflammation restores normal erythropoiesis.
hq_q.f: Ferritin 8 → true iron deficiency, look for blood loss.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: IL-6 in active rheumatoid arthritis -> induces hepatic hepcidin -> degrades ferroportin on macrophages -> traps iron in stores (high ferritin, low serum iron, low TIBC)
tm.g: Anaemia of chronic disease iron panel: LOW serum iron + LOW TIBC/transferrin + NORMAL/HIGH ferritin (vs IDA: low iron + HIGH TIBC + LOW ferritin)
x: Shows marked microcytosis (MCV <70 fL) with normal serum iron and normal TIBC
Pure iron deficiency shows a LOW serum ferritin (<15 to 30 micrograms/L) and a compensatorily HIGH total iron-binding capacity (>72 micromol/L)
Shows HIGH serum iron and high transferrin saturation alongside raised ferritin, with ring sideroblasts in the bone marrow
Shows a macrocytic anaemia (MCV >100 fL) with hypersegmented neutrophils and low serum vitamin B12
f: lifelong MCV of 64 fL with normal serum iron, normal TIBC, normal CRP and HbA2 of 5.2%
Hb 92 g/L, MCV 71 fL, serum iron 4 micromol/L, HIGH total iron-binding capacity (84 micromol/L) and serum ferritin 7 micrograms/L
Hb 88 g/L, HIGH serum iron (38 micromol/L), transferrin saturation 82%, ferritin 450 micrograms/L and bone marrow ring sideroblasts
Hb 90 g/L, MCV 115 fL, sore tongue, absent ankle jerks and positive anti-intrinsic factor antibodies

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has become tired and yellow over 2 weeks.
She is pale and jaundiced. The spleen tip is palpable.
hq_q.w: Antibodies coat red cells, so the direct antiglobulin test is positive. Reticulocytes push the MCV up and bilirubin rises with a normal ALT.
hq_q.f: Negative DAT with spherocytes and a family history → hereditary spherocytosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Autoantibodies tag red cells for destruction in the spleen
tm.g: Haemolysis with a positive DAT is immune haemolysis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to B12 deficiency (Gives a high MCV but low reticulocytes and no positive DAT)
sudden haemolysis after fava beans or nitrofurantoin
the presentation instead showed features specific to Gilbert's syndrome (Haemoglobin would be normal)
negative DAT, spherocytes and an affected father
x: Gives a high MCV but low reticulocytes and no positive DAT
Triggered by oxidants and DAT negative
Haemoglobin would be normal
DAT negative, usually with a family history

hq_q.s: A 54 year old publican attends his GP surgery for a routine hypertension check. He reports mild tiredness at the end of his working week but denies weight change, cold intolerance, sore tongue, diarrhoea or numbness in his feet. On examination, his blood pressure is 146/90 mmHg, there is palmar erythema and facial telangiectasia, and neurological examination is completely normal. Blood tests show: haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-175), MCV 106 fL (80-96), platelets 138 x 10^9/L, serum B12 420 ng/L (normal), serum folate 9.4 micrograms/L (normal), TSH 1.8 mU/L and gamma-GT 245 U/L (<55).
hq_q.w: Chronic alcohol excess is the single commonest cause of an isolated non-megaloblastic macrocytosis (typically MCV 100 to 110 fL) WITHOUT anaemia (here Hb is normal at 148 g/L). Ethanol and its metabolite acetaldehyde exert a direct toxic effect on developing bone marrow erythroblasts and alter red cell membrane lipid composition, enlarging erythrocyte volume independently of folate or vitamin B12 levels. The clues are his occupation, palmar erythema, borderline thrombocytopenia (from direct marrow/splenic effects), normal haematinics (B12/folate) and a markedly elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT 245 U/L). The MCV takes 2 to 4 months (red cell lifespan) to normalise after abstinence.
hq_q.f: B12 of 90 with hypersegmented neutrophils → B12 deficiency.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of his raised mean corpuscular volume (MCV)?

c: serum B12 420 ng/L (normal), serum folate 9.4 micrograms/L (normal)
tm.m: Direct acetaldehyde toxicity on erythroblast development + red cell membrane lipid modification -> round macrocytosis (MCV 100-110 fL) without anaemia + raised gamma-GT
tm.g: Isolated macrocytosis (MCV 100-110 fL) with NORMAL haemoglobin, normal B12/folate/TSH and raised gamma-GT = alcohol excess
x: Ruled out by his normal serum folate (9.4 micrograms/L) and normal haemoglobin
Typically presents in elderly patients with progressive macrocytic anaemia, neutropenia/thrombocytopenia and dysplastic blood film features rather than normal Hb 148 g/L and raised GGT
Ruled out by his completely normal serum TSH of 1.8 mU/L
Ruled out by his normal serum vitamin B12 (420 ng/L), normal haemoglobin and normal neurological examination
f: megaloblastic anaemia (Hb 92 g/L, MCV 114 fL) with hypersegmented neutrophils and serum folate of 1.2 micrograms/L
78 year old non-drinker with progressive macrocytic anaemia (Hb 82 g/L, MCV 112 fL), neutropenia and hypogranular Pelger-Huet neutrophils
weight gain, cold intolerance, slow-relaxing reflexes, MCV 103 fL and serum TSH of 38 mU/L
macrocytic anaemia (Hb 88 g/L, MCV 118 fL), loss of vibration sense at the ankles and serum B12 of 85 ng/L

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old woman takes citalopram. She started clarithromycin for a chest infection 3 days ago. On the ward she has two brief blackouts.
The monitor shows a polymorphic broad complex tachycardia that twists around the baseline and stops by itself. Between episodes she has a pulse and the QTc is 560 ms. She has been given IV magnesium sulfate.
hq_q.w: Torsades de pointes is driven by a long QT. Alongside IV magnesium, stop every QT-prolonging drug (here clarithromycin and citalopram) and correct potassium to the high-normal range; overdrive pacing or isoprenaline is used if it keeps recurring.
hq_q.f: Torsades that does not stop, with no pulse → defibrillate (unsynchronised).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate step alongside the magnesium?

tm.m: Early afterdepolarisations during a prolonged repolarisation trigger twisting VT
tm.g: Torsades: magnesium, stop QT drugs, fix potassium
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Add oral sotalol (Sotalol is a class III drug that lengthens the QT)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Give IV adenosine (Adenosine is for regular narrow complex tachycardia; it does not treat torsades)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Start an amiodarone infusion (Amiodarone prolongs the QT further and can worsen torsades)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Synchronised DC shock now (She is out of the arrhythmia with a pulse; shocks are for sustained, unstable runs)
x: Sotalol is a class III drug that lengthens the QT.
Adenosine is for regular narrow complex tachycardia; it does not treat torsades.
Amiodarone prolongs the QT further and can worsen torsades.
She is out of the arrhythmia with a pulse; shocks are for sustained, unstable runs.

hq_q.s: A 72 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of profuse vomiting, generalized muscle weakness and intermittent palpitations. She takes bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg daily for hypertension. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 92 bpm regular, BP 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, SpO2 98% breathing air. Muscle power is 4/5 symmetrically in all four limbs with depressed deep tendon reflexes.
o: Osborn J waves at the QRS-ST junction
Prominent U waves with flattened T waves
Shortened QT interval with truncated ST segment
Short PR interval with slurred delta waves
Tall tented T waves with flattened P waves
hq_q.w: Hypokalaemia (potassium 2.6 mmol/L secondary to thiazide diuretic therapy and vomiting) delays ventricular repolarisation, producing T-wave flattening or inversion, ST-segment depression, prominent U waves (best seen in V2-V4) and a prolonged QU/QT interval.
hq_q.f: Serum potassium 6.9 mmol/L -> tall tented T waves, flattened/absent P waves, PR prolongation and broad QRS complexes.
hq_q.ql: Which 12-lead ECG abnormality is most likely to be present?

tm.m: Reduced extracellular potassium slows phase 3 potassium efflux across delayed rectifier channels, flattening the T wave and unmasking Purkinje repolarisation as a U wave
tm.g: Hypokalaemia ECG changes: flattened/inverted T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves
x: Positive deflections at the J point (Osborn waves) are characteristic of severe hypothermia (<32°C) rather than thiazide-induced hypokalaemia.
Shortening of the QT interval is caused by hypercalcaemia accelerating ventricular repolarisation, whereas hypokalaemia prolongs the QU interval.
A short PR interval with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) represents pre-excitation via a congenital accessory pathway (Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome).
Tall peaked T waves and loss of P waves are classic features of severe hyperkalaemia rather than hypokalaemia.
f: An elderly patient found unconscious outdoors in winter has a core rectal temperature of 29.5°C and bradycardia.
She has metastatic breast cancer with confusion, polyuria and a corrected serum calcium of 3.45 mmol/L.
A young adult presents with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia and a congenital atrioventricular accessory pathway.
She has acute kidney injury on spironolactone and ramipril with a serum potassium of 6.9 mmol/L.

hq_q.s: A 44 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of severe occipital headache and blurred vision. He stopped his antihypertensive tablets 4 weeks ago. Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 236/138 mmHg in both arms, SpO2 98% breathing air. Fundoscopy demonstrates bilateral optic disc swelling with flame-shaped retinal haemorrhages. Urine dipstick shows blood 2+ and protein 2+.
o: Admit for intravenous labetalol to lower BP gradually
Intravenous labetalol to normalise BP within 1 hour
Restart usual oral tablets and recheck in 1 month
Start oral amlodipine and arrange GP review in 1 week
hq_q.w: Severe hypertension accompanied by acute target-organ damage (bilateral papilloedema, retinal haemorrhages and acute kidney injury) is a hypertensive emergency requiring hospital admission and controlled intravenous labetalol, reducing mean arterial pressure by no more than 20-25% over the first few hours.
hq_q.f: Severe hypertension (>=180/120 mmHg) without papilloedema or acute target-organ damage -> oral antihypertensive therapy and urgent outpatient review.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

c: bilateral optic disc swelling with flame-shaped retinal haemorrhages
tm.m: Cerebral autoregulation shifts upwards in chronic severe hypertension; gradual controlled IV reduction halts fibrinoid necrosis without dropping perfusion below the lower autoregulatory threshold
tm.g: Hypertensive emergency (BP >= 180/120 + papilloedema/retinal haemorrhage/AKI): admit for controlled IV blood pressure reduction (<=25% over first hours)
x: Sublingual nifedipine causes an precipitous, uncontrolled fall in blood pressure, risking stroke and myocardial ischaemia, and is contraindicated.
Dropping blood pressure to normal within an hour in malignant hypertension causes watershed cerebral infarction and ischaemic optic neuropathy.
Delaying inpatient supervision ignores active microvascular fibrinoid necrosis in the retina and kidneys.
Outpatient oral therapy is unsafe in a hypertensive emergency with grade IV hypertensive retinopathy (papilloedema) and acute kidney injury.
f: This option is obsolete and contraindicated in hypertensive emergencies due to unpredictable hypotension.
He has an acute thoracic aortic dissection where systolic BP must be rapidly lowered to 100-120 mmHg within 20 minutes.
He attends clinic with stage 2 hypertension (162/102 mmHg) and no acute target-organ damage.
He is asymptomatic with BP 184/112 mmHg, normal fundoscopy, normal creatinine and a negative urine dipstick.

hq_q.s: A 19 year old woman with type 1 diabetes is brought to the Emergency Department after 24 hours of vomiting and abdominal pain, having omitted her insulin injections while unwell. On examination, she weighs 60 kg, her pulse is 116 bpm, blood pressure is 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate is 28 breaths/min and mucous membranes are dry. Her admission venous blood gas and laboratory results are shown.
o: Give 1 litre of intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride with 40 mmol potassium chloride over 1 hour
Give 1 litre of intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride without potassium over 1 hour
Give an intravenous bolus of 10 units soluble human insulin (Actrapid) stat
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 100 mL over 30 minutes
Start a variable-rate intravenous insulin infusion (sliding scale)
hq_q.w: When a patient with DKA presents with a systolic blood pressure of 90 mmHg or above, JBDS guidelines recommend starting fluid replacement with 1 litre of intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride over the first hour, alongside a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/hour = 6 units/hour for 60 kg). Because her admission serum potassium is 5.8 mmol/L (>5.5 mmol/L) and it is the first resuscitation bag, potassium chloride MUST NOT be added to the initial litre; potassium (40 mmol/L) is added once serum potassium falls into the 3.5 to 5.5 mmol/L range and urine output is confirmed.
hq_q.f: Systolic BP under 90 → 500 ml of crystalloid over 15 minutes, repeated.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial step in her management?

c: 19 year old woman with type 1 diabetes
tm.m: Extracellular hyperosmolality and insulin deficiency shift K+ out of cells initially (K+ 5.8 mmol/L) -> give 1st litre of 0.9% saline over 1 hour WITHOUT potassium to avoid fatal hyperkalaemia
tm.g: DKA with SBP >=90 mmHg and initial K+ >5.5 mmol/L = 1 litre 0.9% sodium chloride over 1 hour WITHOUT potassium (plus fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/h)
x: Potassium must never be added to the first resuscitation litre or when serum potassium exceeds 5.5 mmol/L because of the risk of hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest
UK JBDS guidelines do not use an initial intravenous insulin stat bolus; a continuous fixed-rate infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour is started after fluid resuscitation begins
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate is not used routinely in DKA as it worsens intracellular acidosis and hypokalaemia
DKA requires a weight-based fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/hour) to switch off ketogenesis, not a glucose-titrated variable-rate sliding scale
f: second 1-litre bag of 0.9% sodium chloride (given over 2 hours) once repeat venous potassium has fallen to 4.4 mmol/L and urine output is >0.5 mL/kg/hour
emergency treatment of severe hyperkalaemia (K+ 6.9 mmol/L with ECG changes) using 10 units soluble insulin in 25 g intravenous glucose
life-threatening tricyclic antidepressant toxicity with arterial pH 7.08 and QRS duration 150 ms
perioperative glycaemic control in a fasting patient with type 1 diabetes undergoing elective surgery who has normal blood ketones (0.2 mmol/L)

hq_q.s: A 23 year old man is 4 hours into treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis on the Acute Medical Unit. He is receiving a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour and has completed 2 litres of intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride. He is alert, haemodynamically stable and passing 70 mL/hour of urine. Repeat venous blood gas results at 4 hours are shown.
hq_q.w: Continuous intravenous insulin stimulation of the Na+/K+-ATPase pump drives potassium rapidly into the intracellular compartment as ketoacidosis resolves. Under JBDS DKA guidelines, whenever serum potassium lies between 3.5 and 5.5 mmol/L (here 4.2 mmol/L) and the patient has adequate urine output (>0.5 mL/kg/hour), 40 mmol of potassium chloride per litre must be added to the intravenous replacement fluids. If potassium falls below 3.5 mmol/L, senior review is needed as insulin must be paused temporarily and higher-rate potassium given via central access.
hq_q.f: Potassium 5.8 → no potassium in that bag.
hq_q.ql: How much potassium chloride should be added to his next 1-litre bag of intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride?

c: 4 hours into treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis
tm.m: Ongoing fixed-rate IV insulin drives K+ intracellularly -> serum K+ of 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5 range) requires 40 mmol/L KCl in replacement bags
tm.g: DKA fluid potassium protocol: K+ >5.5 = None; K+ 3.5 to 5.5 = 40 mmol/L; K+ <3.5 = pause insulin + senior review
x: 20 mmol/L is insufficient during active fixed-rate insulin infusion in DKA and allows hypokalaemia to develop
60 mmol/L exceeds standard pre-mixed peripheral DKA fluid bags (40 mmol/L); if K+ falls <3.5 mmol/L, insulin is paused and senior HDU review arranged
80 mmol/L is dangerously concentrated for a peripheral vein and risks severe chemical phlebitis and hyperkalaemic arrhythmia
Omitting potassium when serum K+ is 4.2 mmol/L during fixed-rate insulin infusion will rapidly precipitate severe hypokalaemia
f: routine ward maintenance fluid bag (0.18% NaCl / 4% glucose with 20 mmol/L KCl) in a patient not receiving fixed-rate DKA insulin
patient weights in kg (60 kg) requiring 6 units/hour fixed-rate insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour
total daily maintenance potassium allowance in mmol for an 80 kg surgical inpatient
repeat venous blood gas showing serum potassium of 5.7 mmol/L or complete anuria

hq_q.s: A 79 year old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin is brought to the Emergency Department with drowsiness and profound dehydration after a 7-day history of productive cough and poor fluid intake. On examination, she weighs 60 kg, her pulse is 112 bpm, blood pressure is 102/60 mmHg and mucous membranes are parched. Her admission laboratory results are shown.
o: Give intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride first, introducing low-dose insulin later only if glucose plateaus
Give intravenous 3% hypertonic sodium chloride to match her serum sodium
Give intravenous 5% glucose at 250 mL/hour to lower her serum sodium
Give oral water and gliclazide 80 mg via a nasogastric tube
Start a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately
hq_q.w: With plasma glucose 44 mmol/L, sodium 152 mmol/L, urea 26 mmol/L (calculated osmolality = 2(152) + 44 + 26 = 374 mOsm/kg), blood ketones 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH 7.36, this patient has hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS). Under JBDS guidelines, initial management is intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride alone to restore circulating volume and lower osmolality gradually by 3 to 8 mOsm/kg/hour. Because blood ketones are <=1.0 mmol/L, insulin is withheld initially and started at a low dose (0.05 units/kg/hour) only once plasma glucose stops falling with fluids.
hq_q.f: Ketones 4 and pH 7.1 → DKA, fixed-rate insulin at 0.1 units per kg per hour.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate initial fluid and insulin strategy?

c: 79 year old woman with type 2 diabetes
weighs 60 kg, her pulse is 112 bpm
tm.m: HHS (osmolality 374 mOsm/kg, ketones 0.6 mmol/L, pH 7.36) -> IV 0.9% saline restores renal perfusion and lowers glucose -> withhold insulin until glucose fall plateaus
tm.g: HHS initial management (ketones <=1.0 mmol/L) = IV 0.9% sodium chloride first; add low-dose IV insulin (0.05 units/kg/h) only when glucose stops falling with fluids
x: Hypertonic 3% saline would worsen her severe hypertonicity (374 mOsm/kg) and cellular dehydration
Intravenous 5% glucose adds further glucose and free water, risking both worsening hyperglycaemia and rapid osmotic shifts
A drowsy, hypotensive patient with an 8 to 12 litre fluid deficit requires intravenous crystalloid resuscitation, and sulfonylureas are contraindicated in acute HHS
Starting DKA-dose insulin (0.1 units/kg/hour) before fluid replacement in HHS causes rapid intracellular fluid shift, hypovolaemic shock and cerebral oedema
f: acute symptomatic hyponatraemic seizures (serum sodium 111 mmol/L) requiring a 150 mL bolus of 3% hypertonic saline
later in HHS treatment when plasma glucose drops below 14.0 mmol/L, where 5% or 10% glucose is added alongside 0.9% saline
stable outpatient with newly diagnosed HNF1A-MODY starting oral therapy
22 year old with type 1 diabetes presenting with blood glucose 26 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.1 mmol/L and venous pH 7.12 (DKA)

hq_q.s: A 46 year old man with type 2 diabetes has fingerprick glucose readings of 12 to 16 mmol/L most days. He has had a recent haemolytic anaemia and has been treated for it.
hq_q.w: HbA1c reflects about 3 months of glucose stuck to red cells. If cells die early, there is less time to glycate, so HbA1c reads falsely low.
hq_q.f: Iron deficiency with no haemolysis → HbA1c can read falsely high.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely reason his HbA1c does not match his readings?

tm.m: Young red cells have had less time to collect glucose
tm.g: Haemolysis makes HbA1c falsely low; use glucose readings or fructosamine
f: iron deficiency with normal reticulocytes
the presentation instead showed features specific to Laboratory or sampling error (The pattern is explained by his haemolysis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Poor meter technique (Repeated readings in the same range make this less likely)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Very good control (His glucose readings are high)
x: Old red cells linger and push HbA1c up, not down
The pattern is explained by his haemolysis
Repeated readings in the same range make this less likely
His glucose readings are high

hq_q.s: A 44 year old female pharmacy technician without diabetes is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic with a 3-month history of recurrent episodes of early-morning sweating, tremor, diplopia and confusion before breakfast that resolve within 15 minutes of drinking sweet tea. She has gained 4 kg to stave off attacks. During a supervised 72-hour inpatient fast, she becomes confused at 18 hours; laboratory results taken during the symptomatic episode are shown.
hq_q.w: This patient fulfils Whipple's triad (symptoms of neuroglycopenia, documented low plasma glucose of 1.9 mmol/L during symptoms, and relief of symptoms when plasma glucose is restored). High plasma insulin accompanied by elevated C-peptide proves that the excess insulin is endogenous (since proinsulin is cleaved into equimolar insulin and C-peptide in pancreatic beta-cells, whereas commercial insulin injections contain no C-peptide). A negative plasma and urine sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen excludes secretagogue ingestion, confirming an endogenous pancreatic insulinoma (associated with MEN1 in ~10%).
hq_q.f: High insulin with low C-peptide → injected insulin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: early-morning sweating, tremor, diplopia and confusion before breakfast
tm.m: Autonomous beta-cell neuroendocrine tumour -> co-secretes insulin and C-peptide despite hypoglycaemia -> low glucose + high insulin + high C-peptide + negative sulfonylurea screen
tm.g: Fasting hypoglycaemia + high insulin + high C-peptide + negative sulfonylurea screen = insulinoma (if C-peptide is suppressed = exogenous insulin; if SU screen positive = sulfonylurea misuse)
x: Cortisol deficiency impairs gluconeogenesis and causes fasting hypoglycaemia with appropriately suppressed plasma insulin and C-peptide
Ethanol oxidation depletes hepatic NAD+ and inhibits gluconeogenesis, causing hypoglycaemia with appropriately suppressed insulin and C-peptide
Commercial exogenous insulin suppresses endogenous beta-cell secretion, producing high plasma insulin with a low or undetectable C-peptide
Sulfonylurea ingestion produces identical high insulin and high C-peptide levels, but is ruled out here by the negative urinary sulfonylurea screen
f: postural hypotension, buccal pigmentation, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia with suppressed insulin (<2 mU/L) and C-peptide
malnourished heavy drinker brought in after a 2-day binge with glucose 1.8 mmol/L and undetectable plasma insulin and C-peptide
symptomatic hypoglycaemia (glucose 1.7 mmol/L) with high plasma insulin (48 mU/L) but undetectable C-peptide (<50 pmol/L)
symptomatic hypoglycaemia with high insulin, high C-peptide and a positive urine toxicology screen for gliclazide metabolites

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old woman has had a painful swelling in the front of her neck for 10 days after a viral sore throat. She has palpitations.
Temperature 37.8°C, pulse rate 104 bpm. The thyroid is diffusely tender.
hq_q.w: De Quervain's thyroiditis: inflamed cells leak stored hormone. Treat pain and symptoms. Carbimazole does nothing as no new hormone is being made.
hq_q.f: Painless goitre with positive TSH receptor antibodies → Graves' disease, carbimazole.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: A viral inflammation breaks follicles and releases stored hormone
tm.g: Painful thyroiditis with low uptake: treat symptoms, no antithyroid drugs
f: positive TSH receptor antibodies with eye signs
the presentation instead showed features specific to Levothyroxine (Would worsen the thyrotoxicosis now)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Radioactive iodine (An inflamed gland takes up almost no iodine, and it settles alone)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Thyroidectomy (Not needed for a self-limiting inflammation)
x: Blocks new hormone production, but this is leakage of stored hormone
Would worsen the thyrotoxicosis now
An inflamed gland takes up almost no iodine, and it settles alone
Not needed for a self-limiting inflammation

hq_q.s: A 31 year old nurse presents to the Endocrinology Clinic complaining of a 5 kg weight loss over 2 months, palpitations, anxiety, heat intolerance and oligomenorrhoea. Her mother takes medication for hypothyroidism. On examination, her pulse is 112 bpm regular, she has a fine tremor, there is no proptosis or lid lag, and her thyroid gland is impalpable and non-tender without a bruit. Blood and nuclear medicine results are shown.
hq_q.w: When a patient ingests exogenous thyroid hormone (thyrotoxicosis factitia), elevated circulating T4 and T3 suppress pituitary TSH (<0.01 mU/L), shutting down endogenous thyroid follicular activity. Consequently, the thyroid gland atrophies (impalpable goitre), radionuclide tracer uptake is globally absent, AND serum thyroglobulin is undetectable or very low (because thyroglobulin is only cleaved and released when endogenous colloid is processed into thyroid hormone). By contrast, destructive thyroiditis (De Quervain's or postpartum) also shows absent scan uptake, but follicular destruction leaks huge amounts of thyroglobulin into the bloodstream.
hq_q.f: Absent uptake with a tender gland and high thyroglobulin → thyroiditis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: thyroid gland is impalpable and non-tender
tm.m: Exogenous levothyroxine ingestion -> suppresses pituitary TSH -> shuts down endogenous follicular colloid synthesis -> absent radioiodine uptake + very low serum thyroglobulin
tm.g: Thyrotoxicosis + absent radioiodine uptake + VERY LOW serum thyroglobulin = exogenous levothyroxine use (vs high thyroglobulin in thyroiditis)
x: Causes a painful, tender goitre with absent tracer uptake, but follicular destruction releases high levels of serum thyroglobulin
Produces a diffuse goitre, positive TSH-receptor antibodies, high serum thyroglobulin and diffusely increased radionuclide uptake
Shows a palpable nodule with intense focal tracer uptake and elevated serum thyroglobulin
Presents with a nodular goitre, patchy heterogeneous increased tracer uptake and elevated serum thyroglobulin
f: painful tender goitre after a viral illness with absent radioiodine uptake and markedly elevated serum thyroglobulin
smooth diffuse goitre with bruit, exophthalmos, diffusely increased radioiodine uptake and elevated serum thyroglobulin
single palpable thyroid nodule with focal hot uptake, suppressed surrounding tissue and elevated serum thyroglobulin
older patient with a multinodular goitre, patchy hot and cold areas on uptake scan and elevated serum thyroglobulin

hq_q.s: A 52 year old woman had thyroid tests at a routine check. A repeat 3 months later is unchanged. She has no symptoms, is not pregnant and has no heart disease.
hq_q.w: NICE advises considering levothyroxine for subclinical hypothyroidism when the TSH is 10 or more on two tests 3 months apart, because the risk of progressing to overt hypothyroidism is high, especially with TPO antibodies.
hq_q.f: TSH 7 with a normal free T4 and no symptoms → repeat in 3 months; no treatment yet.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Autoimmune thyroiditis slowly destroys the gland, and the pituitary pushes TSH up first
tm.g: TSH 10 or more on two tests: consider levothyroxine
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Carbimazole (Carbimazole treats an overactive thyroid)
the presentation instead showed features specific to No follow-up needed (With a TSH over 10 and positive antibodies, she is likely to progress)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Radioiodine uptake scan (An uptake scan is for hyperthyroidism or nodules, not a raised TSH)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Repeat tests in 3 months (The TSH is already confirmed above 10 on two tests; another wait adds nothing)
x: Carbimazole treats an overactive thyroid.
With a TSH over 10 and positive antibodies, she is likely to progress.
An uptake scan is for hyperthyroidism or nodules, not a raised TSH.
The TSH is already confirmed above 10 on two tests; another wait adds nothing.

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man presents to his GP with 6 months of progressive lethargy, cold intolerance, erectile dysfunction and dull bifrontal headaches, and mentions he has twice scraped his car wing mirrors and bumped into doorframes on either side. Confrontation visual field testing demonstrates a bitemporal hemianopia, and his ankle reflexes relax slowly. Blood test results are shown.
hq_q.w: A low free T4 (6.0 pmol/L) accompanied by a low or inappropriately normal serum TSH (0.8 mU/L) is the biochemical hallmark of secondary (central) hypothyroidism due to anterior pituitary or hypothalamic disease. Here, a non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma is compressing the optic chiasm (causing bitemporal hemianopia) and pituitary thyrotrophs/gonadotrophs. Crucial clinical rule: always assess the hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenal axis (9 am cortisol/short Synacthen test) and replace hydrocortisone BEFORE starting levothyroxine, as thyroxine accelerates cortisol clearance and precipitates fatal adrenal crisis.
hq_q.f: TSH 38 with a low T4 → primary hypothyroidism.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely thyroid diagnosis?

c: bumped into doorframes on either side
tm.m: Pituitary macroadenoma compresses optic chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia) and pituitary thyrotrophs -> fails to secrete TSH despite low free T4
tm.g: Low free T4 + low or inappropriately normal TSH (+ bitemporal hemianopia/headache) = secondary (central/pituitary) hypothyroidism (give hydrocortisone BEFORE levothyroxine)
x: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is a primary gland failure where low free T4 triggers a markedly elevated pituitary TSH (>10 mU/L)
Exogenous levothyroxine over-replacement causes a suppressed TSH accompanied by an elevated free T4
Primary hypothyroidism always shows an elevated serum TSH in response to a low free T4
Sick euthyroid syndrome occurs in acute severe systemic illness with low free T3 and no chiasmal visual field defect
f: firm rubbery goitre, strongly positive anti-TPO antibodies, free T4 of 6.0 pmol/L and TSH of 45 mU/L
patient on 175 micrograms daily of levothyroxine with palpitations, TSH <0.01 mU/L and free T4 of 31 pmol/L
cold intolerance, dry skin, normal visual fields, free T4 of 6.0 pmol/L and TSH of 36 mU/L
acutely unwell inpatient in intensive care with severe pancreatitis, low free T3, low-normal TSH and normal visual fields

hq_q.s:
A 63-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 2-week history of generalized pruritus and yellowing of her skin and sclerae. She has noticed dark brown urine and pale, putty-coloured stools, without abdominal pain or fever.
Temperature is 36.6°C and heart rate is 72 bpm. Examination confirms scleral icterus and a soft, non-tender abdomen without stigmata of chronic liver disease.
hq_q.w: Marked elevation of alkaline phosphatase (480 IU/L) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (520 IU/L) disproportionate to a modest ALT rise (90 IU/L), accompanied by dark urine and pale stools, is the classic biochemical signature of cholestatic (obstructive) jaundice.
hq_q.f: ALT 1,500 IU/L with ALP 140 IU/L -> acute hepatocellular injury pattern.
hq_q.ql: Which biochemical pattern is demonstrated by these liver function test results?

c: generalized pruritus and yellowing of her skin and sclerae
dark brown urine and pale, putty-coloured stools
tm.m: Biliary obstruction blocks conjugated bilirubin entry into the gut (pale stools) and causes regurgitation into blood and urine (dark urine), while bile acids induce canalicular ALP and GGT synthesis.
tm.g: Disproportionate elevation of ALP and GGT over ALT with dark urine and pale stools -> Cholestatic obstructive pattern
x: Acute hepatocellular injury is characterised by transaminases (ALT and AST) elevated >10 times the upper limit of normal, far exceeding the ALP rise.
Hepatic synthetic failure is defined by hypoalbuminaemia, coagulopathy (prolonged prothrombin time/INR), and hypoglycaemia, whereas her albumin is normal at 38 g/L.
Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (such as Gilbert's syndrome or haemolysis) presents with normal urine and stool colour and completely normal ALP, GGT, and ALT.
Bilirubin, ALP, GGT, and ALT are all above their reference intervals, excluding a normal liver profile.
f: Acute viral hepatitis A presenting with prodromal nausea, ALT 1,850 IU/L, and ALP 135 IU/L
Decompensated cirrhosis with serum albumin 21 g/L and INR 2.4
Asymptomatic 22-year-old fasting with bilirubin 42 µmol/L (unconjugated) and normal ALT, ALP, and GGT
Routine health check showing bilirubin 11 µmol/L, ALP 68 IU/L, GGT 24 IU/L, and ALT 22 IU/L

hq_q.s:
A 22-year-old male medical student presents to his GP after noticing mild yellowing of his sclerae while recovering from a 3-day coryzal illness during which he ate very little. His urine and stool colour are normal, and he feels well.
Examination reveals mild scleral icterus, no pallor, and a soft abdomen with no hepatosplenomegaly.
o: Advise strict lifelong avoidance of dietary fat
Reassure him that this is a benign inherited condition requiring no treatment
hq_q.w: Gilbert's syndrome is an autosomal recessive UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1) promoter polymorphism affecting ~5% of the population. It causes mild, transient unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia triggered by fasting or intercurrent viral illness, with normal liver enzymes and normal reticulocytes; only reassurance is needed.
hq_q.f: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with anaemia, reticulocytosis (8%), raised LDH, and low haptoglobin -> haemolytic anaemia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: recovering from a 3-day coryzal illness during which he ate very little
tm.m: Reduced hepatic UGT1A1 activity (~30% of normal) impairs bilirubin glucuronidation, producing mild unconjugated jaundice during caloric deprivation or viral illness without liver injury or haemolysis.
tm.g: Mild isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia triggered by fasting/illness with normal LFTs and reticulocytes -> Reassure him that this is a benign inherited condition requiring no treatment
x: Caloric restriction and fasting precipitate unconjugated bilirubin rises in Gilbert's syndrome, whereas dietary fat restriction is for biliary colic.
MRCP evaluates extrahepatic and intrahepatic biliary ductal obstruction, which causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and raised ALP.
Liver biopsy is invasive and unnecessary in Gilbert's syndrome, where hepatic histology is completely normal.
Hepatobiliary ultrasound is unnecessary when hyperbilirubinaemia is strictly unconjugated and transaminases and alkaline phosphatase are normal.
f: Symptomatic gallstone biliary colic triggered by fatty meals while awaiting elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Suspected choledocholithiasis or primary sclerosing cholangitis with conjugated jaundice and ALP of 440 IU/L
Unexplained chronic transaminitis (ALT 280 IU/L) with negative viral, metabolic, and autoimmune liver screens
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (bilirubin 85 µmol/L) with ALP 390 IU/L and dark urine

hq_q.s:
A 52-year-old man with heavy alcohol intake is reviewed on the surgical ward 40 hours after admission with acute epigastric pain radiating to his back and vomiting.
Temperature is 38.1°C, heart rate is 108 bpm, blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg, and respiratory rate is 20 breaths/min. His repeat blood results at 40 hours are shown.
o: Mild pancreatitis (1 modified Glasgow criterion met)
Mild pancreatitis (2 modified Glasgow criteria met)
Score cannot be calculated unless serum amylase exceeds 3,000 IU/L
Score cannot be calculated without contrast CT pancreatography
Severe pancreatitis (3 modified Glasgow criteria met)
hq_q.w: The modified Glasgow (Imrie) score assesses acute pancreatitis severity within 48 hours using PANCREAS criteria: PaO2 <8 kPa, Age >55 years, Neutrophils/WCC >15 x 10^9/L, Calcium <2.0 mmol/L, Renal urea >16 mmol/L, Enzymes (LDH >600 or AST >200), Albumin <32 g/L, Sugar (glucose) >10 mmol/L. Here WCC (17.2), Urea (18.0), and Calcium (1.86) meet 3 criteria, predicting severe pancreatitis.
hq_q.f: Modified Glasgow score of 0, 1, or 2 criteria within 48 hours -> predicted mild acute pancreatitis.
hq_q.ql: Which severity classification is indicated by his modified Glasgow score?

c: 40 hours after admission with acute epigastric pain
tm.m: Systemic retroperitoneal inflammation and fat saponification cause leucocytosis (>15), prerenal/inflammatory uraemia (>16), and hypocalcaemia (<2.0); meeting >=3 modified Glasgow criteria predicts severe organ dysfunction.
tm.g: WCC >15, Urea >16, and Calcium <2.0 within 48 hours (3 modified Glasgow criteria) -> Severe pancreatitis (3 modified Glasgow criteria met)
x: Three criteria are met (WCC 17.2 >15, Urea 18.0 >16, Calcium 1.86 <2.0), not 1 criterion.
All three of WCC >15, Urea >16, and Calcium <2.0 are positive, reaching the >=3 threshold for severe pancreatitis.
Serum amylase is diagnostic for acute pancreatitis but forms no part of the modified Glasgow severity score.
The modified Glasgow score is a purely clinical and biochemical prognostic score calculated within 48 hours without requiring CT imaging.
f: Acute pancreatitis in a 45-year-old with WCC 16.5 x 10^9/L but normal urea (6.2), calcium (2.34), PaO2, albumin, and glucose
Acute pancreatitis in a 45-year-old with WCC 16.8 x 10^9/L and urea 17.4 mmol/L, but normal calcium (2.30) and normal remaining parameters
Diagnostic biochemical threshold where lipase or amylase >3 times the upper limit of normal confirms acute pancreatitis
Assessment of local pancreatic necrosis using the Balthazar CT severity index at 72 hours

hq_q.s: A 72 year old man with severe COPD is admitted to the Medical Assessment Unit with an acute infective exacerbation. Over the first hour he has received nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium driven by compressed air, oral prednisolone 30 mg, oral amoxicillin and controlled oxygen via a 28% Venturi mask. One hour later he remains alert and cooperative, with a respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min and SpO2 of 89%. His repeat arterial blood gas on 28% oxygen is shown.
o: Give an intravenous loading dose of aminophylline
Increase oxygen to 15 L/min via a non-rebreathe reservoir mask
Repeat the arterial blood gas in 4 hours without changing treatment
hq_q.w: His repeat arterial blood gas after 1 hour of optimal medical therapy and controlled 28% Venturi oxygen shows persistent decompensated hypercapnic (type 2) respiratory acidosis (pH 7.27 [<7.35], PaCO2 8.2 kPa [>6.5 kPa]). Under NICE NG115 and BTS guidelines, any patient with an acute COPD exacerbation who remains acidotic (pH 7.25 to 7.35 and PaCO2 >6.5 kPa) after 1 hour of bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids and controlled oxygen (targeting SpO2 88% to 92%) should be started immediately on non-invasive bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation (BiPAP), alongside documenting a clear ceiling-of-care escalation plan.
hq_q.f: pH 7.38 with a high bicarbonate → chronic compensated, continue controlled oxygen.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in his management?

c: controlled oxygen via a 28% Venturi mask
One hour later he remains alert
respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min and SpO2 of 89%
tm.m: Persistent hypercapnic acidosis (pH <7.35, PaCO2 >6.5 kPa) after 1 h of medical treatment -> BiPAP inspiratory pressure support unloads fatigued respiratory muscles and blows off CO2
tm.g: Decompensated type 2 respiratory failure in COPD (pH 7.25-7.35, PaCO2 >6.5 kPa) after 1 hour of optimal medical therapy = start non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP)
x: Intravenous aminophylline does not improve alveolar ventilation or reverse respiratory acidosis and carries high arrhythmia toxicity
His SpO2 of 89% is squarely within the target 88% to 92% range; giving 15 L/min oxygen will worsen hypercapnia and precipitate coma
In an alert, cooperative patient with pH 7.27, non-invasive BiPAP is the standard of care and avoids the barotrauma and weaning difficulties of invasive intubation
Leaving a decompensated respiratory acidosis (pH 7.27) untreated for 4 hours risks respiratory muscle exhaustion and cardiac arrest
f: severe acute asthma in HDU refractory to nebulised bronchodilators and IV magnesium sulfate
acute type 1 respiratory failure from massive pulmonary embolism or pneumothorax in a patient without chronic CO2 retention
patient in respiratory arrest, apnoea or profound coma (GCS 5/15) who cannot protect their airway
repeat arterial blood gas at 1 hour showing complete resolution of acidosis with pH 7.38, PaCO2 6.1 kPa and PaO2 8.2 kPa

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old woman presents to the emergency department 6 hours after ingesting 50 aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) 300 mg tablets. She complains of loud ringing in her ears, sweating, nausea, and breathlessness.
Respiratory rate is 30 breaths/min and pulse rate is 114 bpm. Arterial blood gas on air shows pH 7.44, PaCO2 2.9 kPa, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L, and anion gap 24 mmol/L.
o: Acute respiratory alkalosis without metabolic acidosis
Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis
Normal acid-base status on arterial blood gas
hq_q.w: Salicylates directly stimulate the medullary respiratory centre (causing primary respiratory alkalosis with low PaCO2) and uncouple oxidative phosphorylation (causing high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with low bicarbonate). A near-normal pH with both abnormalities confirms a mixed disorder.
hq_q.f: pH 7.52 with low CO2 and normal bicarbonate → acute respiratory alkalosis alone.
hq_q.ql: Which best describes the blood gas?

tm.m: Salicylate directly stimulates medullary ventilation (respiratory alkalosis) and uncouples mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis)
tm.g: Salicylate overdose with low PaCO2, low HCO3-, raised anion gap and near-normal pH -> mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis
f: acute anxiety hyperventilation with pH 7.54, PaCO2 3.1 kPa and bicarbonate 24 mmol/L
diabetic ketoacidosis with pH 7.18, PaCO2 2.8 kPa and bicarbonate 8 mmol/L
persistent pyloric vomiting with pH 7.49, bicarbonate 36 mmol/L and PaCO2 6.4 kPa
pH 7.40, PaCO2 5.3 kPa, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L and anion gap 10 mmol/L
x: Pure acute respiratory alkalosis would not lower serum bicarbonate to 14 mmol/L or raise the anion gap to 24 mmol/L.
Physiological respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis never brings the arterial pH back into the alkaline half of normal (7.44).
Metabolic alkalosis is characterised by an elevated serum bicarbonate (>26 mmol/L) and compensatory hypoventilation (raised PaCO2).
Although the pH is 7.44, a PaCO2 of 2.9 kPa, bicarbonate of 14 mmol/L, and anion gap of 24 mmol/L represent severe opposing acid-base derangements.

hq_q.s: A 68 year old man with a 45 pack-year smoking history presents to the Respiratory Clinic with a 6-week history of progressive breathlessness and a 4 kg weight loss. Chest radiograph demonstrates a moderate right-sided pleural effusion, and an ultrasound-guided diagnostic thoracentesis is performed. Paired pleural fluid and serum biochemistry results are shown.
hq_q.w: Here the pleural fluid protein is 28 g/L (borderline 25 to 35 g/L), so Light's criteria must be applied. An effusion is an exudate if ANY ONE of the three criteria is positive: (1) pleural-to-serum protein ratio >0.5 (here 28/62 = 0.45, negative); (2) pleural-to-serum LDH ratio >0.6 (here 240/200 = 1.20, strongly positive); or (3) pleural LDH >2/3 of the laboratory upper limit of normal for serum LDH (here 240 > 2/3 of 220). Because the LDH ratio is 1.20 (>0.6), this fluid is definitively an exudate, reflecting high local pleural cell turnover (such as pleural malignancy) despite a protein ratio <0.5.
hq_q.f: Pleural protein 18 with LDH 90 → transudate, as in heart failure.
hq_q.ql: Applying Light's criteria to these results, how is the pleural fluid best classified?

c: 6-week history of progressive breathlessness and a 4 kg weight loss
tm.m: High local malignant/inflammatory pleural LDH release -> pleural/serum LDH ratio = 240/200 = 1.2 (>0.6 threshold) -> satisfies Light's criteria for an exudate despite pleural protein of 28 g/L
tm.g: Light's criteria: only ONE of the three ratios needs to be positive (protein ratio >0.5 OR LDH ratio >0.6 OR pleural LDH >2/3 serum ULN) to classify as an exudate
x: Requires milky fluid with pleural fluid triglycerides >1.24 mmol/L
Requires frank pus or infected acidic fluid (pH <7.20) in a febrile patient with pleural sepsis
Requires heavily blood-stained fluid with pleural fluid haematocrit >50% of peripheral blood haematocrit
To classify an effusion as a transudate, ALL THREE of Light's criteria must be negative
f: milky pleural fluid after thoracic duct injury with pleural triglycerides of 4.1 mmol/L
aspirate of frank malodorous pus with pH 6.95 in a patient with swinging fever
bloody pleural fluid after blunt chest trauma with pleural haematocrit 25% and blood haematocrit 42%
pleural protein 22 g/L (serum 68 g/L, ratio 0.32) and pleural LDH 80 IU/L (serum 200 IU/L, ratio 0.40) in left ventricular failure

hq_q.s: A 56 year old man was admitted 6 days ago with right lower lobe community-acquired pneumonia and has remained febrile (38.5°C) with elevated C-reactive protein despite intravenous co-amoxiclav. Bedside thoracic ultrasound demonstrates a moderate right pleural effusion with fine echogenic strands. Ultrasound-guided diagnostic pleural aspiration yields cloudy straw-coloured fluid (not frank pus), and laboratory analysis of the pleural fluid is shown.
o: Continue oral antibiotics alone for a further 7 days
Insert an ultrasound-guided small-bore intercostal chest drain
Instil intrapleural sterile talc slurry for pleurodesis
Perform a single therapeutic aspiration and discharge home
Repeat the thoracic ultrasound scan in 2 weeks
hq_q.w: Even when a parapneumonic pleural aspirate is not frankly purulent, a pleural fluid pH below 7.20 (here pH 7.08, accompanied by low glucose of 1.5 mmol/L and high LDH) defines a complicated parapneumonic effusion. Under British Thoracic Society guidelines, any parapneumonic effusion with a pleural fluid pH <7.20 will not resolve with antibiotics alone and requires prompt insertion of an ultrasound-guided small-bore (12 to 14 Fr) intercostal chest drain alongside continued intravenous antibiotics to prevent progression to a multiloculated fibropurulent empyema.
hq_q.f: pH 7.40 with clear fluid → simple effusion, antibiotics alone.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in his management?

tm.m: Bacterial and neutrophil metabolism in pleural space acidifies fluid (pH <7.20) and activates coagulation cascade (echogenic fibrin strands) -> requires ultrasound-guided intercostal chest drain
tm.g: Non-purulent parapneumonic effusion with pleural fluid pH <7.20 = complicated parapneumonic effusion -> insert ultrasound-guided intercostal chest drain
x: Antibiotics alone fail when pleural fluid pH has dropped below 7.20 because fibrin loculations wall off the infected space
Talc pleurodesis is used for malignant effusions and is contraindicated in acute pleural infection
A single aspiration leaves behind re-accumulating acidic fibrinous fluid; continuous intercostal tube drainage is required
Waiting 2 weeks allows an early fibrinopurulent collection to organise into a thick fibrous cortex requiring surgical thoracotomy/decortication
f: uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion measuring <2 cm with clear fluid and pleural pH 7.38
recurrent malignant pleural effusion from metastatic breast cancer after complete lung re-expansion
palliative symptom relief for a frail patient with a malignant effusion and trapped lung
tiny (<1 cm) resolving simple parapneumonic effusion in an afebrile patient whose CRP has normalised

hq_q.s:
A 36 year old man with bipolar I disorder takes modified-release lithium carbonate 800 mg at 22:00 every night. He attends an afternoon GP appointment at 14:00 the next day feeling completely well with no tremor, nausea, or polyuria.
Blood drawn during that 14:00 appointment returns a serum lithium level of 1.3 mmol/L with normal eGFR (>90 mL/min).
o: Admit for 24 hours of IV fluids
Halve the dose to 400 mg nightly
hq_q.w: Lithium reference ranges (0.4-1.0 mmol/L) apply strictly to blood samples taken 12 hours post-dose. In an asymptomatic patient with normal renal function and a mistimed 16-hour sample, repeat a correctly timed 12-hour level first.
hq_q.f: Timed 12-hour level of 1.6 with tremor and vomiting → stop lithium and admit.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Lithium reference intervals are valid only at 12 hours post-dose; clinical stability and normal renal function warrant a properly timed repeat level
tm.g: Asymptomatic patient with mistimed lithium blood sample -> repeat a properly timed 12-hour post-dose level
f: coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria and dehydration with a 12-hour lithium level of 2.2 mmol/L
obtundation, myoclonus and acute kidney injury with a serum lithium of 4.1 mmol/L
a confirmed 12-hour lithium level of 1.3 mmol/L in a patient whose dose was recently doubled
a confirmed 12-hour level of 1.9 mmol/L accompanied by coarse tremor, diarrhoea and slurred speech
x: Hospital admission for intravenous saline is indicated for symptomatic lithium toxicity or renal impairment, whereas he is completely well with normal eGFR.
Emergency haemodialysis is reserved for severe neurotoxicity (seizures, coma) or lithium levels >4.0 mmol/L.
Halving his maintenance lithium dose on the basis of an untimed sample risks precipitating a manic relapse.
Stopping lithium immediately in a completely asymptomatic man with normal renal function before verifying a 12-hour level risks rebound mania.

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman presents to the emergency department with nausea and right upper quadrant discomfort after taking supratherapeutic doses of paracetamol (approximately sixteen 500 mg tablets daily, 8 g/day) over the past 3 days for severe dental pain.
Plasma paracetamol concentration is 18 mg/L, serum ALT is 450 U/L, and INR is 1.6.
o: Discharge as the level is low
Plot the level on the nomogram
hq_q.w: In a staggered paracetamol overdose over days, the treatment nomogram cannot be used and a low paracetamol level does not exclude poisoning. Anyone with a staggered overdose or hepatotoxicity (ALT 450 U/L, INR 1.6) must start IV acetylcysteine immediately.
hq_q.f: Single overdose with a known time 4 hours ago → plot the level on the nomogram.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Cumulative supratherapeutic paracetamol depletes hepatic glutathione and causes centrilobular necrosis even after plasma drug levels fall
tm.g: Staggered paracetamol overdose or raised ALT/INR regardless of low plasma paracetamol level -> start IV acetylcysteine immediately
f: presenting 30 minutes after swallowing a single acute overdose of 20 paracetamol tablets
a single acute ingestion 4 hours ago with a level below the line and normal ALT and INR
a single acute overdose taken at one known timepoint 4 hours before blood sampling
never appropriate in a staggered overdose with established transaminitis and coagulopathy
x: Activated charcoal is only beneficial within 1 hour of a single acute overdose and has no role after 3 days of staggered ingestion.
A low plasma paracetamol level (18 mg/L) does not exclude life-threatening hepatotoxicity after staggered ingestion, and her ALT (450 U/L) and INR (1.6) already show liver injury.
The paracetamol treatment nomogram is strictly invalid whenever ingestion occurred over more than 1 hour.
Waiting a further 4 hours to repeat the level delays life-saving antidote therapy when acute hepatotoxicity is already present.

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old man with a 30 year history of heavy alcohol dependence was admitted 2 months ago with acute confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia (Wernicke's encephalopathy) after delayed presentation. He is now fully alert and oriented to person, but cannot recall what he ate 10 minutes ago and earnestly describes walking his dog this morning despite being on the ward.
Serum ammonia is 32 µmol/L (normal) and there is no asterixis.
hq_q.w: Korsakoff's syndrome is the chronic, often irreversible amnestic sequela of untreated or late-treated Wernicke's encephalopathy (thiamine/vitamin B1 deficiency). Damage to the mammillary bodies and anterior thalamic nuclei produces profound anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation in an alert, clear sensorium.
hq_q.f: Confusion, ataxia and eye movement problems → Wernicke's, IV Pabrinex now.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: cannot recall what he ate 10 minutes ago
tm.m: Haemorrhagic necrosis of the mammillary bodies and mediodorsal/anterior thalamic nuclei permanently disrupts episodic memory encoding
tm.g: Profound anterograde amnesia and confabulation in a clear sensorium after Wernicke's encephalopathy -> Korsakoff's syndrome
f: gradual decline in memory, word-finding and praxis over 4 years in a non-drinker
acute agitation, visual hallucinations, tachycardia and coarse tremor 3 days after stopping alcohol
drowsiness, asterixis, ascites and a raised venous ammonia of 145 µmol/L
acute global confusion, horizontal nystagmus, sixth nerve palsy and wide-based ataxia
x: Alzheimer's disease progresses insidiously over years across multiple cortical domains (language, praxis, visuospatial function) rather than following acute Wernicke's encephalopathy.
Delirium tremens occurs 48 to 72 hours after alcohol cessation with acute agitation, autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, and clouding of consciousness.
Hepatic encephalopathy causes fluctuating drowsiness, asterixis (flapping tremor), and raised blood ammonia, whereas he is alert with normal ammonia.
Acute Wernicke's encephalopathy is the reversible acute triad of global confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, and ataxia; he is now alert with chronic amnesia.

hq_q.s: A 19 year old student has had a headache, fever and neck stiffness for 12 hours. A lumbar puncture is done after CT head. She has no drug allergies and is not immunocompromised.
hq_q.w: Bacterial meningitis in a young adult is usually meningococcal or pneumococcal. Give IV ceftriaxone without delay, with IV dexamethasone (NICE) to reduce hearing loss and neurological damage. Amoxicillin is added for Listeria over 60 or with immunosuppression.
hq_q.f: Same CSF in a 70 year old → add amoxicillin to cover Listeria.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Steroids damp the inflammatory burst when the bacteria are killed
tm.g: Bacterial meningitis: ceftriaxone plus dexamethasone
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to IV aciclovir (Aciclovir is for viral encephalitis; neutrophils and a low glucose mean bacteria)

the presentation instead showed features specific to IV ceftriaxone and amoxicillin (Amoxicillin covers Listeria, which matters over 60, in pregnancy or with immunosuppression; at 19 the addition is dexamethasone)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV vancomycin (Vancomycin is added for suspected penicillin-resistant pneumococcus, for example after travel; on its own it misses meningococcus)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral ciprofloxacin (Oral ciprofloxacin is prophylaxis for close contacts, not treatment)
x: Aciclovir is for viral encephalitis; neutrophils and a low glucose mean bacteria.
Amoxicillin covers Listeria, which matters over 60, in pregnancy or with immunosuppression; at 19 the addition is dexamethasone.
Vancomycin is added for suspected penicillin-resistant pneumococcus, for example after travel; on its own it misses meningococcus.
Oral ciprofloxacin is prophylaxis for close contacts, not treatment.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man who arrived from Somalia a year ago has had a headache, weight loss and fevers for 3 weeks. He now has double vision. TB meningitis is diagnosed.
There is a right sixth nerve palsy and neck stiffness.
hq_q.w: TB meningitis is treated with four drugs (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol) for 2 months, then rifampicin and isoniazid to complete 12 months, with dexamethasone, which reduces death and disability.
hq_q.f: Lymphocytic CSF with a very high opening pressure in advanced HIV and a positive CSF antigen → cryptococcal meningitis; amphotericin and flucytosine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

c: weight loss and fevers for 3 weeks
tm.m: A thick basal exudate traps cranial nerves and blocks CSF flow; steroids reduce it
tm.g: TB meningitis: four drugs for 12 months plus steroids
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amphotericin and flucytosine (This treats cryptococcal meningitis, usually in advanced HIV with a very high opening pressure)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Isoniazid and rifampicin (Two drugs are the continuation phase; treatment starts with four drugs plus steroids)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV ceftriaxone and aciclovir (This covers bacterial meningitis and herpes encephalitis, not a 3-week lymphocytic TB meningitis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin (This is for bacterial meningitis with resistant pneumococcus; the CSF here is lymphocytic with a 3-week history)
x: This treats cryptococcal meningitis, usually in advanced HIV with a very high opening pressure.
Two drugs are the continuation phase; treatment starts with four drugs plus steroids.
This covers bacterial meningitis and herpes encephalitis, not a 3-week lymphocytic TB meningitis.
This is for bacterial meningitis with resistant pneumococcus; the CSF here is lymphocytic with a 3-week history.

hq_q.s: A 46 year old woman had a sudden severe headache 14 hours ago. CT head is normal. A lumbar puncture is done.
hq_q.w: Blood that does not clear between tubes, with yellow bilirubin pigment formed over 12 hours, means bleeding before the needle went in.
hq_q.f: Red cells falling from 3,200 to 40 with no xanthochromia → traumatic tap.
hq_q.ql: What do these results show?

tm.m: Red cells broken down in the CSF over hours make bilirubin, which turns it yellow
tm.g: Xanthochromia 12 hours after onset confirms subarachnoid blood
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Bacterial meningitis (White cells are normal)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Normal (Thousands of red cells and xanthochromia are not normal)
red cells falling to 40 in tube 3 with no xanthochromia
the presentation instead showed features specific to Viral meningitis (White cells are normal and there is blood)
x: White cells are normal
Thousands of red cells and xanthochromia are not normal
Counts would fall across the tubes, with no xanthochromia
White cells are normal and there is blood

hq_q.s:
A 30 year old woman presents to her GP with a 10-month history of abdominal bloating, pale loose stools and lethargy. She has a history of recurrent sinopulmonary infections since childhood and eats wheat bread and pasta every day.
Pulse rate 80 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg. Abdominal examination is normal. Initial blood tests return.
o: Instruct her to double her gluten intake for 6 weeks
Reassure her that coeliac disease has been excluded
Repeat serum IgA tissue transglutaminase in 6 months
Request IgG-based coeliac serology (IgG tTG or IgG DGP)
hq_q.w: Selective IgA deficiency (total serum IgA <0.07 g/L, here <0.05 g/L, explaining her recurrent sinopulmonary infections) is 10 to 15 times more common in patients with coeliac disease and renders all IgA-based serological tests (IgA tTG and IgA EMA) falsely negative. NICE recommends testing with IgG deamidated gliadin peptide (IgG DGP), IgG tTG or IgG EMA (and referring for duodenal biopsy).
hq_q.f: Normal total IgA with a negative tTG → coeliac is unlikely.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step to investigate her suspected coeliac disease?

c: eats wheat bread and pasta every day
tm.m: Patients with selective IgA deficiency lack IgA-secreting plasma cells, so they cannot mount an IgA anti-tTG response despite florid gluten-induced villous atrophy; they produce IgG autoantibodies instead.
tm.g: Negative IgA tTG with undetectable total IgA (<0.05 g/L) -> request IgG-based coeliac serology (IgG tTG / IgG DGP / IgG EMA)
x: She already eats wheat bread and pasta daily; her negative IgA tTG is caused by selective IgA deficiency (<0.05 g/L), not insufficient gluten intake.
Faecal calprotectin investigates inflammatory bowel disease and does not address her unassessed coeliac disease and iron deficiency (ferritin 7 µg/L).
A negative IgA tTG is invalid when total serum IgA is <0.05 g/L and must never be used to exclude coeliac disease.
Selective IgA deficiency is a permanent primary immunodeficiency, so repeating IgA tTG in 6 months will remain falsely negative.
f: her total serum IgA was normal (2.1 g/L) but she had been avoiding gluten prior to the blood test
her total IgA was normal (2.1 g/L) with a valid negative IgA tTG and normal ferritin, and IBD needed exclusion
she had a negative IgA tTG accompanied by a normal total serum IgA concentration (1.8 g/L) while eating gluten daily
a child with type 1 diabetes and normal total IgA was undergoing scheduled surveillance screening

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old man with acute severe ulcerative colitis has had IV hydrocortisone for 3 days. He still has 8 bloody stools a day.
Temperature 37.6°C, pulse rate 98 bpm. The abdomen is soft and not distended. Abdominal X-ray shows no colonic dilatation.
hq_q.w: If acute severe colitis has not responded after about 3 days of IV steroids (for example more than 8 stools a day, or 3 to 8 with a CRP over 45), rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin is offered, with the surgeons involved. Colectomy follows if rescue fails.
hq_q.f: Same patient with a 7 cm transverse colon on X-ray and peritonism → toxic megacolon; emergency colectomy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Steroid-refractory inflammation needs a different, fast-acting immunosuppressant
tm.g: Day 3 of IV steroids and still severe: rescue therapy
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Continue steroids for 7 more days (Waiting another week risks perforation; the day 3 review decides on rescue)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Emergency colectomy today (Surgery is for failed rescue, toxic megacolon or perforation; he has none yet)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Start azathioprine (Azathioprine takes months to work and is for maintenance)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Switch to oral prednisolone (Stepping down to oral steroids while he is still severe is unsafe)
x: Waiting another week risks perforation; the day 3 review decides on rescue.
Surgery is for failed rescue, toxic megacolon or perforation; he has none yet.
Azathioprine takes months to work and is for maintenance.
Stepping down to oral steroids while he is still severe is unsafe.

hq_q.s:
A 62 year old man presents to his GP with a 3-week history of symmetrical aching and stiffness in his thighs and shoulders. Two months ago he was started on atorvastatin 80 mg once daily following a myocardial infarction.
Examination shows mild proximal quadriceps tenderness with normal 5/5 power and normal pale yellow urine.
o: Stop the statin and recheck CK
hq_q.w: When a patient on a statin develops muscle pain and creatine kinase exceeds 5 times the upper limit of normal (here 4,200 IU/L), stop the statin immediately and recheck CK before considering a lower-dose rechallenge.
hq_q.f: Mild muscle aching on atorvastatin 80 mg with a normal creatine kinase (<5x ULN) -> reassure, or briefly pause and rechallenge at a lower dose.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: symmetrical aching and stiffness in his thighs
tm.m: Marked elevation of serum creatine kinase (>5x ULN) indicates active sarcolemmal myonecrosis that can progress to myoglobinuric rhabdomyolysis if the statin is continued.
tm.g: Statin-associated muscle symptoms with CK >5x upper limit of normal (4,200 IU/L) -> stop the statin and recheck CK
x: Coenzyme Q10 is not recommended by NICE and continuing atorvastatin 80 mg with a CK of 4,200 IU/L risks severe rhabdomyolysis.
Continuing atorvastatin for 6 weeks when CK is >20 times the upper limit of normal carries a high risk of acute rhabdomyolysis and renal failure.
Dose reduction alone is unsafe while CK is 4,200 IU/L; the statin must be stopped completely until symptoms resolve and CK normalises.
Simvastatin 80 mg carries the highest myopathy risk of all statins (MHRA warning) and no statin should be started until CK has returned to normal.
f: never recommended; atorvastatin must be stopped immediately when CK exceeds 5 times the upper limit of normal
asymptomatic mild CK elevation (<5x ULN) after strenuous gym exercise
restarting a lower dose of statin several weeks later AFTER symptoms have resolved and CK has normalised
never appropriate; simvastatin 80 mg is avoided due to high myopathy risk

hq_q.s: A 34 year old man attends his GP after requesting a fasting lipid profile because his father suffered a fatal myocardial infarction aged 44. He is asymptomatic, exercises regularly, never smoked and has a BMI of 22 kg/m2. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 64 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg. Examination reveals firm, nodular thickening of both Achilles tendons and xanthelasmata around the eyelids.
o: Prescribe oral omega-3 fatty acid supplements
Provide dietary advice and repeat lipids in 1 year
Refer to a specialist lipid clinic
Start atorvastatin 20 mg daily without referral
hq_q.w: Under NICE CG71, an adult with total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L or LDL >4.9 mmol/L plus tendon xanthomata and premature family coronary disease meets Simon Broome criteria for familial hypercholesterolaemia and requires specialist lipid clinic referral for DNA and cascade testing.
hq_q.f: Total cholesterol 6.2 mmol/L without tendon xanthomata or family history of premature CHD -> calculate 10-year QRISK3 score.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

c: father suffered a fatal myocardial infarction aged 44
nodular thickening of both Achilles tendons
tm.m: Specialist lipid clinics confirm monogenic LDLR/APOB/PCSK9 mutations, titrate high-intensity statin/ezetimibe/PCSK9i therapy and perform cascade testing of relatives
tm.g: Total cholesterol > 7.5 mmol/L (or LDL > 4.9 mmol/L) with tendon xanthomata / premature family CHD: refer to specialist lipid clinic (do not use QRISK3)
x: NICE CG71 explicitly states that standard cardiovascular risk calculators such as QRISK3 must not be used in suspected familial hypercholesterolaemia because they severely underestimate lifelong risk.
Omega-3 fatty acids do not lower LDL cholesterol and are explicitly not recommended by NICE for primary cardiovascular disease prevention.
Delaying specialist referral and high-intensity statin therapy leaves him exposed to very high risk of premature coronary artery disease.
Although high-intensity statin therapy is indicated, failure to refer to a specialist lipid clinic misses DNA confirmation and cascade testing of first-degree relatives.
f: A 52 year old man with no family history or tendon xanthomata has a routine total cholesterol of 6.1 mmol/L.
This option is not recommended by NICE for familial hypercholesterolaemia or primary CVD prevention.
He has borderline elevated total cholesterol of 5.4 mmol/L with normal LDL, no family history and a QRISK3 score of 4%.
Primary prevention is initiated for polygenic hypercholesterolaemia with a QRISK3 score of 13% and total cholesterol 6.2 mmol/L.

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old woman has a hot, swollen right knee for 2 days. She is otherwise well.
Knee X-ray shows a line of calcium in the cartilage. Aspirate shows weakly positively birefringent rhomboid crystals and no organisms.
hq_q.w: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals, pseudogout, are linked to hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis, hypothyroidism and low magnesium. Here calcium and PTH are both high.
hq_q.f: Transferrin saturation 70% and high ferritin → haemochromatosis.
hq_q.ql: Which underlying condition explains her results?

tm.m: High calcium favours calcium pyrophosphate crystals forming in cartilage
tm.g: Pseudogout with high calcium and PTH is primary hyperparathyroidism
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Gout (Needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals)
a transferrin saturation of 70% with a high ferritin
the presentation instead showed features specific to Rheumatoid arthritis (Symmetrical small joint disease without crystals)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Septic arthritis (No organisms, and the crystals explain it)
x: Needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals
Iron studies are normal
Symmetrical small joint disease without crystals
No organisms, and the crystals explain it

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man with type 2 diabetes treated with modified-release metformin 1 g twice daily attends his GP surgery to discuss his annual renal screening results. He feels well and has no peripheral oedema or urinary symptoms. His clinic blood pressure is 138/84 mmHg. An early-morning urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio was 7.6 mg/mmol 2 months ago and a repeat sample this week is 8.0 mg/mmol (<3.0). His serum creatinine and eGFR results are shown.
o: Add dapagliflozin alone without starting an ACE inhibitor
Refer urgently to the hospital nephrology clinic
Repeat the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio in 12 months
Start an ACE inhibitor (such as ramipril) and titrate to the maximum tolerated dose
Stop metformin immediately due to early diabetic nephropathy
hq_q.w: Confirmed persistent microalbuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio >=3.0 mg/mmol on two early-morning samples) in a patient with type 1 or type 2 diabetes defines diabetic nephropathy (CKD G2 A2). Under NICE NG28 and NG203 guidelines, first-line renoprotective therapy is an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) titrated to the highest licensed dose that the patient can tolerate, regardless of whether blood pressure is below 140/90 mmHg. Once the ACE inhibitor/ARB is titrated to maximum tolerated dose, an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin) is added.
hq_q.f: ACR 80 with eGFR falling fast → nephrology referral.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step in his management?

c: repeat sample this week is 8.0 mg/mmol
tm.m: Confirmed diabetic albuminuria (ACR >=3 mg/mmol) -> angiotensin II blockade dilates the efferent arteriole and lowers intraglomerular pressure -> start and titrate ACEi/ARB first
tm.g: Confirmed urine ACR >=3 mg/mmol in diabetes = start an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) first and titrate to maximum tolerated dose (then add SGLT2 inhibitor)
x: Under NICE NG203/NG28, an SGLT2 inhibitor is added alongside (not instead of) a maximally titrated ACE inhibitor or ARB in diabetic proteinuric CKD
Specialist nephrology referral is required for ACR >=70 mg/mmol (unless caused by diabetes and already treated), ACR >=30 mg/mmol with haematuria, or a sustained eGFR drop >=25%
Microalbuminuria has already been confirmed on two consecutive early-morning samples, so treatment must not be delayed for another year
With an eGFR of 72 mL/min/1.73 m2, metformin remains safe and beneficial; it is only stopped when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2
f: patient with type 2 diabetes and urine ACR 12 mg/mmol who is already taking the maximum tolerated dose of ramipril 10 mg daily
rapidly declining renal function (eGFR dropping from 72 to 44 mL/min/1.73 m2 over 6 months) with dysmorphic haematuria and ACR 85 mg/mmol
annual screening when both early-morning urine ACR readings are normal at 1.1 mg/mmol
progression of chronic kidney disease where eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 (dose reduced below 45 mL/min/1.73 m2)

hq_q.s: A 56 year old woman collapses at home with sudden severe breathlessness and is brought to the Emergency Department resuscitation room. Urgent CT pulmonary angiography shows a large saddle pulmonary embolus straddling the main pulmonary artery bifurcation. Despite a 500 mL crystalloid bolus, her pulse is 128 bpm, blood pressure is 78/42 mmHg, SpO2 is 88% on 15 L/min oxygen and bedside echocardiography shows a severely dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle compressing the left ventricle. She has no bleeding contraindications.
o: Insert an inferior vena cava filter
Start oral apixaban 10 mg twice daily
Start oral warfarin with low-molecular-weight heparin bridging
Start treatment-dose subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin and observe
hq_q.w: A pulmonary embolism causing persistent systemic arterial hypotension (systolic BP <90 mmHg for >15 minutes, here 78/42 mmHg) and obstructive right ventricular shock is a massive (high-risk) pulmonary embolism. Under NICE NG158 and ESC guidelines, immediate systemic intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase (r-tPA, 10 mg bolus followed by 90 mg over 2 hours, or 50 mg bolus in peri-arrest) plus unfractionated heparin is the first-line treatment to actively dissolve the saddle thrombus and relieve acute right ventricular outflow obstruction.
hq_q.f: Stable with a normal BP but a strained right ventricle → anticoagulation and close watch.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate life-saving treatment?

tm.m: Massive saddle PE -> acute RV outflow obstruction and interventricular septal shift -> obstructive cardiogenic shock (SBP <90 mmHg) -> immediate IV alteplase activates plasminogen to lyse clot
tm.g: Massive PE with haemodynamic shock (SBP <90 mmHg) = immediate systemic IV thrombolysis with alteplase
