x: An IVC filter does not relieve existing pulmonary artery obstruction and is reserved for VTE patients with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation
Oral apixaban is first-line for haemodynamically stable PE, not massive PE with shock
Warfarin takes days to achieve therapeutic anticoagulation and does not lyse an acute saddle embolus
Anticoagulation with LMWH alone prevents thrombus extension but does not rapidly recanalise the pulmonary trunk during haemodynamic collapse
f: proximal DVT in a patient who suffered an intracerebral haemorrhage 4 days ago
haemodynamically stable patient with a lobar PE, BP 130/80 mmHg and normal RV function
long-term maintenance anticoagulation for PE in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome
submassive (intermediate-risk) PE with mild RV strain on echo but preserved blood pressure of 124/76 mmHg

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man attends the Emergency Department after passing two black, tarry, foul-smelling stools over the past 24 hours. He has been taking oral ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for 3 weeks for knee osteoarthritis.
Pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98% breathing air. He is alert, haemodynamically stable after initial crystalloid fluid, and has melaena on rectal examination.
o: Immediate emergency theatre endoscopy within 1 hour
Inpatient endoscopy within 24 hours of admission
Outpatient upper GI endoscopy within 4 weeks
Urgent CT mesenteric angiogram within 2 hours
hq_q.w: This patient has acute non-variceal upper GI bleeding with a Glasgow-Blatchford score >0 (urea 12.2 mmol/L, haemoglobin 104 g/L, melaena) and is haemodynamically stable. NICE guidelines (CG141) recommend admitting all patients with a Blatchford score >0 and performing upper GI endoscopy within 24 hours of admission (whereas unstable patients undergo immediate endoscopy after resuscitation).
hq_q.f: Pulse 128 and BP 84/50 → resuscitate, then immediate endoscopy.
hq_q.ql: Within what timeframe should upper gastrointestinal endoscopy be performed?

tm.m: Digestion of intraluminal blood protein by gut bacteria and renal hypoperfusion elevate serum urea (12.2 mmol/L), yielding a high-risk Blatchford score requiring inpatient endoscopy within 24 hours.
tm.g: Haemodynamically stable acute upper GI bleed with Glasgow-Blatchford score >0 -> inpatient endoscopy within 24 hours
x: Immediate emergency endoscopy immediately after resuscitation is reserved for patients with severe acute upper GI bleeding who are haemodynamically unstable.
Discharging an acute melaena patient with Hb 104 g/L and urea 12.2 mmol/L for a 2-week-wait outpatient appointment risks fatal rebleeding at home.
Early discharge for outpatient endoscopy is safe only when the Glasgow-Blatchford score is 0 (normal Hb, normal urea, normal pulse/BP, no melaena).
Upper GI endoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic first line for melaena; CT angiography is used only if endoscopy fails to localise or control bleeding.
f: he presented with profuse fresh haematemesis and persistent haemodynamic instability (pulse 132 bpm, BP 78/46 mmHg)
he had no gastrointestinal bleeding or melaena, but presented to his GP with new dyspepsia and 5 kg weight loss
a 30 year old reported a single dark stool with Hb 148 g/L, urea 4.6 mmol/L, pulse 70 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg and no melaena on exam (GBS 0)
urgent upper GI endoscopy had failed to identify the bleeding source in a patient with ongoing brisk arterial bleeding

hq_q.s: A 46 year old man presents with recurrent epigastric pain, chronic watery diarrhoea and 5 kg weight loss. Repeated upper GI endoscopies have demonstrated multiple refractory peptic ulcers in the second part of the duodenum and proximal jejunum despite high-dose oral omeprazole. He takes no NSAIDs and Helicobacter pylori testing is negative. He underwent lithotripsy for calcium nephrolithiasis last year.
hq_q.w: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumour (gastrinoma) of the pancreas or duodenal wall. Autonomous hypergastrinaemia (fasting gastrin 1,200 ng/L) drives massive gastric acid hypersecretion, causing multiple refractory duodenal and post-bulbar/jejunal ulcers and steatorrhoea/diarrhoea (acid inactivates pancreatic lipase). Coexistent primary hyperparathyroidism (calcium 2.82 mmol/L, PTH 12.0 pmol/L) indicates MEN1.
hq_q.f: Single duodenal ulcer with positive H. pylori → eradication therapy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: proximal jejunum despite high-dose oral omeprazole
tm.m: Autonomous tumour gastrin secretion stimulates parietal cell HCl output and enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia, overwhelming duodenal bicarbonate buffering and inactivating pancreatic enzymes.
tm.g: Multiple/jejunal refractory ulcers + watery diarrhoea + fasting gastrin >1,000 ng/L (+ MEN1 hyperparathyroidism) -> gastrinoma
x: Crohn's disease causes transmural skip lesions and strictures with raised faecal calprotectin, not fasting gastrin of 1,200 ng/L and primary hyperparathyroidism.
Helicobacter pylori causes solitary duodenal bulb or antral ulcers and is excluded here by negative testing and a gastrin level >10 times normal.
Coeliac disease causes duodenal villous atrophy and malabsorption rather than multiple deep post-bulbar peptic ulcers and massive hypergastrinaemia.
NSAIDs inhibit mucosal prostaglandin E2 synthesis, causing gastric or duodenal bulb ulcers with normal fasting gastrin levels.
f: enteroscopy showed skip ulceration and cobblestoning with non-caseating granulomas on biopsy and normal fasting gastrin
he had a solitary duodenal bulb ulcer with a normal serum calcium and a positive stool Helicobacter pylori antigen after stopping PPIs
duodenal biopsies showed persistent subtotal villous atrophy and clonal intraepithelial lymphocytes with no peptic ulceration
urinary salicylate/NSAID toxicology screening was positive in a patient with a solitary gastric antral ulcer and normal fasting gastrin

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man with a 45 pack-year smoking history presents with 5 days of confusion and headache. He takes no regular medications.
Pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 130/78 mmHg. He is clinically euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes and no oedema. Thyroid function and a short Synacthen test are normal.
CT thorax reveals a 4.5 cm central right hilar mass.
hq_q.w: Hypotonic hyponatraemia (sodium 121 mmol/L, serum osmolality 252 mOsm/kg) with concentrated urine (480 mOsm/kg) and natriuresis in a euvolaemic patient confirms SIADH. Ectopic ADH secretion from a central mass is classic for small cell lung carcinoma.
hq_q.f: High calcium with low PTH → squamous cell carcinoma making PTH-related peptide.
hq_q.ql: Which histological type of thoracic malignancy is most likely?

tm.m: Neuroendocrine small cell lung carcinoma cells ectopically secrete ADH (vasopressin), inserting aquaporin-2 channels in renal collecting ducts and retaining free water.
tm.g: Central lung mass + euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with high urine osmolality/sodium (SIADH) -> small cell lung carcinoma
x: Bronchial carcinoid tumours rarely cause SIADH, typically presenting in younger non-smokers with haemoptysis, lobar obstruction or serotonin-mediated flushing.
Adenocarcinoma typically arises in the lung periphery, is the commonest subtype in never-smokers, and does not characteristically secrete ectopic ADH.
Mesothelioma presents as nodular pleural thickening and pleural effusion decades after asbestos exposure rather than a central hilar mass causing SIADH.
Squamous cell carcinoma causes central cavitating lesions and paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia via PTH-related peptide (PTHrP) rather than SIADH.
f: a 30 year old non-smoker presented with recurrent single-lobe pneumonia, episodic facial flushing, diarrhoea and a smooth cherry-red endobronchial lesion
a 54 year old never-smoker had a peripheral right upper lobe spiculated nodule with an EGFR mutation and normal serum sodium
a 72 year old former shipyard worker presented with unilateral chest wall pain, pleural effusion and circumferential pleural rind
he presented with a central cavitating mass, polyuria, polydipsia, adjusted calcium 3.24 mmol/L and suppressed parathyroid hormone

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old woman with newly diagnosed stage II squamous cell lung carcinoma of the left main bronchus is admitted with a 10-day history of worsening confusion, extreme thirst, polyuria and constipation.
Pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg. She has dry mucous membranes and globally brisk reflexes, with no focal bone tenderness.
An isotope technetium-99m whole-body bone scan shows no skeletal metastases.
o: Direct osteolytic bone metastases from the tumour
Secretion of PTH-related peptide by the tumour
hq_q.w: Squamous cell lung carcinoma causes humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy via ectopic parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP). PTHrP raises serum calcium and lowers phosphate via renal phosphaturia while negative feedback suppresses endogenous intact PTH.
hq_q.f: High calcium with a high PTH → primary hyperparathyroidism.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hypercalcaemia?

tm.m: Tumour-derived PTHrP mimics N-terminal PTH at osteoblast RANKL and renal tubular receptors, resorbing bone calcium and excreting phosphate while suppressing native parathyroid glands.
tm.g: Squamous cell lung cancer + high calcium + low phosphate + suppressed PTH + clear bone scan -> PTH-related peptide from the tumour
x: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia with an elevated or inappropriately unsuppressed intact PTH, whereas her PTH is suppressed at 0.6 pmol/L.
Her whole-body isotope bone scan shows no skeletal metastases, and local osteolysis does not typically cause marked renal phosphaturia.
Vitamin D toxicity increases gut phosphate absorption alongside calcium, producing hyperphosphataemia rather than a low phosphate of 0.70 mmol/L.
1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D excess (sarcoidosis or lymphoma) increases intestinal absorption of both calcium and phosphate, causing normal or raised serum phosphate.
f: her intact parathyroid hormone level was elevated at 14.5 pmol/L alongside hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia
she had focal vertebral pain and the bone scan/CT demonstrated multiple punched-out osteolytic metastases with normal serum phosphate
she had been taking high-dose over-the-counter vitamin D supplements with a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D >350 nmol/L and raised phosphate
she had bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, raised serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, suppressed PTH and a high-normal serum phosphate

hq_q.s:
A 70 year old man is being treated with IV antibiotics for Streptococcus gallolyticus endocarditis of his aortic valve. On day 5 he becomes breathless and cannot lie flat.
Pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 104/40 mmHg. There are bibasal crackles and a loud early diastolic murmur. Echocardiogram shows severe aortic regurgitation from a perforated leaflet.
hq_q.w: Heart failure from acute valve destruction is the commonest and most urgent reason for surgery in infective endocarditis, alongside uncontrolled infection and preventing emboli. Antibiotics cannot repair a perforated leaflet.
hq_q.f: Stable on antibiotics with mild regurgitation and a falling CRP → complete the course, then colonoscopy for S. gallolyticus.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: becomes breathless and cannot lie flat
tm.m: Infection destroys the leaflet and causes sudden severe regurgitation
tm.g: Endocarditis with heart failure: urgent surgery
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Add IV gentamicin (Adding gentamicin does not treat the failing valve and risks kidney damage)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Change to IV vancomycin (The organism is sensitive; changing antibiotics does not fix a perforated valve)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Continue antibiotics for 6 weeks (Antibiotics are needed, but he is in heart failure now; waiting risks death)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Repeat echo in 1 week (The echo already shows a perforated leaflet with severe regurgitation)
x: Adding gentamicin does not treat the failing valve and risks kidney damage.
The organism is sensitive; changing antibiotics does not fix a perforated valve.
Antibiotics are needed, but he is in heart failure now; waiting risks death.
The echo already shows a perforated leaflet with severe regurgitation.

hq_q.s:
A 20 year old university student living in halls of residence presents with a 10-day history of a persistent dry cough, low-grade fever, frontal headache and generalized myalgia. Several flatmates have had a similar illness. Over the past 48 hours he has noticed mildly jaundiced sclerae and symmetrical target-like erythematous lesions on his palms.
Temperature 37.8°C, SpO2 96% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows bilateral patchy lower-zone interstitial shadowing.
hq_q.w: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia outbreaks in young adults living in close quarters. Extrapulmonary features include erythema multiforme (target lesions) and IgM cold agglutinin autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (anaemia, raised bilirubin and reticulocytosis).
hq_q.f: Hotel shower, low sodium and abnormal liver tests → Legionella.
hq_q.ql: Which causative organism is most likely responsible?

tm.m: Anti-Mycoplasma IgM autoantibodies cross-react with I-antigen on erythrocyte membranes at peripheral temperatures, triggering complement-mediated extravascular haemolysis.
tm.g: Young adult outbreak + atypical pneumonia + erythema multiforme + positive cold agglutinin haemolysis -> Mycoplasma pneumoniae
x: Chlamydia psittaci follows exposure to infected parrots or cage birds and causes high fever, headache and hepatosplenomegaly without cold agglutinins or target lesions.
Legionella pneumophila follows aerosolised hotel/spa water exposure in older or comorbid adults, causing severe lobar pneumonia, diarrhoea and hyponatraemia.
Staphylococcus aureus causes fulminant cavitating pneumonia with pneumatoceles and empyema following influenza rather than mild atypical pneumonia with cold agglutinins.
Streptococcus pneumoniae causes acute onset rigors, pleuritic pain, rusty sputum and dense lobar consolidation without target lesions or cold agglutinins.
f: he worked in an exotic pet shop handling sick parrots and developed high fever, severe headache, dry cough and splenomegaly
a 60 year old smoker returned from a hotel holiday with high fever, confusion, watery diarrhoea and a serum sodium of 125 mmol/L
he deteriorated rapidly 5 days after proven influenza A infection with high fever, haemoptysis and bilateral cavitating lung abscesses
he presented with sudden-onset rigors, pleuritic pain, rust-coloured sputum, herpes labialis and dense lobar consolidation

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old man presents 7 days after returning from a hotel holiday in Spain with 4 days of high fevers, a dry cough, watery diarrhoea and acute confusion.
Temperature 39.4°C, pulse rate 86 bpm, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 92% breathing air. Crackles are audible at the right base. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.
o: Routine aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures
hq_q.w: Pneumonia after hotel water exposure with confusion, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia (sodium 126 mmol/L) and raised ALT (120 IU/L) indicates Legionnaires' disease. Urinary Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 antigen testing provides rapid diagnostic confirmation.
hq_q.f: Rusty sputum with lobar pneumonia → pneumococcal urinary antigen and blood cultures.
hq_q.ql: Which diagnostic investigation is most appropriate to rapidly confirm the causative pathogen?

tm.m: Legionella pneumophila lipopolysaccharide antigen is filtered by the glomeruli and excreted in urine early in the illness, allowing rapid immunochromatographic detection.
tm.g: Suspected Legionella pneumonia (hotel travel + diarrhoea + confusion + Na 126 + ALT 120) -> urinary Legionella antigen test
x: Respiratory viral PCR detects influenza, RSV and SARS-CoV-2, which do not explain dense lobar consolidation with CRP 290 mg/L, diarrhoea and Na 126 mmol/L after hotel spa exposure.
Legionella pneumophila is a fastidious intracellular bacterium that requires buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar with cysteine and does not grow in standard blood culture bottles.
Cold agglutinins are associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection in young adults with haemolysis and erythema multiforme, not Legionnaires' disease.
Patients with Legionella usually have a dry non-productive cough, and Legionella is a poorly staining intracellular organism that is missed on standard sputum Gram stain.
f: he presented during a winter influenza surge with acute coryza, myalgia, normal sodium and diffuse bilateral viral pneumonitis
he presented with sudden-onset rigors, rust-coloured sputum and high-severity bacteraemic pneumococcal lobar pneumonia
a 20 year old student presented with dry cough, targetoid palmar lesions, jaundice and reticulocytosis
he was expectorating purulent sputum in acute pneumococcal or staphylococcal pneumonia where Gram-positive cocci are readily visualised

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man presents with 1 hour of crushing central chest pain. ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF and right-sided lead V4R. After sublingual glyceryl trinitrate spray, he becomes lightheaded. Temperature 36.4°C, pulse rate 58 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, SpO2 97% breathing air. His jugular venous pressure is elevated 6 cm and lung fields are completely clear on auscultation.
o: Administer a second sublingual GTN spray
Intravenous morphine and glyceryl trinitrate infusion
hq_q.w: Inferior STEMI complicated by hypotension, raised JVP, clear lung fields and ST elevation in V4R indicates right ventricular infarction. Because the right ventricle is preload-dependent, immediate treatment is intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride fluid boluses while avoiding nitrates and diuretics.
hq_q.f: Anterior STEMI with raised JVP, orthopnoea and bibasal pulmonary crackles -> acute left ventricular failure (treat with intravenous loop diuretic).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate hemodynamic intervention while awaiting primary PCI?

c: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF
tm.m: An acutely infarcted right ventricle loses contractile compliance and relies on passive venous return (preload) to maintain transpulmonary blood flow into the left atrium
tm.g: Inferior STEMI + triad of hypotension, raised JVP and clear lungs (ST elevation in V4R) = RV infarction: give IV fluids and avoid nitrates/diuretics
x: Venodilators such as nitrates reduce venous return and right ventricular preload, precipitating profound cardiogenic shock in right ventricular infarction.
Loop diuretics deplete intravascular volume and preload, worsening hypotension when the lung fields are clear and the right ventricle is infarcted.
Both opioids and intravenous nitrates cause venodilation and reduce right ventricular filling pressure, aggravating hypotension.
Beta-blockers are contraindicated in acute myocardial infarction complicated by hypotension (BP 84/50 mmHg) and bradycardia (58 bpm).
f: He has an anterior STEMI with normotension (BP 144/88 mmHg) and ongoing ischaemic chest pain.
He has an extensive anterior STEMI with acute left ventricular failure, hypoxia and widespread bilateral pulmonary crackles.
He has acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with severe hypertension (BP 185/105 mmHg) and bilateral crackles.
He is haemodynamically stable 24 hours after primary PCI with BP 128/78 mmHg and pulse rate 76 bpm.

hq_q.s: A 62 year old man re-presents 3 weeks after an acute anterior myocardial infarction. Over 48 hours he has developed sharp central chest pain worse on lying flat and relieved by sitting forward. Temperature 37.9°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg, SpO2 97% breathing air. Auscultation reveals a pericardial friction rub. ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation and PR depression, with raised ESR and CRP.
hq_q.w: Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis occurring 2 to 6 weeks after an acute MI, characterised by positional pleuritic chest pain, fever, a pericardial friction rub, widespread concave ST elevation and raised inflammatory markers. Treat with aspirin and colchicine.
hq_q.f: Pleuritic chest pain and friction rub occurring within 24-72 hours of a transmural MI -> early peri-infarction fibrinous pericarditis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: 3 weeks after an acute anterior myocardial infarction
tm.m: Release of intracellular myocardial neoantigens following transmural necrosis triggers a delayed immune complex-mediated serositis of the pericardium and pleura
tm.g: Fever + positional pleuritic chest pain + pericardial rub + widespread concave ST elevation 2-6 weeks post-MI = Dressler syndrome
x: Cardiac tamponade presents with Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds and raised JVP) and electrical alternans rather than normotension and a friction rub.
Pulmonary embolism does not cause pain relieved by sitting forward, a pericardial friction rub or widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression.
Reinfarction causes crushing non-positional chest pain, territorial convex ST elevation and a sharp dynamic rise in serum troponin.
A ventricular aneurysm causes persistent localised anterior ST elevation without fever, pleuritic positional pain or a pericardial friction rub.
f: He becomes shocked with BP 78/50 mmHg, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus.
He presents with sudden dyspnoea, hypoxia, unilateral calf swelling and sinus tachycardia without ST elevation.
He stops dual antiplatelet therapy and develops crushing central chest pain with convex ST elevation in V1-V4 and rising troponin.
He is asymptomatic at 6 weeks with persistent ST elevation confined to V1-V4 and a dyskinetic apex on echocardiography.

hq_q.s: A 66 year old man attends the cardiology clinic 6 weeks after a large anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction that was treated late. He is currently asymptomatic. Temperature 36.5°C, pulse rate 68 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, SpO2 98% breathing air. A 12-lead ECG shows deep Q waves and persistent ST-segment elevation across leads V1 to V4. Transthoracic echocardiography reveals a thinned, dyskinetic, bulging left ventricular apex.
o: Complete heart block requiring permanent pacing
hq_q.w: Persistent ST-segment elevation and deep Q waves in V1-V4 weeks after an anterior MI indicates a left ventricular apical aneurysm. Stasis within the dyskinetic apical pouch predisposes to mural thrombus formation and systemic thromboembolism, warranting anticoagulation.
hq_q.f: Sudden cardiogenic shock and new harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge 4 days post-MI -> ventricular septal rupture.
hq_q.ql: Which major complication is he at highest risk of developing from this structural abnormality?

c: 6 weeks after a large anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction
persistent ST-segment elevation across leads V1 to V4
thinned, dyskinetic, bulging left ventricular apex
tm.m: Stasis of blood within the scarred, akinetic apical aneurysm alongside endothelial injury activates the coagulation cascade (Virchow's triad), forming mural thrombus
tm.g: Persistent anterior ST elevation >= 4 weeks post-MI = left ventricular aneurysm -> risk of mural thrombus / systemic embolism and ventricular arrhythmias
x: Endocarditis affects damaged heart valves or prosthetic material rather than a smooth fibrotic left ventricular apical aneurysm.
Aortic dissection arises from cystic medial degeneration and hypertension in the thoracic aorta rather than a scarred left ventricular apex.
Complete atrioventricular block typically complicates acute inferior myocardial infarction affecting the right coronary AV nodal artery in the first week.
Mitral stenosis is a chronic sequela of rheumatic fever rather than anterior myocardial infarction (which is associated with functional mitral regurgitation).
f: A patient with a prosthetic aortic valve presents with persistent fevers, splinter haemorrhages and positive blood cultures for Streptococcus sanguinis.
He has severe uncontrolled hypertension and develops sudden tearing interscapular back pain with unequal arm pulses.
He is 48 hours post-inferior STEMI with bradycardia of 36 bpm, cannon a waves and AV dissociation.
A patient with prior childhood rheumatic fever presents with malar flush, tapping apex beat and a mid-diastolic murmur.

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man has a known brain tumour. He has become drowsy over 2 hours.
GCS 9. BP 194/96 mmHg, pulse rate 46 bpm, and his breathing is irregular.
hq_q.w: Cushing's triad, high blood pressure, slow pulse and irregular breathing, is a late sign of rising pressure in the skull. It needs urgent neurosurgical help.
hq_q.f: High BP with a fast pulse and papilloedema in a known hypertensive → hypertensive emergency.
hq_q.ql: What does this combination of signs mean?

tm.m: The body raises BP to keep blood reaching a squeezed brainstem
tm.g: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing with falling GCS is Cushing's triad
f: a spinal injury above T6 with a full bladder
the presentation instead showed features specific to Beta-blocker overdose (Low BP with a slow pulse)

the presentation instead showed features specific to Hypertensive encephalopathy (Hypertensive encephalopathy raises BP with headache and confusion, but the pulse rises; a slow pulse with irregular breathing means herniation)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sepsis (Low BP with a fast pulse)
x: Spinal cord injury above T6 with a trigger below it
Low BP with a slow pulse
Hypertensive encephalopathy raises BP with headache and confusion, but the pulse rises; a slow pulse with irregular breathing means herniation.
Low BP with a fast pulse

hq_q.s:
A 27 year old woman with recently diagnosed idiopathic intracranial hypertension presents to the neurology clinic with worsening morning headaches and new horizontal double vision that is worst when looking at distant objects or to either side.
Her BMI is 37 kg/m². Examination reveals bilateral papilloedema and impaired abduction of both eyes on lateral gaze. Pupils are equal and reactive, and ptosis is absent.
hq_q.w: The abducens nerve (CN VI) has a long intracranial course over the petrous temporal ridge. Downward brainstem traction from generalized raised intracranial pressure stretches CN VI, causing lateral rectus palsy as a classic false localising sign.
hq_q.f: Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil with 'down-and-out' eye and falling GCS -> oculomotor nerve (CN III) compression from transtentorial uncal herniation (true localising sign).
hq_q.ql: Which cranial nerve palsy is acting as a false localising sign of raised intracranial pressure?

tm.m: Caudal displacement of the brainstem by generalized intracranial hypertension tethers and stretches the abducens nerve over the sharp ridge of the petrous temporal bone.
tm.g: False localising cranial nerve palsy in raised intracranial pressure -> abducens nerve (CN VI)
x: The facial nerve (CN VII) exits the pons into the internal acoustic meatus and causes facial muscle weakness rather than horizontal diplopia on lateral gaze.
An oculomotor (CN III) palsy causes a 'down-and-out' eye, ptosis and a dilated pupil, and in raised ICP is a true ipsilateral localising sign of uncal herniation.
The trigeminal nerve (CN V) mediates facial sensation and mastication and does not innervate extraocular muscles.
A trochlear nerve (CN IV) palsy paralyses the superior oblique muscle, causing vertical/torsional diplopia worse on looking down and in (e.g. walking downstairs).
f: unilateral upper and lower facial weakness with hyperacusis and loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
a fixed dilated ipsilateral pupil, complete ptosis and an eye deviated down and out in uncal herniation
loss of corneal reflex and hemifacial numbness over the forehead, cheek and jaw
vertical diplopia worse when walking down stairs with a compensatory contralateral head tilt

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old man presents with a 4-month history of steadily worsening symmetrical weakness and numbness in both legs and arms, with no preceding illness.
Examination shows both proximal (hip/shoulder) and distal limb weakness, generalized areflexia, and reduced vibration sense. CSF shows protein 1.4 g/L (0.15-0.45) with 2 white cells/mm³, and nerve conduction studies show demyelination and conduction block.
o: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
hq_q.w: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) causes symmetrical proximal and distal weakness, areflexia, raised CSF protein and demyelination progressing for >8 weeks. Unlike Guillain-Barre syndrome, CIDP responds to corticosteroids as well as IVIG.
hq_q.f: Acute ascending weakness and areflexia reaching nadir within 4 weeks after gastroenteritis -> acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (Guillain-Barre syndrome).
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: 4-month history of steadily worsening symmetrical weakness
both proximal (hip/shoulder) and distal limb weakness
tm.m: Chronic T-cell and macrophage-mediated segmental demyelination and remyelination of spinal nerve roots and peripheral nerves causes proximal and distal weakness progressing beyond 8 weeks.
tm.g: Symmetrical proximal + distal demyelinating polyneuropathy with areflexia and raised CSF protein progressing >8 weeks -> CIDP
x: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (Guillain-Barre syndrome) reaches its clinical nadir within 4 weeks, whereas his neuropathy has progressed steadily for 4 months (16 weeks).

Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (HMSN) begins in childhood or adolescence with very slow lifelong distal wasting ('inverted champagne bottle' legs), pes cavus and family history, without proximal hip/shoulder weakness.
Motor neurone disease has no sensory loss, does not slow nerve conduction velocities into the demyelinating range, and combines brisk reflexes with fasciculations.

Vitamin B12 deficiency damages the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, causing absent ankle jerks with brisk knee jerks and extensor plantars rather than four-limb areflexia and conduction block.
f: ascending symmetrical weakness and areflexia peaking 14 days after Campylobacter gastroenteritis
a 19 year old with lifelong high-arched feet (pes cavus), hammer toes, distal calf wasting and an affected father
asymmetrical limb wasting, fasciculations, brisk reflexes and normal sensory conduction studies
megaloblastic anaemia, loss of vibration sense, absent ankle jerks, brisk knee jerks and extensor plantars

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man has tripped often since childhood. His father had the same problem.
He has high-arched feet, thin lower legs and absent ankle reflexes. There is mild distal sensory loss.
hq_q.w: Charcot-Marie-Tooth is an inherited neuropathy: pes cavus, inverted champagne bottle legs and foot drop, usually autosomal dominant.
hq_q.f: Ataxia with diabetes and a cardiomyopathy in a teenager → Friedreich's ataxia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: His father had the same problem
tm.m: A faulty myelin or axon gene makes the longest nerves fail first
tm.g: Lifelong distal weakness, pes cavus and an affected parent is CMT
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (He has no diabetes, and it is mainly sensory)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Friedreich's ataxia (Usually recessive with ataxia, diabetes and heart disease)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Guillain-Barré syndrome (Acute, over days to weeks)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Multiple sclerosis (Central signs such as brisk reflexes)
x: He has no diabetes, and it is mainly sensory
Usually recessive with ataxia, diabetes and heart disease
Acute, over days to weeks
Central signs such as brisk reflexes

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman with late-onset asthma, chronic sinusitis and eosinophilia presents to clinic. Four weeks ago she developed sudden weakness of right ankle dorsiflexion (right foot drop), and yesterday she developed sudden weakness of left wrist and finger extension (left wrist drop) with dorsal web space numbness.
Examination confirms a right common peroneal nerve palsy and a left radial nerve palsy.
hq_q.w: Mononeuritis multiplex is the sequential or simultaneous damage to two or more separate named peripheral nerves (here the right common peroneal and left radial nerves) due to vasa nervorum infarction, typically from systemic vasculitis or diabetes.
hq_q.f: Symmetrical distal 'glove-and-stocking' numbness starting in both feet -> length-dependent symmetrical polyneuropathy.
hq_q.ql: Which clinical term best describes this pattern of peripheral nerve involvement?

c: late-onset asthma, chronic sinusitis and eosinophilia
left wrist and finger extension (left wrist drop)
right common peroneal nerve palsy and a left radial nerve palsy
tm.m: Necrotising vasculitis of the epineurial vasa nervorum arterioles causes acute ischaemic axonal infarction of individual named peripheral nerve trunks in an asymmetrical stepwise pattern.
tm.g: Sequential/asymmetrical lesions of >=2 separate named peripheral nerves (right common peroneal + left radial) -> mononeuritis multiplex
x: A lumbosacral polyradiculopathy affects lower-limb spinal nerve roots and could not explain an acute left radial nerve palsy in the upper limb.
Motor neurone disease causes painless progressive upper and lower motor neurone degeneration without sensory loss over the dorsal web space or asthma/eosinophilia.
A myopathy causes symmetrical proximal shoulder and hip girdle weakness without sensory loss or isolated foot and wrist drops in specific nerve distributions.
Length-dependent polyneuropathy affects the longest axons first, producing symmetrical distal stocking-and-glove sensory loss in both feet before reaching the hands.
f: bilateral radiating leg pain, saddle anaesthesia and lower-limb root weakness from cauda equina compression
progressive painless limb fasciculations, wasting and brisk reflexes with completely normal sensation
symmetrical difficulty rising from a chair and lifting the arms overhead with raised creatine kinase and normal sensation
gradual symmetrical numbness and burning tingling in both feet ascending to the mid-shins in long-standing diabetes

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man presents to the neurology clinic with a 6 month history of unsteady walking that worsens in the dark and shooting pains down both legs.
On examination, he has a wide-based stamping gait, absent ankle and knee reflexes with preserved plantars, and bilateral small, irregular pupils that constrict briskly when focusing on a near target but do not constrict to bright light.
hq_q.w: Bilateral small, irregular pupils displaying light-near dissociation ('accommodation reflex present, pupillary light reflex absent') are Argyll Robertson pupils, classically caused by dorsal midbrain periaqueductal damage in tertiary neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis) or diabetic autonomic neuropathy.
hq_q.f: One large pupil that reacts slowly and has reduced knee jerks → Holmes-Adie pupil.
hq_q.ql: Which condition is classically linked to these pupils?

c: constrict briskly when focusing on a near target
do not constrict to bright light
tm.m: Pretectal dorsal midbrain lesions interrupt the retinotectal light reflex fibres while sparing the more ventral near-accommodation pathway
tm.g: Bilateral small irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react to light -> neurosyphilis (Argyll Robertson pupils)
f: a young woman with a unilateral large pupil that constricts very slowly to near focus and absent knee jerks
fatigable bilateral ptosis and diplopia that worsen towards the end of the day with normal reactive pupils
bilateral symmetrical pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression and drowsiness reversed by naloxone
a unilateral fixed dilated pupil with complete ptosis and the eye deviated down and out
x: A Holmes-Adie tonic pupil is typically unilateral and dilated, with sluggish vermiform constriction to light and slow redilation.
Myasthenia gravis affects nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at skeletal neuromuscular junctions and strictly spares the pupils.
Opioid toxicity causes bilateral symmetrical pinpoint (miotic) pupils that still constrict faintly to a bright light source and reverse with naloxone.
A compressive third nerve palsy causes a unilateral dilated pupil accompanied by complete ptosis and a 'down and out' eye.

hq_q.s:
A 42 year old man had neck manipulation by a chiropractor 2 days ago. He now has pain on the left side of his neck and a headache.
There is a small left pupil and mild left ptosis. An hour ago he had brief weakness of his right hand.
hq_q.w: Cervical manipulation can tear the internal carotid artery intima. Intramural haematoma compresses peri-arterial sympathetic fibres – causing an ipsilateral painful Horner's syndrome (ptosis and miosis) – while intraluminal thrombus embolises to cause contralateral hemisphere TIA or stroke.
hq_q.f: Horner's with shoulder pain and weight loss in a smoker → Pancoast tumour.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: pain on the left side of his neck
tm.m: Intimal tearing of the internal carotid artery injures third-order oculosympathetic fibres and sheds cerebral emboli
tm.g: Painful ipsilateral Horner's syndrome + contralateral hemisphere TIA after neck trauma -> carotid artery dissection
f: progressive shoulder pain, intrinsic hand muscle wasting and ipsilateral Horner's syndrome in a heavy smoker
nightly 45 minute bouts of excruciating left orbital pain with lacrimation and nasal congestion
complete left ptosis with a dilated unreactive pupil and the eye resting down and out
fully reversible shimmering visual aura followed by throbbing headache and normal pupil size
x: A Pancoast tumour causes a subacute preganglionic Horner's syndrome with shoulder pain, C8/T1 hand wasting, and weight loss in a smoker rather than acute post-manipulation TIA.
Cluster headache causes recurrent 30 to 90 minute attacks of excruciating orbital pain with lacrimation and autonomic signs, not contralateral motor TIA.
A left third nerve palsy causes a dilated pupil and 'down and out' eye deviation rather than miosis and contralateral hand weakness.
Migraine with aura does not produce a persistent post-traumatic Horner's syndrome with unilateral neck pain.

hq_q.s: A 56 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus attends her annual rheumatology review. She has taken hydroxychloroquine 200 mg daily (3.2 mg/kg/day) for the past 3 years with good disease control. Her eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73 m², she does not take tamoxifen, and a baseline ophthalmic assessment was normal.
o: Before every adjustment in daily dose
Monthly from the start of treatment
Only if she notices central visual blur
hq_q.w: Royal College of Ophthalmologists guidelines recommend annual retinal screening starting after 5 years of standard-dose hydroxychloroquine in patients without additional risk factors, or after 1 year if dose exceeds 5 mg/kg/day, renal function is impaired, or tamoxifen is co-prescribed.
hq_q.f: eGFR 40 → start yearly screening after 1 year.
hq_q.ql: When should regular retinal screening begin?

tm.m: Cumulative hydroxychloroquine binding to retinal pigment epithelial melanin causes bull's-eye maculopathy after years of exposure
tm.g: Standard-dose hydroxychloroquine without renal impairment or tamoxifen -> annual retinal screening starting at 5 years
f: calculating ideal body weight before initiating a dose above 5 mg/kg/day
never appropriate because toxicity progresses irreversibly between 5-yearly checks once exposure exceeds 5 years
intravitreal anti-VEGF loading phase monitoring in active neovascular age-related macular degeneration
advising a patient on ethambutol to stop tablets immediately and seek review if visual acuity or colour vision changes
x: Dose adjustments within the safe weight-based threshold (<5 mg/kg/day) do not trigger ad-hoc retinal screening before 5 years.
Once the 5 year cumulative exposure threshold is reached, screening must be performed annually rather than every 5 years.
Monthly OCT screening is unnecessary because cumulative retinal toxicity is extremely rare during the first 5 years at standard doses.
Waiting for symptomatic paracentral scotomas or visual loss is unsafe because hydroxychloroquine bull's-eye retinopathy is irreversible once symptomatic.

hq_q.s:
A 54 year old man with a history of gout attends the stone clinic after his second episode of acute renal colic Plain abdominal radiograph (KUB) at presentation showed no visible radiopaque calculus, whereas non-contrast CT KUB demonstrated a 5 mm distal ureteric stone that subsequently passed.
Serum urate is 490 µmol/L (200-430), serum calcium is 2.34 mmol/L (2.20-2.60) and his fasting urine pH is 5.0.
hq_q.w: Uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain X-ray, visible on CT KUB and precipitate in acidic urine (pH <5.5) in patients with gout. Oral potassium citrate alkalinises the urine to dissolve and prevent uric acid calculi.
hq_q.f: Recurrent radiopaque calcium oxalate stones with persistent idiopathic hypercalciuria -> thiazide diuretic (bendroflumethiazide).
hq_q.ql: Which oral medication is most likely to prevent further stones of this type?

c: non-contrast CT KUB demonstrated a 5 mm distal ureteric stone
tm.m: Uric acid has a pKa of 5.35; raising urinary pH above 6.0 with potassium citrate converts insoluble undissociated uric acid into highly soluble urate ions.
tm.g: Radiolucent stone on X-ray + visible on CT + gout + acidic urine (pH 5.0) = uric acid stone -> alkalinise with potassium citrate
x: Thiazide diuretics reduce urinary calcium excretion in hypercalciuric calcium stones, but they raise serum urate and can worsen gout and uric acid stones.
Restricting dietary calcium increases intestinal oxalate absorption and calcium oxalate stone risk, and has no role in uric acid stones.
Dietary oxalate restriction is used for enteric hyperoxaluria and calcium oxalate stones, whereas radiolucent stones at pH 5.0 in gout are uric acid.
Reducing fluid intake concentrates the urine and accelerates crystal supersaturation; patients with any stone type must increase fluid intake to 2.5 to 3 L/day.
f: recurrent radiopaque calcium oxalate stones with persistent idiopathic hypercalciuria
never recommended for renal stone prevention; normal dietary calcium intake should be maintained
recurrent radiopaque calcium oxalate stones with confirmed hyperoxaluria on 24-hour urine collection
syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) causing euvolaemic hyponatraemia

hq_q.s:
A 62 year old woman presents with a 6-month history of dull right loin ache and three episodes of urinary tract infection. Midstream urine cultures have repeatedly grown Proteus mirabilis.
Temperature 37.1°C, BP 134/80 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows blood 2+, leucocytes 3+ and a urine pH of 8.0. Non-contrast CT KUB demonstrates a large branched radiopaque staghorn calculus filling the right renal pelvis and calyces.
hq_q.w: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate, often mixed with calcium carbonate-apatite) stones form in alkaline urine (pH >7.2) infected with urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella or Pseudomonas. Bacterial urease hydrolyses urea into ammonia and bicarbonate, precipitating large branched staghorn calculi.
hq_q.f: Young adult with family history, radio-opaque stones failing shockwave lithotripsy and hexagonal crystals -> cystine stone.
hq_q.ql: Which stone composition is most likely?

tm.m: Bacterial urease splits urinary urea into ammonia, which combines with water to form ammonium and hydroxide ions, alkalinising the urine and precipitating magnesium ammonium phosphate.
tm.g: Recurrent Proteus mirabilis UTI + alkaline urine (pH 8.0) + branched staghorn calculus -> struvite stone
x: Calcium oxalate is the commonest ureteric stone overall (80%) but forms in normal-to-acidic urine independently of Proteus infection and rarely forms full staghorn casts.
Pure calcium phosphate stones form in sterile alkaline urine associated with distal renal tubular acidosis (type 1) or primary hyperparathyroidism rather than Proteus urease infection.
Cystine stones arise from autosomal recessive cystinuria (defective proximal tubular dibasic amino acid transport) in young patients with acidic urine and hexagonal crystals.
Uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain X-ray and precipitate in persistently acidic urine (pH <5.5), not alkaline urine at pH 8.0.
f: a 5 mm radiopaque ureteric calculus in a patient with low fluid intake, sterile urine and urine pH 6.0
nephrocalcinosis and radiopaque stones in a patient with distal renal tubular acidosis, hypokalaemia and sterile alkaline urine
a 19 year old with recurrent stones since childhood, a positive cyanide-nitroprusside test and hexagonal urinary crystals
a radiolucent stone in a patient with gout or ileostomy losses and a fasting urine pH of 5.0

hq_q.s: A 38 year old man with Crohn's disease had 60 cm of terminal ileum removed 2 years ago. He has had two calcium oxalate kidney stones.
o: Excess calcium absorption from the gut
High urine pH from bicarbonate loss
Too much uric acid in the urine
hq_q.w: Without the terminal ileum, bile salts and fat reach the colon. Fat binds calcium, so oxalate stays free and is absorbed in the colon.
hq_q.f: Gout with acid urine → uric acid stones.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely mechanism of his stones?

tm.m: Unabsorbed fat soaks up calcium in the gut, freeing oxalate
tm.g: Ileal disease or resection with oxalate stones is enteric hyperoxaluria
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Excess calcium absorption from the gut (Calcium absorption is reduced, not increased)
the presentation instead showed features specific to High urine pH from bicarbonate loss (Diarrhoea makes the urine more acid)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Infection with urease-making bacteria (Causes struvite, not oxalate)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Too much uric acid in the urine (Causes uric acid stones)
x: Calcium absorption is reduced, not increased
Diarrhoea makes the urine more acid
Causes struvite, not oxalate
Causes uric acid stones

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old retired seamstress attends her GP with a 1-year history of aching pain and knobbly swellings at the joints nearest her fingertips. Her discomfort is worse after knitting and eases with rest, with morning stiffness lasting 10 minutes.
Examination shows hard, non-tender posterolateral bony prominences at the distal interphalangeal joints bilaterally.
hq_q.w: Heberden's nodes are marginal osteophytes at the distal interphalangeal joints characteristic of hand osteoarthritis. Bouchard's nodes are equivalent osteophytic swellings occurring at the proximal interphalangeal joints.
hq_q.f: Hard bony swellings at the proximal interphalangeal joints -> Bouchard's nodes.
hq_q.ql: Which term describes these swellings?

c: hard, non-tender posterolateral bony prominences at the distal interphalangeal joints
tm.m: Articular cartilage loss stimulates marginal endochondral ossification at the distal interphalangeal joint margins
tm.g: Hard bony swellings at the distal interphalangeal joints in osteoarthritis -> Heberden's nodes
x: Represent osteophytes at the proximal interphalangeal joints rather than the distal interphalangeal joints.
Are violaceous scaly plaques over the extensor surfaces of the knuckles seen in dermatomyositis, not bony osteophytes.
Are firm subcutaneous necrobiotic nodules over extensor pressure surfaces such as the olecranon in seropositive rheumatoid arthritis.
Are chalky yellow-white monosodium urate deposits in chronic gout rather than symmetrical posterolateral DIP osteophytes.
f: Hard bony osteophytic swellings located at the proximal interphalangeal joints of the fingers
Violaceous scaly papules over the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints with proximal muscle weakness and heliotrope rash
Firm mobile subcutaneous lumps over the extensor aspect of the elbows in seropositive rheumatoid arthritis
Chalky white deposits over the fingers discharging negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals in chronic gout

hq_q.s: A 70 year old man has had worsening right knee pain on walking for 2 years. Morning stiffness lasts 10 minutes. An X-ray is taken.
hq_q.w: Osteoarthritis shows LOSS: Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis and Subchondral cysts. Key discriminator: Joint space narrowing with osteophytes is osteoarthritis.
hq_q.f: Periarticular erosions and osteopenia in the hands → rheumatoid arthritis.
hq_q.ql: Which X-ray finding is most typical of his likely diagnosis?

c: worsening right knee pain on walking
tm.m: Cartilage wears away and bone remodels at the margins
tm.g: Joint space narrowing with osteophytes is osteoarthritis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Chondrocalcinosis of the menisci (Calcium in cartilage from pyrophosphate disease)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Pencil-in-cup deformity (Psoriatic arthritis)
symmetrical hand swelling with long morning stiffness
the presentation instead showed features specific to Periarticular osteopenia (An early rheumatoid sign)
x: Calcium in cartilage from pyrophosphate disease
Psoriatic arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis
An early rheumatoid sign

hq_q.s:
A 19 year old woman attends general practice after two prolonged nosebleeds this month and heavy menstrual periods since menarche. Last year she required dental packing for oozing that lasted 12 hours after a wisdom tooth extraction. Her mother and maternal uncle have similar bleeding histories.
Examination shows no mucocutaneous telangiectasia. Platelet count is 245 x 10⁹/L, PT is 12 seconds, and APTT is 41 seconds.
hq_q.w: Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, usually autosomal dominant. Deficient von Willebrand factor impairs platelet adhesion (causing epistaxis, menorrhagia, and dental bleeding) and reduces factor VIII levels, mildly prolonging the APTT.
hq_q.f: A boy with bleeding into joints and a long APTT → haemophilia A.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Deficiency of von Willebrand factor impairs GPIb platelet adhesion to subendothelial collagen and accelerates factor VIII degradation
tm.g: Mucocutaneous bleeding + menorrhagia + autosomal dominant family history + normal platelets/mildly raised APTT -> von Willebrand disease
f: a young boy with recurrent spontaneous knee haemarthroses, a normal bleeding time and a maternal uncle affected
recurrent epistaxis with punctate red telangiectasia on the lips and tongue and a normal APTT
petechial rash and epistaxis with an isolated platelet count of 14 x 10⁹/L and normal coagulation screen
acquired bruising with a markedly prolonged prothrombin time and INR in a patient taking oral anticoagulation
x: Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive factor VIII deficiency affecting males with deep haemarthroses and muscle haematomas rather than menorrhagia.
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia causes epistaxis and gastrointestinal bleeding with characteristic ruby-red telangiectasia on the lips, tongue, and fingertips and a normal APTT.
Immune thrombocytopenia causes mucocutaneous bleeding and petechiae due to a markedly low platelet count with normal PT and APTT.
Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, predominantly prolonging the prothrombin time (PT/INR) rather than causing lifelong inherited bleeding.

hq_q.s:
A 15 year old boy presents to the ENT clinic with a 6 month history of progressive left-sided nasal blockage, hyponasal speech, and three episodes of heavy, unprovoked left-sided epistaxis.
Anterior rhinoscopy and flexible nasendoscopy reveal a smooth, lobulated, reddish-purple mass filling the posterior left nasal cavity and nasopharynx. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy.
o: Nasal packing and review in a month
hq_q.w: Unilateral nasal obstruction, recurrent heavy epistaxis, and a smooth reddish posterior nasal mass in an adolescent male indicate juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. Cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) is mandatory before any biopsy because clinic biopsy causes torrential haemorrhage.
hq_q.f: Bleeding from Little's area in a child who picks his nose → antiseptic cream.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

tm.m: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma arises from the sphenopalatine foramen as an unencapsulated vascular tumour lacking contractile smooth muscle
tm.g: Adolescent male with unilateral nasal obstruction, recurrent heavy epistaxis and posterior red mass -> cross-sectional imaging before any biopsy
f: an ulcerated exophytic anterior tongue lesion in an adult smoker requiring histological confirmation
recurrent minor anterior nosebleeds from visible dilated vessels on Little's area in a 9 year old
never appropriate when a unilateral posterior nasal mass is visualised on rhinoscopy
bilateral pale insensate mobile nasal polyps associated with chronic rhinosinusitis and asthma
x: Performing an outpatient punch biopsy of a juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma causes catastrophic, torrential arterial bleeding.
Silver nitrate cautery treats prominent anterior septal vessels in Little's area and ignores a posterior nasopharyngeal tumour.
Packing and waiting a month fails to investigate a locally invasive vascular skull-base tumour.
Intranasal steroid sprays treat bilateral benign inflammatory nasal polyps or allergic rhinitis, not a unilateral vascular neoplasm.

hq_q.s:
Four university flatmates attend the Emergency Department with sudden-onset nausea, abdominal cramps and profuse vomiting starting 2 hours after sharing a takeaway meal of egg fried rice. The rice had been boiled in a large batch earlier that day, left at room temperature on a kitchen counter for 6 hours, and briefly stir-fried before serving.
Temperature 36.7°C, pulse rate 84 bpm. None of the patients has fever or bloody diarrhoea.
hq_q.w: Bacillus cereus is a spore-forming aerobic Gram-positive rod found in uncooked rice. Heat-resistant endospores survive boiling and germinate when cooked rice is left cooling at room temperature, elaborating a preformed, heat-stable emetic toxin (cereulide) that is not destroyed by brief reheating and causes vomiting within 1 to 6 hours.
hq_q.f: Ham sandwiches and cream cakes with vomiting at 2 hours → Staph aureus.
hq_q.ql: Which organism is the most likely cause of this foodborne illness?

tm.m: Heat-stable cereulide dodecadepsipeptide toxin binds 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferent nerves in the stomach, triggering rapid emesis within 1 to 6 hours.
tm.g: Vomiting within 1-6 hours of eating reheated rice left at room temperature -> Bacillus cereus
x: Campylobacter jejuni has a 2 to 5 day incubation period after undercooked poultry and causes febrile bloody diarrhoea rather than rapid vomiting at 2 hours.
Clostridium perfringens causes watery diarrhoea and abdominal cramps 8 to 16 hours after eating reheated meat stews or gravies, with minimal vomiting.
Norovirus has a 12 to 48 hour incubation period and spreads person-to-person or via contaminated shellfish/salads rather than reheated rice at 2 hours.
Salmonella enteritidis has a 12 to 36 hour incubation period after eggs or poultry and causes fever and diarrhoea.
f: they developed fever, severe abdominal cramps and bloody diarrhoea 3 days after eating undercooked chicken
they developed profuse watery diarrhoea and cramps 12 hours after eating a large pot of braised beef stew kept warm on a stove
vomiting and watery diarrhoea developed 30 hours after attending a banquet where a symptomatic food handler had prepared raw salad
fever, headache and watery diarrhoea developed 24 hours after eating lightly cooked scrambled eggs

hq_q.s:
A 16 year old boy presents to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of colicky right iliac fossa abdominal pain, fever and loose stools. He lives on a smallholder farm where his family rear pigs, and he helped clean the farrowing pens last week.
Temperature 38.3°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg. There is localized tenderness in the right iliac fossa.
Ultrasound demonstrates multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, terminal ileal wall thickening and a normal appendix.
hq_q.w: Yersinia enterocolitica is a psychrophilic (cold-tolerant) Gram-negative coccobacillus for which pigs are the primary reservoir (transmitted via undercooked pork, chitterlings, unpasteurised milk or pig contact). It invades Peyer's patches in the terminal ileum and mesenteric lymph nodes, causing terminal ileitis and mesenteric adenitis that closely mimic acute appendicitis ('pseudoappendicitis'), and can trigger erythema nodosum or reactive arthritis.
hq_q.f: Bloody diarrhoea with low platelets and a rising creatinine in a child → E. coli O157 with HUS.
hq_q.ql: Which causative organism is most likely responsible?

tm.m: Yersinia enterocolitica translocates across ileal M cells into Peyer's patches and draining mesenteric lymph nodes, producing necrotising granulomatous lymphadenitis.
tm.g: Pseudoappendicitis (RIF pain + fever + mesenteric adenitis with normal appendix) + pig/pork exposure -> Yersinia enterocolitica
x: Campylobacter jejuni follows undercooked poultry rather than pig husbandry and predominantly causes diffuse bloody enterocolitis.
Clostridioides difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis with profuse watery diarrhoea following broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy.
Escherichia coli O157 follows beef or cattle/sheep petting farm exposure, causing afebrile haemorrhagic colitis and haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
Shigella sonnei has no animal reservoir (humans are the only host) and causes distal colonic dysentery with blood, mucus and tenesmus.
f: he developed febrile bloody diarrhoea 3 days after eating undercooked chicken and subsequently developed ascending areflexic weakness
he developed profuse watery green offensive diarrhoea 10 days after completing a course of oral clindamycin or co-amoxiclav
he developed bloody diarrhoea without fever, haemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 34 x 10^9/L and creatinine 280 µmol/L after a cattle farm visit
an outbreak of acute bloody mucoid dysentery with tenesmus spread person-to-person through a primary school

hq_q.s: A 64 year old man has lost 9 kg over 3 months and has early fullness. He has developed dark, velvety thickened skin in both armpits. He is thin and does not have diabetes.
hq_q.w: Acanthosis nigricans in a thin older person with weight loss can signal gastric cancer. It is usually linked to insulin resistance in younger people.
hq_q.f: An overweight young woman with irregular periods → insulin resistance, check HbA1c.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most appropriate?

tm.m: Tumour growth factors drive the skin to thicken and darken
tm.g: New acanthosis with weight loss and no insulin resistance: look for gastric cancer
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Fasting insulin (Insulin resistance fits young overweight people, not this picture)
an overweight 24 year old with irregular periods
the presentation instead showed features specific to Routine dermatology referral (Misses the likely cancer)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Skin biopsy (The skin change is clinically clear; the cause is elsewhere)
x: Insulin resistance fits young overweight people, not this picture
He does not have diabetes, and it would not find the cause
Misses the likely cancer
The skin change is clinically clear; the cause is elsewhere

hq_q.s:
A 22 year old woman collapsed while standing for 40 minutes in a warm, crowded post office queue. Before falling she felt lightheaded, nauseated and sweaty, with tunnel vision. Witnesses saw her look pale, slump limply and have 8 seconds of brief myoclonic jerks of both arms.
She regained full orientation within 30 seconds of lying flat, with normal ECG and examination.
hq_q.w: Convulsive vasovagal syncope occurs when transient cerebral hypoperfusion during a faint triggers brief (<15 second) myoclonic jerks. A postural trigger, autonomic prodrome, pallor and rapid orientation recovery (<1 minute) distinguish it from epilepsy.
hq_q.f: Unprovoked collapse from sleep with lateral tongue biting, cyanosis, 2-minute tonic-clonic phase and 20 minutes of post-ictal confusion -> generalised tonic-clonic seizure.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: standing for 40 minutes in a warm, crowded post office queue
lightheaded, nauseated and sweaty, with tunnel vision
tm.m: Venous pooling and Bezold-Jarisch vagal bradycardia/vasodilatation transiently reduce cerebral cortical perfusion, releasing brief brainstem reticular myoclonic jerks that cease once supine posture restores blood flow.
tm.g: Prolonged standing trigger + presyncopal prodrome/pallor + brief (<15s) jerks + rapid orientation recovery -> convulsive syncope
x: Hypoglycaemia causes progressive neuroglycopenia and coma that does not resolve spontaneously within 30 seconds of lying flat without glucose administration.
Dissociative seizures typically last 5 to 20 minutes with tightly closed eyes, waxing-and-waning pelvic/head movements and post-event crying rather than an 8-second pale postural faint.
Focal impaired awareness seizures present with an epigastric rising aura, behavioural arrest and lip-smacking automatisms followed by post-ictal confusion rather than a pale postural faint.
True epileptic tonic-clonic seizures last 1 to 3 minutes with sustained tonic stiffening, cyanosis, lateral tongue biting and 15 to 60 minutes of deep post-ictal confusion.
f: sweating, tremor and confusion in an insulin-treated diabetic patient with capillary blood glucose 1.9 mmol/L
a 15-minute episode of waxing-and-waning shaking with tightly closed eyes, side-to-side head movements and normal ictal EEG
a 2-minute episode preceded by deja vu and epigastric rising, with lip-smacking automatisms and post-ictal confusion
an unprovoked 2-minute tonic-clonic convulsion with cyanosis, lateral tongue biting and 30 minutes of post-ictal confusion

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old woman has recurrent episodes of shaking that last 10 to 20 minutes despite two antiseizure drugs. During an attack her eyes remain tightly closed against passive opening, her head shakes from side to side, and limb movements stop and restart.
She weeps afterwards and recalls nurses speaking. Simultaneous ictal video-EEG shows normal waking alpha rhythm without epileptiform activity.
hq_q.w: Dissociative (non-epileptic) seizures feature prolonged (>10 minute) waxing-and-waning movements, forced eye closure, side-to-side head shaking, preserved recall and a normal ictal video-EEG. Manage with clear explanation and psychological therapy.
hq_q.f: Brief 20-second nocturnal hypermotor bicycling attacks arising from sleep with rapid recovery -> frontal lobe epilepsy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: head shakes from side to side
ictal video-EEG shows normal waking alpha rhythm
tm.m: Functional neurological dissociation produces involuntary motor and behavioural episodes without paroxysmal hypersynchronous cortical electrical discharges.
tm.g: Prolonged (10-20 min) waxing-and-waning shaking + tightly closed eyes + side-to-side head movements + normal ictal video-EEG -> dissociative seizure
x: True convulsive status epilepticus lasting 20 minutes causes profound hypoxia, lactic acidosis, open eyes and continuous ictal epileptiform discharges on EEG.
Convulsive syncope lasts under 15 seconds following a postural trigger with facial pallor and limpness, not 20 minutes of waxing-and-waning shaking.
Frontal lobe seizures are typically very brief (<30-60 seconds), clustered out of nocturnal sleep with eyes open and stereotyped hypermotor posturing.

In a true generalised tonic-clonic seizure, the eyes are open during the convulsion, the ictal EEG shows generalised spike-wave activity followed by post-ictal suppression, and the patient has no recall.
f: continuous tonic-clonic seizing with open eyes, cyanosis and continuous ictal spike-wave discharges on EEG
a 10-second pale collapse while standing in a hot room with rapid full recovery on lying flat
stereotyped 20-second nocturnal episodes arising from sleep with eyes open, asymmetric tonic posturing and rapid recovery
a 90-second tonic-clonic convulsion with open eyes, cyanosis, lateral tongue bite and generalised spike-wave on EEG

hq_q.s:
A 6 week old baby has noisy breathing on breathing in, worse when feeding, crying or lying on his back. He is feeding well and gaining weight.
His colour is good and there is no recession.
hq_q.w: Laryngomalacia is a floppy larynx that collapses on breathing in. It usually settles by 18 to 24 months. Refer if feeding, growth or breathing are affected.
hq_q.f: Stridor with poor weight gain and apnoeas → ENT for airway assessment.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: worse when feeding, crying or lying on his back
tm.m: Soft laryngeal tissue folds in on breathing in
tm.g: Thriving baby with positional inspiratory stridor is laryngomalacia
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to IV antibiotics (There is no infection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Nebulised adrenaline (For croup)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral dexamethasone (For croup)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Urgent tracheostomy (Not needed in a well, growing baby)
x: There is no infection
For croup
For croup
Not needed in a well, growing baby

hq_q.s:
A newborn baby girl delivered at term develops central cyanosis and severe subcostal recession in the delivery room whenever she attempts to breastfeed, but turns pink immediately whenever she begins to cry.
On examination, lung fields are clear during crying, heart sounds are normal, and a fine-bore nasogastric catheter cannot be advanced past 3 cm through either nostril.
hq_q.w: Neonates are obligate nasal breathers. Bilateral congenital choanal atresia (often part of CHARGE syndrome) causes paradoxical cyanosis during feeding that resolves when crying opens the oral airway, confirmed by inability to pass a nasal catheter.
hq_q.f: Frothy saliva and choking on the first feed with the tube coiling in the chest → oesophageal atresia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: turns pink immediately whenever she begins to cry
cannot be advanced past 3 cm through either nostril
tm.m: Obligate nasal breathing in neonates causes asphyxia when posterior nasal choanae are occluded, relieved when crying opens the oral airway
tm.g: Neonatal cyanosis worse on feeding and relieved by crying + failure to pass nasal catheter -> bilateral choanal atresia
f: a 3 month old infant with coryza, persistent tachypnoea, chest recession and widespread fine crackles
a 4 week old infant with inspiratory stridor worse when supine and crying, with normal nasal patency
copious frothy saliva and choking on first feed with the nasogastric tube coiling in the upper chest on X-ray
severe micrognathia, posterior displacement of the tongue and a U-shaped cleft palate
x: Viral bronchiolitis presents at 1 to 6 months of age with coryza, cough, tachypnoea, and fine crackles rather than at birth with occluded nostrils.
Laryngomalacia causes positional high-pitched inspiratory stridor from a floppy omega-shaped epiglottis that worsens on crying or feeding, with patent nostrils.
Oesophageal atresia presents with maternal polyhydramnios, frothy oral secretions, choking on feeds, and a nasogastric tube coiling in the upper mediastinum at 10 cm.
Pierre Robin sequence presents with micrognathia, glossoptosis, and a U-shaped cleft palate causing airway obstruction when supine, but nasal catheters pass through the choanae.

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old man who drinks 25 units of vodka daily is admitted to the trauma ward at 10:00 with a displaced intracapsular neck of femur fracture after a mechanical fall. He had his last alcoholic drink at 20:00 yesterday evening.
The ward team prescribes parenteral thiamine and a symptom-triggered chlordiazepoxide chart and monitors for delirium tremens.
o: 12 to 24 hours after his last drink
1 to 2 hours after his last drink
3 to 4 weeks after his last drink
48 to 72 hours after his last drink
7 to 10 days after his last drink
hq_q.w: After stopping alcohol in chronic dependence, simple withdrawal tremor begins at 6 to 12 hours, withdrawal seizures peak at 12 to 48 hours, and delirium tremens (agitation, confusion, hallucinations, and autonomic instability) peaks at 48 to 72 hours.
hq_q.f: Fit at 24 hours → alcohol withdrawal seizure.
hq_q.ql: When are delirium tremens most likely to start?

tm.m: Chronic ethanol exposure downregulates inhibitory GABA-A receptors and upregulates excitatory NMDA glutamate receptors, peaking in hyperexcitability at 48-72 hours
tm.g: Peak onset window for delirium tremens after the last alcoholic drink -> 48 to 72 hours
f: early morning hand tremor, sweating, anxiety and nausea without confusion
acute alcohol intoxication with slurred speech and cerebellar ataxia
relapse prevention follow-up with acamprosate after completing inpatient detoxification
completing a 7-day reducing oral chlordiazepoxide detoxification regimen
x: Six to 12 hours is the onset window for early uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal (tremor, sweating, anxiety, and nausea), before delirium tremens develops.
At 1 to 2 hours after the last drink, blood alcohol concentrations are still elevated and withdrawal has not begun.
Delirium tremens is an acute withdrawal state occurring at 2 to 3 days, not weeks after abstinence.
By 7 to 10 days after alcohol cessation, acute withdrawal and delirium tremens have usually resolved.

hq_q.s: A 28 year old woman is referred to the hypertension clinic with blood pressure poorly controlled despite adherent therapy with amlodipine, indapamide and doxazosin. She has never smoked and has no family history of kidney disease. Temperature 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 168/102 mmHg. Auscultation reveals a systolic-diastolic bruit in the right epigastrium. CT renal angiography demonstrates a 'string-of-beads' appearance of the mid-to-distal right renal artery.
hq_q.w: Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory vascular disease that characteristically affects young women (aged 15-50 years), causing medial fibroplasia of the mid-to-distal renal artery with a classic 'string-of-beads' angiographic appearance and secondary renovascular hypertension responsive to percutaneous transluminal renal angioplasty.
hq_q.f: Older arteriopath (>60 years) with proximal ostial renal artery narrowing and flash pulmonary oedema -> atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

c: systolic-diastolic bruit in the right epigastrium
'string-of-beads' appearance of the mid-to-distal right renal artery
tm.m: Alternating segments of medial fibromuscular ridges and aneurysmal thinning in the distal renal artery reduce renal perfusion pressure, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
tm.g: Young woman with resistant hypertension + renal bruit + 'string-of-beads' renal artery on CT angiography = fibromuscular dysplasia
x: Phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting chromaffin tumour presenting with episodic headache, sweating, pallor and elevated plasma metanephrines.
Atherosclerotic stenosis typically affects the proximal renal artery ostium in older smokers (>55 years) with generalised peripheral or coronary vascular disease.
ADPKD presents with bilaterally enlarged ballotable kidneys containing multiple parenchymal cysts and a positive family history.
Aortic coarctation causes upper-limb hypertension with radio-femoral delay and diminished femoral pulses rather than a beaded distal renal artery.
f: She experiences paroxysmal headaches, drenching sweats and tachycardia with elevated 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines.
A 72 year old smoker with intermittent claudication develops a 35% rise in serum creatinine 1 week after starting ramipril.
Renal ultrasound demonstrates bilaterally enlarged kidneys replaced by numerous fluid-filled cysts alongside hepatic cysts.
A 19 year old man has hypertension in his arms, weak delayed femoral pulses and inferior rib notching on chest X-ray.

hq_q.s: A 66 year old man presents to his GP after developing three separate episodes of tender, erythematous, palpable cord-like superficial veins over his left forearm, right calf and anterior chest wall over the past 8 weeks, each resolving over 10 days as a new lesion appeared elsewhere. Over the same period, he has lost 6 kg in weight and developed a constant dull epigastric ache that radiates straight through to his mid-back. Physical examination reveals epigastric tenderness and mild scleral icterus.
o: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen (pancreatic protocol)
Inherited thrombophilia blood panel (Factor V Leiden and Protein C)
hq_q.w: Recurrent, crops of superficial thrombophlebitis appearing in shifting anatomical locations (arms, trunk and legs) is migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau's sign of malignancy). It is a paraneoplastic hypercoagulable syndrome caused by mucin-secreting adenocarcinomas (most classically carcinoma of the body or tail of the pancreas, as well as gastric or lung adenocarcinoma) releasing tissue factor-bearing microparticles and sialylated mucins that activate factor X. Combined with 6 kg weight loss, jaundice and dull epigastric pain radiating to the back, an urgent pancreatic-protocol contrast CT of the abdomen is mandatory.
hq_q.f: A single tender varicose vein after a knock → superficial thrombophlebitis, compression and NSAIDs.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate urgent diagnostic investigation?

c: three separate episodes of tender, erythematous, palpable cord-like superficial veins
left forearm, right calf and anterior chest wall
lost 6 kg in weight and developed a constant dull epigastric ache that radiates straight through to his mid-back
tm.m: Mucin-secreting pancreatic adenocarcinoma releases tissue-factor microparticles -> systemic activation of coagulation cascade -> migratory superficial thrombophlebitis (Trousseau's sign)
tm.g: Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis (Trousseau's sign) + weight loss + epigastric pain radiating to the back = pancreatic carcinoma -> urgent contrast CT abdomen
x: A lower-limb venous Doppler evaluates local deep vein extension of a single leg thrombophlebitis, but misses the underlying pancreatic malignancy driving migratory lesions across the arms and trunk
Inherited thrombophilias present with venous thromboembolism in young patients (<45 years) with a family history, not new migratory thrombophlebitis and weight loss at age 66
Migratory thrombophlebitis is a sterile paraneoplastic thrombosis, not septic thrombophlebitis from an infected cannula
D-dimer is non-specifically elevated in both superficial thrombophlebitis and malignancy and does not identify the primary tumour
f: isolated superficial thrombophlebitis of the long saphenous vein above the knee to exclude propagation into the femoral vein
24 year old with unprovoked proximal DVT whose mother and sister both had pulmonary emboli in their twenties
purulent erythema and high fever over a peripheral intravenous cannula site left in situ for 6 days
low-probability Wells score assessment in a young patient with acute pleuritic chest pain

hq_q.s: A 34 year old woman attends the Haematology Clinic following a proximal left femoral deep vein thrombosis currently treated with low-molecular-weight heparin. She has a past obstetric history of two unexplained fetal losses at 14 and 18 weeks' gestation. She has no malar rash, arthralgia or renal impairment, and is not currently pregnant. Baseline coagulation tests before starting heparin showed a prolonged APTT that failed to correct on a 50:50 normal plasma mixing study, alongside strongly positive anti-cardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I IgG antibodies repeated 12 weeks apart.
hq_q.w: This woman meets the Revised Sapporo (Sydney) classification criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome (vascular thrombosis + pregnancy morbidity [>=1 unexplained loss of a morphologically normal fetus >=10 weeks] + persistent lupus anticoagulant/anti-cardiolipin/anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I antibodies on two occasions >=12 weeks apart). Note the classic paradox of lupus anticoagulant: in vitro it binds phospholipid reagent in the laboratory tube to prolong the APTT (which fails to correct on 50:50 mixing), whereas in vivo it binds endothelial and platelet beta-2-glycoprotein I to cause severe arterial and venous thrombosis. Long-term oral anticoagulation must be warfarin (target INR 2.0 to 3.0); DOACs are contraindicated due to high recurrent thrombosis risk.
hq_q.f: First provoked DVT after surgery with no antibodies → a DOAC for 3 months.
hq_q.ql: Which oral agent is most appropriate for her long-term anticoagulation?

c: proximal left femoral deep vein thrombosis
two unexplained fetal losses at 14 and 18 weeks' gestation
prolonged APTT that failed to correct on a 50:50 normal plasma mixing study
tm.m: Lupus anticoagulant binds in-vitro phospholipid (prolonging APTT on mixing study) while activating platelets/endothelium in vivo -> triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome -> requires warfarin (avoid DOACs)
tm.g: DVT/PE + recurrent miscarriages (>10 weeks) + prolonged APTT not correcting on 50:50 mix = antiphospholipid syndrome -> long-term warfarin (not DOACs)
x: Direct factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban are inferior to warfarin in antiphospholipid syndrome and carry a higher risk of arterial and venous recurrence
Dabigatran is similarly contraindicated in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome
Low-dose aspirin alone is insufficient after a confirmed venous thromboembolism, which requires full therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin
Rivaroxaban showed significantly higher rates of recurrent thromboembolism and stroke than warfarin in the TRAPS trial of antiphospholipid syndrome
f: first-line oral anticoagulant for a standard proximal DVT in a patient with normal baseline APTT and negative antiphospholipid antibodies
alternative DOAC in non-antiphospholipid VTE when a direct thrombin inhibitor is preferred
pre-conception / early pregnancy prophylaxis (combined with LMWH once pregnant) in obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome WITHOUT prior venous thrombosis
standard once-daily DOAC for provoked lower-limb DVT in a patient without antiphospholipid syndrome

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old man with a 15-year history of recurrent untreated peptic ulcer disease presents to the Emergency Department with a 7-day history of projectile vomiting of large volumes of stale, undigested food eaten several hours earlier. The vomit is never bile-stained, and he has lost 4 kg.
Pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 106/68 mmHg. Examination reveals dehydration, visible epigastric peristalsis and an audible epigastric succussion splash on gentle shaking.
hq_q.w: Chronic cicatricial scarring and oedema from recurrent duodenal bulb or pyloric channel ulcers (or distal antral carcinoma) causes mechanical gastric outlet obstruction (pyloric stenosis). It presents with large-volume non-bilious vomiting of stale food, early satiety, weight loss, an epigastric succussion splash, and a classic hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (Cl 82 mmol/L, K 2.9 mmol/L, HCO3 38 mmol/L) from vomiting gastric HCl.
