hq_q.f: Bile-stained vomiting with distension and colicky pain → small bowel obstruction.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Pyloric stricture blocks chyme entry into the duodenum; vomiting gastric HCl depletes H+ and Cl-, while hypovolaemia activates aldosterone, driving renal K+ and H+ loss (paradoxical aciduria).
tm.g: Non-bilious vomiting of stale food + succussion splash + hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis -> gastric outlet obstruction
x: Diabetic gastroparesis occurs in long-standing poorly controlled diabetes with autonomic neuropathy rather than chronic peptic ulcer scarring.
A tumour at the proximal gastric cardia/fundus obstructs the gastro-oesophageal junction, causing early dysphagia and immediate regurgitation before food enters the stomach.
Obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater in the second part of the duodenum produces dark green, heavily bile-stained vomiting and metabolic acidosis/normal bicarbonate.
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome causes watery secretory diarrhoea and multiple jejunal ulcers rather than mechanical pyloric obstruction with a succussion splash.
f: a patient with a 20-year history of poorly controlled type 1 diabetes, retinopathy and postural hypotension had delayed gastric emptying with a normal pylorus on endoscopy
he had progressive difficulty swallowing solids at the xiphisternum with immediate regurgitation of swallowed food and no succussion splash
he had colicky central abdominal pain, distension and profuse dark-green bilious vomiting following a previous laparotomy
he had multiple jejunal ulcers, chronic watery diarrhoea, hypercalcaemia and a fasting serum gastrin of 1,400 ng/L

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman presents with a 3-week history of headaches and nausea that are worst at home, but clear within hours of arriving at her office. Her husband and two young children have developed similar headaches, and their gas boiler has not been serviced for 4 years.
Pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, SpO2 99% on standard pulse oximetry. Neurological examination is normal.
o: Contrast CT scan of the head
hq_q.w: Headaches and nausea affecting multiple household members that worsen at home and clear away from the building indicate carbon monoxide poisoning. Standard pulse oximetry reads carboxyhaemoglobin as normal SpO2, so measure blood carboxyhaemoglobin by co-oximetry.
hq_q.f: Single patient with morning headache, vomiting and bilateral papilloedema -> contrast CT or MRI head to exclude a space-occupying lesion.
hq_q.ql: Which diagnostic test is most appropriate?

c: worst at home, but clear within hours of arriving at her office
husband and two young children have developed similar headaches
gas boiler has not been serviced for 4 years
tm.m: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with ~240 times the affinity of oxygen to form carboxyhaemoglobin, shifting the oxygen dissociation curve to the left and absorbing 660 nm light identically to oxyhaemoglobin on standard pulse oximeters.
tm.g: Household cluster of headaches/nausea improving away from home + unserviced boiler -> blood carboxyhaemoglobin level (co-oximetry)
x: An intracranial mass lesion does not affect four members of the same family simultaneously or resolve at work.
Lumbar puncture investigates meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage and does not diagnose environmental carbon monoxide poisoning.
Standard two-wavelength pulse oximeters measure carboxyhaemoglobin as if it were oxygenated haemoglobin, giving a falsely reassuring SpO2 reading of 98-100%.
Chronic lead poisoning causes abdominal colic, constipation, peripheral motor neuropathy (wrist drop) and basophilic stippling over months rather than acute headaches that clear within hours at work.
f: a single patient presenting with progressive morning headache, focal hemiparesis and papilloedema
acute fever, neck stiffness and photophobia in a single patient
monitoring arterial oxygenation in acute asthma or pneumonia without carbon monoxide exposure
a battery recycling worker or child eating old paint flakes with abdominal colic, microcytic anaemia and basophilic stippling

hq_q.s: A 68 year old man on the Coronary Care Unit is 3 days post-inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. He becomes lightheaded when sitting upright. Temperature 36.4°C, pulse rate 38 bpm regular, BP 84/52 mmHg, SpO2 96% breathing air. Cannon a waves are visible in the jugular venous pulse. His 12-lead ECG shows P waves at 88/min and narrow QRS complexes at 38/min with complete atrioventricular dissociation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological treatment while preparing for temporary pacing?
hq_q.w: Under Resuscitation Council UK ALS bradycardia guidelines, symptomatic bradycardia with adverse signs (systolic BP <90 mmHg, heart rate <40 bpm) from post-inferior MI complete heart block is treated first-line with intravenous atropine 500 micrograms (repeated up to 3 mg).
hq_q.f: Asymptomatic first-degree heart block (PR interval 240 ms) with normal blood pressure post-inferior MI -> continue cardiac monitoring without atropine or pacing.

c: pulse rate 38 bpm regular, BP 84/52 mmHg
tm.m: Competitive muscarinic (M2) receptor antagonism reverses excessive vagal tone at the ischaemic AV node (supplied by the right coronary artery), accelerating junctional conduction
tm.g: Symptomatic bradycardia / complete heart block with adverse features (BP < 90 mmHg, HR < 40 bpm): IV atropine 500 micrograms bolus first-line (up to 3 mg)
x: Adenosine transiently blocks the AV node and is strictly contraindicated in second- or third-degree heart block as it worsens bradycardia.
Amiodarone suppresses sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodal conduction and would dangerously slow his junctional escape rhythm in complete heart block.
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers depress AV nodal conduction and myocardial contractility, risking asystole in complete heart block.
Beta-blockers are contraindicated in complete heart block and hypotension because they suppress the subsidiary junctional escape pacemaker.
f: He has a haemodynamically stable regular narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia at 184 bpm refractory to vagal manoeuvres.
He develops haemodynamically stable sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia at 170 bpm.
A patient with severe asthma has a regular narrow-complex SVT with normal blood pressure and no AV block.
He is in normal sinus rhythm at 74 bpm with BP 132/80 mmHg awaiting discharge for secondary post-MI prevention.

hq_q.s:
A 62 year old lifelong smoker attends the Respiratory Clinic with 9 months of progressive exertional breathlessness. He has a 45 pack-year smoking history.
Respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 93% breathing air. Examination reveals a barrel-shaped chest, hyperresonant percussion and reduced breath sounds, with no basal velcro crackles or digital clubbing. Full pulmonary function testing is performed.
hq_q.ql: Which pattern of spirometry, lung volumes and gas transfer (TLCO) is most characteristic of pulmonary emphysema?
o: FEV1/FVC 0.54, TLC 128% predicted, RV 145% predicted, TLCO 48% predicted
FEV1/FVC 0.56, TLC 115% predicted, RV 125% predicted, TLCO 98% predicted
FEV1/FVC 0.79, TLC 96% predicted, RV 94% predicted, TLCO 54% predicted
FEV1/FVC 0.82, TLC 64% predicted, RV 68% predicted, TLCO 52% predicted
FEV1/FVC 0.84, TLC 66% predicted, RV 75% predicted, TLCO 96% predicted
hq_q.w: Pulmonary emphysema causes fixed airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC <0.70), hyperinflation and gas trapping (elevated TLC and markedly elevated RV), plus a reduced carbon monoxide transfer factor (TLCO) due to destruction of alveolar-capillary membranes.
hq_q.f: chronic bronchitis or stable asthma with intact alveolar capillary membranes → FEV1/FVC 0.56, TLC 115% predicted, RV 125% predicted, TLCO 98% predicted.

c: no basal velcro crackles or digital clubbing
tm.m: Protease-mediated destruction of alveolar walls reduces elastic recoil (causing premature small-airway collapse, FEV1/FVC <0.70 and high RV/TLC) and obliterates alveolar-capillary beds (low TLCO).
tm.g: Pulmonary emphysema -> obstructive FEV1/FVC (<0.70) + raised TLC and RV + reduced TLCO
x: Airflow obstruction with a preserved or slightly high TLCO (98% predicted) occurs in asthma or isolated chronic bronchitis where alveolar-capillary membranes remain intact.
Normal spirometry and lung volumes with an isolated reduction in TLCO indicate pulmonary vascular disease (such as pulmonary arterial hypertension or chronic thromboembolism).
A high FEV1/FVC ratio (>0.70) with reduced TLC, reduced RV and reduced TLCO represents intrinsic parenchymal restriction such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
A restrictive ventilatory defect with a normal transfer factor (TLCO 96% predicted) occurs in extraparenchymal restriction such as kyphoscoliosis, obesity or neuromuscular weakness.
f: the patient had poorly controlled atopic asthma with airflow obstruction and intact alveolar-capillary gas transfer
a patient with systemic sclerosis or recurrent pulmonary emboli developed pulmonary hypertension with normal lung volumes and isolated low TLCO
the patient had idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with digital clubbing and bibasal end-inspiratory velcro crackles
the patient had extraparenchymal chest wall restriction from severe ankylosing spondylitis or neuromuscular diaphragm weakness

hq_q.s:
A 54 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has had fever, abdominal pain and mild confusion for 1 day. He takes spironolactone and furosemide for ascites.
Temperature 38.3°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg. There is shifting dullness and diffuse abdominal tenderness.
Ascitic tap: cloudy fluid with a neutrophil count of 420 per mm³ and a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 16 g/L.
hq_q.ql: Alongside IV antibiotics, which infusion reduces his risk of hepatorenal syndrome and death?
hq_q.w: Ascitic neutrophils over 250 per mm³ confirm spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Alongside antibiotics, IV albumin on day 1 and day 3 cuts hepatorenal syndrome and death by refilling the underfilled circulation.
hq_q.f: Dehydration without cirrhosis or portal hypertension → 0.9% saline.

tm.m: SBP dilates the gut vessels, the kidneys see too little blood and clamp down; albumin refills the circulation
tm.g: SBP: antibiotics plus IV albumin to prevent hepatorenal syndrome
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to 0.9% saline 1 litre over 2 hours (Saline adds sodium and worsens ascites without the oncotic effect that protects the kidneys in SBP)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fresh frozen plasma (FFP corrects clotting before a procedure; it does not prevent hepatorenal syndrome)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV furosemide (Diuretics are stopped in SBP because they drain the circulation and push the kidneys into failure)

the presentation instead showed features specific to Terlipressin without albumin (Terlipressin treats established hepatorenal syndrome and works with albumin, not instead of it, and is not prevention)
x: Saline adds sodium and worsens ascites without the oncotic effect that protects the kidneys in SBP.
FFP corrects clotting before a procedure; it does not prevent hepatorenal syndrome.
Diuretics are stopped in SBP because they drain the circulation and push the kidneys into failure.
Terlipressin treats established hepatorenal syndrome and works with albumin, not instead of it, and is not prevention.

hq_q.s:
A 22 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has had vomiting and abdominal pain for 2 days. She is breathing deeply.
Pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg. She has had a 1 litre bolus of 0.9% saline and a fixed-rate insulin infusion is being prescribed.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate potassium plan for her next fluid?
o: 40 mmol per litre with each bag
hq_q.w: In DKA, insulin drives potassium into cells. JBDS adds 40 mmol per litre when potassium is 3.5 to 5.5, none above 5.5, and below 3.5 asks for senior review because more is needed, often through a central line in a higher-care area.
hq_q.f: Potassium 4.2 in DKA → 40 mmol per litre in the fluid.

tm.m: Insulin pushes potassium into cells, so a low starting potassium falls further once insulin runs
tm.g: DKA with potassium under 3.5: senior review for extra potassium
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to 20 mmol per litre (20 mmol is too little at any level in DKA; the standard is 40 mmol per litre)
her potassium were 4.2 mmol/L
her potassium were 5.9 mmol/L
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral potassium tablets (She is vomiting and acidotic; replacement must be IV)
x: 20 mmol is too little at any level in DKA; the standard is 40 mmol per litre.
This is the plan for potassium of 3.5 to 5.5; hers is 3.2 and needs more.
Potassium is withheld only when it is above 5.5.
She is vomiting and acidotic; replacement must be IV.

hq_q.s: A 34 year old woman presents to the Endocrine Clinic with a 3-week history of a painful, tender anterior neck swelling radiating to her jaw and ears, accompanied by palpitations, tremor and a 3 kg weight loss. She recovered from a viral upper respiratory tract infection 4 weeks ago. Her pulse is 108 bpm, temperature is 37.8°C, and the thyroid gland is diffusely firm and exquisitely tender without a bruit. TSH is <0.01 mU/L, free T4 is 38 pmol/L (12-22), ESR is 78 mm/hour and TSH-receptor antibodies are negative.
hq_q.ql: What will a technetium-99m pertechnetate thyroid uptake scan show, and what is the most appropriate management?
o: Cold solitary nodule; arrange urgent diagnostic hemithyroidectomy
Diffusely decreased (absent) uptake; start propranolol and an NSAID (or prednisolone if severe)
Diffusely increased uptake; start carbimazole 40 mg once daily
Focal hot nodule with suppression of surrounding tissue; arrange radioiodine therapy
Patchy increased and decreased uptake; start propylthiouracil
hq_q.w: De Quervain's (subacute granulomatous) thyroiditis follows a viral prodrome and presents with a painful, exquisitely tender goitre radiating to the jaw/ears, fever, markedly raised ESR and transient hyperthyroidism caused by leakage of preformed colloid hormone from inflamed follicles. Because pituitary TSH is suppressed and follicular trapping is disrupted, technetium-99m / radioiodine uptake is globally absent (<1%). Thionamides (carbimazole/PTU) are ineffective because no new hormone is being synthesised; management is oral propranolol for adrenergic symptoms plus an NSAID (or oral prednisolone for severe pain).
hq_q.f: painless goitre with bruit, exophthalmos, pretibial myxoedema, and positive TRAB (Graves disease) → Diffusely increased uptake; start carbimazole 40 mg daily.

c: painful, tender anterior neck swelling radiating to her jaw and ears
viral upper respiratory tract infection 4 weeks ago
ESR is 78 mm/hour and TSH-receptor antibodies are negative
tm.m: Post-viral granulomatous follicular inflammation -> leaks preformed T4/T3 -> suppressed TSH + follicular damage causes globally absent tracer uptake -> treat with beta-blocker + NSAID/steroid
tm.g: Painful tender post-viral goitre + high fT4 + raised ESR = De Quervain's thyroiditis -> diffusely absent scan uptake; treat with propranolol + NSAID/prednisolone (not carbimazole)
x: A solitary cold nodule in a euthyroid patient raises suspicion for thyroid malignancy (requiring ultrasound/FNA), not acute painful post-viral thyrotoxicosis
Diffusely increased uptake treated with carbimazole is characteristic of Graves' disease (painless goitre with bruit, orbitopathy and positive TRAB)
A single hyperfunctioning hot nodule with contralateral suppression describes a solitary toxic adenoma
Patchy heterogeneous uptake describes a toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer's disease) in an older patient
f: euthyroid patient with a painless firm 2.5 cm thyroid nodule showing Thy4 suspicious cytology on fine-needle aspiration
painless diffuse goitre with systolic bruit, exophthalmos, pretibial myxoedema and positive TSH-receptor antibodies
painless 3 cm left thyroid nodule with TSH <0.01 mU/L, negative TRAB and isolated focal hyperfunctioning uptake
72 year old woman with a longstanding lumpy goitre, atrial fibrillation and heterogeneous areas of autonomous uptake

hq_q.s:
A 63 year old man with hypertension has sudden severe vertigo, vomiting, hiccups, hoarseness and difficulty swallowing.
There is left ptosis and a small left pupil, an absent gag reflex on the left and left limb ataxia. Pain and temperature sensation are lost on the left side of the face and the right side of the body. Power is normal.
hq_q.ql: Which artery is most likely to be blocked?
hq_q.w: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: vertigo, dysphagia, hoarseness and hiccups, ipsilateral Horner's, ataxia and facial pain and temperature loss, with contralateral body pain and temperature loss. It is caused by PICA or vertebral artery occlusion.
hq_q.f: The same crossed sensory loss with facial weakness and deafness → AICA (lateral pons).

c: left side of the face and the right side of the body
tm.m: The lateral medulla carries the swallowing nuclei, sympathetic fibres and both pain pathways, but not the motor tracts
tm.g: Crossed pain loss, Horner's and bulbar palsy with normal power: PICA, lateral medullary syndrome
f: he also had facial weakness and deafness on the left
the presentation instead showed features specific to Anterior spinal artery (The medial medulla gives contralateral weakness and loss of vibration sense; his power is normal)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Basilar artery (Basilar occlusion causes coma, quadriplegia or locked-in syndrome, not this crossed sensory pattern)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Posterior cerebral artery (PCA infarcts cause a contralateral visual field loss, not bulbar palsy)
x: AICA infarcts the lateral pons, adding facial weakness and deafness rather than hoarseness and dysphagia.
The medial medulla gives contralateral weakness and loss of vibration sense; his power is normal.
Basilar occlusion causes coma, quadriplegia or locked-in syndrome, not this crossed sensory pattern.
PCA infarcts cause a contralateral visual field loss, not bulbar palsy.

hq_q.s:
A 36 year old woman has had 2 days of fluctuating confusion, headache and fever. She has bruises on her legs.
Temperature 38.1°C, GCS 13. There are petechiae over her shins and no neck stiffness. A blood film shows many schistocytes.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
hq_q.w: Fever, confusion, very low platelets and haemolysis with schistocytes and normal clotting is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. It needs urgent plasma exchange with steroids (often caplacizumab and rituximab too). Platelet transfusion is avoided because it can feed new clots.
hq_q.f: Bloody diarrhoea in a child, then kidney failure with schistocytes → haemolytic uraemic syndrome; supportive care.

tm.m: Without ADAMTS13, very large von Willebrand multimers string platelets into clots in small vessels
tm.g: Low platelets + schistocytes + confusion + normal clotting: TTP, plasma exchange
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Cryoprecipitate (Cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen in DIC; her clotting and fibrinogen are normal)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Eculizumab (Eculizumab treats complement-driven atypical HUS; TTP is first treated with plasma exchange)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV immunoglobulin (IVIG treats immune thrombocytopenia, which has no haemolysis or schistocytes)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Platelet transfusion (Platelet transfusion can worsen the small-vessel clots in TTP and is avoided unless bleeding is life threatening)
x: Cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen in DIC; her clotting and fibrinogen are normal.
Eculizumab treats complement-driven atypical HUS; TTP is first treated with plasma exchange.
IVIG treats immune thrombocytopenia, which has no haemolysis or schistocytes.
Platelet transfusion can worsen the small-vessel clots in TTP and is avoided unless bleeding is life threatening.

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old woman presents with a 2-week history of right temporal headache, scalp tenderness when combing her hair, and jaw pain that worsens while chewing. Two hours ago she experienced a sudden curtain-like loss of vision in her right eye.
Examination shows a tender, non-pulsatile right temporal artery, a right relative afferent pupillary defect and a pale, swollen right optic disc. ESR is 94 mm/hour.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
o: Arrange temporal artery biopsy before starting steroids
Start oral prednisolone 15 mg once daily
Start oral prednisolone 40 mg after clinic review
hq_q.w: Giant cell arteritis complicated by acute visual loss (anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy with pale swollen disc and RAPD) requires immediate high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (500 mg to 1 g daily) to protect the fellow eye before biopsy.
hq_q.f: Giant cell arteritis WITHOUT visual symptoms -> start immediate high-dose oral prednisolone (40 to 60 mg daily) today.

c: jaw pain that worsens while chewing
sudden curtain-like loss of vision in her right eye
tm.m: Granulomatous giant-cell inflammation of the posterior ciliary branches of the ophthalmic artery causes acute optic nerve head infarction; immediate intravenous pulse methylprednisolone halts fellow-eye occlusion.
tm.g: Giant cell arteritis WITH visual loss (pale swollen disc, RAPD) -> immediate high-dose IV methylprednisolone
x: Steroid treatment must never be delayed for temporal artery biopsy because contralateral blindness can occur within hours and granulomatous skip lesions remain identifiable for 1 to 2 weeks after starting steroids.
Sumatriptan is a vasoconstrictor used for acute migraine or cluster headache and is contraindicated in ischaemic optic neuropathy and giant cell arteritis.
Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily is the low dose used for isolated polymyalgia rheumatica and is completely insufficient to prevent bilateral blindness in giant cell arteritis.
Delaying corticosteroids until an outpatient clinic review next week in a patient with active visual loss carries a very high risk of permanent bilateral blindness.
f: never appropriate; temporal artery biopsy is always performed AFTER starting immediate corticosteroid therapy
an acute attack of cluster headache in a 35 year old man with unilateral periorbital pain and lacrimation
uncomplicated polymyalgia rheumatica (bilateral shoulder and pelvic girdle morning stiffness) without cranial or visual symptoms
immediate same-day oral prednisolone 40-60 mg is used when giant cell arteritis presents WITHOUT visual loss

hq_q.s:
A 29 year old woman is 33 weeks pregnant with severe pre-eclampsia. Four hours ago she started IV labetalol and a magnesium sulfate infusion. She is now drowsy.
Respiratory rate 8 breaths per minute. Her knee reflexes are absent. Urine output has been 10 ml an hour for 3 hours.
hq_q.ql: Alongside stopping the magnesium, which drug should be given?
hq_q.w: Magnesium is cleared by the kidneys, so oliguria lets it build up. Lost reflexes come first, then slow breathing and cardiac arrest. Stop the infusion and give 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate over 10 minutes.
hq_q.f: Eclamptic seizure → IV magnesium sulfate.

tm.m: Calcium competes with magnesium at the neuromuscular junction and heart
tm.g: Magnesium toxicity: stop the infusion and give IV calcium gluconate
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to IV diazepam (Diazepam deepens sedation and respiratory depression; it is a seizure drug)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV flumazenil (Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, which she has not had)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV lipid emulsion 20% (Lipid emulsion is for local anaesthetic toxicity)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV naloxone (Naloxone reverses opioids, which she has not had)
x: Diazepam deepens sedation and respiratory depression; it is a seizure drug.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, which she has not had.
Lipid emulsion is for local anaesthetic toxicity.
Naloxone reverses opioids, which she has not had.

hq_q.s:
A 27 year old woman has had mild left iliac fossa discomfort and dark vaginal spotting for 2 days. Her last period was 6 weeks ago.
Pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg. The abdomen is soft.
Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a 22 mm left adnexal mass with no fetal heartbeat and no free fluid. Serum hCG is 1,150 IU/L. She can attend follow-up.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?
hq_q.w: NICE offers methotrexate for an unruptured tubal ectopic under 35 mm with no heartbeat, no significant pain and hCG under 1,500 IU/L, if she can attend follow-up.
hq_q.f: Mass of 35 mm or more, a heartbeat or hCG of 5,000 or more → laparoscopic salpingectomy.

c: 22 mm left adnexal mass with no fetal heartbeat
tm.m: Methotrexate stops the fast-dividing trophoblast, so a small, quiet ectopic can be treated without surgery
tm.g: Tubal ectopic under 35 mm, no heartbeat, hCG under 1,500: methotrexate
f: hCG under 1,000 IU/L and falling, with no pain
a 42 mm mass with a visible heartbeat
the presentation instead showed features specific to Laparoscopic salpingotomy (Salpingotomy is for women with damage to the other tube, and still means surgery she does not need)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Repeat hCG in 48 hours (Serial hCG is for a pregnancy of unknown location; here the ectopic is already seen)
x: Expectant care needs hCG of 1,000 IU/L or less and falling; hers is 1,150.
Surgery is first-line with pain, a mass of 35 mm or more, a heartbeat or hCG of 5,000 or more.
Salpingotomy is for women with damage to the other tube, and still means surgery she does not need.
Serial hCG is for a pregnancy of unknown location; here the ectopic is already seen.

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia started clozapine 3 weeks ago. He has had a sore throat, mouth ulcers and fever for 2 days. He has no stiffness or tremor.
Temperature 38.6°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg. There is tonsillar exudate.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most important immediate action?
hq_q.w: Fever and sore throat in the first months of clozapine are agranulocytosis until proven otherwise. Withhold clozapine and check a full blood count with neutrophils the same day.
hq_q.f: Fever with rigidity and a CK of 12,000 on an antipsychotic → neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

c: sore throat, mouth ulcers and fever
tm.m: Clozapine can wipe out neutrophils, and infection then spreads unchecked
tm.g: Sore throat or fever on clozapine: stop it and check the neutrophils today
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Continue clozapine, give penicillin V (Treating the throat while continuing clozapine risks overwhelming sepsis if neutrophils are falling)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Halve clozapine, FBC in 1 week (Agranulocytosis develops in days; a week is far too long to wait)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IM procyclidine (Procyclidine treats acute dystonia; he has no movement disorder)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV dantrolene (Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia or severe NMS; he has no rigidity)
x: Treating the throat while continuing clozapine risks overwhelming sepsis if neutrophils are falling.
Agranulocytosis develops in days; a week is far too long to wait.
Procyclidine treats acute dystonia; he has no movement disorder.
Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia or severe NMS; he has no rigidity.

hq_q.s:
A 3 year old boy has had a fever of 39.4°C for 6 days that has not settled with paracetamol or ibuprofen. He is irritable.
Both eyes are red without discharge. His lips are red and cracked and he has a strawberry tongue. There is a widespread rash on his trunk, his palms and soles are red and swollen, and there is a 2 cm tender node on the right side of his neck.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
hq_q.w: Fever for 5 days or more with red eyes, red cracked lips and strawberry tongue, rash, hand and foot changes and a neck node is Kawasaki disease. IV immunoglobulin (2 g/kg) with aspirin within 10 days of onset cuts the risk of coronary artery aneurysms. He also needs an echocardiogram.
hq_q.f: Fever, sore throat with exudate, sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue but no red eyes → scarlet fever; phenoxymethylpenicillin.

c: palms and soles are red and swollen
tm.m: A medium-vessel vasculitis inflames the coronary arteries, which can balloon into aneurysms
tm.g: Kawasaki: IVIG and aspirin to protect the coronaries
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to IM adrenaline (Adrenaline treats anaphylaxis, with wheeze, stridor or collapse, not 6 days of fever)
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV benzylpenicillin (Antibiotics treat scarlet fever or sepsis; Kawasaki disease is a vasculitis, not an infection)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral prednisolone (Steroids are added for high-risk or resistant Kawasaki disease, but IVIG with aspirin comes first)

the presentation instead showed features specific to Paracetamol and reassurance (This is not a self-limiting viral rash; untreated Kawasaki disease causes coronary aneurysms in up to a quarter of children)
x: Adrenaline treats anaphylaxis, with wheeze, stridor or collapse, not 6 days of fever.
Antibiotics treat scarlet fever or sepsis; Kawasaki disease is a vasculitis, not an infection.
Steroids are added for high-risk or resistant Kawasaki disease, but IVIG with aspirin comes first.
This is not a self-limiting viral rash; untreated Kawasaki disease causes coronary aneurysms in up to a quarter of children.

hq_q.s:
A 46 year old woman had a total thyroidectomy for a multinodular goitre yesterday. Today her voice is hoarse and breathy and her cough is weak. She has no tingling around her mouth and the wound is flat and dry.
Pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 126/80 mmHg, oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Flexible nasendoscopy shows the left vocal cord fixed close to the midline.
o: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve injury
hq_q.w: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies every intrinsic muscle of the larynx except cricothyroid. Injury paralyses the cord on that side close to the midline, so the voice is hoarse and breathy and the cough is weak. It is the complication patients are warned about before thyroid surgery.
hq_q.f: Voice tires and cannot reach high notes but both cords move → external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of her voice change?

c: left vocal cord fixed close to the midline
tm.m: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs beside the inferior thyroid artery, and stretch or division leaves the cord paralysed near the midline
tm.g: Hoarse voice and weak cough with a fixed cord after thyroidectomy is recurrent laryngeal nerve injury
f: a voice that tires and cannot reach high notes with both cords moving
perioral tingling and an adjusted calcium of 1.85 on day 1
the presentation instead showed features specific to Laryngeal oedema from intubation (Gives a hoarse voice that settles over a day or two with both cords moving)
a rapidly swelling tense neck and stridor 4 hours after surgery
x: Weakens cricothyroid, so pitch and stamina suffer, but the cords move and the cough is strong
Her calcium is normal and she has no tingling or cramps
Gives a hoarse voice that settles over a day or two with both cords moving
The wound is flat and dry; a haematoma causes swelling and stridor, not one fixed cord

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man has had pain on opening his bowels for 9 weeks, like passing broken glass, with bright red blood on the paper. He has used a bulk-forming laxative and lidocaine ointment for 6 weeks with little change.
Gentle parting of the buttocks shows a longitudinal tear in the posterior midline with a skin tag at its lower end.
hq_q.w: A fissure present for more than 6 weeks is chronic. NICE advises topical glyceryl trinitrate 0.4% twice a day for 6 to 8 weeks, alongside the laxative, to relax the internal sphincter and let the tear heal. Surgery is kept for fissures that fail medical treatment.
hq_q.f: Fissure for 10 days → stool softeners and a short course of topical lidocaine; GTN is for chronic fissures.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Sphincter spasm cuts blood flow to the posterior midline, so the tear cannot heal until the sphincter relaxes
tm.g: Fissure beyond 6 weeks despite laxatives → topical GTN
f: painless bright red bleeding with a lump that prolapses and reduces itself
failure of 8 weeks of GTN followed by diltiazem ointment
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral metronidazole (Used for perianal sepsis, and he has no abscess or fistula)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Topical hydrocortisone (Soothes itching but does not relax the sphincter or heal a chronic fissure)
x: Treats internal haemorrhoids, which bleed painlessly, not a tear in the anoderm
Effective but risks incontinence, so it follows failed medical treatment
Used for perianal sepsis, and he has no abscess or fistula
Soothes itching but does not relax the sphincter or heal a chronic fissure

hq_q.s:
An 82 year old man in a nursing home has had increasing abdominal distension and no bowel movement or flatus for 3 days. He has long-standing constipation and Parkinson's disease. His abdomen is hugely distended, tympanic and only mildly tender.
Pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg. An abdominal X-ray shows a large dilated loop of bowel shaped like an inverted U, rising from the left iliac fossa towards the right upper quadrant.
hq_q.w: An elderly, constipated man with gross distension and a coffee bean loop rising from the left iliac fossa has a sigmoid volvulus: the sigmoid twists on its long mesentery. Without signs of ischaemia it is decompressed with flexible sigmoidoscopy and a flatus tube.
hq_q.f: The dilated loop starts in the right iliac fossa and points to the left upper quadrant → caecal volvulus.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: A long redundant sigmoid mesentery lets the loop twist, closing both ends so gas cannot escape
tm.g: Coffee bean loop from the left iliac fossa in a constipated elderly patient → sigmoid volvulus
f: a dilated loop from the right iliac fossa pointing to the left upper quadrant
the whole colon dilated with no transition point after a hip operation
the presentation instead showed features specific to Obstructing sigmoid carcinoma (Follows weeks of changing bowel habit and gives a cut-off, not one twisted loop)
bloody diarrhoea, fever and a transverse colon over 6 cm wide in ulcerative colitis
x: Arises from the right iliac fossa and is more common in younger adults
Dilates the colon diffusely with no single twisted loop
Follows weeks of changing bowel habit and gives a cut-off, not one twisted loop
Follows colitis or C. difficile with bloody diarrhoea and systemic toxicity

hq_q.s:
A 71 year old woman has had constant left lower abdominal pain for 2 days with fever and loss of appetite. She has had intermittent constipation for years. She opened her bowels today and is passing flatus.
Temperature 38.3°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 134/80 mmHg. There is tenderness and guarding in the left iliac fossa. The abdomen is not distended.
hq_q.w: Left iliac fossa pain with fever, local guarding and raised inflammatory markers in an older adult is acute diverticulitis, an inflamed sigmoid diverticulum. She is still passing stool and flatus with no distension, so this is not obstruction or volvulus.
hq_q.f: Sudden pain then bloody diarrhoea in a woman with atrial fibrillation and a raised lactate → ischaemic colitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: left lower abdominal pain for 2 days
tm.m: A faecolith blocks the neck of a sigmoid diverticulum, bacteria multiply and the wall becomes inflamed
tm.g: LIF pain, fever and a raised WCC and CRP with the bowels still working → diverticulitis
f: 3 months of looser stools, weight loss and a microcytic anaemia
sudden pain followed by bloody diarrhoea in a woman with atrial fibrillation
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ovarian torsion (Gives sudden severe one-sided pain with vomiting, usually in younger women, and fever comes late)
gross distension and absolute constipation with a coffee bean loop on X-ray
x: Causes a change in bowel habit, weight loss and anaemia, and her haemoglobin is normal
Presents with sudden pain and bloody diarrhoea, and her lactate is normal
Gives sudden severe one-sided pain with vomiting, usually in younger women, and fever comes late
She is passing flatus and the abdomen is not distended

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man has had colicky lower abdominal pain and a swollen abdomen for 4 days. He has not opened his bowels or passed flatus for 2 days and has started to vomit. Over the past 3 months his stools have become looser and he has lost 6 kg. He has never had abdominal surgery.
The abdomen is distended and tympanic with high-pitched bowel sounds. There are no hernias. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated colon down to the sigmoid with no gas in the rectum.
hq_q.w: Large bowel obstruction after months of changing bowel habit, weight loss and an iron deficiency picture is colorectal carcinoma until proven otherwise. It is the commonest cause of large bowel obstruction in the UK. He needs a CT of abdomen and pelvis to confirm the level, stage the tumour and plan decompression.
hq_q.f: Previous laparotomy with dilated small bowel and a collapsed colon → adhesions.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of his bowel obstruction?

c: looser and he has lost 6 kg
dilated colon down to the sigmoid
tm.m: A tumour slowly narrows the lumen, bleeds occultly and finally closes the bowel
tm.g: Large bowel obstruction plus weight loss and a microcytic anaemia → colorectal carcinoma
f: a previous laparotomy with dilated small bowel and a collapsed colon
years of left iliac fossa pain attacks and a smooth tapering narrowing without weight loss
an irreducible tender lump above and medial to the pubic tubercle
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sigmoid volvulus (Gives one twisted loop with sudden distension, not months of weight loss)
x: Cause small bowel obstruction after previous surgery, and he has had none
Can obstruct the colon but does not explain weight loss and iron deficiency
There are no hernias on examination
Gives one twisted loop with sudden distension, not months of weight loss

hq_q.s: A 63 year old man has had rectal bleeding mixed with his stool and a feeling of incomplete emptying for 2 months. Flexible sigmoidoscopy shows an ulcerated mass with rolled edges 6 cm from the anal verge, and a biopsy is taken.
hq_q.w: Six centimetres from the anal verge is the rectum, which is lined by glandular columnar epithelium, so well over 90% of cancers there are adenocarcinomas. Squamous cell carcinoma arises in the anal canal, below the dentate line, within about 4 cm of the verge.
hq_q.f: An ulcerated lesion at the anal margin in a man with HIV and anal warts → squamous cell carcinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely histological type?

tm.m: Columnar mucosa above the dentate line becomes an adenoma and then an adenocarcinoma
tm.g: Rectum means a glandular lining and adenocarcinoma; the anal canal means squamous
f: flushing, diarrhoea and wheeze with liver metastases
the presentation instead showed features specific to Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (A submucosal tumour most often in the stomach, rarely an ulcerated rectal mass)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lymphoma (Rare in the rectum and usually seen with immunosuppression or systemic symptoms)
an ulcerated lesion at the anal margin in a man with HIV and anal warts
x: Rare in the rectum and usually a small yellow submucosal nodule, not an ulcer with rolled edges
A submucosal tumour most often in the stomach, rarely an ulcerated rectal mass
Rare in the rectum and usually seen with immunosuppression or systemic symptoms
Belongs to the anal canal below the dentate line, closer to the verge than 6 cm

hq_q.s:
A 69 year old man has passed blood in his urine on and off for 3 weeks. It is painless and sometimes contains small clots. He smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 40 years and worked in a rubber factory. He has not travelled outside Europe.
Abdominal and rectal examinations are normal. Urine culture shows no growth. Flexible cystoscopy shows a papillary tumour on the bladder wall.
hq_q.w: Over 90% of bladder cancers in the UK are transitional cell, now called urothelial, carcinoma. Smoking and aromatic amines from the rubber and dye industries are the classic causes, and the usual tumour is papillary and presents with painless visible haematuria.
hq_q.f: Grew up beside the Nile with recurrent schistosomiasis → squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely histological type?

c: smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 40 years
tm.m: Carcinogens concentrated in urine sit against the urothelium and drive papillary growth
tm.g: Painless haematuria with smoking or dye work and a papillary bladder tumour → transitional cell carcinoma
f: a tumour at the bladder dome arising from a urachal remnant
a solid kidney mass on CT with a new left varicocele
the presentation instead showed features specific to Small cell carcinoma of bladder (Very rare in the bladder and solid rather than papillary)
recurrent schistosomiasis while growing up in Egypt
x: Rare, arising from urachal remnants at the dome or after bladder exstrophy
Arises in the kidney, and cystoscopy has found the tumour in the bladder
Very rare in the bladder and solid rather than papillary
Linked to schistosomiasis or long-term catheters, and he has neither

hq_q.s:
A 32 year old man is brought to his GP by his sister, who is worried that he has no friends. He works night shifts alone as a security guard and spends his free time doing jigsaws. He says he has never wanted a close relationship and does not mind what others think of him. He shows little emotion during the consultation.
He has no unusual beliefs, odd speech or perceptual disturbances and is not low in mood.
hq_q.w: He is detached by preference: he wants no relationships, is indifferent to praise or criticism and shows flat emotion. That is schizoid personality disorder. Schizotypal adds odd beliefs and speech, and people with avoidant personality disorder want relationships but fear rejection.
hq_q.f: Wants friends but avoids them for fear of being judged → avoidant personality disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: does not mind what others think
no unusual beliefs, odd speech or perceptual disturbances
tm.m: A lifelong preference for solitude and emotional coldness without the odd thinking of the schizophrenia spectrum
tm.g: Does not want people, flat affect and no odd beliefs → schizoid
f: rigid routines, intense narrow interests and social difficulty since early childhood
longs for friends but avoids them because he expects to be ridiculed
the presentation instead showed features specific to Schizophrenia (Needs psychotic symptoms, and he has no unusual beliefs or perceptual disturbance)
magical thinking, odd speech and believing strangers' comments are about him
x: Needs social communication difficulty and restricted, repetitive behaviour from early childhood, which is not described
Avoidant people want relationships and fear rejection, but he does not want them
Needs psychotic symptoms, and he has no unusual beliefs or perceptual disturbance
Adds eccentric beliefs, odd speech and ideas of reference, all absent here

hq_q.s:
A 61 year old man has had central chest tightness at rest for 2 hours. He takes no regular medication and has no history of bleeding.
Pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 148/90 mmHg. His ECG shows 1 mm ST depression in leads V4 to V6. He has been given aspirin 300 mg and fondaparinux. Coronary angiography is planned within 72 hours.
hq_q.w: A rising troponin with ST depression and no ST elevation is an NSTEMI. NICE recommends dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and ticagrelor for 12 months unless the bleeding risk is high, when clopidogrel is used instead. He has no bleeding history and a normal haemoglobin.
hq_q.f: A previous intracranial bleed or other high bleeding risk → clopidogrel with aspirin.
hq_q.ql: Which drug should be added to aspirin?

tm.m: Blocking the platelet P2Y12 receptor on top of aspirin stops more clot forming on the ruptured plaque
tm.g: NSTEMI with a normal bleeding risk → aspirin plus ticagrelor for 12 months
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Apixaban (An anticoagulant, added only when there is another reason such as atrial fibrillation)
a previous haemorrhagic stroke and a transfusion for a bleeding ulcer last year
the presentation instead showed features specific to Dipyridamole (Used after ischaemic stroke, not in acute coronary syndrome)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Warfarin (Has no place in acute coronary syndrome without another indication)
x: An anticoagulant, added only when there is another reason such as atrial fibrillation
A weaker P2Y12 blocker kept for high bleeding risk or when ticagrelor cannot be used
Used after ischaemic stroke, not in acute coronary syndrome
Has no place in acute coronary syndrome without another indication

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old woman has had a cough and wheeze for 4 months, worse at night and after running. She has never smoked. She had eczema as a child. Her chest X-ray is normal.
Spirometry is performed before and 15 minutes after salbutamol.
hq_q.w: Symptoms that vary and are worse at night and with exercise, atopy, obstruction that improves by 450 ml, 19%, after salbutamol and raised eosinophils fit asthma. Reversibility of at least 12% and 200 ml supports the diagnosis. The normal chest X-ray argues against sarcoidosis.
hq_q.f: A 40 pack-year smoker whose obstruction barely changes with salbutamol → COPD.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: worse at night and after running
tm.m: Eosinophilic airway inflammation makes smooth muscle twitchy, so narrowing comes and goes and reverses with a bronchodilator
tm.g: Reversible obstruction of at least 12% and 200 ml with atopy → asthma
f: a 40 pack-year smoker whose FEV1 rises by 50 ml after salbutamol
the presentation instead showed features specific to Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (Can cause a night cough but not reversible airflow obstruction)
dry cough, erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on X-ray
noisy breathing in, normal spirometry between attacks and a flattened inspiratory loop
x: She is a young non-smoker and her obstruction is largely reversible
Can cause a night cough but not reversible airflow obstruction
Usually shows hilar lymphadenopathy on the X-ray and a restrictive pattern
Narrows the larynx on breathing in, with a normal FEV1 and no response to salbutamol

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man has had increasing breathlessness on exertion for 2 years and a cough productive of black sputum. He worked underground in a coal mine for 28 years and has never smoked.
There are fine crackles at both apices. Chest X-ray shows multiple small rounded nodules, most numerous in the upper zones, with no pleural thickening.
hq_q.w: Years of coal dust, black sputum and small rounded upper zone nodules are coal workers' pneumoconiosis. Silicosis also gives upper zone nodules, but it follows quarrying, sandblasting or stonework and classically causes eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes. Asbestosis affects the lower zones with pleural plaques.
hq_q.f: A sandblaster with eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes → silicosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Inhaled coal dust is taken up by alveolar macrophages, which collect around respiratory bronchioles and form nodules
tm.g: Coal miner with upper zone nodules and black sputum → coal workers' pneumoconiosis
f: lagging pipes in a shipyard, calcified pleural plaques and lower zone fibrosis
a pigeon keeper with fevers a few hours after cleaning the loft
20 years of sandblasting and eggshell calcification of the hilar lymph nodes
the presentation instead showed features specific to Tuberculosis (Would bring weight loss, night sweats and cavitation rather than many small nodules over 2 years)
x: Causes lower zone fibrosis with pleural plaques, and his changes are upper zone without pleural disease
Follows organic antigens such as birds or mouldy hay, not coal dust
Follows quartz exposure in quarrying or sandblasting, typically with eggshell hilar calcification
Would bring weight loss, night sweats and cavitation rather than many small nodules over 2 years

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old woman has coughed up large amounts of thick yellow-green sputum every day for several years, about a cupful a day. She had severe whooping cough as a child. She has had 4 chest infections this year. She has never smoked.
Her fingers are clubbed. There are coarse inspiratory crackles at both lung bases that change after coughing.
hq_q.w: Daily copious purulent sputum, recurrent infections, whooping cough in childhood and coarse crackles that shift with coughing are bronchiectasis: permanently dilated bronchi that pool mucus. Clubbing is common. The diagnosis is confirmed on high-resolution CT.
hq_q.f: Fine dry crackles at the end of inspiration that do not clear with coughing, and no sputum → idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Infection damages the bronchial wall, the airways dilate, mucus pools and infection recurs in a vicious cycle
tm.g: Daily copious purulent sputum, recurrent infections and coarse crackles → bronchiectasis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Asthma (Causes variable wheeze and cough without daily purulent sputum or clubbing)
a 40 pack-year smoker with slowly worsening breathlessness and winter infections
fine dry end-inspiratory crackles, clubbing and no sputum in a 70 year old
a 2 week illness with swinging fever, foul sputum and a cavity with a fluid level after a seizure
x: Causes variable wheeze and cough without daily purulent sputum or clubbing
She has never smoked, and her sputum volume is far higher than COPD usually produces
Gives fine dry crackles that do not change with coughing and little sputum
An acute illness with a cavity, not years of daily sputum

hq_q.s:
A 55 year old man has had a daily cough with 2 tablespoons of purulent sputum for 3 years and has needed 5 courses of antibiotics in the past year. He has rheumatoid arthritis.
There are coarse crackles at the right base. Chest X-ray shows thickened bronchial walls at the right base with tramline shadows. Spirometry shows mild airflow obstruction.
hq_q.w: Bronchiectasis is diagnosed on high-resolution CT, which shows bronchi wider than the artery beside them, the signet ring sign, and bronchi that fail to taper. Rheumatoid arthritis is a recognised cause. Sputum culture guides antibiotics but does not make the diagnosis.
hq_q.f: Persistent collapse of one lobe with haemoptysis in a smoker → bronchoscopy to look for an obstructing tumour.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

tm.m: Dilated thick-walled airways are seen directly on thin CT slices, larger than the vessel beside them
tm.g: Suspected bronchiectasis → HRCT confirms it
f: persistent right lower lobe collapse and haemoptysis in a 60 pack-year smoker
the presentation instead showed features specific to Repeat chest X-ray in 6 weeks (Used after pneumonia to check resolution, and X-ray misses much bronchiectasis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility (Tests for asthma and measures obstruction but cannot show dilated bronchi)
the diagnosis is already known and the question is which antibiotic to give for this exacerbation
x: Looks for an obstructing lesion or foreign body, not the airway dilatation itself
Used after pneumonia to check resolution, and X-ray misses much bronchiectasis
Tests for asthma and measures obstruction but cannot show dilated bronchi
Identifies organisms such as Pseudomonas to guide treatment, not the structural diagnosis

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old man who moved from Somalia 2 years ago has had a cough for 8 weeks, with drenching night sweats and 7 kg weight loss. Last week he coughed up streaks of blood. He lives in a shared hostel.
Temperature 37.9°C. Chest X-ray shows patchy consolidation with a cavity in the right upper lobe.
hq_q.w: Weeks of cough, night sweats, weight loss and haemoptysis in a man from a high-incidence country living in crowded housing, with an upper lobe cavity, is pulmonary tuberculosis until proven otherwise. He needs 3 sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli and isolation while he may be infectious.
hq_q.f: A ball inside an old upper lobe cavity with a crescent of air around it → aspergilloma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: cavity in the right upper lobe
tm.m: Mycobacteria thrive in the oxygen-rich apices, and caseating necrosis empties into a bronchus to leave a cavity
tm.g: Chronic cough, sweats, weight loss and an upper lobe cavity in someone from a high-incidence country → TB
f: a mobile mass inside an old cavity with a crescent of air around it
3 days of fever, pleuritic pain and lobar consolidation without a cavity
a 72 year old heavy smoker with haemoptysis and a hilar mass but no fever or sweats
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sarcoidosis (Causes hilar lymphadenopathy and does not usually cavitate or cause haemoptysis)
x: Grows in an existing cavity and causes haemoptysis, but not this febrile illness with weight loss
An acute illness over days, not 8 weeks of sweats and weight loss
Can cavitate, but his age, origin, fevers and sweats point to infection
Causes hilar lymphadenopathy and does not usually cavitate or cause haemoptysis

hq_q.s: A 57 year old man's psoriasis has flared over the past 5 weeks. He has well-demarcated salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale on his elbows, knees and lower back that had been controlled for years with an emollient and calcipotriol. Six weeks ago his cardiologist added a regular drug for exertional angina. He drinks 6 units of alcohol a week and has had no recent sore throat.
hq_q.w: Beta-blockers are a classic trigger for psoriasis flares, along with lithium, antimalarials, NSAIDs and the withdrawal of oral steroids. The flare began within weeks of a new regular anti-anginal, and atenolol is the only beta-blocker offered.
hq_q.f: Flare after a course of oral prednisolone is stopped, or after lithium is started → those drugs instead.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most likely to have caused the flare?

tm.m: Beta-blockade alters signalling in keratinocytes and can trigger or worsen psoriatic plaques
tm.g: Psoriasis flare after a new beta-blocker → stop or switch the beta-blocker
f: ankle swelling and flushing with no change in the skin
the presentation instead showed features specific to Isosorbide mononitrate (Causes headache and postural hypotension)
large painful mouth and perianal ulcers after starting a potassium channel opener
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ranolazine (Can prolong the QT interval but is not a recognised psoriasis trigger)
x: Causes ankle oedema and flushing, not a psoriasis flare
Causes headache and postural hypotension
Causes painful oral, anal and skin ulcers rather than psoriatic plaques
Can prolong the QT interval but is not a recognised psoriasis trigger

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old woman has had intense itching for 3 weeks, worst at night. Her partner has started itching too.
There are small red papules and short grey wavy tracks between her fingers and on the inner wrists, with excoriated papules around her waist. Her face is spared. She is not pregnant and has no allergies.
hq_q.w: Night itch, burrows in the finger webs and wrists and an itchy partner are scabies. First line is permethrin 5% cream over the whole body from the neck down, left on for 8 to 12 hours and repeated after 7 days. All household and close contacts are treated at the same time, even without symptoms.
hq_q.f: Permethrin allergy → malathion 0.5% lotion; crusted scabies in an immunosuppressed patient → oral ivermectin as well.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

tm.m: Sarcoptes mites burrow in the stratum corneum, and the itch is a delayed hypersensitivity to the mites and their faeces
tm.g: Burrows, night itch and itchy contacts → permethrin for her and every contact, twice 7 days apart
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Aqueous cream (An emollient that does not kill mites)
a known allergy to permethrin
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral cetirizine (Can ease the itch but does not treat the infestation)
thick crusted plaques teeming with mites in a man on long-term immunosuppression
x: An emollient that does not kill mites
Second line, used when permethrin cannot be
Can ease the itch but does not treat the infestation
Kept for crusted scabies or treatment failure

hq_q.s: A 58 year old man has had 10 days of malaise and nausea followed by yellow eyes and dark urine. He lives in Hampshire and has not travelled abroad. He enjoys barbecued pork sausages and wild boar. He completed courses of hepatitis A and B vaccine last year before a cruise. He drinks 8 units of alcohol a week and takes no medication.
hq_q.w: Hepatitis E is now one of the commonest causes of acute viral hepatitis in the UK, and most infections caught here come from undercooked pork, game and processed pork products. He is vaccinated against A and B and both tests are negative, and hepatitis C rarely causes acute jaundice. Most cases clear without treatment.
hq_q.f: Unvaccinated, positive hepatitis A IgM after eating shellfish abroad → hepatitis A.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?

c: barbecued pork sausages and wild boar
tm.m: Hepatitis E genotype 3 lives in pigs, and undercooked pork delivers the virus to the liver through the gut
tm.g: Acute hepatitis in the UK with pork exposure and negative A and B → hepatitis E
f: AST twice the ALT, ALT under 300 and 15 years of heavy drinking
a 19 year old with a sore throat, tonsillar exudate and splenomegaly
unvaccinated, with a positive hepatitis A IgM after eating shellfish abroad
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hepatitis C (Acute infection is usually silent, and he has no injecting or blood exposure)
x: He drinks little, and alcohol rarely pushes the ALT above 300 or makes it higher than the AST
Gives a sore throat, lymphadenopathy and a milder hepatitis in young adults
He is vaccinated and the IgM is negative
Acute infection is usually silent, and he has no injecting or blood exposure

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman has noticed red urine on 2 occasions in the past fortnight. She has no pain, fever or urinary frequency. She smokes 15 cigarettes a day.
Abdominal examination is normal.
o: Prescribe nitrofurantoin and review in 1 week
Reassure and repeat dipstick in 3 months
hq_q.w: NICE recommends a suspected cancer referral to urology for anyone aged 45 or over with unexplained visible haematuria and no urinary infection. She is a smoker with painless visible haematuria and sterile urine. She needs cystoscopy and imaging of the upper tracts on the 2 week pathway.
hq_q.f: Dysuria, nitrites and a culture growing E. coli → treat the infection and refer if the blood persists after treatment.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: no pain, fever or urinary frequency
tm.m: Painless bleeding from the urothelium is bladder cancer until cystoscopy shows otherwise
tm.g: Aged 45 or over with unexplained visible haematuria → suspected cancer referral to urology
f: dysuria with nitrite and leucocytes positive and a culture growing E. coli
the presentation instead showed features specific to Reassure and repeat dipstick in 3 months (Visible haematuria in a smoker over 45 cannot wait 3 months)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Refer for routine renal ultrasound (Ultrasound misses many bladder tumours, and the pathway should be urgent)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Send urine for cytology (Misses many low-grade tumours and does not replace cystoscopy)
x: There is no infection, so an antibiotic delays the diagnosis
Visible haematuria in a smoker over 45 cannot wait 3 months
Ultrasound misses many bladder tumours, and the pathway should be urgent
Misses many low-grade tumours and does not replace cystoscopy

hq_q.s:
A 38 year old man has had sudden severe pain in his right loin for 3 hours, coming in waves and spreading to the groin. He cannot keep still and has vomited twice.
Temperature 37.1°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 142/86 mmHg. The abdomen is soft with mild right loin tenderness.
hq_q.w: Sudden colicky loin to groin pain in a restless patient with blood on dipstick and no fever is renal colic from a ureteric stone. A normal temperature and inflammatory markers argue against pyelonephritis. He needs a non-contrast CT KUB within 24 hours and NSAID analgesia.
hq_q.f: Fever of 39°C, rigors, constant loin pain and nitrites → acute pyelonephritis; fever with an obstructing stone → urgent decompression.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: coming in waves and spreading to the groin
tm.m: A stone impacts at a narrow point of the ureter, and peristalsis against it causes colic and bleeding
tm.g: Restless loin to groin colic with haematuria and no fever → ureteric stone
f: central abdominal pain moving to the right iliac fossa with anorexia
fever of 39°C, rigors, constant loin pain and nitrite positive urine
a 72 year old smoker with loin pain, hypotension and a pulsatile mass
the presentation instead showed features specific to Testicular torsion (Presents with scrotal pain and a tender high-riding testis)
x: Pain settles in the right iliac fossa with peritonism, and patients lie still
Needs fever, constant loin pain and raised inflammatory markers, all absent
Unlikely at 38 with a normal blood pressure, though it must be considered in older patients with loin pain
Presents with scrotal pain and a tender high-riding testis

hq_q.s:
A 9 year old boy has had dark brown urine and puffy eyes for 2 days. Two weeks ago he had a sore throat with fever that settled without antibiotics.
BP 134/88 mmHg. There is periorbital swelling and mild ankle swelling.
hq_q.w: A nephritic picture, with haematuria, hypertension, oedema and a raised creatinine, 1 to 3 weeks after a streptococcal throat infection is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. A low C3 and a high anti-streptolysin O titre support it. Most children recover with supportive care.
hq_q.f: Visible haematuria a day or two after a sore throat with normal complement → IgA nephropathy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Immune complexes against streptococcal antigens lodge in the glomeruli and activate complement, which is used up
tm.g: Nephritic picture 2 weeks after a sore throat with a low C3 → post-streptococcal GN
f: a purpuric rash on the buttocks and legs with joint and abdominal pain
visible haematuria starting a day after a sore throat with normal complement
heavy proteinuria, a low albumin and gross oedema with a normal blood pressure and no blood
the presentation instead showed features specific to Urinary tract infection (Does not cause hypertension, oedema, a low complement or a raised titre)
x: Needs the purpuric rash, abdominal pain and arthritis, which he does not have
Bleeding starts within 1 to 2 days of the infection and complement is normal
Gives nephrotic syndrome with heavy proteinuria and no blood or hypertension
Does not cause hypertension, oedema, a low complement or a raised titre

hq_q.s:
A 23 year old woman has had a painful lump on the sole of her foot for 3 months, beneath the ball of the second toe. It hurts most when she squeezes it from side to side. She swims twice a week.
There is a 6 mm rough raised lesion that interrupts the normal skin lines. After gentle paring with a scalpel, several pinpoint black dots appear.
hq_q.w: Plantar warts are caused by human papillomavirus. They interrupt the skin lines, hurt most when squeezed from side to side and show black dots of clotted capillaries when pared. Calluses and corns keep the skin lines and hurt on direct pressure, and a corn shows a translucent central core when pared.
hq_q.f: Pain on direct pressure and a translucent central core when pared → hard corn.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: squeezes it from side to side
tm.m: HPV makes keratinocytes overgrow around small capillaries that clot and show as black dots
tm.g: Black dots, broken skin lines and pain on pinching → plantar wart
f: an enlarging irregular brown-black patch on the sole with pigment spreading onto the nail fold
a diffuse yellow thickening over a pressure point with the skin lines preserved
pain on direct pressure and a translucent central core after paring
the presentation instead showed features specific to Seborrhoeic keratosis (A stuck-on warty lesion of older skin that does not occur on the sole)
x: An irregular pigmented patch, not a rough papule with pinpoint dots after paring
A diffuse thickening with the skin lines running through it
Keeps the skin lines, hurts on direct pressure and has a translucent core
A stuck-on warty lesion of older skin that does not occur on the sole

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old retired farmer has had a slowly growing lesion beside his nose for 18 months. It sometimes bleeds and scabs, then appears to heal.
There is an 8 mm pearly nodule with a rolled edge, fine branching blood vessels over its surface and a small central crust. There are no palpable lymph nodes.
hq_q.w: A slowly growing pearly nodule with a rolled edge, surface telangiectasia and a central crust that bleeds and heals, on sun-damaged facial skin, is a nodular basal cell carcinoma. It invades locally but almost never spreads, so the nodes are not involved. NICE advises a routine rather than a suspected cancer referral.
hq_q.f: A tender crusted nodule on the lower lip that grew over 8 weeks → squamous cell carcinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: bleeds and scabs, then appears to heal
pearly nodule with a rolled edge
tm.m: Nests of basal keratinocyte tumour cells push the skin up into a translucent nodule with stretched vessels on top
tm.g: Pearly rolled edge, telangiectasia and slow growth → BCC
f: a dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin plug that grew over 4 weeks and is now shrinking
a rapidly growing black nodule that bleeds on touch
the presentation instead showed features specific to Seborrhoeic keratosis (A stuck-on warty plaque without a rolled pearly edge)
a tender crusted nodule on the lower lip that grew over 8 weeks
x: Grows within weeks with a central keratin plug and may shrink on its own
Usually pigmented and fast growing, not pearly over 18 months
A stuck-on warty plaque without a rolled pearly edge
Faster growing, crusted and tender, and can spread to nodes

hq_q.s: A 19 year old woman has moderate acne on her face, chest and back with many inflamed papules and pustules but no nodules or scarring. It has not improved after 12 weeks of lymecycline with topical adapalene and benzoyl peroxide. She also asks for contraception. She does not smoke, has no migraine and no personal or family history of venous thrombosis. Her BMI is 23 kg/m².
hq_q.w: Co-cyprindiol, a combined pill containing the anti-androgen cyproterone, is licensed for acne in women when topical treatment and oral antibiotics have failed, and it is also a contraceptive. She has no risk factors for thrombosis. It carries more thrombosis risk than other combined pills, so it is stopped about 3 months after the acne settles.
hq_q.f: Nodules, cysts or scarring, or failure of 2 full courses of treatment → refer to dermatology for isotretinoin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?

c: no personal or family history of venous thrombosis
tm.m: Cyproterone blocks androgen receptors and ethinylestradiol lowers free testosterone, so sebum production falls
tm.g: Failed topical treatment and oral antibiotic, wants contraception, low thrombosis risk → co-cyprindiol
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Desogestrel (A progestogen-only pill that can worsen acne and does not treat it)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Doxycycline (Switching to another tetracycline after one has failed adds resistance without benefit)
nodules and cysts with early scarring despite 2 full courses of treatment
the presentation instead showed features specific to Topical clindamycin (A topical antibiotic on its own breeds resistance and is weaker than what has already failed)
x: A progestogen-only pill that can worsen acne and does not treat it
Switching to another tetracycline after one has failed adds resistance without benefit
For severe, nodular or scarring acne under a dermatologist, and she has none of these
A topical antibiotic on its own breeds resistance and is weaker than what has already failed

hq_q.s:
A 44 year old man has had a severe sore throat for 12 hours and now cannot swallow his saliva. His voice is muffled and he is sitting upright, leaning forward and drooling.
Temperature 39.2°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, respiratory rate 26/min, oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. There is soft inspiratory stridor.
o: Call a senior anaesthetist to secure the airway
Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
hq_q.w: Drooling, a muffled voice, sitting forward and stridor with fever are acute epiglottitis, which can obstruct the airway completely without warning. The priority is a senior anaesthetist and an ENT surgeon to secure the airway, ideally in theatre. Do not lie him flat or examine the throat. IV antibiotics follow once the airway is safe.
hq_q.f: A one-sided tonsillar swelling, trismus and a deviated uvula with a safe airway → peritonsillar abscess for needle aspiration.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate action?

tm.m: A swollen epiglottis can be sucked into the laryngeal inlet, and distress or instruments can trigger complete obstruction
tm.g: Epiglottitis with stridor → the airway first, by a senior anaesthetist, before anything else
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Examine the throat with a tongue depressor (May provoke laryngospasm and complete obstruction)
the airway has already been secured by intubation in theatre
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lateral neck X-ray (Shows the thumb sign but wastes time and takes him away from airway support)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Take a throat swab (Can trigger obstruction and does not change immediate management)
x: May provoke laryngospasm and complete obstruction
Needed soon, but securing the airway takes priority while there is stridor
Shows the thumb sign but wastes time and takes him away from airway support
Can trigger obstruction and does not change immediate management

hq_q.s:
A 31 year old woman with ulcerative colitis extending to the hepatic flexure has had 4 loose stools a day with some blood for 10 days. She is otherwise well and takes no regular medication.
Temperature 36.9°C, pulse rate 78 bpm.
hq_q.w: Fewer than 6 stools a day with no fever, tachycardia or anaemia is a mild to moderate flare. For extensive disease NICE advises a high-dose oral aminosalicylate such as mesalazine, often with a topical one. Oral prednisolone is added if there is no response after about 4 weeks.
hq_q.f: 8 bloody stools a day, fever and tachycardia → acute severe colitis: admit for IV hydrocortisone.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment to induce remission?

tm.m: Mesalazine acts on the inflamed colonic lining and damps down local prostaglandin and leukotriene production
tm.g: Mild to moderate extensive UC → high-dose oral aminosalicylate
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Infliximab (Kept for severe or steroid-refractory disease)
8 bloody stools a day, a temperature of 38°C and a pulse rate of 104 bpm
2 or more flares needing steroids in the past year
no improvement after 4 weeks of high-dose mesalazine
x: Kept for severe or steroid-refractory disease
For acute severe colitis, and she has no systemic features
Maintains remission in steroid-dependent disease but takes months to work
Second line if the aminosalicylate fails

hq_q.s:
A 29 year old woman has had bloating, loose pale stools and tiredness for 8 months. She has type 1 diabetes. She eats a normal diet including bread and pasta.
Abdominal examination is normal.
hq_q.w: Bloating, pale loose stools and iron deficiency with a strongly positive tTG IgA and a normal total IgA in a woman with type 1 diabetes is coeliac disease. She must keep eating gluten until a duodenal biopsy confirms villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia.
hq_q.f: Low total IgA → tTG IgA can be falsely negative, so test IgG-based antibodies.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Gluten triggers T cell damage to the proximal small bowel, so iron, folate and fat are poorly absorbed
tm.g: Strongly positive tTG with normal IgA while eating gluten → coeliac disease
f: mouth ulcers, weight loss, a raised CRP and a tender right iliac fossa mass
diarrhoea starting after drinking stream water on a camping trip, with negative antibody tests
the presentation instead showed features specific to Irritable bowel syndrome (Does not cause iron deficiency or a positive tTG)
bloating and wind only after milk, with normal blood tests
x: Can cause iron deficiency, but the strongly positive tTG with normal IgA points to coeliac disease
Follows untreated water and does not raise tTG
Does not cause iron deficiency or a positive tTG
Causes bloating after dairy without anaemia or antibodies

hq_q.s:
A 63 year old man with type 2 diabetes has had burning pain and pins and needles in both feet for 6 months, worst at night and disturbing his sleep. Paracetamol has not helped.
There is reduced sensation to monofilament and vibration up to the ankles in a stocking distribution. Foot pulses are present and the skin is intact. His eGFR is 74 mL/min/1.73m².
hq_q.w: Burning pain that is worse at night with stocking sensory loss is painful diabetic neuropathy. NICE offers amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin first line, switching between them if one fails. Start low at night and warn about drowsiness and a dry mouth.
hq_q.f: Neuropathic pain confined to a small area in someone who cannot take oral drugs → topical capsaicin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

c: burning pain and pins and needles
tm.m: A tricyclic boosts descending noradrenaline and serotonin inhibition in the spinal cord and dampens pain signals
tm.g: Neuropathic pain → amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Codeine phosphate (Weak opioids do little for neuropathic pain and add constipation and drowsiness)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Ibuprofen (NSAIDs do not help neuropathic pain and can harm the kidneys in diabetes)
a small patch of post-herpetic pain in a man who cannot tolerate oral drugs
severe acute pain needing short-term rescue while a first-line drug is increased
x: Weak opioids do little for neuropathic pain and add constipation and drowsiness
NSAIDs do not help neuropathic pain and can harm the kidneys in diabetes
For localised neuropathic pain when oral drugs are unsuitable
Used only as short-term rescue for acute neuropathic pain, not as long-term treatment

hq_q.s:
A 36 year old man with chronic hepatitis B is admitted to a medical ward with cellulitis of the leg. He is hepatitis B e antigen positive.
He has no cough, diarrhoea or open wounds, and he is not bleeding.
o: Airborne precautions with an FFP3 mask
Contact precautions with a side room, gloves and apron
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask
Protective isolation in a positive pressure room
Standard precautions with safe handling of sharps
hq_q.w: Hepatitis B spreads by blood and body fluids, through sharps injuries, sex and from mother to baby, not through the air or by touch. Standard precautions apply to every patient: hand hygiene, gloves for contact with blood, and careful use and disposal of sharps. A mask adds nothing. Staff should be vaccinated and know their antibody level.
hq_q.f: Smear-positive pulmonary TB or suspected measles → airborne precautions with an FFP3 mask in a negative pressure room.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate infection control approach?

c: no cough, diarrhoea or open wounds
tm.m: The virus needs a route into the blood, so the risk is a needlestick or splash, not breathing near him
tm.g: Bloodborne virus → standard precautions and sharps safety, no mask needed
f: smear-positive cavitating pulmonary tuberculosis
profuse diarrhoea with a positive C. difficile toxin
influenza A with a cough
the presentation instead showed features specific to Protective isolation in a positive pressure room (Protects severely immunosuppressed patients from others)
x: For tuberculosis, measles and chickenpox, which spread through the air
For C. difficile, MRSA and norovirus, which spread by touch and surfaces
For influenza and other respiratory droplets, not bloodborne viruses
Protects severely immunosuppressed patients from others

hq_q.s: A 42 year old woman who is a Jehovah's Witness has a haemoglobin of 64 g/L from heavy menstrual bleeding. The team explains that a blood transfusion would help her quickly. She understands, remembers and weighs the information, and clearly declines blood while accepting iron and tranexamic acid. Her doctor documents her decision and does not transfuse.
hq_q.w: Autonomy is the right of a person with capacity to make decisions about their own body, even ones others think unwise. She has capacity, so her refusal of blood must be respected. Beneficence would push towards transfusion, and justice is about fair use of resources.
hq_q.f: The doctor gives her the full truth about the risks even though it upsets her → veracity.
hq_q.ql: Which ethical principle is the doctor mainly respecting?

tm.m: An informed refusal by an adult with capacity overrides the clinician's view of what is best
tm.g: Capacity plus an informed refusal that is respected → autonomy
f: the team pushes for transfusion because it would help her most
a scarce bed is given to the patient with the greatest clinical need
the doctor avoids a drug because its harms outweigh its benefits
the presentation instead showed features specific to Veracity (Means honesty, which is part of consent but not the principle at stake in this decision)
x: Acting for her good would favour transfusion, which is being set aside
Concerns fairness and the distribution of resources
Means avoiding harm, but withholding blood increases her risk
Means honesty, which is part of consent but not the principle at stake in this decision

hq_q.s:
A 78 year old man has become very breathless over 6 hours and cannot lie flat. He had a myocardial infarction 3 years ago.
Pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 168/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, oxygen saturation 86% breathing air. There are crackles up to both mid zones.
