Chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar shadowing in a bat's wing pattern, upper lobe blood diversion, Kerley B lines at the bases and small bilateral pleural effusions.
hq_q.w: Orthopnoea, bilateral crackles, a very high NT-proBNP and the classic X-ray signs are acute pulmonary oedema from left ventricular failure: bat's wing shadowing, upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines and effusions. Treat with oxygen, sitting him up and IV furosemide, with nitrates if the blood pressure allows.
hq_q.f: Bilateral shadowing with a normal heart size and no effusions 2 days into severe pancreatitis → ARDS.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: A failing left ventricle raises pulmonary venous pressure until fluid leaks into the interstitium and then the alveoli
tm.g: Bat's wing shadowing, upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, effusions and a high BNP → pulmonary oedema
f: bilateral infiltrates with a normal heart size 2 days into severe acute pancreatitis
fever, purulent sputum and consolidation with air bronchograms in both lower lobes
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lymphangitis carcinomatosa (Develops over weeks in someone with known cancer and does not raise BNP like this)
sudden pleuritic pain and a clear chest X-ray after a long flight
x: Follows a major insult such as sepsis or pancreatitis, with normal left heart pressures
Brings fever and a high CRP, and does not cause upper lobe diversion or a raised BNP
Develops over weeks in someone with known cancer and does not raise BNP like this
Usually gives a near-normal X-ray, not bat's wing shadowing

hq_q.s:
A 7 year old boy has had a cold for 5 days and now has a swollen, red left eye and a fever. He says it hurts to look around.
Temperature 38.9°C. The left upper and lower lids are swollen and red. The eye is pushed forward, its movements are reduced and painful, and visual acuity is 6/12 in the left eye and 6/6 in the right.
hq_q.w: Proptosis, painful restricted eye movements and reduced acuity mean the infection is behind the orbital septum: orbital cellulitis. In children it usually spreads from the ethmoid sinuses through the paper-thin lamina papyracea of the medial orbital wall. He needs admission, IV antibiotics and an urgent CT of the orbits and sinuses.
hq_q.f: Swollen red lids with normal eye movements and acuity and no proptosis → preseptal cellulitis.
hq_q.ql: From which structure has the infection most likely spread?

tm.m: Ethmoid infection crosses the lamina papyracea into the orbit behind the septum
tm.g: Orbital cellulitis in a child after a cold → ethmoid sinusitis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Dental abscess (Spreads to the face or maxillary sinus and is an uncommon source in a child after a cold)
a 16 year old with frontal headache and a soft boggy swelling of the forehead above the eyebrow
a tender red swelling just below the inner corner of the eye with a watery eye
the presentation instead showed features specific to Maxillary sinus (Can spread through the orbital floor but is a far less common source than the ethmoids)
x: Spreads to the face or maxillary sinus and is an uncommon source in a child after a cold
The frontal sinuses are small and poorly developed at this age
Dacryocystitis causes a swelling at the inner canthus and rarely orbital cellulitis
Can spread through the orbital floor but is a far less common source than the ethmoids

hq_q.s:
A 28 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has had a painful red right eye for 2 days. Bright light makes it worse and his vision is slightly blurred.
Visual acuity is 6/9 in the right eye. The redness is most marked around the cornea, and the right pupil is small and irregular. There is no discharge.
o: Chloramphenicol eye drops and review in 5 days
hq_q.w: Pain, photophobia, blurred vision, redness around the cornea and a small irregular pupil in someone with ankylosing spondylitis is acute anterior uveitis. It needs same-day slit lamp examination by ophthalmology to confirm it and start steroid and dilating drops. Steroid drops should not be started without slit lamp examination, because they can worsen herpes keratitis.
hq_q.f: Gritty red eyes with sticky discharge, normal acuity and normal pupils → conjunctivitis managed in primary care.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body constricts the pupil and makes it stick to the lens, and moving the iris in light hurts
tm.g: Painful red eye with photophobia, reduced vision and an irregular pupil → same-day ophthalmology
f: gritty red eyes with sticky discharge, normal vision and normal pupils
gritty dry eyes at the end of the day with normal vision and no redness at rest
the presentation instead showed features specific to Prescribe topical prednisolone drops (Steroid drops need slit lamp confirmation first, as they can worsen herpes keratitis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Routine optometrist review (Too slow; a red eye with reduced vision needs same-day specialist review)
x: Treats bacterial conjunctivitis, which does not reduce vision or change the pupil
For dry eye, which does not cause photophobia with an irregular pupil
Steroid drops need slit lamp confirmation first, as they can worsen herpes keratitis
Too slow; a red eye with reduced vision needs same-day specialist review

hq_q.s:
A 79 year old woman says that over the past 3 weeks straight lines in her newspaper look wavy and there is a grey patch in the centre of her vision in the left eye. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day.
Visual acuity is 6/36 in the left eye and 6/9 in the right. Amsler grid testing shows distorted lines in the centre on the left. Fundoscopy shows a raised grey-green area with a small haemorrhage at the left macula.
hq_q.w: Distortion of straight lines with a central blind spot developing over weeks in an older smoker, with a raised macular lesion and haemorrhage, is wet age-related macular degeneration. New vessels leak fluid and blood under the macula. She needs referral to a macular clinic within days for anti-VEGF injections.
hq_q.f: Gradual central blurring over years with yellow drusen and no distortion → dry AMD.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: small haemorrhage at the left macula
tm.m: Choroidal new vessels grow through Bruch's membrane and leak under the macula, lifting and distorting the photoreceptors
tm.g: Wavy lines and a central blind spot developing over weeks → wet AMD
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Cataract (Causes gradual glare and blurring without distortion or a macular haemorrhage)
sudden painless loss of vision with haemorrhages scattered through all 4 quadrants
slow central blurring over years with yellow drusen and no distortion
flashes, floaters and a curtain spreading in from one side
x: Causes gradual glare and blurring without distortion or a macular haemorrhage
Causes sudden painless loss with haemorrhages throughout the retina
Progresses over years with drusen, without new vessels or haemorrhage
Starts with flashes and floaters and a peripheral curtain, not central distortion

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man with polymyalgia rheumatica has taken oral prednisolone for 3 years. Over 6 months his vision has become hazy, he is dazzled by oncoming headlights at night and he finds reading harder.
Visual acuity is 6/18 in both eyes. Intraocular pressures are 16 and 17 mmHg. The red reflex is dull, with a dark central shadow in both eyes. The fundi are hard to see but appear normal.
hq_q.w: Long-term corticosteroids cause posterior subcapsular cataract, which lies in the visual axis and gives early glare from headlights and trouble reading. A dull red reflex with a central shadow confirms an opacity in the lens. Steroids can also raise intraocular pressure, but his pressures are normal.
hq_q.f: Intraocular pressure of 32 mmHg with cupped discs and peripheral field loss on steroids → open-angle glaucoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of his visual symptoms?

tm.m: Steroids alter the lens epithelium so opaque fibres collect under the posterior capsule in the visual axis
tm.g: Long-term steroids with glare and a dull red reflex → posterior subcapsular cataract
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Age-related macular degeneration (Distorts central vision but does not dull the red reflex)
dot and blot haemorrhages and hard exudates with a raised HbA1c
intraocular pressure of 32 mmHg with cupped optic discs and peripheral field loss
the presentation instead showed features specific to Retinal vein occlusion (Causes sudden painless loss with retinal haemorrhages)
x: Distorts central vision but does not dull the red reflex
Steroids can cause diabetes, but the fundi look normal and the problem is in the lens
Steroids can cause it, but his pressures are normal and glaucoma spares central vision until late
Causes sudden painless loss with retinal haemorrhages

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old man is sent to his GP by his optometrist after a routine eye test. He has occasional headaches but otherwise feels well. He has not seen a doctor for 10 years.
The optometrist reports narrowed arterioles with a copper wire appearance, nipping where arteries cross veins, flame-shaped haemorrhages and cotton wool spots in both eyes. The optic discs are normal.
hq_q.w: Copper wiring, arteriovenous nipping, flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots are hypertensive retinopathy, so the first step is to measure his blood pressure. NICE advises same-day specialist referral if the blood pressure is 180/120 mmHg or more with retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema.
hq_q.f: Dot and blot haemorrhages, microaneurysms and hard exudates → diabetic retinopathy: check glucose or HbA1c.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: not seen a doctor for 10 years
tm.m: Chronic high pressure thickens arteriolar walls, and sharp rises damage capillaries so the nerve fibre layer infarcts as cotton wool spots
tm.g: Copper wiring, AV nipping and flame haemorrhages → measure the blood pressure
f: dot and blot haemorrhages, microaneurysms and hard exudates in a man who is always thirsty
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fluorescein angiography (A specialist test that does not come before measuring his blood pressure)
loss of vision in one eye for 4 minutes like a curtain coming down, with a carotid bruit
the presentation instead showed features specific to Urgent CT head (His discs are normal and he has no neurological signs)
x: Diabetic retinopathy gives dot and blot haemorrhages and microaneurysms, not copper wiring
A specialist test that does not come before measuring his blood pressure
For amaurosis fugax or retinal emboli, not this pattern
His discs are normal and he has no neurological signs

hq_q.s:
A 44 year old woman has noticed blood-stained discharge from her right nipple on several occasions over 6 weeks. It comes from a single opening on the nipple. She is not breastfeeding and takes no medication.
There is no palpable lump, skin change or nipple retraction. Pressure at the 9 o'clock position at the edge of the areola produces a bead of bloody fluid from one duct.
hq_q.w: Bloody discharge from a single duct with no lump in a woman in her 40s is most often an intraductal papilloma, a benign wart-like growth in a large duct near the nipple. Ductal carcinoma in situ must be excluded, so she needs triple assessment at the breast clinic.
hq_q.f: Thick green or cream discharge from several ducts with a slit-like retracted nipple around the menopause → duct ectasia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause?

tm.m: A fragile papillary growth in a large duct under the areola bleeds and drains through one opening
tm.g: Bloody discharge from one duct with no lump → intraductal papilloma
f: thick green discharge from several ducts with a slit-like nipple retraction in a 54 year old
a crusted eczema-like nipple that has spread onto the areola
the presentation instead showed features specific to Periductal mastitis (Affects young smokers with pain, inflammation and sometimes an abscess)
milky discharge from both breasts, missed periods and headaches
x: Gives thick coloured discharge from several ducts around the menopause, often with slit-like retraction
Causes an eczema-like rash on the nipple, not discharge from one duct with a normal nipple
Affects young smokers with pain, inflammation and sometimes an abscess
Causes milky discharge from many ducts in both breasts, not blood from one duct

hq_q.s:
A 27 year old woman who is breastfeeding her 3 week old baby has had a painful, red, wedge-shaped area on her left breast for 2 days, with fever and aches. She has kept breastfeeding from both sides and expressing, but it is no better after 24 hours. She has no allergies.
Temperature 38.4°C. There is a tender, warm, red area in the upper outer quadrant with no fluctuant swelling.
o: Stop breastfeeding from the left breast
hq_q.w: Lactational mastitis that has not improved after 12 to 24 hours of effective milk removal needs an antibiotic. Flucloxacillin for 10 to 14 days covers Staphylococcus aureus. Breastfeeding should continue from both breasts, because emptying the breast helps recovery and the milk is safe for the baby.
hq_q.f: A tender fluctuant lump → breast abscess, usually treated with ultrasound-guided aspiration and antibiotics.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

tm.m: Milk stasis lets Staphylococcus aureus from the baby's mouth or the nipple multiply in the breast
tm.g: Mastitis not settling after 24 hours of milk removal → flucloxacillin, and keep feeding
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Cabergoline to stop lactation (Not needed; stopping feeds causes milk stasis and makes mastitis worse)
a penicillin allergy with a rash
a large abscess that has failed repeated needle aspiration, with thinned skin over it
the presentation instead showed features specific to Stop breastfeeding from the left breast (Stopping causes milk stasis and raises the risk of an abscess)
x: Not needed; stopping feeds causes milk stasis and makes mastitis worse
For penicillin allergy, and she has none
For an abscess that fails aspiration, and she has no fluctuant swelling
Stopping causes milk stasis and raises the risk of an abscess

hq_q.s:
A 64 year old man has noticed a painless swelling of his right scrotum that has grown slowly over 8 months. It feels heavy by the end of the day.
There is a smooth, non-tender, fluctuant swelling of the right hemiscrotum. The examiner can get above it, and the testis cannot be felt separately from it. It glows brightly when a pen torch is held against it.
hq_q.w: A painless fluctuant scrotal swelling that transilluminates, that the examiner can get above and in which the testis cannot be felt separately, is a hydrocele: fluid in the tunica vaginalis around the testis. An ultrasound is advised to check the testis inside, especially in younger men.
hq_q.f: A transilluminating swelling above and behind the testis that can be felt separately from it → epididymal cyst.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Fluid collects between the layers of the tunica vaginalis, which wrap around the front and sides of the testis
tm.g: Transilluminates, can get above it and the testis is not felt separately → hydrocele
f: a transilluminating swelling above and behind the testis, which is felt separately
a swelling the examiner cannot get above, with a cough impulse
the presentation instead showed features specific to Testicular tumour (A hard, irregular lump in the testis that does not transilluminate)
a soft swelling like a bag of worms above the left testis that empties on lying down
x: Transilluminates but sits above and behind a testis that is felt separately
The examiner cannot get above it, and there may be a cough impulse
A hard, irregular lump in the testis that does not transilluminate
Feels like a bag of worms, usually on the left, and does not transilluminate

hq_q.s: A 38 year old woman has had episodes of central chest tightness at rest for 2 months, mostly between 4 and 6 am, lasting 10 minutes and easing with glyceryl trinitrate spray. She smokes. During an episode in the emergency department her ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF that settles completely within 15 minutes. Troponin is not raised. Coronary angiography shows smooth, unobstructed coronary arteries. She is started on diltiazem.
o: Lower her heart rate to reduce oxygen demand
Prevent platelet aggregation on a ruptured plaque
Prevent spasm of the coronary arteries
Reduce afterload to improve ventricular function
hq_q.w: Chest pain at rest in the early morning, transient ST elevation that resolves, no troponin rise and normal coronary arteries are vasospastic, or Prinzmetal, angina. Calcium channel blockers relax vascular smooth muscle and are first line to prevent coronary artery spasm. Beta-blockers alone can make spasm worse, and stopping smoking matters.
hq_q.f: Exertional angina with a fixed stenosis → the aim of treatment is to reduce oxygen demand, usually with a beta-blocker.
hq_q.ql: Which is the main purpose of diltiazem in her treatment?

tm.m: Calcium entry drives contraction of coronary smooth muscle, so blocking it stops the artery clamping shut
tm.g: Rest angina with transient ST elevation and normal arteries → calcium channel blocker to prevent spasm
f: exertional angina from a fixed 90% stenosis with a resting heart rate of 96 bpm
the presentation instead showed features specific to Prevent platelet aggregation on a ruptured plaque (Antiplatelets do this, and she has no plaque or troponin rise)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Reduce afterload to improve ventricular function (A minor effect, and her ventricle is not failing)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Stabilise atheromatous plaques (Statins do this, and her arteries have no atheroma)
x: How rate-limiting drugs help fixed stenosis, but her arteries are smooth
Antiplatelets do this, and she has no plaque or troponin rise
A minor effect, and her ventricle is not failing
Statins do this, and her arteries have no atheroma

hq_q.s:
A 34 year old woman has had a fever and headache for 3 days. Today her partner found her confused and saying strange things, and she then had a seizure.
Temperature 38.8°C, GCS 12. There is no neck stiffness or rash. MRI shows high signal in the left temporal lobe.
hq_q.w: Fever with confusion, odd behaviour and a seizure, a lymphocytic CSF with a normal glucose ratio and temporal lobe change on MRI are herpes simplex encephalitis. IV aciclovir should start as soon as it is suspected, without waiting for the CSF HSV PCR.
hq_q.f: Fever, neck stiffness and a turbid CSF full of neutrophils with a low glucose → bacterial meningitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: HSV reaches the temporal lobes along olfactory and trigeminal pathways and causes haemorrhagic inflammation there
tm.g: Fever, behaviour change, seizures and temporal lobe change → HSV encephalitis: give aciclovir
f: neck stiffness, a purpuric rash and CSF with 2000 neutrophils and a low glucose
a ring-enhancing lesion on contrast CT in a man with a dental abscess
the presentation instead showed features specific to Subarachnoid haemorrhage (Starts with a thunderclap headache rather than days of fever, and the CSF shows blood or xanthochromia)
weeks of headache and cranial nerve palsies in a man from Pakistan with a CSF glucose ratio of 0.3
x: Gives a neutrophil CSF with a low glucose and usually neck stiffness
Shows a ring-enhancing mass rather than diffuse temporal lobe change
Starts with a thunderclap headache rather than days of fever, and the CSF shows blood or xanthochromia
Develops over weeks with a very low CSF glucose

hq_q.s:
A 46 year old woman had a sudden, severe occipital headache while lifting a box 14 hours ago, the worst she has ever had. It reached its peak within a minute. She vomited once.
GCS 15. There is mild neck stiffness and no focal neurological deficit. A CT head performed 13 hours after the onset of the headache is normal.
hq_q.w: A thunderclap headache peaking within a minute is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. CT is very sensitive within 6 hours of onset, but after 6 hours a normal CT does not exclude it. NICE advises a lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after the headache began, looking for xanthochromia.
hq_q.f: Normal CT done within 6 hours of onset → SAH is very unlikely and a lumbar puncture is not routinely needed.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next step?

c: reached its peak within a minute
CT head performed 13 hours after the onset
tm.m: Red cells in the CSF break down to bilirubin over about 12 hours, giving xanthochromia that lasts up to 2 weeks
tm.g: Thunderclap headache with a normal CT after 6 hours → LP at 12 hours or more for xanthochromia
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to CT head in 24 hours (CT sensitivity falls further with time, so repeating it does not exclude SAH)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Discharge with analgesia (Missing a warning bleed risks a fatal rebleed)
the presentation instead showed features specific to MRI brain as an outpatient (Far too slow for a possible aneurysmal bleed)
SAH confirmed on CT from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm awaiting coiling
x: CT sensitivity falls further with time, so repeating it does not exclude SAH
Missing a warning bleed risks a fatal rebleed
Far too slow for a possible aneurysmal bleed
Given once SAH is confirmed, to reduce delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm

hq_q.s:
A 74 year old woman has had pain in the right upper abdomen for 2 days, with rigors and yellow skin since yesterday. She had biliary colic 6 months ago and is on the waiting list for a cholecystectomy.
Temperature 39.1°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg. She is jaundiced and tender in the right upper quadrant.
hq_q.w: Fever with rigors, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice is Charcot's triad of ascending cholangitis: a stone blocks the common bile duct and the trapped bile becomes infected. The obstructive LFTs and normal amylase fit. She needs blood cultures, IV antibiotics, fluids and drainage of the bile duct, usually by ERCP.
hq_q.f: Fever and right upper quadrant pain with Murphy's sign but a normal bilirubin → acute cholecystitis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: A stone in the common bile duct stops bile flow, and bacteria climb from the duodenum into the stagnant bile
tm.g: Fever, RUQ pain and jaundice → cholangitis needing antibiotics and drainage
f: fever and right upper quadrant pain with Murphy's sign and a normal bilirubin
epigastric pain going through to the back with an amylase of 1600
an hour of right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal with normal blood tests and no fever
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hepatitis A (Raises the ALT far more than the ALP and does not cause rigors)
x: Inflammation of the gallbladder does not usually cause jaundice or an obstructive picture
The amylase is normal
Brief pain without fever, rigors or jaundice
Raises the ALT far more than the ALP and does not cause rigors

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man has had looser, more frequent stools for 7 weeks. The change began during a 3 week visit to family in India. Two stool cultures and microscopy for ova, cysts and parasites were negative. He has lost 4 kg and feels tired.
Abdominal and rectal examinations are normal.
hq_q.w: A persistent change in bowel habit with weight loss, iron deficiency anaemia and a strongly positive FIT in a man over 60 needs a suspected cancer referral, and colonoscopy with biopsy confirms colorectal cancer. The trip to India is a distractor: negative stool tests and a blood-loss anaemia point to a bowel lesion rather than an infection.
hq_q.f: Bloody diarrhoea, fever and a liver abscess after the same trip → amoebiasis, treated with metronidazole.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

c: microscopy for ova, cysts and parasites were negative
tm.m: A bleeding colonic tumour loses iron slowly and changes bowel habit as it narrows the lumen
tm.g: Over 60 with changed bowel habit, iron deficiency and a positive FIT → colonoscopy, whatever the travel history
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Abdominal ultrasound (Cannot see the colonic lining and gives no tissue diagnosis)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Repeat stool culture (Two negative sets and a blood-loss anaemia make infection unlikely)
bloody diarrhoea, fever and a tender liver with a cystic lesion after the same trip
a 30 year old with bloating, iron deficiency and a normal FIT whose diarrhoea began long before the trip
x: Cannot see the colonic lining and gives no tissue diagnosis
Two negative sets and a blood-loss anaemia make infection unlikely
Amoebiasis gives bloody diarrhoea or a liver abscess, not this picture with negative microscopy
Worth testing in iron deficiency, but coeliac disease does not explain a strongly positive FIT

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old woman with schizophrenia has been well on risperidone for 8 months with no psychotic symptoms. She has not had a period for 5 months, has noticed milky discharge from both nipples and is upset by a reduced sex drive. A pregnancy test is negative. She wants to stay on an antipsychotic.
Her BMI is 31 kg/m².
hq_q.w: Risperidone has caused hyperprolactinaemia, with amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and a low libido. Aripiprazole is a partial dopamine agonist that does not raise prolactin and often lowers it, and it has a low risk of weight gain and diabetes, which matters with her BMI and HbA1c. Amisulpride, sulpiride and haloperidol all raise prolactin, and olanzapine causes the most weight gain.
hq_q.f: Schizophrenia that has not responded to 2 adequate antipsychotic trials → clozapine.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate antipsychotic to switch to?

c: not had a period for 5 months
tm.m: Dopamine normally holds back prolactin release, and D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway lifts that brake
tm.g: Antipsychotic hyperprolactinaemia with metabolic risk → aripiprazole
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amisulpride (Raises prolactin even more than risperidone)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Haloperidol (A potent D2 blocker that raises prolactin and causes extrapyramidal side effects)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Olanzapine (Raises prolactin less but causes marked weight gain and diabetes, and she is already at risk)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sulpiride (Raises prolactin markedly)
x: Raises prolactin even more than risperidone
A potent D2 blocker that raises prolactin and causes extrapyramidal side effects
Raises prolactin less but causes marked weight gain and diabetes, and she is already at risk
Raises prolactin markedly

hq_q.s:
A 21 year old man noticed that the whites of his eyes turned yellow during a 2 day stomach bug, when he was eating very little. He otherwise felt well, and the yellow has nearly gone.
Examination is normal, with no liver or spleen enlargement.
hq_q.w: A mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia that appears with fasting or illness, with normal liver enzymes, haemoglobin and reticulocytes, is Gilbert syndrome. Reduced UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity slows conjugation. It is harmless, needs no treatment and affects about 1 in 20 people.
hq_q.f: Raised unconjugated bilirubin with a low haemoglobin and raised reticulocytes and LDH → haemolytic anaemia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Glucuronidation of bilirubin is slow, and fasting or illness tips the balance so unconjugated bilirubin builds up
tm.g: Isolated unconjugated bilirubin with fasting, normal LFTs and no haemolysis → Gilbert syndrome
f: a newborn with severe unconjugated jaundice that needs phototherapy for months
a raised conjugated bilirubin with normal enzymes and a black liver on biopsy
a falling haemoglobin, reticulocytes of 8% and a raised LDH
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hepatitis A (Would raise the ALT many times over)
x: Causes severe unconjugated jaundice from birth
Raises conjugated bilirubin, which is normal here
His haemoglobin and reticulocytes are normal
Would raise the ALT many times over

hq_q.s:
A 47 year old man has had severe constant epigastric pain going through to his back for 8 hours, with repeated vomiting. He drinks about 50 units of alcohol a week. Sitting forward eases the pain a little.
Temperature 37.8°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg. The epigastrium is tender with guarding.
hq_q.w: Severe epigastric pain going through to the back, eased by sitting forward, with vomiting in a heavy drinker and an amylase more than 3 times the upper limit is acute pancreatitis. Gallstones and alcohol cause most cases. Severity is scored with the modified Glasgow criteria, and a low calcium is one of them.
hq_q.f: Sudden pain with a rigid abdomen and free gas under the diaphragm → perforated duodenal ulcer, though the amylase can be mildly raised.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Pancreatic enzymes activate inside the gland and digest it, and leaking enzymes inflame the retroperitoneum
tm.g: Epigastric pain to the back with amylase over 3 times normal → acute pancreatitis
f: right upper quadrant pain, Murphy's sign and a thickened gallbladder wall with a normal amylase
the presentation instead showed features specific to Inferior myocardial infarction (Can cause epigastric pain, but the troponin is normal)
sudden pain, a board-like abdomen and free air under the diaphragm on an erect chest X-ray
a 74 year old smoker with back pain, collapse and a pulsatile mass
x: Pain is in the right upper quadrant with Murphy's sign, and amylase is not this high
Can cause epigastric pain, but the troponin is normal
Gives sudden peritonitis with a rigid abdomen, and the amylase is rarely over 1000
Unlikely at 47 with a normal blood pressure and no pulsatile mass

hq_q.s:
A 62 year old woman has had tiredness for 4 months and pins and needles in both feet for 6 weeks. She has vitiligo and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. She eats meat and drinks no alcohol.
Her tongue is smooth and red. Vibration sense and joint position sense are reduced in both feet.
hq_q.w: A macrocytic anaemia with glossitis and loss of vibration and joint position sense in a woman with other autoimmune conditions is vitamin B12 deficiency, most likely from pernicious anaemia. Her folate is normal and she is euthyroid. Neurological features mean prompt IM hydroxocobalamin, and folic acid must not be given on its own.
hq_q.f: Macrocytic anaemia with a low folate, a poor diet and no neurological signs → folate deficiency.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?

c: Vibration sense and joint position sense
tm.m: Autoantibodies destroy gastric parietal cells and intrinsic factor, so B12 is not absorbed and both DNA synthesis and myelin suffer
tm.g: Macrocytosis with dorsal column signs and autoimmunity → B12 deficiency
f: a raised GGT, 60 units a week and an MCV of 104 with a normal haemoglobin
a folate of 1.4, a poor diet and no neurological signs
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hypothyroidism (Can cause a mild macrocytosis, but her TSH is normal on treatment)
an 80 year old with low counts in all 3 cell lines and dysplastic cells on the blood film
x: She does not drink
Her folate is normal, and folate deficiency does not damage the dorsal columns
Can cause a mild macrocytosis, but her TSH is normal on treatment
Possible at this age, but her neurological signs and autoimmunity point to B12

hq_q.s:
A 39 year old woman has noticed a painless lump in the front of her neck for 2 months. She feels well.
There is a firm 2.5 cm nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid that moves on swallowing. There is no lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound shows a solid hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications and irregular margins, graded U4.
hq_q.w: A euthyroid woman with a solid nodule that has suspicious ultrasound features, graded U4, needs ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration for cytology, reported on the Thy scale. The result decides between surgery and surveillance. An uptake scan is for nodules with a low TSH, to look for a hot nodule.
hq_q.f: Thyroid nodule with a suppressed TSH and raised free T4 → radioisotope uptake scan to look for a toxic nodule.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

tm.m: Cells drawn from the nodule show whether the follicular cells are benign, indeterminate or malignant
tm.g: Euthyroid solid nodule with suspicious ultrasound → US-guided FNA
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to CT of neck and chest (For staging once cancer is confirmed, or for retrosternal extension)
a nodule with a TSH below 0.01 and a raised free T4
a nodule with diarrhoea, flushing and a family history of phaeochromocytoma
the presentation instead showed features specific to Thyroid peroxidase antibody titre (Support autoimmune thyroiditis but do not assess a nodule)
x: For staging once cancer is confirmed, or for retrosternal extension
Used when the TSH is low, and hot nodules are rarely malignant
Checked when medullary carcinoma is suspected, as in MEN 2
Support autoimmune thyroiditis but do not assess a nodule

hq_q.s:
A 33 year old woman has felt anxious and shaky for 3 months. She has lost 5 kg despite eating more, her periods have become lighter and she cannot tolerate warm rooms. Her GP had suggested anxiety.
Pulse rate 112 bpm, irregularly irregular. She has a fine tremor, warm moist skin and lid lag.
hq_q.w: Weight loss with a large appetite, heat intolerance, tremor, lid lag, lighter periods and atrial fibrillation with a suppressed TSH and high free T4 are thyrotoxicosis. Anxiety can mimic the symptoms but does not change thyroid function. The next step is to find the cause, such as Graves' disease, with TSH receptor antibodies.
hq_q.f: Episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations with surges in blood pressure and normal thyroid tests → phaeochromocytoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Excess thyroid hormone raises the metabolic rate and sensitises tissues to adrenaline
tm.g: Suppressed TSH with a high free T4 and hypermetabolic symptoms → thyrotoxicosis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Excess caffeine intake (Causes tremor and palpitations but not weight loss with abnormal thyroid tests)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Generalised anxiety disorder (Mimics the symptoms but does not suppress the TSH or cause lid lag)
hot flushes and irregular periods in a 49 year old with a normal TSH and a raised FSH
episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations with a BP of 220/120 mmHg and normal thyroid tests
x: Causes tremor and palpitations but not weight loss with abnormal thyroid tests
Mimics the symptoms but does not suppress the TSH or cause lid lag
Unlikely at 33, and it causes flushes rather than heat intolerance with weight loss
Causes episodes with hypertension, and her thyroid tests are abnormal

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man had sudden loss of vision in his left eye this morning, like a curtain coming down from above. It lasted 4 minutes and then fully recovered. He has no headache, jaw pain or scalp tenderness. He smokes and has type 2 diabetes.
Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes. Fundoscopy is normal. There is a left carotid bruit. ESR is 12 mm/h.
hq_q.w: Transient painless loss of vision in one eye, like a curtain, lasting minutes with full recovery, is amaurosis fugax: a retinal TIA, usually from a carotid embolus. The bruit and his vascular risk factors fit. He needs aspirin 300 mg, same-day TIA assessment and carotid Doppler imaging.
hq_q.f: Sudden painless loss that does not recover, with a cherry-red spot at the macula → central retinal artery occlusion.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: lasted 4 minutes and then fully recovered
no headache, jaw pain or scalp tenderness
tm.m: A cholesterol or platelet embolus from the carotid briefly blocks the central retinal artery and then breaks up
tm.g: Transient monocular curtain lasting minutes → amaurosis fugax, treated as a TIA
f: loss of vision that does not recover, with a cherry-red spot at the macula
shimmering zigzag lines in both visual fields over 20 minutes followed by headache
flashes and floaters then a shadow spreading in from one side that persists
the presentation instead showed features specific to Vitreous haemorrhage (Gives floaters or loss that persists, and the fundal view would be obscured)
x: The loss persists, with a pale retina and a cherry-red spot
Gives positive visual symptoms building over 5 to 60 minutes, usually in both visual fields
Starts with flashes and floaters and does not recover within minutes
Gives floaters or loss that persists, and the fundal view would be obscured

hq_q.s:
A 73 year old man has had a dull ache in his right shin for a year, worse at night. His wife says his hats no longer fit and he has become slightly deaf. He feels otherwise well.
His right tibia is bowed and warm to touch.
hq_q.w: A very high ALP with a normal calcium, phosphate and PTH, bone pain, a bowed warm tibia, an enlarging skull and deafness are Paget's disease of bone: overactive, disordered remodelling makes bone bigger but weaker. X-rays and an isotope bone scan show its extent, and bisphosphonates treat the pain.
hq_q.f: New severe localised pain and swelling in a bone already affected by Paget's → osteosarcoma, needing an urgent X-ray and referral.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Overactive osteoclasts and then chaotic osteoblasts lay down large, vascular, weak bone
tm.g: Isolated very high ALP with normal calcium and a bowed warm bone → Paget's disease
f: a PSA of 86 with back pain and sclerotic lesions in the spine
the presentation instead showed features specific to Multiple myeloma (Usually leaves the ALP normal and raises the calcium)
a low calcium and phosphate, a raised PTH and proximal muscle weakness
a calcium of 2.9 with a raised PTH and kidney stones
x: Possible in an older man, but his PSA is normal and the skull and bowing changes fit Paget's
Usually leaves the ALP normal and raises the calcium
Lowers calcium and phosphate and raises the PTH
Raises the calcium and PTH, both normal here

hq_q.s:
An 81 year old woman has become confused and unsteady over 5 days. Three weeks ago she started 2 new medicines: one for low mood and paracetamol for knee pain. Her other medicines are amlodipine, atorvastatin and levothyroxine, all unchanged for years.
She appears euvolaemic, with moist mucous membranes, no oedema and a BP of 138/82 mmHg with no postural drop.
hq_q.w: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with a low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and a high urine sodium is SIADH. SSRIs such as fluoxetine are a common cause, especially in older people in the first few weeks. Her thyroid function is normal. Stop the SSRI and restrict fluids.
hq_q.f: A postural drop, dry mucous membranes and a recently started thiazide → hypovolaemic hyponatraemia from the diuretic.
hq_q.ql: Which drug is most likely to have caused her hyponatraemia?

tm.m: SSRIs increase ADH release, so the kidney holds on to free water and dilutes the plasma sodium
tm.g: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine after starting an SSRI → SIADH from the SSRI
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Amlodipine (Causes ankle oedema and flushing, not SIADH, and the dose has not changed)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Atorvastatin (Not a cause of hyponatraemia, and it has not changed)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Levothyroxine (Treats hypothyroidism, which can lower sodium, and her TSH shows good replacement)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Paracetamol (Not a cause of SIADH)
x: Causes ankle oedema and flushing, not SIADH, and the dose has not changed
Not a cause of hyponatraemia, and it has not changed
Treats hypothyroidism, which can lower sodium, and her TSH shows good replacement
Not a cause of SIADH

hq_q.s:
A 66 year old man with long-standing hypertension has sudden tearing chest pain going through to his back. In the resuscitation room he deteriorates.
Pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg in the right arm and 62/40 mmHg in the left arm. There is a new early diastolic murmur. He is intubated and ventilated and is too unstable to leave the department. ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ST elevation.
hq_q.w: Tearing pain to the back, a difference in blood pressure between the arms and new aortic regurgitation are a type A aortic dissection. CT aortography is the usual first test in a stable patient, but he is too unstable to travel to the scanner. Bedside transoesophageal echocardiography shows the intimal flap, the aortic valve and any tamponade, and can be done in the resuscitation room or theatre.
hq_q.f: The same pain in a patient who is stable → CT aortogram of the whole aorta.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate imaging to confirm the diagnosis?

c: tearing chest pain going through to his back
84/50 mmHg in the right arm and 62/40 mmHg in the left arm
too unstable to leave the department
tm.m: The probe sits in the oesophagus right behind the ascending aorta, so the flap is seen clearly without moving him
tm.g: Suspected dissection: stable → CT aortogram; too unstable to move → bedside TOE
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Chest X-ray (May show a widened mediastinum but can be normal and cannot confirm dissection)
a haemodynamically stable patient with normal renal function
the presentation instead showed features specific to MR angiography (Accurate but slow and not possible in an unstable ventilated patient)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Transthoracic echocardiography (Useful for tamponade and aortic regurgitation, but it misses much of the ascending aorta and arch)
x: May show a widened mediastinum but can be normal and cannot confirm dissection
First choice when stable, but he cannot safely leave the resuscitation room
Accurate but slow and not possible in an unstable ventilated patient
Useful for tamponade and aortic regurgitation, but it misses much of the ascending aorta and arch

hq_q.s:
A 29 year old man is found unresponsive at home with an empty bottle of methadone beside him.
Respiratory rate 6/min, oxygen saturation 84% breathing air, pulse rate 64 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg. His pupils are pinpoint. An arterial blood gas is taken breathing air.
hq_q.w: The pH is low and the PaCO2 high, so the primary problem is a respiratory acidosis from opioid-induced hypoventilation. The bicarbonate is normal because the kidneys have not had time to compensate, so it is acute. A normal lactate and bicarbonate rule out a metabolic acidosis. He needs naloxone and support for his breathing.
hq_q.f: The same gas with a bicarbonate of 34 in a man with severe COPD → chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely acid-base disturbance?

tm.m: Opioids blunt the brainstem response to CO2, so breathing slows and CO2 builds up as carbonic acid
tm.g: Low pH with a high CO2 and normal bicarbonate → acute respiratory acidosis
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Compensated metabolic acidosis (Would show a low bicarbonate and a low CO2)
a pH of 7.50 with a bicarbonate of 38 after days of vomiting
a pH of 7.12, PaCO2 of 8.6 and bicarbonate of 14 with a lactate of 9 after a long seizure
a pH of 7.52 and PaCO2 of 3.1 in a panic attack with tingling fingers
x: Would show a low bicarbonate and a low CO2
Needs a high pH and a high bicarbonate
Would also need a low bicarbonate or a high lactate
Needs a low CO2 and a high pH

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old man has had central chest tightness for 6 weeks when walking uphill, easing within 3 minutes of rest. He smokes and has hypertension.
Examination is normal. His resting ECG is normal. A full blood count, renal function and HbA1c are normal.
hq_q.w: Chest tightness brought on by exertion and relieved by rest within 5 minutes is typical angina. NICE recommends CT coronary angiography as the first-line test for stable chest pain that could be angina, rather than an exercise ECG. Functional imaging follows if CT is inconclusive, and invasive angiography if revascularisation is being considered.
hq_q.f: CT shows a stenosis of uncertain significance → functional imaging such as a myocardial perfusion scan.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first-line investigation?

tm.m: CT shows the coronary lumen and plaque directly and rules out disease with a high negative predictive value
tm.g: Possible stable angina → CT coronary angiography first
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Exercise ECG (No longer recommended to diagnose stable angina, as it misses and over-calls disease)
angina persists despite 2 anti-anginal drugs and revascularisation is being considered
CT shows a 50% to 70% stenosis of uncertain functional significance
the same pain at rest for 40 minutes this morning
x: No longer recommended to diagnose stable angina, as it misses and over-calls disease
Kept for when revascularisation is being considered
Second line when CT is inconclusive or shows disease of uncertain significance
For suspected acute coronary syndrome, and his pain is stable and exertional

hq_q.s:
A 4 year old girl has had high fever and frequent small stools with blood and mucus for 2 days. Today she had a brief generalised seizure while febrile. Three other children at her nursery have had similar diarrhoea this week. The family has no pets and has not travelled.
Temperature 39.6°C. She has lower abdominal tenderness and strains often but passes little.
hq_q.w: High fever, small bloody mucoid stools with straining, a febrile seizure and an outbreak in a nursery point to Shigella, which needs very few organisms to spread from person to person. Shigella sonnei is the usual species in the UK. Stool culture confirms it, and it is notifiable.
hq_q.f: Bloody diarrhoea with little fever, then pallor, bruising and reduced urine a week later → E. coli O157 with haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely causative organism?

tm.m: Shigella invades the colonic lining and spreads from cell to cell, causing ulcerating dysentery, and it often triggers seizures in young children
tm.g: Bloody dysentery with high fever, a seizure and a nursery outbreak → Shigella
f: an adult with crampy pain and bloody diarrhoea after undercooked chicken at a barbecue
bloody diarrhoea with little fever, then pallor, bruising and reduced urine a week later
a 1 year old with vomiting and watery diarrhoea without blood in winter
the presentation instead showed features specific to Salmonella enteritidis (Usually foodborne from eggs or poultry, with watery rather than dysenteric stools)
x: The commonest UK cause of bloody diarrhoea, but it is foodborne, usually from poultry, and rarely spreads through a nursery
Often causes bloody diarrhoea with little or no fever
Causes watery diarrhoea and vomiting without blood
Usually foodborne from eggs or poultry, with watery rather than dysenteric stools

hq_q.s:
A 17 year old girl is brought to her GP by her mother, who has noticed she is eating very little and running every day. She has not had a period for 5 months. She says she is still too fat and is frightened of gaining weight. She denies bingeing or vomiting.
Height 1.65 m, weight 43 kg, BMI 15.8 kg/m². Pulse rate 48 bpm. She has fine downy hair on her arms.
hq_q.w: Restriction and exercise leading to a very low BMI, an intense fear of weight gain with a distorted view of her body, amenorrhoea, bradycardia and lanugo hair are anorexia nervosa. Without bingeing or vomiting her potassium is normal. A BMI this low with a pulse under 50 needs urgent medical assessment of risk.
hq_q.f: A normal BMI with regular binges followed by vomiting and a low potassium → bulimia nervosa.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Starvation shuts down the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis and slows the heart, while the fear of weight gain keeps the restriction going
tm.g: Low BMI with fear of weight gain and restriction → anorexia nervosa
f: the same fears and restriction after losing 15 kg, but with a BMI of 21
restricts food because of a fear of choking, with no concern about weight or shape
a BMI of 22 with weekly binges followed by vomiting and a potassium of 3.0
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hyperthyroidism (Causes weight loss with a fast pulse and no fear of weight gain)
x: Used when the features are present but weight is still in the normal range
Restriction is driven by sensory dislike or fear of choking, not by weight or shape
Needs bingeing with compensation, usually at a normal weight
Causes weight loss with a fast pulse and no fear of weight gain

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man has had a cough with green sputum, fever and right-sided pleuritic pain for 3 days. He is orientated in time, place and person. He has no allergies.
Temperature 38.4°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, respiratory rate 22/min, BP 128/76 mmHg, oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. There is bronchial breathing at the right base. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.
o: Admit for IV co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin
Admit for oral amoxicillin and clarithromycin
Oral amoxicillin at home for 5 days
Oral clarithromycin at home for 5 days
Oral doxycycline at home for 5 days
hq_q.w: His CURB-65 score is 1, for age 65 or over: he is not confused, his urea is 7 or less, his respiratory rate is under 30 and his blood pressure is normal. This is low-severity community-acquired pneumonia, which NICE advises treating at home with oral amoxicillin for 5 days, with advice to return if he worsens.
hq_q.f: CURB-65 of 3, such as confusion, a urea of 9 and age over 65 → high severity: admit for IV co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate management?

c: orientated in time, place and person
tm.m: CURB-65 predicts 30-day mortality, and low scores do well with an oral narrow-spectrum penicillin
tm.g: CURB-65 of 0 or 1 → home with oral amoxicillin for 5 days
f: confusion, a urea of 9.4 and a respiratory rate of 32
a CURB-65 score of 2
the same picture with a penicillin allergy that caused anaphylaxis
the presentation instead showed features specific to Oral doxycycline at home for 5 days (Another penicillin allergy alternative, and he has no allergy)
x: For high-severity pneumonia, CURB-65 of 3 to 5
For moderate severity, CURB-65 of 2, usually with hospital assessment
An alternative for penicillin allergy, and he has none
Another penicillin allergy alternative, and he has no allergy

hq_q.s:
A 41 year old man has had pain in both flanks for months and passed red urine twice in the past year. His mother started dialysis at 55, and his uncle died suddenly from a brain haemorrhage.
BP 162/98 mmHg. Both flanks contain large, irregular, ballotable masses. He has had no weight loss or fever and has no varicocele.
hq_q.w: Bilateral irregular ballotable kidneys, hypertension, haematuria, a raised creatinine and a family history of kidney failure and brain haemorrhage are autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Berry aneurysms cluster in some families. Ultrasound confirms many cysts in both kidneys.
hq_q.f: One kidney mass with haematuria, weight loss, a new left varicocele and polycythaemia → renal cell carcinoma.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: PKD1 or PKD2 mutations let cysts grow from the tubules until they crowd out working nephrons and stretch the capsule
tm.g: Bilateral big kidneys, hypertension and a family history of dialysis or SAH → ADPKD
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Bilateral hydronephrosis (Usually from bladder outflow obstruction, with smooth kidneys and no family history)
a single loin mass with weight loss, a new left varicocele and a haemoglobin of 192
facial angiofibromas, seizures and ash leaf macules with kidney masses
a 3 year old with a smooth abdominal mass on one side that does not cross the midline
x: Usually from bladder outflow obstruction, with smooth kidneys and no family history
Usually a single mass, and he has no weight loss or varicocele
Causes kidney angiomyolipomas with skin and neurological signs, which he lacks
A tumour of young children

hq_q.s:
A 24 year old man has had a headache, fever and vomiting for 18 hours and is drowsy but rousable. A lumbar puncture is being considered.
Temperature 39.1°C, GCS 14. He has neck stiffness and Kernig's sign is positive. There is no rash. Fundoscopy shows swollen optic discs with blurred margins in both eyes.
hq_q.w: Papilloedema is a sign of raised intracranial pressure, and a lumbar puncture then risks herniation of the brain through the foramen magnum. Give IV antibiotics immediately and arrange a CT head before any lumbar puncture. Fever, neck stiffness and Kernig's sign are reasons to suspect meningitis, not reasons to delay.
hq_q.f: A rapidly spreading purpuric rash with shock → treat as meningococcal sepsis and do not delay antibiotics for a lumbar puncture.
hq_q.ql: Which finding is the strongest reason to delay the lumbar puncture?

c: swollen optic discs with blurred margins
tm.m: Removing CSF from below drops the pressure beneath a brain already under high pressure, so it can cone downwards
tm.g: Papilloedema or other signs of raised ICP → antibiotics now and CT first, lumbar puncture later
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Fever of 39.1°C (Expected in meningitis and does not make a lumbar puncture dangerous)
the presentation instead showed features specific to GCS of 14 (Only mildly reduced; a GCS below 9 or a fall of 3 points or more would be a contraindication)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Kernig's sign (A sign of meningeal irritation that supports doing the lumbar puncture)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Neck stiffness (Points to meningitis and is a reason for the lumbar puncture, not against it)
x: Expected in meningitis and does not make a lumbar puncture dangerous
Only mildly reduced; a GCS below 9 or a fall of 3 points or more would be a contraindication
A sign of meningeal irritation that supports doing the lumbar puncture
Points to meningitis and is a reason for the lumbar puncture, not against it

hq_q.s:
A 72 year old man with type 2 diabetes who takes gliclazide is brought in by ambulance after his wife found him sweaty and confused. He cannot follow instructions or swallow safely. A cannula is already in place.
GCS 11, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 146/84 mmHg.
hq_q.w: A hypoglycaemic patient who cannot swallow safely but has IV access needs IV glucose: about 150 ml of 10% glucose or 75 ml of 20% over 10 to 15 minutes. Recheck the glucose after 10 minutes. Sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia can recur for many hours, so he needs admission and a glucose infusion if it returns.
hq_q.f: Unconscious with no IV access → IM glucagon 1 mg.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

c: cannot follow instructions or swallow safely
tm.m: Glucose given into a vein restores fuel to the brain within minutes without relying on the gut or liver glycogen
tm.g: Hypoglycaemia, unable to swallow, IV access → IV 10% or 20% glucose
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Buccal glucose gel (Risks aspiration when he cannot swallow safely and is not advised if consciousness is reduced)
the same picture with no IV access possible
the presentation instead showed features specific to IV 50% glucose (Highly irritant to veins and damages tissue if it leaks, so 10% or 20% is preferred)
alert and able to swallow with a glucose of 3.1
x: Risks aspiration when he cannot swallow safely and is not advised if consciousness is reduced
Used when IV access is not possible; it needs liver glycogen and acts more slowly
Highly irritant to veins and damages tissue if it leaks, so 10% or 20% is preferred
Unsafe when he cannot swallow

hq_q.s: A 23 year old woman has a 5 year history of cutting herself when distressed, intense relationships that end abruptly, and anger she struggles to control. She describes feeling empty and fears that people will leave her. Her mood shifts within hours. She has no psychotic symptoms and no sustained period of low or elevated mood.
hq_q.w: Self-harm, unstable intense relationships, fear of abandonment, emptiness, anger and mood that shifts within hours are emotionally unstable, or borderline, personality disorder. Psychological therapy is the main treatment, and NICE recommends considering dialectical behaviour therapy for women with this diagnosis when reducing recurrent self-harm is the priority. Medicines are not used to treat the disorder itself.
hq_q.f: Flashbacks, nightmares and hypervigilance after an assault → trauma-focused CBT or EMDR for PTSD.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate long-term treatment?

c: no sustained period of low or elevated mood
tm.m: DBT teaches emotion regulation and distress tolerance while validating the person, so self-harm is no longer needed to cope
tm.g: Borderline personality disorder with repeated self-harm → dialectical behaviour therapy
f: 2 months of low mood, loss of interest and early waking with no long-standing relationship difficulties
flashbacks, nightmares and hypervigilance since an assault 6 months ago
the presentation instead showed features specific to Fluoxetine (Drugs do not treat the disorder and are used for coexisting conditions such as depression)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Olanzapine (Sometimes used short term in a crisis, but not as treatment for the disorder)
x: She has no sustained low mood, and standard CBT does not target her emotional instability
A treatment for PTSD, which is not described
Drugs do not treat the disorder and are used for coexisting conditions such as depression
Sometimes used short term in a crisis, but not as treatment for the disorder

hq_q.s:
A 13 year old boy is referred by his school. Over the past 18 months he has stolen from shops, set fire to a bin, been cruel to the family cat and regularly stays out all night without permission. He has hit other pupils and threatened a teacher with a compass.
He is not low in mood, has no psychotic symptoms and does not use drugs.
hq_q.w: A repeated pattern of serious violations of other people's rights and of age-appropriate rules, including theft, fire setting, cruelty to animals, aggression and staying out at night, is conduct disorder. Oppositional defiant disorder is defiance and temper without these serious violations. Antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before 18.
hq_q.f: Angry, argumentative and defiant towards adults but no theft, aggression or cruelty → oppositional defiant disorder.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Persistent antisocial behaviour that breaks major rules and harms others, usually from a mix of temperament and environment
tm.g: Theft, fire setting, cruelty and aggression in a child → conduct disorder
f: the same behaviour continuing in a 22 year old who shows no remorse
fidgety, impulsive and inattentive in every setting since age 5, without cruelty or theft
the presentation instead showed features specific to Autism spectrum disorder (Involves social communication difficulty and rigid routines, not deliberate harm to others)
a 7 year old who argues, loses his temper and refuses rules at home but harms no one
x: Cannot be diagnosed before 18, though conduct disorder often comes before it
Can coexist, but impulsivity and inattention do not explain cruelty and theft
Involves social communication difficulty and rigid routines, not deliberate harm to others
Defiance and temper without serious violations such as theft, cruelty or fire setting

hq_q.s:
An 8 year old boy is brought to his GP because his teacher says he cannot sit still, interrupts constantly and rarely finishes his work. His parents say he is the same at home, loses things every day and runs into the road without looking. This has been the case since he started school 3 years ago.
His hearing test is normal. He makes good eye contact, plays imaginatively and has friends. No staring spells have been seen.
o: Autism spectrum disorder without learning disability
hq_q.w: Hyperactivity, impulsivity and inattention at home and at school for more than 6 months, starting before age 12, are attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. His normal hearing, good social skills and lack of staring spells argue against the alternatives. He should be referred for specialist assessment; drug treatment is not started in primary care.
hq_q.f: Many brief staring spells a day with eyelid flickering and 3 Hz spike and wave on EEG → childhood absence epilepsy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: since he started school 3 years ago
tm.m: Differences in frontostriatal dopamine and noradrenaline signalling weaken inhibition and sustained attention
tm.g: Inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity in 2 settings for over 6 months → ADHD
f: poor eye contact, a need for fixed routines and difficulty making friends
many brief staring spells a day with eyelid flickering and 3 Hz spike and wave on EEG
the presentation instead showed features specific to Hearing impairment from glue ear (His hearing test is normal)
defiance and temper outbursts at home only, with good concentration at school
x: He has good eye contact, imaginative play and friends
Causes brief staring spells, and none have been seen
His hearing test is normal
Describes defiance and temper rather than restlessness and inattention in every setting

hq_q.s:
A 68 year old man with chronic kidney disease has felt weak for 2 days. He recently started spironolactone for heart failure and also takes ramipril.
Pulse rate 52 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg. His ECG shows tall peaked T waves, flattened P waves and a QRS duration of 140 ms.
hq_q.w: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes needs IV calcium gluconate first, 30 ml of 10% over 5 to 10 minutes. It protects the heart within minutes but does not lower the potassium. Insulin with glucose and nebulised salbutamol then shift potassium into cells, and the spironolactone and ramipril are stopped.
hq_q.f: Potassium of 6.6 with a normal ECG → insulin with glucose to shift potassium; calcium is for ECG changes.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first treatment?

tm.m: Calcium restores the gap between resting and threshold potential in cardiac cells, protecting against arrhythmia while potassium is lowered
tm.g: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes → IV calcium gluconate first
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Calcium resonium (Removes potassium through the gut over hours to days, far too slowly)
a potassium of 6.6 with a normal ECG
the presentation instead showed features specific to Nebulised salbutamol (An add-on to insulin that shifts potassium into cells, not the first treatment)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Sodium bicarbonate (Considered with severe acidosis and does not protect the heart)
x: Removes potassium through the gut over hours to days, far too slowly
Lowers potassium within 15 to 30 minutes and comes next, once the heart is protected
An add-on to insulin that shifts potassium into cells, not the first treatment
Considered with severe acidosis and does not protect the heart

hq_q.s:
A 39 year old man has had a painful swollen left knee for 3 weeks, and the whole of the second toe on his right foot is swollen like a sausage. His heels hurt when he first gets up. He has had flaky patches in his scalp for years, which he thought were dandruff. He has had no diarrhoea, urinary symptoms or new sexual partner.
There is a small effusion in the left knee and tenderness where both Achilles tendons insert.
hq_q.w: An asymmetrical oligoarthritis with dactylitis of a whole toe, heel enthesitis, a negative rheumatoid factor and unrecognised scalp psoriasis is psoriatic arthritis. Look for psoriasis in hidden places such as the scalp, natal cleft and umbilicus, and for nail pitting. With no infection beforehand, reactive arthritis is unlikely.
hq_q.f: The same joints 2 weeks after chlamydia or a diarrhoeal illness, with conjunctivitis → reactive arthritis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: no diarrhoea, urinary symptoms or new sexual partner
tm.m: Inflammation starts at entheses, where tendons and ligaments insert into bone, and spreads to joints and whole digits
tm.g: Dactylitis plus enthesitis plus psoriasis anywhere → psoriatic arthritis
f: a hot red first toe joint overnight with a uric acid of 0.56
the same joints 2 weeks after a chlamydia infection, with conjunctivitis and dysuria
symmetrical swelling of the knuckles and wrists with positive anti-CCP
the presentation instead showed features specific to Septic arthritis (A hot, very painful single joint with fever, not dactylitis and enthesitis over weeks)
x: Gives sudden severe attacks, usually of the first toe joint, and his urate is normal
Follows a gut or genital infection, and he has had none
Symmetrical small joint disease, usually seropositive, without dactylitis
A hot, very painful single joint with fever, not dactylitis and enthesitis over weeks

hq_q.s:
A 52 year old woman with plaque psoriasis for 20 years has had pain and stiffness in several fingers for 2 years. Her fingernails are pitted and lifting from the nail bed. Several distal interphalangeal joints are swollen, and her left index finger is shortened and unusually floppy.
An X-ray of both hands is requested.
hq_q.w: Distal interphalangeal joint disease with nail pitting and onycholysis in long-standing psoriasis is psoriatic arthritis. Its X-ray signature is the end of one bone eroded into a pencil shape sitting in a cupped base, with new bone formation nearby. Severe destruction shortens the digit, which can telescope: arthritis mutilans.
hq_q.f: Symmetrical knuckle and wrist disease with periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions → rheumatoid arthritis.
hq_q.ql: Which X-ray finding is most likely?

tm.m: Erosion eats away the end of one phalanx while bone proliferates at the base of the next, so the joint becomes a pencil sitting in a cup
tm.g: Psoriatic DIP disease with nail changes → pencil-in-cup on X-ray
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Chondrocalcinosis of the wrist (The calcified cartilage of calcium pyrophosphate disease)
hard bony swellings at the DIP joints in a 70 year old with no psoriasis
symmetrical swelling of the knuckles and wrists in a woman positive for rheumatoid factor
recurrent hot joints with tophi on the ears
x: The calcified cartilage of calcium pyrophosphate disease
Osteoarthritis, which forms bony Heberden's nodes without nail disease
The pattern of rheumatoid arthritis, which spares the DIP joints
The pattern of chronic tophaceous gout

hq_q.s: A 19 year old man with a severe learning disability needs several dental extractions under general anaesthetic for painful abscesses. He cannot understand or retain information about the procedure, even with pictures and support. His mother, who cares for him, offers to sign the consent form. He has no lasting power of attorney or deputy. The dentist, anaesthetist and family agree the treatment is needed.
o: Apply to the Court of Protection for a decision
Ask his mother to sign the consent form
Best interests decision with his mother and team
Treat him under the Mental Health Act
Wait until he can consent for himself
hq_q.w: He lacks capacity for this decision, and at 19 his mother cannot consent for him unless she holds a relevant lasting power of attorney or is a court-appointed deputy. Under the Mental Capacity Act the treating clinicians decide in his best interests, consulting his mother and others who know him, and record it, often at a best interests meeting.
hq_q.f: No family or friends to consult about serious medical treatment → instruct an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate way to proceed?

c: offers to sign the consent form
tm.m: For an adult who lacks capacity, consent passes to no one; the decision-maker acts in his best interests after consulting others
tm.g: Adult lacking capacity with no LPA or deputy → best interests decision by the clinicians with the family
f: his mother and the team strongly disagree about whether major surgery is in his best interests
he is 15 and lacks Gillick competence
the presentation instead showed features specific to Treat him under the Mental Health Act (Covers treatment of mental disorder, not dental surgery)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Wait until he can consent for himself (His incapacity is lifelong and he is in pain from abscesses now)
x: Kept for serious disputes or decisions such as withdrawing life-sustaining treatment
A parent cannot consent for an adult who lacks capacity
Covers treatment of mental disorder, not dental surgery
His incapacity is lifelong and he is in pain from abscesses now

hq_q.s:
A 26 year old woman has had hard, infrequent stools every 3 to 4 days for 2 months since starting a desk job. She strains and sometimes sees a little bright red blood on the paper. She eats mainly white bread, crisps and ready meals and drinks about 1 litre of fluid a day. She has not tried any changes or remedies. She has no weight loss and no family history of bowel cancer.
Abdominal examination is normal.
hq_q.w: Recent constipation with a low-fibre diet, low fluid intake and inactivity, and no red flags, is managed first with lifestyle advice: more fibre from wholegrains, fruit and vegetables, more fluid and more activity. If that fails, a bulk-forming laxative such as ispaghula is added, then an osmotic laxative.
hq_q.f: New constipation at 64 with weight loss and iron deficiency → urgent investigation for colorectal cancer.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most appropriate first step?

c: white bread, crisps and ready meals
tm.m: Fibre holds water in the stool and adds bulk, which speeds transit and softens the stool
tm.g: Simple constipation with a poor diet and no red flags → fibre, fluid and activity first
f: the presentation instead showed features specific to Bisacodyl tablets (A stimulant laxative for when diet and softer laxatives are not enough)
the presentation instead showed features specific to Lactulose (An osmotic laxative that causes bloating, used after diet and a bulk-forming laxative)
stools still hard after 6 weeks of dietary change and a bulk-forming laxative

the presentation instead showed features specific to Refer for flexible sigmoidoscopy (She is young with no red flags, and small streaks of bright red blood with hard stools fit a fissure or haemorrhoids)
x: A stimulant laxative for when diet and softer laxatives are not enough
An osmotic laxative that causes bloating, used after diet and a bulk-forming laxative
The usual next step if diet and a bulk-forming laxative fail
She is young with no red flags, and small streaks of bright red blood with hard stools fit a fissure or haemorrhoids

hq_q.s:
A 48 year old woman has found it hard to climb stairs and to lift her arms to brush her hair for 3 months. She has become breathless on exertion and has a dry cough. The skin on the sides of her fingers is thickened and cracked. She has no rash on her face or knuckles.
Her shoulder and hip girdle muscles are weak. There are fine crackles at both lung bases.
hq_q.w: Proximal weakness with a very high creatine kinase is an inflammatory myopathy, and with interstitial lung disease and thickened, cracked skin on the fingers, called mechanic's hands, it is the antisynthetase syndrome. Anti-Jo-1 is the classic antibody. Anti-Scl-70 also goes with lung fibrosis, but in systemic sclerosis, which does not raise the CK like this.
hq_q.f: Skin tightening from the fingers up the arms, Raynaud's and lung fibrosis with a normal CK → anti-Scl-70 in diffuse systemic sclerosis.
hq_q.ql: Which antibody is most likely to be positive?

tm.m: Antibodies against histidyl-tRNA synthetase go with inflammation in muscle, lung and joints
tm.g: Myositis plus interstitial lung disease plus mechanic's hands → anti-Jo-1
f: tight skin limited to the fingers and face with calcinosis and Raynaud's
the presentation instead showed features specific to Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (Specific for rheumatoid arthritis)
a malar rash, mouth ulcers, arthritis and proteinuria
skin tightening from the fingers up the arms, Raynaud's and lung fibrosis with a normal CK
x: Marks limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, with Raynaud's and calcinosis, not myositis
Specific for rheumatoid arthritis
Specific for SLE, which causes a rash, arthritis and nephritis
Linked to lung fibrosis in diffuse systemic sclerosis, which does not raise the CK like this

hq_q.s:
A 41 year old man who arrived from Pakistan 18 months ago has had a productive cough for 10 weeks, evening fevers, night sweats and 6 kg weight loss.
Temperature 37.8°C. There are crackles at the left apex. Chest X-ray shows left upper lobe consolidation with a small cavity. An HIV test is negative.
hq_q.w: Suspected active pulmonary TB is confirmed by sending at least 3 sputum samples, including an early morning one, for microscopy for acid-fast bacilli and mycobacterial culture, with rapid molecular testing for rifampicin resistance. Culture also gives drug sensitivities. IGRA and Mantoux tests show exposure, not active disease.
hq_q.f: Cannot produce sputum even after induction → bronchoscopy with lavage.
hq_q.ql: Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

tm.m: Acid-fast bacilli from the cavity are coughed up in sputum, seen with Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine stains and grown in culture
tm.g: Suspected active pulmonary TB → 3 sputum samples for microscopy and culture
f: he cannot produce sputum even after nebulised hypertonic saline
the presentation instead showed features specific to CT chest (Shows the extent of disease but cannot identify the organism)
a healthcare worker with no symptoms and a normal chest X-ray after an exposure
the presentation instead showed features specific to Mantoux test (Detects past exposure or BCG and cannot confirm active TB)
x: Invasive and used when sputum cannot be obtained
Shows the extent of disease but cannot identify the organism
Detects infection but cannot tell latent from active disease
Detects past exposure or BCG and cannot confirm active TB

hq_q.s:
A 58 year old retired builder has had pain on the top of his right shoulder for 6 months. It is worst when he reaches across his body to fasten a seatbelt and when he lifts his arm fully above his head.
There is a bony swelling and point tenderness over the acromioclavicular joint. Pain is reproduced by bringing the arm across the chest. Movement is painful in the last 20 degrees of abduction. External rotation is full.
hq_q.w: Pain on top of the shoulder with local tenderness and swelling of the acromioclavicular joint, pain on bringing the arm across the body and a painful arc at the top of abduction are acromioclavicular joint osteoarthritis. Rotator cuff tendinopathy gives a painful arc in the middle of abduction, and adhesive capsulitis loses external rotation.
hq_q.f: A painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees with pain on resisted abduction → rotator cuff tendinopathy.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

c: point tenderness over the acromioclavicular joint
tm.m: The worn joint is squeezed when the arm crosses the body or reaches the top of elevation
tm.g: ACJ tenderness, pain across the body and a high painful arc → ACJ osteoarthritis
f: global stiffness with loss of external rotation in a woman with diabetes
neck pain with tingling down the arm into the thumb
the presentation instead showed features specific to Glenohumeral joint osteoarthritis (Causes deep pain and loss of movement in every direction, especially rotation)
a painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees with pain on resisted abduction
x: Causes global stiffness, with external rotation lost first, and his is full
Causes neck pain and symptoms down the arm in a dermatome
Causes deep pain and loss of movement in every direction, especially rotation
Gives a painful arc in the middle of abduction, not tenderness over the ACJ

hq_q.s:
A 45 year old woman has had pain and swelling in both hands for 4 months, with morning stiffness lasting 2 hours. Her knuckles and the middle joints of her fingers are affected on both sides, and her wrists ache. She has no rash or skin disease.
Both wrists and several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints are swollen and tender. The distal interphalangeal joints are normal and there is no nail pitting.
hq_q.w: A symmetrical inflammatory arthritis of the small joints of the hands and wrists, sparing the distal interphalangeal joints, with morning stiffness over an hour and positive rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP is rheumatoid arthritis. Anti-CCP is highly specific. She should be referred urgently to rheumatology to start a DMARD such as methotrexate.
hq_q.f: Heberden's nodes at the DIP joints with brief morning stiffness and a normal CRP → osteoarthritis.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Autoimmune synovitis thickens the joint lining, which erodes cartilage and bone at the joint margins
tm.g: Symmetrical small joint synovitis with long morning stiffness and anti-CCP → RA
f: hard bony swellings at the DIP joints with 10 minutes of morning stiffness and a normal CRP
a 72 year old with shoulder and hip girdle stiffness and an ESR of 60 but no joint swelling
DIP joint swelling with nail pitting and plaques on the elbows
the presentation instead showed features specific to Systemic lupus erythematosus (Causes a non-erosive arthritis with a rash, mouth ulcers and other organ involvement)
x: Affects the DIP joints and thumb base with short stiffness and no raised inflammatory markers
Causes girdle stiffness in older people without small joint swelling
Usually asymmetrical with DIP and nail involvement and a negative rheumatoid factor
Causes a non-erosive arthritis with a rash, mouth ulcers and other organ involvement

hq_q.s:
A 29 year old man is brought in by his partner. For 10 days he has slept 2 hours a night, talked rapidly and spent £8,000 on cars he cannot afford. He says he is about to become a billionaire. Two years ago he had 4 months of low mood and could not work. He does not use drugs, and a urine drug screen is negative.
He is overactive, distractible and difficult to interrupt.
hq_q.w: An episode of elevated mood with little sleep, pressured speech, reckless spending and grandiosity lasting more than a week is mania, and with a previous depressive episode this is bipolar affective disorder. A negative drug screen makes a substance cause less likely. He needs urgent specialist assessment.
hq_q.f: Several years of mild ups and downs that never reach mania or major depression → cyclothymia.
hq_q.ql: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

tm.m: Manic and depressive episodes recur in the same person, and disturbed sleep is often the first sign of a relapse
tm.g: Mania for over a week plus past depression → bipolar affective disorder
f: several years of mild mood swings that never reach mania or major depression
mood that changes within hours, with self-harm and fear of abandonment
